'''Allen Joe Fish''' (born November 12, 1942) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Texas]] in [[Dallas]].

==Education and career==

Fish was born in [[Los Angeles]]. He received his [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[Yale University]] in 1965 and his [[Bachelor of Laws]] from [[Yale Law School]] in 1968. He was a Sergeant in the [[United States Army]] Reserve from 1968 to 1974, and was in private practice in [[Dallas]], [[Texas]], from 1968 to 1980. In 1980 he was elected to the 95th Judicial District Court of [[Dallas County, Texas|Dallas County]]. From 1981 to 1983 he was a judge on the Fifth District of the Texas Court of Appeals in Dallas.<ref name="fjc.gov">{{FJC Bio|nid=1380736|inline=yes}}</ref>

=== Federal judicial service ===

On January 31, 1983, Fish was nominated by President [[Ronald Reagan]] to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Texas]] vacated by Judge [[Patrick Higginbotham]]. Fish was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] less than a month later, on February 23, 1983, and received his commission the following day. He served as Chief Judge of the district from 2002 to 2007, assuming [[senior status]] on November 12, 2007.<ref name="fjc.gov"/>

As a single mother, Nelson attended and graduated from the [[University of Texas School of Law]], where she earned a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1993.{{cite web |url=https://secure.sos.state.or.us/orestar/cfDetail.do?page=search&cfRsn=12472 |title=Candidate Information 2012 |last=Brown |first=Kate |date=January 27, 2012 |website=Oregon Secretary of State |publisher=State of Oregon |access-date=January 2, 2018 |page=}}{{cite news |last=Lewton |first=Michael |date=July 2006 |title=Judge Adrienne Nelson |url=https://www.mbabar.org/Resources/AdrienneNelson.html |work=Multnomah Lawyer |location=Portland, Oregon |access-date=January 2, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180103133654/https://www.mbabar.org/Resources/AdrienneNelson.html |archive-date=January 3, 2018 |url-status=dead }} ==Legal career== Nelson moved to [[Portland, Oregon]], in 1993, to be closer to her mother, who had previously relocated to the state. Nelson was a contract analyst for an insurance company for two years. She then worked as an attorney in [[Practice of law|private practice]] in Portland as a [[public defender]],{{Cite news |last=Miller |first=Cheryl |date=July 14, 2022 |title=Biden's Flurry of Judicial Nominations Continues With a Third Batch in One Week |work=[[The National Law Journal]] |url=https://www.law.com/nationallawjournal/2022/07/14/bidens-flurry-of-judicial-nominations-continues-with-a-third-batch-in-one-week/?slreturn=20220615163403 |access-date=July 15, 2022}} with Multnomah Defenders Inc, a non-profit [[public interest law]] firm, from 1996 to 1999, and for the law firm Bennett, Hartman, Morris & Kaplan LLP from 1999 to 2004. Nelson was a senior attorney in Student Legal and Mediation Services for [[Portland State University]] from 2004 to 2006. Nelson served as an [[adjunct professor]] at [[Lewis & Clark Law School]] from 2002 to 2005. Nelson has been a member of the [[American Bar Association]] House of Delegates and the ABA Commission on Disability Rights. She received the Oregon Women Lawyers (OWLs) Judge [[Mercedes Deiz]] Award in 2003, and the [[Oregon State Bar]] President's Public Service Award in 2007.{{dead link|date=September 2022}} She has also served as president of the Multnomah Bar Foundation and president of the Oregon State Bar Foundation Board.{{cite web |url=http://www.reed.edu/reed_magazine/june2014/articles/eliot_circular/new_faces.html |title=New Faces |author= |date=June 2014 |website=Reed magazine |publisher=Reed College |access-date=January 2, 2018 |quote=}} In 2021, a [[Adrienne C. Nelson High School|school]] in [[Happy Valley, Oregon]] was named after Nelson.{{Cite web |date=September 7, 2021 |title=Adrienne C. Nelson High School |url=https://anhs.nclack.k12.or.us/ |access-date=2024-05-15 |website=anhs.nclack.k12.or.us |language=en-US}} ==Judicial service== === Oregon circuit court === Governor [[Ted Kulongoski]] appointed Nelson as a judge on the [[Multnomah County, Oregon|Multnomah County]] [[Oregon circuit courts|Circuit Court]] in February 2006, to replace Sidney Galton. She was re-elected to a new six-year term in 2012.{{cite web |url=http://records.sos.state.or.us/ORSOSWebDrawer/RecordView/6873711 |title=Official Results, May 15, 2012, Primary Election |last=Brown |first=Kate |date=May 2012 |website=Oregon Secretary of State |publisher=State of Oregon |access-date=January 2, 2018 |page=55 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201009112705/http://records.sos.state.or.us/ORSOSWebDrawer/RecordView/6873711 |archive-date=October 9, 2020 |url-status=dead}} === Oregon Supreme Court === Governor [[Kate Brown]] appointed Nelson to the [[Oregon Supreme Court]] in January 2018, to replace justice [[Jack Landau (judge)|Jack Landau]], who retired on December 31, 2017. Nelson's term on the Supreme Court ended in January 2019, but she was elected to a full six year term in November 2018.{{cite web |title=Oregon Supreme Court |url=https://www.americanbar.org/groups/litigation/committees/diversity-inclusion/articles/2019/winter2019-justice-adrienne-nelson-blazes-trails-diversity/ |access-date=10 February 2019 |date=October 9, 2018}} Nelson is the first [[African-American]] to serve on the [[Oregon Supreme Court]], or on any state [[appellate court]] in [[Oregon]]. === United States district court === On July 14, 2022, President [[Joe Biden]] nominated Nelson to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Oregon]].{{Cite press release|title=President Biden Names Twenty-Third Round of Judicial Nominees|date=July 14, 2022|publisher=The White House|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/07/14/president-biden-names-twenty-third-round-of-judicial-nominees/|access-date=July 14, 2022}} {{PD-notice}} President Biden nominated Nelson to the seat vacated by Judge [[Michael W. Mosman]], who assumed [[senior status]] on December 27, 2021.{{Cite web|date=July 14, 2022|title=PN2381 - Nomination of Adrienne C. Nelson for The Judiciary, 117th Congress (2021-2022)|url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/117th-congress/2381|access-date=July 15, 2022|website=www.congress.gov}} On October 12, 2022, a hearing on her nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web|title=Nominations|date=October 9, 2022|publisher=[[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]]|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/10/12/2022/nominations}} On December 1, 2022, her nomination was reported out of committee by a 12–10 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/EBM%20Results%20-%202022-12-011.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – December 1, 2022|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=December 1, 2022}} On January 3, 2023, her nomination was returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]]; she was renominated later the same day.{{Cite press release|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate|date=January 3, 2023|publisher=The White House|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2023/01/03/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-91/}} On February 2, 2023, her nomination was reported out of committee by an 11–9 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/EBM%20Results%20-%202023-02-021.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – February 2, 2023|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=February 2, 2023}} On February 14, 2023, the Senate invoked cloture on her nomination by a 53–44 vote.{{Cite web|date=February 14, 2023|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Adrienne C. Nelson to be U.S. District Judge for the District of Oregon)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00016.htm|access-date=February 14, 2023|website=United States Senate}} On February 15, 2023, she was confirmed by a 52–46 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00017.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Adrienne C. Nelson, of Oregon, to be United States District Judge for the District of Oregon)|website=United States Senate|date=February 15, 2023|access-date=February 15, 2023}} She received her judicial commission on February 23, 2023.{{FJC Bio|nid=13263786|inline=yes}} She is the first [[African-American]] woman to serve on the United States District Court for the District of Oregon.{{Cite web|last=Bernstein|first=Maxine|date=July 14, 2022|title=Oregon Supreme Court Justice Adrienne Nelson nominated to federal bench|url=https://www.oregonlive.com/crime/2022/07/oregon-supreme-court-justice-adrienne-nelson-nominated-to-federal-bench.html|access-date=July 15, 2022|website=oregonlive|language=en}} === Notable cases === On December 10, 2024, Nelson issued an injunction blocking a merger between Kroger and Albertsons. '''Aileen Mercedes Cannon''' (born 1981) is an American lawyer and jurist serving as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida]]. She was appointed in 2020 by President [[Donald Trump]] and confirmed by the [[United States Senate]]. Cannon previously worked for the corporate law firm [[Gibson Dunn]] from 2009 to 2012 and was a federal prosecutor in the Southern District of Florida from 2013 to 2020.

In 2022, Cannon presided over the case of ''[[Trump v. United States (2022)|Donald J. Trump v. United States of America]]''. She ordered the U.S. government to pause using [[FBI search of Mar-a-Lago|materials seized from Trump's private club and residence]] in its investigation and granted Trump's request for a [[special master]] to review the material. The [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit]] reversed and rebuked Cannon after it found she had wrongly exercised [[jurisdiction]] over the case. Cannon then dismissed Trump's lawsuit per orders from the Eleventh Circuit.

Following Trump's indictment in June 2023, Cannon oversaw a [[Federal prosecution of Donald Trump (government documents case)|federal criminal case against Trump]]. Many legal experts, citing her handling of the civil case against Trump, called for her [[recusal]] from the case. Under Cannon, the case was considerably delayed from getting to trial, with Cannon granting multiple requests by Trump to extend pre-trial motions. In July 2024, she dismissed the case entirely, ruling that special counsel [[Jack Smith (lawyer)|Jack Smith]]'s appointment was unconstitutional. The ruling was appealed, but the appeal was dropped after Trump [[2024 United States presidential election|became president]].

Cannon's rulings have received considerable media attention, with many legal experts criticizing her decisions and alleging bias over her handling of Trump's legal cases.

== Early life and education ==
Cannon was born in 1981 in [[Cali]], [[Colombia]].<ref name=Schnell>{{cite news |last1=Schnell |first1=Mychael |title=Five things to know about Aileen M. Cannon, the judge who granted Trump a special master |url=https://thehill.com/regulation/3631564-five-things-to-know-about-aileen-m-cannon-the-judge-who-granted-trump-a-special-master/ |access-date=December 11, 2022 |work=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]] |date=September 7, 2022 |archive-date=December 11, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221211031828/https://thehill.com/regulation/3631564-five-things-to-know-about-aileen-m-cannon-the-judge-who-granted-trump-a-special-master/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=Mazzei>{{Cite news |last1=Mazzei |first1=Patricia |last2=Haberman |first2=Maggie |author-link2=Maggie Haberman |last3=Feuer |first3=Alan |date=September 7, 2022 |title=Trump Ruling Lifts Profile of Judge and Raises Legal Eyebrows |language=en-US |work=[[The New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/09/07/us/politics/aileen-cannon-judge-trump.html |url-status=live |access-date=September 9, 2022 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20220907213453/https://www.nytimes.com/2022/09/07/us/politics/aileen-cannon-judge-trump.html |archive-date=September 7, 2022 }}</ref> She has an elder sister.<ref name="Wilner" /> Her mother had fled Cuba as a girl after the [[Cuban Revolution]] of the 1950s,<ref name=Mazzei/> and her father is from [[Indiana]].<ref name=Wilner>{{cite news |last1=Weaver |first1=Jay |last2=Wilner |first2=Michael |title=Trump-appointed judge at center of ex-president's FBI fight. Who is Aileen Cannon? |url=https://www.miamiherald.com/news/local/article265558746.html |access-date=December 11, 2022 |work=[[Miami Herald]] |date=September 12, 2022 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20220912222835/https://www.miamiherald.com/news/local/article265558746.html |archive-date=September 12, 2022 |url-status=live}}</ref> Cannon grew up in [[Miami|Miami, Florida]], where she attended [[Ransom Everglades School]], a private school.<ref name=Mazzei/><ref name=Wilner/>

Cannon graduated from [[Duke University]] in 2003 with a [[Bachelor of Arts]]. In college, she studied for a semester in [[Spain]] and wrote for Miami's Spanish language newspaper ''[[El Nuevo Herald]]''; her writings included topics such as [[flamenco dancing]], festivals, and [[yoga]].<ref name="Schnell" /><ref name="Wilner" /><ref name="Musgrave">{{cite news |last1=Musgrave |first1=Jane |title=Federal judge now at center of Trump's Mar-a-Lago search a 'stickler for procedure' |url=https://www.palmbeachpost.com/story/news/2022/08/31/federal-judge-decide-special-master-fbi-search-former-president-donald-trump-mar-lago/7940691001/ |access-date=December 11, 2022 |work=[[The Palm Beach Post]] |url-status=dead |date=September 8, 2022 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20221211062112/https://www.palmbeachpost.com/story/news/2022/08/31/federal-judge-decide-special-master-fbi-search-former-president-donald-trump-mar-lago/7940691001/ |archive-date=December 11, 2022}}</ref> Cannon then attended the [[University of Michigan Law School]], where she was an articles editor for the ''[[University of Michigan Journal of Law Reform]]'' and was a quarter-finalist in the school's [[moot court]] competition.<ref name="SJCQ">{{cite web |title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees |work=[[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]] |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Cannon%20SJQ%20-%20PUBLIC.pdf |access-date=10 June 2023 |archive-date=June 22, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230622203425/https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Cannon%20SJQ%20-%20PUBLIC.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> She graduated in 2007 with a [[Juris Doctor]], ''[[Latin honors#United States|magna cum laude]]'', along with membership in the [[Order of the Coif]].<ref name=Schnell/><ref name=Wilner/><ref name="SJCQ" />

Cannon has been a member of the conservative and libertarian [[Federalist Society]] since 2005, when she was a law student.<ref name=Mazzei /><ref name=Tillman>{{cite news |last1=Tillman |first1=Zoe |title=Trump-Appointed Judge Courts Controversy With Mar-a-Lago Order |url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/trump-appointed-judge-courts-controversy-with-mar-a-lago-order |access-date=February 2, 2023 |work=[[Bloomberg News]] |archive-url= https://archive.today/20221211074040/https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/trump-appointed-judge-courts-controversy-with-mar-a-lago-order |archive-date=December 11, 2022 |url-status=live |date=September 6, 2022}}</ref> While being considered for the position of a district judge in 2020, Cannon explained that she joined the Federalist Society because of a "diversity of viewpoints" and also because she "found interesting the organization's discussions about the constitutional separation of powers, the rule of law, and the limited role of the judiciary to say what the law is—not to make the law".<ref name=Schnell/><ref name=Tillman/><ref name=Marimow/>

== Career ==
From 2008 to 2009, Cannon served as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Steven Colloton]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit]] in [[Iowa]].<ref name=Mazzei/> From 2009 to 2012, she was an associate at the [[Washington, D.C.]], office of the corporate law firm [[Gibson Dunn]].<ref name=Schnell/><ref name=Dixon>{{cite news |last1=Dixon |first1=Matt |title=Judge who sided with Trump in Mar-a-Lago case had few high-profile cases |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2022/09/06/judge-mar-a-lago-trump-00055082 |access-date=December 11, 2022 |work=[[Politico]] |date=September 6, 2022 |archive-date=December 11, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221211060452/https://www.politico.com/news/2022/09/06/judge-mar-a-lago-trump-00055082 |url-status=live }}</ref> In one case in 2011, Cannon defended the former leader of the fixed income desk of [[Thomas Weisel Partners]], before the [[Financial Industry Regulatory Authority]]; the former leader was cleared of fraud in the case.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Chutchian |first1=Maria |title=FINRA Clears Thomas Weisel In $16M ARS 'Stuffing' Case |url=https://www.law360.com/articles/284826/finra-clears-thomas-weisel-in-16m-ars-stuffing-case |access-date=February 5, 2023 |work=[[Law360]] |date=November 9, 2011 |archive-date=February 5, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230205071431/https://www.law360.com/articles/284826/finra-clears-thomas-weisel-in-16m-ars-stuffing-case |url-status=live }}</ref>

From 2013 to 2020, Cannon was an [[assistant United States attorney]] for the Southern District of Florida.<ref name="could complicate"/> As a federal prosecutor, Cannon worked in the major crimes division, which included working on drug, firearm, and immigration cases, then moved to the appellate division, working on convictions and sentencings.<ref name=Wilner/><ref name=Marimow>{{cite news |last1=Marimow |first1=Ann |title=In ruling for Trump, low-profile judge Aileen Cannon invites scrutiny |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2022/09/09/who-is-judge-aileen-cannon/ |access-date=December 11, 2022 |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |date=September 9, 2022 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20220909214814/https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2022/09/09/who-is-judge-aileen-cannon/ |archive-date=September 9, 2022}}</ref> In 2018, Cannon was part of the prosecution that won an appellate case involving [[Mutual Benefits Corporation]]'s former lawyer Anthony Livoti Jr., reaffirming his 10-year sentence for fraud related to insurance investment.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Bolado |first1=Carolina |title=Ex-Mutual Benefits Atty Says Co. Wasn't A Ponzi Scheme |url=https://www.law360.com/articles/1038997/ex-mutual-benefits-atty-says-co-wasn-t-a-ponzi-scheme |access-date=February 5, 2023 |work=[[Law360]] |date=May 15, 2018 |archive-date=February 5, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230205070659/https://www.law360.com/articles/1038997/ex-mutual-benefits-atty-says-co-wasn-t-a-ponzi-scheme |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Seal |first1=Dean |title=11th Circ. Affirms Ex-Mutual Benefits Atty's 10-Year Sentence |url=https://www.law360.com/articles/1089509/11th-circ-affirms-ex-mutual-benefits-atty-s-10-year-sentence |access-date=February 5, 2023 |work=[[Law360]] |date=October 4, 2018 |archive-date=February 5, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230205072144/https://www.law360.com/articles/1089509/11th-circ-affirms-ex-mutual-benefits-atty-s-10-year-sentence |url-status=live }}</ref> In 2019, Cannon was part of the prosecution that won an appellate case involving [[Scott W. Rothstein]], which allowed prosecutors to withdraw support for reducing his 50-year sentence for a [[Ponzi scheme]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Hale |first1=Nathan |title=Ponzi Schemer Rothstein Loses Appeal To Trim Sentence |url=https://www.law360.com/articles/1204925/ponzi-schemer-rothstein-loses-appeal-to-trim-sentence |access-date=February 5, 2023 |work=[[Law360]] |date=October 1, 2019 |archive-date=February 5, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230205071818/https://www.law360.com/articles/1204925/ponzi-schemer-rothstein-loses-appeal-to-trim-sentence |url-status=live }}</ref> As a prosecutor, Cannon helped secure convictions for 41 defendants, of which four convictions were from jury trials.<ref name=Kragie/>

Cannon has participated in at least three events funded by [[George Mason University]], a conservative law school, which she did not disclose as required. These included legal colloquia at Sage Lodge in Pray, Montana in 2021 and 2022 and a banquet in 2023.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Thompson |first=Marilyn W. |author-link=Marilyn W. Thompson |last2=Mierjeski |first2=Alex |date=2024-09-17 |title=Judge Aileen Cannon Failed to Disclose a Right-Wing Junket |url=https://www.propublica.org/article/judge-aileen-cannon-trump-documents-case-travel-disclosures |access-date=2024-09-18 |website=ProPublica |language=en}}</ref>

===Notable cases===

It was reported in June 2021 that Cannon ordered Swiss cement company [[LafargeHolcim]] to reach a settlement to compensate an American family under the [[Helms-Burton Act]] for using the family's property in Cuba, which had been seized by the Cuban government in 1960. Before Cannon's order, no one had managed to secure compensation under the Helms-Burton Act for business property confiscated in Cuba.<ref>{{cite news |title=In historic first, Swiss firm settles suit by U.S. family over seized property in Cuba |url=https://www.tampabay.com/news/florida/2021/06/02/in-historic-first-swiss-firm-settles-suit-by-us-family-over-seized-property-in-cuba/ |access-date=February 5, 2023 |work=[[Miami Herald]] |date=June 2, 2021 |archive-date=February 5, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230205094203/https://www.tampabay.com/news/florida/2021/06/02/in-historic-first-swiss-firm-settles-suit-by-us-family-over-seized-property-in-cuba/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

In the case of Christopher Tavorris Wilkins, a 34-year-old man from [[Palm Beach Gardens]] who, in court, threw a chair at and threatened to kill a federal prosecutor, Cannon in April 2022 added six and a half years of imprisonment to his existing 17.5 year sentence for gun charges.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Musgrave |first1=Jane |title=Palm Beach Gardens man learns price of hurling chair at federal prosecutor |url=https://www.palmbeachpost.com/story/news/courts/2022/04/04/christopher-wilkins-punished-throwing-chair-prosecutor/9463460002/ |access-date=February 5, 2023 |work=[[Palm Beach Post]] |date=April 4, 2022 |archive-date=February 5, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230205092645/https://www.palmbeachpost.com/story/news/courts/2022/04/04/christopher-wilkins-punished-throwing-chair-prosecutor/9463460002/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In the case of Paul Vernon Hoeffer, a 60-year-old man from Palm Beach Gardens who pleaded guilty to making death threats against three Democrats: Speaker of the House [[Nancy Pelosi]], Representative [[Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez]], and prosecutor [[Kim Foxx]], with federal sentencing guidelines recommending 33 and 41 months in prison, and prosecutors proposing 41 months, Cannon in April 2022 sentenced Hoeffer to only 18 months in prison and then three years of supervised release, and also fined him just $2,000.<ref name=Tillman/><ref>{{cite news |last1=Gregorian |first1=Dareh |title=Florida man sentenced to 18 months in prison for Pelosi, AOC death threats |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/politics-news/florida-man-sentenced-18-months-prison-pelosi-aoc-death-threats-rcna22631 |access-date=September 24, 2022 |work=[[NBC News]] |date=April 2, 2022 |archive-date=September 24, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220924045631/https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/politics-news/florida-man-sentenced-18-months-prison-pelosi-aoc-death-threats-rcna22631 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Musgrave |first1=Jane |title=Palm Beach County man gets 18 month sentence for death threats to Nancy Pelosi, other top women |url=https://www.palmbeachpost.com/story/news/2022/04/04/paul-hoeffer-gets-18-months-death-threats-pelosi-other-top-women/7272040001/ |access-date=September 24, 2022 |work=[[The Palm Beach Post]] |date=April 4, 2022 |archive-date=November 29, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221129180257/https://www.palmbeachpost.com/story/news/2022/04/04/paul-hoeffer-gets-18-months-death-threats-pelosi-other-top-women/7272040001/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In the case of Juan Antonio Garcia, a 31-year-old former [[Sewall's Point]] police officer, Cannon in July 2022 sentenced him to 25 years in federal prison, a further 20 years of supervision, and a $10,000 fine for soliciting sex from a teenage boy. Sentencing guidelines imposed a range of between 15 years in prison to a life sentence, while federal prosecutors requested over 30 years imprisonment.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Holsman |first1=Melissa |title=Ex-Sewall's Point police officer ordered to prison in lewd texting case involving teen boy |url=https://www.tcpalm.com/story/news/crime/martin-county/2022/07/13/former-sewalls-point-police-officer-juan-garcia-ordered-prison/10040943002/ |access-date=February 5, 2023 |work=[[Treasure Coast Palm]] |date=July 13, 2022 |archive-date=February 5, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230205092137/https://www.tcpalm.com/story/news/crime/martin-county/2022/07/13/former-sewalls-point-police-officer-juan-garcia-ordered-prison/10040943002/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

In the ongoing 18 month-long case of ''United States v. Carver'', Cannon has presided over a complex, multi-defendant health care fraud case in which she has had to rule on issues of attorney-client privilege, defense attempts to suppress evidence or have charges dismissed, and motions to limit the scope of witness testimony. She has generally ruled in the prosecution's favor in each of these matters.<ref name="politico-carver">{{cite news | url=https://www.politico.com/news/2023/06/15/aileen-cannon-criminal-trial-record-00102135 | title=Trump judge's thin criminal trial resume comes with a twist | author-first=Kyle | author-last=Cheney | author-link=Kyle Cheney (journalist) | work=[[Politico]] | date=June 15, 2023 | access-date=June 15, 2023 | archive-date=June 20, 2024 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240620201633/https://www.politico.com/news/2023/06/15/aileen-cannon-criminal-trial-record-00102135 | url-status=live }}</ref>

In a 2023 federal trial of an Alabama man accused of running a child pornography website, Cannon closed the [[jury selection]] to the public on the basis of space restrictions and also failed to swear in the jury. This was described as "a fundamental constitutional error" by legal experts. According to court transcripts from June 12, 2023, Cannon was repeatedly asked by both prosecutors and the defense attorney to open the courtroom. The public defense attorney objected to closing the courtroom, arguing that doing so violates the [[Sixth Amendment to the United States Constitution|Sixth Amendment to the Constitution]], which Cannon overruled. She was forced to restart the jury selection process before the trial ended in a [[plea bargain]] without the jury deliberating. The courtroom in which this took place is the same one in which the 2024 criminal trial ''[[Federal prosecution of Donald Trump (classified documents case)|United States v. Trump]]'' was set to take place, which prompted concern from one legal scholar about how Cannon would handle space restrictions.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Lynch |first1=Sarah N. |last2=Thomsen |first2=Jacqueline |last3=Lynch |first3=Sarah N. |last4=Thomsen |first4=Jacqueline |date=2023-08-04 |title=Exclusive: Trump documents case judge made multiple errors in earlier trial |language=en |work=Reuters |url=https://www.reuters.com/legal/trump-documents-case-judge-made-multiple-errors-earlier-trial-2023-08-04/ |access-date=2023-08-04 |archive-date=August 4, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230804132448/https://www.reuters.com/legal/trump-documents-case-judge-made-multiple-errors-earlier-trial-2023-08-04/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

Cannon presided over the trial of [[Ryan Wesley Routh]], a North Carolina man who attempted to assassinate Trump in [[West Palm Beach, Florida|West Palm Beach]].<ref>{{cite news |url=https://news.sky.com/story/ryan-routh-man-accused-of-trying-to-assassinate-donald-trump-faces-trial-this-week-and-it-could-be-chaotic-13427067 |title=Ryan Routh: Man accused of trying to assassinate Donald Trump goes on trial - and it could be chaotic |date=8 September 2025 |newspaper=Sky News}}</ref> She sentenced Routh to life imprisonment on February 4, 2026.<ref>{{cite news |newspaper=The Guardian |date=4 February 2026 |title=Man who tried to assassinate Trump in Florida sentenced to life in prison |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/feb/04/trump-attempted-assassination-florida-life-sentence}}</ref>

Cannon was the subject of ethics complaints over her handling of this case, but the complaints were dismissed in December 2022 by the Eleventh Circuit's chief judge, [[William H. Pryor Jr.|William Pryor]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Zoppo |first1=Avalon |title=Judge Dismisses Ethics Complaints Accusing Aileen Cannon of Bias in Trump Special Master Order |url=https://www.law.com/nationallawjournal/2022/12/06/judge-dismisses-ethics-complaints-accusing-aileen-cannon-of-bias-in-trump-special-master-order/ |access-date=February 4, 2023 |work=[[The National Law Journal]] |publisher=[[ALM (company)|ALM]] |location=New York City |date=December 6, 2022 |archive-date=February 4, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230204025154/https://www.law.com/nationallawjournal/2022/12/06/judge-dismisses-ethics-complaints-accusing-aileen-cannon-of-bias-in-trump-special-master-order/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

Cannon allegedly received threats in September 2022. A woman from Houston was charged for allegedly leaving Cannon voicemails that stated that the caller was "Donald Trump's hitman, so consider it a bullet from Donald Trump himself" and also stated that "[y]ou’re helping him, ma’am ... He's marked for assassination and so are you". The criminal complaint against the Houston woman stated that she appears to "suffer from severe mental impairments with symptoms including paranoia and delusions".<ref>{{cite news |last1=Sganga |first1=Nicole |last2=Linton |first2=Caroline |title=Texas woman charged with threatening judge who approved Trump special master request |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/judge-aileen-cannon-threats-texas-woman-arrested-trump-special-master/ |access-date=February 4, 2023 |work=[[CBS News]] |date=September 12, 2022 |archive-date=February 4, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230204025255/https://www.cbsnews.com/news/judge-aileen-cannon-threats-texas-woman-arrested-trump-special-master/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Rabinowitz |first1=Hannah |title=Woman arrested for allegedly threatening judge in Mar-a-Lago documents case |url=https://edition.cnn.com/2022/09/12/politics/aileen-cannon-threat-arrest/index.html |access-date=February 4, 2023 |work=[[CNN]] |date=September 12, 2022 |archive-date=June 20, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240620202232/https://edition.cnn.com/2022/09/12/politics/aileen-cannon-threat-arrest/index.html |url-status=live }}</ref> On February 9, 2024, the woman pleaded guilty and was subject to 37 months in federal prison.<ref>{{Cite web |first=Zoë |last=Richards |date=2024-02-10 |title=Texas woman sentenced to 3 years in prison for death threats to judge in Trump's documents case |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/justice-department/texas-woman-gets-3-years-prison-death-threats-judge-trumps-documents-c-rcna138207 |access-date=2024-02-10 |website=NBC News |language=en |archive-date=February 11, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240211010231/https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/justice-department/texas-woman-gets-3-years-prison-death-threats-judge-trumps-documents-c-rcna138207 |url-status=live }}</ref>

====''United States v. Trump'', criminal case====
{{See also|Federal prosecution of Donald Trump (classified documents case)}}
Cannon was assigned in June 2023 to oversee the [[Federal prosecution of Donald Trump (government documents case)|criminal case against former president Donald Trump]]. After an inquiry by ''The New York Times'', the Southern District of Florida's chief clerk confirmed that the assignment was random.<ref name="The New York Times 2023 w265">{{cite news |first=Charlie |last=Savage | title=Judge Aileen Cannon, Who Showed Trump Favor, Gets Documents Case | website=The New York Times |date=June 9, 2023 29, 2023}}</ref><ref name="Bowden 2023 t948">{{cite web |last=Bowden |first=John |title=Trump-appointed judge will stay on Mar-a-Lago documents case unless she recuses |website=The Independent |date=2023-06-12 |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/americas/us-politics/judge-aileen-m-cannon-trump-indictment-b2355852.html |access-date=2023-06-29 |archive-date=June 29, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230629094312/https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/americas/us-politics/judge-aileen-m-cannon-trump-indictment-b2355852.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Yahoo News 2023 x931">{{cite web |first=Ben |last=Adler |title=Calls grow for Judge Aileen Cannon to recuse herself in Trump documents case |website=Yahoo News |date=2023-06-12 |url=https://news.yahoo.com/calls-grow-for-judge-aileen-cannon-to-recuse-herself-in-trump-documents-case-195348307.html |access-date=2023-06-29 |archive-date=June 29, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230629094311/https://news.yahoo.com/calls-grow-for-judge-aileen-cannon-to-recuse-herself-in-trump-documents-case-195348307.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Several legal experts called for Cannon to recuse herself.<ref name="Yahoo News 2023 x931"/> [[Stephen Gillers]], a professor emeritus at the [[New York University School of Law]], opined that Cannon should recuse from the criminal case, as "her impartiality might reasonably be questioned", due to her being "partial to Trump as a former President" in the previous civil case.<ref name=Chotiner>{{Cite magazine |last=Chotiner |first=Isaac |date=2023-06-12 |title=Will the Judge in Trump's Case Recuse Herself—or Be Forced To? |language=en-US |magazine=The New Yorker |url=https://www.newyorker.com/news/q-and-a/will-the-judge-in-trumps-case-recuse-herself-or-be-forced-to |access-date=2023-10-11 |issn=0028-792X |archive-date=October 13, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231013012102/https://www.newyorker.com/news/q-and-a/will-the-judge-in-trumps-case-recuse-herself-or-be-forced-to |url-status=live }}</ref> [[Richard Painter]], [[Norman Eisen]] and [[Fred Wertheimer]], former White House chief ethics lawyers and a good government advocate respectively, jointly called for Cannon's [[recusal]], citing her conduct in the previous civil case, which they described as "fundamentally erroneous ... went well outside the judicial norm and was roundly criticized by the Court of Appeals".<ref name="Yahoo News 2023 x931"/> [[Laurence Tribe]], a professor at [[Harvard Law School]], opined that the "historic trial ... should be, and should be seen to be, entirely unbiased and legally sound", but Cannon being the judge "would cast a long shadow over" the trial.<ref name="Yahoo News 2023 x931"/> However, there was no indication that Cannon would recuse herself, and she soon began issuing orders related to the examination of evidence in the case.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/06/15/us/politics/judge-trump-documents-security-clearances.html |url-status=live |title=Judge Orders Lawyers in Trump Case to Start Getting Security Clearances |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=June 15, 2023 |first1=Alan |last1=Feuer |first2=William |last2=Rashbaum |first3=Maggie |last3=Haberman |archive-url=https://archive.today/20230616234801/https://www.nytimes.com/2023/06/15/us/politics/judge-trump-documents-security-clearances.html |archive-date=June 16, 2023 |access-date=2 October 2024 }}</ref>

This criminal case arose from the [[FBI investigation into Donald Trump's handling of government documents|investigation into his handling of government documents]], which was the subject of a [[#Trump v. United States, civil case|civil case against Trump]] that Cannon coincidentally previously presided over.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Faulders |first1=Katherine |last2=Mallin |first2=Alexander |last3=Bruggeman |first3=Lucien |title=Judge Aileen Cannon, a Trump appointee, initially assigned to oversee his case: Sources |url=https://abcnews.go.com/US/judge-aileen-cannon-trump-appointee-initially-assigned-oversee/story?id=99956910 |access-date=June 10, 2023 |work=[[ABC News (United States)|ABC News]] |date=June 9, 2023 |archive-date=June 9, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230609235323/https://abcnews.go.com/US/judge-aileen-cannon-trump-appointee-initially-assigned-oversee/story?id=99956910 |url-status=live }}</ref> In June 2023, ''The New York Times'' analysed records by [[Bloomberg Law]] of Cannon's handling of criminal cases as a federal judge, finding that before Trump's criminal case, she had presided over 224 criminal cases, of which only four criminal cases went to trial, with a cumulative 14 trial days.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Schmidt |first1=Michael |last2=Savage |first2=Charlie |title=Judge in Trump Documents Case Has Scant Criminal Trial Experience |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/06/14/us/politics/aileen-cannon-judge-trump-documents.html |access-date=June 16, 2023 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=June 14, 2023 |archive-date=June 16, 2023 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20230616010716/https://www.nytimes.com/2023/06/14/us/politics/aileen-cannon-judge-trump-documents.html |url-status=live }}</ref> However ''[[Politico]]'' noted that the ongoing ''Carver'' case, slated for trial in July 2023, featured many of the kinds of pretrial motions and procedures that this case would be expected to see.<ref name="politico-carver"/>

In late June 2023, Cannon ruled against the Department of Justice, denying its request to keep the identities of 84 potential witnesses under seal.<ref name="Guardian June 26, 2023">{{Cite news |last1=Lowell |first1=Hugo |date=June 26, 2023 |title=List of witnesses against Trump cannot be secret in documents case, judge rules |language=en-US |work=The Guardian |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2023/jun/26/donald-trump-witnesses-classified-documents-judge |url-status=live |access-date=June 26, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230627080817/https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2023/jun/26/donald-trump-witnesses-classified-documents-judge |archive-date=June 27, 2023 }}</ref>  In August 2023, Cannon ruled in favor of Trump on the issue of potential conflicts of interest regarding co-defendant [[Walt Nauta]]'s lawyer [[Stanley Woodward (attorney)|Stanley Woodward]] representation of possible witnesses in the case. She rejected the notion that sealed filings were required "to comport with [[grand jury]] secrecy", striking two sealed filings by prosecutors from the court record. Instead, Cannon instructed Woodward and prosecutors to discuss "the legal propriety of using an out-of-district grand jury proceeding" to continue actions in this federal case.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Sharp |first1=Rachel |title=Trump-appointed Judge Aileen Cannon sides with Trump again in classified documents case |url=https://www.the-independent.com/news/world/americas/us-politics/trump-judge-aileen-cannon-court-ruling-b2389395.html |access-date=September 2, 2023 |work=[[The Independent]] |date=August 8, 2023 |archive-date=June 20, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240620202129/https://www.the-independent.com/news/world/americas/us-politics/trump-judge-aileen-cannon-court-ruling-b2389395.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Mallin |first1=Alexander |title=Judge in Trump's classified documents case questions use of out-of-district grand jury in probe |url=https://abcnews.go.com/US/judge-trumps-classified-documents-case-questions-district-grand/story?id=102072911 |access-date=September 2, 2023 |work=[[ABC News (United States)|ABC News]] |date=August 8, 2023 |archive-date=September 2, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230902104724/https://abcnews.go.com/US/judge-trumps-classified-documents-case-questions-district-grand/story?id=102072911 |url-status=live }}</ref> Several legal experts, including notable constitutional scholar Harvard Professor [[Laurence Tribe]], as well as notable former federal prosecutors [[Andrew Weissmann]] and [[Joyce Vance]], indicated that the propriety of the grand jury proceedings were obvious, and that Cannon's questioning of their propriety was alarming.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.vanityfair.com/news/2023/08/egal-experts-blast-judge-aileen-cannons-latest-pro-trump-rulings|title='Dopey and Constitutionally Dubious': Legal Experts Blast Judge Aileen Cannon's Latest Pro-Trump Rulings|date=August 8, 2023|website=[[Vanity Fair (magazine)|Vanity Fair]]|access-date=October 17, 2023|first1=Bess|last1=Levin|archive-date=August 8, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230808235108/https://www.vanityfair.com/news/2023/08/egal-experts-blast-judge-aileen-cannons-latest-pro-trump-rulings|url-status=live}}</ref>

After Trump's legal team in September 2023 requested an extension to the case, Cannon delayed a crucial pre-trial hearing on the [[Classified Information Procedures Act]] (CIPA) from October 2023 to February 2024, while also ruling that she would only ponder on further scheduling in March 2024.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Faulders |first1=Katherine |title=Judge pauses litigation in classified docs case while mulling Trump's request for extension |url=https://abcnews.go.com/US/judge-pauses-litigation-classified-docs-case-mulling-trumps/story?id=103788426 |access-date=October 7, 2023 |work=[[ABC News (United States)|ABC News]] |date=October 7, 2023 |archive-date=October 6, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231006234555/https://abcnews.go.com/US/judge-pauses-litigation-classified-docs-case-mulling-trumps/story?id=103788426 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Lowell |first1=Hugo |title=Trump classified documents trial running about four months behind schedule |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2023/nov/17/trump-classified-documents-trial-delay |access-date=November 20, 2023 |work=[[The Guardian]] |date=November 17, 2023 |archive-date=June 20, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240620202153/https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2023/nov/17/trump-classified-documents-trial-delay |url-status=live }}</ref> While prosecutors asked for a CIPA hearing in March and the defense teams requested for June, Cannon decided in April that the new hearing date should be in May, but when that date approached, the defense teams again requested delay, so Cannon in May granted the defense teams' earlier request of June CIPA hearings.<ref name=Play/><ref name=blown/> ''Politico'' reported that Cannon "has run the pretrial process at a leisurely pace that will make a postponement [of the scheduled May 2024 trial] almost inevitable, according to experts on criminal prosecutions related to classified information"; ''Politico'' further states that if the trial is postponed to after the [[2024 United States presidential election]], Trump could become president and would then be "expected" to instruct the Justice Department to end the case.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Gerstein |first1=Josh |title=How one judge is slowing down one of Trump's biggest criminal cases |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2023/11/22/aileen-cannon-trump-trial-slow-00128391 |access-date=November 23, 2023 |work=[[Politico]] |date=November 22, 2023}}</ref>

In February 2024, Cannon granted Trump's team's motion for the names of witnesses in this case and their testimony to be publicly revealed; this caused the government's prosecutors to ask Cannon to reconsider, citing "significant and immediate risks of threats, intimidation, and harassment" which has been seen in other Trump cases.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Beitsch |first1=Rebecca |title=Special counsel fights judge's order allowing Trump to reveal witness identities in Mar-a-Lago case |url=https://thehill.com/regulation/court-battles/4458476-special-counsel-fights-judges-order-allowing-trump-to-reveal-witness-identities-in-mar-a-lago-case/ |access-date=February 12, 2024 |work=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]] |date=February 9, 2024 |archive-date=February 10, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240210024204/https://thehill.com/regulation/court-battles/4458476-special-counsel-fights-judges-order-allowing-trump-to-reveal-witness-identities-in-mar-a-lago-case/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Garrison |first1=Steve |title=Feds say Mar-a-Lago witnesses face 'significant risks' if identified |url=https://www.courthousenews.com/feds-say-mar-a-lago-witnesses-face-significant-risks-if-identified/ |access-date=February 12, 2024 |work=[[Courthouse News]] |date=February 9, 2024}}</ref> In March 2024, a witness in the case ("Trump Employee 5") and former Mar-a-Lago employee, Brian Butler, identified himself in a media interview and told his story about the incident, citing that in preparation for Cannon's plan to publicize the witness names, he would rather tell his story than "just waiting for it to come out ... I think it's better to at least say what happened than it coming out in the news, people calling me crazy. I'd rather just get it out there."<ref>{{cite news |last1=Fins |first1=Antonio |title=Trump may appear in Fort Pierce federal court today for documents case |url=https://www.palmbeachpost.com/story/news/trump/2024/03/13/trump-legal-cases-before-fort-pierce-federal-court-documents-hearing/72956949007/ |url-status=dead |access-date=April 10, 2024 |work=[[Palm Beach Post]] |date=March 14, 2024 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20240410134909/https://www.palmbeachpost.com/story/news/trump/2024/03/13/trump-legal-cases-before-fort-pierce-federal-court-documents-hearing/72956949007/ |archive-date=April 10, 2024}}</ref> In April 2024, Cannon agreed to censor the potential witnesses' names, but not their statements, from the public; ''Politico'' wrote that it was the "latest decision in which Cannon has sided with prosecutors in an opinion that is primarily critical of their tactics", with Cannon criticizing prosecutors' speed, compliance and basis for their arguments.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Gerstein |first1=Josh |last2=Cheney |first2=Kyle |author-link2=Kyle Cheney (journalist) |title=Siding with special counsel, Cannon agrees to keep witness identities secret |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2024/04/09/cannon-agrees-to-keep-witness-identities-secret-00151402?s=09 |access-date=April 10, 2024 |work=[[Politico]] |date=April 9, 2024 |archive-date=May 8, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240508205041/https://www.politico.com/news/2024/04/09/cannon-agrees-to-keep-witness-identities-secret-00151402?s=09 |url-status=live }}</ref>

In March 2024, Cannon denied without prejudice an attempt by Trump to dismiss the case.<ref>{{cite news |title=Federal judge denies Trump's effort to dismiss classified documents case |url=https://ny1.com/nyc/all-boroughs/politics/2024/03/14/judge-hearing-dismiss-trump-classified-documents-prosecution |access-date=May 8, 2024 |work=[[ny1.com]] |agency=[[Associated Press]] |date=March 14, 2024 |archive-date=May 8, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240508135314/https://ny1.com/nyc/all-boroughs/politics/2024/03/14/judge-hearing-dismiss-trump-classified-documents-prosecution |url-status=live }}</ref> She wrote that Trump's team had raised "various arguments warranting serious consideration", then indicated that the Trump team's arguments about the [[Espionage Act]] being [[Vagueness doctrine|too vague]] could instead be brought up again later in "connection with jury-instruction briefing".<ref>{{cite news |last1=Feuer |first1=Alan |title=Judge Denies One of Trump's Efforts to Derail Documents Case |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/03/14/us/politics/trump-classified-documents-case.html |access-date=May 8, 2024 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=March 14, 2024 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20240315043207/https://www.nytimes.com/2024/03/14/us/politics/trump-classified-documents-case.html |url-status=live |archive-date=March 15, 2024}}</ref> After Trump's team argued that the [[Presidential Records Act]] allowed Trump to retain classified documents, Cannon instructed both prosecutors and Trump's team to craft hypothetical jury instructions regarding the Presidential Records Act, in an action that perplexed observing lawyers and former judges.<ref name=flummoxed>{{cite news |last1=Barrett |first1=Devlin |last2=Stein |first2=Perry |title='Very, very troubling': Judges, lawyers flummoxed by Judge Cannon |url-status=live |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/national-security/2024/03/20/trump-cannon-judge-pra-jury-instructions/ |access-date=May 8, 2024 |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |date=March 20, 2024 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20240416145956/https://www.washingtonpost.com/national-security/2024/03/20/trump-cannon-judge-pra-jury-instructions/ |archive-date=April 16, 2024}}</ref> [[Barbara McQuade]], a law professor and former federal prosecutor, opined that the Presidential Records Act "is just not relevant here in any way it all; it provides no defense. To even allow it to be argued at trial would create confusion for the jury", while former federal judge [[Nancy Gertner]] commented that Cannon's instruction was "very troubling" because it was "giving credence to arguments that are on their face absurd".<ref name=flummoxed/> In April 2024, Cannon denied another motion by Trump to dismiss the case, stating that "the Presidential Records Act does not provide a pre-trial basis to dismiss", while criticizing as "unprecedented and unjust" the prosecutors' request for her to elaborate on whether her jury instructions would include the Presidential Records Act.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Legare |first1=Robert |title=Judge denies Trump's motion to dismiss documents case |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/trump-documents-case-judge-denies-trumps-motion-to-dismiss/ |access-date=May 8, 2024 |work=[[CBS News]] |date=April 4, 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Gerstein |first1=Josh |last2=Cheney |first2=Kyle |author-link2=Kyle Cheney (journalist) |title=Judge denies, for now, a Trump bid to dismiss charges that he hoarded classified documents |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2024/04/04/donald-trump-classified-docs-case-00150642 |access-date=May 8, 2024 |work=[[Politico]] |date=April 4, 2024 |archive-date=May 8, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240508150523/https://www.politico.com/news/2024/04/04/donald-trump-classified-docs-case-00150642 |url-status=live }}</ref>

After the March 2024 hearing on postponing the May 20, 2024 trial, Cannon took until May 7, 2024, to issue an update on the matter.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Cheney |first1=Kyle |author-link1=Kyle Cheney (journalist) |title=Judge Cannon indefinitely postpones Trump's classified docs trial |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2024/05/07/trump-classified-docs-trial-delay-florida-00156680 |access-date=May |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240508005958/https://www.politico.com/news/2024/05/07/trump-classified-docs-trial-delay-florida-00156680 |url-status=live }}</ref> Cannon ruled to indefinitely postpone the trial, citing many pre-trial matters to settle.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Stein |first1=Perry |last2=Barrett |first2=Devlin |title=Judge indefinitely delays Trump's classified documents trial in Florida |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/national-security/2024/05/07/trump-classified-documents-trial-delayed-cannon-florida/ |newspaper=Washington Post |date=7 May 2024 |access-date=2 October 2024 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |first1=Katelyn |last1=Polantz |first2=Hannah |last2=Rabinowitz |first3=Holmes |last3=Lybrand |first4=Tierney |last4=Sneed |title=Federal judge |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240507214417/https://www.cnn.com/2024/05/07/politics/judge-postpones-trump-classified-documents-trial/index.html |url-status=live }}</ref> She accepted Trump's requests to have pre-trial hearings on the appropriateness of the appointment of the special counsel and the potential expansion of recognizing more government agencies as part of the prosecution, which would allow Trump to conduct the [[Discovery (law)|discovery]] process on them.<ref name=Lowell /> Cannon scheduled pre-trial activities to continue up to July 22, 2024, at the earliest.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Jansen |first1=Bart |title=Judge Cannon indefinitely postpones Donald Trump's trial for classified document retention While Donald Trump has continually denounced many of the judges presiding over his legal cases, including [[Tanya Chutkan]], [[Arthur Engoron]] and [[Juan Merchan]], he has not criticized Cannon.<ref Trump has described Cannon as a "highly respected", "very smart", and "very strong judge".<ref>{{cite news |last1=Samuels |first1=Brett |title=Trump praises judge overseeing his classified documents case, saying she 'loves our country' |url=https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/4100155-trump-praises-judge-overseeing-his-classified-documents-case-loves-our-country/ |access-date=May 9, 2024 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Barrett |first1=Devlin |last2=Stein |first2=Perry |title=Trump defends Judge Cannon in fight over classified documents trial 2024}}</ref> ''The Washington Post'' stated in May 2024 that Cannon's "rulings are generally hailed as uniquely wise" by Trump supporters, and she has "been celebrated by adherents of the [[QAnon]] Then his fans call for violence. |url=https://www.reuters.com/investigates/special-report/usa-election-threats-courts/ |access-date=May 15, 2024 |work=[[Reuters]] |date=May 14, 2024 |archive-date=May 16, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240516235921/https://www.reuters.com/investigates/special-report/usa-election-threats-courts/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

After Trump in fundraising emails claimed that during the Mar-a-Lago raid, "Biden's DOJ was authorized to shoot me!" and that Biden was "locked & loaded ready to take me out", prosecutors requested for a gag order on Trump pertaining to law enforcement.<ref name="CNN gag order request">{{Cite news |date=May 24, 2024 |first=Katelyn |last=Polantz |title=Special counsel asks judge for gag order in Trump classified documents case |work=CNN |url=https://edition.cnn.com/2024/05/24/politics/trump-gag-order-trump-classified-documents/index.html |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240525035315/https://edition.cnn.com/2024/05/24/politics/trump-gag-order-trump-classified-documents/index.html |archive-date=May 25, 2024 |url-status=live |access-date=2 October 2024 }}</ref><ref name=Doyle/> Cannon in May 2024 responded by denying the prosecutors' request and instead accusing the prosecutors of being "wholly lacking in substance and professional courtesy" when discussing the issue with the defense team.<ref name=Doyle>{{cite news |last1=Doyle |first1=Katherine |title=Judge denies special counsel's request to impose gag order on Trump over false claim about FBI raid |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/news/rcna154340 |access-date=May 29, 2024 |work=[[NBC News]] |date=May 28, 2024 |archive-date=May 29, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240529002710/https://www.nbcnews.com/news/rcna154340 |url-status=live }}</ref>

On June 20, 2024, ''[[The New York Times]]'' reported that shortly after being assigned the case, two federal judges in South Florida, including the chief judge, [[Cecilia Altonaga]], privately urged Cannon to decline the case and pass it on to other jurists. However, Cannon had not taken their advice.<ref name="NYT June 20, 2024">{{Cite news |last1=Savage |first1=Charlie |last2=Feuer |first2=Alan |date=June 20, 2024 |title=Judge in Trump Documents Case Rejected Suggestions to Step Aside |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/06/20/us/politics/aileen-cannon-trump-classified-documents.html |access-date=2024-06-20 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref name="Guardian June 20, 2024">{{cite web|last=Tait|first=Robert|date=June 20, 2024|url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/article/2024/jun/20/aileen-cannon-trump-classified-documents-case|title=Judge in Trump classified documents case reportedly refused to step aside|work=The Guardian |access-date=2 October 2024}}</ref> Cannon was specifically advised to transfer the case to a jurist in Miami, where they already had a secure facility in which to store and review the sensitive documents, but she declined, and so a new facility had to be constructed at Fort Pierce, at taxpayers' expense.<ref name="Guardian June 20, 2024" />

On July 15, 2024, Cannon dismissed the case against Trump, ruling that "Special Counsel Smith’s appointment violates the [[Appointments Clause]] of the United States Constitution", with a rationale mirroring that of Supreme Court Justice [[Clarence Thomas]]' concurrence in a closely timed case involving Trump.<ref name="Carrie">{{cite news |last1=Johnson |first1=Carrie |title=Judge Cannon dismisses Trump documents case |url=https://www.npr.org/2024/07/15/g-s1-10379/trump-documents-case-dismissed |access-date=July 15, 2024 |work=[[NPR]] |date=July 15, 2024}}</ref> Another decision that invited intense scrutiny from legal commentators and the general public alike, the dismissal incited calls from [[Monica Lewinsky]] for Congress to [[Impeachment in the United States|impeach]] Cannon.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Jouvenal |first=Justin |date=2024-07-16 |title=Dismissal draws new scrutiny to Judge Cannon's handling of Trump case |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/national-security/2024/07/15/judge-cannon-trump-appointee-dismissal/ |access-date=2024-07-16 |newspaper=Washington Post |language=en-US |issn=0190-8286}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Rosenzweig |first=Paul |date=2024-07-15 |title=Judge Cannon Has Gotten It Completely Wrong |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/archive/2024/07/cannon-dismissed-trump-classified-documents/679023/ |access-date=2024-07-16 |website=The Atlantic |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Kochi |first=Sudiksha |title=Monica Lewinsky wants Judge Aileen Cannon overseeing Trump classified docs case impeached |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/elections/2024/06/25/monica-lewinsky-aileen-cannon-impeached/74207722007/ |date=25 June 2024 |access-date=2024-07-16 |website=USA Today |language=en-US}}</ref> Following the re-election of Trump to the presidency, [[Ty Cobb (attorney)|Ty Cobb]] referred to how the ruling could impact future dealings between Trump and the Department of Justice, referring to Cannon as Trump's "pet judge".<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.cnn.com/2024/11/25/politics/video/ty-cobb-trump-retribution-ebof-digvid |publisher=CNN |title=Ty Cobb on what Trump would need to get retribution against special counsel}}</ref>

Trump won the November [[2024 U.S. presidential election]] to secure a second term beginning January 20, 2025.<ref>{{cite news |title=Special counsel who led Trump prosecutions leaves US Justice Department |url=https://www.lemonde.fr/en/united-states/article/2025/01/12/special-counsel-who-led-trump-prosecutions-leaves-us-justice-dept_6736956_133.html |access-date=15 January 2025 |work=[[Le |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250115133841/https://www.lemonde.fr/en/united-states/article/2025/01/12/special-counsel-who-led-trump-prosecutions-leaves-us-justice-dept_6736956_133.html |archive-date=January 15, 2025}}</ref> Cannon on January 7, 2025 ordered Jack Smith, his subordinates, Attorney General [[Merrick Garland]], and the Department of Justice not to release Smith's report on Trump's classified documents case until three days after the 11th Circuit ruled on whether the report could be released (unless the 11th Circuit ordered otherwise).<ref>{{cite news |last1=Gerstein |first1=Josh |title=Cannon temporarily blocks release of Jack Smith report |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2025/01/07/aileen-cannon-blocks-jack-smith-report-release-00196863 |access-date=January 8, 2025 |work=Politico |date=January 7, 2025}}</ref><ref name="Dareh">{{cite news |last1=Barnes |first1=Daniel |last2=Gregorian |first2=Dareh |title=Judge blocks release of special counsel report on Trump's criminal cases |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/news/rcna186604 |access-date=January 8, 2025 |work=NBC News |date=January 7, 2025}}</ref> Cannon intervened after Trump (no longer a defendant) and defendants Walt Nauta and Carlos De Oliveira urged her to block Smith's report.<ref name=Dareh/> In reaction to Cannon's order, Trump responded that Cannon was a "brilliant judge with great courage".<ref>{{cite news |last1=Geoghegan |first1=Tom |first2=James |last2=FitzGerald |first3=Kayla |last3=Epstein |title=Judge blocks release of special counsel's report on Trump |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c99xe7m0vnpo |access-date=January 8, 2025 |work=BBC News |date=January 7, 2025}}</ref> The 11th Circuit on January 9, 2025 declined to block the release of Smith's report.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Beitsch |first1=Rebecca |title=Appeals court denies Trump's bid to block release of Smith Jan. 6 report |url=https://thehill.com/homenews/5078198-appeals-court-denies-trump-bid-to-block-release-of-smith-jan-6-report |access-date=January 10, 2025 |work=The Hill |date=January 9, 2024}}</ref> 

On January 13, 2025, Cannon declined to block the release of Volume I of Smith's report beyond that day; Volume I describes Trump's actions after the 2020 election interfering with the peaceful transfer of power.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Beitsch |first1=Rebecca |title=Cannon allows for release of Smith report on Trump election interference |url=https://thehill.com/regulation/court-battles/5082606-us-district-court-orders-release/ |access-date=January 14, 2025 |work=The Hill |date=January 13, 2025}}</ref> Simultaneously, Cannon blocked the release of Volume II of Smith's report and arranged for a hearing on January 17; Volume II describes the classified documents case and the Department of Justice had proposed sharing it with some members of Congress.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Richer |first1=Alanna |last2=Tucker |first2=Eric |title=Judge clears the way for release of special counsel Smith's report on Trump's 2020 election case |url=https://apnews.com/article/trump-special-counsel-aileen-cannon-d7be86dad89227f12a6f5aac3433b202 |access-date=January 14, 2025 |work=Associated Press |date=January 14, 2025}}</ref> Trump again requested that Cannon block Volume I, but she rejected his request.<ref>{{cite news |first1=Katherine |last1=Faulders |first2=Alexander |last2=Mallin |first3=Peter |last3=Charalambous |first4=Olivia |last4=Rubin |title=Judge denies Trump's last-ditch effort to block midnight release of Jack Smith's final report |url=https://abcnews.go.com/US/trumps-former-defendants-continue-push-block-release-jack/story?id=117620958 |access-date=January 14, 2025 |work=ABC News |date=January 13, 2025}}</ref> In early November, an appeals court unanimously ruled that Cannon delay in ruling on motions to unblock the release of Volume II was "undue delay", and gave her 60 days to act.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Savage |first=Charlie |date=November 23, 2025 |title=As Trump's Inquisitors Face Scrutiny, a Divisive Figure Could Play a New Role |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/11/23/us/politics/trump-florida-cannon-grand-jury.html |access-date=November 23, 2025 |work=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=November 3, 2025 |title=USCA11 Case: 25-13400, In re: AMERICAN OVERSIGHT, In re: KNIGHT FIRST AMENDMENT INSTITUTE AT COLUMBIA UNIVERSITY, |url=https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.ca11.93245/gov.uscourts.ca11.93245.11.0.pdf |access-date=November 23, 2025}}</ref>

On February 23, 2026, Cannon ruled that Smith's final report will not be released, arguing that "it is certainly not customary" for a prosecutor whose case was thrown out to later be allowed to "publicly disseminate large swaths of discovery generated in the case."<ref>{{cite news |last=Cole|first=Devan |date=February 23, 2026 |title=Judge Aileen Cannon bars the release of special counsel report on Trump’s handling of classified documents  |url=https://edition.cnn.com/2026/02/23/politics/aileen-cannon-jack-smith-special-counsel-volume-2-trump-documents |work=[[CNN]]|access-date=February 23, 2026}}</ref>

==Personal life==

Cannon married restaurant executive Josh Lorence in 2008.<ref name=Mazzei/> They have two children and live in [[Vero Beach, Florida]], as of 2022.<ref name=Mazzei/> Cannon is a registered [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]].<ref name="Mazzei" /> She donated $100 to [[Ron DeSantis]]'s gubernatorial campaign in 2018.<ref name=Mazzei/>

[[University of Miami School of Law|University of Miami]] ([[Master of Laws|LLM]]) | footnotes = }} '''Alan Stephen Gold''' (born January 8, 1944) is an inactive [[Senior Status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida]]. ==Early life and education== Gold was born in 1944 in [[New York City]]. He attended [[Miami Beach High School]]. Gold received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] [[Academic degree|degree]] from the [[University of Florida]] in 1966, a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Duke University School of Law]] in 1969, and a [[Master of Laws]] from the [[University of Miami School of Law]] in 1974. ==Career== Gold served as a [[Law clerk|research assistant]] to Judge Charles Carroll of the [[Florida Third District Court of Appeal]] from 1969 to 1970. He was briefly in private practice in [[Miami]] in 1970, before serving as assistant county attorney in the [[Miami-Dade County, Florida|Dade County]] Attorney's Office from 1971 to 1975. ===Federal judicial service=== President [[Bill Clinton]] nominated Gold to the United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida on February 12, 1997, to the seat vacated by Judge [[Jose Alejandro Gonzalez Jr.]] During Gold's confirmation hearings before the Senate, he surprised many when, after being asked which [[Supreme Court of the United States|Supreme Court]] decision troubled him most, he named ''[[Griswold v. Connecticut]]''.{{Cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1997/05/18/weekinreview/impeach-those-liberal-judges-where-are-they.html|title=Impeach Those Liberal Judges! Where Are They?|first=Neil A.|last=Lewis|date=May 18, 1997|via=NYTimes.com}} He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate|Senate]] on June 27, 1997 and received his commission on July 1, 1997. He assumed [[senior status]] on January 10, 2011.{{FJC Bio|nid=1390486|inline=yes}} ===Notable rulings=== During his service on the district court Gold has heard cases including the trial of [[Alberto Gutman]], the [[Political corruption|corruption]] and [[Conspiracy (crime)|conspiracy]] trial of 11 former [[Miami, Florida Police Department|Miami Police Department]] officers[https://www.nytimes.com/2003/04/09/us/partial-verdicts-in-miami-in-police-corruption-trial-182389.html] and a [[racketeering]] and [[fraud]] [[lawsuit]] against [[DuPont]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2001/08/25/business/judge-supports-dupont-in-crop-case.html|title=Judge Supports DuPont in Crop Case|agency=Associated Press|date=August 25, 2001|via=NYTimes.com}} Gold also issued an [[injunction]] in favor of the [[American Civil Liberties Union]] of Florida against the [[Miami-Dade County Public Schools]] in a lawsuit challenging the [[school board]] decision to remove the book ''[[Vamos a Cuba]]'' from school libraries after the book had been challenged by [[Cuban exile]]s.{{Cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2006/07/25/education/25brfs-003.html|title=Judge Blocks Miami Ban on Children's Book|first=Terry|last=Aguayo|date=July 25, 2006|via=NYTimes.com}} Gold also presided over a case involving ten Coral Gables/University of Miami Police officers who were suing the University of Miami for employment related matters along with claims of misreporting crime statistics and police corruption . He dismissed that case on summary judgment in favor of the University, yet failed to disclose to the officers or their counsel (as required by federal statute and judicial rules and canons) the facts that 1) he listed the University as a source of non-investment income on his Federal Financial Disclosure forms for the years he presided over the case; 2) he failed to disclose that his wife was a high level employee of the University during those same years he presided over the case; and 3) his law clerk, was also a paid legal writing instructor at the University's School of Law, again, during the time he presided over the case; and 4)he was a former employee of the University. The officers once this was discovered, but after Gold had already dismissed their case, filed a motion for recusal against Gold and a motion to reopen the case and attached copies of all of the documents supporting their motion.99-CV-02443-ASG - docket entry 346{{better source needed|date=April 2024}} The chief judge ruled that Gold did nothing wrong by not disclosing those details.{{citation needed|date=April 2024}} ==See also== * [[List of Jewish American jurists]] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==Sources== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1390486}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Jose Alejandro Gonzalez Jr.]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida]]}}|years=1997–2011}} {{s-aft|after=[[Robin S.
