[[Vanderbilt University]] ([[Master of Arts in Teaching|MAT]], [[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Aleta Mae Grillos Arthur Trauger'''{{Cite AV media |title=[#107] Judge Aleta Arthur Trauger - TBF Legal History Project |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8T0CLdi-I9U |date=2019-05-01 |last=Cottrell |first=Patricia J. |type=Oral history project interview |language=en |publisher=Tennessee Bar Foundation |place=Nashville, TN |series=Tennessee Bar Foundation Legal History Project |access-date=2024-05-01 |via=[[YouTube]]}}{{rp|0:1:06}} (born 1945){{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VWG8Cd_qvg8C&q=aleta+trauger+born+december+9%2C+1945&pg=PA552|title=Confirmation Hearings on Federal Appointments: Hearings Before the Committee on the Judiciary, United States Senate, One Hundred Fifth Congress, First Session, on Confirmation of Appointees to the Federal Judiciary|first=United States Congress Senate Committee on the|last=Judiciary|date=September 11, 1997|publisher=U.S. Government Printing Office|isbn=9780160386190 |via=Google Books}} is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee]]. ==Education and career== Trauger was born in [[Denver, Colorado]]. She received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in [[English studies|English]] from [[Cornell College]] in 1968, a [[Master of Arts in Teaching]] from [[Vanderbilt University]] in 1972, and a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Vanderbilt University Law School]] in 1976.{{FJC Bio|nid=1390866}} She was a [[law clerk]] and associate in private practice at Barrett Brandt & Barrett in [[Tennessee]] from 1974 to 1977. She began working there while a first-year law student.{{cite web |last=Rexroat |first=Dee Ann |date=November 2019 |title=Aleta Grillos Trauger ’68: Legal pioneer |url=https://news.cornellcollege.edu/2019/11/aleta-grillos-trauger-68-legal-pioneer-report/ |website=[[Cornell College]] |access-date=2024-05-01}} In late 1977, [[United States Attorney|U.S. Attorney]] Hal Hardin hired her as a federal prosecutor; she served as an [[Assistant United States Attorney]] in the Middle District of Tennessee from 1977 to 1979 and from 1980 to 1982, serving in the Northern District of Illinois from 1979 to 1980. In 1981, alongside Bob Lynch Jr, she prosecuted former [[Governor of Tennessee|Tennessee Governor]] [[Ray Blanton|Leonard Ray Blanton]] for [[extortion]], [[conspiracy]], and [[mail fraud]] relating to Blanton's sale of [[liquor license]]s to his friends.{{cite web |date=2024-03-26 |title=Judge Aleta Trauger Opened Doors for Women in Law |url=https://www.uscourts.gov/news/2024/03/26/judge-aleta-trauger-opened-doors-women-law |website=United States Courts |access-date=2024-05-01}} Trauger has credited this case with establishing her reputation and credibility in a male-dominated profession. She was in private practice from 1983 to 1984, and again from 1984 to 1985, returning to private practice from 1985 to 1991. In 1983, Trauger worked as in-house legal counsel for the [[College of Charleston]], the first person to hold the position.{{cite web |title=FJA Officers and Board of Directors {{!}} Executive Committee |url=https://federaljudgesassoc.org/who-we-are/officers-and-board-of-directors/ |website=Federal Judges Association |access-date=2024-05-01}} She was one of the founding members of the Tennessee Lawyers' Association for Women, established July 7, 1989. Trauger served as [[Nashville, Tennessee|Nashville]] Mayor [[Phil Bredesen]]'s first [[chief of staff]] in 1991, leaving the position when she and husband Byron Trauger adopted a baby. ===Federal judicial service=== From 1993 to 1998, she was a [[United States bankruptcy court|United States bankruptcy judge]] for the Middle District of Tennessee. On September 22, 1998, President [[Bill Clinton]] nominated Trauger to a seat on the United States District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee vacated by Judge [[John Trice Nixon]]. She was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on October 21, 1998, and received her commission on October 22, 1998. This made her the first female U.S. District Judge in the Middle District of Tennessee.{{cite web |last=Robertson |first=Seth |date=2016-10-27 |title=Judge Aleta Trauger: Distinguished Service Award Winner |url=https://law.vanderbilt.edu/judge-aleta-trauger-distinguished-service-award-winner/ |website=[[Vanderbilt University Law School]] |access-date=2024-05-01}} ==Notable cases== On March 22, 2000, Trauger heard her first case from the District bench involving the [[Capital punishment|death penalty]]. In the case of ''State of Tennessee v. [[Robert Glen Coe]]'', Trauger issued a stay a mere 16 hours prior to his scheduled execution.{{cite news |date=2000-03-29 |title=Coe Set To Die Next Week |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/coe-set-to-die-next-week/ |newspaper=[[CBS News]] |access-date=2024-05-01}} Coe's attorneys had claimed he was not mentally competent, but did not prove that to Trauger's satisfaction, so she lifted the stay. The [[Tennessee Supreme Court]] then issued a decree setting Coe's execution date for April 5, 2000; Tennessee had not executed an inmate since 1960 when the case came before Trauger.{{cite news |date=2000-03-22 |title=Condemned Tenn. Man Gets Stay |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/condemned-tenn-man-gets-stay/ |newspaper=[[CBS News]] |access-date=2024-05-01}} On March 14, 2014, in the case ''Tanco, et al. v. Haslam, et al.'', Trauger issued a [[Injunction|preliminary injunction]] ordering Tennessee to recognize the marriages of three [[Same-sex relationship|same-sex couples]] consummated out-of-state. In her ruling, Trauger did not directly hold Tennessee's ban [[Constitutionality|unconstitutional]], but stated that, "At some point in the future, likely with the benefit of additional [[precedent]] from circuit courts and, perhaps, the [[Supreme Court of the United States|Supreme Court]], the court will be asked to make a final ruling on the plaintiffs’ claims. At this point, all signs indicate that, in the eyes of the [[Constitution of the United States|United States Constitution]], the plaintiffs’ marriages will be placed on an equal footing with those of [[Heterosexuality|heterosexual couples]] and that [[proscription]]s against same-sex marriage will soon become a footnote in the annals of [[History of the United States|American history]]."{{multiref2 |{{cite news |last=O'Brien |first=Brendan |editor-last1=Bailey |editor-first1=David |editor-last2=Orlofsky |editor-first2=Steve |date=2014-03-18 |title=Tennessee governor to appeal judge's gay-marriage ruling |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/2014/03/18/us-usa-gaymarriage-tennessee-idUSBREA2H2DG20140318/ |newspaper=[[Reuters]] |access-date=2024-05-01}} |{{cite news |last=Hall |first=Heidi |date=2014-03-14 |title=Judge recognizes gay marriages of 3 Tennessee couples |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/nation/2014/03/14/gay-marriage-tennessee-lawsuit/6432547/ |newspaper=[[The Tennessean]] |via=[[USA Today]] |access-date=2024-05-01}} |{{cite news|url=https://www.csmonitor.com/USA/Justice/2014/0315/Judge-calls-Tenn.-gay-marriage-ban-historical-footnote-Do-Southerners-now-agree|title=Judge calls Tenn. gay marriage ban historical 'footnote': Do Southerners now agree?|first=Patrik|last=Jonsson|date=15 March 2014|newspaper=[[The Christian Science Monitor]] }} }} On February 22, 2016, in ''United States of America v. Matt DeHart'', Trauger sentenced [[Matt DeHart]] — an American citizen and former [[Air National Guard|U.S. Air National Guard]] intelligence analyst known for his involvement with the [[Anonymous (hacker group)|Anonymous hacker group]] and [[WikiLeaks]], as well as claims to have received [[Classified information|classified documents]] alleging serious misconduct by the [[Central Intelligence Agency|CIA]] — to 72 months for the [[Pornography|porn]] charges and an additional 18 months for fleeing the country. Journalist Sarah Harrison called the sentencing, “another shameful milestone in the U.S. government's war on digital activists.”{{Cite web |last=Blake |first=Andrew |date=2016-02-23 |title=Matt DeHart, U.S. Vet linked to Anonymous and WikiLeaks, sentenced for child porn |url=http://www.washingtontimes.com/news/2016/feb/23/matt-dehart-us-vet-linked-anonymous-and-wikileaks-/ |website=[[The Washington Times]]}} On March 23, 2017, Trauger issued a preliminary injunction in the case of ''Doe v. Hommrich, et al.'' prohibiting [[Rutherford County, Tennessee|Rutherford County]] from subjecting children to [[solitary confinement]] while the case continued.{{cite news |last=Hale |first=Steven |date=2017-03-23 |title=Judge Grants Injunction in Juvenile Solitary Confinement Case |url=https://www.nashvillescene.com/news/pithinthewind/judge-grants-injunction-in-juvenile-solitary-confinement-case/article_7b91a907-ee0f-5e53-836e-c2a9d879ab91.html |newspaper=[[Nashville Scene]] |access-date=2024-05-01}} That particular case has since settled for $250,000;{{cite news |last=Broden |first=Scott |date=2019-02-25 |title=Family of special-needs boy held in solitary confinement reaches $250K settlement |url=https://www.dnj.com/story/news/2019/02/26/solitary-confinement-special-needs-child-lawsuit-rutherford-county/2952929002/ |newspaper=[[The Daily News Journal]] |access-date=2024-05-01}} however, Trauger had granted the class-action status sought by the [[American Civil Liberties Union|ACLU]] of Tennessee in February 2017. The class encompasses all detainees who were then juveniles held in the Rutherford County [[Youth detention center|Juvenile Detention Center]] from April 15, 2015 through February 17, 2017.{{cite news |last=Willard |first=Michelle |date=2017-02-21 |title=Class action granted in juvenile solitary confinement case |url=https://www.dnj.com/story/news/crime/2017/02/21/class-action-juvenile-solitary-confinement/98205204/ |newspaper=[[The Daily News Journal]] |access-date=2024-05-01}} The class-action settled for $11,000,000, but only twenty-three percent of those eligible to receive a portion could be contacted to file a claim, resulting in only $2.2 million being paid out.{{cite magazine |last=Camp |first=Emma |date=February 2024 |title=Review: Exposing a Broken Juvenile Court System |url=https://reason.com/2024/01/26/the-kids-of-rutherford-county/ |magazine=[[Reason (magazine)|Reason]] |access-date=2024-05-01}} On July 2, 2018, in the case ''Thomas v. Haslam'', Trauger struck down a law that would allow Tennessee officials to revoke [[driver's license]]s of defendants who could not pay their [[court costs]],{{Cite news|date=2018-07-03|url=https://www.wsmv.com/news/federal-judge-drivers-licenses-cant-be-revoked-for-not-paying-court-costs/article_e3a4ace1-30d9-549d-ad4a-31573f84b40c.html|title=Federal judge: Driver's licenses can't be revoked for not paying court costs|first=Kara|last=Apel|website=[[WSMV-TV|WSMV Nashville]]|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200412220418/https://www.wsmv.com/news/federal-judge-drivers-licenses-cant-be-revoked-for-not-paying-court-costs/article_e3a4ace1-30d9-549d-ad4a-31573f84b40c.html|archive-date=April 12, 2020|access-date=2024-05-01}} pointing out before issuing the ruling that the law created an incentive for people to drive on revoked licenses.{{cite news |date=2018-04-06 |title=Tennessee: Judge Questions License Suspension Legality |url=https://www.thenewspaper.com/news/64/6434.asp |newspaper=TheNewspaper.com |access-date=2024-05-01}} In a ruling on a separate [[Class action|class-action lawsuit]] that sued for relief from Tennessee Annotated Code § 55-50-502(a)(1)(H), ''Robinson, et al. v. Purkey'', issued on October 16, 2018, Trauger ruled that Tennessee could likewise not revoke drivers' licenses based on their inability to pay [[Traffic ticket|traffic fines]].{{cite news |last=Tamburin |first=Adam |date=2018-10-18 |title=Tennessee can't revoke driver licenses of people who can't pay traffic fines, judge says |url=https://www.tennessean.com/story/news/2018/10/17/tennessee-driver-licenses-traffic-fines-reinstate/1674099002/ |newspaper=[[The Tennessean]] |access-date=2024-05-01}} On January 3, 2019, Trauger issued a ruling in the case of ''United States v. Matthew Charles'' wherein she ordered Charles' immediate release from prison due to Congressional enactment of the [[First Step Act]]. Charles had been mistakenly granted early in 2016 and ordered back to prison by the Sixth Circuit in 2018 after [[Donald Trump]] chose not to [[Commutation (law)|commute]] Charles' sentence despite his record as a model inmate.{{multiref2 |{{cite magazine | author-link = Mark Joseph Stern | last = Stern |first=Mark Joseph |date=2019-01-03 |title=The New Criminal Justice Reform Law Has Already Righted One Outrageous Injustice |url=https://slate.com/news-and-politics/2019/01/matthew-charles-released-under-first-step-act.html |magazine=[[Slate (magazine)|Slate]] |access-date=2024-05-01}} |{{cite news |last1=Schuppe |first1=Jon |last2=Cornett |first2= Kim |last3=Cho |first3=Michelle |date=2019-01-08 |title='I refused to be bitter or angry': Matthew Charles, released from prison and sent back again, begins life as a free man |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/i-refuse-be-bitter-or-angry-matthew-charles-released-prison-n955796 |newspaper=[[NBC News]] |access-date=2024-05-01}}}} Charles was the first inmate freed under the act authored by [[Dick Durbin]].{{cite magazine |last1=Durbin |first1=Dick |author-link1=Dick Durbin |last2=Charles |first2=Matthew |date=2024-01-26 |title=We're the Senator Who Wrote the First Step Act and the First Man Freed. It's Working {{!}} Opinion |url=https://www.newsweek.com/were-senator-who-wrote-first-step-act-first-man-freed-its-working-opinion-1863739 |magazine=[[Newsweek]] |access-date=2024-05-01}} In the case ''[[League of Women Voters]], et al. v. Hargett, et al.'', Trauger warned that a Tennessee law imposing restrictions on [[voter registration]] had "[[chilling effect]]s" on individuals and organizations attempting to register new voters in Tennessee.{{Cite news|last=Kruesi|first=Kimberlee|date=2019-09-09|url=https://www.washingtontimes.com/news/2019/sep/9/judge-aleta-trauger-tennessee-voter-restrictions-l/|title=Judge warns of 'chilling effects' in Tennessee's new voter law|newspaper=[[The Washington Times]]|agency=[[Associated Press]]}} On September 12, 2019, Trauger ruled that there was no basis that the law would provide more benefit than harm to Tennesseans. The law would have fined groups that pay workers should too many incomplete registration forms be submitted, and would have criminalized intentional infractions of a new set of rules with [[misdemeanor]] charges.{{Cite web|url=https://www.washingtontimes.com/news/2019/sep/12/judge-blocks-tennessee-voter-signup-penalties-citi/|title=Judge Blocks Tennessee Voter Signup Penalties, Citing Harm|first=Jonathan|last=Mattise |last2=Kruesi|first2=Kimberlee|website=[[The Washington Times]]|date=12 September 2019|agency=[[Associated Press]] |access-date=2024-05-01}} [[Tre Hargett]] then wrote to the [[Tennessee General Assembly|Tennessee legislature]] to encourage them to [[repeal]] the law in question, which was done with the repeal going into effect on April 2, 2020. The ACLU then dropped the suit with the plaintiffs requesting reimbursement for legal expenses from the State, which was awarded by the District Court. Tennessee appealed that decision; however, it was upheld by the Supreme Court of the United States on June 12, 2023.{{cite web |title=''League of Women Voters of Tennessee v. Hargett'' Case Summary |url=https://www.aclu.org/cases/league-women-voters-tennessee-v-hargett |website=[[American Civil Liberties Union|ACLU]] |access-date=2024-05-01}} On July 9, 2021, in the case ''Bongo Productions LLC, et al. v. Lawrence et al.'', Trauger issued a preliminary injunction blocking a Tennessee law that would require businesses and other entities that allow [[transgender]] people to use the [[Public toilet|public restroom]] that matches their preferred gender to post a government-prescribed warning sign.{{multiref2 |{{Cite press release|last=Gardner|first=Claire|date=2021-07-09|title=Judge Blocks Tennessee Anti-Trans Restroom Sign Law|url=https://www.aclu-tn.org/judge-blocks-tennessee-anti-trans-restroom-sign-law/|access-date=2021-07-11|website=ACLU of Tennessee|language=en-US}} |{{Cite news|last=Alund|first=Natalie Neysa|date=2021-07-09|title=Federal judge temporarily blocks Tennessee's anti-transgender restroom law|url=https://www.tennessean.com/story/news/2021/07/09/federal-court-blocks-tennessees-anti-trans-restroom-law-going-into-effect/7919265002/|access-date=2021-07-11|newspaper=[[The Tennessean]]|language=en-US}}}} The lawsuit argued that the law violated the [[First Amendment to the United States Constitution|First Amendment]] rights of the businesses by forcing them to post notices that they disagreed with and found offensive.{{cite news |last=Riley|first=John|date=2021-07-12|title=Federal judge blocks Tennessee’s “Business Bathroom Bill” requiring anti-transgender restroom signs|url=https://www.metroweekly.com/2021/07/federal-judge-blocks-tennessees-business-bathroom-bill-requiring-anti-transgender-restroom-signs/|newspaper=[[Metro Weekly]] |access-date=2024-05-01}} The injunction blocked enforcement of the law while the lawsuit was pending, on the grounds that implementation would cause immediate and irreparable harm.{{Cite web|title=Case No. 3:21-cv-00490 – Bongo Productions LLC et al v. Lawrence et al - Order Granting Preliminary Injunction|url=https://www.aclu.org/legal-document/bongo-productions-llc-et-al-v-lawrence-et-al-order-granting-preliminary-injunction|access-date=2021-07-11|website=American Civil Liberties Union|language=en}} The plaintiffs were granted summary judgement on May 17, 2022,{{cite news |last=Yurcaba |first=Jo |date=2022-05-17 |title=Federal judge strikes down Tennessee's transgender bathroom sign law |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/nbc-out/out-politics-and-policy/judge-strikes-tennessees-transgender-bathroom-sign-law-rcna29267 |newspaper=[[NBC News]] |access-date=2024-05-01}} stating in part that the Act failed applicable constitutional standards.{{cite web |date=2022-05-17 |title=Bongo Productions LLC, et al v Lawrence, et al {{!}} Case No. 3:21-cv-0490 {{!}} Summary Judgement |url=https://casetext.com/case/bongo-prods-v-lawrence |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240501105737/https://casetext.com/case/bongo-prods-v-lawrence |url-status=dead |archive-date=May 1, 2024 |website=[[Casetext]] |access-date=2024-05-01}} On March 5, 2024, Trauger issued a ruling regarding ''[[Concord (entertainment company)|Concord Music Group, Inc.]], et al. v. X Corp., d/b/a Twitter'' in which she found that the platform could not be held directly responsible for the infringements that its users engaged in, but that plaintiffs can present the argument that a lack of [[Digital Millennium Copyright Act|DMCA]] enforcement against serial infringers, despite being aware of the problem, makes [[Twitter|X]] liable. The ruling also acknowledged that if plaintiffs prove the platform intentionally delayed or ignored valid DMCA takedown notices, X may be found liable for contributing to the piracy.{{multiref2 |{{cite magazine |last=Donahue |first=Bill |date=2024-03-05 |title=Twitter Music Lawsuit: Judge Allows Publishers’ Copyright Case Against X To Move Forward Bennett was born in Ennis, Texas. He earned a Bachelor of Science degree in Political Science from the [[University of Houston]] in 1988 and a Juris Doctor from the [[University of Texas School of Law]] in 1991.{{cite web |title=Judge Alfred H. Bennett’s Biography |url=https://www.txs.uscourts.gov/page/judge-alfred-h-bennetts-biography |publisher=United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas}} == Legal career == Following law school, Bennett practiced law in Houston, Texas. He began his career as an associate at Fulbright & Jaworski L.L.P. from 1991 to 1994, and later at Solar & Fernandes, L.L.P. from 1994 to 1998. From 1998 to 2008, he operated a solo legal practice, representing individuals and corporate clients in litigation matters before both state and federal courts. During this period, Bennett also completed a 40-hour basic mediation training program through the A.A. White Dispute Resolution Center at the University of Houston in 2007.{{cite web |title=Judge Alfred H. Bennett’s Biography |url=https://www.txs.uscourts.gov/page/judge-alfred-h-bennetts-biography |publisher=United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas}} In addition to private practice, Bennett was active in legal education. From 2003 to 2013, he served as an adjunct professor at the [[Thurgood Marshall School of Law]], where he taught trial advocacy.{{cite web |title=Judge Alfred H. Bennett’s Biography |url=https://www.txs.uscourts.gov/page/judge-alfred-h-bennetts-biography |publisher=United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas}} From 2009 to 2015, Bennett served as the presiding judge of the 61st Civil District Court of Texas in Harris County. While on the state bench, he also served as the administrative judge for the Harris County Civil District Courts from 2010 to 2011.{{cite web |title=Judge Alfred H. Bennett’s Biography |url=https://www.txs.uscourts.gov/page/judge-alfred-h-bennetts-biography|publisher=United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas}} ===Federal judicial service=== On September 18, 2014, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Bennett to serve as a United States district judge for the Southern District of Texas, to the seat vacated by Judge [[Kenneth M. Hoyt]], who assumed [[senior status]] on March 2, 2013.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/09/18/presidential-nominations-and-withdrawal-sent-senate-0|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Presidential Nominations and Withdrawal Sent to the Senate|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=18 September 2014}} On December 16, 2014, Bennett's nomination was returned to the President due to the [[sine die]] adjournment of the [[113th United States Congress|113th Congress]]. On January 7, 2015, President Obama renominated him to the same position.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2015/01/07/presidential-nominations-sent-senate|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=7 January 2015}} Bennett received a hearing before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Judiciary Committee]] on January 21, 2015.{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/nominations-2015-01-21|title=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|website=www.judiciary.senate.gov|date=21 January 2015 }} On February 26, 2015, his nomination was reported out of committee by [[voice vote]].{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%202-26-15%20Update.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – February 26, 2015}} On April 13, 2015, the [[United States Senate]] confirmed Bennett by a 95–0 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1141/vote_114_1_00136.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Alfred H. Bennett, of Texas, to be U.S. District Judge for the Southern District of Texas)|website=senate.gov}} == Notable Cases == === Transgender Prisoner Mistreatment Case (2016) === In ''Zollicoffer v. Livingston'', a transgender prisoner brought a § 1983 action against the Executive Director of the [[Texas Department of Criminal Justice]], alleging Eighth Amendment violations for failing to protect her from sexual assault by other inmates. Bennett acknowledged the “horrific series of assaults, rapes, and abuses” were enough to “offend even the sternest of dispositions,” deferred ruling on whether the director was protected by qualified immunity, and ordered discovery on the issue. The case later settled. === International Kidnapping Case of a Minor (2018) === In ''USA v. Guimaraes'', Bennett presided over a 10-day jury trial in which a Brazilian couple was convicted of the international kidnapping of their grandson. Bennett ordered a sentence below the guidelines while acknowledging “[t]here is no sentence I can impose that will resolve this family fracture.”{{Cite web |date=2018-12-13 |title=Brazilian couple get light sentences in grandson's abduction |url=https://apnews.com/general-news-67ae9471a01546008d16418f335537d8 |access-date=2026-02-03 |website=AP News |language=en}} === Public Corruption Case (2019) === In ''USA v. Delgado'', Bennett sentenced Rodolfo Delgado, a Texas state district judge, to 60 months in prison for conspiracy, bribery, and obstructing justice.{{Cite web |title=  |url=https://www.justice.gov/usao-sdtx/pr/judge-delgado-heads-prison |access-date=2026-02-03 |website=www.justice.gov}} At sentencing, Bennett stated that “such criminal actions will not be tolerated, least of all from individuals conferred with the public trust.” === Houston Busking Case (2022) === In ''Barilla v. City of Houston'', Bennett resolved a dispute between a street performer and the City of Houston by determining the city’s busking and permit ordinances were unconstitutional. The [[Houston City Council]] unanimously rescinded the ordinances the following year.{{Cite news |last=McGuinness |first=Dylan |title=Houston drops its busking ban, three months after a federal judge ruled it unconstitutional |url=https://www.houstonchronicle.com/politics/houston/article/houston-drops-busking-ban-ruling-17893405.php |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250811043006/https://www.houstonchronicle.com/politics/houston/article/houston-drops-busking-ban-ruling-17893405.php |archive-date=2025-08-11 |access-date=2026-02-03 |work=Houston Chronicle |language=en |url-status=live }} === Fourth Amendment Use-of-Force Case (2022-2025) === In ''Barnes v. Felix'', Bennett presided over a Fourth Amendment suit brought on behalf of Ashtian Barnes, who was shot and killed by law enforcement during a traffic stop.  In granting summary judgment to law enforcement, Bennett explained he was “duty bound” by the Fifth Circuit’s “moment of threat” doctrine to focus his analysis on only the two seconds before Barnes was shot. He added, however, that a “more robust examination” would have helped him assess the reasonableness of the shooting. The case [[Barnes v. Felix|went up to the Supreme Court.]] There, a unanimous Court vacated judgment, remanded to the Fifth Circuit, and recognized that a district court “cannot review the totality of the circumstances if it has to put on chronological blinders.”{{Cite web |title=BARNES v. FELIX |url=https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/23-1239 |access-date=2026-02-03 |website=LII / Legal Information Institute |language=en}} == Professional affiliations == In addition to his judicial service, Bennett has been actively involved in professional, civic, and community organizations, with a particular focus on access to justice, legal administration, and community development. From 2011 to 2015, Bennett served on the Texas Access to Justice Commission and chaired its Strategic Planning Committee, contributing to statewide initiatives to improve access to civil legal services.{{cite web |title=Judge Alfred H. Bennett’s Biography |url=https://www.txs.uscourts.gov/page/judge-alfred-h-bennetts-biography |publisher=United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas}} Bennett’s professional affiliations further include involvement with national, state, and local legal organizations, including the [[National Bar Association]], the [[State Bar of Texas]], the Texas Bar College, the Texas Young Lawyers' Association, the Houston Bar Association, and the Houston Lawyers Association. Bennett remains actively engaged with alumni organizations of the University of Houston and the University of Texas School of Law.{{cite web |title=Judge Alfred H. Bennett’s Biography |url=https://www.txs.uscourts.gov/page/judge-alfred-h-bennetts-biography |publisher=United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas}} Bennett is a Life Member of [[Alpha Phi Alpha]] fraternity. == Awards and recognition == * Distinguished Alumni Award, University of Houston Alumni Association (2024).{{cite web |title=UH Alumni Association Announces 2024 Alumni Award Honorees |url=https://houstonalumni.com/uh-alumni-association-announces-2024-alumni-award-honorees/ |publisher=University of Houston Alumni Association}} * Distinguished Alumni of the Year, Thurgood Marshall Legal Society (2019–2020). * Service to the Legal Community Award, The Spouses of Houston Barristers (2017). * The Joyce M. Reynolds Lifetime Achievement Award, Houston Community College (2016). * Honorary Order of the Coif, University of Texas School of Law (2015). * Outstanding Service in the Community, Mexican American Bar Association Foundation (2015). * Father of the Year, Houston Chapter of Jack and Jill of America (2015). * Weldon Berry Judicial Service Award, Houston Lawyers Association (May 2014). * WEBELOS Leader of the Year, Boy Scouts of America, Sam Houston Area Council, W. L. {{nowrap|[[University of Texas, Austin]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]])}} }} '''Alia Moses''' (born January 6, 1962),{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=W6W_avmIJGUC&dq=Alia+Moses+Ludlum+born+1962&pg=PA487 |title=Confirmation Hearings on Federal Appointments: Hearings Before the Committee on the Judiciary, United States Senate, One Hundred Seventh Congress, First Session |date=2003 |publisher=U.S. Government Printing Office |language=en}} formerly known as '''Alia Moses Ludlum''', is the [[United States federal judge|chief United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Texas]]. ==Early life and education== Born in [[Eagle Pass, Texas]], Moses graduated in 1983 from [[Texas Woman's University]] with a [[Bachelor of Business Administration]] degree in Accounting, and in 1986 from the [[University of Texas School of Law]] with a [[Juris Doctor]].{{FJC Bio|nid=1391681}} ==Career== Following law school graduation, Moses was an attorney in the [[Travis County, Texas|Travis County]] Attorney's Office in Austin, Texas from 1986 to 1990. She was an [[assistant United States attorney]] and chief of the [[Del Rio, Texas|Del Rio]] office in the Western District of Texas from 1990 to 1997. She worked as a part-time [[Mediation|mediator]] in private practice from 1997 to 2000. ===Federal judicial service=== Moses began her federal judicial career as a [[United States magistrate judge]] when she was appointed to a four-year part-term in 1997. In 2000, she was promoted to a full-term magistrate judge. On the recommendation of Texas Senators [[Phil Gramm]] and [[Kay Bailey Hutchison]], Moses was nominated by President [[George W. Bush]] on July 11, 2002, to the United States District Court for the Western District of Texas. Her seat was previously held by [[Harry Lee Hudspeth]], who then went into [[senior status]]. Moses was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on November 14, 2002, and received her commission the next day. Moses was appointed to the court under the name of '''Alia Moses Ludlum'''. Moses became chief judge on November 18, 2022, when her predecessor [[Orlando Luis Garcia]] turned 70 years old. ===Notable case=== On October 30, 2023, Moses ordered Border Patrol agents to stop removing [[concertina wire]] installed by the government of Texas with the purpose of deterring migrants.{{Cite web|first1=Uriel J.|last1=García|url=https://www.texastribune.org/2023/10/30/texas-border-lawsuit-concertina-wire-restraining-order-judge/|title=Federal judge orders immigration agents to stop removing Texas' concertina wire on the border|website=The Texas Tribune|date=October 30, 2023|access-date=October 31, 2023}} ===Recognition=== In 2026, a portrait of her was unveiled in the headquarters of the federal judiciary’s Western District of Texas, in San Antonio. All federal judges who become chief judges are thus recognized, with a portrait permanently hanging in the courthouse that is the headquarters for the district which they are assigned.{{Cite web|url=https://twu.edu/news/2026/portrait-adds-legacy-to-us-judge-twu-alum|title=Portrait adds legacy to U.S. judge, TWU alum | TWU|website=twu.edu}} ==See also== *[[List of Hispanic and Latino American jurists]] *[[List of first women lawyers and judges in Texas]] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==Sources== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1391681}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Harry Lee Hudspeth]]}} {{s-ttl|title=Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Texas]]|years=2002–present}} {{s-inc|rows=2}} |- {{s-bef|before=[[Orlando Luis Garcia]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Chief Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Texas]]}}|years=2022–present}} {{s-end}} {{United States 5th Circuit district judges}} {{authority control}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Moses, Alia}} [[Category:1962 births]] [[Category:Living people]] [[Category:21st-century American women judges]] [[Category:Assistant United States attorneys]] [[Category:Hispanic and Latino American judges]] [[Category:Hispanic and Latino American lawyers]] [[Category:Judges of the United States District Court for the Western District of Texas]] [[Category:People from Eagle Pass, Texas]] [[Category:Texas Woman's University alumni]] [[Category:United States district court judges appointed by George W. [[University of Florida]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Allen Cothrel Winsor''' (born 1976)[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Winsor%20SJQ.pdf United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary, "Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees"] is the [[United States federal judge|chief United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Florida]]. == Biography == Winsor received a [[Bachelor of Business Administration#BSBA|Bachelor of Science in Business Administration]] from [[Auburn University]] and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[Fredric G. Levin College of Law]] where he was inducted into the [[Order of the Coif]] and served as editor-in-chief of the [[Florida Law Review]].{{FJC Bio|nid=6631561|inline=yes}} After law school, Winsor served as a [[law clerk]] to Judge [[Edward Earl Carnes]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit]]. From 2003 to 2005, he was an [[Associate lawyer|associate]] at [[King & Spalding]]. He later was a [[Law firm partner|partner]] in the [[Tallahassee]] office of Gray Robinson, where he focused on civil and appellate litigation. He then joined the [[Florida Attorney General]]'s office and served for three years as [[Solicitor General of Florida]], under A.G. [[Pam Bondi]].{{cite web |url=http://www.1dca.org/judges/winsor.html |title=Judge Allen Winsor |last= |first= |date= |website=[[Florida First District Court of Appeal]] |publisher= |access-date=April 10, 2018 |quote=}} In that position, he defended Florida's voter-approved ban on same-sex marriages that was eventually struck down, contending in a legal brief for Florida that recognizing same-sex marriages from other states would ostensibly "impose significant public harm" and that Florida possessed a legitimate interest in restricting marriage as exclusively between men and women.{{Citation needed|date=June 2024}} In 2016, Governor [[Rick Scott]] appointed him to the [[Florida First District Court of Appeal]], where he served until being appointed to the federal district court by President Donald Trump.{{cite web |url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-twelfth-wave-judicial-nominees-twelfth-wave-united-states-attorneys-sixth-wave-united-states-marshals/ |title=President Donald J. Trump Announces Twelfth Wave of Judicial Nominees, Twelfth Wave of United States Attorneys, and Sixth Wave of United States Marshals |last= |first= |date=April 10, 2018 |access-date=April 10, 2018 |via=[[NARA|National Archives]] |work=[[whitehouse.gov]] |quote=}} {{PD-notice}} Ashley Schapitl, a spokeswoman for California Democratic Senator [[Dianne Feinstein]], said Feinstein voted in opposition to Winsor's confirmation because of his role "defending laws that would restrict women's reproductive rights and the prohibition of same-sex marriage." She further mentioned that Winsor assisted Florida in joining an action contesting power plant emissions rules written by the [[Presidency of Barack Obama|Obama administration]]. === Federal judicial service === On April 10, 2018, President [[Donald Trump]] nominated Winsor to serve as a United States District Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Florida]]. He was nominated to the seat vacated by Judge [[Robert Hinkle (judge)|Robert Hinkle]], who assumed [[senior status]] on November 7, 2016.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/ten-nominations-sent-senate-today-2/ "Ten Nominations Sent to the Senate Today", The White House, April 10, 2018] On May 23, 2018, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/05/23/2018/nominations United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Nominations for May 23, 2018] On June 14, 2018, his nomination was reported out of committee by an 11–10 vote.[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%2006-14-18.pdf Results of Executive Business Meeting – June 14, 2018, Senate Judiciary Committee] Democratic Senator [[Bill Nelson]] of Florida supported his nomination.[https://apnews.com/article/823ca7c117f54a1fb5b0ab21713079d7 Democrats oppose Florida judge despite backing from Nelson], ''[[Associated Press]]'', Gary Fineout, June 14, 2018. Retrieved February 2, 2024. On January 3, 2019, his nomination was returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]]. On January 23, 2019, Trump announced his intent to renominate Winsor for a federal judgeship.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-intent-nominate-judicial-nominees/ "President Donald J. Trump Announces Intent to Nominate Judicial Nominees", White House, January 23, 2019] His nomination was sent to the Senate later that day.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/nominations-sent-senate-2/ "Nominations Sent to the Senate", White House, January 23, 2019] On February 7, 2019, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 12–10 vote.[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/02.07.2019%20Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting1.pdf Results of Executive Business Meeting – February 7, 2019, Senate Judiciary Committee] On June 18, 2019, the Senate invoked [[cloture]] on his nomination by a 54–42 vote.[https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=1&vote=00169 On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Allen Cothrel Winsor to be U.S. District Judge for the Northern District of Florida), United States Senate, June 18, 2019] On June 19, 2019, he was confirmed by a 54–44 vote, with Democrat [[Joe Manchin]] voting for him.[https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1161/vote_116_1_00173.htm On the Nomination (Confirmation Allen Cothrel Winsor, of Florida, to be U.S. District Judge for the Northern District of Florida), June 19, 2019] He received his judicial commission on June 21, 2019. He became chief judge in June 2025. == Memberships == He has been a member of the [[Federalist Society]] since 2005. == References == {{Reflist|30em}} == External links == * {{FJC Bio|nid=6631561}} * [https://www.oyez.org/advocates/allen_winsor Appearances at the U.S. Supreme Court] from the [[Oyez Project]] * {{Ballotpedia|Allen_Winsor|Allen Winsor}} * {{LittleSisPeople}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Robert Hinkle (judge)|Robert Hinkle]]}} {{s-ttl|title=Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Florida]]|years=2019–present}} {{s-inc|rows=2}} |- {{s-bef|before=[[Mark E. [[University of Pennsylvania Law School|University of Pennsylvania]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | website = | footnotes = }} '''Allison Dale Burroughs''' (born 1961) is an American lawyer and jurist serving as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts|U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts]]. She was appointed in 2014 by President [[Barack Obama]]. She is best known for ruling that Harvard College's race-conscious admissions process was legal in ''[[Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard]]'' (2019).{{cite web | url=https://www.govinfo.gov/app/details/USCOURTS-mad-1_14-cv-14176/USCOURTS-mad-1_14-cv-14176-4 | title=Students for Fair Admissions, Inc. v. President and Fellows of Harvard College et al}} ==Early life== Allison Dale Burroughs was born in 1961 in [[Boston]].{{cite web | url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Burroughs%20Senate%20Questionnaire%20Final.pdf | title=Senate Judiciary Committee Nomination Questionnaire}} She received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree cum laude from [[Middlebury College]]. She received a [[Juris Doctor]] cum laude in 1988 from the [[University of Pennsylvania Law School]]. She began her legal career as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Norma Levy Shapiro]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania]] from 1988 to 1989. She served as an [[Assistant United States Attorney]] in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania from 1989 to 1995 and in the District of Massachusetts from 1995 to 2005. From 2005 to 2014, she was a partner at [[Nutter McClennen & Fish]], where she represented individuals and corporations in criminal and civil proceedings primarily before federal courts.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/07/31/president-obama-nominates-two-serve-united-states-district-courts|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Obama Nominates Two to Serve on the United States District Courts|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=July 31, 2014}}{{FJC Bio|nid=1394736|inline=yes}} ==Judge== On July 31, 2014, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Burroughs to serve as a United States district judge of the United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts to the seat vacated by Judge [[Rya W. Zobel]], who had assumed [[senior status]] on April 1, 2014.{{cite web|url=http://don411.com/the-white-house-nominations-sent-to-the-senate-allison-dale-burroughs-amit-priyavadan-mehta/#.U9sh6mPG_sV|title=THE WHITE HOUSE NOMINATIONS SENT TO THE SENATE: Allison Dale Burroughs, Amit Priyavadan Mehta, – Created by Don – In category: Human Interest – Tagged with: – Don411.com Media :: Performing Arts News Unabridged -|website=don411.com|date=August 2014}} She received a hearing before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]] on September 17, 2014.[http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/judicial-nominations-2014-09-17 "Judicial Nominations" United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary], September 17, 2014. On November 20, her nomination was reported out of committee by [[voice vote]].{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%2011-20-14.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – November 20, 2014 United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|publisher=}} On December 13, [[Senate Majority Leader]] [[Harry Reid]] filed a motion to invoke [[cloture]] on the nomination. On December 16, Reid withdrew his cloture motion on Burroughs's nomination and the Senate confirmed Burroughs by voice vote. She received her federal judicial commission on December 19 and was sworn in on January 7, 2015.{{cite web|url=http://www.mad.uscourts.gov/general/pdf/announce/010715%20Press%20Release%20-%20USDJ%20Allison%20Burroughs.pdf|title=Press Release|date=January 7, 2015|publisher=United States District Court: District of Massachusetts|access-date=January 22, 2019}} ===Notable cases=== Burroughs is most notable for her order that put a hold on President Donald Trump's travel ban in January 2017 ([[Executive Order 13769]]) and for presiding over ''United States v. Salemme'', ''[[Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard]]'', and ''United States v. Babich''. ''Salemme'' was the last major trial of [[American Mafia]] members. In 2018, Francis Salemme (aka "Cadillac Frank") and co-defendant Paul Weadick were convicted of the murder of Steven A. DiSarro, who disappeared in 1993, and were sentenced to life in prison. In October 2018, Burroughs held a three-week bench trial in ''[[Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard]]'', a lawsuit challenging Harvard's admissions program as discriminatory against Asian Americans.{{cite web|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/education/archive/2018/11/harvard-affirmative-action-trial-wraps-boston/574795/|title=The Stakes for the Harvard Trial Are Higher Now That It's Over|last=Harris|first=Adam|date=November 2, 2018|publisher=The Atlantic|access-date=January 22, 2019}} A decision in favor of the university was announced on October 1, 2019.{{Cite news |last=Hartocollis |first=Anemona |date=October 1, 2019 |title=Harvard Does Not Discriminate Against Asian-Americans in Admissions, Judge Rules |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/10/01/us/harvard-admissions-lawsuit.html |access-date=June 15, 2023 |issn=0362-4331}} ''United States v. Babich'' is a criminal case brought against several former executives of the pharmaceutical company [[Insys Therapeutics]]. The government alleged that the executives violated the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act ([[RICO]]), 18 U.S.C. 1692 ''et seq.'', by engaging in a scheme to sell the fentanyl-based pain medication Subsys by bribing physicians to prescribe it. The indictments led to guilty pleas, including by former Insys CEO Michael Babich. The remaining defendants were tried from January through April 2019.{{cite web|url=https://www.justice.gov/usao-ma/victim-and-witness-assistance-program/united-states-v-michael-babich-alec-burlakoff-richard-simon-sunrise-lee-joseph-rowan-and|title=Press Release|date=January 17, 2019|publisher=United States Department of Justice|access-date=January 22, 2019}} All five remaining defendants, including former billionaire [[John Kapoor]], were convicted of racketeering. Burroughs also presided over a July 2020 lawsuit filed by Harvard and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) that sought to halt an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) policy that required international students in the U.S. on F-1 visas to depart the country if they would not attend in-person classes during the COVID-19 pandemic. Burroughs announced that the Trump administration had agreed to reverse the policy during a July 14 hearing in her Boston courtroom.{{cite web|url=https://www.https://www.wbur.org/edify/2020/07/14/ice-dhs-policy-international-students-leave-america-universities-pandemic|title=Gov't Rescinds Rule Barring Foreign Students From U.S. While Colleges Hold Classes Remotely|date=July 14, 2020|publisher=United States Department of Justice|access-date=July 20, 2020|archive-date=August 19, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130819141428/http://https/|url-status=dead}} In December 2020, Burroughs presided over a lawsuit brought by five Republicans who lost state and federal legislative races in Massachusetts and sought to overturn the election results. At a December 2020 hearing, she said the plaintiffs' requested relief of invalidating the votes of millions of Massachusetts residents was "too late", "misplaced", and "terribly unfair".{{Cite web|url=https://www.bostonherald.com/2020/12/08/former-gop-candidates-sue-massachusetts-seeking-to-throw-out-millions-of-mail-in-early-ballots/|title=Federal judge blasts Republican candidates' request to 'invalidate' Massachusetts election results|date=December 8, 2020}} Burroughs has also presided over several [[class action]]s related to consumer products. '''Alvin Kenneth Hellerstein'''<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-fLiAAAAMAAJ&q=%22Hellerstein,+Alvin%22+1933|title=Biography and Genealogy Master Index 2003|first=Kathy|last=Nemeh|year=2002|publisher=Gale Research International, Limited|isbn=978-0787640552|via=Google Books}}</ref> (December 28, 1933 – October 28, 2026) was an American lawyer and jurist who served as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York|U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York]]. He was appointed in 1998 by President [[Bill Clinton]], and he assumed senior status in 2011.

Hellerstein presided over several high-profile cases, including various litigation brought in the aftermath of the [[September 11 attacks]], a sex-trafficking lawsuit brought against [[Harvey Weinstein]], and the fraud trials of businesswoman [[Charlie Javice]] and investor [[Bill Hwang]]. He presided over the [[Prosecution of Nicolás Maduro and Cilia Flores|federal criminal proceeding]] against [[Venezuela]]'s former president, [[Nicolás Maduro]], until his death in 2026.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Halpert |first1=Madeline |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/live/cwy1x9vwn3dt?post=asset%3A7552c449-28e1-4323-ad09-a88a70d8ed42#post |title=Venezuela's Maduro tells US court 'I am still president' as he pleads not guilty to drugs charges |work=BBC |date=5 January 2026}}</ref>

== Early life, education and career ==
Hellerstein was born in New York City on December 28, 1933, to Rose and Max Hellerstein, and was an [[Orthodox Jew]].<ref>{{cite AV media|url = https://refuseniksactivists.org/item/2188|title = Full, Unedited interview with Alvin K. Hellerstein, 2023|website = Refusenik Activists|date = October 30, 2023|accessdate = October 1, 2025|time = 0:28|quote = My full name is Alvin K. Hellerstein. I was born in New York City, December 28, 1933.}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://gothamist.com/2010/05/03/911_judge.php |title="Judge Has Become "Elvis" of the 9/11 Community": ''Gothamis''t<!-- Bot generated title --> |access-date=May 13, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190513182608/http://gothamist.com/2010/05/03/911_judge.php |archive-date=May 13, 2019 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/05/03/nyregion/03judge.html|title=Empathetic Judge in 9/11 Suits Seen by Some as Interfering|first=Mireya|last=Navarro|newspaper=The New York Times |date=May 2, 2010}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ancestry.com/1940-census/usa/New-York/Alvin-Hellerstein_3r5p0|title=Alvin Hellerstein in the 1940 Census | Ancestry®|website=Ancestry.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UrxFAQAAIAAJ&q=%22Hellerstein,+Alvin%22+1933|title=The American Bench|first1=Marie T.|last1=Finn|first2=Diana R.|last2=Irvine|first3=Mary Lee|last3=Bliss|first4=Gina L. (CON)|last4=Pratton|first5=Samantha (CON)|last5=Morgan|date=July 25, 2009|publisher=Forster-Long|isbn=9780931398582|via=Google Books}}</ref> He attended the [[Bronx High School of Science]], graduating in 1950.<ref name=autogenerated1>{{Cite web|url=https://judges.newyorklawjournal.com/profile/Alvin_K._Hellerstein/Alvin_Hellerstein-100072.xml|title=New York Law Journal | Judges Profiles | Alvin_K._Hellerstein|website=judges.newyorklawjournal.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://umassk12.net/science50/June50Program.pdf|title=The Bronx High School of Science; Nineteenth Commencement Exercises}}</ref> He received a Bachelor of Arts degree from [[Columbia College, Columbia University|Columbia College]] in 1954.<ref name="autogenerated2">{{Cite web|title=Alvin K Hellerstein, United States District Court for the Southern District of New York: Profile and Biography - Bloomberg Markets|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/profile/person/3047466|access-date=September 19, 2020|website=Bloomberg.com}}</ref> He received a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Columbia Law School]] in 1956, and was editor of the ''[[Columbia Law Review]]''.<ref name=autogenerated2 /><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mGkeAQAAMAAJ&q=Alvin+Hellerstein+stroock+%22law+review%22|title=Martindale-Hubbell International Law Directory|date=July 25, 1995|publisher=Martindale-Hubbell|isbn=9781561601103|via=Google Books}}</ref> He was a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Edmund Palmieri]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]] from 1956 to 1957.<ref name=autogenerated2 /><ref name=autogenerated1 />

He was in the [[United States Army]], [[JAG Corps]], as a [[first lieutenant]] from 1957 to 1960.<ref name=autogenerated2 /><ref name=autogenerated3>{{Cite web|url=https://www.americanconference.com/m-a-liability-873i17-nyc/speakers/the-honorable-alvin-k-hellerstein/|title=The Honorable Alvin K. Hellerstein|website=National Advanced Forum on M & A Liability}}</ref> Hellerstein was in the private practice of law, making [[Law firm partner|partner]] in 1969 and ultimately as co-head of the litigation department of [[Stroock & Stroock & Lavan LLP]], in New York City from 1960 to 1998.<ref name=autogenerated2 /><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eun44FV64VMC&q=Alvin+Hellerstein+stroock|title=Confirmation Hearings on Federal Appointments: May 14; June 18; July 16; July 30, 1998; pt. 5. Sept 9; Oct 1, 6-7, 1998| author=United States Congress Senate Committee on the Judiciary|date=July 25, 1997|publisher=U.S. Government Printing Office|isbn=9780160385940 |via=Google Books}}</ref> He was the President and Chairman of the Board of Jewish Education.<ref name=autogenerated3 />

=== Federal judicial service ===
Hellerstein was nominated by President [[Bill Clinton]] to be a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]] on May 15, 1998, to a seat vacated by Judge [[Louis L. Stanton]]. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] through [[unanimous consent]] on October 21, 1998,<ref>{{USCongRec|1998|S12962}}</ref> and received his commission on October 22, 1998. He assumed [[senior status]] on January 30, 2011, until his death.{{Cn|date=November 2026}}

== Notable cases ==
=== World Trade Center ===
* In 2003, Hellerstein agreed to hear a consolidated master case{{what|date=January 2026}} against three airlines, [[ICTS International]] NV, and Pinkerton's [[airport security]] firms, the [[World Trade Center (1973-2001)|World Trade Center]] owners, and [[Boeing]], the aircraft manufacturer. The case was brought by people injured in the [[September 11 attacks]], representatives of those who died, and entities that suffered property damage. In September 2004, just before the three-year [[statute of limitations]] expired, the insurers for the World Trade Center filed suit against [[American Airlines]], [[United Airlines]], and Pinkerton's airport security firm, alleging their negligence allowed the planes to be hijacked.{{Cn|date=November 2026}}
* On January 12, 2006, Hellerstein dismissed the last remaining property-damage claim against New York City, while leaving pending several other suits against other parties, among them the [[Port Authority of New York and New Jersey]]. According to [[Reuters]], "[s]ix insurers sought repayment from the city for expenses arising from the collapse of a 47-story office building near the Twin Towers"; Hellerstein ruled New York had [[Sovereign immunity in the United States|sovereign immunity]].<ref>{{cite news|url=http://news.yahoo.com/s/nm/20060113/bs_nm/financial_newyork_dc | date = January 12, 2006 | title=Judge dismisses Sept 11 suit against NYC | agency = Reuters | work = News.yahoo.com |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060115064148/http://news.yahoo.com/s/nm/20060113/bs_nm/financial_newyork_dc |archive-date=January 15, 2006 }}</ref>
* The World Trade Center [[first responders]] (''e.g.'', police and firefighters) and the city government clashed over payments for health costs of first responders who had survived the collapse of the Twin Towers. On October 17, 2006, Hellerstein rejected New York City's motion to dismiss lawsuits that requested health payments to the first responders.<ref>Anthony DePalma, "Ruling Opens a Door for Thousands of Ground Zero Lawsuits," ''New York Times'', October 18, 2006, B1,</ref>
* On July 7, 2008, Hellerstein ruled against a group of relatives of 9/11 victims and [[ground zero]] recovery workers who had sorted through debris from the collapsed Twin Towers. The group accused New York City of dishonoring human remains that became part of the total debris shipped to city landfills. The judge said that the city was not required to sift through debris from ground zero in search of bits of human remains and remove it to a space where a cemetery might be built (thereby leaving the material from ground zero at [[Fresh Kills]] landfills).<ref name="j goldstein">{{cite web|url=http://www.nysun.com/new-york/judge-rules-for-city-on-search-for-september-11/81405/|title=Judge Rules for City on Search for September 11 Victim Remains |website=The New York Sun|date=July 8, 2008|last=Goldstein|first=Joseph|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080914034533/http://www.nysun.com/new-york/judge-rules-for-city-on-search-for-september-11/81405/|archive-date=September 14, 2008|url-status=dead}}</ref> Hellerstein stated, "Plaintiffs have no property right in an undifferentiated, unidentifiable mass of dirt that may or may not contain the remains of plaintiffs' loved ones."<ref name="bbc 2008" /> He added, "Not every wrong can be addressed through the judicial process."<ref name="j goldstein" /> Hellerstein urged the city to build a memorial and nature reserve at the site. Victims' families' counsel [[Norman Siegel]] criticized the ruling: "We are not prepared to leave hundreds of human remains of 9/11 victims on top of a garbage dump as their final resting place."<ref name="bbc 2008">{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/americas/7494633.stm|title=Judge rejects 9/11 burial claims|website=[[BBC News]]|date=July 8, 2008 }}</ref>
=== "Hope" poster matter ===
Hellerstein presided over the [[Barack Obama "Hope" poster]] case.<ref name=JOLT>{{cite journal|last1=Fisher III|first1=William W.|first2=Frank |last2=Cost |first3=Shepard |last3=Fairey |first4=Meir |last4=Feder |first5=Edwin |last5=Fountain |first6=Geoffrey |last6=Stewart |first7=Marita |last7=Sturken|title=Reflections on the Hope Poster Case|journal=Harvard Journal of Law and Technology|date=Spring 2012|volume=25|issue=2|url=http://jolt.law.harvard.edu/articles/pdf/v25/25HarvJLTech243.pdf|access-date=January 21, 2013}}</ref>  [[Shepard Fairey]], the artist behind the poster, sued the [[Associated Press]]. He sought to establish that his Hope poster did not infringe the AP's copyright of a shot taken by AP freelancer [[Mannie Garcia]]. The AP countersued, accusing Fairey of infringement.<ref>{{cite web|last=Shanahan|first=Ed|title=Judge Rebuffs AP, Lets "Hope" Artist Swap Lawyers|url=http://www.law.com/jsp/iplawandbusiness/PubArticleFriendlyIPLB.jsp?id=1202435330217|access-date=January 21, 2013}}</ref> According to an article co-written by Fairey, "a few days after" his lawsuit was filed, Fairey realized that it contained an error, describing the wrong Garcia photograph as Fairey's source, but Fairey "decided to conceal his mistake" for about eight months, including by "destroy[ing] some documents and fabricat[ing] others."<ref name=JOLT />  When Fairey finally admitted to his attempted cover up, Hellerstein allowed Fairey's original counsel to withdraw.<ref name=JOLT /> In January 2011, the AP and Shepard Fairey settled out of court.<ref name=JOLT />

=== Harvey Weinstein trial ===
Hellerstein presided over a federal lawsuit in the [[Harvey Weinstein sexual abuse allegations|Harvey Weinstein case]]. In April 2019, Hellerstein eliminated 17 claims from the case, but allowed the case to proceed to trial.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.marketwatch.com/story/sex-trafficking-claim-against-harvey-weinstein-can-proceed-but-judge-shrinks-scope-of-case-2019-04-18|title=Sex-trafficking claim against Harvey Weinstein can proceed, but judge shrinks scope of case|agency=Associated Press|website=MarketWatch |date=April 18, 2019 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.alu.edu/alublog/exploring-details-of-harvey-weinstein-trial/ |title=Exploring the Details of the Harvey Weinstein Trial |work=[[Abraham Lincoln University]] |date=April 9, 2020 |access-date=February 19, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200921070213/https://www.alu.edu/alublog/exploring-details-of-harvey-weinstein-trial/ |archive-date=September 21, 2020 |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Michael Cohen prison release ===
On July 23, 2020, Hellerstein granted a [[Injunction#Temporary restraining orders|temporary restraining order]] in favor of President [[Donald Trump]]'s former attorney [[Michael Cohen (lawyer)|Michael Cohen]], ordering that Cohen be released from prison into home confinement.<ref name=NYTCohen>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/aponline/2020/07/23/us/ap-us-michael-cohen-prison.html|title=Judge Orders Michael Cohen to Be Released From Prison|agency=Associated Press|date=July 23, 2020|via=NYTimes.com}}</ref> Cohen had argued that prison officials were preventing his transfer to home confinement out of retaliation for Cohen's refusal to agree not to write a book or contact the media while in home confinement.<ref name=NYTCohen/>

=== David Hu Ponzi Scheme case ===
In April 2022, Hellerstein sentenced [[David Hu (IIG)|David Hu]] of [[IIG Capital]] to 12 years in prison for fraud, [[stealing]] more than $100 million of client's money, running a [[Ponzi scheme]], falsifying financial documents ([[Cooking the books|cooking the book]]), lying to auditors, and other financial crimes.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |date=April 11, 2022 |title=Former Managing Partner Of Manhattan Investment Advisory Firm Sentenced To 12 Years For Defrauding Investors In An Over $120 Million Ponzi-Like Scheme |url=https://www.justice.gov/usao-sdny/pr/former-managing-partner-manhattan-investment-advisory-firm-sentenced-12-years |access-date=March 6, 2023 |website=www.justice.gov |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":7">{{Cite web |date=January 28, 2021 |title=Managing Partner Of Investment Advisory Firm Pleads Guilty To Defrauding Clients And Investors In Over $100 Million Ponzi-Like Fraud Scheme |url=https://www.justice.gov/usao-sdny/pr/managing-partner-investment-advisory-firm-pleads-guilty-defrauding-clients-and |access-date=March 6, 2023 |website=www.justice.gov |language=en}}</ref>

=== U.S. military detainees ===
On December 20, 2004, Hellerstein said he would deny a government request to delay a review of whether certain [[Central Intelligence Agency]] internal files related to [[Iraq]] should be made public.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.wjla.com/news/stories/1204/195735.html |title=ACLU: FBI Ruse Used in Guantanamo Abuse |access-date=June 3, 2005 |url-status=bot: unknown |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050320182051/http://www.wjla.com/news/stories/1204/195735.html |archive-date=March 20, 2005 }}</ref> On June 3, 2005, Hellerstein ordered the government to release four videos from [[Abu Ghraib prison]] and dozens of photographs from the same collection as photos that touched off the Iraqi prisoner abuse scandal a year prior. Hellerstein said the 144 pictures and videos could be turned over in redacted form to protect the victims' identities. The judge ordered the release after he viewed eight of the photos. They were given to the [[U.S. Army]] by a military policeman assigned to Abu Ghraib. On September 29, 2005, in [[American Civil Liberties Union v. Department of Defense|''ACLU v. Department of Defense'']], Hellerstein ordered the release of 87 more photographs and videotapes.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/middle_east/4295324.stm|title=Abu Ghraib images 'must appear'|date=September 30, 2005|via=news.bbc.co.uk}}</ref> In January and September 2017, Hellerstein ordered the release of additional government documents, including those referred to in the [[Senate Intelligence Committee report on CIA torture|Senate torture report]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/us-government-scolded-iraq-detainee-abuse-photos-federal-judge/|title=U.S. government scolded over Iraq detainee abuse photos by federal judge|access-date=November 12, 2017|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.courthousenews.com/judge-peels-off-layer-cia-torture-secrecy/|title=Judge Peels Off Layer of CIA Torture Secrecy|date=September 27, 2017|access-date=November 12, 2017|language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Criminal case of Donald Trump ===
After President [[Donald Trump]] was indicted on [[Prosecution of Donald Trump in New York|state criminal charges by the Manhattan District Attorney's Office]], Trump [[removal jurisdiction|removed]] his criminal case to federal court, where it was assigned to Judge Hellerstein. Judge Hellerstein remanded the criminal case back to state court.<ref>{{Cite news |date=November 6, 2025 |title=Judge to Consider Moving Trump's Hush-Money Conviction to Federal Court |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/11/06/nyregion/trump-conviction-appeal.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251109224422/https://www.nytimes.com/2025/11/06/nyregion/trump-conviction-appeal.html |archive-date=2025-11-09 |access-date=2026-01-05 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="BloombergLaw">{{Cite news |date=December 8, 2025 |title=Trump's Third Immunity Bid Driven by 2nd Cir.: New York Brief |url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/new-york-brief/trumps-third-immunity-bid-driven-by-2nd-cir-new-york-brief |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251211165505/https://news.bloomberglaw.com/new-york-brief/trumps-third-immunity-bid-driven-by-2nd-cir-new-york-brief |archive-date=2025-12-11 |access-date=2026-01-05 |language=en}}</ref> After Trump was convicted in state court, he again removed the case to federal court before Judge Hellerstein, and Hellerstein again remanded the case back to state court. Trump appealed, and the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit|U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit]] assigned the case to Judge Hellerstein to consider whether Trump's conviction should be removed to federal court due to the law of [[presidential immunity]].<ref name="BloombergLaw"/>

In August 2026, Hellerstein again rejected Donald Trump's effort to move his New York criminal conviction from state to federal court.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Mangan |first=Dan |date=2026-08-28 |title=Trump loses bid to transfer New York hush money case to federal court |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/28/trump-hush-money-federal-court.html |access-date=2026-08-28 |website=CNBC |language=en}}</ref> On November 23, 2026, the month after Hellerstein's death, the second US circuit court reversed his decision.<ref name="guard-23nov2026">{{cite news |title=Federal appeals court hands Trump way out of conviction for hush-money payment |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/23/legal-path-erase-donald-trump-hush-money-conviction |access-date=November 23, 2026 |work=[[The Guardian]] |date=November 23, 2026}}</ref>

=== Hugo Carvajal ===
Hellerstein presided over the criminal prosecution of [[Hugo Carvajal]] on [[narcoterrorism]] charges.<ref name=AP25Jun2025>{{cite news|first=Joshua|last=Goodman|title=Former Venezuela spymaster pleads guilty to narcoterrorism charge ahead of trial|publisher=Associated Press|date=June 25, 2025|access-date=June 27, 2025|url=https://apnews.com/article/venezuela-spymaster-guilty-plea-carvajal-e271dc4be0ba8abc69da82315ec62b68}}</ref>

=== Bill Hwang ===
Hellerstein presided over the trial of investor [[Bill Hwang]], and on November 20, 2024, sentenced him to 18 years in prison for his fraudulent scheme at [[Archegos Capital Management]], which caused billions of dollars in losses to banks and contributed to the collapse of [[Credit Suisse]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Goldstein |first1=Matthew |title=Archegos Founder Bill Hwang Is Sentenced to 18 Years |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/11/20/business/bill-hwang-archegos-sentence.html |agency=New York Times}}</ref>

=== Alien Enemies Act ===
In 2025, Hellerstein ruled that President [[Donald Trump]]'s invocation of the [[Alien Enemies Act]] to [[March 2025 American deportations of Venezuelans|deport Venezuelans]] was invalid and unconstitutional. He held that these individuals must receive [[J.G.G. v. Trump|due process]] before being deported, and that the requirements of the [[Alien and Sedition Acts|Alien Enemies Act]] were not satisfied by the President's proclamation.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Jacobs |first1=Shayna |title=N.Y. judge finds Alien Enemies Act use illegal, blocks removals to 'evil' jail |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2025/05/06/new-york-judge-no-deportation-trump-alien-enemies-act/ |agency=Washington Post}}</ref>

=== Charlie Javice, founder of Frank ===
Hellerstein presided over the trial of [[Frank (company)|Frank]] founder [[Charlie Javice]], and on September 29, 2025, sentenced her to seven years in prison for defrauding [[JPMorgan Chase]] out of $175 million in its purchase of the company, which it shuttered in 2023.<ref name="ABC-Javice">{{cite news |title=Charlie Javice sentenced to 7 years in prison for $175M fraud |url=https://abcnews.go.com/Business/charlie-javice-founder-lied-175m-startup-faces-sentencing/story?id=126034577 |access-date=October 1, 2025 |work=ABC News |language=en}}</ref>

=== Kashef v. BNP Paribas ===
Hellerstein presided over a human rights class action trial brought by Sudanese refugees against the French bank [[BNP Paribas]]. The [[bellwether trial]] for the claims of the three plaintiffs lasted five weeks. On October 17, 2025, the jury found [[BNP Paribas]] liable and awarded the three plaintiffs about $20.75 million in total. Observers described it as a landmark verdict holding a bank responsible for a role in human rights abuses.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rowlands |first=Lyndal |title=US jury finds French bank BNP Paribas complicit in Sudan atrocities |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2025/10/18/us-jury-finds-french-bank-bnp-paribas-complicit-in-sudan-atrocities |access-date=2026-10-27 |website=Al Jazeera |language=en}}</ref>  

=== Nicolás Maduro ===
Hellerstein presided over the federal criminal case against Venezuelan president [[Nicolás Maduro]], and his wife [[Cilia Flores]], following the [[2026 United States intervention in Venezuela]],<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/world/2026/01/05/us-venezuela-strikes-nicolas-maduro-live-updates/88022326007/|title='Not guilty' plea for deposed Venezuelan leader Maduro: live updates|first1=Thao|last1=Nguyen|first2=Christopher|last2=Cann|first3=Bart|last3=Jansen|first4=Kathryn|last4=Palmer|publisher=USA Today|date=5 January 2026|accessdate=5 January 2026}}</ref><ref name="NYTimes-Maduro">{{cite news | title=How Manhattan Federal Court Would Handle the Trial of a President |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/01/03/world/americas/maduro-trial-nyc-sdny.html |access-date=January 3, 2026|work=New York Times |language=en}}</ref> which came nearly six years after federal charges against them were filed under ''[[United States v. Maduro, et al.]]'' by the [[First presidency of Donald Trump|first Trump administration]].{{Cn|date=November 2026}}

Following his death in October 2026, his case was reassigned to district judge [[Analisa Torres]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Alvin K. Hellerstein, Federal Judge Who Oversaw Maduro Case, Dies at 92 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/28/nyregion/judge-alvin-hellerstein-dies-maduro-case.html |access-date=28 October 2026 |publisher=The New York Times |date=28 October 2026}}</ref>

== Death ==
Hellerstein died on the morning of October 28, 2026, at the age of 92.<ref>{{cite news |title=Alvin K. Hellerstein, Federal Judge Who Oversaw Maduro Case, Dies at 92 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/28/nyregion/judge-alvin-hellerstein-dies-maduro-case.html |access-date=28 October 2026 |publisher=The New York Times |date=28 October 2026}}</ref>
