'''Amanda Kathleen Brailsford'''<ref name="Questionnaire"/> (born 1967)<ref name="Questionnaire">{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Brailsford%20SJQ%20Public.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=March 21, 2023}}</ref> is the [[United States federal judge|chief United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Idaho]]. She previously served as a judge of the [[Idaho Court of Appeals]] from 2019 to 2023.

== Education ==
Born in [[Twin Falls, Idaho]], Brailsford grew up in [[Hagerman, Idaho|Hagerman]].<ref name="COABio">{{Cite web |title=Hon. Judge Amanda K. Brailsford |url=https://isc.idaho.gov/main/judge_brailsford |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221130031230/https://isc.idaho.gov/main/judge_brailsford |archive-date=November 30, 2022 |access-date=January 18, 2023 |website=isc.idaho.gov}}</ref> She received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] from the [[University of Idaho]] in [[Moscow, Idaho|Moscow]] in 1989 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from its [[University of Idaho College of Law|College of Law]] in 1993.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Hon. Amanda Kathleen Brailsford Profile |url=https://www.martindale.com/attorney/hon-amanda-kathleen-brailsford-896976/ |access-date=January 18, 2023 |website=www.martindale.com}}</ref><ref name="WHBio">{{Cite press release |title=President Biden Names Twenty–Ninth Round of Judicial Nominees |date=January 18, 2023 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2023/01/18/president-biden-names-twenty-ninth-round-of-judicial-nominees/ |access-date=January 18, 2023}} {{PD-notice}}</ref>

== Career ==
Following law school, Brailsford served as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Thomas G. Nelson]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]] from 1993 to 1995.<ref name="COABio" /><ref name="WHBio" /> She worked at the [[Boise]] office of Holland & Hart LLP as an [[Associate lawyer|associate]] from 1995 to 2002, and as a partner from 2003 to 2013.<ref name="COABio" /><ref name="WHBio" /> She was a founding [[law firm partner|partner]] of the law firm of Andersen Banducci PLLC from 2013 to 2017.<ref name="WHBio" />

=== Idaho Court of Appeals ===
On November 30, 2018, Brailsford was appointed as a judge of the [[Idaho Court of Appeals]] by [[List of governors of Idaho|Governor]] [[Butch Otter]] to the seat vacated by the retirement of Judge Sergio Gutierrez.<ref>{{Cite web |date=November 30, 2018 |title=Moeller appointed to Supreme Court, Brailsford picked for Court of Appeals |url=https://www.idahostatejournal.com/news/local/moeller-appointed-to-supreme-court-brailsford-picked-for-court-of-appeals/article_de53c5ff-4b13-54a4-9a7f-975d763e2c69.html |access-date=January 18, 2023 |website=Idaho State Journal |language=en}}</ref> She assumed office in 2019 and left in 2023 to become a federal judge.<ref name="COABio" />

==== Notable rulings ====
In 2022, Brailsford wrote the opinion for the Idaho Court of Appeals affirming an aggravated [[Driving under the influence|DUI]] conviction for Cyrus Buehler. Buehler was accused of being intoxicated while driving his pickup truck that struck a man operating a motorized bicycle.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.idahostatejournal.com/news/local/man-charged-with-felony-dui-for-striking-cyclist-to-plead-guilty-will-likely-file-appeal/article_bb754403-6b2b-58bc-b868-a24b2924f232.html#:~:text=Cyrus%20Wolf%20Buehler%2C%2037%2C%20through%20his%20Pocatello%20attorney%2C,to%20defend%20against%20the%20accusations%2C%20court%20records%20say|title=Man charged with felony DUI for striking cyclist to plead guilty, will likely file appeal|date=27 February 2020 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.idahostatejournal.com/news/local/family-of-severely-injured-bicyclist-says-hospital-plans-to-discharge/article_47aef510-583a-593a-961c-c34bc0091762.html|title=Family of severely injured bicyclist says hospital plans to discharge him prematurely|date=6 February 2018 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite court|litigants=State of Idaho v. Cyrus Wolf Buehler|vol=|reporter=Idaho Supreme Court|opinion=48172|court=Idaho Court of Appeals|date=2022-12-19|url=https://isc.idaho.gov/opinions/48172.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250918075047/https://isc.idaho.gov/opinions/48172.pdf|archive-date=2025-09-18|url-status=live}}</ref>

Also that year, Brailsford wrote the opinion for the court affirming [[Shoshone County, Idaho|Shoshone County]] Sheriff Darrell<!-- Michael--> Gunderson's decision to deny a [[Concealed carry in the United States|concealed weapons license]] to Robert<!-- Ervin --> Peterson. Gunderson disqualified Peterson due to his prior conviction of possessing material sexually exploiting children.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://vettingroom.org/2023/02/16/judge-amanda-brailsford/|title=Judge Amanda Brailsford – Nominee to the U.S. District Court for the District of Idaho|date=16 February 2023}}</ref><ref>{{Cite court|litigants=Robert Ervin Peterson v. Darrell Michael Gunderson, in his official capacity as the Shoshone County Sheriff|vol=|reporter=Idaho Supreme Court|opinion=48781|court=Idaho Court of Appeals|date=2022-07-08|url=https://isc.idaho.gov/opinions/48781.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250905052938/https://isc.idaho.gov/opinions/48781.pdf|archive-date=2025-09-05|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite court|litigants=Robert Ervin Peterson v. Darrell Michael Gunderson, Shoshone County Sheriff|vol=|reporter=Idaho Supreme Court|opinion=48781 Summary|court=Idaho Court of Appeals|date=2022-07-08|url=https://isc.idaho.gov/opinions/48781summ.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250916150713/https://isc.idaho.gov/opinions/48781summ.pdf|archive-date=2025-09-16|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Federal judicial service ===

On January 18, 2023, President [[Joe Biden]] announced his intent to nominate Brailsford to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Idaho|U.S. District Court]] in Idaho.<ref name="WHBio" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Vazquez |first=Maegan |date=January 18, 2023 |title=First on CNN: Biden releases first slate of 2023 judicial nominees |url=https://www.cnn.com/2023/01/18/politics/biden-judicial-nominees-2023/index.html |access-date=January 18, 2023 |website=CNN |language=en}}</ref> On January 31, 2023, her nomination was sent to the [[United States Senate]]. President Biden nominated Brailsford to the seat vacated by Judge [[B. Lynn Winmill]], who assumed [[senior status]] on August 16, 2021.<ref>{{Cite press release|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate|date=January 31, 2023|publisher=The White House|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2023/01/31/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-94/}}</ref> On March 22, 2023, a hearing on her nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Nominations|date=March 21, 2023|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/committee-activity/hearings/03/22/2023/nominations}}</ref> On April 27, 2023, her nomination was reported out of committee by a [[voice vote]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/2023-04-27%20-%20EBM%20-%20Results.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – April 27, 2023|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=May 1, 2023}}</ref><ref>{{Cite press release|title=Idaho Senators Applaud Judiciary Committee Approval of Judge Amanda Brailsford|url=https://www.crapo.senate.gov/media/newsreleases/idaho-senators-applaud-judiciary-committee-approval-of-judge-amanda-brailsford}}</ref> On May 4, 2023, the [[United States Senate]] confirmed her nomination by a voice vote.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/118th-congress/286|title=PN286 — Amanda K. Brailsford — The Judiciary|date=January 31, 2023|website=congress.gov|access-date=May 4, 2023}}</ref> Brailsford received her judicial commission on May 17, 2023,<ref name="FJC">{{FJC Bio|nid=13623536|inline=yes}}</ref> and was sworn in on May 19, 2023.<ref>{{Cite news|date=May 19, 2023|last=Kwan|first=Cory|title=Judge Amanda K. Brailsford becomes Idaho's 13th and first female US District Judge|url=https://www.kivitv.com/news/political/inside-the-statehouse/judge-amanda-k-brailsford-becomes-idahos-13th-and-first-female-us-district-judge|website=kivitv.com|access-date=May 26, 2023}}</ref> She is the first woman to serve on the U.S. District Court in Idaho.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Crawley|first=John|title=Brailsford Confirmed as First Female US Trial Judge in Idaho|url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/daily-labor-report/brailsford-confirmed-in-historic-vote-for-idaho-judiciary|website=news.bloomberglaw.com|date=May 6, 2023}}</ref> She became chief judge of the court in 2026.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.idd.uscourts.gov/Content_Fetcher/index.cfml/Press_Release-New_Chief_Judge__4565.pdf?Content_ID=4565|title=Amanda K. Brailsford Takes Reins as Idaho's Chief District Judge |date=January 2, 2026|website=idd.uscourts.gov|access-date=January 5, 2026}}</ref>

==== Notable cases ====

In ''Creech v. United States District Court for the District of Idaho'', Brailsford received calls to recuse herself from a lawsuit brought by death row inmate [[Thomas Eugene Creech]] alleging prosecutorial fabrication of evidence.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Rodriguez |first1=Richard | url=https://www.ktvb.com/article/news/local/district-court-appeals-removes-federal-judge-creech-case-failing-recuse-herself/277-3cf0861e-50eb-4b10-a4ce-04cc05221552 | title=9th Circuit Court of Appeals removes federal judge in Creech case after failing to recuse herself | website=[[KTVB7]] | date=October 17, 2024 |access-date=October 20, 2024}}</ref> Brailsford had a close personal friendship with Ada County Prosecutor Jan Bennetts, whose office oversaw the prosecution of Creech for the 1981 murder of inmate David Dale Jenson.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Jacobsen |first1=Kate | url=https://www.kivitv.com/news/federal-judge-removed-from-thomas-creech-case-new-appeal-filed | title=Federal judge removed from Thomas Creech case, new appeal filed | website=[[KIVI-TV]] | date=October 18, 2024 |access-date=October 20, 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Zoppo |first1=Avalon | url=https://www.law.com/nationallawjournal/2024/10/17/clear-abuse-of-discretion-9th-circuit-says-judge-should-have-recused-from-death-row-inmates-lawsuit/?slreturn=20241020135721 | title='Clear Abuse of Discretion': 9th Circuit Says Judge Should Have Recused From Death Row Inmate's Lawsuit | website=[[ALM (company)|Law.com]] | date=October 17, 2024 |access-date=October 20, 2024}}</ref> While previously having clerked with and developed a friendship with Bennetts under Judge [[Thomas G. Nelson]] in 1993, Brailsford justified her lack of recusal by saying the two had "lost touch".<ref>{{cite web |last1=Raymond |first1=Nate | url=https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/idaho-judge-removed-death-row-inmates-case-over-friendship-with-prosecutor-2024-10-17/ | title=Idaho judge removed from death-row inmate's case over friendship with prosecutor | website=[[Reuters]] | date=October 17, 2024 |access-date=October 20, 2024}}</ref> Writing for a three judge panel for the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit|Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals]], Judge [[Jay Bybee]] determined that, while Brailsford likely would have been able to hear the case in good faith, her impartiality would have been reasonably questioned due to the unique circumstances of the case, ultimately supporting her removal from the case.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Thomsen |first1=Jacqueline | url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/judges-ties-to-prosecutor-spurs-removal-from-death-row-lawsuit | title=Judge's Ties to Prosecutor Spurs Removal From Death-Row Lawsuit | website=[[Bloomberg Law]] | date=October 17, 2024 |access-date=October 20, 2024}}</ref>

Amit Mehta:
{{Short description|American federal judge (born 1971)}} {{Infobox judge |name = Amit Mehta |image = Mehta A.jpg |caption = Official portrait, 2016 |office = Judge of the [[United States Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court]] |term_start = June 1, 2021 |term_end = |appointer = [[John Roberts]] |predecessor = [[James Boasberg]] |successor = |office1 = Judge of the [[United States District Court for the District of Columbia]] |term_start1 = December 19, 2014 |term_end1 = |appointer1 = [[List of federal judges appointed by Barack Obama|Barack Obama]] |predecessor1 = [[Ellen Segal Huvelle]] |successor1 = |birth_name = Amit Priyavadan Mehta |birth_date = {{birth year and age|1971}} |birth_place = [[Patan, Gujarat]], India |death_date = |death_place = |education = [[Georgetown University]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|BA]])
[[University of Virginia School of Law|University of Virginia]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Amit Priyavadan Mehta''' (born 1971) is an American lawyer and jurist who serves as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Columbia|U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia]]. He was appointed in 2014 by President [[Barack Obama]]. In 2021, Mehta became a judge on the [[United States Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court]]. Mehta presided over cases related to [[January 6 United States Capitol attack|attack on the United States Capitol]] on January 6, 2021, and the [[United States v. Google LLC (2020)|Google antitrust case]]. In 2022, he rejected efforts by [[Donald Trump]] to dismiss lawsuits accusing the former President of legal responsibility in the attacks.{{Cite web |last1=Cheney |first1=Kyle |last2=Gerstein |first2=Josh |date=2022-02-18 |title=Judge rejects Trump effort to toss lawsuits accusing him of Jan. 6 conspiracy |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2022/02/18/trump-january-6-lawsuit-00010249 |access-date=2023-08-14 |website=POLITICO |language=en}} ==Early life and education== Mehta was born in 1971 in [[Patan, Gujarat]], India.{{cite news|url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/world/us/hip-hop-loving-indian-american-judge-rules-against-trump-in-fight-for-his-financial-records/articleshow/69432068.cms|title=Hip-hop loving Indian-American judge rules against Trump in fight for his financial records|last=Rajghatta|first=Chidanand|date=May 21, 2019|work=[[Times of India]]|access-date=21 May 2019}} At the age of one, Mehta emigrated with his parents, Priyavadan and Ragini Mehta, to the United States. His mother worked as a [[laboratory technician]], while his father worked as an engineer.{{Cite web |last=Kulkarni |first=Bhargavi |date=2022-11-30 |title='One of the Most Intelligent Judges': Defense Attorneys Praise Judge Amit Mehta For Conducting a Fair Seditious Conspiracy Trial |url=https://americankahani.com/lead-stories/one-of-the-most-intelligent-judges-defense-attorneys-praise-judge-amit-mehta-for-conducting-a-fair-seditious-conspiracy-trial/ |access-date=2023-06-02 |website=American Kahani |language=en-US}} Mehta was raised in [[Reisterstown, Maryland]], a suburb of [[Baltimore]].{{Cite web |last=Maqsood |first=Zofeen |date=2019-05-25 |title=Newsmaker: Amit Mehta, the Indian American judge who ruled against President Trump - The American Bazaar |url=https://www.americanbazaaronline.com/2019/05/24/newsmaker-amit-mehta-the-indian-american-judge-who-ruled-against-president-trump-437685/,%20https://www.americanbazaaronline.com/2019/05/24/newsmaker-amit-mehta-the-indian-american-judge-who-ruled-against-president-trump-437685/ |access-date=2023-06-02 |language=en-US}} He graduated from [[Franklin High School (Reisterstown, Maryland)|Franklin High School]] in 1989. Mehta graduated from [[Georgetown University]] in 1993 with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in [[economics]], graduating [[Phi Beta Kappa]]. From 1993 to 1994, Mehta worked as a [[paralegal]] at the law firm Patton Boggs (now [[Squire Patton Boggs]]). He then attended the [[University of Virginia School of Law]], where he was an editor of the ''[[Virginia Journal of Social Policy & the Law]]''. He graduated in 1997 with a [[Juris Doctor]] and [[Order of the Coif]] honors. == Early career == After graduating from law school, Mehta spent a year as an associate at the law firm [[Latham & Watkins]] before leaving to be a [[law clerk]] to Judge [[Susan P. Graber]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]] from 1998 to 1999. He was an associate at the law firm Zuckerman Spaeder, LLP from 1999 to 2002, then became a staff attorney at the [[Public Defender Service for the District of Columbia]] from 2002 to 2007. From 2007 to 2014, he rejoined Zuckerman Spaeder, serving as partner from 2010 to 2014. He represented clients in civil and criminal matters before state and federal courts.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/07/31/president-obama-nominates-two-serve-united-states-district-courts|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Obama Nominates Two to Serve on the United States District Courts|date=31 July 2014 |via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|access-date=20 April 2016}}[http://www.zuckerman.com/amit_mehta Official Biography at Zuckerman Spaeder] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140808050845/http://www.zuckerman.com/amit_mehta |date=August 8, 2014 }}{{FJC Bio|nid=1394756|inline=yes}} While in the private sector, he represented former Managing Director of the [[International Monetary Fund]] [[Dominique Strauss-Kahn]]. == Federal judicial service == === Nomination === On July 31, 2014, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Mehta to serve as a United States District Judge of the United States District Court for the District of Columbia, to the seat vacated by Judge [[Ellen Segal Huvelle]], who took [[senior status]] on June 3, 2014.{{cite web|url=http://don411.com/the-white-house-nominations-sent-to-the-senate-allison-dale-burroughs-amit-priyavadan-mehta/#.U9sh6mPG_sV|title=THE WHITE HOUSE NOMINATIONS SENT TO THE SENATE: Allison Dale Burroughs, Amit Priyavadan Mehta|author=Don|work=Don411.com Media :: Performing Arts News Unabridged|access-date=20 April 2016}} He received a hearing before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]] on September 17, 2014.{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/judicial-nominations-2014-09-17|title=Meeting – Hearings & Meetings – United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|date=17 September 2014|publisher=|access-date=20 April 2016}} On November 20, 2014, his nomination was reported out of committee by [[voice vote]].{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%2011-20-14.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – November 20, 2014 United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|publisher=}} On December 13, 2014, Senate Majority Leader [[Harry Reid]] filed a motion to invoke [[cloture]] on the nomination. On December 16, 2014, Reid withdrew his cloture motion on Mehta's nomination, and the Senate proceeded to vote to confirm Mehta in a [[voice vote]].{{cite web|url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/113th-congress/1942|title=PN1942 — Amit Priyavadan Mehta — The Judiciary|date=16 December 2014|publisher=Congress.gov|access-date=20 May 2019}} He received his federal judicial commission on December 19, 2014. === Tenure === {{update|date=December 2022}} [[File:JudgeMehta102715 crop.jpg|thumb|Judge Mehta in 2015]] In May 2019, Mehta ruled that accounting firm [[Mazars]] had to provide its records of [[Donald Trump]]'s accounts from before his presidency to the [[House Oversight Committee]] in response to their subpoena.{{cite web|url=https://www.cnn.com/2019/05/20/politics/mazars-trump-records/index.html|title=Judge orders Trump accounting firm to hand over records to Congress|first=Katelyn|last=Polantz|website=[[CNN]]|date=May 20, 2019}} In a 41-page opinion, he asserted that Congress has the right to investigate potential illegal behavior by a president, including actions both before and after the president assumed office.{{cite news|url=https://www.politico.com/story/2019/05/20/judge-upholds-dem-subpoena-for-trump-financial-records-1335370|title=Judge upholds Dem subpoena for Trump financial records|last1=Desiderio|first1=Andrew|last2=Cheney|first2=Kyle|date=May 20, 2019|work=[[Politico]]|access-date=21 May 2019}} The ruling will be appealed by Trump's personal legal team. In July 2019, Mehta sided with the pharmaceutical firms [[Merck & Co.]], [[Eli Lilly and Company]], and [[Amgen Inc.]] by blocking a [[First presidency of Donald Trump|Trump administration]] rule requiring drugmakers to put prices in television ads, a central part of the president's push to lower the cost of prescription medications. The goal of the rule was to increase transparency; Mehta ruled that requiring big pharmaceutical companies to disclose prices to consumers in television advertisements was something that could be done only by the [[United States Department of Health and Human Services|Department of Health and Human Services]] if mandated by Congress.{{Cite web|url=http://freepdfhosting.com/9f12cc13ab.pdf|title=MERCK & CO., INC., et al., vs US Dept. HHS|last=Mehta|first=Amit|date=July 8, 2019|website=freepdfhosting.com|language=en-US|access-date=2019-07-09}} In 2020, Mehta became the presiding judge in the [[United States v. Google LLC (2020)|''United States v. Google LLC'']] antitrust case.{{Cite web |last=Arbel |first=Tali |date=2021-04-21 |title=Meet Amit Mehta, the judge for Google's antitrust case |url=https://apnews.com/article/donald-trump-district-of-columbia-hip-hop-and-rap-lawsuits-music-dfdd86ca91930cda6ab138cd1393a88e |access-date=2023-06-02 |website=AP NEWS |language=en}} On June 1, 2021, Chief Justice [[John Roberts]] appointed Mehta to the [[United States Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court]].{{cite web |title=FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE SURVEILLANCE COURT FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE SURVEILLANCE COURT OF REVIEW Current and Past Members June 2021 |url=https://www.fisc.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/FISC%20FISCR%20Judges%20June%202021.pdf |accessdate=August 31, 2021}} ==== January 6 Capitol attack-related cases ==== Mehta has presided over several cases related to the [[January 6 United States Capitol attack]]. He has charge of the criminal prosecution of [[Oath Keepers]] founder [[Stewart Rhodes]] for [[seditious conspiracy]].{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/dc-md-va/2022/02/18/stewart-rhodes-jail-seditious-conspiracy/|title=Oath Keepers leader Stewart Rhodes ordered to be jailed until trial on seditious conspiracy|last=Hsu|first=Spencer S.|date=February 18, 2022|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|access-date=19 February 2022}} He is also presiding over three civil lawsuits against Trump and multiple associates, in which several members of Congress and two police officers are suing for damages for physical and emotional injuries they allegedly incurred during the attacks. On February 18, 2022, Mehta issued a lengthy opinion that rejected [[Donald Trump|Trump]]'s claim of "absolute [[Legal immunity|immunity]]" from lawsuits, finding that his actions were not part of his presidential duties, and that there was plausible evidence to suggest he engaged in a [[conspiracy (crime)|conspiracy]] with organized groups to use any means, including violence, to [[Attempts to overturn the 2020 United States presidential election|overturn the results]] of the [[U.S. presidential election, 2020|2020 election]]. The opinion allows the case to proceed, with the plaintiffs demanding documents, depositions, and other evidence from Trump and members of the Oath Keepers and [[Proud Boys]]. Mehta dropped several other co-defendants from the suit, including [[Rudy Giuliani]], [[Donald Trump Jr.]], and Representative [[Mo Brooks]].{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/dc-md-va/2022/02/18/jan6-trump-lawsuit/|title=U.S. judge rejects Trump claim of 'absolute immunity' from Jan. 6 lawsuits|last=Hsu|first=Spencer S.|date=February 18, 2022|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|access-date=19 February 2022}} On January 25, 2024, Mehta sentenced former Trump adviser, [[Peter Navarro]], to four months in jail for contempt of Congress after defying a subpoena related to the congressional investigation into the January 6, 2021, US Capitol attack.{{cite news|url=https://www.cnn.com/2024/01/25/politics/peter-navarro-contempt-congress-sentence/index.html/|title=Former Trump adviser Peter Navarro sentenced to 4 months in jail for defying congressional subpoena|last1=Cole|first1=Devan|last2=Lybrand|first2=Holmes|date=25 January 2024|work=[[CNN]]|access-date=25 January 2024}} ===Google antitrust case=== {{Main|United States v. Google LLC (2020)}} On August 5, 2024, Mehta ruled that [[Google]] is a monopoly and has violated antitrust laws.{{cite web |last1=Feiner |first1=Lauren |title=Judge rules that Google 'is a monopolist' in US antitrust case |url=https://www.theverge.com/2024/8/5/24155520/judge-rules-on-us-doj-v-google-antitrust-search-suit |website=The Verge |date=5 August 2024 }} In September 2025, he ruled that Google would not be required to divest of [[Google Chrome|Chrome]] or [[Android (operating system)|Android]], but would be barred from including [[Google Search|Search]] in exclusive contracts and required to share certain [[Search engine indexing|search index]] and user interaction data with competitors.{{cite news|last=Elias|first=Jennifer|date=September 2, 2025|title=Google stock jumps 8% after search giant avoids worst-case penalties in antitrust case|publisher=CNBC|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2025/09/02/google-antitrust-search-ruling.html|access-date=September 2, 2025}}{{cite news|last=Liedtke|first=Michael|date=September 2, 2025|title=Google avoids breakup in search monopoly case, but judge orders other changes in landmark ruling|publisher=Associated Press|url=https://apnews.com/article/google-search-antitrust-remedies-chrome-846916fda0943c5fa359385044a02c8b|access-date=September 2, 2025}} == Personal life == Mehta is an avid fan of [[hip hop music]]. In a 2015 [[Copyright law of the United States|copyright case]] regarding the similarity of two songs, Mehta noted in a footnote that he was "not a 'lay person' when it comes to hip-hop music and lyrics," and noted he has "listened to hip hop for decades". American rappers [[Jay-Z]], [[Eminem]], [[Kanye West]] and Canadian rapper [[Drake (musician)|Drake]] are among his favorite artists. ==See also== *[[List of Asian American jurists]] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1394756}} *{{Ballotpedia|Amit_Priyavadan_Mehta}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Ellen Segal Huvelle]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States District Court for the District of Columbia]]}}|years=2014–present}} {{s-inc|rows=2}} |- {{s-bef|before=[[James Boasberg]]}} {{s-ttl|title=Judge of the [[United States Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court]]|years=2021–present}} {{s-end}} {{United States DC Circuit district judges}} {{FISA Court}} {{authority control}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Mehta, Amit Priyavadan}} [[Category:1971 births]] [[Category:Living people]] [[Category:American jurists of Indian descent]] [[Category:Georgetown University alumni]] [[Category:Judges of the United States District Court for the District of Columbia]] [[Category:Judges of the United States Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court]] [[Category:Lawyers from Washington, D.C.]] [[Category:People from Reistertown, Maryland]] [[Category:People from Patan district]] [[Category:Public defenders]] [[Category:United States district court judges appointed by Barack Obama]] [[Category:University of Virginia School of Law alumni]] [[Category:Virginia lawyers]] [[Category:American people of Gujarati descent]]

[[Baylor University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Amos Louis Mazzant III''' (born 1965) is the [[United States federal judge|chief United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Texas]] and former [[United States magistrate judge]] of the same court. ==Biography== Mazzant was born in [[Ellwood City, Pennsylvania]].{{cite web|url=http://www2.dallasbar.org/judiciary/profiles.asp?item=97|title=Home – Dallas Bar Association|website=www2.dallasbar.org}} He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree, magna cum laude, in 1987 from the [[University of Pittsburgh]]. He received a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1990 from the [[Baylor Law School]]. Mazzant began his legal career as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Paul Neeley Brown]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Texas]] from 1990 to 1992. From 1992 to 1993, he worked at the law firm of Henderson, Bryant & Wolfe. He served as a law clerk to Magistrate Judge Robert Faulkner from 1993 to 2003 and Magistrate Judge Don D. Bush in 2003, both in the Eastern District of Texas. From 2003 to 2004, he was [[of counsel]] at Wolfe, Tidwell & McCoy, LLP. He served as a justice of the [[Fifth Court of Appeals of Texas|Court of Appeals for the Fifth District of Texas]] at [[Dallas]], from 2004 to 2009. From 2009 to 2014, he served as a [[United States magistrate judge]] in the Eastern District of Texas.[https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/06/26/president-obama-nominates-four-serve-united-states-district-courts "President Obama Nominates Four to Serve on the United States District Court], [[White House Office of the Press Secretary]] (June 26, 2014).{{FJC Bio|nid=1394751|inline=yes}} ===Federal judicial service=== In 2014, Mazzant was recommended to the [[Obama Administration]] as a judicial nominee by U.S. Senator [[Ted Cruz]].{{Cite web|url=https://vettingroom.org/2020/08/19/thirteen-federal-judges-president-trump-may-elevate-to-the-court-of-appeals-in-his-second-term/|title=Thirteen Federal Judges President Trump May Elevate to the Court of Appeals in His Second Term|first=Harsh|last=Voruganti|date=August 19, 2020}} On June 26, 2014, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Mazzant to serve as a United States District Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Texas]], to the seat vacated by Judge [[T. John Ward]], who retired on October 1, 2011.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/06/26/presidential-nominations-sent-senate|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=26 June 2014}} His nomination was part of a bipartisan [[product bundling|package]] of nominees which included [[Robert Pitman]] and [[Robert W. Schroeder III]].{{Cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/06/26/presidential-nominations-sent-senate|title=Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate|date=June 26, 2014|website=whitehouse.gov}} He received a hearing before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]] for September 9, 2014.{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/judicial-nominations-2014-09-09|title=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|website=www.judiciary.senate.gov}} On November 20, 2014 his nomination was reported out of committee by [[voice vote]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%2011-20-14.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – November 20, 2014 United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=8 June 2023}} On December 13, 2014 [[Senate Majority Leader]] [[Harry Reid]] filed a motion to invoke [[cloture]] on the nomination. On December 16, 2014, Reid withdrew his cloture motion on Mazzant's nomination, and the Senate confirmed Mazzant by [[voice vote]]. He received his federal judicial commission on December 19, 2014. He became the chief judge in 2025. Mazzant had been mentioned as someone that President [[Donald Trump]] could nominate to the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit]]—his docket as a district court judge has been '''Amy Sauber Berman Jackson''' (born 1954) is an American lawyer serving as a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Columbia]]. Born and raised in [[Baltimore|Baltimore, Maryland]], she graduated from [[Harvard Law School]] in 1979. After graduation, she served as a [[law clerk ]] until 1980. She then worked as an assistant US attorney until 1984, when she entered private-sector work. She was nominated as a federal judge in 2011 and unanimously confirmed by the [[United States Senate]]. In 2023, she became a senior judge. 

==Early life and education==
Amy Berman was born in 1954, in Baltimore, Maryland,<ref>''Martindale-Hubbell Law Directory'', Vol. 17 ([[Martindale-Hubbell]], 2001).</ref> She is the daughter of Mildred (Sauber) and Barnett Berman, a physician at [[Johns Hopkins Hospital]].<ref>{{Cite news |url= https://www.baltimoresun.com/2004/02/09/dr-barnett-berman-81-internist-army-veteran/ |url-status= live |title= Dr. Barnett Berman, 81, internist, Army veteran |first= Joe |last= Nawrozki |website= [[Baltimore Sun]] |access-date= February 21, 2019 |date= February 9, 2004 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20190219130203/https://www.baltimoresun.com/news/bs-xpm-2004-02-09-0402090061-story.html |archive-date= February 19, 2019 }}</ref> She graduated from [[Harvard College]] in 1976 with a [[Bachelor of Arts]], [[Latin honors#United States|''cum laude'']], and from Harvard Law School in 1979 with a [[Juris Doctor]], ''cum laude''.<ref name= "fjc.gov">{{FJC Bio| nid= 1393656}}</ref>

==Career==
After graduating from law school, Jackson served as a law clerk to Judge [[Harrison Lee Winter]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit]] from 1979 to 1980. From 1980 to 1986, she served as an [[assistant United States attorney]] for the [[District of Columbia]], where she received Department of Justice Special Achievement Awards for her work on high-profile murder and sexual assault cases in 1985 and 1986. From 1986 to 1994, Jackson was an associate and then a [[Partner (business rank)|partner]] at the law firm Venable, Baetjer, Howard and Civiletti (now [[Venable LLP]]).<ref name="NamesThree">{{cite press release |title=President Obama Names Three to United States District Court, 6/17/10 |url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/realitycheck/the-press-office/president-obama-names-three-united-states-district-court-61710 |work=White House Office of the Press Secretary |date=June 17, 2010 |access-date=October 5, 2022 }}</ref>

From 2000 until her appointment as a federal judge, Jackson was a member of the law firm Trout Cacheris & Solomon PLLC in Washington, D.C., where she specialized in complex litigation, criminal investigations and defense, criminal trials, civil trials, and appeals. In 2009 Jackson represented nine-term [[United States House of Representatives|Representative]] for [[Louisiana's 2nd congressional district]] [[William J. Jefferson]] in his [[Political corruption|corruption trial]]. In 2025, Jackson blocked the Trump administration's attempt to oust [[United States Office of Special Counsel]] head [[Hampton Dellinger]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.nytimes.com/live/2025/03/02/us/trump-news-zelensky-europe#dellinger-trump-watchdog-judge-jackson | title=Democrats Invite Fired Federal Workers to Trump's Congressional Address | work=The New York Times | date=March 2, 2025 | last1=Miller | first1=Maya C. }}</ref>

Jackson has served as a legal commentator for [[Fox News]], [[CNN]], [[NBC]], and [[MSNBC]].<ref name="ATTORNEYS, Amy Berman Jackson">{{cite web |url=http://www.troutcacheris.com/attorneys-a-jackson.php |title=ATTORNEYS, Amy Berman Jackson |access-date=March 28, 2011 |publisher=Trout Cacheris PLLC  |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100204130857/http://www.troutcacheris.com/attorneys-a-jackson.php |archive-date=February 4, 2010 }}</ref><ref name="fjc.gov" />

===Federal judicial service===

On June 17, 2010, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Jackson to fill a seat on the United States District Court for the District of Columbia that was vacated by Judge [[Gladys Kessler]], who assumed [[senior status]] in 2007.<ref name="NamesThree"/> She was unanimously rated "well qualified" for the post by the [[American Bar Association]]'s [[Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary]] (the committee's highest rating).<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.americanbar.org/content/dam/aba/migrated/2011_build/federal_judiciary/ratings111.pdf |title=RATINGS OF ARTICLE III JUDICIAL NOMINEES: 11TH CONGRESS |publisher=[[American Bar Association]] |work=[[Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary]] }}</ref> Her nomination lapsed at the end of the [[111th Congress]];<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/111th-congress/1868 |date=June 17, 2010 |title=PN1868 — Amy Berman Jackson — The Judiciary, 111th Congress (2009–2010) |work=Congress.gov }}</ref> Obama renominated her on January 5, 2011, at the beginning of the [[112th Congress]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/112th-congress/26 |title=PN26 — Amy Berman Jackson — The Judiciary 112th Congress (2011–2012) |work=Congress.gov|date=March 17, 2011 }}</ref> The United States Senate confirmed Jackson on March 17, 2011, by a 97–0 vote.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=112&session=1&vote=00045|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Amy Berman Jackson, of the District of Columbia, to be U.S. District Judge)|publisher=United States Senate}}</ref> She received her commission the next day. She assumed [[senior status]] on May 1, 2023.<ref name="fjc.gov"/>

===Selected opinions===

====Labor law====
In ''Chamber of Commerce v. National Labor Relations Board'' (2012), Jackson ruled that the [[National Labor Relations Board]] had the statutory authority to promulgate a federal regulation requiring the posting of workplace posters informing workers of the [[right to organize]] and [[collective bargaining|collectively bargain]], but also struck down the portions of the regulation in which the NLRB made a "blanket advance determination that a failure to post [the notice] will always constitute an unfair labor practice" and tolled the [[statute of limitations]] in unfair labor practice actions involving a failures to post.<ref>{{cite news|title=Judge Clears Rule on Union Posters at Work |newspaper=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/03/03/business/judge-clears-rule-on-union-posters-at-work.html |agency=[[Associated Press]] |date=March 3, 2012 |access-date=October 5, 2022 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|author=Kevin Bogardus|date=March 2, 2012|title=Judge: NLRB can require employers to display union posters|url=https://thehill.com/business-a-lobbying/213903-judge-nlrb-can-require-union-posters-in-the-workplace|newspaper=The Hill}}</ref><ref name=Rubenstein>{{cite news|author=Abigail Rubenstein|title=Biz Groups Urge DC Circ. Not To Reconsider NLRB Poster Rule|work=Law360|date=August 21, 2013|url=https://www.law360.com/articles/466667/biz-groups-urge-dc-circ-not-to-reconsider-nlrb-poster-rule}}</ref> The next year, the D.C. Circuit vacated the NLRB rule, finding that it contravened Section 8(c) of the [[National Labor Relations Act]], the provision protecting most employers' speech.<ref name=Rubenstein/>

In 2015, Jackson ruled against a coalition of businesses who challenged an NLRB rule expediting union elections.<ref>{{cite news |first=Daniel |last=Wiessner |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/unions-election-idUSL1N10A3TX20150730 |title=Business groups lose challenge to NLRB election rules |work=[[Reuters]] |date=July 30, 2015 |access-date=October 5, 2022 }}</ref><ref>''[https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=283076418686383814 Chamber of Commerce v. National Labor Relations Bd.]'', 118 F. Supp. 3d 171 (2015).</ref>

====EPA & Spruce Mine permit====
Also in March 2012, Jackson overturned a decision by the [[United States Environmental Protection Agency|Environmental Protection Agency]] (EPA) that revoked a permit for the [[Spruce 1]] mine project in [[Logan County, West Virginia]], on the ground that the EPA did not have power under the [[Clean Water Act]] to rescind the permit.<ref>{{cite news|last=Broder|first=John M.|title=Court Reverses E.P.A. on Big Mining Project|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/03/24/science/earth/court-reverses-epa-saying-big-mining-project-can-proceed.html|newspaper=The New York Times|date=March 24, 2012}}</ref> That ruling was reversed by the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit in April 2013.<ref>{{cite news|last=Broder|first=John M.|title=Court Backs E.P.A. Veto of Mining Permit|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2013/04/24/science/earth/court-backs-epa-veto-of-mining-permit.html|newspaper=The New York Times|date=April 24, 2013}}</ref> On September 30, 2014, Jackson ruled in the EPA's favor, allowing its veto of the permit to stand.<ref>{{cite news|title=EPA wins another round on Spruce Mine veto|url=http://www.wvgazette.com/article/20140930/GZ01/140939918 |first=Ken Jr. |last=Ward |access-date=October 5, 2022 |newspaper=The Charleston Gazette|date=September 30, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141006104604/http://www.wvgazette.com/article/20140930/GZ01/140939918 |archive-date=October 6, 2014 }}</ref>

====Jesse Jackson Jr.====
Jackson presided at the August 2013 sentencing of former U.S. Representative [[Jesse Jackson Jr.]] and his wife, [[Sandi Jackson]]. After accepting guilty pleas to misuse of campaign funds, she sentenced Representative Jackson to 30 months and his wife to 12 months in prison.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://rollcall.com/2013/08/14/jesse-jackson-jr-and-wife-sentenced-to-jail-time/ |first=Matt |last=Fuller |title=Jesse Jackson Jr. and Wife Sentenced to Jail Time |date=August 14, 2013 |work=Roll Call}}</ref>

====''Bishop of D.C. v. Sebelius''====
In December 2013, in the case of ''Roman Catholic Archbishop of Washington v. Sebelius'', Jackson ruled for the [[Department of Health and Human Services]] under Secretary [[Kathleen Sebelius]] and against the [[Roman Catholic Diocese of Washington]] in its constitutional [[Test case (law)|test case]] challenge to the [[contraceptive mandate]] under the [[Affordable Care Act]] as applied to the church's [[District of Columbia]] employees.<ref name="Bloomberg">{{cite web|url=https://www.insurancejournal.com/news/national/2013/12/23/315288.htm |first1=Andrew |last1=Zajac |first2=Joel |last2=Rosenblatt |title=Judge Rejects Catholic Church Challenge to Obamacare Birth Control Coverage |date=December 23, 2013 |work=Bloomberg |via=insurancejournal.com |access-date=October 5, 2022 }}</ref> The [[United States Department of Health and Human Services]] and other agencies made accommodations for religious organizations, under which such organizations did not have to "provide, pay for, or facilitate access to contraception" if they certify their objection to doing so.<ref name="Bloomberg"/><ref name="Archdiocese">{{cite web |url=https://rewirenewsgroup.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/Roman-Cath.-Archb.-of-Wash.-Dist.-Ct.-Order.pdf |title=Roman Catholic Archbishop of Washington v. Sebelius |quote=1:13-cv-01441-ABJ |date=December 20, 2013 |access-date=October 5, 2022 }}</ref> Jackson rejected the archdiocese's argument that the act of "self-certifying" in itself constitutes a substantial burden on the archdiocese's right to freely exercise religion.<ref name="Archdiocese"/>

====Benghazi wrongful death case====
In May 2017, Jackson dismissed a wrongful death suit filed against former [[United States Secretary of State|Secretary of State]] [[Hillary Clinton]] by the parents of two of the Americans killed in [[2012 Benghazi attack|the 2012 attack on the American diplomatic compound in Benghazi]], Libya, on the basis of the [[Westfall Act]].<ref>{{cite news |first=Eric |last=DuVall |url=https://www.upi.com/Top_News/US/2017/05/27/Judge-dismisses-wrongful-death-suit-against-Clinton-over-Benghazi/5811495910092/ |title=Judge dismisses wrongful death suit against Clinton over Benghazi |date=May 27, 2017 |work=UPI |access-date=October 5, 2022 }}</ref>

====Paul Manafort and Rick Gates====
In October 2017, Jackson was assigned to preside over the criminal case that Special Counsel [[Robert Mueller]] brought against [[Paul Manafort]] and [[Rick Gates (political consultant)|Rick Gates]] as part of his [[Special Counsel investigation (2017–present)|investigation]] into [[Russian interference in the 2016 United States elections|Russian interference in the 2016 election cycle]]. She accepted their "not guilty" pleas, granted bail, confiscated their passports, and ordered them held under house arrest. She also warned defense lawyers not to discuss the case outside of court.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.npr.org/2017/11/02/561692221/manafort-and-gates-to-remain-restricted-to-their-homes-judge-says|title=Manafort And Gates To Remain Restricted To Their Homes, Judge Says|last=Lucas|first=Ryan|date=November 2, 2017|work=NPR|access-date=November 4, 2017}}</ref> On June 15, 2018, after the prosecution accused Manafort of attempted [[witness tampering]], Jackson revoked his bail and sent him to jail until his upcoming federal trials.<ref>{{Cite news |first1=David |last1=Voreacos |first2=Steven T. |last2=Dennis |first3=David |last3=McLaughlin |first4=Andrew M. |last4=Harris |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2018-06-15/manafort-sent-to-jail-after-judge-cancels-house-arrest-jig5977k |title=Manafort Heads to Jail After Judge Faults Witness Tampering |date=June 15, 2018 |work=Bloomberg.com |access-date=June 15, 2018 |language=en}}</ref> On February 23, 2018, Gates pleaded guilty to one count of [[Making false statements|false statements]] and one count of [[conspiracy against the United States]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite news|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2018/02/23/former-trump-campaign-official-rick-gates-pleads-guilty-on-two-counts.html|title=Former Trump campaign official Rick Gates pleads guilty to lying and conspiracy against the US|last=Breuninger|first=Kevin|date=February 23, 2018|work=CNBC|access-date=February 23, 2018}}</ref> The plea bargain to which Gates agreed included his cooperation with the Mueller investigation.<ref name=":1">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/06/16/us/politics/rick-gates-russia.html|title=How the Russia Investigation Entangled a Manafort Protégé|last1=Confessore|first1=Nicholas|date=June 16, 2017|work=The New York Times|access-date=October 30, 2017|last2=Meier|first2=Barry|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> On September 14, 2018, Manafort pleaded guilty to two counts of conspiracy against the United States and his plea bargain similarly included an agreement to cooperate with Mueller's investigation.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/09/14/us/politics/manafort-plea-deal.html|title=Paul Manafort Agrees to Cooperate With Special Counsel; Pleads Guilty to Reduced Charges|last1=LaFraniere|first1=Sharon|date=September 14, 2018|work=The New York Times|access-date=September 15, 2018|last2=Vogel|first2=Kenneth|language=en-US}}</ref> But on February 13, 2019, Jackson ruled that Manafort had lied to Mueller's office, to the FBI, and to a grand jury after having pleaded guilty regarding his interactions with [[Konstantin Kilimnik]], a man the FBI believed had ties to Russian intelligence agencies. Jackson ruled that the Special Counsel was no longer bound by the original terms of Manafort's plea, which included the prosecution having committed to advocating a sentence reduction for him.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/legal-issues/us-judge-finds-paul-manafort-lied-to-mueller-probe-about-contacts-with-russian-aide/2019/02/13/c5209f7a-2f2c-11e9-86ab-5d02109aeb01_story.html |title=Federal judge finds Paul Manafort lied to Mueller probe about contacts with Russian aide |author=Spencer S. Hsu |newspaper=The Washington Post |date=February 13, 2019}}</ref> Trump pardoned Manafort on December 23, 2020, the same day he pardoned Roger Stone.<ref name=pardons/>

====Alex van der Zwaan====
On April 3, 2018, Jackson sentenced a former associate of Gates, Dutch attorney [[Alex van der Zwaan]], who practiced in London, to one month in prison and a $20,000 fine.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.buzzfeed.com/zoetillman/a-lawyer-who-admitted-lying-to-the-special-counsels-office|title=A Lawyer Who Admitted Lying To The Special Counsel's Office Was Just Sentenced To One Month In Jail|last=Tillman|first=Zoe|date=April 3, 2018|work=Buzzfeed|access-date=May 8, 2021}}</ref> Van der Zwaan had pleaded guilty to a single count of [[Making false statements|making a false statement]] to investigators regarding alleged [[Russian interference in the 2016 United States elections]].<ref>{{cite news|last1=Viswanatha|first1=Aruna|last2=Quentin Wilber|first2=Del|title=Associate of Gates Pleads Guilty to Lying to Mueller Team |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/special-counsels-office-files-criminal-charges-against-alex-van-der-zwaan-1519137989|access-date= May 8, 2021|work=[[The Wall Street Journal]]|date= February 20, 2018}}</ref> Upon release he was deported to Holland.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cnn.com/2018/06/05/politics/alex-van-der-zwaan-deported/index.html|title=Only person to serve time in Mueller investigation deported|last1=Polantz|first1=Katelyn|last2=Kopan|first2=Tal|date=June 5, 2018|publisher=CNN|access-date=May 8, 2021}}</ref> In December 2020, Trump pardoned him.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Haberman |first1=Maggie |last2=Schmidt |first2=Michael S. |date=2020-12-23 |title=Trump Pardons Two Russia Inquiry Figures and Blackwater Guards |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/12/22/us/politics/trump-pardons.html |access-date=May 8, 2021}}</ref>

====Roger Stone====
In January 2019 Jackson was assigned the case of [[Roger Stone]], who had been an informal advisor to 2016 presidential candidate [[Donald Trump]], after a grand jury had indicted Stone on seven counts including making false statements, obstruction of justice, and witness tampering.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2019-01-25/roger-stone-arrested-in-florida-as-part-of-special-counsel-probe|title=Trump Associate Roger Stone Arrested in Florida as Part of Special Counsel Probe|first1=Andrew M.|last1=Harris|first2=David|last2=Kocieniewski|first3=David|last3=Voreacos|website=Bloomberg|date=January 25, 2019|access-date=January 25, 2019}}</ref> On February 15, 2019, Jackson imposed a limited gag order on Stone and his attorneys.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.cnn.com/2019/02/15/politics/roger-stone-gag-order/index.html|title=Judge puts gag order on Roger Stone and attorneys|last=Polantz|first=Katelyn|date=February 15, 2019|work=CNN|access-date=February 21, 2019}}</ref> On February 18, Stone posted an [[Instagram]] photo of Jackson.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.huffpost.com/entry/roger-stone-judge-instagram_n_5c6b1233e4b0b9cc78ff507e|title=Roger Stone Attacks Judge Presiding Over His Case In Bizarre Instagram Post|last=Campbell|first=Andy|date=February 18, 2019|work=Huffington Post|access-date=February 21, 2019}}</ref> Stone took his post down and apologized, but on February 21, Jackson tightened the terms of his gag order, saying, "From this moment on, the defendant may not speak publicly about this case—period."<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.cnn.com/2019/02/19/politics/roger-stone-gag-order/index.html|title=Judge calls new hearing on gag order after Roger Stone's inflammatory post|last=Polantz|first=Katelyn|date=February 19, 2019|work=CNN|access-date=February 21, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.foxnews.com/politics/roger-stone-apologizes-to-judge-for-instagram-post-my-wife-is-kicking-me|title=Judge rips into Roger Stone, bars him from speaking publicly on case: 'There will be no third chance'|last=Re|first=Gregg|date=February 21, 2019|work=Fox News|access-date=February 23, 2019}}</ref> In February 2020, the [[United States Department of Justice|Department of Justice]] prosecutors recommended a seven-to-nine-year federal prison sentence for Stone. Trump characterized the recommendation as unfair and "a miscarriage of justice". But the [[United States Department of Justice|Department of Justice]] under Attorney General [[William Barr]] recommended a shorter sentence, indicating that it should be "far less." Irate, the four lead prosecutors resigned from the case.<ref>{{Cite news |first1=Dartunorro |last1=Clark |first2=Michael |last2=Kosnar |first3=Dareh |last3=Gregorian |first4=Tom |last4=Winter |date=February 11, 2020 |access-date=October 5, 2022 |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/politics-news/doj-backpedalling-sentencing-recommendation-trump-ally-roger-stone-n1134961|title=All four Roger Stone prosecutors resign from case after DOJ backpedals on sentencing recommendation |website=[[NBC News]] }}</ref> Trump criticized Jackson's earlier judicial rulings on Twitter.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/nation/2020/02/12/trump-stone-judge/|title=Trump attacks federal judge, prosecutors in Twitter tirade defending Roger Stone|last=Chiu|first=Allyson|date=February 12, 2020|newspaper=The Washington Post|access-date=20 February 2020}}</ref> On February 20, 2020, Jackson said before Stone's sentencing: "He was not prosecuted, as some have claimed, for standing up for the president. He was prosecuted for covering up for the president." Jackson denied that Stone was being punished for his politics or his allies.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.nbcwashington.com/news/politics/made-of-steel-judge-amy-berman-jackson-set-to-sentence-roger-stone-after-trumps-attacks/2220486/ |title='Made of Steel': Judge Amy Berman Jackson Sentences Roger Stone After Trump's Attacks |work=[[NBC]] |first=Noreen |last=O'Donnell |date=February 20, 2020 |access-date=February 22, 2020 }}</ref> She sentenced him to 40 months in federal prison and a $20,000 fine.<ref>{{Cite news |date=February 20, 2020 |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/2020/02/20/roger-stone-sentencing-hearing-underway/4798388002/ |title=Truth still matters': Judge sentences Roger Stone to 40 months in prison for obstructing Congress' Russia investigation|last3=Wu|first1=Kristine |last1=Phillips |first2=Kevin |last2=Johnson |first3=Nicholas |website=[[USA Today]] |language=en-US |access-date=2020-02-22}}</ref> Stone's lawyers moved to disqualify Jackson; Jackson denied the motion on the basis of lack of "factual or legal support" for it.<ref>{{cite news |first=John |last=Bowden |url=https://thehill.com/regulation/484289-judge-denies-roger-stones-motion-to-disqualify-her |title=Judge denies Roger Stone's motion to disqualify her |work=The Hill |date=February 23, 2020 }}</ref> Jackson criticized Trump's personal attacks on the Stone jury foreperson after the verdict.<ref name=attacks>{{cite news |first=Katelyn |last=Polantz |url=https://www.cnn.com/2020/02/25/politics/roger-stone-hearing-juror-amy-berman-jackson/index.html |title=Judge Amy Berman Jackson criticizes Trump's attacks on Roger Stone juror |work=[[CNN]] |date=February 25, 2020 |access-date=May 9, 2021 }}</ref> Trump tweeted, "There has rarely been a juror so tainted as the forewoman in the Roger Stone case. Look at her background. She never revealed her hatred of 'Trump' and Stone. She was totally biased, as is the judge. Roger wasn't even working on my campaign. Miscarriage of justice. Sad to watch!"<ref name=attacks/>

Trump commuted Stone's sentence in July 2020, shortly before Stone was scheduled to report to federal prison. He pardoned Stone on December 23, 2020, four weeks before [[Joe Biden]] was sworn in.<ref name=pardons>{{cite news |url=https://www.npr.org/2020/12/23/949820820/trump-pardons-roger-stone-paul-manafort-and-charles-kushner |title=Trump Pardons Roger Stone, Paul Manafort And Charles Kushner |work=[[National Public Radio]] |first1=Anita |last1=Kelly |first2=Ryan |last2=Lucas |first3=Vanessa |last3=Romo |date=December 23, 2020 |access-date=May 9, 2021 }}</ref>

====Mueller investigation memo====
{{further|Barr letter}}
In May 2021, Jackson found that the Justice Department under Barr had inappropriately failed to release a memo by the [[Special Counsel]] about alleged obstruction of justice. Her opinion described Barr as having summarized "what he'd hardly had time to skim, much less study closely, [which] prompted an immediate reaction, as politicians and pundits took to their microphones and Twitter feeds to decry what they feared was an attempt to hide the ball."<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/judge-orders-justice-dept-to-release-trump-obstruction-memo/2021/05/04/bb13b820-ad18-11eb-82c1-896aca955bb9_story.html |title=Judge orders Justice Dept. to release Trump obstruction memo |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |first=Eric |last=Tucker |agency=[[Associated Press]] |date=May 4, 2021 |access-date=May 5, 2021 }}</ref> Former U.S. Attorney [[Joyce Vance]] believed that Berman could refer Barr for investigation by the [[Office of Professional Responsibility]] or to the Justice department's [[Inspector General]], with possibilities of censure, disbarment or prosecution. Either the IG or the OPR could further refer the case to the DOJ's [[Public Integrity Section]], which could initiate an investigation and/or prosecution.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.msnbc.com/opinion/judge-amy-berman-jackson-s-barr-rebuke-opens-door-doj-n1266692 |title=Judge Amy Berman Jackson's rebuke opens door to DOJ accountability |work=[[MSNBC]] |first=Joyce |last=Vance |date=May 7, 2021 |access-date=May 11, 2021 }}</ref>

==== CFPB ====
On March 28, 2025, Jackson blocked the Trump administration from dismantling the [[Consumer Financial Protection Bureau]] (CFPB) and ordered the reinstatement of its employees.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://abcnews.go.com/Politics/judge-blocks-dismantling-consumer-financial-protection-bureau-orders/story?id=120277275|title=Judge blocks dismantling of Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, orders employees reinstated|website=ABC News|date=2025-03-28|access-date=2025-03-30}}</ref> On August 15, 2025, a three-judge panel of the Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit overturned Jackson's ruling, 2-1, allowing the administration to proceed with plans to significantly reduce the CFPB staff. Judge [[Cornelia Pillard]] dissented.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.npr.org/2025/08/15/nx-s1-5403868/appeals-court-ruling-cfpb-layoffs|title=CFPB Staff Layoffs Can Proceed, Appels Court Rules|website=National Public Radio|date=2025-08-15}}</ref>

==Affiliations==
Jackson served on the board of the Washington D.C. Rape Crisis Center and has also been a member of the Parent Steering Committee of the Interdisciplinary Council on Developmental and Learning Disorders.<ref name="ATTORNEYS, Amy Berman Jackson"/>

==Personal life==
Jackson was married to Darryl W. Jackson, a lawyer and a senior Republican political appointee.<ref name=Hsu2019>{{cite news |first=Spencer S. |last=Hsu |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/legal-issues/paul-manafort-is-about-to-face-another-sentencing-judge-amy-berman-jackson/2019/03/09/ebdea46a-41cc-11e9-a0d3-1210e58a94cf_story.html |title=Paul Manafort is about to face another sentencing judge: Amy Berman Jackson |newspaper=Washington Post |date=March 11, 2019 }}</ref> He worked in the [[Office of Export Enforcement]] as Assistant Secretary of Commerce for [[George W. Bush]] in 2005 after leaving the [[Arnold & Porter]] firm.<ref>{{cite web|title=Darryl Jackson -- Department of Commerce|url=https://georgewbush-whitehouse.archives.gov/results/leadership/bio_813.html|quote=On October 7, 2005, the United States Senate confirmed President Bush's nomination of Darryl W. Jackson, of the District of Columbia, to be Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Export Enforcement}}</ref> They have two sons, one of whom is Matt Jackson, who won 13 consecutive games on ''[[Jeopardy!]]'', earning $411,612.<ref>{{cite web|title='Jeopardy!' mastermind Matt Jackson loses in classiest way possible |url=https://mashable.com/archive/matt-jackson-loses-jeopardy |last=Ellis |first=Johnathan |work=[[Mashable]] |date=October 14, 2015 |access-date=February 20, 2020}}</ref><ref name="NYT-Profile">{{Cite news |last=LaFraniere |first=Sharon |date=February 20, 2020 |title=Judge in Roger Stone Trial Confronts a High-Pressure Decision |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/02/20/us/politics/amy-berman-jackson-roger-stone.html |access-date=February 20, 2020 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> While appearing on the trivia show, he said, "My mom is white, liberal and Jewish, and my dad is black, Christian and conservative."<ref name="WashingtonPost"/><ref name=Hsu2019/>

In her spare time, Jackson writes music and sings.<ref name="NYT-Profile" />

{{Short description|American judge (born 1973)}} {{Infobox officeholder | honorific_prefix = | name = Amy M. Baggio | honorific_suffix = | image = Judge Amy Baggio.png | alt = | caption = | office = Judge of the [[United States District Court for the District of Oregon]] | term_start = August 22, 2024 | term_end = | appointer = [[List of federal judges appointed by Joe Biden|Joe Biden]] | predecessor = [[Marco A. Hernandez]] | successor = | office1 = Judge of the [[Multnomah County, Oregon|Multnomah County]] [[Oregon circuit courts|Circuit Court]] | term_start1 = March 19, 2019 | term_end1 = August 22, 2024 | appointer1 = [[Kate Brown]] | predecessor1 = Marilyn Litzenberger | successor1 = Jeff Auxier | pronunciation = | birth_name = Amy Margaret Baggio | birth_date = {{birth year and age|1973}} | birth_place = [[Pittsburgh]], Pennsylvania, U.S. | death_date = | death_place = | death_cause = | party = | spouse = | education = [[Wake Forest University]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|BA]])
[[Lewis & Clark Law School| Lewis & Clark College]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Amy Margaret Baggio''' (born 1973){{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/baggio_sjq.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=December 13, 2023}} is an American lawyer who has served as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Oregon]] since 2024. A native of [[Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania]], prior to appointment to the bench, she had a career in criminal defense, including as a federal public defender. She also previously served as a judge of the [[Multnomah County, Oregon|Multnomah County]] [[Oregon circuit courts|Circuit Court]] from 2019 to 2024. == Early life and education == Baggio was born in [[Pittsburgh]]. Baggio received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] in speech communication, ''[[cum laude]]'', in 1995 from [[Wake Forest University]] in Winston-Salem, North Carolina, and a [[Juris Doctor]] in 2001 from [[Lewis & Clark Law School]] in Portland, Oregon.{{Cite press release |title=President Biden Names Forty-Second Round of Judicial Nominees |date=November 15, 2023 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2023/11/15/president-biden-names-forty-second-round-of-judicial-nominees/ |access-date=November 15, 2023}} {{PD-notice}}{{cite news |last1=Wong |first1=Peter |title=Multnomah judge named to U.S. District Court |url=https://www.portlandtribune.com/news/multnomah-judge-named-to-u-s-district-court/article_77c2f084-8440-11ee-afbc-032717768b16.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231119113936/https://www.portlandtribune.com/news/multnomah-judge-named-to-u-s-district-court/article_77c2f084-8440-11ee-afbc-032717768b16.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=November 19, 2023 |access-date=10 October 2024 |work=PortlandTribune.com |date=15 November 2023 |language=en}} == Early life and career == From 2001 to 2002, Baggio served as a staff attorney in the [[Portland, Oregon|Portland]] Office of the Metropolitan Public Defender. From 2002 to 2005, she served as a research and writing attorney and then from 2005 to 2012 as an [[federal public defender|assistant federal public defender]], both within the Office of the Federal Public Defender for the District of Oregon. From 2013 to 2019, she worked as a [[sole practitioner]] at her own criminal law defense firm, Baggio Law, also in [[Portland, Oregon|Portland]]. On March 19, 2019, [[Oregon Governor]] [[Kate Brown]] appointed Baggio to serve as a judge of the [[Multnomah County, Oregon|Multnomah County]] [[Oregon circuit courts|Circuit Court]] in Portland, to fill the vacancy left by the retirement of Judge Marilyn Litzenberger.{{Cite web |title=The Honorable Amy Baggio: Multnomah County Circuit Court Judge |url=https://mbabar.org/about/mba-news/the-honorable-amy-baggio--multnomah-county-circuit-court-judge/ |access-date=November 15, 2023 |website=mbabar.org}} In 2021, Baggio presided over a case that raised questions about the quality of medical care at the [[Snake River Correctional Institution]]. Baggio ruled that the prison's masking compliance had been inadequate and "creates an unjustifiable risk" throughout the prison.{{Cite web |date=April 19, 2021 |title=Oregon prison COVID-19 lawsuit ruling hailed as a landmark |url=https://www.oregonlive.com/politics/2021/04/oregon-prison-covid-19-lawsuit-ruling-hailed-as-a-landmark-for-prisoners-rights.html |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |date=November 15, 2023 |title=President Biden nominates Oregon judge for the federal bench |url=https://oregoncapitalchronicle.com/2023/11/15/biden-nominates-oregon-judge-for-the-federal-bench/ |language=en-US}} === Federal judicial service === On June 1, 2023, Baggio was one of six names U.S. senators [[Ron Wyden]] and [[Jeff Merkley]] submitted to the White House.{{Citation |title=Names of 6 finalists forwarded to White House for upcoming federal court vacancy in Oregon |url=https://www.oregonlive.com/crime/2023/06/names-of-6-finalists-forwarded-to-white-house-for-upcoming-federal-court-vacancy-in-oregon.html|language=en |access-date=2023-06-01}} On November 15, 2023, President [[Joe Biden]] announced his intent to nominate Baggio to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Oregon]]. On November 27, 2023, her nomination was sent to the Senate. President Biden nominated Baggio to the seat being vacated by Judge [[Marco A. Hernandez]], who subsequently assumed [[senior status]] on August 21, 2024.{{Cite press release |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |date=November 27, 2023 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2023/11/27/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-130/}} On December 13, 2023, a hearing on her nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web|title=Nominations|date=December 12, 2023|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/committee-activity/hearings/12/13/2023/nominations}} On January 3, 2024, her nomination was returned to the president under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]]{{Cite web |date=January 3, 2024 |title=PN1155 — Amy M. Baggio — The Judiciary |url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/118th-congress/1155 |access-date=January 9, 2024 |website=congress.gov}} and she was renominated on January 8, 2024.{{Cite press release |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |date=January 3, 2024 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2024/01/08/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-133/}} On January 18, 2024, her nomination was reported out of committee by a 12–9 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/2024-01-18_-_ebm_-_results1.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – January 18, 2024|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=January 19, 2024}}{{Cite press release |title=Senate Judiciary Committee Advances Twenty Judicial Nominations, One Executive Nomination to the Full Senate |date=January 18, 2024 |publisher=United States Senate Judiciary Committee |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/press/releases/senate-judiciary-committee-advances-twenty-judicial-nominations-one-executive-nomination-to-the-full-senate |access-date=January 18, 2024}} On February 6, 2024, the Senate invoked cloture on her nomination by a 54–43 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1182/vote_118_2_00037.htm|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Amy M. Baggio to be United States District Judge for the District of Oregon)|website=United States Senate|date=February 6, 2024|access-date=February 6, 2024}} Later that day, her nomination was confirmed by a 54–44 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1182/vote_118_2_00038.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Amy M. Baggio, of Oregon, to be U.S. District Judge for the District of Oregon)|website=United States Senate|date=February 6, 2024|access-date=February 6, 2024}} She received her judicial commission on August 22, 2024,{{FJC Bio|nid=13761496|inline=yes}} and was sworn in the next day.{{Cite press release|title=Hon. Amy Baggio Appointed as a U.S. District Judge for the District of Oregon|url=https://ord.uscourts.gov/index.php?view=article&id=2312:hon-amy-baggio-appointed-as-a-u-s-district-judge-for-the-district-of-oregon&catid=218|website=ord.uscourts.gov|access-date=August 23, 2024}} === Notable cases === * Baggio and Ruben Iniquez, who also worked as an assistant federal public defender, were appointed to represent [[List of Afghan detainees at Guantanamo Bay|Nazar Chaman Gul]] in his case filed in [[United States District Court for the District of Columbia|U.S. District Court]]. Baggio and Iniquez helped secure the release of Gul, an [[Afghans|Afghan]] imprisoned at [[Guantanamo Bay detention camp|Guantanamo Bay Prison]] since 2003, in what turned out to be a case of mistaken identity.{{Cite web |date=November 16, 2023 |title=Multnomah judge named to District Court |url=https://www.portlandtribune.com/news/multnomah-judge-named-to-u-s-district-court/article_77c2f084-8440-11ee-afbc-032717768b16.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231119113936/https://www.portlandtribune.com/news/multnomah-judge-named-to-u-s-district-court/article_77c2f084-8440-11ee-afbc-032717768b16.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=November 19, 2023 |language=en-US}} * In 2023, Baggio sentenced Tusitala "Tiny" Toese, a member of the [[Proud Boys]], to an additional two years in prison beyond the minimum sentence for his role in a 2021 brawl in east [[Portland, Oregon|Portland]].{{Cite web |date=July 21, 2023 |title=Tusitala 'Tiny' Toese hit with more prison time for 2021 Proud Boys clash in Portland; 'You lose,' victim taunts |url=https://www.oregonlive.com/crime/2023/07/tusitala-tiny-toese-hit-with-more-prison-time-for-2021-proud-boys-clash-in-portland-you-lose-victim-taunts.html |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |date=November 15, 2023 |title=President Biden nominates Oregon judge to federal bench |url=https://www.heraldandnews.com/news/president-biden-nominates-oregon-judge-for-federal-bench/article_64a6f04a-8404-11ee-9dd4-5b840f698661.html |language=en-US}} == See also == * [[List of Oregon judges]] == References == {{Reflist}} == External links == *{{FJC Bio|nid=13761496}} *{{Ballotpedia|Amy_Baggio}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Marco A. '''Amy Mil Totenberg''' (born 1950) is a  [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Georgia]].  She previously worked in private practice in [[Atlanta]] and also formerly served as a [[special master]] for the [[United States District Court for the District of Maryland]].

==Early life and education==
[[File:Jill, Nina, and Amy Totenberg celebrate the return of their father's Stradivarius violin.jpg|thumb|Left to right: Sisters Jill, [[Nina Totenberg]], and Amy celebrate the return of their father’s Stradivarius violin in August 2015]]
Amy Totenberg was born in [[New York City]], the daughter of Melanie Francis (Eisenberg),<ref name=fdr>Stated on ''[[Finding Your Roots]]'', January 27, 2021</ref> a real estate broker, and violinist [[Roman Totenberg]].<ref>{{cite news |work = [[The New York Times]] |date = May 9, 2012 |access-date = May 9, 2012 |title = Roman Totenberg, Violinist and Teacher, Dies at 101 |url = https://www.nytimes.com/2012/05/09/arts/music/roman-totenberg-violinist-and-teacher-dies-at-101.html |first = Bruce |last = Weber }}</ref> Her father was a Polish Jewish immigrant, who lost many of his family members in the [[Holocaust]].<ref name=fdr/> Her mother was of German Jewish and Polish Jewish descent from an upper-class family that had lived in San Francisco and New York.<ref name=fdr/> Her eldest sister, [[Nina Totenberg]], is a [[Supreme Court of the United States|Supreme Court]] correspondent for [[National Public Radio|NPR]].<ref name="NPR biography">{{cite web |url = https://www.npr.org/templates/story/story.php?storyId=2101289 |title = Nina Totenberg; NPR Biography |date = September 25, 2007 |publisher = [[National Public Radio]] |access-date = January 11, 2011 }}</ref> Another sister, Jill Totenberg, is a businesswoman.<ref name="NYT2002">{{cite news |url = https://www.nytimes.com/2002/04/21/style/weddings-vows-jill-totenberg-and-brian-foreman.html |title = WEDDINGS: VOWS; Jill Totenberg and Brian Foreman |work = The New York Times |date = April 21, 2002 |first = Jenny |last = Allen |access-date = August 7, 2015 }}</ref>

Totenberg earned an [[Bachelor of Arts|Artium Baccalaureus]], ''[[magna cum laude]]'', in 1974 from [[Harvard University|Harvard-Radcliffe College]] and a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1977 from [[Harvard Law School]].<ref name="TotenbergWH">{{cite web |url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/president-obama-nominates-judge-leonard-stark-and-amy-totenberg-united-states-distr |title=President Obama Nominates Judge Leonard Stark and Amy Totenberg to the United States District Court |date=March 17, 2010 |access-date=September 17, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170216172822/https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/president-obama-nominates-judge-leonard-stark-and-amy-totenberg-united-states-distr |archive-date=2017-02-16 |via=[[NARA|National Archives]] |work=[[whitehouse.gov]] |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="fjc.gov">{{FJC Bio|nid=1393621|inline=yes}}</ref>

==Career==
Upon graduating from Harvard-Radcliffe, Totenberg worked as a summer intern at the law firm of James M. Haviland in [[Charleston, West Virginia]].  In 1975 she was a legal assistant for Education/Instrucción in [[Roxbury, Massachusetts]], and held this position into 1977.<ref name="Totenberg">{{cite web |url=http://judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/111thCongressJudicialNominations/upload/AmyTotenberg-PublicQuestionnaire.pdf |title=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees |work=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary |publisher=The United States Senate |access-date=September 17, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101006173927/http://judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/111thCongressJudicialNominations/upload/AmyTotenberg-PublicQuestionnaire.pdf |archive-date=6 October 2010 |url-status=dead }}</ref> After graduating from law school, she served as a partner for The Law Project in [[Atlanta]] from 1977 until 1982. She served as a sole legal practitioner in Atlanta from 1982 until 1994. Between 1988 and 1993, Totenberg worked part-time for the city of [[Atlanta]] as a [[pro tem]]  Municipal Court Judge.<ref name="Totenberg"/> From 1994 until 1998, Totenberg served as the first-ever general counsel for Atlanta's school system.<ref name="TotenbergWH"/> From 1998 until becoming a federal judge in 2011, Totenberg served as a sole legal practitioner and arbitrator in Atlanta, working part-time as a special master and court monitor for several United States district courts.<ref name="TotenbergWH"/>  She also worked from 2004 until 2007 as an adjunct professor at the [[Emory University School of Law]].<ref name="Totenberg"/><ref name="fjc.gov"/>

===Federal judicial service===
In February 2009, Totenberg submitted a resume and letter of interest for a United States district judgeship vacancy. After an interview by a committee appointed by the Georgia Democratic Congressional delegation, Totenberg was among the applicants whose names were submitted to the [[White House]]. On March 17, 2010, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Totenberg to fill the judicial vacancy on the United States District Court for the Northern District of Georgia that had been created by the decision by Judge [[Jack Tarpley Camp Jr.]] to assume [[senior status]] at the end of 2008.<ref name="TotenbergWH"/> Totenberg was reported out of the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]] on December 1, 2010, by a [[voice vote]].<ref>{{cite news | first = Bill | last = Rankin | title = Senate approves Totenberg, Jones to federal bench in Atlanta | date = 2011-02-28 | publisher = Cox Media Group | work = The Atlanta Journal-Constitution }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/112thCongress.cfm |title=Judicial Nominations and Confirmations: 112th Congress |website=judiciary.senate.gov |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110108213625/http://judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/112thCongress.cfm |archive-date=January 8, 2011}}</ref> Senators returned Totenberg's nomination to President Obama at the end of the [[111th United States Congress|111th Congress]], however, and he resubmitted the nomination on January 5, 2011. The Senate confirmed Totenberg by a [[voice vote]] on February 28, 2011. She received her commission on March 1, 2011. She assumed [[senior status]] on April 3, 2021.<ref name="fjc.gov"/>
