'''Ana Cecilia Reyes''' (born 1974) is an Uruguayan-born American lawyer who has served as [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Columbia]] since 2023. She was nominated to the position by President [[Joe Biden]], and is both the first [[Hispanic and Latino Americans|Latina]] and the first openly [[LGBTQ]] person to serve as a district court judge in Washington, D.C.<ref name="blade">{{Cite news |last=Chibbaro Jr. |first=Lou |date=February 17, 2023 |title=Ana Reyes confirmed as first LGBTQ federal judge in D.C. |url=https://www.washingtonblade.com/2023/02/17/ana-reyes-confirmed-as-first-lgbtq-federal-judge-in-d-c/,%20https://www.washingtonblade.com/2023/02/17/ana-reyes-confirmed-as-first-lgbtq-federal-judge-in-d-c/ |access-date=June 14, 2024 |website=Washington Blade |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==

Reyes was born in 1974 in [[Montevideo]], [[Uruguay]].<ref name="Questionnaire">{{cite web |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Reyes%20SJQ%20Public%20Final%20for%20OneDrive.pdf |title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees |publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary |access-date=June 21, 2022}}</ref> She moved to [[Spain]] and later immigrated to [[Louisville, Kentucky]], as a child.<ref name="teacher">{{Cite news |last=Page |first=Sydney |date=December 1, 2020 |title=A D.C. lawyer learned English as a child from a teacher who tutored her each day. She found her to say thank you. |language=en-US |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/2020/12/01/dc-lawyer-learned-english-child-when-her-teacher-tutored-her-free-each-day-she-just-found-her-say-thank-you/ |access-date=May 1, 2022 |issn=0190-8286}}</ref><ref name="Ali 2022" /> After her arrival in the United States, her first-grade teacher helped her learn English. She received media attention in 2020 for reuniting with her first-grade teacher after over 40 years.<ref name="teacher" />

Reyes graduated from [[Transylvania University]] in 1996 with a [[Bachelor of Science]], ''[[Latin honors#United States|summa cum laude]]''. From 1996 to 1997, Reyes worked for [[Feminist Majority Foundation]] on its unsuccessful drive to defeat the [[1996 California Proposition 209]], which sought to prohibit state governmental institutions from considering race, sex, or ethnicity, specifically in the areas of [[government jobs|public employment]], [[government contract|public contracting]], and public education.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Ness |first=Carol |date=September 15, 1996 |title=Two faces of Prop. 209: More alike than different Honor students from immigrant families back opposite sides |page=C1 |work=[[San Francisco Examiner]] |id={{ProQuest|270443792}}}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Ness |first1=Carol |title=2 Peas at Odds |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/1996/09/29/2-peas-at-odds/ |access-date=March 20, 2025 |work=[[Chicago Tribune]] |date=August 19, 2021 |orig-date=September 29, 1996}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Morse |first=Rob |date=August 8, 1996 |title=The boys of Freedom Summer '96 |url=https://www.sfgate.com/news/article/The-boys-of-Freedom-Summer-96-3130260.php |page=A1 |work=San Francisco Examiner |id={{ProQuest|270436770}}}}</ref>

Reyes then attended [[Harvard Law School]], where she was an editor of the ''[[Harvard Law Review]]'' and a semi-finalist in the [[Ames Moot Court Competition]].<ref name="Questionnaire" /> She graduated in 2000 with a [[Juris Doctor]], ''magna cum laude''.<ref name="FJCBio" /> Reyes later received a [[Master of Public Policy|master's in international public policy]] from the [[Paul H. Nitze School of Advanced International Studies]], with honors, in 2014.<ref name="Ali 2022" /><ref name="WHBio">{{Cite press release |title=President Biden Names Seventeenth Round of Judicial Nominees |date=April 27, 2022 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/04/27/president-biden-names-seventeenth-round-of-judicial-nominees/ |access-date=April 27, 2022}} {{PD-notice}}</ref>

== Career ==
After law school, Reyes served as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Amalya Kearse]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit]] from 2000 to 2001. She then entered private practice at the law firm [[Williams & Connolly]], becoming a partner in 2009.<ref name="Ali 2022">{{cite news |last1=Ali |first1=Shirin |title=President Biden's judicial nominee could become the first Hispanic woman and LGBTQ person to serve on the court |url=https://thehill.com/changing-america/respect/diversity-inclusion/3468872-president-bidens-judicial-nominee-could-become-the-first-hispanic-woman-and-lgbtq-person-to-serve-on-the-court/ |access-date=May 2, 2022 |work=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]] |date=April 27, 2022}}</ref><ref name="WHBio" /> Reyes focused on [[cross-border legal issues]] and [[international arbitration]], while also taking on pro bono work to represent asylum seekers and refugee organizations.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Tillman |first=Zoe |date=October 31, 2011 |title=Ana Reyes |volume=34 |page=20 |work=[[The National Law Journal|The National Law Journal & Legal Times]] |location=New York |issue=9 |id={{ProQuest|902451216}}}}</ref> The [[Women's Bar Association of the District of Columbia]] named her "Woman Lawyer of the Year" in 2017.<ref name="teacher" /> In September 2021, Chief Judge [[Beryl Howell]] asked Reyes to serve as the Chair of the Magistrate Judge Merit Selection Panel.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.wc.com/News/176901/Ana-Reyes-to-Chair-Magistrate-Judge-Merit-Selection-Panel | title=Ana Reyes to Chair Magistrate Judge Merit Selection Panel – Williams & Connolly LLP }}</ref> Reyes is known to bring her pet [[Golden Retriever]], Scout, to work.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Koenig |first=Bryan |date=January 26, 2024 |title=Judge Reyes Talks Big Trials, Preparation And Dogs At Work – Law360 |url=https://www.law360.com/articles/1790189/judge-reyes-talks-big-trials-preparation-and-dogs-at-work |access-date=June 14, 2024 |website=Law360 |language=en}}</ref>

=== Federal judicial service ===
[[File:Ana C. Reyes (Judge).jpg|thumb|Reyes in 2022]]
On April 27, 2022, President [[Joe Biden]] announced his intent to nominate Reyes to serve as a United States district judge of the [[United States District Court for the District of Columbia]]. She had been recommended for the position by Delegate [[Eleanor Holmes Norton]].<ref name="blade" /> On May 19, 2022, her nomination was sent to the Senate. President Biden nominated Reyes to the seat being vacated by Judge [[Colleen Kollar-Kotelly]], who announced her intention to assume [[senior status]] upon confirmation of a successor.<ref>{{Cite press release|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate|date=May 19, 2022|publisher=The White House|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/05/19/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-67/}}</ref> A hearing on her nomination was held before the [[Senate Judiciary Committee]] on June 22, 2022.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Nominations|date=June 22, 2022|publisher=[[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]]|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/06/22/2022/nominations}}</ref> On August 4, 2022, her nomination reported out of committee by a 11–9–2 vote.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/EBM%20Results%20-%202022-08-04.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – August 4, 2022|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=August 4, 2022}}</ref>

On January 3, 2023, Reyes' nomination was returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]]; she was renominated later the same day.<ref>{{Cite press release|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate|date=January 3, 2023|publisher=The White House|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2023/01/03/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-91/}}</ref> On February 2, 2023, her nomination was reported out of committee by an 11–9 vote.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/EBM%20Results%20-%202023-02-021.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – February 2, 2023|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=February 2, 2023}}</ref> On February 15, 2023, the Senate invoked cloture on her nomination by a 52–47 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|date=February 15, 2023|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Ana C. Reyes to be U.S. District Judge for the District of Columbia)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00018.htm|access-date=February 15, 2023|website=United States Senate}}</ref> Later that day, her nomination was confirmed by a 51–47 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|date=February 15, 2023|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Ana C. Reyes, of the District of Columbia to be U.S. District Judge for the District of Columbia)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00020.htm|access-date=February 15, 2023|website=United States Senate}}</ref> She received her judicial commission on February 21, 2023.<ref name="FJCBio">{{FJC Bio|nid=13263791|inline=yes}}</ref> Reyes was sworn in on February 22, 2023.<ref>{{Cite web|date=February 22, 2023|title=Ana C. Reyes Sworn in as United States District Judge|url=https://www.dcd.uscourts.gov/sites/dcd/files/J.%20Reyes%20Announcement%20Final%2020230223.pdf|website=dcd.uscourts.gov|access-date=May 27, 2023}}</ref> She became the first Hispanic woman and openly LGBTQ person to serve as a district court judge in Washington, D.C.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Stern|first=Seth|date=February 15, 2023|title=First Latina, LGBTQ Judge Confirmed to DC District Court|url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/first-latina-lgbtq-judge-confirmed-to-dc-district-court|access-date=February 15, 2023|website=Bloomberg Law|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Raymond|first=Nate|date=April 27, 2022|title=Exclusive: Biden's latest judicial nominees dominated by public defenders|url=https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/exclusive-bidens-latest-judicial-nominees-dominated-by-public-defenders-2022-04-27/|access-date=April 27, 2022|website=Reuters|language=en}}</ref><ref name="Ali 2022" />

=== Notable rulings ===
==== Position on Hunter Biden investigation ====
Reyes criticized the [[United States Department of Justice]] (DOJ) in the House Select Committee on April 5, 2024, for refusing to allow attorneys involved in the [[Hunter Biden laptop controversy]] to comply with subpoenas issued by House Republicans. She accused the DOJ of hypocrisy in prosecuting Trump administration official [[Peter Navarro]], noting that he had been imprisoned for not complying with House committee subpoenas.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Barnes |first1=Daniel |last2=Richards |first2=Zoë |date=April 6, 2024 |title=Judge berates Justice Department for defying House GOP subpoenas tied to Biden impeachment inquiry |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/justice-department/judge-berates-doj-republican-subpoenas-hunter-biden-probe-rcna146681 |access-date=March 19, 2024 |website=NBC News}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=April 5, 2024|title='Are you kidding me?': Biden-appointed judge torches DOJ for blowing off Hunter Biden-related subpoenas from House GOP |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2024/04/05/biden-appointed-judge-torches-doj-00150884 |website=Politico}}</ref>

==== Trump tax return whistleblower case ====
In January 2024, Reyes sentenced [[Charles Littlejohn|Charles E. Littlejohn]], who leaked the [[tax returns of Donald Trump]] along with several other wealthy taxpayers to the media, to five years in prison. Reyes denounced Littlejohn's decision to leak Trump's tax returns as a "an attack on our constitutional democracy", stating: "When you target the sitting president of the United States, you're targeting the office and when you're targeting the office of the president of the United States, you're targeting democracy—you're targeting our constitutional system of government." Reyes added that Trump was under no legal obligation to release his tax returns, compared the whistleblower's actions to the [[January 6 United States Capitol attack]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Faler |first=Brian |date=January 29, 2024 |title=Trump tax return leaker sentenced to 5 years in prison |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2024/01/29/irs-charles-littlejohn-tax-prison-trump-00138367 |access-date=June 13, 2024 |website=Politico}}</ref> During the trial, Reyes told Littlejohn that "I have reacted so strongly to your case because it engenders the same fear that Jan. 6 does". Reyes' decision to sentence Littlejohn to five years in prison received attention for being over six to twelve times longer than the four-to ten-month sentence recommended by the [[United States Federal Sentencing Guidelines]].<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Lord |first=Bob |date=May 19, 2024 |title=A Whistleblower Exposed Trump's Tax Avoidance. Biden Should Pardon Him |url=https://www.rollingstone.com/politics/political-commentary/charles-littlejohn-whistleblower-trump-tax-biden-pardon-1235022648/ |access-date=June 13, 2024 |magazine=Rolling Stone |language=en-US|archive-url=https://archive.today/20240519181802/https://www.rollingstone.com/politics/political-commentary/charles-littlejohn-whistleblower-trump-tax-biden-pardon-1235022648/|archive-date=May 19, 2024|url-status=live}}</ref>

==== Assa Abloy antitrust case ====
In 2023, Reyes presided over an [[United States antitrust law|antitrust]] case brought by the DOJ against [[Assa Abloy]]'s acquisition of [[Spectrum Brands]]' hardware and home improvement (HHI) division.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Koenig |first=Bryan |date=June 13, 2024 |title=At Assa Abloy Trial: Air Of Secrecy, Judge's Cryptic Warning – Law360 UK |url=https://www.law360.co.uk/articles/1601501/at-assa-abloy-trial-air-of-secrecy-judge-s-cryptic-warning |access-date=June 14, 2024 |website=Law360 |language=en}}</ref> Reyes reportedly favored the lawsuit ending in a settlement rather than a trial. During the trial, Reyes indicated interest in reinterpreting the burden of proof in "litigate-the fix" merger cases; while the burden is generally on merging companies to prove a deal would not harm competition, Reyes expressed interest for putting the burden of proof on DOJ lawyers.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Shaffer |first=Sara |date=May 8, 2023 |title=The Antitrust Agenda: How Judge Ana Reyes' Pro-Settlement Bent in Assa Abloy/Spectrum Brands Case Led to Mediation; May 12 Items on FTC Calendar; Key Takeaway from AELP Event |url=https://thecapitolforum.com/the-antitrust-agenda-how-judge-ana-reyes-pro-settlement-bent-in-assa-abloy-spectrum-brands-case-led-to-mediation-may-12-items-on-ftc-calendar-key-takeaway-from-aelp-event/ |access-date=June 13, 2024 |website=The Capitol Forum |language=en}}</ref>

==== Second Trump administration ====
Reyes heard ''Storch v. Hegseth'' about the [[2025 dismissals of U.S. inspectors general]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Kunzelman|first1=Michael |last2=Boone|first2=Rebecca |title=Federal judge refuses to reinstate eight former inspectors general fired by Trump administration |url=https://apnews.com/article/inspectors-general-fired-trump-ruling-87145a36a311ce6d4c2e2e4c3276c17d |work=[[AP News]] |date=September 24, 2025 |language=en}}</ref>

In ''[[Trump v. Miot]]'', Reyes blocked the [[second Trump administration]] from terminating [[Temporary protected status of Haitians in the United States]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=LUIS ANDRES HENAO |last2=HANNAH SCHOENBAUM |title=Judge blocks Trump administration from ending protections for Haitians |url=https://apnews.com/article/haiti-springfield-immigration-ruling-202aef9c838bec43d19d6f1d67766b77 |work=[[AP News]] |date=February 2, 2026 |language=en}}</ref>

Reyes heard ''DC Preservation League v. Department of Interior'' about the [[East Potomac Park Golf Course#Second Trump presidency|Trump administration and the East Potomac Park Golf Course]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Montague |first1=Zach |title=Judge Orders Trump Administration to Answer for Tree Removals at D.C. Golf Course |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/12/us/politics/judge-trees-golf-trump.html |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=October 12, 2026 |language=en}}</ref>

Rubio'' about [[Deportation in the second Trump administration#Iran|the Trump administration deporting Iranians]] to Iran.<ref>{{cite news |last1=KUNZELMAN |first1=MICHAEL |last2=SANTANA |first2=REBECCA |last3=RIDDLE |first3=SAFIYAH |title=AP Exclusive: Trump administration held talks with Iran on deporting Iranians during the war |url=https://apnews.com/article/iran-immigration-deportation-flights-emails-1f245367d432b2683a546936014a1f90 |work=[[AP News]] |date=November 5, 2026 |language=en}}</ref>

===== Transgender military ban =====
{{See also|Executive Order 14183}}
In February 2025, Reyes presided over hearings for a preliminary injunction against President Trump's [[Executive Order 14183]], which banned transgender people from serving in the military. During the hearings, Reyes described that order as an attempt to label "an entire category of people dishonest, dishonorable, undisciplined, immodest, who lack integrity – people who have taken an oath to defend this country, who have been under fire, people who have taken fire for this country", saying that it showed an "unadulterated animus" towards the transgender community, and that portions of it were "frankly ridiculous".<ref>{{Cite news |last=Kheel |first=Rebecca |date=February 18, 2025 |title='Unadulterated Animus': Judge Tears into Trump Administration at Hearing on Transgender Military Ban |url=https://www.military.com/daily-news/2025/02/18/unadulterated-animus-judge-tears-trump-administration-hearing-transgender-military-ban.html |access-date=February 23, 2025 |website=[[Military.com]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |first=Michael |last=Kunzelman |date=February 18, 2025 |title=Judge questions motives for Trump's order banning transgender troops |url=https://apnews.com/article/trump-transgender-troops-executive-order-8373e8f3c4d59a7f99962f62a611be0b |access-date=February 23, 2025 |work=[[AP News]] |language=en}}</ref> On February 21, 2025, the DOJ filed a judicial misconduct complaint against Reyes signed by [[Chad Mizelle]]. The complaint, submitted to the DC Circuit, alleges that Reyes displayed "hostile and egregious misconduct" during the hearings. Specific claims include alleged inappropriate language such as questioning a DOJ attorney's religious beliefs. The complaint<ref>{{cite news |last=Wiessner |first=Daniel |title=US Justice Department accuses judge reviewing Trump transgender military ban of misconduct |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/us/us-justice-department-accuses-judge-reviewing-trump-transgender-military-ban-2025-02-22/ |work=[[Reuters]] |date=February 22, 2025 |access-date=February 22, 2025}}</ref> was dismissed by Chief Judge [[Sri Srinivasan]] of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit on September 29, 2025.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Kunzelman |first1=Michael |title=Court official dismisses Justice Department's misconduct complaint against a federal judge in DC |url=https://apnews.com/article/justice-department-judge-complaint-transgender-executive-order-150dec66b471ecc3f6224d6324d44dbe |access-date=December 27, 2025 |work=AP News |date=November 25, 2025 |language=en}}</ref>

[[Columbia Law School|Columbia University]] ([[Juris Doctor|J.D.]]) | occupation = | profession = | known_for = | cabinet = | committees = | portfolio = | awards = | signature = | signature_alt = | website = | footnotes = }} '''Analisa Nadine Torres''' (born 1959) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]]. ==Early life and education== Analisa Torres's father, Frank Torres, served for many years as a [[New York Supreme Court]] justice in [[the Bronx]], and as a Democratic member of the [[New York State Assembly]]; and her grandfather [[Felipe N. Torres]] (d. 1994) served as a Family Court judge and was also an assemblyman.{{cite news |last=Gregorian |first=Dareh |title=New judge in NYPD stop-and-frisk case, "Analisa Torres, has been critical of police tactic in past" |date=November 1, 2013 |work=[[Daily News (New York)|Daily News]] |url-access=limited |url=https://www.nydailynews.com/2013/11/01/new-judge-in-nypd-stop-and-frisk-case-analisa-torres-has-been-critical-of-police-tactic-in-past/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230908023545/https://www.nydailynews.com/2013/11/01/new-judge-in-nypd-stop-and-frisk-case-analisa-torres-has-been-critical-of-police-tactic-in-past/|url-status=live|archive-date=September 8, 2023}}Eric Pace (April 5, 1994). [https://www.nytimes.com/1994/04/05/obituaries/felipe-n-torres-96-former-legislator-and-retired-judge.html Felipe N. Torres, 96, Former Legislator And Retired Judge], ''[[The New York Times]]'' Torres received her [[Bachelor of Arts|Artium Baccalaureus]] degree, ''[[magna cum laude]]'', in 1981 from [[Harvard College]] and her [[Juris Doctor]] in 1984 from [[Columbia Law School]].{{cite web |title=Senate Confirms Gillibrand Recommended Judge Analisa Torres to Sit on Federal Bench |url=https://www.gillibrand.senate.gov/news/press/release/senate-confirms-gillibrand-recommended-judge-analisa-torres-to-sit-on-federal-bench |website=Kirsten Gillibrand United States Senator|date=April 18, 2013 |access-date=January 16, 2018}} ==Career== Torres spent the early portion of her legal career as a real estate associate at three [[New York City]] law firms ([[Kaye Scholer]] from 1984 to 1985, [[Coudert Brothers]] from 1985 to 1987, and [[Patterson Belknap Webb & Tyler|Patterson, Belknap, Webb & Tyler]] from 1988 to 1992). From 1992 to 1999, she clerked for Justice Elliot Wilk of the New York Supreme Court; she served as a commissioner of the [[New York City Planning Commission]] from 1993 to 1995. From 2000 to 2002, Torres was a judge of the [[New York City Criminal Court]]. From 2003 to 2004, she was a judge on the [[New York City Civil Court]]. She served as an acting justice of the New York Supreme Court in the Bronx from 2004 to 2009, and became an elected justice of that court in 2010, handling criminal felony cases, serving until 2013.{{cite web |url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2012/11/14/president-obama-nominates-seven-united-states-district-courts |work=[[whitehouse.gov]] |title=President Obama Nominates Seven to the United States District Courts |via=[[NARA|National Archives]] |date=November 14, 2012}}{{cite web |url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/112thCongressJudicialNominations/upload/Torres-Senate-Questionnaire-Public-Final-WD.pdf |title=Senate Judiciary Committee Nomination Questionnaire |publisher=|access-date=November 28, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170217143926/http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/112thCongressJudicialNominations/upload/Torres-Senate-Questionnaire-Public-Final-WD.pdf|archive-date=February 17, 2017|url-status=dead}}{{FJC Bio|nid=1394176|inline=yes}} === Federal judicial service === On November 14, 2012, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Analisa Torres to serve as a United States district judge for the United States District Court in the Southern District of New York, to the seat vacated by Judge [[Naomi Reice Buchwald]], who assumed senior status on March 21, 2012. On January 2, 2013, Torres's nomination was returned to the President, due to the [[sine die]] adjournment of the Senate. On January 3, 2013, she was renominated to the same office. Her nomination was reported by the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] on February 14, 2013, by [[voice vote]].{{cite web |url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2013/01/03/president-obama-re-nominates-thirty-three-federal-judgeships |work=[[whitehouse.gov]] |title=President Obama Re-nominates Thirty-Three to Federal Judgeships |via=[[NARA|National Archives]] |date=January 3, 2013}} The Senate confirmed Torres's nomination on April 18, 2013, by voice vote. She received her commission on April 23, 2013. == Personal life == Torres had been married since 1983 to Constantino Ramón Argimon, the son of Venezuelans living in [[Caracas]].{{Cite news |date=1982-10-17 |title=Miss Torres And Student Plan Nuptials |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1982/10/17/style/miss-torres-and-student-plan-nuptials.html |access-date=2026-11-01 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} == See also == * [[List of African American federal judges]] * [[List of African American jurists]] * [[List of Hispanic and Latino American jurists]] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== * {{FJC Bio|nid=1394176}} * {{Ballotpedia|Analisa_Torres}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Naomi Reice Buchwald]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]]}}|years=2013–present}} {{s-inc}} {{s-end}} {{United States 2nd Circuit district judges}} {{authority control}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Torres, Analisa}} [[Category:1959 births]] [[Category:Living people]] [[Category:20th-century American lawyers]] [[Category:20th-century American women lawyers]] [[Category:20th-century African-American lawyers]] [[Category:21st-century American women judges]] [[Category:African-American judges]] [[Category:Columbia Law School alumni]] [[Category:Harvard College alumni]] [[Category:Hispanic and Latino American judges]] [[Category:Hispanic and Latino American lawyers]] [[Category:Judges of the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]] [[Category:Kaye Scholer associates]] [[Category:Lawyers from New York City]] [[Category:New York state court judges]] [[Category:New York Supreme Court justices]] [[Category:Patterson Belknap Webb & Tyler people]] [[Category:United States district court judges appointed by Barack Obama]]

Haggerty}} | footnotes = }} '''Ancer Lee Haggerty''' (born August 26, 1944){{cite web|url=http://www.jtbf.org/index.php?src=directory&view=biographies&srctype=detail&refno=71|title=JTBF}} is an [[United States federal judge|inactive senior United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Oregon]]. At the time of his nomination to the federal bench by President [[Bill Clinton|Clinton]] in 1993, he was serving as an [[Oregon circuit court]] judge. ==Early life and education== Haggerty was born in [[Vanport, Oregon]]. He graduated from the [[University of Oregon]] with a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree in 1967, and after service in the [[United States Marine Corps]] from 1967 to 1970, entered [[University of California College of the Law, San Francisco]], earning a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1973. ==Career== Haggerty was a [[law clerk]] for the metropolitan public defender in [[Portland, Oregon]] in 1973. He was a staff attorney of Metropolitan Public Defender in Portland from 1973 to 1977. He was in private practice of law in Portland from 1977 to 1988. He was a judge to the [[Multnomah County, Oregon|Multnomah County]] District Court, Oregon from 1989 to 1990. He was a judge to the Multnomah County Circuit Court, Oregon from 1990 to 1993. ===Federal judicial service=== Haggerty was nominated by President [[Bill Clinton]] on November 19, 1993, to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Oregon]]. He was nominated to a seat vacated by Judge [[Owen M. Panner]]. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on March 25, 1994, and received commission on March 28, 1994. He served as chief judge from 2002 to 2009.{{cite news|url=http://www.ord.uscourts.gov/news/xv1.pdf|title=Courthouse News|volume=XV|issue=1|date=January 20, 2009|publisher=United States District Court for the District of Oregon|page=2|access-date=2009-03-10}}{{Dead link|date=October 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} He took [[senior status]] on August 26, 2009, and took inactive senior status at the end of 2014, meaning that he remains a member of the court, but no longer hears cases or participates in court business.{{cite news|author1-link=Bryan Denson|last1=Denson|first1=Bryan|title=Ancer Haggerty, presiding judge in two notorious neo-Nazi cases in Portland, hangs up robes|url=http://www.oregonlive.com/portland/index.ssf/2014/12/ancer_haggerty_presiding_judge.html|work=[[The Oregonian]]|date=December 31, 2014}} ===Notable case=== Haggerty was the presiding judge in the trial of [[White Aryan Resistance]] (WAR) founder and leader, [[Tom Metzger]], over his involvement in the 1988 murder of [[Mulugeta Seraw]] by skinhead members of Portland's East Side White Pride. == See also == * [[List of African-American federal judges]] * [[List of African-American jurists]] * [[List of first minority male lawyers and judges in Oregon]] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1381616}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Owen M. [[Yale Law School|Yale University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | footnotes = }} '''Andrea Robin Wood''' (born March 2, 1973) is an American attorney serving as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois]]. ==Early life and education== Wood was born March 2, 1973, in [[St. Louis, Missouri]].{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/113thCongressJudicialNominations/upload/Wood-Senate-Questionnaire-Public-Final.pdf|title=Senate Judiciary Committee Nomination Questionnaire|publisher=|access-date=2013-05-13|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131018040030/http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/113thCongressJudicialNominations/upload/Wood-Senate-Questionnaire-Public-Final.pdf|archive-date=2013-10-18|url-status=dead}} She received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from the [[University of Chicago]] in 1995 and a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1998 from [[Yale Law School]]. == Career == Wood served as a law clerk to Judge [[Diane Wood]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit]] from 1998 to 1999. From 1999 to 2004, she worked as an associate at the law firm of [[Kirkland & Ellis]], where she was responsible for litigation, primarily in federal court. In 2004, she became a senior attorney at the [[U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission]], where she managed complex investigations and litigation involving [[securities law]]. In 2007, she became senior trial counsel in the Division of Enforcement, serving until her appointment to the bench in 2013.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2013/04/30/president-obama-announces-intent-nominate-three-serve-united-states-dist|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Obama Announces Intent to Nominate Three to Serve on the United States District Court|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=30 April 2013}}{{FJC Bio|nid=1394291|inline=yes}} ===Federal judicial service=== On May 6, 2013, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Wood to serve as a United States district judge of the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois, to fill the vacancy left by Judge [[William J. Hibbler]], who died on March 19, 2012. She received a hearing before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] on June 19, 2013. On July 18, 2013, her nomination was reported out of committee by [[voice vote]].{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/Materials113thCongress.cfm#District|title=Senate Judiciary Committee Nomination Page|access-date=2013-07-19|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131217035140/http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/Materials113thCongress.cfm#District|archive-date=2013-12-17|url-status=dead}} The [[United States Senate]] confirmed her nomination on October 14, 2013 by [[voice vote]]. She received her commission on October 15, 2013. At the time she was sworn in, she was the youngest United States district court judge.{{cite web|url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2013/10/14/sec-lawyer-in-chicago-confirmed-by-us-senate-for-federal-judge/|title=SEC lawyer in Chicago confirmed by U.S. Senate for federal judge|website=[[Chicago Tribune]] |date=14 October 2013 |publisher=}} == See also == * [[List of African-American federal judges]] * [[List of African-American jurists]] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1394291}} *{{Ballotpedia|Andrea_R._Wood}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[William J. He served as a [[United States Magistrate Judge]] of the same court from 2016 to 2023. == Education == Schopler received a Bachelor of Arts, ''[[summa cum laude]]'', from [[Dartmouth College]] in 1994 and he received a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Harvard Law School]], ''[[cum laude]]'', in 1997.{{Cite press release|title=President Biden Names Twenty-Third Round of Judicial Nominees|date=June 29, 2022|publisher=The White House|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/07/14/president-biden-names-twenty-third-round-of-judicial-nominees/|access-date=July 14, 2022}}{{PD-notice}} == Career == Schopler was a [[Sole practitioner|solo practitioner]] in [[Chapel Hill, North Carolina]], from 1997 to 1998. In 1998, Schopler became an assistant [[public defender]] for [[Courts of North Carolina|district 15B in North Carolina]]. He returned to private practice that same year. Schopler was named to the North Carolina Capital Roster for [[capital murder]] cases.{{cite web | url=https://trellis.law/judge/andrew.g.schopler | title=Judge Andrew G. Schopler for U.S. District Court, Southern District of California in California }} From 1998 to 2004, he worked at Rudolf and Maher in [[Chapel Hill, North Carolina]]. From 2004 to 2016, he was an [[assistant United States attorney]] in the [[United States Attorney|United States Attorney's Office]] for the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of California|Southern District of California]]. === Military service === Schopler has served in the [[California Army National Guard]] since 2014, holding the rank of [[Major (United States)|major]].{{Cite news |last=Rodriguez |first=Katherine |date=March 7, 2023 |title=Magistrate Judge Andrew G. Schopler Gets U.S. Senate Confirmation to Serve as a District Judge |url=https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/ce9/2023/Schopler_CAS_Confirmed.pdf |access-date=December 4, 2024 |work=United States Courts for the Ninth Circuit}} In 2018, he deployed to [[Afghanistan]] as part of his duties as a [[Judge advocate general|Judge Advocate General]] (JAG) officer for [[United States Northern Command#Subordinate unified commands|Special Operations Command North]] (SOCNORTH), a [[United States Army Special Forces|Green Beret]] unit. During this deployment, he worked on [[special operations]] across [[Afghanistan]] and was awarded the [[Bronze Star Medal]] for his service. Beginning in 2021, Schopler was involved in [[2020–2021 U.S. troop withdrawal from Afghanistan|Operation North Star]], aiding in the evacuation of [[Citizenship of the United States|U.S. citizens]] and at-risk Afghan allies from Afghanistan. His military commendations include the [[Meritorious Service Medal (United States)|Meritorious Service Medal]], [[Commendation Medal#Army|Army Commendation Medal]], [[Achievement Medal#Army, Air Force, Space Force, and Coast Guard|Army Achievement Medal]], [[Reserve Good Conduct Medal#U.S. Army Reserve Components Achievement Medal|Army Reserve Components Achievement Medal]] (with [[Oak leaf cluster|Bronze Oak Leaf Cluster]]), [[National Defense Service Medal]], [[Afghanistan Campaign Medal]] (with [[Service star|Bronze Star Device]]), [[Global War on Terrorism Service Medal]], [[Armed Forces Reserve Medal]] (with [[Armed Forces Reserve Medal#For mobilization – the "M" device|"M" Device]]), [[Army Service Ribbon]], [[NATO Medal#Non-Article 5 Medal|Non-Article 5 NATO Medal]], [[List of decorations awarded by the United States National Guard#California|California State Service Ribbon]], and the [[Parachutist Badge (United States)|Parachutist Badge]]. === Federal judicial service === [[File:Andrew G Schopler.jpg|thumb|right|250px|U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee hearing]] Schopler served as [[United States Magistrate Judge]] of the Southern District of California from September 30, 2016 to March 10, 2023.{{Cite web |date=October 11, 2016 |title=Azano prosecutor becomes federal magistrate judge |url=https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/sd-me-schopler-judge-20161011-story.html |access-date=July 14, 2022 |website=San Diego Union-Tribune |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |date=July 14, 2022 |title=Biden nominates two for San Diego federal court bench |url=https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/news/courts/story/2022-07-14/biden-nominates-two-for-san-diego-federal-court-bench |access-date=July 14, 2022 |website=San Diego Union-Tribune |language=en-US}} On July 14, 2022, President [[Joe Biden]] nominated Schopler to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States District Judge]] of the same court. His nomination received the support of Senators [[Alex Padilla]] and [[Dianne Feinstein]].{{Cite web|title=Feinstein, Padilla Support Nomination of Judges Simmons, Schopler to Southern District Court |url=https://www.feinstein.senate.gov/public/index.cfm/2022/7/feinstein-padilla-support-nomination-of-judges-simmons-schopler-to-southern-district-court|access-date=July 14, 2022|website=United States Senator for California|language=en}} President Biden nominated Schopler to the seat vacated by Judge [[Larry Alan Burns]], who assumed [[senior status]] on January 22, 2021.{{Cite web|date=July 14, 2022|title=PN2383 – Nomination of Andrew G. Schopler for The Judiciary, 117th Congress (2021–2022)|url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/117th-congress/2383|access-date=July 15, 2022|website=www.congress.gov}} On December 13, 2022, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web|title=Nominations|date=December 12, 2022|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/12/13/2022/nominations}} On January 3, 2023, his nomination was returned to the president under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]]. He was renominated on January 23, 2023.{{Cite press release|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate|date=January 23, 2023|publisher=The White House|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2023/01/23/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-92/}} On February 9, 2023, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 15–6 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/2023-02-09%20-%20EBM%20-%20Results.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – February 9, 2023|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=February 9, 2023}} On March 7, 2023, the Senate invoked [[cloture]] on his nomination by a 57–39 vote.{{Cite web|date=March 7, 2023|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Andrew G. Schopler to be U.S. District Judge for the Southern District of California)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00042.htm|access-date=March 7, 2023|website=United States Senate}} His nomination was confirmed later that day by a 56–39 vote.{{Cite web|date=March 7, 2023|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Andrew G. Schopler, of California, to be U.S. District Judge for the Southern District of California)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00043.htm|access-date=March 7, 2023|website=United States Senate}} He received his judicial commission on March 10, 2023.{{FJC Bio|nid=13363936|inline=yes}} == References == {{Reflist}} == External links == *{{FJC Bio|nid=13363936}} *{{Ballotpedia|Andrew_Schopler}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Larry Alan Burns]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of California]]}}|years=2023–present}} {{s-inc}} {{s-end}} {{United States 9th Circuit district judges}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Schopler, Andrew G.}} [[Category:1971 births]] [[Category:Living people]] [[Category:20th-century American lawyers]] [[Category:21st-century American lawyers]] [[Category:Assistant United States attorneys]] [[Category:California lawyers]] [[Category:Dartmouth College alumni]] [[Category:Harvard Law School alumni]] [[Category:Judges of the United States District Court for the Southern District of California]] [[Category:People from Chapel Hill, North Carolina]] [[Category:Public defenders]] [[Category:United States Army reservists]] [[Category:United States district court judges appointed by Joe Biden]] [[Category:United States magistrate judges]]

[[Baylor University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Andrew Scott Hanen''' (born 1953) is an American lawyer who serves as a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas]]. ==Early life and education== Hanen was born in 1953,"Andrew Scott Hanen". ''The Complete Marquis Who's Who Biographies.'' Accessed February 17, 2015 via LexisNexis. in [[Elgin, Illinois]] and raised in [[Waco, Texas]].Molly Hennessy-Fiske, [http://www.latimes.com/nation/nationnow/la-na-immigration-lawsuit-hanen-20150217-story.html U.S. Judge Andrew Hanen has history of opposing Obama immigration policies], ''Los Angeles Times'' (February 17, 2015). He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]], with honors, from [[Denison University]] in 1975, majoring in [[economics]] and [[political science]]. He received his [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Baylor Law School]] in 1978. ==Career== Hanen began his legal career as a briefing attorney to [[Joe R. Greenhill]], chief justice of the [[Supreme Court of Texas]], from 1978 to 1979. He then worked in private practice in [[Houston, Texas|Houston]] from 1979 to 2002.{{FJC Bio|nid=1391491|inline=yes}} In 1992, Hanen was nominated by then-President [[George H. W. Bush]] to be a [[United States District Judge|United States district judge]], but the nomination lapsed. ===Federal judicial service=== On January 23, 2002, he was nominated by President [[George W. Bush]] to a seat on the [[United States District Court]] for the [[Southern District of Texas]] vacated by [[Filemon Vela Sr.]], who assumed [[senior status]]. Hanen was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on May 9, 2002, by a 97–0 vote.{{cite web|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Andrew S. Hanen, of Texas, to be U.S. District Judge)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1072/vote_107_2_00105.htm|access-date=June 9, 2023}} He received his commission on May 10, 2002. He assumed [[senior status]] on January 2, 2025. Hanen maintained chambers in [[Brownsville, Texas]] from 2002 until 2018, when he relocated to Houston, also within the Southern District.{{Cite web|last=Reagan|first=Mark|date=2018-03-24|title=Judge moving to spot in Houston|url=https://www.themonitor.com/2018/03/24/judge-moving-to-spot-in-houston/|access-date=2020-11-02|website=The Monitor|language=en-US}} ===Notable cases=== During the sentencing of a convicted child smuggler in December 2013, Hanen sharply criticized the [[United States Department of Homeland Security]] in an opinion that "veered far from the matter at hand" and "that quickly won rave reviews on right-wing news sites." Not only did he criticize the policy of reuniting children with their [[illegal immigrant]] mothers, he further rebuked the department for not prosecuting this child's mother.{{cite news|last1=Linda Greenhouse|author-link=Linda Greenhouse|title=The Supreme Court's Silent Failure on Immigration|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/06/26/opinion/sunday/the-supreme-courts-silent-failure-on-immigration.html?ref=todayspaper|access-date=26 June 2016|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=June 25, 2016|page=SR2}} Hanen wrote, "DHS should cease telling the citizens of the United States that it is enforcing our border security laws because it is not. Even worse, it is helping those who violate these laws."{{cite news|last1=Von Spakovsky|first1=Hans A.|title=Federal Judge: The Obama Administration Aids and Abets Human Trafficking|url=http://www.nationalreview.com/corner/366830/federal-judge-obama-administration-aids-and-abets-human-trafficking-hans-von-spakovsky|access-date=26 June 2016|work=[[National Review]]|date=20 December 2013}} In February 2015, Hanen granted the State of Texas's motion for a nationwide [[preliminary injunction]] barring President [[Barack Obama]] from carrying out the [[Deferred Action for Parents of Americans]] (DAPA) program. In ''[[United States v. Texas (2016)|United States v. Texas]]'', that ruling was affirmed by an equally divided [[Supreme Court of the United States]] on June 23, 2016 (with an eight-member bench due to the death of Justice [[Antonin Scalia]]). Hanen made national news for related assertions and sanctions which were later withdrawn. On May 19, 2016, while the case was awaiting a decision at the Supreme Court, Hanen demanded that some 3,000 [[United States Department of Justice|Department of Justice]] lawyers in 26 states take ethics classes, and ordered other sanctions for those who argued ''[[Texas v. United States (2016)|Texas v. United States]]'', involving President Obama's immigration executive actions.{{cite news |last=Shear |first=Michael |date=May 19, 2016 |title=Federal Judge in Texas Demands Justice Dept. Lawyers Take Ethics Class |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/05/20/us/andrew-hanen-immigration-texas-court.html?_r=0 |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |location=[[New York City|New York]] |access-date=May 20, 2016|quote=In a blistering order, Judge Andrew S. Hanen of Federal District Court in Brownsville accused the Justice Department lawyers of lying to him during arguments in the case, and he barred them from appearing in his courtroom.}}Aaron Nelsen (June 7, 2016). [http://www.expressnews.com/news/local/article/Federal-judge-stays-his-sanctions-order-7968882.php "Federal judge stays his sanctions order"], ''[[San Antonio Express-News]]''. Hanen did not explain why he extended his sanctions to attorneys who had no involvement in the case.Julia Preston (May 31, 2016). [https://www.nytimes.com/2016/06/01/us/justice-dept-says-judge-in-immigration-case-is-out-of-bounds.html Justice Dept. Says Judge in Immigration Case Is Out of Bounds], ''[[The New York Times]]''. Hanen accused Justice Department's lawyers of lying to him during arguments in the case, and barred them from appearing in his courtroom. He accused the department of "a calculated plan of unethical conduct".{{cite news |last1=Palazzolo |first1=Joe |last2=Gershman |first2=Jacob |date=May 19, 2016 |title=Furious Federal Judge Orders Justice Department Lawyers to Undergo Ethics Training |url=https://blogs.wsj.com/law/2016/05/19/furious-federal-judge-orders-justice-department-lawyers-to-undergo-ethics-training/ |newspaper=[[The Wall Street Journal]] |location=[[New York City|New York]] |access-date=May 20, 2016 |quote=The problem, according to Judge Hanen, is the Justice Department assured him that the federal government wouldn't begin implementing the program — which the judge apparently took to mean any part of it — before February 2015, giving him time to weigh the legal issues. He also claimed the Justice Department misled him about how many three-year extensions were granted.}} Hanen further ordered [[United States Attorney General|Attorney General]] [[Loretta Lynch]] to appoint someone within the department to ensure compliance with his order. Hanen also ordered U.S. immigration officials to turn over, within weeks, the names and addresses of 50,000 people who received deferral under the expanded deferred action initiative. The [[National Immigration Law Center]], the [[American Civil Liberties Union]] (ACLU) Immigrants' Rights Project, and the ACLU of Texas petitioned the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]] to vacate the order or postpone the deadline. Separately, the Justice Department argued in a filing in the district court that Hanen's ordered sanctions "exceed the scope of [the court's] authority and unjustifiably impose irreparable injury on the Department of Justice, the Department of Homeland Security and thousands of innocent third parties."Brent Kendall (May 31, 2016). [https://blogs.wsj.com/law/2016/05/31/justice-department-pushes-back-on-sweeping-sanction/ Justice Department Pushes Back on Sweeping Sanction], ''[[The Wall Street Journal]]''. The Justice Department also argued that additional ethics courses could cost up to $7.8 million over five years. On June 7, 2016, Hanen stayed his order requiring ethics courses for federal attorneys and requiring U.S. immigration officials to turn over the names and addresses until August 22, 2016. On January 19, 2017, Hanen withdrew the sanctions in the order issued on May 19, 2016, as well as his demand that [[Immigration and Customs Enforcement]] (ICE) turn over personal information of 50,000 DACA recipients, stating: "This Court finds upon [DOJ's] newly filed evidence, that the statements in question, though repeated on multiple occasions, were not the product of a bad faith intent to deceive the Court or that they were made with malice."{{Cite web|url=https://www.aila.org/infonet/texas-et-al-v-us-documentation|title=AILA - Resources on the Lawsuit Challenging DAPA and DACA Expansion|website=www.aila.org}} On July 16, 2021, Hanen ruled that the [[Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals]] (DACA) program was unconstitutional, and provisionally blocked approvals of all new applications nationwide while allowing the receipt of such new applications. The ruling did not immediately cancel the protected status of existing recipients.[https://www.cnn.com/2021/07/16/politics/daca-ruling-hanen/index.html Federal judge blocks new DACA applications and says program is illegal], ''[[CNN]]'', Priscilla Alvarez, Tierney Sneed and Rachel Janfaza, July 16, 2021. Retrieved July 17, 2021.[https://www.nytimes.com/2021/07/16/us/court-daca-dreamers.html Judge Rules DACA Is Unlawful and Suspends Applications], ''[[New York Times]]'', Miriam Jordan, July 16, 2021. Retrieved July 17, 2021. On January 28, 2022, Hanen blocked enforcement of Texas's [[Anti-BDS laws|anti-BDS law]]. The case was brought about by Palestinian-American contractor Rasmy Hassouna, who had refused to renew his business's, A&R Engineering and Testing Inc., contract with the city of Houston due to the law. Hanen ruled that the law violated Hassouna's [[First Amendment to the United States Constitution|First Amendment]] right to [[Freedom of speech in the United States|freedom of speech]].{{cite web|last=Folmar|first=Chloe|url=https://thehill.com/homenews/state-watch/591949-federal-judge-blocks-enforcement-of-texass-anti-bds-law|title=Federal judge blocks enforcement of Texas's anti-BDS law|work=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]]|date=January 29, 2022|accessdate=January 29, 2022}} On September 13, 2023, Hanen again held that DACA was unlawful, and extended the ongoing injunction preventing the government from processing new applications for the program. He declined the request, from the states challenging DACA, to order that the program be ended within two years.{{Cite news |date=2023-09-13 |title=Federal judge again declares that DACA is illegal with issue likely to be decided by Supreme Court |language=en |work=[[Associated Press]] |url=https://apnews.com/article/immigration-daca-dreamers-51ba8c941993ffa26e1251aef84b0284 |access-date=2023-09-14}} ===2020 Texas voting case=== {{see also|2020 United States presidential election in Texas}} Two days before a decision was rendered in this case, ''[[Slate (magazine)|Slate Magazine]]'' had described him as "one of the most notoriously partisan conservatives in the federal judiciary."{{cite web| author-link = Mark Joseph Stern | last = Stern |first=Mark Joseph|url=https://slate.com/news-and-politics/2020/10/texas-drive-through-voting-throw-out-ballots.html|title=Texas Republicans Ask Federal Judge to Throw Out 117,000 Legally Cast Ballots|work=[[Slate (magazine)|Slate]]|date=2020-10-31|access-date=2020-10-31|language=en}} On November 2, 2020, Hanen heard a suit against officeholder [[Chris Hollins (politician)|Chris Hollins]], the Harris County Clerk, filed by Texas state representative [[Steve Toth]] and a group of Texas Republican candidates who sought to invalidate about 127,000 drive-thru votes in [[Harris County, Texas]]. [https://www.latimes.com/world-nation/story/2020-11-02/federal-judge-throws-out-republican-challenge-to-texas-drive-thru-voting Federal judge in Texas rejects Republican challenge to drive-through voting], ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'', Molly Hennessy-Fiske, November 2, 2020. Retrieved July 17, 2021. Toth said Harris County exceeded its state constitutional authority by allowing drive-thru voting as an alternative to walk-in voting during the [[COVID-19 pandemic in Texas|COVID-19 pandemic]], a change Toth argued could be determined solely by the [[Texas Legislature]]. Democrats countered that his request would disenfranchise all voters who had previously cast drive-thru votes in good faith.{{cite news|title=Federal judge sets hearing Monday on challenge to ballots from drive-thru voting in Texas' largest county|url=https://www.cnn.com/2020/10/31/politics/texas-ballots-drive-thru-voting-hearing-monday/index.html|date=October 31, 2020|work=CNN}}{{cite Report}} Hanen dismissed the Republicans' lawsuit, stating they needed to prove the existence of an "evil motive" to have the ballots thrown out and he said they failed to do so.{{Cite web|title=Federal Judge Dismisses Effort To Throw Out Drive-Through Votes In Houston|url=https://www.npr.org/2020/11/02/930365888/federal-judge-dismisses-effort-to-throw-out-drive-through-votes-in-houston|access-date=2020-11-02|website=NPR.org|date=2 November 2020 |language=en|last1=Naylor |first1=Brian }}{{Cite web|last=Mangan|first=Dan|date=2020-11-02|title=Judge rejects GOP bid to toss 127,000 drive-thru ballots in Harris County, and that drive-through voting could proceed on election day, but because the statute allowed for casting votes in "buildings," and he ruled that tent voting could not be included.{{cite web|url=https://slate.com/news-and-politics/2020/11/houston-area-harris-county-closes-drive-thru-voting-locations-election-day.html|title=Houston-Area County Closes Drive-Thru Voting Locations on Election Day Over Fear of GOP Lawsuits|last=Hannon|first=Elliot|work=[[Slate (magazine)|Slate]]|date=2020-11-03|access-date=2021-07-22}} Hanen's judgment retained the validity of the early drive-up votes that had been cast prior to his decision. It did not dismiss the possibility of whether those drive-thru sites comported with the state's election law. It did not preclude votes cast subsequent to his decision from being challenged, saying, "I would not vote in a drive-thru out of my concern whether that's legal or not." He ordered Harris County to retain and segregate records of any drive-thru ballots cast on Election Day because of the possibility of future legal challenges. Hollins chose to close nine of Harris County's 10 drive-thru voting sites on Election Day. He said, "I cannot in good faith encourage voters to cast their votes in tents if that puts their votes at risk." Hanen's decision was appealed by the Republican plaintiffs to the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]], but their appeal was rejected. Republican activist Steve Hotze and three Republican candidates sued the Clerk, Hollins, seeking to halt drive-through voting after the [[Texas Supreme Court]] ruled that the manner of voting could proceed. Richard Mithoff, a Harris County attorney said, "We're very grateful that we saved 127,000 votes from both parties," standing with Hollins and other Texas Democrats outside the federal courthouse in downtown Houston. Hollins said the county's staff of 11,000 election workers were ready to count the early drive-through votes. Republicans requested that the courts stop the county from tabulating the votes until after the resolution of their claims. Before the decision, Harris County Clerk Chris Hollins said that drive-through voting would continue on election day at 10 sites, in addition to in-person voting at more than 800 polling places. More than a million registered voters in the county still had not cast ballots, he said, adding that Republicans had filed almost a dozen lawsuits to constrict the intended expanded ability to exercise the franchise. "They will have the same access to the polls that their neighbors have had," Hollins said. "We're proud to be upholding democracy at a time when it is under attack." He said the case was just the latest in nearly a dozen lawsuits brought by Texas Republicans to block expanded voter access. In October, Republican Gov. [[Greg Abbott]] had limited every county to a single drop site for mailed votes, forcing Harris County to close 11 additional sites and voters to drive several hours to drop off their ballots. Republicans also successfully sued to block Harris County from mailing ballots to all those eligible unless they requested them. Hollins had previously said that drive-through voting would continue on election day at 10 sites, in addition to in-person voting at more than 800 polling places. More than 1 million registered voters in the county had yet to vote. After Hanen's decision, he kept the [[Toyota Center]] arena site open, since it comported with existing law. Regarding election day voting, as a result of the court rejecting the claim, "They will have the same access to the polls that their neighbors have had." "…We're proud to be upholding democracy at a time when it is under attack." He noted the case was the latest in nearly a dozen lawsuits brought by Texas Republicans to block expanded voter access. In November, Republican Governor Greg Abbott limited every county to a single drop site for mailed votes. That forced the county to have to close eleven other sites and caused some voters to need to drive many hours to drop their ballots off. Republicans also had successfully sued to stop Harris County from mailing ballots to every eligible voter in lieu of requests for such ballots. Hanen's decision was appealed by Republicans to the [[Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals]]. At stake in the legal contest over drive-through voting sites were almost 9% of all the votes cast in the third-most populous county in the U.S. The effort by Hollins that re-opened drive-through voting sites this year was intended to address safety issues resulting from the pandemic. Republicans who sued argued drive-through voting was offered illegally and strategically in areas with Democratic majorities. Curbside voting in Harris County previously had been limited to disabled voters, and drive-through voting in 2020 was unrestricted. Retiree Peter Nasser, had been protesting outside the courthouse "to protect my vote," saying Republicans were "scared to death of losing Texas." [[Temple University Beasley School of Law|Temple University]] ([[Master of Laws|LLM]]) }} '''Angel Kelley''' (born 1967) is an American attorney and judge serving as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts]]. She is a former associate justice of the [[Massachusetts Superior Court]]. == Early life and education == Kelley was born in [[New Rochelle, New York]], in 1967, growing up with three brothers. Her father was an overnight truck driver originally from [[Selma, Alabama]]; her mother had immigrated from [[Japan]] following [[World War II]] after marrying a U.S. soldier and found work as a supermarket meat packer in New York following a divorce.{{Cite web |title=Judge Kelley Tells Her Rare Story in Rising to a Judgeship – Chelsea Record |url=https://chelsearecord.com/2021/01/21/judge-kelley-tells-her-rare-story-in-rising-to-a-judgeship/ |access-date=2026-04-28 |website=chelsearecord.com}} Following her father's death, Kelley attended college and received her [[Bachelor of Arts]] from [[Colgate University]] in 1989, her [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Georgetown University]] in 1992, and her [[Master of Laws]] in trial advocacy from [[Temple University]] in 2003.[https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/05/12/president-biden-announces-third-slate-of-judicial-nominees/ "President Biden Announces Third Slate of Judicial Nominees", White House, May 12, 2021] {{PD-notice}}{{better source|date=February 2025}}{{cite web|url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/kelley-angel|title=Kelley, Angel|publisher=Federal Judicial Center|access-date=February 17, 2025}} == Legal and academic career == Kelley began her legal career as a staff attorney at [[The Legal Aid Society]] in the Juvenile Rights Division in [[Brooklyn]], [[New York (state)|New York]] from 1993 to 1997. From 1997 to 2005, she was an attorney for the [[Port Authority of New York and New Jersey]]. From 2007 to 2009, Kelley served as an [[Assistant United States Attorney]] for the [[United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts|United States Attorney's Office for the District of Massachusetts]]. From 1992 to 2005, she was a part-time instructor at [[Columbia University]]. From 2004 to 2005 she was a part-time instructor at [[New York University]]. From 2005 to 2007, she was a clinical instructor at [[Harvard Law School]]. Since 2012, she has been a part-time [[adjunct professor]] at [[Suffolk University Law School]]. Since 2016, she has been a volunteer instructor at [[Emory University School of Law]] and since 2018, she has been a part-time adjunct professor at [[Boston University School of Law]].{{Cite web '''Angela M. Martinez''' (born 1972)<ref name="Questionnaire">{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/martinez_sjq.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=March 19, 2024|archive-date=March 20, 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240320000837/https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/martinez_sjq.pdf|url-status=bot: unknown}}</ref> is an American lawyer who has served as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Arizona]] since 2024. She previously served as a [[United States magistrate judge]] of the same court from 2023 to 2024.

== Education ==

Martinez earned a [[Bachelor of Arts]] from the [[University of Arizona]] in 1995 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the University of Arizona [[James E. Rogers College of Law]] in 2000.<ref name="WHBio">{{Cite press release |title=President Biden Names Forty-Sixth Round of Judicial Nominees and Announces Two New Nominees to Serve as U.S. Attorney |date=February 21, 2024 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2024/02/21/president-biden-names-forty-sixth-round-of-judicial-nominees-and-announces-two-new-nominees-to-serve-as-u-s-attorney/ |access-date=February 21, 2024}} {{PD-notice}}</ref>

== Career ==

Martinez served as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[John Roll]] of the United States District Court for the District of Arizona from 2000 to 2002. From 2002 to 2004, she was an [[Associate lawyer|associate]] at Lewis and Roca, L.L.P. in [[Phoenix, Arizona|Phoenix]] and [[Tucson]]. From 2005 to 2009, she served as an [[assistant United States attorney]] in the District of Arizona and from 2012 to 2013, she was an [[Associate lawyer|associate]] at Farhang & Medcoff, P.L.L.C. From 2013 to 2015, she served as a law clerk for Judge [[Jennifer Zipps]] of the United States District Court for the District of Arizona. From 2015 to 2023, Martinez was previously an assistant United States attorney in the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Arizona.<ref name="WHBio" />

=== Federal judicial service ===

On March 30, 2023, she was appointed to serve as a [[United States magistrate judge]] of the District of Arizona.<ref>{{Cite web |date=March 30, 2023 |title=GENERAL ORDER 23-09 |url=https://www.azd.uscourts.gov/sites/azd/files/general-orders/23-09.pdf |access-date=February 21, 2024 |website=United States District Court for the District of Arizona}}</ref>

On February 21, 2024, President [[Joe Biden]] announced his intent to nominate Martinez to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Arizona]].<ref name="WHBio" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Hansen |first=Ronald J. |date=February 21, 2024 |title=President Joe Biden set to nominate 2 women to become federal judges in Arizona |url=https://www.azcentral.com/story/news/local/arizona/2024/02/21/joe-biden-to-nominate-angela-martinez-and-krissa-lanham-as-us-judges/72676524007/ |access-date=February 21, 2024 |website=The Arizona Republic |language=en-US}}</ref> On February 27, 2024, her nomination was sent to the Senate. President Biden nominated Martinez to the seat being vacated by Judge [[James A. Soto]], who subsequently assumed [[senior status]] on July 1, 2024.<ref>{{Cite press release |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |date=February 27, 2024 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2024/02/27/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-138/}}</ref> On March 20, 2024, a hearing on her nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Nominations|date=March 19, 2024|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/committee-activity/hearings/03/20/2024/nominations}}</ref> On April 18, 2024, her nomination was reported out of committee by a 13–8 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/2024-04-18_-_ebm_-_results.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – April 18, 2024|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=April 18, 2024}}</ref><ref>{{Cite press release |title=Senate Judiciary Committee Advances Ten Nominations to the Full Senate |date=April 18, 2024 |publisher=United States Senate Judiciary Committee |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/press/releases/senate-judiciary-committee-advances-ten-nominations-to-the-full-senate |access-date=April 18, 2024}}</ref> On May 21, 2024, the [[United States Senate]] invoked cloture on her nomination by a 64–29 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|date=May 21, 2024|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Angela M. Martinez to be United States District Judge for the District of Arizona)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1182/vote_118_2_00175.htm|access-date=May 21, 2024|website=United States Senate}}</ref> On May 22, 2024, her nomination was confirmed by a 66–28 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1182/vote_118_2_00177.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Angela M. Martinez, of Arizona, to be U.S. District Judge for the District of Arizona)|website=United States Senate|date=May 21, 2024|access-date=May 21, 2024}}</ref> Martinez is Biden's 200th judge to be confirmed.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Freking |first=Kevin |last2=Min Kim |first2=Seung |date=May 22, 2024 |title=Senate set to confirm 200th federal judge under Biden as Democrats surpass Trump's pace |url=https://apnews.com/article/biden-judges-trump-senate-200-confirmed-63b764d071d9c084b6669eabab527240 |access-date=May 22, 2024 |website=AP News |language=en}}</ref>
She received her judicial commission on July 2, 2024.<ref>{{FJC Bio|nid=13761691|inline=yes}}</ref>

[[Columbia Law School]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | alma_mater = | occupation = | profession = | known_for = | salary = | net_worth = | cabinet = | committees = | portfolio = | awards = | signature = | signature_alt = | website = | footnotes = }} '''Anita Jane Brody''' (née '''Blumstein'''; born May 25, 1935), also known as '''Anita Blumstein Brody''', is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania]]. ==Education and career== Brody was born in [[Brooklyn]], [[New York (state)|New York]]. She earned a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[Wellesley College]]{{cite web|title=Wellesley in Philadelphia Law Mentoring Event - Brown Bag Lunch With Judge Brody|url=http://web.wellesley.edu/Alum/Clubs/Clubs/Philadelphia/W-I-P%20Protegee%20Project.html|publisher=Wellesley College|accessdate=March 10, 2017|date=November 1, 2006|archive-date=March 12, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170312052442/http://web.wellesley.edu/Alum/Clubs/Clubs/Philadelphia/W-I-P|url-status=dead}} in 1955, and a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Columbia Law School]] in 1958. Brody was a deputy assistant state attorney general in [[New York (state)|New York]] from 1958 to 1959. From 1973 to 1981, she was in private practice in [[Philadelphia]]. In 1981, Brody was appointed by Pennsylvania Governor [[Richard Thornburgh]], and then elected a Judge of the [[Pennsylvania Court of Common Pleas|Court of Common Pleas]] for [[Montgomery County, Pennsylvania|Montgomery County]], Pennsylvania, which is part of the [[Philadelphia Metropolitan Area]].{{cite web|url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/brody-anita-blumstein|title=Brody, Anita Blumstein - Federal Judicial Center|website=www.fjc.gov}} In 1989, she was the Republican nominee for a seat on the [[Supreme Court of Pennsylvania|Pennsylvania Supreme Court]], but was defeated by Democrat [[Ralph Cappy]].{{Cite news |last=Roddy |first=Dennis B. |date=1989-11-08 |title=Crappy state court victor |pages=1 |work=The Pittsburgh Press |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=g94cAAAAIBAJ&dq=ralph+cappy+anita+brody&pg=PA1&article_id=5195,4388191 |access-date=2023-11-22}} ==Federal judicial service== Brody was nominated by President [[George H. W. Bush]] on November 22, 1991, to the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania]], to a new seat created as a result of the passage of 104 Stat. 5089. She was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on September 2, 1992, and received her commission on October 2, 1992. ==Notable cases== Brody presided over the case to decide whether a group of lawsuits by former NFL players against the [[National Football League|NFL]] would be heard in federal court or whether the cases would be heard by an arbitrator in accordance with the league's [[collective bargaining]] agreement, as the league has requested. In an April 9, 2013 hearing, the NFL's lawyer, [[Paul Clement]], admitted it would be difficult for the NFL to make the argument that an arbitrator should hear the cases of former players who never signed the collective bargaining agreement. The medical condition [[chronic traumatic encephalopathy#American football|chronic traumatic encephalopathy]] (sometimes referred to simply as CTE) resulting from concussions is a factor in the suits.[https://www.nytimes.com/2013/04/10/sports/football/judge-hears-nfl-arguments-to-dismiss-head-trauma-cases.html?hpw Judge hears NFL arguments to dismiss head trauma cases], nytimes.com, April 10, 2013. In June 2024, Brody presided over a case regarding the [[SS United States|SS United States Conservancy]] and its Pier 82 landlord, Penn Warehousing. The landlord had continued to up the rent of the conservancy keeping ''United States'' at her berth. Brody ruled that Penn Warehousing did not break any contract rules, and that ''United States'' would have to find a new home within ninety days. The conservancy also has to raise funds for insurance, repairs, tugs, surveys, and preparations for the move.{{Cite web |last=Conde |first=Ximena |date=2024-06-14 |title=SS United States must leave its South Philadelphia berth by mid-September, judge rules |url=https://www.inquirer.com/news/ss-united-states-south-philadelphia-ruling-20240614.html |access-date=2024-06-15 |website=www.inquirer.com |language=en}}{{Cite web |title=Iconic Ocean Liner SS United States Ordered to Leave Berth by September |url=https://maritime-executive.com/article/iconic-ocean-liner-ss-united-states-order-to-leave-berth-by-september |access-date=2024-06-15 |website=The Maritime Executive |language=en}} ==References== {{Reflist}} ==Sources== * {{FJC Bio|271|nid=1378321|name=Anita Blumstein Brody}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=Seat established by 104 Stat. 5089}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania]]}}|years=1992–2009}} {{s-aft|after=[[L.
