Arthur J. Schwab:
{{Short description|American judge (born 1946)}} {{Infobox officeholder | honorific_prefix = | name = Arthur James Schwab | honorific_suffix = | image = ArthurJSchwab.jpg | alt = | caption = | office = [[Senior Status|Senior Judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania]] | term_start = January 1, 2018 | term_end = | office1 = Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania]] | term_start1 = September 17, 2002 | term_end1 = January 1, 2018 | nominator1 = | appointer1 = [[List of federal judges appointed by George W. Bush|George W. Bush]] | predecessor1 = [[Maurice Blanchard Cohill Jr.]] | successor1 = [[Robert J. Colville]] | pronunciation = | birth_name = Arthur James Schwab | birth_date = {{Birth year and age|1946|}} | birth_place = [[Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania|Pittsburgh]], [[Pennsylvania]] | death_date = | death_place = | death_cause = | resting_place = | resting_place_coordinates = | citizenship = | party = | other_party = | height = | spouse = | partner = | relations = | children = | parents = | mother = | father = | relatives = | education = [[Grove City College]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|AB]])
[[University of Virginia School of Law|University of Virginia]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | alma_mater = | occupation = | profession = | known_for = | salary = | net_worth = | cabinet = | committees = | portfolio = | awards = | signature = | signature_alt = | website = | footnotes = }} '''Arthur James Schwab''' (born 1946){{Cite web |title=Judge Schwab |url=http://www.pawd.uscourts.gov/documents/judge/schwab_b.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141217033729/http://www.pawd.uscourts.gov/documents/judge/schwab_b.pdf |archive-date=2014-12-17 |accessdate=2014-12-17}} is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania]]. ==Early life, education, and career== Born in [[Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania|Pittsburgh]], [[Pennsylvania]], Schwab received an [[Bachelor of Arts|Artium Baccalaureus]] from [[Grove City College]], Pennsylvania in 1968 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Virginia School of Law]] in 1972. He served in the [[Pennsylvania National Guard]] from 1968 to 1978, and was a [[law clerk]] in a [[Pennsylvania]] private practice in 1972, and to Chief Judge [[Collins J. Seitz]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit]] from 1972 to 1973. He was in private practice in Pennsylvania from 1973 to 2002. He began teaching as an adjunct professor at [[Grove City College]], Pennsylvania, in 2001. ==Federal judicial service== On January 23, 2002, Schwab was nominated by President [[George W. Bush]] to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania]] vacated by [[Maurice B. Cohill, Jr.]] Schwab was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on September 13, 2002; received commission on September 17, 2002; and sworn-in to office on January 1, 2003.{{Cite web|title=Arthur J. Schwab {{!}} Western District of Pennsylvania {{!}} United States District Court|url=https://www.pawd.uscourts.gov/arthur-j-schwab|access-date=2020-06-21|website=www.pawd.uscourts.gov}} He assumed [[senior status]] on January 1, 2018. In 2008, the ''Pittsburgh Post-Gazette'' reported Schwab had the "lowest ranking among federal judges" by 797 lawyers in the Allegheny County Bar Association.{{cite web|url=https://www.post-gazette.com/local/neighborhoods/2008/06/25/Judge-in-Wecht-case-gets-rock-bottom-ranking-from-lawyers/stories/200806250235|title=Judge in Wecht case gets rock-bottom ranking from lawyers|work=Pittsburgh Post-Gazette|access-date=18 December 2014}} In 2011, he was accused of bias and recused himself from seventeen ongoing cases.{{cite web|url=http://www.fromthesidebar.com/2011/11/21/accused-of-bias-judge-recuses-himself-from-17-ongoing-cases/|title=Accused of Bias, Judge Recuses Himself from 17 Ongoing Cases|accessdate=18 December 2014}} ===Tommy Chong case=== In 2003, Schwab presided over the case involving [[Tommy Chong]]'s trial for conspiracy to distribute drug paraphernalia (bongs), and sentenced him to nine months in federal prison, as well as a hefty financial penalty. {{cite news | title=Tommy Chong gets the joint | date=September 13, 2003 | publisher= post-gazette.com| url=http://old.post-gazette.com/columnists/20030913roddy102col2p2.asp| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141217023421/http://old.post-gazette.com/columnists/20030913roddy102col2p2.asp| url-status=dead| archive-date=December 17, 2014}} ===Cyril Wecht case=== In 2008, Schwab presided over and was eventually removed from the [[Cyril Wecht]] federal trial, a case that caused considerable controversy. The defendant, a prominent Democrat in Pennsylvania, alleged that Judge Schwab was biased and the prosecution was political in nature and sought unsuccessfully to have the judge removed. Among the decisions Judge Schwab made was seeking to keep the names of jurors anonymous, a tactic usually reserved for criminal cases where the jurors may be in danger. This was overturned by the Third Circuit Court of Appeals. After Schwab declared the original trial a mistrial, he was criticized for not following proper procedures before declaring a mistrial, such as polling the jury which would have determined if the defendant should be retried on all counts or just one.{{cite news | author=Jason Cato | title=Panel criticizes Wecht judge | date=2008-08-05 | publisher=Pittsburgh Tribune-Review | url=http://www.pittsburghlive.com/x/pittsburghtrib/news/specialreports/wecht/trial/s_581110.html | access-date=2009-05-19 | archive-url=https://archive.today/20130131074935/http://www.pittsburghlive.com/x/pittsburghtrib/news/specialreports/wecht/trial/s_581110.html | archive-date=2013-01-31 | url-status=dead }} One month later, he was removed from presiding over the retrial. The Appellate court cited a "combative tenor" in the proceedings and hoped for "reduced level of rancor."{{cite news | author=Jason Cato | title=Federal appeals court removes Wecht judge | date=2008-09-06 | publisher=Pittsburgh Tribune-Review | url=http://www.pittsburghlive.com/x/pittsburghtrib/news/s_586835.html | access-date=2009-05-19 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080906192529/http://www.pittsburghlive.com/x/pittsburghtrib/news/s_586835.html | archive-date=2008-09-06 | url-status=dead }} On May 14, 2009, the new judge in the case tossed out most of the evidence against Wecht stating it was seized under unconstitutional warrants{{cite news|author=Jason Cato |title=Judge tosses evidence in remaining Wecht corruption charges |date=2009-05-14 |publisher=Pittsburgh Tribune-Review |url=http://www.pittsburghlive.com/x/pittsburghtrib/news/specialreports/wecht/trial/s_625211.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130104113454/http://www.pittsburghlive.com/x/pittsburghtrib/news/specialreports/wecht/trial/s_625211.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=2013-01-04 }} On June 2, all charges were dropped against Wecht. {{cite news | author=Jason Cato | title=Charges against Cyril H. Wecht to be dismissed | date=2009-05-14 | publisher= Pittsburgh Post Gazette| url=http://www.postgazette.com/pg/09153/974440-455.stm}} ===West Penn Allegheny Health System v UPMC case=== In 2012, Schwab presided over the [[Allegheny Health Network|West Penn Allegheny Health System]] v [[University of Pittsburgh Medical Center]] (UPMC) case, and in a rare move, the 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals removed him from case. According to ''Pittsburgh Post Gazette'', "It's rare for a federal judge to get yanked from a case, and twice in four years gets everyone's attention." {{cite news | author=Jason Cato | title=Experts: Pulling judge from case is rare; impeachment even rarer | date=2012-03-30 | publisher= Pittsburgh Post Gazette| url=https://www.post-gazette.com/local/region/2012/03/30/Experts-Pulling-judge-from-case-is-rare-impeachment-even-rarer/stories/201203300124}} ===Juarez-Escobar Case=== On December 16, 2014, Schwab wrote that President Obama's [[Immigration reform#Obama.27s executive actions of November.2C 2014|executive action]] on immigration was [[unconstitutional]]{{cite news | title=US judge says Obama immigration action invalid | date=2014-12-16 | newspaper= Washington Post | url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/courts_law/us-judge-says-obama-immigration-action-invalid/2014/12/16/86fed65e-8566-11e4-abcf-5a3d7b3b20b8_story.html| archive-url=https://archive.today/20141217162133/http://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/courts_law/us-judge-says-obama-immigration-action-invalid/2014/12/16/86fed65e-8566-11e4-abcf-5a3d7b3b20b8_story.html| url-status=dead| archive-date=2014-12-17}} in a case involving a Honduran man facing criminal charges for returning to the United States after being deported.{{cite news | title=Federal Judge Calls Obama's Immigration Actions Unlawful | date=2014-12-16 | work= New York Times | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2014/12/17/us/federal-judge-calls-obamas-immigration-actions-unlawful.html |accessdate=2014-12-17}}'' United States v. Juarez-Escobar'', no. 14-0180 (W.D. Penn., Dec. 16, 2014) ([https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/volokh-conspiracy/wp-content/uploads/sites/14/2014/12/Juarez-Escobar.pdf memorandum opinion and order]). Accessed Dec. 17, 2014. Whether discussion of the presidential order was necessary or appropriate to resolve the case before the court was questioned in the ''[[Washington Post]]''.{{cite news | title=District Court Declares Obama Immigration Action Unconstitutional (Updated) | date=2014-12-17 | newspaper= Washington Post | url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/volokh-conspiracy/wp/2014/12/16/district-court-declares-obama-immigration-action-unconstitutional/ | accessdate=2014-12-17}} ==References== {{reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1391631}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Maurice Blanchard Cohill Jr.]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania]]}}|years=2002–2018}} {{s-aft|after=[[Robert J. Arun Subramanian:
{{Short description|American federal judge (born 1979)}} {{Use mdy dates|date=July 2025}} {{Infobox officeholder | honorific_prefix = | name = Arun Subramanian | honorific_suffix = | image = Arun Subramanian.jpg | alt = | caption = Subramanian in 2022 | office = Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]] | term_start = April 13, 2023 | term_end = | appointer = [[List of federal judges appointed by Joe Biden|Joe Biden]] | predecessor = [[Alison Nathan]] | successor = | pronunciation = | birth_name = Arun Srinivas Subramanian | birth_date = {{Birth year and age|1979}} | birth_place = [[Pittsburgh]], Pennsylvania, U.S. | death_date = | death_place = | death_cause = | party = | spouse = | education = [[Case Western Reserve University]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|BA]])
[[Columbia Law School|Columbia University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Arun Srinivas Subramanian''' (born 1979){{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Subramanian%20SJQ%20Public%20Final.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=December 12, 2022}} is an American lawyer and jurist serving as a [[United States federal judge|U.S. district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York|U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York]]. He was appointed in 2023 by President [[Joe Biden]]. Before his appointment, Subramanian was a [[partner (business rank)|partner]] at the law firm [[Susman Godfrey LLP]]. == Early life and education == Subramanian was born in [[Pittsburgh]] in 1979. His family were Indian [[Tamils]] who had immigrated to the United States. His father was a [[control systems engineer]] and his mother was a [[bookkeeper]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.india.com/news/world/meet-arun-subramanian-1st-indian-american-to-become-new-york-district-court-judge-manhattan-federal-district-court-5932978/|title=Meet Arun Subramanian}}{{Cite news|url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/nri/us-canada-news/arun-subramanian-becomes-first-indian-american-judge-of-new-york-district-court/articleshow/98489326.cms|title=Arun Subramanian becomes first Indian-American judge of New York district court| website=[[The Times of India]] |date=March 8, 2023 }} Subramanian graduated from [[Case Western Reserve University]] in 2001 with a [[Bachelor of Arts]], ''[[Latin honors|summa cum laude]]''. He then attended [[Columbia Law School]], where he was the executive articles editor of the ''[[Columbia Law Review]]''. He graduated in 2004 with a [[Juris Doctor]] with James Kent Scholar and Harlan Fiske Stone Scholar honors.{{Cite press release |title=President Biden Names Twenty-Sixth Round of Judicial Nominees |date=September 2, 2022 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/09/02/president-biden-names-twenty-sixth-round-of-judicial-nominees/ |access-date=September 2, 2022}} {{PD-notice}} == Career == After law school, Subramanian was a [[law clerk]] to Judge [[Dennis Jacobs]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit|U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit]] from 2004 to 2005, to Judge [[Gerard E. Lynch]] of the Southern District of New York from 2005 to 2006, and to Justice [[Ruth Bader Ginsburg]] of the [[Supreme Court of the United States|U.S. Supreme Court]] from 2006 to 2007. From 2007 to 2023, he was in private practice at the law firm [[Susman Godfrey LLP]] in New York City, where he focused on [[commercial law]] and [[bankruptcy law]].{{cite web | url=https://www.americanbazaaronline.com/2022/09/05/biden-names-arun-subramanian-as-new-york-district-court-judge-450836/ | title=Biden names Arun Subramanian as New York district court judge | date=September 5, 2022 }} === Federal judicial service === Subramanian was recommended to President [[Joe Biden]] by Senator [[Chuck Schumer]].{{Cite web|last=Balk|first=Tim|date=June 9, 2022|title=Sen. Schumer recommends 3 candidates for spots on federal bench in New York's Eastern, Southern Districts|url=https://www.nydailynews.com/2022/06/09/sen-schumer-recommends-3-candidates-for-spots-on-federal-bench-in-new-yorks-eastern-southern-districts/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240928024241/https://www.nydailynews.com/2022/06/09/sen-schumer-recommends-3-candidates-for-spots-on-federal-bench-in-new-yorks-eastern-southern-districts/|url-status=live|archive-date=September 28, 2024|access-date=September 2, 2022|url-access=limited|website=New York Daily News}} On September 2, 2022, President Biden announced his intent to nominate Subramanian to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]]. On September 6, 2022, his nomination was sent to the Senate. President Biden nominated Subramanian to the seat vacated by Judge [[Alison Nathan]], who was elevated to the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit]] on March 31, 2022.{{Cite press release|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate|date=September 6, 2022|publisher=The White House|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/09/06/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-80/}} On December 13, 2022, a hearing on his nomination was held before the Senate Judiciary Committee.{{Cite web|title=Nominations|date=December 12, 2022|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/12/13/2022/nominations}} On January 3, 2023, his nomination was returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]]. He was renominated on January 23, 2023.{{Cite press release|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate|date=January 23, 2023|publisher=The White House|location=Washington, She also is a former [[United States attorney]]. == Early life and education == Born in [[St. Louis, Missouri]], Fleissig earned a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in 1976 from [[Carleton College]] and a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1980 from [[Washington University School of Law]].[https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/president-obama-nominates-five-serve-united-states-district-court-bench President Obama Nominates Five to Serve on the United States District Court Bench], ''[[whitehouse.gov]]'' (January 20, 2010). During her third year of law school, she worked as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Edward Louis Filippine]], a judge on the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri.[https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/presidential-nominations-sent-senate-2 Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate], ''[[whitehouse.gov]]'' (January 20, 2010).{{FJC Bio|nid=1393236}} == Career == From 1980 until 1991, Fleissig worked for a St. Louis law firm, first as an associate (from 1980 until 1989), and then as a partner (from 1989 until 1991). In 1991, Fleissig became an [[assistant United States attorney]] in St. Louis, a post she held until being named United States Attorney in 2000. She served as United States Attorney from 2000 until 2001, when she again became an Assistant United States Attorney. Later in 2001, Fleissig became a [[United States magistrate judge]], a position she held until becoming a United States District Judge in 2010. === Federal judicial service === In February 2009, Fleissig submitted her resume for a federal district court vacancy in St. Louis to United States Senator [[Claire McCaskill]]. In August 2009, McCaskill personally interviewed Fleissig. After interviews with representatives of the [[United States Department of Justice]] and the White House, Fleissig was nominated on January 20, 2010 to the position by President Obama, to replace Judge [[E. Richard Webber]], who assumed [[senior status]] on June 30, 2009. On March 4, 2010, the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]] sent Fleissig's nomination to the full Senate. The Senate confirmed Fleissig on June 7, 2010 by a 90–0 vote.{{Cite web|date=June 7, 2010|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Audrey Goldstein Fleissig, of Missouri, to be United States District Judge for the Eastern District of Missouri)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1112/vote_111_2_00177.htm|publisher=[[United States Senate]]|access-date=April 15, 2023}} She received her commission on June 9, 2010. As of Oct. 1, 2018, she is Chair of the [[Committee on Court Administration and Case Management]] (CACM) of the [[Judicial Conference of the United States]], and has continued in that role through at least June 2019.{{cite web| title=Chief Justice Names New Conference Committee Chairs| url=http://www.uscourts.gov/news/2018/10/04/chief-justice-names-new-conference-committee-chairs| publisher=Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts| date=October 4, 2018| access-date=October 4, 2018}}{{cite web| title=September 24, 2019 Agenda Book| author=[[Advisory Committee on Criminal Rules]]| date=September 6, 2019| url=https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/2019-09_criminal_rules_agenda_book.pdf| page=191| access-date=March 21, 2020}} Fleissig assumed [[senior status]] on April 14, 2023, her 68th birthday. == References == {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1393236}} *{{Ballotpedia|Audrey_Fleissig}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[E. [[Harvard Law School|Harvard University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Barry Lynn Winmill''' (born 1952) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Idaho]]. ==Early life and education== Born and raised in [[Blackfoot, Idaho]], Winmill grew up on a dairy farm.[http://www.fedbar.org/PDFs/Past-Judicial-Profiles/Ninth-Circuit_1/Winmill-Hon-B-Lynn.aspx Betty H. Richardson, Judicial Profile: Hon. B. Lynn Winmill Chief U.S. District Judge, District of Idaho] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190928195731/http://www.fedbar.org/PDFs/Past-Judicial-Profiles/Ninth-Circuit_1/Winmill-Hon-B-Lynn.aspx |date=2019-09-28 }}, ''The Federal Lawyer'', [[Federal Bar Association]]. He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[Idaho State University]] (ISU) in [[Pocatello, Idaho|Pocatello]] in 1974,[https://www.fjc.gov/node/1389946 B. Lynn Winmill], ''[[Biographical Directory of Federal Judges]]'', [[Federal Judicial Center]]. where he was student body president. Winmill earned his [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Harvard Law School]] in 1977. ==Legal career== Following law school, Winmill was in private practice for two years in [[Denver]], [[Colorado]], and back in Pocatello from 1979 to 1987. == Judicial career == === State judicial service === Appointed by Governor [[Cecil Andrus]] in 1987, Winmill was a state judge in the [[Courts of Idaho|Idaho District Court]] (Sixth District) in Pocatello from 1987 to 1995. From 1992 to 1995, he served as the administrative district judge and chair of the state's Evidence Rules Committee. Winmill was concurrently an adjunct professor at ISU (1991–1995), and a finalist on three occasions for the [[Idaho Supreme Court]], but he was never nominated.{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=H7VeAAAAIBAJ&sjid=KDAMAAAAIBAJ&pg=3163%2C2598348 |newspaper=Lewiston Morning Tribune |location=Idaho |agency=Associated Press |title=Pocatello judge confirmed as new federal justice |date=August 12, 1995 |page=7A }} ===Federal judicial service=== On May 24, 1995, Winmill was nominated by President [[Bill Clinton]] to a seat on the U.S. District Court for the District of Idaho, vacated by Judge [[Harold L. Ryan]], who assumed [[senior status]] in early 1993.{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=6RxOAAAAIBAJ&sjid=uOwDAAAAIBAJ&pg=5334%2C5974440 |newspaper=Deseret News |location=Salt Lake City, Utah |agency=Associated Press |title=Idaho judge nominated for federal bench |date=April 10, 1995 |page=A10 }}{{efn|Clinton's original nominee for the vacancy was lawyer John Tait of [[Lewiston, Idaho|Lewiston]]. That nomination was one of many that year blocked for political reasons.[https://lmtribune.com/obituaries/john-reid-tait/article_90cee511-174b-556d-8064-6cff7a8ed5b5.html Obituary: John Reid Tait], ''[[Lewiston Morning Tribune]]'' (February 12, 2012). The state's Republican [[United States Senate|U.S. Senators]], [[Larry Craig]] and [[Dirk Kempthorne]], opposed Tait's nomination.}} The [[American Bar Association]]'s [[Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary]], which rates judicial nominees, unanimously rated Winmill as "well qualified" for the post (the committee's highest rating).[https://www.americanbar.org/content/dam/aba/migrated/2011_build/federal_judiciary/ratings104.pdf Ratings of Article III Judicial Nominees, 104th Congress (1995-1996)], [[American Bar Association]] [[Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary]]. Confirmed by the Senate by [[voice vote]] on August 11, 1995,[https://www.congress.gov/nomination/104th-congress/412 PN412 — B. Lynn Winmill — The Judiciary], 104th Congress (1995-1996), [[Congress.gov]]. Winmill received his commission three days later. He served as chief judge for over 19 years, from 1999 to January 1, 2019,Demi Harris, [https://www.kivitv.com/chief-judges-to-step-down-as-the-chiefs-after-a-combine-33-years-of-service Chief Judges to step down after a combined 33 years of service] (December 21, 2018), and assumed senior status on August 16, 2021. ===Noteworthy cases=== Winmill granted the ''[[habeas corpus]]'' petition of Charles Fain, a [[Wrongful conviction|wrongfully convicted]] man who spent 18 years on Idaho's death row. Winmill ordered [[DNA testing]] that was previously unavailable; the new testing exonerated Fain, who was released from prison. Winmill and Fain later made joint speaking appearances. In 1999, Winmill presided over the trial of Allan Elias, a southeastern Idaho businessman, on charges arising from a 1996 incident in which Elias ordered an employee, who lacked safety training or proper [[Personal protective equipment|protective equipment]], to clean the inside of a large tank that stored a toxic mixture of [[phosphoric acid]] and [[cyanide]].Associated Press, [https://www.nytimes.com/2000/04/30/us/businessman-sentenced-to-prison-for-exposing-worker-to-cyanide.html Businessman Sentenced to Prison For Exposing Worker to Cyanide], Associated Press (April 30, 2000). The employee suffered severe brain damage, and Elias was convicted of "knowingly endangering the safety and health of his employees, illegally disposing of hazardous cyanide waste and making a false statement to the [[Occupational Safety and Health Administration]]." In 2000, Winmill sentenced Elias to 17 years in prison, the longest-ever sentence in the United States for an environmental crime.Virginia Sutcliffe, [https://www.ehstoday.com/news/ehs_imp_33275 Idaho Man Given Longest-Ever Sentence for Environmental Crime], ''[[EHS Today]]'' (May 3, 2000). In ''Western Watersheds Project v. Fish and Wildlife Service'' (2007),''[https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=10053865102918105288 Western Watersheds Project v. Fish & Wildlife Service]'', 535 F. Supp. 2d 1173 (D. Idaho 2007). Winmill ordered the [[United States Fish and Wildlife Service]] (FWS) to reconsider its decision not to list the [[sage-grouse]] as an [[Endangered species|endangered]] or [[threatened species]] under the [[Endangered Species Act]]. In an opinion highly critical of FWS officials, Winmill singled out deputy assistant secretary [[Julie A. MacDonald]] for criticism, and held that the agency had impermissibly disregarded scientific evidence in making its decision to deny protection to the sage-grouse.Rebecca Boone, [https://missoulian.com/news/local/judge-orders-sage-grouse-protections-reconsidered/article_ab1b3472-8fb7-58bd-9004-be9ff1e42f8f.html Judge orders sage grouse protections reconsidered], Associated Press (December 5, 2007).[https://www.nytimes.com/2007/12/15/opinion/15sat4.html Bird in the Brush], ''New York Times'' (December 15, 2007). In ''[[Animal Legal Defense Fund]] v. Otter'' (2015), Winmill struck down the "[[ag gag]]" law passed by the [[Idaho Legislature]] in 2012, ruling that the statute—which, among other things, banned the audio or visual recording of agricultural operations—violated the [[Free Speech Clause]] of the [[First Amendment to the United States Constitution]]. In January 2018, the [[U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]] upheld most of the ruling.Mateusz Perkowski, [https://www.capitalpress.com/state/idaho/th-circuit-strikes-down-most-of-idaho-s-ag-gag/article_32160617-bd0f-5753-9fc5-c030cf0070fb.html 9th Circuit strikes down most of Idaho's 'ag gag' law], ''Capital Press'' (January 4, 2018).Dan Flynn, [https://www.foodsafetynews.com/2018/01/split-decision-on-idahos-ag-gag-law-might-extend-beyond-agriculture/ Split decision on Idaho's Ag-Gag Law Might Extend Beyond Agriculture], ''Food Safety News'' (January 5, 2018).''[https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11695750170308697399 Animal Legal Defense Fund v. Otter]'', 118 F. Supp. 3d 1195 (D. Idaho 2015), ''affirmed in part and reversed in part sub nom.'' ''[https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16712217464617617239 Animal Legal Defense Fund v. Wasden]'', 878 F.3d 1184 (9th Cir. 2018). In ''Edmo v. Idaho Department of Correction'' (2018), Winmill ruled in favor of a [[transgender]] inmate diagnosed with [[gender dysphoria]], who challenged the state's refusal to provide [[gender confirmation surgery]]. Winmill ruled that the state's disregard of the "generally accepted medical standards for the treatment of gender dysphoria" constituted [[deliberate indifference]] to the inmate's medical needs, in violation of the [[Eighth Amendment to the United States Constitution]].{{cite web|author=Tommy Simmons|url=https://www.idahostatejournal.com/news/local/state-ordered-to-pay-for-surgery-for-transgender-prison-inmate/article_c43c405e-1e9b-57f2-9829-f774e12737d0.html|title=State Ordered to Pay for Surgery for Transgender Prison Inmate|newspaper=Idaho State Journal|date=December 14, 2018}}{{cite web|title=Case Summary & History: Adree Edmo v. Idaho Department of Correction et al.|publisher=National Center for Lesbian Rights|url=http://www.nclrights.org/cases-and-policy/cases-and-advocacy/edmo-v-idaho-department-of-correction-et-al/|access-date=2019-09-28|archive-date=2019-09-28|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190928142933/http://www.nclrights.org/cases-and-policy/cases-and-advocacy/edmo-v-idaho-department-of-correction-et-al/|url-status=dead}} On August 13, 2026, in ''Seyb v. Members of the Idaho Board of Medicine, et al'' (2024), Winfill ruled in favor of the plaintiff, finding that the state's ''de facto'' [[Abortion law|abortion ban]], legislated via Idaho's Defense of Life and the Fetal Heartbeat Acts, violates [[due process]] and equal protection clauses under the [[14th Amendment]].{{Cite web |date=2026-08-14 |title=A federal judge blocks Idaho from prosecuting doctors for health-protecting abortions |url=https://apnews.com/article/idaho-abortion-ban-health-judge-a342b48b2042ed47d1e3738e3224802a |access-date=2026-08-19 |website=AP News |language=en}} ==Personal life== Winmill is married; he and his wife Judy have four children and fourteen grandchildren. He has served as a member of the board of the Idaho Humanities Council; as a member of the Board of Visitors of [[Brigham Young University]]'s [[J. Reuben Clark Law School]]; and as a co-founder of the Idaho Legal History Society, which sponsored the performance of an original play marking the hundredth anniversary of the high-profile trial of [[Big Bill Haywood]]. ==Notes== {{Notelist}} ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1389946}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Harold L. [[Harvard Law School|Harvard University]] ([[Bachelor of Laws|LLB]]) | footnotes = }} '''Barbara Jacobs Rothstein''' (born 1939) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Washington]]. == Biography == Born in [[Brooklyn]],Christina Stolicky, [https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-news-tribune-federal-judge-balances/130165095/ Federal judge balances justice and inspires women]", ''The Tacoma News Tribune'' (January 27, 1983), p. D-2. Rothstein received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[Cornell University]] in 1960 and a [[Bachelor of Laws]] from [[Harvard Law School]] in 1966. She was in private practice in [[Boston]], [[Massachusetts]] from 1966 to 1968. She worked for the Washington State Attorney General's Office from 1968 to 1977, where she worked as assistant attorney general and chief trial attorney for the [[Consumer Protection]] and [[Antitrust]] Division. She was also an adjunct professor at the [[University of Washington Law School]] from 1975 to 1977. She was a judge of the [[King County Superior Court|Superior Court of Washington]] in [[King County, Washington|King County]], [[Washington (state)|Washington]] from 1977 to 1980.{{FJC Bio|2065|nid=1387206|name=Barbara Jacobs Rothstein}} === Federal judicial service === On December 3, 1979, Rothstein was nominated by President [[Jimmy Carter]] to a new seat on the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Washington]] created by 92 Stat. 1629. She had been recommended to Carter by Senators [[Henry M. Jackson]] and [[Warren Magnuson]], who had "decided to use a merit commission to select the appointment rather than the usual method of selecting through the political process". She was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on February 20, 1980, and received her commission the same day. She served as Chief Judge from 1987 to 1994. From 2003 to 2011, she was the Director of the [[Federal Judicial Center]]. She assumed [[senior status]] on September 1, 2011, and is currently serving by designation on the [[United States District Court for the District of Columbia]]. ===Notable cases=== In February 2020, Rothstein, sitting by designation with the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit]] in Florida, was a member of a 3-judge panel in ''Jones et al. v. DeSantis'', a 2020 voting rights case. [[2018 Florida Amendment 4]] permitted former felons to vote, however DeSantis signed a law that required former felons to pay all legal fees before being eligible to vote again, despite some of them not knowing how much they owed. District judge [[Robert Hinkle (judge)|Robert Hinkle]] struck down that law, and the panel kept the injunction against the law. However, the panel was reversed in a sharply divided en banc decision that September.{{Cite web|url=https://www.uscourts.gov/courts/ca11/201914551.pdf|title=KELVIN LEON JONES, BONNIE RAYSOR, et al., PLAINTIFFS-APPELLEES, versus GOVERNOR OF FLORIDA, FLORIDA SECRETARY OF STATE, DEFENDANTS-APPELLANTS|website=uscourts.gov|date=February 19, 2020|access-date=November 29, 2021}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.courthousenews.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/fla-felons-ca11.pdf|title=KELVIN LEON JONES, ROSEMARY MCCOY, et al., PLAINTIFFS-APPELLEES, versus GOVERNOR OF FLORIDA, FLORIDA SECRETARY OF STATE, DEFENDANTS-APPELLANTS|website=Courthouse News|date=September 11, 2020|access-date=November 29, 2021}} In August 2025, Rothstein tossed many conditions the Trump administration tried to impose on existing grants, which included not using the funds for abortion, DEI, or "gender ideology", as well as requirements that the grant recipients cooperate with ICE. Rothstein ruled that Congress, not the president, holds the power to set conditions on federal funding.{{Cite web|url=https://www.courthousenews.com/local-governments-score-win-in-case-over-conditions-on-federal-grants/|title=Local governments score win in case over conditions on federal grants|website=Courthouse News|date=2025-08-12|access-date=2026-03-29}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.courthousenews.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/federal-grants-preliminary-injunction-ruling.pdf|title=King County v. '''Barry Ted Moskowitz''' (born August 17, 1950) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of California]].

==Education and career==

Moskowitz was born in [[Paterson, New Jersey]]. He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[Rutgers University]] in 1972 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Rutgers Law School]] in 1975. He was a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Leonard I. Garth]] on the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit]] from 1975 to 1976. He was an [[assistant United States attorney]] for the District of New Jersey from 1976 to 1982. He was in private practice in [[Wayne, New Jersey]] from 1982 to 1985, and was then again an assistant United States attorney, this time in the Southern District of California, from 1985 to 1988.

===Federal judicial service===

From 1986 to 1995, Moskowitz was a [[United States magistrate judge]] of the Southern District of California. On June 30, 1995, Moskowitz was nominated by President [[Bill Clinton]] to a new seat on the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of California]] created by 104 Stat. 5089. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on December 22, 1995, and received his commission on December 26, 1995. He was elevated to chief judge on January 23, 2012 <ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.uscourts.gov/News/TheThirdBranch/12-03-01/Judicial_Milestones.aspx |title=The Third Branch |access-date=2012-03-26 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120414053254/http://www.uscourts.gov/News/TheThirdBranch/12-03-01/Judicial_Milestones.aspx |archive-date=2012-04-14 }}</ref> He assumed [[senior status]] on January 23, 2019.

'''Bernard Alvin Friedman'''<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.floridabar.org/mybarprofile/111275|title=Bernard Alvin Friedman|work=The Florida Bar}}</ref> (born September 23, 1943) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan]].

==Education and career==

Born in [[Detroit]], [[Michigan]], Friedman received a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Detroit College of Law]], now [[Michigan State University College of Law]] in 1968. He was in the [[United States Army]], JAG Corps from 1967 to 1968, reaching the rank of lieutenant. He continued at this rank in the [[United States Army Reserve]] JAG Corps from 1968 to 1973. Friedman was a felony trial attorney of [[Wayne County, Michigan|Wayne County]] prosecutor's office, Michigan from 1969 to 1970. He was in private practice in Detroit from 1970 to 1974, and in [[Southfield, Michigan|Southfield]], Michigan from 1974 to 1982. He was a judge on the 48th district court, Michigan from 1982 to 1988.<ref name="fjc.gov">{{cite web|url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/friedman-bernard-.|title=Friedman, Bernard A. - Federal Judicial Center|website=www.fjc.gov}}</ref>

==Federal judicial service==

On February 2, 1988, Friedman was nominated by President [[Ronald Reagan]] to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan]] vacated by judge [[Robert Edward DeMascio]]. Friedman was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on April 19, 1988, and received his commission on April 20, 1988. He served as chief judge from June 16, 2004 until he assumed [[senior status]] on January 1, 2009.<ref name="fjc.gov"/> When he took senior status, he was replaced by judge [[Gershwin A. Drain]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://archive.freep.com/article/20120929/NEWS01/309290074/-Dream-come-true-for-new-U-S-judge |title='Dream come true' for new U.S. Judge | Detroit Free Press | freep.com |access-date=2014-11-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141125115045/http://archive.freep.com/article/20120929/NEWS01/309290074/-Dream-come-true-for-new-U-S-judge |archive-date=2014-11-25 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Notable decisions==

=== Overturning Michigan's same-sex marriage ban ===

On March 21, 2014, Friedman struck down Michigan's constitutional and statutory bans on same-sex marriage. As he did not immediately issue a stay on his ruling, more than three hundred marriage licenses were issued to same-sex couples before the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit|Sixth Circuit Court]] issued a stay on Friedman's ruling the next day, pending appeals. The federal government announced it would recognize the marriages that took place during the brief period it was legal.

On August 22, 2015, Friedman presided over the wedding of the plaintiffs who he had originally ruled in favor of, after the U.S. Supreme Court had ruled two months earlier that all state bans on same-sex marriage were unconstitutional.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/nation/2015/08/22/michigan-couple-gay-marriage-case-exchange-vows/32217531/|title=Michigan couple in gay marriage case exchange vows|website=[[USA Today]] }}</ref>

===Overturning the Federal ban on female genital mutilation (FGM)===

On November 20, 2018, he ruled that the federal law against [[female genital mutilation]] (FGM) is unconstitutional because the law overreaches the federal government's enumerated powers as defined by the "necessary and proper" clause and the "Interstate commerce" clause.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.detroitnews.com/story/news/local/detroit-city/2018/11/20/judge-dismisses-key-count-genital-mutilation-case/2066855002/|title=Genital mutilation ban ruled unconstitutional; judge drops charges}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://content-static.detroitnews.com/pdf/2018/US-v-Nagarwala-dismissal-order-11-20-18.pdf|title=OPINION AND ORDER GRANTING DEFENDANTS' MOTION TO DISMISS COUNTS ONE THROUGH SIX OF THE THIRD SUPERSEDING INDICTMENT}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://reason.com/volokh/2018/11/20/federal-female-genital-mutilation-ban-ex|title=Federal Female Genital Mutilation Ban Exceeds Congress's Power, Holds District Court|date=20 November 2018}}</ref>

Howell Signature.svg | signature_alt = | website = | footnotes = }} '''Beryl Alaine Howell''' (born December 3, 1956) is an American attorney and jurist who serves as a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Columbia|U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia]]. She was appointed to the District of Columbia federal court in 2010 by President [[Barack Obama]], and she served as its chief judge from 2016 to 2023. As chief judge, she supervised federal [[grand juries]] in the district, including for the [[Mueller special counsel investigation]] into [[Russian interference in the 2016 United States elections]] and investigations into [[attempts to overturn the 2020 United States presidential election]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/opinion/op-ed/la-oe-neuborne-mueller-grand-juries-20181129-story.html|title=Trump may fire Mueller, but he can't fire Mueller's grand jury|last=Neuborne|first=Burt|website=[[Los Angeles Times]]|date=November 29, 2018 |access-date=November 30, 2018}}{{cite news |last1=Savage |first1=Charlie |title=Gavel to Pass to New Chief Judge Overseeing Grand Jury in Trump Inquiry |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/03/13/us/politics/trump-judge-james-boasberg.html |work=The New York TImes |date=March 13, 2023}} ==Early life and education== Howell was born in 1956 in [[Fort Benning]]. She is the daughter of an [[U.S. Army]] officer.{{Cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/public-safety/meet-the-judge-who-just-released-200-secret-government-surveillance-requests/2016/09/23/4ddb1266-7b50-11e6-beac-57a4a412e93a_story.html|title=This judge just released 200 secret government surveillance requests|last=Hsu|first=Spencer|date=September 26, 2016|newspaper=Washington Post}} She attended elementary and secondary school in six states and Germany.{{Cite press release |title=President Obama Names Five to United States District Court |date=July 14, 2010 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://whitehouse.gov/the-press-office/president-obama-names-five-united-states-district-court-0 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170118172241/https://www.whitehouse.gov/the-press-office/president-obama-names-five-united-states-district-court-0 |archive-date=January 18, 2017 |access-date=March 1, 2023 |url-status=bot: unknown }} {{PD-notice}} Howell graduated from [[Bryn Mawr College]] in 1978 with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] in [[philosophy]] with honors. From 1978 to 1980, Howell worked as a legal assistant at the law firm Shanley & Fisher (now part of [[Faegre Drinker]]). She then attended [[Columbia Law School]], graduating in 1983 with a [[Juris Doctor]] as a Harlan Fiske Stone Scholar.{{FJC Bio|nid=1393581}} ==Career== After law school, Howell was a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Dickinson R. Debevoise]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of New Jersey]] from 1983 to 1984. From 1985 to 1987, she was in private practice as an associate at the [[New York City]] law firm of [[Schulte Roth & Zabel]]. From 1987 to 1993, Howell was an [[assistant United States attorney]] for the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York]], where she became deputy chief of the Narcotics section.{{cite web|url=https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2011/03/riaa-lobbyist-becomes-federal-judge-rules-on-file-sharing-cases/ |title=RIAA lobbyist becomes federal judge, rules on file-sharing cases |date=March 28, 2011 |last=Anderson | first=Nate |publisher=[[Ars Technica]] |access-date=March 4, 2013}} From 1993 to 2003, Howell served on the staff of the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]] as a senior advisor to Chairman [[Patrick Leahy]], including as the committee's [[general counsel]] starting in 1997. While working for Senator Leahy, Howell helped craft the [[Freedom of Information Act (United States)#The Electronic Freedom of Information Act Amendments of 1996|E-FOIA amendments]], which expanded electronic access to government records.{{cite web |url=http://www.brynmawr.edu/sandt/2003_october/practicing.html |title=Practicing at the Intersection of Law, Policy and Technology |work=Science and Technology newsletter |publisher=[[Bryn Mawr College]] |date=October 2003 |access-date=March 4, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130105080931/http://www.brynmawr.edu/sandt/2003_october/practicing.html |archive-date=January 5, 2013 |url-status=dead }} She also helped Sen. Leahy fend off proposals to impose new limits on the FOIA. In 2001, she was honored by the Coalition to Support and Expand the Freedom of Information Act, and in 2004, her FOIA work was honored by the [[Society of Professional Journalists]]. Howell was involved in crafting numerous pieces of legislation for the investigation and prosecution of [[computer crime]] and [[copyright infringement]], including the [[Anti-Cybersquatting Consumer Protection Act]], the [[National Information Infrastructure Protection Act]], the [[Computer Fraud and Abuse Act]], the [[Communications Assistance for Law Enforcement Act]] (CALEA),{{cite web| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071012022052/http://www.strozllc.com/professionals/xprProfessionalDetails1.aspx?xpST=ProfessionalDetail&professional=6 | title=Stroz Friedberg LLC – Professionals – Howell, Beryl A. |publisher= Stroz Friedberg, LLC |archive-date=October 12, 2007 |url=http://www.strozllc.com/professionals/xprProfessionalDetails1.aspx?xpST=ProfessionalDetail&professional=6 |access-date=March 6, 2013 }} the [[No Electronic Theft Act]] (NET Act), the [[Digital Millennium Copyright Act]] (DMCA), and the [[Digital Theft Deterrence and Copyright Damages Improvement Act of 1999]]. Howell was involved in national security issues, including the creation of the [[USA PATRIOT Act]], which she defended in 2005 in an article for the ''[[Pennsylvania Bar Association]] Quarterly''. The [[Center for Democracy and Technology]] lists Howell as a "board alum".{{cite web|url=https://www.cdt.org/staff | title=Staff | publisher=[[Center for Democracy and Technology]] |access-date=March 4, 2013}} From 2004 to 2010, she served as a member of the United States Sentencing Commission after being appointed by President [[George W. Bush]]. === Champion Award === In November 2023 at a meeting of the Women's White Collar Defense Association, Howell received the Champion Award for people who advance opportunities for women in "the white collar field".{{Cite web |title=Awards Program - Women's White Collar Defense Association |url=https://www.wwcda.org/event/awards-program |access-date=2023-12-16 |website=www.wwcda.org}} In her acceptance speech, she said: "My D.C. judicial colleagues and I regularly see the impact of big lies at the [[Criminal proceedings in the January 6 United States Capitol attack|sentencing of hundreds, hundreds of individuals who have been convicted for offense conduct on Jan. 6, 2021]], when they disrupted the certification of the 2020 presidential election at the U.S. Capitol." She also cited historian [[Heather Cox Richardson]]’s book, ''Democracy Awakening''.{{Citation |title=2023 WWCDA Awards Gala Full Video | date=November 30, 2023 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sNDnJWh1gzE |access-date=2023-12-16 |publisher=YouTube |language=en}} The next month, Representative [[Elise Stefanik]], a Republican from New York, filed a complaint of judicial misconduct in which she alleged that Howell's remarks were "conduct unbecoming of a federal judge".{{Cite web |last=Rajkumar |first=Shruti |date=2023-12-16 |title=Rep. Elise Stefanik Lodges Complaint Against Judge Who Oversaw Jan. 6, Trump Cases |url=https://www.huffpost.com/entry/elise-stefanik-complaint-against-judge-beryl-howell_n_657ccab5e4b036ecab4508f0 |access-date=2023-12-16 |website=HuffPost |language=en}} ===Lobbying=== From 2004 to 2009,{{cite web|url=http://www.opensecrets.org/revolving/rev_summary.php?id=31911|title=Revolving Door: Beryl A Howell Employment Summary – OpenSecrets|website=www.opensecrets.org}}[https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2012/11/us-copyright-surveillance-machine-about-be-switched-on U.S. Copyright Surveillance Machine About To Be Switched On, Promises of Transparency Already Broken], [[Electronic Frontier Foundation]], November 15, 2012. 17, 2014 |url-status=dead }} ===Federal judicial service=== [[File:Naturalization-30 (29613128232).jpg|thumb|Howell presiding over a [[naturalization ceremony]], 2016]] On July 14, 2010, Howell was nominated by President [[Barack Obama]] to the United States district judge of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia seat being vacated by Judge [[Paul L. Friedman]], who assumed [[senior status]] on December 31, 2009.{{Cite press release |title=Presidential Nominations and Withdrawal Sent to the Senate, 7/14/10 |date=July 14, 2010 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://www.whitehouse.gov/the-press-office/presidential-nominations-and-withdrawal-sent-senate-71410 |access-date=July 14, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100716103629/http://www.whitehouse.gov/the-press-office/presidential-nominations-and-withdrawal-sent-senate-71410 |archive-date=July 16, 2010 |url-status=bot: unknown }} She was confirmed by the U.S. Senate on December 22, 2010. She received her judicial commission on December 27, 2010. She served as the chief judge from March 17, 2016, to March 17, 2023. She assumed senior status on February 1, 2024. A 2015 analysis by Ravel Law found Howell to be the second most-cited district court judge appointed in the previous five years.{{Cite news|url=https://abovethelaw.com/2015/04/judging-the-judges-who-are-the-most-cited-new-jurists-on-the-federal-bench/?rf=1|title=Judging The Judges: Who Are the Most-Cited New Jurists On The Federal Bench?|last=Kassam|first=Kerry|date=April 23, 2015|work=Above the Law}} === Notable decisions === ==== Hodge v Talkin ==== In 2011, Harold Hodge Jr. stood outside the U.S. Supreme Court wearing a sign that protested the American government's treatment of black and Hispanic people.{{cite web|url=http://thecaucus.blogs.nytimes.com/2013/06/13/supreme-court-issues-new-rule-barring-protests-on-plaza/?_php=true&_type=blogs&_r=0 |title=Supreme Court Issues New Rule Barring Protests on Plaza |work=New York Times |date=June 13, 2013 |access-date=September 25, 2014}} He did so in violation of a 1949 federal law that makes such protests a crime. Hodge sued the [[Marshal of the United States Supreme Court]] and the [[U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia]] under the [[First Amendment to the United States Constitution|First Amendment]]. In a June 2013 decision, Howell struck down the law as violating the First Amendment's guarantee of free speech.{{cite web |url=http://watchdog.org/172646/supreme-court-speech/ |title=Protester challenges Supreme Court speech-free zone |publisher=Watchdog.org |access-date=September 25, 2014 |archive-date=September 16, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150916033856/http://watchdog.org/172646/supreme-court-speech/ |url-status=dead }} The judge wrote, "The absolute prohibition on expressive activity in the statute is unreasonable, substantially overbroad and irreconcilable with the First Amendment." The defendants appealed the decision to the [[U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia]], which reversed Howell's decision and reinstated the law as it applies to the Supreme Court Plaza and steps. ''Hodge v. Talkin'', 799 F. 3d 1145 (D.C. Cir. 2015). ==== FEC and anonymous dark money ==== In 2018, Howell struck down a regulation of the [[Federal Election Commission]] allowing [[dark money]] groups, certain nonprofit organizations engaged in political activities, to conceal their donors. She wrote that the regulation "blatantly undercuts the congressional goal of fully disclosing the sources of money flowing into federal political campaigns, and thereby suppresses the benefits intended to accrue from disclosure."{{cite news |last1=Griffiths |first1=Brent D. |title=Judge's ruling invalidates FEC regulation allowing anonymous donations to 'dark money' groups |url=https://www.politico.com/story/2018/08/04/campaigns-dark-money-groups-donors-anonymous-ruling-762440 |access-date=May 22, 2021 |work=Politico |date=August 4, 2018}} The Supreme Court later declined to review the decision.{{cite news |last1=Lee |first1=Michelle Ye Hee |last2=Barnes |first2=Robert |title=Political nonprofits must now name many of their donors under federal court ruling after Supreme Court declines to intervene |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/political-nonprofits-must-now-name-many-of-their-donors-under-federal-court-ruling-after-supreme-court-declines-to-intervene/2018/09/18/851ea210-bb72-11e8-9812-a389be6690af_story.html |access-date=May 22, 2021 |newspaper=Washington Post |date=September 18, 2018}} ==== Robert Mueller grand jury ==== {{Main|Mueller special counsel investigation}} In that same year, Howell became the supervising judge for the grand jury working for special counsel [[Robert Mueller]]'s investigation into [[Russian interference in the 2016 United States elections]]. On October 25, 2019, she ruled in favor of the [[United States House Committee on the Judiciary|House Judiciary Committee]], which had sought grand jury materials from the [[Mueller special counsel investigation|Mueller investigation]], finding their [[Impeachment inquiry into Donald Trump|impeachment inquiry]] into President [[Donald Trump]] to be a judicial proceeding.{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/10/25/us/politics/house-impeachment-subpoenas.html|title=Impeachment Inquiry Is Legal, Judge Rules, Giving Democrats a Victory|first1=Charlie|last1=Savage|first2=Emily|last2=Cochrane|newspaper=The New York Times |date=October 25, 2019}} Justice Department attorneys had previously asserted that congressional investigators had "not yet exhausted [their] available [[Discovery (law)|discovery]] tools,” arguments Howell said "smack of farce," as the administration had openly stated it would [[Stonewalling|stonewall]] the investigation.{{Cite web|url=https://lawandcrime.com/high-profile/federal-judge-calls-trump-admins-legal-arguments-a-farce-in-order-filled-with-jabs-at-doj-attorneys/|title=Federal Judge Calls Trump Admin's Legal Arguments a 'Farce' in Order Filled with Jabs at DOJ Attorneys|website=lawandcrime.com|date=October 25, 2019 }} ==== Executive Order 14230 against Perkins Coie ==== {{See also|Perkins Coie#Targeting by Donald Trump}} On March 6, 2025, citing the firm's association with [[Fusion GPS]] and [[George Soros]], President Trump issued Executive Order [[wikisource:Executive Order 14230|14230]] titled "Addressing Risks from Perkins Coie LLP." The order suspended security clearances for the firm's employees, restricted their access to federal buildings, directed agencies to review and potentially terminate contracts with the firm, and ordered the government not to hire attorneys from the firm.{{Cite web |date=March 6, 2025|title=Addressing Risks from Perkins Coie LLP|url=https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/03/addressing-risks-from-perkins-coie-llp/|website=The White House}} In May 2025, Judge Howell issued a permanent injunction blocking the executive order in its entirety; citing "No American president has ever before issued executive orders like the one... this action draws from a playbook as old as Shakespeare who penned the phrase ''"[[Let's kill all the lawyers|The first thing we do, let's kill all the lawyers]]"''... The importance of independent lawyers to ensuring the American judicial systems fair and impartial administration of justice has been recognized in this country since its founding era in 1770... The instant case presents an unprecedented attack on these founding principles."{{cite web |date=May 2, 2025|title=Judge permanently blocks Trump's executive order targeting Democratic-tied law firm Perkins Coie | CNN Politics|url=https://www.cnn.com/2025/05/02/politics/perkins-coie-trump-executive-order|website=[[CNN]]}}{{cite web |title=The ruling against Trump's law firm order shows how to respond in this moment|url=https://www.lawdork.com/p/judge-howell-trump-perkins-coie-final-order}}{{Cite web |title=Trump order punishing law firm Perkins Coie ruled unconstitutional - The Washington Post|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2025/05/02/trump-perkins-coie-law-firms-lawsuit/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250503214736/https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2025/05/02/trump-perkins-coie-law-firms-lawsuit/|archive-date=2025-05-03|access-date=2026-02-14}}{{cite web |date=May 5, 2025|title=A judge used Trump's own words to expose his real agenda|url=https://www.msnbc.com/opinion/msnbc-opinion/judge-used-trumps-words-expose-real-agenda-rcna204827|website=[[MSNBC]]}}{{cite web |title=Judge strikes down Trump's executive order targeting law firm Perkins Coie|url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2025/5/3/judge-strikes-down-trumps-executive-order-targeting-law-firm-perkins-coie}}{{cite web |last1=Parloff|first1=Roger|date=April 25, 2025|title=A Reporter's Notes of the April 23 Perkins Coie Hearing|url=https://www.lawfaremedia.org/article/a-reporter-s-notes-of-the-april-23-perkins-coie-hearing|work=Lawfare}} ==== Warrentless arrests of suspected undocumented immigrants ==== In December 2025, Howell limited warrantless immigration arrests in Washington D.C., ruling that Federal immigration officers cannot make an arrest without a warrant unless they can show probable cause that the person is a flight risk.{{Cite web |date=2025-12-02|title=Judge limits warrantless immigration arrests in DC|url=https://www.politico.com/news/2025/12/02/immigration-arrests-order-dc-00674125?cid=apn|access-date=2025-12-22|website=Politico}} ==Personal life== Howell is married to Michael Rosenfeld, an executive producer at [[National Geographic Society|National Geographic Television & Film]]. [[University of Florida]] ([[Bachelor of Science|BS]])
[[University of Miami School of Law|University of Miami]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | occupation = | profession = | known_for = | salary = | net_worth = | cabinet = | committees = | portfolio = | awards = | signature = | signature_alt = | website = | footnotes = }} '''Beth Francine Bloom''' (born 1962){{Cite web |url=http://www.lawdiary.com/docs/subscribers/FL_Judicial_Biographies.pdf |title=BIOGRAPHIES OF STATE AND COUNTY COURT JUDGES IN FLORIDA |date=June 1, 2016 |access-date=May 21, 2021 |archive-date=July 30, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170730052812/http://www.lawdiary.com/docs/subscribers/FL_Judicial_Biographies.pdf |url-status=dead }} is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida]] and former [[Florida]] [[Florida Circuit Courts|circuit court judge]]. ==Biography== Bloom received an [[Associate of Arts]] degree in 1982 from [[Broward Community College]]. She received a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree in 1984 from the [[University of Florida]]. She received a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1988 from the [[University of Miami School of Law]]. From 1988 to 1995, she served at the law firm of Floyd, Pearson, Richman, Greer, Weil, Brumbaugh & Russomanno, P.A., where she handled a broad range of [[civil litigation]]. From 1992 to 1993, she served as a traffic magistrate judge concurrently with her private practice. From 1995 to 2010, she was a county judge in [[Miami-Dade County, Florida|Miami-Dade County]] within the Eleventh Judicial Circuit and served as an associate administrative judge of the Criminal Division in 2010. From 2010 to 2014, she served as an appellate judge in the [[Eleventh Judicial Circuit Court of Florida|Eleventh Judicial Circuit]].{{cite press release|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/02/05/president-obama-announces-intent-nominate-four-serve-united-states-distr|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Obama Announces Intent to Nominate Four to Serve on the United States District Courts|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=5 February 2014}}{{FJC Bio|nid=1394591|inline=yes}} ===Federal judicial service=== [[File:Beth Bloom.jpg|thumb|alt=Bloom at her confirmation hearing]] On February 6, 2014, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Bloom to serve as a United States district judge of the United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida, to the seat vacated by Judge [[Donald L. Graham]], who assumed [[senior status]] on December 15, 2013.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/02/06/presidential-nominations-sent-senate|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=6 February 2014}} She received a hearing before the [[United States Senate Judiciary Committee]] on April 1, 2014.{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/judicial-nominations-2014-04-01|title=Nominations|publisher=Committee on the Judiciary|work=United States Senate|date=1 April 2014}} On May 8, 2014, her nomination was reported out of committee by [[voice vote]].{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%20-%2005-08-14.pdf|title=Executive Business Meeting|publisher=Committee on the Judiciary|work=United States Senate|date=8 May 2014}} On June 19, 2014, [[Senate Majority Leader]] [[Harry Reid]] filed a motion to invoke [[cloture]] on the nomination. On June 23, 2014, the [[United States Senate]] invoked [[cloture]] on her nomination by a 53–31 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=113&session=2&vote=00204| title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture on the Nomination of Beth Bloom, of Florida, to be U.S. District Judge)|publisher=United States Senate|date=23 June 2014}} On June 24, 2014, she was confirmed by a 95–0 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=113&session=2&vote=00208| title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Beth Bloom, of Florida, to be U.S. District Judge)|publisher=United States Senate|access-date=24 June 2014}} She received her judicial commission on June 25, 2014. ==See also== * [[List of Jewish American jurists]] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1394591}} *{{Ballotpedia|Beth_Bloom}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Donald L. {{Short description|American judge (born 1953)}} {{Infobox officeholder | honorific_prefix = | name = Beth Labson Freeman | honorific_suffix = | image = Judge Beth Freeman2.jpg | alt = | caption = | office = Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of California]] | term_start = February 26, 2014 | term_end = | appointer = [[List of federal judges appointed by Barack Obama|Barack Obama]] | predecessor = ''Seat established by 104 Stat. 5089'' | successor = | pronunciation = | birth_name = Beth Ann Labson | birth_date = {{Birth date and age|1953|11|21}} | birth_place = [[Washington, D.C.]], U.S. | death_date = | death_place = | death_cause = | resting_place = | resting_place_coordinates = | citizenship = | party = | other_party = | height = | spouse = | partner = | relations = | children = | parents = | mother = | father = | relatives = | education = [[University of California, Berkeley]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|BA]])
[[Harvard Law School|Harvard University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | occupation = | profession = | known_for = | salary = | net_worth = | cabinet = | committees = | portfolio = | awards = | signature = | signature_alt = | website = | footnotes = }} '''Beth Ann Labson Freeman''' (born November 21, 1953) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of California]]. ==Early life and education== Freeman was born Beth Ann Labson in 1953, in [[Washington, D.C.]]{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/113thCongressJudicialNominations/upload/Freeman-Senate-Questionnaire-Public-Final.pdf|title=Senate Judiciary Committee Nomination Questionnaire|publisher=|access-date=2013-07-11|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131107021444/http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/113thCongressJudicialNominations/upload/Freeman-Senate-Questionnaire-Public-Final.pdf|archive-date=2013-11-07|url-status=dead}} She received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in 1976 from the [[University of California at Berkeley]]. She received a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1979 from [[Harvard Law School]]. == Career == From 1979 to 1981, she worked at [[Fried, Frank, Harris, Shriver & Jacobson]] and from 1981 to 1983, she worked at Lasky, Haas, Cohler and Munter. From 1983 to 2001, she served as deputy county counsel at the [[San Mateo County]] Counsel's Office. From 1987 to the present, she has been affiliated with Peninsula Temple Beth El, a [[Reform Judaism]] [[synagogue]] where, prior to 2012, she served the community in various official capacities. From 2001 to 2014, she served as a judge on the [[California Superior Courts|San Mateo County Superior Court]], serving as assistant presiding judge from 2009 to 2010 and [[Presiding Judge]] from 2011 to 2012. As a [[county judge]], she presided over a broad array of civil and criminal matters.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2013/06/20/president-obama-announces-intent-nominate-three-serve-united-states-dist|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Obama Announces Intent to Nominate Three to Serve on the United States District Court|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=20 June 2013}}{{FJC Bio|nid=1394361|inline=yes}} ===Federal judicial service=== [[File:Freeman Swearing In.jpg|thumb|New District Judge Beth Labson Freeman receives the oath of office from Northern District Chief Judge [[Claudia Ann Wilken]] ''(April 24, 2014)'']] On June 20, 2013, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Freeman to serve as a United States District Judge of the United States District Court for the Northern District of California, to a new seat created on October 3, 2011, pursuant to 28 U.S.C. 133(b)(1), following the appointment of [[Jeremy Fogel]] as Director of the [[Federal Judicial Center]]. On October 31, 2013, the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] reported Freeman's nomination to the full Senate. After the first session of the 113th Congress ended, Freeman's nomination was returned to President Obama, who renominated Freeman in January 2014. The Senate Judiciary Committee reported Freeman's nomination to the full Senate on January 16, 2014.{{Cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/Materials113thCongress.cfm|title=Judicial Nomination Materials: 113th Congress|access-date=2014-02-13|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131217035140/http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/Materials113thCongress.cfm|archive-date=2013-12-17|url-status=dead}} On February 12, 2014, Senate Majority Leader [[Harry Reid]] filed for [[cloture]] on Freeman's nomination. On February 25, 2014, the [[United States Senate]] invoked cloture on Freeman's nomination by a 56–42 vote, with one senator voting present.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1132/vote_113_2_00042.htm|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture on the Nomination of Beth Labson Freeman, of California, to be U.S. District Judge)|website=www.senate.gov}} Freeman's nomination was confirmed later that day by a 91–7 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=113&session=2&vote=00043|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Beth Labson Freeman, of California, to be U.S. District Judge for the Northern District)|website=www.senate.gov}} Freeman received her judicial commission on February 26, 2014. ===Notable cases=== On December 22, 2020, Judge Freeman handed down a [[nationwide injunction]] blocking enforcement of President Donald Trump's [[executive order]] barring federal contractors from training employees on various concepts rooted in [[critical race theory]], finding the measure cuts into the constitutional freedoms of LGBTQ [[advocacy groups]] who filed a legal challenge.{{Cite web|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/money/2020/12/23/trump-diversity-training-ban-executive-order-blocked-federal-judge/4033590001/|title=Donald Trump executive order banning diversity training blocked by federal judge|website=[[USA Today]]}} In her ruling, Judge Freeman wrote that the administration's directive to [[List of federal agencies in the United States|federal agencies]] to cancel training contracts involving “critical race theory,” “white privilege,” “intersectionality,” “systemic racism,” “positionality,” “racial humility,” and “unconscious bias” was likely unconstitutional.[https://www.lambdalegal.org/sites/default/files/legal-docs/downloads/diversity_ca_20201222_order-granting-part-nationwide-preliminary-injunction.pdf Court document] lambdalegal.org On September 30, 2022, Judge Freeman issued a partial dismissal on two lawsuits (consolidated into one) against San Jose's gun control ordinance (which was enacted in response to the [[2021 San Jose shooting]]) with leave to amend in part and without leave to amend in part.{{Cite web |date=September 30, 2022 |title=First Dismissal of San Jose Gun Control Ordinance Lawsuit leave to amend in part and without leave to amend in part.{{Cite web |date=July 13, 2023 |title=Second Dismissal of San Jose Gun Control Ordinance Lawsuit |url=https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.cand.391018/gov.uscourts.cand.391018.107.0.pdf |access-date=July 14, 2023}}{{Cite news |last=Greschler |first=Gabriel |date=July 14, 2023 |url=https://www.mercurynews.com/2023/07/14/legal-challenge-against-san-joses-gun-insurance-law-dealt-serious-blow/ |access-date=July 14, 2023}} On September 18, 2023, she ruled that social media and technology corporations ability to collect data of users, including children, is protected speech, thus rendering a California privacy law unenforceable for unconstitutionality.{{Cite [[Rutgers University–Newark|Rutgers University, Newark]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''William John Martini''' (born February 10, 1947) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of New Jersey]], having been in active service from November 14, 2002, to February 10, 2015. Martini is one of 24 judges seated on the New Jersey District Court, and his highest profile case to date was the corruption trial for former [[Newark, New Jersey|Newark]] Mayor [[Sharpe James]]. Before his judicial service, Martini was a [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]] [[politician]] who represented [[New Jersey's 8th congressional district]] in the [[United States House of Representatives|House of Representatives]], where he served from January 3, 1995 to January 3, 1997. ==Early life and career== Martini was born in [[Passaic, New Jersey]]. He graduated from [[Passaic High School]]. He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[Villanova University]] in [[Philadelphia]], and received his [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Rutgers School of Law—Newark]] in 1972. Martini clerked for the Hon. Joseph P. Hanrahan, on the Superior Court of New Jersey, from 1972 to 1973. Martini then worked as an assistant in the [[Hudson County, New Jersey|Hudson County]] prosecutor's office in 1973. The following year, he was named an [[assistant United States attorney]] in the [[U.S. Attorney for the District of New Jersey|U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of New Jersey]], and served in that post until 1977. He went into private practice after that. Martini would eventually land in [[Passaic County, New Jersey|Passaic County]] again, and won election to the city council in [[Clifton, New Jersey]] in 1990. He would add a position on the Passaic County [[Board of County Commissioners (New Jersey)|Board of Chosen Freeholders]] in 1992.{{cite news |last=Barry |first=Jan |title=Passaic County GOP tightens grip |work=[[The Record (North Jersey)|The Record]] |date=November 4, 1992 |access-date=August 9, 2008 |url=http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1P1-22651877.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121021064056/http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1P1-22651877.html |archive-date=October 21, 2012 |via=[[HighBeam Research]] |url-access=subscription |location=Bergen County, NJ |url-status=usurped}} In 1994, the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]] nominated Martini for Congress in [[New Jersey's 8th congressional district]]. He faced off against one-term incumbent [[Herb Klein (politician)|Herbert Klein]], who had fallen out of favor with the voters. That, and the wave of the 1994 [[Republican Revolution]], helped Martini defeat Klein and flip one of the 54 seats in the House of Representatives the Republicans gained that year.{{cite news |last=Voreacos |first=David |title=Martini Edges Klein in Race for 8Th District |work=[[The Record (North Jersey)|The Record]] |date=November 9, 1994 |access-date=August 9, 2008 |url=http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1P1-22560992.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121021064108/http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1P1-22560992.html |archive-date=October 21, 2012 |via=HighBeam Research |url-access=subscription |location=Bergen County, NJ |url-status=usurped}} In addition, he was the first Republican to win an election in the district since [[Gordon Canfield]] won his last re-election bid in 1958. Two years later, Martini was defeated for re-election in 1996 by [[Paterson, New Jersey|Paterson]] mayor [[Bill Pascrell]] in his final run for political office. This made him one of eight Republican Representatives elected in the 1994 Republican Revolution to be defeated in their re-election bids.{{cite news |last=Goodnough |first=Abby |title=Democrats Pick Up Seat as Pascrell Defeats Martini in Expensive Eighth District Race |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=November 6, 1996 |access-date=August 9, 2008 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1996/11/06/nyregion/democrats-pick-up-seat-pascrell-defeats-martini-expensive-eighth-district-race.html}} In 1999, the Governor [[Christine Todd Whitman]] named Martini to the Board of Commissioners of the [[Port Authority of New York and New Jersey]], a post in which he served for three years.[http://www.panynj.biz/pr/3-99.html "WILLIAM J. MARTINI SWORN IN AS COMMISSIONER OF THE PORT AUTHORITY OF NEW YORK AND NEW JERSEY"], [[Port Authority of New York and New Jersey]] press release dated January 13, 1999. Accessed August 9, 2008. === Federal judicial service === On January 23, 2002, Martini was nominated for a judgeship of the United States District Court of New Jersey by President [[George W. Bush]], was confirmed on November 14, 2002 and received his commission on November 19, 2002. He assumed [[senior status]] on February 10, 2015.{{FJC Bio|nid=1391656|inline=yes}} ===Sharpe James case=== Martini sentenced [[Sharpe James]], former mayor of [[Newark, New Jersey|Newark]], to 27 months in prison for corruption. State and federal prosecutors wanted the maximum allowable sentence of 15 to 20 years although federal guidelines would only allow a 5 to 12 year potential sentence. Martini said that James' years as a public servant played a role in his decision, but would not discuss the case further. U.S. Attorney [[Chris Christie]] announced that he would appeal Martini's sentence.Cunningham, Jennifer H. [http://myheraldnews.com/view.html?type=stories&action=detail&sub_id=41095 "Judge defends James sentencing"]{{Dead link|date=November 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}, ''[[Herald News]]'', August 6, 2008. Accessed August 9, 2008. ===''Hassan v. City of New York''=== In February 2014, Martini dismissed a federal lawsuit brought by eight New Jersey Muslims alleging they were unlawfully targeted for surveillance by the New York Police Department because of their religion. The suit accused the NYPD of spying on Muslims in mosques, restaurants and schools. In his decision. Martini wrote "The more likely explanation for the surveillance was to locate budding terrorist conspiracies." Associated Press. [https://www.nytimes.com/2014/02/21/nyregion/judge-finds-surveillance-of-mosques-was-allowed.html "Judge Finds Surveillance of Mosques Was Allowed"], ''[[New York Times]]'', February 21, 2014. Accessed February 21, 2014. Baher Azmy, Legal Director at the [[Center for Constitutional Rights]] (which served as co-counsel in the case) responded to Judge Martini's ruling: "In addition to willfully ignoring the harm that our innocent clients suffered from the NYPD's illegal spying program, by upholding the NYPD's blunderbuss Muslim surveillance practices, the court's decision gives legal sanction to the targeted discrimination of Muslims anywhere and everywhere in this country, without limitation, for no other reason than their religion." Center for Constitutional Rights. [http://ccrjustice.org/newsroom/press-releases/court-gives-nypd-green-light-conduct-religious-surveillance/ "Court Gives NYPD Green Light to Conduct Religious Surveillance"], February 20, 2014. Accessed February 21, 2014. The plaintiffs appealed the dismissal of their case, and numerous organizations filed ''amicus curiae'' briefs.Center for Constitutional Rights (including litigation timeline and briefs) [http://www.ccrjustice.org/hassan] Accessed January 13, 2015. The [[United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit|Court of Appeals]] reversed Martini's decision and remanded the case in October 2015. It was eventually settled in April 2018.[https://ccrjustice.org/home/press-center/press-releases/settlement-reached-nypd-muslim-surveillance-lawsuit "Settlement Reached in NYPD Muslim Surveillance Lawsuit"], ''[[Center for Constitutional Rights]]'', April 9, 2018. From 2010 to 2014, he served as an assistant U.S. attorney in the U.S. Attorney's Office for the [[United States District Court for the District of Columbia|District of Columbia]]. From 2014 to 2023, Long served as an assistant U.S. attorney in the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Louisiana in [[New Orleans]]. From February 2020 to July 2021, Long was detailed to serve as the deputy chief of staff to [[Federal Bureau of Investigation|FBI]] Director [[Christopher A. Wray]] in [[Washington, D.C.]]{{cite web |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2023/06/07/biden-judicial-picks-edwards-scott-long-00100661| title=Biden rolls out 2 new red-state judicial picks| date=June 7, 2023| first=Betsy|last=Woodruff| publisher=Politico, US}}{{cite web |url=https://thehill.com/homenews/administration/4038161-biden-names-two-louisiana-judicial-nominee-picks/| title=Biden names two Louisiana judicial nominee picks| date=June 7, 2023| first=Alex|last=Gangitano | publisher=The Hill, US}} === Notable cases === * In 2016, Long prosecuted retired [[New Orleans Saints]] player [[Darren Sharper]] who was accused of drugging and raping women.
