[[University of Chicago Law School|University of Chicago]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Carl John Nichols''' (born 1970) is an American lawyer and jurist who has served as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Columbia]] since 2019. He has concurrently served as a judge of the [[United States Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court]] since 2024 and is the Presiding Judge of that court. == Early life == Nichols was born in 1970 in [[Rhinebeck, New York]].[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Nichols%20SJQ.pdf United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees: Carl J. Nichols] He spent most of his childhood in [[Simsbury, Connecticut]]. He left for college and received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] in 1992 from [[Dartmouth College]], where he majored in [[philosophy]] and graduated with high honors. He spent some time at the [[University of Edinburgh]] in Scotland as an exchange student from Dartmouth. After graduating, he spent one year as a [[paralegal]] at a law firm before attending the [[University of Chicago Law School]], where he was a member of the ''[[University of Chicago Law Review]]''. He graduated in 1996 with a [[Juris Doctor]], graduating [[Order of the Coif]]. == Career == While in law school, Nichols was a summer associate at [[Gibson Dunn|Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher]] in 1995.{{cite web |title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees: Carl John Nichols |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/download/nichols-sjq |publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary |format=PDF |access-date=June 26, 2026}} After law school, Nichols was a [[law clerk]] to Judge [[Laurence Silberman]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit]] from 1996 to 1997. He then clerked for Justice [[Clarence Thomas]] of the [[Supreme Court of the United States|U.S. Supreme Court]] from 1997 to 1998.{{cite web|url=https://www.buzzfeed.com/zoetillman/trump-is-expected-to-nominate-a-former-justice-department|title=Trump Is Expected To Nominate A Seasoned Former Justice Official For A Judgeship After His First Pick Bombed|first=Zoe|last=Tillman|date=March 12, 2018|website=[[BuzzFeed]]|access-date=March 13, 2018}} From 1998 to 2005, Nichols was in private practice at the law firm [[Boies Schiller Flexner LLP]], becoming a partner in 2002. He later joined the [[United States Department of Justice]] as a deputy assistant attorney general for the Federal Programs Branch of the [[United States Department of Justice Civil Division|Civil Division]], and then as principal deputy [[Associate Attorney General|associate attorney general]]. He left the government in 2009 and joined [[Wilmer Cutler Pickering Hale and Dorr]], where he worked as a partner until 2019.{{cite web|url=https://www.wilmerhale.com/carl_nichols/|title=Carl J. Nichols – WilmerHale|author=|date=|website=[[WilmerHale]]|access-date=March 13, 2018|archive-date=April 8, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170408180242/https://www.wilmerhale.com/carl_nichols/|url-status=dead}} === Federal judicial service === Nichols was mentioned as a potential judicial nominee in March 2018. On June 7, 2018, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to nominate Nichols to serve as a United States district judge of the [[United States District Court for the District of Columbia]].{{cite web |url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-fifteenth-wave-judicial-nominees-fourteenth-wave-united-states-attorney-nominees-ninth-wave-united-states-marshal-nominees/ |title=President Donald J. Trump Announces Fifteenth Wave of Judicial Nominees, Fourteenth Wave of United States Attorney Nominees, and Ninth Wave of United States Marshal Nominees|last=|first=|date=June 7, 2018|access-date=June 7, 2018|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|quote=}}{{PD-notice}} On June 18, 2018, his nomination was sent to the Senate. President Trump nominated Nichols to the seat vacated by [[Richard W. Roberts]], who assumed [[senior status]] on March 16, 2016.{{Cite web|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/seventeen-nominations-one-withdrawal-sent-senate-today/|title=Seventeen Nominations and One Withdrawal Sent to the Senate Today – The White House|website=trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov}} On August 22, 2018, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/committee-activity/hearings/08/22/2018/nominations|title=Nominations | United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|website=www.judiciary.senate.gov}} On October 11, 2018, his nomination was reported out of committee by an 11–10 vote.[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/10-11-18%20Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting1.pdf Results of Executive Business Meeting – October 11, 2018, Senate Judiciary Committee] On January 3, 2019, his nomination was returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]]. On January 23, 2019, President Trump announced his intent to renominate Nichols for the same federal judgeship.{{Cite web|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-intent-nominate-judicial-nominees/|title=President Donald J. Trump Announces Intent to Nominate Judicial Nominees – The White House|website=trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov}} His nomination was sent to the Senate later that day.{{Cite web|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/nominations-sent-senate-2/|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate – The White House|website=trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov}} On February 7, 2019, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 12–10 vote.[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/02.07.2019%20Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting1.pdf Results of Executive Business Meeting – February 7, 2019, Senate Judiciary Committee] On May 21, 2019, the Senate invoked cloture on his nomination by a 55–42 vote.[https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1161/vote_116_1_00121.htm On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Carl J. Nichols to be U.S. District Judge for the District of Columbia)], United States Senate, May 21, 2019 On May 22, 2019, his nomination was confirmed by a 55–43 vote.[https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=1&vote=00125 On the Nomination (Confirmation Carl J. Nichols, of the District of Columbia, to be U.S. District Judge for the District of Columbia)], United States Senate, May 22, 2019 He received his judicial commission on June 25, 2019.{{FJC Bio|nid=6489111|inline=yes}} ==Notable cases== ===''American Foreign Service Association v. Trump'' === On February 7, 2025, in [[Department of Government Efficiency#United States Agency for International Development (USAID)|a case involving the shutdown of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID)]], Nichols issued a [[temporary restraining order]] that blocked the government from putting 2,200 [[USAID]] employees on administrative leave as was planned to happen by midnight that evening, reinstating 500 USAID employees who had already been placed on administrative leave, and pausing an order that recalled USAID employees posted overseas to the United States.{{cite news |last1=Tanis |first1=Fatma |last2=Bond |first2=Shannon |title=Judge pauses Trump order to put USAID employees on administrative leave |url=https://www.npr.org/sections/goats-and-soda/2025/02/07/g-s1-47224/usaid-freeze-judge-trump |access-date=8 February 2025 |work=NPR |date=8 February 2025 |language=en}}''AFSA v. Trump'', no. 25-352 (February 7, 2025 D.D.C.), [https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.dcd.277213/gov.uscourts.dcd.277213.15.0_2.pdf order of February 7, 2025]. On February 21, Nichols declined to extend the injunction. Nichols ruled that "the record now reflects that no USAID employee stationed abroad has been or imminently will be required to return to the United States within thirty days." Nichols ruled, in effect, that discontinuing housing, visa sponsorship, and security was not tantamount to "requiring" employees stationed abroad to return.{{Cite news |date=2025-02-21 |title=Judge Ends Block on Trump Plan to Put USAID Workers on Leave (3) |url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/daily-labor-report/judge-lifts-block-on-trump-plan-to-put-usaid-employees-on-leave |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250425104224/https://news.bloomberglaw.com/daily-labor-report/judge-lifts-block-on-trump-plan-to-put-usaid-employees-on-leave |archive-date=2025-04-25 |access-date=2026-06-23 |language=en}} === Trial of Steve Bannon === Nichols was the judge for the 2022 trial in which [[Steve Bannon#2022 contempt of Congress conviction|a jury convicted Steve Bannon of contempt of Congress]].{{Cite web |date=2021-11-12 |title=Stephen K. Bannon Indicted for Contempt of Congress |url=https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/stephen-k-bannon-indicted-contempt-congress |access-date=2022-07-18 |website=www.justice.gov |language=en}}{{Cite web |last=Reilly |first=Ryan J. |date=2022-07-18 |title=Steve Bannon's contempt of Congress trial begins despite his attempts to delay it |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2022/07/18/steve-bannons-contempt-of-congress-trial-begins-despite-his-attempts-to-delay-it.html |access-date=2022-07-18 |website=CNBC |language=en}}''U.S. v. Bannon'', no. 21-670 (D.D.C.), [https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.dcd.237438/gov.uscourts.dcd.237438.137.0_15.pdf order of July 27, 2022]. === ''United States v. Miller'' === In March 2022, Nichols ruled that Garret Miller, one of the defendants [[Criminal charges in the 2021 United States Capitol attack|criminally charged in connection with the 2021 U. S. Capitol attack]], could not be charged with obstructing Congress's certification of the 2020 presidential election without a showing that Miller had tampered with official documents or records as part of the attack.{{cite news |last1=Hsu |first1=Spencer S. |title=U.S. judge dismisses lead charge against Jan. 6 Capitol riot defendant |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/dc-md-va/2022/03/08/judge-tosses-jan-6-obstruction-charge/ |access-date=March 8, 2022 |newspaper=Washington Post |date=March 8, 2022}}''U.S. v. Miller'', no. 21-119 (March 7, 2022 D.D.C.), [https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.dcd.227582/gov.uscourts.dcd.227582.72.0.pdf order]. Nichols's ruling is contrary to those of all seven other U.S. District Court judges who had considered the same issue, and may affect up to 275 similar criminal prosecutions. The U.S. Supreme Court agreed with Nichols in [[Fischer v. United States (2024)|''Fischer v. United States'']], resulting in hundreds of charges being dropped and sentences changed. ===Dominion defamation lawsuits === On August 11, 2021, Nichols denied motions to dismiss lawsuits brought by [[Dominion Voting Systems]] alleging that [[Sidney Powell]] (1:21-cv-00040 (CJN)), [[Rudy Giuliani]] (1:21-cv-00213 (CJN)), and [[Mike Lindell]] (1:21-cv-00445 (CJN)) defamed and damaged Dominion by their statements alleging fraud and misconduct in the 2020 presidential election. Those lawsuits, therefore, were allowed to proceed.{{cite news |last1=Wolfe |first1=Jan |last2=Thomas |first2=David |title=Trump allies including Giuliani lose bid to dismiss Dominion vote machine lawsuits |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/us/trump-allies-giuliani-powell-lose-bid-dismiss-dominion-lawsuits-2021-08-11/ |access-date=13 August 2021 |work=Reuters |date=12 August 2021 |language=en}}[https://deadline.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/08/dominion-1.pdf Order of United States District Court for the District of Columbia (signed by Nichols) reported by ''Deadline'' (PDF)] === ''TikTok v. Trump'' === {{main|TikTok v. Trump}} On Sunday, September 27, 2020, Judge Nichols, granting in part the motion of plaintiffs [[TikTok]] and [[ByteDance]], issued a preliminary injunction partially enjoining (i.e., temporarily stopping) the [[Department of Commerce]]'s implementation of President [[Donald Trump]]'s August 6, 2020, [[Executive Order|executive order]] prohibiting certain transactions related to TikTok. The portion of the prohibition that Nichols enjoined would have barred [[Apple Inc.|Apple]] and [[Google]] from offering TikTok in their app stores, and would have taken effect just before midnight that night.{{cite news |last1=Shepardson |first1=David |title=U.S. judge blocks Trump administration's ban on new TikTok downloads |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-usa-tiktok-ban/judge-plans-to-decide-on-tiktok-u-s-app-store-ban-by-end-of-day-idUSKBN26I0PT |access-date=28 September 2020 |work=Reuters |date=28 September 2020 |language=en}} On December 7, 2020, Judge Nichols granted a second preliminary injunction requested by TikTok and ByteBance, enjoining the remainder of the Commerce Department's implementation of that executive order.{{cite news |last1=Shu |first1=Catherine |title=Second federal judge rules against Trump administration's TikTok ban |url=https://techcrunch.com/2020/12/07/second-federal-judge-rules-against-trump-administrations-tiktok-ban/ |access-date=9 December 2020 |work=TechCrunch |date=7 December 2020}} The case (then captioned ''TikTok v. Biden'') was dismissed by joint stipulation of the parties on July 21, 2021, following President [[Biden]]'s decision to rescind President Trump's August 6, 2020, executive order.{{cite news |last1=Fung |first1=Brian |title=TikTok, Biden administration agree to drop litigation over Trump-era app store ban |url=https://www.cnn.com/2021/07/22/tech/tiktok-trump-ban-dismissed/index.html |access-date=13 August 2021 |work=CNN |date=22 July 2021}}{{cite web |title=Stipulation of Dismissal – #71 in TIKTOK INC. v. TRUMP (D.D.C., 1:20-cv-02658) |url=https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/18455532/71/tiktok-inc-v-trump/ |website=CourtListener |access-date=13 August 2021 |language=en-us}} ===''Donald J. Trump v. Committee on Ways and Means'' === On August 1, 2019, Nichols issued a temporary order that barred the State of New York from handing over state tax returns to the U.S. House Committee on Ways and Means and established a briefing and hearing schedule.{{cite web|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2019/08/01/judge-temporarily-bars-ny-from-giving-trumps-state-tax-returns-to-congress.html|title= Judge temporarily bars NY from giving Trump's state tax returns to Congress |website= [[CNBC]] |date=August 1, 2019 |access-date=August 1, 2019}} The state, through its attorney general and co-defendant [[Letitia James]], promptly asked Nichols to dismiss the lawsuit or transfer it to a federal court in New York, on the ground that it cannot be maintained against them where the defendants neither reside nor act.{{cite news |last1=Polantz |first1=Katelyn |title=Trump has been clobbered by the courts |url=https://www.ktvz.com/news/politics/trump-has-been-clobbered-by-the-courts/1131792254 |access-date=16 October 2019 |agency=CNN |publisher=KTVZ |date=October 13, 2019 |archive-date=October 16, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191016152109/https://www.ktvz.com/news/politics/trump-has-been-clobbered-by-the-courts/1131792254 |url-status=dead }} On November 11, 2019, Nichols dismissed the lawsuit, finding that the court did not have jurisdiction over the New York Attorney General or the commissioner of the New York Department of Taxation and Finance.{{cite news|url=https://abcnews.com/Politics/judge-dismisses-trump-lawsuit-ny-officials-house-committee/story?id=66918561|title=Judge dismisses Trump lawsuit against NY officials, House committee over taxes|last=Bruggeman|first=Lucien|date=November 11, 2019|work=ABC News|access-date=11 November 2019}} === Trial of Sean Dunn === Nichols presided over the [[trial of Sean Dunn]], who was acquitted of assaulting a federal agent by throwing a [[Subway (restaurant)|Subway]] sandwich at him.{{Cite news |last=McQuade |first=Barbara |date=2025-11-08 |title=U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro wasted our money pursuing sandwich thrower |url=https://www.msnbc.com/opinion/msnbc-opinion/jeanine-pirros-case-dc-sandwich-thrower-was-downright-lawless-rcna242612 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251114230014/https://www.msnbc.com/opinion/msnbc-opinion/jeanine-pirros-case-dc-sandwich-thrower-was-downright-lawless-rcna242612 |archive-date=2025-11-14 |access-date=2025-11-14 |work=[[MSNBC]]}} == Affiliation == Nichols has been a member of the [[Federalist Society]]; once from 2003 to 2008 and again in 2018. == See also == * [[List of law clerks for {{Short description|American judge (born 1970)}} {{Infobox officeholder | honorific_prefix = | name = Carlos E. Mendoza | honorific_suffix = | image = Carlos E. Mendoza-portrait (cropped).jpg | alt = | caption = | office = Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Middle District of Florida]] | term_start = June 27, 2014 | term_end = | nominator = | appointer = [[List of federal judges appointed by Barack Obama|Barack Obama]] | predecessor = [[John Antoon]] | successor = | pronunciation = | birth_name = | birth_date = {{Birth date and age|1970|02|18}} | birth_place = [[Hialeah, Florida|Hialeah]], [[Florida]], U.S. | death_date = | death_place = | death_cause = | resting_place = | resting_place_coordinates = | citizenship = | party = | other_party = | height = | spouse = | partner = | relations = | children = | parents = | mother = | father = | relatives = | education = [[College of Central Florida|Central Florida Community College]] ([[Associate of Arts|AA]])
[[West Virginia University]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|BA]], [[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | occupation = | profession = | known_for = | salary = | net_worth = | cabinet = | committees = | portfolio = | awards = | signature = | signature_alt = | website = | footnotes = | allegiance = {{flag|United States}} | branch = [[File:Seal of the United States Marine Corps.svg|23px]] [[United States Marine Corps Reserve]] (1989–1995)
{{navy|United States}} (1997–2005) | rank = [[File:US-O3 insignia.svg|23px]] [[Lieutenant (navy)|Lieutenant]] | battles = [[Operation Desert Shield]] [[Operation Desert Storm]] | unit = [[File:Seal of the United States Navy Judge Advocate General's Corps.png|23px]] [[United States Navy Judge Advocate General's Corps]] }} '''Carlos Eduardo Mendoza''' (born February 18, 1970) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Middle District of Florida]] and former [[Florida]] [[Florida Circuit Courts|circuit court judge]]. ==Biography== Mendoza enlisted in the [[United States Marine Corps]] after graduation from high school and participated in combat operations during [[Operation Desert Shield]] and [[Operation Desert Storm]]. He received an [[Associate of Arts]] degree in 1991 from [[College of Central Florida|Central Florida Community College]]. He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree, magna cum laude, in 1993 from [[West Virginia University]]. He received a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1997 from the [[West Virginia University College of Law]]. He began his legal career by serving as a [[Judge Advocate]] in the [[Judge Advocate General's Corps]] of the [[United States Navy]] from 1997 to 2005. From 2005 to 2008, he was an Assistant State Attorney in the Seventh Judicial Circuit of Florida. From 2008 to 2011, he served as an Assistant City Attorney for [[St. Augustine, Florida|St. Augustine]], [[Florida]]. From 2011 to 2014, he served as a [[Florida Circuit Courts|Circuit Court Judge]] in the [[Seventh Judicial Circuit Court of Florida|Seventh Judicial Circuit]].[https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/02/05/president-obama-announces-intent-nominate-four-serve-united-states-distr "President Obama Announces Intent to Nominate Four to Serve on the United States District Courts" White House, February 5, 2014]{{FJC Bio|nid=1394586|inline=yes}} ===Federal judicial service=== On February 6, 2014, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Mendoza to serve as a United States District Judge of the United States District Court for the Middle District of Florida, to the seat vacated by Judge [[John Antoon]], who assumed [[senior status]] on June 3, 2013.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/02/06/presidential-nominations-sent-senate|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=6 February 2014}} He received a hearing before the [[United States Senate Judiciary Committee]] on April 1, 2014.{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/judicial-nominations-2014-04-01|title=Nominations|publisher=Committee on the Judiciary|work=United States Senate|date=1 April 2014}} On May 8, 2014, his nomination was reported out of committee by [[voice vote]].{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%20-%2005-08-14.pdf|title=Executive Business Meeting|publisher=Committee on the Judiciary|work=United States Senate|date=8 May 2014}} On June 19, 2014, [[Senate Majority Leader]] [[Harry Reid]] filed a motion to invoke [[cloture]] on the nomination. On June 23, 2014, the [[United States Senate]] invoked [[cloture]] on his nomination by a 53–31 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=113&session=2&vote=00203| title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture on the Nomination of Carlos Mendoza, of Florida, to be U.S. District Judge)|publisher=United States Senate|date=23 June 2014}} On June 24, 2014, his nomination was confirmed by a 94–0 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=113&session=2&vote=00207|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Carlos Eduardo Mendoza, of Florida, to be U.S. District Judge)|publisher=United States Senate|access-date=24 June 2014}} He received his judicial commission on June 27, 2014. ==See also== *[[List of Hispanic and Latino American jurists]] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1394586}} *{{Ballotpedia|Carlos_E._Mendoza}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[John Antoon]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Middle District of Florida]]}}|years=2014–present}} {{s-inc}} {{s-end}} {{United States 11th Circuit district judges}} {{authority control}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Mendoza, Carlos E.}} [[Category:1970 births]] [[Category:Living people]] [[Category:Assistant United States attorneys]] [[Category:Florida lawyers]] [[Category:Florida state court judges]] [[Category:Hispanic and Latino American judges]] [[Category:Judges of the United States District Court for the Middle District of Florida]] [[Category:District attorneys]] [[Category:United States district court judges appointed by Barack Obama]] [[Category:United States Marine Corps officers]] [[Category:United States Marine Corps reservists]] [[Category:United States Navy officers]] [[Category:West Virginia University College of Law alumni]] [[Category:Hispanic and Latino American lawyers]]
Carlton W. Reeves:
{{Use mdy dates|date=April 2023}} {{Short description|American judge (born 1964)}} {{Use American English|date=March 2026}} {{Infobox judge |name = Carlton Reeves |image = Carlton Reeves (cropped).jpg |caption = Reeves in 2022 |office = Chair of the [[United States Sentencing Commission]] |president = [[Joe Biden]]
[[Donald Trump]] |term_start = August 5, 2022 |term_end = |predecessor = [[Charles Breyer]] (acting) |successor = |office1 = Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Mississippi]] |appointer1 = [[List of federal judges appointed by Barack Obama|Barack Obama]] |term_start1 = December 20, 2010 |term_end1 = |predecessor1 = [[William H. Barbour Jr.]] |successor1 = |birth_name = Carlton Wayne Reeves |birth_date = {{birth date and age|1964|4|11}} |birth_place = [[Fort Hood]], [[Texas]], U.S. |death_date = |death_place = |education = [[Jackson State University]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|BA]])
[[University of Virginia]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) |awards = [[Thomas Jefferson Foundation]] Medal (2019){{cite web | url=https://www.monticello.org/press/news-releases/2019-thomas-jefferson-award-recipients/ | title=UVA, Monticello Announce Recipients of 2019 Thomas Jefferson Foundation Medals }} }} '''Carlton Wayne Reeves''' (born April 11, 1964) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Mississippi]] and chair of the [[United States Sentencing Commission]]. Reeves was the district court judge in ''[[Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization]]'' (2022), the case that resulted in the Supreme Court overturning ''[[Roe v. Wade]]'' (1973). ==Early life and education== Reeves was born in 1964 in [[Fort Hood, Texas]],[http://judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/111thCongressJudicialNominations/upload/CarltonReeves-PublicQuestionnaire.pdf Senate Judiciary Committee Questionnaire: Carlton Wayne Reeves] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101105042324/http://judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/111thCongressJudicialNominations/upload/CarltonReeves-PublicQuestionnaire.pdf |date=November 5, 2010 }}, (April 26, 2010). and was raised in rural [[Yazoo City, Mississippi]].{{cite news|title=The Man Behind The Speech: Judge Carlton Reeves Takes On Mississippi's Past|url=https://www.npr.org/sections/codeswitch/2015/03/02/387477815/the-man-behind-the-speech-judge-carlton-reeves-takes-on-mississippis-past|access-date=June 29, 2016|newspaper=[[National Public Radio]]|date=March 2, 2015}} Reeves was one of seven children, with three sisters and three brothers.{{r|atlantic}} Reeves was a student in the first integrated public-school class in Mississippi.{{cite web | last=Holding | first=Reynolds | title=The Judge Who Told the Truth About the Mississippi Abortion Ban | website=The Atlantic | date=November 30, 2021 | url=https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/archive/2021/11/supreme-court-mississippi-abortion-ban/620833/ | access-date=December 2, 2021}} As a teenager, Reeves cleaned the office of Judge [[William H. Barbour Jr.]], whom he would later replace on the federal bench. Reeves was the first person in his family to attend a four-year college, and graduated in 1986 ''[[magna cum laude]]'' from [[Jackson State University]].[https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/president-obama-names-three-united-states-district-court President Obama Names Three to the United States District Court] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170216172457/https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/president-obama-names-three-united-states-district-court |date=February 16, 2017 }}, ''[[whitehouse.gov]]'' (April 28, 2010). Reeves then attended the [[University of Virginia School of Law]], graduating in 1989 as a Ritter Scholar. After law school, Reeves served as a [[law clerk]] for Justice [[Reuben V. Anderson]], the first [[African American]] judge to serve on the [[Supreme Court of Mississippi|Mississippi Supreme Court]].{{FJC Bio|nid=1393566|inline=yes}} ==Career== Reeves began his legal career in 1991 as a staff attorney for the Supreme Court of Mississippi; later that year, he entered private practice as an associate at the [[Jackson, Mississippi]] office of regional law firm Phelps Dunbar. From 1995 to 2001, Reeves served as Chief of the Civil Division for the Office of the [[United States Attorney]] for the Southern District of Mississippi. In 2001, Reeves returned to private practice to found his own firm, Pigott Reeves Johnson, in Jackson. During his time in private practice, Reeves served on the boards of a number of civic organizations, including the [[ACLU]] of Mississippi, the Mississippi Center for Justice, and the [[Magnolia Bar Association]]. ===Federal judicial service=== On April 28, 2010, Reeves was nominated by President [[Barack Obama]] to fill a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Mississippi]] vacated by Judge [[William H. Barbour Jr.]] Reeves was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on December 19, 2010, by [[voice vote]].Associated Press, [http://www.wxvt.com/Global/story.asp?S=13710751 Reeves confirmed as US judge for south Mississippi]{{dead link|date=November 2016 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}, (December 19, 2010). Reeves is the second African American to serve on the federal judiciary in [[Mississippi]]. He received his commission on December 20, 2010. ===Notable decisions=== ====''Campaign for Southern Equality v. Bryant''==== {{Main|Same-sex marriage in Mississippi}} On November 25, 2014, Reeves ruled in the case of ''[[Campaign for Southern Equality v. Bryant]]'' that Mississippi’s same-sex marriage ban violated the [[Due Process Clause|Due Process]] and [[Equal Protection Clause]]s of the [[Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution|Fourteenth Amendment]]. Reeves' opinion noted the connection between racism and homophobia, and how that connection had long operated to oppress both black and LGBT Mississippians.{{cite news | title = Federal Judge Overturns Mississippi's Ban On Same-Sex Marriage | author = Ack Ford | publisher = Think Progress| date = November 25, 2014 | url = http://thinkprogress.org/lgbt/2014/11/25/3597274/mississippi-marriage-decision/}} Reeves held that, just as the state's views on race had led it to oppress blacks for generations, "Mississippi’s traditional beliefs about gay and lesbian citizens ... [took] away fundamental rights owed to every citizen. It is time to restore those rights."{{cite court |litigants= Campaign for Southern Equality v. Bryant |opinion= Case 3:14-cv-00818-CWR-LRA |pinpoint= Doc. 30 |court= S.D. Miss. |date= 2014 |url= https://www.southernequality.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/11/Mississippi-Order.pdf |access-date= June 29, 2016 |archive-date= April 1, 2016 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160401041732/https://www.southernequality.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/11/Mississippi-Order.pdf |url-status= dead }}{{Cite web |url=https://www.southernequality.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/11/Mississippi-Order.pdf |title=Archived copy |access-date=November 15, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160401041732/https://www.southernequality.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/11/Mississippi-Order.pdf |archive-date=April 1, 2016 |url-status=bot: unknown }} ====''United States v. Butler''==== {{Main|Murder of James Craig Anderson}} On February 10, 2015, Reeves sentenced three young white men for their roles in the death of a 48-year-old black man named James Craig Anderson.{{cite news | title = Deryl Dedmon, two others sentenced from 7–50 years in hate crime | author = Therese Apel | publisher = The Clarion-Ledger| date = February 12, 2015 | url = http://www.clarionledger.com/story/news/2015/02/10/deryl-dedmon-two-others-to-be-sentenced-in-hate-crime-tuesday/23166397/}} They were part of a group that beat Anderson and then killed him by running over his body with a truck, yelling "white power" as they drove off.{{cite news|last=Severson|first=Kimberly|title=Killing of Black Man Prompts Reflection on Race in Mississippi|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/08/23/us/23jackson.html?hp|access-date=August 22, 2011|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=August 22, 2011}} In handing down sentences of between 7 and 50 years in prison for the defendants, Reeves gave a widely publicized speech that remarked on how the killing of Anderson fit into Mississippi's "tortured past" of lynchings and racism.{{cite news|title=A Black Mississippi Judge's Breathtaking Speech To 3 White Murderers|url=https://www.npr.org/sections/codeswitch/2015/02/12/385777366/a-black-mississippi-judges-breathtaking-speech-to-three-white-murderers|access-date=June 29, 2016|newspaper=[[National Public Radio]]|date=February 13, 2015}} While noting that the defendants had "ripped off the scab of the healing scars of Mississippi," Reeves asserted that the integrated, race-neutral operation of Mississippi's modern-day justice system was "the strongest way" for the state to reject the racism of the past. ====''Barber v. Bryant''==== {{Main|Religious Liberty Accommodations Act}} On June 30, 2016, Reeves issued a ruling that halted Mississippi's [[Religious Liberty Accommodations Act]] from going into effect.{{cite news|title= Federal Judge Halts Mississippi Anti-LGBT Law From Going Into Effect|url=https://www.buzzfeed.com/chrisgeidner/federal-judge-halts-mississippi-anti-lgbt-law-from-going-int|access-date=June 30, 2016|newspaper=[[BuzzFeed News]]|date=June 30, 2016}} The Act provided protection to entities and individuals who refused to provide marriage-related goods and services to LGBT individuals. Reeves' holding noted that "[r]eligious freedom was one of the building blocks of this great nation, and after the nation was torn apart, the guarantee of equal protection under [the] law was used to stitch it back together. But [the Act] does not honor that tradition of religiou[s] freedom, nor does it respect the equal dignity of all of Mississippi's citizens. It must be enjoined." In June 2017 a panel of judges from the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]] reversed Judge Reeves ruling in a 3–0 decision, finding that the plaintiffs lacked standing. The [[Religious Liberty Accommodations Act]] was reinstated.{{cite web |last1=Campbell |first1=Larrison |title='Religious freedom' law upheld by federal appeals court |date=June 22, 2017 |url=https://mississippitoday.org/2017/06/22/5th-circuit-dismisses-case-against-house-bill-1523/ |publisher=Mississippi Today |access-date=June 22, 2017}} ====''Moore v. Bryant''==== On September 8, 2016, Reeves issued a ruling dismissing a lawsuit seeking to have the Mississippi state flag, which contains the [[Stars and Bars (flag)|Stars and Bars]] emblem of the [[Confederate States of America|Confederacy]] declared unconstitutional. The basis of the dismissal is the plaintiff's failure to allege a specific injury and thus an inability to demonstrate the standing necessary to bring an action in federal court.Moore v. Bryant (Case No. 3:16-CV-151-CWR-FKB S.D. Miss. September 8, 2016). ====''Jackson v. Currier''==== {{main|Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization}} On November 20, 2018, Reeves issued a written ruling in ''Jackson Women's Health Organization v. Currier'' (Mary Currier in her official capacity as the State Health Officer of the State of Mississippi).{{cite web |title=Jackson v Currier |url=https://www.reproductiverights.org/sites/crr.civicactions.net/files/documents/Jackson-v-Currier-Order.pdf |access-date=November 23, 2018}} The ruling struck down a Mississippi law, passed in March 2018, that outlawed most abortions after the 15th week of pregnancy.{{cite news |title=U.S. Judge Strikes Down Mississippi Ban on Abortions After 15 Weeks |url=https://www.nytimes.com/reuters/2018/11/21/us/politics/21reuters-mississippi-abortion.html |access-date=November 23, 2018 |agency=Reuters |date=November 20, 2018}} Reeves had previously issued an [[injunction]], effectively preventing the law from taking effect. His ruling included strong statements about the law, calling it "pure gaslighting" as well as an unconstitutional limitation on women's due-process rights.{{cite news |last1=Schmidt |first1=Samantha |title='Pure gaslighting': Federal judge strikes down Mississippi ban on abortions after 15 weeks |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/social-issues/pure-gaslighting-federal-judge-strikes-down-mississippi-ban-on-abortions-after-15-weeks/2018/11/21/02dd0670-ed9f-11e8-96d4-0d23f2aaad09_story.html |access-date=November 23, 2018 |newspaper=Washington Post |date=November 21, 2018}} His ruling also invalidated a similar Louisiana law, which had been written as contingent on the outcome of the Mississippi lawsuit. Reeves' decision was upheld by the U.S. Court of Appeals. In October 2020, shortly after Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg's death, the Attorney General for Mississippi filed a petition with the U.S. Supreme Court seeking review of the ruling.{{Cite web|last=Warren|first=Anthony|title=AG Fitch taking abortion ban ruling to U.S. Supreme Court|url=https://www.wlbt.com/2020/10/23/ag-fitch-taking-abortion-ban-ruling-us-supreme-court/|access-date=October 25, 2020|website=WLBT News|date=October 23, 2020 |language=en-US}} The Court granted ''[[certiorari]]'' to the petition on May 17, 2021, limiting the case to the single question "Whether all pre-viability prohibitions on elective abortions are unconstitutional." The case was heard in December 2021, and in June 2022 the Supreme Court ruled in favor of Mississippi, overturning its prior rulings in favor of abortion rights in ''Roe v. Wade'' and ''Planned Parenthood v. Casey''. This not only reversed Reeves' initial decision in the same case, but also obviated his decision enjoining as unconstitutional a subsequent Mississippi statute that purported to ban abortion as of six weeks past the patient's last menstrual period.{{cite news|url=https://www.vice.com/en/article/here-we-go-again-this-judge-blocked-another-mississippi-abortion-ban-and-hes-tired/|title="Here We Go Again:" This Judge Blocked Another Mississippi Abortion Ban and He's Tired|last=Sherman|first=Carter|date=May 24, 2019|work=Vice News|access-date=May 24, 2019}} ====''Jackson Women's Health Org. v. Dobbs''==== Mississippi Governor [[Phil Bryant]] signed a law scheduled to go into effect on July 1, 2019, that would ban abortions later than six weeks of pregnancy. The [[Center for Reproductive Rights]] challenged the law. Because of his decision finding the prior, less restrictive, "15-week" law in the ''Currier'' case to be unconstitutional, Reeves began his decision by writing, "Here we go again. Mississippi has passed another law banning abortions prior to viability."{{cite news|url=https://www.vice.com/en/article/here-we-go-again-this-judge-blocked-another-mississippi-abortion-ban-and-hes-tired/|title="Here We Go Again:" This Judge Blocked Another Mississippi Abortion Ban and He's Tired|last=Sherman|first=Carter|date=May 24, 2019|work=Vice News|access-date=May 24, 2019}} He inquired, "Doesn't it boil down to six is less than fifteen?", adding that the new law "smacks of defiance to this court." Reeves noted that although there were exceptions for situations where the mother's life or health is endangered should pregnancy be taken to term, the law does not allow for exceptions in the cases of pregnancies resulting from rape or incest.[https://www.clarionledger.com/story/news/2019/05/21/mississippi-abortion-law-ban-federal-court-ruling-fetal-heartbeat-bill/3691727002/ Federal judge's questions point toward striking down Mississippi's latest abortion ban], "Clarion Ledger", Sarah Fowler, May 21, 2019. Retrieved May 22, 2019. Subsequently, the Supreme Court accepted ''[[Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization]]''.{{r|vice}} ====''Jamison v. McClendon''==== On August 4, 2020, Reeves wrote an opinion upholding the grant of [[qualified immunity]] in a case against a Richland, Mississippi police officer.{{Cite web|last=Stern (Slate)|first=Mark|title=Jamison v McClendon|url=https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/7013933-Jamison-v-McClendon.html|access-date=September 18, 2020|website=www.documentcloud.org|language=en}} The opinion stated that the two-hour traffic stop of Clarence Jamison by Officer Nick McClendon ''should'' have resulted in a Fourth Amendment violation, but he was limited to uphold prior decisions by the US Supreme Court. Reeves' ruling gives a history of minority deaths that have occurred over the decades, and argues that the doctrine of qualified immunity must be done away with.{{cite news|last=Marcus|first=Ruth|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=August 6, 2020|title=A federal judge delivers a blistering lesson|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/the-supreme-court-invented-qualified-immunity-now-a-judges-blistering-opinion-shows-why-it-must-go/2020/08/05/f72778e6-d74a-11ea-930e-d88518c57dcc_story.html|access-date=August 14, 2020}}{{Cite web|last=Steier|first=Richard|date=August 31, 2020|title=Judge: Change Law That Shielded Cop's Misconduct Civilly|url=https://thechiefleader.com/news/news_of_the_week/judge-change-law-that-shielded-cops-misconduct-civilly/article_79ee17ce-ebbb-11ea-b16c-1377d1d96f60.html|access-date=September 1, 2020|website=The Chief|language=en}} [[Austin Sarat]], writing in [[Justia]], compares Reeves' opinion to "great dissents written by Supreme Court justices".{{cite web|url=https://verdict.justia.com/2020/08/11/memorializing-miscarriages-of-justice|title=Memorializing Miscarriages of Justice|last=Sarat|first=Austin|date=August 11, 2020|website=Justia|access-date=August 14, 2020}} CNN quotes a portion of the opinion:{{cite web|url=https://www.cnn.com/2020/08/04/politics/qualified-immunity-federal-judge/index.html|title=Federal judge pens scathing opinion on qualified immunity|last1=Ehrlich|first1=Jamie|last2=de Vogue|first2=Ariane|website=CNN|date=August 4, 2020|access-date=August 14, 2020}} {{blockquote|text=The Constitution says everyone is entitled to equal protection of the law -- even at the hands of law enforcement. Over the decades, however, judges have invented a legal doctrine to protect law enforcement officers from having to face any consequences for wrongdoing. The doctrine is called "qualified immunity." In real life it operates like absolute immunity.}} ====''J.W. v. City of Jackson''==== On March 23, 2023, Reeves issued a lengthy opinion holding that the City of Jackson had violated the due process rights of over 1,000 children by intentionally misleading them to consume lead contaminated water. The plaintiffs brought bodily integrity claims and state-created danger claims, but under Fifth Circuit case law, only the bodily integrity claims survived. Reeves' opinion criticized the circuit court for not recognizing the right to state-created danger, stating that "The Fifth Circuit’s categorical bar on holding government actors accountable for the dangers they create or enhance has also had nightmarish consequences for ordinary citizens." Reeves dismissed some defendants, including the mayor, on qualified immunity grounds.{{cite web | title=Lawsuit moving forward against Jackson, MSDH over lead in drinking water | website=WLBT | date=May 3, 2023 | url=https://www.wlbt.com/2023/05/03/lawsuit-moving-forward-against-jackson-msdh-over-lead-drinking-water/ | access-date=June 29, 2023}} ====''United States of America v. Bullock''==== On June 28, 2023, Reeves struck down the felon-in possession statute as applied against the defendant, Jesse Bullock. The opinion is a critique of both the Supreme Court's expansion of Second Amendment rights in ''[[New York State Rifle & Pistol Association, Inc. v. Bruen]]'' and originalism.{{cite web | last=Pierson | first=Brendan | title=Mississippi judge, dismissing gun charge, assails Supreme Court gun ruling | website=Reuters | date=June 29, 2023 | url=https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/mississippi-judge-dismissing-gun-charge-assails-supreme-court-gun-ruling-2023-06-29/ | access-date=June 29, 2023}} ==== ''Green v. Thomas''==== In an order denying qualified immunity for police detective Jacquelyn Thomas,{{cite web | website=DocumentCloud | title=No.3:23-CV-126-CWR-ASH | url=https://s3.documentcloud.org/documents/24674613/green-v-thomas.pdf | date=May 20, 2024 | access-date=May 23, 2024}} Reeves critiqued the Supreme Court's establishment and expansion of qualified immunity.{{cite web | author-link = Mark Joseph Stern | last = Stern | first=Mark Joseph | title=In an Extraordinary Opinion, a Federal Judge Delivers a Scathing Warning About the Supreme Court | website=Slate Magazine | date=May 22, 2024 | url=https://slate.com/news-and-politics/2024/05/supreme-court-judge-carlton-reeves-warning-abortion-police-civil-rights.html | access-date=May 23, 2024}}{{cite magazine | last=Ford | first=Matt | title=A Federal Judge Just Called Out the Supreme Court | magazine=The New Republic | date=May 22, 2024 | url=https://newrepublic.com/article/181825/federal-judge-just-called-supreme-court | access-date=May 23, 2024}} === Appointment to United States Sentencing Commission === On May 11, 2022, President [[Joe Biden]] announced his intent to nominate Reeves to serve as a member of the [[United States Sentencing Commission]].{{Cite press release |title=President Biden Nominates Bipartisan Slate for the United States Sentencing Commission |date=May 11, 2022 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/05/11/president-biden-nominates-bipartisan-slate-for-the-united-states-sentencing-commission/ |access-date=May 11, 2022}} On May 12, 2022, his nomination was sent to the Senate, he has been nominated to fill the position and chairmanship left vacant by Judge [[Patti B. Saris]], whose term expired.{{Cite press release |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |date=May 12, 2022 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/05/12/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-66/}} {{PD-notice}} On June 8, 2022, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web |title=Nominations |date=June 8, 2022 |publisher=[[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]] |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/06/08/2022/nominations}} On July 21, 2022, his nomination was reported out of committee by a voice vote, with six Republican senators voting “no” on record.{{cite web|url= https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/EBM%20Results%20-%202022-07-21.pdf|title= Results of Executive Business Meeting – July 21, 2022|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=July 21, 2022}} On August 4, 2022, the [[United States Senate]] confirmed his nomination by a voice vote.{{cite web|title=PN2084 - Nomination of Carlton W. Reeves for United States Sentencing Commission, 117th Congress (2021-2022)|website=Congress.gov|date=August 4, 2022 |url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/117th-congress/2084|access-date=August 5, 2022}} == See also == * [[List of African-American federal judges]] * [[List of African-American jurists]] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1393566}} *{{Ballotpedia|Carlton_W._Reeves}} *[https://www.npr.org/blogs/codeswitch/2015/02/12/385777366/a-black-mississippi-judges-breathtaking-speech-to-three-white-murderers "A Black Mississippi Judge's Breathtaking Speech To 3 White Murderers", February 13, 2015, NPR] {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[William H. [[University of Virginia School of Law|University of Virginia]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Carol Bagley Amon''' ({{nee|Bagley}}; born April 23, 1946) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York]]. ==Education== Carol Ann Bagley was born in [[Richmond, Virginia]]. She received a [[Bachelor of Science]] from [[College of William and Mary|College of William & Mary]] in 1968, then a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[University of Virginia School of Law]] in 1971.{{FJC Bio|nid=1377166|inline=yes}} == Career == Amon was a staff attorney of the [[COMSAT|Communications Satellite Corporation]] in [[Washington, D.C.]] from 1971 to 1973. She was then a trial attorney of Narcotics Task Force of the [[United States Department of Justice]] from 1973 to 1974. She was an [[Assistant United States Attorney|assistant United States attorney]] of the Eastern District of New York from 1974 to 1986. She was chief of frauds from 1978 to 1980, and then chief of general crimes from 1981 to 1982. She was a senior litigation counsel from 1984 to 1986. During her tenure at the United States Attorney's office, she received the John Marshall Award, the highest honor conferred by the Department of Justice.{{Cite web |date=5 June 2017 |title=Honoring Women at UVA Law |url=https://www.law.virginia.edu/about/honoring-women-uva-law |access-date=22 January 2025 |website=[[University of Virginia School of Law]] |language=en}} In 1983, Amon successfully prosecuted four members of the [[Provisional Irish Republican Army]] (Provisional IRA) who conspired to obtain guns, explosives and missiles for their [[Provisional Irish Republican Army campaign|armed campaign]].{{Cite news |last1=Fried |first1=Joseph P. |date=March 1983 |title=CASE OUTLINED AGAINST 4 ON TRIAL FOR DEALING IN GUNS FOR I.R.A. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1983/03/01/nyregion/case-outlined-against-4-on-trial-for-dealing-in-guns-for-ira.html |access-date=22 January 2025 |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |page=2}} ===Federal judicial service=== Amon was a [[United States magistrate judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York]] from 1986 to 1990. She was nominated by President [[George H. W. Bush]] to be a United States District Judge of that court on May 18, 1990, to a seat vacated by [[Mark Americus Costantino|Mark A. Costantino]]. She was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on August 3, 1990, and received her commission on August 7, 1990. She served as Chief Judge from 2011 to 2016. She took [[senior status]] on November 30, 2016. In 2009, Amon sentenced [[National Basketball Association|NBA]] referee [[Tim Donaghy]] to 15 months in federal prison for his role in fixing NBA games.{{Cite news |date=29 July 2008 |title=Donaghy sentenced to 15 months in gambling case |url=https://www.espn.com/nba/news/story?id=3509440 |access-date=20 November 2022 |work=[[ESPN.com]]}} ==References== {{Reflist}} ==Sources== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1377166}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Mark Americus Costantino]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York]]}}|years=1990–2016}} {{s-aft|after=[[Rachel Kovner]]}} {{s-bef|before=[[Raymond Dearie]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Chief Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York]]}}|years=2011–2016}} {{s-aft|after=[[Dora Irizarry]]}} {{s-end}} {{United States 2nd Circuit senior district judges}} {{Chief Judge of the United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York}} {{Authority control}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Amon, Carol}} [[Category:1946 births]] [[Category:Living people]] [[Category:20th-century American women judges]] [[Category:21st-century American judges]] [[Category:21st-century American women judges]] [[Category:Assistant United States attorneys]] [[Category:College of William & Mary alumni]] [[Category:Judges of the United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York]] [[Category:Lawyers from Richmond, Virginia]] [[Category:United States district court judges appointed by George H. She also served as a [[United States magistrate judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri]] from 1990 to 1994.{{FJC Bio|nid=1386251|inline=yes}} ===Federal judicial service=== On July 15, 1994, Perry was nominated by President [[Bill Clinton]] to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri]] vacated by Judge [[Clyde S. Cahill]]. She was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on October 6, 1994, and received her commission the following day. She served as chief judge from 2009 to 2016. Perry assumed [[senior status]] on December 31, 2018. ====Notable ruling==== On August 18, 2014 Perry denied motions by the [[American Civil Liberties Union|ACLU]] for temporary restraining orders against six police officers to prevent the enforcement of a 5-second rule in [[Ferguson, Missouri]]. Perry cited the need for law enforcement's protection of property and the availability of a "free-speech zone".{{cite web|url=http://www.stltoday.com/news/local/metro/judge-denies-aclu-motion-for-an-order-to-stop-police/article_fb22afea-3720-5b45-8d4a-2d923e793925.html|title=Judge denies ACLU motion for an order to stop police tactics|first=Margaret S.|last=Gillerman|date=18 August 2014 |access-date=2014-08-23|archive-date=2018-07-08|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180708081950/https://www.stltoday.com/news/local/metro/judge-denies-aclu-motion-for-an-order-to-stop-police/article_fb22afea-3720-5b45-8d4a-2d923e793925.html|url-status=live}} However, at the time of this ruling the free speech zone was off-limits to the public.{{cite web|url=https://www.aclu.org/blog/free-speech-racial-justice/there-no-5-second-rule-first-amendment-ferguson|title=There Is No 5-Second Rule for the First Amendment, Ferguson|first=Lee|last=Rowland|date=August 21, 2014|access-date=September 11, 2019|url-status=live|archive-date=September 29, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180929155648/https://www.aclu.org/blog/free-speech/freedom-press/there-no-5-second-rule-first-amendment-ferguson}} ==References== {{Reflist}} ==Sources== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1386251}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Clyde S. [[Fordham University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Cathy Seibel''' (born 1960) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]]. ==Early life and education== Born in [[West Islip, New York]], Seibel graduated from [[Princeton University]] with her [[Bachelor of Arts|Artium Baccalaureus]] degree in 1982 and later from [[Fordham University School of Law]] with a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1985.{{Cite journal|date=2020-12-01|journal=Fonseca, Journal of Communication|issue=21|doi=10.14201/fjc202021|issn=2172-9077|doi-access=free|title=Núm. 21 (2020): Adolescentes en serie. Jóvenes protagonistas en la ficción televisiva | Fonseca, Journal of Communication }} At Fordham, Seibel served as Editor-in-Chief of the [[Fordham Law Review]]. ==Career== Following law school graduation, Seibel worked as a [[law clerk]] for United States District Judge [[Joseph M. McLaughlin]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York]] from 1985 to 1987. From 1987 to 1991, Seibel was an [[assistant United States attorney]] for the Southern District of New York with the U.S. Attorney's Office. Seibel was assigned to serve as special assistant United States attorney for the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Washington]] from 1991 to 1993. From 1993 to 1997, Seibel was assistant United States attorney for the Southern District of New York before serving as AUSA-in-Charge of the White Plains branch from 1997 to 1999. Seibel was a senior trial counsel with the United States Attorney's Office from 1999 to 2005. She was appointed deputy U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York, where she served from 2005 to 2008. ===Federal judicial career=== Seibel was nominated to the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York by President [[George W. Bush]] on March 11, 2008 to a seat vacated by the death of Judge [[Richard C. Casey]]. Seibel was confirmed by the [[United States Senate|Senate]] on July 22, 2008 and received her commission on July 30, 2008. [[Yale University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Cecilia María Altonaga''' (born December 26, 1962) is an American lawyer and jurist serving as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida|U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida]]. She was appointed in 2003 by President [[George W. Bush]] and is the first [[Cuban Americans|Cuban-American]] woman to be appointed as a chief judge and a federal judge in the United States. ==Biography== Altonaga was born in [[Baltimore]], [[Maryland]], to parents who escaped from the communist regime in [[Cuba]].Lisette Garcia, "[https://www.newspapers.com/clip/114899096/the-miami-herald/ County judge attains new benchmark]", ''[[Miami Herald]]'' (August 29, 1999), Neighbors Sunday Profile, p. 4. She attended [[Notre Dame Academy (Miami, Florida)|Notre Dame Academy]] in Miami, graduating in 1980,Melissa Sanchez, "Cuban-American judge inspires teens", ''Miami Herald'' (April 3, 2011), p. B3. and then received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] from [[Florida International University]] in 1983. Altonaga earned her [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Yale Law School]] in 1986.{{FJC Bio|nid=1391821}} She worked as an attorney in the Miami Dade County Attorney's Office from 1986 to 1987, and then served as a [[law clerk]] to [[Edward B. Davis]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida]] from 1987 to 1988 before returning to the County Attorney's Office as an assistant County Attorney until 1996. In 1996, Governor [[Lawton Chiles]] appointed her as a [[County court (Florida)|County Court]] Judge on [[Florida]]'s Eleventh Judicial Circuit Court. In 1999, she was elevated to circuit court judge in that district by Governor [[Jeb Bush]]. == Federal judicial service== On January 15, 2003, President [[George W. Bush]] nominated Altonaga to be a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida]]. She was nominated to the seat vacated by [[Shelby Highsmith]] who assumed [[senior status]] on March 15, 2002. She was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on May 6, 2003, and received her commission the following day. During her time on the federal bench, Altonaga has been noted for her strong support of the recently created [[Florida International University College of Law]], having served as the keynote speaker in the 2004 Convocation, judged several [[moot court]] competitions, and employed FIU law students as summer [[intern]]s.{{citation needed|date=July 2021}} She became chief judge on July 1, 2021.{{cite web|url=https://www.flsd.uscourts.gov/sites/flsd/files/news/PressReleaseJudgeAltonagaChiefJudge_0.pdf|title=Judge Cecilia M. Altonaga Succeeds Judge K. Michael Moore As Chief United States District Judge for the Southern District of Florida|publisher=[[United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida]]|date=July 1, 2021|accessdate=July 6, 2021}} ===Notable cases and rulings=== On June 14, 2007, Altonaga ruled that [[US Sugar Corporation]]'s practice of pumping untreated [[wastewater]] into [[Lake Okeechobee]] was in violation of the [[Clean Water Act]]. Largely as a result of this decision, on June 25, 2008 the state of Florida announced plans to purchase {{convert|300|sqmi|km2}} of land controlled by US Sugar, which will be used to restore vital water flow between [[Lake Okeechobee]] and the [[Everglades National Park]], helping to ensure its survival in the face of competition for water from surrounding development.{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2008/jun/24/conservation.usa|title=Florida to buy 187,000 farmland acres to preserve Everglades|last=Schor|first=Elana|date=2008-06-24|publisher=Guardian|access-date=2008-06-25}} She also presided over the trial of [[Charles McArther Emmanuel]], son of former Liberian dictator [[Charles Taylor (Liberian politician)|Charles Taylor]], for torture.{{cite news|url=https://news.yahoo.com/s/ap/20090109/ap_on_re_us/taylor_s_son|title=Taylor's son gets 97 years in prison for torture|last=Anderson|first=Curt|date=2009-01-09|publisher=[[Associated Press]]|access-date=2009-01-09}} {{Dead link|date=October 2010|bot=H3llBot}} In September 2006, Dubai Sheikh [[Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum]] was accused of encouraging the abduction and enslavement of thousands of boys for use as jockeys in [[camel racing]]. A [[class action]] suit was filed in the state of Florida in the United States.{{cite news| url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/americas/dubai-princes-accused-of-masterminding-trade-in-jockey-slaves-416101.html | work=The Independent | location=London | title=Dubai princes accused of masterminding trade in jockey slaves | first=Andrew | last=Gumbel | date=2006-09-15 | access-date=2010-05-13}}{{cite news| url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/middle_east/5346430.stm | work=BBC News | title=Dubai's ruler accused of slavery | date=2006-09-14 | access-date=2010-05-13}}[http://www.nysun.com/foreign/dubai-leader-faces-charges-of-enslavement/62611/ A Dubai Leader Faces Charges of Enslavement – September 14, 2007 - The New York Sun][http://www.hwwilson.com/currentbio/cover_bios/cover_bio_4_08.htm Cover Bio from Current Biography Monthly Magazine – April 2008] In July 2007, Altonaga granted a motion to dismiss the suit because none of the involved parties resided in the United States.{{citation needed|date=April 2022}} In 2012, Altonaga disqualified the entire firm of [[Morgan & Morgan]] from a class action suit for "deplorable behavior" in connection with depositions for the case, including insisting on holding them in a [[Dunkin' Donuts]], appearing dressed in t-shirt and shorts, bragging about playing [[Angry Birds]] during depositions, and drawing and then showing off "pictures of male genitalia".{{cite news|last1=Zaretsky|first1=Staci|title=Things That (website)|Above the Law]]|date=17 May 2012}} On December 5, 2016, Altonaga rejected the [[U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission]]'s $450,000 penalty against Michael Boudreaux, the City of [[Miami]]'s budget director, for deceiving municipal bond investors, instead fining him $15,000.{{cite news|last1=Aubin|first1=Dena|title=Judge slashes SEC's proposed fine for ex-Miami budget director|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/usa-miami-sec-idUSL1N1E11AU|access-date=8 December 2016|work=[[Reuters]]|date=6 December 2016}} In 2021, Altonaga was assigned to preside over the Trump]] filed a defamation lawsuit against [[ABC News (United States)|ABC News]] and [[George Stephanopoulos]] for an airing of ''This Week'', arguing that Stephanopoulos harmed Trump's reputation by claiming that Trump was found liable for raping the writer [[E. Jean Carroll]] in a New York case.{{Cite web|last1=Jackson|first1=David|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/2024/03/19/donald-trump-lawsuit-george-stephanopoulos-abc/73033183007/|title=Donald Trump files lawsuit against George Stephanopoulos, ABC News after interview with GOP lawmaker|date=March 19, 2024|website=USA Today}}{{Cite web|last1=Wendling|first1=Mike|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-us-canada-68582953|title=Trump sues ABC News and host Stephanopoulos over rape claim|date=March 19, 2024|website=BBC}}{{Cite web|last1=Battaglio|first1=Stephen|url=https://www.latimes.com/entertainment-arts/business/story/2024-03-19/trump-sues-abcs-george-stephanopoulos-for-liable|title=Trump sues ABC News and George Stephanopoulos for defamation|date=March 19, 2024|website=Los Angeles Times}} Altonaga, presiding over the suit brought by Trump, denied a motion to dismiss by Stephanopoulos, finding that the technical definition used by the judge in the New York case did not examine the findings made by the jury.{{cite news|url=https://www.cnn.com/2024/07/24/media/trump-lawsuit-abc-george-stephanopoulos-rape-claim/index.html |title=Judge won't dismiss Trump's defamation suit against ABC News and George Stephanopoulos|first1=Marshall|last1=Cohen|work=[[CNN]]|date=July 24, 2024}} ===Supreme Court speculation=== In July 2005, following the retirement of Justice [[Sandra Day O'Connor]], Altonaga's name was raised as a potential [[George W. Bush Supreme Court candidates|George W. Bush Supreme Court candidate]],Linda P. Campbell, "Latinas for Bush's short list", ''[[Fort Worth Star-Telegram]]'' (September 8, 2005), p. 13B.Margaret Talev, "High court focus shifts to next nominee", ''The Herald Rock Hill'' (September 20, 2005), p. 3A: "Potential candidates include: ... "Cecilia Altonaga, a Cuban American U.S. district court judge in Florida". a position for which she was promoted by Florida's Hispanic community.McNelly Torres and Madeline Baro Diaz, "Case made for Hispanic justice from Florida", ''[[South Florida Sun Sentinel]]'' (July 9, 2005), p. 5B. However, it constitutes an extremely rare occurrence for a sitting District Court judge to be appointed to the Supreme Court, with the most recent occurrence being [[Edward Terry Sanford]] in 1923. At 43, Altonaga was younger than most other Hispanics or women who were being mentioned as possible nominees, which might have made her a more attractive choice to the President. President Bush went through several other nominees, and ultimately succeeded in nominating Judge [[Samuel Alito]] for the position. ==Personal life== Altonaga married attorney George Mencio in 1986. Meredith |url=https://www.kybar.org/members/?id=32548472 |website=kybar.org |location= |publisher=Kentucky Bar Association |access-date=June 19, 2025}} (born 1981) is a [[United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Kentucky|District Court for the Eastern District of Kentucky]]. He previously served as the first [[Solicitor General of Kentucky|solicitor general of Kentucky]] from 2019 to 2021. == Early life and education == A native of [[Lexington, Kentucky]], Meredith is the son of [[Stephen Meredith (politician)|Stephen Meredith]], a member of the [[Kentucky Senate]]. He later worked for Ransdell & Roach before joining the administration of [[Governor of Kentucky|Governor]] [[Matt Bevin]] in 2015 as chief deputy general counsel. In December 2019, [[Attorney General of Kentucky|Attorney General]] [[Daniel Cameron (American politician)|Daniel Cameron]] appointed Meredith as the commonwealth's first solicitor general, a position he would continue to hold until 2021.{{Cite web |last=Wolfson |first=Mike Trautmann, Joe Sonka and Andrew |title=Who is Chad Meredith, the anti-abortion Republican President Biden plans to make a judge? |url=https://www.courier-journal.com/story/news/politics/mitch-mcconnell/2022/07/05/who-chad-meredith-bidens-anti-abortion-pick-kentucky-judge/7790119001/ |access-date=2022-07-05 |website=The Courier-Journal |language=en-US}} === Consideration for judicial nomination in first Trump administration === In 2020, Meredith was [[vetted]] to possibly be nominated by President [[Donald Trump]] to the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Kentucky]] following the elevation of Judge [[Justin R. Walker]] to the [[United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit]]. However, Meredith was passed over in favor of [[Benjamin Beaton]].{{Cite web |last=Wolfson |first=Andrew |title=Young conservative who clerked for Ginsburg nominated to the federal bench in Louisville |url=https://www.courier-journal.com/story/news/politics/mitch-mcconnell/2020/08/12/young-conservative-who-clerked-ruth-bader-ginsburg-nominated-federal-judge/3359966001/ |access-date=2025-06-20 |website=The Courier-Journal |language=en-US}} Following this, Meredith joined [[Squire Patton Boggs]] as [[of counsel]] to their global litigation practice group.{{Cite web |title=Kentucky Solicitor General Joins Squire Patton Boggs {{!}} 01 {{!}} 2022 {{!}} News {{!}} Squire Patton Boggs |url=https://www.squirepattonboggs.com/en/news/2022/01/kentucky-solicitor-general-joins-squire-patton-boggs |access-date=2025-11-14 |website=www.squirepattonboggs.com |language=en}} === Consideration for nomination under Biden === In late-June 2022, it was reported that President [[Joe Biden]] would nominate Meredith to serve as a judge of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Kentucky]].{{cite web |url=https://www.cnn.com/2022/06/30/politics/biden-federal-judgeship-kentucky-conservative-anti-abortion-lawyer/index.html |title=Biden intends to nominate a conservative, anti-abortion lawyer to federal judgeship, Kentucky Democrats say |last1=Vazquez |first1=Maegan |last2=Diaz |first2=Daniella |last3=Lee |first3=MJ |publisher=CNN |date=June 30, 2022 |website=cnn.com |access-date=July 5, 2022}} The nomination announcement was originally scheduled for June 24, the same day the ''[[Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization]]'' decision was released. The plan to nominate Meredith, which was struck between Biden and Senate Minority Leader [[Mitch McConnell]], was criticized by Democrats due to Meredith's anti-abortion stances.{{Cite web |last=Stern |first=Mark Joseph |date=2022-07-01 |title=The Biden-McConnell Deal to Make an Anti-Abortion Advocate a Federal Judge Is Still On |url=https://slate.com/news-and-politics/2022/07/biden-mcconnell-chad-meredith-abortion-kentucky-judge.html |access-date=2022-07-05 |website=Slate Magazine |language=en}}{{Cite news |date=2022-07-01 |title=Biden's Planned Nomination of Anti-Abortion Judge Outrages Left |language=en |work=Bloomberg.com |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2022-07-01/potential-biden-kentucky-judicial-nominee-outrages-progressives |access-date=2022-07-05}} Despite McConnell's support, the nomination was never formally put forward by Biden in accordance with the [[Blue slip (U.S. Senate)|blue slip]] rule due to opposition from Senator [[Rand Paul]].{{Cite web |date=2025-06-19 |title=President Donald Trump's latest judicial pick is someone that Joe Biden almost nominated |url=https://apnews.com/article/trump-kentucky-judges-mitch-mcconnell-chad-meredith-a0af0a9a4db445d0cb65633c3fc3680f |access-date=2025-06-20 |website=AP News |language=en}} === Nomination to district court under Trump === On June 18, 2025, President Trump announced his intention to nominate Meredith to the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Kentucky to a seat vacated by Judge [[Danny C. Reeves]]. The nomination was formally transmitted to the [[United States Senate]] on June 23, 2025, was approved by the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]] on September 11 by a 12–10 vote.{{cite web |last=Ward |first=Jasper |date=June 19, 2025 |title=Trump taps Kentucky lawyer for judgeship after scrapped Biden nomination |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/us/trump-taps-kentucky-lawyer-judgeship-after-scrapped-biden-nomination-2025-06-19/ |website=reuters.com |location= |publisher=Reuters |access-date=June 19, 2025}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/119th-congress/368|title=PN368 - Nomination of Stephen Chad Meredith for The Judiciary, 119th Congress (2025-2026)|date=June 23, 2025|website=www.congress.gov}}{{Cite web |title=Senate Judiciary Committee Advances Chad Meredith's Federal Judgeship Nomination {{!}} Marshall County Daily.com |url=https://www.marshallcountydaily.com/2025/09/12/senate-judiciary-committee-advances-chad-merediths-federal-judgeship-nomination/ |access-date=2025-09-15 |website=www.marshallcountydaily.com |language=en-US}} Paul stated that he would support Meredith's nomination despite his previous opposition in 2022. '''Charles Adam Pannell Jr.''' (born January 24, 1946) is an inactive [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Georgia]].

==Education and career==

Pannell was born in [[DeKalb County, Georgia]]. He received an [[Bachelor of Arts|Artium Baccalaureus]] degree from the [[University of Georgia]] in 1967 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Georgia School of Law]] in 1970. He was in the [[United States Army]] Reserves in the [[Judge Advocate General's Corps, United States Army|Judge Advocate General's Corps]] from 1971 to 1997. He was an [[assistant United States attorney]] of the Northern District of Georgia from 1971 to 1972, and in private practice in Georgia from 1972 to 1976. He was a special assistant attorney general of the State of Georgia from 1974 to 1976, and then a [[district attorney]] of Georgia's Conasauga Judicial Circuit from 1977 to 1979. He was a Superior court judge of the Conasauga Judicial Circuit from 1979 to 1999.

===Federal judicial service===

On July 14, 1999, Pannell was nominated by President [[Bill Clinton]] to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Georgia]] vacated by [[Frank M. Hull]]. Pannell was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on October 15, 1999, and received his commission on October 26, 1999. Pannell assumed [[senior status]] on January 31, 2013,<ref>{{FJC Bio|nid=1391056|inline=yes}}</ref> and inactive senior status on September 30, 2024.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.gand.uscourts.gov/news/hon-charles-pannell-jr-take-inactive-senior-status-effective-september-30-2024|title=Hon. Charles A. Pannell, Jr., to Take Inactive Senior Status Effective September 30, 2024|work=United States District Court, Northern District of Georgia|date=September 11, 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240921025045/https://www.gand.uscourts.gov/news/hon-charles-pannell-jr-take-inactive-senior-status-effective-september-30-2024|url-status=live|archive-date=September 21, 2024}}</ref>

Kornmann then received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[College of St. Thomas]] in 1959 and a [[Bachelor of Laws]] from [[Georgetown University Law Center]] in 1962. He was in the [[South Dakota National Guard]] from 1963 to 1972 and the [[United States Army]] from 1968 to 1972. He became a captain. He was a Legislative assistant to U.S. Senator [[George McGovern]] in 1963. Kornmann was an Executive secretary of [[South Dakota Democratic Party]] from 1963 to 1965. He was in private practice in [[Aberdeen, South Dakota|Aberdeen]], South Dakota from 1965 to 1995, also working as an assistant city attorney for the City of Aberdeen from 1970 to 1986. ==Federal judicial service== On January 23, 1995, Kornmann was nominated by President [[Bill Clinton]] to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the District of South Dakota]] vacated by [[John Bailey Jones]]. On March 24, 1995, Kornmann was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]]. On May 7, 1995, he took the oath of office and began his position.{{Cite web |last=Gallagher |first=Patrick |date=2022-12-30 |title=Ours to Use and Enjoy {{!}} Aberdeen Magazine |url=https://aberdeenmag.com/2022/12/ours-to-use-and-enjoy/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230128123556/https://aberdeenmag.com/2022/12/ours-to-use-and-enjoy/ |archive-date=January 28, 2023 |access-date=2026-09-02 |language=en-US}} ==References== {{Reflist}} ==Sources== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1383476}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[John Bailey Jones]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States District Court for the District of South Dakota]]}}|years=1995–2008}} {{s-aft|after=[[Roberto Lange]]}} {{s-end}} {{United States 8th Circuit senior district judges}} {{authority control}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Kornmann, Charles B.}} [[Category:1937 births]] [[Category:Living people]] [[Category:Judges of the United States District Court for the District of South Dakota]] [[Category:United States district court judges appointed by Bill Clinton]] [[Category:United States Army officers]] [[Category:University of St. Thomas (Minnesota) alumni]] [[Category:Georgetown University Law Center alumni]] [[Category:People from Aberdeen, South Dakota]] [[Category:South Dakota Democrats]] [[Category:20th-century American judges]] [[Category:21st-century American judges]] [[Category:South Dakota National Guard personnel]] [[Category:People from Watertown, South Dakota]]
