[[Howard University]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|BA]], [[Bachelor of Laws|LLB]]) | footnotes = }} '''Consuelo Bland Marshall''' (born September 28, 1936) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Central District of California]]. ==Education and career== Born in [[Knoxville, Tennessee]], Marshall received an [[Associate of Arts]] degree from [[Los Angeles City College]] in 1956. She received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[Howard University]] in 1958. She received a [[Bachelor of Laws]] from [[Howard University School of Law]] in 1961. She was a deputy city attorney of Los Angeles City Attorney's Office from 1962 to 1967. She was in private practice of law in [[Los Angeles]], [[California]] from 1968 to 1970. She was a Commissioner of the Juvenile Court of the [[Los Angeles County Superior Court]] from 1971 to 1976. She was a judge of the Civil and Criminal Division of the Inglewood Municipal Court in [[Inglewood, California|Inglewood]], California from 1976 to 1977. She was a judge of the Criminal Division of the Los Angeles County Superior Court from 1977 to 1980.{{FJC Bio|1485|nid=1384346|name=Consuelo Bland Marshall}} ===Federal judicial service=== Marshall was nominated by President [[Jimmy Carter]] on June 20, 1980, to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Central District of California]] vacated by Judge [[Robert Firth (judge)|Robert Firth]]. She was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on September 29, 1980, and received her commission on September 30, 1980. She served as the first woman and first African-american woman Chief Judge from 2001 to 2005.{{cite journal |last1=BERMAN |first1=HON. HOWARD L. |title=TRIBUTE TO CHIEF UNITED STATES DISTRICT JUDGE CONSUELO B. MARSHALL |journal=Congressional Record |date=13 December 2005 |url=https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CRECB-2005-pt21/html/CRECB-2005-pt21-Pg28174-2.htm |access-date=2 July 2026}} She assumed [[senior status]] on October 24, 2005. === Landmark rulings === A notable decision was rendered by Judge Marshall in the matter ''Preferred Communications Inc. v. City of Los Angeles.''{{Cite web |title=Preferred Communications, Inc., a California Corporation, plaintiff-appellant, v. City of Los Angeles, California, a Municipal Corporation; and Department of Water and Power, a Municipal utility, Defendants-appellees, 754 F.2d 1396 (9th Cir. 1985) |url=https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F2/754/1396/319225/ |access-date=2024-01-14 |website=Justia Law |language=en}} The [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]] and later the [[Supreme Court of the United States|U.S. Supreme Court]] found that the City of Los Angeles violated the First Amendment through its procedure relative to the [[South Los Angeles|South Central Los Angeles]] [[Cable television in the United States|Cable Television Franchise]] specifically by depriving Preferred Communications Inc. access to the public utility lines.{{Cite web |title=CITY OF LOS ANGELES and Department of Water and Power, Petitioners v. PREFERRED COMMUNICATIONS, INC. |url=https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/476/488 |access-date=2024-01-14 |website=LII / Legal Information Institute |language=en}} Marshal would dismiss the case twice; and, twice, Marshall was reversed, in two higher courts. In sum, twelve senior [[Bench (law)|members of the bench]] superseded Marshall's dismissal of the case; three judges from the 9th Circuit{{Cite web |title=Preferred Communications, Inc., a California Corporation v. City of Los Angeles, California, a..., 754 F.2d 1396 – CourtListener.com |url=https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/447985/preferred-communications-inc-a-california-corporation-v-city-of-los/ |access-date=2024-01-14 |website=CourtListener |language=en-us}} and nine [[List of justices of the Supreme Court of the United States|justices]] in the [[Supreme Court of the United States|U.S. Supreme Court.]] The Ninth Circuit summarizes:   
"...[w]e affirm the district court's decision insofar as it pertains to the plaintiff's antitrust claims and reverse its dismissal of the First Amendment claim," {{Cite web |title=Preferred Communications, Inc., a California Corporation, plaintiff-appellant, v. City of Los Angeles, California, a Municipal Corporation; and Department of Water and Power, a Municipal utility, Defendants-appellees, 754 F.2d 1396 (9th Cir. 1985) |url=https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F2/754/1396/319225/ |access-date=2024-01-14 |website=Justia Law |language=en}}
and, subsequently, the [[Supreme Court of the United States of America]] "dismissed as improper" {{Cite web |title=City of Los Angeles v. Preferred Communications (1986) |url=https://firstamendment.mtsu.edu/article/city-of-los-angeles-v-preferred-communications/ |access-date=2024-01-14 |website=The Free Speech Center |language=en-US}} Marshall's ruling, stating:
"...[t]he complaint should not have been dismissed. The activities in which respondent allegedly seeks to engage plainly implicate First Amendment interests."
Multiple delays permeate the timeline of events before and after the separate rulings from the higher courts. *In 1983 the case was filed in district court for the Central District of California.{{Cite journal |last=Corn-Revere |first=Robert |date=1994-01-01 |title=New Technology and the First Amendment: Breaking the Cycle of Repression |url=https://repository.uclawsf.edu/hastings_comm_ent_law_journal/vol17/iss1/11 |journal=UC Law SF Communications and Entertainment Journal |volume=17 |issue=1 |pages=247 |issn=1061-6578}} ''(#83-5846 cbm)'' * In 1985 the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]] unanimously overturned Marshall's decision.(#''754 f 2d)'' * In 1986 the Supreme Court rendered unanimous judgment (9-0), to reverse Marshall and upheld the Ninth Circuit's 3-0 ruling ''(#476 U.S. 488, 1986'') * In 1992 Judge Marshall would issue her final ruling in defiance of the mandate issued by two higher courts having deferred the case in sum for five years subsequent to the Supreme Court decision.{{Cite web| title=Preferred Communications: Preamble to Breakup of Local Cable Franchising | url=https://digitalcommons.pace.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1505&context=plr | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100619113108/http://digitalcommons.pace.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1505&context=plr | archive-date=2010-06-19}} While it was the opinion of [[Supreme Court Chief Justice]] [[William Rehnquist|William H. Rehnquist]] that: "the City of Los Angeles was obligated to allow [Preferred Communications Inc.] use of its physical capacity to further speech," the Plaintiff(s) were deprived a jury trial to determine damages for roughly a decade. Between 1983 and 1992, legal hardship and economic disenfranchisement were the product of continual delays; further, no public hearing was ever granted to plaintiff(s) in their effort to assert their first amendment rights under the U.S. constitution. [[Georgetown University Law Center|Georgetown University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | party = }} '''Corey Landon Maze''' (born 1978){{Cite web |url=https://vettingroom.org/2018/12/07/corey-maze/ |title=Corey Maze – Nominee for the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Alabama |last=Voruganti |first=Harsh |date=2018-12-07 |website=The Vetting Room |language=en |access-date=2019-10-18}} is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Alabama]]. == Education == Maze earned his [[Bachelor of Arts]], ''[[summa cum laude]]'', from [[Auburn University]] and his [[Juris Doctor]], ''[[cum laude]]'', from the [[Georgetown University Law Center]].[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-fourteenth-wave-judicial-nominees-thirteenth-wave-united-states-attorney-nominees-eighth-wave-united-states-marshal-nominees/ "President Donald J. Trump Announces Fourteenth Wave of Judicial Nominees, Thirteenth Wave of United States Attorney Nominees, and Eighth Wave of United States Marshal Nominees" White House, May 10, 2018] {{PD-notice}} == Career == From 2008 to 2011, Maze served as the Solicitor General of Alabama. Before his appointment as Solicitor General, Maze prosecuted criminal trials and appeals for five years as an Assistant Attorney General. During that period, he argued three cases in the Supreme Court of the United States and won three "Best Brief Awards" from the National Association of Attorneys General. From 2011 to 2019, Maze served as chief of the Attorney General's Special Litigation unit and acted as the state's primary counsel in complex civil matters such as the [[Deepwater Horizon oil spill|2010 oil spill]] in the Gulf of Mexico and the ongoing opioid crisis. === Federal judicial service === On May 10, 2018, President [[Donald Trump]] nominated Maze to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Alabama]].{{cite news|title=Donald Trump nominates Alabama's Corey Maze for federal judgeship|url=http://altoday.com/archives/23542-donald-trump-nominates-alabamas-corey-maze-for-federal-judgeship|access-date=15 May 2018|publisher=Alabama Today|date=May 10, 2018}} On May 15, 2018, his nomination was sent to the [[United States Senate|Senate]]. He was nominated to the seat vacated by Judge [[Virginia Emerson Hopkins]], who subsequently assumed [[senior status]] on June 22, 2018.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/fifteen-nominations-one-withdrawal-sent-senate-today/ "Fifteen Nominations and One Withdrawal Sent to the Senate Today" White House, May 15, 2018] On October 17, 2018, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/10/17/2018/nominations United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Nominations for October 17, 2018] On January 3, 2019, his nomination was returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]]. On January 23, 2019, President Trump announced his intent to renominate Maze for a federal judgeship.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-intent-nominate-judicial-nominees/ "President Donald J. Trump Announces Intent to Nominate Judicial Nominees", White House, January 23, 2019] His nomination was sent to the Senate later that day.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/nominations-sent-senate-2/ "Nominations Sent to the Senate", White House, January 23, 2019] On February 7, 2019, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 13–9 vote.[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/02.07.2019%20Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting1.pdf Results of Executive Business Meeting – February 7, 2019, Senate Judiciary Committee] On June 11, 2019, the Senate invoked cloture on his nomination by a 62–34 vote.[https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=1&vote=00151 On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture on the Nomination of Corey Landon Maze, of Alabama, to be United States District Judge for the Northern District of Alabama)], United States Senate, June 11, 2019 On June 12, 2019, his nomination was confirmed by a 62–34 vote.[https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=1&vote=00156 On the Nomination (Confirmation Corey Landon Maze, of Alabama, to be U.S. District Judge for the Northern District of Alabama)], United States Senate, June 12, 2019 He received his judicial commission on June 18, 2019.{{FJC Bio|nid=6594536|inline=yes}} == Memberships == He has been a member of the [[Federalist Society]] since 2017.[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Maze%20SJQ.pdf United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees: Corey L. The elder Carney [[Immigration to the United States|immigrated to the United States]] to further his medical career. Cormac was raised in [[Long Beach, California]], where he attended [[St. Anthony High School (California)|St. Anthony High School]]. Carney received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from the [[University of California, Los Angeles]] (UCLA) in 1983 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Harvard Law School]] in 1987. He attended the [[U.S. Air Force Academy]] for one year before transferring to UCLA.{{cite web|author=Abdollahi, Panteha|title=Judicial Profile: Hon. Cormac J. Carney, U.S. District Judge, Central District of California|work=The Federal Lawyer|date=June 2010|pages=48–50|url=http://fedbar.org/Resources_1/Judicial-Profiles/Judicial-PDFs/Carney-Profile.aspx|publisher=Federal Bar Association|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20111021053417/http://fedbar.org/Resources_1/Judicial-Profiles/Judicial-PDFs/Carney-Profile.aspx|archivedate=October 21, 2011}} ==Football career== Carney was a wide receiver on the [[UCLA Bruins football team]].{{Cite web | url=http://www.uclabruins.com/sports/m-footbl/spec-rel/062405aaa.html | title=Cormac Carney To Be Inducted into CoSIDA Academic All-America Hall of Fame | work=UCLABruins.com | date=June 24, 2005 | accessdate=August 14, 2011 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120405155144/http://www.uclabruins.com/sports/m-footbl/spec-rel/062405aaa.html | archive-date=2012-04-05 | url-status=dead }} He was named to the GTE/CoSIDA [[Academic All-America]] football team, and inducted into the CoSIDA Academic All-America Hall of Fame in 2005. He was also named to the [[1981 All-Pacific-10 Conference football team|1981]] and [[1982 All-Pacific-10 Conference football team]]s. A highlight of his college football career was UCLA's victory over [[1983 Michigan Wolverines football team|Michigan]] in the [[1983 Rose Bowl]]. He played for the [[USFL]] team [[Memphis Showboats]] in the 1984 season. Carney made 37 receptions for 701 yards and 2 touchdowns. ==Legal career== Carney practiced law in [[Los Angeles, California|Los Angeles]] for four years with [[Latham & Watkins]] and eleven years with [[O'Melveny & Myers]]. ==Judicial career== ===California state court=== In October 2001, Carney was appointed by [[California Governor]] [[Gray Davis]] to the bench of the [[Orange County Superior Court]].Rachanee Srisavasdi, [https://www.ocregister.com/2009/12/15/broadcom-judge-was-shaped-by-football/ Broadcom judge was shaped by football], ''Orange County Register'' (December 15, 2009). He served on the state bench, presiding over civil and criminal trials, until his appointment to the federal district court.[https://www.presstelegram.com/2014/07/17/judge-cormac-carney-who-ruled-in-death-penalty-case-was-a-long-beach-athlete Judge Cormac Carney who ruled in death penalty case was a Long Beach athlete], ''Press-Telegram'' (Long Beach, Calif.) (July 17, 2014). ===Federal judicial service=== On January 7, 2003, Carney was nominated by President [[George W. Bush]] to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Central District of California]] vacated by [[Carlos R. Moreno]].{{Cite press release |title=Judge Cormac J. Carney Succeeds Judge Virginia A. Phillips as Chief Judge of the Central District of California |date=June 1, 2020 |url=http://www.cacd.uscourts.gov/news/judge-cormac-j-carney-succeeds-judge-virginia-phillips-chief-judge-central-district-california |access-date=June 7, 2020}} A substantial majority of the [[American Bar Association]]'s [[Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary]] rated Carney as "qualified" for the post, while a minority of the committee members abstained. (ABA rankings of judicial nominees are on a three-part scale: well-qualified, qualified, and not qualified.)[https://www.americanbar.org/content/dam/aba/administrative/federal_judicary/ratings108.pdf Ratings of Article III Judicial Nominees: 108th Congress], [[American Bar Association]]'s [[Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary]] (last updated January 10, 2008). Carney was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on April 7, 2003, on an 80–0 vote,[https://www.congress.gov/nomination/108th-congress/19 PN19 — Cormac J. Carney — The Judiciary: 108th Congress (2003–2004)], Congress.gov. and received his commission on April 9, 2003. He assumed [[senior status]] on May 31, 2024.{{FJC Bio|nid=1391806|inline=yes}} ====Notable decisions==== * In 2009, Carney dismissed [[fraud]] and [[conspiracy]] charges against two executives of [[Broadcom Corporation]], a [[telecommunications]] company, because of [[prosecutorial misconduct]]. Carney also [[vacated]] a guilty plea by Broadcom co-founder [[Henry Samueli]] and dismissed a civil case brought by the [[Securities and Exchange Commission]] against four Broadcom executives. Carney found that the government had violated the defendants' [[right to a fair trial]] and right to [[due process]] by, among other things, engaging in conduct that "intimidated and improperly influenced" three important defense witnesses to try to prevent them from testifying and by leaking confidential grand jury proceedings.[https://www.nytimes.com/2009/12/16/technology/companies/16broadcom.html Charges Dismissed Against 2 Broadcom Executives], Associated Press (December 15, 2009).Rachanee Srisavasdi, Larry Welborn & Michael Mello, [https://www.ocregister.com/2009/12/15/broadcom-fraud-charges-dismissed/ Broadcom fraud charges dismissed], ''Orange County Register'' (December 15, 2009). * In ''Jones v. Davis'' (2014), Carney issued an opinion and order declaring the [[Capital punishment in California|California death penalty]] to be [[unconstitutional]], writing that the system's arbitrariness and lengthy delays led to only a "random few" being executed by the state and violated the [[Eighth Amendment to the United States Constitution|Eighth Amendment]]'s ban on [[cruel and unusual punishment]]. (California at the time had 740 prisoners sentenced to die, but had executed only 13 people since 1978, the last one in 2006.) In a 29-page order, Carney vacated the death sentence of Ernest Dewayne Jones, who was sentenced to death in 1995 for rape and murder. The order was appealed by then-[[California Attorney General]] [[Kamala Harris]].Mark Berman, [https://www.latimes.com/local/la-me-death-penalty-appeal-20140822-story.html Atty. Gen. Harris seeks to overturn ban on California executions], ''Los Angeles Times'' (August 21, 2014).Mark Berman, [https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/post-nation/wp/2015/11/12/federal-appeals-court-reverses-ruling-that-said-californias-death-penalty-system-is-unconstitutional/ Federal appeals court reverses ruling that said California’s death penalty system is unconstitutional], ''Washington Post'' (November 12, 2015).[https://www.reuters.com/article/us-usa-deathpenalty-california/u-s-appeals-court-rejects-challenge-to-california-death-penalty-idUSKCN0T12BA20151112 U.S. appeals court rejects challenge to California death penalty], Reuters (November 12, 2015). The [[U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]] overturned Carney's ruling in November 2015; in a unanimous decision of three-judge panel, the appellate court noted that "Many agree with Petitioner that California's capital punishment system is dysfunctional and that the delay between sentencing and execution in California is extraordinary," but held that the district court could not consider "novel constitutional theories" in reviewing a [[habeas corpus]] case. * In ''[[Fazaga v. FBI]]'' (2012), Carney dismissed most of plaintiffs' claims on the grounds of the [[state secrets privilege]]. In 2019, the Ninth Circuit affirmed in part and reversed in part, reviving some of plaintiffs' claims.{{cite journal | title = Fazaga v. FBI | journal = [[Harvard Law Review]]|url=https://harvardlawreview.org/2020/03/fazaga-v-fbi/|volume = 33 | pages = 1774 | year = 2020 }}[http://www.metnews.com/articles/2020/fazaga072120.htm No En Banc Rehearing in Case in Which State Secrets Defense Is Denied FBI], ''Metropolitan News-Enterprise'' (July 21, 2020). The Supreme Court ruled unanimously on March 4, 2022, reversing the Ninth Circuit and remanding the case. The opinion, written by Justice [[Samuel Alito]], stated that Section 1806(f) of FISA does not override the state secrets privilege, as was ruled by the Ninth Circuit.{{Cite news |title=SUPREME COURT OF THE UNITED STATES |url=https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/21pdf/20-828_5ie6.pdf}} * In ''United States v. Rundo'' (2019), Carney dismissed [[criminal conspiracy]] charges and [[rioting]] against Robert Rundo, the leader of the [[white supremacist]] [[Rise Above Movement]] group, and three of this followers, stemming from their attack on counter-demonstrators and a police officer in [[2017 Berkeley protests|Berkeley, California, in July 2017]]. Carney ruled that the [[Anti-Riot Act of 1968]] was [[Facial challenge|facially overbroad]] in violation of the First Amendment. In 2021, the Ninth Circuit reversed Carney's ruling. Applying the ''[[Brandenburg v. Ohio]]'' standard, the court of appeals, in a ''[[per curiam]]'' decision, agreed that the portions of the act that make it a crime to organize a riot, or to encourage, urge, or promote a future act of violence, were unconstitutional, but held that the Act's prohibitions on "speech that instigates (incites, participates in, or carries on) an imminent riot" and the Act's prohibition on "conduct such as committing acts of violence in furtherance of a riot, and aiding and abetting of that speech or conduct" were constitutional, since they addressed speech and actions directed to inciting or producing [[imminent lawless action]] and likely to incite or produce such action.Bob Egelko, [https://www.sfchronicle.com/local/article/Rioting-charges-stemming-from-2017-Berkeley-melee-16001721.php Rioting charges stemming from 2017 Berkeley melee restored against white supremacists], ''San Francisco Chronicle'' (March 4, 2021).''United States v. Rundo'', 497 F. Supp. 3d 872 (C.D. Cal. 2019), ''reversed'', 990 F.3d 709 (9th Cir. 2021) (per curiam). Later, Carney dismissed the case again.{{Cite web|url=https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/us-dis-crt-c-d-cal-sou-div/115856212.html|title=UNITED STATES v. RUNDO (2024)|website=Findlaw}}{{Cite web |last=Campbell |first=Cheri Mossburg, Josh |date=2024-02-23 |title=A highly unusual ruling to dismiss a case against 2 White nationalists is put on hold by a federal appeals court |url=https://www.cnn.com/2024/02/22/us/rise-above-movement-ruling-on-hold/index.html |access-date=2024-07-22 |website=CNN |language=en}}{{Cite news |last=Feuer |first=Alan |date=2024-02-22 |title=Charges Against Two White Nationalists Are Dismissed as 'Selective Prosecution' |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/02/21/us/politics/rise-above-selective-prosecution.html |access-date=2024-07-22 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} This time, Carney said the two men were being [[Selective prosecution|selectively prosecuted]], claiming that members of Antifa and other groups were not prosecuted for similar crimes. The controversial ruling was immediately put on hold by the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals.{{Cite news |last1=Mossburg |first1=Cheri |last2=Campbell |first2=Josh |date=February 23, 2024 |title=A highly unusual ruling to dismiss a case against 2 White nationalists is put on hold by a federal appeals court |url=https://www.cnn.com/2024/02/22/us/rise-above-movement-ruling-on-hold/index.html |work=[[CNN]]}} The Ninth Circuit then reversed Carney a second time and reinstated the case on 18 July 2024, rejecting the defendants' arguments that they had been singled out for prosecution over "[[Antifa (United States)|Antifa]] and [[Far-left politics|far-left]] groups."{{Cite web|url=https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2024/07/18/24-932.pdf|title=United States v. Rundo, No. 24-932 (9th Cir. 2024)}} * In 2019, Carney sentenced [[Adau Mornyang]], an Australian model, to three years of probation and 100 hours of community service for causing an airline flight disturbance; Mornyang had pleaded guilty to felony interference with a flight crew and misdemeanor assault.Andrew Dalton, [https://apnews.com/article/67b11ad0ceaf4e879107db93f48bc391 Australian model sentenced for airline flight disturbance], Associated Press (July 15, 2019). * From March 2020 until May 2021, during the [[COVID-19 pandemic in the United States|COVID-19 pandemic]], the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California temporarily halted both [[jury trial]]s and [[bench trial]]s to prevent the spread of the coronavirus.Meghann M. Cuniff, [https://www.latimes.com/socal/daily-pilot/entertainment/story/2021-04-14/orange-county-judge-softens-stance-on-trial-delays-amid-may-10-resumption Orange County judge softens stance on trial delays amid May 10 resumption], ''Los Angeles Times'' (April 14, 2021).Meghann M. Cuniff, [https://www.latimes.com/socal/daily-pilot/entertainment/story/2021-01-27/orange-county-federal-judge-dismisses-criminal-cases-over-lack-of-jury-trials Orange County federal judge dismisses criminal cases over lack of jury trials], ''Los Angeles Times'' (January 27, 2021). Carney was one of a minority of judges who believed that trials should continue, believing that doing so was crucial for preserving the parties' rights. Beginning in September 2020, he sought to summon [[jury pool]]s to select jurors for trial, but this effort was blocked by Chief Judge [[Philip S. Gutierrez]]. In five criminal cases, Carney dismissed federal charges [[with prejudice]] on [[speedy trial]] grounds.[https://www.latimes.com/socal/daily-pilot/entertainment/story/2021-02-25/u-s-judge-drops-charges-in-fifth-criminal-case-citing-suspects-right-to-a-speedy-trial Citing suspect's right to a speedy trial, U.S. judge drops charges in fifth criminal case as jury ban lingers], ''Los Angeles Times'' (February 25, 2021). The controversial decision led to an appeal by federal prosecutors to the Ninth Circuit. In April 2021, the Ninth Circuit reversed Carney's dismissal of the indictment in ''United States v. Olson'', holding that Carney had misread the "ends of justice provision" of the [[Speedy Trial Act]] and that Carney's view (that a speedy trial is required unless it is impossible to hold a trial) was "an unnecessarily inflexible interpretation of a provision meant to provide necessary flexibility to district courts to manage their criminal cases."Meghann M. Cuniff, [https://www.latimes.com/socal/daily-pilot/entertainment/story/2021-04-27/9th-circuit-reversal-in-pandemic-jury-trial-dismissal-could-foreshadow-four-pending-appeals 9th Circuit reversal in pandemic jury trial dismissal could foreshadow 4 pending appeals], ''Los Angeles Times'' (April 27, 2021).''United States v. Olsen'', 494 F. Supp. 3d 722 (C.D. Cal. 2020), ''reversed'', 995 F.3d 683 (9th Cir. 2021). * On March 20, 2023, Carney in ''Boland v. Bonta'' issued a preliminary injunction against requiring handguns to have certain mechanical features (including [[microstamping]]) under the State of California's "Unsafe Handgun Act" (UHA).{{Cite web |last=Pierson |first=Brendan |date=20 March 2023 |title=Judge blocks California law requiring safety features for handguns |url=https://news.yahoo.com/judge-blocks-california-law-requiring-203520968.html |access-date=2023-03-20 |website=Yahoo News |language=en-US}} Throughout his ruling, Carney justified his decision by, amongst other considerations, pointing to logical contradictions he observed within the UHA, making an argument about the use of Off-Roster Handguns by law enforcement departments throughout the state by stating "If C.L.I.'s (Chamber Load Indicator[s]) and M.D.M.'s (Magazine Disconnect Mechanism[s]) truly increased the overall safety of a firearm, law enforcement surely would use them. But they do not. Instead, they choose to use 'newer, improved and safer generations of handguns' that are Off-Roster."{{Cite web |title=California law mandating handgun safety features violates Second Amendment, judge says |url=https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/us/california-law-mandating-handgun-safety-features-violates-second-amendment-judge-says/ar-AA18Ut59 |access-date=2023-03-22 |website=MSN |language=en-US}} In the conclusion of his ruling, Carney wrote "The Second Amendment enshrines a fundamental constitutional right for law-abiding citizens to keep and bear arms for self-defense."{{Cite web |title=Federal Judge Blocks California Handgun Law Preventing Production of New Models |url=https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/us/federal-judge-blocks-california-handgun-law-preventing-production-of-new-models/ar-AA18RLUk |access-date=2023-03-21 |website=MSN |language=en-US}} The Court's opinion effectively halts enforcement of the UHA after 14 consecutive days have passed from the date of the ruling.{{Cite web |last=Edwards |first=Cam |title=Federal judge issues injunction against CA microstamping requirement and other aspects of "Unsafe Handguns Act" |url=https://bearingarms.com/camedwards/2023/03/20/federal-judge-issues-injunction-against-ca-microstamping-requirement-and-other-aspects-of-unsafe-handguns-act-n68616 |access-date=2023-03-20 |website=bearingarms.com |date=20 March 2023 |language=en}}{{Cite news |date=20 March 2023 |title=UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT. CENTRAL DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA. SOUTHERN DIVISION |url=https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.cacd.858747/gov.uscourts.cacd.858747.60.0_1.pdf}} * On December 20, 2023, Carney in ''May v. Bonta'' and ''Carralero v. Bonta'' (consolidated into one) issued a preliminary injunction against a major portion of "sensitive places" as defined in California's SB 2.{{Cite web |date=December 20, 2023 |title=May v. Bonta Preliminary Injunction |url=https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.cacd.898535/gov.uscourts.cacd.898535.45.0.pdf |access-date=December 21, 2023}}{{Cite web |date=December 20, 2023 |title=Carralero v. Bonta Preliminary Injunction |url=https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.cacd.899875/gov.uscourts.cacd.899875.41.0.pdf |access-date=December 21, 2023}} ====Tenure as chief judge==== Carney succeeded [[Virginia A. Phillips]] as Chief Judge of the Central District of California on June 1, 2020. However, he stepped down on June 26, 2020 in light of allegations that he had made racially insensitive comments regarding the Clerk of the Court, Kiry Gray, who is [[African American]]. Carney referred to Gray as "street smart" and telling her "it was not like I was the police officer standing on your neck."{{Cite web |last=Hamilton |first=Matt |date=June 28, 2020 |title=Chief federal judge in L.A. steps down over racially insensitive comments about Black court official |url=https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2020-06-28/chief-district-judge-los-angeles-steps-down-racially-insensitive-comments |access-date=June 30, 2020 |website=Los Angeles Times |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |last=Hamilton |first=Matt |date=July 6, 2020 |title='All he saw to me was my skin color': Clerk faces backlash from judge's comment |url=https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2020-07-06/judge-carney-resignation-follow |access-date=August 19, 2020 |website=Los Angeles Times |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |date=June 29, 2020 |title=Chief federal judge in LA resigns over racially charged comment about Black court official |url=https://abc7.com/6279712/ |access-date=June 30, 2020 |website=ABC7 Los Angeles |language=en}} Carney apologized to Gray for the remark.[https://apnews.com/article/862c15ea2a0e6a5a8da2c23c20213600 Top US judge in LA steps down over remark called insensitive], Associated Press (June 29, 2020). '''Cristal C. Brisco''' ({{nee|'''Clark'''}}; born 1981)<ref name="Questionnaire">{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/brisco_sjq.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=December 13, 2023}}</ref> is an American lawyer who has served as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Indiana]] since 2024. She previously served as a judge of the [[St. Joseph County, Indiana|St. Joseph County]] [[Courts of Indiana|Superior Court]] from 2021 to 2024.

== Education ==

Brisco received a [[Bachelor of Arts]], ''[[cum laude]]'', from [[Valparaiso University]] in 2002 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[Notre Dame Law School]] in 2006.<ref name="WHBio">{{Cite press release |title=President Biden Names Forty-Second Round of Judicial Nominees |date=November 15, 2023 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2023/11/15/president-biden-names-forty-second-round-of-judicial-nominees/ |access-date=November 15, 2023}} {{PD-notice}}</ref>

== Career ==

Brisco began her career as an associate at [[Barnes & Thornburg]] where she worked from 2006 to 2013. From 2013 to 2017, she served as [[corporation counsel]] for the [[South Bend, Indiana|City of South Bend]] during Mayor [[Pete Buttigieg]]'s Administration.<ref name="South Bend, IN Black History Month Celebration 2022">{{Cite web |date=February 24, 2022 |title=South Bend Black History Month Celebration 2022 |url=https://www.southbendin.gov/initiative/black-history-month-celebration-2022/ |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name="Cristal Brisco named St. Joseph Superior Court judge">{{Cite web |date=June 21, 2021 |title=Brisco named St. Joseph Superior Court judge |url=https://www.southbendtribune.com/story/news/local/2021/06/21/magistrate-cristal-brisco-named-st-joseph-superior-court-judge/7775147002/ |language=en-US}}</ref> From 2017 to 2018, she was [[general counsel]] to [[Saint Mary's College (Indiana)|Saint Mary's College, Notre Dame]]. From 2018 to 2021, she served as a magistrate judge on the [[St. Joseph County, Indiana|St. Joseph County]] Circuit Court in [[Mishawaka, Indiana]]. On June 3, 2021, she was appointed by Governor [[Eric Holcomb]] to serve as a judge of the [[St. Joseph County, Indiana|St. Joseph County]] [[Courts of Indiana|Superior Court]] in South Bend, Indiana<ref>{{Cite web |date=June 7, 2021 |title=Cristal Brisco '06 J.D. appointed as St. Joseph Superior Court judge |url=https://law.nd.edu/news-events/news/cristal-brisco-st-joseph-superior-court-judge/ |access-date=November 15, 2023 |website=The University of Notre Dame Law School |language=en}}</ref> and concurrently served as a judge on the Indiana Commercial Court from 2022 to 2024.<ref name="WHBio" />

=== Federal judicial service ===

On November 15, 2023, President [[Joe Biden]] announced his intent to nominate Brisco to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Indiana]].<ref name="WHBio" /> On November 27, 2023, her nomination was sent to the Senate. President Biden nominated Brisco to the seat vacated by Judge [[Theresa Lazar Springmann]], who assumed [[senior status]] on January 23, 2021.<ref name="TIL">{{Cite web |date=November 15, 2023 |title=Brisco, Lund nominated to IN Northern District Court |url=https://www.theindianalawyer.com/articles/brisco-lund-nominated-to-in-northern-district-court |access-date=November 15, 2023 |website=The Indiana Lawyer |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite press release |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |date=November 27, 2023 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2023/11/27/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-130/}}</ref> On December 13, 2023, a hearing on her nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Nominations|date=December 12, 2023|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/committee-activity/hearings/12/13/2023/nominations}}</ref> On January 3, 2024, her nomination was returned to the president under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]]<ref>{{Cite web |date=January 3, 2024 |title=PN1157 — Cristal C. Brisco — The Judiciary |url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/118th-congress/1157 |access-date=January 9, 2024 |website=congress.gov}}</ref> and she was renominated on January 8, 2024.<ref>{{Cite press release |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |date=January 3, 2024 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2024/01/08/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-133/}}</ref> On January 18, 2024, her nomination was reported out of committee by a 14–7 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/2024-01-18_-_ebm_-_results1.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – January 18, 2024|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=January 19, 2024}}</ref><ref>{{Cite press release |title=Senate Judiciary Committee Advances Twenty Judicial Nominations, One Executive Nomination to the Full Senate |date=January 18, 2024 |publisher=United States Senate Judiciary Committee |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/press/releases/senate-judiciary-committee-advances-twenty-judicial-nominations-one-executive-nomination-to-the-full-senate |access-date=January 18, 2024}}</ref> On January 24, 2024, the Senate invoked cloture on her nomination by a 68–29 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1182/vote_118_2_00019.htm|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Cristal C. Brisco to be U.S. District Judge for the Northern District of Indiana)|website=United States Senate|date=January 24, 2024|access-date=January 24, 2024}}</ref> Later that day, her nomination was confirmed by a 67–32 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1182/vote_118_2_00021.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Cristal C. Brisco, of Indiana, to be United States District Judge for the Northern District of Indiana)|website=United States Senate|date=January 24, 2024|access-date=January 24, 2024}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|last=Raymond|first=Nate|title=US Senate confirms two Biden judicial nominees in Republican-led states|url=https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/us-senate-confirms-two-biden-judicial-nominees-republican-led-states-2024-01-24/|website=Reuters|access-date=January 24, 2024}}</ref> She received her judicial commission on January 26, 2024.<ref>{{FJC Bio|nid=13761456|inline=yes}}</ref> She became the first Black woman to sit as a judge on the federal court serving northern Indiana.<ref name="Two Valpo grads nominated to fill federal judicial vacancies">{{Cite web |date= November 15, 2023 |title=Two Valpo grads nominated to fill judicial vacancies |url=https://www.nwitimes.com/news/local/crime-courts/federal-judicial-vacancies-valparaiso-university/article_9fc4feb4-83d8-11ee-a5b4-2b2b9d89294f.html |language=en-US}}</ref>

She received her [[Juris Doctor]] degree from the [[Washington College of Law]] in 2007.{{Cite press release |title=President Biden Names Ninth Round of Judicial Nominees |date=November 3, 2021 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/11/03/president-biden-names-ninth-round-of-judicial-nominees/ |access-date=November 3, 2021}} {{PD-notice}} == Career == From 2007 until 2010, Silva worked as an assistant state attorney in the [[Miami-Dade]] State Attorney's Office, serving as assistant chief of litigation for the [[domestic violence]] unit in 2010. She was deputy chief of the criminal division from 2013 to 2018 and chief of the criminal division from 2018 to 2019. During her time as a federal prosecutor, Silva assisted with the criminal investigation into the [[2017 Las Vegas shooting]] that killed 58 people in the initial shooting and injured about 500 others. In the years after, two more victims have died of shooting-related injuries.{{Cite web|url=https://www.reviewjournal.com/news/politics-and-government/nevada/nominees-for-us-judgeships-in-nevada-appear-headed-for-confirmation-2497061/|title = Nominees for US judgeships in Nevada appear headed for confirmation|date = 15 December 2021}}{{cite web | url=https://www.cnn.com/2023/04/07/us/las-vegas-2017-shooting-stephen-paddock-letters | title=Before Las Vegas mass shooting, a friend of the gunman implored him not to 'shoot or kill innocent people,' newspaper reports | website=[[CNN]] | date=8 April 2023 }} From 2019 to 2022, Silva served as a judge on the Eighth Judicial District Court, Department IX, in [[Clark County, Nevada|Clark County]] after being appointed by [[Governor of Nevada|Nevada Governor]] [[Steve Sisolak]].{{Cite web |title=Cristina D. Mahan]], who assumed [[senior status]] on June 29, 2018.{{Cite press release |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |date=November 3, 2021 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/11/03/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-43/}} {{PD-notice}} On December 15, 2021, a hearing on her nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web |title=Nominations |date=December 8, 2021 |publisher=[[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]] |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/12/08/2021/nominations}} On January 3, 2022, her nomination was returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]];{{Cite web |date=January 3, 2022 |title=PN1357 - Nomination of Cristina D. He was in the [[United States Air Force]] from 1974 to 1979. While in the Air Force, he was an Assistant Staff Judge Advocate in the [[United States Air Force Judge Advocate General's Corps|Judge Advocate General's Corps]] with the rank of Captain. He was an [[Assistant United States Attorney]] of the Eastern District of Louisiana from 1979 to 1987 and held the same office in the Eastern District of Tennessee from 1987 to 1995. ==Federal judicial service== Collier is a United States district judge of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Tennessee]]. He was nominated by President Bill Clinton on February 13, 1995, to a new seat created by 104 Stat. 5089. He was confirmed by the Senate on May 8, 1995, and received his commission on May 10, 1995. He served as chief judge from 2005 to 2012. [[University at Buffalo Law School|University at Buffalo]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | footnotes = }} '''Cynthia Marie Rufe''' (née '''Favata'''; born 1948) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania]]. ==Early life and education== Born in [[Philadelphia, Pennsylvania]], Rufe graduated from [[Adelphi University]] with her [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in 1970 and later from [[University at Buffalo Law School]] with a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1977. ==Career== Following law school graduation, Rufe served as a [[public defender]] in [[Bucks County, Pennsylvania|Bucks County]], Pennsylvania, spending much of her tenure there in the juvenile division. She became a deputy [[public defender]] in 1980. Soon thereafter, she left government service to practice privately. She practiced in her own firm for 11 years, gaining prominence in the local legal community. In 1994, she was elected as a judge of the Bucks County [[Pennsylvania Courts of Common Pleas|Court of Common Pleas]], where she served for eight years, until 2002. ===Federal judicial service=== On the recommendation of Senators [[Arlen Specter]] and [[Rick Santorum]], Rufe was nominated to the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania by President [[George W. Bush]] on January 23, 2002 to a seat vacated by Judge [[Norma Levy Shapiro]]. Rufe was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on April 30, 2002 and received her commission on May 3, 2002. She assumed [[senior status]] on December 31, 2021.{{FJC Bio|nid=1391516|inline=yes}} In February 2026, she ruled that panels depicting enslaved lives must be reinstated at the [[President's House (Philadelphia)|President's House]] site in Philadelphia.{{cite news |last1=Mackey |first1=Robert |title=US judge orders Trump administration to restore Philadelphia slavery exhibit |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/feb/16/philadelphia-slavery-exhibit |access-date=February 19, 2026 |work=The Guardian |date=February 17, 2026}}{{cite news |last1=Mitman |first1=Hayden |title=Judge sets deadline for Trump Administration to restore slavery exhibit |url=https://www.nbcphiladelphia.com/news/local/trump-administration-appeals-restoration-of-slavery-exhibit-at-presidents-house/4354746/ |access-date=19 February 2026 |work=NBC10 Philadelphia |date=18 February 2026}} In her judgement she quoted from [[George Orwell]]{{'s}} dystopian ''[[Nineteen Eighty-Four]]'' and wrote: {{blockquote|As if the Ministry of Truth in George Orwell's 1984 now existed, with its motto "Ignorance is Strength," this Court is now asked to determine whether the federal government has the power it claims—to dissemble and disassemble historical truths when it has some domain over historical facts. It does not.{{cite web |title=City of Philadelphia v. [[UCLA School of Law|University of California, Los Angeles]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Cynthia Valenzuela Dixon''' ({{nee|'''Valenzuela'''}}; born 1969){{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/valenzuela_sjq.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=May 21, 2024}} is an American lawyer who has served as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Central District of California]] since 2024. She previously served as a judge of the [[State Bar Court of California]] from 2016 to 2024. == Education == Valenzuela Dixon earned a [[Bachelor of Arts]] from the [[University of Arizona]] in 1991 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[UCLA School of Law]] in 1995.{{Cite press release |title=President Biden Names Forty-Eighth Round of Judicial Nominees |date=April 24, 2024 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2024/04/24/president-biden-names-forty-eighth-round-of-judicial-nominees/ |access-date=April 24, 2024}} {{PD-notice}} == Career == From 1995 to 1998, she was a special assistant at the [[United States Commission on Civil Rights]] in [[Los Angeles]]; from 1998 to 2000, she was a trial attorney in the [[United States Department of Justice Civil Rights Division|U.S. Department of Justice's Civil Rights Division]] in [[Washington, D.C.]]; from 2000 to 2006, she served as an [[assistant U.S. attorney]] in the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Central District of California. From 2006 to 2011, she was the head of national litigation at the [[Mexican American Legal Defense and Educational Fund]] in Los Angeles; from 2011 to 2016, she worked as the Criminal Justice Act Supervising Attorney for the Central District of California in Los Angeles. From 2016 to 2024, she served as a judge of the [[California State Bar Court]] in Los Angeles since her appointment by the [[California Supreme Court]]. === Federal judicial service === On April 24, 2024, President [[Joe Biden]] announced his intent to nominate Valenzuela Dixon to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Central District of California]]. He received a [[Juris Doctor]] from Harvard Law School ''[[cum laude]]'' in 1969 and served as the Supreme Court Note and Developments Editor of the Harvard Law Review.{{cite web|title=Hornby, David Brock - Federal Judicial Center|url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/hornby-david-brock|website=Federal Judicial Center|accessdate=13 November 2017|ref=FJC Bio}}{{cite web|last1=Reiss|first1=Christina|title=Learning from the Best, the Brightest, and the Kindest: An Interview with the Honorable D. Brock Hornby|url=http://www.med.uscourts.gov/news/portrait-unveiling-ceremony-judge-d-brock-hornby|publisher=United States District Court, District of Maine|accessdate=13 November 2017|ref=Portrait}}{{cite web|title=Court History, District of Maine|url=http://www.med.uscourts.gov/court-history|accessdate=13 November 2017|ref=DMeHistory}} ==Career== Following law school, Hornby was a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[John Minor Wisdom]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]] in New Orleans (1969–70).{{cite book|title=Almanac of the Federal Judiciary|publisher=2018 WL 246294|location=Westlaw|ref=Almanac}} Hornby taught law at the [[University of Virginia School of Law]] (1970-1974), becoming an Associate Professor and receiving tenure in 1973. He became a naturalized United States citizen in Abingdon Virginia. Hornby engaged in the private practice of law at Perkins, Thompson, Hinckley & Keddy in [[Portland, Maine|Portland]], [[Maine]] (1974–82; partner from 1975). He held various officer and board positions including that of President (1977–79) at the Portland Society of Art (1975–84), which then operated both the Portland Museum of Art and the Portland School of Art (now Maine College of Art) during a period when the School attained national accreditation and the Museum embarked on its ambitious expansion program engaging Henry M. Cobb of Pei Cobb Freed & Partners to design the new Museum building with the support of Charles Shipman Payson. Hornby served as trustee and member of various committees (including the executive committee) of Westbrook College (1979–85, 1986–90) (now part of University of New England). He served on the board of the Chamber of Commerce of the Greater Portland Region (1979–82). He also served on the boards of various other charitable and civic endeavors.{{cite web|last1=Coffin|first1=Frank|title=Remarks at the Induction of United States District Judge D. Brock Hornby|url=http://files.mainelaw.maine.edu/Coffin/Public_Speeches/pdf/VI-JudgeHornby.pdf|accessdate=15 November 2017|date=June 11, 1990}} ==Judicial service== [[File:Judge D. Brock Hornby (cropped).jpg|thumb|right|Hornby in 2018]] Hornby was the first full-time [[United States magistrate judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Maine]] (1982-1988). He was succeeded by Magistrate Judge David M. Cohen. In 1988, Maine Governor John A. McKernan appointed Hornby an associate justice of the [[Maine Supreme Judicial Court]] to fill a seat vacated by Justice David Nichols. Hornby served there until 1990 and was succeeded by Justice Morton A. Brody.{{cite web|title=Justices of the Supreme Judicial Court of the State of Maine, 1820 to 2009|url=http://www.cleaves.org/sjcbios1.htm#DBH|website=Cleaves Law Library|accessdate=13 November 2017|ref=Cleaves}} President [[George H. W. Bush]] appointed Hornby a United States District Judge in the District of Maine in 1990 to fill a seat made vacant by the appointment of [[Conrad Cyr]] to the First Circuit. Hornby was confirmed by the [[U.S. Senate]] on April 27, 1990. He served as [[Chief judge (United States)|chief judge]] of the court from 1996 to 2003. Hornby assumed [[senior status]] on May 1, 2010, and inactive senior status on February 28, 2022.{{cite web|url=https://www.med.uscourts.gov/sites/med/files/Judge-Hornby-Inactive-Senior-Status-Announcement.pdf|title=D. Brock Hornby Takes Inactive Senior Status|work=U.S. District Court, District of Maine|year=2022}} Hornby was succeeded in the position by [[Nancy Torresen]]. ==Awards for judicial service== In 2009, Hornby received the 27th Annual Edward J. Devitt Distinguished Service to Justice Award. The Devitt Award is the highest honor that can be bestowed on a federal judge.{{cite web|title=Dwight D. Opperman Foundation - The Devitt Award|url=http://www.oppermanfoundation.org/devitt-award|accessdate=13 November 2017|ref=Opperman}}{{Dead link|date=July 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}{{cite news|last1=Harrison|first1=Judy|title=Hornby gets top honor in federal judiciary|url=http://bangordailynews.com/2009/09/14/politics/hornby-gets-top-honor-in-federal-judiciary/|accessdate=13 November 2017|work=Bangor Daily News|date=September 14, 2009|ref=BDN}}{{cite web|title=Maine Jurist Receives Devitt Award|url=http://www.uscourts.gov/ttb/2009-06/article10.cfm?WT.cg_n=TTB&WT.cg_s=June09_article10_tableOfContents|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100410103937/http://www.uscourts.gov/ttb/2009-06/article10.cfm?WT.cg_n=TTB&WT.cg_s=June09_article10_tableOfContents|url-status=dead|archive-date=10 April 2010|publisher=The Third Branch: Newsletter of the Federal Courts|accessdate=13 November 2017|ref=Third Branch}} In 2014, Hornby received an Honorary Doctor of Laws degree and the [[Morton A. Brody Distinguished Judicial Service Award]] from Colby College, given to a judge "who embodies the qualities of integrity, compassion, humanity, and judicial craftsmanship exhibited by Judge Brody."{{cite web|title=Morton A. Brody Distinguished Judicial Service Award: D. Brock Hornby|url=http://www.colby.edu/events/morton-a-brody-distinguished-judicial-service-award-d-brock-hornby/|publisher=Colby College|accessdate=13 November 2017|ref=Colby}}{{cite web|title=Goldfarb Award Past Recipients. 2014: D. Brock Hornby|url=http://www.colby.edu/goldfarb/brodyaward/past-recipients/861-2/|publisher=Goldfarb Center for Public Affairs and Civic Engagement|accessdate=13 November 2017|ref=Colby}}{{cite journal|title=The Honorable D. Brock Hornby Receives 2014 Morton A. Brody Distinguished Judicial Service Award|journal=Goldfarb Magazine|date=2013–2014|page=9|url=http://www.colby.edu/goldfarb/wp-content/uploads/sites/98/2014/09/14-107_GC-2014-Goldfarb-Magazine_v10.pdf|accessdate=13 November 2017}} In April 2014, the Maine Legislature passed a resolution recognizing Hornby's achievement.{{cite web|title=Senate Legislative Record, One Hundred and Twenty-Sixth Legislature|url=http://lldc.mainelegislature.org/Open/LegRec/126/Senate/LegRec126vSD_pSA0001-0099_Sentiments.pdf|publisher=Maine State Legislature|ref=MeLegis|pages=69–70}} ==Other activities during judicial service== '''Writing and speaking''' As a judge, apart from judicial opinions, Hornby has focused his writing on less formal genres. He is a frequent contributor to the Green Bag, an "entertaining journal of law" dedicated to good legal writing.{{cite web|title=Green Bag literature|url=http://www.greenbag.org/green_bag_press/green_bag_press.html|accessdate=13 November 2017|ref=Green Bag}} Hornby's writing has also appeared in publications such as Judicature, The ALI Reporter, the Maine Bar Journal, The Federal Lawyer, The Journal of Appellate Practice and Process, In Camera, FCCA Journal, Judges' Journal, Litigation, and FJC Directions. While the federal judiciary was seeking salary restoration, Hornby also wrote and spoke on that topic.{{cite web|last1=Hornby|first1=D. Brock|title=Judicial Compensation and the Quality of the Judiciary|url=http://www.metrocorpcounsel.com/articles/8770/judicial-compensation-and-quality-judiciary|website=Metropolitan Corporate Counsel|accessdate=13 November 2017|date=September 1, 2007}}{{Dead link|date=July 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}{{cite web|last1=Hornby|first1=D. Brock|title=Judicial Salaries: An Urgent Need Unmet|url=http://www.fedbar.org/Resources_1/Federal-Lawyer-Magazine/2009/The%20Federal%20Lawyer%20October%202009/Features/Judicial-Salaries-An-Urgent-Need-Unmet.aspx?FT=.pdf|publisher=The Federal Lawyer|accessdate=13 November 2017|date=October 2009}}{{Dead link|date=July 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} The Green Bag has published "Beatitudes and Jeremiads"{{cite web |url=http://greenbag.org/v17n4/v17n4_ex_post_hornby.pdf |title=Beatitudes and Jeremiads |website=Green Bag |language=en-US |access-date=2019-12-09|ref=Beatitudes}} as well as several chapters of Hornby's "Fables in Law: Legal Lessons from Field, Forest, and Glen," Aesopian legal fables for lawyers, judges, and law professors.{{cite web|title=Fables in Law, Chapter 13 |url=http://greenbag.org/v22n3/v22n3_ex_post_hornby.pdf |publisher=Green Bag |accessdate=2019-12-09|ref=Fables}} Judicature has published three "imagined conversations" among fictitious former law school classmates now well along in their careers, on the topics of judicial opinion writing, the decline in federal civil trials, and public attention to federal judges. Hornby uses his characters, including the federal trial lawyer Talagud Storey and the general counsel Manny G. Risk, to canvas the major issues surrounding these topics. Hornby has also written about criminal sentencing and summary judgment. Hornby has taught other judges in the United States and in foreign countries.{{cite web|title=Maine Life Fellow D. Brock Hornby|url=http://www.americanbarfoundation.org/fellows/news/191|publisher=American Bar Foundation|ref=ABF|date=June 22, 2009}} He has spoken publicly at commencements and ceremonies honoring other judges and lawyers.{{cite web|title=U.S. District Court Judge D. Brock Hornby to Speak at Maine Law's Commencement|url=https://usm.maine.edu/publicaffairs/us-district-court-judge-d-brock-hornby-speak-maine-laws-commencement|publisher=University of Southern Maine|accessdate=13 November 2017}}{{cite web|title=Judge Hornby Asks Maine Law Graduates to Value and Preserve Constitutional Democracy|url=https://usm.maine.edu/publicaffairs/judge-hornby-asks-maine-law-graduates-value-and-preserve-constitutional-democracy|publisher=University of Southern Maine|accessdate=13 November 2017}}{{cite journal|title=Remarks at Ceremony for the Honorable Sandra Day O'Connor By the Honorable D. Brock Hornby, Judge of the United States District Court for the District of Maine and ALI Council member|journal=Proceedings of ALI Annual Meetings: 83rd Annual Meeting, Proceedings 2006|page=248|publisher=The American Law Institute}}{{cite journal|title=Presentation by Judge D. Brock Hornby of John Minor Wisdom Award to Guy Miller Struve, Esquire, Life Member of the American Law Institute|journal=Proceedings of ALI Annual Meetings: 88th Annual Meeting, Proceedings 2011|date=May 16, 2011|page=58|publisher=The American Law Institute}} For many years he updated pattern jury instructions for district courts within the First Circuit Court of Appeals (now updated by Judge Torresen){{cite web|title=Portrait Unveiling Ceremony for Judge D. Brock Hornby|url=https://www.ali.org/news/articles/portrait-unveiling-ceremony-judge-d-brock-hornby/|publisher=American Law Institute|accessdate=16 November 2017|date=August 31, 2016}}{{cite web|title=District of Maine 2017 Revisions to Pattern Criminal Jury Instructions for the District Courts of the First Circuit, Preface to the 1998 Edition|url=http://www.med.uscourts.gov/pdf/crpjilinks.pdf|accessdate=16 November 2017|archive-date=5 September 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170905041811/http://www.med.uscourts.gov/pdf/crpjilinks.pdf|url-status=dead}} and a case-based manual for opening statements and closing arguments in jury trials.{{cite web|last1=Hornby|first1=Brock|title=Summary of First Circuit Authority and Local Rules Concerning Opening Statements and Closing Arguments|url=http://www.med.uscourts.gov/pdf/OpeningAndClosing.pdf|accessdate=16 November 2017|date=June 15, 2017|archive-date=4 March 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180304100003/http://www.med.uscourts.gov/pdf/OpeningAndClosing.pdf|url-status=dead}} '''Committees and boards''' Hornby has served on numerous committees and boards. When Hornby became a United States District Judge, Chief Justice Rehnquist appointed him to the Judicial Conference's [[Committee on Court Administration and Case Management]] (CACM) (1990-2000; chair 1997–2000) and as chair of the FJC's Committee on District Judge Education (1995–98). Hornby served on the Judicial Conference itself from 2000 to 2003. The Chief Justice appointed him to the executive committee (2002–03), the Judicial Conduct and Disability Act Study Committee (2004–06), and as chair of the Committee on the Judicial Branch (2005-2012). In 2007, Chief Justice Roberts appointed Hornby chair of an ad hoc committee to secure federal judge salary restoration. Hornby's committee duties have included testifying before Congress.{{cite web|title=Statement of Judge D. Brock Hornby on Behalf of the Judicial Conference of the United States Before the Committee on the Judiciary, Hearing on Judicial Security and Independence|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/hornby_testimony_02_14_07.pdf|publisher=United States Senate}} Judge Hornby was elected to the Council of the American Law Institute in 1996 (ALI member since 1979), and took emeritus status in 2017. He was an Adviser on the Restatement of the Law (Third), Restitution and Unjust Enrichment and Chair of the Awards Committee.{{cite web|title=ALI Members - The Hon. D. Brock Hornby|url=https://www.ali.org/members/member/102945/|publisher=The American Law Institute|accessdate=13 November 2017}} Hornby was a Member of the National Academies' Standing Committee on Science, Technology, and Law (2006–13). ==Selected publications== "History Lessons: Instructive Legal Episodes from Maine's Early Years — Episode 3: An Enslaved Man Suing in Federal Court," vol. 26, no. 2 Green Bag 2d 101 (Winter 2023). [[Yale Law School|Yale University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Dabney Langhorne Friedrich''' (née '''Patricia Dabney Langhorne'''; born 1967){{cite web |title=Friedrich, Dabney Langhorne |url=https://www.fjc.gov/node/4022586 |publisher=Federal Judicial Center |access-date=14 June 2019}} is an American attorney and jurist serving as a [[United States federal judge|United States district court judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Columbia]]. She previously served as a member of the [[United States Sentencing Commission]]. ==Early life and education== Patricia Dabney Langhorne was born in 1967, in [[Pensacola, Florida]]. She graduated from [[Trinity University (Texas)|Trinity University]] in 1988 with a [[Bachelor of Arts]], ''[[Latin honors|magna cum laude]]''. She spent one year at [[University College, Oxford]], receiving a Diploma in Legal Studies in 1989. She then attended [[Yale Law School]], where she was a senior editor of the ''[[Yale Journal on Regulation]]''. She graduated in 1992 with a [[Juris Doctor]].{{cite news|title=WEDDINGS; Dabney Langhorne, Matthew Friedrich|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2001/01/21/style/weddings-dabney-langhorne-matthew-friedrich.html?mcubz=1|access-date=June 12, 2017|work=New York Times|date=January 21, 2001}}{{cite web |title=Senate Judiciary Questionnaire – Dabney L. Friedrich |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Friedrich%20SJQ.pdf |access-date=1 September 2023}} ==Career== Langhorne started her legal career as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Thomas F. Hogan]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Columbia]]. She served as an associate counsel to the president during the [[George W. Bush administration]], as chief crime counsel to Senator [[Orrin Hatch]], as an [[assistant United States attorney]] in the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia|Eastern District of Virginia]], as a trial attorney at the [[United States Department of Justice]], and as an assistant United States attorney in the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of California|Southern District of California]].{{cite news|last1=Tillman|first1=Zoe|title=The White House Is Preparing To Make A Move On The DC Federal Trial Court|url=https://www.buzzfeed.com/zoetillman/the-white-house-is-interviewing-candidates-for-the-dc|access-date=June 12, 2017|publisher=BuzzFeed News|date=April 14, 2017}}{{cite web|title=Dabney Friedrich|url=https://ballotpedia.org/Dabney_Friedrich|publisher=Ballotpedia|access-date=June 12, 2017}} In 2006, Friedrich was nominated by President [[George W. Bush]]{{Cite web|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate|url=https://georgewbush-whitehouse.archives.gov/news/releases/2006/08/20060802-4.html|access-date=2021-12-13|website=georgewbush-whitehouse.archives.gov}} as a member of the [[United States Sentencing Commission]] (and ultimately confirmed by the Senate on February 28, 2007{{Cite web|date=2007-02-28|title=PN34 - Nomination of Dabney Langhorne Friedrich for United States Sentencing Commission, 110th Congress (2007-2008)|url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/110th-congress/34|access-date=2021-12-13|website=www.congress.gov}}), a position she held until 2016.{{cite web|url=https://ballotpedia.org/Dabney_Friedrich|title=Dabney Friedrich - Ballotpedia|publisher=}} In that capacity, she helped establish sentencing policies and practices for the federal criminal justice system by promulgating guidelines for congressional review and recommending changes in criminal statutes.{{cite web|url=https://www.whitehouse.gov/the-press-office/2017/05/08/president-donald-j-trump-announces-judicial-candidate-nominations|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170509012131/https://www.whitehouse.gov/the-press-office/2017/05/08/president-donald-j-trump-announces-judicial-candidate-nominations|url-status=dead|archive-date=2017-05-09|title="President Donald J. Trump Announces Judicial Candidate Nominations" White House, May 8, 2017|publisher=}} === Federal judicial service === On May 8, 2017, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to nominate Friedrich to serve as a United States district judge of the United States District Court for the District of Columbia, to a seat vacated by [[Reggie Walton]], who assumed [[senior status]] on December 31, 2015.{{cite web|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2017/06/07/president-donald-j-trump-announces-judicial-candidate-nominations|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Donald J. Trump Announces Judicial Candidate Nominations}} She was formally nominated on June 7, 2017.{{cite web|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2017/06/07/twelve-nominations-sent-senate-today|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Twelve Nominations Sent to the Senate Today}} On July 25, 2017, the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] held a hearing on her nomination.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/07/25/2017/nominations|title=Nominations - United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|website=www.judiciary.senate.gov|date=July 25, 2017 }} Her nomination was reported out of [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|committee]] by a [[voice vote]] on September 14, 2017.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/09-14-17%20Results%20of%20Exeuctive%20Business%20Meeting.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – September 14, 2017|publisher=Senate Judiciary Committee}} On November 16, 2017, the [[United States Senate]] invoked cloture on her nomination by a 93–4 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=115&session=1&vote=00279|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Dabney Langhorne Friedrich, of California, to be U.S. District Judge for the District of Columbia)|website=United States Senate}} On November 27, 2017, her nomination was confirmed by a 97–3 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=115&session=1&vote=00281|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Dabney Langhorne Friedrich, of California, to be United States District Judge for the District of Columbia)|website=United States Senate}} She received her judicial commission on December 1, 2017.{{FJC Bio|nid=4022586|inline=yes}} Friedrich is a [[feeder judge]]. Since 2019, she has sent more of her clerks to the [[Supreme Court of the United States|Supreme Court]] than any other district court judge in the country.{{cite news|title=These Judges Feed the Most Law Clerks to the U.S. Supreme Court|url=https://www.law.com/nationallawjournal/2023/07/19/katsas-sutton-top-list-of-judges-who-feed-most-law-clerks-to-supreme-court/|access-date=July 20, 2024|work=Law.com|date=July 19, 2023}} ==== Concord Management and Consulting ==== In June 2018, Friedrich rejected Russian-owned [[Concord Management and Consulting]]'s request that she examine the instructions provided to the grand jury before the jury indicted the company. Concord accused Special Counsel [[Robert Mueller]]'s prosecutors of giving faulty instructions, tainting the grand jury's decision to approve charges.{{cite news|url=https://www.cnn.com/2018/06/15/politics/concord-ruling-special-counsel-russian-company/index.html|title=Judge rejects request by Russian firm to review Mueller's grand jury instructions|website=[[CNN]]|date=June 15, 2018|last=Cohen|first=Marshall}} On August 13, 2018, in the case of ''United States v. Concord Management and Consulting LCC'', she ruled against the defendant, one of 16 Russian entities charged by Special Counsel [[Robert Mueller]], when it sought to void its indictment on the ground that Mueller's appointment to his position violated constitutional separation of powers. In a 41-page opinion, she held that although "no statute explicitly authorizes the Acting Attorney General to make the appointment, Supreme Court and D.C. Circuit precedent make clear that the Acting Attorney General has the necessary statutory authority," "the appointment does not violate core separation-of-powers principles. Nor has the Special Counsel exceeded his authority under the appointment order by investigating and prosecuting Concord."{{cite web|url=https://assets.documentcloud.org/documents/4754539/Concord-Management-20180813.pdf|title=United States of America v. Concord Management & Consulting LLC, USDC/D.DC 18-cr-0032-2 (DLF)|date=August 13, 2018}}{{cite web|title=US judge rejects Russian company's bid to dismiss Mueller charges|url=https://thehill.com/policy/national-security/401543-us-judge-rejects-russian-companys-bid-to-dismiss-mueller-charges/|website=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]]|date=August 13, 2018|access-date=August 13, 2018|last=Chalfant|first=Morgan}} In January 2019, Friedrich strongly rebuked the attorneys for [[Concord Management and Consulting]] for repeatedly making personal attacks on Mueller's team. The rebuke was triggered by a January 4 filing that questioned the trustworthiness of Mueller's office. Friedrich called Concord's recent filings "unprofessional, inappropriate, and ineffective," and said their "relentless personal attacks" would not affect her decision.{{cite web|title=A Judge Told The Defense In The Russian Troll Farm Case To "Knock It Off" With Attacks On Mueller's Office|url=https://www.buzzfeednews.com/article/zoetillman/russian-troll-farm-robert-mueller-lawyer|website=[[BuzzFeed News]]|date=January 7, 2019|access-date=January 7, 2019|last=Tillman|first=Zoe}} ==== ''Alabama Association of Realtors v. HHS'' ==== In May 2021, Friedrich vacated the temporary federal [[eviction]] [[Moratorium (law)|moratorium]] issued by the [[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]], which had been extended multiple times since being enacted by the previous [[First presidency of Donald Trump|Trump administration]]. She ruled that the [[Public Health Service Act]] did not grant the CDC the legal authority to impose a nationwide eviction moratorium. Under the [[Presidency of Joe Biden|Biden administration]], the CDC had sought an extension of the eviction moratorium, through June 30.{{Cite web|last=Rummler|first=Orion|title=Federal judge overturns CDC's eviction moratorium|url=https://www.axios.com/eviction-moratorium-cdc-judge-22290142-d045-4f50-88eb-4ee71642c0c4.html|access-date=2021-05-05|website=Axios|date=May 5, 2021 |language=en}} ==== Trial of Pan Am Flight 103 bombing suspect ==== As of 2026, Friedrich is presiding over the planned trial of 1988 Pan Am 103 bombing suspect [[Abu Agila Masud|Abu Agila Mohammad Mas'ud Kheir Al-Marimi]] In August 2026, Friedrich temporarily delayed Al-Marimi's trial which was planned to being that month, citing the case's complex nature, some newly discovered evidence and "the need for the defense to determine how best to defend this case." {{Cite web |date=2026-08-24 |title=Judge postpones U.S. trial for Libyan man accused in deadly 1988 Lockerbie bombing, citing new evidence - CBS News |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/lockerbie-bombing-suspect-us-trial-postponed-new-evidence/ |access-date=2026-11-23 |website=www.cbsnews.com |language=en-US}} On October 5, 2026, Friedrich officially set for Al-Marimi's trial to begin on January 19, 2027.{{Cite web |date=2026-10-05 |title=Lockerbie bombing trial date set as judge warns against further delay |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c699zvzenxp7o |access-date=2026-11-23 |website=www.bbc.com |language=en-GB}} ==References== {{Reflist|30em}} ==External links== * {{FJC Bio|nid=4022586}} * [http://www.dcd.uscourts.gov/content/district-judge-dabney-l-friedrich Biography at District Court for the District of Columbia] * {{Ballotpedia|Dabney_Friedrich|Dabney Friedrich}} {{s-start}} {{s-gov}} {{s-bef|before=Michael E. [[UCLA School of Law|University of California, Los Angeles]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | occupation = | profession = | known_for = | salary = | net_worth = | cabinet = | committees = | portfolio = | awards = | signature = | signature_alt = | website = | footnotes = }} '''Dale Alan Drozd''' (born 1955) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of California]] and former [[United States magistrate judge|Chief United States magistrate judge]] of the same court. ==Early life and education== Drozd was born in 1955, in [[Los Angeles County, California]]. He is a 1973 graduate of [[Servite High School]], in [[Anaheim, California|Anaheim]]. He attended the [[University of Southern California]] from 1973 to 1975, graduated from [[San Diego State University]] with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in 1977, and he received a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1980 from the [[University of California, Los Angeles, School of Law]].{{cite web| url=http://www.caed.uscourts.gov/caednew/index.cfm/judges/all-judges/5017/ |title=Chief Magistrate Judge Dale A. Drozd |publisher= United States District Court, Eastern District of California| access-date= October 16, 2013}}{{FJC Bio|nid=1394801|inline=yes}} == Career == After graduation Drozd served as a law clerk to Judge [[Lawrence K. Karlton]] of the United States District Judge Eastern District of California from 1980 to 1982 and was in private practice of law for 15 years in [[San Francisco]] and [[Sacramento, California|Sacramento]]. === Federal judicial service === The judges of the United States District Court of the Eastern District of California appointed Drozd to be a [[United States magistrate judge]] in 1997 and he was appointed as chief United States magistrate judge of the same court in 2010. He served as chief judge from January 1, 2011, until his appointment as district judge. On November 12, 2014, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Drozd to serve as a judge on the United States District Court for the [[Eastern District of California]], to the seat vacated by [[Anthony W. Ishii]], who assumed [[senior status]] on October 31, 2012.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/11/12/president-obama-nominates-two-serve-united-states-district-courts|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Obama Nominates Two to Serve on the United States District Courts|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=November 12, 2014}}{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/11/12/presidential-nominations-sent-senate|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=November 12, 2014}} On December 16, 2014, his nomination was returned to the president due to the [[sine die]] adjournment of the [[113th United States Congress|113th Congress]]. On January 7, 2015, President Obama renominated him to the same position.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2015/01/07/presidential-nominations-sent-senate|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=January 7, 2015}} He received a hearing before the [[United States Senate Judiciary Committee]] on May 6, 2015.{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/nominations-2015-05-06|title=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|website=www.judiciary.senate.gov}} On June 4, 2015, his nomination was reported out of committee by [[voice vote]] with [[Senator Vitter]] recorded as voting no.{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%20for%2006-04-152.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – June 4, 2015}} On October 5, 2015, the [[United States Senate]] confirmed him by a 69–21 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=114&session=1&vote=00274|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Dale A.
