[[University of Utah College of Law|University of Utah]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | footnotes = }} '''Dale Albert Kimball'''{{cite web|url=https://archive.org/stream/confirmationhear972unit#page/574/mode/2up/search/%22Dale+Albert%22|title=Biographical Information (Public)|page=574|work=Confirmation hearings on federal appointments: Hearings before the Committee on the Judiciary, United States Senate, One Hundred Fifth Congress|date=1997 }} (born 1939){{cite web|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=A7dFAQAAIAAJ&q=%22Kimball,+Dale+A%22+1939|title=Judicial Staff Directory 2008/Winter|first=Claudia Driggins|last=Henley|date=10 December 2007|publisher=CQ Press|via=Google Books}} is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Utah]].{{cite web|url=http://www.utd.uscourts.gov/judges/kimball.html|title=JUDGE DALE A. KIMBALL|website=www.utd.uscourts.gov|access-date=2008-12-16|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170107013849/http://www.utd.uscourts.gov/judges/kimball.html|archive-date=2017-01-07|url-status=dead}} ==Early life and education== Kimball was born in [[Provo, Utah|Provo]], [[Utah]], grew up on a dairy farm in [[Draper, Utah|Draper]], Utah, and worked in the fields where his family grew alfalfa, sugar beets, and grain. He continued to work on the family farm throughout his schooling, including his time in law school. His family sold their farm to the Catholic Diocese in 1996 and it is now the site of the Skaggs Catholic Center, which houses Juan Diego High School. Kimball first became interested in law while taking a commercial law class from E.L. Crawford at Jordan High School.{{cite web|url=http://www.fedbar.org/Chapters/Utah-Chapter/Judicial-Profiles/US-District-Judge-Dale-Kimball.aspx?FT=.pdf|title=Judicial Profile: Dale Kimball|publisher=|access-date=2011-10-24|archive-date=2012-04-15|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120415092946/http://www.fedbar.org/Chapters/Utah-Chapter/Judicial-Profiles/US-District-Judge-Dale-Kimball.aspx?FT=.pdf|url-status=dead}} Kimball graduated magna cum laude from [[Brigham Young University]] with a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree in [[political science]]. In 1967, he received his [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Utah College of Law]], graduating [[Order of the Coif]] and second in his class. While attending law school, Kimball was a member of the [[Phi Kappa Phi]] honor society and was the Case Note Editor of the Utah Law Review. ==Career== After graduating from law school, Kimball began his legal practice at Van Cott, Bagley, Cornwall & McCarthy in [[Salt Lake City]], Utah, where Kimball maintained a full-time general practice until 1974. In 1974, Kimball became a full-time law professor at BYU's [[J. Reuben Clark Law School]]. In his second year as a full-time professor, Kimball also co-founded the law firm formerly known as Kimball, Parr, Waddoups, Brown & Gee. The firm is now known as Parr, Brown, Gee & Loveless. Kimball continued to teach part-time at BYU from 1976 to 1980. From 1975 until his appointment as a United States District Judge in 1997, Kimball maintained a full-time legal practice, primarily in commercial litigation. === Federal judicial service === On September 4, 1997, President [[Bill Clinton]] nominated Kimball as a United States district judge of the [[United States District Court for the District of Utah]]. Kimball's nomination was confirmed by the United States Senate on October 21, 1997, and he received his commission on October 24, 1997. On November 24, 1997, Kimball was sworn in as a United States District Judge. Kimball replaced the Judge [[David K. Winder]], who took [[senior status]] in June 1997. After twelve years as a full-time district court judge, Kimball took senior status on November 30, 2009.{{FJC Bio|nid=1390526|inline=yes}} ===Notable cases=== During his time on the bench, Kimball has presided over many notable cases, such as the [[Brian David Mitchell]] criminal trial, case no. 2:08cr125DAK.[Case Number 2:08cr125DAK][Case Number 2:03cv688DAK] In the case of ''Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance v. Norton'', Case No. 2:99cv852DAK,[Case Number 2:99cv852DAK] Judge Kimball's decision was reversed by the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit|Tenth Circuit]], but the [[Supreme Court of the United States|United States Supreme Court]] then reversed the Tenth Circuit and affirmed Judge Kimball (9-0), ''[[Norton v. Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance|Norton v SUWA]]'', 542 U.S. 55 (2004). More than 800 of his memorandum decisions appear on Westlaw. In 1999, Kimball sat [[by designation]] with the Tenth Circuit of Appeals, authoring two published opinions and two unpublished opinions: ''Zeran v. Diamond Broadcasting, Inc.'', 203 F.3d 714 (10th Cir, 2000); and ''United States v. Moore'', 198 F.3d 793 (10th Cir. 1999); ''Hutchinson v. Pfeil'', 201 F.3d 448 (10th Cir. 1999) (unpublished); ''Standard v. Union Pacific Railroad Co.'', 198 F.3d 258 (10th Cir. 1999) (unpublished). In May 2009, to help with the congested dockets of a neighboring district, Kimball sat by designation in the [[United States District Court for the District of Idaho]]. ===Brian David Mitchell and Wanda Barzee=== After defendant [[Brian David Mitchell]] was declared incompetent to stand trial in Utah state court for the alleged [[Kidnapping of Elizabeth Smart|kidnapping]] of [[Elizabeth Smart]], he and co-defendant [[Wanda Barzee]] were indicted by a federal grand jury for kidnapping and unlawful transportation of a minor. On May 25, 2011, Judge Kimball sentenced Mitchell to life in prison under the federal sentencing guidelines and the sentencing factors found in 18 U.S.C. § 3553a. Mitchell decided not to appeal. After being declared competent to stand trial as a result of forced medication ordered by the state court, Wanda Barzee entered into a plea agreement with the federal government. Judge Kimball sentenced Barzee on November 17, 2009, to 15 years in prison.{{cite web|url=http://www.sltrib.com/ci_14492043|title=Utah Local News - Salt Lake City News, Sports, Archive - The Salt Lake Tribune|first=The Salt Lake|last=Tribune|website=www.sltrib.com|access-date=2011-12-23|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100304170434/http://www.sltrib.com/ci_14492043|archive-date=2010-03-04|url-status=dead}} ==Community and professional service== Kimball is a member of [[the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints]] and has served in many leadership positions within the church, including [[Bishop (Latter Day Saints)|bishop]], high councilor, [[Stake president#Stake officers|stake president]], and [[Regional representative of the Twelve]].''Deseret News'', May 3, 2003 === Former activities === * Chairman of Utah State Bar Judicial Performance Evaluation Committee * Chairman of Utah State Bar Ethics and Discipline Committee * Chairman of Utah State Bar Committee on the Unauthorized Practice of Law * Counselor to the Inn of the American Inn of Court I * Member of Utah Federal District Court, Mediation/Arbitration Panels * Chairman of Pioneer Theater Board * Member of Deseret News Publishing Company Board of Directors and Member of * Executive Committee * Member of Alta View Hospital Board of Governors * Member of Jordan Education Foundation Board * Trustee of University of Utah College of Law Alumni Board * Member of Board of Salt Lake chapter of [[J. Reuben Clark Law Society]] * Member of Judicial Conference Committee on Administration of the Bankruptcy System * Member of Tenth Circuit Judicial Conference === Current activities === * Fellow of the American Bar Foundation * Master of the Bench for the American Inn of Court I * Member of the Board of Federal Bar Association, Salt Lake Chapter * Member of the Judicial Conference Committee on Criminal Law ==Awards and publications== Kimball graduated second in his class at the University of Utah College of Law and was elected to the [[Order of the Coif]]. Order of the Coif is an honorary scholastic society consisting of members graduating in the top ten percent of their class. In 1996, Kimball was honored by the Utah State Bar as the "Distinguished Lawyer of the Year". In 2010, Kimball was honored by the Federal Bar Association, Salt Lake Chapter as the "Judge of the Year". ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1390526}} *[https://web.archive.org/web/20170107013849/http://www.utd.uscourts.gov/judges/kimball.html Judge Dale A. He then received his [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Yale Law School]] in 2005.{{cite press release|title=President Biden Names Eighth Round of Judicial Nominees|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/09/30/president-biden-names-eighth-round-of-judicial-nominees/|date=September 30, 2021|publisher=White House Press Office}} ==Career== Ho served as a [[law clerk]] to Judge [[Barbara S. Jones]] of the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York from 2005 to 2006 and Associate Judge [[Robert S. Smith]] of the [[New York Court of Appeals]] from 2006 to 2007.{{Cite web |title=Fried Frank Fellowship Opens Doors |url=https://www.friedfrank.com/siteFiles/Site%20Pages/Fried%20Frank%20Fellowship%20Opens%20Doors%20.pdf |access-date=October 5, 2021 |website=www.friedfrank.com |archive-date=October 22, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211022185147/https://www.friedfrank.com/siteFiles/Site%20Pages/Fried%20Frank%20Fellowship%20Opens%20Doors%20.pdf |url-status=dead }} Through a one-year Fried Frank Civil Rights Fellowship, he worked for the law firm [[Fried, Frank, Harris, Shriver & Jacobson]] as an [[NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund|NAACP Legal Defense & Educational Fund, Inc.]] (NAACP LDF) Fellow from 2007 to 2009. He then worked as a staff attorney with the NAACP LDF from 2009 to 2013,{{Cite press release|title=LDF Issues Statement on President Biden's New Judicial Nominees |url=https://www.naacpldf.org/press-release/ldf-issues-statement-on-president-bidens-new-judicial-nominees/ |access-date=October 5, 2021 |website=www.naacpldf.org}} where he worked on [[legislative redistricting]] projects, including anti-[[gerrymandering]] efforts.{{cite news |last1=Service |first1=Ronnie EllisCNHI News |title=Lawmaker wants prisoners to be counted in redistricting |url=https://www.richmondregister.com/news/local_news/lawmaker-wants-prisoners-to-be-counted-in-redistricting/article_1734fe88-0acc-56be-b3fe-e2a7069a2928.html |access-date=March 25, 2021 |work=Richmond Register |date=August 24, 2011 |language=en}} In 2013, Ho became Director of the [[American Civil Liberties Union]] (ACLU) Voting Rights Project. In 2014, Ho began teaching election law as an Adjunct Assistant Professor of Law at [[Brooklyn Law School]] starting in 2013, and a [[racial justice]] [[law clinic|clinic]] as an adjunct professor at the [[New York University School of Law]] starting in 2014.{{cite news |last1=Kalmbacher |first1=Colin |title=Biden Nominates ACLU Voting Rights Head to Federal Judgeship in New York; Progressives Praise Choice of 'Democracy's Lawyer' |url=https://lawandcrime.com/judiciary/biden-nominates-aclu-voting-rights-head-to-federal-judgeship-in-new-york-progressives-praise-choice-of-democracys-lawyer/ |access-date=October 1, 2021 |work=Law & Crime |date=September 30, 2021}}[https://www.brooklaw.edu/contact-us/ho-dale/ "Dale Ho,"] Brooklyn Law School.[https://congress.gov/116/meeting/house/110060/witnesses/HHRG-116-HA08-Bio-HoD-20191017-U1.pdf "Dale Ho,"] Congress.gov. In 2019, Ho was one of five ACLU lawyers featured in the documentary ''[[The Fight (2020 film)|The Fight]]'', produced by actress [[Kerry Washington]], which followed his preparation, oral argument, and reaction in the United States Supreme Court proceedings around ''[[Department of Commerce v. New York]]''{{cite news |last1=Kenigsberg |first1=Ben |title='The Fight' Review: Pressing the Case, or Cases |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/07/30/movies/the-fight-review.html |access-date=March 19, 2021 |work=The New York Times |date=July 30, 2020}} (see ''Notable cases'', below). === Notable cases === In 2018, Ho was a lead attorney in ''[[Fish v. Kobach]]'', in which the district court ruled that it was illegal to require documentary proof of citizenship in order to [[Voter registration in the United States|register to vote]].{{cite news |last1=Desrochers |first1=Daniel |url=https://www.mcclatchydc.com/news/politics-government/article254643767.html |title=Attorney who helped toss Kobach's voter registration law nominated for federal judgeship|access-date=October 1, 2021 |publisher=McClatchy |date=September 30, 2021}}{{cite news |last1=Cassens Weiss |first1=Debra |title=Judge strikes down Kansas voter ID law and orders Kris Kobach to take additional CLE |url=https://www.abajournal.com/news/article/judge_strikes_down_kansas_voter_id_law_and_orders_kris_kobach_to_take_addit |access-date=March 19, 2021 |work=ABA Journal |language=en}} Ho argued the case before the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit]], which affirmed the Kansas district court's ruling.{{cite news|url=https://apnews.com/article/donald-trump-kansas-voting-rights-elections-us-supreme-court-f12295c7870a94eb7749d94fa5e7019b|work=Associated Press|title=Supreme Court won't revive Kansas voter registration ID law|date=December 14, 2020}} Ho argued twice against the [[First presidency of Donald Trump|Trump administration]] in front of the [[Supreme Court of the United States]]. In ''[[Department of Commerce v. New York]]'' (2019), Ho represented a coalition of immigrant advocacy groups who successfully challenged [[Donald Trump]]'s plan to include a citizenship question on the [[2020 United States census]] questionnaire.{{cite news |last1=Sherman |first1=Mark |last2=Gresko |first2=Jessica |title=Justices to weigh Trump census plan to exclude noncitizens |url=https://apnews.com/article/virus-outbreak-immigration-us-supreme-court-courts-67f13dacddd136420b4bc49ac301f273 |access-date=March 26, 2021 |work=Associated Press|date=October 16, 2020}} In ''[[Trump v. New York]]'' (2020), the ACLU unsuccessfully challenged the Trump administration's plan to exclude [[Illegal immigration to the United States|illegal immigrants]] from the [[United States congressional apportionment|U.S. congressional apportionment]] process. === Federal judicial service === From the start of President [[Joe Biden]]'s [[Presidency of Joe Biden|administration]], Ho had been considered a potential nominee for a federal judgeship.{{cite news |last1=Kragie |first1=Andrew |title=65 Names To Watch When Biden Picks Circuit Judges – Law360 |url=https://www.law360.com/articles/1338187/65-names-to-watch-when-biden-picks-circuit-judges |access-date=March 26, 2021 |work=www.law360.com |date=January 3, 2021 |language=en}} The public criminal defense and voting rights attorney was a candidate of the Biden administration's program to open up the field to practitioners outside the traditional pool of corporate lawyers and prosecutors.Luc Cohen. [https://www.aol.com/news/dale-ho-judge-deciding-whether-180341178.html?soc_src=social-sh&soc_trk=ma AOL website] Retrieved 20 February 2025. On June 7, 2021, [[U.S. Senate Majority Leader]] [[Chuck Schumer]] recommended Ho for a federal judgeship to the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]].{{cite news |last1=Alder |first1=Madison |title=Schumer Recommends Voting Rights Lawyers for Federal Bench |url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/schumer-recommends-voting-rights-lawyers-for-federal-bench |access-date=June 7, 2021 |work=Bloomberg Law |date=June 7, 2021 |language=en}} On September 30, 2021, Biden nominated Ho to serve as a judge of that court,{{Cite web|url=https://lawandcrime.com/judiciary/biden-nominates-aclu-voting-rights-head-to-federal-judgeship-in-new-york-progressives-praise-choice-of-democracys-lawyer/|title = Biden Nominates ACLU Voting Rights Head to Federal Judgeship in New York; Progressives Praise Choice of 'Democracy's Lawyer'|date = September 30, 2021}} to the seat vacated by Judge [[Katherine B. Forrest]], who resigned on September 11, 2018.{{Cite press release |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |date=September 30, 2021|publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/09/30/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-37/}} {{PD-notice}} On December 1, 2021, a hearing on his nomination was held Judiciary]] |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/11/24/2021/nominations}} During his confirmation hearing, Ho apologized for his "overheated rhetoric" on social [[Harvard Law School|Harvard University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | footnotes = }} '''Dale Susan Fischer''' (born October 17, 1951) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Central District of California]]. ==Early life and education== Fischer was born in [[Orange, New Jersey]]. She received her [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from the [[University of South Florida]] in 1977, and her [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Harvard Law School]] in 1980.{{FJC Bio|nid=1392061|inline=yes}} ==Private practice== Fischer was in private practice in California for 17 years, from 1980 to 1997, during which she also volunteer briefly for the [[Los Angeles City Attorney's Office]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CHRG-108shrg93184/html/CHRG-108shrg93184.htm|title=CONFIRMATION HEARINGS ON FEDERAL APPOINTMENTS|website=govinfo.gov}} She practiced as a business litigator at the law firms [[Heller Ehrman]] and [[Kindel & Anderson]].[https://abtl.org/profiles/fischer.pdf "ABTL Judge Interview Project: Federal District Court Judge Dale Fischer (Central District of CA)"]{{Cite web|url=http://www.metnews.com/articles/fisc050503.htm|title=Superior Court Judge Dale Fischer Nominated to U.S. District Court|website=metnews.com}} ==Judicial career== ===State judicial service=== Fischer was a judge on the Los Angeles [[Municipal Court]] from 1997 to 2000, hearing criminal cases. She was then a judge on the [[Los Angeles County Superior Court]], hearing criminal cases from 2000 to 2003. ===Federal judicial service=== On May 1, 2003, Fischer was nominated by President [[George W. Bush]] to a new seat on the [[United States District Court for the Central District of California]] created by 116 Stat. 1758. She was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on October 27, 2003, and received her commission on November 5, 2003. She assumed [[senior status]] on May 1, 2024. ====Notable cases==== In 2008, she oversaw the case of private investigator [[Anthony Pellicano]]. Fischer sentenced Pellicano to 15 years in prison for running an illegal [[wiretapping]] operation, wiretapping billionaire [[Kirk Kerkorian]]'s former wife. The sentence significantly exceeded the five-year, 10-month term recommended by probation officials.{{Cite news|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/BL-LB-7002|title=Judge Fischer Goes Large, Hands Pellicano 15 Years|first=Dan|last=Slater|website=The Wall Street Journal|date=16 December 2008 }} In 2018, Judge Fischer issued a nationwide injunction and receivership over West H&A-a company who had frauduently hijacked more than 2,000 defaulted mortgages nationwide and coinvinced the distressed borrowers to begin paying their mortgage payments to West H&A instead of their real lender. Nationstar Mortage LLC, represented by Jered Ede and Jane Kutepova, sought and obtained the first-of-its kind injunction and receivership after discovering several of its borrowers had begun paying West H&A thinking they had cured their defaults. West H&A was operated by Patrick Soria, who Fischer found in civil and criminal contempt after Nationstar demonstrated Soria had violated Judge Fischer's order. Soria was then prosecuted by the DOJ. In 2021, Soria was sentenced to more than 12 years in prison for orchestrating the fraud scheme causing more than $7 million in losses. Fischer said the scheme was "the most brazen and heartless" she had presided over in her career. {{Cite news|url=https://kfiam640.iheart.com/content/2021-08-02-weho-man-sentenced-to-over-12-years-in-prison-for-real-estate-fraud|title=WeHo Man Sentenced to Over 12 Years in Prison for Real Estate Fraud|last=City News Service|date=August 2, 2021|website=KFIAM640}} In 2023 the criminal [[securities fraud]] case of [[Terren Peizer]], the CEO and chairman of publicly traded healthcare company Ontrak, was assigned to Fischer.{{Cite web|url=https://www.lexology.com/library/detail.aspx?g=d852e2cb-3338-435f-8475-8a9d1120b2ec|title=DOJ and SEC bring charges for insider trading and fraudulent scheme using purported 10b5-1 plans|first=Cydney S.|last=Posner|date=March 6, 2023|website=Lexology}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.ft.com/content/0a74de62-2758-4590-9c1f-6d18aef8f6d4|title=One-time Milken associate now at centre of novel insider trading case; US authorities accuse investor of violating rules on stock sales plans for corporate executives|date=March 20, 2023|work=The Financial Times}} After Peizer was charged with [[insider trading]] by the SEC, which alleged that he sold $20 million of Ontrak stock while he was in possession of material nonpublic negative information related to the company’s largest customer,{{Cite web|url=https://www.sec.gov/news/press-release/2023-42|title= SEC Charges Ontrak Chairman Terren Peizer With Insider Trading|date=March 1, 2023|website=SEC.gov}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.jdsupra.com/legalnews/client-alert-doj-and-sec-used-data-3325885/|title=Client Alert: DOJ and SEC Used Data Analytics to Target Insider Trading with 10b5-1 Plans|website=JD Supra|date=March 15, 2023}} the [[U.S. Department of Justice]] announced [[criminal charge]]s of securities fraud against Peizer, charging that thereby he had avoided $12 million in losses.{{Cite web|url=https://www.justice.gov/criminal-vns/case/united-states-v-terren-s-peizer|title=UNITED STATES V. TERREN S. PEIZER; PENDING CRIMINAL DIVISION CASES; Court Docket: 2:23-CR-89|date=March 1, 2023|website=The United States Department of Justice}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.justice.gov/opa/speech/assistant-attorney-general-kenneth-polite-jr-delivers-keynote-aba-s-38th-annual-national|title=Assistant Attorney General Kenneth A. Polite, Jr. Delivers Keynote at the ABA's 38th Annual National Institute on White Collar Crime|date=March 3, 2023|website=The United States Department of Justice}} Peizer was convicted of insider trading and securities fraud, and could face up to 65 years in prison.{{Cite web|url=https://ktla.com/news/local-news/santa-monica-man-used-anti-insider-trading-measure-to-commit-fraud-doj/|title=Santa Monica man used anti-insider-trading measure to commit fraud: DOJ|date=March 1, 2023|publisher=KTLA|access-date=March 29, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230328043228/https://ktla.com/news/local-news/santa-monica-man-used-anti-insider-trading-measure-to-commit-fraud-doj/|archive-date=March 28, 2023|url-status=dead}}Dave Michaels (June 21, 2024). [[Indiana University Maurer School of Law|Indiana University, Bloomington]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | party = }} '''Damon Ray Leichty''' (born 1971) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Indiana]]. == Education and career == Leichty earned his [[Bachelor of Arts]], ''[[summa cum laude]]'', from [[Wabash College]], a [[Master of Letters]] from the [[University of Aberdeen]], and his [[Juris Doctor]], ''[[cum laude]]'', from the [[Indiana University Maurer School of Law]].[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-sixteenth-wave-judicial-nominees-sixteenth-wave-united-states-attorney-nominees-eleventh-wave-united-states-marshal-nominees/ "President Donald J. Trump Announces Sixteenth Wave of Judicial Nominees, Sixteenth Wave of United States Attorney Nominees, and Eleventh Wave of United States Marshal Nominees" White House, July 13, 2018] {{PD-notice}} After graduation from law school, Leichty served as a [[law clerk]] to Judge [[Robert Lowell Miller Jr.]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Indiana]]. He went on to join the [[South Bend]] office of the law firm of [[Barnes & Thornburg]], where he became a partner. His practice focused on complex [[civil litigation]], including federal [[product liability]] cases. Leichty has been an [[adjunct professor]] at [[Notre Dame Law School]] since 2017, where he teaches [[product liability]] law.[https://law.nd.edu/directory/damon-leichty/ Notre Dame Law School faculty profile] == Federal judicial service == On July 13, 2018, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to nominate Leichty to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Indiana]]. On July 17, 2018, his nomination was sent to the Senate. President [[Donald Trump]] nominated Leichty to the seat vacated by Judge [[Robert Lowell Miller Jr.]], who assumed [[senior status]] on January 11, 2016.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/ten-nominations-sent-senate-today-4/ "Ten Nominations Sent to the Senate Today", White House, July 17, 2018] In early 2017, Leichty interviewed with Republican Senator [[Todd Young]] in April but was not selected by the [[White House]] until April 2018 when he interviewed with Democratic Senator [[Joe Donnelly]].{{cite web | url=https://vettingroom.org/2018/11/16/damon-leichty/ | title=Damon Leichty – Nominee to the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Indiana | date=16 November 2018 }} On November 13, 2018, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/11/13/2018/nominations United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Nominations for November 13, 2018] On January 3, 2019, his nomination was returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]]. On January 23, 2019, President Trump announced his intent to renominate Leichty for a federal judgeship.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-intent-nominate-judicial-nominees/ "President Donald J. Trump Announces Intent to Nominate Judicial Nominees", White House, January 23, 2019] His nomination was sent to the Senate later that February 7, 2019, Senate Judiciary Committee] On July 9, 2019, the Senate invoked cloture on his nomination by an 87–11 vote.[https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=1&vote=00193 On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Damon Ray Leichty to be U.S. District Judge for the Northern District of Indiana)], United States Senate, July 9, 2019 On July 10, 2019, his nomination was confirmed by an 85–10 '''Dan Aaron Polster''' (born 1951) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Ohio]]. Polster mediated a settlement between the city of [[Cleveland]] and the family of [[Killing of Tamir Rice|Tamir Rice]], a 12-year-old black boy who was killed by a white police officer in 2014. In December 2017, a federal judicial panel selected Polster to preside over more than 3,000 consolidated prescription opioid-related lawsuits in [[multidistrict litigation]] known as the National Prescription Opiate Litigation. A trial for the litigation began in October 2021.

==Education and career==

Born in [[Cleveland]], Polster received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] from [[Harvard College]] in 1972 and earned a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Harvard Law School]] in 1976. He was a trial attorney in the [[Antitrust]] Division of the [[United States Department of Justice]] from 1976 to 1982, and an [[assistant United States attorney]] in the Northern District of Ohio from 1982 to 1998.<ref>{{Cite web |title=FJA Officers and Board of Directors – Federal Judges Association |url=https://www.federaljudgesassoc.org/who-we-are/officers-and-board-of-directors/ |access-date=August 17, 2022 |language=en-US}}</ref>

===Federal judicial service===

On July 31, 1997, Polster was nominated by President [[Bill Clinton]] to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Ohio]] vacated by [[David Dudley Dowd Jr.]] Polster was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on July 31, 1998, and received his commission on August 3, 1998. He assumed [[senior status]] on January 31, 2021.<ref>{{FJC Bio|nid=1390761|inline=yes}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Caniglia |first1=John |title=Two federal judges in Cleveland will take senior status, giving President Biden seats to fill on the Northern Ohio bench; a third jurist is considering a similar move |url=https://www.cleveland.com/court-justice/2021/01/two-federal-judges-in-cleveland-will-take-senior-status-giving-president-biden-seats-to-fill-on-the-northern-ohio-bench-a-third-is-considering-a-similar-move.html |access-date=September 14, 2021 |work=cleveland.com |date=January 29, 2021 |language=en}}</ref>

=== Notable rulings and commentary ===

Polster helped to mediate a lawsuit over limits on protests at the [[2016 Republican National Convention]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Gerstein |first1=Josh |title=Judge reports settlement in GOP convention protest suit |url=https://www.politico.com/blogs/under-the-radar/2016/06/republican-national-convention-protest-lawsuit-224770 |work=POLITICO |date=June 24, 2016 |language=en}}</ref>

Polster mediated a settlement between the city of [[Cleveland]] and the family of [[Killing of Tamir Rice|Tamir Rice]], a 12-year-old black boy who was killed by a white police officer in 2014.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Palmer |first1=Kim |title=Cleveland to pay $6 million to settle police killing of black boy |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/ohio-police-shooting-idINKCN0XN0HL |access-date=October 25, 2021 |work=Reuters |date=April 26, 2016 |language=en}}</ref> Rice's mother said "It's disturbing that I had to put a price on my son, that I was forced to make a decision I didn't want to make." She said she is angry and frustrated that no one has been held accountable for her son's death.<ref>{{cite news |title=Tamir Rice's mother remains frustrated 2 years after death |url=https://apnews.com/article/f4337d7f57a44f258ac2b40e724be34a |access-date=October 25, 2021 |publisher=Associated Press |date=November 20, 2016}}</ref> The settlement meant that there would not be answers to some of the questions raised in the civil lawsuit, including whether dispatchers passed along sufficient information to the police and whether the department erred in hiring the officer who killed Rice. Some experts have questioned whether the settlement will lead to adequate reforms of the police department.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Heisig |first1=Eric |title=Cleveland to pay $6M to Tamir Rice's family to settle lawsuit |url=https://www.cleveland.com/court-justice/2016/04/city_of_cleveland_to_pay_6_mil.html |access-date=October 25, 2021 |work=cleveland.com |date=April 25, 2016 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Graham |first1=David A. |title=Will a $6 Million Tamir Rice Settlement Help Reform Cleveland Cops? |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/national/archive/2016/04/tamir-rice-settlement-cleveland/479691/ |access-date=October 25, 2021 |work=The Atlantic |date=April 25, 2016}}</ref>

In February 2017, Polster said that comments made by [[Donald Trump]] criticizing federal judges called the president's legitimacy into question.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Heisig |first1=Eric |title=Cleveland federal judge comments on Trump's attacks on judiciary |url=https://www.cleveland.com/court-justice/2017/02/cleveland_federal_judge_says_t.html |access-date=October 25, 2021 |work=cleveland |date=February 9, 2017 |language=en}}</ref>

Polster mediated settlements in 700 cases involving medical contract dye.<ref name=nyt/> Of mediation, Polster has said "Sometimes I feel like I am a therapist, or a rabbi or a priest. I had to train myself to lean in to the emotions. For lawyers, it is just the facts–forget the feelings and emotions."<ref name=interview>{{cite news |title=An Interview With Judge Dan Polster |url=https://nyfamilymediation.com/news/an-interview-with-judge-dan-polster/ |access-date=October 25, 2021 |work=Family Mediation LLP |date=April 11, 2018}}</ref> He has said "I can do things, as a judge, that no one else can, ''because'' I am the judge. I also use my courtroom in the mediation. Mediation is qualitatively different if the party is sitting in the very courtroom, the very seat, he or she will be in if the case is tried in front of the jury box. I use that!"<ref name=interview/>

Polster rejected arguments from Ohio Secretary of State [[Frank LaRose]] to limit the use of ballot drop boxes in the 2020 election.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Timm |first1=Jane |title=With Election Day looming, voting rights are still being decided in court. Here's what to know. |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2020-election/election-day-looms-who-s-winning-legal-war-over-mail-n1243223 |work=NBC News |date=October 17, 2020 |language=en}}</ref> LaRose immediately appealed the decision.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Carr Smyth |first1=Julie |title=Judge again blocks restrictions on ballot drop boxes in Ohio |url=https://apnews.com/article/election-2020-voting-rights-elections-courts-cleveland-8e178cef9e4fbc55273ec87ad46551a1 |access-date=October 25, 2021 |work=AP NEWS |date=October 8, 2020 |language=en}}</ref> The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit granted an injunction against Polster's ruling, leaving the ultimate decision to be made after election day. The appeals court ruled that "Ohio's restrictions are reasonable and non-discriminatory" and that the state "offers many ways to vote."<ref name=wapo>{{cite news |last1=Kranish |first1=Michael |title=Ohio's drop-box dispute shows how voting rights groups and Democrats fear Trump's influence |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/ohio-voting-drop-box-trump/2020/10/27/02343b08-1534-11eb-82af-864652063d61_story.html |access-date=October 25, 2021 |work=Washington Post}}</ref> The plaintiffs dropped the case on October 22, facing the possibility of $40,000 in court costs.<ref name=wapo/>

===Multidistrict opioid litigation===

In December 2017, a federal judicial panel selected Polster to preside over more than 3,000 consolidated prescription opioid-related lawsuits in [[multidistrict litigation]] known as the National Prescription Opiate Litigation.<ref>{{cite web|title=MDL 2804: National Prescription Opiate Litigation|url=https://www.ohnd.uscourts.gov/mdl-2804|publisher=[[United States District Court for the Northern District of Ohio]]}}</ref> The multidistrict litigation is a master case designed to simultaneously resolve all opioid lawsuits against drug companies and pharmacies. The defendants include makers of prescription painkillers, companies that distribute them, and pharmacies that dispense them. Legal experts have described the opioid litigation as the largest and most complex civil lawsuit in U.S. history.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Achenbach |first1=Joel |last2=Bernstein |first2=Lenny |title=A federal judge vowed to tackle the opioid crisis. Drug companies say that's a sign of bias. |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/health/a-federal-judge-vowed-to-tackle-the-opioid-crisis-drug-companies-say-thats-a-sign-of-bias/2019/09/15/94b12f8a-d7ab-11e9-a688-303693fb4b0b_story.html |access-date=September 15, 2021 |work=Washington Post |date=September 15, 2019}}</ref>

During the case's first hearing in January 2018, Polster told lawyers that he planned to dispense with legal norms like [[Discovery (law)|discovery]] and ordered lawyers to immediately prepare for settlement discussions. ''The New York Times'' reported that many lawyers on both sides "were scathing, questioning his grasp of the issues and predicting that a stepped-up timetable was bound to collapse."<ref name=nyt>Hoffman, Jan. [https://www.nytimes.com/2018/03/05/health/opioid-crisis-judge-lawsuits.html "Can This Judge Solve the Opioid Crisis?"], ''[[The New York Times]]'', March 5, 2018.</ref><ref>Heisig, Eric. [http://www.cleveland.com/court-justice/index.ssf/2018/01/heres_why_a_federal_judge_pres.html "Here's why a federal judge presiding over opioid lawsuits thinks settling is important"], ''[[Cleveland.com]]'', January 19, 2018.</ref> In September 2019, attorneys for eight drug distributors sought to disqualify Polster from the case, saying his public comments about his intention to get plaintiffs help showed evidence of bias. Attorneys cited Polster's January 2018 remark that "My objective is to do something meaningful to abate the [opioid] crisis and to do it in 2018."<ref>{{cite news |last1=Gillespie |first1=Mark |title=Drug company attorneys seek to disqualify Judge Dan Aaron Polster |url=https://www.clevelandjewishnews.com/news/local_news/drug-company-attorneys-seek-to-disqualify-judge-dan-aaron-polster/article_6442221f-b77d-5a6e-b8b5-4c4520b5f53d.html |access-date=September 15, 2021 |work=Cleveland Jewish News |agency=Associated Press |date=September 14, 2019 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Journal |first1=A. B. A. |title=Opioid sellers say judge must recuse because he pushed settlement; 1 defendant files for bankruptcy |url=https://www.abajournal.com/news/article/opioid-makers-say-judge-must-recuse-because-he-pushed-settlement-one-defendant-files-for-bankruptcy |access-date=September 15, 2021 |work=ABA Journal |date=September 16, 2019 |language=en}}</ref> Polster declined to step aside.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Bernstein |first1=Lenny |title=Judge in landmark opioid trial declines to step aside |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/health/judge-in-landmark-opioid-trial-declines-to-step-aside/2019/09/26/ddac54d4-e062-11e9-8dc8-498eabc129a0_story.html |access-date=September 15, 2021 |work=Washington Post |date=September 26, 2019}}</ref>

In April 2019, Polster barred the media from court proceedings in the opioid lawsuit. The [[Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press]] criticized this move, saying "the public is presumed to have the right of access to proceedings in civil cases."<ref>{{cite news |last1=Heisig |first1=Eric |title=Federal judge bars media from court proceeding on upcoming trial on opioid epidemic in Cleveland |url=https://www.cleveland.com/court-justice/2019/04/federal-judge-bars-media-from-court-proceeding-on-upcoming-trial-on-opioid-epidemic-in-cleveland.html |access-date=September 15, 2021 |work=cleveland.com |date=April 23, 2019 |language=en}}</ref> Polster issued a gag order limiting the ability of attorneys to speak publicly about the litigation.<ref>{{cite news |title=Judge issues gag order in opioid lawsuit settlement talks |url=https://apnews.com/article/4746f68231e340d2814ad32c25636da5 |access-date=October 25, 2021 |publisher=Associated Press |date=February 6, 2018}}</ref> An investigation by [[Reuters]] "showed that Polster has been more willing to seal documents than other judges involved in opioid litigation, raising concerns that important information about the crisis remains secret."<ref name=reuters/>

In June 2019, a three-judge panel of the Sixth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that Polster's blocking of the release of court records in opioid cases was inappropriate.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.claimsjournal.com/news/national/2019/06/24/291635.htm|title=US Appeals Court Says Judge Went Too Far on Drug Data Order|date=June 24, 2019|website=Claims Journal|language=en-US|access-date=June 25, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.reuters.com/investigates/special-report/usa-courts-secrecy-judges/|title=How judges added to the grim toll of opioids|last=Lesser|first=Benjamin|last2=Levine|first2=Dan|website=Reuters|language=en|access-date=June 25, 2019|last3=Girion|first3=Lisa|last4=Dowdell|first4=Jaimi}}</ref>

In April 2020, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit issued a sharp rebuke of Polster, writing that his pretrial ruling allowing plaintiffs to add new claims more than a year after the deadline was a "clear abuse of discretion."<ref>{{cite news |last1=Heisig |first1=Eric |title=Appeals court again rebukes Cleveland federal judge over opioid litigation narrowing case against large pharmacy chains |url=https://www.cleveland.com/court-justice/2020/04/appeals-court-again-rebukes-cleveland-federal-judge-over-opioid-litigation-narrowing-case-against-large-pharmacy-chains.html |access-date=October 25, 2021 |work=cleveland.com |date=April 15, 2020 |language=en}}</ref> Judge [[Raymond Kethledge]] wrote that multidistrict litigation is "not some kind of judicial border country, where the rules are few and the law rarely makes an appearance."<ref>{{cite news |last1=Bronstad |first1=Amanda |title=6th Circuit Panel: MDL Judge's Ruling in Opioid Case Was 'Clear Abuse of Discretion' |url=https://www.law.com/2020/04/15/6th-circuit-panel-mdl-judges-ruling-in-opioid-case-was-clear-abuse-of-discretion/?slreturn=20210815143249 |access-date=September 15, 2021 |work=Law.com |date=April 15, 2020 |language=en}}</ref>

In September 2020, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit reversed Polster's 2019 approval of the nation's first "negotiation class." Judge [[Eric L. Clay]] wrote that "the district court simply is not authorized by the structure, framework, or language of Rule 23," referring to [[Federal Rules of Civil Procedure|Federal Rule 23 of Civil Procedure]], which governs class action lawsuits.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Bronstad|first1=Amanda |title=Appeals court nixes 'negotiation class' created for opioid settlement |url=https://www.benefitspro.com/2020/09/29/appeals-court-reverses-negotiation-class-created-for-opioid-settlement-412-104587/?slreturn=20210814163202 |access-date=September 15, 2021 |work=BenefitsPRO |date=September 29, 2020 |language=en}}</ref>

Polster has a history of encouraging parties to settle their cases outside of court.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Heisig |first1=Eric |title=Appeals court blasts Cleveland judge's secrecy in opioid litigation, decision to block public release of DEA painkiller data |url=https://www.cleveland.com/court-justice/2019/06/appeals-court-blasts-cleveland-judges-decision-to-block-public-release-of-opioid-data-collected-by-dea.html |access-date=October 25, 2021 |work=cleveland.com |date=June 20, 2019 |language=en}}</ref> He has been clear about his preference for a settlement rather than a trial in the opioid litigation, saying at an initial hearing that "we don't need a lot of briefs and we don't need trials."<ref name=reuters>{{cite news |last1=Hals |first1=Tom |last2=Raymond |first2=Nate |title=Judge's unorthodox approach has huge opioid settlement within reach |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-opioids-litigation-judge/judges-unorthodox-approach-has-huge-opioid-settlement-within-reach-idUSKBN1WX1AT |access-date=October 25, 2021 |work=Reuters |date=October 18, 2019 |language=en}}</ref> Polster warned pharmaceutical companies that they would face bankruptcy if they did not settle.<ref>{{cite news |title=Pharmacies Face Peril Without Opioid Settlements, Judge Says |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2021-04-07/pharmacies-face-peril-without-opioid-settlements-judge-says |access-date=September 15, 2021 |work=Bloomberg.com |date=April 7, 2021 |language=en}}</ref> ''Legal Newsline'' wrote that in doing so, Polster "demonstrated why plaintiff lawyers love the strategy so much: Because it is extremely effective at extracting settlements from the companies they sue."<ref>{{cite news |last1=Fisher |first1=Daniel |title=Opioid judge threatens pharmacies with bankruptcy if they don't settle |url=https://legalnewsline.com/stories/580881752-opioid-judge-threatens-pharmacies-with-bankruptcy-if-they-don-t-settle |access-date=September 15, 2021 |work=Legal Newsline |date=March 23, 2021 |language=en}}</ref>

The multidistrict opioid litigation is thought to have wide-reaching legal implications. Writing for ''National Review'', Jack Fowler said "Somewhat off America's radar screen is a legal case, of the huge-implications variety, that is not only vast and complex but also a nose-thumbing to those (naïvely?) believing that social policy should be set by the people's legislative representatives, and not by judges."<ref>{{cite news |last1=Fowler |first1=Jack |title=Is Settling the Opioid Crisis the Job of a Maverick Judge? |url=https://www.nationalreview.com/2021/06/is-settling-the-opioid-crisis-the-job-of-a-maverick-judge/ |access-date=September 15, 2021 |work=National Review |date=June 24, 2021}}</ref> In ''The Wall Street Journal'', Yale law professor Abbe Gluck wrote, "What began as a single opioid lawsuit in Ohio is now the only such case that matters. Every significant opioid lawsuit in the U.S. has been lumped together into a giant case before one federal judge in Cleveland who has declared his extraordinary ambition to 'solve' the crisis in 2018." Gluck asked, "Is a federal courtroom, presided over by a single judge, a better forum for making policy than 50 state legislatures or Congress?"<ref>{{cite news |last1=Gluck |first1=Abbe R. |title=Can a Judge Solve the Opioid Crisis? |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/can-a-judge-solve-the-opioid-crisis-1525731873 |access-date=September 15, 2021 |work=Wall Street Journal |date=May 7, 2018}}</ref>

The trial, which was originally scheduled for October 2020, was delayed due to [[COVID-19 pandemic in the United States|COVID-19]]. A number of companies settled prior to trial, while other companies, including [[Walmart]] and [[Walgreens]], elected to go to trial. Polster initially said he would automatically disqualify any potential jurors who were not vaccinated against COVID-19. He later reversed this order.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Raymond |first1=Nate |title=Opioid MDL judge reverses order requiring COVID vaccines for jurors |url=https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/opioid-mdl-judge-reverses-order-requiring-covid-vaccines-jurors-2021-06-23/ |work=Reuters |date=June 23, 2021 |language=en}}</ref>

The trial began in October 2021.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Gillispie |first1=Mark |title=Trial against pharmacy chains' opioid sales begins |url=https://www.seattletimes.com/business/trial-against-pharmacy-chains-opioid-sales-set-to-begin/ |access-date=October 25, 2021 |work=The Seattle Times |publisher=Associated Press |date=October 4, 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Pierson |first1=Brendan |title=Rite Aid settles bellwether opioid case with Ohio counties |url=https://www.reuters.com/legal/litigation/rite-aid-settles-bellwether-opioid-case-with-ohio-counties-2021-08-26/ |access-date=September 15, 2021 |work=Reuters |date=August 26, 2021 |language=en}}</ref> In the trial, lawyers for the plaintiffs claimed the pharmacies "dispensed like a vending machine" and failed to identify signs of drug misuse. A lawyer for one of the defendant companies said that others, including doctors, were instead to blame for the rise in prescriptions.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Segall |first1=Grant |title=Pharmacy chains failed to prevent opioid misuse, U.S. jury hears |url=https://www.reuters.com/business/healthcare-pharmaceuticals/pharmacy-chains-face-first-trial-over-us-opioid-epidemic-2021-10-04/ |website=Reuters |access-date=November 10, 2021 |language=en |date=October 5, 2021}}</ref>

Three weeks into the six week trial, a juror committed grave misconduct by giving fellow jurors a printout from her home computer that cast doubt on testimony by a witness from [[Walgreens]]. All four defendants in the trial—Walgreens, Walmart, Giant Eagle Inc., and CVS—sought a mistrial due to the juror's misconduct. The Ohio counties' lead trial lawyer initially said it would be appropriate to declare a mistrial, but later changed his mind. Polster denied the mistrial motions.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Frankel |first1=Alison |title=When juror misconduct doesn't matter: opioid MDL edition |url=https://www.reuters.com/legal/litigation/when-juror-misconduct-doesnt-matter-opioid-mdl-edition-2021-10-26/ |access-date=November 2, 2021 |work=Reuters |date=October 26, 2021 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Felten |first1=Eric |title=With Rogue Juror, Opioid Plaintiffs Face New Setback Most Foul {{!}} RealClearInvestigations |url=https://www.realclearinvestigations.com/articles/2021/11/18/latest_opioid_trial_augurs_reversals_most_frequent_804088.html |access-date=December 1, 2021 |work=www.realclearinvestigations.com |date=November 18, 2021 |language=en}}</ref>

On November 23, 2021, the jury found CVS, Walgreens, and Walmart liable for creating a public nuisance by contributing to the U.S. opioid crisis. The jury only decided liability, and now Polster will decide how much the companies will have to pay in damages.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Moyer |first1=Liz |title=Biden Took Action to Lower Oil Prices. Why It May Do the Opposite. |url=https://www.barrons.com/articles/things-to-know-today-51637748120 |access-date=December 1, 2021 |work=www.barrons.com |date=November 24, 2021}}</ref> The companies have announced plans to appeal the verdict, saying that pharmacists only dispensed prescriptions written by licensed health care providers.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Mann |first1=Brian |title=3 of America's biggest pharmacy chains have been found liable for the opioid crisis |url=https://www.npr.org/2021/11/23/1058539458/a-jury-in-ohio-says-americas-big-pharmacy-chains-are-liable-for-the-opioid-epide |access-date=December 1, 2021 |work=NPR.org |date=November 23, 2021 |language=en}}</ref> Some experts expect the verdict to be set aside due to [[juror misconduct]], and for an appeals court to order a retrial.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Feeley |first1=Jef |title=Why Jury's Opioid Verdict Against Pharmacy Chains May Not Survive Appeal |url=https://www.insurancejournal.com/news/national/2021/11/30/643742.htm |access-date=December 1, 2021 |work=Insurance Journal |date=November 30, 2021}}</ref> Similar public nuisance arguments in other opioid lawsuits have been rejected in California and Oklahoma.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Hoffman |first1=Jan |title=The Core Legal Strategy Against Opioid Companies May Be Faltering |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/11/11/health/opioids-lawsuits-public-nuisance.html |access-date=December 1, 2021 |work=The New York Times |date=November 11, 2021}}</ref> The editorial board of ''The Wall Street Journal'' critiqued the Ohio verdict, writing "The jury verdict distorts product liability and public-nuisance law since opioids are legal products and pharmacies had no control over how they were used by customers. If the verdict stands, or the companies settle, the precedent could lead to similar nuisance suits across much of the U.S. economy."<ref>{{cite news |author=The Editorial Board |title=Opinion {{!}} The Great Ohio Opioid Stick-Up |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/the-great-ohio-opioid-stick-up-dan-polster-cvs-walmart-walgreens-jury-11637709510 |access-date=December 1, 2021 |work=Wall Street Journal |date=November 23, 2021}}</ref>

In August 2022, Polster ruled that CVS, Walgreens, and Walmart pharmacies must pay $650.5 million in damages to Lake County and Trumbull County in Ohio for contributing to the opioid epidemic in those areas.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Hoffman |first=Jan |date=August 17, 2022 |title=CVS, Walgreens and Walmart Must Pay $650.5 Million in Ohio Opioids Case |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/08/17/health/opioids-cvs-walmart-walgreens.html |access-date=August 17, 2022 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

The seat was vacated by Judge [[Donald W. Molloy]], who assumed [[senior status]] in August 2011.{{Cite web | author=The White House: Office of the Press Secretary | url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2011/05/04/nomination-s-sent-senate | title=Nominations Sent to the Senate | date=May 4, 2011 | via=[[NARA|National Archives]] | work=[[whitehouse.gov]] | access-date=May 7, 2011}} Christensen's nomination was reported from the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]] on October 6, 2011. The Senate confirmed his nomination on December 5, 2011, by voice vote. He received his commission on December 6, 2011. He served as chief judge from March 19, 2013 to March 19, 2020. He took senior status on November 7, 2025. === Notable rulings === In late August 2018, Christensen placed a 14-day hold on grizzly bear hunting in Wyoming and Idaho after the [[United States Fish and Wildlife Service|U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service]] lifted federal protections for grizzlies in [[Yellowstone National Park]] areas in 2017.{{cite web |last1=Associated Press |title=Judges halts first unable to vote at all. [[San Diego State University]] ([[Bachelor of Science|BS]])
[[McGeorge School of Law|University of the Pacific]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | footnotes = }} '''Dana Makoto Sabraw''' (born July 3, 1958) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of California]]. He was nominated by President [[George W. Bush]] in 2003. ==Early life and education== Sabraw is [[Hāfu|half-Japanese]]; his Japanese mother met his father in 1954 when he was a [[United States Army]] soldier stationed in [[Japan]] during the [[Korean War]]. They married in 1955. His father was a teacher of special-needs students and his mother taught [[English as a second language]].{{cite news|url=https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/sdut-vista-judge-takes-seat-in-federal-court-2003oct06-story.html|title=Vista judge takes seat in federal court|last=Marshall|first=Scott|date=October 6, 2003|work=San Diego Union Tribune}} Sabraw was born in [[San Rafael, California|San Rafael]], [[California]] in 1958,[https://www.fjc.gov/node/1392011 Sabraw, Dana Makoto], ''History of the Federal Judiciary'', [[Federal Judicial Center]]. and grew up in the [[Sacramento]] suburb of [[Carmichael, California]].Kristina Davis, [https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/news/courts/sd-me-judge-sabraw-20180719-story.html Who is Dana Sabraw, the judge behind the family reunification case?], ''San Diego Union-Tribune'' (July 22, 2018). He received an [[Associate of Arts]] degree from [[American River Junior College]] in 1978, a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree from [[San Diego State University]] in 1980, and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[McGeorge School of Law]] at [[University of the Pacific (United States)|University of the Pacific]] in 1985. ==Career== His first job was working as a [[Wrestling|wrestling instructor]], [[Strength and conditioning coach|conditioning instructor]], and later a [[lifeguard]] for the [[San Juan Unified School District]] in [[Carmichael, California]] From 1976 to 1977.[https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=uc1.c078036695&view=1up&seq=535 Confirmation hearing on federal appointments : hearing before the Committee on the Judiciary, United States Senate, One Hundred Eighth Congress, first session. pt.4 (2003)] From 1977 to 1982, he worked at many businesses and colleges which included [[Westmont College|Westmont]] and the [[University of the Pacific (United States)|University of the Pacific]]. Sabraw was in private practice for six years at the [[Santa Barbara, California|Santa Barbara]] law firm of Price, Postel & Parma before joining the [[San Diego]] office of the international law firm [[Baker McKenzie]] in 1992. === State court service === Sabraw was a judge on the [[North County (San Diego area)|North County]] Municipal Court, County of San Diego, from 1995 to 1998. He was a judge on the [[San Diego County Superior Court]] from 1998 to 2003. Governor [[Pete Wilson]] appointed Sabraw to both posts. ===Federal judicial service === Sabraw was nominated by President [[George W. Bush]] on May 1, 2003, to be a United States District Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of California]], to a new seat created by 116 Stat. 1758. The [[American Bar Association]]'s [[Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary]] unanimously rated Sabraw "well qualified" for the judgeship.[https://www.americanbar.org/content/dam/aba/migrated/2011_build/federal_judiciary/ratings108.pdf Ratings of Article III Judicial Nominees: 108th Congress] (last updated January 10, 2008). Sabraw was unanimously confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] in a 95-0 vote on September 25, 2003. He received his commission the following day. He was the chief judge from January 22, 2021 until January 22, 2025. ====Notable cases==== In 2016 Sabraw presided over a case brought against the State of California by a group of [[anti-vaccine movement|anti-vaccine parents]] who challenged [[California Senate Bill 277|S.B. 277]], a California law that required all schoolchildren in public and private schools to be fully vaccinated against a number of diseases.Paul Sisson, [http://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/sdut-vaccination-order-judge-sabraw-2016aug26-htmlstory.html Judge denies injunction against vaccine law], ''San Diego Union-Tribune'' (August 26, 2018). Sabraw rejected the activists' claim that the law was a violation of the constitutional rights to [[free exercise of religion]] or to equal public education, writing that "the fundamental rights under the [[First Amendment to the United States Constitution]] do not overcome the State's interest in protecting a child's health" and that the Constitution "does not require the provision of a religious exemption to vaccination requirements, much less a personal belief exemption." After Sabraw rejected the plaintiffs' application for an injunction, the group dropped the lawsuit.Jane Meredith Adams, [https://edsource.org/2016/parent-group-withdraws-suit-against-school-vaccination-law/568949 Parent group withdraws suit against school vaccination law], ''EdSource'' (September 1, 2016). In February 2018, Sabraw was assigned a case in which the [[American Civil Liberties Union]] (ACLU) sued the [[First presidency of Donald Trump|Donald Trump administration]] on behalf of a [[Democratic Republic of the Congo|Congolese]] woman who had been separated from her 7-year-old daughter in November when she presented herself at the [[San Ysidro Port of Entry]] seeking asylum. The case later became a class-action suit challenging the administration's [[Trump administration family separation policy|policy of separating families]] who cross the U.S.-Mexico border.{{cite news|url=https://www.voiceofsandiego.org/topics/government/a-readers-guide-to-the-family-separation-case/|title=A Reader's Guide to the Family Separation Case|last=Srikrishnan|first=Maya|date=August 1, 2018|work=Voice of San Diego|access-date=31 December 2018}}{{cite news|url=https://www.politico.com/story/2018/06/19/family-separation-trump-administration-lawsuit-654822|title=New lawsuit challenges Trump administration over family separation|last=Gerstein|first=Josh|date=June 19, 2018|work=Politico|access-date=21 June 2018}} In June 2018, Sabraw denied the government's motion to dismiss the case, finding that plaintiffs alleged sufficient grounds to proceed with their claim that the policy violates plaintiffs' [[Due Process Clause|constitutional right to due process]].{{cite news|url=https://slate.com/news-and-politics/2018/06/district-court-judge-rules-that-trump-administration-child-separations-would-be-unconstitutional.html|title=District Court Judge Denounces Forced Child Separation as "Brutal" and Clear Constitutional Violation|last=Stahl|first=Jeremy|date=June 6, 2018|work=Slate|access-date=21 June 2018}} Later that month, Sabraw entered a [[nationwide injunction]] ordering an end to most family separations at the border and requiring the immediate reunification of all children separated from their family members under the policy.{{cite news|url=https://www.cnn.com/2018/06/26/politics/federal-court-order-family-separations/index.html|title=Federal judge orders reunification of parents and children, end to most family separations at border|last=Jarrett|first=Laura|date=June 27, 2018|publisher=CNN|access-date=31 December 2018}}{{cite court|litigants=Ms. L. v. U.S. Immigration & Customs Enforcement|vol=310 |reporter=F.Supp.3d|opinion=1133|court=S.D. Cal.|date=2018|url=https://casetext.com/case/ms-l-v-us-immigration-customs-enforcement|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200923213946/https://casetext.com/case/ms-l-v-us-immigration-customs-enforcement|url-status=dead|archive-date=September 23, 2020}} He continued to oversee the process of family reunification, requiring regular reports from the administration. In July 2018, Sabraw suspended family deportations for one week, until family unifications could be completed.{{cite web|title=U.S. judge suspends deportations of reunited immigrant families|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-usa-immigration/u-s-judge-suspends-deportations-of-reunited-immigrant-families-idUSKBN1K615F|work=Reuters|author=Marty Graham|date=July 16, 2018}} In August 2018, Sabraw ruled that it is the government's burden to reunite separated migrant families.{{Cite web |url=https://abcnews.go.com/US/News/us-government-argues-aclu-locate-reunite-hundreds-migrant/story?id=57020100 |title=Government's job to reunite migrant parents deported without kids, not ACLU: Judge |last=Pearle |first=Lauren |date=August 3, 2018|work=ABC News}} However, in January 2020, he ruled in support of the Trump administration's separation of 900 children from their parents on the grounds that the parents were unfit or dangerous, given doubts about paternity, criminal history, or having communicable diseases. He distinguished these cases from those where he had earlier ruled against the Trump administration because their purpose had been to deter immigration across the southern border altogether. In so ruling, he rejected the ACLU's claim that the administration had reverted to previous abusive family separations, although he did also grant the ACLU position that the government would have to administer DNA tests to remove paternity doubts, something the Trump administration had fought.{{Cite web|url=https://thehill.com/regulation/court-battles/478105-judge-rules-in-favor-of-administration-on-family-separations-at|title = Judge rules in favor of administration on family separations at border|date = 13 January 2020}} In April 2018, he presided over the case of a [[U.S. Border Patrol]] agent who pleaded guilty to smuggling drugs across the border, sentencing him to 70 months in federal prison.{{cite news|url=https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/news/courts/sd-me-lopez-sentence-20180425-story.html|title=Border Patrol agent who picked up drugs along fence for apparent traffickers gets prison|last=Davis|first=Kristina|date=April 25, 2018|work=The San Diego Union-Tribune|access-date=31 December 2018}} On March 31, 2023, he granted a preliminary injunction against major portions of California's handgun roster in a case called ''Renna v. Bonta''. ===Recognition=== ''[[The San Diego Union-Tribune]]'' named Sabraw its 2018 "San Diego Person of the Year" for his order ending the Trump administration's family separation policy, stating that Sabraw's ruling "ended a shameful chapter in our country's history" and adding: "His honest, thoughtful oversight of a complex case shouldn't be forgotten."{{cite news|last=The San Diego Union-Tribune Editorial Board|date=December 28, 2018|title=Dana Sabraw: the 2018 San Diego person of the year|work=The San Diego Union-Tribune|url=https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/opinion/editorials/sd-dana-sabraw-person-of-the-year-20181228-story.html|access-date=31 December 2018}} ==Personal life== Sabraw lives in [[Scripps Ranch, San Diego]]. He is married to [[Summer Stephan]], a career prosecutor with the [[San Diego County District Attorney]]'s office who was elected District Attorney in June 2018.{{cite web|url=http://www.sdcda.org/office/meet-da.html|title=Summer Stephan, San Diego County District Attorney|work=San Diego County District Attorney|access-date=21 June 2018}} They have three children. [[University of Chicago]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Daniel Joe Calabretta''' (né '''Powell''', born 1978){{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2014/12/14/fashion/weddings/jonathan-calabretta-daniel-powell.html|title=Jonathan Calabretta, Daniel Powell|work=The New York Times|date=2014-12-14}}{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Calabretta%20SJQ%20Public%20Final.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=October 9, 2022}} is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of California]]. == Early life and education == Calabretta was born in [[Union City, Tennessee]],{{Cite web |title=Senate Confirms Daniel J. Calabretta for Federal Judgeship in Eastern District of California - New CAED |url=https://www.caed.uscourts.gov/caednew/index.cfm/news/senate-confirms-daniel-j-calabretta-for-federal-judgeship-in-eastern-district-of-california/ |access-date=2023-02-20 |website=www.caed.uscourts.gov}} to Kathleen G. Van Ness. He was adopted by Charles L. Silber. He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] from [[Princeton University]] in 2000 and a [[Juris Doctor|J.D.]] degree from the [[University of Chicago Law School]] in 2003.{{Cite press release|title=President Biden Names Twenty-Fourth Round of Judicial Nominees|date=July 29, 2022|publisher=The White House|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/07/29/president-biden-names-twenty-fourth-round-of-judicial-nominees/|access-date=July 29, 2022}}{{PD-notice}} == Legal and academic career == Calabretta served as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[William A. Fletcher]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]] from 2003 to 2004 and [[Associate Justice]] [[John Paul Stevens]] of the [[United States Supreme Court]] from 2004 to 2005. From 2005 to 2008, he was an [[associate lawyer|associate]] at [[Munger, Tolles and Olson]]. From 2008 to 2013, he served as a deputy attorney general in the [[California Department of Justice]]. From 2013 to 2018, he served as deputy legal affairs secretary in the Office of Governor [[Jerry Brown]]. Calabretta taught a "Direct Democracy in California" course at [[UC Davis School of Law]] in 2021 and 2022 and at [[Lincoln Law School of Sacramento]] in 2022. == Judicial career == === State court service === In 2018, [[California Governor]] [[Jerry Brown]] appointed Calabretta to serve as a judge of the [[Sacramento County Superior Court]].{{Cite web |date=November 29, 2018 |title=Daniel J. Calabretta, '03: Appointed to a Judgeship in the Sacramento County Superior Court |url=https://www.law.uchicago.edu/news/daniel-j-calabretta-03-appointed-judgeship-sacramento-county-superior-court |access-date=July 29, 2022 |website=www.law.uchicago.edu}}{{cite web |title=Governor Brown Appoints 12 Superior Court Judges |url=https://archive.gov.ca.gov/archive/gov39/2018/11/29/governor-brown-appoints-12-superior-court-judges-2/index.html}}{{cite web |title=Governor Newsom Announces Judicial Appointments 1.29.24 |date=30 January 2024 |url=https://www.gov.ca.gov/2024/01/29/governor-newsom-announces-judicial-appointments-1-29-24/}} === Federal judicial service === On July 29, 2022, President [[Joe Biden]] announced his intent to nominate Calabretta to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of California]].{{Cite web|date=July 29, 2022|title=Biden nominates Sacramento Superior Court's Calabretta for federal judgeship|url=https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article263958676.html|access-date=July 29, 2022|website=[[The Sacramento Bee]]}} On August 1, 2022, his nomination was sent to the Senate. President Biden nominated Calabretta to the seat vacated by Judge [[John Mendez]], who assumed [[senior status]] on April 27, 2022.{{Cite press release|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate|date=August 1, 2022|publisher=The White House|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/08/01/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-78/}} On October 12, 2022, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web|title=Nominations|date=October 9, 2022|publisher=[[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]]|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/10/12/2022/nominations}} On December 1, 2022, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 12–10 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/EBM%20Results%20-%202022-12-011.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – December 1, 2022|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=December 1, 2022}} On January 3, 2023, his nomination was returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]]; he was renominated later the same day.{{Cite press release|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate|date=January 3, 2023|publisher=The White House|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2023/01/03/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-91/}} On February 2, 2023, his nomination was reported out of committee by an 11–9 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/EBM%20Results%20-%202023-02-021.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – February 2, 2023|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=February 2, 2023}} On February 15, 2023, the Senate invoked cloture on his nomination by a 52–46 vote.{{Cite web|date=February 15, 2023|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Daniel J. Calabretta to be U.S. District Judge for the Eastern District of California)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00019.htm|access-date=February 15, 2023|website=United States Senate}} On February 16, 2023, his nomination was confirmed by a 51–45 vote.{{Cite web|date=February 16, 2023|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Daniel J. Calabretta, of California, to be U.S. District Judge for the Eastern District of California)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00022.htm|access-date=February 16, 2023|website=United States Senate}} He received his judicial commission on February 21, 2023.{{FJC Bio|nid=13268821|inline=yes}} He is the first openly [[LGBT|gay]] judge to serve on the Eastern District of California.{{Cite web|last1=Raymond|first1=Nate|date=July 29, 2022|title=Biden nominates abortion rights lawyer in U.S. Supreme Court case to federal judgeship|url=https://www.reuters.com/legal/world/us/biden-nominates-abortion-rights-lawyer-us-supreme-court-case-federal-judgeship-2022-07-29/|access-date=July 29, 2022|website=Reuters|language=en}}{{Cite press release |title=Senate Confirms Judge Daniel J. He received a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1981 from the [[University of Kansas School of Law]]. He has spent his entire law career at the law firm of Stinson Morrison Hecker LLP (now Stinson LLP) in [[Wichita, Kansas|Wichita]],{{cite web|url=http://www.stinsonleonard.com/Content/News_and_Events/News_Releases/2014_News_Releases/Stinson_Leonard_Street_LLP_Completes_Merger/|title=Firm Completes Merger – Stinson Leonard Street LLP|website=www.stinsonleonard.com|access-date=May 1, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140317211744/http://www.stinsonleonard.com/Content/News_and_Events/News_Releases/2014_News_Releases/Stinson_Leonard_Street_LLP_Completes_Merger/|archive-date=March 17, 2014|url-status=dead}} starting as an [[Associate lawyer|associate]] in 1981 and becoming a [[Law firm partner|partner]] in 1988. He has represented businesses and governmental entities in complex [[civil litigation]] in federal and state courts. He also served as [[General Counsel|general counsel]] to the [[Kansas City Royals]].{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2013/08/01/president-obama-nominates-six-serve-united-states-district-courts|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Obama Nominates Six to Serve on the United States District Courts|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=August 1, 2013}} He has also served as a member of the board of directors and executive committee of the Providence Medical Center and St. John Hospital.{{FJC Bio|nid=1394441|inline=yes}} ===Federal judicial service=== On August 1, 2013, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Crabtree to serve as a judge of the United States District Court for the District of Kansas, to the seat vacated by Judge [[John Watson Lungstrum]], who assumed [[senior status]] on November 2, 2010. On January 16, 2014, his nomination was reported out of committee by a [[voice vote]].{{cite web|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting - January 16, 2014|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/ExecutiveBusinessMeetingResults-01-16-2014.pdf|work=United States Senate|publisher=Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=January 16, 2014}} On April 11, 2014, Senate Majority Leader [[Harry Reid]] filed a motion to invoke [[cloture]] on the nomination. On April 29, 2014, the [[United States Senate]] invoked cloture on his nomination by a 57–39 vote.{{cite web|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture on the Nomination of Daniel D. Crabtree, of Kansas, to be U.S. District Judge)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1132/vote_113_2_00114.htm|publisher=United States Senate|access-date=April 29, 2014}} On April 30, 2014, his nomination was confirmed by a 94–0 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=113&session=2&vote=00121|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Daniel D. Crabtree, of Kansas, to be U.S. District Judge for the District of Kansas)|publisher=United States Senate|access-date=April 30, 2014}} He received his judicial commission on May 1, 2014. He assumed [[senior status]] on August 11, 2025. ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1394441}} *{{Ballotpedia|Daniel_D._Crabtree}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef | before = [[John Watson Lungstrum]] }} {{s-ttl | title = {{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States District Court for the District of Kansas]]}} | years = 2014–2025 }} {{S-aft | after = [[Tony Mattivi]] }} {{s-end}} {{United States 10th Circuit senior district judges}} {{authority control}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Crabtree, Daniel D.}} [[Category:1956 births]] [[Category:Living people]] [[Category:20th-century American lawyers]] [[Category:21st-century American lawyers]] [[Category:Judges of the United States District Court for the District of Kansas]] [[Category:Kansas lawyers]] [[Category:Ottawa University alumni]] [[Category:United States district court judges appointed by Barack Obama]] [[Category:University of Kansas School of Law alumni]]
