[[University of Virginia]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Daniel Desmond Domenico ''' (born 1972) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Colorado]] and a United States circuit judge - designate of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit]]. == Biography == Domenico earned his [[Bachelor of Arts]], ''magna cum laude'', from [[Georgetown University]], and his [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Virginia School of Law]], where he was inducted into the [[Order of the Coif]] and served as an editor of the ''[[Virginia Law Review]]''. After graduating from law school, he was an associate at [[Hogan Lovells|Hogan & Hartson]] from 2000 to 2003 and then served as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Timothy Tymkovich]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit]] from 2003 to 2004. In 2004, Domenico was counsel to [[John Thune]]'s ultimately successful [[2004 United States Senate election in South Dakota|campaign for U.S. Senate]]. From 2006 to 2015, he served as the [[Solicitor General]] of [[Colorado]], where he oversaw major litigation for the state and represented governors from both the Democratic Party and Republican Party. During his tenure as Solicitor General, he argued in state and federal courts, including the [[Supreme Court of the United States]], and received the Supreme Court Best Brief Award from the [[National Association of Attorneys General]]. At the time of his appointment, he was the youngest state solicitor general in the country, and his nine years of service made him the longest serving solicitor general in Colorado history. He has also served as an [[adjunct professor]] of natural resources and advanced [[constitutional law]] at the [[Sturm College of Law]]. From 2015 to 2019, Domenico served as [[Principal (commercial law)|principal]] of Kittredge, LLC.[https://web.archive.org/web/20170928222558/https://www.whitehouse.gov/the-press-office/2017/09/28/president-donald-j-trump-announces-eighth-wave-judicial-candidates " President Donald J. Trump Announces Eighth Wave of Judicial Candidates" White House, September 28, 2017] {{PD-notice}} In early 2017, President [[Donald Trump]] appointed [[Neil Gorsuch]] to the [[Supreme Court of the United States]]. Trump considered nominating Domenico to succeed Gorsuch on the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit]], but ultimately chose [[Colorado Supreme Court]] Justice [[Allison H. Eid]], who was successfully confirmed.{{Cite web |url=https://abovethelaw.com/2017/05/circuit-court-nominees-in-the-trump-administration-a-nationwide-round-up/ |title=Circuit Court Nominees In The Trump Administration: A Nationwide Round-Up |last=Lat |first=David |author-link=David Lat |date=May 1, 2017 |website=[[Above the Law (website)|Above the Law]] |language=en-US |access-date=May 8, 2019}} == Federal judicial service == === District Court service === On September 28, 2017, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to nominate Domenico to an undetermined seat on the [[United States District Court for the District of Colorado]]. On October 2, 2017, he was officially nominated to the seat vacated by Judge [[Robert E. Blackburn]], who assumed [[senior status]] on April 12, 2016.[https://web.archive.org/web/20171002211505/https://www.whitehouse.gov/the-press-office/2017/10/02/eight-nominations-sent-senate-today "Eight Nominations Sent to the Senate Today" White House, October 2, 2017] On January 3, 2018, his nomination was returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.congress.gov/congressional-record/2018/1/3/daily-digest|title=Congressional Record|website=www.congress.gov}} On January 5, 2018, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to renominate Domenico to a federal judgeship.{{Cite web|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-renomination-21-judicial-nominees/|title=President Donald J. Trump Announces Renomination of 21 Judicial Nominees – The White House|website=trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov}} On January 8, 2018, his renomination was sent to the [[United States Senate|Senate]].{{Cite web|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/nominations-sent-senate-today-2/|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate Today – The White House|website=trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov}} On January 24, 2018, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/committee-activity/hearings/01/24/2018/nominations|title=Nominations | United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|website=www.judiciary.senate.gov}} On February 15, Domenico's nomination was reported out of committee by an 11–10 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/02-15-18%20Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – February 15, 2018, Senate Judiciary Committee}} On January 3, 2019, his nomination was returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]]. [[University of North Dakota School of Law|University of North Dakota]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | footnotes = }} '''Daniel Lee Hovland''' (born November 10, 1954) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of North Dakota]]. ==Education and career== Hovland was born in [[Moorhead, Minnesota]]. He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[Concordia College, Moorhead|Concordia College]] in 1976 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of North Dakota School of Law]] in 1979. He was a [[law clerk]] to Judge [[Ralph J. Erickstad]] of the [[North Dakota Supreme Court]] from 1979 to 1980. He was an assistant attorney general of Office of the Attorney General for the State of North Dakota from 1980 to 1983. He was in private practice in [[Bismarck, North Dakota]], from 1983 to 2002. He was a Commissioner, Bismarck Park & Recreation District, North Dakota from 1992 to 2002. He was an administrative law judge in the Office of Administrative Hearings of North Dakota from 1994 to 2002.{{FJC Bio|nid=1391666|inline=yes}} ===Federal judicial service=== Hovland was nominated by President [[George W. Bush]] on June 26, 2002, to a seat vacated by Judge [[Patrick Anthony Conmy]]. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on November 14, 2002, and received his commission on November 26, 2002. He served as chief judge from 2002 through 2009 and reassumed that role on November 1, 2016, until assuming [[senior status]] on November 10, 2019.{{Cite web |url=http://www.ndd.uscourts.gov/announce/Press_Release_Chief_Judge_DLH.pdf |title=Press Release: Daniel Hovland assumed Chief Judge position on 11/1/2016, United States District Court for the District of North Dakota, November 1, 2016 |access-date=November 18, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170114061053/http://www.ndd.uscourts.gov/announce/Press_Release_Chief_Judge_DLH.pdf |archive-date=January 14, 2017 |url-status=dead }} ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1391666}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Patrick Anthony Conmy]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States District Court for the District of North Dakota]]}}|years=2002–2019}} {{s-aft|after=[[Daniel M. '''Daniel Mack Traynor''' (born 1970)<ref name="Questionnaire">{{Cite web |title=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees: Daniel Mack Traynor |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Daniel%20Mack%20Traynor%20Senate%20Questionnaire%20-%20PUBLIC.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201008014704/https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Daniel%20Mack%20Traynor%20Senate%20Questionnaire%20-%20PUBLIC.pdf |archive-date=October 8, 2020}}</ref> is a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit]].

== Education ==

Traynor earned his [[Bachelor of Arts]] from the [[University of North Dakota]] and his [[Juris Doctor]], with distinction, from the [[University of North Dakota School of Law]], where he served as an associate editor on the ''North Dakota Law Review''.<ref name="WHBio">{{Cite web|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-judicial-nominees-united-states-marshal-nominee-4/|title=President Donald J. Trump Announces Judicial Nominees and United States Marshal Nominee – The White House|website=trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov}}</ref><ref name="SJCQ">{{cite web |last=Traynor |first=Daniel Mack |date=May 14, 2026 |title=Senate Judiciary Committee Questionnaire |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/traynor_sjq.pdf |website=www.judiciary.senate.gov |location= |publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary |access-date=May 14, 2026}}</ref>

== Legal career ==

Upon graduation from law school, Traynor served as a law clerk to Chief Justice [[Gerald W. VandeWalle]] of the [[North Dakota Supreme Court]]. From 1998 to 2019, he was a [[shareholder]] at the Traynor Law Firm in [[Devils Lake, North Dakota]], where his practice focused on insurance defense, personal injury – branches of [[insurance law]] – and business litigation.<ref name="WHBio" />

== Federal judicial service ==

=== District Court service ===

On August 28, 2019, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to nominate Traynor to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] for the [[United States District Court for the District of North Dakota]]. On September 19, 2019, his nomination was sent to the Senate. He was nominated to the seat vacated by Judge [[Daniel L. Hovland]], who assumed [[senior status]] on November 10, 2019.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/eight-nominations-three-withdrawals-sent-senate/|title=Eight Nominations and Three Withdrawals Sent to the Senate – The White House|website=trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov}}</ref> Traynor was recommended for the district court by Senator [[Kevin Cramer]], who announced his support for the nomination.<ref>{{Cite press release |title=Senator Kevin Cramer on President Trump's Nomination of Daniel Traynor to be U.S. District Judge for North Dakota |date=August 28, 2019 |location=Bismarck, North Dakota |url=https://www.cramer.senate.gov/senator-kevin-cramer-president-trumps-nomination-daniel-traynor-be-us-district-judge-north-dakota |access-date=August 28, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://bismarcktribune.com/news/local/crime-and-courts/president-trump-nominates-devils-lake-attorney-for-nd-federal-judgeship/article_807a5956-84c9-5391-bd3e-c95c83a2e170.html |title=President Trump nominates Devils Lake attorney for ND federal judgeship |last=Dura |first=Jack |website=Bismarck Tribune |date=28 August 2019 |language=en |access-date=2019-08-29}}</ref> On September 25, 2019, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/committee-activity/hearings/09/25/2019/nominations|title=Nominations | United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|website=www.judiciary.senate.gov}}</ref> On October 31, 2019, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 12–10 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/103119%20Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – October 31, 2019, Senate Judiciary Committee}}</ref> On December 18, 2019, the [[United States Senate]] invoked [[cloture]] on his nomination by a 51–42 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=1&vote=00405|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Daniel Mack Traynor, of North Dakota to be U.S. District Judge for the District of North Dakota) |website=www.senate.gov|access-date=2019-12-18}}</ref> On December 19, 2019, his nomination was confirmed by a 51–41 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=1&vote=00418|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Daniel Mack Traynor to be U.S. District Judge for the District of North Dakota)|website=www.senate.gov|access-date=2019-12-19}}</ref> He received his judicial commission on January 13, 2020.<ref name="fjc">{{FJC Bio|nid=7544351|inline=yes}}</ref> His service on the district court terminated on July 28, 2026, upon elevation to the court of appeals.

=== Court of Appeals service ===

On May 11, 2026, President Trump announced his intention to nominate Traynor to the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit]] to an undesignated seat.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/116558181455512054|title=Donald J. Trump (@realDonaldTrump)|website=Truth Social}}</ref> On May 12, 2026, Trump nominated Traynor to the seat on the Eighth Circuit being vacated by Judge [[Ralph R. Erickson]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/119th-congress/999/6|title=PN999-6 – Nomination of Daniel Mack Traynor for The Judiciary, 119th Congress (2025–2026)|date=May 12, 2026|website=www.congress.gov}}</ref> On July 16, 2026 his nomination was reported to the full Senate by a 11–10 vote. On July 22, 2026, the Senate invoked cloture on his nomination by a 51–46 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1192/vote_119_2_00206.htm|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Daniel Mack Traynor to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the Eighth Circuit)|website=www.senate.gov.|access-date=July 23, 2026}}</ref> On July 23, 2026, his nomination was confirmed by a 48–47 vote.<ref> {{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1192/vote_119_2_00208.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Daniel Mack Traynor, of North Dakota, to United States Circuit Judge for the Eighth Circuit)|website=www.senate.gov|access-date=July 23, 2026}}</ref> He received his judicial commission on July 24, 2026.<ref name="fjc"/>

=== Notable cases ===
Traynor dismissed ''[[Corner Post, Inc. v. Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System]]'' in 2022, ruling that the suit was outside of the [[statute of limitations]]. In 2025, after the [[Supreme Court of the United States]]' ruling, Traynor ruled that the [[Federal Reserve]] "had acted outside the scope of its authority" under the [[Durbin amendment]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Scarcella |first1=Mike |title=US judge vacates Fed's debit card 'swipe fees' rule, but pauses order for appeal |url=https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/us-judge-vacates-feds-debit-card-swipe-fees-rule-pauses-order-appeal-2025-08-07/ |publisher=[[Reuters]] |date=August 7, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=North Dakota Retail Association v. Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, 1:21-cv-00095 |url=https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/59869712/north-dakota-retail-association-v-board-of-governors-of-the-federal/ |work=[[CourtListener]] |language=en-us}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Weinberger |first1=Evan |title=Fed's Debit Card Swipe Fee Rule Tossed in Win for Retailers (2) |url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/banking-law/feds-debit-card-swipe-fee-rule-tossed-in-win-for-retailers |work=news.[[bloomberglaw.com]] |date=August 7, 2025 |language=en}}</ref>

== Memberships ==

Traynor is a member of the [[North Dakota State Board of Higher Education]] and former chair of the Disciplinary Board of the North Dakota Supreme Court.<ref name="WHBio" /> He has been a member of the [[Federalist Society]] since 2016.<ref name="Questionnaire" />

Hurley, U.S. District Court Judge.jpg | alt = | caption = | office = [[Senior status|Senior Judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida]] | term_start = February 24, 2009 | term_end = | office1 = Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida]] | term_start1 = March 11, 1994 | term_end1 = February 24, 2009 | appointer1 = [[List of federal judges appointed by Bill Clinton|Bill Clinton]] | predecessor1 = [[James Carriger Paine]] | successor1 = [[Kathleen M. Williams]] | pronunciation = | birth_name = | birth_date = {{Birth date and age|1943|02|24}} | birth_place = [[Fitchburg, Massachusetts]], U.S. | death_date = | death_place = | death_cause = | resting_place = | resting_place_coordinates = | citizenship = | party = | other_party = | height = | spouse = | partner = | relations = | children = | parents = | mother = | father = | relatives = | education = [[Saint Anselm College]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|AB]])
[[George Washington University Law School|George Washington University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | footnotes = }} '''Daniel Thomas Kozaki Hurley'''{{cite journal|journal=The Florida Bar Journal|volume=42|page=407|url=https://archive.org/details/sim_florida-bar-journal_1968-06_42_6/page/406/mode/2up|title=List of Current Applicants For Admission to The Florida Bar}} (born February 24, 1943){{Cite web |url=http://www.lawdiary.com/docs/subscribers/FL_Judicial_Biographies.pdf |title=BIOGRAPHIES OF FEDERAL COURT JUDGES SITTING IN FLORIDA |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170730052812/http://www.lawdiary.com/docs/subscribers/FL_Judicial_Biographies.pdf |archive-date=July 30, 2017 |access-date=May 9, 2018}} is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida]]. == Early life and education == Hurley was born in [[Fitchburg, Massachusetts]]. Both sides of his family were of [[Irish American|Irish ancestry]]; they had [[Immigration to the United States|immigrated to the United States]] and settled in Fitchburg after the [[Great Famine (Ireland)|Great Famine of Ireland]]. Hurley had decided to become a [[Priesthood (Catholic Church)|Catholic priest]] in the eighth grade. He attended a [[Catholic school|Catholic]] [[high school]] (where he was senior class president) before attending [[Saint Anselm College]], where he was [[student government]] president. After receiving his [[Bachelor of Arts|Artium Baccalaureus]] [[Academic degree|degree]] from Saint Anselm in 1964, Hurley attended [[St. Vincent de Paul Regional Seminary]], a Catholic [[seminary]] in [[Boynton Beach, Florida]] operated by the [[Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Miami|Diocese of Miami]] After a year at seminary, Hurley was sent to [[Washington, D.C.]], to work toward a [[master's degree]] in [[Relationship counseling|marriage counseling]]. Working in Washington led Hurley to change career paths. He entered [[George Washington University Law School]], and while he was a law student, he worked as a [[legislative aide]], in the House Post Office, and attended sessions of [[United States Congress|Congress]] and the [[Supreme Court of the United States|Supreme Court]]. Hurley received his [[Juris Doctor]] in 1968. == Career == Hurley served as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[John H. Pratt]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Columbia]] from 1968 to 1969 and for Judge [[Roger Robb]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit]] in 1969. In 1969 Hurley was a volunteer for the [[Moratorium to End the War in Vietnam|Vietnam Moratorium Committee]]. From 1970 to 1972 Hurley was assistant county solicitor for [[Palm Beach County, Florida]]. From 1973 to 1975 Hurley was assistant state attorney for the [[Florida Circuit Courts|Fifteenth Judicial Circuit of Florida]] and from 1975 to 1977 Hurley served as a judge on the county court of Palm Beach County. Hurley served as a judge on the Fifteenth Judicial Circuit from 1977 to 1979, on the [[Florida Fourth District Court of Appeal]] from 1979 to 1986, and again on the Fifteenth Judicial Circuit from 1986 to 1994. The return to circuit court was unusual; this was because Hurley missed the human contact of the [[trial court]] and disliked the isolation of the [[appellate court]]. ==Federal judicial service== President [[Bill Clinton]] nominated Judge Hurley to the United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida on November 10, 1993, to the seat vacated by [[James Carriger Paine]]. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on March 10, 1994, and he received his commission on March 11, 1994. He assumed [[senior status]] on February 4, 2009{{FJC Bio|nid=1382596|inline=yes}} and retired around 2018.{{Cite web|url=https://www.flsd.uscourts.gov/sites/flsd/files/adminorders/2017-38.pdf|title=In Re: Amended Magistrate Judge Pairing Assignment for Miami, Fort Lauderdale, West Palm Beach, Fort Pierce, and Key West|website=flsd.uscourts.gov|date=2017-07-05|access-date=2026-05-11}}{{Cite web|url=http://sdfla.blogspot.com/2018/03/west-palm-beach-state-courthouse.html|title=West Palm Beach State Courthouse dedicated to Judge Daniel T.K. Hurley (Guest Post by Ron Herman)|website=SDFLA blogspot|date=2018-03-02|access-date=2026-05-11}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.flsd.uscourts.gov/sites/flsd/files/adminorders/2020-45.pdf|title=In Re: Amended Magistrate Judge Pairing Assignment for Miami, Fort Lauderdale, West Palm Beach, Fort Pierce, and Key West|website=flsd.uscourts.gov|date=2020-07-09|access-date=2026-05-11}} === E-waste recycling case === In 2018, Hurley ruled that [[Eric Lundgren]], a [[California]] man who built a sizable business out of recycling [[electronic waste]], had infringed upon [[Microsoft]]'s products, valuing [[restore disk]]s Microsoft themselves provided for free at $700,000.{{cite news|last1=Jackman|first1=Tom|title=Reporter|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/true-crime/wp/2018/04/24/recycling-innovator-eric-lundgren-loses-appeal-on-computer-restore-discs-must-serve-15-month-prison-term/?noredirect=on|newspaper=The Washington Post|access-date=24 April 2018}} Despite the fact that the disks could only be used on machines already having a valid license and provided for free, Hurley ruled that the disks could be valued at $25 a piece, qualifying Lungren for a 15-month prison sentence and a $50,000 fine. Hurley also denied Lundgren's request to remain free pending his appeal, but the U.S. Court of Appeal for the 11th Circuit granted the request as Lundgren was about to surrender for imprisonment.{{Cite web|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/amphtml/news/true-crime/wp/2018/02/15/eric-lundgren-e-waste-recycling-innovator-faces-prison-for-trying-to-extend-lifespan-of-pcs/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180218161636/https://www.washingtonpost.com/amphtml/news/true-crime/wp/2018/02/15/eric-lundgren-e-waste-recycling-innovator-faces-prison-for-trying-to-extend-lifespan-of-pcs/|url-status=dead|archive-date=2018-02-18|title=Eric Lundgren, 'e-waste' recycling innovator, faces prison for trying to extend life span of PCs|website=www.washingtonpost.com|access-date=2018-04-27}} Hurley retired shortly after sentencing Lundgren.{{Cite web|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/peterhigh/2017/06/20/a-recycling-entrepreneur-has-been-sentenced-to-15-months-in-prison/|title=A Recycling Entrepreneur Has Been Sentenced To 15 Months In Prison|website=Forbes|date=2017-06-20|access-date=2026-05-12}} In an unpublished per curiam opinion issued April 11, 2018, the Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeal ultimately affirmed Lundgren's conviction and sentence. United States of America v. Eric Lundgren, Eleventh Circuit Case No. 17-12466. '''Darrel James Papillion''' (born 1968) is an American lawyer from [[Louisiana]] who serves as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana]].

== Early life and education ==

Papillion was born in 1968 in [[Eunice, Louisiana]].<ref name="FJC">{{FJC Bio|nid=13675556|inline=yes}}</ref> He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] from [[Louisiana State University|Louisiana State University and A&M College]] in 1990 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[Paul M. Hebert Law Center]] at [[Louisiana State University]] in 1994.<ref name="WHBio">{{Cite press release |title=President Biden Names Thirty-First Round of Judicial Nominees and Announces New Nominees to Serve as U.S. Attorney |date=March 20, 2023 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2023/03/20/president-biden-names-thirty-first-round-of-judicial-nominees-and-announces-new-nominees-to-serve-as-u-s-attorney/ |access-date=March 20, 2023}} {{PD-notice}}</ref>

== Career ==

From 1994 to 1995, Papillion served as a [[law clerk]] for Associate Justice [[Catherine D. Kimball]] of the [[Louisiana Supreme Court]]. From 1995 to 1999, he was an [[Associate lawyer|associate]] at McGlinchey Stafford A.P.L.C. and from 1999 to 2001, he was an associate at Moore, Walters & Thompson, A.P.L.C. From 2001 to 2009, he was a [[Law firm partner|partner]] at Moore, Walters, Thompson, Thomas, Papillion & Cullens, A.P.L.C. From 2009 to 2023, he was a partner with Walters, Papillion, Thomas, Cullens, LLC in [[Baton Rouge, Louisiana]].<ref name="WHBio" />  As a lawyer, he focused on [[product liability]], [[personal injury law|personal injury]], and [[wrongful death]] cases.<ref name="NOLA">{{Cite web|url=https://www.nola.com/news/politics/president-taps-baton-rouge-trial-lawyer-to-new-orleans-court/article_ae8a1376-c754-11ed-8f1f-b74a4c1c1dbb.html|title=Joe Biden taps Baton Rouge trial lawyer Darrel Papillion to New Orleans federal court|first=Mark |last=Ballard|website=NOLA.com|date=March 20, 2023 }}</ref> Since 2000, he has been an [[adjunct professor]] at [[Paul M. Hebert Law Center]] and from 2005 to 2006 he was an adjunct professor at [[Southern University Law Center]].<ref name="Martindale">{{Cite web |title=Darrel J. Papillion Profile {{!}} Baton Rouge, LA Lawyer {{!}} Martindale.com |url=https://www.martindale.com/attorney/darrel-j-papillion-590308/ |access-date=March 20, 2023 |website=www.martindale.com}}</ref>

From 2013 to 2014, he was president of the Baton Rouge Bar Association and from 2016 to 2017 he served as president of the Louisiana State Bar Association.<ref name="auto2">{{Cite web |title=Darrel J. Papillion Installed as 76th President of the Louisiana State Bar Association |url=https://www.lsba.org/NewsArticle.aspx?Article=970ddee2-23eb-4172-a645-541c329ae29b |access-date=March 20, 2023 |website=www.lsba.org}}</ref> From 2020 until becoming a federal judge, Papillion served on the Board of Directors of the [[Innocence Project]] of New Orleans.<ref name="Questionnaire">{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Papillion%20SJQ%20Public.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=April 17, 2023}}</ref><ref name="Darrel James Papillion Fact Sheet">{{Cite web |date=April 13, 2023 |title=AFJ: Darrel James Papillion Fact Sheet |url=https://www.afj.org/document/darrel-james-papillion-fact-sheet/ |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Notable cases ===

* Papillion served as co-counsel in ''Johnson v. [[Kyle Ardoin|Ardoin]]'', a [[Voting Rights Act of 1965|Voting Rights Act]] challenge to Louisiana's 2011 congressional districts. Papillion represented the plaintiffs, nine [[African Americans|African American]] voters who alleged the congressional map violated Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/new-congressional-maps-in-southern-states-dilute-black-votes-critics-say | title=New congressional maps in southern states dilute Black votes, critics say | website=[[PBS]] | date=September 4, 2022 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.voanews.com/a/6502133.html | title=Black Representation at Heart of Louisiana Redistricting Battle | date=March 27, 2022 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/court-cases/johnson-v-ardoin | title=Johnson v. Ardoin | Brennan Center for Justice }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.cullensgroup.com/team/darrel-papillion | title=Darrel Papillion, J.D. | Cullens Group | access-date=March 21, 2023 | archive-date=March 21, 2023 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230321055735/https://www.cullensgroup.com/team/darrel-papillion | url-status=dead }}</ref>
* Papillion represented plaintiffs in ''English v. Ardoin'' seeking declaratory and injunctive relief preventing Louisiana's Secretary of State from using the 2010 congressional districts reapportionment and redistricting map. The plaintiffs claimed the plan was violating the [[Constitution of the United States|United States]] and Louisiana constitutions.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/world/us/us-supreme-court-reinstates-louisiana-electoral-map-faulted-racial-bias-2022-06-28/|title=U.S. Supreme Court allows Louisiana electoral map faulted for racial bias|first=Andrew|last=Chung|newspaper=Reuters |date=June 29, 2022|via=www.reuters.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://casetext.com/case/english-v-ardoin|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230404222100/https://casetext.com/case/english-v-ardoin|url-status=dead|archive-date=April 4, 2023|title=English v. Ardoin, 335 So. 3d 272 | Casetext Search + Citator|website=casetext.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last1=Ballard |first1=Mark |last2=Karlin |first2=Sam |date=June 6, 2022 |title=Louisiana lawmakers must redraw maps, come up with second majority-minority district, judge rules |url=https://www.theadvocate.com/baton_rouge/news/politics/elections/louisiana-lawmakers-must-redraw-maps-come-up-with-second-majority-minority-district-judge-rules/article_6811742e-e5e2-11ec-aa09-2b81c381c9e8.html |website=The Advocate |language=en}}</ref>

=== Federal judicial service ===

On March 20, 2023, President [[Joe Biden]] announced his intent to nominate Papillion to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana]].<ref name="NOLA" /> On March 21, 2023, his nomination was sent to the Senate. President Biden nominated Papillion to the seat vacated by Judge [[Carl Barbier]], who assumed [[senior status]] on January 1, 2023.<ref>{{Cite press release |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |date=March 21, 2023 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2023/03/21/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-101/}}</ref> He had the support of Senators [[Bill Cassidy]] and [[John Kennedy (Louisiana politician)|John Kennedy]].<ref>{{Cite news|last=Raymond|first=Nate|title=Biden nominates four new federal judges across three states|url=https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/biden-nominates-four-new-federal-judges-across-three-states-2023-03-20/|access-date=April 21, 2023|website=reuters.com|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|last=Alder|first=Madison|title=Louisiana Trial Attorney Among Four New Biden Judicial Picks|url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/louisiana-trial-attorney-among-four-new-biden-judicial-picks|access-date=April 21, 2023|website=news.bloomberglaw.com|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|last=Press-Herald|first=Minden|title=Kennedy supports Louisiana's Papillion: "He's a real lawyer's lawyer"|url=https://press-herald.com/kennedy-supports-louisianas-papillion-hes-a-real-lawyers-lawyer/|website=press-herald.com|access-date=April 21, 2023}}</ref> On April 18, 2023, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Nominations|date=April 17, 2023|publisher=[[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]]|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/committee-activity/hearings/04/18/2023/nominations}}</ref> During his confirmation hearing, he was questioned by Senators [[Mike Lee]] and [[Marsha Blackburn]] over his role in prosecuting Tony Spell, a Louisiana pastor who defied state restrictions during the [[COVID-19 pandemic]].<ref>{{Cite news|last=Ballard|first=Mark|title=New Orleans judicial nominee grilled on Tony Spell prosecution|url=https://www.nola.com/news/politics/judicial-nominee-questioned-about-tony-spell-prosecution/article_20e4e55c-de18-11ed-86ed-5f1db9c1b47f.amp.html|access-date=April 21, 2023|website=nola.com|language=en}}</ref> On May 11, 2023, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 15–6 vote.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/2023-05-11%20-%20EBM%20-%20Results.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – May 11, 2023|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=May 11, 2023}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|last=Ballard|first=Mark|title=Senate committee sets up final Senate vote on confirmation of Darrel Papillion to federal bench|url=https://www.nola.com/news/politics/judiciary-panel-advances-darrel-papillion-to-confirmation/article_0991a3b6-ea7c-11ed-b445-e7fc3be7d2d3.amp.html|website=nola.com|access-date=May 11, 2023|language=en}}</ref> On May 17, 2023, the [[United States Senate]] invoked cloture on his nomination by a 63–33 vote.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00129.htm|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Darrel James Papillion to be United States District Judge for the Eastern District of Louisiana)|website=United States Senate|date=May 17, 2023|access-date=May 17, 2023}}</ref> On May 30, 2023, his nomination was confirmed by a 59–31 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00133.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Darrel James Papillion, of Louisiana, to be U.S. District Judge for the Eastern District of Louisiana)|website=United States Senate|date=May 30, 2023|access-date=May 30, 2023}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|date=May 30, 2023|last=Ballard|first=Mark|title=Senate confirms Baton He received his judicial commission on June 1, 2023.<ref name="FJC" />

== Personal life==
He married his wife, Shirley, in 1991 at St. Joan of Arc Catholic Church in [[Oberlin, Louisiana]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=August 8, 1991 |title=Shirley Cezar married Darrel Papillion |pages=5 |work=Basile Weekly |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/23874066/shirley-cezar-married-darrel-papillion/ |access-date=April 7, 2023}}</ref> In 2018, Papillion was considered for an earlier bench opening but withdrew from consideration when his wife was diagnosed with [[cancer]] and later died.<ref name="NOLA" /> Papillion is [[Catholic Church|Catholic]].<ref name="auto1">{{Cite web |title=Darrel J. Papillion, Member {{!}} Walters, Papillion, Thomas, Cullens |url=https://www.lawbr.net/staff/darrel-j-papillion |access-date=April 7, 2023 |website=www.lawbr.net |archive-date=April 7, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230407131126/https://www.lawbr.net/staff/darrel-j-papillion |url-status=dead }}</ref>

[[George Washington University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Darrin Phillip Gayles''' (born 1966)[https://www.blackpast.org/african-american-history/darrin-phillip-gayles-1966/ BlackPast Darrin Phillip Gayles (1966- )] is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida]] and former [[Florida Circuit Courts|Florida Circuit Court judge]]. == Education and legal career == Gayles received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in 1990 from [[Howard University]]. He received a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1993 from the [[George Washington University Law School]]. He began his career as an assistant state attorney in the Miami-Dade State Attorney's Office from 1993 to 1997. From 1997 to 1999, he served as an assistant district counsel at the [[United States Immigration and Naturalization Service]]. From 1999 to 2004, he served as an [[assistant United States attorney]] for the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida|Southern District of Florida]].{{Cite web |date=February 5, 2014 |title=President Obama Announces Intent to Nominate Four to Serve on the United States District Courts |url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/02/05/president-obama-announces-intent-nominate-four-serve-united-states-distr |website=[[whitehouse.gov]] |via=[[NARA|National Archives]]}}{{FJC Bio|nid=1394576|inline=yes}} == Judicial career == === State judicial service === In 2004, Gayles became a judge, serving as a county judge in [[Miami-Dade County, Florida|Miami-Dade County]] within the Eleventh Judicial Circuit. From 2011 to 2014, he served as a [[Florida Circuit Courts|circuit court judge]] on the [[Eleventh Judicial Circuit Court of Florida]]. === Federal judicial service === On February 6, 2014, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Gayles to serve as a United States District Judge of the United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida, to the seat vacated by Judge [[Patricia A. Seitz]], who assumed [[senior status]] on November 16, 2012.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/02/06/presidential-nominations-sent-senate|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=February 6, 2014}} He received a hearing before the [[United States Senate Judiciary Committee]] on April 1, 2014.{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/judicial-nominations-2014-04-01|title=Nominations|publisher=Committee on the Judiciary|work=United States Senate|date=April 1, 2014}} On May 8, 2014, his nomination was reported out of committee by a [[voice vote]].{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%20-%2005-08-14.pdf|title=Executive Business Meeting|publisher=Committee on the Judiciary|work=United States Senate|date=May 8, 2014}} On June 16, 2014, the [[United States Senate]] invoked [[cloture]] by a 55–37 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=113&session=2&vote=00194|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture on the Nomination of Darrin P. Gayles, of Florida, to be U.S. District Judge)|publisher=United States Senate|access-date=June 16, 2014}} On June 17, 2014, his nomination was confirmed by a 98–0 vote,{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=113&session=2&vote=00197|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Darrin P. Gayles, of Florida, to be U.S. District Judge)|publisher=United States Senate|access-date=June 19, 2014}} making him the first openly [[gay]] [[African-American]] federal judge.{{cite news|last=Weaver|first=Jay|title=Miami's Gayles confirmed as first openly gay black male judge on federal bench|url=http://www.miamiherald.com/2014/06/17/4183778/miamis-gayles-confirmed-as-first.html|access-date=June 17, 2014|newspaper=Miami Herald |date=June 17, 2014}}{{cite web|url=http://miamiherald.typepad.com/gaysouthflorida/2014/02/obama-nominates-four-for-federal-judgeships-including-gay-miami-dade-judge-darrin-gayles.html|title=Obama nominates four for federal judgeships, including gay Miami-Dade Judge Darrin Gayles – Steve Rothaus' Gay South Florida|website=miamiherald.typepad.com}} He received his judicial commission on June 19, 2014. [[File:Darrin Gayles.jpg|thumb|right|250px|Darrin P. Gayles U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee hearing]] ===Cases=== Sitting with the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit|Eleventh Circuit]] in July 2020, Gayles dissented when the court upheld an Alabama voter ID law without a trial even though evidence showed that voters of color were twice as likely to lack ID as white voters. Gayles wrote "The majority opinion essentially argues that we should not penalize Alabama’s legislators for Alabama’s past; rather, we should start with a clean slate when reviewing the Photo ID Law. But this is not what the law commands us to do. Alabama’s history of voter suppression is relevant here and provides a wealth of direct and circumstantial evidence that should be considered at trial."{{Cite web|url=https://cases.justia.com/federal/appellate-courts/ca11/18-10151/18-10151-2020-07-21.pdf?ts=1595356240|title=18-10151 Greater Birmingham Ministries v. Secretary of State for Alabama|website=Justia|date=July 21, 2020|access-date=August 18, 2021}} In 2025, Gayles was assigned [[Donald Trump]]'s lawsuit against ''[[The Wall Street Journal]]'' and [[Rupert Murdoch]] after the WSJ ran a story on an [[Jeffrey Epstein's birthday book|alleged lette]]r Trump wrote to sex offender [[Jeffrey Epstein]] for his 50th birthday.{{cite news|url = https://www.politico.com/news/2025/07/21/wall-street-lawsuit-judge-donald-trump-00465363|title = Trump's lawsuit against Wall Street Journal now has a judge — and it's not Aileen Cannon|last = Cheney|first = Kyle|work = [[Politico]]|date = July 21, 2025|accessdate = July 21, 2025}} In April 2026, Gayles dismissed the lawsuit citing a failure to "adequately allege actual malice".{{Cite news |date=2026-04-13 |title=Judge dismisses Trump’s lawsuit against Wall Street Journal and Murdoch |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/apr/13/trump-lawsuit-wall-street-journal-murdoch-dismissed |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260413164206/https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/apr/13/trump-lawsuit-wall-street-journal-murdoch-dismissed |archive-date=2026-04-13 |access-date=2026-04-13 |work=the Guardian |language=en}} == See also == * [[List of African-American federal judges]] * [[List of African-American jurists]] * [[List of first minority male lawyers and judges in the United States]] * [[List of first minority male lawyers and judges in Florida]] * [[List of LGBT jurists in the United States]] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== * {{FJC Bio|nid=1394576}} * {{Ballotpedia|Darrin_P._Gayles}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Patricia A. He previously served as an [[assistant United States attorney]] in the Eastern District of North Carolina. ==Education and early life== Bragdon was born in 1977 in [[Warren, Ohio]].{{cite web |date=September 18, 2025 |title=Senate Judiciary Committee Questionnaire |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/bragdon_sjq.pdf |location= |publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary |access-date=September 18, 2025}} He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in [[government]] from [[Campbell University]] in 1999 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Virginia School of Law]] in 2002, where he was editor of the [[Virginia Law Review]]. Williams]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit]] from 2002 to 2003. ==Career== Bragdon worked as an [[Associate lawyer|associate]] at Burr and Forman in their [[Birmingham, Alabama]] office from 2003 to 2006. He then [[law clerk|clerked]] for Associate Justice [[Clarence Thomas]] of the [[United States Supreme Court]] from 2006 to 2007. Bragdon was hired to be an [[assistant United States attorney]] for the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of North Carolina|United States Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of North Carolina]] in 2007. He was promoted to chief of appeals for that office in 2021.{{Cite web|url=https://www.budd.senate.gov/2025/08/22/budd-tillis-applaud-nomination-of-four-nc-judges/|title=Budd, Tillis Applaud Nomination of Four NC Judges|first=samara|last=st.john|date=August 23, 2025}} ===Federal judicial service=== On August 22, 2025, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intention to nominate Bragdon to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Middle District of North Carolina]] vacated by Judge [[Loretta Copeland Biggs]].{{Cite web|url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/trump-taps-federal-prosecutors-for-north-carolina-federal-courts|title=Trump Taps Federal Prosecutors for North Carolina Trial Courts|date=August 22, 2025}} The nomination was transmitted to the [[United States Senate]] on September 15, 2025.{{Cite web|url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/119th-congress/520/1|title=PN520-1 - Nomination of David A. Bragdon for The Judiciary, 119th Congress (2025-2026)|date=September 17, 2025|website=www.congress.gov}} On September 17, 2025, a confirmation hearing was held for him and other nominees before the Senate Judiciary Committee.{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/committee-activity/hearings/nominations-09-17-2025|title=LOCATION CHANGE: Nominations | United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|website=www.judiciary.senate.gov}} October 9, 2025, the committee voted in favor of his nomination by a 12–10 [[party-line vote]].{{Cite web |date=October 9, 2025 |title=RESULTS OF EXECUTIVE BUSINESS MEETING |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/7724bc11-ea93-6871-6706-e3abbb21e374/2025-10-09_EBM_Results.pdf |access-date=December 4, 2025 |website=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary}} On December 1, 2025, the U.S. Senate voted to invoke [[cloture]] on his nomination by a vote of 50–41.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1191/vote_119_1_00624.htm|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: David A. Bragdon to be U.S. District Judge for the Middle District of North Carolina)|website=www.senate.gov}} The following day, his nomination was confirmed by a 53–45 vote.{{Cite web |date=December 2, 2025 |title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: David A. Bragdon, of North Carolina, to be U.S. District Judge for the Middle District of North Carolina) |url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1191/vote_119_1_00625.htm |access-date=December 4, 2025 |website=senate.gov}} He received his judicial commission on December 12, 2025.{{FJC Bio|nid=13762085|inline=yes}} == See also == * [[List of law clerks for the tenth seat of the Supreme Court of the United States]] ==References== {{Reflist}} == External links == * {{FJC Bio|nid=13762085}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef | before = [[Loretta Copeland Biggs]] }} {{s-ttl | title = {{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Middle District of North Carolina]]}} | years = 2025–present }} {{S-inc}} {{s-end}} {{United States 4th Circuit district judges}} {{Authority control}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Bragdon, David Alan}} [[Category:1977 births]] [[Category:Living people]] [[Category:21st-century American judges]] [[Category:21st-century American lawyers]] [[Category:Assistant United States attorneys]] [[Category:Campbell University alumni]] [[Category:Judges of the United States District Court for the Middle District of North Carolina]] [[Category:Law clerks of the Supreme Court of the United States]] [[Category:North Carolina lawyers]] [[Category:People from Warren, Ohio]] [[Category:United States district court judges appointed by Donald Trump]] [[Category:University of Virginia School of Law alumni]] {{US-judge-stub}}

[[University of Virginia School of Law|University of Virginia]] ([[Master of Laws|LLM]]) | footnotes = }} '''David Alan Faber''' (born October 21, 1942) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of West Virginia]]. ==Education and career== Feber was born in [[Charleston, West Virginia]]. He graduated from [[Sissonville High School]] and received an [[Bachelor of Arts|Artium Baccalaureus]] degree from [[West Virginia University]] in 1964 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Yale Law School]] in 1967. He was in private practice in Charleston from 1967 to 1968. He was in the [[United States Air Force]], [[JAG Corps]] from 1968 to 1972, and was then in the [[United States Naval Reserve]] from 1973 to 1977. He returned to private practice in Charleston from 1972 to 1981, and was in the West Virginia Air National Guard from 1978 to 1992. He was the [[United States Attorney]] for the Southern District of West Virginia from 1981 to 1986, again returning to private practice in Charleston from 1987 to 1991, also serving as a special part-time [[assistant United States attorney]] for the Northern District of West Virginia from 1988 to 1990.{{FJC Bio|nid=1380591|inline=yes}} Faber earned his [[Doctor of Philosophy]] in history from the [[University of Cambridge]]. He earned his [[Master of Laws]] from the [[University of Virginia School of Law]]. ===Federal judicial service=== On August 1, 1991, Faber was nominated by President [[George H. W. Bush]] to a new seat on the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of West Virginia]] created by 104 Stat. 5089. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on November 21, 1991, and received his commission on November 25, 1991. He served as Chief Judge from 2002 to 2007, assuming [[senior status]] on December 31, 2008. '''David Augustin Ruiz''' (born 1973)<ref name="Questionnaire">{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Ruiz%20SJQ%20Public%20Final.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=November 15, 2021}}</ref> is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Ohio]]. He served as a [[United States magistrate judge]] of the same court from 2016 to 2022.

== Education ==

Ruiz received his [[Bachelor of Arts]] from [[Ohio State University]] in 1997 and his [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[Ohio State University Moritz College of Law]] in 2000.<ref name="WHBio">{{Cite press release |title=President Biden Names Eighth Round of Judicial Nominees |date=September 30, 2021 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/09/30/president-biden-names-eighth-round-of-judicial-nominees/ |access-date=September 30, 2021}} {{PD-notice}}</ref>

== Legal career ==

From 2001 to 2003, Ruiz worked in private practice in [[Pittsburgh]], [[Pennsylvania]]. From 2003 to 2010, he worked as a senior attorney at Calfee Halter & Griswold in [[Cleveland]]. From 2010 to 2016, he served as an [[Assistant United States Attorney]] in the Northern District of Ohio.<ref name="WHBio" /> Prior to Ruiz becoming a United States magistrate judge, he served as a [[pro bono]] attorney for [[The Legal Aid Society]] of Cleveland.<ref>{{Cite web| title=Short Takes | page=1 | url=https://lasclev.org/wp-content/uploads/2011/05/04-16-07-Crains-Legal-Affairs.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211217174519/https://lasclev.org/wp-content/uploads/2011/05/04-16-07-Crains-Legal-Affairs.pdf | archive-date=2021-12-17}}</ref>

== Federal judicial service ==

Ruiz was sworn in as a [[United States magistrate judge]] on October 1, 2016.<ref>{{Cite web |title=David A. Ruiz |url=https://www.uscourts.gov/judicial-milestones/david-ruiz |access-date=September 30, 2021 |website=United States Courts |language=en}}</ref> He filled the vacancy left by the retirement of Judge Kenneth S. McHargh on September 30, 2016.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Kenneth S. McHargh |url=https://www.uscourts.gov/judicial-milestones/kenneth-s-mchargh |access-date=September 30, 2021 |website=United States Courts |language=en}}</ref>

On September 30, 2021, President [[Joe Biden]] nominated Ruiz to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Ohio]]. President Biden nominated Ruiz to the seat vacated by Judge [[Solomon Oliver Jr.]], who assumed [[senior status]] on February 15, 2021.<ref name="September30">{{Cite press release|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate|date=September 30, 2021|publisher=The White House|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/09/30/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-37/}} {{PD-notice}}</ref> On November 17, 2021, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Nominations|date=November 17, 2021|publisher=[[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]]|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/11/10/2021/nominations|access-date=December 20, 2021|archive-date=December 20, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211220231817/https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/11/10/2021/nominations|url-status=dead}}</ref> During his confirmation hearing, Senator [[Marsha Blackburn]] questioned whether he had enough of a background in criminal proceedings to serve as a judge.<ref>{{Cite news|date=November 17, 2021|last=Eaton|first=Sabrina|title=Senate Judiciary Committee grills three Northeast Ohio judicial nominees on past cases|url=https://www.cleveland.com/news/2021/11/senate-judiciary-committee-grills-three-northeast-ohio-judicial-nominees-on-past-cases.html|website=cleveland.com|access-date=June 13, 2023}}</ref>
On December 16, 2021, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 14–8 vote.<ref>{{Cite news|date=December 16, 2021|last=Eaton|first=Sabrina|title=Senate Judiciary Committee signs off on three prospective Northeast Ohio judges|url=https://www.cleveland.com/news/2021/12/senate-judiciary-committee-signs-off-on-three-prospective-northeast-ohio-judges.html|website=cleveland.com|access-date=June 13, 2023}}</ref><ref name="PN1214">{{Cite web|date=December 16, 2021|title=PN1214 - Nomination of David Augustin Ruiz for The Judiciary, 117th Congress (2021–2022)|url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/117th-congress/1214|access-date=December 20, 2021|website=www.congress.gov}}</ref> On January 3, 2022, his nomination was returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]];<ref name="PN1214"/> he was renominated the same day.<ref>{{Cite press release|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate|date=January 3, 2022|publisher=The White House|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/01/03/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-53/}} {{PD-notice}}</ref> 

On January 13, 2022, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 14–8 vote.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Mark%20up%201.13.22%20Results.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – January 13, 2022|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=January 13, 2022}}</ref> On February 1, 2022, the Senate invoked cloture on his nomination by a 59–38 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|date=February 1, 2022|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: David Augustin Ruiz to be U.S. District Judge for the Northern District of Ohio)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1172/vote_117_2_00016.htm|access-date=February 1, 2022|website=United States Senate}}</ref> Later that day, his nomination was confirmed by a 62–35 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|date=February 1, 2022|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: David Augustin Ruiz to be U.S. District Judge for the Northern District of Ohio)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1172/vote_117_2_00017.htm|access-date=February 1, 2022|website=United States Senate}}</ref> He received his judicial commission on February 8, 2022.<ref>{{FJC Bio|nid=11445751|inline=yes}}</ref> 
He was sworn in on February 10, 2022.<ref>{{Cite web|date=February 10, 2022|title=David A. Ruiz and Bridget Meehan Brennan Sworn In as United States District Judges|url=https://www.ohnd.uscourts.gov/news/david-ruiz-and-bridget-meehan-brennan-sworn-united-states-district-judges|website=ohnd.uscourts.gov|access-date=May 28, 2023}}</ref> He became the first [[Hispanic]] district court judge in Ohio.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Diamond|first=Jeremy|date=September 30, 2021|title=Biden nominates 10 more to federal bench, with continued focus on diversity|url=https://www.cnn.com/2021/09/30/politics/federal-judicial-nominees-joe-biden/index.html|access-date=September 30, 2021|website=CNN}}</ref>

'''David Alan Ezra''' (born June 27, 1947)<ref>{{cite book|url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=pur1.32754076879414&seq=232|title=Confirmation Hearings on Federal Appointments: Hearings before the Committee on the Judiciary, United States Senate, One Hundredth Congress, First Session, Part 7|year=1989|publisher=U.S. Government Printing Office|page=222}}</ref> is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Hawaii]]. Since January 2013, Ezra has been designated by the [[Chief Justice of the United States]] to serve on the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Texas]], San Antonio and Austin Divisions to help ease the heavy workload for the federal judges in Texas. Judge Ezra is often designated to sit on the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit where he holds the record for the most designated sittings of any judge in that Court’s history.<ref name=":0" />

==Early life and education==

Born in [[Columbus, Ohio]], Ezra’s family moved to Hawaii when he was quite young and he grew up in Hawaii. Ezra graduated from St. Louis High School in Honolulu and received a [[Bachelor of Business Administration]] from [[St. Mary's University, Texas|St. Mary's University]] ''[[Latin honors#magna cum laude|magna cum laude]]'' in 1969, followed by a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[St. Mary's University School of Law]] in 1972, where he graduated first in his class.<ref>{{cite web|title=Bio: The Honorable David A. Ezra (Retired), Lecturer in Law|url=https://www.law.hawaii.edu/person/honorable-david-ezra|website=University of Hawaii|publisher=William S. Richardson School of Law|access-date=March 27, 2017|archive-date=March 28, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170328195724/https://www.law.hawaii.edu/person/honorable-david-ezra|url-status=dead}}</ref> He served in the US Marine Corps from 1966-1968. He also served as a commissioned officer in the [[United States Army]] from 1971 to 1976.

==Career==

Ezra was in private practice in [[Honolulu]], [[Hawaii]] from 1972 to 1988, becoming a partner in the law firm of Anthony, Hoddick, Reinwald, and O'Connor in 1980. Ezra became the Managing Partner of the law firm of Ezra, O'Connor, Moon and Tam in 1981.<ref name="fjc.gov">{{FJC Bio|nid=1380586|inline=yes}}</ref> He was an [[adjunct professor]] of law at the [[William S. Richardson School of Law]] from 1978 to 2013.  He has been the jurist in residence at St. Mary’s University School of Law since 2016.{{citation needed|date=January 2026}}

Ezra is a member of both the Hawaii and Texas Bars.{{citation needed|date=August 2026}}

===Federal judicial service===
On November 18, 1987, Ezra was nominated by President [[Ronald Reagan]] to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the District of Hawaii]] vacated by Judge [[Samuel Pailthorpe King]]. Ezra was unanimously confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on May 19, 1988, and received his commission on May 20, 1988.<ref name="fjc.gov"/> He served as chief judge from 1999 to 2005.<ref>{{cite news|title=Former attorney general, prosecutors nominated for federal judge|url=http://www.staradvertiser.com/2015/06/16/breaking-news/former-attorney-general-prosecutors-nominated-for-federal-judge/|access-date=March 27, 2017|work=Honolulu Star Advertiser|date=June 16, 2015}}</ref>

Ezra was the youngest federal judge ever appointed to the District of Hawaii and the first federal judge from Hawaii to be elected to the [[Judicial Conference of the United States]]. Ezra also served as Secretary, Vice President, and [[President (corporate title)|President]] of the District Judges Association of the Ninth Circuit and served multiple terms on the Ninth Circuit Judicial Council. He also served as Vice President of the Federal Judges Association and remains a member of the Board of Directors. Ezra was appointed and served on the Judicial Conference Committee on the Administration of the Bankruptcy System and was its long range planning chairman. In 2010 Ezra was appointed to the Council on Budget and Finance of the [[Judicial Conference of the United States]]. In 2023 Ezra was appointed to the Committee which oversees Oscar, the federal judicial law clerk hiring system. Ezra continues to be designated to serve on federal courts both within and outside the Ninth Circuit, particularly in complex cases, and is often designated to sit on the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals where he holds the record for the most designated sittings of any judge in that Court’s history. He assumed [[senior status]] on June 27, 2012, having served as an active judge in regular service longer than any other judge in Hawaii history.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Zimmerman|first1=Malia|title=Hawaii's Longest Serving Active Federal Judge – David Ezra – Moves to Senior Status This Summer, But Controversial Cases Still on His Docket|url=http://www.hawaiireporter.com/hawaiis-longest-serving-active-federal-judge-david-ezra-moves-to-senior-status-this-summer-but-controversial-cases-still-on-his-docket|access-date=March 27, 2017|work=Hawaii Reporter|date=February 21, 2012}}</ref> Ezra continues to carry a full caseload.

Ezra was awarded the University of Hawaii Lifetime Achievement Award; the St. Mary’s University Lifetime Achievement Award; The St. Mary’s University School of Law Rosewood Gavel Award; The Federal Bar of Austin, Texas “Judge David Alan Ezra” Extraordinary Achievement Award which they named after him.

In January 2013, Ezra was designated by the Chief Justice [[John Roberts]] to the Western District of Texas, San Antonio and Austin Divisions, to help ease the heavy workload for the federal judges in that state.<ref name=":0">{{cite news|title=Hawaiian Judge Coming to Alamo City|url=http://www.mysanantonio.com/news/local_news/article/Hawaiian-judge-coming-to-Alamo-City-4145437.php|newspaper=San Antonio Express News|date=December 26, 2012}}</ref> Ezra maintains chambers and courtrooms in both San Antonio and Austin, but does the bulk of his court work in Austin, Texas.

In September 2023, Ezra ruled that a controversial floating border barrier in the Rio Grande River violates federal law and must be removed. Texas Governor Greg Abbott had ordered deployment of the floating barrier in July as part of Operation Lone Star, his multibillion-dollar effort to fight illegal immigration and smuggling at the U.S.-Mexico border.<ref>{{Cite web|title=The floating border barrier in the Rio Grande must be removed, a federal judge rules|website=[[NPR]] |url=https://www.npr.org/2023/09/06/1198028921/texas-floating-border-barrier-rio-grande-abbott-judge-mexico-immigration}}</ref>
 
Ezra presided over ''[[United States v. Texas (2024)|United States v. Texas]]'', a legal challenge to [[Texas Senate Bill 4 (2023)|Texas Senate Bill 4]] which empowers state and local police officers to arrest migrants who cross from [[Mexico]] without authorization.<ref>{{Cite news|title=TA Legal Showdown on the Border Between the U.S. and Texas: What to Know
|work=The New York Times |date=27 March 2024 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/02/15/us/texas-border-law-challenge-explainer.html |last1=Goodman |first1=J. David |last2=Sandoval |first2=Edgar }}</ref> Ezra struck down S.B. 4 in February 2024, and the 5th circuit affirmed Ezra's ruling on March 26, 2024.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ca5.uscourts.gov/opinions/pub/24/24-50149-CV2.pdf|title=24-50149 United States of America vs. State of Texas|website=ca5.uscourts.gov|date=March 26, 2024|access-date=April 20, 2024}}</ref>

'''David Briones''' (born February 26, 1943) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Texas]].

==Education and career==
Born in [[El Paso, Texas|El Paso]], [[Texas]], Briones was in the [[United States Army]] from 1964 to 1966, then received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from the [[University of Texas at El Paso]] in 1969 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Texas School of Law]] in 1971. He was in private practice in El Paso from 1971 to 1991. He was a judge on the El Paso County Court at Law Number One from 1991 to 1994.

===Federal judicial service===
On August 25, 1994, Briones was nominated by President [[Bill Clinton]] to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Texas]] vacated by [[Lucius Desha Bunton]]. Briones was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on October 7, 1994, and received his commission on October 11, 1994. He assumed [[senior status]] on February 26, 2009. He was succeeded by Judge [[David C. Guaderrama]]<ref>{{cite web |url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2011/09/14/president-obama-nominates-judge-david-campos-guaderrama-united-states-di|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]| title=President Obama Nominates Judge David Campos Guaderrama to the United States District Court |via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=September 14, 2011 }}</ref>

On December 10, 2019, Briones blocked President Donald Trump from using federal military funds for the border wall.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://thehill.com/regulation/court-battles/473991-federal-judge-in-texas-blocks-trump-from-using-military-funds-for|title=Federal judge in Texas blocks Trump from using military funds for border wall|first=Zack|last=Budryk|date=December 10, 2019|website=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]]}}</ref> On January 8, 2020, the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]] stayed Briones' [[nationwide injunction]], pending disposition of the appeal.

Guaderrama received his [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in 1975 from [[New Mexico State University]] and his [[Juris Doctor]] in 1979 from the [[University of Notre Dame Law School]]. ==Career== He entered solo private practice in 1979 and became a partner of Guaderrama and Guaderrama from 1980 to 1986. He served as Chief Public Defender of [[El Paso County, Texas]], from 1987 to 1994. Guaderrama served as District Judge of the 243rd [[District Court of Texas]] in [[El Paso County, Texas|El Paso County]] from 1995 to 2010. Judges of Texas district courts are elected in partisan elections: Guaderrama ran under the [[Texas Democratic Party|Democratic Party]] banner.{{cite web|url=http://www.co.el-paso.tx.us/elections/2006-11-07/final.shtm|title=El Paso County: election results|access-date=2012-04-26|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120304045911/http://www.co.el-paso.tx.us/elections/2006-11-07/final.shtm|archive-date=2012-03-04|url-status=dead}} ===Federal judicial service=== In October 2010, he was appointed magistrate judge of the United States District Court for the Western District of Texas.{{FJC Bio|nid=1393966|inline=yes}} On September 14, 2011, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Guaderrama to be a United States district judge of the United States District Court for the Western District of Texas,{{cite web | author=The White House: Office of the Press Secretary | url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2011/09/14/president-obama-nominates-judge-david-campos-guaderrama-united-states-di | title=President Obama Nominates Judge David Campos Guaderrama to the United States District Court | date=September 14, 2011 | via=[[NARA|National Archives]] | work=[[whitehouse.gov]] | access-date=September 17, 2011}} to the seat vacated by Judge [[David Briones]] who assumed senior status on February 26, 2009. On November 2, 2011, he received a hearing before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] and his nomination was reported to the floor on December 1, 2011. Guaderrama's nomination was confirmed by [[voice vote]] on April 26, 2012. He received his commission on April 30, 2012. He served in the [[United States Navy]] from January 1969 to October 1972 and became a [[Yeoman (United States Navy)|Yeoman Second Class]]. He then received a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of South Carolina School of Law]] in 1975, and was in private practice in [[Charleston, South Carolina|Charleston]], [[South Carolina]] until 1977. He was an assistant deputy solicitor for the Ninth Judicial Circuit in Charleston, South Carolina from 1977 to 1980. He was a city attorney of [[Isle of Palms, South Carolina|Isle of Palms]], South Carolina from 1980 to 1985. He was in private practice in Charleston from 1981 to 1990,{{cite web|url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/norton-david-c.|title=Norton, David C.|publisher=Federal Judicial Center|work=Biographical Directory of Article III Federal Judges, 1789-present}} and was a [[Law firm partner|partner]] at the [[law firm]] of Holmes & Thomson.Dave Munday, [https://www.postandcourier.com/archives/my-whole-life-i-wanted-to-be-just-like-my/article_d38aaf44-c20b-5b0e-9cce-0e93cd60bd44.html 'My whole life I wanted to be just like my father'], ''Post & Courier'' (September 3, 2014). ==Federal judicial service== On April 18, 1990, Norton was nominated by President [[George H. W. Bush]] to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the District of South Carolina]] that was vacated by Judge [[Solomon Blatt Jr.]] Norton was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on June 28, 1990, and received his commission on July 12, 1990. He served as Chief Judge from 2007 to 2012. Norton is a member of the Board of Advisors of the [[Charleston School of Law]].[http://charlestonlaw.edu/about/board-of-directors-and-board-of-advisors/board-of-advisors/ Board of Advisors], Charleston School of Law (last accessed December 10, 2017). {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200814004930/https://charlestonlaw.edu/about/board-of-directors-and-board-of-advisors/board-of-advisors/|date=2020-08-14}}. ===Notable cases=== * Norton presided over the criminal case of [[Michael Slager]], a police officer who killed Walter Scott, an unarmed black man, in April 2015 after a traffic stop in [[North Charleston, South Carolina]]. Scott was fleeing the officer when he was shot five times in the back. Slager pleaded guilty to federal charges of violating Scott's civil rights. Norton sentenced Slager to 20 years' imprisonment, a sentence within the [[Federal Sentencing Guidelines]].{{Cite news|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/2017/12/07/judges-ruling-walter-scott-shooting-could-sentence-former-police-officer-up-24-years/930667001/|title=Ex-S.C. cop gets 20 years in prison for fatally shooting Walter Scott, an unarmed black man|last=Stanglin|first=Doug|date=December 7, 2017|work=USA Today}}{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/12/07/us/michael-slager-sentence-walter-scott.html|title=White ex-cop gets 20 years for Walter Scott slaying|author=Alan Blinder|date=December 7, 2017|work=New York Times}} * In July 2017, Norton found that plaintiffs with [[mesothelioma]] still needed to prove defendants [[proximate cause|specifically caused]] their diseases, even though every exposure to [[asbestos]] is unsafe.{{Bluebook journal |first=|last=Note| title=Recent Case: District of South Carolina Holds the Every Exposure Theory Insufficient to Demonstrate Specific Causation Even if Legal Conclusions Are Scientifically Sound| volume=131 | journal=[[Harvard Law Review|Harv. '''David Gonzalez Estudillo''' (born 1973)<ref name="Questionnaire">[https://web.archive.org/web/20210608210624/https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Estudillo%20SJQ%20Public%20Final.pdf United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees: David Estudillo]</ref> is an American lawyer serving as the [[United States federal judge|chief United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Washington]]. He is a former Washington state court judge.

== Early life and education ==

Estudillo was born and raised in [[Sunnyside, Washington]], where his parents owned a small grocery store.<ref>{{Cite web |date=August 31, 2015 |title=Superior Court judge earned his way through life |url=https://columbiabasinherald.com/news/2015/aug/31/superior-court-judge-earned-his-way-through-2/ |access-date=April 29, 2021 |website=Columbia Basin Herald |language=en}}</ref> He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] from the [[University of Washington]] in 1996 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Washington School of Law]] in 1999.<ref name="WHBio">[https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/04/29/president-biden-announces-second-slate-of-judicial-nominees/ "President Biden Announces Second Slate of Judicial Nominees", White House, April 29, 2021] {{PD-notice}}</ref>

== Career ==

After graduating law school, Estudillo began his legal career at Jeffers, Danielson, Sonn & Aylward in [[Wenatchee]]. From 2002 to 2005, he was an attorney with Scheer and Zehnder in the [[Seattle]] office, where his practice focused on complex [[civil litigation]]. From 2005 to 2015, he was a solo practitioner at Estudillo Law Firm PLLC, where he focused on [[immigration law]] and general [[civil litigation]].<ref name="WHBio" /> The firm represented detained and non-detained clients before the [[Executive Office for Immigration Review]] and [[Board of Immigration Appeals]]. He also represented people seeking immigration benefits through applications filed with [[United States Citizenship and Immigration Services]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Escobar |first1=Ted |title=Superior Court judge earned his way through life |url=https://columbiabasinherald.com/news/2015/aug/31/superior-court-judge-earned-his-way-through-2/ |access-date=15 December 2021 |work=Columbia Basin Herald |date=31 August 2015 |language=en}}</ref> In 2015, he was appointed by [[Governor of Washington|Washington Governor]] [[Jay Inslee]] to serve as a judge for the [[Grant County, Washington|Grant County]] [[List of Superior Court Districts in Washington|Superior Court]] from September 1, 2015, until his elevation as a federal judge in 2021, preceded by Evan Sperline and succeeded by Anna Gigliotti.<ref>{{Cite press release |title=Inslee appoints David. G. Estudillo to Grant County Superior Court |date=August 19, 2015 |url=https://www.governor.wa.gov/news-media/inslee-appoints-david-g-estudillo-grant-county-superior-court |access-date=April 29, 2021 |archive-date=April 29, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210429140455/https://www.governor.wa.gov/news-media/inslee-appoints-david-g-estudillo-grant-county-superior-court |url-status=dead }}</ref>

=== Federal judicial service ===
[[File:David G. Estudillo.jpg|thumb|Estudillo during his hearing with the Senate Judiciary Committee]]
On April 29, 2021, President [[Joe Biden]] nominated Estudillo to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] for the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Washington]] to the seat vacated by Judge [[Ronald B. Leighton]], who assumed [[senior status]] on February 28, 2019.<ref>[https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/04/29/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-15/ "Nominations Sent to the Senate", White House, April 29, 2021]</ref> On June 9, 2021, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].<ref>[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/06/02/2021/nominations United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Nominations for June 9, 2021]</ref> On July 15, 2021, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 15–7 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – July 15, 2021|date=July 15, 2021|publisher=Senate Judiciary Committee|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%20July%2015.pdf|access-date=November 25, 2022}}</ref> On September 14, 2021, the Senate invoked [[cloture]] on his nomination by a 52–42 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|date=September 14, 2021|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: David G. Estudillo to be U.S. District Judge for the Western District of Washington)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1171/vote_117_1_00361.htm|access-date=February 17, 2022|website=United States Senate}}</ref> Later that day, his nomination was confirmed by a 54–41 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=117&session=1&vote=00362|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: David G. Estudillo, of Washington, to be United States District Judge for the Western District of Washington)|date=September 14, 2021|website=United States Senate|access-date=September 14, 2021}}</ref> He received his judicial commission on October 7, 2021.<ref>{{FJC Bio|nid=10719696|inline=yes}}</ref> He was sworn in on October 15, 2021.<ref>{{Cite web|date=October 20, 2021|title= THE WESTERN DISTRICT OF WASHINGTON WELCOMES DISTRICT JUDGE DAVID G. ESTUDILLO|url=https://www.wawd.uscourts.gov/sites/wawd/files/Judge%20Estudillo%20announcement.pdf|website=wawd.uscourts.gov|access-date=May 27, 2023}}</ref> He became the chief judge on September 3, 2022, succeeding [[Ricardo S. Martinez]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=New Chief District Judge in the Western District of Washington|url=https://www.wawd.uscourts.gov/news/new-chief-district-judge-western-district-washington|access-date=September 6, 2022|website=www.wawd.uscourts.gov}}</ref>
