'''David Grant Campbell''' (born December 6, 1952) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Arizona]].

==Early life and education==
Born in [[Salt Lake City, Utah]], Campbell received a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree from the [[University of Utah]] in 1976 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[S.J. Quinney College of Law]] at the University of Utah in 1979.<ref name="fjc">{{cite web|url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/campbell-david-g|title=Campbell, David G. - Federal Judicial Center|website=www.fjc.gov}}</ref>

==Career==
Campbell served as a [[law clerk]] to Judge [[J. Clifford Wallace]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]] from 1979 to 1980, and to Associate Justice [[William H. Rehnquist]] of the [[Supreme Court of the United States]] for the 1982 Term.<ref name="fjc"/> He worked in private practice in the interim year, and returned to private practice in 1982, working most notably at Osborn Maledon in [[Phoenix, Arizona]].<ref name="udenver-iaals">{{cite web|
title=David G. Campbell|
type=biography|
url=https://online.iaals.du.edu/profile/david-g-campbell|
access-date=October 18, 2020|
website=Institute for the Advancement of the American Legal System|
publisher=[[University of Denver]]|
archive-date=October 18, 2020|
archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201018133935/https://online.iaals.du.edu/profile/david-g-campbell|
url-status=dead}}</ref>
Outside of formal legal practice, Campbell served as an adjunct professor of law at the [[Arizona State University College of Law]], and as a visiting professor of law at [[Brigham Young University Law School]],<ref name="fjc"/> where he was named professor of the year in 1990.<ref name="lds"/>

===Federal judicial service===
Campbell was nominated to serve as judge of the [[United States District Court for the District of Arizona]] by President [[George W. Bush]] on March 13, 2003, to a new seat created by 116 Stat. 1758.<ref name="fjc"/> The [[United States Senate]] confirmed him on July 8, 2003 by 92–0 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1081/vote_108_1_00263.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation David G. Campbell, of Arizona, to be U.S. District Judge)|website=United States Senate|date=July 8, 2003|access-date=June 22, 2023}}</ref> He received his commission on July 15, 2003.<ref name="fjc"/> Judge Campbell was a member of the Advisory Committee on Federal Rules of Civil Procedure from 2005 to 2011, and chaired the committee from 2011 to 2015,<ref name="rules-agenda">
{{cite web|
url=https://www.uscourts.gov/rules-policies/records-rules-committees/agenda-books|
title=Agenda Books|
website=Committee on Rules and Practice and Procedure and the Advisory Committees|
publisher=[[Administrative Office of the United States Courts]]|
access-date=October 18, 2020}}</ref> while the Advisory Committee approved important changes to discovery-related rules that ultimately became effective in December 2015.
From 2016 to 2020, Judge Campbell chaired the Committee on Rules of Practice and Procedure for the federal courts, which oversees the Civil, Criminal, Appellate, Bankruptcy, and Evidence advisory committees.<ref name="rules-agenda"/>  Judge Campbell currently serves as chair of the federal courts' Committee on International Judicial Relations.  
He assumed [[senior status]] on July 31, 2018.<ref name="fjc"/>

Judge Campbell has worked with the courts of Botswana, Namibia, South Africa, and other countries on judicial case management<!--
  and [[court annexed mediation]]{{cn|date=October 2020|reason=First of all, what *is* "court annexed mediation," a reader can't be expected to know, hence the redlink. There are a bunch of facially plausible PDF sources produced by https://www.google.com/search?q="david+campbell"+"court+annexed+mediation" but I've not taken the time to dig into them - {{u|Jhawkinson}} }}
-->.<ref name="udenver-iaals"/>

He is a member of the [[American Law Institute]]<ref name="ali">
{{cite web|
url=https://www.ali.org/members/member/433190/|
title=Elected Member: The Hon. David G. Campbell|
website=[[American Law Institute]]|
language=en|
access-date=October 18, 2020}}</ref> and a Fellow of the [[American Bar Foundation]].<ref name="abf">
{{cite web|
url=http://www.americanbarfoundation.org/searchresults.aspx?q=%22David+G.+Campbell%22|
title=Search results - American Bar Foundation|
website=[[American Bar Foundation]]|
access-date=October 18, 2020}}</ref>

==Personal==
Campbell is a member of [[the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints]] (LDS Church). He served as a [[LDS missionary]] in the England Birmingham [[mission (LDS Church)|Mission]] and has been a [[bishop (Latter Day Saints)|bishop]] in the LDS Church. Campbell and his wife Stacey are parents to three daughters and two sons.<ref name="lds">{{cite web|
url=https://www.thechurchnews.com/archive/2004-11-06/lds-federal-judges-raising-the-bar-26260|
title=LDS federal judges raising the bar|
publisher=[[Church News]]|
date=November 6, 2004|
access-date=October 18, 2020}}{{Dead link|date=September 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref>

{{nowrap|[[Notre Dame Law School|Notre Dame University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]])}} | footnotes = }} '''David George Larimer''' (born March 3, 1944) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of New York]]. ==Education and career== Larimer was born in [[Rochester, New York]]. He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[St. John Fisher College]] in 1966 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Notre Dame Law School]] in 1969. He served as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Joseph C. McGarraghy]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Columbia]] from 1969 to 1970. After this, he was an [[assistant United States attorney]] for the District of Columbia in [[Washington, D.C.]] from 1970 to 1973. In the following years, Larimer worked as an assistant United States attorney of the Western District of New York in Rochester from 1973 to 1975. He was in private practice in Rochester from 1975 to 1979. An adjunct instructor of law, Larimer taught at St. John Fisher College from 1978 to 1981. He was a chief appellate law assistant for the Supreme Court, Appellate Division Fourth Department in Rochester from 1979 to 1981. He was in private practice in Rochester from 1982 to 1987.{{FJC Bio|nid=1383641|inline=yes}} ===Federal judicial service=== Larimer was [[United States magistrate judge]] for the [[United States District Court for the Western District of New York]] from 1983 to 1987. On May 5, 1987, Larimer was nominated by President [[Ronald Reagan]] to a new seat created by 98 Stat. 333, confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on November 5, 1987, and received his commission on November 6, 1987. He served as Chief Judge from 1996 to 2002. He assumed [[senior status]] on March 3, 2009. Judge [[Frank P. Geraci Jr.]], of New York, was nominated by President [[Barack Obama]] on Monday, May 14, 2012 to the Senate and confirmed by voice vote on Thursday, December 13, 2012, as his replacement.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2012/05/14/presidential-nominations-sent-senate|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=14 May 2012}}{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2012/05/14/president-obama-nominates-two-serve-us-district-court|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Obama Nominates Two to Serve on the US District Court|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=14 May 2012}} As of December 2025, the Western District of New York's website lists Larimer as inactive.{{Cite web|url=https://www.nywd.uscourts.gov/district-judges|title=District Judges|website=nywd.uscourts.gov|access-date=December 13, 2025}} ==References== {{Reflist}} ==Sources== * {{FJC Bio|nid=1383641}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=Seat established by 98 Stat. 333}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of New York]]}}|years=1987–2009}} {{s-aft|after=[[Frank P. '''David Herrera Urias''' (born 1967)<ref name="Questionnaire">{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Urias%20SJQ%20Public%20Final.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=November 2, 2021}}</ref> is an American lawyer serving as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of New Mexico]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=David Urias|url=https://www.lawyer.com/david-herrera-urias.html|access-date=2021-09-08|website=www.lawyer.com|language=en}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Born in [[Pecos, Texas]], Urias was raised in [[Albuquerque, New Mexico]], the son of Estella Urias and David D. Urias. He has two siblings.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Albuquerque Journal Obituaries|url=http://obits.abqjournal.com/obits/search?page=271&query=JOHNNY|access-date=2021-09-08|website=obits.abqjournal.com}}</ref> He earned a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from the [[University of New Mexico]] in 1997 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of New Mexico School of Law]] in 2001.<ref name="WHBio">{{Cite web |date=September 8, 2021 |title=President Biden Names Seventh Round of Judicial Nominees |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/09/08/president-biden-names-seventh-round-of-judicial-nominees/ |access-date=September 8, 2021 |website=The White House |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Career ==
In 2001 and 2002, Urias served as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Vanessa Ruiz]] of the [[District of Columbia Court of Appeals]]. After his clerkship, Urias won the Fried Frank Civil Rights Fellowship.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Fried Frank Fellowship Opens Doors |url=https://www.friedfrank.com/siteFiles/Site%20Pages/Fried%20Frank%20Fellowship%20Opens%20Doors%20.pdf |access-date=2021-10-05 |website=www.friedfrank.com |archive-date=2021-10-22 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211022185147/https://www.friedfrank.com/siteFiles/Site%20Pages/Fried%20Frank%20Fellowship%20Opens%20Doors%20.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> From 2002 to 2004, he was an associate at [[Fried, Frank, Harris, Shriver & Jacobson]] in [[New York City]]. From 2004 to 2008, he worked as a staff attorney for the [[Mexican American Legal Defense and Educational Fund]]. He joined Freedman Boyd Hollander Goldberg Urias & Ward, P.A. in 2008.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Vella|first=Lauren|date=2021-09-08|title=Biden nominates three Latinos to the federal bench|url=https://thehill.com/homenews/administration/571273-biden-nominates-three-latinos-to-the-federal-bench|access-date=2021-09-08|website=TheHill|language=en}}</ref>

=== Federal judicial service ===
On September 8, 2021, President [[Joe Biden]] announced his intent to nominate Urias to serve as a United States district judge of the [[United States District Court for the District of New Mexico]].<ref name="WHBio" /> On September 20, 2021, his nomination was sent to the Senate. President Biden nominated Urias to the seat to be vacated by Judge [[Martha Vázquez]], who subsequently assumed [[senior status]] in 2022.<ref name="September20">{{Cite press release|title=Nominations and Withdrawal Sent to the Senate|date=September 20, 2021|publisher=The White House|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/09/20/nominations-and-withdrawal-sent-to-the-senate-3/}} {{PD-notice}}</ref> On November 3, 2021, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Nominations|date=October 27, 2021|publisher=[[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]]|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/10/27/2021/nominations}}</ref> During his confirmation hearing, he was criticized by Senator [[Marsha Blackburn]] over his affiliation with the [[American Civil Liberties Union|ACLU]] of [[New Mexico]].<ref>{{Cite news|date=November 3, 2021|last=Wagner|first=Rose|title=GOP works to trip judicial nominees on road to confirmation with focus on activist pasts|url=https://www.courthousenews.com/gop-works-to-trip-judicial-nominees-on-road-to-confirmation-with-focus-on-activist-pasts/|website=Courthouse News|access-date=July 7, 2023}}</ref> On December 2, 2021, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 12–10 vote.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%2012.2.21.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – December 2, 2021|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=December 3, 2021}}</ref> On December 17, 2021, the [[United States Senate]] invoked cloture on his nomination by a 45–25 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1171/vote_117_1_00512.htm|title= On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: David Herrera Urias to be U.S. District Judge for the District of New Mexico)|website=[[United States Senate]]|access-date=December 17, 2021}}</ref> His nomination was confirmed that same day by a 45–26 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=117&session=1&vote=00513|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: David Herrera Urias, of New Mexico, to be U.S. District Judge for the District of New Mexico)|date=December 17, 2021|website=[[United States Senate]]|access-date=December 17, 2021}}</ref> He received his judicial commission on January 14, 2022,<ref>{{FJC Bio|nid=11226126|inline=yes}}</ref> was sworn in by Judge [[James O. Browning]] on January 21, 2022.<ref>{{Cite press release|date=January 21, 2022|title= Nomination of David Herrera Urias to Fill United States District Court Judicial Vacancy|url=https://www.nmd.uscourts.gov/sites/nmd/files/2022-Jan%2021_Press%20Release_Appointment%20of%20Daivd%20Urias%20as%20U.S.%20District%20Judge.pdf|website=nmd.uscourts.gov|access-date=July 5, 2025}}</ref>

==== Notable rulings ==== 

In September 2023, New Mexico Governor [[Michelle Lujan Grisham]] issued a public health order suspending the right to carry either open or concealed firearms at most public places in the Albuquerque area. Urias granted a temporary restraining order, and in response Grisham narrowed the order to only prohibit guns in public parks and playgrounds. In October 2023, after the temporary restraining order had expired, Urias declined a request by gun rights advocates to block the firearm restrictions while legal challenges over the order's constitutionality move forward.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Lee |first1=Morgan |title=Federal judge won't block suspension of right to carry guns in some New Mexico parks, playgrounds |url=https://abcnews.go.com/Health/wireStory/federal-judge-block-suspension-carry-guns-new-mexico-103909649 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231012044241/https://abcnews.go.com/Health/wireStory/federal-judge-block-suspension-carry-guns-new-mexico-103909649 |url-status=dead |archive-date=October 12, 2023 |access-date=15 November 2023 |work=ABC News |agency=Associated Press |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Goldberg |first1=Julia |title=Judge Lets Gov. Lujan Grisham Gun Ban Stand—for Now |url=https://www.sfreporter.com/news/morningword/2023/10/12/judge-lets-gov-lujan-grisham-gun-ban-standfor-now/ |access-date=15 November 2023 |work=Santa Fe Reporter |date=12 October 2023 |language=en}}</ref>

'''David Hittner''' (born July 10, 1939) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas]]. He also has served by temporary assignment on the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]], as well as the U.S. District Courts for the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York|Southern District of New York]] and the District of Arizona. His tenure as a federal judge began in 1986, when he was nominated for the lifetime position by President [[Ronald Reagan]] and unanimously confirmed by the [[United States Senate]]. Prior to his appointment to the federal bench in 1986, Hittner served from 1978 to 1986 as the elected judge of the 133rd Judicial District Court of [[Harris County, Texas]], based in [[Houston]].<ref name="fjc.gov">{{FJC Bio|nid=1382211|inline=yes}}</ref>

==Early life==
Hittner was born in [[Schenectady, New York|Schenectady]], [[New York (state)|New York]],<ref name="fjc.gov" /> but moved with his family to [[Brooklyn]], New York when he was a year old. His father, J. George Hittner, was an electrician and a member of the [[Freemasonry|Masons]] fraternal service organization. His mother, Sophie Moskowitz Hittner, was a bookkeeper and homemaker. Hittner was a [[Boy Scouts of America|Boy Scout]], earning 81 merit badges and attaining [[Eagle Scout (Boy Scouts of America)|Eagle Scout]] rank.<ref name=":6" /> He followed his hometown team, the [[History of the Brooklyn Dodgers|Brooklyn Dodgers]], and met his childhood hero, [[Jackie Robinson]], the first African-American to play major league baseball.<ref name=":6" />

==Education, military service and early career==
Hittner received his undergraduate degree from New York University, serving as the president of his graduating class.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Rosenthal |first=Lee H. |date=2005 |title=Judge David Hittner: A View through Chambers, A Tribute to United States District Judge David Hittner |url=https://heinonline.org/HOL/Page?collection=journals&handle=hein.journals/stexlr46&id=574&men_tab=srchresults |journal=South Texas College of Law - Law Review |volume=46 |issue=3 |pages=557}}</ref> Hittner received his [[Juris Doctor]] degree from New York University School of Law. He passed the New York bar exam, and served two years in the Army as an infantry captain and paratrooper.<ref name="fjc.gov" /> Hittner then moved to Houston to pursue his legal career.

After passing the Texas bar, Hittner joined a private firm, gaining expertise in litigation and courtroom procedure. Hittner also developed an interest in family law and in 1975 was among the first class of Texas lawyers certified as family law specialists.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Certification Matters |url=https://www.texasbar.com/AM/Template.cfm?Section=articles&Template=/CM/HTMLDisplay.cfm&ContentID=38575 |access-date=2023-06-21}}</ref>

== Judicial career ==
=== State court service ===
Hittner twice campaigned for election to judgeships in Harris County's Courts of Domestic Relations. Those races were unsuccessful, but in 1978 Democratic Texas Governor Dolph Briscoe appointed Hittner to the 133rd Judicial District Court of Harris County. He subsequently won election twice, serving until 1986.<ref name="fjc.gov" />

=== Federal judicial service ===
On April 22, 1986, President Reagan nominated Hittner to succeed Judge [[George Edward Cire]] on the United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas. Hittner was confirmed by the U. S. Senate on June 6, 1986, and he received his commission on June 9, 1986. He assumed [[senior status]] on November 11, 2004, and initially maintained a full-time caseload. In addition to his regular duties as a state and federal judge, Hittner became an expert in [[summary judgment]]s, a teacher and a mentor. From 1981 until 2007, he conducted a [[continuing legal education]] program for state and federal court practitioners entitled "Saturday Morning in Court", with the focus on the critical minutiae of trial practice. The program prompted a laudatory note from Chief Justice [[Warren E. Burger|Warren Burger]], who recalled overseeing a similar project early in his legal career.<ref>Nov. 3, 1982 letter from Chief Justice Warren Burger to David Hittner, Judge of the 133rd Judicial District Court based in Houston</ref> Hittner has been an adjunct professor at South Texas College of Law Houston.<ref>{{Cite web | title=South Texas College of Law Home Page | url=http://www.stcl.edu | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/19961222182516/http://stcl.edu:80/ | access-date=2026-02-11 | archive-date=1996-12-22}}</ref>

===Notable cases===

Hittner was a member of a three-judge panel that held three of Texas' 30 congressional districts, as drawn by the state legislature in 1990, were unconstitutional. They were drawn based on racial minority populations in an effort to [[Gerrymandering in the United States|influence election results]]. The panel's decision was twice affirmed by the U.S. Supreme Court.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Verhovek |first=Sam Howe |date=1994-08-18 |title=Redraw Lines Of 3 Districts, Texas Is Told |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/08/18/us/redraw-lines-of-3-districts-texas-is-told.html |access-date=2023-06-21 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> In 1995, Hittner blocked the execution of death row inmate Calvin Burdine and ordered a new trial. Burdine's court-appointed counsel in state court had dozed off during significant parts of the proceedings. Hittner's decision was affirmed by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit, and the U.S. Supreme Court declined to review the decision further.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Best Court Ruling 2002 |url=https://www.houstonpress.com/best-of/2002/people-and-places/best-court-ruling-6604307 |access-date=2023-06-21 |website=Houston Press |language=en}}</ref>

In 2001, Hittner sentenced Matthew Marshall to 10 years in federal prison for leading a group that [[cross burning|burned a cross]] in the front yard of an African-American family in the Houston suburb of [[Katy, Texas|Katy]].<ref>{{Cite news |title=Ringleader gets 10 years for Katy cross burning |newspaper=Chron |url=https://www.chron.com/news/houston-texas/article/ringleader-gets-10-years-for-katy-cross-burning-1993409.php |access-date=2023-08-03}}</ref> In 2004, Hittner presided over criminal proceedings against former [[Enron]] assistant treasurer Lea Weingarten Fastow, the wife of Enron executive Andrew Fastow. She eventually pleaded guilty to filing a false federal tax return and served one year in federal prison.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Lea Fastow gets the maximum: one year in prison |url=https://www.chron.com/business/enron/article/lea-fastow-gets-the-maximum-one-year-in-prison-1981501.php |access-date=2023-08-03}}</ref>

Hittner sentenced [[Allen Stanford|R. Allen Stanford]] to a total of 110 years in federal prison for orchestrating a 20-year investment fraud scheme.<ref>{{cite news|date=June 14, 2012|title=Allen Stanford jailed for 110 years for $7bn Ponzi|work=BBC News|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-us-canada-18450893}}</ref> Stanford, the former chairman of Stanford International Bank, was found guilty of misappropriating more than $7 billion from his bank and financial institutions to finance his personal business and lifestyle. During the six-week trial in 2012, Stanford was convicted on 13 of 14 counts of conspiracy, fraud, obstruction and money laundering. The jury also found that 29 financial accounts located abroad—worth approximately $330 million—were proceeds of Stanford's fraud and should be forfeited.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2012-06-14 |title=Office of Public Affairs {{!}} Allen Stanford Sentenced to 110 Years in Prison for Orchestrating $7 Billion Investment Fraud Scheme {{!}} United States Department of Justice |url=https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/allen-stanford-sentenced-110-years-prison-orchestrating-7-billion-investment-fraud-scheme |access-date=2023-08-03 |website=www.justice.gov |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2009-11-18 |title=Finra's flaws exposed: Special report on Madoff and Stanford scams calls for reform |url=https://www.investmentnews.com/finras-flaws-exposed-special-report-on-madoff-and-stanford-scams-calls-for-reform-24328 |access-date=2023-08-03 |website=InvestmentNews |language=en-US}}</ref> At the time, the Stanford trial was the largest financial fraud case ever tried to a jury in federal court.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Cohn |first=Scott |date=2019-02-20 |title=Victims of that other Ponzi scheme—Allen Stanford's—say they have been short-changed |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2019/02/20/allen-stanfords-ponzi-scheme-victims-say-they-have-been-short-changed.html |access-date=2023-06-21 |website=CNBC |language=en}}</ref> In 2016, Hittner sentenced the organizer of a [[sex trafficking]] ring that operated in Houston's East End to life in federal prison. Hortencia "Tencha" Medeles, then 70, was the leader of an international sex-trafficking ring that forced women, including minors, into prostitution. During the trial in 2015, jurors learned that Medeles owned a three-building complex in southeast Houston. Hidden doorways and staircases led from a downstairs cantina to a brothel upstairs where 17 rooms were rented out for sexual activities. Evidence presented in the case showed rooms were rented out 64,296 times during a 19-month period ending in 2013.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Sex trafficking brothel madam heads to federal prison |url=https://www.chron.com/news/houston-texas/houston/article/Madam-of-sex-trafficking-brothel-heads-to-federal-6771822.php |access-date=2023-08-03}}</ref> In 2016, Hittner granted the agreed dismissal of a wrongful death civil rights lawsuit filed by the family of [[Death of Sandra Bland|Sandra Bland]], an African-American woman who died in a Texas county jail days after a traffic violation and controversial arrest. Her death was ruled a suicide. Following a judge-approved mediation, the lawyers representing Bland's family told Hittner that a legal settlement, $1.9 million, had resolved their claims.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-11-02 |title=Judge formally dismisses Sandra Bland lawsuit after deal |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/nation-world/ct-sandra-bland-lawsuit-dismissed-20161102-story.html |access-date=2023-06-21 |website=Chicago Tribune}}</ref>

In 2023, Hittner ruled that Texas Senate Bill 12, legislation that [[Drag panic|criminalized drag performances in the presence of minors]], was unconstitutional on five counts. He issued a permanent injunction against SB12.<ref>{{Cite magazine |date=2023-12-06 |title=The Drag Queens Fighting Performance Bans in Texas |url=https://www.newyorker.com/news/letter-from-the-southwest/the-drag-queens-fighting-performance-bans-in-texas |access-date=2023-12-11 |magazine=The New Yorker}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-09-26 |title=Judge rules Texas' drag ban unconstitutional |url=https://spectrumlocalnews.com/tx/south-texas-el-paso/news/2023/09/26/judge-rules-texas--drag-ban-unconstitutional |access-date=2023-12-11 |website=Spectrum News 1}}</ref>

* Creator of "Saturday Morning in Court," a continuing legal education lecture series, presented nationwide from 1981 to 2007.<ref name=":2">{{Cite news |last=Gorham |first=Marilynne |date=July 2006 |title=Judicial Profile: Hon. David Hittner Senior U.S. District Judge, Southern District of Texas |url=https://www.fedbar.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/HittnerJuly2006_3-pgs-pdf-3.pdf |work=Federal Bar Association Judicial Profile |pages=3}}</ref><ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |last=Davidson |first=Mark |date=2005 |title=Judge David Hittner-Last and Best of His Kind |url=https://heinonline.org/HOL/Page?handle=hein.journals/stexlr46&id=581&collection=journals&index= |journal=South Texas College of Law - Law Review |volume=46 |issue=3 |pages=571}}</ref>
* Creator of "Humor in the Courtroom: Does it Really Exist?" a keynote presentation delivered across the United States and Canada from 1981 to 2007.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Breaux |first=Natasha |date=2020-09-24 |title=Houston Federal Judge David Hittner Loves Jury Trials and Good Humor |url=https://texaslawbook.net/houston-federal-judge-david-hittner-loves-jury-trials-and-good-humor/ |access-date=2025-10-22 |website=The Texas Lawbook |language=en-US}}</ref>
* Law school and college lecturer at schools throughout the country, including Harvard Law School, the University of Texas School of Law, Tulane Law School, University of Houston Law Center, South Texas College of Law, and the U.S. Military Academy at West Point.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":1" />

== Personal life and  memberships ==
Hittner has three children, four grandchildren, and two great-grandchildren.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last=Rosenthal |first=Lee H. |date=2005 |title=Judge David Hittner: A View Through Chambers |url=https://heinonline.org/HOL/Page?collection=journals&handle=hein.journals/stexlr46&id=578&men_tab=srchresults |journal=South Texas College of Law - Law Review |volume=46 |issue=3 |pages=562}}</ref>

He is a Master Mason, a member of the Scottish Rite of Freemasonry and the Shriners - embracing a family tradition that included his father and later his son. Masonic honors include the Thirty-Third Degree (1991); the Sam Houston Medal, the highest recognition of the Grand Lodge of Texas (2004); and the Thirty-Third Degree with Grand Cross - the rarest honor in Masonry (2019).<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |last=Daughtery |first=Deon |date=June 29, 2012 |title=Stanford Judge David Hittner opens up about his history, memorabilia and his favorite president |url=https://www.bizjournals.com/houston/blog/2012/06/federal-judge-david-hittner-opens-up.html |website=Houston Business Journal}}</ref>

Hittner became a Cub Scout in 1947 and has maintained his membership in the Boy Scouts of America throughout adulthood. He has been a scoutmaster and for more than 40 years he has served as a member of both the Sam Houston Area Council Board of Directors and the National Jewish Committee on Scouting. He has been a voting delegate on the National Council of the Boy Scouts of America. His adult recognitions include the Silver Beaver Award (1974,) the Silver Antelope Award (1988) and the Distinguished Eagle Scout Award (1989).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Distinguished Eagle Scout Award — Sam Houston Area Council |url=https://shacbsa.org/distinguished-eagle-scout-award |access-date=2025-02-24 |website=shacbsa.org}}</ref><ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last=Jones |first=Edith H |date=2005 |title=In Honor of David Hittner: A Tribute to United States District Judge David Hittner |url=https://heinonline.org/HOL/Page?handle=hein.journals/stexlr46&div=30&g_sent=1&casa_token=&collection=journals |journal=South Texas College of Law - Law Review |volume=46 |issue=3 |pages=553–556}}</ref>

Prior to his military service, he was a competitive flatwater canoeist and later served as a regional officer of the American Canoe Association.<ref name=":4" /> He is a member of the American Legion, the Association of the United States Army and the 82nd Airborne Division Association.<ref name=":5" />

He is the founder and former president of the [[Brooklyn Dodgers]] Fan Club of Houston.<ref>https://www.chron.com/opinion/outlook/article/a-tale-of-two-home-runs-and-lessons-for-a-1483791.php</ref> Hittner has played the acoustic 12-string and [[electric bass]] guitars in the Texas Barflies, a country-western band.<ref name=":3" />

[[University of Kentucky]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''David Jason Hale''' (born June 30, 1967) is the [[United States federal judge|chief United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Kentucky]] and former [[United States attorney]] for the Western District of Kentucky. ==Biography== Hale was born on June 30, 1967{{cite web|url=http://www.lawyercentral.com/david-j-hale-interactive-profile--20-267536.html|title=Attorney David J Hale – Lawyer in Louisville KY|website=www.lawyercentral.com|access-date=March 28, 2016|archive-date=June 12, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180612162125/https://www.lawyercentral.com/david-j-hale-interactive-profile--20-267536.html|url-status=dead}} at the [[United States Army]] hospital at [[Fort Campbell]], [[Kentucky]].{{cite web|url=http://www.mainjustice.com/2010/02/12/meet-david-j-hale/|title=Biography at Main Justice|publisher=|access-date=August 27, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131112234000/http://www.mainjustice.com/2010/02/12/meet-david-j-hale/|archive-date=November 12, 2013|url-status=dead}}{{cite web|url=https://www.justice.gov/usao/biographies/hale.html|title=Official Biography at the United States Department of Justice|publisher=|access-date=November 22, 2020|archive-date=October 22, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141022015138/http://www.justice.gov/usao/biographies/hale.html|url-status=dead}} He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in 1989 from [[Vanderbilt University]]. He received a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1992 from the [[University of Kentucky College of Law]]. From 1992 to 1994, he was an associate at the law firm of Brown, Todd and Heyburn. From 1995 to 1999, he served as an [[assistant United States attorney]] for the Western District of Kentucky. He joined the law firm of Reed, Weitkamp, Schell & Vice, PLLC, in 1999, becoming a partner in 2002, serving until his appointment as United States attorney.{{cite web |url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/president-obama-nominates-five-serve-us-attorneys |title=President Obama Nominates Five to Serve as United States Attorney |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170216173234/https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/president-obama-nominates-five-serve-us-attorneys |via=[[NARA|National Archives]] |work=[[whitehouse.gov]] |date=January 20, 2010 |archive-date=February 16, 2017 }}{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/06/19/president-obama-announces-nominates-two-serve-united-states-district-cou|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Obama Announces Nominates Two to Serve on the United States District Courts|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=June 19, 2014}}{{FJC Bio|nid=1394686|inline=yes}} ===United States attorney=== On January 20, 2010, [[Barack Obama|President Obama]] nominated Hale to serve as the United States Attorney for the Western District of Kentucky, in place of [[David L. Huber]] who had resigned. His nomination was reported by the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] on April 22, 2010, and he was confirmed by the [[United States Senate|Senate]] on April 29, 2010. He took the oath of office on May 7, 2010. ===Federal judicial service=== On June 19, 2014, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Hale to serve as a United States District Judge of the United States District Court for the Western District of Kentucky, to the seat vacated by Judge [[Charles Ralph Simpson III]], who assumed [[senior status]] on February 1, 2013.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/06/19/presidential-nominations-sent-senate|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=June 19, 2014}} On July 29, 2014, a hearing before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]] was held on his nomination.{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/judicial-nominations-2014-07-29|title=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|website=www.judiciary.senate.gov}} On September 18, 2014, his nomination was reported out of committee by a [[voice vote]].{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%209-18-14.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – September 18, 2014|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary}} On December 1, 2014, Senate Majority Leader [[Harry Reid]] filed for [[cloture]] on his nomination. On December 3, 2014, the [[United States Senate]] invoked cloture on his nomination by a 65–31 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=113&session=2&vote=00303|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture on David J. Hale, of Kentucky, to be U.S. District Judge for the Western District of Kentucky)|website=United States Senate|access-date=December 3, 2014}} He was later confirmed by a [[voice vote]] that same day.{{cite web|url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/113th-congress/1805|title=PN1805 — David J. Hale — The Judiciary|publisher=congress.gov|access-date=November 5, 2022}} He received his judicial commission on December 10, 2014. He became the court's chief judge in 2025. ===Notable case=== On March 31, 2017, Hale ruled against the dismissal of a lawsuit accusing Donald Trump of inciting violence against protesters in [[Louisville, Kentucky]]. During a campaign rally on March 1, 2016, Trump repeatedly said "get 'em out of here" while pointing at anti-Trump protesters. According to the protesters, as they were escorted out they were repeatedly shoved and punched by his supporters.{{Citation|last=Right Side Broadcasting Network|title=Full Speech: Donald Trump Holds Rally in Louisville, KY (3-1-16)|date=March 1, 2016|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0Hzc9yL3_n8&t=29m9s|access-date=April 2, 2017}}{{Citation|last=Conservative Outfitters|title=Senior Citizen Veteran Fights Protester at Louisville Trump Rally|date=March 2, 2016|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ILwalNSS3vY|access-date=April 2, 2017}} Trump's attorneys moved for dismissal of the case, arguing he was protected by free speech laws, and wasn't trying to get his supporters to resort to violence.{{Cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/the-fix/wp/2017/04/02/a-judge-rules-trump-may-have-incited-violence-and-trump-again-has-his-own-mouth-to-blame/|title=Analysis {{!}} A judge rules Trump may have incited violence … and Trump again has his own mouth to blame|newspaper=Washington Post|access-date=April 2, 2017}} ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1394686}} *{{Ballotpedia|David_J._Hale}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Charles Ralph Simpson III]]}} {{s-ttl|title=Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Kentucky]]|years=2014–present}} {{s-inc|rows=2}} |- {{s-bef|before=[[Gregory N. [[University of Oklahoma College of Law|University of Oklahoma]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | footnotes = }} '''David Lynn Russell''' (born July 7, 1942) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Oklahoma]] and a former United States district judge of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Oklahoma]] and the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Oklahoma]]. He served as the [[United States Attorney for the Western District of Oklahoma|United States attorney for the Western District of Oklahoma]] from 1975 to 1977 and again from 1981 to 1982. ==Education and career== Russell was born in [[Sapulpa, Oklahoma]]. He received a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree from [[Oklahoma Baptist University]] in 1963 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Oklahoma College of Law]] in 1965. He was in the [[United States Navy]], JAG Corps, from 1965 to 1968, continuing to serve as a reservist until 1971 and achieving the rank of lieutenant commander. He was an assistant attorney general of the State of Oklahoma from 1968 to 1969, and was then a legal advisor to Governor [[Dewey Bartlett]] from 1969 to 1971. He entered private practice in [[Oklahoma City]] from 1971 to 1972, but when Bartlett was elected to the [[United States Senate]], Russell became his chief legislative assistant from 1972 to 1975. Russell was then the [[United States attorney]] for the Western District of Oklahoma from 1975 to 1977, returning to private practice in Oklahoma City from 1979 to 1981, but again serving in the United States attorney post from 1981 to 1982.{{FJC Bio|nid=1387246|inline=yes}} ===Federal judicial service=== On December 4, 1981, Russell was nominated by President [[Ronald Reagan]] to a joint seat on the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Oklahoma]], [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Oklahoma]], and [[United States District Court for the Western District of Oklahoma]], vacated by Judge [[Frederick Alvin Daugherty]]. Russell was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on December 16, 1981, and received his commission on December 17, 1981. On December 1, 1990, he was reassigned by [[operation of law]] to serve on only the Western District of Oklahoma, where he served as Chief Judge from 1994 to 2001. He received a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree from [[Cornell University]] in 1959. He received a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Syracuse University College of Law]] in 1963. He was in private practice of law in [[Utica, New York|Utica]], New York from 1963 to 1991. He was an assistant district attorney (part-time), Oneida County District Attorney's Office from 1966 to 1967. ==Federal judicial service== Hurd served as a [[United States magistrate judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of New York]] from 1991 to 1999. Hurd is a United States district judge of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of New York]]. He was nominated by President [[Bill Clinton]] on February 12, 1999, to a seat vacated by [[Constantine George Cholakis]]. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on September 13, 1999, and received his commission on September 22, 1999. On November 1, 2021, Hurd informed President Biden that he intended to take [[senior status]] effective upon the confirmation of his successor. On July 14, 2022, one day after Biden nominated Jorge Alberto Rodriguez of [[Clifton Park, New York|Clifton Park]], an [[Albany, New York|Albany]]-based assistant attorney general, Hurd wrote another letter to President Biden. In the letter, Hurd wrote “Please be advised that I immediately [[rescind]] my decision to take senior status as a United States District Judge for the Northern District of New York". “I will take senior status if a confirmed successor lives in this area and is permanently assigned to the United States Courthouse in Utica, New York. Otherwise, I shall remain on full-time active status until I retire or die.”{{Cite web |last=Gavin |first=Robert |date=2022-08-08 |title=Biden pick for New York federal judgeship in limbo |url=https://www.timesunion.com/news/article/Law-Beat-17350929.php |access-date=2022-08-08 |website=Times Union |language=en-US}} On August 8, 2022, [[Kirsten Gillibrand]]'s chief of staff Jess Fassler said “It has always been the expectation that Judge Hurd’s successor would sit in the Utica courthouse, and Jorge Rodriguez has committed to doing so”.{{Cite web |date=August 9, 2022 |title=Biden pick for New York federal judgeship in limbo |url=https://www.syracuse.com/state/2022/08/biden-pick-for-new-york-federal-judgeship-in-limbo.html |access-date=August 9, 2022 |website=Tribune News Service}}{{cite web | url=https://www.timesunion.com/news/article/Gillibrand-s-office-says-Biden-pick-committed-17359359.php | title=Gillibrand's office says Biden pick 'committed' to holding court in Utica | date=August 8, 2022 }} On August 10, 2022, Hurd wrote a letter to Biden to officially rescind his senior status and remain in active service.{{Cite web |last=Alder |first=Madison |date=August 10, 2022 |title=Federal Judge Who Rescinded Departure Insists He's Staying |url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/federal-judge-who-rescinded-departure-insists-hes-staying |access-date=August 11, 2022 |website=news.bloomberglaw.com |language=en}} On March 27, 2024, Hurd wrote a new letter to Biden stating that he intended to take senior status upon confirmation of a successor. The news of his decision coincided with an announcement from the [[Administrative Office of the United States Courts|Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts]] that "there is no plan to close the courthouse" in Utica.{{Cite web |last=Raymond |first=Nate |date=April 4, 2024 |title=N.Y. federal judge who rescinded semi-retirement changes his mind, again |url=https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/ny-federal-judge-who-rescinded-semi-retirement-changes-his-mind-again-2024-04-04/ |access-date=July 23, 2024 |website=reuters.com |language=en}} On July 31, Biden nominated [[Anthony J. Brindisi, of New York, to be United States District Judge for the Northern District of New York)|website=United States Senate|date=December 4, 2024|access-date=December 4, 2024}} Hurd assumed [[senior status]] on December 9, 2024.{{FJC Bio|nid=1391031|inline=yes}} ==Notable cases== In August 2001, Hurd became the first judge to apply [[Abortion in New York|New York's abortion clinic access law]], passed in 1999.{{cite web | title=Family Fined in First Ruling Based on State Abortion Clinic Access Law | website=The New York Times | date=2001-08-28 | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2001/08/28/nyregion/family-fined-in-first-ruling-based-on-state-abortion-clinic-access-law.html | access-date=2024-06-09}} On February 20, 2003, Hurd ruled that New York authorities cannot punish a state trial judge for political activity. Albany judge Thomas J. Spargo had handed out doughnuts and gasoline coupons during his campaign, bought drinks for voters, spoke at political fundraising rallies, and loudly protested against the 2000 election recount process in Florida. However, Hurd said he had no opinion on whether Spargo's actions "would bring disrespect to the judiciary". Hurd cited ''[[Republican Party of Minnesota v. '''David Ogden Nuffer''' (born 1952) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Utah]].

==Biography==

Nuffer was born in 1952 in [[Portland, Oregon|Portland]], [[Oregon]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/112thCongressJudicialNominations/upload/DavidNuffer-PublicQuestionnaire.pdf|title=United States Senate Questionnaire|publisher=|access-date=2012-03-22|archive-date=2016-03-04|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304052831/http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/112thCongressJudicialNominations/upload/DavidNuffer-PublicQuestionnaire.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree, cum laude, from [[Brigham Young University]] (BYU) in 1975 and a [[Juris Doctor]], cum laude, from the [[J. Reuben Clark Law School]] at (BYU) in 1978. He served in private practice from 1978 until 2002. He was formerly a [[United States magistrate judge]] of the United States District Court for the District of Utah. He served in a part-time capacity while remaining a practicing [[lawyer]] starting in 1995 and became full-time in 2003, serving until his elevation to District Judge in 2012.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.utd.uscourts.gov/judges/nuffer_resume.html|title=Judge Nuffer – Resume|access-date=2008-06-19|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080516063455/http://www.utd.uscourts.gov/judges/nuffer_resume.html|archive-date=2008-05-16|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.legalspan.com/catalog2/faculty.asp?UserID=200801221138552720952%20%20%20%20%20&OwnerColor=%238A261E&recID=20080122-272095-113855|title=David Nuffer- U.S. Magistrate Judge, District of Utah|access-date=2008-06-19|archive-date=2011-07-13|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110713195453/http://www.legalspan.com/catalog2/faculty.asp?UserID=200801221138552720952%20%20%20%20%20&OwnerColor=|url-status=dead}}</ref> Since 2001 he has been an [[adjunct professor]] at BYU. He served as president of the Utah State Bar from 2000 to 2001.<ref name="fjc.gov">{{FJC Bio|nid=1393926|inline=yes}}</ref>

===Federal judicial service===

On June 29, 2011, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Nuffer to serve as a United States District Judge for the United States District Court for the District of Utah.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2011/06/29/president-obama-nominates-two-united-states-district-court|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Obama Nominates Two to the United States District Court|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=29 June 2011}}</ref> He would replace Judge [[Dale A. Kimball]], who assumed senior status in 2009. The [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] held a hearing on his nomination on September 20, 2011 and reported it to the floor on October 13, 2011. On March 22, 2012, the [[United States Senate]] confirmed Nuffer by a 96–2 vote.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=112&session=2&vote=00057|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation David Nuffer, of Utah, to be United States District Judge for the District of Utah)|website=www.senate.gov}}</ref> He received his commission on March 23, 2012.<ref name="fjc.gov"/> He served as Chief Judge from 2014 to 2018. He assumed [[senior status]] on April 2, 2022.<ref name="fjc.gov"/>

On March 1, 2018, the District of Utah established a southern region serving the southern part of the state. In April 2019, Nuffer moved to southern Utah, becoming the first district judge in Utah to reside off the [[Wasatch Front]]. He has chambers in the  St. George.  The federal court leases offices and a courtroom there.{{citation needed|date=April 2022}}

David O. Carter:
{{Short description|American judge (born 1944)}} {{other people|David Carter|David Carter (disambiguation)}} {{Infobox officeholder | name = David Carter | office = Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Central District of California]] | appointer = [[Bill Clinton]] | term_start = October 22, 1998 | term_end = | predecessor = [[William J. Rea]] | successor = | birth_name = David Ormon Carter | birth_date = {{birth date and age|1944|3|28}} | birth_place = [[Providence, Rhode Island]], U.S. | death_date = | death_place = | spouse = Mary Cohee | education = [[University of California, Los Angeles]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|BA]], [[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | allegiance = {{flag|United States}} | branch = {{flag|United States Marine Corps}} | service_years = 1967–1969 | rank = [[First lieutenant|First Lieutenant]] | battles = [[Vietnam War]] | mawards = [[Bronze Star Medal|Bronze Star]]
[[Purple Heart]] }} '''David Ormon Carter'''{{cite book|date=1999|title=Hearings Before the Committee on the Judiciary, United States Senate, One Hundred Fifth Congress, Second Session on Confirmation of Appointees to the Federal Judiciary. Part 5|publication-place=Washington, D.C.|publisher=U.S. Government Printing Office|page=382|hdl=2027/pur1.32754071095347|hdl-access=free|isbn=0-16-058115-X}} (born March 28, 1944) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Central District of California]].{{cite news|last1=Weinstein|first1=Henry|last2=Haldane|first2=David|date=October 22, 1998|title=O.C. Jurist Is Confirmed as Federal Judge|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1998-oct-22-me-35060-story.html|work=Los Angeles Times|access-date=2013-10-24}} ==Education and military service== In college he lettered in cross country and track on the teams of [[Jim Bush]]. Carter received his [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree [[cum laude]] in 1967 and his [[Juris Doctor]] in 1972 from the [[University of California, Los Angeles]] and [[UCLA School of Law]], respectively. After graduating from college, Carter accepted a commission in the [[United States Marine Corps]]. He served in the [[Vietnam War]] where he fought in the [[Battle of Khe Sanh]], receiving a [[Bronze Star Medal|Bronze Star]] for [["V" device|valor]] in 1968. He was medically discharged as a [[First lieutenant|First Lieutenant]] after receiving a [[Purple Heart]].{{Cite web |date=2022-03-30 |title=Who is the OC judge who said Trump ‘more likely than not’ committed a crime? |url=https://www.ocregister.com/2022/03/30/who-is-the-o-c-judge-who-said-trump-more-likely-than-not-committed-a-crime/ |access-date=2026-08-27 |website=Orange County Register |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |last=Diamond |first=Barbara |date=2012-05-31 |title=Judge delivers moving Memorial Day speech |url=https://www.latimes.com/socal/daily-pilot/ocnow/tn-cpt-0601-memorial-20120531-story.html |access-date=2026-08-27 |website=Daily Pilot |language=en-US}} ==Early career== Carter began his legal career as an Assistant District Attorney with the [[Orange County, California|Orange County]] District Attorney's Office in 1972 where he became the senior deputy [[district attorney]] in charge of the office's homicide division. Carter filed charges and was the initial prosecutor in the case of serial killer [[William Bonin]], also known as "The Freeway Killer," who became the first person executed by [[lethal injection]] in [[California]] in 1996.{{Cite web |date=1996-02-11 |title='Freeway Killer' Bonin Nears Date With Execution |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1996-02-11-mn-34809-story.html |access-date=2026-08-27 |website=Los Angeles Times |language=en-US}} ==Judicial career== ===Orange County Superior Court=== {{external media | width = 210px | float = right | headerimage= | audio1 = [https://www.sciencehistory.org/distillations/podcast/rethinking-ink “Rethinking Ink”], ''Distillations'' Podcast Episode 220, [[Science History Institute]]}} In 1981, Carter joined the bench as a Municipal Court Judge in [[Orange County, California]]. One year later, he became an Orange County Superior Judge, a position that he held until joining the federal judiciary in 1998. Carter initiated a variety of programs to assist in the rehabilitation of convicted felons, including a [[Tattoo#Removal|tattoo removal]] program for gang members,{{cite magazine|last=Klett|first=Joseph|date=March 28, 2018|title=Second Chances|url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/distillations/magazine/second-chances|magazine=Distillations|access-date=2018-06-27}} and was active in planning the county's [[Law Day]] festivities. ===United States District Court=== {{BLP sources section|date = October 2022}} Carter was nominated by President [[Bill Clinton]] on June 25, 1998, to fill a seat vacated by [[William J. Rea]]. Carter was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on October 21, 1998, and received his commission the following day.{{FJC Bio|nid=1390796|inline=yes}} He now sits in the Southern Division of the [[Central District of California]] in [[Santa Ana, California|Santa Ana]], California.{{cite web|url=https://www.cacd.uscourts.gov/honorable-david-o-carter|title=Honorable David O. Carter|website=United States District Court, Central District of California|access-date=2023-04-01}} As a jurist, Carter is known for his intellect, courteous judicial demeanor, work ethic, and expertise in complex criminal cases.{{cite book|date=2006|title=Almanac of the Federal Judiciary|publication-place=New York|publisher=Aspen Law & Business}} Although he is assigned to the [[Central District of California]], Carter also regularly sits [[by designation]] in the [[United States District Court for the District of Idaho]] and on occasion in the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]] and in the [[District Court of Guam|District of Guam]]. In addition to his judicial functions, Carter lectured fellow judges at the California Judges College, the Judicial Criminal Law Institute, and the Ninth Circuit Judicial Conference. He also speaks frequently with judges abroad, including engagements in [[Brazil]], [[Bosnia and Herzegovina|Bosnia]], [[China]], the [[Philippines]], [[Central Asia]], [[Pakistan]], [[Afghanistan]], and [[Malawi]]. Carter teaches an undergraduate course on international narcotics trade at the [[University of California, Irvine]], where he has received the school's Distinguished Professors Award three times.{{Cite web |title=Bio {{!}} The Sedona Conference® |url=https://www.thesedonaconference.org/bio/34071 |access-date=2026-08-27 |website=www.thesedonaconference.org}}{{Non primary source needed|date=August 2026}} ==Notable cases== ===Gay-Straight Alliance (''Colin ex rel. Colin v. Orange Unified School District'')=== In the first ruling of its kind, Carter issued a [[preliminary injunction]] in 2000 ordering [[Orange County, California|Orange County]] public school officials to allow a [[Gay-straight alliance|Gay-Straight Alliance]] club organized by students to meet on campus. Carter held that the [[Equal access act|Equal Access Act]] requires a [[public high school]], which accepts federal funding and establishes a limited open forum for non-curriculum-related student groups, to allow a student group promoting [[homosexual]] tolerance to meet on campus.{{cite court|litigants=Colin ex rel. Colin v. Orange Unified Sch. Dist.|vol=83|reporter=F. Supp. 2d|opinion=1135|court=C.D. Cal.|date=2000|url=https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2443692/colin-ex-rel-colin-v-orange-unified-school-dist/}} Plaintiff's attorney explained, "The judge's opinion was resounding. He really regarded this case as important and understood the real-life issues."{{cite news|last=Kane|first=Rich|date=December 5, 2013|title=Anthony Colin Made El Modena High School a Safer Place|url=https://www.ocweekly.com/anthony-colin-made-el-modena-high-school-a-safer-place-6429366/|work=OC Weekly|access-date=2023-04-01}} The case settled after Carter issued the injunction when the school board agreed to recognize the Gay-Straight Alliance organization. Although the case was politically controversial, Orange County School Board member Linda Davis later admitted at a board meeting on November 18, 2000 that Carter's legal ruling was correct: "We know the law is on their side, but our community members don't want it."{{cite magazine|last=Dowling-Sendor|first=Benjamin|date=July 2000|title=Equal Access Means Equal|url=http://www.asbj.com/2000/07/0700schoollaw.html|magazine=American School Board Journal|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20010308101002/http://www.asbj.com/2000/07/0700schoollaw.html|archive-date=2001-03-08}} ===Mexican Mafia trials (''United States v. Fernandez, et al.'')=== Between 2000 and 2001, Carter presided over the longest criminal trial in the history of the [[Central District of California]].{{cite court|litigants=United States v. Fernandez|vol=172|reporter=F. Supp. 2d|opinion=1252|court=C.D. Cal.|date=2001|url=https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2443692/colin-ex-rel-colin-v-orange-unified-school-dist/}} This case involved the prosecution of more than forty alleged members of the [[Mexican mafia|Mexican Mafia]] on charges of [[murder]], [[attempted murder]], [[Conspiracy (crime)|conspiracy]] to murder, [[extortion]], [[robbery]], and various [[drug trafficking]] and [[firearm]]s crimes. Much of the case involved a triple [[homicide]] that occurred in 1998.{{cite news|last=Rosenzweig|first=David|date=November 10, 2001|title=Jury Convicts 3, Clears 2 in Mexican Mafia Case|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2001-nov-10-me-2584-story.html|work=Los Angeles Times|access-date=2023-04-01}} The case was severed into three trials, with Carter presiding over each, and lasted for a combined 18 months. Following the conviction of Mariano "Chuy" Martinez on murder charges, the prosecution sought the [[death penalty]], making it the first capital case to be tried in [[Los Angeles]] federal court since 1950.{{cite news|last=Rosenzweig|first=David|date=February 15, 2001|title=Mexican Mafia Figure Convicted of 3 Murders|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2001-feb-15-me-25661-story.html|work=Los Angeles Times|access-date=2023-04-01}} A jury ultimately spared Martinez, sentencing him instead to [[Life sentence|life imprisonment]]. ===Anna Nicole Smith (''In re Marshall'')=== In 2002, Carter awarded over $88 million in damages to former [[Playboy Playmate|''Playboy'' Playmate]] Vickie Lynn Marshall, also known as [[Anna Nicole Smith]], in the battle over the estate of her late husband, billionaire [[J. Howard Marshall]]. The case came to Carter on appeal following a federal bankruptcy court ruling that awarded Smith $475 million of her late husband's $1.6 billion fortune. Carter concluded that Howard's son, [[E. Pierce Marshall]], interfered with Smith's attempts to collect her [[inheritance]]. "The evidence of willfulness, maliciousness, and fraud is overwhelming," Carter wrote in his 54-page opinion.{{cite court|litigants=In re Marshall|vol=275|reporter=B.R.|opinion=5|pinpoint=57|court=C.D. Cal.|date=2002|url=https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1862439/in-re-marshall/}} Upon finding that Smith had a reasonable expectation that she would receive a portion of her husband's estate without interference, Carter held that Smith was entitled to collect $44.3 million in [[punitive damages]] and $44.3 million in [[Damages#Compensatory damages|compensatory damages]] against Pierce Marshall.{{cite magazine|last=Hylton|first=Hilary|date=February 16, 2007|title=The Legal Afterlife of Anna Nicole Smith|url=http://www.time.com/time/arts/article/0,8599,1591324,00.html|magazine=Time|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070219031901/http://www.time.com/time/arts/article/0,8599,1591324,00.html|archive-date=2007-02-19}} The [[Ninth circuit|Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals]] vacated Carter's order on the grounds that he lacked [[jurisdiction]] to hear the case because [[federal jurisdiction]] interfered with [[Texas]] [[probate court]] proceedings.{{cite court|litigants=In re Marshall|vol=392|reporter=F.3d|opinion=1118|court=9th Cir.|date=2004|url=https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/788710/in-re-vickie-lynn-marshall-debtor-e-pierce-marshall/}} The [[Supreme Court of the United States]] reversed the Ninth Circuit, concluding in a unanimous opinion that Carter properly exercised jurisdiction over Smith's claim and remanded the case for further proceedings.{{cite court|litigants=Marshall v. Marshall|vol=547|reporter=U.S.|opinion=293|court=U.S.|date=2006|url=https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/145660/marshall-v-marshall/}} However, on remand from the Supreme Court, the Ninth Circuit determined that Carter should have deferred to the earlier decision of the Texas probate court, and directed Carter to enter judgment for Marshall.{{cite court|litigants=In re Marshall|vol=600|reporter=F.3d|opinion=1037|court=9th Cir.|date=2010|url=https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/408/in-re-marshall/}} ===Aryan Brotherhood trials (''United States v. Mills, et al.'')=== Carter has been involved in the proceedings arising from the 2002 [[indictment]] on [[racketeering]] charges of forty alleged members of the [[Aryan Brotherhood]] ("AB"), a notorious [[prison gang]].{{cite news|author=|date=March 13, 2006|title=Members of prison gang go on trial|url=https://www.ocregister.com/2006/03/13/members-of-prison-gang-go-on-trial/|work=The Orange County Register|access-date=2007-06-29}} This indictment alleges that the AB ordered thirty-two murders over a 23-year period and charges forty-one AB gang members and associates with violations of the federal [[Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act|RICO Act]].{{cite web|url=http://fl1.findlaw.com/news.findlaw.com/hdocs/docs/crim/usmills101702ind.pdf|title=Indictment|last1=Yang|first1=Debra W.|last2=Gordon|first2=John S.|date=February 2002|website=FindLaw|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160610094505/http://fl1.findlaw.com/news.findlaw.com/hdocs/docs/crim/usmills101702ind.pdf|archive-date=2016-06-10}} Twenty-six defendants were eligible for the [[death penalty]], making this the largest capital indictment in federal history.{{cite news|last=Duersten|first=Matthew|date=February 3, 2005|title=Who'll Stop the Reign?|url=https://www.laweekly.com/wholl-stop-the-reign/|work=LA Weekly|access-date=2007-06-23}} Twenty of the defendants charged in the indictment were assigned to Carter, including two of the three commissioners of the AB's federal faction, [[Barry Mills (Aryan Brotherhood)|Barry "The Baron" Mills]] and [[Tyler Bingham|Tyler "The Hulk" Bingham]]. Following a six-month trial, a jury convicted both Mills and Bingham of committing Violent Crimes in Aid of Racketeering (VICAR) and murder. The jury deadlocked on the death penalty,{{cite news|author=|date=September 15, 2006|title=2 Aryan Inmates Spared Death Penalty|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/2-aryan-inmates-spared-death-penalty/|work=CBS News|agency=Associated Press|access-date=2023-04-01}} and both have been sentenced and are now serving life terms at [[ADX Florence]], the federal system's sole [[supermax]] facility. The trials of several remaining defendants are currently ongoing before Carter and other judges in the [[Central District of California]]. ===''MGA Entertainment v. Mattel''=== Carter presided over a $500 million lawsuit between [[MGA Entertainment]] and [[Mattel]] over the origins and ownership of the [[Bratz]] line of fashion dolls. Ultimately, Mattel was ordered to pay $137 million in attorney's fees and costs.{{cite news|last=Sistrunk|first=Jeff|date=December 20, 2013|title=Mattel Can't Duck $137M in Legal Fees in Bratz Row|url=https://www.law360.com/articles/497664/mattel-can-t-duck-137m-in-legal-fees-in-bratz-row|url-access=limited|work=Law360|access-date=2023-04-01}} ===''Barnett v. Obama''=== In 2009, Carter dismissed a lawsuit, ''Barnett v. Obama'', challenging President Barack Obama's election and assumption of office because of claims that Obama was not a [[Barack Obama citizenship conspiracy theories|natural born citizen of the United States]], commenting that [[Federal impeachment in the United States|the power to remove a sitting president from office]] resides with Congress, not the judiciary.{{cite news|last=Holmes|first=Baxter|date=October 29, 2009|title='Birthers' Lawsuit Challenging Obama's Election Is Dismissed|url=http://latimesblogs.latimes.com/lanow/2009/10/birthers-lawsuit-challenging-obamas-election-dismissed.html|work=Los Angeles Times|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091031193427/http://latimesblogs.latimes.com/lanow/2009/10/birthers-lawsuit-challenging-obamas-election-dismissed.html|archive-date=2009-10-31}}{{cite news|last=Winger|first=Richard|date=October 29, 2009|title=Alan Keyes Loses Lawsuit on Presidential Qualifications|url=https://ballot-access.org/2009/10/29/alan-keyes-loses-lawsuit-on-presidential-qualifications/|work=Ballot Access News|access-date=2023-04-01}} ===''United States v. McGraw-Hill''=== Carter presided over a civil action brought by the [[U.S. Department of Justice]] against [[Standard & Poor's]]. The $5 billion lawsuit claimed that [[Standard & Poor's|S&P]] engaged in fraud when it gave high ratings to [[mortgage-backed securities]] and [[collateralized debt obligations]] before the [[2008 financial crisis]]. Carter denied a motion to dismiss, noting that S&P's argument that those ratings were mere [[puffery]] was "deeply and unavoidably troubling when you take a moment to consider its implications." S&P claimed that this action is retaliation for its [[United States federal government credit-rating downgrades|2011 downgrade of United States debt]].{{cite news|last=Henning|first=Peter J.|date=September 9, 2013|title=S.&P.'s Counterattack on the Government|url=https://archive.nytimes.com/dealbook.nytimes.com/2013/09/09/sps-counterattack-on-the-government/|work=The New York Times|access-date=2023-04-01}} In 2015, S&P settled with the DoJ for $1.375 billion.{{cite press release|author=|date=February 3, 2015|title=Justice Department and State Partners Secure $1.375 Billion Settlement with S&P for Defrauding Investors in the Lead Up to the Financial Crisis|url=https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-and-state-partners-secure-1375-billion-settlement-sp-defrauding-investors|publisher=United States Department of Justice|access-date=2023-04-01}} === Cases involving the homeless === In 2018, Judge Carter was the judge presiding in a case involving clearing homeless people from the [[Santa Ana River Trail]] in [[Orange County, California]].{{cite news|last=Goffard|first=Christopher|date=February 20, 2018|title=Meet the Judge at the Center of O.C. Riverbed Homeless Case Who Is Known for His Unconventional, Hands-on Approach|url=https://www.latimes.com/local/lanow/la-me-ln-judge-carter-profile-20180220-story.html|work=Los Angeles Times|access-date=2021-03-26}} Known for his unconventional approach, he helped broker a deal between the residents of the river trail and the county, whereby many of the residents were placed in motels for a month.{{cite news|last=Taxin|first=Amy|date=February 15, 2018|title=Judge Brings Officials, Lawyers to Soon-to-be-closed Homeless Camp|url=https://www.csmonitor.com/USA/Justice/2018/0215/Judge-brings-officials-lawyers-to-soon-to-be-closed-homeless-camp|work=The Christian Science Monitor|agency=Associated Press|access-date=2021-03-26}} In 2019, Carter was removed from presiding over a case involving homeless plaintiffs challenging anti-camping ordinances in five South Orange County cities due to concerns about his bias. His statements and actions in the Santa Ana River Trail case were cited in the order removing him from the case: "The Court finds that in view of the combination of circumstances, a reasonable observer would conclude based on appearances that the District Judge [Carter] is not unbiased."{{cite news|url=https://www.ocregister.com/2019/06/14/south-orange-county-cities-win-request-to-remove-judge-david-o-carter-from-hearing-homeless-lawsuit/|title=South Orange County cities win request to remove Judge David O. Carter from hearing homeless lawsuit|newspaper=[[The Orange County Register]]|date=June 14, 2019|last=Walker|first=Theresa}} In 2021, he was the judge in a case involving removing homeless people from [[Echo Park, Los Angeles]].{{cite news|last=Weber|first=Christopher|date=March 26, 2021|title=Los Angeles Park Closed After Protest to Save Homeless Camp|url=https://apnews.com/article/los-angeles-1f083f4d56bbb865f76b8e79547208ff|work=AP News|access-date=2021-03-26}} On April 21, 2021, Carter ruled in a 110-page opinion brief that homeless people on [[Skid Row, Los Angeles|Skid Row]], in Los Angeles, must be offered housing by October 18.{{cite magazine|last=Cuniff|first=Meghann|date=April 21, 2021|title='A Legacy of Racism': Judge Issues Bold Order to House Skid Row's Homeless|url=https://www.lamag.com/citythinkblog/skid-row-homeless-injunction-judge-david-o-carter/|magazine=Los Angeles Magazine|access-date=2023-04-01}} Both the city and county of Los Angeles appealed, and Carter's ruling was overturned on September 23, 2021, by a unanimous vote of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit|9th Circuit Court of Appeals]].{{cite news|last1=Oreskes|first1=Benjamin|last2=Dolan|first2=Maura|last3=Zahniser|first3=David|date=September 23, 2021|title=Appeals Court Strikes Down Sweeping Order to House L.A.'s Skid Row Homeless Population|url=https://www.latimes.com/homeless-housing/story/2021-09-23/appeals-court-strikes-down-sweeping-order-to-house-l-a-s-skid-row-homeless|work=Los Angeles Times|access-date=2022-10-24}} ===''Eastman v. Thompson''=== In 2022, Judge Carter ordered [[John Eastman]] to turn over certain documents to the [[United States House Select Committee on the January 6 Attack]]. In his order, the judge said "the Court finds it more likely than not that [[Donald Trump|President Trump]] corruptly attempted to obstruct the Joint Session of Congress on January 6, 2021."{{cite news|last1=Cheney|first1=Kyle|last2=Gerstein|first2=Josh|last3=Wu|first3=Nicholas|date=March 28, 2022|title=Trump Likely Committed Felony Obstruction, Federal Judge Rules|url=https://www.politico.com/news/2022/03/28/trump-judge-felony-obstruction-insurrection-00020918|work=Politico|access-date=2022-03-28}} In the civil suit, Eastman had claimed [[attorney-client privilege]], but Carter rejected the claim because attorney-client privilege does not apply if the discussion involved a crime, and "the illegality of the plan was obvious."{{cite news|last1=Barnes|first1=Daniel|last2=Gregorian|first2=Dareh|date=March 28, 2022|title=Trump Probably Broke the Law in an Effort to Obstruct Jan. 6 Proceedings, Judge Says|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/donald-trump/federal-judge-finds-trump-likely-not-tried-illegally-disrupt-electoral-rcna21857|work=NBC News|access-date=2022-03-28}} In that opinion Carter coined the term “this was a coup in search of a legal theory.”{{cite web | title=Federal Judge Finds Trump Most Likely Committed Crimes over 2020 Election (Published 2022) | website=[[The New York Times]] | date=28 March 2022 | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/03/28/us/politics/trump-election-crimes.html?smid=nytcore-ios-share&referringSource=articleShare }} ===''United States v. Shirley Weber'' (voter data)=== On January 15, 2026, Carter ruled that the federal government could not force California to hand over sensitive voter information, such as voters' names, addresses, birthdates, drivers license and Social Security numbers. Carter wrote: “The centralization of this information by the federal government would have a chilling effect on voter registration which would inevitably lead to decreasing voter turnout as voters fear that their information is being used for some inappropriate or unlawful purpose.
