{{nowrap|[[Boston College]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]])}} | signature = | signature_alt = | website = | footnotes = }} '''Ellen Judith Huvelle''' ([[Maiden and married names|''née'']] '''Segal'''; born June 3, 1948) is an inactive [[United States federal judge|Senior United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Columbia]].{{cite news |url = http://www.dcd.uscourts.gov/huvelle-bio.html |title = Judge Ellen Segal Huvelle |publisher = [[United States Department of Justice]] |access-date = 2008-06-11 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080617183042/http://www.dcd.uscourts.gov/huvelle-bio.html |archive-date = 2008-06-17 |url-status = dead }} She has overseen several significant cases. In a case decided in May 2001, Huvelle "upheld federal regulations that restrict the sale of consumers' names, Social Security numbers, dates of birth, addresses and phone numbers." {{cite news | url=https://money.cnn.com/2001/05/16/living/q_bankrate/ | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030219011414/http://money.cnn.com/2001/05/16/living/q_bankrate/ | url-status=dead | archive-date=February 19, 2003 | title= For privacy, opt out: Protect your private information from stalkers, telemarketers, identity thieves | publisher=[[CNN Money]] | author=Holden Lewis | author-link=Holden Lewis | date=May 16, 2001 | access-date=2008-05-08 }} Later that year, Huvelle heard requests by family members of [[Vince Foster]] seeking access to pictures of his body taken after his death. In November 2005, she accepted the [[guilty plea]] in the high-profile prosecution of [[lobbyist]] [[Michael Scanlon]]. Huvelle assumed [[senior status]] on June 3, 2014.{{cite web|url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/huvelle-ellen-segal|title=Huvelle, Ellen Segal - Federal Judicial Center|website=www.fjc.gov}} ==Early life and career== Born in [[Boston]], [[Massachusetts]], Huvelle grew up in Newton, Massachusetts and graduated from [[Newton North High School|Newton High School]] in 1966.[https://www.classmates.com/siteui/yearbooks/4182722862?page=243&searchTerm=Segal&yearbookViewerEnabled=true&swipeEnabled=true Newton High School (Class of 1966)]. ===Education=== She received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[Wellesley College]] in 1970 and a [[Urban planning education|Master in City Planning]] from the [[Yale School of Architecture]] in 1972. With her father and brother both lawyers, Huvelle focused on the law and in 1975 earned a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[Boston College Law School]]. ===Early career=== In 1973 she was a law clerk for the appellate division of the [[Suffolk County, Massachusetts|Suffolk County District Attorney's Office]] in Massachusetts. In 1974 she was a [[public defender]] for the [[Committee for Public Counsel Services]] in [[Boston]]. ===Legal career=== Following law school, she served as [[law clerk]] to [[Chief Justice]] [[Edward F. Hennessey]] of the [[Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court]] from 1975 to 1976. From 1976 until 1984, Huvelle was an associate at the firm of [[Williams & Connolly]] in [[Washington, D.C.]] and in 1984, she became the first female partner at that firm, where she remained until 1990. In 1983, Huvelle was one of three attorneys who drafted an [[amicus brief]] on behalf of the [[Motion Picture Association of America]] in the [[landmark case]] of ''[[Sony Corp. of America v. Universal City Studios, Inc.]]''. As a partner at Williams & Connolly, Huvelle represented several notable clients including hotel magnate [[Leona Helmsley]] and fight promoter [[Don King (boxing promoter)|Don King]]. ==Judicial service== ===District of Columbia superior court service=== Huvelle was appointed by President [[George H. W. Bush]] as an Associate Judge of the [[District of Columbia Superior Court]] in September 1990 and served in the Civil, Criminal and Family Divisions until her appointment to the federal bench.[https://www.congress.gov/nomination/101st-congress/1181/1 Pres. Nom. 1,181], 101st Cong. (1990). While serving on that court, she was a lecturer at the [[University of Virginia School of Law]] from 1997 to 1999. ===Federal judicial service=== On March 25, 1999, Huvelle was nominated by President [[Bill Clinton]] to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the District of Columbia]], vacated by [[John Garrett Penn]].[https://www.congress.gov/nomination/106th-congress/180 Pres. Nom.180], 106th Cong. (1999). She was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on October 15, 1999, receiving her commission on October 26, 1999. [[United States Senate|Senator]] [[Patrick Leahy]] cited the long delays in Huvelle's confirmation as United States District Judge as a troubling example of problems in the confirmation process. {{cite news | url=http://leahy.senate.gov/press/200112/121101b.html | title=Statement of Senator Patrick Leahy on Judicial Nominations | publisher=[[United States Senate]] | author=Patrick Leahy | author-link=Patrick Leahy | date=December 11, 2001 | access-date=2008-05-08 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080501082540/http://leahy.senate.gov/press/200112/121101b.html |archive-date = 2008-05-01}} She took [[senior status]] on June 3, 2014. Huvelle has been a Fellow of the [[American Bar Association]], a member of the Edward Bennett Williams Inn of Court, and has taught [[trial practice]] at [[Harvard Law School]]'s Trial Advocacy Workshop and at the [[University of Virginia School of Law]].{{cite news |url = http://www.dcd.uscourts.gov/huvelle-bio.html |title = Judge Ellen Segal Huvelle |publisher = [[United States Department of Justice]] |access-date = 2008-05-08 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080511193735/http://www.dcd.uscourts.gov/huvelle-bio.html |archive-date = 2008-05-11 |url-status = dead }} ==Notable opinions== ===Privacy and "opt out"=== According to ''[[CNN]]'' Huvelle played a key role in ensuring that ordinary consumers can opt out of information collection on their personal information. ===''A.C.L.U. v. '''Emmet Gael Sullivan''' (born June 4, 1947)<ref>{{Cite book |last=Affairs |first=United States Congress Senate Committee on Governmental |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qqE1AAAAIAAJ&q=Nomination+of+Robert+I.+Richter |title=Nominations for Superior Court of the District of Columbia: Hearing Before the Committee on Governmental Affairs, United States Senate, Ninety-eighth Congress, Second Session, on the Nominations of Emmet G. Sullivan, Colleen C. Kollar-Kotelly, Rufus G. King III, Susan R. Holmes, Noel A. Kramer, Robert I. Richter, and Robert S. Tignor, to be Associate Judges of the Superior Court of the District of Columbia, September 11, 1984 |date=1984 |publisher=U.S. Government Printing Office |pages=10 |language=en}}</ref> is an American attorney and jurist serving as a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Columbia]].<ref name=UrbinaBio>
{{cite web
 |url         = http://www.dcd.uscourts.gov/sullivan-bio.html
 |title       = Emmet G. Sullivan
 |publisher   = [[US District Court]]
 |access-date  = June 28, 2008
 |url-status     = dead
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20080618003116/http://www.dcd.uscourts.gov/sullivan-bio.html
 |archive-date = June 18, 2008
}}</ref>

He earned his undergraduate and law degrees from [[Howard University]]. He worked in private practice for more than a decade at Houston & Gardner, becoming a name [[Partner (business rank)#Law firms|partner]] in 1980. He was appointed to the [[Superior Court of the District of Columbia]] in 1984 by President [[Ronald Reagan]], to the [[District of Columbia Court of Appeals]] as an Associate Judge in 1992 by President [[George H. W. Bush]], and to the federal bench in 1994 by President [[Bill Clinton]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://jnc.dc.gov/sites/default/files/dc/sites/jnc/publication/attachments/Record-JNC-Recs-Desigs-Oct13.pdf|title=Report of District of Columbia Judicial Nomination Commission}}</ref>

==Early life==
Sullivan was born in [[Washington, D.C.]], in 1947 and attended local schools. He graduated from [[McKinley Technology High School]] in 1964. In 1968, he received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in political science from [[Howard University]], a [[historically black university]], and in 1971 a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[Howard University School of Law]].<ref name=WashingtonPost2.4.21/>

== Career ==
Upon graduation from law school, Sullivan received a [[Reginald Heber Smith]] Fellowship in [[poverty law]] from the [[University of Pennsylvania]]. He was assigned to the Neighborhood Legal Services Program in Washington, D.C., where he worked for one year. The following year, he served as a [[law clerk]] to Superior Court Judge [[James A. Washington Jr.]], a former professor and dean of [[Howard University School of Law]].{{fact|date=August 2026}}

In 1973, Sullivan joined the law firm of Houston & Gardner, co-founded by [[Charles Hamilton Houston]], who had expanded Howard University Law School as its dean, and led litigation for the [[NAACP]] to overturn racially restrictive laws. Sullivan became a partner and was actively engaged in the general practice of law with that firm.{{fact|date=August 2026}}

In August 1980, his partner, William C. Gardner, was appointed as an Associate Judge of the Superior Court of the District of Columbia. Sullivan was a name partner in the successor firm of Houston, Sullivan & Gardner. He also taught as an adjunct professor at the Howard University School of Law and has served as a member of the visiting faculty at Harvard Law School's Trial Advocacy Workshop.{{fact|date=August 2026}}

Sullivan was appointed by [[Ronald Reagan|President Reagan]] to the [[Superior Court of the District of Columbia]] on October 3, 1984. On November 25, 1991, Sullivan was appointed by [[George H. W. Bush|President George H. W. Bush]] to serve as an Associate Judge of the [[District of Columbia Court of Appeals]].{{fact|date=August 2026}}

===Federal judicial service===
Sullivan was nominated by President [[Bill Clinton]] on March 22, 1994, to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the District of Columbia]] vacated by Judge [[Louis F. Oberdorfer]]. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on June 15, 1994, and received his commission on June 16, 1994.<ref name="fjc">{{FJC Bio|nid=1388436|inline=yes}}</ref> Sullivan assumed [[senior status]] on April 3, 2021.<ref name="fjc"/><ref name=WashingtonPost2.4.21>{{Cite news|last1=Hsu|first1=Spencer S.|last2=Marimow|first2=Ann E.|date=February 4, 2021|title=U.S. judge in Flynn case takes senior status, joining wave of jurists allowing Biden to name successors|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|url=https://washingtonpost.com/local/legal-issues/judge-emmet-sullivan-retiring/2021/02/04/8788f754-66f5-11eb-8c64-9595888caa15_story.html|access-date=February 4, 2021}}</ref>

===Notable cases===
Sullivan presided over a number of [[habeas corpus]] petitions in the early 21st century submitted on behalf of men detained by the United States military at the [[Guantanamo Bay detention camp]] as part of President [[George W. Bush]]'s response to the [[9/11 attacks]] of terrorism.<ref name=GuantanamoHabeasRespondentResponse>{{cite web|url=http://www.pegc.us/archive/OK_v_Bush/govt_resp_to_GK_20060815.pdf|title=Respondents' response to Court's August 7, 2006 order|date=August 15, 2006|publisher=[[United States Department of Defense]]|access-date=June 23, 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080627111630/http://www.pegc.us/archive/OK_v_Bush/govt_resp_to_GK_20060815.pdf|archive-date=June 27, 2008|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Sullivan presided over the 2008 trial of U.S. [[United States Senate|Senator]] [[Ted Stevens]], who was convicted of seven felony ethics violations in October. During the trial, the judge refused requests by the defense for a mistrial to be declared, after information was revealed that the prosecution had withheld exculpatory [[Brady disclosure|''Brady'' material]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/10/03/us/03stevens.html|title=Judge Berates Prosecutors in Trial of Senator|first=Neil A.|last=Lewis|work=The New York Times |date=October 2, 2008|via=NYTimes.com}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://abcnews.go.com/TheLaw/story?id=5937338&page=1|title=Judge Denies Stevens Mistrial Request|first1=Jason|last1=Ryan|first2=Theresa|last2=Cook|date=October 2, 2008|work=ABC News|access-date=August 11, 2018}}</ref> Eight days after the guilty verdict, Stevens narrowly lost his reelection bid.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2008/11/18/AR2008111803227.html |first=Paul |last=Kane |title=Sen. Ted Stevens Loses Reelection Bid |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |date=November 19, 2008|access-date=August 11, 2018}}</ref> As more evidence of prosecutorial misconduct became known in early 2009, Judge Sullivan held four prosecutors in civil [[contempt of court]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/02/14/us/politics/14stevens.html |first=Neil A. |last=Lewis |title=4 Prosecutors in Stevens Case Held in Contempt |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=February 13, 2009 |access-date=August 11, 2018}}</ref> On April 1, 2009, following a [[United States Department of Justice|Justice Department]] probe that found additional evidence of [[prosecutorial misconduct]], the Department of Justice recommended that Stevens' conviction be dismissed.<ref name="dcbar">{{cite web|url=https://www.dcbar.org/bar-resources/publications/washington-lawyer/articles/october-2009-ted-stevens.cfm|first=Anna Stolley|last=Perskey|title=A Cautionary Tale: The Ted Stevens Prosecution|publisher=Washington Lawyer|date=October 2009|access-date=August 11, 2018|archive-date=December 8, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151208142411/https://www.dcbar.org/bar-resources/publications/washington-lawyer/articles/october-2009-ted-stevens.cfm|url-status=dead}}</ref> On April 7, 2009, Sullivan set aside the conviction and appointed a lawyer to investigate the prosecution team for criminal contempt.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.cnn.com/2009/POLITICS/04/07/ted.stevens/index.html|work=CNN|title=Sen. Ted Stevens's conviction set aside|date=April 7, 2009}}</ref> Subsequently, one of the four prosecutors held in contempt committed suicide.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2010/09/27/AR2010092706613.html |first=Paul |last=Duggan |title=Justice Dept. lawyer kills self |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |date=September 28, 2010 |access-date=August 11, 2018}}</ref> Ultimately, Sullivan dismissed the civil contempt charges,<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2010/10/12/AR2010101206934.html |first=Spencer S.|last=Hsu |title=Judge lifts civil contempt findings against Justice Department lawyers in Ted Stevens case |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |date=October 12, 2010 |access-date=August 11, 2018}}</ref> and no additional charges were brought against the three surviving prosecutors.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.politico.com/blogs/under-the-radar/2012/03/appeals-court-wont-delay-stevens-report-117444 |first=Josh |last=Gerstein |title=Appeals court won't delay Stevens report |publisher=Politico |date=March 14, 2012 |access-date=August 11, 2018}}</ref>

In 2014, Sullivan was presiding over a case, ''[[Judicial Watch]] v. [[IRS]],''<ref>{{cite news |title=Motion for Status Conference |author=Judicial Watch |newspaper=Judicial Watch |date=June 27, 2014 |url=http://nblo.gs/Zd7kv |access-date=August 15, 2014 |archive-date=August 18, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140818085138/http://nblo.gs/Zd7kv |url-status=dead }}</ref> related to an ongoing investigation into the [[2013 IRS controversy]]. There was a fruitless attempt to determine where the deleted emails of former IRS employee [[Lois Lerner]] had gone, what damage to her computer hard drive occurred, and what steps the IRS had taken to recover the information contained in the emails and on the hard drive.<ref>{{cite news |title=Judge Prods IRS on Effort to Save Lois Lerner's E-Mail |author=Andrew Zajac |newspaper=[[Bloomberg L.P.|Bloomberg]] |date=August 14, 2014 |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/2014-08-14/judge-prods-irs-on-effort-to-save-lois-lerner-s-e-mail.html |access-date=August 15, 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Group: Inquiry ordered into lost IRS emails |author=Kevin G. Hall |newspaper=[[Fort Worth Star-Telegram]] |date=August 14, 2014 |url=http://www.star-telegram.com/2014/08/14/6044045/group-inquiry-ordered-into-lost.html |access-date=August 15, 2014 |archive-date=August 19, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140819084141/http://www.star-telegram.com/2014/08/14/6044045/group-inquiry-ordered-into-lost.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In 2015, Sullivan presided over a [[Freedom of Information Act (United States)|FOIA]] lawsuit involving the matter of [[Hillary Clinton email controversy|Hillary Clinton's private email use while Secretary of State]].<ref>{{cite news|author1=Jason Donner|title=Judge orders State Dept. to work on recovering emails, suggests Clinton violated policy|url=https://www.foxnews.com/politics/judge-orders-state-dept-to-work-on-recovering-emails-suggests-clinton-violated-policy/|access-date=August 27, 2015|work=Fox News|date=August 20, 2015}}</ref>

According to the [[American Civil Liberties Union]] (ACLU), a woman and her child fled domestic abuse in El Salvador to seek asylum in the U.S. However, the mother was removed from her detention facility and likely put on a plane on August 9, 2018, despite Justice Department promises that she and others would not be deported before the judge could rule on their cases. Sullivan demanded, "Turn that plane around." He threatened to hold those responsible for the removal in contempt of court, starting with Attorney General [[Jeff Sessions]], if the situation was not rectified. A [[United States Department of Homeland Security|Department of Homeland Security]] official stated, "We are complying with the court's requests...the plaintiffs will not disembark and will be promptly returned to the United States."<ref>[https://www.wkrg.com/news/local-news/judge-threatens-to-hold-jeff-sessions-in-contempt/1357404405 Judge threatens to hold Jeff Sessions in contempt Mobile native's Justice Department deported woman] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180810153353/https://www.wkrg.com/news/local-news/judge-threatens-to-hold-jeff-sessions-in-contempt/1357404405 |date=August 10, 2018 }}, ''[[WKRG]]'', Peter Albrecht, August 9, 2018. Retrieved August 10, 2018.</ref>

====''Blumenthal v Trump''====
{{Main|Blumenthal v Trump}}
Judge Sullivan presided over a [[Legal affairs of the first Donald Trump presidency|lawsuit involving President Trump]], which challenged payments by foreign governments to Trump-owned hotels.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/federal-judge-allows-trump-to-appeal-lawsuit-over-foreign-payments-accepted-by-his-hotels/2019/08/21/7e288a38-c428-11e9-b72f-b31dfaa77212_story.html|title=Federal judge allows Trump to appeal lawsuit over foreign payments accepted by his hotels |last1=Fahrenthold |first1=David A. |last2=Marimow |first2=Ann E. |date=August 21, 2019 |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]}}</ref> Sullivan granted in part and denied in part the Trump team's [[motion to dismiss]] for lack of standing;<ref>335 F.Supp.3d 45</ref> denied the motion to dismiss for failure to state claim;<ref>373 F.Supp.3d 191</ref> and certified [[interlocutory appeal]].<ref name=":0">Blumenthal v. Trump, 19-5237, 2020 WL 593891 (D.C. Cir. Feb. 7, 2020) (No. 1:17-cv-01154)</ref> On February 7, 2020, in a [[per curiam decision|''per curiam'' decision]], the [[United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit]] held that individual members of Congress lacked standing to bring action against the president.<ref name=":0" /><ref>United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia, opinion PER CURIAM, February 7, 2020 https://www.cadc.uscourts.gov/internet/opinions.nsf/2EFD382E65E33B3C852585070055D091/$file/19-5237-1827549.pdf {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210215025018/https://www.cadc.uscourts.gov/internet/opinions.nsf/2EFD382E65E33B3C852585070055D091/$file/19-5237-1827549.pdf |date=February 15, 2021 }}</ref> The court, finding in favor of Trump, reversed and remanded Sullivan's holding that the members of Congress had [[Standing (law)#United States|standing to sue]] and instructed him to [[Prejudice (legal term)|dismiss]] the complaint.<ref name=":1">Blumenthal v. Trump, 19-5237, 2020 WL 593891, at *5 (D.C. Cir. Feb. 7, 2020)</ref>

Circuit Court of Appeals]], asking that Sullivan be ordered to drop the charges, challenging his decision to appoint Gleeson, and asking that he be removed from the case.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.foxnews.com/politics/flynn-attorney-files-writ-to-shut-down-judge-sullivans-efforts-to-keep-case-alive|title=Flynn attorney files emergency appeal to shut down Judge Sullivan's orders, boot him from case|last=Re|first=Gregg|date=May 20, 2020|work=Fox News|access-date=22 May 2020}}</ref><ref name=writ>{{Cite web|url=https://sidneypowell.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/Petition-filed.pdf%27Flynn|title=writ of mandamus petition'}}{{Dead link|date=March 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> On May 21, citing ''US v Fokker Servs, BV'', 818 F.3d 733 (DC Cir 2016), the D.C. Circuit ordered Sullivan to respond to the writ of mandamus by June 1, 2020, and invited the government to respond within the same 10-day period.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cadc.uscourts.gov/internet/orders.nsf/14CA50587730CED08525856F006906EF/$file/20-5143LDSN.pdf|title='DC Circuit Court Of Appeals May 21, 2020 Order'|access-date=May 21, 2020|archive-date=May 22, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200522052158/https://www.cadc.uscourts.gov/internet/orders.nsf/14CA50587730CED08525856F006906EF/%24file/20-5143LDSN.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> On June 1, as part of his response,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/f/?id=00000172-716b-d526-a77e-f9ef46250000|title=Brief For Judge Emmet G. Sullivan In Response To May 21, 2020 Order|publisher=Politico|date=June 1, 2020|access-date=June 2, 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/news/2020/06/01/judge-questions-unusual-justice-department-filing-in-flynn-case-294330|title=DOJ urges appeals court to force dismissal of Flynn case|author=Cheney, Kyle|publisher=Politico|date=June 1, 2020|access-date=June 2, 2020|archive-date=February 15, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210215154304/https://www.politico.com/news/2020/06/01/judge-questions-unusual-justice-department-filing-in-flynn-case-294330|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=sullie.response>{{Cite news|last1=Re|first1=Gregg|title=Judge's lawyers hint at 'reason to question' DOJ's motives in new Michael Flynn case filing; DOJ fires back|work=Fox News|url=https://www.foxnews.com/politics/judge-sullivans-lawyers-cite-unusual-developments-as-providing-reason-to-question-dojs-motion-to-dismiss|date=June 1, 2020|access-date=June 2, 2020}}</ref> Sullivan argued that the ''Fokker'' decision does not apply because it did not consider a situation where the defendant pleaded guilty twice and the prosecutor changed course; Sullivan moved to dismiss.<ref name=sullie.response/> Oral arguments before a D.C. Retrieved June 15, 2020.</ref> Sullivan was next due to hear the case on July 16, 2020.<ref>[https://www.lawfaremedia.org/article/oral-argument-summary-re-michael-flynn Oral Argument Summary: In re: Michael Flynn], ''[[Lawfare]]'', Benjamin Wittes, June 12, 2020. On June 24, 2020, in a 2-1 decision, the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals panel granted Flynn's petition for a writ of mandamus, ordering Judge Sullivan to dismiss the case. "In this case, the district court's actions will result in specific harms to the exercise of the Executive Branch's exclusive prosecutorial power. The contemplated proceedings would likely require the Executive to reveal the internal deliberative process behind its exercise of prosecutorial discretion, interfering with the Article II charging authority." The decision also vacated Judge Sullivan's amicus appointment on mootness grounds.<ref name=writ.granted>{{cite news|url=https://www.cadc.uscourts.gov/internet/opinions.nsf/79798A0FA0633B7985258591004DD3E7/$file/20-5143-1848728.pdf|title=In re Michael T. Judge Sullivan's options were either to request the full appellate court to review the case or to grant the DOJ's motion to dismiss the charges in accordance with the writ of mandamus.<ref name=hearing.nixed>{{cite news|url=https://www.foxnews.com/politics/flynn-case-hearing-deadlines-nixed-after-court-ordered-to-allow-dismissal|title=Flynn case hearing, deadlines nixed after court-ordered to allow dismissal|last=Blitzer|first=Ronn|date=June 25, 2020|work=Fox News|access-date=9 July 2020}}</ref>

7-30-2020</ref> In addition to vacating the June 24, 2020 panel decision, the Order directs all parties to be prepared to "address whether there are 'no other adequate means to attain the relief' desired" (citation omitted).<ref name=en.banc.granted /> On August 11, the full appeals court heard arguments from the DOJ and from Flynn's attorney.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/2020/08/11/michael-flynn-appeals-court-hears-case-trump-ally/5581317002/|title=Michael Flynn's efforts to force federal judge to dismiss case faces a skeptical appeals court|last=Phillips|first=Kristine|date=August 11, 2020|work=USA Today|access-date=11 August 2020}}</ref> On August 31, the appeals court declined to order dismissal of Flynn's prosecution.<ref name="Appeals court keeps case alive">{{cite web|url=https://apnews.com/d996f8036f0598b9c2dd81e6af3d7df5 |title=Appeals court keeps Flynn case alive, won't order dismissal |publisher=[[Associated Press]] |date=31 August 2020 |access-date=31 August 2020 |author=Tucker, Eric}}</ref> In an ''[[en banc]]'' hearing, eight of the D.C. Circuit judges ruled in favor of allowing Sullivan to adjudicate the case. Only the two judges who ruled in favor of Flynn in June 2020, appointed by Presidents [[George W. Bush]] and [[Donald Trump]] ruled against the decision. In their dissent, they reversed their earlier position that the case should not be taken from Sullivan and assigned to another judge.<ref>[https://www.politico.com/news/2020/08/31/judge-can-move-forward-with-flynn-hearing-appeals-court-says-406066 Appeals court deals setback to Flynn's attempt to end DOJ case],  ''[[Politico]]'', Josh Gerstein, August 31, 2020. Retrieved August 31, 2020.</ref>

On November 25, 2020, Trump issued Flynn a full [[Federal pardons in the United States|presidential pardon]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-us-canada-55080923 |access-date=November 28, 2020 |title=Michael Flynn: Trump pardons ex-national security adviser|date=November 26, 2020|work=BBC News }}</ref>  On December 8, 2020, Judge Sullivan dismissed the case as moot because of the presidential pardon. In his 43-page opinion he commented that the pardon was "extraordinarily broad", noted that such a pardon does not render the recipient "innocent", and pointed out that acceptance of a pardon implies an admission of guilt.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.cnn.com/2020/12/08/politics/michael-flynn/index.html|title=Judge formally dismisses Michael Flynn case after Trump pardon|last=Polantz|first=Katelyn|date=December 8, 2020|work=CNN|access-date=9 December 2020}}</ref>

A man who left a graphic death threat on Sullivan's voicemail during the Flynn proceeding was sentenced in July 2021 to 18 months in prison.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/news/2021/07/19/threatened-flynn-judge-prison-500189|title=Man who threatened Flynn-case judge sentenced to 18 months|first=Josh|last=Gerstein|website=POLITICO|date=July 19, 2021 }}</ref>

====Post Office====
On October 28, 2020, Sullivan ordered USPS to lift limits on extra trips and overtime leading up to Election Day. He also ordered the Postal Service to update him on the number of trips occurring each day at a national, regional, and local level.<ref>[https://www.news4jax.com/news/2020/10/28/federal-judge-orders-usps-to-lift-limits-on-extra-trips-overtime-one-week-before-election/ Federal judge orders USPS to lift limits on extra trips, overtime, one week before election], ''[[WJXT]]'', October 28, 2020. Retrieved February 17, 2021.</ref> On November 3, Sullivan ordered the USPS to "sweep its facilities" in crucial swing states by 3 p.m. that day. The USPS failed to meet the deadline.<ref>[https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/usps-ordered-to-sweep-swing-state-facilities-for-ballots-1 USPS ordered to sweep swing state facilities for Ballots], ''[[Bloomberg Law]]'', November 3, 2020. Retrieved February 17, 2021.</ref> After the USPS failure to comply with the court-ordered ballot sweep, Sullivan ordered Postmaster General [[Louis DeJoy]] to appear in court.<ref>[https://www.marketwatch.com/story/u-s-postal-service-officials-ordered-to-court-hearing-after-failure-to-comply-with-federal-judges-ballot-sweep-order-01604510041 U.S. Postal Service officials ordered to appear in court after failing to comply with federal judge's ballot-sweep order], ''[[Associated Press]]'', November 4, 2020. Retrieved February 17, 2021.</ref> Sullivan has also ordered the Postal Service to sweep their facilities for ballots twice a day in states with extended deadlines. At a post-election hearing in early November, Sullivan said that DeJoy "is either going to have to be deposed or appear before me and testify under oath about why some measures were not taken."<ref>[https://www.reuters.com/article/us-usa-election-post-office/u-s-appeals-ruling-that-barred-postal-service-changes-before-election-idUSKBN2872QB U.S. appeals ruling that barred Postal Service changes before election], ''[[Reuters]]'', David Shepardson, November 27, 2020. Retrieved June 4, 2021.</ref>

====Title 42====
On November 15, 2022, Sullivan ruled that [[Title 42 expulsion]], a tool used by presidents [[Donald Trump]] and [[Joe Biden]] to forbid asylum seekers from remaining in the United States was a violation of the [[Administrative Procedure Act (United States)|Administrative Procedure Act]], noting that the Title was an "arbitrary and capricious" violation of the Act. The ruling required the United States government to process all asylum seekers under immigrant law as previous to Title 42's implementation, and Sullivan specifically called out the [[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention|CDC]] for intentionally ignoring the negative effects that Title 42 would bring about, as well as failing to allow migrants to reside with legal US residents. The ruling was celebrated by the [[American Civil Liberties Union|ACLU]], the plaintiff in the case.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Alvarez |first=Priscilla |date=2022-11-15 |title=Federal judge blocks Title 42 rule that allowed expulsion of migrants at US-Mexico border, restoring access for some asylum seekers {{!}} CNN Politics |url=https://www.cnn.com/2022/11/15/politics/title-42-migrants/index.html |access-date=2022-11-15|publisher=[[CNN]]|language=en-US}}</ref>

[[New York University School of Law|New York University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | footnotes = }} '''Eric Nicholas Vitaliano''' (born 1948) is an American judge and politician. He was a member of the [[New York State Assembly|New York State Assembly]] and is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York]]. Vitaliano was nominated by President [[George W. Bush]] on October 6, 2005, to a seat vacated by [[Arthur Spatt]]. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on December 21, 2005, and received commission on January 19, 2006. == Early life == Vitaliano was born in [[West New Brighton, Staten Island]] in 1948. He attended [[St. Peter's Boys High School]]. While at college he became a member of the [[The Bronx|Bronx]] [[Young Democrats of America]].{{Cite web |title=Collection: PM-03: Assemblyman Eric N. Vitaliano Papers {{!}} College of Staten Island ArchivesSpace |url=https://archivesspace.library.csi.cuny.edu/repositories/2/resources/31 |access-date=2023-02-27 |website=archivesspace.library.csi.cuny.edu}} Vitaliano received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] from [[Fordham College]] in 1968, followed by a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[New York University School of Law]] in 1971. == Career == After law school, Vitaliano clerked for [[United States District Judge]] Mark A. Constantino of the [[Eastern District of New York]], and worked for seven years for the [[Manhattan]] law firm of [[Simpson Thacher & Bartlett]]. From 1979 to 1981 he served as Chief of Staff to Congressman [[John M. Murphy (New York politician)|John M. Murphy]].{{citation needed|date=December 2018}} He was a member of the [[New York State Assembly]] from 1983 to 2001, sitting in the [[185th New York State Legislature|185th]], [[186th New York State Legislature|186th]], [[187th New York State Legislature|187th]], [[188th New York State Legislature|188th]], [[189th New York State Legislature|189th]], [[190th New York State Legislature|190th]], [[191st New York State Legislature|191st]], [[192nd New York State Legislature|192nd]], [[193rd New York State Legislature|193rd]] and [[194th New York State Legislature]]s. In a 1997 special election, he ran for Congress in [[New York's 13th congressional district|13th District]], but was defeated by Republican [[Vito Fossella]].[https://www.nytimes.com/1997/08/23/nyregion/duos-and-bandwagons-in-staten-island-race.html ''Duos and Bandwagons In Staten Island Race''] by Jonathan P. Hicks, in ''[[The New York Times]]'' on August 23, 1997 In November 2001, Vitaliano was elected to the [[New York City Civil Court]].{{citation needed|date=December 2018}} ===New York State assembly === As a member of the New York State Assembly, Vitaliano supported many political causes throughout his career. He supported the closure of the [[Fresh Kills Landfill]] and lobbied for the order of consent from the [[New York State Department of Environmental Conservation]] that was required to begin the closure process. In 1996, he shaped the bill whose successful passage of legislation eventually enabled the landfill to close in 2001. In addition to this, Vitaliano also served as the senior New York City member of the Legislative Commission on Solid Waste Management and served as vice-chairman of the Joint Legislative Commission on Toxic Substances and Hazardous Wastes.{{Cite news |last=Ap |date=1996-05-31 |title=Assembly Votes to Force S.I. Dump to Close |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1996/05/31/nyregion/assembly-votes-to-force-si-dump-to-close.html |access-date=2023-03-02 |issn=0362-4331}} Vitaliano was also supported an increase of public transportation on Staten Island. He frequently lobbied to ensure satisfactory express bus service from the [[Metropolitan Transportation Authority]] from the Island to [[New York City]]. He also supported the one-way toll for the [[Verrazzano–Narrows Bridge]], which eventually was enacted on a federal level. === Run for Congress === In 1997, after fourteen years in the State Assembly, Vitaliano decided to run for [[United States Congress|Congress]]. A climax of his campaign was the day President [[Bill Clinton]] came to Staten Island in support of his candidacy. His attempt was unsuccessful and he lost to his [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] opponent, [[New York City Council]]man [[Vito Fossella]].{{Cite news |last=Hicks |first=Jonathan P. |date=1997-06-17 |title=S.I. Democrats Pick Nominee For Congress |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1997/06/17/nyregion/si-democrats-pick-nominee-for-congress.html |access-date=2023-03-02 |issn=0362-4331}} ===Federal judicial service=== In 2005, he was recommended to the Eastern District bench by Senator [[Charles Schumer]]. Vitaliano was officially nominated to the court by President [[George W. Bush]] on October 6, 2005, to the seat vacated by [[Arthur Donald Spatt]], confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on December 21, 2005, and received his commission on January 19, 2006. He assumed [[senior status]] on February 28, 2017.{{FJC Bio|nid=1392331|inline=yes}} ===Notable case=== In July 2011, wide attention came to his [[injunction]] that essentially nullified a set of decisions by the federal, state and city governments over the last years, which had removed two historic buildings from classification as federally designated parkland. One, the Tobacco Warehouse, a Civil War-era structure in Dumbo, was on the verge of conversion to the new home of Brooklyn's leading theater company. Judge Vitaliano held it was “crystal clear” that the National Park Service and others had exceeded their authority.{{cite news |date=July 14, 2011 |title=Ruling Ends Theater's Bid for Brooklyn Waterfront |newspaper=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/07/14/nyregion/st-anns-warehouse-loses-bid-for-waterfront-site.html |access-date=November 2, 2012}} == Personal life == Vitaliano has [[glaucoma]] and is legally blind.[https://nypost.com/2015/07/06/legally-blind-judge-still-running-courtroom/ ''Legally blind judge still running courtroom''] by Selim Algar, in ''[[New York Post]]'' on July 6, 2015 ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1392331}} {{s-start}} {{s-par|us-ny-hs}} {{s-bef|before=[[Victor L. [[New York University School of Law|New York University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | party = }} '''Eric Ross Komitee''' (born 1970) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York]]. ==Education== Komitee earned his [[Bachelor of Arts]], with high honors, from [[Emory University]] in 1992, where he was inducted into [[Phi Beta Kappa]], and his [[Juris Doctor]], ''[[cum laude]]'', from the [[New York University School of Law]] in 1995, where he served as the senior notes and comments editor of the ''[[New York University Law Review]]''.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-fourteenth-wave-judicial-nominees-thirteenth-wave-united-states-attorney-nominees-eighth-wave-united-states-marshal-nominees/ "President Donald J. Trump Announces Fourteenth Wave of Judicial Nominees, Thirteenth Wave of United States Attorney Nominees, and Eighth Wave of United States Marshal Nominees" White House, May 10, 2018] {{PD-notice}} ==Legal career== After graduating from law school, he served as a [[law clerk]] to Judge [[James Larry Edmondson]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit]] from 1995 to 1996. He has practiced from 1996 to 2000 as an [[Associate lawyer|associate]] in the Government Enforcement and White Collar Crime group of [[Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom]] and as an associate in the corporate practice group of [[Cravath Swaine & Moore]]. He previously served for eight years as an [[Assistant United States Attorney]] for the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York|Eastern District of New York]] from 2000 to 2008, rising to serve as Chief of the Business and Securities Fraud Section from 2006 to 2008. From 2008 to 2019, he served as General Counsel of [[Viking Global Investors]] in New York City. == Federal judicial service == In August 2017, Komitee was one of several candidates pitched to New York senators [[Chuck Schumer]] and [[Kirsten Gillibrand]] by the White House as judicial candidates for vacancies on the federal courts in New York.{{Cite web |url=https://www.buzzfeed.com/zoetillman/the-white-house-has-pitched-a-nominee-for-manhattans |title=The White House Has Pitched A Nominee For Manhattan's Powerful US Attorney Opening |last=Tillman |first=Zoe |date=August 7, 2017 |publisher=[[BuzzFeed]] |access-date=May 10, 2018}} On May 10, 2018, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to nominate Komitee to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] for the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York]]. On May 15, 2018, his nomination was sent to the [[United States Senate|Senate]]. He was nominated to the seat that was vacated by Judge [[Eric N. Vitaliano]], who assumed [[senior status]] on February 28, 2017. On August 1, 2018, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/08/01/2018/nominations United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Nominations for August 1, 2018] On September 13, 2018, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 21–0 vote.[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/09-13-18%20Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting.pdf Results of Executive Business Meeting – September 13, 2018 Senate Judiciary Committee] On January 3, 2019, his nomination was returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]].{{cite news |title=Trump Drops Obama Picks, N.Y., Calif. Names From Judges List |url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/trump-drops-obama-picks-n-y-calif-names-from-judges-list-1 |access-date=15 February 2019 |publisher=Bloomberg Law |date=January 23, 2019}} On April 8, 2019, President Trump announced the renomination of Komitee to the district court.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-judicial-nominations/ "President Donald J. Trump Announces Judicial Nominations", White House, April 8, 2019] On May 21, 2019, his nomination was sent to the Senate. On June 20, 2019, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 21–1 vote.[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%20June%2020%202019.pdf Results of Executive Business Meeting – June 20, 2019, Senate Judiciary Committee] On December 2, 2019, the Senate invoked [[cloture]] on his nomination by an 81–5 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=1&vote=00368|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Eric Ross Komitee to be U.S. District Judge for the Eastern District of New York)|date=December 2, 2019|website=[[United States Senate]]|access-date=December 3, 2019|language=en}} On December 3, 2019, his nomination was confirmed by an 86–4 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=1&vote=00369|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Eric Ross Komitee, of New York, to be U.S. District Judge for the Eastern District of New York )|date=December 3, 2019|website=[[United States Senate]]|access-date=December 3, 2019|language=en}} He received his judicial commission on December 5, 2019.{{FJC Bio|nid=7460631|inline=yes}} == See also == * [[List of Jewish American jurists]] ==References== {{Reflist|30em}} == External links == *{{FJC Bio|nid=7460631}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Eric N. '''Eric Claude Schulte''' (born 1972)<ref name="Questionnaire">{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/schulte_sjq.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=March 6, 2024}}</ref> is an American lawyer who is serving as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of South Dakota]].

== Education ==

Schulte earned a [[Bachelor of Arts]] from the [[University of South Dakota]] in 1994 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of South Dakota School of Law]] in 1999.<ref name="WHBio">{{Cite press release |title=President Biden Names Forty-Fifth Round of Judicial Nominees and One New Nominee to Serve as U.S. Marshal |date=February 7, 2024 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2024/02/07/president-biden-names-forty-fifth-round-of-judicial-nominees-and-one-new-nominee-to-serve-as-u-s-marshal/ |access-date=February 7, 2024}} {{PD-notice}}</ref>

== Career ==

From 1999 to 2000, Schulte served as a [[law clerk]] to the South Dakota Second Judicial Circuit in [[Sioux Falls]]. From 2000 to 2005, he served as an [[Associate lawyer|associate]] with Davenport, Evans, Hurwitz & Smith, L.L.P. and served as a [[Law firm partner|partner]] with the same firm from 2006 to 2024.<ref name="WHBio" />

=== Federal judicial service ===

In December 2023, Schulte was seen as a top contender for nomination to the federal bench.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Whitney |first=Stu |date=December 23, 2023 |title=Sioux Falls lawyer favored as federal judge nominee |url=https://www.dakotanewsnow.com/2023/12/23/sioux-falls-lawyer-favored-federal-judge-nominee/ |access-date=February 7, 2024 |website=www.dakotanewsnow.com |language=en}}</ref> He was recommended to the White House by Senators [[John Thune]] and [[Mike Rounds]].<ref name="RCJ">{{Cite web |last=Whitney |first=Stu |date=February 6, 2024 |title=Camela Theeler tabbed as candidate for South Dakota federal judge |url=https://rapidcityjournal.com/news/local/camela-theeler-tabbed-as-candidate-for-south-dakota-federal-judge/article_fc5e6d62-c448-11ee-82bd-6be6c1a25365.html |access-date=February 7, 2024 |website=Rapid City Journal |language=en}}</ref> On February 7, 2024, President [[Joe Biden]] announced his intent to nominate Schulte to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of South Dakota]].<ref name="WHBio" /> On February 8, 2024, his nomination was sent to the Senate. President Biden nominated Schulte to the seat being vacated by Judge [[Karen Schreier]], who announced her intent to assume [[senior status]] upon confirmation of a successor.<ref>{{Cite press release |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |date=February 8, 2024|publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2024/02/08/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-137/}}</ref> On March 6, 2024, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Nominations |date=March 6, 2024 |publisher=[[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]] |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/committee-activity/hearings/03/06/2024/nominations}}</ref> On April 11, 2024, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 12–9 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/2024-04-11_-_ebm_-_results.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – April 11, 2024|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=April 11, 2024}}</ref> The Republicans on the committee opposed his nomination because of Schulte's prior writings on the issue of “[[Voting Rights Act of 1965#Preclearance requirement|preclearance]]”.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Whitney|first=Stu|title=South Dakota judicial nominees pass committee, head to full US Senate vote|url=https://www.dakotanewsnow.com/2024/04/11/south-dakota-judicial-nominees-pass-committee-head-full-us-senate-vote/?outputType=amp|website=Dakota News Now|access-date=April 11, 2024}}</ref> On May 15, 2024, the [[United States Senate]] confirmed his nomination by a 61–33 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1182/vote_118_2_00167.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Eric C. Schulte, of South Dakota, to be United States District Judge for the District of South Dakota)|website=United States Senate|date=May 15, 2024|access-date=May 15, 2024}}</ref> He received his judicial commission on June 3, 2024.<ref>{{FJC Bio|nid=13761661|inline=yes}}</ref>

{{Short description|American judge (born 1968)}} {{Use American English|date=July 2026}} {{Use mdy dates|date=July 2023}} {{Infobox officeholder | name = Esther Salas | image = Esther Salas (cropped).jpg | office = Judge of the [[United States District Court for the District of New Jersey]] | appointer = [[Barack Obama]] | term_start = June 14, 2011 | term_end = | predecessor = [[Katharine Sweeney Hayden]] | successor = | birth_date = {{birth year and age|1968|}} | birth_place = {{nowrap|[[Monterey Park, California]], U.S.}} | death_date = | death_place = | party = | spouse = {{marriage |Mark Anderl|1993}} | children = 1 {{efn|group=upper-alpha|Deceased}} | education = [[Rutgers University–New Brunswick|Rutgers University, New Brunswick]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|BA]])
[[Rutgers University–Newark|Rutgers University, Newark]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Esther Salas''' (born 1968) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of New Jersey]] sitting in [[Newark, New Jersey]]. She previously served as a [[United States magistrate judge]] of the same court from 2006 until her confirmation as a district judge in 2011. Salas is the first [[Hispanic]] woman to serve as a United States magistrate judge and as a United States District Judge in the District of New Jersey.{{Cite web|title=Local roots|url=https://archive.hudsonreporter.com/2011/07/24/local-roots/|date=July 24, 2011|access-date=July 20, 2020|website=Hudson Reporter|language=en-US|archive-date=October 1, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201001172711/https://archive.hudsonreporter.com/2011/07/24/local-roots/|url-status=dead}} == Early life== Salas is from [[Monterey Park, California]], and is the daughter of a [[Cuban immigration to the United States|Cuban mother]] and a [[Mexican immigration to the United States| Mexican father]].[http://law.newark.rutgers.edu/home/hon-esther-salas-94-first-latina-new-jersey-district-court "Spotlight on: Hon. Esther Salas ’94 – First Latina on New Jersey District Court"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160408201839/http://law.newark.rutgers.edu/home/hon-esther-salas-94-first-latina-new-jersey-district-court |date=April 8, 2016 }}. [[Rutgers School of Law–Newark|Rutgers School of Law]]. accessed July 28, 2011. Her father is [[Jewish]] and her mother is [[Roman Catholic]].{{Cite magazine|author=Chris Sagona|url=https://njmonthly.com/articles/politics-public-affairs/immigration-stories-esther-salas/|title=Immigration Stories: Esther Salas, From Union City to the Federal Bench|date=February 6, 2018|magazine=New Jersey Monthly}} At the age of five, she, her mother, Aurelia Salas, along with her siblings, moved to [[Union City, New Jersey]]. Though she lost contact with her father when she moved from the West Coast, she would later reconnect with him during the course of the background check she underwent upon being appointed a federal judge. In 1978, her mother's home burned down.{{Cite web|url=https://www.vice.com/en/article/suspect-in-killing-of-judges-son-was-a-racist-who-left-a-long-sexist-paper-trail/|title=Suspect in Killing of Judge’s Son Was a Racist Who Left a Long, Sexist Paper Trail|first=David|last=Gilbert|website=Vice.com|date=July 21, 2020|access-date=November 6, 2026}} Growing up [[indigent]], Salas recalls having to translate for her divorced mother at the welfare office, and later helping friends with various problems facing their lives, an activity that led to her pursuit of a career focusing on human services. Salas attended [[Emerson High School (Union City, New Jersey)|Emerson High School]] in Union City, where her extracurricular activities included cheerleading. After graduating from high school in 1987, she attended [[Rutgers University–New Brunswick]], where she lived on campus and was active in clubs and activities.{{cite web | url=https://www.rutgers.edu/news/first-scholarship-honor-judges-slain-son-awarded | title=First Scholarship in Honor of Judge's Slain Son Awarded }} Salas graduated from Rutgers in 1991 and in 1994 from [[Rutgers School of Law–Newark|Rutgers University School of Law in Newark]] with a Juris Doctor.{{cite web |url=http://blogs.app.com/capitolquickies/2010/12/02/cecchi-salas-nominated-as-federal-judges-in-new-jersey/ |title=Cecchi, Salas nominated as federal judges in New Jersey |last1=Symons |first1=Michael |date=December 2, 2010 |newspaper=[[Asbury Park Press]]|access-date=December 2, 2010}} She credits her success during her education and during her later professional life to the Minority Student Program.{{FJC Bio|nid=1393721|inline=yes}} == Career == Following law school graduation, Salas served as a [[law clerk]] to Eugene J. Codey Jr., of the [[Superior Court of New Jersey]]. From 1995 to 1997, Salas worked for Garces & Grabler, P.C., where she practiced criminal matters in superior and municipal courts. Between 1997 and 2006, she served as an [[Public defender#Federal Public Defender systems|Assistant Federal Public Defender]] for the District of New Jersey, representing indigent defendants in federal matters. Salas served as president of the Hispanic Bar Association of New Jersey from 2001 to 2002, and as president of the Hispanic Bar Foundation of New Jersey. She has also been a member of the Governor's Hispanic Advisory Committee for Policy Development, the Supreme Court Committee on Minority Concerns, and the Supreme Court Committee on Women in the Courts. === Federal judicial service === In 2006, Salas was selected from a group of 99 applicants as [[United States magistrate judge]] for the [[United States District Court for the District of New Jersey|District of New Jersey]], becoming the first Latina in that position, in which she served for five years. On August 31, 2010, Senators [[Frank Lautenberg]] and [[Robert Menendez]] announced they would recommend to President [[Barack Obama]] that Salas be nominated as a federal district judge on the same court.Ryan, Joe. [http://www.nj.com/news/index.ssf/2010/08/senators_support_two_magistrat.html "Menendez, Lautenberg support magistrates from Newark to become federal judges"]. [[NJ.com]]. August 31, 2010 Obama nominated her on December 1, 2010, to a seat vacated by [[Katharine Sweeney Hayden]] who assumed [[senior status]] on May 30, 2010. The [[American Bar Association]]'s [[Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary]], which rates the qualifications of federal judicial nominees, unanimously rated Salas "well qualified" for the judgeship (the committee's highest rating).[https://web.archive.org/web/20170728191905/https://www.americanbar.org/content/dam/aba/uncategorized/2011/ratings112.authcheckdam.pdf Ratings of Article III Judicial Nominees: 112th Congress], [[American Bar Association]] [[Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary]]. The nomination expired without Senate action at the end of the [[111th Congress]].[https://www.congress.gov/nomination/111th-congress/2370 PN2370 — Esther Salas — The Judiciary], 111th Congress (2009–2010), Congress.gov. Obama renominated Salas on January 5, 2011, at the beginning of the [[112th Congress]], and the Senate confirmed her by [[voice vote]] on June 14, 2011 and she received her commission the same day,[https://www.congress.gov/nomination/112th-congress/35 PN35 — Esther Salas — The Judiciary], 112th Congress (2011–2012), Congress.gov. making her the first Latina on the District Court of New Jersey.[https://law.newark.rutgers.edu/us-district-court-judge-esther-salas-%E2%80%9994-honoree-minority-student-program-banquet-tribute-alumni U.S. District Court Judge Esther Salas '94 Is Honoree at Minority Student Program Banquet & Tribute to Alumni Judges]. [[Rutgers University]]. March 13, 2012[http://law.newark.rutgers.edu/home/hon-esther-salas-94-first-latina-new-jersey-district-court Hon. Esther Salas '94 – First Latina on New Jersey District Court] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160408201839/http://law.newark.rutgers.edu/home/hon-esther-salas-94-first-latina-new-jersey-district-court |date=April 8, 2016 }}. Rutgers University. Retrieved July 10, 2015. === Notable cases === The U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey has a busy docket; according to a 2018 profile, Salas "presides over as many as 485 civil matters and 50 criminal cases" at any given time. *In 2013, Salas presided over a criminal case against the former [[Chief Information Technology Officer|chief information technology officer]] for the office of [[Dawn Zimmer]], the mayor of [[Hoboken, New Jersey]]. The administrator pleaded guilty to hacking into Zimmer's email account to disclose her emails, and the emails of others, to other persons within [[Hoboken City Hall]].Hack, Charles (March 21, 2013). [https://www.nj.com/jjournal-news/2013/03/hoboken_mayors_former_technolo.html Hoboken mayor's former technology administrator tells judge he hacked her e-mails, shared them]. ''[[The Jersey Journal]]''. Salas sentenced the man to five years' probation.Alexander W. Silady, [https://www.nj.com/hudson/2013/08/former_hoboken_it_manager_sentenced_to_probation_for_stealing_emails.html Former Hoboken IT manager sentenced to probation for stealing emails], ''The Jersey Journal'' (August 2, 2013). *Salas was the judge responsible for the trial of ''[[Real Housewives of New Jersey]]'' star [[Teresa Giudice]] and her husband, Giuseppe "Joe" Giudice. Both were sentenced for [[bank fraud]] on October 2, 2014.Maag, Christopher (October 5, 2014). [https://web.archive.org/web/20141228053339/http://www.northjersey.com/news/real-housewives-judge-esther-salas-shaped-by-her-personal-reality-1.1102637?page=all 'Real Housewives' Judge Esther Salas shaped by her personal reality]. ''[[The Record (North Jersey)|The Record]]''. *In 2018, Salas issued an order temporarily blocking [[U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement]] (ICE) from deporting certain [[Christianity in Indonesia|Indonesian Christians]] in New Jersey who were present without authorization in the U.S. and were subject to [[Removal proceedings|orders of removal]], but were seeking legal status. The order dealt with about 50 Christians who had fled persecution in Indonesia and had lived in New Jersey for many years before being targeted by immigration enforcement actions.David Porter, [https://apnews.com/a0d70566ab48401dbad22d096286b8cb Judge temporarily halts deportation of Indonesian Christians], Associated Press (February 3, 2018). *In 2018, Salas sentenced Farad Roland, a leader of the Newark "South Side Cartel" set of the [[Bloods]] street gang, to 45 years in prison for his role in a series of crimes from 2003 to 2010, including five fatal shootings, a carjacking and drug dealing.Alex Napoliello, [https://www.nj.com/essex/2018/01/bloods_leader_facing_death_penalty_accepts_plea_de.html Gang leader, facing death penalty, accepts deal of 45 years in prison], NJ Advance Media for NJ.com (January 26, 2018). The sentence accepted a plea agreement reached between the defendant and federal prosecutors. Salas had earlier ruled that Roland's [[intellectual disability]] made him ineligible to be [[federal death penalty|sentenced to death]] under the [[Eighth Amendment to the United States Constitution]], which prohibits cruel and unusual punishment, and under the [[Federal Death Penalty Act]].[https://apnews.com/014835d3654a413dab3852418360fc44 Judge bars death penalty in Newark gang slayings], Associated Press (December 18, 2017). *Salas is the judge presiding over the class-action lawsuit against [[Deutsche Bank]] (''Karimi v. Deutsche Bank Aktiengesellschaft et al.''), which alleges that Deutsche Bank had poor financial reporting practices and made misleading statements to securities investors, resulting from Deutsche Bank's desire to obscure its anti-[[money laundering]] deficiencies and its poor monitoring of high-risk customers such as [[Jeffrey Epstein]], [[Danske Bank money laundering scandal|Danske Bank in Estonia]], and [[FBME Bank]].{{cite press release|publisher=Faruqi & Faruqi LLP|date=July 16, 2020|title=Deutsche Bank Deadline Alert: Faruqi & Faruqi, LLP Encourages Investors Who Suffered Losses Exceeding $250,000 In Deutsche Bank Aktiengesellschaft To Contact The Firm|url=https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2020/07/16/2063666/0/en/DEUTSCHE-BANK-DEADLINE-ALERT-Faruqi-Faruqi-LLP-Encourages-Investors-Who-Suffered-Losses-Exceeding-250-000-In-Deutsche-Bank-Aktiengesellschaft-To-Contact-The-Firm.html}}{{Cite web|title=Securities Class Action Clearinghouse: Case Page|url=http://securities.stanford.edu/filings-case.html?id=107463|website=securities.stanford.edu}} == Personal life == Salas is married to attorney Mark A. Anderl (born 1957) since 1993, with whom she had a son, Daniel Anderl (July 13, 2000 – July 19, 2020). She was a [[criminal defense attorney]] and former [[Essex County, New Jersey|Essex County]] assistant prosecutor. Salas and her family are Catholic.{{cite web | url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4JPlcbW5aJs | title=Complete statement from Judge Esther Salas after son killed, husband shot | website=[[YouTube]] | date=August 3, 2020 }} === Home attack === On July 19, 2020, an assailant targeted Salas's family at their home. Daniel, aged 20, opened the door when the assailant knocked. The assailant then opened fire, killing Daniel at the scene. His father Mark was also shot multiple times and left in a critical but stable condition.{{cite web|url=https://newjerseyglobe.com/judiciary/son-of-federal-judge-slain-husband-in-critical-condition/|title=Son of federal judge slain, husband in critical condition|first1=David|last1=Wildstein|newspaper=New Jersey Globe|date=July 19, 2020|access-date=July 20, 2020|language=en-US}}{{cite web|url=https://apnews.com/fecbf88ebc2b33e35c291a43ad52939a|title=Son of US District Judge Esther Salas killed, husband shot|work=Associated Press|date=July 19, 2020|access-date=July 20, 2020|language=en-US}}{{cite web |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/07/19/nyregion/shooting-nj-judge-esther-salas.html |title=Husband and Son of a Federal Judge, Esther Salas, Are Shot in New Jersey |last1=Vigdor |first1=Neil |last2=Ortiz |first2=Aimee |last3=Armstrong |first3=Kevin |date=July 19, 2020 |newspaper=The New York Times |access-date=July 20, 2020}} Salas was in the basement at the time of the attack and was not injured. The [[Federal Bureau of Investigation]] led the investigation into the attack on Salas' family home in conjunction with the [[U.S. Marshals Service]] and local law enforcement.{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/07/20/nyregion/esther-salas.html|title='Anti-Feminist' Is Identified as Suspect in Killing of Son of Federal Judge in N.J.|newspaper=The New York Times|first1=Nicole|last1=Hong|first2=William K.|last2=Rashbaum|first3=Mihir|last3=Zaveri|date=July 20, 2020|access-date=July 20, 2020}} The following day, the FBI identified 72-year-old attorney [[Roy Den Hollander]] as the primary suspect; Den Hollander was found dead from a [[self-inflicted gunshot wound]] in the town of [[Rockland, New York|Rockland]] in [[upstate New York]].{{cite news|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/politics/archive/2020/07/judge-esther-salas-shooting-suspect-left-pro-trump-paper-trail/614425/|title=The New Jersey Shooting Suspect Left a Pro-Trump Paper family|publisher=CNN|date=July 21, 2020|access-date=July 21, 2020}} Den Hollander was a self-described [[Antifeminism|antifeminist]] previously known for filing unsuccessful lawsuits against "ladies night" promotions at bars and nightclubs, as well as suing [[Columbia University]] for offering [[women's studies]] classes.{{cite web|first1=Tim|last1=Elfrink|first2=Devlin|last2=Barrett|title='Anti-feminist' lawyer identified as suspect in deadly shooting at federal judge's home|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/nation/2020/07/19/esther-salas-fedex-shooting/|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=July 19, 2020|access-date=July 20, 2020}} Den Hollander had appeared before Salas in connection with a lawsuit he brought challenging the military's male-only [[Conscription in the United States|draft]].{{cite news|url=https://www.cnn.com/2020/07/20/us/suspect-shooting-at-judge-salas-home/index.html|title=Suspect in fatal shooting at home of Judge Esther Salas described himself as an 'anti-feminist' lawyer, once argued a case before the judge|publisher=CNN|last1=Levenson|first1=Eric|last2=Murphy|first2=Paul P.|last3=Polantz|first3=Katelyn|date=July 20, 2020|access-date=July 20, 2020}} In various writings, Den Hollander ranted about his hatred of women, used racist and sexist terms to disparage Salas, and spoke of his personal grievances. Den Hollander described himself as a "[[Men's rights movement|men's rights]]" activist but was ejected from the [[National Coalition for Men]] and is also a suspect in the shooting death of a men's rights lawyer, [[Marc Angelucci]], at his home in [[Crestline, California]], earlier the same month.{{cite news|last=Richard|first=Winton|url=https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2020-07-21/fbi-deliveryman-suspect-new-jersey-judge-family-attack-california-lawyer-killing|title=FBI investigates whether suspect in judge family attack is behind California lawyer's slaying|newspaper=The Los Angeles Times|date=July 21, 2020|access-date=July 21, 2020}} Salas was interviewed for a ''[[60 Minutes]]'' report in February 2021 about this attack, in which ''60 Minutes'' also revealed the discovery of the gunman's planning for an attack on Justice [[Sonia Sotomayor]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/esther-salas-sonia-sotomayor-60-minutes-2021-02-19/|title = Federal judge whose son was killed in attack says gunman targeted Sonia Sotomayor| website=[[CBS News]] Eumi K. Lee:
{{Short description|American judge (born 1972)}} {{Infobox officeholder | honorific_prefix = | name = Eumi K. Lee | honorific_suffix = | image = Eumi K. Lee, U.S. District Court Judge.jpg | alt = | caption = | office = Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of California]] | term_start = May 7, 2024 | term_end = | appointer = [[List of federal judges appointed by Joe Biden|Joe Biden]] | predecessor = [[William Orrick III]] | successor = | office1 = Judge of the [[Alameda County Superior Court]] | term_start1 = December 7, 2018 | term_end1 = May 7, 2024 | appointer1 = [[Jerry Brown]] | predecessor1 = Alison M. Tucher | successor1 = Thomas Eagle Weathers | pronunciation = | birth_name = Eumi Kim Lee | birth_date = {{birth year and age|1972}} | birth_place = [[Madison, Wisconsin]], U.S. | death_date = | death_place = | death_cause = | party = [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] | spouse = | education = [[Pomona College]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|BA]])
[[Georgetown University Law Center|Georgetown University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Eumi Kim Lee''' (born 1972){{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/lee_sjq.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=September 5, 2023}} is an American lawyer who has served as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of California]] since 2024. She previously served as a judge of the [[Alameda County Superior Court]] from 2018 to 2024. == Education == Lee received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] from [[Pomona College]] in 1994 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Georgetown University Law Center]], ''[[Latin honors#United States|cum laude]]'', in 1999.{{Cite press release |title=President Biden Names Thirty-Sixth Round of Judicial Nominees |date=July 27, 2023 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2023/07/27/president-biden-names-thirty-sixth-round-of-judicial-nominees/ |access-date=July 27, 2023}} {{PD-notice}} == Career == From 1999 to 2000, Lee served as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Jerome Turner]] of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Tennessee]]. From 2000 to 2001, she was an [[Associate lawyer|associate]] at [[Keker, Van Nest & Peters LLP]] in [[San Francisco]]. From 2001 to 2002, she served as a law clerk for Judge [[Warren J. Ferguson]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]]. From 2002 to 2005, she was again an associate at the same law firm. From 2005 to 2018, she was a [[clinical professor]] of law at the [[University of California College of the Law, San Francisco]] (formerly the University of California, Hastings College of the Law). From 2006 to 2012, she was [[of counsel]] and a [[consultant]] at Gonzalez and Leigh and from 2009 to 2012, she was an ethics trainer for [[San Diego Gas & Electric]], [[Southern California Gas Company]] and [[Southern California Edison]].{{Cite web |date=December 7, 2018 |title=Governor Brown Appoints 13 Superior Court Judges {{!}} Governor Edmund G. Brown Jr. |url=https://archive.gov.ca.gov/archive/gov39/2018/12/07/governor-brown-appoints-13-superior-court-judges/index.html|access-date=2023-07-27 |website=www.ca.gov}} On December 7, 2018, Lee was appointed by [[California Governor]] [[Jerry Brown]] to serve as a judge of the [[Alameda County Superior Court]], to fill the vacancy left by the elevation of Judge Alison M. Tucher to the [[California Courts of Appeal]]. She was the first [[Korean Americans|Korean-American]] judge ever appointed to the Alameda County Superior Court.{{Cite web |date=December 11, 2018 |title=Welcome to the Alameda County Bench Eumi Lee! » Alameda County Bar Association |url=https://www.acbanet.org/2018/12/11/welcome-to-the-alameda-county-bench-eumi-lee/ |access-date=July 27, 2023 |website=Alameda County Bar Association |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |last=Tae-hee |first=Lee |date=December 11, 2018 |title=Korean-American judges gaining presence in US |url=https://www.koreaherald.com/view.php?ud=20181211000462 |access-date=July 27, 2023 |website=The Korea Herald |language=en}} === Federal judicial service === On July 27, 2023, President [[Joe Biden]] nominated Lee to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of California]]. President Biden nominated Lee to the seat vacated by Judge [[William Orrick III]], who assumed [[senior status]] on May 17, 2023.{{Cite press release|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate|date=July 27, 2023 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2023/07/27/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-117/}} On September 6, 2023, a hearing on her nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web|title=Nominations|date=September 5, 2023|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/committee-activity/hearings/09/06/2023/nominations}} During her confirmation hearing, Lee was questioned on a journal article she wrote regarding the treatment of [[transgender]], [[illegal immigrant]], and [[women prisoners]] in California. Lee responded that the article was a summary of remarks made during conference panel discussion and not her own opinions.{{Cite web |date=November 2, 2023 |title=Judiciary Panel Unexpectedly Delays Votes on Biden Judge |url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/judiciary-panel-unexpectedly-delays-votes-on-biden-judge-picks?source=newsletter&item=read-text®ion=digest |language=en-US}} On November 9, 2023, her nomination was reported out of committee by an 11–10 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/2023-11-09_-_ebm_-_results.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – November 9, 2023|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=November 9, 2023}}{{Cite news|last=Headley|first=Tiana|title=Judiciary Democrats at Full Strength Advance Biden Court Picks|url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/judiciary-democrats-at-full-strength-advance-biden-court-picks|website=Bloomberg Law|access-date=November 9, 2023}} On November 13, 2023, her nomination was returned to the Judiciary Committee because of issues regarding [[proxy voting]] in committee.{{Cite web|url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/ip-law/senate-returns-two-district-court-nominations-to-judiciary-panel|title=Senate Returns Two District Court Nominations to Judiciary Panel|publisher=Bloomberg Law|access-date=November 14, 2023}} On November 30, 2023, during the first committee vote, her nomination failed to be reported out of committee by an 10–0–9 vote with all committee Republicans in attendance not voting, along with Democratic Senator [[Chris Coons]]. In a second vote, her nomination was reported out of committee by an 11–10 [[party-line vote]].{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/2023-11-30_-_ebm_-_results.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – November 30, 2023|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=November 30, 2023}} On January 3, 2024, her nomination was returned to the president under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]]{{Cite web |date=January 8, 2023 |title=PN906 — Eumi K. Lee — The Judiciary |url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/118th-congress/906 |website=congress.gov}} and she was renominated on January 8, 2024.{{Cite press release |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |date=January 8, 2024 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2024/01/08/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-133/}} On January 18, 2024, her nomination was reported out of committee by an 11–10 [[party-line vote]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/2024-01-18_-_ebm_-_results1.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – January 18, 2024|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=January 19, 2024}}{{Cite press release |title=Senate Judiciary Committee Advances Twenty Judicial Nominations, One Executive Nomination to the Full Senate |date=January 18, 2024 |publisher=United States Senate Judiciary Committee |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/press/releases/senate-judiciary-committee-advances-twenty-judicial-nominations-one-executive-nomination-to-the-full-senate |access-date=January 18, 2024}} On March 20, 2024, the Senate invoked cloture on her nomination by a 50–49 vote, with Senator [[Joe Manchin]] voting against the motion.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1182/vote_118_2_00097.htm|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Eumi K. Lee to be U.S. District Judge for the Northern District of California)|website=United States Senate|date=March 20, 2024|access-date=March 20, 2024}} Later that day, her nomination was confirmed by a 50–49 vote, with Senator Manchin voting against confirmation.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1182/vote_118_2_00098.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Eumi K. Lee, of California, to be U.S. District Judge for the Northern District of California)|website=United States Senate|date=March 20, 2024|access-date=March 20, 2024}} She received her judicial commission on May 7, 2024.{{FJC Bio|nid=13761571|inline=yes}} == Community involvement == Prior to her appointment to the bench, she was a member of the [[Bar Association of San Francisco]].{{Cite web |date=December 11, 2018 |title=Members Appointed as Superior Court Judges |url=https://www.sfbar.org/blog/members-appointed-as-superior-court-judges/ |access-date=July 27, 2023 |website=The Bar Association of San Francisco |language=en-US}} Lee is a [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrat]]. == See also == * [[List of Asian American jurists]] * [[List of first women lawyers and judges in
