[[UC Berkeley School of Law|University of California, Berkeley]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | occupation = | profession = | known_for = | salary = | net_worth = | cabinet = | committees = | portfolio = | awards = | signature = | signature_alt = | website = | footnotes = }} '''Indira Talwani''' (born October 6, 1960){{cite book |last1=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary |title=Confirmation Hearings on Federal Appointments: Hearings Before the Committee on the Judiciary, United States Senate, One Hundred Thirteenth Congress, First Session, Part 7 |date=2013 |publisher=Government Publishing Office |page=230 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Mwvrn3CpXvwC |access-date=April 29, 2025}} is an American lawyer and jurist serving as a [[United States federal judge|U.S. district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts]]. She was appointed in 2014 by President [[Barack Obama]]. ==Biography== Talwani graduated from [[Phillips Exeter Academy]] in 1978 and received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree, ''[[cum laude]]'', in 1982 from [[Radcliffe College]]. She received a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1988 from [[UC Berkeley School of Law]], graduating [[Order of the Coif]].{{cite news | url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/world/us/who-is-indira-talwani-the-indian-american-judge-who-blocked-trumps-deportation-order/articleshow/120300195.cms | title=Who is Indira Talwani, the Indian-American judge who blocked Trump's deportation order? | work=The Times of India | date=April 16, 2025 }}{{cite web|url=http://www.segalroitman.com/pages/talwani.shtml|title=Biography at Segal Roitman LLP|publisher=|access-date=September 25, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130927190659/http://www.segalroitman.com/pages/talwani.shtml|archive-date=September 27, 2013|url-status=dead}} Talwani began her legal career as a [[law clerk]] to Judge [[Stanley Alexander Weigel]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of California]], from 1988 to 1989. She served as an associate at the [[San Francisco, California]], law firm of Altshuler Berzon LLP, from 1989 to 1995 and as a partner at that law firm, from 1996 to 1999. From 1999 to 2014, she served as a partner at the [[Boston]], Massachusetts, law firm of Segal Roitman LLP, where she focused her practice on [[civil litigation]] at the state and federal trial court and appellate levels.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2013/09/24/president-obama-nominates-two-serve-united-states-district-courts|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Obama Nominates Two to Serve on the United States District Courts|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=September 24, 2013}}{{FJC Bio|nid=1394486|inline=yes}} ===Federal judicial service=== {{See also|2025 SNAP shutdown|Laken Riley Act#Legacy}} On September 24, 2013, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Talwani to serve as a United States district judge of the United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts, to the seat vacated by Judge [[Mark L. Wolf]], who assumed [[senior status]] on January 1, 2013.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2013/09/24/presidential-nominations-sent-senate|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=September 24, 2013}} On February 6, 2014, her nomination was reported out of committee.{{cite web|title=Executive Business Meeting|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/hearings/hearing.cfm?id=138603a26950ad873303535a6318f123&2|work=United States Senate|publisher=Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=February 6, 2014|archive-date=February 14, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140214063426/http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/hearings/hearing.cfm?id=138603a26950ad873303535a6318f123&2|url-status=dead}} Cloture was filed on her nomination on May 6, 2014.{{cite web|url=https://democrats.senate.gov/2014/05/06/cloture-filed-on-4-judicial-nominations-talwani-peterson-rosenstengal-rosenbaum/|title=Cloture filed on 4 judicial nominations (Talwani, Peterson, Rosenstengal, Rosenbaum)|publisher=|access-date=May 31, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161121144432/https://democrats.senate.gov/2014/05/06/cloture-filed-on-4-judicial-nominations-talwani-peterson-rosenstengal-rosenbaum/|archive-date=November 21, 2016|url-status=dead}} On May 8, 2014, the [[United States Senate|Senate]] invoked [[cloture]] on her nomination by a 55–41 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=113&session=2&vote=00134|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture on the Nomination of Indira Talwani, of Massachusetts, to be U.S. District Judge)|publisher=United States Senate|access-date=May 8, 2014}} Later that day, her nomination was confirmed by a 94–0 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=113&session=2&vote=00137| title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Indira Talwani, of Massachusetts, to be U.S. District Judge)|publisher=United States Senate|access-date=May 8, 2014}} She received her judicial commission on May 12, 2014. Talwani presided over the sentencing of many parents involved in the [[2019 college admissions bribery scandal|Operation Varsity Blues]] college admissions scandal, including actress [[Felicity Huffman]]. Talwani sentenced Huffman to 14 days in prison, 1 year supervised release, a $30,000 fine, and 250 hours of community service after Huffman pleaded guilty to [[conspiracy]] to commit [[mail fraud]], and [[honest services fraud|honest services mail fraud]] for her role in the scandal. Huffman served 11 out of her 14 days.{{Cite web|url=https://www.justice.gov/usao-ma/pr/first-parent-college-admissions-case-sentenced-prison|title=First Parent in College Admissions Case Sentenced to Prison|date=September 13, 2019}} On July 28, 2025, Talwani ordered the Trump administration to continue Medicaid funding for [[Planned Parenthood]], blocking enforcement of that provision of the "One Big Beautiful Bill" signed earlier that month.{{Cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/jul/28/planned-parenthood-medicaid-ruling-trump?CMP=oth_b-aplnews_d-1|title=Judge orders Trump administration to continue Medicaid funding to Planned Parenthood|website=The Guardian|date=2025-07-28|access-date=2025-12-16}} Talwani's ruling kept Planned Parenthood funded for six weeks, until the 1st Circuit permitted the Trump administration to end Planned Parenthood funding in September.{{Cite web|url=https://www.reuters.com/world/court-allows-trump-administration-end-planned-parenthoods-medicaid-funding-2025-09-11/|title=Court allows Trump administration to end Planned Parenthood's Medicaid funding|website=Reuters|date=2025-09-11|access-date=2025-12-16}} {{See also|Parole for Cubans, Haitians, Nicaraguans, and Venezuelans}} Talwani blocked Trump administration from revoking immigration parole by issuing a temporary restraining order that extends the “family reunification parole” status of immigrants who were set to see it expire on January 14, 2026 as part of the administration’s broad crackdown on immigration.{{Cite web|url=https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/world/judge-blocks-trump-administration-from-revoking-immigration-parole/ar-AA1TXVNM/|title=Judge blocks Trump administration from revoking immigration parole|website=Politico|date=2026-01-11|access-date=2026-01-11}} On June 25, 2026 Talwani blocked Trump's attempt to force individual States to release their voting rolls, using the post office to threaten to refuse delivery of votes by mail. In a 37 page ruling she stated that "The Constitution does not grant the President any specific powers over elections".{{cite web|url=https://www.democracydocket.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/2026-06-25-Order.pdf |format=PDF|title=Donald J. Trump v State of Missouri, et al.|website=Democracydocket.com|access-date=July 10, 2026}} On July 17, 2026 Talwani ruled that the [[Office of Management and Budget]] and the Trump administration can’t change grant terms after the fact, and can't use an obscure clause relating to agency priorities to make billions of dollars in funding cuts. She granted a summary judgment preventing the administration from relying on the clause to make cuts and denied a motion by the government to dismiss the case.{{cite web|url=https://www.reuters.com/world/trump-administration-cannot-cancel-grants-disfavored-causes-us-judge-rules-2026-07-17/ |title=US judge says Trump administration cannot revoke grants that conflict with its priorities |website=reuters.com|access-date=July 18, 2026}} On August 28, 2026 Talwani issued a Temporary Restraining Order to pause the Trump administration plan to control the delivery of mail-in ballots pursuant to [[Executive Order 14399]].{{cite news |last=Cheney |first=Kyle |title=Judge blocks Trump's mail-in voting plan, again |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2026/08/27/judge-blocks-trumps-mail-in-voting-plan-again-01053826 |work=Politico |date=August 27, 2026 |access-date=August 28, 2026}} On September 14, 2026, the Supreme Court declined to lift Talwani's stay, meaning the Trump administration's executive order will not take effect for the 2026 midterm elections.{{Cite web|url=https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/09/supreme-court-denies-trump-administrations-request-to-implement-parts-of-usps-rule-on-mail-in-vo/|title=Supreme Court denies Trump administration’s request to implement parts of rule on mail-in voting|website=SCOTUSblog|date=2026-09-14|access-date=2026-09-16}} ==See also== *[[List of Asian American jurists]] *[[List of first women lawyers and judges in Massachusetts]] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1394486}} *{{Ballotpedia|Indira_Talwani}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Mark L. [[University of Copenhagen Faculty of Law]] (C.Juris)
[[University of Alabama School of Law|University of Alabama]] (MCLaw, [[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | alma_mater = | occupation = | profession = | known_for = | salary = | net_worth = | cabinet = | committees = | portfolio = | awards = | signature = | signature_alt = | website = | footnotes = }} '''Inge Prytz Johnson''' (born December 19, 1945) is an inactive [[United States federal judge|Senior United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Alabama]]. ==Early life and education== Born in [[Svendborg]], [[Denmark]], Johnson received a Certificate of English Law from [[City of London College]] in 1968 and a Juris Certificate from the [[University of Copenhagen Faculty of Law]] in 1969. In 1970, Johnson moved to the [[United States]], and attended the [[University of Alabama School of Law]] and graduated with a M.C.Law degree. She received a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Alabama School of Law]] in 1973. ==Career== Following law school graduation, Johnson started her legal career as a private practice attorney licensed in the nation of [[Denmark]] from 1970 to 1971. During this time, Johnson also served as a part-time faculty member for the [[University of Copenhagen Faculty of Law]]. After receiving her license to practice law in the United States, Johnson started her legal career as a private practice attorney in [[Alabama]] from 1973 to 1979. In 1978, Johnson held a part-time Municipal judge for the City Court of [[Muscle Shoals, Alabama|Muscle Shoals]] from 1978 to 1979. In 1979, Johnson was elected by the people of Alabama to become a [[Circuit Court|Circuit court]] judge in the 31st Judicial Circuit Court of Alabama until her appointment to the federal bench in 1999. Johnson was the Chief Judge of the Court from 1980 to 1999. ===Federal judicial service=== On the recommendation of U.S. Senator [[Richard Shelby]], Johnson was nominated by President [[Bill Clinton]] on August 31, 1998, to a seat vacated by [[James Hughes Hancock]]. Johnson was confirmed by the [[United States Senate|Senate]] on October 8, 1998, and received commission on October 9, 1998. '''Irene Cornelia Berger''' (born September 27, 1954) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of West Virginia]].

== Early life and education ==

A native of [[Faraday, West Virginia|Faraday]] in [[McDowell County, West Virginia|McDowell County]], [[West Virginia]],<ref name=wvrecord_20090917>Lawrence Smith, [http://www.wvrecord.com/news/221144-manchin-already-seeking-replacement-for-berger Manchin already seeking replacement for Berger], ''[[West Virginia Record]]'' (September 17, 2009).</ref> Berger graduated from [[West Virginia University]] in 1976 with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in mathematics<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://eberly.wvu.edu/eberly_news/2008/4/30/wvu-eberly-college-of-arts-and-sciences-honors-outstanding-alumni |title=Eberly College of Arts & Sciences | Eberly News | WVU Eberly College of Arts and Sciences honors outstanding alumni |access-date=2009-10-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100612232711/http://eberly.wvu.edu/eberly_news/2008/4/30/wvu-eberly-college-of-arts-and-sciences-honors-outstanding-alumni |archive-date=2010-06-12 |url-status=dead }}</ref> and from [[West Virginia University College of Law]] with a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1979.<ref name=whgov_20090708>[https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the_press_office/President-Obama-Nominates-Irene-Berger-Roberto-Lange-to-Serve-on-the-District-Court-Bench/ President Obama Nominates Irene Berger, Roberto Lange to Serve on the District Court Bench], ''whitehouse.gov'' (July 8, 2009).</ref><ref name="fjc.gov">{{FJC Bio|nid=1392951|inline=yes}}</ref>

== Career ==

After graduating from law school, Berger worked as a staff attorney for the Legal Aid Society of Charleston, where her clients largely were low-income individuals facing domestic, consumer and tenant-landlord disputes.<ref name=whgov_20090708/> She held that position from June 1979 until January 1982. In February 1982, Berger became assistant prosecuting attorney for [[Kanawha County, West Virginia|Kanawha County]].<ref name=whgov_20090708/> She held that position for more than 12 years. In May 1994, Berger joined the United States Attorney's office for the Southern District of West Virginia as an [[assistant United States attorney]].<ref name=whgov_20090708/> In July 1994, West Virginia Gov. [[Gaston Caperton]] appointed Berger to be a [[Kanawha County, West Virginia|Kanawha County]] circuit judge.<ref name=wvrecord_20090917/><ref name="fjc.gov"/>

=== Federal judicial service ===

On July 8, 2009, Berger was nominated by President [[Barack Obama]] to serve as a United States District Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of West Virginia]], to replace [[David A. Faber]], who assumed [[senior status]].<ref name=wvrecord_20090917/> The [[United States Senate]] confirmed Berger on October 27, 2009, by a 97–0 vote.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=111&session=1&vote=00328 |title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Irene Cornelia Berger of West Virginia to be U.S. District Judge)|work=United States Senate|date=2009-10-27|access-date=2009-10-27}}</ref> She received her commission on November 9, 2009.<ref name="fjc.gov"/> She is the first African-American female federal judge in West Virginia's history.<ref name=wvrecord_20090917/>

Lemelle''' (born 1950){{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Cmlw3xWy5EQC&pg=PA858|page=858|title==Hearings before the Committee on the Judiciary, United States Senate, One Hundred Fifth Congress, Second Session, on Confirmations of Appointees to the Federal Judiciary, February 4; February 25; March 18; March 24; April 29, 1998|publisher=U.S. Government Printing Office|year=1998}} is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana]]. ==Early life and education== Born in [[Opelousas, Louisiana|Opelousas]], [[Louisiana]], Lemelle received a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree from [[Xavier University of Louisiana]] in 1971 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Loyola University New Orleans School of Law]] in 1974. He was a [[law clerk]] for Robert Collins of the [[Orleans Parish]] Criminal District Court from 1972 to 1974.{{cite web|url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/lemelle-ivan-l.-r.|title=Lemelle, Ivan L. R. - Federal Judicial Center|website=www.fjc.gov}} ==Career== Lemelle was an [[assistant district attorney]] of [[Orleans Parish]] from 1974 to 1977. He was in private practice in [[New Orleans]] from 1977 to 1981. He was an assistant city attorney of New Orleans from 1977 to 1978. He was an assistant state attorney general of Louisiana Department of Justice from 1980 to 1984. ===Federal judicial service=== Lemelle served as [[United States magistrate judge]] of the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana from 1984 to 1998. On February 12, 1997, Lemelle was nominated by President [[Bill Clinton]] to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana]] vacated by Judge [[Veronica D. Wicker]]. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on April 3, 1998, and received his commission on April 7, 1998. He assumed [[senior status]] on June 29, 2015. ===Notable cases=== * In 2009, Lemelle was assigned the [[Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act]] (RICO) case alleged against [[Renée Gill Pratt]] and [[Mose Jefferson]], brother of former [[U.S. representative]] [[William J. Jefferson]], who simultaneously stood indicted on sixteen counts in federal court in [[Virginia (U.S. state)|Virginia]]. On 2009 July 28, Lemelle delayed the start of the racketeering trial to 2010 January 25.[http://www.nola.com/news/t-p/neworleans/index.ssf?/base/news-11/124884542991340.xml&coll=1 "Trial delayed for Gill Pratt, Jefferson kin"] in ''Times-Picayune'', 2009 July 29, Saint Tammany Edition, p. B3. Besides Gill Pratt and Mose Jefferson, other defendants in the racketeering case were [[Betty Jefferson]] and her daughter [[Angela Jefferson Coleman]]. [[Brenda Jefferson Foster]], younger sister of Mose Jefferson and Betty Jefferson, had entered a guilty plea in the racketeering case and obtained a promise of leniency in exchange for agreeing to testify against her siblings. The ''bribery'' trial of Mose Jefferson alone was still set to begin on 2009 August 10. In two separate trials during August 2009, William J. Jefferson was convicted on 11 felony counts related to bribery; Mose Jefferson, on four.The August 2009 trials concerned bribery ''per se'', separate and apart from Mose Jefferson's indictment for racketeering, that trial being set by Lemelle to commence on January 25, 2010. * In 2009, Lemelle heard a real estate fraud case against Michael O'Keefe Jr. (born c. 1959), the son of former [[Louisiana State Senate]] President [[Michael O'Keefe (Louisiana politician)|Michael H. O'Keefe Sr.]] The younger O'Keefe was at the time the president of Citywide Mortgage Company of New Orleans. He pleaded guilty to making false statements during a transaction with the [[United States Department of Housing and Urban Development]]. The scam involved fraudulent appraisals, credit documents, and loan applications. O'Keefe was ordered to pay nearly $700,000 in restitution. He also served in prison for nearly two years.{{cite web|url=http://mortgagefraudblog.com/citywide_president_pleads_guilty/|title="Citywide President Pleads Guilty", April 21, 2009|publisher=mortgagefraudblog.com|access-date=June 21, 2013|archive-date=June 25, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130625071151/http://mortgagefraudblog.com/citywide_president_pleads_guilty/|url-status=dead}} * On September 11, 2009, Lemelle visited Kentwood High School and O. W. Dillon Memorial Elementary School (both in [[Kentwood, Louisiana]]), Roseland Elementary School (in [[Roseland, Louisiana]]), and Northwood Preparatory High School (in [[Amite, Louisiana]])—all in [[Tangipahoa Parish, Louisiana|Tangipahoa Parish]]. The three schools are subject to potential changes, depending on Lemelle's ruling on a 4-decades-old desegregation-related settlement.Sylvia Schon, "Deseg judge visits schools" in [[Daily Star (Hammond)|''Daily Star'' (Hammond)]], 2009 September 13, pp. 1A, 7A. ==Legacy== In November 2020, it was proposed by the New Orleans City Council Street Renaming Commission that Capdevielle Street (named after [[Paul Capdevielle]], a [[Confederate States of America|Confederate]] hero and former mayor) be renamed for Lemelle. He was the only living person proposed for such an honor. The decision process was ongoing as of February 2021.{{Cite web|last=Adelson|first=Jeff|title=New names for 38 New Orleans streets, parks; see all latest recommendations|url=https://www.nola.com/news/politics/article_7707bf0c-6c84-11eb-a819-9b2a7abec4eb.html|access-date=2021-02-23|website=New Orleans Advocate|date=11 February 2021 |language=en}} ==Personal life== Lemelle is [[Catholic Church|Catholic]], raised in Holy Ghost Catholic Church in Opelousas, the largest [[Black Catholicism|Black Catholic]] church in the country.The Honorable Ivan Lemelle (The HistoryMakers A2010.054), interviewed by Denise Gines, June 8, 2010, The HistoryMakers Digital Archive. [[Duke University School of Law|Duke Law School]] ([[Master of Laws|LLM]]) | party = }} '''John Campbell "Cam" Barker''' (born 1980) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Texas]]. == Education and career == Barker earned his [[Bachelor of Science]] from [[Texas A&M University]], ''[[summa cum laude]]'', in [[computer engineering]].{{Cite web |url=https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/news/releases/ag-paxton-applauds-senate-confirmation-texas-deputy-solicitor-general-cam-barker-us-district-court |title=AG Paxton Applauds Senate Confirmation of Texas Deputy Solicitor General Cam Barker to the U.S. District Court in Tyler |website=Texas Attorney General |language=en |access-date=2019-05-29}} As an undergraduate, he was inducted into [[Tau Beta Pi]],[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Barker%20SJQ.pdf “Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees,”] United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary hired by Microsoft as a programmer,[https://txed.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/courtdocuments/Investiture%20of%20J.%20Campbell%20Barker.pdf “Investiture Ceremony”], United States District Court for the Eastern District of Texas and co-authored a paper published in the IEEE Transactions on Multimedia.{{Cite web |title=Wavelet-Based VBR Video Traffic Smoothing |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/3424214_Wavelet-Based_VBR_Video_Traffic_Smoothing |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230628092124/https://www.researchgate.net/publication/3424214_Wavelet-Based_VBR_Video_Traffic_Smoothing |archive-date=2023-06-28 |access-date=2026-01-27 |website=ResearchGate |language=en}} Barker then earned his [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Texas School of Law]] with highest honors, graduating first in his class. While on the law review there, Barker published an article on copyright statutory damagesBarker, J. Cam, [https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=660601 “Grossly Excessive Penalties in the Battle Against Illegal File-Sharing: The Troubling Effects of Aggregating Minimum Statutory Damages for Copyright Infringement,”] 83 Tex. L. Rev. 525 (2004). that was cited by the district court in ''[[Sony BMG v. Tenenbaum]]'', 721 F. Supp. 2d 85 (D. Mass. 2010). Upon graduation from law school, Barker served as a law clerk to Judge [[William Curtis Bryson]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit]] and Judge [[John M. Walker Jr.]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit]]. After his clerkships, he served as a trial attorney in the Department of Justice's [[United States Department of Justice Criminal Division|Criminal Division]] for four years and was detailed as a [[Special Assistant United States Attorney]] for the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia|Eastern District of Virginia]] in 2009. Barker prosecuted three members of the [[MS-13]] gang who were convicted of conspiracy and racketeering.{{cite news |last1=Voruganti |first1=Harsh |title=J. Campbell Barker – Nominee to the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Texas |url=https://vettingroom.org/2018/02/21/cam-barker/ |access-date=7 October 2019 |publisher=Vetting Room |date=February 21, 2018}} Barker was given the Department of Justice's Meritorious Award three times while serving under U.S. Attorneys General [[Michael Mukasey]] and [[Eric Holder]]. Also, while at the Department of Justice, the [[American Inns of Court]] selected Barker to visit London and study English law as one of two annual Pegasus Scholars.American Inns of Court, [https://home.innsofcourt.org/AIC/Awards_and_Scholarships/Pegasus_Scholarships/Pegasus_Scholarship_Recipients.aspx “Pegasus Scholarship Recipients: 2011”.] From 2011 to 2015, Barker practiced commercial and [[intellectual property]] law at Yetter Coleman LLP in Texas, where he was named a partner. While at the firm, Barker was twice named to the Pro Bono College of the [[State Bar of Texas]] and was named Appellate Lawyer of the Week by Texas Lawyer magazine for helping an immigrant reverse a decision denying him asylum.John Council, [https://www.law.com/texaslawyer/almID/1202619109636/appellate-lawyer-of-the-week-pro-bono-political-persecution-protection/ “Appellate Lawyer of the Week: Pro Bono Political Persecution Protection”], Texas Lawyer (Sept. 16, 2013). From 2015 to 2019, Barker served as Deputy Solicitor General of Texas under [[Solicitor General of Texas|Solicitors General]] [[Scott A. Keller]] and [[Kyle D. Hawkins]], in which he helped to represent the state of Texas on appeal before federal and state courts in civil and criminal actions.{{Cite web |title=President Donald J. Trump Announces Tenth Wave of Judicial Nominees – The White House |url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-tenth-wave-judicial-nominees/ |access-date=2026-01-27 |website=trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov}} For his work there, Barker twice earned a Best Brief Award from the [[National Association of Attorneys General]]. While a sitting judge, Barker graduated in 2023 from [[Duke University School of Law|Duke Law School]] with a [[Master of Laws]] in judicial studies.{{Cite web |title=Wayback Machine |url=https://judicialstudies.duke.edu/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/2021-MJS-Bios-Photos.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241201154724/https://judicialstudies.duke.edu/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/2021-MJS-Bios-Photos.pdf |archive-date=2024-12-01 |access-date=2026-01-27 |website=judicialstudies.duke.edu}} In 2024, a version of his Master of Laws thesis paper was published in the Washington University Law Review with the title "Standing Orders: A Survey of Individual Judges’ Regulation of Practice in All Future Cases Before Them.{{cite web | title=Standing Orders: A Survey of Individual Judges' Regulation of Practice in All Future Cases Before Them – Washington University Law Review | url=https://wustllawreview.org/2024/11/05/standing-orders-a-survey-of-individual-judges-regulation-of-practice-in-all-future-cases-before-them/ }} === Federal judicial service === On January 23, 2018, President [[Donald Trump]] nominated Barker to the seat on the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Texas]] vacated by Judge [[Leonard Davis (judge)|Leonard Davis]], who retired on May 15, 2015.{{cite news|url=https://www.dallasnews.com/news/politics/2018/01/23/trump-nominates-four-texans-fill-judge-posts|title=Trump nominates four federal judges for Texas, including another Paxton aide to replace controversial 'Satan's plan' nominee|date=January 23, 2018|newspaper=[[The Dallas Morning News]]}}{{cite web|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/four-nominations-sent-senate-today-6/|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Four Nominations Sent to the Senate Today}} On May 9, 2018, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web |title=Nominations {{!}} United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/committee-activity/hearings/05/09/2018/nominations |access-date=2026-01-27 |website=www.judiciary.senate.gov |language=en}} On June 7, 2018, his nomination was reported out of committee by an 11–10 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/06-07-18%20Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – June 7, 2018, Senate Judiciary Committee}} On January 3, 2019, his nomination was returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]]. On January 23, 2019, President Trump announced his intent to renominate Barker for a federal judgeship.{{Cite web |title=President Donald J. Trump Announces Intent to Nominate Judicial Nominees – The White House |url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-intent-nominate-judicial-nominees/ |access-date=2026-01-27 |website=trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov}} His nomination was sent to the Senate later that day.{{Cite web |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate – The White House |url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/nominations-sent-senate-2/ |access-date=2026-01-27 |website=trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov}} On February 7, 2019, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 12–10 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/02.07.2019%20Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting1.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – February 7, 2019|publisher=Senate Judiciary Committee}} On April 30, 2019, the Senate invoked cloture on his nomination by a 52–46 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1161/vote_116_1_00084.htm|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture J. Campbell Barker to be U.S. District Judge for the Eastern District of Texas)|website=United States Senate|date=April 30, 2019}} On May 1, 2019, his nomination was confirmed by a 51–47 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=1&vote=00085|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation J. Campbell Barker, of Texas, to be U.S. District Judge for the Eastern District of Texas)|website=United States Senate|date=May 1, 2019}} He received his judicial commission on May 3, 2019.{{FJC Bio|nid=6379986|inline=yes}} == Notable rulings == On February 25, 2021, Barker struck down the [[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]]'s federal [[COVID-19 eviction moratoriums in the United States|eviction moratorium]].{{cite web|last=Millhiser|first=Ian|url=https://www.vox.com/2021/2/26/22302149/eviction-moratorium-trump-judge-campbell-barker-terkel-cdc-commerce-clause-constitution|title=A Trump judge's order striking down the federal eviction moratorium, briefly explained|publisher=Vox|date=February 26, 2021}} On March 9, 2024, Barker vacated the [[National Labor Relations Board]]'s final rule on [[Joint employment (US Law)|joint-employer]] status, issued in October 2023,{{cite web|url=https://www.nlrb.gov/news-outreach/news-story/board-issues-final-rule-on-joint-employer-status|title=Board Issues Final Rule on Joint-Employer Status|publisher=[[National Labor Relations Board]]|date=October 26, 2023}} that was set to be in effect 3 days later. He had previously stayed the rule until the 11th.{{cite web|url=https://www.nlrb.gov/news-outreach/news-story/nlrbs-joint-employer-rule-vacated-by-us-district-judge|title=NLRB's Joint-Employer Rule Vacated by U.S. District Judge|publisher=National Labor Relations Board|date=March 9, 2024}} On August 26, 2024, Barker paused President [[Joe Biden|Biden]]'s Keeping Families Together initiative which aims to offer a path to citizenship for immigrants who are married to U.S. citizens and living in the United States illegally.{{Cite web |title=Texas judge blocks Biden citizenship plan for migrant spouses |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cdxleplk81wo |access-date=2024-08-27 |website=www.bbc.com |date=August 27, 2024 |language=en-GB}} This was placed on temporary hold due to a lawsuit from 16 states, citing it could be harmful to them. On November 7, 2024, Barker ruled that the Biden administration lacked the authority to establish the program and to bypass Congress to create immigration legislation by executive order.{{Cite web |last=Galvan |first=Astrid |date=November 7, 2024 |title=Federal judge strikes down Biden program for undocumented immigrants |url=https://www.axios.com/2024/11/07/biden-immigration-citizenship-marriage-texas-ruling?utm_source=pocket-newtab-en-us |access-date=November 8, 2024 |website=Axios}} == See also == * [[Donald Trump judicial appointment controversies]] == References == {{Reflist}} == External links == * {{FJC Bio|nid=6379986}} * {{Ballotpedia|J._Campbell_Barker|J. [[University of Tennessee College of Law|University of Tennessee]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | footnotes = }} '''John Daniel Breen''' (born July 10, 1950)''U.S. Public Records Index'', Vol 1 (Provo, UT: Ancestry.com Operations, Inc.), 2010. is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Tennessee]]. ==Education and career== Breen was born in [[Jackson, Tennessee]]. He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[Spring Hill College]] in 1972 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Tennessee College of Law]] in 1975. He was in private practice in Jackson from 1975 to 1991. ==Federal judicial service== He served as [[United States magistrate judge]] of the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Tennessee from 1991 to 2003 before being nominated as a federal judge. On January 7, 2003, Breen was nominated by President [[George W. Bush]] to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Tennessee]] vacated by [[Julia Smith Gibbons]]. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on March 13, 2003 and received his commission on March 14, 2003. He served chief judge from August 8, 2013 to March 18, 2017. He assumed [[senior status]] on March 18, 2017. ===Notable case=== Breen presided over the case of Daniel Cowart and Paul Schlesselman, the perpetrators in the [[Barack Obama assassination plot in Tennessee]]. In 2010, Breen convicted the two of [[conspiracy (crime)|conspiracy]] to murder Obama and other African-American people and sentenced Cowart and Schlesselman to 14 and 10 years in federal prison respectively; both suspects pleaded guilty to conspiracy to their charges.{{cite web|title=Obama assassination plot: Paul Schlesselman sentenced to 10 years for plotting murder spree|url=http://www.nydailynews.com/news/national/2010/04/16/2010-04-16_obama_assassination_plot_paul_schlesselman_sentenced_to_10_years_for_plotting_mu.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100418032120/http://www.nydailynews.com/news/national/2010/04/16/2010-04-16_obama_assassination_plot_paul_schlesselman_sentenced_to_10_years_for_plotting_mu.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=April 18, 2010|work=New York Daily News|accessdate=January 9, 2011|date=April 16, 2010}}{{cite press release|url=http://memphis.fbi.gov/dojpressrel/pressrel10/me102210.htm|title=Tennessee Man Sentenced for Conspiring to Commit Murders of African-Americans|publisher=Federal Bureau of Investigation, Memphis|date=October 22, 2010|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://archive.today/20110805165411/http://memphis.fbi.gov/dojpressrel/pressrel10/me102210.htm|archive-date=August 5, 2011}} ==References== {{Reflist}} ==Sources== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1391771}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Julia Smith Gibbons]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Tennessee]]}}|years=2003–2017}} {{s-aft|after=[[Mark Norris (judge)|Mark Norris]]}} {{s-bef|before=[[Jon Phipps McCalla]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Chief Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Tennessee]]}}|years=2013–2017}} {{s-aft|after=[[S. [[Valparaiso University School of Law|Valparaiso University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | party = }} '''James Patrick "J. P." Hanlon''' (born 1970) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Indiana]]. == Education == Hanlon earned his [[Bachelor of Arts]] from [[DePauw University]] and his [[Juris Doctor]], ''[[magna cum laude]]'', from the [[Valparaiso University School of Law]], where he was an editor of the school's law review.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-twelfth-wave-judicial-nominees-twelfth-wave-united-states-attorneys-sixth-wave-united-states-marshals/ "President Donald J. Trump Announces Twelfth Wave of Judicial Nominees, Twelfth Wave of United States Attorneys, and Sixth Wave of United States Marshals" White House, April 10, 2018] {{PD-notice}} == Career == After graduating from law school, he served as a [[law clerk]] to Judge [[Robert Lowell Miller Jr.]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Indiana]]. From 1998 to 2001, Hanlon practiced as an associate in the [[labor and employment law]] practice group at [[Seyfarth Shaw LLP]] in [[Chicago]]. From 2001 to 2006, he served for five years as an [[assistant United States attorney]] for the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Indiana|Southern District of Indiana]]. During that period, he tried twelve jury and two bench trials to successful resolution on behalf of the government, and argued multiple cases on appeal before the [[Seventh Circuit]]. Before becoming a judge, he was a partner in the [[Indianapolis]] office of Faegre Baker Daniels LLP, where he served as co-chair of the firm's [[white collar criminal defense]] and investigations practice. Before Faegre Baker Daniels was formed through the merger of Baker & Daniels LLP and Faegre & Benson LLP in 2012, he had been a partner with Baker & Daniels LLP since 2006.{{Cite press release |title=PRESIDENT TRUMP TO NOMINATE J.P. HANLON '92 TO SERVE AS US DISTRICT COURT JUDGE |date=April 10, 2018 |publisher=[[DePauw University]] |url=https://www.depauw.edu/news-media/latest-news/details/33619/ |access-date=April 11, 2018 |archive-date=April 11, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180411111503/https://www.depauw.edu/news-media/latest-news/details/33619/ |url-status=dead }} Hanlon has served as an [[adjunct professor]] at the [[Indiana University Robert H. McKinney School of Law]], where he taught courses on white collar crime. == Federal judicial service == On April 10, 2018, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to nominate Hanlon to serve as a United States District Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Indiana]].{{Cite web |url=https://www.seattletimes.com/nation-world/fort-wayne-indianapolis-attorneys-nominated-for-us-bench/ |title=Fort Wayne, Indianapolis attorneys nominated for US bench |date=April 10, 2018 |publisher=[[The Seattle Times]]}} On April 12, 2018, his nomination was sent to the [[United States Senate|Senate]]. He was nominated to the seat that was vacated by Judge [[William T. Lawrence (judge)|William T. Lawrence]], who assumed [[senior status]] on July 1, 2018.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/twenty-nine-nominations-sent-senate-today/ "Twenty-Nine Nominations Sent to the Senate Today", The White House, April 12, 2018] On June 6, 2018, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/06/06/2018/nominations United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Nominations for June 6, 2018] On June 28, 2018, his nomination was reported out of committee by a [[voice vote]].[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%2006-28-18.pdf Results of Executive Business Meeting – June 28, 2018, Senate Judiciary Committee] On October 11, 2018, his nomination was confirmed by a [[voice vote]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/115th-congress/1831|title=PN1831 — James Patrick Hanlon — The Judiciary|last=|first=|date=April 12, 2018|website=[[United States Senate]]|access-date=October 11, 2018|language=en}} He received his judicial commission on November 5, 2018.{{FJC Bio|nid=5375106|inline=yes}} He was sworn in on November 13, 2018.{{Cite press release|date=November 13, 2018|title=James Patrick Hanlon sworn in as United States District Judge|url=https://www.insd.uscourts.gov/sites/insd/files/JPH%20sworn%20in%20press%20release.pdf|website=insd.uscourts.gov|access-date=May 28, 2023}} === Notable cases === On June 30, 2021, Hanlon issued an [[injunction]] against Indiana's "abortion reversal law", blocking the law while it makes its way through the courts.{{Cite web|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/2021/06/30/indiana-abortion-clinic-reversal-law-federal-judge-eric-holcomb/7814452002/|title=Federal judge blocks Indiana 'abortion reversal' law|website=USA Today|date=June 30, 2021|access-date=June 30, 2021}}{{Caselaw source|case=''All-Options, Inc. v. Attorney General of Indiana''|courtlistener=https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/59914507/all-options-inc-v-attorney-general-of-indiana/}} On June 16, 2023, he issued an order stopping an Indiana ban on [[puberty blocker]]s and hormones for transgender minors from taking effect as scheduled July 1.{{Cite web |last=Associated Press |date= 16 June 2023|title="A federal judge has blocked much of Indiana's ban on gender-affirming care for minors." June 16, 2023. |url=https://www.npr.org/2023/06/16/1182931422/judge-blocks-indiana-ban-gender-affirming-care-minors |website=National Public Radio.}} The injunction was vacated by the Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit.{{Caselaw source|case=''K.C. v. The Individual Members of the Licensing Board of Indiana''| courtlistener=https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/67142836/kc-v-the-individual-members-of-the-medical-licensing-board-of-indiana/}} == References == {{Reflist}} == External links == * {{FJC Bio|nid=5375106}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[William T. J. Paul Oetken:
{{Short description|American judge (born 1965)}} {{Use mdy dates|date=January 2022}} {{Infobox judge | name = Paul Oetken | image = | caption = Oetken in 2015 | office = Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]] | appointer = [[Barack Obama]] | term_start = July 20, 2011 | term_end = | predecessor = [[Denny Chin]] | successor = | birth_name = James Paul Oetken | birth_date = {{birth year and age|1965|}} | birth_place = [[Louisville, Kentucky]], U.S. | death_date = | death_place = | spouse = {{marriage|Makky Pratayot|2014}} | education = [[University of Iowa]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|BA]])
[[Yale University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''James Paul Oetken''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|ɛ|t|k|ɪ|n}} {{respell|EHT|kin}}; born 1965), known professionally as '''J. Paul Oetken''', is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]]. He is the first [[coming out|openly]] [[gay]] man to be confirmed as an [[Article Three of the United States Constitution|Article III judge]]. == Early life and education == Oetken was born in 1965,{{Cite web |title=J. Paul Oetken |url=https://lgbthistorymonth.com/sites/default/files/icon_multimedia_pdfs/2022/Oetken-LGBT_HistoryMonthBio2022%2028.pdf |access-date=May 6, 2025 |website=lgbthistorymonth.com}} in [[Louisville, Kentucky]].{{Cite web|author=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|url=http://judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/112thCongressJudicialNominations/upload/JPaulOetken-PublicQuestionnaire.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees: J. Paul Oetken|date=January 24, 2011|access-date=March 17, 2011|archive-date=July 21, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110721062320/http://judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/112thCongressJudicialNominations/upload/JPaulOetken-PublicQuestionnaire.pdf|url-status=dead}} He was valedictorian and class president at [[Regis High School (Iowa)|Regis High School]] in Cedar Rapids, Iowa. He earned a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from the [[University of Iowa]] in 1988, and a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Yale Law School]] in 1991.{{cite news| url=http://www.metroweekly.com/poliglot/2011/01/obama-nominates-oetken-for-ny.html| title=Obama Nominates Oetken for N.Y. Federal Court Spot|first=Chris|last=Geidner|work=Metro Weekly|date=January 26, 2011|access-date=March 17, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110218160603/http://www.metroweekly.com/poliglot/2011/01/obama-nominates-oetken-for-ny.html|archive-date=February 18, 2011|url-status=dead}} Oetken served as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Richard Cudahy]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit]] from 1991 to 1992. Then, he clerked for Judge [[Louis F. Oberdorfer]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Columbia]] from 1992 to 1993. Lastly, he clerked for Associate Justice [[Harry Blackmun]] of the [[United States Supreme Court]] from 1993 to 1994.{{cite book| last1=Murdoch|first1=Joyce|last2=Price|first2=Deb|title=Courting Justice: Gay Men And Lesbians V. The Supreme Court| url=https://archive.org/details/courtingjusticeg00murd|url-access=registration|year=2001|publisher=Basic Books|isbn=978-0-465-01514-6| pages=[https://archive.org/details/courtingjusticeg00murd/page/416 416–418]}}{{FJC Bio|nid=1393731|inline=yes}} == Career == During the mid-1990s, Oetken worked as an associate with the law firm of [[Jenner & Block]]. In 1997, he joined the [[Office of Legal Counsel]] in the United States Department of Justice as an attorney-advisor, where he worked until becoming an associate counsel to the president of the United States in the office of the [[White House Counsel]] in 1999. He held that job until President [[Bill Clinton]] left office in 2001. From 2001 until 2003, Oetken worked as an [[associate lawyer|associate]] at the law firm of [[Debevoise & Plimpton]], including as counsel in 2003 and 2004.{{Cite web | author=The White House: Office of the Press Secretary | url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2011/01/26/president-obama-names-six-united-states-district-court | title=President Obama Names Six to United States District Court | date=January 26, 2011 | via=National Archives | work=whitehouse.gov | access-date=March 17, 2011}} In 2004, Oetken joined [[Cablevision]] Systems Corporation as its associate general counsel, until 2011 when he left to join the federal bench. === Federal judicial service === On January 26, 2011, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Oetken to serve on the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]] to replace Judge [[Denny Chin]], who was elevated to the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit]].{{cite press release | author=The White House: Office of the Press Secretary | url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2011/01/26/presidential-nominations-sent-senate-0 | title=Presidential nominations sent to the Senate | date=January 26, 2011 | via=National Archives | work=whitehouse.gov | access-date=March 17, 2011}} New York Senator [[Charles Schumer]] recommended Oetken to the post.{{cite news | url=http://www.nyrealestatelawblog.com/2010/09/schumer_woul_like_j_paul_oetke.html | work=NY Real Estate Law Blog | title=Schumer wants J. Paul Oetken to serve | first=Lucas A. | last=Ferrara | date=September 27, 2010 | access-date=March 17, 2011 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110714220139/http://www.nyrealestatelawblog.com/2010/09/schumer_woul_like_j_paul_oetke.html | archive-date=July 14, 2011 | url-status=dead }} Schumer recommended Oetken a year after he recommended former [[Assistant United States Attorney]] Daniel S. Alter, also openly gay,{{cite news | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/01/28/nyregion/28judge.htm | work=The New York Times | title=Obama Nominee for Judge Could Be First Openly Gay Man on the Federal Bench | first=Benjamin | last = Weiser | date=January 27, 2011 | access-date=March 17, 2011}} whom the White House declined to nominate after concluding, because of statements that had been attributed to Alter, that his nomination was unlikely to survive the 60-vote threshold needed to overcome a [[filibuster]] in the Senate.{{cite web | url=http://www.washingtonblade.com/2010/10/20/white-house-rejects-gay-judicial-nominee/ | work=Washington Blade | title=White House rejects gay judicial nominee | first=Chris | last=Johnson | date=October 20, 2010 | access-date=March 17, 2011}} Schumer stated that diversity was a consideration in his recommendations for federal judgeships, and that he was "shocked to learn" that no openly gay men had served on the federal bench. The Senate confirmed Oetken on July 18, 2011, by an 80–13 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=112&session=1&vote=00112|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation J. Paul Oetken, of New York, to be U.S. District Judge for the Southern District of New York)|website=www.senate.gov}} He received his commission on July 20, 2011. At the time of his confirmation, Oetken was the second openly gay [[Article III judge]] in the country, after [[Deborah Batts]],{{cite news | url=http://www.washingtonblade.com/2011/03/13/senate-hearing-set-for-gay-judicial-nominee/ | title=Senate hearing set for gay judicial nominee | first=Chris | last=Johnson | work=Washington Blade | date=March 13, 2011 | access-date=March 17, 2011}} and the first openly [[gay men|gay male]] federal judge.{{Cite news |last=Lalwani |first=Nikita |date=July 19, 2011 |title=Oetken LAW '91 confirmed as federal judge |language=en |url=https://yaledailynews.com/blog/2011/07/19/oetken-law-91-confirmed-as-federal-judge/ |access-date=June 20, 2023}} == Personal life == Oetken lives with his husband, Makky Pratayot, in [[Manhattan]].{{cite news|url=http://www.metroweekly.com/news/?ak=6723|title=Judge Oetken: Gay lawyer dons his robe, taking his place on the federal bench in Manhattan – and in history|work=[[Metro Weekly]]|date=November 3, 2011}} They were married on September 6, 2014, at [[the Jane]] by Judge [[Alison Nathan]].{{cite news | url = https://www.nytimes.com/2014/09/07/fashion/weddings/makky-pratayot-j-paul-oetken.html | title = Makky Pratayot, J. Paul Oetken | work = The New York Times | date = September 7, 2014 }} == See also == * [[Joe Biden Supreme Court candidates]] * [[List of law clerks for the second seat of the Supreme Court of the United States]] * [[List of LGBT jurists in the United States]] * [[Lev Parnas]] == References == {{Reflist}} == External links == *{{FJC Bio|nid=1393731}} *{{Ballotpedia|J._Paul_Oetken}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Denny Chin]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]]}}|years=2011–present}} {{s-inc}} {{s-end}} {{United States 2nd Circuit district judges}} {{Authority control}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Oetken, J. [[Harvard Law School|Harvard University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | party = [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]]{{Cite web |url=https://www.cleveland.com/court-justice/2019/06/new-judge-appointed-to-cuyahoga-county-common-pleas-court-bench.html |title=New judge appointed to Cuyahoga County Common Pleas Court bench |last=Shaffer |first=Cory |date=June 21, 2019 |website=cleveland |language=en |access-date=February 28, 2020}} | caption = Calabrese in 2020 }} '''Jude Philip Calabrese''' (born 1971) is an American lawyer and jurist who serves as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Ohio]]. He formerly served as a judge of the [[Cuyahoga County, Ohio|Cuyahoga County]] [[Ohio Courts of Common Pleas|Court of Common Pleas]] from 2019 to 2020. == Early life and education == Calabrese was born in 1971 in [[Evanston, Illinois]]. He graduated from the [[College of the Holy Cross]] with a [[Bachelor of Arts]], ''[[Latin honors#Distinctions|summa cum laude]]'', in [[classics]] and [[religious studies]] in 1993 with membership in [[Phi Beta Kappa]] and [[Alpha Sigma Nu]].{{Cite web |last=Calabrese |first=J. Philip |date=2020 |title=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Philip%20Calabrese%20SJQ%20-%20PUBLIC.pdf |access-date=March 29, 2024 |website=[[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]]}} As an undergraduate, Calabrese was a legislative assistant to state representatives [[Eric Fingerhut]] and [[Judy Robson]], and state senator [[Lynn Adelman]]. After graduating from Holy Cross, Calabrese earned a [[Fulbright Program|Fulbright scholarship]] to study ancient history at the [[American School of Classical Studies at Athens]] from 1993 to 1994.{{Cite web |title=Past Award Recipients: Fulbright |url=https://www.holycross.edu/outcomes-after-holy-cross/office-distinguished-fellowships-and-graduate-studies/our-record-success/past-award-recipients |access-date=2023-10-15 |website=[[College of the Holy Cross]] |language=en}} In 1997, he enrolled at [[Harvard Law School]], graduating with a [[Juris Doctor]] (J.D.), ''cum laude'', in 2000. He had been a [[summer associate]] at the law firm of [[Jones Day]] in 1998 and 1999. == Career == After finishing law school, Calabrese served as a law clerk to Judge [[Alice M. Batchelder]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit]]. He was a partner with Porter, Wright, Morris & Arthur, where he co-chaired the firm's class action practice. Since fall 2017, he has served as an adjunct professor at [[Case Western Reserve University School of Law]].{{Cite web |title=J. Philip Calabrese Resume |url=https://www.judgephilcalabrese.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/Resume.pdf |access-date=February 28, 2020 |publisher=judgephilcalabrese.com |archive-date=February 29, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200229050221/https://www.judgephilcalabrese.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/Resume.pdf |url-status=dead }}{{Cite web|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-judicial-nominees-united-states-attorney-nominee-united-states-marshal-nominee/|title=President Donald J. Trump Announces Judicial Nominees, a United States Attorney Nominee, and a United States Marshal Nominee|language=en-US|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|access-date=February 27, 2020}} He has been a member of the [[City Club of Cleveland]] since 2001 and of the [[Federalist Society]] since 2005. === State court service === On June 21, 2019, Governor [[Mike DeWine]] appointed Calabrese as a judge of the [[Cuyahoga County, Ohio|Cuyahoga County]] [[Ohio Courts of Common Pleas|Court of Common Pleas]] to fill the vacancy left by Judge [[Pamela Barker]]'s appointment to the United States District Court for the Northern District of Ohio.{{Cite web |url=http://www.courtnewsohio.gov/bench/2019/calabreseAppt_062119.asp |title=Governor Appoints Cuyahoga County Common Pleas Judge |date=June 21, 2019 |website=www.courtnewsohio.gov |access-date=February 28, 2020}}{{Cite web |last=Heisig |first=Eric |date=2020-02-26 |title=President Donald Trump nominates Cuyahoga County judge for federal bench |url=https://www.cleveland.com/court-justice/2020/02/president-donald-trump-nominates-cuyahoga-county-judge-for-federal-bench.html |access-date=2023-10-15 |website=[[Cleveland.com]] |publisher=[[The Plain Dealer]] |language=en}} He was sworn into office on July 3, 2019.{{Cite web |url=https://cp.cuyahogacounty.us/court-information/news/posts/court-welcomes-judge-j-philip-calabrese/ |title=Court Welcomes Judge J. Philip Calabrese |date=July 3, 2019 |website=cp.cuyahogacounty.us |language=en |access-date=February 28, 2020 |archive-date=February 29, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200229044528/https://cp.cuyahogacounty.us/court-information/news/posts/court-welcomes-judge-j-philip-calabrese/ |url-status=dead }} His state court service ended in 2020 after he became a federal judge. === Federal judicial service === On February 26, 2020, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to nominate Calabrese to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Ohio]]. On March 3, 2020, his nomination was sent to the Senate. President Trump nominated Calabrese to the seat vacated by Judge [[Christopher A. '''James Rodney Gilstrap''' (born May 1, 1957) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Texas]]. He is notable for presiding over more than one quarter of all [[patent infringement]] cases filed in the nation and is often referred to by various sources as the country's single "busiest patent judge."<ref name="motherboard">{{cite web|url=https://www.vice.com/en/article/the-small-town-judge-who-sees-a-quarter-of-the-nations-patent-cases/|title=The Small Town Judge Who Sees a Quarter of the Nation's Patent Cases|author=Kaleigh Rogers|date=May 5, 2016|work=Motherboard|publisher=VICE|access-date=September 26, 2016|archive-date=September 20, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160920073458/http://motherboard.vice.com/read/the-small-town-judge-who-sees-a-quarter-of-the-nations-patent-cases|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Jess">{{Cite web |url=https://www.law360.com/articles/628732/judge-gilstrap-keeps-eastern-district-s-tight-ship-afloat |title=Judge Gilstrap Keeps Eastern District's Tight Ship Afloat |last=Krochtengel |first=Jess |publisher=[[Law360]] |language=en |access-date=April 3, 2018 |url-access=registration |archive-date=April 3, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180403174828/https://www.law360.com/articles/628732/judge-gilstrap-keeps-eastern-district-s-tight-ship-afloat |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Gilstrap was born in [[Pensacola, Florida]]. He is an [[Eagle Scout (Boy Scouts of America)|Eagle Scout]]. He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] from [[Baylor University]] in 1978, where he graduated ''magna cum laude''.<ref name="kcentv">{{cite web |url=http://www.kcentv.com/story/16210540/baylor-law-alumnus-rodney-gilstrap-confirmed-as-federal-judge |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130127150034/http://www.kcentv.com/story/16210540/baylor-law-alumnus-rodney-gilstrap-confirmed-as-federal-judge |url-status=dead |archive-date=January 27, 2013|title=Baylor Law Alumnus Rodney Gilstrap Confirmed as Federal Judge  |author=KCENTV  |date=December 7, 2011 |access-date=July 16, 2012 }}</ref> As an undergraduate he was inducted into [[Phi Beta Kappa]]. He also earned a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Baylor Law School]] in 1981,<ref name=whgov_20110519>{{Cite web | author=The White House: Office of the Press Secretary | url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2011/05/19/president-obama-nominates-three-united-states-district-court | title=President Obama Nominates Three to the United States District Court | date=May 19, 2011 | access-date=June 12, 2011 | archive-date=February 2, 2017 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170202052708/https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2011/05/19/president-obama-nominates-three-united-states-district-court | via=[[NARA|National Archives]] | work=[[whitehouse.gov]] | url-status=live }}</ref> where he was associate editor of the ''Baylor Law Review.'' While on the review, he published the article ''Video Recorders: Copyright Infringement'', 33 Baylor Law Review 695 (1981).<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/JamesGilstrap-PublicQuestionnaire.pdf |title=Judge J. Rodney Gilstrap Public Questionnaire |publisher=Senate Judiciary Committee |access-date=January 30, 2017 |archive-date=January 31, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170131063946/http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/JamesGilstrap-PublicQuestionnaire.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> Gilstrap later served as president of the Baylor Law Alumni Association.<ref name="kcentv" /><ref name="fjc.gov">{{FJC Bio|nid=1393871|inline=yes}}</ref>

==Career==
After graduation from law school, Gilstrap entered private practice in the town of [[Marshall, Texas]] as an Associate with the firm of Abney, Baldwin & Searcy from 1981 to 1984.<ref name=Marshall>{{Cite news |url=https://marshallnewsmessenger.com/2011/05/20/gilstrap-tapped-to-be-federal-judge/ |title=Gilstrap tapped to be federal judge |last=Richardson |first=Robin Y. |date=May 20, 2011 |work=Marshall News Messenger |access-date=April 3, 2018 |language=en |archive-date=February 2, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170202061006/https://www.marshallnewsmessenger.com/news/2011/may/20/gilstrap-tapped-to-be-federal-judge/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="fjc.gov"/> He later became a founding Partner of Smith & Gilstrap in Marshall from 1984 to 1989, where his practice covered oil and gas, [[real estate]], [[probate law]] and occasionally [[patent law|patent cases]].<ref name=Marshall/><ref name="PriorArt">{{Cite web |url=http://thepriorart.typepad.com/the_prior_art/2011/06/gilstrapnomination.html |title=Straight Outta Marshall: Local Lawyer Gilstrap Tapped to Replace Ward |last=Goldberg |first=Andrew |website=The Prior Art Blog |access-date=January 28, 2017 |archive-date=December 25, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161225171358/http://thepriorart.typepad.com/the_prior_art/2011/06/gilstrapnomination.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Among the patent cases Gilstrap worked on while at Smith & Gilstrap included defending [[Capital One Financial]] Corporation in a patent suit brought by LML Patent Corporation alleging [[patent infringement]] by several banks on patents covering payment services and the representation of a company called Bluestone Innovations Texas in a patent infringement suit brought against a number of foreign companies involving [[Light-emitting diode]]s (or [[LED]]) technology.<ref name="Berkeley">{{Cite web |url=https://www.law.berkeley.edu/files/careers/Profiles_of_Other_Federal_Judges.pdf |title=Profiles of Other Federal Judges |publisher=Berkeley Law |access-date=January 28, 2017 |archive-date=May 14, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160514050757/https://www.law.berkeley.edu/files/careers/Profiles_of_Other_Federal_Judges.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> Gilstrap served as a [[Harrison County, Texas|Harrison County]] Judge from 1989 to 2002.<ref name=Michael>{{Cite web |url=http://mcsmith.blogs.com/eastern_district_of_texas/2011/05/judge-rodney-gilstrap-of-marshall-named-for-eastern-district-judgeship.html |title=Judge Rodney Gilstrap of Marshall Named for Eastern District Judgeship |last=Smith |first=Michael C. |date=May 19, 2011 |website=Eastern District of Texas Federal Court Practice |access-date=April 3, 2018 |archive-date=April 3, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180403174306/http://mcsmith.blogs.com/eastern_district_of_texas/2011/05/judge-rodney-gilstrap-of-marshall-named-for-eastern-district-judgeship.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Gilstrap also served 16 years on the Courthouse Preservation Council in Marshall, and also served as the Chair of the Unauthorized Practice of Law Committee with the State Bar of Texas.<ref name=Michael/> In 2004, Gilstrap co-authored an article with Leland de la Garza which appeared in the [[Texas Bar Journal]]: ''UPL: Unlicensed, Unwanted and Unwelcome'' 67 [[Texas Bar Journal]] 798 (2004). While and after serving as a Harrison County Judge, Gilstrap was practicing at Smith & Gilstrap until he became appointed to the federal bench in 2011.<ref name="fjc.gov"/>

===Federal judicial service===
On May 19, 2011, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Gilstrap to a seat on [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Texas]].<ref name=whgov_20110519/><ref name=Marshall/> Gilstrap was rated as Unanimously Qualified by the [[American Bar Association]] and had a hearing before the [[Senate Judiciary Committee]] on July 28, 2011.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://ballotpedia.org/James_Gilstrap |title=James Gilstrap |website=Ballotpedia |language=en-US |access-date=April 3, 2018 |archive-date=November 12, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181112024315/https://ballotpedia.org/James_Gilstrap |url-status=live }}</ref> On September 15, 2011, the [[Senate Judiciary Committee]] reported his nomination to the Senate floor by voice vote. The Senate confirmed his nomination by [[voice vote]] on December 5, 2011.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/executive_calendar/xcalv.pdf|title=Senate Executive Calendar|publisher=[[Senate of the United States]]|access-date=February 16, 2018|archive-date=February 15, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180215070525/https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/executive_calendar/xcalv.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> He received his commission on December 6, 2011.<ref name="fjc.gov"/> He became the chief judge on March 1, 2018, after [[Ron Clark (judge)|Ron Clark]] assumed [[senior status]].<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.txed.uscourts.gov/?q=news/new-chief-judge-eastern-district-texas |title=New Chief Judge for Eastern District of Texas |date=February 26, 2018 |access-date=April 3, 2018 |publisher=United States District Court |language=en |archive-date=May 2, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180502101727/http://www.txed.uscourts.gov/?q=news%2Fnew-chief-judge-eastern-district-texas |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Patent law experience ==

===The busiest patent judge in the country===
According to [[Lex Machina]] and other sources, Gilstrap is the [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] that hears the most patent cases in the country and has been referred to by many sources as the nation's single "busiest patent judge".<ref name="motherboard" /><ref name="Jess" /> In 2016, for example, 1,119 cases were brought before Gilstrap, who saw more new cases than the next 10 highest ranking judges – 2016 was also the fourth year in a row where Gilstrap had more patent cases than any other federal judge.<ref name="Lex">{{Cite press release |title=Lex Machina's Fourth Annual Patent Litigation Year in Review Report Shows 22 Percent Decline in Patent Filings in 2016 |date=March 2, 2017 |publisher=Lex Machina |url=https://lexmachina.com/media/press/report-shows-22-percent-decline-in-patent-filings-in-2016 |language=en-US |access-date=April 3, 2018 |archive-date=April 3, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180403234752/https://lexmachina.com/media/press/report-shows-22-percent-decline-in-patent-filings-in-2016/ |url-status=live }}</ref>  In 2015, over 28% of the nation's patent cases were filed before him.<ref name="motherboard" /> Gilstrap and [[United States Magistrate Judge]] [[Roy S. Payne]], who are the only two judges based out of the [[Marshall, Texas|Marshall]] division of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Texas]], also have the most patent cases filed before them out of the predominant share of the nation's patent cases that are filed in the Eastern District of Texas.<ref name="motherboard" /><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://lexmachina.com/14318
