'''James V. Selna''' (born February 22, 1945)<ref name="Bio">[https://www.cacd.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/documents/JVS/AD/Resume.pdf Biography of James V. Selna], U.S. District Court for the Central District of California.</ref> is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Central District of California]].

==Early life, education, and military service==
Selna was born in [[San Jose, California|San Jose]], [[California]], on February 22, 1945.<ref name="Bio"/> He received an [[Bachelor of Arts|A.B.]] degree from [[Stanford University]] in 1967.<ref name="fjc.gov">{{cite web|url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/selna-james-v.|title=Selna, James V.|publisher=[[Federal Judicial Center]]}}</ref> He graduated with distinction and [[Phi Beta Kappa]].<ref name="Bio"/> In 1970, Selna received a [[Juris Doctor|J.D.]] from [[Stanford Law School]],<ref name="fjc.gov"/> where he served on the ''[[Stanford Law Review]]''.<ref name="Bio"/>

Selna was a captain in the [[U.S. Army Reserve]] from 1967 to 1978.<ref name="fjc.gov"/>

==Career in private practice and as state judge==
Selna was in private practice in [[California]] from 1970 to 1998,<ref name="fjc.gov"/> at the law firm of [[O'Melveny & Myers]], working first from the firm's Los Angeles office and then its [[Newport Beach]] office.<ref name="Bio"/> While in private practice, Selna was involved in a number of significant cases, including ''Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum Commission v. National Football League'', an [[antitrust]] case involving the [[Oakland Raiders]]' move to Los Angeles,<ref name="Bio"/> in which Selna was one of the attorneys representing the [[National Football League|NFL]].<ref>''The American Lawyer Guide to Leading Law Firms, 1983-84'', Vol. 1 (Am-Law Publishing, 1983), p. 939.</ref>

He was a judge on the [[California superior courts|Superior Court]], Orange County, California from 1998 to 2003.<ref name="fjc.gov"/>

==Federal judicial service==

Selna was nominated by President [[George W. Bush]] to be a Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Central District of California]] on January 29, 2003, to a seat vacated by [[John Spencer Letts]].<ref name="fjc.gov"/> A substantial majority of the [[American Bar Association]]'s [[Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary]] rated Selna "well qualified" for the position, with a minority abstaining.<ref>[https://www.americanbar.org/content/dam/aba/migrated/2011_build/federal_judiciary/ratings108.authcheckdam.pdf Ratings of Article III Judicial Nominees, 108th Congress], [[American Bar Association]]'s [[Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary]] (last updated January 10, 2008).</ref> Selna was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on March 27, 2003, by a unanimous vote of 97–0.<ref>[https://www.congress.gov/nomination/108th-congress/278 PN278 — James V. Selna — The Judiciary], 108th Congress (2003-2004), Library of Congress.</ref> He received his commission the same day.<ref name="fjc.gov"/> He assumed [[senior status]] on March 3, 2020.

===Notable cases===
Selna was assigned the case of ''Farnan v. Capistrano Unified School District'', in which Chad Farnan, a [[Mission Viejo, California]] high school student, alleged that his [[AP European History]] teacher at [[Capistrano Valley High School]] had violated the [[Establishment Clause]] of the [[First Amendment to the United States Constitution|First Amendment]] to the [[United States Constitution]] by making a number of classroom statements in 2007 that the student interpreted as disparaging religion.<ref name="MartindaleNoInjunction">Scott Martindale, [https://www.ocregister.com/2009/07/13/no-injunction-against-teacher-who-insulted-christians-judge-rules/ No injunction against teacher who insulted Christians, judge rules], ''Orange County Register'' (July 13, 2009).</ref><ref>Scott Martindale, [https://www.ocregister.com/2012/02/21/supreme-court-wont-hear-appeal-of-students-anti-christian-lawsuit/ Supreme Court won’t hear appeal of student's anti-Christian lawsuit],  ''Orange County Register'' (February 21, 2012).</ref> In May 2009, Selna granted, in part, the by-then-former student's motion for summary judgment, ruling that one statement of the many cited by the student—a comment that [[creationism]] was "superstitious nonsense"—did violate the Establishment Clause. Selna ruled, however, that 20 other statements complained of by Farnar did not violate the Establishment Clause.<ref>{{cite web|author=Andrew Brown|url=https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2009/may/11/creationism-schools-science-us|title=Enemies of creationism may be hindering science teachers|date=May 11, 2009|newspaper=The Guardian}}</ref> Selna also determined that the teacher was protected by [[qualified immunity]] and entered judgment denying the Farnan's request for declaratory, injunctive or monetary relief, and inviting the defendants to apply for recovery of attorney fees and costs.<ref name="MartindaleNoInjunction"/><ref>[http://ncse.com/webfm_send/1658 Judgment], ''Farnarn v. Capistrano  Unified School District'' (C.D. Cal. Sept. 24, 2009).</ref>  In August 2011, the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit|Ninth Circuit]] affirmed Selna's finding of qualified immunity, but because it found the immunity issue to be dispositive, vacated that portion of the judgment that dealt with the constitutionality of the teacher's comments.<ref>''[http://www.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2011/08/19/09-56689.pdf C.F. v. Capistrano Unified School Dist.]'', 654 F.3d 975 (9th Cir. 2011).</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://ncse.com/news/2011/08/vindication-corbett-006835 |title=Vindication for Corbett |date=19 August 2011 |publisher=National Center for Science Education |access-date=19 August 2011}}</ref>

In 2007, Selna ruled in favor of [[Broadcom]] in a major [[patent infringement]] suit against [[Qualcomm]].<ref name="Qualcomm">[https://www.nytimes.com/2007/08/11/business/11broadcom.html Judge Sides With Broadcom in Qualcomm Patent Fight], Bloomberg News (August 11, 2007).</ref> The jury found that Qualcomm had infringed three of Broadcom's patents and returned a $19.64 million award to Qualcomm; Selna doubled that to $39.3 million in damages and legal fees, finding that the infringement was intentional.<ref name="Qualcomm"/> The following year, Selna found Qualcomm in [[Contempt of court|contempt]] for violating an injunction ordering it to stop using technology subject to the Broadcom patents.<ref>[https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2008-aug-29-fi-qual29-story.html Qualcomm found in contempt], Bloomberg News (August 29, 2008).</ref>

Selna presided over a complex [[class action]] [[multi-district litigation]] against [[Toyota]] involving the "[[sudden acceleration]]" issue (see [[2009–11 Toyota vehicle recalls]]).<ref>Stuart Pfeifer, [https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2010-may-28-la-fi-toyota-lawsuit-20100529-story.html Judge orders Toyota to turn over documents to plaintiffs' lawyers], ''Los Angeles Times'' (May 28, 2010).</ref><ref>Stuart Pfeifer, [https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2010-may-15-la-fi-toyota-20100515-story.html Judge selects lawyers in Toyota litigation], ''Los Angeles Times'' (May 15, 2010).</ref>

In 2015, Selna presided over a case brought by an operator of sober-living homes against the city of [[Costa Mesa, California]]. The operator challenged the city's ordinance requiring "sober-living homes in single-family neighborhoods to obtain special permits and be at least 650 feet from one another." Selna rejected the operator's claim that the ordinance improperly discriminated against recovering [[substance abuse]]rs and dismissed the suit.<ref>Bradley Zint, [http://www.latimes.com/socal/daily-pilot/news/tn-dpt-me-1016-yellowstone-recovery-20151015-story.html Judge dismisses sober-living case], ''Los Angeles Times'' (October 15, 2015).</ref><ref>Bradley Zint, [http://www.latimes.com/tn-dpt-me-0415-solid-landings-20150413-story.html Costa Mesa housing permit isn't unfair to addicts, judge tentatively rules], ''Los Angeles Times'' (April 13, 2015).</ref>

In 2016, Selna oversaw the case of [[Peter "Sana" Ojeda]], a leader of the [[Mexican Mafia]] in [[Orange County, California]]. After Ojeda was convicted of [[racketeering]], Selna sentenced him to 15 years in federal prison, finding that Ojeda remained a danger to the community despite his advanced age.<ref>Brittny Mejia, [http://www.latimes.com/local/lanow/la-me-ln-mexican-mafia-oc-boss-sentenced-15-years-20160509-story.html Mexican Mafia's O.C. boss sentenced to 15 years in federal prison], ''Los Angeles Times'' (May 9, 2016).</ref>

On August 16, 2023, he rejected a proposed [[United States dollar|$]]200 million settlement in a class-action lawsuit prompted by [[Kia Challenge|a rise in thefts of vehicles]] manufactured by [[South Korea]]n automakers [[Hyundai Motor Company|Hyundai]] and [[Kia]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://apnews.com/article/hyundai-kia-settlement-tentative-rejection-f1ad760620101c55ac3b5cf934aab298 | title=Judge declines to approve Hyundai/Kia class action settlement, noting weak proposed remedies | website=[[Associated Press News]] | date=17 August 2023 }}</ref> On November 17, 2023, he rejected requests by Kia and Hyundai to halt lawsuits from American cities suing the automakers.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Steinberg |first=Julie |date=November 20, 2023 |title=Kia, Hyundai Must Face US Cities' Claims Cars Are Easy to Steal |url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/litigation/us-cities-advance-auto-theft-lawsuits-against-kia-hyundai |work=Bloomberg Law}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Selna had previously served as a member of the board of trustees for the [[Orange County Museum of Art]] and Newport Harbor Art Museum, and as a member of the board of directors for the Orange County Business Committee for the Arts.<ref name="Bio"/>

She served as a judge of the 3rd District of the [[Michigan Court of Appeals]] from 2007 to 2021. == Education == Beckering received her [[Bachelor of Arts]] from the [[University of Michigan]] in 1987 and her [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Wisconsin Law School]] in 1990.[https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/06/30/president-biden-names-fifth-round-of-judicial-nominees/ "President Biden Names Fifth Round of Judicial Nominees", White House, June 30, 2021] {{PD-notice}}{{Cite web |title=Jane M. Beckering Judge Profile on Martindale.com |url=https://www.martindale.com/attorney/hon-jane-m-beckering-719219/ |access-date=2021-07-06 |website=www.martindale.com}} == Legal career == Beckering started her career at McDermott, Will & Emery, LLP, in [[Chicago, Illinois]], then returned to [[Grand Rapids, Michigan]], and later founded the law firm of Buchanan & Beckering, PLC. She was a lawyer for 17 years, first in [[Chicago]] and then in [[Grand Rapids]] before she became a judge in 2007. In 2006 as a lawyer Beckering sought the Democratic nomination{{efn|In Michigan, judicial elections are nonpartisan but candidates are nominated by political parties.}} for the [[Michigan Supreme Court]]. She made it to the general election ballot but placed a distant third behind incumbents [[Maura Corrigan]] and [[Michael Cavanagh (judge)|Michael Cavanagh]]. == Judicial career == === State court service === Beckering was appointed a Judge of the [[Michigan Court of Appeals]] by [[Michigan Governor]] [[Jennifer Granholm]] to replace Judge [[Janet T. Neff]], who was appointed as a federal district court judge. She took office on September 10, 2007.{{Cite news |last=Czurak |first=David |date=September 10, 2007 |title=Beckering Takes A Seat |url=https://grbj.com/uncategorized/beckering-takes-a-seat/ |access-date=July 6, 2021 |website=Grand Rapids Business Journal |language=en-US}} Beckering is vice president of the Grand Rapids Bar Association, with a term set to expire on January 1, 2025.{{Cite web |title=COA Third District Judges |url=https://courts.michigan.gov/Courts/COA/judges/Pages/BiosD3.aspx#JMB |access-date=2021-07-06 |website=courts.michigan.gov |archive-date=2021-07-09 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210709185357/https://courts.michigan.gov/Courts/COA/judges/Pages/BiosD3.aspx#JMB |url-status=dead }} Her service terminated upon her elevation as a federal judge. === Federal judicial service === On June 30, 2021, President [[Joe Biden]] announced his intent to nominate Beckering to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Michigan]]. Neff]], who assumed [[senior status]] on March 1, 2021.[https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/07/13/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-24/ "Nominations Sent to the Senate", White House, July 13, 2021] A hearing on her nomination before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] was scheduled to take place on August 11, 2021, but was postponed.{{Cite web|title=Nominations: Wednesday, August 11, 2021|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/08/04/2021/nominations|access-date=August 10, 2021|website=www.judiciary.senate.gov|language=en}} On October 6, 2021, a hearing on her nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web|title=Nominations|date=October 6, 2021|publisher=[[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]]|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/09/29/2021/nominations}} On October 28, 2021, her nomination was reported out of committee by a 12-9–1 vote.{{Cite web|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – October 28, 2021|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/EBM%20Results%2010.28.21.pdf|access-date=November 25, 2022|website=www.judiciary.senate.gov}} On December 17, 2021, the [[United States Senate]] invoked cloture on her nomination by a 46–24 vote.{{Cite web|url= https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1171/vote_117_1_00516.htm|title= On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Jane M. McKinney School of Law]] in 1983.[https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/president-obama-nominates-five-serve-united-states-district-court-bench President Obama Nominates Five to Serve on the United States District Court Bench], ''[[whitehouse.gov]]'' (January 20, 2010).{{FJC Bio|nid=1393226|inline=yes}} == Career == From 1983 until 1990, Magnus-Stinson worked as an associate for a law firm in [[Indianapolis]]. From 1991 until 1995, she worked for then-Governor [[Evan Bayh]], first as an executive assistant in 1991 and then as Counsel to the Governor from 1991 until 1995. She also served as Bayh's Deputy Chief of Staff from 1994 until 1995. From 1995 until 2007, Magnus-Stinson served as a Superior Court judge on the [[Courts in Indiana|Marion County Superior Court]], in the Criminal Division. === Federal judicial service === In January 2007, Magnus-Stinson became a [[United States magistrate judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Indiana]], a position she held until becoming a federal district judge in 2010. In November 2008, Magnus-Stinson notified Senator Bayh, who by that point had become one of Indiana's two senators, of interest in a district court judgeship. After Magnus-Stinson underwent a series of interviews with officials from the [[United States Department of Justice]] and the Office of the [[White House Counsel]], President Obama on January 20, 2010, nominated Magnus-Stinson to the seat on the Southern District of Indiana, to replace Judge [[Larry J. McKinney]], who assumed [[senior status]] on July 4, 2009.[https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/presidential-nominations-sent-senate-2 Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate], ''[[whitehouse.gov]]'' (January 20, 2010). On March 11, 2010, the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]] reported Magnus-Stinson's nomination out of committee. The [[United States Senate]] confirmed Magnus-Stinson by a [[voice vote]] on June 7, 2010. She received her commission on June 9, 2010. She served as the chief judge from November 23, 2016.{{Cite web |url=http://www.insd.uscourts.gov/sites/insd/files/JMS%20Chief%20Judge%20PR%20FINAL.pdf |title=United States District Court for the Southern District of Indiana Announces New Chief Judge |publisher=UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT SOUTHERN DISTRICT OF INDIANA |publication-date=November 28, 2016}} and served until March 20, 2021. She assumed [[senior status]] on July 1, 2024.{{Cite news|date=September 1, 2023|last=Carson|first=Daniel|title=Magnus-Stinson assuming senior status next summer|url=https://www.theindianalawyer.com/articles/magnus-stinson-assuming-senior-status-next-summer|website=The Indiana Lawyer|access-date=September 12, 2023}} == References == {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1393226}} *{{Ballotpedia|Jane_Magnus-Stinson}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Larry J. Hebert Law Center]].{{FJC Bio|nid=1393796|inline=yes}} == Career == Milazzo began her career as an elementary school teacher. She then began working in 1986 as a paralegal for a Napoleonville, Louisiana law firm. In 1989, she shifted to being a law clerk while attending law school. From 1992 until 1998, she served as an associate at her family's law firm, and from 1998 until 2008, she was a partner in that firm. In 2008, Milazzo was elected a state district judge in Louisiana. === Federal judicial service === On March 16, 2011, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Milazzo to fill a seat on the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana that had been vacated by Judge [[Mary Ann Vial Lemmon]], who assumed [[senior status]] on January 1, 2011.{{Cite web | author=The White House: Office of the Press Secretary | url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2011/03/16/nominations-sent-senate | title=Nominations Sent to the Senate | date=March 16, 2011 | via=[[NARA|National Archives]] | work=[[whitehouse.gov]] | access-date=March 27, 2011}} On October 11, 2011, the [[United States Senate]] confirmed Milazzo by a 98–0 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1121/vote_112_1_00158.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Jane Margaret Triche-Milazzo, of Louisiana, to be U.S. District Judge)|website=United States Senate|date=October 11, 2011|access-date=May 30, 2023}} She received her judicial commission the following day. Milazzo was appointed to the bench under the name Jane Margaret Triche-Milazzo, but has since changed her name to Jane Margaret Triche Milazzo. == Personal life== Milazzo is the daughter of former Louisiana politician [[Risley C. Triche]] and Clara Triche of Napoleonville, Louisiana.{{Cite web |url=http://www.23rdjdc.org/DivisionD.aspx |title=23rd Judicial District Court of Louisiana - Honorable Jane Triche-Milazzo |access-date=2011-03-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110718210051/http://www.23rdjdc.org/DivisionD.aspx |archive-date=2011-07-18 |url-status=dead }} She is married to John W. Hall {{!}} District of Connecticut {{!}} United States District Court|website=www.ctd.uscourts.gov|access-date=2019-05-28}} ==Education and career== Born in [[Lowell, Massachusetts|Lowell]], [[Massachusetts]], Hall received an [[Bachelor of Arts|Artium Baccalaureus]] degree from [[Mount Holyoke College]] in 1970. She went on to earn a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[New York University School of Law]] three years later. After obtaining her J.D., Hall entered [[practice of law|private practice]] for two years. Then, she landed a position as a [[trial attorney]] in the [[United States Department of Justice Antitrust Division]], which she held until 1979. She was then a Special [[Assistant United States Attorney]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia|Eastern District of Virginia]] in 1979. From 1980 to 1997, she was in private practice in [[Hartford, Connecticut|Hartford]], [[Connecticut]]. ==Federal judicial service== Hall was nominated by President [[Bill Clinton]] on June 5, 1997, to a seat vacated by [[T. F. Gilroy Daly]]. She was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on September 11, 1997, and received her commission on September 18, 1997. She served as Chief Judge of the [[United States District Court for the District of Connecticut]] from September 2013 to September 2018. She assumed [[senior status]] on January 21, 2021. Hall was featured in the Serial podcast ''[[The Retrievals]]''.{{Cite web |date=2023-06-29 |title=The Retrievals on Apple Podcasts |url=https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/the-retrievals/id1691599042 |access-date=2023-07-25 |website=Apple Podcasts |language=en-US}} She presided over the sentencing of former nurse Donna Monticone, who stole hundreds of vials of fentanyl from patients at the Yale Reproductive Endocrinology and Infertility Lab, where she worked.{{Cite web |date=2021-05-25 |title=District of Connecticut {{!}} Former Nurse Sentenced for Tampering with Fentanyl Vials Intended for Patients at Fertility Clinic {{!}} United States Department of Justice |url=https://www.justice.gov/usao-ct/pr/former-nurse-sentenced-tampering-fentanyl-vials-intended-patients-fertility-clinic |access-date=2023-07-25 |website=www.justice.gov |language=en}} The fentanyl was supposed to be used to administer moderate sedation to patients undergoing egg retrievals, but Monticone used the fentanyl herself and replaced it with saline solution. As detailed in The Retrievals, Monticone attended a number of these egg retrieval procedures knowing the patients were being given saline solution instead of sedation and witnessing their cries of pain.{{Cite web |title=The Retrievals Episode 2 |url=https://the-retrievals.simplecast.com/episodes/episode-2-the-nurse-CfKVwl_z |access-date=2023-07-25 |website=the-retrievals.simplecast.com}} Despite numerous letters from victims detailing the immense physical and psychological pain Monticone caused, and despite sentencing guidelines that called for 4 to 5 years in prison, Hall only sentenced Monticone to four nonconsecutive weekends in prison. ==References== {{Reflist}} ==Sources== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1390496}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[T. [[Wayne State University Law School|Wayne State University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | footnotes = }} '''Janet Theresa Neff''' (born 1945) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Michigan]]. ==Early life and education== Neff was born in [[Wilkinsburg, Pennsylvania]]. She graduated from [[University of Pittsburgh]] with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in 1967 and later from [[Wayne State University Law School]] with a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1970. ==Career== Following law school graduation, Neff was an assistant city attorney for the city of [[Grand Rapids, Michigan]], from 1971 to 1973. She was in private practice in Michigan from 1973 to 1978 and from 1980 to 1988. She was a Commissioner, [[Michigan Supreme Court]] from 1978 to 1980. She became an [[assistant United States attorney]] of the U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Michigan in 1980. She was a judge on the [[Michigan Court of Appeals]] from 1989 to 2007. ===Federal judicial service=== Neff was nominated to the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Michigan]] by President [[George W. Bush]] on March 19, 2007, to a seat vacated by Judge [[David McKeague]].{{FJC Bio|nid=1392606|inline=yes}} Despite the blocking of her confirmation vote by U.S. Senator [[Sam Brownback]] from Kansas because she had attended a same-sex commitment ceremony,[https://www.reuters.com/article/us-usa-congress-judge/senate-rejects-brownbacks-concerns-about-judge-idUSN0931175220070709 Senate rejects Brownback's concerns about judge], ''[[Reuters]]'', July 9, 2007. Retrieved December 22, 2017. Neff was confirmed by the [[United States Senate|Senate]] on July 9, 2007, by an 83–4 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1101/vote_110_1_00240.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Janet T. Neff, of Michigan, to be U.S. District Judge)}} She received her commission on August 6, 2007. She assumed [[senior status]] on March 1, 2021. Neff took inactive senior status on October 1, 2024.{{Cite web|url=https://www.miwd.uscourts.gov/sites/miwd/files/Admin%20Order%2024-CA-079.pdf|title=IN THE MATTER OF REASSIGNMENT OF CASES ASSIGNED TO THE HONORABLE JANET T. NEFF|website=miwd.uscourts.gov|date=2024-10-01|access-date=2025-12-26}} ==Notable cases== In 1991, Neff said in the [[Michigan Court of Appeals]] that a refusal of lifesaving treatment had to be contemporaneous and informed in the case of [[Werth v. Taylor]].190 Mich. App. 141 (1991). In 2015, Neff dismissed a lawsuit against [[Eaton County, Michigan]]. The lawsuit was brought by the family of two murder victims, Michael and Terri Greene, who were murdered during a home invasion by an Eaton County jail inmate, Christopher Perrien, who was released by the jail each day to go to a work release job at a company that did not exist. The county failed to verify that the company was real before releasing Perrien on work release status.{{Cite web|last=Palmer|first=Ken|title=Judge tosses family's suit against Eaton Co., She was in private practice in [[Corpus Christi, Texas|Corpus Christi]], Texas from 1981 to 1993.{{cite book | title=Confirmation Hearings on Federal Appointments: Hearings Before the Committee on the Judiciary, United States Senate, One Hundred Third Congress, First Session on Confirmations of Appointees to the Federal Judiciary | publisher=U.S. Government Printing Office | issue=v. 4, pt. 2 | year=1995 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3zlqdRdXH0oC&pg=PA638 | access-date=October 11, 2021 | page=638}}{{cite web | title=Judge Janis Graham Jack is our 2016 Texan of the Year | website=Dallas Morning News Interactives | date=December 23, 2016 | url=http://interactives.dallasnews.com/2016/texan-of-the-year/ | access-date=October 12, 2021}} ===Federal judicial service=== On November 19, 1993, Jack was nominated by President [[Bill Clinton]]{{cite report |title=Judicial Nominations by President Clinton During the 103rd–106th Congresses |publisher=Congressional Research Service |date=September 20, 2006 |url=https://www.everycrsreport.com/reports/98-510.html|author=Denis Steven Rutkus |id=98-510 GOV|access-date=June 17, 2026}} to a new seat on the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas]] created by 104 Stat. 5089. She was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on March 10, 1994, and received her commission on March 11, 1994. She assumed [[senior status]] on June 1, 2011.{{FJC Bio|nid=1382701|inline=yes}} Jack left the court on October 14, 2025.{{Cite web|url=https://www.txs.uscourts.gov/page/history-district-judges|title=History of District Judges|website=Southern District of Texas|access-date=December 3, 2025}} ===Notable rulings=== In June 2005, Jack threw out about 9,000 suits against US Silica corp.Kimberly Strassel, "Ulizio: He fought the Tort Bar—and Won", ''[[Wall Street Journal]]'', May 2, 2009.{{cite report|title=Judicial Hellholes 2005 |publisher=American Tort Reform Association |date=2005|url=https://www.judicialhellholes.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/JH2005.pdf|access-date=June 17, 2026}} In 2015, Jack ruled in favor of plaintiffs in a class action suit (''M.D. v. Abbott'') on behalf of 10,000-plus foster children in care of the State of Texas, saying leaders were violating the constitutional rights of the children in its long-term foster care.{{cite web | title=M.D. v. Abbott | website=Civil Rights Litigation Clearinghouse | url=https://www.clearinghouse.net/detail.php?id=12435 | access-date=October 11, 2021}} With much of her ruling sustained on appeal, Jack continues to supervise the case as late as 2024, holding the State in contempt of court and often expressing "disgust" at the State of Texas’ failure to care for foster children.”Editorial: Righteous anger, disgust at treatment of foster kids,” San Antonio Express-News, October 17, 2020.{{cite web | last=Bohra | first=Neelam | title=Judge says Texas officials need to speed up foster care reforms | website=The Texas Tribune | date=February 9, 2021 | url=https://www.texastribune.org/2021/02/09/texas-foster-care-lawsuit-judge/ | access-date=October 11, 2021}}{{Cite web |last=Oxner |first=Reese |date=2022-03-30 |title=Judge loses trust in Texas' child abuse investigation of foster care facility and calls for federal inquiry |url=https://www.texastribune.org/2022/03/30/refuge-texas-rangers-federal-investigation/ |access-date=2022-03-31 |website=The Texas Tribune |language=en}} On October 11, 2024, however, the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit reversed her contempt order, held that the State of Texas had substantially complied with her previous orders, and removed her from the case.{{Cite web |date=October 11, 2024 |title=United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit |url=https://www.ca5.uscourts.gov/opinions/pub/24/24-40248.CV0.pdf |access-date=8 Oct 2025 |website=ca5.uscourts.gov}} ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1382701}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=Seat established by 104 Stat. 5089}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas]]}}|years=1994–2011}} {{s-aft|after=[[David S. {{nowrap|[[University of Notre Dame]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]])}} | website = | footnotes = }} '''Janis Lynn Sammartino''' (born April 24, 1950) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of California]]. ==Early life and education== Sammartino was born in [[Philadelphia]]. She graduated from [[Occidental College]] with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in 1972 and later from [[Notre Dame Law School]] at the [[University of Notre Dame]] with a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1975.{{FJC Bio|nid=1392626|inline=yes}} ==Legal career== Following law school graduation, Sammartino worked as a [[law clerk]] for [[Courts of Indiana|St. Joseph County Superior Court]] Judge Douglas Seely from 1975 to 1976. She was a deputy city attorney of [[San Diego]] City Attorney's Office from 1976 to 1994. Sammartino was a judge on the [[San Diego, California|San Diego]] [[State court (United States)|Municipal Court]] from 1994 to 1995. She was a judge on the [[San Diego County Superior Court]] from 1995 to 2007. ==Judicial career== Sammartino was nominated to the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of California]] by President [[George W. Bush]] on March 19, 2007, to a seat vacated by the death of Judge [[Judith Keep]]. She was confirmed by the [[United States Senate|Senate]] on September 10, 2007, on a 99–0 vote{{Cite web |date=March 19, 2007 |title=PN353 — 110th Congress (2007-2008) — Janis Lynn Sammartino — The Judiciary |url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/110th-congress/353 |access-date=April 15, 2024 |website=congress.gov}} and received her commission on September 21, 2007. ===Notable cases=== On May 17, 2017, Sammartino sentenced [[Rear Admiral]] Robert Gilbeau, the first active duty admiral ever convicted of a felony, to 18 months in prison for his involvement in the [[Fat Leonard scandal]], although Gilbeau will still be allowed to continue collecting his nearly $10,000 monthly pension.{{cite news|last1=Craig Whitlock|author-link=Craig Whitlock|last2=Tony Perry|title=Former admiral sentenced to 18 months in 'Fat Leonard' case|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/investigations/former-admiral-sentenced-to-18-months-in-fat-leonard-case/2017/05/17/1a11869c-3b06-11e7-a058-ddbb23c75d82_story.html|access-date=May 18, 2017|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|date=May 17, 2017}} ==References== {{Reflist}} ==Sources== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1392626}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Judith Keep]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of California]]}}|years=2007–present}} {{s-inc}} {{s-end}} {{United States 9th Circuit district judges}} {{Authority control}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Sammartino, Janis Lynn}} [[Category:1950 births]] [[Category:Living people]] [[Category:21st-century American women judges]] [[Category:California state court judges]] [[Category:Judges of the United States District Court for the Southern District of California]] [[Category:Lawyers from Philadelphia]] [[Category:Notre Dame Law School alumni]] [[Category:Occidental College alumni]] [[Category:Superior court judges in the United States]] [[Category:United States district court judges appointed by George W. '''Jasmine Hyejung  Yoon'''<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.martindale.com/attorney/jasmine-hyejung-yoon-5048892/|title=Jasmine Hyejung Yoon Profile | Washington, DC Lawyer | Martindale.com|website=www.martindale.com}}</ref> (born 1980)<ref name="Questionnaire">{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/yoon_sjq.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=February 7, 2024}}</ref> is an American lawyer and jurist serving as a [[United States federal judge|U.S. district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Virginia]]. She was appointed in 2024 by President [[Joe Biden]]. She previously was the vice president of [[Business Ethics|Corporate Integrity, Ethics, and Investigations]] at [[Capital One]].

== Education ==
Yoon received her [[Bachelor of Arts]] from the [[University of Virginia]] in 2003, where she was a [[Jefferson Scholarship|Jefferson Scholar]], and her [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Virginia School of Law]] in 2006.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2024/01/10/president-biden-names-forty-fourth-round-of-judicial-nominees/|title=President Biden Names Forty-Fourth Round of Judicial Nominees|website=[[White House]]|date=January 10, 2024|access-date=January 10, 2024}} {{PD-notice}}</ref>

== Career ==
From 2006 to 2009, she was an associate at [[Crowell & Moring]] LLP in [[Washington, D.C.]] in its White Collar and Regulatory Enforcement group. From 2009 to 2010, she served as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[James C. Cacheris]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia]]. From 2010 to 2016, Yoon was an assistant U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia as a member of the [[White Collar Crime]]s and [[political corruption|Public Corruption]] Unit.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.law.virginia.edu/news/201107/jasmine-yoon-06-fights-financial-fraud|title=Jasmine Yoon '06 Fights Financial Fraud|website=UVA Law|date=July 7, 2011|access-date=January 10, 2024}}</ref> From 2019 to 2022, Yoon was an Interim University Counsel and Associate University Counsel at the [[University of Virginia]] in [[Charlottesville, Virginia|Charlottesville]]. From 2022 to 2024, she was the Vice President of Corporate Integrity, Ethics, and Investigations at [[Capital One]].

=== Federal judicial service ===
On January 10, 2024, President [[Joe Biden]] announced his intent to nominate Yoon as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Virginia]]. On February 1, 2024, President Biden nominated Yoon to a seat being vacated by Judge [[Michael F. Urbanski]], who subsequently assumed [[senior status]] on July 4, 2024.<ref>{{Cite press release |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |date=February 3, 2024 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2024/02/03/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-136/}}</ref> On February 8, 2024, a hearing on her nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Nominations|date=February 7, 2024|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/committee-activity/hearings/02/08/2024/nominations}}</ref> On March 7, 2024, her nomination was reported out of committee by a 14–7 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/2024-03-07_-_ebm_-_results.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – March 7, 2024|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=March 7, 2024}}</ref> On March 11, 2024, the [[United States Senate]] invoked [[cloture]] on her nomination by a 52–38 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1182/vote_118_2_00085.htm|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Jasmine Hyejung Yoon to be U.S. District Judge for the Western District of Virginia)|website=United States Senate|date=March 11, 2024|access-date=March 11, 2024}}</ref> On March 12, 2024, her nomination was confirmed by a 55–41 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1182/vote_118_2_00086.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Jasmine Hyejung Yoon, of Virginia, to be United States District Judge for the Western District of Virginia)|website=United States Senate|date=March 12, 2024|access-date=March 12, 2024}}</ref> She  received her judicial commission on July 8, 2024.<ref>{{FJC Bio|nid=13761546|inline=yes}}</ref> Yoon became the first Asian American judge to serve on the Western District of Virginia.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/biden-names-first-6-new-judicial-nominees-2024-2024-01-10/|title=Biden names first 6 new judicial nominees of 2024|website=Reuters|date=January 10, 2024|access-date=January 10, 2024}}</ref>  On October 4, 2024, a formal investiture ceremony was held at the University of Virginia School of Law.<ref>{{Cite tweet |number=1844065287831945293 |user=UVALaw |title=U.S. Judge Jasmine Yoon’s investiture ceremony took place at #UVALaw last week. Yoon, the first Asian American federal judge in Virginia, posed with her 2006 classmates, including Dean Leslie Kendrick ’06 and U.S. Attorney Chris Kavanaugh ’06. |date=October 9, 2024 |access-date=October 30, 2024}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Yoon is married to [[Christopher R. Kavanaugh]]. who served as [[United States Attorney]] for the Western District of Virginia from 2021 to 2024.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://roanoke.com/news/local/government-politics/jasmine-yoon-will-be-nominated-for-western-district-judgeship/article_85524fea-afbc-11ee-b7d4-8376bceabca1.html|title=Jasmine Yoon will be nominated for Western District judgeship|website=The Roanoke Times|date=January 10, 2024|access-date=January 10, 2024}}</ref>

[[File:National Defense Service Medal ribbon.svg|23px]] [[National Defense Service Medal]]}} }} '''Jason Kenneth Pulliam''' (born 1971) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Texas]]. == Education == Pulliam received a [[Bachelor of Arts]], ''[[cum laude]]'', and a [[Master of Arts]] from [[Brooklyn College]]. He received his [[Juris Doctor]], ''cum laude'', from the [[Thurgood Marshall School of Law]] at [[Texas Southern University]].[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-judicial-nominees-united-states-attorney-nominee-united-states-marshal-nominees/ "President Donald J. Trump Announces Judicial Nominees, a United States Attorney Nominee, and United States Marshal Nominees" White House, March 1, 2019] {{PD-notice}} == Career == Pulliam served in the [[United States Marine Corps]] and was a Judge Advocate from 2000 to 2004. From 2017 to 2019, Pulliam was of counsel with Prichard Young, where his practice focused on complex civil litigation matters. === Judicial career === Pulliam served as a Justice on [[Texas Courts of Appeals|Texas' Fourth Court of Appeals]] after being appointed to the court by Governor [[Rick Perry]] on January 8, 2015.{{cite web |url=https://www.mysanantonio.com/news/local/article/Governor-appoints-local-judge-to-4th-Court-of-6002989.php |title=Governor appoints local judge to 4th Court of Appeals |last=Casady |first=Michelle |date=January 9, 2015 |website=San Antonio Express-News |access-date=March 2, 2019}} His term ended on December 31, 2016. He also previously served as a judge for the [[Bexar County, Texas|Bexar County]] Court at Law,{{cite web |url=http://jasonforjudge.com/administrative-judge-for-the-county-courts/ |title=Administrative Judge for the County Courts |date=July 9, 2017 |language=en-US |access-date=March 2, 2019 |archive-date=March 2, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190302210357/http://jasonforjudge.com/administrative-judge-for-the-county-courts/ |url-status=dead }} handling both civil and criminal matters. ==== Federal judicial service ==== On March 1, 2019, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to nominate Pulliam to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] for the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Texas]]. President Trump nominated Pulliam to the seat vacated by [[Sam Sparks]], who assumed [[senior status]] on December 31, 2017. On March 5, 2019, his nomination was sent to the Senate.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/ten-nominations-one-withdrawal-sent-senate/ "Ten Nominations and One Withdrawal Sent to the Senate", White House, March 5, 2019] On May 22, 2019, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web |title=Nominations |date=May 22, 2019 |publisher=[[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]] |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/committee-activity/hearings/05/22/2019/nominations}} On June 20, 2019, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 12–10 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%20June%2020%202019.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – June 20, 2019|publisher=Senate Judiciary Committee}} On July 30, 2019, the [[United States Senate]] invoked [[cloture]] on his nomination by a 54–34 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=1&vote=00248|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Jason K. Pulliam to be United States District Judge for the Western District of Texas)|website=United States Senate|date=July 30, 2019}} On July 31, 2019, his nomination was confirmed by a 54–36 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=1&vote=00256|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Jason K. Pulliam, of Texas, to be U.S. District Judge for the Western District of Texas)|website=United States Senate|date=July 31, 2019}} He received his judicial commission on August 5, 2019.{{FJC Bio|nid=6840711|inline=yes}} == Personal life == On August 23, 2012, Pulliam and court [[bailiff]] Charles Cook witnessed a mugging and apprehended two suspects on foot until police arrived. the two occupants until police arrived.{{cite news|last=Tedesco|first=John|date=August 24, She received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[Wellesley College]] in 1968, then a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Washington University School of Law]] in 1971, and a [[Master of Laws]] from [[Yale Law School]] in 1982. She was an attorney with the Civil Rights Division of the [[United States Department of Justice]] in [[Washington, D.C.]] from 1971 to 1973. She was then an [[assistant United States attorney]] for the Eastern District of Missouri from 1973 to 1978. She was corporate counsel to [[Southwestern Bell Telephone Company]] in St. Louis from 1978 to 1981.{{FJC Bio|nid=1381736|inline=yes}} == Judicial career == ===State judicial service=== In 1982, Hamilton became a circuit judge for Missouri's Twenty-second Judicial Circuit, and in 1988, she was elevated to the [[Missouri Court of Appeals]], Eastern District. During her service as a state court judge, Hamilton was an adjunct professor, teaching at [[Saint Louis University School of Law|Saint Louis University Law School]] from 1986 to 1987, and in 1989, and at Washington University School of Law from 1987 to 1992. ===Federal judicial service=== On August 3, 1990, President [[George H. W. Bush]] nominated Hamilton to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri]] vacated by Judge [[John Francis Nangle]]. She was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on September 28, 1990, and received her commission on October 1, 1990. She served as Chief Judge from 1995 to 2002. She took [[senior status]] on July 1, 2013 and inactive senior status in December 2022.{{Cite web|url=https://www.moed.uscourts.gov/sites/moed/files/documents/publications/2022_Jul_Dec_Report.pdf|title=Reviewing July—December 2022 & Looking Ahead at Events to Come in January—June 2023|website=moed.uscourts.gov|date=2023-01-01|access-date=2026-01-09}} ==References== {{Reflist}} ==Sources== * {{FJC Bio|nid=1381736}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[John Francis Nangle]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri]]}}|years=1990–2013}} {{s-aft|after=[[Ronnie L. [[Yale Law School|Yale University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Jeannette Anne Vargas''' (born 1973){{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/vargas_sjq.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=April 17, 2024}}{{Cite press release |title=Manhattan U.S. Attorney Preet Bharara Announces Appointments in Civil Division |date=September 9, 2010 |publisher=U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York |url=https://www.justice.gov/archive/usao/nys/pressreleases/September10/civildivisionappointmentspr.pdf |access-date=March 21, 2024}} is an American lawyer who has served as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]] since 2024. She previously served as an [[assistant United States attorney]] in the [[United States Attorney for the Southern District of New York|U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York]] from 2002 to 2024. ==Early life== Vargas earned a [[Bachelor of Arts]], ''[[Latin honors#magna cum laude|magna cum laude]]'', from [[Harvard College]] in 1995 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Yale Law School]] in 2000.{{Cite press release |title=President Biden Names Forty-Seventh Round of Judicial Nominees and Announces One New Nominee to Serve as U.S. Marshal |date=March 20, 2024 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2024/03/20/president-biden-names-forty-seventh-round-of-judicial-nominees-and-announces-one-new-nominee-to-serve-as-u-s-marshal/ |access-date=March 20, 2024}} {{PD-notice}} == Career == From 2000 to 2001, Vargas worked as an associate at [[Simpson Thacher & Bartlett]] in [[New York City]]. From 2001 to 2002, she was a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Sonia Sotomayor]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit]]. From 2002 to 2024, she served as an assistant United States attorney in the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York. In that role, from 2010 to 2014, she served as chief of the Tax and Bankruptcy Unit, from 2014 to 2016, she was senior trial counsel and she served as deputy chief in the Civil Division from 2016 to 2024. === Federal judicial service === Vargas was recommended to the Biden administration by Senator [[Kirsten Gillibrand]].{{Cite press release |title=Gillibrand Announces Her Recommendation For U.S. District Court For The Southern District Of New York, Jeannette Vargas, Has Been Nominated By President Biden |date=March 20, 2024 |publisher=Senator Gillibrand Press Release Office |url=https://www.gillibrand.senate.gov/news/press/release/gillibrand-announces-her-recommendation-for-u-s-district-court-for-the-southern-district-of-new-york-jeannette-vargas-has-been-nominated-by-president-biden/ |access-date=March 21, 2024}} On March 20, 2024, President [[Joe Biden]] announced his intent to nominate Vargas to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]]. On March 21, 2024, her nomination was sent to the Senate. President Biden nominated Vargas to the seat vacated by Judge [[Paul G. Gardephe]], who assumed [[senior status]] on August 9, 2023.{{Cite press release |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |date=March 21, 2024|publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2024/03/21/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-141/}} On April 17, 2024, a hearing on her nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web|title=Nominations|date=April 16, 2024|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/committee-activity/hearings/04/17/2024/nominations}} On May 9, 2024, her nomination was reported out of committee by an 11–10 [[party-line vote]].{{Cite press release |title=Senate Judiciary Committee Advances the Protecting Older Americans Act, Four Judicial Nominations to the Full Senate |date=May 9, 2024 |publisher=United States Senate Judiciary Committee |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/press/releases/senate-judiciary-committee-advances-the-protecting-older-americans-act-four-judicial-nominations-to-the-full-senate |access-date=May 9, 2024}} On September 10, 2024, the [[United States Senate]] invoked [[cloture]] on her nomination by a 52–43 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1182/vote_118_2_00233.htm|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Jeannette A. Vargas, of New York, to be U.S. District Judge for the Southern District of New York)|website=United States Senate|date=September 10, 2024|access-date=September 10, 2024}} Later that day, her nomination was confirmed by a 51–43 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1182/vote_118_2_00234.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Jeannette A. Vargas, of New York, to be U.S. District Judge for the Southern District of New York)|website=United States Senate|date=September 10, 2024|access-date=September 10, 2024}} She received her judicial commission on November 6, 2024.{{FJC Bio|nid=13761858|inline=yes}} == Notable rulings == === DOGE ruling === In response to a February 2025 lawsuit filed by Attorney General [[Letitia James]] of New York, Vargas issued an injunction prohibiting [[Department of Government Efficiency|DOGE]] from accessing Treasury systems.{{Cite news |last=Meko |first=Hurubie |date=2025-02-22 |title=Federal Judge Banishes Musk's DOGE Aides From Treasury Dept. Systems |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/02/21/nyregion/sdny-doge-elon-musk-treasury-injunction.html |access-date=2025-02-23 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} On April 11, 2025 she decided in favor of the [[Second presidency of Donald Trump|Trump administration]]. The New York Times wrote: "Judge Vargas acknowledged that her preliminary injunction had been ordered in part because of what the court identified as issues with the Treasury’s “hasty implementation and gaps in training” for the DOGE team members. "However, 'based on existing record,' Judge Vargas wrote that the mitigation, training and vetting procedures that the government has detailed in its filings are adequate to satisfy her concerns."{{Cite news |last=Meko |first=Hurubie |date=2025-04-11 |title=Judge Says One DOGE Member Can Access Sensitive Treasury Dept. Data |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/04/11/nyregion/doge-treasury-lawsuit.html |access-date=2025-04-13 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} === Drake-Kendrick Lamar defamation case === {{Main|Drake–Kendrick Lamar feud|Not Like Us#Legal actions}} In 2024, rappers [[Drake (musician)|Drake]] and [[Kendrick Lamar]]—who were both signed to the same record company, [[Universal Music Group]] (UMG)—exchanged aggressive [[diss tracks]]. In particular, Lamar's "[[Not Like Us]]" described Drake as a "certified pedophile." Drake sued UMG for [[defamation]], alleging that Lamar's accusations were false and that UMG knew they were false, but boosted the visibility of Lamar's accusations to make money at Drake's expense.{{Cite news |title=Drake's Lawyers Cite Kendrick's Halftime Show in Defamation Lawsuit Over 'Not Like Us' |url=https://www.billboard.com/pro/drake-lawyers-kendrick-lamar-super-bowl-halftime-show-lawsuit/}}{{Cite web |last=Monroe |first=Jazz |date=2025-01-15 |title=Drake Federally Sues Universal Music Group Over Kendrick Lamar's “Defamatory” Diss Song “Not Like Us” |url=https://pitchfork.com/news/drake-withdraws-legal-action-against-spotify-and-universal-music-group-over-not-like-us-streams/ |access-date=2025-10-11 |website=Pitchfork |language=en-US}} In October 2025, Judge Vargas granted UMG's motion to dismiss the lawsuit. She held that New York State defamation law disfavored legal liability for statements of opinion and would not allow Drake to sue UMG for publishing and amplifying Lamar’s opinion.{{Cite news |date=2025-10-09 |title=Judge Dismisses Drake's Lawsuit Over Kendrick Lamar's 'Not Like Us' |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/10/09/arts/music/drake-kendrick-lamar-not-like-us-lawsuit-dismissed.html |access-date=2025-10-11 |work=The New York Times |language=en}}{{Cite web |date=2025-10-10 |title=Drake's lawsuit over Kendrick Lamar diss track Not Like Us is dismissed |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cd9y104g7kno |access-date=2025-10-11 |website=www.bbc.com |language=en-GB}} She concluded that in context, Lamar's lyrics were opinions, even if they were worded similarly to factual assertions, as a [[Reasonable person|reasonable listener]] would understand that rap battles are not "fact-checked verifiable content." For support, she noted that Drake had previously dared Lamar to accuse him in "[[Taylor Made Freestyle]]", and had also accused Lamar of domestic violence. She dismissed Drake's argument that some [[social media]] commenters thought Lamar was stating facts, because "[i]n a world in which billions of people are active online, support for almost any proposition, no matter how farfetched, fantastical or unreasonable, can be found with little effort."{{Cite web |last=Vargas |first=Jeannette |date=2025-10-09 |title=Opinion and Order: Aubrey Drake Graham v. UMG Recordings, Inc. |url=https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.nysd.635046/gov.uscourts.nysd.635046.96.0.pdf |access-date=2025-10-11 |website=CourtListener |publisher=U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York}} == See also == * [[List of Hispanic and Latino American jurists]] == References == {{Reflist}} == External links == *{{FJC Bio|nid=13761858}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Paul G.
