'''Jerry Wayne Blackwell''' (born 1962)<ref name="Questionnaire">{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Blackwell%20SJQ%20Public%206-28-22.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary |access-date=July 26, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220726194008/https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Blackwell%20SJQ%20Public%206-28-22.pdf |archive-date=July 26, 2022 |url-status=dead}}</ref> is an American lawyer who serves as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Minnesota]]. Before becoming a judge, he was one of the prosecutors in the [[trial of Derek Chauvin]] for the murder of [[George Floyd]].

== Education ==

On a [[Morehead-Cain Scholarship]], Blackwell earned a [[Bachelor of Science]] from the [[University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill]] in 1984. He received a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of North Carolina School of Law]] in 1987.<ref name="WHBio">{{Cite web |date=June 15, 2022 |title=President Biden Names Nineteenth Round of Judicial Nominees |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/06/15/president-biden-names-nineteenth-round-of-judicial-nominees/ |access-date=June 15, 2022 |website=The White House |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Jerry W. Blackwell |url=https://www.top100civildefenselitigators.com/listing/jerry-w-blackwell-2/ |access-date=June 15, 2022 |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Career ==

From 1987 to 2022, Blackwell was a lawyer in private practice.<ref name="FJCBio">{{FJC Bio|nid=12916001|inline=yes}}</ref> He worked as a partner at [[Robins Kaplan LLP]] in [[Minneapolis]] from 1987 to 1996 and Nilan Johnson Lewis from 1996 to 2000. From 2000 to 2006, he was a partner at Blackwell Igbanugo in [[Edina, Minnesota]],<ref name="split">Sam Black, [https://www.bizjournals.com/twincities/stories/2006/11/20/story3.html "Disputes lead to split of top black-owned law firm"], ''[[Minneapolis/St. Paul Business Journal]]'', November 19, 2006. {{Subscription required}}</ref> one of the nation's largest Black-owned law firms before it was dissolved.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Wagner |first=Rose |date=June 15, 2022 |title=Seven new judicial nominees put Biden over the 100-pick marker |url=https://www.courthousenews.com/seven-new-judicial-nominees-put-biden-over-the-100-pick-marker/ |access-date=June 15, 2022 |website=www.courthousenews.com}}</ref> In 2006, he co-founded the law firm Blackwell Burke in Minneapolis.<ref name="split" /><ref name="WHBio" />

=== Notable cases ===

During his career, Blackwell represented [[Prince (musician)|Prince]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Prince: 5 years after his death, how the Purple One lives on |url=https://www.startribune.com/prince-5-years-after-his-death-his-legacy-overstuffed-vault-superfans-critics-paisley-park/600045087/ |access-date=July 19, 2022 |website=Star Tribune}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=The Prince 'Purple House' in Chanhassen is leveled |url=https://prince.org/msg/7/43129 |access-date=July 19, 2022 |website=prince.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Voruganti |first=Harsh |date=July 18, 2022 |title=Jerry Blackwell – Nominee to the U.S. District Court for the District of Minnesota |url=https://vettingroom.org/2022/07/18/jerry-blackwell/ |access-date=July 19, 2022 |website=The Vetting Room |language=en}}</ref>

In 2020, Blackwell obtained a posthumous pardon of Max Mason, a Black man falsely convicted in [[Duluth, Minnesota]], of raping a white woman in 1920.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Shropshire |first=Terry |date=March 30, 2021 |title=Who is Jerry Blackwell, the prosecutor in Derek Chauvin's murder trial? |url=https://rollingout.com/2021/03/30/who-is-jerry-blackwell-the-prosecutor-in-derek-chauvins-murder-trial/ |access-date=July 19, 2022 |website=Rolling Out |language=en-US}}</ref>

Blackwell was a special assistant state attorney general for the prosecution during the [[trial of Derek Chauvin]], the Minneapolis police officer who murdered [[George Floyd]].<ref>{{Cite news |title=Biden's Planned Nominee Would Be DC Circuit's First Latino (2) |url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/biden-plans-to-nominate-d-c-circuits-first-latino |website=news.bloomberglaw.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Jerry W. Blackwell, prosecutor in the Derek Chauvin trial, to speak with Jones and Lovelace on Race, Policing, and Activism |url=https://law.duke.edu/news/jerry-w-blackwell-prosecutor-derek-chauvin-trial-speak-jones-and-lovelace-race-policing-and/ |access-date=June 15, 2022 |website=Duke University School of Law |language=en}}</ref> Blackwell served as a ''[[pro bono]]'' prosecutor and delivered the opening statement and closing argument for the prosecution.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://news.yahoo.com/biden-nominates-prosecutor-helped-convict-164546942.html | title=Biden nominates prosecutor who helped convict Derek Chauvin to become a federal judge | date=June 15, 2022 }}</ref> In closing, he said to the jury, "You were told, for example, that Mr. Floyd died because his heart was too big. You heard that testimony. Now having seen all the evidence, having heard all the evidence, you know the truth. And the truth of the matter is that the reason George Floyd is dead is because Mr. Chauvin's heart was too small."<ref>{{Cite web |title=Derek Chauvin's 'heart was too small,' prosecutor says in last word to jury |url=https://news.yahoo.com/derek-chauvin-heart-too-small-213400241.html |access-date=July 19, 2022 |website=news.yahoo.com |date=April 19, 2021 |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Federal judicial service ===

On June 15, 2022, President [[Joe Biden]] nominated Blackwell to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Minnesota]] to the seat vacated by Judge [[Susan Richard Nelson]], who assumed [[senior status]] on December 31, 2021.<ref>{{Cite press release|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate|date=June 15, 2022|publisher=The White House|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/06/15/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-71/}}</ref> On July 27, 2022, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Nominations|date=July 26, 2022|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/07/27/2022/nominations}}</ref> On September 15, 2022, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 13–8 vote, Senator [[Thom Tillis]] "passed" on the vote.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/EBM%20Results%20-%202022-09-15.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – September 15, 2022|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=September 15, 2022}}</ref> On December 1, 2022, the [[United States Senate]] invoked cloture on his nomination by a 54–42 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1172/vote_117_2_00368.htm|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Jerry W. Blackwell to be U.S. District Judge for the District of Minnesota)|date=December 1, 2022|website=United States Senate|access-date=December 1, 2022}}</ref> On December 7, 2022, his nomination was confirmed by a 51–43 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|date=December 7, 2022|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Jerry W. Blackwell, of Minnesota, to be United States District Judge for the District of Minnesota)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1172/vote_117_2_00383.htm|access-date=December 7, 2022|website=United States Senate}}</ref> He received his judicial commission on December 20, 2022.<ref name="FJCBio" />

== Personal life ==

Blackwell is a hobby farmer and beekeeper.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Meet the prosecutor who helped convict Derek Chauvin |url=https://www.mprnews.org/story/2021/05/24/meditation-coach-beekeeper-prosecutor-meet-the-man-who-helped-convict-derek-chauvin |access-date=July 19, 2022 |website=MPR News |date=May 24, 2021 |language=en}}</ref>

[[Yale Law School|Yale University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | occupation = | profession = | known_for = | salary = | net_worth = | cabinet = | committees = | portfolio = | awards = | signature = | signature_alt = | website = | footnotes = }} '''Jesse Matthew Furman''' (born 1972) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]]. == Early life and education == Furman is the son of psychologist [[Gail Furman|Gail (née Gorman)]] and real estate developer [[Jay Furman]].{{Cite web|title=In Memoriam: Jay Furman, 1942-2015 |publisher=[[New York University School of Law]] News|date=January 5, 2015 |url=http://www.law.nyu.edu/news/memoriam-jay-furman }} He earned a [[Bachelor of Arts]] from [[Harvard College]] in 1994 and then was a [[Henry Fellowship|Henry Fellow]] at the [[University of Oxford]] from 1994 to 1995.{{Cite web | author=White House: Office of the [[White House Press Secretary|Press Secretary]] | url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2011/06/07/president-obama-nominates-four-united-states-district-court | title=President Obama Nominates Four to the United States District Court | date=June 7, 2011 | via=[[NARA|National Archives]] | work=[[whitehouse.gov]] | access-date=June 8, 2011}} He received a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Yale Law School]] in 1998. From 1998 to 1999, Furman served as a [[law clerk]] for then United States District Judge and future [[United States Attorney General]] [[Michael Mukasey]]. From 1999 to 2000, he clerked for [[United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit]] Judge [[José A. Cabranes]].{{cite web |title=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/JesseFurman-PublicQuestionnaire.pdf |website=judiciary.senate.gov |access-date=June 4, 2024}} From 2002 to 2003, he clerked for Associate Justice [[David Souter]].{{FJC Bio|nid=1393896|inline=yes}} == Career == Furman worked as a lawyer at the [[law firm]] Wiggin & Dana from 2000 to 2002 and again from 2003 to 2004. In 2004, he became a federal prosecutor in the Southern District of New York, where he served as an [[Assistant United States Attorney]]. From 2007 to 2009, he worked in the office of the United States Attorney General as Counselor to the Attorney General. A 2005 ''[[New York Observer]]'' article named him as a potential future Supreme Court nominee.{{cite news |first=Anna |last=Schneider-Mayerson |title=The Little Supremes |url=http://www.observer.com/node/51498 |work=[[The New York Observer]] |date=2005-11-03 |access-date=2015-06-10 |archive-date=October 13, 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081013062520/http://www.observer.com/node/51498 }} === Federal judicial service === On June 7, 2011, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Furman to a seat on the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York that had been vacated by Judge [[Alvin Hellerstein]], who assumed [[senior status]] in January 2011.{{Cite web| author=The White House: Office of the Press Secretary|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2011/06/07/nominations-sent-senate|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate|date=June 7, 2011|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|access-date=June 8, 2011}} On September 15, 2011, the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] reported his nomination to the Senate floor by a [[voice vote]]. On February 15, 2012, Senate Majority Leader [[Harry Reid]] filed [[cloture]] on Furman's nomination.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/galleries/pdcl/|title=U.S. Senate Periodical Press Gallery|access-date=2012-08-21 |url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120502100722/https://www.senate.gov/galleries/pdcl/|archive-date=2012-05-02 }} The Senate vitiated the cloture motion on February 16 and confirmed Furman on February 17, by a 62–34 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=112&session=2&vote=00021|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Jesse M. Furman, of New York, to be United States District Judge)|website=www.senate.gov}} He received his commission the same day. ===Notable cases=== {{Main|2020 United States Census|Department of Commerce v. New York|Detention of Mahmoud Khalil}} On March 24, 2018, [[United States Secretary of Commerce]] [[Wilbur Ross]] announced his decision to add a question about citizenship status to the [[2020 United States Census|2020 Census]] questionnaire, asserting that it was necessary to help the [[United States Department of Justice|Justice Department]] enforce the [[Voting Rights Act of 1965]].{{cite web |last1=Hansi Lo Wang |title=How The 2020 Census Citizenship Question Ended Up In Court |url=https://www.npr.org/2018/11/04/661932989/how-the-2020-census-citizenship-question-ended-up-in-court |website=NPR.org |access-date=1 April 2020}} Two groups of plaintiffs filed lawsuits in the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]] to block the question.{{cite web |last1=Hansi Lo Wang |title=More Than 2 Dozen States, Cities Sue To Block Census Citizenship Question |url=https://www.npr.org/2018/04/03/599159295/17-states-7-cities-sue-to-remove-2020-census-citizenship-question |website=NPR.org|date=3 April 2018 }} The cases were assigned to Furman, who rejected the plaintiffs' claim that adding the question violated the [[Article One of the United States Constitution#Clause 3: Apportionment of Representatives and taxes|Enumeration Clause]] of the U.S. Constitution but held that Ross's decision violated the [[Administrative Procedure Act (United States)|Administrative Procedure Act]] and that the Voting-Rights-Act-enforcement rationale was a pretext designed to conceal the true reasons for adding the question.{{cite web |last1=Hansi Lo Wang |title=Judge Orders Trump Administration To Remove 2020 Census Citizenship Question |url=https://www.npr.org/2019/01/15/671283852/judge-orders-trump-administration-to-remove-2020-census-citizenship-question |website=NPR.org |access-date=1 April 2020}} Furman entered an order blocking implementation of Ross's decision. On June 27, 2019, the Supreme Court affirmed Furman's order, agreeing that the Voting-Rights-Act-enforcement rationale was pretextual.{{cite news |last1=Liptak |first1=Adam |title=Supreme Court Leaves Census Question on Citizenship in Doubt |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/06/27/us/politics/census-citizenship-question-supreme-court.html |website=[[The New York Times]] |date=27 June 2019 |access-date=1 April 2020}} The Court's decision left open the possibility that Ross could try again to add the citizenship question to the 2020 Census, but the Trump administration did not make a second attempt.{{cite web |last1=Hansi Lo Wang |title=Trump Backs Off Census Citizenship Question Fight |url=https://www.npr.org/2019/07/11/739858115/trump-expected-to-renew-push-for-census-citizenship-question-with-executive-acti |website=NPR.org |access-date=1 April 2020}} On March 10, 2025, Furman later, Furman granted Khalil two [[attorney-client privilege|attorney-client-privileged]] phone calls, but also ruled that he would remain detained.{{cite Jessica G. L. Clarke:
{{Short description|American judge (born 1983)}} {{Infobox judge | name = Jessica Clarke | image = Judge Clarke's Photo.jpg | office = Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]] | appointer = [[List of federal judges appointed by Joe Biden|Joe Biden]] | term_start = April 20, 2023 | term_end = | predecessor = [[Colleen McMahon]] | successor = | birth_name = Jessica Gloria Lynn Clarke | birth_date = {{birth year and age|1983}} | birth_place = [[Akron]], [[Ohio]], U.S. | death_date = | death_place = | education = [[Northwestern University]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|BA]])
[[Ohio State University Moritz College of Law|Ohio State University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Jessica Gloria Lynn Clarke''' (born 1983){{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Clarke%20SJQ%20Public%20Final%20for%20Box1.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=January 11, 2022}} is an American lawyer from [[New York (state)|New York]] who serves as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]]. == Education == Clarke received her [[Bachelor of Arts]] from [[Northwestern University]] in 2005 and her [[Juris Doctor]], ''[[cum laude]]'', from the [[Ohio State University Moritz College of Law]] in 2008.{{Cite press release |title=President Biden Names Eleventh Round of Judicial Nominees |date=December 15, 2021 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/12/15/president-biden-names-eleventh-round-of-judicial-nominees/ |access-date=December 15, 2021}} {{PD-notice}} == Career == Clarke began her law career as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Solomon Oliver Jr.]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Ohio]] from 2008 to 2010. From 2010 to 2016, she served as a trial attorney in the Housing & Civil Enforcement Section of the [[United States Department of Justice Civil Rights Division|Civil Rights Division of the United States Department of Justice]]. She then worked at the [[boutique law firm]] Emery Celli Brinckerhoff Abady Ward & Maazel LLP, first as an associate from 2016 to 2018 and then as [[of counsel]] from 2018 to 2019. From 2019 to 2023, she served as chief of the Civil Rights Bureau at the New York State Office of Attorney General under [[Letitia James]], overseeing the bureau's work on violations of civil rights law in New York.{{Cite web|url=https://www.huffpost.com/entry/chuck-schumer-judicial-nominees-biden_n_612f8a5fe4b05f53eda226f0|title = Chuck Schumer Recommends 3 Progressive Women for Federal Judgeships|date = September 2021}} === Federal judicial service === On December 15, 2021, President [[Joe Biden]] nominated Clarke to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]] to a seat vacated by Judge [[Colleen McMahon]], who assumed [[senior status]] on April 21, 2021.{{Cite press release|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate|date=December 15, 2021|publisher=The White House|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/12/15/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-52/|access-date=December 15, 2021}} On January 12, 2022, a hearing on her nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web|title=Nominations|date=January 11, 2022|publisher=[[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]]|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/01/05/2022/nominations}} During her hearing, Republican senators questioned her over her role in an investigation related to the New York City police response to [[George Floyd protests]]. James recommended that New York City decriminalize minor infractions to reduce "negative contact with the police, particularly in communities of color."{{Cite web|last=Raymond|first=Nate|title=U.S. Senate confirms civil rights lawyer to New York federal bench|url=https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/us-senate-confirms-civil-rights-lawyer-new-york-federal-bench-2023-03-16/|publisher=Reuters|date=March 16, 2023}} On February 10, 2022, the committee failed to report her nomination by an 11–11 vote.{{cite web|last1=Wagner|first1=Rose|title=Three judicial nominees make it through blue-slip debacle and out of committee|url=https://www.courthousenews.com/three-judicial-nominees-make-it-through-blue-slip-debacle-and-out-of-committee/|website=Courthouse News Service|access-date=12 February 2022}}{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/EBM%20Results%20-%202022-02-10.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – February 10, 2022|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=February 24, 2022}} On June 23, 2022, the [[United States Senate]] discharged the committee from further consideration of her nomination by a 50–49 vote.{{Cite web|date=June 22, 2022|title=On the Motion (Motion to Discharge Jessica G. L. Clarke to be U.S. District Judge for the Southern District of New York from the Committee on the Judiciary)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1172/vote_117_2_00239.htm |access-date=June 23, 2022|publisher=United States Senate|location=Washington, D.C.}} On January 3, 2023, her nomination was returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]]; she was renominated later the same day.{{Cite press release|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate|date=January 3, 2023|publisher=The White House|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2023/01/03/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-91/}} On February 9, 2023, her nomination was reported out of committee by an 11–10 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/2023-02-09%20-%20EBM%20-%20Results.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – February 9, 2023|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=February 9, 2023}} On March 16, 2023, the Senate invoked cloture on her nomination by a 49–45 vote.{{Cite web|date=March 16, 2023|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Jessica G.L. Clarke to be U.S. District Judge for the Southern District of New York)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00060.htm|access-date=March 16, 2023|website=United States Senate}} Later that day, her nomination was confirmed by a 48–43 vote.{{Cite web|date=March 16, 2023|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Jessica G.L. Clarke, of New York, to be U.S. District Judge for the Southern District of New York)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00062.htm|access-date=March 16, 2023|website=United States Senate}} She received her judicial commission on April 20, 2023.{{FJC Bio|nid=13408976|inline=yes}} == See also == * [[List of African-American federal judges]] * [[List of African-American jurists]] * [[Joe Biden judicial appointment controversies]] == References == {{Reflist}} == External links == *{{FJC Bio|nid=13408976}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Colleen McMahon]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]]}}|years=2023–present}} {{s-inc}} {{s-end}} {{United States 2nd Circuit district judges}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Clarke, Jessica G. She previously worked at the law firm Relman Colfax PLLC, joining in 2012 and as a [[Partner (business rank)|partner]] from 2019 to 2021. == Early life and education == Cobb was born in [[Springfield, Ohio]]. After graduating from [[Mercy High School (Farmington Hills, Michigan) |Mercy High School]] in Farmington Hills, Michigan,{{Cite web |title=Judge Jia M. Cobb '98 United States District Court for the District of Columbia {{!}} Mercy High School |url=https://www.mhsmi.org/headlines/21/12/10/judge-jia-m-cobb-98-united-states-district-court-district-columbia |access-date=2022-09-23 |website=www.mhsmi.org}} she attended [[Northwestern University]], graduating in 2002 with a [[Bachelor of Arts]], [[Latin honors#United States|''magna cum laude'']]. She then attended [[Harvard Law School]], where she was a coordinating editor of the ''[[Harvard Law Review]]''. She graduated in 2005 with a [[Juris Doctor]], ''cum laude''.{{Cite web|date=2021-06-15|title=President Biden Announces 4th Slate of Judicial Nominations|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/06/15/president-biden-announces-4th-slate-of-judicial-nominations/|access-date=2021-06-15|website=The White House|language=en-US}} == Career == Cobb began her career as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Diane Wood]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit]] from 2005 to 2006. Cobb supervised incoming attorneys and was a member of the Forensic Practice Group.{{cite web | url=https://www.dcd.uscourts.gov/content/district-judge-jia-m-cobb | title=District Judge Jia M. Cobb | District of Columbia | United States District Court }} Cobb also taught law at the [[Washington College of Law]] and [[Harvard Law School]]. She worked as a legal partner at Relman Colfax, a national plaintiff-side [[civil rights]] law firm from 2012 to 2021.{{Cite news|last=Hulse|first=Carl|date=2021-06-15|title=A leading voting rights expert is among Biden's new round of judicial nominees.|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/06/15/us/politics/biden-judges.html|access-date=2021-06-15|issn=0362-4331}} Cobb previously served as an elected member of the District of Columbia Bar's Criminal Law and Individual Rights Section Steering Committee. === Federal judicial service === On June 15, 2021, President [[Joe Biden]] nominated Cobb to serve as a United States district judge of the [[United States District Court for the District of Columbia]]. She was nominated to the seat vacated by Judge [[Emmet G. Sullivan]], who assumed [[senior status]] on April 3, 2021.{{Cite web|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/06/15/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-20/|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate|date=June 15, 2021|website=The White House}} Cobb was previously recommended for the position by House Delegate [[Eleanor Holmes Norton]].{{Cite web|date=2021-03-25|title=Norton Recommends Jia Cobb for U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia|url=https://norton.house.gov/media-center/press-releases/norton-recommends-jia-cobb-for-us-district-court-for-the-district-of|access-date=2021-06-15|website=Congresswoman Eleanor Holmes Norton|language=en}} On July 14, 2021, a hearing on her nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/07/07/2021/nominations|title=Nominations | United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|website=www.judiciary.senate.gov|date=14 July 2021 }} On August 5, 2021, her nomination was reported out of committee a 13–9 vote.{{Cite web|date=August 5, 2021|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – August 5, 2021|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%20August%205,%202021.pdf|publication-place=Washington, D.C.}} On October 26, 2021, the [[United States Senate]] invoked cloture on her nomination by a 51–46 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1171/vote_117_1_00427.htm|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Jia M. [[University of Washington School of Law|University of Washington]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | party = }} ''' Jill Aiko Otake''' (born 1973) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Hawaii]]. == Biography == Jill Otake was born in 1973, in [[Honolulu]].{{cn|date=May 2023}} She graduated from the [[ʻIolani School]] and earned a [[Bachelor of Science]], ''cum laude'', from [[Georgetown University]], where she majored in the [[Russian language]]. Otake received her [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Washington School of Law]] in 1998{{FJC Bio|nid=5019306|inline=yes}} and was selected for [[the Order of Barristers]].[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-ninth-wave-judicial-nominees-tenth-wave-united-states-attorney-nominees/ " President Donald J. Trump Announces Ninth Wave of Judicial Nominees and Tenth Wave of United States Attorney Nominees " White House, December 20, 2017] {{PD-notice}} After graduating from law school, Otake [[law clerk|clerked]] for Associate Justice [[Simeon R. Acoba Jr.]] of the [[Supreme Court of Hawaii|Hawaii Supreme Court]]. She worked for five years as a deputy prosecuting attorney in [[King County, Washington]]. Otake then spent nine years as a supervisor and as an [[assistant United States attorney]] for the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Washington|Western District of Washington]]. Immediately before becoming a judge, Otake was Special Counsel to the United States Attorney and Acting Chief of the Special Crime section as an assistant United States attorney for the [[United States District Court for the District of Hawaii|District of Hawaii]]. She was deputy chief of that office from 2014 to 2018. Otake is a recipient of the [[Federal Bureau of Investigation]] Certificate of Recognition, [[Internal Revenue Service]] Excellence Award, and numerous [[U.S. Department of Justice]] Performance Awards. Otake was an instructor for the inaugural Hawaii Federal Trial Academy, sponsored by the Federal Bar Association and the [[United States District Court for the District of Hawaii]].{{cite news |last1=Schuster |first1=Brett |title=NAPABA Applauds Nomination of Jill Otake to the U.S. District Court for the District of Hawaii |url=https://napaba.site-ym.com/page/1217_otake_nom?&hhsearchterms=%22jill+and+otake%22 |access-date=September 13, 2018 |publisher=National Asian Pacific American Bar Association |date=December 20, 2017}} Otake is co-chair of the [[Hawaii State Bar Association]]'s Professionalism and Risk Management Committee and was also a volunteer attorney for Volunteer Legal Services Hawaii. She is also a mentor for Hawaii women lawyers. Otake has taught trial advocacy at [[Seattle University Law School]]; served as co-president of the Asian Bar Association of Washington; and served on the [[United States District Court for the District of Hawaii]]'s Chief Probation Officer Selection Committee. She was a [[fellow]] of the 2016 Hawaii State Bar Association's Leadership Institute. She currently serves on the [[ʻIolani School|'Iolani School]] Board of Governors.{{Cite web |title=Board of Governors - 'Iolani School |url=https://www.iolani.org/school/board-of-governors |access-date=2023-02-01 |website=www.iolani.org |language=en-US}} == Federal judicial service == [[File:Jill Otake Swearing In.png|thumb|right|Judge Jill A. Otake is honored in the Aloha Tradition after taking the oath of office.]] Otake was recommended to the White House by [[United States Senate|U.S. Senators]] [[Mazie Hirono]] and [[Brian Schatz]].[http://www.staradvertiser.com/2015/06/16/breaking-news/former-attorney-general-prosecutors-nominated-for-federal-judge/ "Former attorney general, prosecutors nominated for federal judge" Honolulu Star-Advertiser, June 16, 2015]{{cite web|title=Hirono & Schatz Announce Nomination of Jill Otake to U.S. District Court|date=December 20, 2017 |url=https://www.hirono.senate.gov/press-releases/hirono-and-schatz-announce-nomination-of-jill-otake-to-us-district-court}} On December 21, 2017, her nomination was sent to the [[United States Senate]]. On December 20, 2017, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to nominate Otake to serve as a United States District Judge of the [[United States District Court for the District of Hawaii]]. She was nominated to the seat vacated by Judge [[Susan Oki Mollway]], who assumed [[senior status]] on November 6, 2015. The [[American Bar Association]]'s Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary rated Otake unanimously "Well Qualified."{{Cite web|url=https://www.americanbar.org/content/dam/aba/uncategorized/GAO/Web%20rating%20Chart%20Trump%20115.authcheckdam.pdf|title=STANDING COMMITTEE ON THE FEDERAL JUDICIARY : RATINGS OF ARTICLE III AND ARTICLE IV JUDICIAL NOMINEES|date=December 13, 2018|website=American Bar Association|access-date=July 20, 2019}}[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/four-nominations-sent-senate-today-5/ "Four Nominations Sent to the Senate Today" White House, December 21, 2017] On March 7, 2018, a hearing on her nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/03/07/2018/nominations United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Nominations for March 7, 2018] On April 12, 2018, her nomination was reported out of committee by [[voice vote]].[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/04-12-18%20Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting.pdf Results of Executive Business Meeting – April 12, 2018, Senate Judiciary Committee] On August 1, 2018, the Senate confirmed her nomination by a [[voice vote]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/115th-congress/1338|title=PN1338 — Jill Aiko Otake — The [[Yale University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Jill Annette Niederhauser Parrish''' (born August 16, 1961) is an American lawyer who serves as the [[United States federal judge|chief United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Utah]]. She served as a justice of the [[Utah Supreme Court]] from 2003 to 2015. Parrish grew up in [[Utah]] and received her [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[Weber State University]] in 1982.{{cite web|url=https://www.nndb.com/people/524/000168020/ |title=Jill N. Parrish |publisher=Nndb.com |date= |access-date=June 10, 2012}} In 1985 she received her [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Yale Law School]]. Parrish then served as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[David Kent Winder]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Utah]]. Parrish also served as an [[assistant United States attorney]] in the Civil Division of the United States Attorney’s Office for the District of Utah from 1995 until her appointment to the [[Utah Supreme Court]]. == Early life and education == Parrish was born Jill Annette Niederhauser in [[Ogden, Utah]], on August 16, 1961, the daughter of Ed and Beulah Niederhauser. She lived in Ogden until she left for law school in 1982. Parrish graduated from [[Ogden High School (Ogden, Utah)|Ogden High School]] in 1979. She attended [[Weber State University]], graduating with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] in Communication and Political Science in 1982. She attended Yale Law School, graduating with a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1985.{{Cite web|url=https://www.sltrib.com/news/1589674-155/court-federal-parrish-judge-utah-bench|title=Obama nominates Jill Parrish for federal court judge|last=Tribune|first=Thomas Burr The Salt Lake|website=The Salt Lake Tribune|language=en-US|access-date=April 28, 2016}} During her time at [[Yale]], Parrish was on the Yale Moot Court Team.{{FJC Bio|nid=1394781|inline=yes}} == Early legal career == After graduating from law school, Parrish served as a [[law clerk]] to Judge [[David Kent Winder]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Utah]]. Upon completion of her clerkship in 1986 she joined the [[Salt Lake City]] law firm of Parr, Waddoups, Brown, Gee & Loveless as an associate. She became a shareholder at the firm in 1990. During her time at Parr, Waddoups, Parrish’s focus was on commercial litigation. One high-profile case was Gold Standard, Inc. v. Getty Oil Co.,{{cite web |url=http://www.leagle.com/decision/19961975915P2d1060_11970.xml/GOLD%20STANDARD,%20INC.%20v.%20GETTY%20OIL%20CO.|title=Gold Standard, Inc. v. Getty Oil Co |publisher=Leagle.com |date=January 11, 1996 |access-date=August 5, 2014}} 915 P.2d 1060, (Utah 1996). Gold Standard, Inc and [[Getty Oil]] Co. entered into a joint mining venture. When Gold Standard failed to fund its portion in the venture, Getty Oil reduced its share. Gold Standard sued Getty Oil claiming wrongful conversion, [[breach of contract]] and [[fraud]]. Parrish represented the defendant, Getty Oil Co. The trial court granted a partial summary judgment in favor of Getty Oil Co. The Utah Supreme court affirmed the trial court's partial [[summary judgment]] in 1996. From 1995 to 2003, Parrish served as an [[assistant United States attorney]] in the Civil Division of the United States Attorney's Office for the District of Utah, where she supervised the financial litigation unit. Parrish started at the United States Attorney's office during Scott M. Matheson's tenure as the United States attorney. While at the U.S. Attorney’s office, Parrish worked on cases involving [[Revised Statute 2477]]SUWA. {{cite web|url=http://www.suwa.org/site/PageServer?pagename%3Dwork_rs2477 |access-date=November 17, 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100906071802/http://www.suwa.org/site/PageServer?pagename=work_rs2477 |archive-date=September 6, 2010 |title=Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance: RS2477 }} (commonly known as, [[RS 2477]].) In the Civil division, Parrish also represented the United States in torts and in environmental and employment cases. RS 2477 became a law shortly after the [[American Civil War]] as part of the Mining act of 1866. The law states that "the right-of-way for the construction of highways across public lands, not reserved for public uses, is hereby granted." RS 2477 was repealed by the [[United States Congress]] in 1976, but any existing rights-of-way were protected as long as they were in compliance with the statute. Controversy arose in the 1980s when several Utah officials argued that passage of a vehicle alone amounted to construction of a highway. This would give right of way for construction of a highway on any one of the numerous dirt trails and tracks throughout Southern Utah. This brought controversy because the construction of highways on these trails allegedly would be devastating to Utah wildlife. Parrish was involved in the lengthy litigation process that involved these roads in Southern Utah. The laws regarding RS 2477 claims are still not well defined and continue to stir up controversy.{{cite web| url=http://suwa.convio.net/site/PageServer?pagename=rs2477_background | title=Background on the Current RS 2477 Policy Landscape| publisher=Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance| access-date=August 5, 2014}} == Judicial career == === Utah Supreme Court === Parrish was appointed to the [[Utah Supreme Court]] in January 2003, by Governor [[Mike Leavitt]], following the retirement of Justice [[Richard C. Howe]].Elizabeth Neff, "[https://web.archive.org/web/20030429233541/http://www.sltrib.com/2003/Feb/02272003/Utah/33295.asp Senate OKs Two Supreme Court Justices]", ''Salt Lake Tribune'', February 27, 2003). Parrish served as chair of both the Supreme Court Committee on Civility and Professionalism and the State Law Library Oversight Committee. She was a member of the Court Technology Committee until October 2010. She is a past president of the Utah Chapter of the Federal Bar Association{{cite web |url=https://www.fedbar.org/Chapters/Utah-Chapter.aspx |title=Utah Chapter |publisher=Fedbar.org |date= |access-date=June 10, 2012}} and formerly served as the State Court Liaison to that organization. Parrish served as the Supreme Court representative on the Utah Judicial Council.{{cite web |url=http://www.utcourts.gov/knowcts/adm/ |title=Utah State Courts – Court Governance |publisher=Utcourts.gov |date=May 23, 2012 |access-date=June 10, 2012}} ===Federal judicial service=== On September 18, 2014, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Parrish to serve as a [[United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Utah]], to the seat vacated by Judge [[Dee Benson]], who assumed [[senior status]] on January 1, 2014.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/09/18/president-obama-nominates-seven-serve-united-states-district-courts|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Obama Nominates Seven to Serve on the United States District Courts|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=September 18, 2014}} On December 16, 2014, her nomination was returned to the President due to the [[sine die]] adjournment of the [[113th United States Congress|113th Congress]]. On January 7, 2015, President Obama renominated her to the same position.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2015/01/07/presidential-nominations-sent-senate|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=January 7, 2015}} She received a hearing before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Judiciary Committee]] on January 21, 2015.{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/nominations-2015-01-21|title=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|website=www.judiciary.senate.gov}} On February 26, 2015, her nomination was reported out of committee by [[voice vote]].{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%202-26-15%20Update.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – February 26, 2015|publisher=}} On May 21, 2015, the [[United States Senate]] confirmed her by a 100–0 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=114&session=1&vote=00184|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Jill N. Parrish, of Utah, to be United States District Judge)|website=www.senate.gov}} She received her judicial commission on August 17, 2015. A formal [[investiture]] for Parrish was held on November 23, 2015.{{cite web| url=https://www.sltrib.com/home/3218273-155/new-federal-judge-in-utah-formally | title=New federal judge in Utah formally takes oath of office | publisher=[[The Salt Lake Tribune]] | date=November 23, 2015 | access-date=December 8, 2015 | author=Harvey, Tom}} She became chief judge on October 1, 2025. == Selected opinions == === Utah Department of Transportation v. G. Kay, Inc. === On September 26, 2003, Justice Parrish authored her first opinion for the Utah Supreme court in the case of Utah Department of Transportation v. G. Kay, Inc.{{cite court |url=http://www.utcourts.gov/opinions/supopin/utahdept09262003.htm |litigants=Utah Dept of Transp. v. G. Kay, Inc |reporter=UT |court=Utah Supreme |volume=40 |opinion=20020063 |date=September 26, 2003 |accessdate=August 5, 2014}} 78 P.3d 612 (Utah 2003). In this case, the Utah Department of Transportation (UDOT) condemned property owned by G. Kay, Inc. to make the Legacy Nature Preserve, a 2,100-acre area that was to be set aside to mitigate the environmental impacts of the construction of the proposed Legacy highway. When UDOT moved to condemn the land owned by G. Kay, Inc., G. Kay moved to dismiss UDOT’s complaint, because they did not have the authority to condemn its property. The court affirmed that UDOT did have the authority to condemn the property to mitigate the environmental impact of the construction of the Legacy Parkway Project (Legacy Highway.) Chief Justice Durham, Associate Chief Justice Durrant, Justice Wilkins, and Judge Nehring concurred in Justice Parrish's opinion. === State v. Jeffs === State v. Jeffs,{{cite court |url=http://www.utcourts.gov/opinions/supopin/Jeffs072710.pdf |litigants=State of Utah v. Jeffs| reporter=UT| opinion=20080508 |volume=49 |date=July 27, 2010 |court=Utah Supreme |accessdate=August 5, 2014}} ( No. 20080408, Filed July 27, 2010, 2010 UT 49). The state of Utah charged [[Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints]] (FLDS) leader [[Warren Jeffs]] with two counts of rape as an accomplice against Elissa Wall. Wall was a student at Alta Academy, an FLDS school where Jeffs was both a teacher and the principal. Wall had been taught by Jeffs, both in school and in church, that to disobey his teachings or those of his counselors was to be denied spiritual salvation. Jeffs’ two rape charges were the result of sexual intercourse that ensued between Elissa Wall, who was 14 at the time, and her 19-year-old cousin, Allen Steed, after Jeffs allegedly forced Wall to marry Steed. Jeffs was convicted after a jury trial in 2007 and sentenced to two consecutive terms of five years to life. Jeffs raised seven issues that he thought invalidated the jury verdict. On July 27, 2010, the Utah Supreme court reversed Jeffs’ two convictions of rape and remanded for a new trial on the grounds that "the trial court’s instructions to the jury regarding lack of consent were in error." Justice Parrish authored the court’s decision with Chief Justice Durham, Associate Chief Justice Durrant, and Justice Nehring in concurrence. Justice Parrish wrote in the conclusion of the court’s decision that "We regret the effect our opinion today may have on the victim of the underlying crime, to whom we do not wish to cause additional pain. However, we must ensure that the laws are applied evenly and appropriately." === State v. Willis === In State v. Willis{{cite court |url=http://www.utcourts.gov/opinions/supopin/willis110504.htm |litigants=State of Utah v. Willis |reporter=UT |date=November 5, 2004 |court=Utah Supreme |volume=93 |opinion=20020703 |accessdate=June 10, 2012}} 100 P.3d 1218 (Utah, 2006) The defendant, Wade Willis challenged the constitutionality of the Utah code that prohibits certain "restricted persons" including those who are on probation for a felony, from possessing firearms. Willis, who was on probation for a third degree felony, was found in possession of a nine-millimeter handgun. Willis was charged with a second degree felony under Utah Code section 76-10-503(2)(a) which prohibits convicted felons from possessing a firearm. Willis argues that this violates his right to bear arms, a right guaranteed by the Utah constitution (Article 1, Section 6.) Justice Parrish and the court in a unanimous opinion, rejected his argument. Parrish stated "that there is no evidence in the legislative history to suggest the existence of an intent to extend the right of gun possession to felons." === American Bush v. City of South Salt Lake === In American Bush v. City of South Salt Lake,{{cite court |volume=40 |litigants=American Bush v. City of South Salt Lake |url=http://www.utcourts.gov/opinions/supopin/AmericanBush072806.pdf |title=Utah Supreme |opinion=20020117 |reporter=UT |date=July 28, 2006 |accessdate=August 5, 2014}} 140. P.3d 1235 (Utah 2006). the City of South Salt Lake passed an ordinance that prohibited [[sexually oriented business]] employees from "[a]ppear[ing] in a state of nudity before a patron on the premises of a sexually oriented business." American Bush, Paradise Modeling and Leather and Lace filed an action in state court claiming that this ordinance violated their free speech rights as defined by the Utah State Constitution. The court granted summary judgment in favor of the City of South Salt lake, stating that the right to "communicate freely their thoughts and opinions" did not extend to nude dancing in sexually oriented businesses. Justice Parrish, with Associate Chief Justice Wilkins and Justice Durrant in concurrence, affirmed the court’s summary judgment. === University of Utah v. Shurtleff === [[University of Utah]] v. Shurtleff{{cite court |url=http://www.utcourts.gov/opinions/supopin/UnivofUtah090806.pdf |title=University of Utah v. Shurtleff | court=Utah Supreme |opinion=20030877 |volume=51 |reporter=UT |date=September 8, 2006 |accessdate=August 5, 2014}} 144 P.3d 1109 (Utah, 2006). Utah Attorney General Mark Shurtleff issued Opinion No. 01-002, which claimed that the University’s policy prohibiting firearms on campus violated Utah’s Uniform Firearms Act, The University sued the Attorney general for a [[declaratory judgement]] claiming that, under Article X, Section 4 of the [[Utah Constitution]], they could disregard Utah Law when it interfered with academic affairs. During the appeals process, Utah Legislature passed section 63-98-102, which prohibits state and local entities from enforcing policies that inhibit the possession of firearms on public or private property. Justice Parrish with Associate Chief Justice Wilkins, Justice Durrant, and Justice Nehring in concurrence gave the opinion that the University of Utah did not have the power to disregard Utah Law. Chief Justice Durham dissented. == Public speeches == On October 12, 2005, Parrish delivered a speech at the Admissions Ceremony for new inductees to the [[Utah State Bar]] that was published in the ''Utah Bar Journal'' in its January/February 2006 issue. In her speech ''Lessons From Kindergarten'', Justice Parrish advises that to achieve success in the legal profession, you need more than just knowledge of the law. You need "those other characteristics and qualities that you bring to bear in your professional life- the really important things, the lessons you learned in Kindergarten." Parrish advised new lawyers to share, play fair, practice with professionalism and civility, be responsible and work hard, and maintain a sense of perspective.{{cite journal| last=Parrish| first=Jill| date=January 24, 2006| title=Lessons From Kindergarten| journal=Utah Bar Journal| volume=19| number=1| pages=42–44| url=http://www.utahbar.org/utah-bar-journal/view-from-the-bench/lessons-from-kindergarten/| access-date=September 5, 2014}}{{Dead link|date=February 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }} == References == {{Reflist}} == External links == *{{FJC Bio|nid=1394781}} *{{Ballotpedia|Jill_Parrish}} *[https://web.archive.org/web/20110725185923/http://www.utahbar.org/barjournal/pdf/2006_jan_feb.pdf Utah Bar Journal Vol. 19 No. 1] *[http://www.utcourts.gov/judgesbios/showGallery.asp?dist=10&ct_type=S/ Utah State Courts: Supreme Court Justices] *[http://www.utcourts.gov/opinions/ Utah State Courts: Appellate Court Opinions] *[https://web.archive.org/web/20101129011824/http://www.justice.gov/usao/ut/division.html United States Attorney's Office: District of Utah] {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Richard C. '''Jimm Larry Hendren''' (born June 11, 1940 in [[Gravette, Arkansas]]) is an inactive [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Arkansas]].

==Education and career==

Hendren graduated with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from the [[University of Arkansas]] in 1964 and then received a [[Bachelor of Laws]] from the [[University of Arkansas School of Law]] in 1965. Later that year Hendren would join the [[JAG Corps]] of the [[United States Navy]], returning in 1968, for a year, to his private practice in [[Bentonville, Arkansas]], which he would expand in later years. In 1970 Hendren became a [[United States Naval Reserve]] [[Lieutenant Commander]], a position he would hold until 1983. Meanwhile, in 1977, he became a [[probate judge]] (Chancellor) of Arkansas' Sixteenth Chancery District, before returning again to his private practice.<ref name="fjc.gov">{{cite web|url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/hendren-jimm-larry|title=Hendren, Jimm Larry - Federal Judicial Center|website=www.fjc.gov}}</ref>

==Federal judicial service==

Hendren was nominated by [[George H. W. Bush]] as a United States District Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Arkansas]] on November 5, 1991, to a new seat created by ''104 Statute 5089''. The nomination was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on March 13, 1992, and Hendren received his commission on March 18, 1992. He served as the Chief Judge from 1997 until he assumed [[senior status]] on December 31, 2012.<ref name="fjc.gov"/>

==Notable case==

Hendren is well known for ruling in favor of Billy Ray and Mary Nell Counts, a couple in [[Cedarville, Arkansas]], in the 2003 [[lawsuit]] ''Counts et ux. v. Cedarville School Board''. The court decided that the local school's rule requiring parents' written consent to read the ''[[Harry Potter]]'' books was [[unconstitutional]].<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.ala.org/ala/alonline/currentnews/newsarchive/2003/april2003/judgesmitesharry.cfm|publisher=American Library Association|title=Judge Smites Harry Potter Restrictions in Arkansas|accessdate=2007-03-13|date=2003-04-28|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20070311193153/http://www.ala.org/ala/alonline/currentnews/newsarchive/2003/april2003/judgesmitesharry.cfm|archivedate=2007-03-11}}</ref> The district court's opinion can be found [https://web.archive.org/web/20090225145909/http://www.prbsklaw.com/documents/02-2155-mo-wp.pdf here], and the decision was cited as [[precedent]] in subsequent [[censorship]] cases.<ref>{{cite web|title=Fayetteville Rethinks Restricted Reads|work=American Library Association|url=http://www.ala.org/ala/alonline/currentnews/newsarchive/2005abc/september2005abc/fayetteback.cfm|year=2005|accessdate=2007-05-30|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20070606224253/http://www.ala.org/ala/alonline/currentnews/newsarchive/2005abc/september2005abc/fayetteback.cfm|archivedate=2007-06-06}}</ref>

She received her [[Associate of Arts]] [[Academic degree|degree]] from [[Rockland Community College]] in 1972, her [[Bachelor of Arts]] from [[Roger Williams College]] in 1973, and her [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Antioch School of Law]] in 1976. ==Career== Lenard worked for the Office of the [[State Attorney]] in the [[Florida Circuit Courts|11th Judicial Circuit of Florida]] ([[Miami-Dade County, Florida|Dade County]]) from 1976 to 1982, serving as assistant state attorney from 1976 to 1978, as chief of the [[Consumer fraud|Consumer Fraud]] Division from 1978 to 1980, and as chief of the Consumer and Economic Crime Division from 1980 to 1982. Lenard served as a Dade [[County court (Florida)|County Court]] judge from 1982 to 1993 and as a circuit judge for the Family Division of the 11th Judicial Circuit from 1993 to 1995. ===Federal judicial service=== President [[Bill Clinton]] nominated Lenard to the United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida on September 29, 1995, to the seat vacated by Judge [[James Lawrence King]]. She was confirmed by the [[United States Senate|Senate]] on December 22, 1995, and received her commission on December 26, 1995. She assumed [[senior status]] on July 1, 2017.{{FJC Bio|nid=1383816|inline=yes}} ===Notable case=== Lenard was the presiding judge in the third trial of the [[Seas of David|Liberty City Seven]], after the first two trials ended in [[mistrial (law)|mistrials]].{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/04/24/us/24miami.html|title=Six Suspects Will Be Tried a Third Time in Sears Plot|first=Carmen|last=Gentile|work=The New York Times |date=24 April 2008|via=NYTimes.com}} She has also presided over the Moisés Maionica case;{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/01/26/world/americas/26suitcase.html|title=Venezuelan Pleads Guilty in Cover-Up of Suitcase of Cash|first=Alexei|last=Barrionuevo|work=The New York Times |date=26 January 2008|via=NYTimes.com}} the [[Lawsuit|civil trial]] of Juan López Grijalba, a [[Honduran Army]] [[colonel]], who was found responsible killings and kidnappings in [[Honduras]] during the 1980s and was ordered to pay $47 million to several [[torture]] victims and surviving relatives;{{cite web|url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html|title=World Briefing - [[New York Law School]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | footnotes = }} '''Joan Marie Azrack''' (born in 1951) is an American lawyer who serves as a [[senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York]]. She is a former [[United States magistrate judge]] of the same court. ==Biography== Azrack was born in 1951, in [[Neptune Township, New Jersey]].{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Azrack%20Senate%20Questionnaire%20Final.pdf|title=Senate Judiciary Committee Nomination Questionnaire}} She received a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree in 1974 from [[Rutgers University]]. She received a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1979 from [[New York Law School]]. She began her career as a trial attorney in the [[United States Department of Justice Criminal Division|Criminal Division]] of the [[United States Department of Justice]] from 1979 to 1981. From 1982 to 1990, she was an [[Assistant United States Attorney]] in the Eastern District of New York, where she served as Deputy Chief of the Narcotics Section from 1985 to 1986 and as Deputy Chief of the Criminal Division and Chief of the Business and Securities Fraud Section from 1986 to 1990. From 1988 to 1991, Azrack was a visiting instructor at [[Harvard Law School]].{{Cite web|title=Profiles – Joan Azrack|url=https://judges.newyorklawjournal.com/profile/U.S._District_Court,_Eastern_District/Joan_Azrack/Joan_Azrack-100007.xml|website=New York Law Journal}}{{Cite web |date=September 18, 2014 |title=President Obama Nominates Seven to Serve on the United States District Courts |url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/09/18/president-obama-nominates-seven-serve-united-states-district-courts |website=[[whitehouse.gov]] |via=[[NARA|National Archives]]}}{{FJC Bio|nid=1394716|inline=yes}} ===Federal judicial service=== From 1990 to 2014 she served as a [[United States magistrate judge]] in the Eastern District and as chief United States magistrate judge from 2000 to 2005.{{cite web|url=http://www.nyed.uscourts.gov/General_Information/Court_Phone_Book/Magistrate-Judges/JMA/jma.html|title=Joan M. Azrack|publisher=United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York|access-date=December 14, 2010|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110421072649/http://www.nyed.uscourts.gov/General_Information/Court_Phone_Book/Magistrate-Judges/JMA/jma.html|archive-date=April 21, 2011}} On September 18, 2014, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Azrack to serve as a United States district judge of the United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York, to the seat vacated by Judge [[Joanna Seybert]], who assumed [[senior status]] on January 13, 2014.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/09/18/presidential-nominations-and-withdrawal-sent-senate-0|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Presidential Nominations and Withdrawal Sent to the Senate|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=September 18, 2014}} She received a hearing before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]] on November 13, 2014.{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/nominations-2014-11-13|title=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|website=www.judiciary.senate.gov}} On December 11, 2014, her nomination was reported out of committee by [[voice vote]].{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%2012-11-14.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – December 11, 2014}} On Saturday, December 13, 2014 [[Senate Majority Leader]] [[Harry Reid]] filed a motion to invoke [[cloture]] on the nomination. On December 16, 2014, Reid withdrew his cloture motion on Azrack's nomination, and the Senate proceeded to vote to confirm Azrack in a [[voice vote]]. She received her federal judicial commission on December 19, 2014. [[Northwestern University School of Law|Northwestern University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | footnotes = }} '''Joan Marilyn Humphrey Lefkow''' ({{nee|'''Humphrey'''}}; born January 8, 1944) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois]]. ==Education and career== Lefkow was born in [[Nemaha County, Kansas]]. She attended [[Wheaton College (Illinois)|Wheaton College]] in Illinois, where she received an [[Bachelor of Arts|Artium Baccalaureus]] degree, and obtained her [[Juris Doctor]] [[(J.D.)]] at [[Northwestern University School of Law]] in 1971. After graduation, she became a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Thomas E. Fairchild]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit]]. From 1972 to 1975, Lefkow was a staff attorney at the Legal Assistance Foundation of Chicago. After that, she served as an administrative law judge for the [[Illinois]] Fair Employment Practices Commission from 1975 to 1979. She was an instructor at [[University of Miami School of Law]] in 1980 and 1981 before becoming the executive director of the [[Cook County, Illinois|Cook County]] Legal Assistance Foundation from 1981 to 1982. From 1982 to 1997 she was a [[United States magistrate judge]], and from 1997 to 2000 a [[U.S. Bankruptcy Court|United States Bankruptcy Judge]] of the Northern District of Illinois. ===Federal judicial service=== Lefkow was nominated by President [[Bill Clinton]] on May 11, 2000, to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois]] vacated by Judge [[Ann Claire Williams]], and confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on June 30, 2000. She received her commission on July 11, 2000.{{cite web|url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/lefkow-joan-humphrey|title=Lefkow, Joan Humphrey - Federal Judicial Center|website=www.fjc.gov}} Lefkow assumed [[senior status]] on September 1, 2012. ===Matthew Hale=== In May 2000, Judge Lefkow presided over the enforcement of a high-profile [[trademark infringement]] case against the [[World Church of the Creator]] (WCOTC), an organization run by [[white supremacist]] leader [[Matthew F. Hale]]. The [[Oregon]]-based [[Church of the Creator (New Age movement)|TE-TA-MA Truth Foundation]]—described by the [[Southern Poverty Law Center]] as "a peace-loving, multicultural church"—sued Hale's church for using the name "Church of the Creator." WCOTC argued against the validity of the suit because Hale's church had been using the name since 1973, but the Foundation had trademarked it in 1987, and no contest was filed against the trademark within a five-year period, making their ownership legally incontestable.{{cite web|url=https://www.splcenter.org/fighting-hate/intelligence-report/2003/world-church-creator-turmoil-after-leader-matt-hale-imprisoned|title=World Church of the Creator In Turmoil After Leader Matt Hale Imprisoned}} In January 2002, Lefkow ruled in favor of Hale, but her decision was overturned on appeal. On July 25, Lefkow ruled against Hale, saying that his church infringed the Church of the Creator's trademark. (Hale's organization has since been renamed the [[Creativity Movement]].) An [[injunction]] was issued on November 19 forbidding Hale's church from using the term "Church of the Creator." Hale's World Church of the Creator was ordered to stop using the name on the [[Internet]], and to remove or cover up the phrase "Church of the Creator" on all of Hale's publications and products. In response to this decision, Hale sued Lefkow on December 24, claiming that her order violated the Constitution in requiring the "destruction" of the group's bibles."Supremacist disagrees with ruling, sues judge", ''Peoria Journal Star'', December 27, 2002. At around the same time, threats were made against Lefkow on the Internet, and her home address, and family photographs of her husband and children, were posted on the [[Stormfront (website)|Stormfront]] website.[http://www.splcenter.org/intel/news/item.jsp?aid=11 "Family of judge targeted by hate group murdered"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091019144143/http://www.splcenter.org/intel/news/item.jsp?aid=11 |date=October 19, 2009}}, splcenter.org; accessed November 18, 2014. Meanwhile, an undercover [[FBI]] informant, posing as Hale's "security" chief, taped a conversation with Hale where he asked about Lefkow's home address, and discussed her impending "extermination."[https://www.nytimes.com/2005/03/01/national/01judge.html?adxnnl=1&adxnnlx=1109818886-sbR2Qy0kSe5cnCOoigiOow 2 Bodies Found at Residence of U.S. Judge], nytimes.com, March 1, 2005; accessed November 18, 2014. On January 8, 2003, Hale was arrested on charges of plotting to murder Lefkow. The FBI informant in that trial received several death threats, and Lefkow initially was protected by a detail of the [[United States Marshals Service]].{{Cite news |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/chicago-tribune-judge-stays-on-hale-civi/149642809/ |title=Judge stays on Hale civic case |first=John |last=McCormick |newspaper=[[Chicago Tribune]] |page=2-3 |date=2003-03-04 |access-date=2024-06-19 |via=Newspapers.com}} On April 24, Judge Lefkow ruled that the Creativity Movement had failed to stop using the name "World Church of the Creator," and should be fined $1,000 a day until it complied.Robinson, Mike, "White Supremacist Group Fined $1,000 a Day", ''Kansas City Star'', April 24, 2003. On April 6, 2005, Hale was sentenced to a 40-year prison term for soliciting the undercover FBI informant to kill Judge Lefkow. His conviction and sentence were affirmed in 2006. A subsequent application to void them, on grounds including ineffective assistance of counsel, was rejected, and his appeal from that decision was affirmed on March 5, 2013.{{cite web|url=https://pdfserver.amlaw.com/nlj/7thCirHalevUS.pdf|title=U.S. Court of Appeals decision|access-date=March 7, 2013}} In a separate proceeding, sympathizer [[Bill White (neo-nazi)|Bill White]] was convicted and sentenced to prison for threatening the life of the foreman of the jury that convicted Hale in Judge Lefkow's courtroom, although the conviction was overturned on appeal.{{cite news|title=Judge throws out conviction of white supremacist|first=Annie |last=Sweeney|work=Chicago Tribune|date=April 20, 2011|url=http://www.chicagotribune.com/news/local/ct-met-charges-dismissed-white-suprem20110419,0,5037177.story }} ==Double homicide at Lefkow's home== On February 28, 2005, Lefkow returned home to find the bodies of both her husband and mother in the basement of her home on the [[North Side, Chicago|North Side]] of [[Chicago]]. According to an anonymous federal source, both Michael Francis Lefkow, 64, and Donna Grace Glenn Humphrey, 89, had been shot multiple times. The Cook County medical examiner's office stated that the victims were killed with [[.22 caliber]] shots to the head. No weapon was found at the scene, but two .22-caliber casings were recovered; evidence of a break-in was found as well. Initial suspicions focused on the possibility that hate groups were involved. On March 4, the FBI announced a $50,000 reward for information leading to the identification of anyone involved in the slayings.Babwin, Don. [http://www.daily-chronicle.com/articles/2005/03/05/news/news03.txt FBI Offers Reward for Ill. Killing Info]{{Dead link|date=February 2020 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}, March 5, 2005 AP story from ''The Daily Chronicle'' archives; accessed November 18, 2014. On March 8, investigators announced that DNA samples had been obtained from a cigarette butt found inside the kitchen sink. Further evidence was recovered in and around the home, including a fingerprint, a bloody footprint, and a soda can.''Associated Press''. [http://www.kare11.com/news/news_article.aspx?storyid=76460 Report: DNA Found Inside Judge's Home], kare11.com, March 8, 2005; accessed November 18, 2014. Lefkow and her children were again placed under the protection of the [[United States Marshals Service]].[https://www.usatoday.com/news/nation/2005-07-13-lefkow_x.htm Judge Lefkow returns to bench after slayings], USAToday.com, July 13, 2005; accessed November 18, 2014. On May 18, 2005, Judge Lefkow testified before the [[U.S. Congress]] on the problem of providing security for judges, placing some of the blame for the attack on her family on rhetoric against judges issued by persons such as [[Pat Robertson]]. [http://www.chicagotribune.com/news/nationworld/chi-050518lefkowstatement-story.html Joan Lefkow testimony, quoted in the Chicago Tribune on May 18, 2005] a radio host and [[FBI]] informant [[Hal Turner]] asserted in September of that year that comments of his (which called for Lefkow's death) may have inspired the murders.[http://www.adl.org/main_extremism/turner_own_words.htm Comments by Hal Turner] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060602111003/http://www.adl.org/main_Extremism/turner_own_words.htm |date=June 2, 2006}}, adl.org; accessed November 18, 2014. ===Perpetrator=== On March 10, 2005, the [[Chicago Police Department]] and federal agents announced a possible break in the case. According to investigators, a van was stopped during a traffic stop in [[West Allis, Wisconsin]], at 6:00{{nbsp}}p.m. on March 9. As West Allis police officer Rick Orlowski approached the vehicle, the driver, identified as 57-year-old Polish electrician Bart Allen Ross (born Bartłomiej Ciszewski), shot and killed himself. Later that night, a suicide note was found in the car, confessing to the murders of Lefkow's husband and mother, allegedly providing details about the crimes which would have been known only to the actual murderer.{{Cite news |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/kentucky-new-era-report-judges-mother/149643185/ |title=Report: Judge's mother, husband slayings tied to Wisconsin suicide |newspaper=[[Kentucky New Era]] |publication-place=Hopkinsville |place=Chicago |agency=AP |page=8 |date=2005-03-10 |access-date=2024-06-19 |via=Newspapers.com}} Ross had been a plaintiff in a medical malpractice case that Lefkow had dismissed. Investigators found over three hundred .22 caliber shells in the vehicle, casings of the same caliber that were found in the Lefkow home.Coen, Jeff; Heinzmann, David. [http://www.chicagotribune.com/news/local/chi-050310lefkow,1,487378.story?coll=chi-newsbreaking-hed&ctrack=2&cset=true "Wisconsin death has Lefkow tie"]. ''Chicago Tribune'', March 10, 2005; accessed November 18, 2014. DNA evidence from Ross allegedly matched the cigarette butt found in Lefkow's home. Ross sent a handwritten letter to [[WMAQ-TV]] describing breaking into the Lefkow home with a plan to kill the judge.[https://edition.cnn.com/2005/US/03/11/judge.bodies/index.html "Revenge likely motive in judge killings case"], ''CNN'', March 11, 2005; accessed November 18, 2014. Financially stable, with a house, prior to contracting a rare mouth cancer, Ross underwent multiple surgeries and treatments. These completely cured his cancer, but left him massively disfigured, in constant pain, financially wiped out with deep debt, and living in his van. His attempts to sue the medical system may have been intended to jump-start the remainder of his life, but with no actual case of wrongdoing, they were inevitably dismissed.[http://www.chicagotribune.com/news/nationworld/chi-0503110282mar11-story.html "Decade of despair boiled over to paranoia"], ''Chicago Tribune'', March 11, 2005; accessed May 21, 2018. ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1391246}} *[http://www.splcenter.org/intel/intelreport/article.jsp?pid=59 Southern Poverty Law Center Intelligence Report], splcenter.org; accessed November 18, 2014. {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Ann Claire Williams]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois]]}}|years=2000–2012}} {{s-aft|after=[[Manish S. [[St. John's University School of Law|St. John's University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | footnotes = }} '''Joanna Seybert''' (born September 18, 1946) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York]]. ==Education and career== Seybert received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from the [[University of Cincinnati]] in 1967 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[St. John's University School of Law]] in 1971. She began her legal career as a trial attorney for the [[Legal Aid Society]] in [[New York City]] from 1971 to 1973. She served as a senior trial attorney for the Federal Defender Services of the Legal Aid Society in [[Brooklyn]], [[New York (state)|New York]] from 1973 to 1975. She was an attorney in private practice in [[Woodbury, Nassau County, New York]] in 1976 and 1979. She was a senior staff attorney for the Legal Aid Society in [[Nassau County, New York]] from 1976 to 1979. She served as Chief of the Major Litigation Bureau in Nassau County Attorney's Office from 1980 to 1987. She was a Judge of the Nassau County District Court from 1987 to 1991 and a Judge of the Nassau County Court from 1992 to 1993. ===Federal judicial service=== She was nominated to the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York]] by President [[Bill Clinton]] on September 24, 1993, to a new seat created by 104 Stat. 5089, confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on November 20, 1993, and received her commission on November 24, 1993. Dishman''' ({{nee|'''Warmbrod'''}}; born 1979) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Oklahoma]]. == Education == Dishman earned her [[Bachelor of Business Administration]], ''[[cum laude]]'', from [[Southern Methodist University]] and her [[Juris Doctor]], ''[[summa cum laude]]'', from the [[University of Oklahoma College of Law]], where she served as editor-in-chief of the ''Oklahoma Law Review''.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-judicial-nominees-united-states-attorney-nominees-united-states-marshal-nominees/ "President Donald J. Trump Announces Judicial Nominees, United States Attorney Nominees, and United States Marshal Nominees" White House, August 14, 2019] {{PD-notice}} == Legal career == Upon graduation from law school, Dishman served as a [[law clerk]] to Judges [[Edward C. Prado]] and [[Carolyn Dineen King]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]]. She spent five years as an attorney in the [[San Antonio]] office of [[Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld]]. From 2012 to 2019, she was a [[shareholder]] at McAfee & Taft in [[Oklahoma City]], where her practice focused on complex [[civil litigation]] in federal and state courts and where she served as President of the Oklahoma City Chapter of the [[Federal Bar Association]]. == Federal judicial service == On August 14, 2019, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to nominate Dishman to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] for the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Oklahoma]].{{cite web|last1=Casteel|first1=Chris |title=Trump taps Oklahoma City attorney for federal judgeship|url=https://oklahoman.com/article/5638650/trump-taps-oklahoma-city-attorney-for-federal-judgeship|date=August 15, 2019 |publisher=[[The Oklahoman]]|access-date=August 17, 2019}} On September 9, 2019, her nomination was sent to the Senate. President Trump nominated Dishman to the seat vacated by Judge [[Vicki Miles-LaGrange]], who assumed [[senior status]] on November 5, 2018.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/seventeen-nominations-two-withdrawals-sent-senate/ "Seventeen Nominations and Two Withdrawals Sent to the Senate", White House, September 9, 2019] On September 25, 2019, a hearing on her nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/09/25/2019/nominations United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Nominations for September 25, 2019] On October 31, 2019, her nomination was reported out of committee by a 17–5 vote.[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/103119%20Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting.pdf Results of Executive Business Meeting – October 31, 2019, Senate Judiciary Committee] On December 18, 2019, the [[United States Senate]] invoked [[cloture]] on her nomination by a 76–17 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=1&vote=00406|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Jodi W. Dishman to be U.S. District Judge for the Western District of Oklahoma) |website=www.senate.gov|access-date=2019-12-18}} On December 19, 2019, her nomination was confirmed by a 75–17 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=1&vote=00419|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Jodi W. Dishman, of Oklahoma, to be U.S. District Judge for the District of Oklahoma)|website=www.senate.gov|access-date=2019-12-19}} She received her judicial commission on December 20, 2019.{{FJC Bio|nid=7544441|inline=yes}} ==Personal life== She is married to Brent Dishman, whom Governor [[Kevin Stitt]] appointed as District Judge on the [[Oklahoma County District Court]] on October 11, 2021.{{cite web |title=Governor Stitt Appoints Brent Dishman to serve as Oklahoma County Judge |url=https://oklahoma.gov/governor/newsroom/newsroom/2021/october/governor-stitt-appoints-brent-dishman-to-serve-as-oklahoma-count.html |date=October 11, 2021 |access-date=18 April 2022}}{{cite web |title=Oklahoma County - OSCN |url=https://www.oscn.net/courts/oklahoma |date=April 18, 2022}} They have two sons.{{cite web |title=College of the Ozarks to celebrate graduates with events beginning May 12, 2019 |url=https://www.cofo.edu/content/PR/pressRelease.aspx?id=9491dff2-aaef-4c53-834e-8f1de0a2477c |publisher=College of the Ozarks |access-date=18 October 2019 |date=May 6, 2019}} == References == {{Reflist}} == External links == *{{FJC Bio|nid=7544441}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Vicki Miles-LaGrange]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Oklahoma]]}}|years=2019–present}} {{s-inc}} {{s-end}} {{United States 10th Circuit district judges}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Dishman, Jodi W.}} [[Category:1979 births]] [[Category:Living people]] [[Category:21st-century American lawyers]] [[Category:21st-century American women judges]] [[Category:Judges of the United States District Court for the Western District of Oklahoma]] [[Category:Lawyers from Memphis, Tennessee]] [[Category:Oklahoma lawyers]] [[Category:Southern Methodist University alumni]] [[Category:United States district court judges appointed by Donald Trump]] [[Category:University of Oklahoma College of Law alumni]] {{US-federal-judge-stub}}
