He also served as a judge of the [[United States Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court]] from 2018 to 2025. ==Biography== John J. Tharp Jr. was born in [[Camp Lejeune]], [[North Carolina]].{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/JohnTharp-PublicQuestionnaire.pdf|title=Senate Judiciary Committee Questionnaire}}{{cite web|url=http://www.martindale.com/John-J-Tharp-Jr/928686-lawyer.htm|title=John Joseph Tharp, Jr. Lawyer Profile on Martindale.com|website=www.martindale.com}} He received his [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree, ''summa cum laude'', from [[Duke University]] in 1982. Following his graduation, he served for five years in the [[United States Marine Corps]] as a commissioned officer, attaining the rank of captain.[http://www.mayerbrown.com/lawyers/profile.asp?hubbardid=T706998110 Tharp's profile at mayerbrown.com] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110927004436/http://www.mayerbrown.com/lawyers/profile.asp?hubbardid=T706998110 |date=2011-09-27 }} He received his [[Juris Doctor]], ''magna cum laude'', from the [[Northwestern University School of Law]] in 1990. He served as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Joel Flaum]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit]] from 1990 to 1991. He worked as an associate at [[Kirkland & Ellis]] from 1991 to 1992. He served as an [[assistant United States attorney]] in the Northern District of Illinois from 1992 to 1997. From 1997 until 2012, he was an [[Associate lawyer|associate]] and then a [[Law firm partner|partner]] at the [[white shoe law firm]] of [[Mayer Brown]] LLP. He was the co-chair of the [[securities law|securities litigation and enforcement]] practice at that firm.[https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2011/11/10/president-obama-nominates-four-serve-us-district-court-bench "President Obama Nominates Four to Serve on the US District Court Bench" White House, November 10, 2011]{{FJC Bio|nid=1393986|inline=yes}} ===Federal judicial service=== On July 31, 2008, President [[George W. Bush]] nominated Tharp to replace [[Mark Filip]] on the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois.{{cite web|url=https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/nominations-sent-the-senate-22|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate|work=The American Presidency Project|date=July 31, 2008|access-date=June 18, 2023}} The nomination generated no controversy, but was made with less than six months remaining in the [[Presidency of George W. Bush|Bush presidency]] and was returned after not being acted upon by the [[110th Congress]]. On July 5, 2011, Senator [[Mark Kirk]], an Illinois Republican, recommended to President Barack Obama, a Democrat, that Tharp be appointed to the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois.{{cite news | url = https://www.chicagotribune.com/2011/07/06/kirk-nominates-ex-prosecutor-for-federal-judge/ | title = Kirk nominates ex-prosecutor for federal judge | date = July 6, 2011 | work = [[Chicago Tribune]] | first=Rick | last=Pearson}} The recommendation stemmed from a long-standing tradition in Illinois that, when the state is represented in the Senate by a Democrat and a Republican, the senator from the president's party gets to recommend candidates for two in every three judicial vacancies and the other senator chooses candidates for one in three. On November 10, 2011, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Tharp to be a district judge on the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois, filling the vacancy created by Judge [[Blanche M. Manning]], who assumed [[senior status]] in 2010. Tharp received his hearing by the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] on January 26, 2012, and his nomination was reported to the Senate floor on February 16, 2012, by a voice vote, with Senator [[Mike Lee]] recording the only no vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/ExecutiveBusinessMeetingResults-02-16-2012.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting - February 16, 2012|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=May 25, 2023}} On May 14, 2012, the [[United States Senate]] confirmed Tharp by an 86–1 vote, with Senator [[Mike Lee]] casting the lone nay vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=112&session=2&vote=00090|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation John J. Tharp, Jr., of Illinois, to be United States District Judge for the Northern District of Illinois)|website=www.senate.gov}} "I'm honored by both the nomination and the confirmation," Tharp told the ''Chicago Tribune'' shortly after the vote. "It's a real credit to both our senators that they worked together to get this done."{{cite news| url=http://www.chicagotribune.com/news/local/breaking/chi-senate-confirms-oak-park-lawyer-as-new-chicagobased-federal-judge-20120514,0,1983587.story | work=Chicago Tribune | first=Bob | last=Goldsborough | title=Senate confirms Oak Park lawyer as new Chicago-based federal judge}} He received his commission on May 16, 2012. He assumed [[senior status]] on September 30, 2026. ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1393986}} *{{Ballotpedia|John_Tharp,_Jr.|John Tharp}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Blanche M. '''John Wheadon deGravelles''' (born in 1949)<ref>{{cite web |title=John W deGravelles |url=https://www.lawyercentral.com/john-w-degravelles-interactive-profile--20-279694.html |website=Lawyer Central |publisher=Lawyer Central Network, LLC |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130703034538/https://www.lawyercentral.com/john-w-degravelles-interactive-profile--20-279694.html |archive-date=3 July 2013 |date=2013}}</ref> is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Middle District of Louisiana]], based in the capital city of [[Baton Rouge, Louisiana|Baton Rouge]].

==Biography==

DeGravelles is the son of the late Charles deGravelles and Virginia deGravelles, Louisiana [[Republican Party (United States)|Republicans]] who were once members of the [[Republican National Committee]]. The senior deGravelleses were on the RNC at the same time in 1968. DeGravelles has a twin brother, Charles Nations deGravelles, an [[Episcopal Church in the United States|Episcopalian]] [[archdeacon]], were born on November 2, 1949, in [[Lafayette, Louisiana|Lafayette]], [[Louisiana]].<ref>[http://degravelles.com/resume/ Law Firm Resume] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140524045059/http://degravelles.com/resume/ |date=2014-05-24 }}</ref> His sister, [[Ann McBride Norton]], who died in 2020, was head of the public interest group [[Common Cause]] from 1995 to 1999.<ref name="sister obit">{{cite news |last1=Seelye |first1=Katharine Q. |title=Ann McBride Norton, First Woman to Run Common Cause, Dies at 75 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/05/12/us/politics/ann-mcbride-norton-first-woman-to-run-common-cause-dies-at-75.html |access-date=9 July 2025 |work=[[New York Times]] |date=12 May 2020}}</ref>

DeGravelles received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in 1971 from [[Louisiana State University]] in Baton Rouge. He received a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1974 from the Louisiana State University [[Paul M. Hebert Law Center]] with [[Order of the Coif]] designation.<ref>[http://degravelles.com/about-us/john-w-degravelles/ Law Firm Biography] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140314191838/http://degravelles.com/about-us/john-w-degravelles/ |date=2014-03-14 }}</ref><ref name="fjc.gov">{{FJC Bio|nid=1394621|inline=yes}}</ref>

From 1974 to 1986, he worked at the law firm of Dué, Dodson, deGravelles, Robinson & Caskey (and its predecessor firms), becoming a [[Law firm partner|partner]]  in 1976. He was a solo practitioner from 1986 to 1987. Starting in 1987, he was a partner at deGravelles, Palmintier, Holthaus & Frugé LLP (and its predecessor firms). During his career, he has handled a wide variety of civil litigation in state and federal courts.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/03/13/president-obama-nominates-john-w-degravelles-serve-united-states-distric|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Obama Nominates John W. deGravelles to Serve on the United States District Court for the Middle District of Louisiana|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=13 March 2014}}</ref><ref name="fjc.gov"/>

During his career, deGravelles has been actively engaged in legal education and scholarship. Beginning in 1994, deGravelles became a member of the [[adjunct faculty]] at [[Louisiana State University]] [[Paul M. Hebert Law Center]] where he taught courses in Maritime Torts, Advanced Litigation, Pre-Trial Litigation, and Federal Courts.<ref name="fjc.gov"/>

Since 1993, deGravelles has served as a member of the faculty of [[Tulane University Law School]]'s Summer Program in [[Rhodes, Greece|Rhodes]], [[Greece]], teaching Maritime Personal Injury Law. In association with Tulane Law School, deGravelles has presented lectures on various topics of [[Admiralty law|maritime law]] in [[St. Petersburg, Russia|St. Petersburg]], [[Russia]]; [[Istanbul]], [[Turkey]]; [[Odesa]], [[Ukraine]]; and [[Thessaloniki]], [[Greece]]. In 2015, deGravelles served as a member of the faculty of the LSU Law School's summer program in [[Lyon]], [[France]], teaching maritime law.<ref name="fjc.gov"/>

DeGravelles was awarded a Fulbright Scholarship to teach American Maritime Private International Law at the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki Law School in Thessaloniki, Greece, during the fall semester of 2001. While there, he also gave lectures on the American judicial system. In March, 2011, in association with the Center for International Legal Studies, deGravelles taught a course on the American judicial system at the Lugansk State University of the International Affairs Law School in [[Lugansk]], Ukraine.

During his career, deGravelles has been active in legal organizations. From 1992 to 1993, he served as president of the Louisiana Association for Justice, formerly the Louisiana Trial Lawyers Association. In 1998, he was the president of the Louisiana chapter of the American Board of Trial Advocates. He was a member of the national board of governors of the [[American Association for Justice]] (formerly the American Trial Lawyers Association) from 1993 to 1996 and again from 2011 to 2014. He was admitted as a Fellow of the International Academy of Trial Lawyers in 2006 and the Litigation Counsel of American in 2009.  In 2015, he was elected President of the Dean Henry George McMahon [[American Inns of Court|American Inn of Court]], Inn No. 71.  He has been since 1974 a member of the [[American Bar Association|American]] and Baton Rouge [[bar association]]s and the Maritime Law Association since 1996.{{citation needed|date=April 2023}}

===Federal judicial service===

On March 13, 2014, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated deGravelles to serve as a United States district judge of the United States District Court for the Middle District of Louisiana, to the seat vacated by Judge [[James Joseph Brady]], a Democrat who assumed [[senior status]] on December 31, 2013.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/03/13/presidential-nominations-sent-senate|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=13 March 2014}}</ref> He received a hearing before the [[United States Senate Judiciary Committee]] on May 20, 2014.<ref>{{cite web|title=May 20, 2014: Judicial Nominations|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/judicial-nominations-2014-05-20|publisher=United States Senate}}</ref> On June 19, 2014, his nomination was reported out of committee by a [[voice vote]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%20-%2006-19-14.pdf|title=Executive Business Meeting|publisher=Committee on the Judiciary|work=United States Senate|access-date=19 June 2014}}</ref> On July 16, 2014, Senate Majority Leader [[Harry Reid]] filed a motion to invoke [[cloture]] on deGravelles nomination. On July 22, 2014, the Senate invoked cloture on his nomination by a 57–39 vote.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=113&session=2&vote=00236|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture on John W. deGravelles, of Louisiana, to be U.S. District Judge)|publisher=United States Senate|access-date=22 July 2014}}</ref> Later that day, deGravelles was confirmed by a 100–0 vote.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=113&session=2&vote=00239|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation John W. deGravelles, of Louisiana, to be U.S. District Judge, Middle District of Louisiana)|publisher=United States Senate|access-date=22 July 2014}}</ref> He received his judicial commission on July 23, 2014.<ref name="fjc.gov"/>

===Notable cases===

*On August 31, 2014, deGravelles partially blocked enforcement of Louisiana's new [[abortion]] law which took effect on September 1. The measure requires those performing abortions to have admitting privileges at a hospital within thirty miles of the abortion facility.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/judge-blocks-louisianas-new-abortion-law/ | title=Enforcement of new Louisiana abortion law blocked | website=[[CBS News]] | date=September 2014 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2014/09/01/us/politics/judge-blocks-abortion-law-in-louisiana.html | title=Judge Blocks Abortion Law in Louisiana | newspaper=The New York Times | date=September 2014 }}</ref>
*In October 2015, deGravelles issued a [[temporary restraining order]] that blocked the administration of then Governor [[Bobby Jindal]] from defunding [[Planned Parenthood]] within the state. Jindal spokesman Mike Reed said the state would appeal deGravelles' ruling.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2015/10/planned-parenthood-abortion-louisiana-jindal-medicaid/ | title=A Federal Judge Gave an Epic Defense of Planned Parenthood That Everyone Should Read }}</ref>
*In November 2024, deGravelles issued a preliminary injunction blocking a new Louisiana law requiring public schools to display the Ten Commandments, ruling that the statute is unconstitutional. Louisiana Attorney General [[Liz Murrill]] promised to appeal.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Wall |first=Patrick |date=2024-11-12 |title=Louisiana law requiring the Ten Commandments in schools is unconstitutional, judge rules |url=https://www.theadvocate.com/baton_rouge/news/education/louisiana-ten-commandments-law-ruling-unconstitutional/article_25444e77-70d7-5065-bcfe-a63bcb06036a.html#tncms-source=featured-top |access-date=2024-11-12 |website=The Advocate |language=en}}</ref> 
*In December 2025, deGravelles permanently blocked enforcement of the Louisiana Secure Online Child Interaction and Age Limitation Act, which required social media companies to verify user ages and implement parental consent mechanisms.<ref>''NetChoice v. Murrill'', 3:25-cv-00231 (M.D. La. December 15 2025), Dkt. No. 78, available at https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/69750810/netchoice-v-murrill/</ref> The Louisiana Attorney General filed an appeal in the Fifth Circuit in January 2026.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Netchoice v. Murrill, 26-30016 - CourtListener.com |url=https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/73295493/netchoice-v-murrill/ |access-date=2026-06-16 |website=CourtListener |language=en-us}}</ref>
*On May 3, 2026 deGravelles ruled Senate Bill 256 unconstitutional and blocked the state from eliminating the office of  [[Court clerk|Clerk]] of the [[Orleans Parish]] Criminal District Court, which would have prevented [[Calvin Duncan (legal advocate)|Calvin Duncan]], elected to the position in November 2025, from taking Office.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Masson |first=Rob |last2=Brooks |first2=Jesse |last3=Press |first3=The Associated Press |date=2026-05-04 |title=Louisiana exoneree’s first day as elected clerk gets messy after court intervenes |url=https://www.fox8live.com/2026/05/04/fifth-circuit-grants-stay-calvin-duncan-lawsuit-consolidation-law-takes-effect/ |url-status=live |access-date=2026-05-05 |website=Fox8live.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-11-16 |title=A New Orleans man who had his murder conviction tossed wins election as city’s chief record keeper |url=https://apnews.com/article/new-orleans-clerk-calvin-duncan-dc0ca1c86bcc313b4e5af43ed623fa15 |access-date=2026-05-05 |website=AP News |language=en}}</ref>

[[West Virginia University College of Law|West Virginia University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | footnotes = }} '''Jon David Levy''' (born March 18, 1954) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Maine]] and served as an associate justice of the [[Maine Supreme Judicial Court]] from 2002 to 2014. ==Biography== Levy received a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree in 1976 from [[Syracuse University]]. He received a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1979 from the [[West Virginia University College of Law]] where he was the lead article editor of the Law Review and graduated [[Order of the Coif]]. He served as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[John Thomas Copenhaver Jr.]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of West Virginia]] from 1979 to 1981. From 1981 to 1982, he was appointed by Judge [[William Wayne Justice]] to serve as a special court monitor of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas]]. From 1983 to 1995, he was an attorney in private practice in [[York, Maine]]. From 1995 to 2002, he served as a judge of the [[Courts of Maine|Maine District Court]], serving as deputy chief judge from 2000 to 2001 and chief judge from 2001 to 2002. From 2002 until his confirmation as a federal judge in 2014, he served as an associate justice of the [[Maine Supreme Judicial Court]].{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2013/09/19/president-obama-nominates-eight-serve-united-states-district-courts|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Obama Nominates Eight to Serve on the United States District Courts|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=19 September 2013}}{{cite web |url=http://www.courts.state.me.us/maine_courts/supreme/justices_bios.html#jabar |title=Biography |access-date=September 4, 2013 |archive-date=May 23, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140523104331/http://www.courts.state.me.us/maine_courts/supreme/justices_bios.html#jabar |url-status=dead }}{{FJC Bio|nid=1394461|inline=yes}} ===Federal judicial service=== On September 19, 2013, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Levy to serve as a United States district judge of the United States District Court for the District of Maine, to the seat vacated by Judge [[George Z. Singal]], who assumed [[senior status]] on July 31, 2013.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2013/09/19/presidential-nominations-sent-senate|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=19 September 2013}} On January 16, 2014 his nomination was reported out of committee by a 15–2 vote.{{cite web|title=Executive Business Meeting|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/ExecutiveBusinessMeetingResults-01-16-2014.pdf|work=United States Senate|publisher=Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=16 January 2014}} On April 11, 2014 [[Harry Reid|Senate Majority Leader Reid]] filed a motion to invoke [[cloture]] on the nomination. On April 29, 2014 the [[United States Senate]] invoked [[cloture]] on his nomination by a 63–34 vote.{{cite web|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture on the Nomination of Jon David Levy, of Maine, to be U.S. District Judge)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=113&session=2&vote=00116|access-date=29 April 2014}} On April 30, 2014, his nomination was confirmed by a 75–20 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=113&session=2&vote=00123|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Jon David Levy, of Maine, to be U.S. District Judge for the District of Maine)|publisher=United States Senate|access-date=30 April 2014}} He received his judicial commission on May 2, 2014. He served as chief judge from January 1, 2019[https://www.med.uscourts.gov/news/judge-jon-d-levy-begin-term-chief-judge "Judge Jon D. Levy to Begin Term as Chief Judge", United States District Court for the District of Maine, December 31, 2018] to March 18, 2024.{{Cite press release |title=New Chief U.S. District Judge Term beginning on March 18, 2024 |date=February 29, 2024 |publisher=United States District Court for the District of Maine |url=https://www.med.uscourts.gov/news/new-chief-us-district-judge-term-beginning-march-18-2024 |access-date=April 5, 2024}} He assumed [[senior status]] on May 6, 2024. On May 3, 2024, Levy dismissed a lawsuit filed by Amber Lavigne against Great Salt Bay Community School in [[Damariscotta, Maine]]. Lavigne contended that the school board and individual school officers had violated her “right to control and direct the care, custody, education, upbringing and healthcare decisions of her children,” by providing her then 13-year-old daughter with a chest binder and instructions on using it, and by referring to the child using a new name and pronouns, without consulting Lavigne. Levy held that the school district and individual school personnel could not be held legally liable for providing transgender care to minors without parental permission.{{cite news |title=Judge dismisses lawsuit by mother who said school hid teen's gender expression |url=https://apnews.com/article/transgender-lawsuit-school-informing-parents-maine-e531efdeecb20d8625cb3859a1c3185d |access-date=7 May 2024 |agency=Associated Press |publisher=Associated Press |date=7 May 2024}} ==See also== *[[List of Jewish American jurists]] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1394461}} *{{Ballotpedia|Jon_Levy}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Leigh Saufley]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Justice of the [[Maine Supreme Judicial Court]]}}|years=2002–2014}} {{s-aft|after=[[Jeffrey Hjelm]]}} {{s-bef|before=[[George Z. He then earned a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[Valparaiso University School of Law]] in 1981.{{FJC Bio|nid=1393136|inline=yes}} == Career == From 1981 until 1989, DeGuilio served as an associate for a [[Schererville, Indiana]] law firm, during which time he also served part-time as a deputy prosecutor and public defender for [[Lake County, Indiana]] and as a City Councilman (1984–1987) in Hammond. From 1989 until 1993, DeGuilio served as a prosecuting attorney for Lake County and then from 1993 until 1999 he was the [[United States attorney]] for the Northern District of Indiana. In 1999, he served briefly as a partner in the [[South Bend, Indiana]] office of the [[Barnes & Thornburg]] law firm before taking a job with Peoples Bank SB/NorthWest Indiana Bancorp in 1999. From 1999 until 2001, he served as a senior vice president and trust officer, and from 2001 was the bank's general counsel and corporate secretary until becoming a federal judge. === Federal judicial service === In January 2009, DeGuilio informed Indiana Senator [[Evan Bayh]] of his interest in a vacant federal district judgeship. On January 20, 2010, President Obama nominated DeGuilio to the position, which was vacated by Judge [[Allen Sharp]], who took [[senior status]] in November 2007 and died in 2009.[https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/presidential-nominations-sent-senate-2 Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate], ''whitehouse.gov'' (January 20, 2010). He received his judicial commission on May 13, 2010. He became chief judge on June 1, 2020.{{cite web|url=https://www.innd.uscourts.gov/sites/innd/files/2020-17.pdf|title=In The Matter Of Designating A Chief Judge For The United States District Court, Northern District Of Indiana|publisher=United States District Court for the Northern District of Indiana|date=May 29, 2020|access-date=June 9, 2020}} He assumed [[senior status]] on July 17, 2023. == References == {{Reflist}} == Sources == *{{FJC Bio|nid=1393136}} *{{Ballotpedia|Jon_E._DeGuilio|Jon DeGuilio}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Allen Sharp]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Indiana]]}}|years=2010–2023}} {{s-aft|after=[[Gretchen S. Jon S. Tigar:
{{Short description|American judge (born 1962)}} {{Infobox officeholder | name = Jon S. Tigar | image = File:Judge Tigar BW Desk Photo.jpeg | office = Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of California]] | appointer = [[List of federal judges appointed by Barack Obama|Barack Obama]] | term_start = January 18, 2013 | term_end = | predecessor = [[Saundra Brown Armstrong]] | successor = | birth_name = | birth_date = {{Birth year and age|1962}} | birth_place = [[London]], United Kingdom | death_date = | death_place = | parents = [[Michael Tigar]] | education = [[Williams College]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|BA]])
[[University of California, Berkeley]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Jon S. Tigar''' (born 1962) is an American lawyer serving as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of California]]. He was previously a California state court judge on the [[Alameda County Superior Court]] from 2002 to 2013. == Early life and education == Tigar is the son of attorney [[Michael Tigar]].{{cite news | first=Nick | last=Yulico | url=http://www.metnews.com/articles/judg122801.htm | title=Davis Nominates Santa Clara Judge to Sixth District Court of Appeal | work=Metropolitan News-Enterprise | date=December 28, 2001 | access-date=December 22, 2012}} He graduated from [[Williams College]] in 1984 with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in [[economics]] and [[English literature]]. He spent two years working as a [[paralegal]], then attended the [[UC Berkeley School of Law]], where he was an articles editor of the ''[[California Law Review]]'' and a [[research assistant]] to professor [[Melvin Eisenberg]].{{cn|date=September 2023}} He graduated in 1989 with a [[Juris Doctor]] degree{{cite web |date=11 June 2012 |title=President Obama Nominates Two to Serve on the US District Court |url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2012/06/11/president-obama-nominates-two-serve-us-district-court |work=[[whitehouse.gov]] |via=[[NARA|National Archives]]}} and [[Order of the Coif]] honors.{{cite web |title=Senate Judiciary Committee Questionnaire – Jon S. Tigar |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/download/tigar-senate-questionnaire-public-final-wd |access-date=9 November 2022}} == Career == After graduating from law school, Tigar served as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Robert Smith Vance]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit]] from 1989 to 1990.{{cite web |date=11 June 2012 |title=President Obama Nominates Two to Serve on the US District Court |url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2012/06/11/president-obama-nominates-two-serve-us-district-court |work=[[whitehouse.gov]] |via=[[NARA|National Archives]]}}{{FJC Bio|nid=1394116|inline=yes}} During Tigar's clerkship, Vance was killed by a [[mail bomb]] sent to his home.{{Cite web|title=Judge Vance Murder|url=https://www.fbi.gov/history/famous-cases/judge-vance-murder|access-date=2021-06-10|website=Federal Bureau of Investigation|language=en-us}} From 1990 until 1992, Tigar served as a litigation [[Associate lawyer|associate]] for the law firm [[Morrison & Foerster]]. He then served as a [[public defender]] in San Francisco from 1993 until 1994. Tigar practiced complex [[commercial litigation]], and became a [[Law firm partner|partner]], at the law firm [[Keker, Van Nest & Peters LLP|Keker & Van Nest]] from 1994 until 2002. From 2002 to 2013, Tigar served as a judge on the Alameda County Superior Court. Tigar is an elected member of the [[American Law Institute]], for which he served as an adviser to the [[Restatements of the Law|Restatement (Third) of Torts: Liability for Economic Loss]] and now serves in the same capacity on the forthcoming [https://www.ali.org/project/torts-defamation-and-privacy Restatement (Third) of Torts: Defamation and Privacy].{{Cite web|url=https://www.ali.org/projects/show/torts-defamation-and-privacy/#_participants|title=ALI, Restatement of the Law Third, Torts: Defamation and Privacy: Participants}} Tigar has taught Pretrial Litigation at [[UC Berkeley School of Law]]. He previously served as a member of the California Judicial Council's Advisory Committee on Civil Jury Instructions and the Ninth Circuit's Jury Instructions Committee. From 2016 to 2019, he was the Judicial Representative to the Section of Antitrust Law of the [[American Bar Association]]. He is a Fellow of the [[American Bar Foundation]]. === Federal judicial service === On June 11, 2012, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Tigar to be a judge on the [[United States District Court]] for the Northern District of California, taking the seat vacated by Judge [[Saundra Brown Armstrong]], who assumed [[senior status]] on March 23, 2012. The [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]] held a hearing on his nomination on July 11, 2012, and reported his nomination to the floor on August 2, 2012. The Senate confirmed his nomination by [[unanimous consent]] on December 21, 2012. He received his commission on January 18, 2013. ==Notable decisions== * On April 2, 2015, Tigar ordered the [[California Department of Corrections]] ("CDCR") to provide a [[gender reassignment surgery]] to a transgender inmate, finding that such surgery was the only adequate medical treatment for the inmate's gender dysphoria.{{Cite news|url=https://www.latimes.com/local/lanow/la-me-la-california-inmate-sex-change-20150402-story.html|title=Ryan Parker, "Federal Judge Orders California Prison Inmate Be Granted Sexual Reassignment," L.A. Times (Apr. 2, 2015)}} * Since August 2017, Tigar has presided over ''[[Plata v. Schwarzenegger|Plata v. Newsom]]'', a case concerning the constitutional adequacy of medical care in the California state prison system. On September 27, 2021, Tigar ordered that all [[California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation|CDCR]] staff, including medical and custody staff, be vaccinated against [[COVID-19]], subject to medical and religious exemption.{{Cite web|title="Judge orders California prison guards to get vaccinated," S.F. Chronicle (Sept. 27, 2021)|date=27 September 2021 |url=https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Judge-orders-California-prison-guards-to-get-16491863.php}} Tigar found that because the undisputed evidence showed that staff were the means for COVID to enter the prisons, allowing prison employees to remain unvaccinated violated incarcerated persons' [[Eighth Amendment to the United States Constitution|Eighth Amendment]] [[Constitutional rights]]. On April 25, 2022, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals vacated Tigar's order, finding that CDCR's refusal to require its custody staff to accept the vaccine did not constitute deliberate indifference.''Plata v. Newsom'', No. 21-16696, 2022 WL 1210694 (9th Cir. Apr. 25, 2022). * On November 19, 2018, Tigar issued a [[nationwide injunction]] barring the [[Donald Trump|Trump administration]] from enforcing a rule that would deny asylum to anyone who entered the United States somewhere other than at a designated port of entry.{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/11/20/us/judge-denies-trump-asylum-policy.html|title=Miriam Jordan, "Federal Judge Blocks Trump's Proclamation Targeting Some Asylum Seekers," NY Times (Nov. 20, 2018)|work=The New York Times |date=20 November 2018 |last1=Jordan |first1=Miriam }} Complaining about the ruling, President Trump characterized Tigar as an "Obama judge"—prompting Chief Justice [[John Roberts]] to respond, "We do not have Obama judges or Trump judges, Bush judges or Clinton judges. What we have is an extraordinary group of dedicated judges doing their level best to do equal right to those appearing before them. That independent judiciary is something we should all be thankful for."{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/11/21/us/politics/trump-chief-justice-roberts-rebuke.html|title=Adam Liptak, "Chief Justice Defends Judicial Independence After Trump Attacks 'Obama Judge,'" NY Times (Nov. 21, 2018)|work=The New York Times |date=21 November 2018 |last1=Liptak |first1=Adam }} [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]] upheld Tigar's injunction,{{Cite news|url=http://www.abajournal.com/news/article/9th_circuit_says_new_asylum_restrictions_likely_violate_federal_law_bybee_w/|title=Debra Cassens Weiss, "9th Circuit: New Asylum Restrictions Likely Violate Federal Law; Bybee Wrote Opinion," ABA Journal (Dec. 10, 2018)}}{{Cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2018/dec/07/trump-asylum-ban-immigration-us-court|title="Court Refuses to Allow Trump Asylum Ban for Immigrants Entering Illegally," The Guardian (Dec. 7, 2018)}} and the Supreme Court allowed it to remain in place pending appeal.{{Cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/courts_law/supreme-court-denies-trump-administration-request-to-immediately-enforce-new-asylum-rules/2018/12/21/e9cdaf32-03c8-11e9-b6a9-0aa5c2fcc9e4_story.html|title=Robert Barnes, "Supreme Court Denies Trump Administration Request to Immediately Enforce New Asylum Rules," Washington Post (Dec. 21, 2018)}} On February 2, 2021, [[President Biden]] signed Executive Order 14010 revoking Proclamation 9880 of May 9, 2019 (Addressing Mass Migration Through the Southern Border of the United States),{{Cite web|title=Executive Order 14010—Creating a Comprehensive Regional Framework To Address the Causes of Migration, To Manage Migration Throughout North and Central America, and To Provide Safe and Orderly Processing of Asylum Seekers at the United States Border {{!}} The American Presidency Project|url=https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/executive-order-14010-creating-comprehensive-regional-framework-address-the-causes|access-date=2021-04-01|website=www.presidency.ucsb.edu}} thereby abrogating the rule limiting asylum claims. * On July 24, 2019, Tigar issued a [[nationwide injunction]] that barred the [[Donald Trump|Trump administration]] from denying asylum to persons who crossed through but did not apply for asylum in a third country.{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/07/24/us/asylum-ruling-tro.html|title=Miriam Jordan and Zolan Kanno-Youngs, "Trump's Latest Attempt to Bar Asylum Seekers Is Blocked After a Day of Dueling Rulings," NY Times (July 24, 2019)|work=The New York Times |date=24 July 2019 |last1=Jordan |first1=Miriam |last2=Kanno-Youngs |first2=Zolan }} In August, the Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit found the administration's asylum policy "likely violated federal regulatory law" but narrowed Tigar's injunction to apply only within the Ninth Circuit.{{Cite news|url=https://www.politico.com/story/2019/08/16/immigration-asylum-donald-trump-1667003|title=Ted Hesson, "Trump Scores Partial Win On Asylum Ban As Court Narrows Injunction," Politico (Aug. 16, 2019)}} On September 9, 2019, Tigar reinstated the nationwide scope of the injunction.{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/09/09/us/migrants-asylum-injunction.html|title=Sarah Mervosh, "Judge Reinstates Nationwide Injunction on Trump Asylum Rule," NY Times (Sep. 9, 2019)|work=The New York Times |date=9 September 2019 |last1=Mervosh |first1=Sarah }} The Supreme Court stayed both orders on September 11, 2019, without addressing the legality of the administration's asylum policy.{{Cite news|title=Faith E. Pinho, "Ruling Opens the Way for Sex, Rock and 'Gangster' Talk on License Plates," L.A. Times (Nov. 25, 2020)|url=https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2020-11-25/controversial-personalized-license-plates-court-ruling}} On July 6, 2020, the Ninth Circuit affirmed the injunction blocking the third country asylum bar and upheld the nationwide scope of the injunction. * In November 2020, Tigar issued an order enjoining the [[California Department of Motor Vehicles]] from enforcing a ban on personalized license plate configurations it found “offensive to good taste and decency” on the grounds that the regulation violated the [[First Amendment to the United States Constitution]].{{Cite news|last=|first=|date=|title=Faith E. Pinho, "Ruling Opens the Way for Sex, Rock and 'Gangster' Talk on License Plates," L.A. Times (Nov. 25, 2020)|work=|url=https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2020-11-25/controversial-personalized-license-plates-court-ruling|access-date=March 31, 2021}} Tigar wrote that the DMV's “good taste and decency” standard created “a facial distinction between societally favored and disfavored ideas” and that “the public expression of ideas may not be prohibited merely because the ideas are themselves offensive to some of their hearers.”{{Cite news|title=Bob Egelko, "California's Ban on Some 'Offensive' Vehicle License Tags Ruled Violation of Free Speech," S.F. Chronicle (Nov. 25, 2020)|url=https://www.sfchronicle.com/news/article/California-s-ban-on-some-offensive-15752102.php}} * On June 9, 2025, Tigar issued an order enjoining the Trump administration from enforcing the provisions of particular Executive Orders that required the termination of all "equity-related" contracts and grants and the termination of all funding for any programs that "promote gender ideology." The plaintiffs in the case were "a group of nonprofit organizations that provide healthcare, social services, and advocacy for LGBTQ communities—many specifically serving transgender individuals—and that rely heavily on federal funding to carry out their missions."{{Cite web |title=U.S. Northern District of California Grants Limited Preliminary Injunction of DEI-Related Executive Orders |url=https://www.jdsupra.com/legalnews/u-s-northern-district-of-california-7597032/ |access-date=2025-06-27 |website=JD Supra |language=en}} "The Court reasoned that the vagueness of the language 'equity-related' and the lack of any definition is likely to inhibit the exercise of freedom of expression because it provides no guidance to grantees as to how they can modify their expression to avoid termination or from even assessing what grants are implicated."''Id.'' * Tigar has presided over [[securities fraud]] lawsuits involving some of America’s largest corporations, including [[Netflix]], [[Facebook]], [[Super Micro Computer]], [[Twitter]], [[Wells Fargo Bank]], and [[Yelp]]. Writing in the [[The New York Times|New York Times]], financial writer [[Gretchen Morgenson]] called Judge Tigar’s ruling in the Wells Fargo case “[https://www.nytimes.com/2017/11/03/business/wells-fargo-board.html both unusual and welcome].”{{Cite news |last= |first= |date= |title=Gretchen Morgenson, "Bringing Accountability to the Boardroom,” N.Y. Times (Nov. 3, 2017) |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/11/03/business/wells-fargo-board.html |access-date=November 7, 2024 |work=}} == References == {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1394116}} *{{Ballotpedia|Jon_S._Tigar}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Saundra Brown Armstrong]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of California]]}}|years=2012–present}} {{s-inc}} {{s-end}} {{United States 9th Circuit district judges}} {{authority control}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Tigar, Jon Steven}} [[Category:1962 births]] [[Category:Living people]] [[Category:Judges of the United States District Court for the Northern District of California]] [[Category:Public defenders]] [[Category:Superior court judges in the United States]] [[Category:United States district court judges appointed by Barack Obama]] [[Category:UC Berkeley School of Law alumni]] [[Category:Williams College alumni]] [[Category:British emigrants to the United States]] [[Category:People associated with Morrison & Foerster]]

Hawley To Serve As U.S. Magistrate Judge In Central Illinois |url=https://www.ilcd.uscourts.gov/sites/ilcd/files/MJ%20Information%20Release.pdf}} He received a [[Juris Doctor]], ''cum laude'', from [[DePaul University College of Law]] in 1997.{{Cite press release |title=President Biden Names Fifty-Second Round of Judicial Nominees |date=July 3, 2024 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2024/07/03/president-biden-names-fifty-second-round-of-judicial-nominees/ |access-date=July 3, 2024}} {{PD-notice}} == Career == From 1997 to 1998, Hawley served as a [[law clerk]] to Judge [[Michael P. McCuskey]] on the Illinois Third District Appellate Court and again on the U.S. District Court for the Central District of Illinois in 1998. From 1998 to 1999, he served as a law clerk for Justice [[James D. Heiple]] on the [[Illinois Supreme Court]]. From 1999 to 2014, Hawley served in the Federal Public Defender's Office for the Central District of Illinois. === Federal judicial service === On February 28, 2014, Hawley was selected to serve as a [[United States magistrate judge]] for the U.S. District Court for the Central District of Illinois to fill the vacancy left by the retirement of Judge John A. Gorman. On July 3, 2024, President [[Joe Biden]] announced his intent to nominate Hawley to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Central District of Illinois]].{{Cite web |date=July 3, 2024 |title=President Joe Biden taps local judge to be a federal district judge |url=https://www.centralillinoisproud.com/news/local-news/president-joe-biden-taps-local-judge-to-be-a-federal-district-judge/ |access-date=July 3, 2024 |website=ciproud.com}} On July 8, 2024, his nomination was sent to the Senate. On November 30, 2022, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web|title=Nominations|date=November 30, 2022|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/11/30/2022/nominations}} On January 3, 2023, his nomination was returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]]. '''Jordan Emery Pratt''' (born 1987) is an American lawyer who has served as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Middle District of Florida]] since 2025. He served as a judge of the [[Florida Fifth District Court of Appeal]] from 2023 to 2025. He has served as deputy general counsel of the [[Small Business Administration|United States Small Business Administration]], senior counsel in the Office of Legal Policy of the [[United States Justice Department]] and deputy solicitor general in the [[Florida Attorney General|Florida Attorney General's Office]].

==Education==

Pratt was born in 1987 in [[Tampa, Florida]].<ref>{{cite web |last = Pratt |first = Jordan Emery |date = June 24, 2025 |title = Pratt's Senate Judiciary Committee Questionnaire |url = https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/pratt_sjq.pdf |website = judiciary.senate.com |publisher = United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary |access-date = June 24, 2025}}</ref> He graduated from [[Jesuit High School (Tampa)|Jesuit High School]] in 2006 in Tampa. He graduated as a co-[[valedictorian]] of his undergraduate class at the [[University of Florida]], receiving a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in [[criminology]] in 2009. He received his [[Juris Doctor]], ''[[magna cum laude]]'' and [[Order of the Coif]], from the [[University of Florida Levin College of Law]] in 2012,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.martindale.com/attorney/mr-jordan-e-pratt-168527816/|title=Jordan E Pratt Profile | Daytona Beach, FL Lawyer | Martindale.com|website=www.martindale.com}}</ref> where he was a law review editor and president of the school's [[Federalist Society]] and [[Christian Legal Society]] chapters. During his second summer in law school (2011), he [[intern]]ed for Judge [[Jeffrey Sutton]] on the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://firstliberty.org/news/first-liberty-attorney-jordan-pratt-appointed-state-appellate-judge/|title=First Liberty Attorney Jordan Pratt Appointed to Become State Appellate Judge}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://newsdipper.co.uk/judge-jordan-pratt-florida-appeal-court-journey|title=The Rise of Judge Jordan Pratt: A Distinguished Career in Law and Justice - News Dipper|date=February 13, 2025}}</ref>

==Career==

After graduating from law school, Pratt was a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Harvey Schlesinger]] of the [[United States District Court for the Middle District of Florida]] from 2012 to 2014 and Judge [[Jennifer Walker Elrod]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]] from 2014 to 2015.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.jaxdailyrecord.com/news/2023/nov/02/from-the-bench-fifth-district-court-of-appeal-judge-jordan-pratt/|title=From the bench: 5th District Court of Appeal Judge Jordan Pratt|date=November 2, 2023|website=Jax Daily Record}}</ref> He served as deputy solicitor general in the [[Florida Attorney General|Florida Attorney General's Office]] from 2015 to 2019.<ref name="auto1">{{Cite web|url=https://afj.org/nominee/jordan-e-pratt/|title=Jordan E. Pratt|website=Alliance for Justice}}</ref> Pratt then served as deputy general counsel of the [[Small Business Administration|United States Small Business Administration]] from 2019 to 2020 and senior counsel in the [[Office of Legal Policy]] of the [[United States Justice Department]] between 2020 and 2021. From 2021 to 2023, he was senior counsel at [[First Liberty Institute]].<ref name="auto1"/>  From 2023 to 2025, he served as a judge of the [[Florida Fifth District Court of Appeal]].<ref name="auto">{{Cite web|url=https://floridapolitics.com/archives/740441-donald-trump-names-5-florida-judges-to-u-s-district-judge-posts-across-the-state/|title=Donald Trump names 5 Florida Judges to U.S. District Judge posts across the state|first=Jacob|last=Ogles|date=May 29, 2025}}</ref>

=== Federal judicial service ===

On May 28, 2025, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intention to nominate Pratt to the [[United States District Court for the Middle District of Florida]].<ref name="auto"/> On June 16, 2025, Pratt's nomination was sent to the Senate. President Trump nominated Pratt to the seat to be vacated by Judge [[Steven Douglas Merryday]], who subsequently assumed [[senior status]] on August 31, 2025.<ref>{{Cite web |date=June 16, 2025 |title=PN346-6 — Jordan Emery Pratt — The Judiciary |url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/119th-congress/346/6 |access-date=June 18, 2025 |website=congress.gov}}</ref> On July 21, 2025, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 12–10 [[party-line vote]].<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/2025-07-17_ebm_results2.pdf | title=Results of committee executive business meeting | website=www.judiciary.senate.gov}}</ref> On October 28, 2025, the [[United States Senate]] invoked [[cloture]] on his nomination by a 52–47 vote.<ref>{{Cite web |title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Jordan Emery Pratt to be U.S. District Judge for the Middle District of Florida) |url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1191/vote_119_1_00591.htm |access-date=November 6, 2025 |website=www.senate.gov}}</ref> Later that same day, his nomination was confirmed by a 52–47 vote.<ref>{{Cite web |title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Jordan Emery Pratt, of Florida, to be U.S. District Judge for the Middle District of Florida) |url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1191/vote_119_1_00592.htm |access-date=November 6, 2025 |website=www.senate.gov}}</ref> He received his judicial commission on November 3, 2025.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Jordan Pratt {{!}} Middle District of Florida {{!}} United States District Court |url=https://www.flmd.uscourts.gov/judges/jordan-pratt |access-date=November 6, 2025 |website=www.flmd.uscourts.gov}}</ref><ref>{{FJC Bio|nid=13762072|inline=yes}}</ref>

'''Jose E. Martinez''' (born July 28, 1941)<ref>[https://www.lawdiary.com/docs/subscribers/FL_Judicial_Biographies.pdf BIOGRAPHIES OF FEDERAL COURT JUDGES SITTING IN FLORIDA, December 2018]</ref> is an American lawyer who serves as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida]].

==Early life and education==
Martinez was born in 1941 in [[Santo Domingo]], [[Dominican Republic]]. He received a [[Bachelor of Business Administration]] degree from the [[University of Miami]] in 1962 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Miami School of Law]] in 1965.

==Career==
Martinez served in the [[United States Navy Reserve|United States Naval Reserve]] from 1964 to 1993, and was a [[United States Navy|Navy]] legal officer from 1965 to 1968.

Martinez served as a [[law clerk]] in private practice in 1965. He was an [[assistant United States attorney]] for the Southern District of Florida from 1968 to 1970. Martinez was in private practice in Florida from 1970 to 2002. From 1972 to 1974, he was regional director of the [[Drug Enforcement Administration|Office for Drug Abuse Law Enforcement]] of the [[United States Department of Justice|Department of Justice]].

=== Federal judicial service ===
President [[George W. Bush]] nominated Martinez to the United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida on January 23, 2002, to the seat vacated by Judge [[Edward B. Davis]]. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate|Senate]] on September 13, 2002, and received his commission on September 17, 2002.<ref>{{FJC Bio|nid=1391616|inline=yes}}</ref>

Martinez was the judge in ''[[Sinaltrainal v. Coca-Cola]]''.{{citation needed|date=April 2024}}

'''Joseph Francis Bataillon''' (born October 3, 1949) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Nebraska]].

==Education and career==

Bataillon was born in [[Omaha, Nebraska]]. He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[Creighton University]] in 1971 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Creighton University School of Law]] in 1974. Bataillon was a deputy [[public defender]] for [[Douglas County, Nebraska]] from 1974 to 1980. He was in private practice in Omaha from 1980 to 1997.

===Federal judicial service===

On January 7, 1997, Bataillon was nominated by President [[Bill Clinton]] to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the District of Nebraska]] vacated by Judge [[Lyle Elmer Strom]]. Bataillon was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on September 11, 1997, and received his commission on September 18, 1997. He served as chief judge from 2004 to 2011. He assumed [[senior status]] on October 3, 2014.

===Notable case===

In 2003-05, Bataillon heard ''[[Citizens for Equal Protection v. Bruning]]'', a federal constitutional challenge to a voter initiative constitutional amendment that prohibited Nebraska from recognizing same-sex marriages or unions known as [[Nebraska Initiative Measure 416 (2000)|Nebraska Initiative Measure 416]]. In November 2005, Bataillon ruled that Initiative Measure 416 was unconstitutional under the [[Equal Protection Clause]], the [[First Amendment to the United States Constitution|First Amendment]], and the [[Contract Clause]]'s prohibition on [[bill of attainder|bills of attainder]]. In so doing, Bataillon became the first judge in the U.S. to invalidate a state marriage amendment defining marriage as between a man and a woman on federal constitutional grounds.

In July 2006, the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit]] reversed Bataillon's decision on all three arguments and held that "laws limiting the state-recognized institution of marriage to heterosexual couples ... do not violate the Constitution of the United States."

In 2015, the Eighth Circuit's ruling was invalidated by the [[United States Supreme Court]]'s decision in ''[[Obergefell v. Hodges]]''.

==Personal life==
Bataillon is married to Pam Bataillon, who ran for [[1998 Nebraska gubernatorial election|lieutenant governor of Nebraska in 1998]].<ref name=unopposed>{{cite news|title=Pam Bataillon Campaigns|newspaper=Omaha World-Herald|date=May 8, 1998|page=22|access-date=June 22, 2023|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/892237740/}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Pam Bataillon Entering Race|newspaper=Omaha World-Herald|date=February 23, 1998|page=9|access-date=June 22, 2023|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/892060626/}}</ref>

Salisbury Township, PA|work=United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit|date=August 5, 2022}} (born 1955) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania]]. ==Early life and education== Leeson was born in 1955, in [[Allentown, Pennsylvania]] and received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree, cum laude, in 1977 from [[DeSales University]] in [[Center Valley, Pennsylvania]]. He received a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1980 from the [[Columbus School of Law|Catholic University of America Columbus School of Law]].{{citation needed|date=May 2023}} ==Career== Upon graduation from law school, he became a founding partner of the law firm of Leeson, Leeson & Leeson in [[Bethlehem, Pennsylvania]]. The firm conducted a general civil practice with an emphasis on litigation. In 2014, a fire heavily damaged the historic 19th century building that was owned and occupied by the firm. The building was subsequently reconstructed. Leeson earned certification as a civil trial advocate from the National Board of Trial Advocacy and also served as an arbitrator for the [[American Arbitration Association]]. He served as a solicitor for several municipalities in Pennsylvania.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/06/13/president-obama-announces-intent-nominate-five-serve-united-states-distr|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Obama Announces Intent to Nominate Five to Serve on the United States District Courts|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=13 June 2014}}{{FJC Bio|nid=1394701|inline=yes}} In 2017, he was awarded an honorary Doctor of Law degree from [[DeSales University]].{{citation needed|date=May 2023}} Leeson previously held elected public office as a member of the city council in Bethlehem, where he served as vice president and chair of the finance committee. He also was elected as a member of the Northampton County Government Study Commission where he co-authored the Home Rule Charter for [[Northampton County, Pennsylvania|Northampton County]]. He has served as chair of the boards of the Lehigh Valley Public Telecommunications Corporation (WLVT-TV, WLVR-FM, and LehighValleyNews.com), the Lehigh Valley Community Foundation, the Lehigh–Northampton Airport Authority, and the Janet Johnston Housenick and William D. Housenick Memorial Foundation. He formerly served as a member of the board of commissioners of the Pennsylvania Public Television Network, and as a member of the administrative board of directors of the Pennsylvania Catholic Conference. He currently serves as a member of the Board of Trustees of DeSales University. ===Federal judicial service=== On June 16, 2014, President [[Barack Obama]] [https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/06/13/president-obama-announces-intent-nominate-five-serve-united-states-distr nominated Leeson] to serve as a United States District Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania]] to the seat vacated by Judge [[Eduardo C. Robreno]], who assumed [[senior status]] on August 31, 2013.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/06/16/presidential-nominations-sent-senate|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=16 June 2014}} On July 24, 2014, a hearing before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]] was held on his nomination.{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/judicial-nominations_2014-07-24|title=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|website=www.judiciary.senate.gov|date=24 July 2014 }} On September 18, 2014, his nomination was reported out of committee by a [[voice vote]].{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%209-18-14.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – September 18, 2014 United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|publisher=}} On December 3, 2014, Senate Majority Leader [[Harry Reid]] filed a cloture motion on his nomination. On December 4, 2014, the [[United States Senate]] invoked cloture on Leeson’s nomination by a 66–26 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=113&session=2&vote=00310|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture on the Nomination of Joseph F. Leeson, Jr., of Pennsylvania, to be U.S. District Judge)|publisher=[[United States Senate]]|date=4 December 2014|access-date=30 January 2015}} Later that day, Leeson was confirmed by a 76–16 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=113&session=2&vote=00312|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Joseph F. [[Rutgers Law School|Rutgers University]] ([[Bachelor of Laws|LLB]]) | footnotes = }} '''Joseph Henry Rodriguez''' (born December 12, 1930) is an inactive [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of New Jersey]]. ==Education and career== Rodriguez was born in [[Camden, New Jersey]], to Mario, a survivor of the 1918 sinking of the passenger liner [[SS Carolina|SS ''Carolina'']], and Carmen Martinez Chapel Rodriguez. Rodriguez received an [[Bachelor of Arts|Artium Baccalaureus]] degree from [[La Salle University]] in 1955 and a [[Bachelor of Laws]] from [[Rutgers School of Law–Camden]] in 1958. He was in private practice in Camden from 1959 to 1982. He was the Chairman of the New Jersey State Board of Higher Education from 1971 to 1973, and of the State Commission of Investigation from 1974 to 1979. He was a public advocate/public defender for the State of New Jersey from 1982 to 1985.{{FJC Bio|nid=1387071|inline=yes}} ===Federal judicial service=== On February 28, 1985, Rodriguez was nominated by President [[Ronald Reagan]] to a new seat on the [[United States District Court for the District of New Jersey]] created by 98 Stat. 333. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on May 3, 1985, and received his commission on May 10, 1985. He assumed [[senior status]] on May 22, 1998. In 2007, Rodriguez wrote for a unanimous panel of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit]] when it held that challengers had no [[standing (law)|standing]] to bring claims of racially [[exclusionary zoning]].{{cite journal|title=Recent Case: Third Circuit Denies Standing to Bring Claim of Racial Discrimination in Zoning|journal=[[Harvard Law Review]]|date=2007|volume=120|page=1105|url=https://harvardlawreview.org/wp-content/uploads/pdfs/taliaferro_v_darby.pdf|accessdate=25 October 2017}} In October 2025, [[The Philadelphia Inquirer]] reported that Rodriguez had become inactive the previous month.[https://www.inquirer.com/news/new-jersey/nj-federal-judge-joseph-rodriguez-first-hispanic-camden-20251020.html "New Jersey’s first Hispanic federal judge retires after 40 years on the bench"] ==See also== *[[List of Hispanic and Latino American jurists]] *[[List of first minority male lawyers and judges in New Jersey]] ==References== {{Reflist|2}} ==Sources== * {{FJC Bio|nid=1387071}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=Seat established by 98 Stat. 333}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States District Court for the District of New Jersey]]}}|years=1985–1998}} {{s-aft|after=[[Faith S. '''Joseph Martin Hood''' (born 1942) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Kentucky]].

==Education and career==

Born in [[Ashland, Kentucky|Ashland]], [[Kentucky]], Hood received a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree from the [[University of Kentucky]] in 1965 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Kentucky College of Law]] in 1972. He was in the [[United States Army]] as a Captain from 1966 to 1970. He was a [[law clerk]] to Judge [[Howard David Hermansdorfer]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Kentucky]] from 1972 to 1976, and was then a [[United States magistrate judge]] for the same court from 1976 to 1990.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/hood-joseph-martin|title=Hood, Joseph Martin|website=www.fjc.gov|language=en|access-date=2017-05-01}}</ref>

==Federal judicial service==
[[File:Joseph M. Hood portrait 2007.jpg|thumb|right|Judicial portrait of Hood, 2007, by Marcia Cone.]]
On January 24, 1990, Hood was nominated by President [[George H. W. Bush]] to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Kentucky]] vacated by Judge [[Scott Elgin Reed]]. Hood was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on April 27, 1990, and received his commission on April 30, 1990. He served as Chief Judge from 2005 to 2007, assuming [[senior status]] on October 14, 2007.<ref name=":0" /> He has been a member of the [[Judicial Conference of the United States]] since 2016.

'''Joseph Normand Laplante''' (born July 27, 1965) is an American attorney and jurist serving as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of New Hampshire]].

==Early life and education==

Laplante was born in [[Nashua, New Hampshire]]. He received an [[Bachelor of Arts|Artium Baccalaureus]] degree from [[Georgetown University]] in 1987. He received a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[Georgetown University Law School]] in 1990.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Joseph N. Laplante |url=https://www.law.georgetown.edu/faculty/joseph-n-laplante/ |access-date=2022-07-12 |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Career ==
Laplante worked in private practice in New Hampshire, from 1990 to 1993. He was a senior assistant attorney general in the Office of the Attorney General of the State of New Hampshire, from 1993 to 1998. He was a trial attorney in the Criminal Division of the [[United States Department of Justice]], from 1998 to 1999. He was an [[Assistant United States Attorney|assistant United States attorney]] in the United States Attorney's Office for the District of Massachusetts from 2000 to 2002 and served as first assistant United States attorney in the United States Attorney's Office for the District of New Hampshire from 2002 to 2007.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Judiciary |first=United States Congress Senate Committee on the |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nSnStEpeERIC&dq=Joseph+Normand+Laplante+georgetown&pg=PA342 |title=Confirmation Hearings on Federal Appointments: Hearing Before the Committee on the Judiciary, United States Senate, One Hundred Tenth Congress, First Session |date=2009 |publisher=U.S. Government Printing Office |language=en}}</ref>

Laplante was nominated by President [[George W. Bush]] on June 13, 2007, to a seat vacated by [[Joseph A. Diclerico Jr.]] and subsequently confirmed by the Senate on December 14, 2007 by a vote of 97-0,<ref>{{cite web | title=Meet Joseph Laplante, judge who blocked Trump on birthright citizenship despite Supreme Court ruling | date=10 July 2025 | url=https://www.hindustantimes.com/world-news/us-news/meet-joseph-laplante-judge-who-blocked-donald-trump-on-birthright-citizenship-despite-supreme-court-ruling-101752170291497.html }}</ref> receiving his commission on December 28, 2007.<ref name="FJC">{{FJC Bio|nid=1392671|inline=yes}}</ref> He served as chief judge from 2011 to 2018.<ref name="FJC"/>

==Other activities==
Laplante is a member of the Webster-Batchelder American Inn of Court, and has served on two New Hampshire Bar Association committees: the New Lawyer’s Committee (past chairman), and the Professionalism Committee (past chairman). He is also an advisory board member of the St. Paul’s School Advanced Studies Program, a program that he attended as a student in 1982.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Institute |first1=The American Law |title=Members |url=https://www.ali.org/members/member/453534/ |website=American Law Institute |access-date=15 November 2023 |language=en}}</ref>

Judge Laplante has served on the Nashua Region Board of the New Hampshire Charitable Foundation (chairman 2006–08), the Nashua Police Athletic League and Youth Safe Haven (chairman 2003–08), and the St. Christopher School Advisory Board. He coordinates the youth wrestling program (K-8th grade) for the Boys & Girls Club of Greater Nashua, and volunteers at the Corpus Christi Food Pantry.

He is a boxing referee, licensed to officiate both professional and amateur bouts.<ref>{{cite web |title=- CONFIRMATION HEARINGS ON FEDERAL APPOINTMENTS |url=https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CHRG-110shrg47206/html/CHRG-110shrg47206.htm |website=www.govinfo.gov |access-date=15 November 2023}}</ref>

'''Joseph Scott Van Bokkelen''' (born June 7, 1943) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Indiana]].

==Education and career==
Van Bokkelen was born in Born in [[Chicago]], Illinois and attended [[Mooresville High School (Indiana)|Mooresville High School]]. He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[Indiana University Bloomington]] in 1966 and a [[Juris Doctor]] f rom [[Indiana University Maurer School of Law|Indiana University School of Law]] in 1969. He was a Deputy attorney general of Office of the Indiana Attorney General from 1969 to 1970. He was an Assistant attorney general of Office of the Indiana Attorney General from 1971 to 1972. He was an [[Assistant United States Attorney]] of the United States Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Indiana from 1972 to 1975. He was in private practice in [[Indiana]] from 1975 to 2001. He was the [[United States Attorney]] for the Northern District of Indiana from 2001 to 2007.

==Federal judicial service==
[[File:Richard Lugar and Joe Van Bokkelen.jpg|thumb|left|Van Bokkelen with [[Richard Lugar]] in 2007]]
On January 9, 2007, Van Bokkelen was nominated by President [[George W. Bush]] to a seat  on the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Indiana]] vacated by [[Rodolfo Lozano]]. Van Bokkelen was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on June 28, 2007, and received his commission on July 18, 2007. He assumed [[senior status]] on September 29, 2017. Van Bokkelen took inactive senior status as of July 7, 2025.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.innd.uscourts.gov/sites/innd/files/2025-06.pdf|title=IN RE: ASSIGNMENT OF CIVIL CASES|website=innd.uscourts.gov|date=2025-07-07|access-date=2025-12-26}}</ref>
