Gibson]] on the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit]].{{FJC Bio|nid=1393266|inline=yes}}Dena Bunis, [http://www.ocregister.com/news/tucker-254425-judge-law.html Senate sends O.C. judge to federal bench], ''[[The Orange County Register]]'' (June 21, 2010). == Career == From 1987 until 2002, Staton was an attorney with the [[San Francisco]] and [[Newport Beach]] offices of the law firm [[Morrison & Foerster]], first as an [[Associate lawyer|associate]] (1987–1994) and then as a [[Law firm partner|partner]] (1995–2002). In 2002, Staton became a judge on [[Orange County Superior Court]], based in [[Santa Ana, California|Santa Ana]]. She was appointed to the position by [[Governor of California|Governor]] [[Gray Davis]] to fill the vacancy created when Judge Richard D. Fybel was elevated to the [[California Courts of Appeal|California Court of Appeal]] in Orange County.Allison Lomas, [http://www.metnews.com/articles/appt102102.htm Davis Appoints Attorneys With Diverse Careers to Southern California Courts], ''Metropolitan News-Enterprise'' (October 21, 2002). === Federal judicial service === On February 4, 2010, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Staton to fill the vacancy in the [[United States District Court for the Central District of California|Central District]] created by Judge [[Alicemarie Huber Stotler]], who assumed [[senior status]] in January 2009.[https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/presidential-nomination-sent-senate-2-4-10 Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate 2/4/10] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170216173116/https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/presidential-nomination-sent-senate-2-4-10 |date=2017-02-16 }}, ''[[whitehouse.gov]]'' (February 4, 2010). On March 18, 2010, the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]] reported Staton's nomination to the full Senate, which unanimously confirmed Staton on June 21, 2010, in a voice vote.{{cite web|url=http://news.richmond.edu/news/article/-/2113/breaking-the-logjam-of-nominations-to-the-federal-trial-courts.html|title=Breaking the Logjam of Nominations to the Federal Trial Courts Breaking the Logjam of Nominations to the Federal Trial Courts – University of Richmond|access-date=2017-02-08|archive-date=2017-02-11|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170211080109/http://news.richmond.edu/news/article/-/2113/breaking-the-logjam-of-nominations-to-the-federal-trial-courts.html|url-status=dead}} She received her commission on June 22, 2010. Staton was appointed to the bench under the name of Josephine Staton Tucker and served under that name until September 20, 2013. She assumed senior status on September 19, 2026. ==Notable cases== === Friedrichs v. California Teachers Association === Staton presided over a challenge brought by several Orange County public school teachers to the California Teachers Union's exclusive bargaining system on constitutional grounds. The [[9th Circuit Court of Appeals]] affirmed her ruling in favor of the teachers union,{{Cite web| title=Rebecca Friedrichs, et al., v. California teachers association, et al. | url=https://assets.documentcloud.org/documents/1292811/teacher-friedrichs-plaintiffs-appeals-brief0814.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170202025412/https://assets.documentcloud.org/documents/1292811/teacher-friedrichs-plaintiffs-appeals-brief0814.pdf | archive-date=2017-02-02}} and this ruling was upheld by an evenly divided [[U.S. Supreme Court]] in a 4-4 ''[[per curiam]]'' decision in ''[[Friedrichs v. California Teachers Ass'n]]''.{{cite web|url=https://www.oyez.org/cases/2015/14-915|title=Friedrichs v. California Teachers Association|publisher=oyez.org}} [[Justice Scalia]] had been the expected 5th vote to overturn the controlling 1977 ''[[Abood]]'' decision, but his 2016 death shortly after the case was argued meant there was a deadlocked decision.{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/03/30/us/politics/friedrichs-v-california-teachers-association-union-fees-supreme-court-ruling.html|title=Victory for Unions as Supreme Court, Scalia Gone, Ties 4–4|first=Adam|last=Liptak|newspaper=The New York Times |date=29 March 2016}} Subsequently, ''[[Abood]]'' was overturned in ''[[Janus v. AFSCME]]'' in 2018, which effectively overturned Staton's ruling in ''Friedrichs''.{{cite web |url = https://www.nytimes.com/2018/06/27/us/politics/supreme-court-unions-organized-labor.html |title = Supreme Court Ruling Delivers a Sharp Blow to Labor Unions |first = Adam |last = Liptak |date = 27 June 2018 |access-date = 9 December 2019 |work = [[The New York Times]]}} === Afghan family travel ban case === In the wake of President [[Donald Trump]]'s controversial [[Executive Order 13769]] restricting immigration from seven Muslim-majority countries, certain individuals with valid U.S. visas continued to be detained at borders and airports despite a nationwide temporary restraining order having been issued by U.S. District Judge [[James Robart]] in [[Washington v. Trump (2017)|Washington v. Trump]]. In a case that drew international attention, Staton issued an emergency [[temporary restraining order]] on March 4, 2017, to prevent an Afghan family from being separated—and the wife and three small children sent to a detention facility in Texas—after all five had arrived at [[Los Angeles International Airport]] with [[Special Immigrant Visa]]s and were detained for almost two days without access to counsel.{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/03/04/us/afghan-family-detained-los-angeles-visas.html|title=An Afghan Family, With Visas in Hand, Is Detained in Los Angeles|first=Nicholas|last=Kulish|newspaper=The New York Times |date=4 March 2017}} Staton held a hearing on March 6, 2017, after which the [[Department of Homeland Security]] released the family for provisional resettlement in Washington state{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/local/california/la-me-ln-afghan-family-detained-20170306-story.html|title=Afghan family detained in L.A. despite having special visas will be freed|first=Cindy|last=Carcamo|date=6 March 2017|via=LATimes.com}} and ultimately granted them permanent residency status.{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/local/lanow/la-me-ln-afghan-family-granted-residency-20170418-story.html|title=Afghan family detained at LAX is granted permanent residency|first=Melissa|last=Etehad|date=18 April 2017|via=LATimes.com}} Special immigrant visas were created for citizens from Iraq and Afghanistan whose lives were at risk because they had worked for the U.S. military or government, and the visa requires intense State Department vetting and interviews before being approved. At the hearing it was revealed that the visas had been issued because the father had worked for the U.S. military in Afghanistan for more than 10 years and had received death threats from the [[Taliban]]. === Constitutionality of CFPB === In a case involving a long-running investigation by the [[Consumer Financial Protection Bureau]] (CFPB) into the fraudulent consumer debt relief practices of Morgan Drexen and its proxy law firm, Staton ruled that the CFPB was a constitutionally formed federal bureau.{{cite web|url=http://www.lenderlawwatch.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/9/2019/05/Seila-District-Court-opinion.pdf|title=Seila District Court opinion|date=25 August 2017}} The defendant had argued that the CFPB violated constitutional separation of powers because it was headed by a single Director who exercises substantial executive power but can only be removed by the President for cause. Staton cited the Supreme Court decision in ''[[Morrison v. Olson]]'' to hold that the for-cause removal restriction protecting the CFPB's Director does not "impede the President’s ability to perform his constitutional duty" to ensure that the laws are faithfully executed. Prior to the ruling, a three judge panel of the [[DC Circuit Court of Appeals]] had found the CFPB's structure unconstitutional in a ruling written by then-Judge [[Brett Kavanaugh]], but an [[en banc]] decision by the DC Circuit reversed that decision and found the CFPB to be constitutional.{{cite web|url=http://www.abajournal.com/news/article/full_dc_circuit_upholds_structure_of_consumer_financial_protection_bureau|title=Full DC Circuit upholds structure of Consumer Financial Protection Bureau|first=Debra|last=Weiss|work=ABA Journal |date=31 January 2018|via=abajournal.com}} Staton's ruling was unanimously affirmed by the Ninth Circuit.{{cite web|url=https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2019/05/06/17-56324.pdf|title=CFPB v. Seila Law LLC}} The case, [[Seila Law v. Consumer Financial Protection Bureau]], was argued before the [[U. S. Supreme Court]] on March 3, 2020.{{cite web |url=https://www.scotusblog.com/case-files/cases/seila-law-llc-v-consumer-financial-protection-bureau/ |title=Seila Law LLC v. Consumer Financial Protection Bureau |work=[[SCOTUSblog]] |access-date=9 December 2019}} On June 29, 2020, the Supreme Court in a 5–4 decision ruled that the CFPB structure, with a sole director that could only be terminated for cause, was unconstitutional as it violated the separation of powers, vacating the lower court judgement and remanding the case for review. The Court found that the statute concerning the director of the CFPB was [[severability|severable]] from the rest of the statute establishing the agency, and thus "The agency may therefore continue to operate, but its Director, in light of our decision, must be removable by the President at will."{{cite web | url = https://www.cnbc.com/2020/06/29/supreme-court-leaves-consumer-regulator-standing-but-backs-presidents-ability-to-fire-director.html | title = Supreme Court leaves consumer regulator standing but backs president's ability to fire director | first1 = Dan | last1 = Mangan | first2 = Tucker | last2 = Higgens | date = June 29, 2020 | access-date = June 29, 2020 | work = [[CNBC]] }} === Kids' climate change case === On January 17, 2020, on a 2–1 vote, a Ninth Circuit panel reversed an Oregon district court ruling in [[Juliana v. United States|Juliana, et al. v. United States of America]], et al., a [[climate justice]]-based [[lawsuit]] filed in 2015 by 21 youth plaintiffs including [[Xiuhtezcatl Martinez]] against the [[Federal government of the United States|United States]] and several of its [[Federal government of the United States#Executive branch|executive branch]] positions and officers, formerly including President [[Barack Obama]] and currently, President [[Donald Trump]]. The plaintiffs, on behalf of themselves and future generations, sought relief under the U.S. Constitution for longstanding U.S. governmental policy contributing to global climate disruption and caused by man-made greenhouse gas emissions. The majority agreed that the government had not rebutted the plaintiffs' science-based allegations of a looming climate catastrophe, but found a lack of standing on the part of the plaintiffs, with Judge [[Andrew D. Hurwitz]] holding that "it is beyond the power of an Article III court to order, design, supervise, or implement the plaintiffs' requested remedial plan. As the opinions of their experts make plain, any effective plan would necessarily require a host of complex policy decisions entrusted, for better or worse, to the wisdom and discretion of the executive and legislative branches."{{cite web|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/kids-climate-change-lawsuit-tossed-out-by-federal-appeals-court/ | title = Kids' climate change lawsuit tossed out by federal appeals court | first = Irana | last =Ivanova | date = January 17, 2020 | access-date = January 19, 2020 | work = [[CBS News]] }} In dissent, Staton, sitting on the 9th Circuit panel by designation, characterized the majority as shirking its judicial responsibility to rectify a grave constitutional wrong in the manner the [[U.S. Supreme Court]] laudably did in its landmark [[Brown v. Board of Education]] decision, stating, "My colleagues throw up their hands, concluding that this case presents nothing fit for the Judiciary."{{cite web|url=https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2020/01/17/18-36082.pdf|title=Juliana 9th Circuit opinion|date=27 January 2020}} She further argued, "No case can singlehandedly prevent the catastrophic effects of climate change predicted by the government and scientists. But a federal court need not manage all of the delicate foreign relations and regulatory minutiae implicated by climate change to offer real relief, and the mere fact that this suit cannot alone halt climate change does not mean that it presents no claim suitable for judicial resolution."[https://www.registerguard.com/news/20200117/us-court-dismisses-suit-by-youths-over-climate-change U.S. court dismisses suit by youths over climate change] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201031020958/https://www.registerguard.com/news/20200117/us-court-dismisses-suit-by-youths-over-climate-change |date=2020-10-31 }}, ''[[Register-Guard]]'', Gillian Flaccus (AP), January 18, 2020. Retrieved January 19, 2020. In an analogy from her impassioned dissent that became widely cited in the news media,{{cite web |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/science/archive/2020/01/read-fiery-dissent-childrens-climate-case/605296/ |first=Robinson |last=Meyer |title=A Climate-Lawsuit Dissent That Changed My Mind |website=[[The Atlantic]]|date=January 22, 2020|access-date=January 31, 2020}}{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/01/17/climate/juliana-climate-case.html |first=John |last=Schwartz |title=Court Quashes Youth Climate Change Case Against Government |website=[[New York Times]]|date=January 17, 2020|access-date=January 31, 2020}}{{cite web|url=https://time.com/5767438/climate-lawsuit-kids/ |first=Madeleine |last=Carlisle |title=A Federal Court Threw Out A High Profile Climate Lawsuit. Here's What It Might Mean For The Future of Climate Litigation |website=[[Time Magazine]]|date=January 18, 2020|access-date=January 31, 2020}} Staton stated that "[i]n these proceedings, the government accepts as fact that the United States has reached a tipping point crying out for a concerted response -- yet presses ahead toward calamity. It is as if an asteroid were barreling toward Earth and the government decided to shut down our only defenses. Seeking to quash this suit, the government bluntly insists that it has the absolute and unreviewable power to destroy the Nation."[https://www.cnn.com/2020/01/17/politics/climate-childrens-lawsuit/index.html Appeals court throws out lawsuit by children seeking to force action on climate crisis], ''[[CNN]]'', Dan Berman, January 17, 2020. Retrieved January 19, 2020. The plaintiffs in Juliana subsequently requested a full ''[[en banc]]'' review by the 9th Circuit of the panel's decision.[http://climatecasechart.com/case/juliana-v-united-states/ Climate Case Status chart] Retrieved June 29, 2020. The petition was denied.{{cite web |url=https://www.bloomberglaw.com/public/desktop/document/KelseyRoseJulianaetalvUSAetalDocketNo18360829thCirDec272018CourtD/10?1612999900 |title=Kelsey Rose Juliana, et al v. USA, et al, Docket No. 18-36082 (9th Cir. Dec 27, 2018), Court Docket |website=www.bloomberglaw.com |access-date=February 10, 2021}} === Coronavirus quarantine case === In a case that drew national media attention, Staton issued a temporary restraining order at the request of the City of [[Costa Mesa]] on February 21, 2020, in response to a hasty plan by the State of California and the U.S. federal government to ship dozens of patients testing positive for coronavirus, then quarantined at [[Travis Air Force Base]] in [[Solano County]], to a former assisted living center in [[Orange County, California]].{{cite web|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/health/health-news/federal-judge-blocks-effort-transfer-coronavirus-patients-california-city-n1140786/ | title = Federal judge blocks effort to transfer coronavirus patients to California city | first = Alicia | last = Victoria Lozano | date = February 22, 2020 | access-date = March 25, 2020 | work = [[NBC News]] }} Staton scheduled an expedited hearing for the following Monday, after which she continued the TRO in place pending a showing by the State of California as to its plan to house the patients in a densely populated part of the county. Prior to the hearing, the federal government had planned to ship the non-California resident former passengers of the {{ship||Diamond Princess|ship|2}} cruise ship from Travis to a former army base in [[Anniston, Alabama]], but Governor [[Kay Ivey]] of Alabama lobbied [[President Trump]] to include them in the group to be sent to Orange County, California, instead.{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/02/23/us/coronavirus-quarantine-california-alabama.html/ | title = Don't Send Them Here: Local Officials Resist Plans to House Coronavirus Patients | first = Farah | last = Stockman | date = February 23, 2020 | access-date = March 25, 2020 | work = [[New York Times]] }} At the hearing it became apparent that neither the State of California nor the Federal Government had developed a rationale for the plan,{{cite web|url=https://www.ocregister.com/2020/02/24/hed-goes-here-on-outcome-of-court-hearing// | title = Injunction stays in place on using Fairview Developmental Center in Costa Mesa to house coronavirus patients | first = Alica | last = Robinson | date = February 24, 2020 | access-date = March 25, 2020 | work = [[Orange County Register]] }} so the TRO was continued for another week to allow the authorities to do so. Prior to the next scheduled hearing, as the [[COVID-19 pandemic]] evolved, the state and federal governments withdrew their plan to house the Travis patients at the Fairview Developmental Center location.{{cite web|url=https://www.ocregister.com/2020/03/01/hearing-canceled-on-feds-scrapped-plan-to-house-coronavirus-patients-in-o-c/ | title = Hearing canceled on Feds' scrapped plan to house Coronavirus patients in O.C. | date = March 1, 2020 | access-date = March 25, 2020 | work = [[Orange County Register]] }} == References == {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1393266}} *{{Ballotpedia|Josephine_S._Tucker|Josephine Staton}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Alicemarie Huber Stotler]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Central District of California]]}}|years=2010–2026}} {{s-vac}} {{s-end}} {{United States 9th Circuit district judges}} {{authority control}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Staton, Josephine L.}} [[Category:1961 births]] [[Category:Living people]] [[Category:21st-century American women judges]] [[Category:California state court judges]] [[Category:Harvard Law School alumni]] [[Category:Judges of the United States District Court for the Central District of California]] [[Category:People associated with Morrison & Foerster]] [[Category:United States district court judges appointed by Barack Obama]] [[Category:William Jewell College alumni]]

[[Yale University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | party = }} '''Joshua Michael Divine''' (born 1990) is an American lawyer and jurist who serves as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri]] and of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Missouri]]. From January 2023 to 2025, he was [[Solicitor General of Missouri|solicitor general of Missouri]]. ==Education== Divine was born in 1990 at [[Yokota Air Base]], near [[Tokyo]], Japan.{{cite web |last = Divine |first = Joshua Michael |date = June 3, 2025 |title = Divine's Senate Judiciary Committee Questionnaire |url = https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/divine_sjq.pdf |website = judiciary.senate.com |publisher = United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary |access-date = June 3, 2025}} He received a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree in mathematics with highest honors from the [[University of Northern Colorado]] in 2012. He was a columnist for the student newspaper ''[[The Mirror (UNC newspaper)|The Mirror]]''. Following graduation from UNCO, Divine worked briefly as a day laborer, [[Law School Admission Test|LSAT]] instructor, and [[paralegal]]. He then attended [[Yale Law School]], where he was a ''Forum'' editor of ''[[The Yale Law Journal]]'' and a member of the school's [[Federalist Society]] chapter.{{Cite web |title=The Yale Law Journal - Masthead: Volume 125 |url=https://www.yalelawjournal.org/masthead/volume-125 |access-date=2025-08-02 |website=www.yalelawjournal.org}} He received a [[Juris Doctor]] from Yale in 2016.{{Cite web|url=https://www.kttn.com/missouri-ag-staffers-nominated-by-trump-for-federal-judge-positions/|title=Missouri AG staffers nominated by Trump for federal judge positions|work=KTTN News|date=May 7, 2025}} ==Career== Divine served as a [[law clerk]] to Judge [[William H. Pryor Jr.]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit]] from 2016 to 2017. He then served as a deputy solicitor general in the Office of the [[Missouri Attorney General]] from 2017 to 2019, before working as the deputy counsel to United States Senator [[Josh Hawley]]. From 2020 to 2021, Divine served as a law clerk to Justice [[Clarence Thomas]] of the [[Supreme Court of the United States]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/st-louis-post-dispatch-judge-continues/171891108/|title= County judge to step down for a job with AG |first1= Kurt|last1=Erickson|work=St. Louis Post-Dispatch|date=December 29, 2022|pages=A1, A3|via=newspapers.com}} Divine then worked as [[counsel|Chief Counsel]] to Senator Hawley, and in December 2022, was named by [[Missouri Attorney General]] [[Andrew Bailey (politician)|Andrew Bailey]] to serve as Solicitor General of Missouri in 2023. In that capacity, he successfully challenged [[Economic policy of the Joe Biden administration#Student loan forgiveness|student loan forgiveness]] efforts by President [[Joe Biden]]. === Federal judicial service === On May 6, 2025, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to nominate Divine to serve as a United States district judge of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri]] and the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Missouri]].{{Cite web |date=May 6, 2025 |title=White House Press Release - President Donald J. Trump Announces Judicial Candidate Nominations |url=https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/white-house-press-release-president-donald-j-trump-announces-judicial-candidate-1 |access-date=May 13, 2025 |website=www.presidency.ucsb.edu}} On May 12, 2025, his nomination was sent to the Senate. President Trump nominated Divine to the seat vacated by Judge [[Rodney W. Sippel]], who assumed [[senior status]] on January 28, 2023. On June 26, his nomination was favorably reported out of committee by a 12–10 [[party-line vote]].{{Cite web |date=June 26, 2025 |title=Results of Executive Business Meeting |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/2025-06-26_ebm_results.pdf |access-date=June 26, 2025 |website=U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee}} On July 17, the Senate invoked [[cloture]] on his nomination by a 52–46 vote.{{Cite web |date=July 17, 2025 |title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Joshua M. Divine to be U.S. District Judge for the Eastern and Western Districts of Missouri) |url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1191/vote_119_1_00412.htm |access-date=July 22, 2025 |website=www.senate.gov}} On July 22, his nomination was confirmed by a 51–46 vote.{{Cite web |date=July 22, 2025 |title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Joshua M. Divine, of Missouri, to be United States District Judge for the Eastern and Western Districts of Missouri) |url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1191/vote_119_1_00420.htm |access-date=July 22, 2025 |website=www.senate.gov}} He received his judicial commission on July 24, 2025.{{FJC Bio|nid=13762033}}{{Cite web |title=Hon. Joshua M. Divine Sworn In as United States District Judge for Eastern District of Missouri {{!}} Eastern District of Missouri {{!}} United States District Court |url=https://www.moed.uscourts.gov/news/2025/hon-joshua-m-divine-sworn-united-states-district-judge-eastern-district-missouri |access-date=2025-08-03 |website=www.moed.uscourts.gov}} ==== Notable cases ==== Divine was one of the first judges to rule in favor of the Trump administration's policy of detaining without bond immigrants facing deportation. As of November 2025, Judge Divine was one of "only eight judges nationwide" to rule that way, with more than 200 ruling the other way.{{Cite web |date=2025-11-28 |title=More than 220 judges have now rejected the Trump admin’s mass detention policy |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2025/11/28/trump-detention-deportation-policy-00669861 |access-date=2026-02-21 |website=POLITICO |language=en}}{{Cite web |title=Mejia Olalde v. Nov. 10, 2025) |url=https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.moed.223800/gov.uscourts.moed.223800.26.0.pdf}}{{Cite web |date=2026-02-12 |title=Even Trump’s own appointees are ruling against ICE’s mass detention strategy |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2026/02/12/donald-trump-judges-mandatory-detention-rulings-00778256 |access-date=2026-02-22 |website=POLITICO |language=en}} The [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]], the first federal appellate court to rule on the issue, ruled the same way as Judge Divine.{{Cite web |date=2026-02-07 |title=Appeals court affirms Trump policy of jailing immigrants without bond |url=https://apnews.com/article/fifth-circuit-immigrant-detainees-denied-bond-f5265ecf771d1f8e9f20d48bddfb1a25 |access-date=2026-02-22 |website=AP News |language=en}} == Selected publications == * Divine, Joshua M. [[Harvard Law School|Harvard University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | party = }} '''Joshua David Wolson''' (born 1974) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania]]. ==Early life and education== Wolson was born in [[Ann Arbor, Michigan]], in 1974. He attended and graduated from [[Parkland High School (Pennsylvania)|Parkland High School]] in [[South Whitehall Township, Pennsylvania]], and then attended the [[University of Pennsylvania]], where he graduated with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] ''[[magna cum laude]]'' in 1996. Three years later, in 1999, he was awarded his [[Juris Doctor]] ''cum laude'' from [[Harvard Law School]].[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-fourteenth-wave-judicial-nominees-thirteenth-wave-united-states-attorney-nominees-eighth-wave-united-states-marshal-nominees/ "President Donald J. Trump Announces Fourteenth Wave of Judicial Nominees, Thirteenth Wave of United States Attorney Nominees, and Eighth Wave of United States Marshal Nominees" White House, May 10, 2018] {{PD-notice}} ==Career == After graduating from Harvard Law School in 1999, he served as a [[law clerk]] to Judge [[Jan E. DuBois]], a federal judge in the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania|U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania]] from 1999 to 2000. He then joined [[Covington & Burling]] in [[Washington, D.C.]], where he served for eight years as an [[Associate lawyer|associate]] in the firm's [[litigation]] and [[antitrust]] groups. He returned to [[Philadelphia]] and joined Dilworth Paxson's litigation group in 2008, becoming a [[Law firm partner|partner]] in 2010. He represented plaintiffs and defendants in complex litigation matters, including antitrust, [[RICO]], [[intellectual property]], [[procurement]], and [[civil rights]] disputes. He also served as a co-chair of the firm's Plaintiffs' Rights Practice Group and a member of the firm's executive committee. == Federal judicial service == On May 10, 2018, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to nominate Wolson to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] for the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania]] after the seat was vacated by Judge [[James Knoll Gardner]], who assumed senior status on April 3, 2017. On May 15, 2018, Wolson's nomination was sent to the [[United States Senate|Senate]]. On July 11, 2018, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/07/11/2018/nominations United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Nominations for July 11, 2018] On September 13, 2018, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 13–8 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/09-13-18%20Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – September 13, 2018|publisher=Senate Judiciary Committee}} On January 3, 2019, his nomination was returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]]. On January 23, 2019, President Trump announced his intent to renominate Wolson for a federal judgeship.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-intent-nominate-judicial-nominees/ "President Donald J. Trump Announces Intent to Nominate Judicial Nominees", White House, January 23, 2019] His nomination was sent to the Senate later that day.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/nominations-sent-senate-2/ "Nominations Sent to the Senate", White House, January 23, 2019] On February 7, 2019, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 14–8 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/02.07.2019%20Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting1.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – February 7, 2019|publisher=Senate Judiciary Committee}} On May 1, 2019, the Senate invoked cloture on his nomination by a 64–35 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1161/vote_116_1_00090.htm|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture Joshua Wolson to be U.S. District Judge for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania)|website=United States Senate|date=May 1, 2019}} On May 2, 2019, his nomination was confirmed by a 65–33 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1161/vote_116_1_00093.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Joshua Wolson, of Pennsylvania, to be U.S. District Judge for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania)|website=United States Senate|date=May 2, 2019}} He received his judicial commission on May 28, 2019.{{FJC Bio|nid=6385006|inline=yes}} Wolson occupies the same federal judgeship seat for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania that he previously clerked for, having clerked for Judge Jan E. DuBois, who preceded Judge James K. Gardner, who ultimately preceded Wolson.{{Cite web |last=Voruganti |first=Harsh |date=2018-07-18 |title=Joshua Wolson – Nominee to the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania |url=https://vettingroom.org/2018/07/18/joshua-wolson/ |access-date=2026-06-29 |website=The Vetting Room |language=en}} Wolson has demonstrated a commitment to his local Pennsylvania community. In February 2025, Wolson returned to his alma mater, Parkland High School in South Whitehall Township, to hold a live hearing in front of the school's AP American Government students and members of the school's law club.{{Cite web |last=Moughan |first=Layne |title=Order in the… High School? |url=https://phstrumpet.org/5200/news/order-in-the-high-school/ |access-date=2026-06-29 |website=The Trumpet}} After the hearing, Wolson answered questions from the students in attendance. === Notable cases and rulings === On the bench, Wolson has gained notoriety for using pop culture references, especially in introductions, to illustrate legal concepts.{{Cite web |title=A Motion to Reconsider A Motion For Leave To File a Motion To Reconsider A Motion To Reconsider |url=https://ipde.com/blog/2023/06/13/a-motion-to-reconsider-a-motion-for-leave-to-file-a-motion-to-reconsider-a-motion-to-reconsider/ |access-date=2026-06-30 |website=ipde.com |language=en}}{{Cite web |title=Federal judge cites The Simpsons in wage ruling {{!}} Eric Meyer posted on the topic |url=https://www.linkedin.com/posts/emeyer_theemployerhandbook-employmentlaw-humanresources-activity-7328720871349456897-QTau |access-date=2026-06-30 |website=LinkedIn |language=en}}{{Cite web |date=2021-04-15 |title=Pennsylvania Court Quotes Taylor Swift Song in Decision on Free Speech |url=https://www.newsweek.com/pennsylvania-court-quotes-taylor-swift-song-decision-free-speech-1583896 |access-date=2026-06-30 |website=Newsweek |language=en}} For example, in a 2021 free speech lawsuit, ''Crash Proof Retirement, LLC v. Paul M. Price'', Wolson quoted [[Taylor Swift]] to explain that critical opinions do not inherently amount to commercial speech for the basis of a [[Lanham Act]] claim, writing:
If free speech means anything, it means that you do not get to sue people because you don't like their opinion of you. In the immortal words of Taylor Swift, although "haters gonna hate, hate, hate . . . ," sometimes you just have to "shake it off." "Shake it off," however, Crash Proof Retirement did not. Instead, it sued Paul M. Price . . . .{{Cite web |title=State Bar of Texas {{!}} Articles |url=https://www.texasbar.com/AM/Template.cfm?Section=articles&Template=/CM/HTMLDisplay.cfm&ContentID=61875 |access-date=2026-06-29 |website=www.texasbar.com}}
Wolson has also made references to Philadelphia. On February 18, 2021, in ''Julie Darrup v. Wal-Mart Stores East, LP'', Wolson wrote:
Philadelphia has much to recommend it. World class cuisine. Great universities. Gritty. But one thing that Philadelphia, and the Eastern District of Pennsylvania as a whole, lacks is any connection to this case. The case arises from a slip-and-fall at a Walmart store in Coal Township, Pennsylvania, in the Middle District of Pennsylvania. Even though the accident occurred there, Plaintiff Julie Darrup channels her inner W.C. Fields and argues that she'd rather be in Philadelphia. The problem is that she never lived in this District, never got treatment in this District, and never had any other connection to this District. The Court will therefore grant Walmart's Motion to transfer this case to the Middle District of Pennsylvania pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a).{{Cite web |title=DARRUP v. WAL-MART STORES EAST, LP et al, No. 1:2021cv00314 - Document 14 (M.D. Pa. 2021) |url=https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/pennsylvania/pamdce/1:2021cv00314/128157/14/ |access-date=2026-06-30 |website=Justia Law |language=en}}
Similarly, in a March 10, 2021 ruling in ''Tomei v. Office of the 32nd Judicial District of Delaware County'', Wolson combined references to both pop culture and Philadelphia sports:
The Court does not have the power to make the world a perfect place. If it could, Jim Fregosi would not have pulled Roger Mason in Game 6 of the 1993 World Series, the Phillies wouldn't have traded Ryne Sandberg for Ivan DeJesus, and the 76ers would have drafted Brad Daugherty instead of trading for Roy Hinson. And, of course, Simba would have never gone down into that gorge. But courts only have the power to grant relief afforded under the law. Instead, parties must live with the wisdom of Timon: "Look kid. Bad things happen, and you can't do anything about it . . . ."{{Cite web |date=2021-03-10 |title=TOMEI v. OFFICE OF THE 32ND JUDICIAL DISTRICT DELAWARE COUNTY, 2:20-cv-02429 |url=https://app.midpage.ai/document/tomei-v-office-of-the-10400598 |access-date=2026-06-30 |website=Midpage |language=en}}
In a March 2026 ruling, Wolson employed sci-fi analogies to explain a patent dispute between Moderna, Arbutus Biopharma, and Genevant Sciences regarding the lipid nanoparticle (LNP) delivery technology used in COVID-19 vaccines. Framing the allegations that Moderna infringed on patents during the government's [[Operation Warp Speed]], Wolson wrote:
In Star Trek, members of Starfleet must observe the Prime Directive, even as they jump into or come out of warp speed. In this case, Arbutus Biopharma Corp. and Genevant Sciences GmbH (collectively, "Arbutus") claim that during the U.S. Government's own Operation Warp Speed to find a vaccine for Covid-19, Moderna Inc. and ModernaTX, Inc. (collectively, "Moderna") violated the Prime Directive of patent law: don't copy other people's inventions. Moderna asks me to hold as a matter of law that when it jumped to warp speed to make a Covid-19 vaccine, it did so for the Government . . . .{{Cite web |last=Wolson |first=Joshua |date=February 2, 2026 |title=Arbutus Biopharma Corporation and Genevant Sciences GmbH v. Moderna, Inc. and ModernaTX, Inc. |url=https://www.ded.uscourts.gov/sites/ded/files/opinions/22-252_1.pdf |access-date=June 29, 2026}}
Wolson's subsequent [[summary judgment]] rulings on the eve of trial spurred a $2.25 billion settlement, the largest disclosed patent settlement in pharmaceutical industry history.{{Cite web |title=Genevant Sciences Wins $2.25 Billion Settlement in COVID-19 Patent Litigation Case {{!}} Williams & Connolly LLP |url=https://www.wc.com/News/248103/Genevant-Sciences-Wins-225-Billion-Settlement-in-COVID-19-Patent-Litigation-Case |access-date=2026-06-29 |website=www.wc.com}}{{Cite web |last=Bhatti |first=Pomy |date=2026-03-03 |title=Genevant Sciences and Arbutus Biopharma Announce $2.25 Billion Global Settlement With Moderna |url=https://www.genevant.com/genevant-sciences-and-arbutus-biopharma-announce-2-25-billion-global-settlement-with-moderna/ |access-date=2026-06-29 |website=Genevant Sciences |language=en-GB}} == Memberships == On his Senate Judiciary Committee questionnaire, Wolson reported being a member of the [[Federalist Society]], the [[American Bar Association]], [[Republican Jewish Coalition]], and the Republican National Lawyers Association.[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Wolson%20SJQ1.pdf United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees: Joshua D. '''Joy Flowers Conti''' (born 1948)<ref>{{Cite web |title=Joy Flowers Conti, Senior District Judge |url=https://www.pawd.uscourts.gov/content/joy-flowers-conti-senior-district-judge |access-date=2021-04-26 |website=www.pawd.uscourts.gov}}</ref> is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania]].

==Early life and education==
Born in [[Kane, Pennsylvania|Kane]], [[Pennsylvania]], Conti grew up in an army family and graduated from high school in Germany.<ref>{{cite web|author=Brian Bowling |url=http://triblive.com/x/pittsburghtrib/news/pittsburgh/s_711498.html |title=Newsmaker: Judge Joy Flowers Conti |publisher=TribLIVE |date=2010-11-30 |accessdate=2017-10-26}}</ref> Conti graduated from [[Duquesne University]] with her [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in 1970 where she was a member of [[Alpha Phi]]. She later graduated from [[Duquesne University School of Law]] with a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1973, where she was editor-in-chief of the ''Duquesne Law Review''.<ref name=pabar>{{cite web|url=http://www.pabar.org/site/Public/Media/NewsReleases/2016/10-26-2016 |title=Chief Judge Joy Flowers Conti, U.S. District Court for the Western of Pennsylvania, to Receive Award from PBA Business Law Section |publisher=Pabar.org |date=2016-10-26 |accessdate=2017-10-26}}</ref>

==Legal career==
Conti began her legal career working as a [[law clerk]] for Justice Louis L. Manderino, [[Supreme Court of Pennsylvania]] from 1973 to 1974. She was in private practice in [[Pennsylvania]] from 1974 to 1976 and again from 1982 to 2002. In 1974, Conti was the first female lawyer hired by Kirkpatrick, Lockhart, Johnson & Hutchinson, now known as [[K&L Gates|K&L Gates, LLP]].<ref name=pabar/> Conti was a professor of law at Duquesne University School of Law from 1976 to 1982. She was a Hearing examiner (part-time) for the  Bureau of Occupational and Professional Affairs, Department of State in Pennsylvania from 1978 to 1982. She returned to Kirkpatrick & Lockhart in 1982.<ref name=pabar/> In 1996, she joined [[Buchanan Ingersoll & Rooney]] concentrating her practice on bankruptcy, healthcare, general corporate, and nonprofit corporation law.<ref name=pabar/>

==Federal judicial career==
In 2002, Conti was nominated to the United States District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania by President [[George W. Bush]] on January 23, 2002 to a seat vacated by [[Alan N. Bloch]].  Conti was confirmed by the [[United States Senate|Senate]] on July 29, 2002 on a Senate vote and received her commission on July 31, 2002. She served as chief judge from 2013, upon the resignation of [[Sean J. McLaughlin]], till 2018. She assumed [[senior status]] on December 6, 2018.

'''Judith Ellen Levy''' (born 1958) is an American lawyer who has served as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan]] since 2014.

==Early life==
Levy was born in 1958 in [[Bloomington, Indiana]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/113thCongressJudicialNominations/upload/Levy-Senate-Questionnaire-Final.pdf |title=Senate Judiciary Committee Nomination Questionnaire |date= |access-date=December 5, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170224132403/http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/113thCongressJudicialNominations/upload/Levy-Senate-Questionnaire-Final.pdf |archive-date=February 24, 2017 |url-status=dead }}</ref> She received a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree in 1981 from the [[University of Michigan]] and a [[Juris Doctor]], cum laude, in 1996 from the [[University of Michigan Law School]].
Levy worked at the [[Michigan Medicine|University of Michigan Hospital]] and served as the bargaining chairman for Local 1583 of the [[American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees]] for six years.<ref>[https://quod.lib.umich.edu/u/umregproc/ACW7513.1992.001?rgn=main;view=fulltext ''Proceedings of the Board of Regents (1992–1993)'' Ann Arbor: University of Michigan Board of Regents]</ref>

Levy is openly gay and has three daughters.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.hrc.org/blog/entry/openly-gay-attorney-one-of-six-nominated-to-district-court-today/ |title=Openly Gay Attorney One of Six Nominated to District Court Today, Human Rights Campaign blog |publisher=Hrc.org |date=July 26, 2013 |access-date=December 5, 2013 |archive-date=December 19, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131219033024/http://www.hrc.org/blog/entry/openly-gay-attorney-one-of-six-nominated-to-district-court-today/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

She is Jewish. 
<ref>https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1_4gFznrC3U&t=220s</ref>

==Career==
From 1996 to 1999, she worked as a [[law clerk]] to Judge [[Bernard A. Friedman]] of the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan. From 1999 to 2000, she was a trial attorney for the [[United States Equal Employment Opportunity Commission]]. From 2000 to 2014, Levy served as an [[Assistant United States Attorney]] in the Eastern District of Michigan, and was Chief of the Civil Rights Unit in 2010–2014.<ref name="whitehouse1">{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2013/07/25/president-obama-nominates-six-serve-united-states-district-court |title=President Obama Nominates Six to Serve on the United States District Court |date=July 25, 2013 |via=[[NARA|National Archives]] |work=[[whitehouse.gov]] |access-date=December 5, 2013}}</ref><ref name="fjc.gov">{{FJC Bio|nid=1394396|inline=yes}}</ref>

===Federal judicial service===
On July 25, 2013, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Levy to serve as a federal judge on the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan]], to the seat vacated by Judge [[Nancy Garlock Edmunds]], who assumed [[senior status]] on August 1, 2012.<ref name="whitehouse1"/> On March 11, 2014, the [[United States Senate]] invoked cloture on her nomination by a 56–42 vote.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1132/vote_113_2_00064.htm|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture on the Nomination of Judith Ellen Levy, of Michigan, to be U.S. District Judge)|website=www.senate.gov}}</ref> On March 12, 2014, her nomination was confirmed by a 97–0 vote.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=113&session=2&vote=00069|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Judith Ellen Levy, of Michigan, to be U.S. District Judge for the Eastern District of Michigan)|website=www.senate.gov}}</ref> She received her judicial commission on March 14, 2014.<ref name="fjc.gov"/> With her confirmation and receiving of commission, she became the first openly [[lesbian]] federal judge in Michigan.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Resnikoff |first=Ned |date=March 17, 2014 |title=Senate confirms first openly lesbian federal judge in Michigan |url=https://www.msnbc.com/msnbc/mich-gets-first-out-lesbian-federal-judge-msna287711 |access-date=June 20, 2023 |website=MSNBC.com |language=en}}</ref>

==== Notable rulings ====

On November 10, 2021, Levy approved a $626 million settlement for the people of [[Flint, Michigan|Flint]] who were affected by the [[Flint water crisis]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Stelloh |first=Tim |date=November 10, 2021 |title=Judge approves $626 million settlement in Flint water crisis |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/judge-approves-626-million-settlement-flint-water-crisis-rcna5183 |access-date=November 10, 2021 |website=[[NBC News]] |language=en}}</ref>

In December 2025, Levy declined to impose an additional two-year sentence related to illegal immigration charges on Honduran national [[Edys Renan Membreno Diaz]], who had previously been convicted and sentenced for raping a disabled woman. While giving her ruling, Levy referred to Diaz as an "ambassador for living up to our immigration restrictions" and praised him for his "family devotion and willingness to perform work that it claimed Americans find undesirable."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Zimmermann |first=David |date=December 13, 2025 |title=Obama-appointed judge under fire for light sentence and praise of illegal immigrant who raped woman with cerebral palsy |url=https://www.washingtonexaminer.com/news/justice/3917059/obama-judge-light-sentence-praise-of-illegal-immigrant-raped-woman-cerebral-palsy/ |access-date=January 6, 2026 |website=[[Washington Examiner]] |language=en}}</ref>

[[Penn State Dickinson Law]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Julia Kathleen Munley''' (born 1965){{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Munley%20SJQ%20Public.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=June 6, 2023}} is an American judge who is serving as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Middle District of Pennsylvania]]. She previously served on the [[Pennsylvania courts of common pleas|Lackawanna County Court of Common Pleas, 45th district]]. == Education == Munley received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] from [[Marywood University]] in 1987 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[Penn State Dickinson Law]] in 1992.{{Cite press release |title=President Biden Names Thirty-Third Round of Judicial Nominees |date=May 3, 2023 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2023/05/03/president-biden-names-thirty-third-round-of-judicial-nominees/ |access-date=May 3, 2023}} {{PD-notice}} == Career == From 1992 to 1993, Munley served as a [[law clerk]] to Judge Stephen J. McEwen of the [[Pennsylvania Superior Court]]. From 1993 to 1995, she was an associate with Masterson, Braunfeld, Maguire & Brown and from 1995 to 2001 she was an associate at Mazzoni & Karam Law Offices in [[Scranton, Pennsylvania]]. From 2001 to 2016, she worked as a [[trial attorney]] and partner at Munley Law in Scranton. From 2016 to 2023, she served as a judge on the Court of Common Pleas of Lackawanna County in Pennsylvania's 45th Judicial District. She was appointed as a judge by Governor [[Tom Wolf]] to fill the vacancy left by the retirement of Judge Robert Mazzoni.{{Cite web |last1=Bugda |first1=Jayne Ann |last2=Butash |first2=Joseph |date=June 30, 2016 |title=Julia Munley Appointed Interim County Judge |url=https://www.pahomepage.com/news/julia-munley-appointed-interim-county-judge/ |access-date=May 3, 2023 |website=PAhomepage.com |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |title=Julia Munley |url=https://scranton.psu.edu/person/julia-munley |access-date=May 3, 2023 |website=Penn State Scranton |language=en}} === Federal judicial service === On May 3, 2023, President [[Joe Biden]] announced his intent to nominate Munley to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Middle District of Pennsylvania]]. On May 4, 2023, her nomination was sent to the Senate. President Biden nominated Munley to the seat vacated by Judge [[Robert D. Mariani]], who assumed [[senior status]] on September 30, 2022.{{Cite press release |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |date=May 4, 2023 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2023/05/04/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-105/}} On June 7, 2023, a hearing on her nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web|title=Nominations|date=June 6, 2023|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|location=Washington, web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00256.htm|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Julia Kathleen Munley to be United States District Judge for the Middle District of Pennsylvania)|website=United States Senate|date=October 17, 2023|access-date=October 17, 2023}} Her nomination was confirmed later that day by a 52–45 vote.{{Cite '''Julia Eleanor Kobick''' (born 1983)<ref name="Questionnaire">{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Kobick%20SJQ%20Public%20Final1.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=November 29, 2022}}</ref> is an American lawyer who is serving as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts]] since 2023.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Biden nominates abortion rights lawyer in U.S. Supreme Court case to federal judgeship|url=https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/politics/biden-nominates-abortion-rights-lawyer-in-us-supreme-court-case-to-federal-judgeship/ar-AA106I1k|access-date=July 29, 2022|website=MSN|language=en-US}}</ref> She previously served as deputy state solicitor in the [[Massachusetts Attorney General|Office of the Massachusetts Attorney General]].

== Education ==

Kobick earned a [[Bachelor of Arts]], ''[[cum laude]]'', from [[Harvard University]] in 2005 and a [[Juris Doctor]], ''magna cum laude'', from [[Harvard Law School]] in 2010.<ref name="Questionnaire" /><ref name="WHBio">{{Cite press release |title=President Biden Names Twenty-Fourth Round of Judicial Nominees |date=July 29, 2022 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/07/29/president-biden-names-twenty-fourth-round-of-judicial-nominees/ |access-date=July 29, 2022}} {{PD-notice}}</ref>

== Career ==

From 2005 to 2007, Kobick was a second and third grade teacher at P.S. 86, [[Kingsbridge Heights|Kingsbridge Heights Elementary School]]; during the same period she was a corps members with [[Teach For America]].{{citation needed|date=August 2023}}  From 2007 to 2011, she was a resident [[tutor]] at [[Cabot House]].{{citation needed|date=August 2023}} She served as a summer [[Associate lawyer|associate]] during the summer of 2009 with [[Hogan Lovells]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.law360.com/cases/5342fd22d0a47d4ca700aeac | title=Zogenix, Inc. V. Patrick }}</ref>{{failed verification|date=August 2023}}  Kobick served as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[F. Dennis Saylor IV]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts]] from 2010 to 2011, for Judge [[Michael Chagares]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit]] from 2011 to 2012, and for [[Associate Justice]] [[Ruth Bader Ginsburg]] of the [[United States Supreme Court]] from 2012 to 2013. From 2013 to 2021, she served as a deputy attorney general in the Office of the Massachusetts Attorney General. She became deputy state solicitor, the state's title for the deputy [[solicitor general]], in 2021 and left in 2023 to become a federal judge.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Micek |first=John L. |date=2023-11-08 |title=Mass. lawyer confirmed as 150th Biden-appointed federal judge |url=https://www.masslive.com/politics/2023/11/mass-lawyer-confirmed-as-150th-biden-appointed-federal-judge.html |access-date=2026-07-17 |website=masslive |language=en}}</ref>

=== Notable cases ===

In 2017, Kobick was part of the legal team that sued the [[First presidency of Donald Trump|Trump administration]] for its rollback of the [[Affordable Care Act]]'s [[contraceptive mandate|contraceptive coverage mandate]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.mass.gov/news/ag-healey-sues-the-trump-administration-for-roll-back-of-contraception-coverage-mandate|title=AG Healey Sues the Trump Administration for Roll Back of Contraception Coverage Mandate | Mass.gov|website=www.mass.gov}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last1=Pear |first1=Robert |last2=Ruiz |first2=Rebecca R. |last3=Goodstein |first3=Laurie |date=October 6, 2017 |title=Trump Administration Rolls Back Birth Control Mandate |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/10/06/us/politics/trump-contraception-birth-control.html |access-date=November 29, 2022 |website=The New York Times |language=en-US}}</ref>

In 2022, Kobick defended Massachusetts' [[mask mandate]] during the [[COVID-19 pandemic]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.law360.com/articles/1489103 | title=End of Mask Order Moots Legal Challenge, Mass. Justices Say - Law360 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://vettingroom.org/2022/09/30/julia-kobick/ | title=Julia Kobick – Nominee to the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts | date=September 30, 2022 }}</ref>

In 2022, Kobick was part of the legal team defending Massachusetts' "[[right to repair]]" law. The law mandated access to car diagnostic and repair systems.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.law360.com/articles/1461292 | title='Irritated' Judge Nearing Verdict on Mass. Car Data Law - Law360 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.repairerdrivennews.com/2022/09/06/judge-looks-to-resolve-2-major-outstanding-issues-in-mass-right-to-repair-case/ | title=Judge looks to resolve 2 'major outstanding issues' in Mass. 'right to repair' case | date=September 6, 2022 }}</ref>

In November 2026, Kobick issued a nationwide injunction enjoining enforcement of the [[United States Department of Homeland Security]]'s rule sharply limiting the use of Curricular Practical Training by international students on [[F visa]]<nowiki/>s.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Court Orders Injunction and Stay in Federal CPT Advisories {{!}} ISSO |url=https://isso.columbia.edu/news/court-orders-injunction-and-stay-federal-cpt-advisories |access-date=2026-11-18 |website=isso.columbia.edu}}</ref>

=== Federal judicial service ===

On July 29, 2022, President [[Joe Biden]] announced his intent to nominate Kobick to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts.<ref name="WHBio" /> On August 1, 2022, her nomination was sent to the Senate. President Biden nominated Kobick to the seat vacated by Judge [[William G. Young]], who assumed [[senior status]] on July 1, 2021.<ref>{{Cite press release |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |date=August 1, 2022 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/08/01/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-78/}}{{PD-notice}}</ref> On November 30, 2022, a hearing on her nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Nominations|date=November 29, 2022|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/11/30/2022/nominations}}</ref> During her hearing, she was repeatedly questioned by Senator [[Josh Hawley]] about an argument she made before the Supreme Court, claiming the [[Second Amendment to the United States Constitution|Second Amendment]] did not apply to stun guns because they did not exist when the Amendment was written; an argument which had previously been rejected unanimously by the Court, and which the Court again rejected when she made it.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Kutner|first=Brad|title=US Senate Judiciary Panel Grills Handful of Biden District Court Nominees|url=https://www.law.com/nationallawjournal/2022/11/30/us-senate-judiciary-panel-grills-handful-of-biden-district-court-nominees/|language=en|access-date=May 11, 2023}}</ref> On January 3, 2023, her nomination was returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]]. She was renominated on January 23, 2023.<ref>{{Cite press release |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |date=January 23, 2023 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2023/01/23/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-92/}}</ref> On February 9, 2023, her nomination was reported out of committee by an 11–10 vote.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/2023-02-09%20-%20EBM%20-%20Results.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – February 9, 2023|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=February 9, 2023}}</ref> On November 7, 2023, the Senate invoked cloture on her nomination by a 52–46 vote, with Senator [[Joe Manchin]] voting against the motion to invoke cloture on her nomination.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00296.htm|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Julia E. Kobick to be United States District Judge for the District of Massachusetts)|website=United States Senate|date=November 7, 2023|access-date=November 7, 2023}}</ref> Later that day, Kobick was confirmed by a 52–46 vote, with Senator Manchin voting against confirmation.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00297.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation,: Julia E. Kobick, of Massachusetts, to be United States District Judge for the District of Massachusetts)|website=United States Senate|date=November 7, 2023|access-date=November 7, 2023}}</ref> Kobick's confirmation made her the 150th judge confirmed during the [[Presidency of Joe Biden|Biden presidency]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=November 7, 2023 |title=Senate confirms Biden's 150th judge |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/joe-biden/senate-confirms-bidens-150th-judge-rcna123849 |access-date=November 7, 2023 |website=NBC News |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite press release |title=Statement from President Joe Biden on 150th Judicial Confirmation |date=November 7, 2023 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2023/11/07/statement-from-president-joe-biden-on-150th-judicial-confirmation/ |access-date=November 7, 2023}}</ref> She received her judicial commission on November 13, 2023.<ref>{{FJC Bio|nid=13761336|inline=yes}}</ref>

[[Florida State University College of Law|Florida State University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Julie Simone Sneed''' ({{nee|'''Guider'''}}; born 1969) is an American lawyer who has served as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Middle District of Florida]] since 2024. She previously served as a [[United States magistrate judge]] of the same court from 2015 to 2024. == Education == Sneed received a [[Bachelor of Science]] from the [[University of Florida]] in 1991 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[Florida State University College of Law]] in 1994.{{Cite press release |title=President Biden Names Forty-First Round of Judicial Nominees |date=November 1, 2023 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2023/11/01/president-biden-names-forty-first-round-of-judicial-nominees/ |access-date=November 1, 2023}} {{PD-notice}} == Career == Sneed was a [[law clerk]] for Judge Chris W. Altenbernd on the [[Florida Second District Court of Appeal]] from 1995 to 1997 and for Judge [[James D. Whittemore]] of the United States District Court for the Middle District of Florida from 2000 to 2004. From 1997 to 2000, she was a litigation [[Associate lawyer|associate]] at Trenam, Kemker, Scharf, Barkin, Frye, O’Neill & Mullis, P.A. in [[Tampa]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.bbb.org/us/fl/tampa/profile/eminent-domain-lawyer/trenam-kemker-scharf-barkin-frye-oneill-mullis-pa-0653-90171584|title=Trenam, Kemker, Scharf, Barkin, Frye, O'Neill & Mullis, P.A. | Better Business Bureau® Profile|website=www.bbb.org}} From 2004 to 2012, she was an associate and later a partner at Fowler White Boggs Banker, P.A. in their Tampa office. From 2012 to 2015, she worked as a partner at [[Akerman LLP]]. From 2015 to 2024, she served as a United States magistrate judge for the Middle District of Florida.{{Cite web |title=Julie S. Sneed {{!}} United States Courts |url=https://www.uscourts.gov/judicial-milestones/julie-s-sneed |access-date=November 1, 2023 |website=www.uscourts.gov |language=en}} === Federal judicial service === On November 1, 2023, President [[Joe Biden]] announced his intent to nominate Sneed to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Middle District of Florida]]. Her nomination was part of a bipartisan package of nominees which included [[David S. Leibowitz|David S. Leibowitz.]] On November 6, 2023, her nomination was sent to the Senate. President Biden nominated Sneed to the seat vacated by Judge [[Roy B. Dalton Jr.]], who assumed [[senior status]] on July 9, 2022.{{Cite press release |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |date=November 6, 2023|publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. 12–9 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/2024-01-18_-_ebm_-_results1.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – January 18, 2024|publisher=United States Senate {{Short description|American judge (born 1965)}} {{Use American English|date=March 2025}} {{Use mdy dates|date=March 2025}} {{Infobox judge | name = Julien Neals | image = Julien Neals.jpg | office = Judge of the [[United States District Court for the District of New Jersey]] | term_start = June 22, 2021 | term_end = | appointer = [[List of federal judges appointed by Joe Biden|Joe Biden]] | predecessor = [[Bill Martini]] | successor = | birth_name = | birth_date = {{Birth year and age|1965|}} | birth_place = [[Newark, New Jersey]], U.S. | death_date = | death_place = | education = [[Morehouse College]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|BA]])
[[Emory University School of Law|Emory University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | party = }} '''Julien Xavier Neals''' (born 1965){{cite web |title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Neals%20Senate%20Questionnaire%20Final.pdf |publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary |access-date=November 13, 2022}}{{Cite web |last=Voruganti |first=Harsh |date=April 21, 2021 |title=Julien Neals – Nominee to the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey |url=https://vettingroom.org/2021/04/21/julien-neals-nominee-to-the-u-s-district-court-for-the-district-of-new-jersey/ |access-date=April 28, 2021 |website=The Vetting Room |language=en}} is an American lawyer serving as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of New Jersey]]. == Education == [[File:Julian Neals 1983.jpg|thumb|left|upright=0.8|Neals in the [[Morehouse College]] yearbook, 1983]] Neals attended high school at [[Seton Hall Preparatory School]]. He then received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] from [[Morehouse College]] in 1986. He received a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Emory University School of Law]] in 1991.{{Cite web |title="President Obama Nominates Two to Serve on the United States District Courts" White House, February 26, 2015 |date=26 February 2015 |url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2015/02/26/president-obama-nominates-two-serve-united-states-district-courts |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210121124127/https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2015/02/26/president-obama-nominates-two-serve-united-states-district-courts |archive-date=January 21, 2021 |access-date=March 3, 2021}} == Career == He began his legal career as a [[law clerk]] to Judge Seymour Margulies of the [[New Jersey Superior Court]] in [[Hudson County, New Jersey|Hudson County]] from 1991 to 1992. From 1992 to 2006 and in 2014, he worked at Chasan, Leyner & Lamparello, P.C., in [[Secaucus, New Jersey]], first as an associate, and later as a partner, where he practiced general litigation in state and federal courts. From 2006 to 2014, he worked for the [[Newark, New Jersey|City of Newark]], as Chief Judge of the Newark Municipal Court from 2006 to 2008, as Corporation Counsel from 2008 to 2010, and as Business Administrator from 2010 to 2014. From January 2015 until his confirmation, he served as County Counsel for [[Bergen County, New Jersey|Bergen County]]. == Federal judicial service == === Expired nomination to district court under Obama === On February 26, 2015, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Neals to serve as a United States District Judge of the United States District Court for the District of New Jersey, to the seat vacated by Judge [[Faith S. Hochberg]], who retired on March 6, 2015.{{Cite web |url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2015/02/26/presidential-nominations-sent-senate |title="Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate" White House, February 26, 2015 |date=26 February 2015 |access-date=March 3, 2021 |archive-date=October 30, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201030031923/https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2015/02/26/presidential-nominations-sent-senate |url-status=live }} He received a hearing before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Judiciary Committee]] on September 30, 2015.{{Cite web |url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/nominations-09-30-15 |title="Nominations", United States Senate Judiciary Committee, September 30, 2015 |access-date=September 24, 2015 |archive-date=September 25, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150925112043/http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/nominations-09-30-15 |url-status=live }} On November 5, 2015, his nomination was favorably reported out of committee by [[voice vote]].{{Cite web |url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%2011-05-15.pdf |title=United States Senate Judiciary Committee: Results of Executive Business Meeting – November 5, 2015 |access-date=2015-11-05 |archive-date=2015-12-22 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151222112535/http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%2011-05-15.pdf |url-status=live }} However, Senate Majority Leader [[Mitch McConnell]] refused to schedule the nomination for a Senate vote. The nomination expired on January 3, 2017, with the end of the [[114th United States Congress|114th Congress]].{{cite news|url=https://www.courier-journal.com/story/news/politics/mitch-mcconnell/2021/06/08/mitch-mcconnell-votes-against-joe-bidens-first-judicial-nominee/7603323002/|title=Mitch McConnell blocked an Obama judicial nominee but couldn't pull it off a second time|last=Watkin|first=Morgan|date=June 8, 2021|work=Courier-Journal|access-date=9 June 2021}} === Renomination to district court under Biden === On March 30, 2021, President [[Joe Biden]] announced his intent to renominate Neals to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] for the [[United States District Court for the District of New Jersey]].{{Cite web|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/03/30/president-biden-announces-intent-to-nominate-11-judicial-candidates/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210330150653/https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/03/30/president-biden-announces-intent-to-nominate-11-judicial-candidates/|url-status=live|title=President Biden Announces Intent to Nominate 11 Judicial Candidates|date=March 30, 2021|archive-date=March 30, 2021|website=The White House}} On April 19, 2021, his nomination was sent to the Senate. President Biden nominated Neals to the seat vacated by Judge [[Bill Martini]], who assumed [[senior status]] on February 10, 2015.{{Cite web|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/04/19/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-11/|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate|date=April 19, 2021|website=The White House}} Neals was recommended by Senator [[Cory Booker]].{{Cite journal|url=https://slate.com/news-and-politics/2023/02/cory-booker-judicial-appointments-biden-judges.html|title=The Curious Case of Cory Booker's Judicial Appointments|first=Alexander|last=Sammon|journal=Slate |date=February 24, 2023|via=slate.com}} On April 28, 2021, a hearing on his nomination was held before the Senate Judiciary Committee.{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/04/21/2021/nominations|title=Nominations | United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|website=www.judiciary.senate.gov|date=28 April 2021 }} On May 20, 2021, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 16–6 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%20May%2020,%202021.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – May 20, 2021, Senate Judiciary web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=117&session=1&vote=00219|website=United States Senate|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Julien Xavier Neals to be U.S. District Judge for the District of New Jersey)|date=June 7, 2021|access-date=June 7, 2021}} On June 8, 2021, his nomination was confirmed by a 66–33 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=117&session=1&vote=00220|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Julien Xavier Neals to be U.S. District [[Fordham University School of Law|Fordham University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | footnotes = }} '''Kevin Michael Moore''' (born July 17, 1951) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida]]. ==Early life and education== Moore was born in 1951 in [[Coral Gables, Florida]], the fifth of seven children, to Thomas Francis Moore, Jr. and Janet Fay Moore. He received his [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[Florida State University]] in 1972 and his [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Fordham University School of Law]] in 1976.{{FJC Bio|nid=1385306|inline=yes}} ==Career== [[File:Florida-representatives-take-oath-miami-federal-courthouse.jpg|thumb|Chief Judge Kevin Michael Moore, swearing in Members of Congress [[Carlos Curbelo (politician)|Carlos Curbelo]], [[Frederica Wilson]], [[Mario Díaz-Balart]], and [[Ileana Ros-Lehtinen]]. ''(February 2015)'']] Moore served as an [[assistant United States attorney]] for the Southern District of Florida from 1976 to 1981, as supervisory assistant United States attorney for the Northern District of Florida from 1981 to 1982, and as assistant United States attorney for the Northern District of Florida from 1983 to 1987. Moore served as the [[United States attorney]] for the Northern District of Florida from 1987 to 1989. From 1989 to 1992, Moore served as director of the [[United States Marshals Service]] at the [[United States Department of Justice]]. ===Federal judicial service=== Moore was nominated by President [[George H. W. Bush]] on October 4, 1991, to the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida]], to the seat vacated by Judge [[Eugene P. Spellman]]. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate|Senate]] on February 6, 1992, and received his commission on February 10, 1992. He served as chief judge from July 1, 2014, until July 1, 2021. === Intent to nominate to United States Sentencing Commission === On August 12, 2020, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to nominate Moore to serve as chair of the United States Sentencing Commission.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-intent-nominate-appoint-individuals-key-administration-posts-081220/ "President Donald J. A ''Courier Journal'' report on Caldwell's appointment as U.S. attorney in 1991 noted that she had dated senator [[Mitch McConnell]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/politics/longtime-ky-federal-judge-to-vacate-seat-paving-way-for-biden-conservative-pick/ar-AAZ4WwZ|title=Longtime Ky. federal judge to vacate seat, paving way for Biden conservative pick|website=MSN}} {{dead link|date=September 2026}} McConnell, who recommended Caldwell for that position, said at the time that she was well qualified and should not be barred from the position because of their personal relationship.{{Cite web|url=https://www.courier-journal.com/story/news/politics/2022/07/01/kentucky-judge-leaves-opening-spot-bidens-gop-pick-chad-meredith/7784121001/|title=Kentucky federal judge to step down, opening seat for Biden's anti-abortion GOP nominee|first=Joe|last=Sonka|website=The Courier-Journal}} ==Federal judicial service== Caldwell was nominated by [[President of the United States|President]] [[George W. '''Karen Elizabeth Schreier''' (born 1956) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of South Dakota]] and was the 36th [[United States Attorney for the District of South Dakota|United States Attorney]] for the District of South Dakota.

== Early life and education ==

Born in [[Sioux Falls, South Dakota|Sioux Falls]], [[South Dakota]], Schreier earned an [[Bachelor of Arts|Artium Baccalaureus]] degree from [[Saint Louis University (United States)|Saint Louis University]] in 1978 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[Saint Louis University School of Law]] in 1981.<ref name=fjc_schreier>{{cite web|url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/schreier-karen-e.|title=Schreier, Karen E. - Federal Judicial Center|website=www.fjc.gov}}</ref>

== Career ==
Schreier worked as a [[law clerk|judicial law clerk]] for [[South Dakota Supreme Court]] Justice [[Francis G. Dunn]] from 1981 until 1982.<ref name=fjc_schreier/> Schreier worked in private law practice in Sioux Falls from 1982 until 1993. She was elected as Chairwoman of the [[South Dakota Democratic Party]] in 1992,<ref>{{cite news|date=January 27, 1992|title=Democrats name chairman, nominate slates for primary|work=[[Rapid City Journal]]|location=[[Rapid City, South Dakota]]|page=B2|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/527472831|access-date=April 20, 2024}}</ref> and stepped down at the end of the year.<ref>{{cite news|date=December 7, 1992|title=Democrats elect Kip Scott|work=[[Rapid City Journal]]|location=[[Rapid City, South Dakota]]|page=B4|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/528741447/|access-date=April 20, 2024}}</ref> Schreier was one of the Democratic Party's electors for [[Bill Clinton]] and [[Al Gore]] in [[1992 United States presidential election in South Dakota|1992]].

She was recommended by Senator [[Tom Daschle]] to serve as [[United States Attorney for the District of South Dakota]] in 1993,<ref>{{cite news|date=March 20, 1993|title=5 South Dakotans tapped for federal jobs|last=Kranz|first=David|work=[[Argus Leader]]|location=[[Sioux Falls, South Dakota]]|page=1A|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/239873722/|access-date=April 20, 2024}}</ref> and was nominated to the position by President [[Bill Clinton]] on July 19, 1993.<ref>{{cite news|date=July 20, 1993|title=Schreier tapped for U.S. attorney|work=[[Argus Leader]]|location=[[Sioux Falls, South Dakota]]|page=B1|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/239933303/|access-date=April 20, 2024}}</ref> Prior to her confirmation by the U.S. Senate, Schreier was appointed as interim U.S. Attorney by Attorney General [[Janet Reno]] on July 29, 1993, becoming the first woman to serve as U.S. Attorney in South Dakota.<ref>{{cite news|date=July 31, 1993|title=State's new U.S. attorney sets agenda|last=Trautmann|first=Mike|work=[[Argus Leader]]|location=[[Sioux Falls, South Dakota]]|page=2B|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/239936400/|access-date=April 20, 2024}}</ref> On September 21, 1993, the United States Senate confirmed her nomination by [[voice vote]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/103rd-congress/489?q=%7B%22search%22%3A%22schreier%22%7D&s=2&r=11|title=PN489 — Karen Elizabeth Schreier — Department of Justice|website=congress.gov|access-date=April 20, 2024}}</ref>

== Federal judicial service ==

On March 8, 1999, President [[Bill Clinton]] nominated Schreier to be a United States District Judge of the [[United States District Court for the District of South Dakota]] to replace [[Richard Battey]], who had taken [[senior status]] on January 1, 1999.<ref name=fjc_battey>{{cite web|url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/battey-richard-howard|title=Battey, Richard Howard - Federal Judicial Center|website=www.fjc.gov}}</ref> The [[United States Senate]] confirmed Schreier on June 30, 1999, as part of a package of nominees it approved in a 94–4 vote.<ref>[https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=106&session=1&vote=00190 U.S. Senate Roll Call Votes], ''senate.gov''</ref> Schreier received her commission on July 7, 1999.<ref name=fjc_schreier/> She served as [[Chief judge (United States)|Chief Judge]] from January 1, 2006, to January 1, 2013. She assumed [[senior status]] on May 15, 2024.<ref name=fjc_schreier/>
