[[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrat]] (1993–2001) | other_party = | height = | spouse = | partner = | relations = | children = | parents = | mother = | father = | relatives = | education = {{nowrap|[[University of North Carolina]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|BA]], [[Juris Doctor|JD]])}} | occupation = | profession = | known_for = | salary = | net_worth = | cabinet = | committees = | portfolio = | awards = | signature = | signature_alt = | website = | footnotes = }} '''Lance Michael Africk''' (born December 1, 1951) is a [[United States federal judge|senior United States district judge]] for the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana]]. ==Education and career== The [[New York City]]-born Africk''U.S. Public Records Index'', Volume 1 (Provo, UT: Ancestry.com Operations, Inc.), 2010. received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] from the [[University of North Carolina]] at [[Chapel Hill, North Carolina|Chapel Hill]] in 1973, and two years later a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of North Carolina School of Law]]. From 1975 to 1976, he was a [[law clerk]] to James Gulotta, a judge of the [[Louisiana Courts of Appeal|Louisiana 4th Circuit Court of Appeals]]. He entered the private practice of law in [[Louisiana]] from 1976 to 1977, and was thereafter Director of the Career Criminal Bureau for the [[Orleans Parish]] District Attorney's Office from 1977 to 1980. He returned to private practice until 1982, and then became an Assistant [[United States Attorney]] for the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana]] until 1990. In 1986, he began teaching as an instructor at the [[University of New Orleans]].{{FJC Bio|nid=1391471|inline=yes}} ===Federal judicial service=== Africk became a [[United States magistrate judge]] for the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana]] in 1990. After the election of [[Bill Clinton]] in [[1992 United States presidential election|1992]], Africk changed his party affiliation from Republican to Democrat. He did not obtain nomination for a judgeship under Clinton.{{cite web|last=Crouere|first=Jeff|title=Inside Jefferson Parish|url=http://www.bestofneworleans.com/gambit/inside-jefferson-parish/Content?oid=1239984|work=Gambit Weekly|accessdate=March 31, 2011|date=February 19, 2002}} On January 23, 2002, by which time he had returned to Republican registration, Africk was nominated by President [[George W. Bush]] to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana]] vacated by [[Edith Brown Clement]]. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on April 17, 2002,{{cite web|title=Presidential Nomination: Lance Michael Africk|url=https://georgewbush-whitehouse.archives.gov/news/nominations/9.html|publisher=White House|accessdate=March 31, 2011}} and received his commission the same day. He assumed [[senior status]] on October 1, 2024. More [[Conservative (politics)|conservative]] Republicans opposed Bush's selection of Africk, whose past Democratic affiliation caused them discomfiture; the publication ''Gambit Weekly'' reported that shipbuilder Donald Thomas "Boysie" Bollinger of [[Lockport, Louisiana|Lockport]] in [[Lafourche Parish, Louisiana|Lafourche Parish]], a major GOP donor and the son of former party chairman [[Donald G. Bollinger]], was the driving force behind the Africk nomination. ===Notable case=== On March 31, 2011, Africk sentenced former [[New Orleans Police Department|New Orleans police officer]] David Warren to 25 years and 9 months in federal prison on a federal civil rights violation of committing [[manslaughter]] with a firearm in the case of the [[death of Henry Glover]]. Africk sentenced another former officer, Greg McRae, to 17 years and 3 months in prison and three years of supervised release on [[obstruction of justice]] and another [[civil rights]] charge.{{cite news|last=Robertson|first=Campbell|title=2 Former Officers Sentenced in Post-Katrina Killing|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/04/01/us/01police.html|newspaper=The New York Times|date=March 31, 2011}} "Henry Glover was not at the strip mall to commit suicide. He was there to retrieve some baby clothing. You killed a man. Despite your tendentious arguments to the contrary, it was no mistake," Africk told Warren.{{cite news|last=Kunzelman |first=Michael |title=Ex-cops go to prison in post-Katrina killing |url=http://www.ajc.com/news/nation-world/ex-cops-go-to-892584.html |newspaper=Atlanta Journal-Constitution |date=March 31, 2011 |agency=Associated Press |archiveurl=https://archive.today/20240525071029/https://www.webcitation.org/5xbRk7nni?url=http://www.ajc.com/news/nation-world/ex-cops-go-to-892584.html |archivedate=May 25, 2024 |url-status=dead }} On December 17, 2012, the Fifth Circuit vacated Warren's conviction and one of the convictions related to McRae, ordering new trials on those charges. The three-judge panel found, among other concerns, that the trials of the two men should have been conducted separately. In 2013, Warren was acquitted.{{Cite web |last=Times-Picayune |first=NOLA com {{!}} The |title=Jury acquits David Warren, ex-cop who shot Henry Glover after Katrina |url=https://www.nola.com/news/crime_police/jury-acquits-david-warren-ex-cop-who-shot-henry-glover-after-katrina/article_650e0302-9d69-5ebd-b4d2-744a9b35fa49.html |access-date=2023-03-14 |website=NOLA.com |date=12 December 2013 |language=en}} In 2014, Africk resentenced McRae to the same punishment. He dismissed calls for leniency on the grounds of Warren's acquittal, calling it "irrelevant." He said McRae's crime was separate and should be punished individually.
"You did not merely burn a corpse, you, a law enforcement officer, burned a corpse to obstruct justice."{{Cite web |last=Simerman |first=John |title=Federal judge keeps 17-year sentence for officer who burned body |url=https://www.nola.com/news/article_aca4eb09-931e-5c79-b1dd-1daf8d0bb415.html |access-date=2023-03-14 |website=NOLA.com |date=18 August 2014 |language=en}}
In 2015, McRae was granted a resentencing hearing after his obstruction of justice conviction was overturned entirely.{{Cite web |last=SIMERMAN |first=JOHN |title=Appeals court drops charge, orders new sentencing for former NOPD officer who burned Henry Glover's body in a car on the Algiers levee |url=https://www.nola.com/news/appeals-court-drops-charge-orders-new-sentencing-for-former-nopd-officer-who-burned-henry-glover/article_fa0945ce-b61a-5ce1-b72c-a31af578cb7f.html |access-date=2023-03-15 |website=NOLA.com |date=August 2015 |language=en}} In 2016, Africk reduced McRae's sentence to 11 years and nine months, which was within the federal guidelines. However, he rejected calls for a greater reduction on the grounds that McRae was mentally disturbed at the time of the crime. He said a long prison sentence was still warranted due to the severity of the crime.
"The facts behind your conviction deal with much more than the burning of an automobile. By hiding behind a [[blue wall of silence]], you were hiding the truth."{{Cite web |last=SIMERMAN |first=JOHN |title=Judge reduces ex-NOPD officer's sentence in post-Katrina burning of Henry Glover's body |url=https://www.nola.com/news/judge-reduces-ex-nopd-officers-sentence-in-post-katrina-burning-of-henry-glover-s-body/article_f5b92867-e91c-5fc3-a3d1-7082e474c9a7.html |access-date=2023-03-14 |website=NOLA.com |date=5 February 2016 |language=en}}
==Other interests== Africk served as the 54th president of the [[Sugar Bowl]] Committee in 2011–2012,{{cite news|title=Judge Lance Africk Named 54th Sugar Bowl President|date=February 20, 2011|url=http://allstatesugarbowl.org/site.php?pageID=19&newsID=317|work=Sugar Bowl}} and oversaw the game in which the [[University of Michigan Wolverines]] defeated [[2011 Virginia Tech Hokies football team|Virginia Tech]] in an overtime win. '''Lance Edward Walker''' (born March 13, 1972) is the [[United States federal judge|chief United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Maine]]. He was formerly a justice of the [[Maine Superior Court]].

== Education==

Walker was born on March 13, 1972, in [[Milo, Maine]].<ref name="LawyerCentral">{{Cite web |url=https://www.lawyercentral.com/lance-e-walker-interactive-profile--20-324698.html |title=Lawyer Central Profile |access-date=April 11, 2018 |archive-date=April 11, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180411174716/https://www.lawyercentral.com/lance-e-walker-interactive-profile--20-324698.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> His father was an engineer for the [[Canadian Pacific Railway]]. When Walker was in fifth grade, his family moved to [[Dover-Foxcroft, Maine]], where his parents owned a hardware store and travel agency.<ref name=bangor>{{cite news |last1=Harrison |first1=Judy |title=Judge Walker formally sworn in a day after he tosses out Poliquin's suit |url=https://bangordailynews.com/2018/12/15/news/bangor/judge-walker-formally-sworn-in-a-day-after-he-tosses-out-poliquins-suit/ |access-date=7 October 2019 |publisher=Bangor Daily News |date=December 15, 2018}}</ref> In 1990, Walker graduated from [[Foxcroft Academy]]. He earned his [[Bachelor of Arts]] in philosophy from the [[University of Maine]] and obtained a [[Juris Doctor]] with honors from the [[University of Maine School of Law]].<ref name="Questionnaire">[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Walker%20SJQ.pdf "United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees"] {{PD-notice}}</ref>

== Career ==

In 1999 he was in private practice in [[Bangor, Maine]]. Upon graduation from law school, Walker served as a [[law clerk]] to Justices Atwood, Marden, and Studstrup of the [[Maine Superior Court]] for one year. Before his nomination to the bench by [[Governor of Maine]] [[Paul LePage]], he worked in private practice at the [[Portland, Maine]], law firm of Norman Hanson & DeTroy. For approximately thirteen years he handled [[personal injury]] and [[products liability]] claims for insurance companies. He tried twenty cases to verdict.<ref name="Questionnaire" />

=== State judicial service ===

Walker was nominated to the state district court by Governor [[Paul LePage]] on February 7, 2014,<ref>{{Cite press release |title=Governor LePage Announces Judicial Nominees |date=February 7, 2014 |url=http://www.maine.gov/tools/whatsnew/index.php?topic=Gov+News&id=614339&v=article2011 |access-date=April 10, 2018}}</ref> and his appointment was unanimously confirmed by the [[Maine Senate]] soon thereafter. Walker was sworn into office on May 2, 2014.<ref>{{Cite press release |title=Governor Administers Oath To Judicial Appointees |date=May 2, 2014 |url=http://www.maine.gov/tools/whatsnew/index.php?topic=Gov+News&id=619733&v=article2011 |access-date=April 10, 2018}}</ref>

On May 26, 2015, Walker was nominated to the [[Maine Superior Court]] by Governor [[Paul LePage]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.pressherald.com/2015/05/26/lepage-nominates-3-judges-to-maine-superior-court/ |title=LePage nominates three judges to Maine Superior CoWurt |last=Russell |first=Eric |date=May 26, 2015 |publisher=[[Portland Press Herald]] |access-date=April 10, 2018}}</ref>  He was unanimously confirmed by the Maine Senate.  He was sworn in on June 17, 2015.<ref>{{Cite tweet |number=611192740811022336 |user=Governor_LePage |title=Honored to swear in Judge Lance E. Walker as Justice of the Maine Superior Court. #mepolitics |date=June 17, 2015}}</ref> Walker's service on the state bench terminated when he became a federal judge.

=== Federal judicial service ===

Walker was recommended to the White House for a federal judgeship by U.S. Senators [[Susan Collins]] and [[Angus King]] of Maine.<ref>{{Cite press release |title=Senators Collins, King Announce the Nomination of Maine Superior Court Justice Lance Walker to U.S. District Court for the District of Maine |date=April 10, 2018 |url=https://www.collins.senate.gov/newsroom/senators-collins-king-announce-nomination-maine-superior-court-justice-lance-walker-us |access-date=April 10, 2018}}</ref>

On April 10, 2018, President [[Donald Trump]] nominated Walker to serve as a United States district judge of the [[United States District Court for the District of Maine]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.pressherald.com/2018/04/10/portland-judge-nominated-to-federal-bench/ |title=Trump nominates Maine Superior Court judge to federal bench |last=Miller |first=Kevin |date=April 10, 2018 |publisher=[[Portland Press Herald]]}}</ref> He was nominated to the seat vacated by Judge [[John A. Woodcock Jr.]], who assumed [[senior status]] on June 27, 2017.<ref>[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/ten-nominations-sent-senate-today-2/ "Ten Nominations Sent to the Senate Today", The White House, April 10, 2018]</ref> On June 6, 2018, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].<ref>[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/06/06/2018/nominations United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Nominations for June 6, 2018]</ref> On June 28, 2018, his nomination was reported out of committee by a [[voice vote]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%2006-28-18.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – June 28, 2018|publisher=Senate Judiciary Committee}}</ref> On October 11, 2018, his nomination was confirmed by [[voice vote]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/115th-congress/1810|title=PN1810 — Lance E. Walker — The Judiciary|date=April 10, 2018|website=[[United States Senate]]|access-date=October 11, 2018}}</ref> He received his judicial commission on October 17, 2018.<ref>{{FJC Bio|nid=5375111|inline=yes}}</ref> Walker became chief judge on March 18, 2024.<ref>{{Cite press release |title=New Chief U.S. District Judge Term beginning on March 18, 2024 |date=February 29, 2024 |publisher=United States District Court for the District of Maine |url=https://www.med.uscourts.gov/news/new-chief-us-district-judge-term-beginning-march-18-2024 |access-date=April 5, 2024}}</ref>

Walker rejected challenges to Maine's [[instant-runoff voting|ranked-choice voting]] system by former Republican U.S. Representative [[Bruce Poliquin]], who was seeking to have ranked-choice voting declared unconstitutional in order to initiate a new election after narrowly losing his seat to [[Jared Golden]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Harrison |first1=Judy |title=Judge rejects Poliquin's challenge to ranked-choice voting |url=https://bangordailynews.com/2018/12/13/politics/judge-rejects-poliquins-challenge-to-ranked-choice-voting/ |access-date=7 October 2019 |publisher=Bangor Daily News |date=December 14, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181214124614/https://bangordailynews.com/2018/12/13/politics/judge-rejects-poliquins-challenge-to-ranked-choice-voting/ |archive-date=December 14, 2018 |url-status=live}}</ref>

== Memberships ==

On his Senate Judiciary Committee questionnaire, Walker reported being a member of the [[Federalist Society]], the [[National Rifle Association of America]], the Woodlands Club, Scarborough Fish & Game Club, and the Maine [[Audubon Society]].<ref name="Questionnaire" />

==Political activities==
He was appointed by Governor [[Paul LePage]] in 2012 to serve on the Board of the Combat Sports Authority of Maine. He served on the board from 2012 to 2013.

'''Laura Anne Taylor Swain'''<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vZPLQiWklXIC&pg=PA261|page=261|title=Hearings before the Committee on the Judiciary, United States Senate, One Hundred Sixth Congress, Second Session, on Confirmations of Appointees to the Federal Judiciary, May 25, June 15, July 12, and July 25, 2000|publisher=U.S. Government Printing Office|year=2001}}</ref> ({{nee|'''Taylor'''}}; born 1958)<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.thehistorymakers.org/biography/honorable-laura-taylor-swain |title=The Honorable Laura Taylor Swain's Biography |date=April 28, 2018 |website=The HistoryMakers |language=en |access-date=March 14, 2020}}</ref> is an American lawyer and jurist serving as the chief judge of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]]. She was appointed to the Southern District of New York in 2000 by President [[Bill Clinton]] and has served as its chief judge since 2021. She also serves as an Adjunct Professor at the [[Benjamin N. Cardozo School of Law]], which is the law school of [[Yeshiva University]].<ref name="a636">{{cite web | title=A Life in Judicial Service | website=Hunter College High School Alumnae/i Association | url=https://hchsaa.org/a-life-in-judicial-service/ | access-date=2026-08-27}}</ref>

== Education and career ==

Swain was born in 1958, in [[Brooklyn]]. She graduated from [[Radcliffe College]] of [[Harvard University]] in 1979 with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] and from [[Harvard Law School]] in 1982 with a [[Juris Doctor]].<ref name="fjc">{{FJC Bio|nid=1391251|inline=yes}}</ref> From 1982 until 1983, Swain worked as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Constance Baker Motley]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]].<ref name=fjc/> From 1983 until 1996, Swain worked in private legal practice in [[New York City]], practicing as an associate, and then counsel, in the areas of [[ERISA]], [[employee benefits]], [[executive compensation]] and [[employment law]] for the firm [[Debevoise & Plimpton]].<ref name=fjc/><ref>[http://schumer.senate.gov/1-Senator%20Schumer%20Website%20Files/pressroom/press_releases/PR00183.html] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030925212140/http://schumer.senate.gov/1-Senator%20Schumer%20Website%20Files/pressroom/press_releases/PR00183.html|date=September 25, 2003}}</ref>

Swain also served as a member of the New York State Board of Law Examiners from 1986 to 1996. She chaired the advisory committee for the Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure from 2007 to 2010.{{cn|date=May 2024}}

=== Federal judicial service ===

Swain was a [[United States bankruptcy court|United States bankruptcy judge]] for the Eastern District of New York from November 1, 1996, to July 11, 2000.<ref>[http://schumer.senate.gov/1-Senator%20Schumer%20Website%20Files/pressroom/press_releases/PR00183.html] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141221155823/http://schumer.senate.gov/1-Senator%20Schumer%20Website%20Files/pressroom/press_releases/PR00183.html|date=December 21, 2014}}</ref> On April 25, 2000, President Clinton nominated Swain to be a United States District Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]] to the seat vacated by Judge [[Thomas P. Griesa]]. She was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on June 16, 2000, and received her commission on July 11, 2000.<ref name=fjc/> She became chief judge on April 10, 2021, after [[Colleen McMahon]] assumed [[senior status]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Brown |first=Stephen Rex |title=Manhattan Federal Court gets new chief judge amid coronavirus pandemic |url=https://www.nydailynews.com/2021/04/01/manhattan-federal-court-gets-new-chief-judge-amid-coronavirus-pandemic/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231216201153/https://www.nydailynews.com/2021/04/01/manhattan-federal-court-gets-new-chief-judge-amid-coronavirus-pandemic/ |url-status=live |archive-date=December 16, 2023 |access-date=April 1, 2021 |website=nydailynews.com|url-access=limited |date=April 2021 }}</ref>

=== Puerto Rico debt crisis ===
On May 5, 2017, Chief Justice [[John Roberts]] appointed Judge Swain to oversee the [[debt restructuring]] case in the [[Puerto Rican government-debt crisis]].<ref>{{cite news|last1=Goldstein|first1=Matthew|title=Judge in Puerto Rico's Debt Lawsuit Handled Major Financial Cases|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/05/05/business/dealbook/judge-puerto-rico-case.html|access-date=May 6, 2017|work=[[The New York Times]]|date=May 5, 2017}}</ref>

=== Copyright and authorship cases ===
Swain's tenure on the District Court bench has included some of the Southern District of New York's high-profile book authorship disputes. In particular, she presided over ''Lapine v. Seinfeld'' and ''Hoover v. Boncompangi''.  Both cases were widely covered by the press, and were rich fodder for New York's tabloid newspapers.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nydailynews.com/gossip/2007/10/19/2007-10-19_jessica_seinfelds_recipes_stir_up_plagia.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071021005522/http://www.nydailynews.com/gossip/2007/10/19/2007-10-19_jessica_seinfelds_recipes_stir_up_plagia.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=October 21, 2007|title=Jessica Seinfeld's recipes stir up plagiarism accusations|website=NY Daily News|access-date=December 21, 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nydailynews.com/gossip/2009/01/31/2009-01-31_sister_pact_book_flap_settled_between_na.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090202102357/http://www.nydailynews.com/gossip/2009/01/31/2009-01-31_sister_pact_book_flap_settled_between_na.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=February 2, 2009|title=Sister pact! Book flap settled|website=NY Daily News|access-date=December 21, 2014}}</ref>

=== ''Lapine v. Seinfeld'' ===
This action was filed{{when?|date=March 2026}} by author Missy Chase Lapine against comedian [[Jerry Seinfeld]] and his wife, [[Jessica Seinfeld]], asserting that the couple used ideas for Jessica Seinfeld's cookbook ''Deceptively Delicious: Simple Secrets to Get Your Kids Eating Good Food'' from Lapine's book ''The Sneaky Chef: Simple Strategies for Hiding Healthy Foods in Kids' Favorite Meals''.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://blogs.wsj.com/law/2008/01/08/food-fight-author-sues-seinfelds-over-childrens-cookbook/|title=Food Fight! Author Sues Seinfelds Over Children's Cookbook|author=Peter Lattman|newspaper=Wall Street Journal|date=January 8, 2008 |access-date=December 21, 2014}}</ref><ref name="auto">{{cite web|url=https://online.wsj.com/public/resources/documents/seinfeldcomplaint.pdf|title=Seinfeld Complaint|publisher=Online.wsj.com|access-date=December 21, 2014}}</ref>

The Seinfelds denied Lapine's claim. Lapine claimed she experienced substantial financial loss.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://amlawdaily.typepad.com/Lapine.pdf|title=Seinfeld v Lapine|publisher=Amlawdaily.typepad.com|access-date=December 21, 2014}}</ref>

As a result of comments made by Mr. Seinfeld about the authorship dispute on the ''[[Late Show with David Letterman]]'', Lapine included a cause of action for defamation to her suit.<ref name="auto"/>

=== ''Hoover v. Boncompagni'' ===
This action was filed{{when?|date=March 2026}} by [[Tatiana Boncompagni Hoover]] against her older sister Natasha Boncompagni.  Hoover, a New York socialite, professional author, and wife of an heir to the Hoover cleaning founder, accused her sister of making unauthorized electronic copies of her book ''Hedge Fund Wives''.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://blogs.wsj.com/law/2008/10/27/of-copyright-family-feuds-hedge-fund-wives-goes-to-court/|title=Of Copyright & Family Feuds: "Hedge Fund Wives" Goes to Court|author=Dan Slater|newspaper=Wall Street Journal|date=October 27, 2008 |access-date=December 21, 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://online.wsj.com/public/resources/documents/hedgefundwives.pdf|title=Hedge Fund Wives Complaint|publisher=Online.wsj.com|access-date=December 21, 2014}}</ref>

The court granted an emergency temporary restraining order preventing the older sister from further distribution of the pre-publication manuscript.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://blogs.wsj.com/law/2008/10/29/in-boncompagni-copyright-suit-tatiana-gets-tro/|title=In Boncompagni Copyright Suit, Tatiana Gets TRO|author=Dan Slater|newspaper=Wall Street Journal|date=October 29, 2008 |access-date=December 21, 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://online.wsj.com/public/resources/documents/boncompagnitro.pdf|title=Boncompagnito Complaint|publisher=Online.wsj.com|access-date=December 21, 2014}}</ref>

The case reached closure in early 2009 when Swain entered a consent order stating, "The Defendant has announced to the Court that she is not a co-author of ''Hedge Fund Wives'' and has no authorship or co-authorship rights to the work. The Defendant agrees to release any registered or pending copyrights that she has relating to ''Hedge Fund Wives'', and any domain names or other property relating to ''Hedge Fund Wives'' or the Plaintiff’s first novel, ''Gilding Lily''."<ref>{{cite news|url=https://blogs.wsj.com/law/2009/01/30/a-sisterly-settlement-the-boncompagnis-bury-the-hatchet/|title=A Sisterly Settlement: The Boncompagnis Bury the Hatchet|newspaper=Wall Street Journal|date=January 30, 2009 |access-date=December 21, 2014 |last1=Jones |first1=Ashby }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://online.wsj.com/public/resources/documents/boncompagnisettlement.pdf|title=Boncompagnito Settlement|publisher=Online.wsj.com|access-date=December 21, 2014}}</ref>

=== Defamation case ===

On February 19, 2021, Swain dismissed a defamation lawsuit filed by [[Devin Nunes]] against [[CNN]]. Nunes sought $435 million in damages and claimed that on November 22, 2019, CNN published a false news article and engaged in a conspiracy theory to damage his reputation. Swain noted that under California law, a retraction must be demanded in writing within 20 days of publication, which Nunes failed to request.<ref>https://www.sfgate.com/news/article/Judge-rejects-Rep-Devin-Nunes-defamation-suit-15965052.php ''SF Gate.'' February 19, 2021. Retrieved February 19, 2021.</ref>

'''Lawrence Leroy Piersol''' (born October 21, 1940) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of South Dakota]].

==Early life and education==
Born in [[Vermillion, South Dakota|Vermillion]], [[South Dakota]], Piersol received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from the [[University of South Dakota]] in 1962 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of South Dakota School of Law]] in 1965.

==Career==
Piersol attended [[The Judge Advocate General's Legal Center and School]] at the [[University of Virginia]] and entered [[Judge Advocate General's Corps, United States Army]], where he served in from 1965 to 1968. He was in private practice in [[Sioux Falls, South Dakota|Sioux Falls]], South Dakota from 1968 to 1993. A member of the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]], he served in the [[South Dakota House of Representatives]], serving as Minority Whip (1971 to 1972) and Majority Leader (1973 to 1974).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.usd.edu/press/news/news.cfm?nid=1851|title=News|publisher=}}</ref>

==Federal judicial service==
On August 6, 1993, Piersol was nominated by President [[Bill Clinton]] to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the District of South Dakota]] vacated by [[Donald J. Porter]]. Piersol was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on November 20, 1993, and received his commission on November 22, 1993. He served as chief judge from 1999 to 2005 and assumed senior status on July 31, 2009.

'''Lee Hyman Rosenthal''' (born November 30, 1952) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas]].

== Education and early life ==

Born to a [[Jewish American|Jewish]] father,<ref>{{Cite web |title=HAROLD M. HYMAN |url=https://jhvonline.com/harold-m-hyman-p32260-124.htm |access-date=2025-03-25 |website=jhvonline.com}}</ref> Rosenthal received her [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from the [[University of Chicago]] in 1974 and her [[Juris Doctor|J.D.]] degree from the [[University of Chicago Law School]] in 1977, where she was an editor of the Law Review.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://lawreview.uchicago.edu/sites/lawreview.uchicago.edu/files/uploads/About/Mastheads/v44.pdf|title=The University of Chicago Law Review|publisher=lawreview.uchicago.edu|date=1976|accessdate=2016-10-13|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161013080825/https://lawreview.uchicago.edu/sites/lawreview.uchicago.edu/files/uploads/About/Mastheads/v44.pdf|archive-date=2016-10-13|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="fjc.gov">{{FJC Bio|nid=1387151|inline=yes}}</ref>

== Career ==

After graduating from law school, Rosenthal completed a one-year [[Law clerk|clerkship]] with Chief Judge [[John Robert Brown (judge)|John Robert Brown]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]]. Rosenthal practiced with the [[Houston]] law firm [[Baker Botts]] from 1978 to 1992, becoming a partner in 1985.<ref name="thesedonaconference1">{{cite web|url=http://www.thesedonaconference.org/people/profiles/RosenthalLee|title=Hon. Lee H. Rosenthal | The Sedona Conference®|publisher=Thesedonaconference.org|accessdate=2014-08-22}}</ref>

=== Federal judicial service ===

On March 20, 1992, Rosenthal was nominated by President [[George H. W. Bush]] to be a United States district judge of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas]] to a new seat authorized by 104 Stat. 5089. She was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on May 12, 1992, and received her commission on May 13, 1992.<ref name="fjc.gov"/> She became chief judge on November 13, 2016.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.txs.uscourts.gov/content/new-chief-judge-lee-h-rosenthal|title=New Chief Judge Lee H. Rosenthal - Southern District of Texas|website=www.txs.uscourts.gov}}</ref> and served until November 29, 2022, one day before she turned 70. She assumed [[senior status]] on December 1, 2024.<ref name="fjc.gov"/>

Rosenthal chaired the Judicial Conference Committee on Rules of Practice and Procedure, to which she was appointed in 2007 by Chief Justice [[John Roberts]]<ref name="autogenerated1">[http://www.rice.edu/ricemagazine/2008/2008_Issue1/sallyport/RosenthalBoard.html]{{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081127003113/http://www.rice.edu/ricemagazine/2008/2008_Issue1/sallyport/RosenthalBoard.html|date=27 November 2008}}</ref> The committee supervises the rule-making process in the federal courts and oversees and coordinates the work of the Advisory Committees on the Federal Rules of Evidence and of Civil, Criminal, Bankruptcy and Appellate Procedure.{{citation needed|date=October 2016}}

Prior to 2007, Rosenthal was a member, then chair, of the Judicial Conference [[Advisory Committee on Civil Rules|Advisory Committee on the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure]]. Chief Justice [[William H. Rehnquist]] appointed her to that committee in 1996, and as chair in 2003.<ref name="thesedonaconference1"/><ref name="autogenerated1"/> Under her tenure, the discovery rules were amended to address the impact of changes in information technology in 2006. In 2007, the entire set of civil rules was edited to be clearer and simpler without changing substantive meaning. The work clarifying and simplifying the rules used in the trial courts won the committee the 2007 "Reform in Law" Award from the Burton Awards for Legal Achievement, an award issued with the [[Library of Congress]] and the Law Library of Congress.<ref name="autogenerated1"/>

==Law reform==

Rosenthal was elected to the [[American Law Institute]] (ALI) and in 2007 was elected to its council. She currently serves on ALI's executive committee as an adviser on four of ALI's projects: The Restatement of Employment Law; Privacy Law Principles; Aggregate Litigation; and Rules of Transnational Civil Procedure.<ref name="thesedonaconference1"/><ref name="autogenerated1"/> She is a member of the board of editors for the ''Manual for Complex Litigation'', published by the [[Federal Judicial Center]].<ref>{{cite book | last = | first = | author-link = | title =Manual For Complex Litigation | publisher =Federal Judicial Center | series = | volume = | edition = 4| date =2004 | location =Washington, D.C. | pages = | language = | url =https://public.resource.org/scribd/8763868.pdf | doi = | id = | isbn = | mr = | zbl = | jfm = }}</ref>

Rosenthal is a member of the [[Rice University]] Board of Trustees<ref name="autogenerated1"/> and a member of the [[Duke University School of Law]] Board of Visitors.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.law.duke.edu/news/story?id=6899&u=11|title=Welcoming new board members|publisher=Law.duke.edu|date=2011-09-28|accessdate=2014-08-22}}</ref> She is also an adjunct faculty at the [[University of Houston Law Center]].<ref>{{cite web|author=The State of Texas and The University of Houston Law Center|url=https://www.law.uh.edu/faculty/adjunct/main.asp?PID=4755|title=University of Houston Law Center Adjunct Faculty|publisher=Law.uh.edu|date=2011-10-01|accessdate=2014-08-22}}</ref>

==Reputation==

Rosenthal was selected as the trial judge of the year by the Texas Association of Civil Trial and Appellate Specialists in 2000 and again in 2006.<ref name="thesedonaconference1"/> She has received the Houston Bar Association's highest bar-poll evaluation for judges three times — in 1999, 2005 and 2007.<ref name="autogenerated1"/> In the 2007 poll, 80.5% of respondents rated her "outstanding" and 16.5% rated her "acceptable".<ref>{{cite web|
url=http://www.hba.org/folder-poll-results/Eval07.pdf|
title=Judicial Poll Results|
author=Houston Bar Association|
accessdate=May 28, 2018|
archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110724005831/http://www.hba.org/folder-poll-results/Eval07.pdf|
archivedate=July 24, 2011
|date=July 24, 2011 }}</ref>

[[Harvard University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Lee Philip Rudofsky''' (born 1979) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Arkansas]], serving since 2019. In September 2026, Rudofsky was nominated by President [[Donald Trump]] to a seat on the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit]], but Trump withdrew his nomination in November 2026. ==Early life== Rudofsky was born in New York City in 1979 to Edward S. and Susan Rudofsky. He was raised in the city, where his father practiced as a commercial litigation attorney.{{cite web |title=Rudofsky, Lee Philip |url=https://fjc.gov |website=fjc.gov |publisher=Federal Judicial Center}} He spent his early childhood years in [[Brooklyn]], where his family resided in the [[Gerritsen Beach, Brooklyn|Gerritsen Beach]] neighborhood. He attended public primary schools and graduated from [[Stuyvesant High School]] in [[Manhattan]].{{cite web |title=Lee Rudofsky Report |url=https://afj.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/Rudofsky-Report-FINAL.pdf |website=afj.org |publisher=Alliance for Justice}}{{cite web |title=Edward Rudofsky |url=https://fedsoc.org |website=fedsoc.org |publisher=The Federalist Society}} == Education and early career == Rudofsky received a [[Bachelor of Science]] in 2001 and a [[Master of Public Administration]] in 2002 from [[Cornell University]]. He then earned a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Harvard Law School]] in 2005. After law school, Rudofsky served as a [[law clerk]] to Justice [[Robert J. Cordy]] of the [[Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court]]. He then clerked for Judge [[Andrew Kleinfeld]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]]. He subsequently became an associate at the law firm [[Kirkland & Ellis]]. He next served as deputy general counsel to the [[Mitt Romney 2012 presidential campaign]]. In 2015, Rudofsky became [[Solicitor General]] of [[Arkansas]]. He left that post in 2018 to become senior director for global anti-corruption compliance at [[Walmart]].{{cite web |url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-judicial-nominees-united-states-marshal-nominee-3/ |title=President Donald J. Trump Announces Judicial Nominees and United States Marshal Nominee |last= |first= |date=July 1, 2019 |access-date=July 1, 2019 |via=[[NARA|National Archives]] |work=[[whitehouse.gov]] |quote=}} {{PD-notice}}{{cite web |url=https://arkansasag.gov/media-center/news-releases/lee-rudofsky-as-solicitor-general |title=Lee Rudofsky as Solicitor General | Arkansas Attorney General |website=arkansasag.gov |access-date=2019-07-02 |archive-date=2019-07-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190702060503/https://arkansasag.gov/media-center/news-releases/lee-rudofsky-as-solicitor-general/ |url-status=dead }}{{cite web |url=https://arkansasag.gov/media-center/news-releases/rutledge-names-nicholas-bronni-as-solicitor-general |title=Rutledge Names Nicholas Bronni as Solicitor General | Arkansas Attorney General |website=arkansasag.gov |access-date=2019-07-02 |archive-date=2019-07-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190702060507/https://arkansasag.gov/media-center/news-releases/rutledge-names-nicholas-bronni-as-solicitor-general/ |url-status=dead }} He has been a member of the [[Federalist Society]] since 2002.[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Lee%20Rudofsky%20SJQ%20-%20PUBLIC.pdf United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees: Lee Rudofsky] == Federal judicial service == ===U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Arkansas=== On July 1, 2019, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to nominate Rudofsky to serve as a United States District Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Arkansas]]. Rudofsky was nominated to the seat vacated by Judge [[James Leon Holmes]], who assumed [[senior status]] on March 31, 2018. On July 8, 2019, his nomination was sent to the [[United States Senate]].[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/four-nominations-sent-senate/ "Four Nominations Sent to the Senate", White House, July 8, 2019] Senator [[Tom Cotton]] recommended his nomination.{{Cite press release |title=Cotton Applauds Nomination of Lee Rudofsky for District Court Judge for Eastern District of Arkansas |date=July 1, 2019 |url=https://www.cotton.senate.gov/?p=press_release&id=1170 |quote="Lee Rudofsky is an outstanding choice to serve as district court judge. Lee understands that the proper role for a judge is to interpret the Constitution and the laws as written, and I look forward to his confirmation."}} On July 31, 2019, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/07/31/2019/nominations United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Nominations for July 31, 2019] On October 17, 2019, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 12–10 web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=1&vote=00346|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture Lee Philip Rudofsky to be U.S. District Judge for the Eastern District of Arkansas)|date=November 6, 2019|website=[[United States Senate]]|access-date=November 7, 2019}} On November 7, 2019, his nomination was confirmed by a 51–41 vote.{{Cite web|url= https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=1&vote=00350|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Lee Philip Rudofsky, of Arkansas, to be U.S. District Judge for the Eastern District of Arkansas)|last=|first=|date=November 7, 2019|website=[[United States Senate]]|access-date=November 7, 2019|language=en}} He received instead concluding that provision could only be enforced by lawsuits filed directly by the [[Attorney General of the United States]].{{Cite joins|date=February 17, 2022}} ===Nomination to U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit=== In September 2026, Rudofsky was nominated by President [[Donald Trump]] to a seat on the [[United States [[Rutgers Law School|Rutgers University]], [[Camden, New Jersey]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]] 1976) | footnotes = }} '''Legrome Derek Davis''' (born 1952) is an inactive [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania]]. Davis attended [[Princeton University]] and then [[Rutgers Law School]]. Most of his career as an attorney was spent in the office of the [[District Attorney of Philadelphia]]. In 1987, Pennsylvania Governor [[Bob Casey Sr.|Robert P. Casey Sr.]] nominated Davis to fill a position as a judge on [[Pennsylvania courts of common pleas|Philadelphia's Court of Common Pleas]], in [[First Judicial District of Pennsylvania|Pennsylvania's First Judicial District]], after a number of judges had lost their positions in a corruption scandal. Davis, among other Casey nominees, was chosen without consultation with [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]] leaders and his nomination was rejected in [[Pennsylvania State Senate|Pennsylvania's State Senate]]. Davis and four others, known as the "Casey Five", successfully ran for the Philadelphia judgeships later in 1987 with some significant endorsements, but with opposition from the city's Democratic party. In 1998 and 1999, Davis was nominated by President [[Bill Clinton]] to serve as a district court judge of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania]]. Although supported by Pennsylvania Senators [[Rick Santorum]] and [[Arlen Specter]], both [[Republican Party (United States)|Republicans]], Davis was not appointed in either of those instances. In 2002, again with the support of Specter and Santorum, Davis was nominated to the same federal judgeship by President [[George W. Bush]], and was appointed as a United States district judge. He retired in 2017, and became a senior judge. During his judicial career, Davis, a Democrat, was supported by both Democratic leaders (such as Clinton, Casey, [[Ed Rendell]], and [[Wilson Goode]]) and Republican leaders (such as Bush, Santorum, Spector, and [[Ronald D. Castille]]). He was also viewed favorably as a judge by both prosecuting and defense attorneys. ==Early life and education == Davis was born in 1952, in [[Columbus, Ohio]]. Davis's father was a [[sergeant]] in the [[United States Air Force]] and while growing up Davis lived in Alaska, Texas, Massachusetts, Oklahoma, England, and Kansas. He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[Princeton University]] in 1973 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Rutgers Law School]], [[Camden, New Jersey|Camden]], in 1976.{{cite web|title=The President Nominates Francis M. Allegra and Legrome D. Davis to serve on the Federal Bench|url=http://clinton6.nara.gov/1998/07/1998-07-30-francis-allegra-and-legrome-davis-named-to-federal-bench.html|publisher=The White House|date=July 30, 1998|access-date=November 17, 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100705123848/http://clinton6.nara.gov/1998/07/1998-07-30-francis-allegra-and-legrome-davis-named-to-federal-bench.html|archive-date=July 5, 2010|url-status=dead}} == Legal career == === Lawyer === Davis was an assistant district attorney in Philadelphia from 1977 to 1980. He was hired by [[Ed Rendell]], then the [[District Attorney of Philadelphia]] (D.A.) (later Pennsylvania's governor and chair of the [[Democratic National Committee]]{{Cite web |title=Governor Edward Gene Rendell {{!}} PHMC > Pennsylvania Governors |url=https://www.phmc.state.pa.us/portal/communities/governors/1951-2015/edward-rendell.html |access-date=2026-05-26 |website=www.phmc.state.pa.us}}). Davis left the D.A.'s office in 1980, and spent a year as an attorney for the Pennsylvania Crime Commission. He returned to the D.A.'s office as an assistant deputy district attorney from 1981 to 1987. During his time in the D.A.'s office, he was chief of the rape unit. After leaving the D.A.'s office a second time, Davis spent part of 1987 in the general counsel's office at the [[University of Pennsylvania]]. He was briefly in private practice in 1987, as an [[associate attorney]] with the Philadelphia law firm of [[Ballard Spahr|Ballard, Spahr, Andrews & Ingersoll]] (now Ballard Spahr). In 2002, Pennsylvania [[United States Senate|United States Senator]] [[Arlen Specter]] observed that Davis handled many complicated prosecutions for the district attorney's office. Davis was hired originally by then [[District Attorney of Philadelphia]] [[Ed Rendell]] to join the D.A.'s office. In 1998, Rendell observed that Davis "was a great trial lawyer and a great supervisor in the D.A.'s office".{{Cite news |last=Lloyd |first=Linda |date=August 1, 1998 |title=Praise rains down on judicial nominee Davis |work=[[The Philadelphia Inquirer]] |pages=B1, B4}} === Philadelphia Court of Common Pleas === In 1987, a number of judges were removed from Pennsylvania's [[First Judicial District of Pennsylvania|First Judicial District]] in the Philadelphia Court of Common Pleas for corruption. Pennsylvania Governor [[Bob Casey Sr.|Robert P. Casey, Sr.]] (a Democrat{{Cite web |date=2019-01-15 |title=Robert P. Casey |url=https://www.nga.org/governor/robert-p-casey/ |access-date=2026-05-26 |website=National Governors Association}}) nominated replacement judges to [[Pennsylvania State Senate|Pennsylvania's State Senate]], including Davis. The senate did not accept three of Casey's nominations, including Davis, [[John W. Herron]], and [[C. Darnell Jones II|C. Darnell Jones, II]]. These three and two other Casey nominees (Mark I. Bernstein, and Edward R. Summers), later known as the "Casey Five", chose to run for judicial positions on Philadelphia's Court of Common Pleas later in 1987 (as Democrats{{Cite news |date=May 29, 1987 |title=Casey judge must get another vote of support |work=The Philadelphia Inquirer |pages=26A}}). Casey had chosen Davis, Herron, and Jones without the input of any political party leaders; and though running as Democrats, the three were not endorsed by any political party in the election; all five were actively opposed by some Democratic party leaders, such as state senator [[Vince Fumo|Vincent Fumo]]; difficult obstacles to overcome in Philadelphia judicial elections. In addition to Casey, they did receive support from office holders Mayor [[Wilson Goode]] (a Democrat) and [[District attorney|District Attorney]] [[Ronald D. Castille]] (a Republican{{Cite news |last=Hepp |first=Christopher |date=June 5, 1985 |title=Castille Blast Foe for Hiring Dealer |work=[[Philadelphia Daily News]] |pages=32}}), along with former District Attorney [[Ed Rendell]] who was running for mayor against Goode in Philadelphia's Democratic [[primary election]]s.{{Cite web |last=Kromer |first=John |date=2020 |title=Philadelphia Battlefields: Disruptive Campaigns and Upset Elections in a Changing City (Temple University Press) |url=https://www.phila3-0.org/the_price_of_a_judge_excerpt_from_philadelphia_battlefields |website=www.phila3-0.org}}{{Cite web |last1=Goldman |first1=Mary |last2=Hearn |first2=Peter |last3=Jones |first3=Ernest E. |date=2007-11-01 |title=Letters, Judges too good to throw out |url=https://www.inquirer.com/philly/opinion/20071101_Letters___Judges_too_good_to_throw_out.html |access-date=2024-07-28 |website= |language=en}}{{Cite web |last=Lounsberry |first=Emilie |date=2008-09-27 |title=Three from area are appointed federal judges |url=https://www.inquirer.com/philly/news/local/20080927_Three_from_area_are_appointed_federal_judges.html |access-date=2024-07-28 |website= |language=en}}{{Cite news |date=April 16, 1987 |title=Casey spearheads effort to elect 5 as judges |work=Courier-Post (Camden, New Jersey) |pages=7B}}{{Cite news |last=Baer |first=John |date=May 11, 1987 |title=It's Not That Easy To Judge |work=Philadelphia Daily News |pages=22}}{{Cite news |last=Tulsky|first=Fredric N.|date=April 16, 1987|title=Goode supports Casey on judicial nominees|work=The Philadelphia Inquirer|pages=4–B}} Democratic city chairman [[Bob Brady|Robert Brady]] unsuccessfully attempted to convince Goode to withdraw his endorsement, in favor of the candidates supported by Philadelphia's Democratic party. All of the "Casey Five" judges were elected.{{Cite news |last=Goldwyn |first=Ron |last2=Days |first2=Michael |last3=Schneider |first3=Howard |date=May 9, 1987 |title=Goode Firm On Slating 'Casey Five' |work=Philadelphia Daily News |pages=5, 10}} Davis served as a judge on Philadelphia's Court of Common Pleas from 1987 to 2002, in that court's criminal division.{{Cite web |last=D'Annunzio |first=P.J. |date=September 28, 2017 |title=Pa. Eastern District Judge Legrome Davis Takes Senior Status |url=https://www.law.com/thelegalintelligencer/almID/1202799219683/ |access-date=2024-07-29 |website=The Legal Intelligencer |language=en}} During part of that time, he was the criminal division's supervising judge.{{Cite news |last=Lloyd |first=Linda |date=January 27, 1999 |title=Clinton backs Phila. judge for federal court |work=The Philadelphia Inquirer |pages=R5}}{{Cite news |date=September 10, 1995 |title=Notice To Public, Change In Courtroom Locations |work=The Philadelphia Inquirer |pages=A15}} In 1990, he developed and presided over an expedited felony disposition program known as the "rocket docket", with input from both prosectors in the D.A.'s office and criminal defense attorneys. This program reduced the court's backlog of felony cases by 34% by the end of the year. In 1996, Davis overturned the criminal convictions of 60 people who had been arrested for drug offenses and later convicted, based on the fabricated testimony and misconduct of a group of Philadelphia police officers who confessed to manufacturing evidence against innocent people as well as drug users, among other things.{{Cite web |title=Phila. judge tosses out 60 convictions - UPI Archives |url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1996/03/20/Phila-judge-tosses-out-60-convictions/7225827298000/ |access-date=2026-05-26 |website=UPI |language=en}} In 1998, when Davis was being considered for a [[United States district court]] judgeship, then Philadelphia mayor Ed Rendell said of Davis, "He's smart. He's got a wonderful temperament. He's just a great choice". At the same time, highly positioned attorneys from both the Philadelphia D.A.'s office and the [[Defender Association of Philadelphia]] (public defenders) agreed that Davis would make an excellent federal judge; with the chief of the public defenders office, Ellen T. Greenlee, stating that Davis "'has the respect of everyone in the system'". ===Federal judicial service=== ==== Expired nominations to district court under Clinton ==== Davis was nominated to serve as a United States district judge of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania]] by President [[Bill Clinton]] on two occasions, July 30, 1998{{Cite web |date=October 21, 1998 |title=PN1316 — Legrome D. Davis — The Judiciary |url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/105th-congress/1316 |access-date=June 1, 2024 |website=congress.gov}} and January 26, 1999.{{Cite web |date=December 15, 2000 |title=PN34 — Legrome D. Davis — The Judiciary |url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/106th-congress/34 |access-date=June 1, 2024 |website=congress.gov}} Each time, he was nominated to the seat vacated by Judge [[Edmund V. Ludwig]], who assumed [[senior status]] on May 20, 1997. Both nominations lapsed.{{FJC Bio|nid=1391481|inline=yes}} ==== Renomination to district court under Bush ==== On January 23, 2002, Davis was nominated by President [[George W. Bush]] to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania]] vacated by [[Edmund V. Ludwig]]. Davis was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on April 18, 2002, and received commission on April 23, 2002. During the 2002 hearings on his confirmation, Davis was presented to the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] by Pennsylvania Senator [[Rick Santorum]]. Santorum observed that although he was a [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] and Davis a [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrat]], he considered Davis "an outstanding nominee and someone who I have been very, very strongly supportive of for several years", and that the administration of President [[George W. Bush]] was also "very enthusiastic" in supporting Davis's confirmation as a federal judge. Santorum also observed that he and Pennsylvania Senator Arlen Specter (also a Republican{{Cite web |title=Biographical Directory of the United States Congress, Specter, Arlen 1930–2012 |url=https://bioguide.congress.gov/search/bio/S000709 |access-date=2026-05-26 |website=bioguide.congress.gov}} and strong Davis supporter), used a panel to review judicial candidates for federal judgeships, and Davis had the highest score of those undergoing that panel process at the time.{{Cite web |date=March 19, 2002 |title=Hearings before the Committee On The Judiciary, United States Senate, One Hundred Seventh Congress, Second Session, S. Hrg. 107-584, Pt. 3, Serial No. J-107-23, pp. 463, 468 |url=https://www.congress.gov/107/chrg/shrg85707/CHRG-107shrg85707.htm |website=congress.gov}} Davis assumed [[senior status]] on September 28, 2017.{{Cite web |date=September 28, 2017 |title=Pa. Eastern District Judge Legrome Davis Takes Senior Status |url=https://www.law.com/article/almID/1202799219683/ |access-date=2026-05-26 |website=Law.com |language=en}} He was reported as being retired by at least April 2022. He has taught advanced trial advocacy in criminal cases at [[Drexel University]]'s [[Thomas R. Kline School of Law (Drexel University)|Thomas R. Kline School of Law]].{{Cite web |date=2018-12-20 |title=Drexel University Thomas R. Kline School of Law, Clinical and Affiliated Faculty |url=https://drexel.edu/law/faculty/clinical_affiliated/ |access-date=2026-05-26 |website=Drexel University Kline School of Law |language=en}} Among the cases over which Davis presided as a federal judge was ''Langbord v. United States'', a lengthy litigation involving a dispute over the ownership of ten [[1933 double eagle|1933 double eagle $20 gold coins]] between the family in possession of the coins and the United States Government. Davis upheld the government's position that the coins were subject to forfeiture under a 1933 law, and was affirmed on appeal.{{Cite web |title=Legrome D. Davis, Judicial Biography |url=https://www.paed.uscourts.gov/sites/paed/files/documents/Judge_DavisL.pdf |website=United States District Court, Eastern District of Pennsylvania}} Davis was chosen by the [[Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation]] to preside over a complex [[multidistrict litigation]] case arising out of a [[2015 Philadelphia train derailment|2015 Amtrak train derailment]] that led to eight deaths and over 200 injuries.{{Cite news |last=Roebuck |first=Jeremy |date=October 13, 2015 |title=All Amtrak Train 188 lawsuits will be heard in Phila. |url=https://www.inquirer.com/philly/news/20151014_All_Amtrak_Train_188_lawsuits_will_be_heard_in_Phila_.html?query=legrome%20davis%20amtrak |work=The Philadelphia Inquirer}} In the early 2010s, he ruled in favor of the parents of [[Autism|autistic]] students in a [[class action]] against the [[School District of Philadelphia]], in allowing parents to play a role in the placement of their children when those children were transferred from one school building to another (''P.V., a minor, by and through his Parents, Pedro Valentin and Yolanda Cruz, individually, and on behalf of all others similarly situated, et al., v. The School District of Philadelphia et al.'').{{Cite web |title=Court Upholds Earlier Ruling: School District of Philadelphia Must Involve Parents in Process of Transferring Students with Autism {{!}} The Public Interest Law Center |url=https://pubintlaw.org/cases-and-projects/court-upholds-earlier-ruling-school-district-of-philadelphia-must-involve-parents-in-process-of-transferring-students-with-autism/ |access-date=2026-05-25 |website=pubintlaw.org |language=en}} == Personal life == Davis's daughter Katherine Davis became a middle school and elementary school principal in Philadelphia, before being selected as the 15th president of the 186-year old [[Central High School (Philadelphia)|Central High School]] in Philadelphia; the first woman and person of color to lead that school.{{Cite web |last=Mezzacappa |first=Dale |date=April 25, 2022 |title=Philly's historic Central High gets its first woman, Black president |url=https://whyy.org/articles/phillys-historic-central-high-first-woman-black-president/ |access-date=2026-05-26 |website=WHYY |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |last=Graham |first=Kristen |date=2022-04-29 |title=Central High's new president is the first Black and first female leader in the storied school's history |url=https://www.inquirer.com/news/central-high-principal-kate-davis-20220429.html |access-date=2026-05-26 |website=Inquirer.com |language=en}} == See also == * [[List of African-American federal judges]] * [[List of African-American jurists]] ==References== {{reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1391481}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Edmund V. He received a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1991 from [[Columbia Law School]]. He served as a [[law clerk]] to Judge [[Rya W. Zobel]] of the United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts from 1991 to 1992. He worked in private practice at the law firm of Mintz, Levin, Cohn, Ferris, Glovsky and Popeo P.C., from 1992 to 1994. From 1994 to 1996, he served in the Office of the Attorney General of [[Massachusetts]] as assistant attorney general and, from 1996 to 1997, as opinions coordinator in the same office. He served as an [[federal public defender|assistant federal public defender]] in [[Boston]], from 1997 to 2005.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2013/12/19/president-obama-nominates-eight-serve-united-states-district-courts|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Obama Nominates Eight to Serve on the United States District Courts|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=19 December 2013}}{{FJC Bio|nid=1394556|inline=yes}} ===Federal judicial service=== In 2005, he was appointed as a [[United States magistrate judge]] in the District of Massachusetts, becoming chief United States magistrate judge in 2012. On December 19, 2013, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Sorokin to serve as a United States district judge of the United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts, to the seat vacated by Judge [[Joseph L. Tauro]], who assumed [[senior status]] on September 26, 2013.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2013/12/19/presidential-nominations-sent-senate|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=19 December 2013}} He received a hearing before the [[United States Senate Judiciary Committee]] on February 25, 2014.{{cite web|title=Nominations|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/nominations-2014-02-25|work=United States Senate|publisher=Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=25 February 2014}} On March 27, 2014, his nomination was reported out of committee by a [[voice vote]].{{cite web|title=Executive Business Meeting|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%20-%2003-27-14.pdf|work=United States Senate|publisher=Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=27 March 2014}} On June 5, 2014, [[United States Senate Majority Leader|Senate Majority Leader]] [[Harry Reid]] filed for [[cloture]] on the nomination. On June 9, 2014, the [[United States Senate]] invoked [[cloture]] on his nomination by a 52–33 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=113&session=2&vote=00177|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture on the Nomination of Leo T. Sorokin, of Massachusetts, to be U.S. District Judge)|publisher=United States Senate|access-date=9 June 2014}} On June 10, 2014, his nomination was confirmed by a 91–0 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=113&session=2&vote=00180|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation of Leo T. Sorokin, of Massachusetts, to be United States District Judge for the District of Massachusetts)|publisher=United States Senate|access-date=10 June 2014}} He received his judicial commission on June 10, 2014. In 2025, he ordered the U.S. government to provide 48 hours notice before deporting a doctor from [[Lebanon]] with a H1B visa who had returned to the U.S.{{Cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/03/16/us/brown-university-rasha-alawieh-professor-deported.html|title=Brown University Professor and Doctor Is Deported to Lebanon Despite a Judge's Order|work=The New York Times |date=Mar 16, 2025|accessdate=Mar 17, 2025 |last1=Goldstein |first1=Dana }} ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1394556}} *{{Ballotpedia|Leo_Sorokin}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Joseph L. [[File:35th Fighter Wing.png|23px]] [[35th Fighter Wing]] }} '''Leon Schydlower''' (born 1971){{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/schydlower_sjq.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=January 23, 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250720023028/https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/schydlower_sjq.pdf|archive-date=July 20, 2025}} is an American lawyer who has served as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Texas]] since 2024. He previously served as a [[United States magistrate judge]] of the same court from 2015 to 2024. == Education == Schydlower's father is an immigrant from Cuba.{{Cite web|url=https://www.elpasotimes.com/story/news/2024/03/30/el-paso-federal-judge-leon-schydlower-reflects-on-senate-confirmation-senator-ted-cruz-john-cornyn/73098320007/|title='I'm incredibly honored': El Pasoan Leon Schydlower sworn in as new U.S. District Court judge|first=Aaron|last=Martinez|website=El Paso Times}} In 1989, Schydlower graduated from [[Hanks High School]] in eastern [[El Paso]].{{Cite web|url=https://kfoxtv.com/news/local/president-biden-nominates-el-pasoan-for-west-texas-us-district-court-joe-biden-judge-leon-schydlower-congresswoman-veronica-escobar-special-assistant-us-attorney-us-navy-judge-advocate-generals-corps-kemp-smith-law-firm-university-of-texas-school-of-law|title=President Biden nominates El Pasoan for West Texas U.S. District Court|first=Drew|last=Pittock|date=December 19, 2023|website=KFOX}} Schydlower received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] from the [[University of Texas at Austin]] in 1993 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Texas School of Law]] in 1995.{{Cite press release |title=President Biden Names Forty-Third Round of Judicial Nominees |date=December 19, 2023 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2023/12/19/president-biden-names-forty-third-round-of-judicial-nominees/ |access-date=December 19, 2023}} {{PD-notice}} == Career == From 1996 to 1998, Schydlower served as a trial attorney on active duty in the [[United States Navy]] [[Judge Advocate General's Corps]]. He was in the [[United States Navy Reserve]] from 2000 to 2004 and has served in the [[Air Force Reserve Command|U.S. Air Force Reserve]] Judge Advocate General's Corps since 2010, where he holds the rank of [[Lieutenant colonel (United States)|lieutenant colonel]]. From 1998 to 2000, he worked as a [[Assistant United States Attorney|special assistant United States attorney]] in the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Hawaii.{{Cite web |title=Schydlower, Leon {{!}} Federal Judicial Center |url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/schydlower-leon |access-date=2024-11-27 |website=www.fjc.gov}} From 2000 to 2002, he was a partner and associate at [[El Paso]]'s Kemp Smith law firm. From 2002 to 2015, he was a [[sole practitioner]]. From 2015 to 2024, he served as a [[United States magistrate judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Texas]].{{Cite web |title=Leon Schydlower {{!}} United States Courts |url=https://www.uscourts.gov/judicial-milestones/leon-schydlower |access-date=December 19, 2023 |website=www.uscourts.gov |language=en}} He was sworn in and had a formal [[investiture]] on January 13, 2016.{{Cite web |title=U.S. Magistrate Judge Leon Schydlower Investiture |url=https://www.elpasotimes.com/picture-gallery/news/2016/01/13/us-magistrate-judge-leon-schydlower-investiture/78772636/ |access-date=December 19, 2023 |website=El Paso Times |language=en-US}} === Federal judicial service === On December 19, 2023, President [[Joe Biden]] announced his intent to nominate Schydlower to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Texas]]. His nomination received support from Senators [[John Cornyn]] and [[Ted Cruz]].{{Cite web |last=Jefferson |first=Greg |date=December 19, 2023 |title=Biden to nominate two to federal bench based in San Antonio |url=https://www.expressnews.com/news/article/judicial-nominees-in-san-antonio-18561958.php |access-date=December 19, 2023 |website=San Antonio Express-News |language=en}} On January 10, 2024, his nomination was sent to the Senate. President Biden nominated Schydlower to the seat vacated by Judge [[Philip Ray Martinez]], who died on February 26, 2021.{{Cite press release |title=Nominations Press Release Attached |date=January 10, 2024|publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2024/01/10/nominations-press-release-attached/}} On January 24, 2024, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web|title=Nominations|date=January 23, 2024|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/committee-activity/hearings/01/24/2024/nominations}} On February 7, 2024, his nomination was withdrawn and he was renominated to the seat vacated by Judge [[Frank Montalvo]], who assumed [[senior status]] on December 1, 2022.{{Cite press release |title=Nominations and Withdrawals Sent to the Senate |date=February 7, 2024|publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2024/02/07/nominations-and-withdrawals-sent-to-the-senate-12/}} On February 29, 2024, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 20–1 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/2024-02-29_-_ebm_-_results.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – February 29, 2024|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=February 29, 2024}} On March 22, 2024, the [[United States Senate]] confirmed his nomination by a 90–8 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1182/vote_118_2_00104.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Leon Schydlower, of Texas, to be United States District Judge for the Western District of Texas)|website=United States Senate|date=March 22, 2024|access-date=March 22, 2024}} He received his judicial commission on March 26, 2024.{{FJC Bio|nid=13761586|inline=yes}} '''Leonard Terry Strand''' (born July 14, 1965) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Iowa]] and a former [[United States magistrate judge]] of the same court.

==Education==

Strand was born on July 14, 1965, raised in [[Sioux City, Iowa]], and graduated from [[West High School (Sioux City, Iowa)|West High School]] as [[valedictorian]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=2016|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Strand%20Senate%20Questionnaire%20Final.pdf|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181230074558/https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Strand%20Senate%20Questionnaire%20Final.pdf|archive-date=December 30, 2018|access-date=|website=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary}}</ref> He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree, with high distinction and [[Phi Beta Kappa]], in 1987 from the [[University of Iowa]].<ref name=":0" /> He received a [[Juris Doctor]], with highest distinction, first in his class, and [[Order of the Coif]], in 1990 from the [[University of Iowa College of Law]].<ref name=":0" /> During law school, he worked at [[Vinson & Elkins]] in [[Houston]] and Simmons Perrine Moyer Bergman in [[Cedar Rapids, Iowa|Cedar Rapids]] and also contributed to ''[[The Journal of Corporation Law]]''.<ref name=":0" />

== Career ==
After graduating from law school, Strand joined Simmons Perrine Moyer Bergman as an associate. He was a partner at the firm from 1996 to 2012. During his service with the firm, he specialized in commercial litigation and employment law and served on the firm's management committee.<ref name=":0" /> He was also briefly an arbitrator for the [[American Arbitration Association]].<ref name=":0" />

===Federal judicial service===

From June 7, 2012, to February 12, 2016, Strand served as a [[United States magistrate judge]] for the Northern District of Iowa.<ref>{{cite web|date=21 July 2015|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Obama Nominates Judge Leonard Terry Strand to Serve on the United States District Court for the Northern District of Iowa|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2015/07/21/president-obama-nominates-judge-leonard-terry-strand-serve-united-states}}</ref><ref name="fjc.gov">{{FJC Bio|nid=1394841|inline=yes}}</ref>

On July 21, 2015, President [[Barack Obama]], at the recommendation of Senator [[Chuck Grassley]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.grassley.senate.gov/news/news-releases/grassley-recommends-two-outstanding-iowans-federal-judgeships|title=Grassley Recommends Two Outstanding Iowans for Federal Judgeships – Chuck Grassley|website=www.grassley.senate.gov}}</ref> nominated Strand to serve as a United States district judge of the United States District Court for the Northern District of Iowa, to the seat vacated by Judge [[Mark W. Bennett]], who assumed [[senior status]] on June 4, 2015.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/114th-congress/675|title=PN675 – Nomination of Leonard Terry Strand for The Judiciary, 114th Congress (2015–2016)|date=11 February 2016|website=www.congress.gov}}</ref> <!--Previous reference is a temporary placeholder reference until the White House updates its website--> He received a hearing before the [[United States Senate Judiciary Committee]] on October 21, 2015.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/nominations-10-21-15|title=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|website=www.judiciary.senate.gov|date=21 October 2015 }}</ref> On November 5, 2015, his nomination was reported out of committee by [[voice vote]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%2011-05-15.pdf|title=United States Senate Judiciary Committee: Results of Executive Business Meeting – November 5, 2015|publisher=}}</ref> On February 11, 2016, the [[United States Senate]] confirmed his nomination by a 93–0 vote.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=114&session=2&vote=00023|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Leonard Terry Strand, of South Dakota, to be U.S. District Judge for the Northern District of Iowa)|website=www.senate.gov}}</ref> He received his commission on February 12, 2016.<ref name="fjc.gov" /> Strand's investiture occurred on April 21, 2016.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.iand.uscourts.gov/e-web/notice.nsf/ee15040a4773b461862573bf005138dd/e49948718fbad91f86257f800053c48d/$FILE/Leonard%20T%20Strand%20Investiture.pdf|title=United States District Court for the Northern District of Iowa, Investiture of Judge Leonard T. Strand April 21, 2016|publisher=}}</ref> He served as the chief judge from February 12, 2017 to February 12, 2024.<ref name="fjc.gov" />

[[Yale University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Leslie Abrams Gardner''' (''[[née]]'' '''Leslie Joyce Abrams'''; born December 6, 1974) is the [[United States federal judge|chief United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Middle District of Georgia]]. Prior to being appointed to the bench, she was an [[assistant United States attorney]].{{Cite web|title=Leslie Abrams Gardner, United States District Court for the Middle District of Georgia: Profile and Biography|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/profile/person/18674683|access-date=2021-03-19|website=Bloomberg.com|language=en}} ==Biography== Gardner is the daughter of the Reverend Carolyn and the Reverend Robert Abrams, originally of [[Hattiesburg, Mississippi]]. She was one of six children. Her older sister [[Stacey Abrams]] is the former House Minority Leader in the [[Georgia General Assembly]]. Gardner received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in 1997 from [[Brown University]]. She received a [[Juris Doctor]] in 2002 from [[Yale Law School]]. She began her career serving as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Marvin J. Garbis]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Maryland]]. She served as an [[Associate lawyer|associate]] at the law firm of [[Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom]] LLP, from 2003 to 2006 and again from 2007 to 2010. She served as an associate at the law firm of [[Kilpatrick Townsend & Stockton]], from 2006 to 2007. From 2010 to 2014, she served as an assistant U.S. attorney in the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Georgia|Northern District of Georgia]].{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/03/11/president-obama-nominates-leslie-joyce-abrams-serve-united-states-distri|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Obama Nominates Leslie Joyce Abrams to Serve on the United States District Court for the Middle District of Georgia|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=March 11, 2014}}{{FJC Bio|nid=1394646|inline=yes}} Gardner married her husband, Jimmie Gardner, in 2018; he had been [[exonerate]]d two years prior for spending more than 25 years in prison for accusations of sexual assault.{{cite web |last1=Rubin |first1=Leslie |title=Man whose convictions were overturned after 27 years in prison settles suit for $3 million |url=https://wchstv.com/news/local/man-whose-convictions-were-overturned-after-27-years-in-prison-settles-suit-for-3-million |publisher=WCHS-TV |access-date=18 November 2023}} In November 2023, the [[Tampa Police Department]] released a statement stating her husband had been arrested on allegations of [[human trafficking]].{{cite web |last1=Rodriguez |first1=Nathaniel |title=Stacey Abrams' brother-in-law arrested in Tampa for human trafficking, attacking teen: police |url=https://www.wfla.com/news/hillsborough-county/stacey-abrams-brother-in-law-arrested-in-tampa-for-human-trafficking-attacking-teen-police/ |publisher=WFLA-TV |access-date=18 November 2023}} ===Federal judicial service=== On March 11, 2014, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Gardner to serve as a United States district judge for the [[United States District Court for the Middle District of Georgia]], to the seat being vacated by Judge [[Willie Louis Sands]], who subsequently assumed [[senior status]] on April 12, 2014.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/03/11/presidential-nominations-sent-senate|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=March 11, 2014}} She received a hearing before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] on May 13, 2014.{{cite web|title=Judicial Nominations|date=May 13, 2014 |url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/judicial-nominations-2014-05-13|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary}} On June 19, 2014, her nomination was reported out of committee by [[voice vote]].{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%20-%2006-19-14.pdf|title=Executive Business Meeting|publisher=Committee on the Judiciary| work=United States Senate|access-date=June 19, 2014}} On November 12, 2014, Senate Majority Leader [[Harry Reid]] filed for [[cloture]] on her nomination. On November 17, 2014, the [[United States Senate]] invoked [[cloture]] on her nomination by a 68–28 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=113&session=2&vote=00277| title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture on the Nomination of Leslie Joyce Abrams, of Georgia, to be U.S. District Judge)|publisher=[[United States Senate]]|access-date=November 17, 2014}} On November 18, 2014, her nomination was confirmed by a 100–0 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=113&session=2&vote=00281| title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Leslie Joyce Abrams, of Georgia, to be U.S. District Judge)|publisher=[[United States Senate]]|access-date=November 18, 2014}} She received her judicial commission on November 20, 2014. Gardner became the first African-American woman federal judge to serve on a federal district court in Georgia.{{cite journal |title=First Two African American Female Judges Confirmed to Serve on Georgia Federal Bench |journal=American Bar Association |date=12 February 2015 |url=https://www.americanbar.org/groups/diversity/women/publications/perspectives/2015/winter/first_two_african_american_female_judges_confirmed_serve_georgia_federal_bench/ |access-date=4 July 2026}} She became chief judge on June 1, 2024.{{Cite news|date=May 31, 2024|last=Grant|first=Ty|title=Chief Judge named for Middle District of Ga.|url=https://www.walb.com/2024/05/31/chief-judge-district-court-named-middle-district-ga/?outputType=amp|website=walb.com|access-date=June 8, 2024}} In May 2024, [[NPR]] revealed that Gardner had this on her required annual financial disclosure report for that year, in violation of federal law.{{Cite web |last1=Dreisbach |first1=Tom |last2=Johnson |first2=Carrie |date=2024-05-01 |title=When judges get free trips to luxury resorts, disclosure is spotty |url=https://www.npr.org/2024/05/01/1247512187/federal-judges-disclosures-luxury-trips |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240501093641/https://www.npr.org/2024/05/01/1247512187/federal-judges-disclosures-luxury-trips |archive-date=2024-05-01 |access-date=2024-05-07 |website=[[NPR]]}} In response, court clerk David Bunt told NPR that the financial disclosures were incomplete due to an "oversight" and that Gardner was updating her disclosure reports. == See also
