[[New York University School of Law|New York University]] ([[Master of Laws|LLM]]) | signature = | signature_alt = }} '''Loretta A. Preska''' (born 1949) is an American lawyer who serves as a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]].{{Cite web |title=Hon. Loretta A. Preska {{!}} U.S District Court |url=https://www.nysd.uscourts.gov/hon-loretta-preska |access-date=2023-12-21 |website=www.nysd.uscourts.gov}} Born in Albany, Preska received law degrees from [[Fordham University School of Law]] and [[New York University School of Law]]. She practiced law in New York City from 1973 to 1992 at the [[law firm]]s of [[Cahill Gordon & Reindel]] and Hertzog, Calamari & Gleason (now [[Winston & Strawn]]). President [[George H. W. Bush]] appointed her to the district bench in 1992. She served as [[Chief judge (United States)|chief judge]] of the court for a seven-year term from 2009 to 2016, and took [[senior status]] in 2017. President [[George W. Bush]] nominated Preska to the [[U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit]] in 2008,{{Cite web |title=Judicial Nominations - Loretta A. Preska |url=https://georgewbush-whitehouse.archives.gov/infocus/judicialnominees/preska.html |access-date=2023-12-21 |website=georgewbush-whitehouse.archives.gov}} but the [[United States Senate|Senate]] did not act on the nomination. {{TOC limit|4}} ==Early life and education== Preska was born in [[Albany, New York|Albany]], [[New York (state)|New York]],{{cite web|url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/preska-loretta|title=Preska, Loretta A.|publisher=Federal Judicial Center|work=Biographical Directory of Article III Federal Judges, 1789–present}}''[https://books.google.com/books?id=q_kEf5pJduUC Confirmation Hearings on Appointments to the Federal Judiciary, May 14, June 4, 18, and July 1, 1992, Pt. 9, Serial No. J-102-7]'', United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary, 102nd Congress, 1st Session (1993), pp. 317–30. in 1949, to her father, Victor, an engineer at [[Benét Laboratories]] at [[Watervliet Arsenal]], and her mother, Etta Mae, a registered nurse.Phil Schatz, [https://www.fedbar.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/Preska-Dec2013_4-pgs-pdf-5.pdf Judicial Profile: Hon. Loretta A. Preska: Chief U.S. District Judge, Southern District of New York], ''The Federal Lawyer'' (December 2013). She is of [[Lithuanian American|Lithuanian descent]].''[https://books.google.com/books?id=q_kEf5pJduUC Confirmation Hearings on Appointments to the Federal Judiciary, May 14, June 4, 18, and July 1, 1992, Pt. 9, Serial No. J-102-7]'', United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary, 102nd Congress, 1st Session (1993), p. 220.[https://www.westpointcoh.org/interviews/the-judicial-front-in-the-war-on-terror The Judicial Front in the War on Terror: Interview with Loretta Preska], Center for Oral History, United States Military Academy, West Point, New York. She grew up in the Albany suburb of [[Delmar, New York|Delmar]], where she was active in the [[Girl Scouts of the USA|Girl Scouts]] and graduated from [[Bethlehem Central High School]]. She earned her [[Bachelor of Arts|B.A.]] degree in chemistry from the [[College of Saint Rose]] (1970), her [[Juris Doctor|J.D.]] from [[Fordham University School of Law]] (1973),{{cite news|title=Captain of the Mother Court: Judge Loretta Preska|url=https://www.law360.com/articles/510134/the-captain-of-the-mother-court-judge-loretta-preska|work=[[Law360]]|date=February 19, 2014}} and her [[Master of Laws|LL.M]] from [[New York University School of Law]] (1978). Her LL.M work focused on trade regulation. ==Legal career== Preska was an attorney in private practice in [[New York City]] from 1973 until 1992. She worked at [[Cahill Gordon & Reindel]] from 1973 to 1982, and then at Hertzog, Calamari & Gleason{{efn|Hertzog, Calamari & Gleason merged into [[Winston & Strawn]] in 1999.[https://www.lawfuel.com/blog/corporate-law-corporate-attorney-david-hertzog-rejoins-winston-strawn/ Corporate Law – Corporate Attorney David Hertzog Rejoins Winston & Strawn] (press release), Winston & Strawn via ''Lawfuel'' (May 19, 2009).}} from 1982 until her appointment to the federal bench. She primarily practiced commercial civil litigation in the federal courts,''[https://books.google.com/books?id=q_kEf5pJduUC Confirmation Hearings on Appointments to the Federal Judiciary, May 14, June 4, 18, and July 1, 1992, Pt. 9, Serial No. J-102-7]'', United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary, 102nd Congress, 1st Session (1993), pp. 204–06. but also represented several officers of [[EF Hutton]] in [[grand jury]] proceedings in connection with a case in which the company entered criminal guilty pleas. She cites [[Floyd Abrams]] as a friend and mentor. ==Federal judicial service== Preska was nominated by President [[George H. W. Bush]] on March 31, 1992, to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]] vacated by Judge [[Robert Joseph Ward]]. Senator [[Al D'Amato]] recommended the nomination.[https://www.strose.edu/outcomes/alumni-stories/honorable-loretta-a-preska/ Alumni Stories, Honorable Loretta A. Preska '70, H '95], College of St. Rose (last accessed September 6, 2020).[https://www.nytimes.com/1992/08/16/nyregion/update-a-small-whittling-down-of-federal-bench-vacancies.html A Small Whittling Down of Federal Bench Vacancies], ''New York Times'' (August 16, 1992), p. 43. Preska was [[advice and consent|confirmed]] by the [[United States Senate]] on August 11, 1992,[https://www.congress.gov/nomination/102nd-congress/1003 PN1003 — Loretta A. Preska — The Judiciary: 102nd Congress (1991–1992)], Congress.gov. by [[unanimous consent]]. She received her commission the following day. Her confirmation was part of a "bipartisan package" that also including the confirmation of [[Sonia Sotomayor]] (who later became a [[Supreme Court of the United States|Supreme Court]] justice). Sotomayor was confirmed by the Senate to the district bench the same day, also unanimously. Preska served as chief judge of the court for a seven-year term from June 1, 2009, to May 31, 2016, succeeding [[Kimba M. Wood]] in the role.[https://www.law.com/newyorklawjournal/almID/1202659180362/Meet-the-Judges-Southern-District-Chief-Judge-Loretta-Preska/ Meet the Judges: Southern District Chief Judge Loretta Preska], ''New York Law Journal'' (June 13, 2014). As chief judge, Preska pressed for more adequate funding for the federal judiciary, *Reed Albergotti, [https://www.wsj.com/articles/BL-LB-45691 Judge Preska: Budget Cuts Hurting SDNY], ''Wall Street Journal'' (August 26, 2013). *[[Joe Palazzolo]], [https://www.wsj.com/articles/BL-LB-46494 U.S. Attorney, Chief Judge Decry Budget Cuts], ''Wall Street Journal'' (December 2, 2013). which suffered from the effects of the [[Great Recession]] and [[United States budget sequestration in 2013|budget sequestration]]. In 2010, as chief judge, Preska issued an order permitting [[criminal defense attorney]]s to carry [[mobile phone]]s into the courthouse; previously, only federal prosecutors were permitted to do so. The rule change followed several years of lobbying by the [[Federal Bar Council]].John Eligon, [https://cityroom.blogs.nytimes.com/2010/02/19/now-cellphones-for-the-defense-too/ Now, Cellphones for the Defense, Too], ''New York Times'' (February 19, 2010). She took [[senior status]] on March 1, 2017. ===Consideration for higher courts === In 2007, it was reported that Preska was on President [[George W. Bush]]'s short list of [[George W. Bush Supreme Court candidates|potential Supreme Court nominees]].[[Jan Crawford]] Greenburg, [https://abcnews.go.com/Politics/SupremeCourt/story?id=3235598 EXCLUSIVE: Women, Minorities Top Bush's Supreme Court Short List], ABC News, June 1, 2007 On September 9, 2008, Bush nominated Preska to a judgeship on the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit|U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit]] to replace Judge [[Chester J. Straub]], who retired.[https://georgewbush-whitehouse.archives.gov/news/releases/2008/09/20080909-8.html Nominations and Withdrawals Sent to the Senate] (press release), White House Office of the Press Secretary (September 9, 2008). The [[American Bar Association]]'s [[Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary]] unanimously rated Preska "well qualified" for the circuit judgeship, the committee's highest rating.[https://www.americanbar.org/content/dam/aba/administrative/federal_judicary/ratings110.pdf Ratings of Article III Judicial Nominees: 110th Congress], American Bar Association Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary (last updated November 20, 2008). The Senate did not act on the nomination, and it expired in January 2009 at the end of the [[110th Congress]],[https://www.congress.gov/nomination/110th-congress/1989 PN1989 — Loretta A. Preska — The Judiciary: 110th Congress (2007–2008)], Congress.gov. upon the [[sine die adjournment]] of the Senate. ===Tenure and notable cases=== Preska is considered a conservative judge,Tom Wrobleski, [https://www.silive.com/news/2011/12/staten_islanders_quick_to_chid.html Staten Islanders quick to chide judge for wiping her feet on the flag], ''Staten Island Advance'' (December 30, 2011). and served on the advisory board of the [[Federalist Society]]. Preska has presided over a number of notable cases. ====Civil cases==== =====Commercial, copyright, and contract litigation===== In ''[[Leibovitz v. Paramount Pictures Corp.]]'' (1996), Preska ruled that an image of the actor [[Leslie Nielsen]] seemingly pregnant that mimicked a similar photo of [[Demi Moore]] was [[fair use]] as [[parody]]. Her ruling was upheld by the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit|Second Circuit]] in 1998.''Leibovitz v. Paramount Pictures Corp.'', [https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=17425848561284943775 948 F. Supp. 1214] (S.D.N.Y. 1996), ''aff'd'', [https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=18427314453578523770 137 F.3d 109 ](2d Cir. 1998).[https://www.fedbar.org/blog/get-over-yourself-parody-and-fine-art/ Get Over Yourself: Parody and Fine Art], Federal Bar Association (November 10, 2016). In ''National Basketball Association v. Motorola, Inc.'' (1997), Preska ruled in favor of the [[National Basketball Association|NBA]], granting a [[permanent injunction]] blocking [[Motorola Inc.]] and a statistics company from transmitting real-time basketball scores and other statistics through its "SportsTrax" pager service. Preska ruled that the service was a commercial misappropriation rather than mere media coverage, but dismissed the NBA's copyright and [[Lanham Act]] false-advertising claims. On appeal, the Second Circuit vacated the injunction, finding that the service was neither an unlawful misappropriation nor a Lanham Act violation. *''Nat't Basketball Ass'n v. Sports Team Analysis & Tracking Sys., Inc.'', [https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=9178872622147772198 939 F. Supp. 1071] (S.D.N.Y. 1996), ''rev'd'', [https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=10739824072419550811 105 F.3d 841] (2d Cir. 1997). * Larry Neumeister, [https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/business/1997/01/31/nba-loses-court-fight-over-score-pager-service/724ec960-cebf-4596-bfe0-5a95a5977d13/ NBA Loses Court Fight Over Score Pager Services], ''Washington Post'' (January 31, 1997). Preska presided over the case of ''Mastercard International Inc. v. Fédération Internationale de Football Association'' (2006), brought by [[MasterCard]] against [[FIFA]] after the soccer association awarded sponsorship deals for the next two [[FIFA World Cup|World Cup]]s to MasterCard's rival [[Visa Inc.|Visa]].Martha Graybow, [https://www.reuters.com/article/us-soccer-mastercard-fifa/mastercard-and-fifa-settle-world-cup-sponsor-fight-idUSL2190109720070621 MasterCard and FIFA settle World Cup sponsor fight], Reuters (June 21, 2007).''[https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=564739269925245482 Mastercard International Inc. v. Fédération Internationale De Football Association]'', 464 F. Supp. 2d 246 (S.D.N.Y. 2006). Preska ruled in December 2006 that FIFA had violated its previous 16-year sponsorship contract with MasterCard, which included a clause granting MasterCard a [[right of first refusal]]. The parties subsequently settled the case. In ''Zuckerman v. Metropolitan Museum of Art'' (2018), Preska ruled in favor of the [[Metropolitan Museum of Art]], dismissing a lawsuit seeking the return of [[Picasso]]'s painting ''[[The Actor (painting)|The Actor]]'' to the heir of its original owners, [[Paul Friedrich Leffmann|Paul and Alice Leffmann]]. The Leffmanns were a [[German Jewish]] couple who sold the painting in 1938 to finance their flight from [[Nazi Germany|Nazis]]. The painting was acquired by the Met in 1952. Preska ruled that the Leffmanns' heir could not show, under New York law, that the painting was sold under duress. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed the dismissal on the ground that the claim was raised too late (72 years after the work was sold and 58 years after it was donated to the art museum). *''Zuckerman v. Metropolitan Museum of Art'', [https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=1524653119321347593 307 F. Supp. 3d 304] (S.D.N.Y. 2018), aff'd, [https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2716212276291412621 928 F. 3d 186] (2d Cir. 2019). *[https://apnews.com/f8330db760664eda966efad6ef56d663 Judge rules against heir who wanted Met to return a Picasso], Associated Press (February 7, 2018). *[https://www.artforum.com/news/us-appeals-court-dismisses-ownership-claim-over-picasso-painting-80175 US Appeals Court Dismisses Ownership Claim over Picasso], ''Art Forum'' (June 27, 2019). =====Defamation litigation===== In 1998, Preska presided over a [[defamation]] suit brought by [[Richard Jewell]] against the ''[[New York Post]]''. Jewell, who was wrongly suspected of being the [[Centennial Olympic Park bombing|Centennial Olympic Park bomber]], alleged that several articles, headlines, photographs, and [[editorial cartoon]]s in the newspaper had libeled him. Preska dismissed claims based on a photograph and an editorial cartoon, but allowed the remainder of the claims to proceed. *[https://apnews.com/432b680cbaedbe28bdac15155ebec263 Jewell Libel Suit To Proceed], Associated Press (October 1, 1998). *''[https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4401132485484697581 Jewell v. NYP Holdings, Inc.]'', 23 F. Supp. 2d 348 (1998). The ''Post'' subsequently settled the case for an undisclosed sum. Paul Farhi, [https://web.archive.org/web/20191210215432/https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/style/what-clint-eastwoods-new-movie-gets-every-wrong-about-the-female-reporter-who-broke-the-richard-jewell-story/2019/12/10/fca0d8b4-1b69-11ea-8d58-5ac3600967a1_story.html?outputType=amp What Clint Eastwood's new movie gets very wrong about the female reporter who broke the Richard Jewell story], ''Washington Post'' (December 10, 2019). In 2019, Preska disqualified the law firm of [[Boies Schiller Flexner LLP]] from representing [[Virginia Roberts Giuffre|Virginia Giuffre]] in her lawsuit against professor emeritus [[Alan Dershowitz]], but denied Dershowitz's motion to dismiss the suit, in which Giuffre alleged that Dershowitz falsely claimed that she fabricated her sexual-abuse accusations against [[Jeffrey Epstein]], and thus defamed her.''[https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=14386338337951473666 Giuffre v. Dershowitz]'', 410 F. Supp. 3d 564 (S.D.N.Y. 2019).Tom Jackman & Deanna Paul, [https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/public-safety/david-boies-thrown-out-of-libel-suit-he-filed-against-alan-dershowitz/2019/10/16/5e9b9ea2-f052-11e9-89eb-ec56cd414732_story.html David Boies thrown out of libel suit he filed against Alan Dershowitz], ''Washington Post'' (October 16, 2020).Tom Winter, Sarah Fitzpatrick and Adiel Kaplan, [https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/justice-department/judge-denies-alan-dershowitz-s-motion-dismiss-epstein-related-defamation-n1067476 Judge denies Alan Dershowitz's motion to dismiss Epstein-related defamation suit], NBC News (October 16, 2019). In 2020, Preska denied a motion by British socialite [[Ghislaine Maxwell]], an Epstein associate charged with recruiting girls abused by Epstein, to block the public release of her 2016 deposition testimony in a civil case. Preska stayed her ruling pending Maxwell's appeal to the Second Circuit.Larry Neumeister, [https://apnews.com/article/jeffrey-epstein-new-york-ghislaine-maxwell-courts-u-s-news-4c828dd12aa264b814ce2a6d8c2f1bb1 Epstein's ex-girlfriend tries late bid to seal testimony], Associated Press (July 29, 2020). =====Labor litigation===== Preska presided over long-running litigation between Local 100 of the [[Hotel Employees and Restaurant Employees Union]] and New York's [[Metropolitan Opera]].Ralph Blumenthal, [https://www.nytimes.com/2003/01/31/movies/judge-rules-for-the-met-in-opera-s-labor-dispute.html Judge Rules for the Met In Opera's Labor Dispute], ''New York Times'' (January 31, 2003). In June 2000, Preska found the union to be in [[Contempt of court|contempt]], determining that the union had defamed the Met and engaged in harassment of Met board members. Preska enjoined the union from distributing leaflets at the opera, but at the 2000 season opening, the union held a demonstration. In February 2001, a panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit vacated the injunction, holding that "While the injunction presents serious questions under the First Amendment and libel law, we hold that the injunction is impermissibly [[Vagueness doctrine|vague]] because it fails to provide the Union with adequate notice of what conduct is being enjoined."''Metropolitan Opera Ass'n, Inc. v. Local 100, Hotel Employees & Restaurant Employees Union'', 239 F.3d 172 (2d Cir. 2001). In November 2002, however, the Second Circuit held that [[Lincoln Center]] could permissibly block the union from holding a rally in Lincoln Plaza,Thomas J. Lueck, [https://www.nytimes.com/2002/11/19/nyregion/justices-uphold-lincoln-center-s-ban-on-rallies.html Justices Uphold Lincoln Center's Ban on Rallies], ''New York Times'' (November 19, 2002). holding that the location was not a "[[public forum]]" and that Lincoln Center management had a consistent policy of limiting "expression in the plaza to events having an artistic or performance-related component." In January 2003, in a strongly worded 148-page decision, Preska ruled in favor of the Met in its defamation and harassment suit against the union, writing that the union and its counsel had withheld evidence in violation of the [[Discovery (law)|discovery]] rules and had not been truthful to the court. She ordered the union to pay the Met's sizable legal fees.''Metropolitan Opera Ass'n, Inc. v. Local 100, Hotel Employees & Restaurant Employees Union'', 212 F.R.D. 178 (S.D.N.Y. 2003). In 2015, Preska approved a settlement agreement between the federal government and the [[International Brotherhood of Teamsters]], terminating the [[consent decree]] that had been in place for 25 years. The consent decree required certain reforms to combat organized crime influence and corruption within the union, and had been entered into in 1989 to settle a civil racketeering suit brought against the Teamsters by the government. Under the settlement, a five-year transition away from federal monitoring of the union began. *David Shepardson, [https://www.detroitnews.com/story/business/2015/02/17/judge-approves-end-us-decree-overseeing-teamsters/23585351/ Judge approves end to U.S. decree overseeing Teamsters], ''Detroit News'' (February 17, 2015). *Todd Spangler, [https://www.freep.com/story/news/local/michigan/2015/01/14/teamsters-settlement-order-uaw-organized-crime/21755335/ Agreement ends federal oversight of Teamsters union], ''Detroit Free Press'' (January 14, 2015). =====Other litigation===== In ''[[Bloomberg L.P. v. Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System]]'' (2009), Preska presided over a [[Freedom of Information Act (United States)|Freedom of Information Act]] suit brought by [[Bloomberg L.P.]] against the [[Federal Reserve System]], seeking to compel the Fed to provide documents revealing the identity of recipients of bailouts from the [[Troubled Asset Relief Program]] during the [[2008 financial crisis]], along with the types and amounts of collateral provided. Preska sided with [[Bloomberg News]] reporters, concluding that the Fed's claims that disclosure would cause an "imminent competitive harm" to borrowers were merely conjecture. The Second Circuit affirmed this ruling. *''[https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=595858462510045956 Bloomberg L.P. v. Bd. of Governors of the Federal Reserve System]'', 649 F. Supp. 2d 262 (2009), ''aff'd'', [https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=3477959921372842887 601 F.3d 143] (2d Cir. 2010) *{{cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-federalreserve-bloomberg-lawsuit/federal-reserve-loses-suit-demanding-transparency-idUSTRE57O03P20090825|work=Reuters|title=Federal Reserve loses suit demanding transparency|date=August 25, 2009}} In [[Microsoft Corp. v. United States|a 2014 case]], [[Microsoft]] challenged a federal [[search warrant]] for a customer's email records, on the ground that the data was stored on servers in a [[data center]] in Ireland and could not be produced to the U.S. authorities without an Irish warrant. The [[magistrate judge]] denied Microsoft's [[motion to quash]] the warrant, and following a hearing, Preska upheld the magistrate judge's ruling in a decision from the bench, holding that "It is a question of control, not a question of the location of that information." * ''In re Warrant to Search a Certain E-Mail Account Controlled and Maintained by Microsoft Corp.'', [https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=7140299424734352333 15 F. Supp. 3d 466] (S.D.N.Y. 2014), ''aff'd'', 2014 WL 4629624 (S.D.N.Y. August 29, 2014), ''rev'd'', [https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=13435051576607435520 829 F.3d 197] (2d. Cir. 2016), ''rehearing en banc denied'', [https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4004560388364424542 855 F.3d 53] (2d Cir. 2017). *{{cite news |title=Judge orders Microsoft to turn over data held overseas |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |author=Ellen Nakashima |author-link=Ellen Nakashima |date=July 31, 2014 |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/national-security/judge-orders-microsoft-to-turn-over-data-held-overseas/2014/07/31/b07c4952-18d4-11e4-9e3b-7f2f110c6265_story.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140806110605/https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/national-security/judge-orders-microsoft-to-turn-over-data-held-overseas/2014/07/31/b07c4952-18d4-11e4-9e3b-7f2f110c6265_story.html |archive-date=2014-08-06 |url-access=subscription}}{{cbignore}} *{{cite web|author=Joseph Ax|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-usa-tech-warrants-idUSKBN0G024I20140731|title=Microsoft ordered by U.S. judge to submit customer's emails from abroad|work=Reuters|date=July 31, 2014}} *{{cite news|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/2014-07-31/microsoft-fails-to-block-u-s-warrant-for-ireland-e-mail.html|work=Bloomberg L.P.|first=Bob|last=Van Voris|title=Microsoft Fails to Block U.S. Warrant for Ireland E-Mail|date=August 1, 2014}} In 2016, the Second Circuit reversed on appeal, determining that the [[Stored Communications Act]] of 1986 did not [[Extraterritorial jurisdiction|apply extraterritorially]]. *Wingfield, Nick & Cecilia Kang, [https://www.nytimes.com/2016/07/15/technology/microsoft-wins-appeal-on-overseas-data-searches.html?_r=0 Microsoft Wins Appeal on Overseas Data Searches], ''New York Times'' (July 14, 2016). * Jonathan Stempel, [https://www.reuters.com/article/us-microsoft-usa-warrant/microsoft-wins-landmark-appeal-over-seizure-of-foreign-emails-idUSKCN0ZU1RJ Microsoft wins landmark appeal over seizure of foreign emails], Reuters (July 16, 2016). The case went to the Supreme Court, but was dismissed as moot due to Congress's enactment of the [[CLOUD Act]] in 2018, which created a process for U.S. investigators to access data stored overseas.[https://www.sullcrom.com/us-supreme-court-dismisses-us-v-microsoft-as-moot-after-cloud-act-signed-into-law U.S. Supreme Court Dismisses U.S. v. Microsoft as Moot After CLOUD Act Signed Into Law], Sullivan & Cromwell LLP (April 19, 2018). In ''[[Consumer Financial Protection Bureau v. RD Legal Funding, LLC]]'' (2018), Preska overturned the entirety of Title X of the [[Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act]], which created the [[Consumer Financial Protection Bureau]]. Preska ruled that the law establishing the CFPB's structure was unconstitutional because it established that the agency's single director could be removed by the president only [[for cause]].Debra Cassens Weiss, [https://www.abajournal.com/news/article/judge_rules_consumer_financial_protection_bureau_is_unconstitutionally_stru Judge rules Consumer Financial Protection Bureau is unconstitutionally structured and can't sue], ''ABA Journal'' (June 22, 2018).Pratin Vallabhaneni & Margaux Curie, [https://www.whitecase.com/publications/alert/us-supreme-court-rules-cfpbs-leadership-structure-unconstitutional-leaves-cfpb US Supreme Court Rules CFPB's Leadership Structure is Unconstitutional but Leaves CFPB Intact], White & Case (July 8, 2020). Preska disagreed with the ''en banc'' decision of the [[U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit]] that upheld the constitutionality of the CFPB's structure, and sided with the dissenter in that case, then-Judge [[Brett Kavanaugh]], who believed that the protections for the CFPB director violated the Constitution's [[Take Care Clause]]. (The U.S. Supreme Court ultimately ruled, in a 5–4 decision in ''[[Seila Law v. Consumer Financial Protection Bureau|Seila Law v. CFPB]]'' (2020), that the law's mandate that a CFPB director be removed only "for cause" was unconstitutional, but severed that portion of the statute, allowing the CFPB to continue operating while making its director removable at the will of the president.) ====Criminal cases==== In 2008, [[Susan Lindauer]], a former journalist and [[congressional aide]] charged with acting as an [[Foreign Agent Registration Act|unregistered foreign agent]] of [[Saddam Hussein]]'s Iraqi government, was released after Preska ruled her [[United States federal laws governing defendants with mental diseases or defects|unfit to stand trial]], saying that she was "highly intelligent" and "generally capable of functioning at a high level in many ways," but suffered from a mental disease or defect that left her with "a lack of connection with reality" and rendered her "unable to understand the nature and consequences of the proceedings against her or to assist properly in her defense."{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/09/17/nyregion/17lindauer.html?_r=1&|work=The New York Times|first=Benjamin|last=Weiser|title=Woman Accused of Iraq Ties Is Ruled Unfit for Trial Again|date=September 17, 2008}} Preska's ruling affirmed earlier rulings by Judge [[Michael B. Mukasey]]. In 2011, Preska sentenced [[Piracy off the coast of Somalia|Somali pirate]] [[Abduwali Muse]] to 33 years in prison for his leadership of a group of pirates who [[Maersk Alabama hijacking|seized the ''Maersk Alabama'']] and held its crew hostage. In pronouncing sentence, Preska cited the defendant's "depraved acts of physical and psychological violence" including forcing Captain [[Richard Phillips (merchant mariner)|Richard Phillips]] to undergo a [[mock execution]].{{cite news| url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-us-canada-12486129|work=BBC News|title=Somali pirate sentenced to 33 years in US prison|date=February 16, 2011}} Preska oversaw the criminal case against [[Hector Monsegur|Hector Xavier Monsegur]] ("Sabu"), a computer hacker who assisted [[Anonymous (group)|Anonymous]] and others in cyberattacks targeting credit card companies, various governments, and media outlets. Monsegur became a government informant immediately after his arrest in early 2011, and pleaded guilty in August 2011 to twelve counts of hacking, fraud, and [[identity theft]]. In 2014, Preska sentenced Monsegur to time served (seven months in jail) and a $1,200 fine; federal prosecutors requested, and Preska granted, the lenient sentence due to Monsegur's "extraordinary" cooperation with the government.Tina Susman, [https://www.latimes.com/nation/nationnow/la-na-nn-hacker-sabu-sentenced-20140527-story.html Hacker-turned-informant Sabu is a free man after N.Y. sentencing], ''Los Angeles Times'' (May 27, 2014).Benjamin Weiser, [https://www.nytimes.com/2014/05/28/nyregion/hacker-who-helped-disrupt-cyberattacks-is-allowed-to-walk-free.html Hacker Who Helped Disrupt Cyberattacks Is Allowed to Walk Free], ''New York Times'' (May 28, 2014). Information from Monsegur helped lead the authorities to at least eight co-conspirators, including [[Jeremy Hammond]], and helped to stymie at least 300 cyberattacks. Hammond pleaded guilty in 2013 to hacking the private intelligence firm [[Stratfor]], and Preska sentenced him to the maximum 10 years.Aaron Katersky, [https://abcnews.go.com/Blotter/jeremy-hammond-anonymous-stratfor-hacker-10-years/story?id=20904069 Anonymous Stratfor Hacker Given 10 Years], ABC News (November 15, 2013). In 2009, [[Ahmed Ghailani|Ahmed Khalfan Ghailani]], the first detainee brought from the [[Guantanamo Bay detention camp]] to stand trial in a U.S. civilian court (as opposed to a [[Guantanamo military commission]]), appeared before Preska to plead not guilty.{{cite web|last=Honan |first=Edith |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-usa-guantanamo-ghailani/first-guantanamo-suspect-moved-to-u-s-for-trial-idUSTRE5581MS20090609|title=First Guantanamo suspect moved to U.S. for trial |work=[[Reuters]] |date=June 9, 2009}}{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/06/10/nyregion/10gitmo.html?_r=0|work=The New York Times|first=Benjamin|last=Weiser|title=A Plea of Not Guilty for Guantánamo Detainee|date=June 10, 2009}} In 2010, Ghailani subsequently was convicted by a jury of conspiracy in the [[1998 United States embassy bombings|1998 bombing of U.S. embassies in Kenya and Tanzania]], and in 2011 was sentenced to life in prison. *Benjamin Weisner, [https://www.nytimes.com/2010/11/18/nyregion/18ghailani.html Detainee Acquitted on Most Counts in '98 Bombings], ''New York Times'' (November 18, 2010). *Chad Bray, [https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10001424052748704698004576104073143860398 Embassy Bomber Gets Life in Prison], ''Wall Street Journal'' (January 26, 2011). Ghailani's trial and sentencing were by a different Southern District judge, [[Lewis A. Kaplan]]. In 2014, Preska sentenced [[Eric Stevenson (politician)|Eric Stevenson]], a former [[New York State Assembly|New York state assemblyman]] from [[the Bronx]], to three years in prison for bribery.Sean Gardiner, [https://www.wsj.com/articles/new-york-state-assemblyman-is-sentenced-after-bribery-conviction-1400723486?tesla=y New York State Assemblyman Is Sentenced After Bribery Conviction], ''Wall Street Journal'' (May 22, 2014). In 2019, Preska sentenced [[Patrick Ho]], a former [[Hong Kong]] ophthalmologist and government official, to three years in prison for conspiring to bribe African government officials (specifically, the [[President of Chad|presidents of Chad]] and [[President of Uganda|Uganda]]) to secure oil rights for [[CEFC China Energy|CEFC China]], an energy company. *Matthew Goldstein, [https://www.nytimes.com/2019/03/25/business/cefc-china-patrick-ho-bribery.html Ex-Hong Kong Official Gets Lighter Sentence in Bribery Case], ''New York Times'' (March 25, 2019). *[https://apnews.com/article/24b657a2dd0c28cb182c9102bd7497a1 Hong Kong businessman ends prison sentence in bribery scheme], Associated Press (June 9, 2020). In 2017, Preska sentenced former [[Rikers Island]] guard Brian Coll to 30 years in prison for beating inmate Ronald Spear to death in 2012. Coll had been convicted the preceding year of deprivation of civil rights resulting in death, [[obstruction of justice]], falsifying records, and [[Conspiracy (crime)|conspiracy]]. Coll repeatedly kicked Spear, a seriously ill pretrial detainee in the jail complex's infirmary unit, in the head while other guards held the inmate face-down on the floor. During the sentencing hearing, Preska criticized a "culture of violence and poor treatment of inmates" at Rikers and referred to the "particularly vicious and callous" nature of Coll's attack on Spear. *Thomas MacMillan, [https://www.wsj.com/articles/former-nyc-jail-guard-sentenced-to-30-years-in-death-of-inmate-1505335025 Former NYC Jail Guard Sentenced to 30 Years in Death of Inmate], ''Wall Street Journal'' (September 13, 2017). *Benjamin Weiser, [https://www.nytimes.com/2017/09/13/nyregion/rikers-brian-coll-ronald-spear-sentencing-brutality.html Ex-Rikers Guard Is Sentenced to 30 Years in Fatal Beating of Inmate], ''New York Times'' (September 13, 2017). Preska oversaw the proceedings against [[Chuck Person]], a former NBA player and assistant coach of the [[Auburn Tigers men's basketball]] team, who was implicated in a [[2017–18 NCAA Division I men's basketball corruption scandal|college basketball corruption scandal]].[https://apnews.com/fa8a56366c12446c8a0630a104136e00 Judge upholds charges against ex-Auburn Coach Chuck Person], Associated Press (January 3, 2019). Preska denied Person's motion to dismiss the charges.''[https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=14403977030114474963 United States v. Person]'', 373 F. Supp. 3d 452 (S.D.N.Y. 2019). In 2019, after he pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit bribery, Preska sentenced him to two years of probation and 200 hours of community service. She found that "no purpose would be served" by sending the remorseful Person to prison; rejected prosecutors' argument that Person was motivated by "insatiable greed"; and cited Person's long record of charitable giving.Larry Neumeister, [https://apnews.com/42c9f7eb4cc54facac46038e558582d8 Former Auburn assistant basketball coach avoids prison], Associated Press (July 17, 2019). =====Steven Donziger===== {{See also|Steven Donziger#Criminal contempt charge}} In a 2021 [[bench trial]], Preska found attorney [[Steven Donziger]] guilty of six counts of criminal contempt; in a 245-page opinion, Preska said that Donziger had "repeatedly and willfully" defied court orders. He faces a maximum six-month jail sentence.{{cite news |last1=Milman |first1=Oliver |title=Lawyer Steven Donziger found guilty of withholding evidence in Chevron case |url=https://www.theguardian.com/business/2021/jul/26/lawyer-steven-donziger-guilty-chevron |access-date=28 July 2021 |work=The Guardian |date=27 July 2021 |language=en}}{{cite news |last1=Randazzo |first1=Sara |title=Chevron Foe Steven Donziger Found Guilty of Contempt in Ecuador Saga |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/chevron-foe-steven-donziger-found-guilty-of-contempt-in-ecuador-saga-11627311839 |access-date=29 July 2021 |work=Wall Street Journal |date=26 July 2021}}[https://apnews.com/article/business-environment-and-nature-141973cbb5eb49b767da77e36948e376 Judge convicts NY lawyer who fought Chevron of contempt], Associated Press (July 26, 2021). Preska wrote that she did not question the sincerity of Donziger's longrunning legal battle against [[Chevron Corporation|Chevron]] on behalf of Ecuadorians over [[Lago Agrio oil field|pollution in Ecuador's rainforest]], but that Donziger was not entitled to "take the law into his own hands." The [[United Nations]]' Human Rights Council criticized the situation and said that Donziger had not been granted a fair trial. With regards to Preska, "[...] The Working Group is of the view that Judge P did not act in a manner which was independent, objective and impartial in relation to Mr. Donziger's case. Consequently, the Working Group concludes that the imposition of pre-trial detention upon Mr. Donziger violated Article 9 (3) of the Covenant." The council was also critical of how Judge [[Lewis A. Kaplan|Kaplan]] appointed Preska to hear Donziger's case and of Preska's dismissal of Donziger's challenge to her appointment.[https://thehill.com/policy/energy-environment/574786-un-rules-that-steven-donziger-house-arrest-violates-international UN rules that Steven Donziger house arrest violates international laws] ''[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]]''[https://static1.squarespace.com/static/5ac2615b8f5130fda4340fcb/t/61537ea231d36d4b49f955fe/1632861862416/2021-09-24-advance-un-human-rights-working-group-on-arbitrary-detention-letter.pdf Opinion No. 24/2021 concerning Mr. Steven Donziger (United States of America)] Human Rights Council - Working Group on Arbitrary Detention == Personal life== In 1983, Preska married Thomas J. Kavaler, with whom she attended law school. Kavaler was the editor-in-chief of the ''[[Fordham Law Review]]'' and is a partner at [[Cahill Gordon & Reindel]].[https://www.nytimes.com/1983/09/12/style/loretta-preska-weds-a-fellow-lawyer.html Loretta Preska Weds Thomas J. He was a [[United States Merchant Marine Academy]] Cadet Midshipman from 1945 to 1947. He was a [[United States Marine Corps Reserve]] First Lieutenant from 1950 to 1952. He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[Yale University]] in 1950. He received a [[Juris Doctor]] and [[Bachelor of Laws]] from the [[University of Virginia School of Law]] in 1955. He was in private practice of law in New York City from 1955 to 1985.{{FJC Bio|2274|nid=1388246|name=Louis Lee Stanton}} ==Federal judicial service== Stanton was nominated by President [[Ronald Reagan]] on June 12, 1985, to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]] vacated by Judge [[Henry Frederick Werker]]. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on July 16, 1985, and received commission on July 18, 1985. He assumed [[senior status]] on October 1, 1996. ==Notable cases== Stanton was the judge in the lawsuit ''[[Viacom International Inc. v. YouTube, Inc.|Viacom Int'l, Inc.v. YouTube, Inc.]]'', in which Viacom sued YouTube alleging direct and indirect copyright infringement of Viacom's copyrighted works. In response to a formal [[motion to compel]] discovery, Stanton ordered Google to provide Viacom with YouTube user data. This decision received criticism from the [[Electronic Frontier Foundation]] and privacy advocates.{{cite web|url=http://ap.google.com/article/ALeqM5gFJIDFx4LzK1pGKWT0NpWgkN-6mQD91MIVO00 |title=Court court of "ignoring the protections of the federal [[Video Privacy Protection Act]]."{{cite web | url=http://www.appscout.com/2008/07/judge_google_must_hand_over_yo_1.php | title=Judge: Google Must the defendants' and plaintiffs' employees.{{Cite news|title=Lawyers in YouTube lawsuit reach user privacy deal |last=Auchard |first=Eric |publisher=[[Reuters]] |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/newsOne/idUSSP21085220080715 |date=July 15, 2008 }} In 2010, and in 2013, Stanton ruled in Google's favor in a motion for summary judgment.{{Cite news| title = US judge tosses out Viacom copyright suit against YouTube |author=Lefkow, Chris| publisher = AFP| url = https://www.google.com/hostednews/afp/article/ALeqM5h_AfErLSMMGD417l8aR0CYib0aNQ| archive-url = date=June 23, 2010}} Stanton was the judge in the civil complaint filed by the [[U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission]] (SEC) against [[Bernard Madoff]].{{Cite news| title = Judge in Madoff case |date=December 30, 2008}} In another case Stanton ruled to dismiss the case of the Federal Trade Commission and New York attorney general against Quincy Bioscience of Madison, Wisconsin. Quincy was accused of saying that its [[Prevagen]] dietary supplement advertising claims were misleading. His ruling was overturned and the case was returned to the lower court.{{Cite news| title = Court Orders A Trial in Prevagen Lawsuit |last = Terrell |first = Kenneth | url =https://www.aarp.org/politics-society/advocacy/info-2019/prevagen-lawsuit.html |publisher = [[AARP]] |date= February 26, 2019 |accessdate= March 1, 2019}} In 2021, Stanton ruled that Locast, a streaming non-profit, must cease online streamed redistribution of live local television stations. She graduated from [[Wake Forest University]] with her [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in 1984 and later from [[University of Virginia School of Law]] with a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1988.{{FJC Bio|nid=1391916|inline=yes}} ==Career== Following law school graduation, Flanagan served as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Malcolm Jones Howard]] of the United States District Court for the Eastern District of North Carolina from 1988 to 1989. She was a private practice attorney in [[Washington, D.C.]] from 1989 to 1990 and [[North Carolina]] from 1990 to 1999. ===Federal judicial service=== Between 1995 and 2003, Flanagan served as a [[United States magistrate judge]] for the United States District Court for the Eastern District of North Carolina. Bush on January 29, 2003, to a seat vacated by Judge [[James Carroll Fox]].{{cite web |title=Nominations Senate to the Senate |url=https://georgewbush-whitehouse.archives.gov/news/releases/2003/01/20030129-16.html |website=georgewbush-whitehouse.archives.gov |access-date=March 1, 2025 |date=January 29, 2003}} She was confirmed by the [[United States Senate|Senate]] on July 17, 2003, and received her commission the next day. ==References== {{Reflist}} ==Sources== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1391916}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[James Carroll Fox]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of North Carolina]]}}|years=2003–present}} {{s-inc}} {{s-end}} {{United States 4th Circuit district judges}} {{authority control}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Flanagan, Louise Wood}} [[Category:1962 births]] [[Category:Living people]] [[Category:Wake Forest University alumni]] [[Category:University of Virginia School of Law alumni]] [[Category:Judges of the United States District Court for the Eastern District of North Carolina]] [[Category:United States district court judges appointed by George W. {{short description|American judge (born 1968)}} {{Infobox officeholder |name = Lydia Griggsby |image = Lydia Kay Griggsby (cropped).jpg |caption = Griggsby in 2017 |office = Judge of the [[United States District Court for the District of Maryland]] |appointer = [[Joe Biden]] |term_start = July 20, 2021 |term_end = |predecessor = [[Catherine C. [[Georgetown University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Lydia Kay Griggsby''' (born January 16, 1968){{Cite web |last=Voruganti |first=Harsh |date=April 6, 2021 |title=Judge Lydia Griggsby – Nominee to the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland |url=https://vettingroom.org/2021/04/06/judge-lydia-griggsby/ |access-date=May 13, 2021 |website=The Vetting Room |language=en}} is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Maryland]]. She is a former judge of the [[United States Court of Federal Claims]] and chief counsel for privacy and information policy for the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]]. She is the first woman of color to serve as a judge on the [[United States District Court for the District of Maryland]].{{Cite web |last=Fenton |first=Justin |date=March 30, 2021 |title=Biden to nominate two Maryland women to become federal judges, including the first woman of color |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2021/03/30/biden-to-nominate-two-maryland-women-to-become-federal-judges-including-the-first-woman-of-color/ |access-date=March 31, 2021 |website=baltimoresun.com}} == Early life and education == Griggsby was born and raised in [[Baltimore|Baltimore, Maryland]], and attended the [[Park School of Baltimore]] in [[Baltimore|Baltimore, Maryland]].{{Cite web |title=African American Heritage Spotlight: Judge Lydia Griggsby |url=https://www.uscourts.gov/data-news/judiciary-news/2022/02/17/african-american-heritage-spotlight-judge-lydia-griggsby |access-date=2025-09-29 |website=www.uscourts.gov |language=en}} Her parents were both educators who graduated from [[Historically black colleges and universities|Historically Black Colleges and Universities]] (HBCUs). She received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from the [[University of Pennsylvania]] in 1990 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[Georgetown University Law Center]] in 1993.{{Cite web |title=Lydia K. Griggsby, Judge, U.S. District Court (Maryland) |url=https://msa.maryland.gov/msa/mdmanual/39fed/02usd/html/msa18530.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com |access-date=2025-09-29 |website=msa.maryland.gov}}{{AI-retrieved source|date=March 2026|checked=no}} She is also a member of [[Delta Sigma Theta]] sorority. == Career == Griggsby began her legal career as an associate with the [[law firm]] of [[DLA Piper|DLA Piper LLP]], from 1993 to 1995. She served as a trial attorney in the Commercial Litigation Branch of the [[United States Department of Justice Civil Division|Civil Division]] of the [[United States Department of Justice]], from 1995 to 1998. She served as an Assistant United States Attorney in the [[Washington, D.C.|District of Columbia]], from 1998 to 2004. She worked as Counsel for the [[United States Senate Select Committee on Ethics]], from 2004 to 2005. She served as Privacy Counsel for the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]] from 2004 to 2008, and as Chief Counsel for Privacy and Information Policy for senator [[Patrick Leahy]]{{Cite web |date=30 March 2021 |title=A look at President Biden's first 11 judicial nominees |url=https://news.yahoo.com/look-president-bidens-first-11-144606553.html}} on the same committee until 2014.{{Cite web |date=April 10, 2014 |title=President Obama Nominates Three to Serve on the U.S. Court of Federal Claims |url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/04/10/president-obama-nominates-three-serve-us-court-federal-claims |website=[[White House]]}} === Assistant U.S. Attorney service === Griggsby served as a trial attorney in the Commercial Litigation Branch of the Civil Division of the [[United States Department of Justice]] from 1995 to 1998. She then served as an [[Assistant United States Attorney]] in the [[District of Columbia]] from 1998 to 2004. Notably, she represented the United States in a [[Clean Air Act (United States)|Clean Air Act]] enforcement action against [[Toyota]] for violations involving more than two million vehicles sold between 1996 and 1998, helping to secure a settlement that required the company to spend $20 million on cleaner vehicle projects, strengthen emissions compliance, and pay a $500,000 civil penalty.{{Cite web |last=Voruganti |first=Harsh |date=2021-04-06 |title=Judge Lydia Griggsby – Nominee to the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland |url=https://vettingroom.org/2021/04/06/judge-lydia-griggsby/ |access-date=2025-09-29 |website=The Vetting Room |language=en}}{{Cite web |last=US EPA |first=OECA |date=2013-05-09 |title=Toyota Motor Corporation Settlement |url=https://www.epa.gov/enforcement/toyota-motor-corporation-settlement |access-date=2025-09-29 |website=www.epa.gov |language=en}} After her service as a federal prosecutor, Griggsby worked as Counsel for the [[United States Senate Select Committee on Ethics]] from 2004 to 2005. She then served as Privacy Counsel for the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]] from 2004 to 2008, and as Chief Counsel for Privacy and Information Policy for [[Patrick Leahy|Senator Patrick Leahy]] on the same committee until 2014.{{Cite web |title=Lydia Kay Griggsby, District Judge {{!}} District of Maryland {{!}} United States District Court |url=https://www.mdd.uscourts.gov/lydia-kay-griggsby-district-judge |access-date=2025-09-29 |website=www.mdd.uscourts.gov}} In that capacity, she was the lead Senate counsel on several pieces of legislation enacted by Congress to reform the [[Freedom of Information Act (United States)|Freedom of Information Act]], including the [[OPEN Government Act of 2007]] and the [[Freedom of Information Act (United States)|OPEN FOIA Act of 2009]], as well as on legislation amending the [[Video Privacy Protection Act]]. === Federal judicial service === On April 10, 2014, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Griggsby to serve as a Judge of the [[United States Court of Federal Claims]], to the seat vacated by Judge [[Francis Allegra]], whose term expired October 21, 2013.{{Cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/04/10/presidential-nominations-sent-senate|title=Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate|date=April 10, 2014|website=[[White House]]}} A hearing on her nomination before the [[United States Senate Judiciary Committee]] was held on June 4, 2014.{{cite web|title=June 4, 2014: Judicial Nominations|date=4 June 2014 |url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/judicial-nominations-2014-06-04|publisher=United States Senate}} On June 12, 2014, her nomination was reported out of committee by [[voice vote]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%20-%2006-12-14.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting - June 12, 2014}} On December 3, 2014, Senate Majority Leader [[Harry Reid]] filed for cloture on her nomination. On December 4, 2014, the Senate invoked cloture on Griggsby's nomination by a 53–36 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=113&session=2&vote=00311|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture on the Nomination of Lydia Kay Griggsby, of Maryland, to be a Judge of the U.S. Court of Federal Claims)|website=www.senate.gov}} Later that day, her nomination was confirmed by a [[voice vote]]. She received her commission on December 5, 2014.{{FJC Bio|nid=10270716|inline=yes}} She took the oath of office on December 15, 2014.{{Cite web|url=http://www.uscfc.uscourts.gov/node/2703|title=Lydia Kay Griggsby took the oath of office on December 15, 2014, as Judge of the United States Court of Federal Claims.|website=www.uscfc.uscourts.gov|access-date=2019-08-06}} Her service on the claims court terminated on July 23, 2021, when she was sworn in as an [[Federal tribunals in the United States#Article III courts|Article III]] district court judge. On March 30, 2021, President [[Joe Biden]] announced his intent to nominate Griggsby to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] for the [[United States District Court for the District of Maryland]].{{Cite web|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/03/30/president-biden-announces-intent-to-nominate-11-judicial-candidates/|title=President Biden Announces Intent to Nominate 11 Judicial Candidates|date=March 30, 2021|website=The White House}} On April 19, 2021, her nomination was sent to the Senate. President Biden nominated Griggsby to the seat vacated by Judge [[Catherine C. Blake]], who assumed [[senior status]] on April 2, 2021.{{Cite web|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/04/19/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-11/|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate|date=April 19, 2021|website=The White House}} On May 12, 2021, a hearing on her nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/05/05/2021/nominations|title=Nominations | United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|website=www.judiciary.senate.gov|date=12 May 2021 }} On June 10, 2021, her nomination was reported out of committee by a 16–6 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%20June%2010,%202021.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – June 10, 2021, Senate Judiciary Committee}} On June 16, 2021, the [[United States Senate]] invoked cloture on her nomination by a 57–41 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1171/vote_117_1_00235.htm|title= On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Lydia Kay Griggsby to be U.S. District Judge for the District of Maryland)|website=www.senate.gov}} Her nomination was confirmed later that day by a 59–39 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1171/vote_117_1_00237.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Lydia Kay Griggsby, of Maryland, to be U.S. District Judge for the District of Maryland)|website=www.senate.gov}} She received her judicial commission on July 20, 2021. She was sworn in on July 23, 2021.{{Cite press release|title=Swearing-In of Lydia Kay Griggsby as United States District Judge|date=July 23, 2021|publisher=United States District Court for the District of Maryland|url=https://www.mdd.uscourts.gov/news/swearing-lydia-kay-griggsby-united-states-district-judge-2021-07-23t000000|access-date=August 10, 2021}} === Notable cases === Griggsby has presided over several notable cases. In 2022, Judge Griggsby intervened in [[NAACP]] v. [[Baltimore County, Maryland|Baltimore County]] when she granted a preliminary injunction blocking the [[Baltimore County, Maryland#Law and government|Baltimore County Council's]] redistricting plan, finding it likely violated the [[Voting Rights Act of 1965|Voting Rights Act]] by diluting Black voters' electoral power.{{Cite web |title=VICTORY: Federal Judge Orders Baltimore County to Submit Redistricting Plan that Complies with Voting Rights Act |url=https://www.aclu-md.org/press-releases/victory-federal-judge-orders-baltimore-county-submit-redistricting-plan-complies/ |access-date=2025-09-29 |website=ACLU of Maryland |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |last=Lee |first=John |date=2022-02-23 |title=Judge strikes down Baltimore County's redistricting map |url=https://www.wypr.org/wypr-news/2022-02-22/judge-strikes-down-baltimore-countys-redistricting-map |access-date=2025-09-29 |website=WYPR |language=en}} She ordered the county to submit a remedial map, and later accepted a revised plan that included one majority-Black district.{{Cite web |title=Baltimore County NAACP et al v. Baltimore County et al |url=https://www.aclu-md.org/cases/baltimore-county-naacp-et-al-v-baltimore-county-et-al/ |access-date=2025-09-29 |website=ACLU of Maryland |language=en-US}} In 2023, she oversaw the criminal trial of former Baltimore City State's Attorney [[Marilyn Mosby]] (Maryland v. Mosby), who was charged with perjury and making false statements on mortgage applications.{{Cite web |date=2023-11-09 |title=District of Maryland {{!}} Former Baltimore City State's Attorney Marilyn Mosby Convicted on Two Counts of Perjury {{!}} United States Department of Justice |url=https://www.justice.gov/usao-md/pr/former-baltimore-city-states-attorney-marilyn-mosby-convicted-two-counts-perjury |access-date=2025-09-29 |website=www.justice.gov |language=en}} A jury found Mosby guilty on both counts of perjury related to withdrawals from her city retirement account, and later on two counts of making false mortgage applications in connection with vacation homes in Florida.{{Cite web |date=2024-05-23 |title=Baltimore's former top prosecutor spared prison for mortgage fraud and perjury |url=https://apnews.com/article/marilyn-mosby-baltimore-prosecutor-sentencing-8f2419edd3ff404cdf24434777e6eefe |access-date=2025-09-29 |website=AP News |language=en}} Griggsby sentenced Mosby to twelve months of home confinement followed by supervised release. In 2025, Griggsby presided over [[GLMA: Health Professionals Advancing LGBTQ+ Equality|GLMA]] v. [[National Institutes of Health|NIH]],{{Cite web |title=GLMA v. National Institutes of Health |url=https://lambdalegal.org/case/glma-v-national-institutes-of-health/ |access-date=2025-09-29 |website=Lambda Legal |language=en-US}} a lawsuit filed by Lambda Legal on behalf of LGBTQ+ health researchers and advocacy groups after the [[Department of Health and Human Services]] revoked existing National Institutes of Health grants and blocked new applications for review.{{Cite web |title=Judge rules in favor of LGBTQ+ health researchers after HHS revoked funding for "radical" programs |url=https://www.gaytoday.com/index.php/2025/08/06/judge-rules-in-favor-of-lgbtq-health-researchers-after-hhs-revoked-funding-for-radical-programs/ |access-date=2025-09-29 |website=www.gaytoday.com}}{{Cite web |last=Reinmann |first=Molly |last2=CNN |date=2025-08-05 |title=Judge Pauses Termination of LGBTQ Health Research Grants |url=https://www.outsmartmagazine.com/2025/08/nih-lgbtq-research-halted/ |access-date=2025-09-29 |website=OutSmart Magazine |language=en-US}} The plaintiffs alleged that the policy unlawfully targeted LGBTQ+-related programs. Griggsby granted a preliminary injunction, finding that the administration's actions constituted unlawful discrimination in violation of the [[Fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution|Fifth Amendment]] and Section 1557 of the [[Affordable Care Act]], and ordered that funding be restored while the case proceeded. In 2026, Griggsby presided over United States v. [[Tom Goldstein]], a former [[Supreme Court of the United States|United States Supreme Court]] advocate accused of tax fraud.{{Cite web |last=Toobin |first=Jeffrey |date=December 28, 2025 |title=He Was a Supreme Court Lawyer. Then His Double Life Caught Up With Him. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/12/28/magazine/thomas-goldstein-supreme-court-gambling.html#:~:text=Thomas%20Goldstein%20was%20a%20superstar,now%20land%20him%20in%20prison. |website=The New York Times Magazine}} == Abusive workplace == On February 10, 2026, [[NPR]] published an article about a December 17, 2025, [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit]] order where Griggsby acknowledged her chambers had "resulted in an abusive workplace" following a complaint by a former law clerk who alleged bullying, harsh verbal criticism, inadequate guidance, and intimidating behavior during the clerkship resulting in their resignation and transfer along with their co-clerk.{{Cite news |last=Johnson |first=Carrie |date=2026-02-10 |title=Federal judge acknowledges 'abusive workplace' in court order |url=https://www.npr.org/2026/02/10/nx-s1-5709042/judges-accountability |access-date=2026-02-13 |work=NPR |language=en}} The order, signed by Chief Judge [[Albert Diaz (judge)|Albert Diaz]], concluded that after an investigation—which involved meeting with former clerks—clerk's feared asking questions, were subjected to intense questioning about large caseloads, and experienced stress-related health effects.{{Cite web |last=Machina® |first=Lex |title=Md. Federal Judge Owns Up To Creating 'Abusive' Workplace - Law360 |url=https://www.law360.com/articles/2440863/md-federal-judge-owns-up-to-creating-abusive-workplace |access-date=2026-02-13 |website=www.law360.com |language=en}} Griggsby disputed some specific allegations while acknowledging that aspects of her management style had created an abusive environment and expressing regret for the impact on staff. As corrective action, the order stated that she agreed to undertake workplace-focused training and mentorship, meet regularly with the circuit's Director of Workplace Relations, and encourage future clerks to raise concerns through appropriate judicial channels, concluding that these steps constituted appropriate remedial measures. The matter drew criticism from advocacy group Legal Accountability Project, which argued the response was insufficient and highlighted broader concerns about accountability mechanisms within the federal judiciary.{{Cite web |last=Raymond |first=Nate |date=February 11, 2026 |title=US judge acknowledges 'abusive workplace' after ex-clerk files complaint |url=https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/us-judge-acknowledges-abusive-workplace-after-ex-clerk-files-complaint-2026-02-11/ |website=Reuters}} == Personal life == Griggsby is a member of the [[National Presbyterian Church]] and serves as a [[Deacon]].{{Cite web |title=Justice, Service and Faith: A Fireside Chat with a Federal Judge |url=https://nationalpres.org/event/justice-service-and-faith-a-fireside-chat-with-a-federal-judge/ |access-date=2026-02-13 |website=National Presbyterian Church |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |title=Staff & Leaders |url=https://nationalpres.org/welcome/leaders-staff/ |access-date=2026-02-13 |website=National Presbyterian Church |language=en-US}} == See also == * [[List of African-American federal judges]] * [[List of African-American jurists]] * [[List of Native American jurists]] == References == {{Reflist}} == External links == * {{FJC Bio|nid=10270716}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Francis Allegra]]}} {{s-ttl|title=Judge of the [[United States Court of Federal Claims]]|years=2015–2021}} {{s-aft|after=[[Philip Hadji]]}} |- {{s-bef|before=[[Catherine C. Blake]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States District Court for the District of Maryland]]}}|years=2021–present}} {{s-inc}} {{s-end}} {{United States 4th Circuit district judges}} {{Authority control}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Griggsby, Lydia Kay}} [[Category:1968 births]] [[Category:20th-century American lawyers]] [[Category:20th-century American women lawyers]] [[Category:21st-century American lawyers]] [[Category:21st-century American women judges]] [[Category:African-American judges]] [[Category:Georgetown University Law Center alumni]] [[Category:Judges of the United States Court of Federal Claims]] [[Category:Judges of the United States District Court for the District of Maryland]] [[Category:Lawyers from Washington, D.C.]] [[Category:Living people]] [[Category:United States Article I federal judges appointed by Barack Obama]] [[Category:United States Department of Justice lawyers]] [[Category:United States district court judges appointed by Joe Biden]] [[Category:United States Senate lawyers]] [[Category:University of Pennsylvania alumni]] [[Category:20th-century African-American lawyers]] [[Category:African-American women lawyers]] [[Category:21st-century African-American lawyers]]
