{{Short description|American judge (born 1939)}} {{Use American English|date=July 2026}} {{Use mdy dates|date=July 2026}} {{Infobox officeholder | name = Lynn Adelman | image = Lynn_Adelman.jpg | office = Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Wisconsin]] | term_start = December 23, 1997 | term_end = | appointer = [[List of federal judges appointed by Bill Clinton|Bill Clinton]] | predecessor = [[Thomas John Curran]] | successor = | state_senate1 = Wisconsin | district1 = [[Wisconsin's 28th Senate district|28th]] | term_start1 = January 3, 1977 | term_end1 = December 23, 1997 | predecessor1 = [[James Devitt (politician)|James Devitt]] | successor1 = [[Mary Lazich]] | party = [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] | birth_name = Lynn Steven Adelman | birth_date = {{Birth date and age|1939|10|01}} | birth_place = [[Milwaukee]], Wisconsin, U.S. | death_date = | death_place = | spouse = {{marriage|Elizabeth L. "Betty" Halmbacher|1976}} | education = [[Princeton University]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|BA]])
[[Columbia University]] ([[Bachelor of Laws|LLB]]) }} '''Lynn Steven Adelman'''{{cite book|title=The Nassau Herald|year=1961|page=2|publisher=Princeton University}} (born October 1, 1939) is an American lawyer and former politician. He has served as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] for the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Wisconsin]] since December 1997.{{cite web|url=https://www.wied.uscourts.gov/judges/lynn-adelman|title=Lynn Adelman | Eastern District of Wisconsin | United States District Court|website=Wied.uscourts.gov|access-date=November 24, 2019}} Prior to becoming a federal judge, he served 20 years as a [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] member of the [[Wisconsin Senate]], representing southwest [[Milwaukee County]] and neighboring municipalities from 1977 to 1997. He also ran three times for the U.S. House of Representatives in 1974, 1982, and 1984. ==Early life and education== Adelman was born in [[Milwaukee]]. He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[Princeton University]] in 1961 and a [[Bachelor of Laws]] from [[Columbia Law School]] in 1965. == Career == Adelman was a research assistant at Columbia from 1965 to 1966. He was a trial attorney for the Legal Aid Society of Wisconsin from 1967 to 1968, and then entered private practice in Milwaukee in 1968.{{FJC Bio|nid=1390426|inline=yes}} In 1993, Adelman represented Todd Mitchell, a black man convicted of a racially motivated attack against a 14-year old white boy, in ''[[Wisconsin v. Mitchell]]'', a landmark [[First Amendment to the United States Constitution|first amendment]] case.{{Cite web|url=https://www.c-span.org/video/?39931-1/supreme-court-hate-crimes-case|title=Supreme Court Hate Crimes Case | C-SPAN.org|website=www.c-span.org}}{{ussc|name=Wisconsin v. Mitchell|volume=508|page=476|pin=479|year=1993}} ===Political career=== [[File:1972_WI_Cong_09.svg|thumb|right|Wisconsin's 9th congressional district 1972–1981.]] Adelman made his first bid for elected office in 1974, running for [[U.S. House of Representatives]] and seeking to oust ten-term Republican incumbent [[Glenn Robert Davis]] from [[Wisconsin's 9th congressional district]]. Davis, who was a close ally of then-president [[Richard Nixon]], was politically wounded by the [[Watergate scandal]] and Nixon's other recent controversies. Adelman focused much of his campaign on issues of executive overreach and the need for Congress to re-assert its authority.{{cite news|url= https://www.newspapers.com/article/ozaukee-county-news-graphic-adelman/172430541/ |title= Adelman speaks to county Democrats |newspaper= Ozaukee County News Graphic |date= June 20, 1973 |page= 52 |accessdate= May 15, 2025 |via= [[Newspapers.com]] }} Davis, however, was defeated in the Republican primary by moderate Republican [[Bob Kasten]]. The general election was one of the most hotly-contested in the state, with both campaigns breaching [[campaign finance]] limits that had existed at that time—Adelman spent about $104,000 and Kasten spent about $89,000 (adjusted for inflation, $677,000 and $579,000, respectively).{{cite news|url= https://www.newspapers.com/article/west-bend-news-kasten-adelman/172435274/ |title= Adelman, Kasten both boiled over |newspaper= West Bend News |first= Marc |last= Eisen |accessdate= May 15, 2025 |via= [[Newspapers.com]] }} Kasten defeated Adelman with 52% of the vote.{{Cite news|url= https://www.newspapers.com/article/west-bend-news-kasten-adelman/172431514/ |title= Some ousters altered local politics |newspaper= West Bend News |date= March 3, 1975 |page= 25 |accessdate= May 15, 2025 |via= [[Newspapers.com]] }} In the aftermath of the election, Adelman was critical of some of Kasten's early votes in Congress and seemed intent on a rematch in 1976.{{Cite news|url= https://www.newspapers.com/article/west-bend-news-kasten-adelman/172434549/ |title= Adelman raps Kasten oil vote |newspaper= West Bend News |date= March 6, 1975 |page= 2 |accessdate= May 15, 2025 |via= [[Newspapers.com]] }} Rather than running again for Congress in 1976, Adelman moved south from [[Shorewood, Wisconsin]]—in northern Milwaukee County—to [[New Berlin, Wisconsin]]—in southeast [[Waukesha County, Wisconsin|Waukesha County]]. The move immediately sparked speculation that Adelman would instead run for [[Wisconsin Senate]] against Republican incumbent [[James Devitt (politician)|James Devitt]] in the [[Wisconsin's 28th Senate district|28th Senate district]].{{cite news|url= https://www.newspapers.com/article/waukesha-daily-freeman-adelman/172454042/ |title= Adelman to Face Devitt? |newspaper= Waukesha Daily Freeman |date= July 18, 1975 |page= 3 |accessdate= May 15, 2025 |via= [[Newspapers.com]] }} Shortly after Adelman's move, newspapers broke the story that Devitt was the subject of a [[John Doe law (Wisconsin)|John Doe investigation]] relating to campaign finance violations during his run for governor in 1974.{{Cite news|url= https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-capital-times-devitt/172473637/ |title= John Doe Investigation of Devitt Gifts Sought |newspaper= [[The Capital Times]] |date= March 25, 1976 |page= 1 |accessdate= May 15, 2025 |via= [[Newspapers.com]] }} Adelman officially announced his candidacy in June 1976.{{cite news|url= https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-waukesha-county-freeman-adelman/172473133/ |title= It's Official: Adelman to Challenge Devitt |newspaper= Waukesha Freeman |date= June 8, 1976 |page= 3 |accessdate= May 15, 2025 |via= [[Newspapers.com]] }} Devitt was indicted a month later.{{cite news|url= https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-waukesha-county-freeman-devitt-charg/172473714/ |title= Devitt is Indicted on 2 Charges |newspaper= Waukesha Freeman |date= July 23, 1976 |page= 1 |accessdate= May 15, 2025 |via= [[Newspapers.com]] }} Despite the indictment, Devitt won renomination against two Republican challengers. Adelman won the general election in a landslide, receiving nearly two thirds of the vote. [[File:1982_WI_Cong_04.svg|thumb|right|Wisconsin's 4th congressional district 1982–1991.]] While serving his second term in the state Senate, Adelman made two more runs for U.S. House of Representatives—the 1980s redistricting had shifted Adelman from the 9th congressional district to the [[Wisconsin's 4th congressional district|4th district]]. In the first election under those new maps, Adelman launched a [[primary challenge]] against 17-term incumbent congressman [[Clement Zablocki]]. Zablocki had not had a competitive primary or general election since winning the office in 1948.{{cite news|url= https://www.newspapers.com/article/wisconsin-state-journal-adelman-zablocki/172474875/ |title= Adelman v. Zablocki |newspaper= [[Wisconsin State Journal]] |date= May 26, 1982 |page= 6 |accessdate= May 16, 2025 |via= [[Newspapers.com]] }} In the campaign, Adelman sought to tie Zablocki to the economic policies of the Reagan administration in the midst of the [[early 1980s recession]]. Zablocki was sometimes seen as too conservative for his safely Democratic district, but he fended off the criticisms and distanced himself from Reagan, winning the primary with 60% of the vote.{{cite news|url= https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-waukesha-county-freeman-adelman-zabl/172475586/ |title= Candidates spar on economy |newspaper= Waukesha Freeman |date= July 9, 1982 |first= Steven |last= Walters |page= 1 |accessdate= May 16, 2025 |via= [[Newspapers.com]] }} Zablocki died just a year later and Adelman made another run in the special election to succeed him in the spring of 1984. He lost the primary to state senator [[Jerry Kleczka]]—another popular Polish Catholic from Milwaukee's south side. Adelman went on to win re-election four more times in the 28th Senate district. Through much of his tenure in the Senate, he served on the committee overseeing the judiciary, and was chairman in the years when Democrats held the majority.{{cite web|url= https://www.wisconsinhistory.org/Records/Article/CS4713 |title= Adelman, Lynn S. 1939 |website= [[Wisconsin Historical Society]] |date= 4 April 2016 |accessdate= May 16, 2025 }} === Federal judicial service === [[File:Doors Open Milwaukee 2023 37 (Federal Building--courtroom of Hon. Lynn Adelman).jpg|thumb|Courtroom of Hon. Lynn Adelman in [[Milwaukee]]'s [[Federal Building (Milwaukee, Wisconsin)|Federal Building]]]] In 1997, Adelman chose to apply for appointment as [[U.S. district judge]] in the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Wisconsin|Eastern District of Wisconsin]] to fill the vacancy created when district judge [[Thomas John Curran]] took [[senior status]] at the beginning of that year. He was one of nineteen applicants, which included nine other state judges, two U.S. magistrate judges, and prominent state attorneys, including [[Maxine Aldridge White]], [[Joan F. Kessler]], and the then-chairman of the [[Democratic Party of Wisconsin]] Mark Sostarich.{{cite news|url= https://www.newspapers.com/article/wisconsin-state-journal-adelman-judge/172476060/ |title= 19 apply for federal judgeship |newspaper= [[Wisconsin State Journal]] |date= January 19, 1997 |page= 24 |accessdate= May 16, 2025 |via= [[Newspapers.com]] }} Adelman's application rose above the others as state Republicans embraced his candidacy and Republican then-governor [[Tommy Thompson]] wrote a glowing recommendation, describing Adelman as "thoughtful, fair, and open-minded." Newspapers at the time speculated that Republican praise for Adelman was at least partly motivated by their desire to flip his seat in a special election and thereby regain the majority in the state Senate. Adelman was nominated to the seat by President Clinton on September 8, 1997. He received a hearing by the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee]] on October 29, 1997. He was confirmed by the full [[United States Senate]] by [[voice vote]] on November 13, 1997,{{cite web|url= https://www.congress.gov/nomination/105th-congress/609 |title= PN609 - Nomination of Lynn S. Adelman for The Judiciary, 105th Congress (1997–1998) |website= [[Congress.gov]] |year= 1997 |accessdate= May 16, 2025 }} and received his commission on December 23, 1997. ===Notable cases=== ====''Frank, et al vs Walker''==== The [[Wisconsin]] Voter ID law was a law passed by then Wisconsin governor [[Scott Walker (politician)|Scott Walker]] in 2011.{{cite web|url=https://ballotpedia.org/Lynn_Adelman|title=Lynn Adelman|website=Ballotpedia|access-date=November 24, 2019}} This law made voters of Wisconsin show a state-issued photo ID at the polls before they could vote. The reasoning behind this law was that Scott Walker wanted to stop the voter fraud that was allegedly happening within the state of Wisconsin. Adelman ruled, on April 29, 2014, that this law violated the [[Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution|fourteenth amendment]] and thus the law was unconstitutional. Adelman made this ruling because in the trial he saw no evidence of voter fraud and concluded that the law was unfair to minority voters because "Blacks and Latinos are more likely than whites to lack an ID". Adelman was overturned on appeal with the Appeals Court offering a particularly stunning rebuke:
“the district judge found as a fact that the majority of the Supreme Court was wrong about benefits such as better record keeping and promoting public confidence. Maybe that testimony will eventually persuade the Justices themselves, but in our hierarchical judicial system a district court cannot declare a statute unconstitutional just because he thinks (with or without the support of a political scientist) that the dissent was right and the majority wrong.” [Frank v. Walker, 768 F.3d 744, 750 (7th Cir. 2014)] The Panel continued: “The district judge heard from one political scientist, whose view may or may not be representative of the profession's. After a majority of the Supreme Court has concluded that photo ID requirements promote confidence, a single district judge cannot say as a “fact” that they do not, even if 20 political scientists disagree with the Supreme Court.” [ Frank v. Walker, 768 F.3d 744, 750 (7th Cir. 2014)]{{cite court |litigants=Frank v. Walker |vol=768 |reporter=F.3d |opinion=744 |pinpoint=750 |court=7th Cir. |date=2014 |url=https://casetext.com/case/frank-v-walker-27/case-details |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211018085516/https://casetext.com/case/frank-v-walker-27/case-details |url-status=dead |archive-date=October 18, 2021 }}
====''Johnny Kimble vs Wisconsin's Department of Workforce Development, et al.''==== In this case Johnny Kimble sued former Equal Rights Division Secretary [[Sheehan Donoghue]] for not giving him a pay raise based on his race and gender. The Equal Rights Division job is to investigate discrimination claims and to judge whether the claim of discrimination is true. Johnny Kimble is an ex employee of the Equal Rights Division and ran the office in Milwaukee.{{cite news|url=http://archive.jsonline.com/news/milwaukee/87074052.html|title=State equal-rights officials suffered discrimination, court rules|author=Vielmetti, Bruce|date=March 8, 2010|work=Journal Sentinel|access-date=November 24, 2019}} Sheehan Donoghue was appointed to this position in 1991 by then governor of Wisconsin [[Tommy Thompson]]. Adelman's ruling on this case was that Johnny Kimble was denied pay raises because of his race and that the Department of Workforce Development was to pay Johnny Kimble what he lost. This ruling was made on February 25, 2010. Adelman said that Sheehan Donoghue made statements that contradicted to what she said and what other witnesses said, she also got defensive and evasive during the questioning, and the evidence on the case did not support her claims. The evidence they found was when the Milwaukee office did well she credited the office, not Johnny, but when the Madison office did well she credited the section chief, who was white. Also, whenever Johnny said they need technical support she ignored him, but when it was a white employee, she promised help. ====''St. Augustine School v. Evers''==== In June 2017, Adelman found that [[Tony Evers]], then [[Superintendent of Public Instruction of Wisconsin]], did not violate the Constitution's [[Free Exercise Clause]] nor its [[Establishment Clause]] when he denied bussing to an independent Catholic school because there was a nearby archdiocesan school.{{Bluebook journal|last=|first=|title=Recent Case: Seventh Circuit Holds Denial of Busing to Catholic School Under Wisconsin Statute Does Not Violate Free Exercise or Establishment Clauses|volume=132|journal=[[Harvard Law Review|Harv. L. Rev.]]|page=2344|url=http://harvardlawreview.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/2344-2351_Online.pdf|year=2019}} In his opinion, Adelman referenced Wikipedia articles on [[Traditionalist Catholic]] and [[Montessori education]].{{cite court|litigants=St. Augustine School v. Evers|vol=276|reporter=F. Supp. 3d|opinion=890|court=E.D. Wis.|year=2017|url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=14895342753351508405}} His judgment was affirmed by a divided panel of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit]] in October 2018.{{cite court|litigants=St. Augustine School v. Evers|vol=906 |reporter=F.3d|opinion=591|court=7th Cir.|year=2018|url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=8116620098576159983}} ====''United States vs. Sujata Sachdeva''==== In this trial, [[Koss Corporation]]'s Chief Financial Advisor Sujata Sachdeva was charged with [[Embezzlement|embezzling]] $34 million from the company. The other person involved in the embezzlement was Julie Mulvaney who was a senior accountant at Koss Corporation.{{cite web|url=https://www.sec.gov/litigation/litreleases/2010/lr21640.htm|title=Sujata Sachdeva and Julie Mulvaney|website=www.sec.gov|access-date=November 24, 2019}} The Koss Corporation is a manufacturer of [[headphones]]. Sachdeva used almost all of the $34 million she embezzled, from the Koss Corporation, to go on a wild shopping spree. The shopping spree consisted of shopping at designer, jewelry, department stores, and other high-end retailers. Sachdeva, along with Mulvaney, tried to cover up the embezzlement by creating false accounting records. Mulvaney created falsified journal records to cover Sachdeva's spending spree. Sachdeva's attorney's argued that Sachdeva was mentally ill with [[alcoholism]], diagnosed [[bipolar disorder]], and a [[shopping addiction]], when she went on the shopping spree. The sentence the federal prosecutor wanted was 15–20 years in prison, and the lawyers for Sachdeva wanted the sentenced reduce to 6–7 years in prison, because of her mental condition. Adelman sentenced Sachdeva to 11 years in federal prison on November 17, 2010. Adelman gave some leniency to Sachdeva because of her cooperation with the [[Federal Bureau of Investigation|FBI]]. ====''United States vs. William White''==== William White, a [[Neo-Nazism|Neo-Nazi]] who ran the Virginia-based American Nationalist Socialist Workers Party, posted the address, name, and telephone numbers of a juror in [[Chicago]] who convicted a white supremacist to his website. The prosecutors claimed that White did this in hopes that the juror would be harmed for the conviction of the [[White supremacy|white supremacist]]. Adelman at first dismissed the indictment of White, because he did not threaten or actually caused harm to the man and he obtained the information legally, and that what White did was covered over the [[First Amendment to the United States Constitution|First Amendment]]. This judgement by Adelman was overturned and White went on to trial and was convicted by a [[jury]] in Chicago. After this sentencing Adelman reversed it for the same reasons he dismissed the case in the first place. Then on February 20, 2013, Adelman did sentence White to three and half years in [[prison]] for soliciting violence to a juror. When this sentencing happened, White was already in jail for other threats and intimidation practices. ====''United States vs. Hannah Dugan''==== In April 2025, federal agents arrested Wisconsin circuit court judge [[Hannah Dugan]] and charged her with obstructing a federal proceeding and concealing a person from arrest. The situation arose from the case of Eduardo Flores-Ruiz, an undocumented immigrant who was appearing in Dugan's courtroom as a defendant. After being informed that federal agents were waiting outside the main courtroom entrance to detain Flores-Ruiz for deportation, Dugan allowed him to leave out of an alternate door. Dugan was indicted on May 13, and the case was randomly assigned to Adelman.{{cite news|url= https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/crime/2025/05/13/judge-lynn-adelman-to-hear-the-federal-case-against-hannah-dugan/83537010007/ |title= What to know about Lynn Adelman, the federal judge who will hear the Hannah Dugan case |first= Cary |last= Spivak |date= May 13, 2025 |newspaper= [[Milwaukee Journal Sentinel]] |accessdate= May 15, 2025 }} The case received a rush of national attention as Democrats and legal experts denounced the arrest as an assault on the independence of the judiciary and an attempt by the [[Second presidency of Donald Trump|Donald Trump administration]] to intimidate political opponents. Dugan's attorneys moved to dismiss the case on the basis of judicial immunity, official acts, and the Tenth Amendment. They wrote "The government's prosecution of Judge Dugan is virtually unprecedented and entirely unconstitutional".{{cite news |last1=Smith |first1=Mitch |title=Wisconsin Judge Accused of Obstructing Immigration Agents Seeks Dismissal of Case |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/05/14/us/judge-hannah-dugan-ice-wisconsin.html |access-date=14 May 2025 |work=The New York Times |date=14 May 2025}} On August 26, 2025 Adelman ruled against Dugan, stating "There is no basis for granting immunity simply because some of the allegations in the indictment describe conduct that could be considered 'part of a judge's job'" and that Dugan "went well beyond her judicial role."{{Cite web |last=Perez |first=Chris |date=2025-08-26 |title='She had no authority': Judge must face the music for allegedly obstructing Trump ICE agents |url=https://lawandcrime.com/high-profile/she-had-no-authority-judge-must-face-the-music-for-allegedly-obstructing-trump-ice-agents-as-there-is-no-basis-for-granting-immunity-ruling-says/ |access-date=2025-08-26 |website=Law & Crime |language=en}} After Dugan was convicted by the jury, Adelman denied her motions for acquittal and/or a new trial.{{cite web|url=https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.wied.111897/gov.uscourts.wied.111897.117.0.pdf|format=PDF|title=UNITED STATES OF AMERICA : Case No. 25-CR-89 : HANNAH C. DUGAN v United States|website=Storage.courtlistener.com|access-date=June 25, 2026}} On June 16, 2026, Adelman upheld the 2025 obstruction of justice verdict, declining the [[appeal]] of Dugan's 2025 [[felony]] conviction.{{Cite web |date=2026-06-16 |title=Judge upholds the conviction of former Wisconsin judge Hannah Dugan for helping immigrant evade ICE |url=https://apnews.com/article/hannah-dugan-judge-trump-immigration-ice-f7b658ea094b975add2559990f655748 |access-date=2026-06-16 |website=AP News |language=en}} On July 8, 2026, Adelman ordered Dugan to pay a fine of $5000 and declined to sentence her to serve any time in prison.{{Cite web |date=2026-07-08 |title=Former Wisconsin Judge Hannah Dugan avoids jail time for obstructing arrest of illegal immigrant |url=https://www.foxnews.com/politics/former-wisconsin-judge-hannah-dugan-avoids-jail-time-obstructing-arrest-illegal-immigrant |access-date=2026-07-08 |website=Fox News |language=en}} ====Federal lawsuits against Joseph Mensah==== Adelman has presided over three separate [[civil trial]] lawsuits against former Milwaukee Police Department officer Joseph Mensah involving three people who Mensah shot to death, including ''Estate Of Antonio Gonzalez v. On September 11, 2025 the same day a second [[mistrial]] was ruled in Cole's case due to a [[hung jury]], Adelman scheduled for a third civil trial against Mensah for Cole's death to start on May 4, 2026. On April 28, 2026, a third civil trial against Mensah over Cole's death would be avoided, with Cole's family in the process of finalizing an agreed settlement.{{cite news|url=https://wisconsinexaminer.com/briefs/confidential-settlement-agreement-close-to-completion-in-joseph-mensah-shooting-of-alvin-cole/|title=Confidential settlement agreement close to completion in Joseph Mensah shooting of Alvin Cole|first=Isiah|last=Holmes|work=Wisconsin Examiner|date=April 28, 2026|accessdate=July 8, 2026}}{{cite news|url=https://www.jsonline.com/story/communities/north/2026/04/28/attorneys-say-theyre-close-to-confidential-settlement-in-mensah-case/89820578007/?gnt-cfr=1&gca-cat=p&gca-uir=false&gca-epti=z119969p115850l116050c115850u004869e1101xxv119969&gca-ft=291&gca-ds=sophi|title=Joseph Mensah civil case nears settlement with no third trial|first=Bridget|last=Fogarty|work=Milwaukee Journal Sentinel|date=April 28, 2026|accessdate=July 8, 2026}} ===Criticism of the Supreme Court under John Roberts=== In February 2020, Adelman wrote an article criticizing the recent record of the [[Supreme Court of the United States]] under Chief Justice [[John Roberts]] The article singled out Chief Justice Roberts and accused him of actively participating in "undermining American democracy," through activist decisions on [[Suffrage|voting rights]] and [[campaign finance]] by corporate interests. Adelman wrote, "Instead of doing what it can to ensure the maintenance of a robust democratic republic, the Court's decisions ally it with the most anti-democratic currents in American politics, forces that would be pleased if unlimited money could be spent on elections and if minorities could be deterred from voting."{{Cite web|url=https://journals.law.harvard.edu/lpr/wp-content/uploads/sites/89/2020/03/Adelman.pdf|title=The Roberts Court's Assault on Democracy|website=Harvard Law & Policy Review|date=February 2020|access-date=November 28, 2021}} The article specifically cited a number of partisan 5–4 decisions, such as ''[[Shelby County v. Holder]]'', (which struck down part of the [[Voting Rights Act of 1965]]), ''[[Rucho v. Common Cause]]'', (which decided that federal courts could not rule on cases of [[gerrymandering]]), ''[[Citizens United v. FEC]]'', (which allowed unlimited corporate spending on elections), and ''[[Janus v. AFSCME]]'' (which held that it was unconstitutional for public employee [[Trade union|unions]] to require [[collective bargaining]] fees). The article created waves in legal circles because of the unusually blunt criticism of the Court coming from a sitting federal judge.{{cite news|url= https://www.washingtonpost.com/nation/2020/03/11/lynn-adelman-roberts-trump/ |title= 'Assault on Democracy': A sitting federal judge takes on John Roberts, Trump and Republicans |last= Barbash |first= articles where Adelman had also directly criticized conservatives while serving as a federal judge.{{cite news|url= Evans]] assumed [[senior status]].Adam Korbitz, [http://www.wisbar.org/AM/Template.cfm?Section=News&Template=/CM/ContentDisplay.cfm&ContentID=89976 Kohl, Feingold forward four names to President Obama for Seventh Circuit], ''State Bar of Wisconsin'' (January 25, 2010). {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100214114354/http://www.wisbar.org/AM/Template.cfm?Section=News |date=February 14, 2010}} Adelman was recommended along with [[Victoria F. Nourse]], Richard Sankovitz and Dean Strang, but was not selected for the spot. ==Personal life and family== Lynn Adelman is the eldest of three sons born to Albert Adelman and his wife Edith (''{{nee}}'' Margoles) Adelman. {{Short description|American judge (born 1941)}} {{for|the Canadian artist and academic|Lynn Hughes (artist)}} {{Infobox officeholder | honorific_prefix = | name = Lynn Nettleton Hughes | honorific_suffix = | image = Lynn Nettleton Hughes.jpg | alt = | caption = | office = [[Senior Status|Senior Judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas]] | term_start = February 12, 2023 | term_end = | office1 = Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas]] | term_start1 = December 17, 1985 | term_end1 = February 12, 2023 | appointer1 = [[List of federal judges appointed by Ronald Reagan|Ronald Reagan]] | predecessor1 = [[Robert J. O'Conor Jr.]] | successor1 = [[Nicholas Ganjei]] | birth_name = Lynn Nettleton Hughes | birth_date = {{birth year and age|1941}} | birth_place = [[Houston]], Texas, U.S. | death_date = | death_place = | education = [[University of Alabama]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|BA]])
[[University of Texas School of Law|University of Texas]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]])
[[University of Virginia School of Law|University of Virginia]] ([[Master of Laws|LLM]]) | alma_mater = }} '''Lynn Nettleton Hughes''' (born 1941) is an inactive [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas]]. He gained attention for being removed from a number of cases for showing bias and failing to follow federal rules.{{cite web |last1=Weiss |first1=Debra Cassens |title=5th Circuit Keeps Count: It has kicked federal judge off 6 cases, thrice reversed his discovery refusals |url=https://www.abajournal.com/web/article/5th-circuit-keeps-count-it-has-kicked-federal-judge-off-six-cases-thrice-reversed-his-discovery-refusals |website=ABAJournal |publisher=ABA |access-date= July 27, 2022}} Hughes has been involuntarily removed from so many cases that the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit|Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]] has describe removing him as "[[déjà vu]] all over again."{{Cite web|url=https://www.law360.com/articles/1497445|title=5th Circ. Rebuke Of Judge Hughes Is 'Déjà Vu All Over Again'|website=Law360.com}} ==Education and career== Hughes was born in [[Houston]]. He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from the [[University of Alabama]] in 1963 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Texas School of Law]] in 1966. He was in private practice in Houston from 1966 to 1979. He was President of Southwest Resources in Houston from 1969 to 1970. He was a judge on the 165th Judicial District, State of Texas from 1979 to 1980. He was a judge on the 189th Judicial District, State of Texas from 1981 to 1985. He was an adjunct professor at the [[South Texas College of Law]] from 1973 to 2003. He was an adjunct professor at the University of Texas School of Law from 1990 to 1991. He received a [[Master of Laws]] from the [[University of Virginia School of Law]] in 1992.{{FJC Bio|nid=1382501|inline=yes}} Since approximately 2008, Hughes has been a lecturer focusing on ethical issues for the 35,000-member [[American Association of Petroleum Geologists]].{{cite web |url=http://hosted.ap.org/dynamic/stories/U/US_GULF_OIL_SPILL_JUDGE_CONFLICTS?SITE=MALOW&SECTION=HOME&TEMPLATE=DEFAULT |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210613203852/http://hosted.ap.org/dynamic/stories/U/US_GULF_OIL_SPILL_JUDGE_CONFLICTS?SITE=MALOW&SECTION=HOME&TEMPLATE=DEFAULT |url-status=dead |archive-date=June 13, 2021 |title=Lowell Sun June 6, 2010 Many Gulf federal judges have oil links |work=[[Lowell Sun]] |access-date=6 June 2010}} === Federal judicial service === Hughes was nominated by President [[Ronald Reagan]] on October 16, 1985, to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas]] vacated by Judge [[Robert J. O'Conor Jr.]] He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on December 16, 1985, and received his commission on December 17, 1985. He assumed inactive [[senior status]] on February 12, 2023.{{cite web|url=https://www.txs.uscourts.gov/page/history-district-judges|title=History of District Judges|work=United States District & Bankruptcy Court, Southern District of Texas}} == Rulings and appeals == ===Sex discrimination ruling and reversal on appeal=== In the case of ''Equal Employment Opportunity Commission v. Houston Funding II, Ltd. et al.'', Case Number H-11-2442 (S.D. Tex. Feb. 2, 2012), Donnicia Venters, a mother represented by the [[Equal Employment Opportunity Commission|EEOC]], claimed that she was fired from Houston Funding due to her request to be allowed to pump [[breastfeeding|breastmilk]] upon her return to work after giving birth. Houston Funding claimed that it had fired Venters for abandoning her job for over two months after giving birth. Venters sued Houston Funding, alleging that the company had [[sex discrimination|discriminated against her based on her sex]].{{cite web|last=Plushnick-Masti |first=Ramit |url=https://www.seattletimes.com/#.TzWBce4ozM8.facebook |title=Judge: Firing for lactation not sex discrimination |publisher=The Seattle Times |date=February 9, 2012 |url-access=limited |access-date=March 10, 2012}} Citing several previous District Court opinions which had already ruled on the issue, Judge Hughes explained that breastfeeding is not covered by Title VII of the Civil Rights Act. In the ruling, Hughes writes, "Even if the company's claim that she was fired for abandonment is meant to hide the real reason – she wanted to pump breast milk – lactation is not pregnancy, childbirth or a related medical condition. She gave birth on Dec. 11, 2009. After that day, she was no longer pregnant and her pregnancy-related conditions ended. Firing someone because of lactation or breast-pumping is not sex discrimination."{{cite web|url=https://www.scribd.com/doc/81200704/EEOC-v-Houston-Funding-II-LTD-Case-No-H-11-2442-S-D-Tex-Feb-2-2011 |title=EEOC v Houston Funding II, LTD, Case No. H-11-2442 (S.D. Tex. Feb. 2, 2011) |publisher=Scribd.com |access-date=March 10, 2012}}{{cite news|last=Winter|first=Jessica|title=Subject for Debate: Are Women People?|url=https://ideas.time.com/2012/03/07/subject-for-debate-are-women-people/?iid=op-article-mostpop1|magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]] |date=March 7, 2012}} Hughes was overruled by the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals which held that Venters had established a ''[[prima facie]]'' case of sex discrimination under [[Civil Rights Act of 1964#Title VII – equal employment opportunity|Title VII]].{{cite web |url=http://www.ca5.uscourts.gov/opinions%5Cpub%5C12/12-20220-CV0.wpd.pdf |title=Equal Employment Opportunity Commission v. Houston Funding II, Ltd., No. 12-20220 |website=ca5.uscourts.gov}} Critically, the Fifth Circuit found Hughes to be so biased that it took the unusual step of reassigning the case to a district court judge on remand.{{citation needed|date=October 2022}} ===Sexism controversy=== Upon dismissing the indictment in a case titled ''United States v. Swenson'', Judge Hughes sharply criticized a female prosecutor on the case, saying "It was a lot simpler when you guys wore dark suits white shirts and navy ties . . . we didn’t let girls do it in the old days." The Fifth Circuit reversed, and stated that Judge Hughes' comments were "demeaning, inappropriate and beneath the dignity of a federal judge."{{cite web|last=Council |first=John |url=https://www.law.com/texaslawyer/2018/07/05/fifth-circuit-criticizes-houston-federal-judge-for-alleged-sexist-remarks/ |title=Fifth Circuit Criticizes Houston Federal Judge for Alleged Sexist Remarks |publisher=Texas Lawyer |date=July 5, 2018|access-date=July 6, 2018}} The Fifth Circuit reassigned the case to another judge, finding Hughes to be too biased. ===Reversed in an employment discrimination case=== The [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]] reversed the judge in an employment discrimination case and took the rare step of reassigning it to another judge and said this:
From the outset of these suits, the district judge’s actions evinced a prejudgment of Miller’s claims. At the beginning of the Initial Case Management Conference, the judge dismissed sua sponte Miller’s claims against TSUS and UHS, countenancing no discussion regarding the dismissal. Later in the same conference, the judge responded to the parties’ opposition to consolidating Miller’s two cases by telling Miller’s counsel, “I will get credit for closing two cases when I crush you. . . . How will that look on your record?” And things went downhill from there. The court summarily denied Miller’s subsequent motion for reconsideration, denied Miller’s repeated requests for leave to take discovery (including depositions of material witnesses), and eventually granted summary judgment in favor of SHSU and UHD, dismissing all claims. Miller now appeals the district court’s rulings and asks for her cases to be reassigned on remand. Mindful of the fundamental right to fairness in every proceeding—both in fact, and in appearance, we REVERSE, REMAND, and direct that these cases be REASSIGNED to a new district judge for further proceedings.''Miller v. Sam Hous. State Univ.'', 986 F.3d 880 (5th Cir. 2021)
The Fifth Circuit also notes that previous to the ''Miller'' case Hughes handled another case, ''McKoy'', in a similar fashion – which also resulted in the case being similarly reversed and remanded.
In support of her position, Miller refers us to McCoy v. Energy XXI GOM, LLC, 695 F. App’x 750 (5th Cir. 2017). In that case, the same district judge [, i.e. Hughes,] imposed substantially similar discovery restrictions to those imposed here. ''Id.'' at 753. Specifically, the district judge denied almost all requests for discovery and “permitted only the deposition of [the plaintiff]” and “the disclosure by the defendants of certain documents pertaining to the specific [object] at issue,” certain photographs, and a video. ''Id.'' On appeal, we reversed and remanded the case on summary judgment grounds, finding genuine issues of material fact existed, even with the limited discovery that had been permitted. ''Id.'' at 758. But we also noted that “[t]he district court abused its discretion in refusing to allow [the plaintiff] to conduct sufficient discovery . . . to support the allegations he ha[d] fairly raised[.]” ''Id.'' at 759.
===''Sua sponte'' reassignment in the ''Khan'' case=== In ''U.S. v. Khan'', the Fifth Circuit took what it self-described as the "rare" move of reassigning a criminal case on appeal, doing so despite the absence of a request from either party, given the bias displayed by Judge Hughes in the trial court proceedings.{{Cite web|title=5th Circ. Rips Texas Judge For Hostility Toward DOJ Attys - Law360|url=https://www.law360.com/articles/1382559/5th-circ-rips-texas-judge-for-hostility-toward-doj-attys|access-date=2021-06-14|website=Law360.com|language=en}} Hughes engaged in personally insulting conduct, attacking individual attorneys for the federal government, which caused the Fifth Circuit to conclude that his behavior "reveal[ed] a level of prejudice" that was unacceptable for a federal judge. Because Hughes had supervised the trial court proceedings for more than four years, the Fifth Circuit lamented that "reassignment is regrettable," but concluded that "it is nonetheless necessary for the reasons we have stated."{{Cite web|title=UNITED STATES v. KHAN (2021)|url=https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/us-5th-circuit/2126185.html|access-date=2024-09-26|website=Findlaw|language=en}} The absence of a request for reassignment meant that the Fifth Circuit's decision to reassign is called "[[sua sponte]]." In general, federal courts limit their decisions to the issues presented by the parties. ''United States v. Sineneng-Smith'', 140 S. Ct. 1575 (2020). Moreover, in general, federal appellate courts are extremely hesitant to require reassignment of a judge after an appeal, particularly if the judge has substantial experience with a case.{{Cite web|title=Legal News & Analysis on Litigation, Policy, Deals : Law360|url=https://www.law360.com/subscribe/free_trial?target_url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.law360.com%2Farticles%2F1036762%2Fattachments%2F0|access-date=2021-06-14|website=Law360.com|language=en}} === Upheld in COVID-19 vaccination requirement suit=== In ''Jennifer Bridges v. Houston Methodist Hospital'' Hughes ruled that private employers have the right to require COVID-19 vaccinations as a condition for employment, even while the vaccine was only available under an [[Emergency Use Authorization]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/20860668-houston-methodist-lawsuit-order-of-dismissal|title=DocumentCloud|website=Documentcloud.org|access-date=28 July 2022}} He dismissed the case by rejecting the arguments of the plaintiffs because Texas law only permits employees to sue for wrongful termination if they were required by their employer to engage in illegal conduct, while receiving the COVID-19 vaccine is legal. He further noted that individual plaintiffs would still be able to seek medical or religious accommodations under the [[Americans With Disabilities Act of 1990]] and [[Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964]]. He found that the vaccine has been authorized for emergency use by the FDA, and that the plaintiffs were not clinical trial participants, and were therefore not being utilized as test subjects. He rejected the notion that requirement for vaccination violated the [[Nuremberg Code]] and described the comparison of vaccination to the Holocaust was "reprehensible". This opinion was upheld by the Fifth Circuit in June 2022.{{cite web|url=https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCOURTS-ca5-21-20311/pdf/USCOURTS-ca5-21-20311-0.pdf|title=Jennifer Bridges; Bob Nevens; Maria Trevino; Ricardo Zelante; Latricia Blank; et al., Plaintiffs—Appellants, versus The Methodist Hospital, doing business as Houston Methodist; Methodist Health Centers, doing business as Houston Methodist The Woodlands Hospital, Defendants—Appellees.|website=Govinfo.gov|access-date=2022-07-28}} ==Criticism for bias== Hughes has repeatedly been chastised for failing to follow the law of the appellate court which supervises him.{{Cite web|url=https://www.law360.com/articles/1481454/attachments/0|title = Legal News & Analysis on Litigation, Policy, Deals |website=Law360.com}} In a 2022 case, the Fifth Circuit found "record support" for the "serious accusation" that Hughes "had prejudged the case...from the outset." In reversing Hughes and reassigning the case to a new judge on remand, the Fifth Circuit highlighted that it has repeatedly "reassigned this district judge's cases before," and highlighted five separate instances over as many years, in which the Fifth Circuit found that a "reasonable observer" would likely question Hughes' "impartiality," noting his overt bias and explicit sexism had forced the Court of Appeals to strip him of cases. Hughes was also reprimanded for explicitly attacking a female attorney representing the United States of America in open court. While on the record, Hughes stated that "It was a lot simpler when you guys wore dark suits, white shirts and navy ties...We didn't let girls do it in the old days."{{cite web|url=https://www.ca5.uscourts.gov/opinions/pub/21/21-20270-CR0.pdf|title=United States of America, Plaintiff—Appellee/Cross-Appellant, versus Brenda Rodriguez, Defendant—Appellant/Cross-Appellee|website=Ca5.uscourts.gov|access-date=2022-07-28}} In a rebuke on appeal, the Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit reversed Hughes - who had dismissed the prosecution as a punitive sanction - and reprimanded Hughes that his "comments are demeaning, inappropriate, and beneath the dignity of a federal judge.” {{cite web|url=https://images.law.com/contrib/content/uploads/documents/401/9248/Swenson.pdf|title=UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, Plaintiff - Appellant v. SIMONE SWENSON, Defendant - Appellee|website=Images.law.com|access-date=2022-07-28}} After the decision, Hughes subsequently banned the same female attorney from ever appearing before him again as a punishment for raising his misconduct to the attention of the court of appeals. The Fifth Circuit again intervened, vacating his order and finding that he had "abused his discretion." Judge [[James Ho]] concurred in the vacatur, noting that "it’s hard to imagine a less persuasive way for a judge to rebut the charge that he discriminated against a female attorney than by expelling her from his courtroom—not just in one case, but in every case that she may bring for the rest of her career." ==See also== * [[List of United States federal judges by longevity of service]] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== * {{FJC Bio|nid=1382501}} * [https://www.txs.uscourts.gov/content/lynn-n-hughes-united-states-district-judge Official Page] {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Robert J. He also has been a [[United States Democratic Party|Democratic]] [[United States|American]] [[politician]], and a former member of the [[Missouri House of Representatives]] from southwest [[Missouri]]'s 134th district. He served five terms from January 5, 1983, to January 6, 1993. ==Biography== Harpool was born in 1956 in [[Springfield, Missouri]]. He received a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree, ''cum laude'', in 1977 from [[Southwest Missouri State University]]. He received a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1980 from the [[University of Missouri Columbia School of Law]]. From 1983 to 1993, he served as a member of the [[Missouri House of Representatives]]. From 1980 to 2001, he served at Daniel, Clampett, Lilly, Dalton, Powell & Cunningham. From 2002 to 2003, he served at Cunningham, Harpool & Cardonnier LLC. From 2004 to 2006, he served at Lathrop & Gage LLP. He ran unsuccessfully for the [[Missouri Senate]] from the 30th district in 2006. From 2006 to 2014, he was a shareholder at Baird, Lightner, Millsap & Harpool, PC, in Springfield, where he handled a broad array of [[civil litigation]].{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2013/08/01/president-obama-nominates-six-serve-united-states-district-courts |title=President Obama Nominates Six to Serve on the United States District Courts |date=2013-08-01 |via=[[NARA|National Archives]] |work=[[whitehouse.gov]] |access-date=2017-02-26}} Harpool was the plaintiff's lawyer of a high-profile court case involving the Republic School District.{{cite web|url=https://abcnews.com/US/special-student-sues-missouri-school-district-rapes/story?id=14325659 |title=Special Needs Student Sues Missouri School District Over Rapes |website=Abcnews.go.com |date=2011-08-17 |access-date=2017-02-26}}{{cite web|url=http://www.news-leader.com/article/20110817/NEWS12/108170372/Suit-filed-against-Republic-School-District |title=Suit filed against Republic School District | Springfield News-Leader | news-leader.com |access-date=2014-03-26 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140328000050/http://www.news-leader.com/article/20110817/NEWS12/108170372/Suit-filed-against-Republic-School-District |archive-date=2014-03-28 }}{{FJC Bio|nid=1394416|inline=yes}} ===Personal=== He married the former Cindy McCord in 1978 and they have six children.{{citation needed|date=March 2014}} ==State senate redistricting== Harpool was the chair of the Missouri Senate redistricting committee. On August 18, 2011 the map submitted by the committee was turned down by the Republican members of the committee. While on the committee he focused on population growth and census data to redraw the district boundaries. Senator [[John Lamping]] and many in opposition voiced their concerns over the proposed map because it would eliminate his district altogether. Citing population trends and census data, Harpool argued that [[Saint Louis County, Missouri|Saint Louis County]] must lose the seat in order for fair representation to the faster-growing areas like [[Greene County, Missouri|Greene]], [[Stone County, Missouri|Stone]], and [[Barry County, Missouri|Barry]] counties in southwestern Missouri.{{cite web|url=http://news.stlpublicradio.org/post/commission-mo-senate-redistricting-facing-deadline-next-week |title=Commission on Mo. Senate redistricting facing deadline next week | St. Louis Public Radio |website=News.stlpublicradio.org |date=2011-05-25 |access-date=2017-02-26}}{{cite web|url=http://www.semissourian.com/story/1753781.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120910164938/http://www.semissourian.com/story/1753781.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=2012-09-10 |title=State News: Senate committee for redistricting finally throws in the towel (8/17/11) | Southeast Missourian newspaper, Cape Girardeau, MO |website=Semissourian.com |date=2011-08-17 |access-date=2017-02-26 }} ==Federal judicial service== On August 1, 2013, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Harpool to serve as a United States District Judge of the United States District Court for the Western District of Missouri, to the seat vacated by Judge [[Richard Everett Dorr]], who died on April 24, 2013. His nomination passed through the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2013/08/01/presidential-nominations-sent-senate-1 |title=Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate |date=2013-08-01 |via=[[NARA|National Archives]] |work=[[whitehouse.gov]] |access-date=2017-02-26}}{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/01/06/presidential-nominations-sent-senate-0 |title=Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate |date=2014-01-06 |via=[[NARA|National Archives]] |work=[[whitehouse.gov]] |access-date=2017-02-26}} On Thursday March 13, 2014 [[Harry Reid|Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid]] filed a motion to invoke [[cloture]] on the nomination. On March 26, 2014, cloture was invoked by a 56–43 vote.{{cite web|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture on the Nomination of M. Douglas Harpool, of Missouri, to be U.S. District Judge)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=113&session=2&vote=00081|publisher=United States Senate|access-date=26 March 2014}} He was later confirmed that same day by a 93–5 vote.{{cite web|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation M. Douglas Harpool, of Missouri, to be U.S. District Judge)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=113&session=2&vote=00085|publisher=United States Senate|access-date=26 March 2014}} He received his judicial commission on March 28, 2014. Garibaldi of the [[Supreme Court of New Jersey|New Jersey Supreme Court]], from 1989 to 1990. From 1998 to 2000, she was a partner at the law firm of Tompkins, McGuire, Wachenfeld & Barry, LLP, where her practice focused on civil litigation in Federal and State courts.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/06/26/president-obama-nominates-four-serve-united-states-district-courts|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Obama Nominates Four to Serve on the United States District Courts|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=26 June 2014}} ===Federal judicial service=== From 2000 to 2014, she served as a [[United States magistrate judge]] in the District of New Jersey.{{FJC Bio|nid=1394671|inline=yes}} On June 26, 2014, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Arleo to serve as a United States district judge of the United States District Court for the District of New Jersey, to the seat vacated by Judge [[Dennis M. He received his [[Juris Doctor]] in 1979 from the [[Pace University School of Law]]. He began his career as an associate at the [[law firm]] of Bartels, Pykett & Aronwald (now Aronwald & Pykett). From 1980 to 1986, he served as an assistant district attorney in the Nassau County District Attorney's Office. He spent most of the period from 1986 to 2001 serving as an [[assistant United States attorney]] in the Middle District of Pennsylvania, except from 1993 to 1997, during which he was a partner at the law firm of Hourigan, Kluger, Spohrer & Quinn PC. He earned a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in 1978 from [[Valdosta State University]] and a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1981 from the [[Walter F. George School of Law]] at [[Mercer University]].[https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/president-obama-nominates-four-serve-united-states-district-court-bench President Obama Nominates Four to Serve on the United States District Court Bench] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170216173115/https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/president-obama-nominates-four-serve-united-states-district-court-bench |date=2017-02-16 }}, ''[[whitehouse.gov]]'' (February 4, 2010).{{FJC Bio|nid=1393261|inline=yes}} == Career == From 1981 to 1985, Treadwell served as an [[Associate lawyer|associate]] for the [[Atlanta]] law firm of Kilpatrick & Cody (now [[Kilpatrick Stockton]]). He then served as an associate for the [[Macon, Georgia]] law firm Chambless, Higdon & Carson LLP from 1985 until 1987 and then as a partner with that firm from 1987 until 2000. From 2000 until 2010, Treadwell was a partner in the [[Macon, Georgia]] firm Adams, Jordan & Treadwell, where he specialized in [[personal injury]] and [[wrongful death]].Amy Leigh Womack, [http://www.macon.com/2010/02/05/1011439/treadwell-nominated-for-federal.html Macon attorney Treadwell nominated for federal judgeship]{{dead link|date=June 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}, ''[[The Telegraph (Macon)|Macon Telegraph]]'' (February 5, 2010). He also has been an adjunct professor at his alma mater, the Walter F. George School of Law at Mercer University, since 1998. === Federal judicial service === On February 4, 2010, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Treadwell to serve on the [[United States District Court for the Middle District of Georgia]], to fill the vacancy created by Judge [[Hugh Lawson (judge)|Hugh Lawson]], who assumed [[senior status]] at the end of 2008.[https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/presidential-nomination-sent-senate-2-4-10 Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate 2/4/10] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170216173116/https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/presidential-nomination-sent-senate-2-4-10 |date=2017-02-16 }}, ''[[whitehouse.gov]]'' (February 4, 2010). On March 18, 2010, the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]] reported Treadwell's nomination out of committee by a [[voice vote]].{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/ExecutiveBusinessMeetingResults-03-18-2010.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting - March 18, 2010|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=April 24, 2023}} The [[United States Senate]] confirmed Treadwell on June 21, 2010 by an 89–0 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1112/vote_111_2_00196.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Marc T. Treadwell, of Georgia, to be United States District Judge for the Middle District of Georgia)|publisher=[[United States Senate]]|access-date=November 1, 2022}} He received his commission on June 22, 2010. He served as Chief Judge from July 1, 2020{{cite web|url=https://www.gamd.uscourts.gov/sites/gamd/files/Press_Release_Chief_Judge_Middle_District.pdf|title=NEWS RELEASE|publisher=United States District Court Middle District of Georgia|work=Office of the Clerk|date=July 1, 2020|access-date=July 7, 2020}} to May 31, 2024.{{Cite news|date=May 31, 2024|last=Grant|first=Ty|title=Chief Judge named for Middle District of Ga.|url=https://www.walb.com/2024/05/31/chief-judge-district-court-named-middle-district-ga/?outputType=amp|website=walb.com|access-date=June 8, 2024}} ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1393261}} *{{Ballotpedia|Marc_Thomas_Treadwell}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Hugh Lawson (judge)|Hugh Lawson]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Middle District of Georgia]]}}|years=2010–present}} {{s-inc}} {{s-bef|before=[[Clay D. She graduated from the [[University of Texas at Austin]] with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in 1973 and from [[University of Houston Law Center]]{{cite web|url=https://www.mcdonaldworley.com/blog/involved-in-serious-auto-accident-what-to-remember-to-do/ |title=Houston Laws|date=7 March 2017 }} with a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1978. ==Career== Crone started her legal career in private practice in [[Houston]], Texas from 1978 to 1992. Bush]] nominated Crone on May 1, 2003, to a new seat created by 116 Stat. 1758. She was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on September 30, 2003, and received her commission on October 3, 2003. ==Notable case== On October 4, 2016, Crone entered a [[nationwide injunction]] blocking President [[Barack Obama]]’s Fair Pay and Safe Workplaces rule, known to its opponents as the [[blacklisting]] rule.{{cite news|last1=Trottman|first1=Melanie|title=Construction Trade Group Wins Injunction Blocking U.S. Federal Workplace Rule|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/construction-trade-group-wins-injunction-blocking-u-s-federal-workplace-rule-1477407170|accessdate=26 October 2016|work=[[The Wall Street Journal]]|date=25 October 2016}} Judge Crone found the [[Due Process Clause]] and [[Free Speech Clause]] of the [[United States Constitution]] forbid the President from requiring federal contractors to disclose mere [[allegation]]s that the contractor had violated labor laws. ==References== {{Reflist}} ==Sources== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1392021}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=Seat established by 116 Stat. 1758}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Texas]]}}|years=2003–present}} {{s-inc}} {{s-end}} {{United States 5th Circuit district judges}} {{authority control}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Crone, Marcia Ann Cain}} [[Category:1952 births]] [[Category:Living people]] [[Category:University of Texas at Austin alumni]] [[Category:University of Houston Law Center alumni]] [[Category:United States magistrate judges]] [[Category:Judges of the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Texas]] [[Category:United States district court judges appointed by George W. [[University of Colorado Law School]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | footnotes = }} '''Marcia Smith Krieger''' (born March 3, 1954)[https://books.google.com/books?id=hQU8AQAAIAAJ&q=Marcia+S.+Krieger+judge+1954 The Martindale-Hubbell Law Directory, page 369] is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Colorado]]. ==Early life and education== Born in [[Denver, Colorado]], Krieger graduated from [[Lewis and Clark College]] with her [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in 1975 and later from [[University of Colorado Law School]] with a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1979. ==Career== Following law school graduation, Krieger worked in private practice in Colorado from 1979 to 1994. In 1994 she became a United States Bankruptcy Judge for the District of Colorado where she worked until her nomination to the federal bench in 2002. Krieger was also an Adjunct lecturer for the [[University of Colorado at Boulder]] from 1999 to 2001. ===Federal judicial career=== Krieger was nominated to the United States District Court for the District of Colorado by President George W. Bush on September 10, 2001, to a seat vacated by Judge [[Daniel B. Sparr]], who assumed [[senior status]]. Krieger was confirmed by the [[United States Senate|Senate]] on January 25, 2002, and received her commission on January 30, 2002. She served as the chief judge from January 1, 2013, to March 3, 2019. She assumed [[senior status]] on March 3, 2019.{{FJC Bio|nid=1391406|inline=yes}} ===Notable cases=== In 2003, Krieger sentenced [[Scott Lee Kimball]] to [[time served]] and three years' [[supervised release]] for passing bad checks in Alaska, as well as full restitution and a $5,000 fine, per a plea agreement between him and the government that took into account Kimball's service up to that point as an FBI informant. Unbeknownst to her, the FBI or anyone else involved in his case, Kimball had already committed three of the four [[serial murder]]s he would later plead guilty to; he is currently serving a 70-year sentence. At the sentencing, Krieger expressed some reservations about Kimball's reticence about his own financial situation in the face of his willingness to inform on others, but since she could not find any legal precedent for refusing the downward departure from the [[Federal Sentencing Guidelines]] the prosecution asked for in exchange for his demonstrated cooperation, she granted it.{{cite web|title=Criminal Action 03-CR-23, ''United States v. Kimball'', Reporter's Transcript: Sentencing Hearing (Order)|url=http://scottleekimball.com/wp-content/uploads/2003/12/sentencing.pdf|publisher=[[United States District Court for the District of Colorado]]|date=December 2, 2003|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160618223149/http://scottleekimball.com/wp-content/uploads/2003/12/sentencing.pdf|archive-date=June 18, 2016|access-date=August 7, 2021}} In 2010, Krieger denied a new trial for former [[Qwest]] Chief Executive Officer [[Joseph Nacchio]]'s 2007 conviction of [[insider trading]] charges. Nacchio's legal team claimed that testimony former Qwest [[Chief Financial Officer]] Robin Szeliga gave in a [[Lawsuit|civil lawsuit]] related to the case differed from testimony given in the [[Criminal procedure|criminal trial]]. Krieger disallowed the request on the basis that the testimony in the civil trial was not substantially different from the criminal trial and that minor differences were unlikely to result in an acquittal.{{cite news |title=Judge Denies New Trial for Ex-Qwest CEO Nacchio |date=January 12, 2010 |work=ABC News |url=https://abcnews.go.com/Business/wireStory?id=9545686}}{{dead link|date=November 2026|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}} In 2018, Krieger declined a request to return an imprisoned transgender woman, Lindsay Saunders-Velez, to her cell after her lawyers argued that the "punishment pod" she had been assigned to after a minor infraction housed several male inmates who had tormented her previously. Krieger said that the attorneys had not proved a risk of “imminent and irreparable injury”. Hours after the judge issued her ruling, Saunders-Velez was allegedly raped. She was taken to a hospital with rectal and other injuries. A nurse there noted that the alleged rapist might be HIV positive.[https://web.archive.org/web/20180503162217/http://time.com/5264056/transgender-inmate-raped-lawsuit-colorado/ "Time" A Transgender Inmate Says She Was Raped in a 'Discriminatory and Dangerous' Colorado Men's Prison, May 3, 2018] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1391406}} *[http://www.cod.uscourts.gov/JudicialOfficers/ActiveArticleIIIJudges/HonMarciaSKrieger.aspx Marcia S. [[University of Washington School of Law|University of Washington]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | footnotes = }} '''Marco Antonio Hernandez''' (born 1957) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Oregon]]. ==Early life and education== Hernandez was born in [[Nogales, Arizona]], in 1957 and is of Hispanic descent.{{cite web|url=https://www.justice.gov/archive/olp/ma-hernandez-resume.htm|title=Marco A. Hernandez|work=Office of Legal Policy|publisher=United States Department of Justice|access-date=20 July 2010}} He moved to [[Oregon]] at 17 and began work as a dishwasher, and then as a janitor before working his way through community college while working as a teacher's aide. Hernandez then moved on to a four-year school and received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from Western Oregon State College (now known as [[Western Oregon University]]) in 1983.[https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/president-obama-names-five-united-states-district-court-0 President Obama Names Five to United States District Court] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170216171747/https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/president-obama-names-five-united-states-district-court-0 |date=2017-02-16 }}, ''[[whitehouse.gov]]'' (July 14, 2010). He then attended the [[University of Washington School of Law]] and earned his [[Juris Doctor]] in 1986.{{FJC Bio|nid=1393596|inline=yes}} ==Career== After law school he returned to Oregon where he spent three years working for [[Legal Aid]] Services of Oregon where he often represented farm workers.{{cite news|url=http://www.oregonlive.com/news/index.ssf/2010/07/obama_nominates_two_men_as_jud.html|title=Obama nominates two for U.S. District Court judgeships in Oregon|last=Tomlinson|first=Stuart|date=July 14, 2010|work=[[The Oregonian]]|access-date=19 July 2010}} Following his time with [[legal aid]], Hernandez then joined the [[Washington County, Oregon|Washington County]] [[District Attorney]]'s office as a deputy prosecutor in 1989.{{cite news|url=http://blog.oregonlive.com/hillsboroargus/2010/07/county_judge_nominated_to_fede.html|title=County judge nominated to federal bench – again|last=Christensen|first=Nick|date=July 17, 2010|work=[[The Hillsboro Argus]]|access-date=19 July 2010}} Shortly before leaving office in January 1995, [[List of governors of Oregon|Governor]] [[Barbara Roberts]] appointed Hernandez to be [[Washington County, Oregon|Washington County]] [[Oregon Circuit Court|Circuit Court]] Judge.Peter Wong, [http://www.statesmanjournal.com/article/20100714/UPDATE/100714059 Obama names two as federal judges in Oregon]{{dead link|date=June 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}, ''[[Statesman Journal]]'' (July 14, 2010). In 2001, he allowed a claim for [[loss of companionship]] in a pet case to go to trial, the first time such a claim was allowed to go to trial in the United States.{{cite journal|last=Duckler|first=Geordie L.|author2=Dana M. Campbell|date=June 2001|title=Nature of the Beast|journal=Oregon State Bar Bulletin|publisher=[[Oregon State Bar]]|url=http://www.osbar.org/publications/bulletin/01june/beast.htm}} Hernandez served as [[Presiding Judge]] of the County's Circuit Court from 2002 to 2005. He won re-election to a new six-year term on the court in May 2008. He has also served as the judge for the county's Mental Health Court,{{cite news|url=http://blog.oregonlive.com/breakingnews/2008/03/court_of_hope.html|title=Washington County Mental Health Court gives some a chance to turn their lives around|last=Gregory|first=Roger|date=March 28, 2008|work=[[The Oregonian]]|access-date=20 July 2010}} and as presiding judge from 2002 until 2005. ==Federal judicial nominations== In January 2008, Hernandez was one of three candidates recommended by a six-member judicial selection committee to replace [[Garr King]] on the [[United States District Court for the District of Oregon]].James Pitkin, {{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20130209145913/http://blogs.wweek.com/news/2008/01/25/immerguts-out-the-final-three-who-are-in-for-a-federal-judge-appointment/|title=Immergut’s Out: The Final Three Who Are In For A Federal Judge Appointment}}, ''[[Willamette Week]]'' (January 25, 2008). President [[George W. Bush]] selected Hernandez to fill the vacancy on the District Court of Oregon and submitted his nomination on July 23, 2008.Holly Danks, [http://www.oregonlive.com/politics/oregonian/index.ssf?/base/news/1216866396224170.xml&coll=7 Politics could sink local judge's federal nomination], ''[[The Oregonian]]'' (July 24, 2008). [[List of United States senators from Oregon|Senators]] [[Gordon H. Smith]] and [[Ron Wyden]] supported the nomination, but it was made with less than six months remaining in the [[Presidency of George W. Bush|Bush presidency]].James Pitkin, {{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20130210064834/http://blogs.wweek.com/news/2009/07/28/ron-wyden-adds-marco-hernandez-as-the-sixth-name-to-judges-list/|title=Ron Wyden Adds Marco Hernandez As The Sixth Name to Judges’ List}}, ''[[Willamette Week]]'' (July 28, 2009). The nomination was not acted upon by the [[110th Congress]] and was thus returned.{{cite web|url=http://judges.law.yale.edu/?q=content/marco-hernandez|title=Marco A. '''Margaret Merrell Miller Garnett'''<ref name = Questionnaire/> (born 1971) is an American lawyer from New York who is serving as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]].

== Education ==
Born in [[West Point, New York]], in 1971,<ref name="Questionnaire">{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/garnett_sjq.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=July 26, 2023|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20230726215431/https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/garnett_sjq.pdf|archive-date = July 26, 2023}}</ref> Garnett received a Bachelor of Arts in English and Government from the [[University of Notre Dame]] in 1992, a Master of Arts in 1995 and a [[Master of Philosophy]] in Political Science in 1997, both from [[Yale University]] and a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Columbia Law School]] in 2000.<ref name="WHBio">{{Cite press release |title=President Biden Names Thirty-Fifth Round of Judicial Nominees and One New Nominee to Serve as U.S. Attorney|date=June 28, 2023 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2023/06/28/president-biden-names-thirty-fifth-round-of-judicial-nominees-and-one-new-nominee-to-serve-as-u-s-attorney/ |access-date=June 28, 2023}} {{PD-notice}}</ref>

== Career ==

After graduating from law school, Garnett started her career as an [[Associate lawyer|associate]] at [[Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz]] in New York City from 2000 to 2004.

She served as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Gerard E. Lynch]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]].

From 2005 to 2017, Garnett was an [[Assistant United States Attorney]] in the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York, which included service as a Chief of the [[Violent Crime]]s/Violent and [[Organized Crime]] Unit from 2011 to 2014 and as a Chief of Appeals from 2016 to 2017.

During 2017–2018, she served as Executive Deputy Attorney General for Criminal Justice in the New York State Attorney General's Office.

From 2018 to 2021, she was commissioner of the [[New York City Department of Investigation]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=October 13, 2021 |title=New York City's Top Corruption Watchdog Leaving for Federal Role (Published 2021) |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/10/13/nyregion/margaret-garnett-investigation-department.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250810151819/https://www.nytimes.com/2021/10/13/nyregion/margaret-garnett-investigation-department.html |archive-date=August 10, 2025 |access-date=January 27, 2026 |work=The New York Times |language=en |url-status=live }}</ref>

From 2021 to May 2023, she was the deputy United States attorney for the Southern District of New York.<ref name="WHBio" /> From May 2023 to 2024, she served as [[Special Counsel]] to the United States attorney in that same district.<ref name="WHBio" /><ref>{{Cite press release |title=U.S. Attorney Damian Williams Announces The Selection Of Deputy U.S. Attorney And Special Counsel |date=May 18, 2023 |publisher=United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York |url=https://www.justice.gov/usao-sdny/pr/us-attorney-damian-williams-announces-selection-deputy-us-attorney-and-special-counsel |access-date=June 28, 2023 |archive-date=July 1, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230701140649/https://www.justice.gov/usao-sdny/pr/us-attorney-damian-williams-announces-selection-deputy-us-attorney-and-special-counsel |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="NYLJ">{{Cite web |last=Wester |first=Jane |date=May 18, 2023 |title=SDNY Deputy US Attorney Moves to Special Counsel Role While Biden Considers Her for Judgeship |url=https://www.law.com/newyorklawjournal/2023/05/18/sdny-deputy-us-attorney-moves-to-special-counsel-role-while-biden-considers-her-for-judgeship/ |access-date=June 28, 2023 |website=New York Law Journal |language=en |archive-date=July 23, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230723051621/https://www.law.com/newyorklawjournal/2023/05/18/sdny-deputy-us-attorney-moves-to-special-counsel-role-while-biden-considers-her-for-judgeship/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Federal judicial service ===

Garnett was recommended to the [[Presidency of Joe Biden|White House]] by Senator [[Chuck Schumer]].<ref name="NYLJ" /> On June 28, 2023, President [[Joe Biden]] announced his intent to nominate Garnett to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]].<ref name="WHBio" /> On July 11, 2023, her nomination was sent to the Senate. President Biden nominated Garnett to the seat vacated by Judge [[Vincent L. Briccetti]], who assumed [[senior status]] on April 21, 2023.<ref>{{Cite press release |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |date=July 11, 2023 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2023/07/11/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-113/ |access-date=February 1, 2025 |archive-date=January 21, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250121201237/https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2023/07/11/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-113/ |url-status=live }}</ref>  On July 26, 2023, a hearing on her nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Nominations|date=July 25, 2023|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/committee-activity/hearings/07/26/2023/nominations}}</ref> On September 14, 2023, her nomination was reported out of committee by a 12–9 vote.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/2023-09-14_-_ebm_-_results.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – September 14, 2023|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=September 14, 2023}}</ref> On November 28, 2023, the [[United States Senate]] invoked [[cloture]] on her nomination by a 49–46 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00316.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Margaret M. Garnett to be U.S. District Judge for the Southern District of New York)|website=United States Senate|date=November 28, 2023|access-date=November 28, 2023|archive-date=November 29, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231129114024/https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00316.htm|url-status=live}}</ref> Her nomination was confirmed later that day by a 49–46 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00317.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Margaret M. Garnett, of New York, to be U.S. District Judge for the Southern District of New York)|website=United States Senate|date=November 28, 2023|access-date=November 28, 2023|archive-date=November 29, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231129114024/https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00317.htm|url-status=live}}</ref> She received her judicial commission on January 9, 2024.<ref>{{FJC Bio|nid=13761361|inline=yes}}</ref>

=== Notable rulings ===
On January 30, 2026, Judge Garnett ruled that federal prosecutors cannot seek the death penalty and dismissed the [[Federal death penalty|death-eligible]] counts from [[Luigi Mangione|Luigi Mangione's indictment]].<ref>{{Cite news|title=Federal Judge Drops Death Penalty Charge Against Luigi Mangione|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/01/30/nyregion/death-penalty-luigi-mangione.html|work=The New York Times|date=January 30, 2026|access-date=January 30, 2026|issn=0362-4331|language=en-US|first1=Benjamin|last1=Weiser|first2=Hurubie|last2=Meko}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Garnett lives in [[Brooklyn]]. She and her husband, Seth, a [[script supervisor]], have two children. She is the granddaughter of two generals, and her father served as an Army officer.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Margaret Garnett '00: The Gift of Doing What's Right |url=https://www.law.columbia.edu/news/archive/margaret-garnett-00-gift-doing-whats-right |access-date=June 28, 2023 |website=law.columbia.edu |language=en |archive-date=July 1, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230701140649/https://www.law.columbia.edu/news/archive/margaret-garnett-00-gift-doing-whats-right |url-status=live }}</ref>

Guzman.jpg | alt = | caption = | office = Judge of the [[United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts]] | term_start = March 3, 2023 | term_end = | appointer = [[List of federal judges appointed by Joe Biden|Joe Biden]] | predecessor = [[Timothy S.
