[[Boston University School of Law|Boston University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Margaret Rose Guzman''' (born 1960){{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Guzman%20SJQ%20Public%20Final.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=September 19, 2022}} is an American attorney serving as a [[United States federal judge|United States District Judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts]]. She previously served as a judge of the Ayer District Court in [[Middlesex County, Massachusetts]]. == Education == Guzman initially enrolled at the [[University of Southern Maine]] for her undergraduate education but transferred to [[Clark University]] where she earned a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in 1989. She received her [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[Boston University School of Law]] in 1992.{{Cite web |last=STAFF |first=TELEGRAM & GAZETTE |title=Guzman and Keamy are nominated for judgeships |url=https://www.telegram.com/story/news/state/2009/06/19/guzman-keamy-are-nominated-for/51956103007/ |access-date=2022-07-13 |website=The Worcester Telegram & Gazette |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |last=Lynch |first=Melissa |date=2020-09-21 |title=The Clark community recalls the life and legacy of Ruth Bader Ginsburg |url=https://clarknow.clarku.edu/2020/09/21/the-clark-community-recalls-the-life-and-legacy-of-ruth-bader-ginsburg/ |access-date=2022-07-13 |website=Clark Now {{!}} Clark University |language=en}} == Career == From 1992 to 2005, Guzman served as a [[public defender]] for the [[Massachusetts Committee for Public Counsel Services]]. She was a [[sole practitioner]] in [[Worcester, Massachusetts]], from 2005 to 2009. From 2009 to 2017, she served as a judge on [[Massachusetts District Court|Dudley District Court]].{{cite web|url=https://vettingroom.org/2022/08/18/judge-margaret-guzman/|title=Judge Margaret Guzman – Nominee to the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts | date=18 August 2022 }} In 2012, the special counsel for the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court noted that Guzman had acquitted all 149 defendants who appeared before her in bench trials on [[drunk driving]] charges. The report, which did not allege judicial misconduct, called for reform of procedures to ensure that lawyers did not engage in [[judge shopping]].{{cite web | url=https://www.patriotledger.com/story/news/courts/2012/11/02/high-rates-acquittal-when-drunken/37952237007/ | title=High rates of acquittal when drunken-driving cases go to bench trials }} She joined the [[Massachusetts District Court|Ayer District Court]] in 2017 and left in 2023 to become a federal judge.{{Cite press release |title=President Biden Names Twenty-Second Round of Judicial Nominees |date=July 13, 2022 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/07/13/president-biden-names-twenty-second-round-of-judicial-nominees/ |access-date=July 13, 2022}} === Federal judicial service === On July 13, 2022, [[President of the United States|President]] [[Joe Biden]] nominated Guzman to serve as a United States District Judge of the [[United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts]]. President Biden nominated Guzman to the seat vacated by Judge [[Timothy S. Hillman]], who assumed [[senior status]] on July 1, 2022.{{Cite press release|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate|date=July 13, 2022|publisher=The White House|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/07/13/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-74/}}{{PD-notice}} On September 21, 2022, a hearing on her nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web|title=Nominations |date=September 21, 2022|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/09/21/2022/nominations}} Conservatives and law enforcement attacked her nomination, claiming that she is reflexively pro-criminal defendant and pointing out that Guzman had acquitted all 149 defendants who appeared before her in bench trials on [[drunk driving]] charges while serving as a judge on Dudley District Court.{{Cite web|date=November 2, 2012|last1=Burrell|first1=Chris|last2=Simpson|first2=Neal|title=High rates of acquittal when drunken-driving cases go to bench trials|url=https://www.patriotledger.com/story/news/courts/2012/11/02/high-rates-acquittal-when-drunken/37952237007/|website=patriotledger.com|access-date=June 4, 2023}} On December 1, 2022, her nomination was reported out of committee by a 12–10 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/EBM%20Results%20-%202022-12-011.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – December 1, 2022|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=December 1, 2022}} On January 3, 2023, her nomination was returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]]; she was renominated later the same day.{{Cite press release |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |date=January 3, 2023 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2023/01/03/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-91/}} On February 2, 2023, her nomination was reported out of committee by an 11–9 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/EBM%20Results%20-%202023-02-021.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meaning – February 2, 2023|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=February 2, 2023}} On February 28, 2023, the Senate invoked cloture on her nomination by a 49–48 vote, with the Vice President [[Kamala Harris]] [[List of tie-breaking votes cast by the vice president of the United States|voting for the affirmative]].{{Cite web|date=February 28, 2023|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Margaret R. Guzman to be U.S. District Judge for the District of Massachusetts)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00031.htm|access-date=February 28, 2023|website=United States Senate}} On March 1, 2023, her nomination was confirmed by a 49–48 vote, with the vice president casting the tie-breaking vote.{{Cite web|date=March 1, 2023|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Margaret R. Guzman, of Massachusetts, to be U.S. District Judge for the District of Massachusetts)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00032.htm|access-date=March 1, 2023|website=United States Senate}} She received her judicial commission on March 3, 2023.{{FJC Bio|nid=13333861|inline=yes}} She is the first [[Hispanic and Latino Americans|Hispanic]] judge to serve on the District Court for the District of Massachusetts.{{Cite web|last=Stoico|first=Nick|date=July 13, 2022|title=Biden nominates Judge Guzman for Mass. federal court; would be first Hispanic judge - The Boston Globe|url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/2022/07/13/metro/biden-nominates-judge-guzman-mass-federal-court-would-be-first-hispanic-judge/|access-date=July 13, 2022|website=BostonGlobe.com|language=en-US}} == Notable cases == In December 2023, Guzman allowed a lawsuit against [[3M]] and other corporations to proceed. The lawsuit was filed by Massachusetts homeowners who had their water tested and found that their drinking water contained excessive and potentially dangerous amounts of [[PFAS]].{{cite web |title=Biden Judge Rules that Proposed Class Action Against Corporations for Contaminating Drinking Water Should Proceed |url=https://www.pfaw.org/blog-posts/biden-judge-rules-that-proposed-class-action-against-corporations-for-contaminating-drinking-water-should-proceed/ |website=People For the American Way |date=January 3, 2024 |access-date=October 23, 2026}}{{cite web |title=Ryan v. Greif |url=https://webservices.courthousenews.com/sites/Data/AppellateOpinionUploads/2023-26-12--14-53-40-USDC%20Massachusetts-4_22cv40089.pdf |website=Courthouse News Service |date=December 21, 2023 |access-date=February 20, 2024}} === 2026 sentencing controversy and recusal === On January 23, 2026, Guzman sentenced Moises and Kiersten Soto to 18 years in federal prison following their convictions for sex trafficking. During a recess in the sentencing hearing, a member of Guzman's staff handed federal prosecutors an envelope intended for the victim, who was not present. Prosecutors subsequently disclosed that the envelope contained a handwritten card from Guzman, a bracelet, and several seashells. Defense attorneys said they were not informed of the communication until five days after sentencing.{{cite news |last=Stoico |first=Nick |title=Judge's note, gift to victim sparks bid for new trial in Worcester couple's sex trafficking case |url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/06/27/metro/judge-bias-allegations-soto-sex-trafficking-case/ |work=The Boston Globe |date=June 27, 2026 |access-date=October 23, 2026}} Defense counsel subsequently sought a new trial and resentencing, arguing that the communication raised questions about Guzman's impartiality and demonstrated potential bias toward the prosecution's principal witness. Federal prosecutors opposed a new trial, maintaining that the gesture represented sympathy for the victim after the jury's guilty verdict, but agreed that resentencing before a different judge was appropriate. Guzman recused herself from the case on February 20, 2026, one day after defense counsel filed a motion for a new trial. The proceedings were reassigned to U.S. District Judge [[Myong J. Joun]]. On July 20, 2026, Joun vacated both defendants' original 18-year prison sentences. She became chief judge of the court on February 1, 2021.{{Cite web |last=Geberer |first=Raanan |date=January 7, 2021 |title=New Chief Judge Named in Federal E.D. Courthouse |url=https://brooklyneagle.com/articles/2021/01/06/new-chief-judge-named-in-federal-e-d-courthouse/ |access-date=January 23, 2020 |website=Brooklyn Eagle |language=en-US}} == Early life and education == Brodie was born Margo Kitsy Williams in [[St. John's, Antigua and Barbuda|St. John's]], [[Antigua]]. She earned a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in 1988 from [[St. Francis College]] in [[Brooklyn]] and then a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1991 from the [[University of Pennsylvania Law School]].{{Cite press release| url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2011/06/07/president-obama-nominates-four-united-states-district-court | title=President Obama Nominates Four to the United States District Court | publisher = [[White House]], Office of the Press Secretary | location = Washington, D.C.| date=June 7, 2011 | access-date=January 19, 2019}}{{FJC Bio|nid=1393901|inline=yes}} == Career == Brodie worked for the New York City Law Department from 1991 until 1994, and then at the law firm Carter, Ledyard & Millburn from 1994 until 1999. She then joined the office of the [[United States Attorney for the Eastern District of New York|United States attorney for the Eastern District of New York]] in 1999 as an [[assistant United States attorney]]. Brodie was Deputy Chief of the General Crimes Section from 2006 to 2007, Chief of the General Crimes Section from 2007 until 2009, Counselor to the Criminal Division from 2009 to 2010, and deputy chief of the Criminal Division from 2010 to 2012. === Federal judicial service === On June 7, 2011, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Brodie to a seat on the United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York that had been vacated by Judge [[Allyne R. Ross]], who assumed [[senior status]] in April 2011.{{Cite web | author=The White House: Office of the Press Secretary|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2011/06/07/nominations-sent-senate|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate|date=June 7, 2011|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|access-date=June 8, 2011}} She received a hearing before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] on September 7, 2011. Her nomination was reported out of committee by a voice vote on October 6, 2011, and was placed on the Senate Executive Calendar the same day.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/ExecutiveBusinessMeetingResults-10-06-2011.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting - October 6, 2011|website=judiciary.senate.gov}} On February 27, 2012, the [[United States Senate]] confirmed Brodie by an 86–2 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=112&session=2&vote=00023|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Margo Kitsy Brodie, of New York, to be U.S. District Judge for the Eastern District of New York)|website=www.senate.gov}} She received her commission on February 29, 2012. {{nowrap|[[Duke University School of Law]] ([[Master of Laws|LLM]])}} | occupation = | profession = | known_for = | salary = | net_worth = | cabinet = | committees = | portfolio = | awards = | signature = | signature_alt = | website = | footnotes = }} '''Marina Garcia Marmolejo''' (born 1971) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas]]. ==Early life and education== Garcia Marmolejo was born in [[Nuevo Laredo]], [[Tamaulipas]], [[Mexico]] and is a [[United States nationality law#Naturalization|naturalized United States citizen]].{{cite web |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/MarinaMarmolejo-PublicQuestionnaire.pdf |title=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary, Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees |publisher=United States Senate |access-date=1 November 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101105045125/http://judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/111thCongressJudicialNominations/upload/MarinaMarmolejo-PublicQuestionnaire.pdf |archive-date=2010-11-05 |url-status=dead}}[http://www.kcbd.com/Global/story.asp?S=12887555 Ex-prosecutor nominated for south Texas judge]{{dead link|date=June 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}, ''[[Associated Press]]'' (July 28, 2010). She received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from the [[University of the Incarnate Word]] in 1992.[https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/president-obama-names-marina-marmolejo-united-states-district-court President Obama Names Marina Marmolejo to the United States District Court] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170216171634/https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/president-obama-names-marina-marmolejo-united-states-district-court |date=2017-02-16 }}, ''[[whitehouse.gov]]'' (July 28, 2010). In 1993, Garcia Marmolejo served as a substitute teacher in the United Independent School District in [[Laredo, Texas]]. From 1993 to 1996, she worked as a [[research assistant]] to Professor Raul M. Sanchez at [[St. Mary's University School of Law]], where she also worked as a Property tutor and a student attorney at the Criminal Justice Clinic.{{FJC Bio|nid=1393781|inline=yes}} She then attended [[St. Mary's University, Texas|St. Mary's University]] in [[San Antonio, Texas]], where she earned a [[Master of Arts]] degree and her [[Juris Doctor]], both in 1996. In 2020, Garcia Marmolejo earned her [[Master of Laws]] in Judicial Studies from [[Duke University School of Law]].{{Cite web |title=Master of Judicial Studies Program 2018-2020: Participant Biographies |url=https://judicialstudies.duke.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/2018-MJS-Bios-Photos.pdf |website=Duke University School of Law}} Her LL.M. thesis, ''Jack of All Trades, Masters of None: Giving Jurors the Tools They Need to Reach the Right Verdict'', was selected for publication in the George Mason Law Review.{{Cite journal |last=Garcia Marmolejo |first=Marina |date=2020–2021 |title=Jack of All Trades, Masters of None: Giving Jurors the Tools They Need to Reach the Right Verdict |url=https://heinonline.org/HOL/Page?handle=hein.journals/gmlr28&id=153&div=&collection= |journal=George Mason Law Review |volume=28 |pages=149}} ==Career== Before becoming a federal judge, Garcia Marmolejo began her legal career as an [[Federal public defender#Federal Public Defender systems|Assistant Federal Public Defender]]. From 1996 to 1998, served as a federal defender in the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Texas|Western District of Texas]], and from 1998 to 1999, she served as a federal defender in the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas|Southern District of Texas]].{{Cite web |date=August 4, 2010 |title=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary - Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/MarinaMarmolejo-PublicQuestionnaire.pdf}} She earned the highest performance evaluation each year. In 1999, she served as an [[assistant United States attorney]] for the Southern District of Texas. For her prosecutorial work, Garcia Marmolejo received awards from the [[United States Department of Homeland Security|Department of Homeland Security]], [[Drug Enforcement Administration]], [[Federal Bureau of Investigation]], and [[U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement|Immigration and Customs Enforcement]]. As a federal public defender and federal prosecutor, Garcia Marmolejo tried over 30 cases to verdict.{{Cite web |title=The Hon. Marina Garcia Marmolejo - St. Mary's Law |url=https://law.stmarytx.edu/academics/faculty/the-hon-marina-garcia-marmolejo/ |access-date=2022-10-23 |website=St. Mary's Law |language=en-US}} In 2007, she moved into private practice and helped open the [[San Antonio]] office of Thompson & Knight, where she served as [[Of Counsel]]. In 2009, Marmolejo was hired to be a [[law firm partner|partner]] with the law firm of [[Reid Collins & Tsai|Reid Collins Tsai LLP]] in their [[Austin, Texas|Austin]] office. === Federal judicial service === During the [[111th Congress]], Democrats from the [[Texas's congressional delegations#United States House of Representatives|Texas House delegation]] and Republican [[U.S. Senator]]s [[John Cornyn]] and [[Kay Bailey Hutchison]] agreed to recommend Marmolejo for a [[Laredo, Texas|Laredo]] vacancy on the Southern District of Texas.Gary Martin, [http://www.chron.com/disp/story.mpl/metropolitan/7129494.html Obama names Laredo lawyer to federal judge post], ''[[Houston Chronicle]]'' (July 28, 2010).Gary Martin, [http://www.chron.com/disp/story.mpl/chronicle/6988308.html Texas Dems criticize Obama on slow judicial appointments], ''[[Houston Chronicle]]'' (May 3, 2010). On July 28, 2010, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Marmolejo to replace [[Samuel B. Kent]].[https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/presidential-nominations-sent-senate-72810 Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate, 7/28/10] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170216171631/https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/presidential-nominations-sent-senate-72810 |date=2017-02-16 }}, ''[[whitehouse.gov]]'' (July 28, 2010). The Senate confirmed Marmolejo by [[unanimous consent]] on October 3, 2011,{{Cite web |url=http://judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/112thCongress.cfm |title=Judicial Nominations and Confirmations: 112th Congress |access-date=2011-10-15 |archive-date=2011-01-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110108213625/http://judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/112thCongress.cfm |url-status=dead }} and she received her judicial commission on October 4, 2011. Since taking the bench, Garcia Marmolejo has heard over 12,000 cases, presided over nearly 100 trials, and maintained a reversal rate of less than 1%. Notably, Garcia Marmolejo is credited with being the first jurist to conclude that after the First Step Act of 2018, a judge has the discretion to look beyond the U.S. Sentencing Commission's policy statements to determine what constitutes an "extraordinary and compelling" circumstance to justify compassionate release.{{Cite web |last=Santos |first=Michael |date=June 24, 2019 |title=Federal District Court Uses Compassionate Release as a Second Look Resentencing Provision |url=https://prisonprofessors.com/federal- district-court-judge-uses-compassionate-release-as-a-second-look-resentencing-provision/ |website=Prison Professors}} According to the legal database Westlaw, more than 450 cases have cited her opinion on this issue.{{Cite web |title=United States v. Cantu |url=https://1.next.westlaw.com/Document/I7fed3110916b11e9a3ecec4a01914b9c/View/FullText.html?originationContext=typeAhead&transitionType=Default&contextData=(sc.Default) |access-date=October 23, 2022 |website=Westlaw}} In 2022, she became a Jurist in Residence at her alma mater, St. Mary's University School of Law. She also founded St. Mary's clerkship mentorship program. ===Consideration for Fifth Circuit=== Marmolejo had been considered a candidate for a vacancy on the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]], along with District Judge [[Xavier Rodriguez]].{{cite web | url=http://www.expressnews.com/news/local/article/Another-federal-judge-may-go-5026374.php | title=Another federal judge may go | publisher=[[San Antonio Express-News]] | date=December 1, 2013 | access-date=April 24, 2015 | author=Contreras, Guillermo}} ==See also== *[[List of Hispanic and Latino American jurists]] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1393781}} *{{Ballotpedia|Marina_Marmolejo}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Samuel B. '''Mark A. Kearney''' (born 1962) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania]].

==Biography==

Kearney received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree, cum laude, in 1984 from [[Villanova University]]. He received a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1987 from [[Villanova University School of Law]]. From 1987 to 1988, he served as a [[law clerk]] to Vice Chancellor [[Maurice A. Hartnett III]] of the [[Delaware Court of Chancery]]. He served as an associate at the law firm of Elliott, Mannino & Flaherty, P.C., from 1988 to 1990. From 1990 to 2014, he served at the law firm of Elliott, Greenleaf & Siedzikowski, P.C., in [[Blue Bell, Pennsylvania|Blue Bell]], Pennsylvania, serving as a shareholder from 1995 to 2014. He handled complex commercial litigation before both federal and state courts.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/06/13/president-obama-announces-intent-nominate-five-serve-united-states-distr|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Obama Announces Intent to Nominate Five to Serve on the United States District Courts|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=13 June 2014}}</ref><ref name="fjc.gov">{{FJC Bio|nid=1394691|inline=yes}}</ref> He served as the 2009 President of the Montgomery Bar Association (Pennsylvania) as it celebrated 125 years of service and as the 2014-15 President of the Pennsylvania Bar Institute (the largest CLE provider on Pennsylvania law) as it recognized 50 years of providing continuing legal education.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.mainlinemedianews.com/kingofprussiacourier/news/whitpain-based-lawyer-mark-kearney-confirmed-as-federal-judge/article_18c44f05-24ac-5b6f-9a05-d3f6fe9a9c17.html|title=Whitpain-based lawyer Mark Kearney confirmed as federal judge|date=8 December 2014}}</ref> He was repeatedly recognized as Top 50 litigation star in Pennsylvania by Benchmark Litigation and received the honor of "Trial Lawyer of the Year" while in practice.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.elliottgreenleaf.com/index.php/mark-a-kearney-honored-as-trial-lawyer-of-the-year/|title=Mark A. Kearney honored as Trial Lawyer of the Year|date=11 November 2014}}</ref> He is a member of the Villanova Law School's Board of Consultors.{{citation needed|date=May 2023}}

===Federal judicial service===
On June 16, 2014, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Kearney to serve as a United States district judge of the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, to the seat vacated by Judge [[J. Curtis Joyner]], who assumed [[senior status]] on May 1, 2013.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/06/16/presidential-nominations-sent-senate|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=16 June 2014}}</ref> On July 24, 2014, a hearing before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]] was held on his nomination.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/judicial-nominations_2014-07-24|title=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|website=www.judiciary.senate.gov}}</ref> On September 18, 2014, his nomination was reported out of committee by a [[voice vote]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%209-18-14.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – September 18, 2014 United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|publisher=}}</ref> On December 1, 2014, Senate Majority Leader [[Harry Reid]] filed for [[cloture]] on his nomination. On December 3, 2014, the [[United States Senate]] invoked [[cloture]] on his nomination by a 60–36 vote.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=113&session=2&vote=00304|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture on Mark A. Kearney, of Pennsylvania, to be U.S. District Judge for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania)|publisher=United States Senate|access-date=3 December 2014}}</ref> He was confirmed later that day by [[voice vote]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/113th-congress/1776|title=PN1776 — Mark A. Kearney — The Judiciary|publisher=congress.gov|access-date=5 November 2022}}</ref> He received his judicial commission on December 4, 2014.<ref name="fjc.gov"/>

===Notable cases===
On February 19, 2016, Kearney issued a ruling in which he held that the [[First Amendment to the United States Constitution]] does not protect the right of citizens to film police activity in a public area.<ref>{{cite web|title=Fields v. Philadelphia|url=https://advance.lexis.com/document/?pdmfid=1000516&crid=9e6fc33d-a830-4635-966d-1227e6ecd43c&pddocfullpath=%2Fshared%2Fdocument%2Fcases%2Furn%3AcontentItem%3A5J4W-S691-F04F-409F-00000-00&pddocid=urn%3AcontentItem%3A5J4W-S691-F04F-409F-00000-00&pdcontentcomponentid=6413&pdshepid=urn%3AcontentItem%3A5J51-HVH1-DXC7-G1WX-00000-00&pdteaserkey=sr1&pditab=allpods&ecomp=9f4Lk&earg=sr1&prid=5860b75b-9dce-4646-b9c5-ff428de6c605|date=2016}}</ref> One commentator opined this ruling is contrary to a consistent line of cases at the federal and state level.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Turley|first1=Jonathan|title=Federal Court: First Amendment Does Not Generally Protect Public Filming Of Police In Public|date=24 February 2016 |url=https://jonathanturley.org/2016/02/24/federal-court-first-amendment-does-not-generally-protect-public-filming-of-police-in-public/|access-date=4 March 2016}}</ref> Kearney explained the governing law in the Third Circuit did not allow him - as a trial judge - to recognize this new constitutional claim in the exceptionally narrow facts presented in the case.<ref>{{cite web|title=Fields v. Philadelphia|url=https://phillylawblog.files.wordpress.com/2016/02/the-trial-court-opinion.pdf|access-date=4 March 2016}}</ref> In July 2017, [[United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit]] Judge [[Thomas L. Ambro]], joined by Judge [[L. Felipe Restrepo]] and partially by Judge [[Richard Lowell Nygaard]], reversed Kearney's judgment but granted [[qualified immunity]] to the police officers involved.<ref>{{Bluebook journal |first=|last=Note| title=Recent Case: Third Circuit Holds Bystanders Have First Amendment Right to Record Police but Grants Qualified Immunity to Officers Involved | volume=131 | journal=[[Harvard Law Review|Harv. L. Rev.]] | page=2049 | url=https://harvardlawreview.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/2049-2056_Online.pdf| year=2018}}</ref>

Kearney also granted injunctions prohibiting state actors from treating female low risk inmates significantly different than male low risk inmates under the Equal Protection Clause<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.readingeagle.com/news/article/second-female-inmate-at-berks-county-prison-wins-gender-bias-suit|title=Second female inmate at Berks County Prison wins gender bias suit|date=22 May 2019}}</ref> and to stop Pennsylvania from interfering with the ongoing construction of the Scudder Falls Bridge in Bucks County under the Compact Clause.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.law360.com/articles/1185039/pa-can-t-stop-bridge-agency-from-using-elevators|title=Pa. Can't Stop Bridge Agency From Using Elevators|date=5 August 2019}}</ref>

In 2016, the court of appeals designated Kearney to hear over 70 cases in the Western District of Pennsylvania and in 2017, over 50 cases in the District of Delaware.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.delawareonline.com/story/money/2017/05/30/delaware-court-meet-case-demand-visiting-judges/354631001/|title=Delaware court to solve judicial shortage with visiting judges|date=30 May 2017}}</ref> Kearney has held businesses accountable for not being licensed to collect debt from a borrower under the Pennsylvania Consumer Credit Code<ref>{{cite web|url=https://cornerstonesupport.com/pa-court-case-emphasizes-the-importance-of-debt-buyer-licensing/|title=PA Court Case Emphasizes the Necessity of Licensing for Debt Buyers|date=17 June 2019}}</ref> and reviewed false advertisement claims against the Morgan and Morgan law firm's legal marketing strategy allegedly confusing Pennsylvanians as to who would be litigating on their behalf.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-otc-marketing/is-this-the-case-that-will-upend-legal-marketing-idUSKBN1HK2VV|title=Is this the case that will upend legal marketing?|newspaper=Reuters |date=13 April 2018}}</ref> He received national press complimenting his "model" handling of the antitrust case brought by Rockfon against Armstrong World Industries in the District of Delaware.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.law.com/thelegalintelligencer/2018/03/02/should-a-judges-personal-judicial-experience-affect-antitrust-pleadings/|title=Should a Judge's Personal Judicial Experience Affect Antitrust Pleadings?|date=2 March 2018}}</ref>

He held the Pennsylvania Supreme Court's ''Gallagher v. Geico'' decision is retroactive, allowing relief to insureds denied stacking benefits in their insurance policy.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.law.com/thelegalintelligencer/2019/04/24/seismic-insurance-stacking-decision-applies-retroactively-federal-judge-rules/|title='Seismic' Insurance Stacking Decision Applies Retroactively, Federal Judge Rules|date=24 April 2019}}</ref> He also found a Fifth Amendment right not to be forced to reveal confidential telephone passcodes for investigatory purposes.<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://slate.com/technology/2015/09/court-rules-that-defendants-don-t-have-to-provide-smartphone-passcodes.html|title=Federal Judge Says Law Enforcement Can't Make You Hand Over Your Smartphone Passcode|journal=Slate |date=25 September 2015 |last1=Newman |first1=Lily Hay }}</ref>

In the wake of the #MeToo era, Kearney denied a University's motion to dismiss a male professor's erroneous outcome claims based on anti-male bias.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://pennrecord.com/stories/512389395-fired-university-of-the-arts-professor-can-proceed-with-lawsuit-alleging-civil-rights-violation|title=Fired University of the Arts professor can proceed with lawsuit alleging civil rights violation|date=2 April 2019}}</ref> In a physical and emotional assault lawsuit brought by a porn star, Kearney denied reality star Josh Duggar's motion to compel Danica Dillion's disclosures.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://radaronline.com/exclusives/2016/01/josh-duggar-porn-star-sex-battery-lawsuit-judge-shuts-down-reality-star-again/|title=Judge Shuts Down Josh Duggar in Porn Star Battery Lawsuit - Again!|date=11 January 2016}}</ref>

In criminal cases, Kearney dismissed an indictment against two men because the prosecutors and agents waited too long to bring them to trial even though they knew where to find them for years before unsealing the indictment.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://advance.lexis.com/document/?pdmfid=1000516&crid=61e1a933-0e2b-46fa-8b28-e9490bdc78b1&pddocfullpath=%2Fshared%2Fdocument%2Fcases%2Furn%3AcontentItem%3A5VN5-TT91-JG02-S2Y6-00000-00&pddocid=urn%3AcontentItem%3A5VN5-TT91-JG02-S2Y6-00000-00&pdcontentcomponentid=6413&pdshepid=urn%3AcontentItem%3A5VM4-3231-DXC8-71RH-00000-00&pdteaserkey=sr1&pditab=allpods&ecomp=9f4Lk&earg=sr1&prid=64a30f20-7d52-4689-8e80-39b95879cf9d|title=United States v. Akindele|date=2019}}</ref>{{primary source inline|date=May 2023}}

In April and July 2020, Kearney found a hotel franchisor could be liable for sex trafficking in its hotels and could turn and sue downstream franchisees and abusers accused of sex trafficking in company hotels in the same case.  In one of the first cases in the country, his ruling addressed respective potential liabilities of hotels, local hotel franchise owners, and traffickers under the William Wilberforce Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of 2008.<ref>{{Cite web|last1=July 07|first1=Max Mitchell {{!}}|last2=PM|first2=2020 at 03:10|title=US Judge Rules Marriott Can Bring 3rd Parties Into Sex Trafficking Case|url=https://www.law.com/thelegalintelligencer/2020/07/07/marriott-can-bring-third-parties-into-sex-trafficking-lawsuit-us-judge-rules/|website=The Legal Intelligencer|language=en}}</ref>

Under the False Claims Act, Kearney held an electricians union could recover over $1,000,000 for a contractor's false billing of electricians’ work efforts on a rail project funded by the United States<ref>{{Cite web|title=Union Gets $1 Million Win in False Claims Suit Against Fairfield|url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/federal-contracting/union-gets-1-million-win-in-false-claims-suit-against-fairfield|website=news.bloomberglaw.com|language=en|date=6 February 2020}}</ref> and later awarded approximately $1.4 million in attorney fees to the union (reducing the request) after success for over a decade of litigation.<ref>{{Cite web|last1=April 13|first1=P. J. D'Annunzio {{!}}|last2=PM|first2=2020 at 06:36|title=Local 98 Wins $1.4M in Lawyer Fees for Suit Over Non-Union SEPTA Projects|url=https://www.law.com/thelegalintelligencer/2020/04/13/local-98-wins-1-4m-in-lawyer-fees-for-suit-over-non-union-septa-projects/|website=The Legal Intelligencer|language=en|date=13 April 2020}}</ref>

Kearney granted an employer's motion to dismiss a claim by a former employee who also served as a U.S. Naval reservist seeking paid leave for when he left work for short voluntary military service after exploring Congress's use of  “defined benefits and seniority” guaranteed under the Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act.<ref>{{Cite web|title=FedEx Worker Loses Military Leave Pay Suit - Law360|url=https://www.law360.com/articles/1293792/fedex-worker-loses-military-leave-pay-suit|website=www.law360.com|language=en|date=21 July 2020}}</ref>

In a monumental environmental case brought by Greenwich Terminals, Gloucester Terminals, and the [[Philadelphia Regional Port Authority|Philadelphia Port Authority]], Judge Kearney evaluated the sanctity of plans to dig a major port from the [[Delaware River]]. These port operators sued the [[United States Army Corps of Engineers]] and its officials under the [[Administrative Procedure Act]], contesting the Corps’ issuance of dredging and construction permits for the Edgemoor Port Project on the Delaware River. The challengers alleged that the Corps failed to adequately consider the impacts of the project’s turning basin and maintenance dredging on river navigation and public safety and neglected to obtain a required Statement of No Objection from the Philadelphia Port Authority. Judge Kearney examined whether the Corps fulfilled their statutory duties under the [[Clean Water Act]], the [[Rivers and Harbors Act]], and its own procedural guidance. Judge Kearney’s review highlighted material flaws in the Corps’ reasoning, including their reliance on unverified data from the applicant, their failure to consider navigation and safety in the public interest review, and their unjustified departure from requiring a Statement of No Objection. Judge Kearney vacated both the [[Clean Water Act#Section 404: Discharges of dredged or fill materials|section 404/10 permit]] and the [[Rivers and Harbors Act#Section 14: Section 408 permissions|section 408 authorization]], instructing the Corps to reconsider the project in accordance with applicable law. This was a major decision for the economic and environmental impacts of the ports to [[Philadelphia]].
<ref>{{cite web |title=Philaport lawsuit halts Edgemoor port project |url=https://delawarecurrents.org/2024/01/15/philaport-lawsuit-port-wilmington/ |website=Delaware Currents |date=15 January 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Philadelphia port expansion plan halted by judge |url=https://whyy.org/articles/philadelphia-port-delaware-expansion-plan-halted/ |website=WHYY |date=January 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Judge halts Delaware River port expansion over safety and procedural concerns |url=https://www.inquirer.com/business/philaport-holt-lawsuit-army-corps-delaware-edgemoor-20241029.html |website=The Philadelphia Inquirer |date=29 October 2024}}</ref>

In [[Joseph Jung]] et al. v. [[Philadelphia|City of Philadelphia]] et al., Judge Kearney presided over a case in which seven vehicle owners sought to invalidate Philadelphia’s traffic camera enforcement schemes. Jung and others challenged the facial validity of [[Pennsylvania]]’s red light and speed camera statutes, and the [[Philadelphia Parking Authority]]’s issuance of violation notices under both substantive and procedural [[due process]] doctrines. Judge Kearney distinguished between [[Legislation|legislative]] and [[Executive (government)|executive]] action, demonstrating the statutes’ civil nature under the [[Kennedy v. Mendoza-Martinez|Mendoza-Martinez]] factors; explaining why neither the facial statutory presumptions nor the City’s form violation notices implicated any [[Fundamental rights in the United States|fundamental rights]]. Judge Kearney concluded that the $100–$150 fines were not constitutionally significant deprivations and the available appeal process which included administrative review and [[State court (United States)|state court]] access, satisfied procedural due process. Judge Kearney dismissed Jung and others’ [[Civil Rights Act of 1871|§ 1983]] claims with prejudice after two failed attempts to state a claim.<ref>{{cite web |title=Federal judge upholds Philly red light and speed camera programs |url=https://www.inquirer.com/transportation/ppa-red-light-speed-cameras-fines-lawsuit-20250226.html |website=The Philadelphia Inquirer |date=26 February 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Jung v. City of Philadelphia Docket |url=https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/69663773/jung-v-city-of-philadelphia/ |website=CourtListener |access-date=25 July 2025}}</ref>

Judge Kearney navigated an employment discrimination case in ''Ionnae Alvarado-Jones v. [[Victoria's Secret]] Stores, LLC'', where Ms. Alvarado-Jones alleged workplace [[sexual harassment]], [[retaliation]], and constructive discharge. While Ms. Alvarado-Jones reserved her Federal [[Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964|Title VII]] claims by timely filing with the [[Equal Employment Opportunity Commission|EEOC]], Ms. Alvarado-Jones failed to timely request dual filing with the [[Pennsylvania Human Relations Commission]] and neglected to file any complaint with the [[Philadelphia Commission on Human Relations]]. The employer moved to dismiss Ms. Alvarado-Jones’s state and municipal law claims. Applying § 9-1122, Judge Kearney reaffirmed the requirement of exhaustion before the Philadelphia Commission, insofar as the [[Philadelphia City Council]]’s procedural scheme forecloses attempts to later file with Philadelphia City Council after pursuing remedies elsewhere.<ref>{{cite web |title=Victoria's Secret Employee Files Sexual Harassment Lawsuit in Philadelphia |url=https://www.phillymag.com/news/2025/04/14/victorias-secret-philadelphia-lawsuit/ |website=Philadelphia Magazine |date=14 April 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Victoria's Secret employee alleges harassment, retaliation in Philly lawsuit |url=https://www.inquirer.com/business/retail/victoria-secret-employee-lawsuit-sexual-harassment-20250417.html |website=The Philadelphia Inquirer |date=17 April 2025}}</ref>

In 2025, Judge Kearney ruled that council officials of [[Yardley, Pennsylvania|Yardley Borough]], [[Bucks County, Pennsylvania]], violated the [[First Amendment to the United States Constitution|First Amendment]] by deleting a [[Facebook]] comment posted by Mr. Earl Markey which criticized a sitting councilman. The borough argued [[qualified immunity]], labelling the comment as a “personal attack”, that the online platform was meant for moderated discussions and it was not to be considered a public platform. Judge Kearney rejected the borough’s arguments, noting recent appellate court precedent which protected political speech on government run social media pages. Despite borough officials revising their policy, reimbursing Mr. Markey’s legal fees and offering to repost the comment, Judge Kearney held the deletion unconstitutional, reinforcing the right to criticize public officials in digital forums, holding local governments accountable for online censorship.<ref>{{cite news |title=Judge: Yardley Officials Illegally Deleted Criticism on Facebook |url=https://www.inquirer.com/politics/pennsylvania/yardley-facebook-comment-first-amendment-lawsuit-20250705.html |work=The Philadelphia Inquirer |date=5 July 2025}}</ref>

[[Georgetown Law Center|Georgetown University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | party = }} '''Mark Christopher Scarsi''' (born 1964) is an American lawyer who has served as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Central District of California]] since 2020. Scarsi was confirmed with broad bipartisan support by an 83–12 vote. Prior to his confirmation, Scarsi served as a corporate litigator in Los Angeles. == Early life, education, and career == Scarsi was born in 1964 in [[Syracuse, New York]]. He studied [[computer science]] at [[Syracuse University]], graduating in 1987 with a [[Bachelor of Science]].{{cite news |last1=Herbert |first1=Geoff |title=Judge in Hunter Biden tax case is Syracuse native, SU graduate |url=https://www.syracuse.com/news/2024/06/judge-in-hunter-biden-tax-case-is-syracuse-native-su-graduate.html |access-date=5 June 2024 |work=[[syracuse.com]] |date=5 June 2024 |language=en}} From 1987 to 1993, Scarsi worked as a [[software engineer]] for [[GE Aviation]] and [[Lockheed Martin]], designing and developing detection and signal processing computer systems for U.S. defense applications. He also did graduate study in computer science at Syracuse, receiving a [[Master of Science]] in 1993. He then attended [[Georgetown University Law Center]], graduating in 1996 with a [[Juris Doctor]], ''[[Latin honors#United States|magna cum laude]]'', and [[Order of the Coif]] honors.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-eighteenth-wave-judicial-nominees-eighteenth-wave-united-states-attorney-nominees-thirteenth-wave-united-states-marshal-nominees/ "President Donald J. Trump Announces Eighteenth Wave of Judicial Nominees, Eighteenth Wave of United States Attorney Nominees, and Thirteenth Wave of United States Marshal Nominees" White House, October 10, 2018] {{PD-notice}}{{cite web |title=Senate Judiciary Committee Questionnaire – Mark C. Scarsi |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/download/mark-scarsi-sjq&download=1 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201012120429/https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Mark%20Scarsi%20SJQ%20-%20PUBLIC.pdf |archive-date=October 12, 2020}} == Career == After graduating from law school, Scarsi was in private practice at the [[Los Angeles]]-based [[intellectual property]] law firm Christie, Parker & Hale (now part of [[Lewis Roca Rothgerber Christie]]) from 1996 to 1998. From 1998 to 2007, Scarsi was in practice at [[O'Melveny & Myers]], becoming a [[partner (business rank)|partner]] in 2003. In 2007, he joined [[Milbank, Tweed, Hadley & McCloy]], where he served as the chair of the firm's Global Intellectual Property Practice and as the Los Angeles office's managing partner. Scarsi noted he only became a [[Federalist Society]] member in 2017 prior to his judicial nomination.[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Mark%20Scarsi%20SJQ%20-%20PUBLIC.pdf "Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees", United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary] === Federal judicial service === On October{{nbsp}}10, 2018, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to nominate Scarsi to serve as a [[United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Central District of California]]. On November{{nbsp}}13, 2018, his nomination was sent to the Senate. President Trump nominated Scarsi to the seat vacated by Judge [[George H. King (judge)|George H. King]], who retired on January{{nbsp}}6, 2017.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/twenty-six-nominations-sent-senate/ "Twenty Six Nominations Sent to the Senate", White House, November 13, 2018] On January{{nbsp}}3, 2019, his nomination was returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]]. On January 30, 2019, [[Donald Trump|President Trump]] announced his intent to renominate Scarsi to the district court.{{Cite web |url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-intent-nominate-judicial-nominees-2/ |title=President Donald J. Trump Announces Intent to Nominate Judicial Nominees |date=January 30, 2019 |language=en-US |via=[[NARA|National Archives]] |work=[[whitehouse.gov]] |access-date=January 31, 2019}} On February{{nbsp}}6, 2019, his nomination was sent to the Senate.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/twelve-nominations-sent-senate/ "Twelve Nominations Sent to the Senate", The White House, February 6, 2019] A hearing on his nomination before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] was held on November{{nbsp}}13, 2019.[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/11/13/2019/nominations United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Nominations for November 13, 2019] On January{{nbsp}}3, 2020, his nomination was once again returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the United States Senate.{{Cite web |url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/116th-congress/375 |title=PN375 – Nomination of Mark C. Scarsi for The Judiciary, 116th Congress (2019–2020) |date=January 3, 2020 |website=www.congress.gov |access-date=January 4, 2020}} On January{{nbsp}}9, 2020, he was renominated to the same seat.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/seven-nominations-sent-senate-5/ "Seven Nominations Sent to the Senate", White House, January 9, 2020] On March{{nbsp}}5, 2020, his nomination was reported out of committee by [[voice vote]].[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/030520%20Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting.pdf Results of Executive Business Meeting – March 5, 2020, Senate Judiciary Committee] On September{{nbsp}}14, 2020, the Senate invoked [[cloture]] on his nomination by a 77–12 vote.[https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=2&vote=00169 "On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Mark C. Scarsi to be U.S. District Judge for the Central District of California) United States Senate, September 14, 2020] On September{{nbsp}}15, 2020, his nomination was confirmed by an 83–12 vote.[https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=2&vote=00170 On the Nomination (Confirmation: Mark C. Scarsi, of California, to be U.S. District Judge for the Central District of California) United States Senate, September 15, 2020] He received his judicial commission on September{{nbsp}}18, 2020.{{FJC Bio|nid=8894336|inline=yes}} Prior to [[Pardon of Hunter Biden|President Biden's pardon]] of [[Hunter Biden]] in December 2024, he presided over Hunter Biden's case related to tax charges. '''Mark Eaton Walker''' (born 1967) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Florida]].

==Biography==

Born in [[Winter Garden, Florida]], he received his [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from the [[University of Florida]] in 1989, graduating first in his class.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|date=17 February 2012|title=Senate Judiciary Committee Questionnaire, The Hon. Mark E. Walker|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/MarkWalker-PublicQuestionnaire.pdf|access-date=23 July 2020|website=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary}}</ref>  He received his [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[Fredric G. Levin College of Law]] at the University of Florida in 1992, ''[[magna cum laude]]''. From 1983 to 1993, during high school and during breaks in the academic year in college, Walker worked at a [[Winn-Dixie]], the same store where his father worked.<ref name=":1">{{Cite news|last=Burlew|first=Jeff|date=13 December 2009|title=Judge presiding over Hoffman murder trial known for fairness|work=Tallahassee Democrat}}</ref> Walker identified his experience working at Winn-Dixie as "the job that, more than any other, helped prepare him to be a lawyer and interact with people."<ref name=":1" /> After graduating from law school second in his class, he clerked for Judge [[Emmett Ripley Cox]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit]] from 1993 to 1994.<ref name=":0" /> He clerked for Justice [[Stephen H. Grimes]] of the [[Florida Supreme Court]] from 1994 to 1996.<ref name=":0" /> He clerked for Judge [[Robert Hinkle (judge)|Robert Hinkle]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Florida]] from 1996 to 1997.<ref name=":0" /> In July 1997 he spent a short period in private practice, but soon left to work as an assistant public defender for Florida's second judicial circuit.<ref name=":0" /> He served as an assistant public defender from 1997 to 1999.<ref name=":0" /> He worked in [[practice of law|private practice]] from 1999 to 2009 specializing in civil litigation and criminal defense.<ref name=":0" /> From 2009 to 2012, he served as a [[Circuit court (Florida)|state circuit judge]] in [[Tallahassee]].<ref name="WH2012">{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2012/02/16/president-obama-nominates-three-serve-us-district-court|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Obama Nominates Three to Serve on the US District Court|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=16 February 2012}}</ref><ref name="fjc.gov">{{FJC Bio|nid=1394066}}</ref>

===Federal judicial service===

On February 16, 2012, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Walker to serve as United States district judge for the United States District Court for the Northern District of Florida.<ref name=WH2012/> He replaced Judge [[Stephan P. Mickle]], who assumed [[senior status]] in 2011. His nomination was reported out of committee on June 7, 2012 by a [[voice vote]], with one senator voting "nay".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/ExecutiveBusinessMeetingResults-06-07-2012.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting - June 7, 2012|access-date=2012-12-06}}</ref> The [[United States Senate]] confirmed Walker on December 6, 2012 by a 94–0 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1122/vote_112_2_00224.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Mark E. Walker, of Florida, to be United States District Judge for the Northern District of Florida)|access-date=2022-11-01}}</ref> He received his commission on December 7, 2012.<ref name="fjc.gov"/> He became chief judge in June 2018.<ref name="fjc.gov"/>

==Notable rulings==

=== ''Hand v. Scott'' ===

In January 2018, Walker ruled against Florida and ordered [[Florida governor]] [[Rick Scott]] to restore the voting rights of felons after their release from prison.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.tampabay.com/florida-politics/buzz/2018/02/01/federal-judge-strikes-down-floridas-system-for-restoring-felon-voting-rights/|title=Judge strikes down Florida's system for denying felons' voting rights|first=Steve|last=Bousquet}}</ref>

=== ''League of Women Voters v. Detzner'' ===

In July 2018, Walker invalidated as unconstitutional Florida's total prohibition on early voting sites on college and university campuses.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/grade-point/wp/2018/07/25/stark-pattern-of-discrimination-judge-makes-it-easier-for-college-students-to-vote/|title='Stark pattern of discrimination': Judge makes it easier for college students to vote|first=Susan|last=Svrluga|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] }}</ref> Walker determined the prohibition violated the First, Fourteenth, and Twenty-Sixth Amendments and the law revealed a "stark pattern of discrimination" against younger voters. Consequently, in the 2018 midterms, nearly 60,000 people voted at the on-campus early voting locations.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://thinkprogress.org/it-can-be-hard-for-college-students-to-get-to-the-polls-floridas-new-law-is-making-it-even-harder-aa140bb798f9/|title='It can be hard for college students to get to the polls. Florida's new law is making it even harder.
|first=Danielle|last=Maclean|website=[[ThinkProgress]]
|date=20 July 2019
}}</ref>

=== ''Keohane v. Jones, et al.'' ===

Walker ordered the [[Florida Department of Corrections]] to continue providing a [[transgender woman]] prisoner with hormone treatment and ordered them to provide the prisoner with women's undergarments and grooming products.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.tampabay.com/florida-politics/buzz/2018/08/23/this-ends-now-florida-prison-system-ordered-to-accommodate-transgender-inmate/|title='This ends now': Florida prison system ordered to accommodate transgender inmate}}</ref> The prisoner was diagnosed with [[gender dysphoria]] but has been housed in a male-only correctional facility. Walker's ruling was ultimately reversed by the [[Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=March 11, 2020 |title=Appeal from the United States District Court for the Northern District of Florida |url=https://media.ca11.uscourts.gov/opinions/pub/files/201814096.pdf }}</ref>

=== ''Madera-Rivera v. Detzner'' ===

In September 2018, Walker decided another significant voting rights case, in which he granted a preliminary injunction against the [[Florida Secretary of State|Florida secretary of state]], directing him to ensure that Spanish speaking voters have access to ballots in the Spanish language for the November 2018 elections.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.npr.org/2018/09/07/645753328/judge-orders-florida-officials-to-provide-sample-ballots-in-spanish|title=Judge Orders Florida Officials To Provide Sample Ballots In Spanish|first=Vanessa|last=Romo|website=NPR |date=7 September 2018 }}</ref> This decision, made on the basis of Section 4(e) of the Voting Rights Act, was especially critical, as Florida was grappling with a recent influx of Puerto Ricans fleeing the aftermath of 2017's [[Hurricane Maria]].

=== ''League of Women Voters v. Scott'' ===

After the 2018 midterms, Walker ruled in favor of then-governor Rick Scott who oversaw the state's ongoing recount in which he was a candidate for U.S. Senate. “Though sometimes careening perilously close to a due process violation, Scott’s most questionable conduct has occurred in his capacity as a candidate rather than as governor," Walker wrote. Though Scott's actions were “reckless and haphazard“ and “Scott has toed the line between imprudent campaign-trail rhetoric and problematic state action. But he has not crossed that line."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.buzzfeednews.com/article/dominicholden/florida-rick-scott-oversee-election-judge|title=A Judge Says Florida Republican Gov. Rick Scott Can Keep Overseeing Florida's Election|first=Dominic|last=Holden|website=[[BuzzFeed News]] |date=16 November 2018 }}</ref>

=== Anti-riot law ===

On September 9, 2021, Walker blocked Florida's anti-riot law as a violation of the [[First Amendment]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.abcactionnews.com/news/state/floridas-gop-backed-anti-riot-law-blocked-by-judge |title=Florida's GOP-backed 'anti-riot' law blocked by judge|website=ABC News|date=September 9, 2021|access-date=October 27, 2021}}</ref>

=== University of Florida professors ===

In another free speech case, on January 4, 2022, Walker refused to dismiss a lawsuit filed by professors at the University of Florida after the University tried to stop them from testifying in a voting rights lawsuit.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/michaeltnietzel/2022/01/04/federal-judge-denies-university-of-floridas-motion-to-dismiss-professors-first-amendment-lawsuit/?sh=3b8b7d8e1534|title=Federal Judge Denies University Of Florida's Motion To Dismiss Professors' First Amendment Lawsuit|website=Forbes|date=January 4, 2022|access-date=January 5, 2022}}</ref>

The ruling eventually blocked the law as incompatible with the First Amendment.<ref>{{cite web|first=Tim|last=Cushing|access-date=2022-11-22|title=Federal Court Blocks Florida's 'Stop WOKE' Act, Calls It 'Positively Dystopian' |url=https://www.techdirt.com/2022/11/21/federal-court-blocks-floridas-stop-woke-act-calls-it-positively-dystopian/|date=2022-11-21|website=Techdirt}}</ref>

=== ''League of Women Voters v. Laurel M. Lee'' ===

On March 30, 2022, Walker ruled that Florida Senate Bill 90 violated the Voting Rights Act, issued a permanent [[injunction]] against the law’s restrictions on [[absentee ballot]] drop boxes, and required Florida to obtain [[Voting Rights Act of 1965#Preclearance requirement|preclearance]] from federal courts before enacting election laws.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ax |first=Joseph |title=Florida judge blocks new GOP-backed voting law |url=https://gazette.com/florida-judge-blocks-new-gop-backed-voting-law/article_551a8afa-b12a-11ec-8bdd-4f28e5e558a3.html |access-date=2022-03-31 |website=Colorado Springs Gazette |date=31 March 2022 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Federal Judge Rules Florida's New Voting Restrictions Are Unconstitutional |url=https://www.newsweek.com/florida-voting-restrictions-federal-ruling-1693885 |access-date=2022-03-31 |website=MSN |date=31 March 2022 |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last1=Daniels |first1=Eugene |last2=Okun |first2=Eli |title=POLITICO Playbook PM: Advocates applaud Biden's transgender policy moves |url=https://politi.co/3JZUvvZ |access-date=2022-03-31 |website=POLITICO |date=31 March 2022 |language=en}}</ref>

In an outline of the legislative history of the bill, Walker wrote, "And the exact justification for SB 90 as a whole, and for its constituent parts, is difficult to pin down, with sponsors and supporters offering conflicting or nonsensical rationales."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Walker |first=Mark E. |date=March 31, 2022 |title=TALLAHASSEE DIVISION LEAGUE OF WOMEN VOTERS OF FLORIDA, INC., et al., Plaintiffs, v. LAUREL M. LEE, in her official capacity as Florida Secretary of State, et al. |url=https://www.democracydocket.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/2022-03-31-Final-Order-Following-dckt-665_0.pdf |access-date=March 31, 2022 |website=[[Democracy Docket]]}}</ref>

On May 5, 2022, the 11th Circuit Court of Appeals lifted Walker's order, pending appeal:  "The lower court’s ruling relying on an analysis of racism in Florida’s history is 'problematic,' and 'failed to properly account for what might be called the presumption of legislative good faith,' according to the order issued Friday by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit.
Additionally, the state has 'a substantial argument' that another provision in the law governing 'line warming' activities outside polling places 'passes constitutional muster,' though the lower court found it to be 'unconstitutionally vague and overbroad,' according to the order.
The court also noted the next statewide election is in August, while local elections are ongoing—too close for interfering with state laws administering elections, the judges wrote."  The appeals court did not reach the merits, which will be decided in the main appeal.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/eleventh-circuit-sides-with-desantis-on-election-law-court-order | title=Eleventh Circuit Sides with DeSantis on Election-Law Court Order }}</ref>

=== ''Florida State Conference of Branches and Youth Units of the NAACP, et al v. Cord Byrd, et al.'' ===
On July 3, 2023, Judge Walker granted a preliminary injunction against SB 7020, a Florida law that barred non-citizens from handling or collecting voter registration forms, and third-party voter registration groups from retaining personal information collected when registering new voters.<ref>{{Cite news |date=July 3, 2023 |title=US judge blocks portions of new Florida elections law |language=en |work=AP News |url=https://apnews.com/article/elections-immigration-florida-government-41b49bbb0406d188488ff622481808bb |access-date=July 4, 2023}}</ref>

===Florida Amendment 4 intimidation (2024)===
In October 2024, the Florida Department of Health threatened to bring criminal charges against local TV stations for airing an advertisement in support of [[2024 Florida Amendment 4|Amendment 4]]—a proposed constitutional amendment to prohibit the Florida legislature from restricting [[Abortion in Florida|abortion]] before [[fetal viability]]—which it claimed to contain false information regarding current state law. The health department sent out cease-and-desist letters and contracted for $1.4 million with two law firms to pursue litigation against the stations, claiming that the ads constitute a "sanitary nuisance" because it ""threatens or impairs"" the health of Florida residents. In response, a lawsuit was filed by Floridians Protecting Freedom, the group that organized the amendment's ballot initiative.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cnn.com/2024/10/08/media/florida-tv-abortion-rights-ad-fcc-desantis/index.html|title=Florida is threatening to prosecute TV stations over an abortion rights ad.}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://apnews.com/article/florida-abortion-commercial-desantis-lawsuit-979cd3059d79c92a2b8038585fa922e0|title=Abortion rights group sues after Florida orders TV stations to stop airing ad}}</ref>

Judge Walker issued a temporary restraining order against the Florida Department of Health. In his written opinion, he heavily condemned the health department's decision, commenting "[[It's the economy, stupid|it's the First Amendment, stupid]]".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://floridaphoenix.com/2024/10/17/federal-judge-rebukes-attorney-defending-desantis-admins-threats-to-broadcasters/|title=U.S. judge blocks DeSantis admin’s threats to broadcasters over Amendment 4 ads
}}</ref>

=== ''Computer & Communications Industry Association et al v. Uthmeier'' ===
On June 3, 2025, He would grant a [[Injunction|Preliminary Injunction]] to Florida HB 3 claiming that the law violated the First Amendment and failed [[Intermediate scrutiny|Intermediate Scrutiny]].<ref>[https://apnews.com/article/florida-social-media-ban-minors-lawsuit-678e71c6c6183b87435b7f51feb71fbe Federal judge blocks Florida from enforcing social media ban for kids while lawsuit continues] | AP News</ref>

Mark G. Mastroianni:
{{Short description|American judge (born 1964)}} {{Infobox officeholder | honorific_prefix = | honorific_suffix = | image = Mark Mastroianni (cropped).jpg | alt = | caption = Mastroianni in 2015 | office = Judge of the [[United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts]] | term_start = June 5, 2014 | term_end = | appointer = [[List of federal judges appointed by Barack Obama|Barack Obama]] | predecessor = [[Michael Ponsor]] | successor = | office1 = District Attorney of [[Hampden County, Massachusetts|Hampden County]] | term_start1 = January 5, 2011 | term_end1 = June 5, 2014 | predecessor1 = William Bennett | successor1 = James Orenstein | pronunciation = | birth_name = | birth_date = {{Birth year and age|1964}} | birth_place = {{nowrap|[[Springfield, Massachusetts]], U.S.}} | death_date = | death_place = | death_cause = | resting_place = | resting_place_coordinates = | citizenship = | party = | other_party = | height = | spouse = | partner = | relations = | children = | parents = | mother = | father = | relatives = | education = [[American International College]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|BA]])
[[Western New England University School of Law|Western New England University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | occupation = | profession = | known_for = | salary = | net_worth = | cabinet = | committees = | portfolio = | awards = | signature = | signature_alt = | website = | footnotes = }} '''Mark Gerald Mastroianni''' (born 1964) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts]]. He has served on the court since 2014. Prior to joining the federal bench, he was [[district attorney]] of [[Hampden County, Massachusetts]]. ==Early life and education== Mastroianni graduated from [[Cathedral High School (Springfield, Massachusetts)|Cathedral High School]] in [[Springfield, Massachusetts]].[https://businesswest.com/blog/mark-mastroianni-finds-a-comfort-zone-behind-the-bench/ Mark Mastroianni Finds A Comfort Zone Behind The Bench], ''BusinessWest'' (August 11, 2015). He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree, ''magna cum laude'', in 1986, from the [[American International College]]. He received a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1989 from [[Western New England School of Law]].{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2013/09/24/president-obama-nominates-two-serve-united-states-district-courts|title=President Obama Nominates Two to Serve on the United States District Courts|publisher=White House Press Office|date=September 24, 2013}}{{FJC Bio|nid=1394536|inline=yes}} ==Career== Mastroianni began his career in the Hampden District Attorney's Office as an assistant district attorney in 1990. From 1995 to 2011, he worked as an attorney in private practice as a sole practitioner, focusing his practice on criminal defense matters in state and federal court. He then became district attorney for [[Hampden County, Massachusetts]], serving as the chief law enforcement officer of the county and managing an office of nearly 140 employees. Under Mastroianni, the D.A.'s Office opened an unsolved-crime unit and a [[Forensic DNA|DNA unit]], allowing several [[cold case]]s to be solved. ===Federal judicial service=== When a vacancy on the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts opened, Mastroianni interviewed for the position before a committee to screen and recommend possible candidates, convened by Senator [[Elizabeth Warren]] and led by former District Judge [[Nancy Gertner]]. Mastroianni submitted his application in early 2013, went through several rounds of interviews, and received the recommendation. On September 24, 2013, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Mastroianni to serve on the court, to the seat vacated by Judge [[Michael Ponsor]], who assumed [[senior status]] on August 15, 2011.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2013/09/24/presidential-nominations-sent-senate|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=24 September 2013}} Mastroianni was rated "well qualified" for the post by a substantial majority of the [[American Bar Association]]'s [[Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary]].[https://www.americanbar.org/content/dam/aba/uncategorized/GAO/WebRatingChart.pdf ABA Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary Ratings for 113th Congress], [[American Bar Association]]'s [[Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary]]. He received a hearing before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] on February 11, 2014. His nomination was reported out of committee by voice vote on March 6, 2014.{{cite web|title=Judicial Nomination Materials: 113th Congress|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/Materials113thCongress.cfm|work=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|publisher=United States Senate|access-date=6 March 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131217035140/http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/Materials113thCongress.cfm|archive-date=17 December 2013|url-status=dead}} On May 22, 2014 [[Senate Majority Leader]] [[Harry Reid]] filed for cloture on the nomination. On June 3, 2014, the Senate invoked [[cloture]] on his nomination by a 56–39 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=113&session=2&vote=00168|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture on the Nomination of Mark G. Mastroianni, of Massachusetts, to be U.S. District Judge)|publisher=United States Senate|access-date=3 June 2014}} On June 4, 2014, Mastroianni was confirmed by a 92–2 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=113&session=2&vote=00171|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Mark G. Mastroianni to be U.S. District Judge for the District of Massachusetts)|publisher=United States Senate|access-date=4 June 2014}} He received his judicial commission the following day, and was ceremonially sworn in on August 1, 2014.Stephanie Barry, [https://www.masslive.com/news/2014/08/springfields_us_district_judge.html Springfield's U.S. District Judge Mark G. Mastroianni ceremonially sworn in at Springfield Museums, reflects on new challenge], ''The Republican'' (Springfield, Mass.) (August 1, 2014). ===Notable cases=== Mastroianni presided over a [[trademark]] case involving the name "[[fire cider]]" (a mixture of herbs, [[apple cider vinegar]], and other ingredients). After a [[Pittsfield, Massachusetts]]-based company registered the phrase as a trademark in 2012, others brought suit, contending that the phrase is a longstanding phrase in [[herbalism]] that cannot be trademarked. In 2019, Mastroianni issued a decision siding with the challengers and holding that "fire cider" is a generic term.Josh Landes, [https://www.wamc.org/post/fire-cider-trademark-battle-ends-name-declared-generic Fire Cider Trademark Battle Ends With Name Declared Generic], WAMC (November 4, 2019).Zoe Greenberg, [https://www.bostonglobe.com/metro/2019/10/20/herbalists-defended-their-brew-court-they-won/r94hvWnBghLvdwsnw7W7JN/story.html Zoe Greenberg, Herbalists defended their brew in court. They won], ''Boston Globe'' (October 20, 2019).''[https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=8179494286338875792 Shire City Herbals, Inc. v. Blue]'' (D. Mass. Sept. 30, 2019). In 2017, Mastroianni dismissed a [[defamation]] lawsuit brought by Katherine Mae McKee against comedian [[Bill Cosby]]. After McKee accused Cosby of raping her in 1974, a Cosby representative published a public letter in 2014 questioning her credibility, prompting the woman to sue for defamation. In dismissing McKee's suit, Mastroianni held that the [[Free Speech Clause]] of the [[First Amendment to the United States Constitution]] gave broad liberty to for individuals publicly accused of misconduct to defend themselves without fear of being held liable for defamation.Graham Bowley, [https://www.nytimes.com/2017/02/16/arts/cosby-judge-dismisses-civil-defamation-suit.html Cosby Judge Dismisses Civil Defamation Suit], ''New York Times'' (February 16, 2017).''[https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=15598524150684083212 McKee v. Cosby]'', 236 F. Supp. 3d 427 (D.
