{{nowrap|[[University of Texas at Austin]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]])}} | children = 5 | website = {{URL|https://www.txnd.uscourts.gov/judge/judge-matthew-kacsmaryk|District Court Website}} }} ''' Matthew Joseph Kacsmaryk''' ({{IPAc-en|k|æ|s|ˈ|m|ær|ɪ|k}};{{YouTube|Y9w1nYp7Zvsborn}}{{YouTube|8iOC0_guybY}} born 1977) is an American lawyer who serves as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] in the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Texas]]. He was nominated to the position by President [[Donald Trump]] in 2017 and sworn in for the position in 2019. Conservative groups and the Texas Attorney General tend to file cases in Kacsmaryk's jurisdiction so that he is likely to hear those cases, as he reliably rules against Democratic policies and for Republican policies.{{cite news|author=Alexandra Hutzler|url=https://abcnews.com/Politics/unprecedented-texas-abortion-pill-ruling-sparks-debate-judge/story?id=98531203|title=Unprecedented Texas abortion pill ruling sparks debate about 'judge shopping'|date=April 13, 2023|publisher=ABC News}} His court has been hospitable to conservative lawsuits that many lawyers consider meritless.{{Cite news |last=Enrich |first=David |date=2025-02-07 |title=Trump Lawsuits Against Media Gain Momentum |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/02/07/business/media/trump-media-lawsuits.html |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} In 2023, he presided over [[Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine v. FDA|a lawsuit]] regarding the [[Food and Drug Administration]] (FDA)'s approval of abortion medication [[mifepristone]] in 2000, and had issued a preliminary ruling suspending the approval of the drug, marking the first time a court tried to invalidate the approval of a drug over the FDA's objection.{{cite news |last1=Belluck |first1=Pam |author1-link=Pam Belluck |last2=Jewett |first2=Christina |date=April 10, 2023 |title=Drug Company Leaders Condemn Ruling Invalidating F.D.A. Approval of Abortion Pill |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/04/10/health/abortion-ruling-pharma-executives.html |access-date=April 10, 2023 |work=The New York Times}} His injunction was lifted unanimously by the [[Supreme Court of the United States]] on June 13, 2024, restoring access to mifepristone under current FDA regulations. Kacsmaryk previously worked for the law firm [[Baker Botts]] in 2003 to 2008, then worked as a federal prosecutor in Texas from 2008 to 2013, and then worked for the [[conservative Christian]] legal organization [[First Liberty Institute]] from 2014 to 2019. ==Early life and career== Kacsmaryk was born in 1977 in [[Gainesville, Florida]]. His mother, Dorothy, was a microbiologist; Kacsmaryk's sister, Griffith, recalled that she chose to stay home with her children and was passionate about anti-abortion issues.{{cite news |last1=Kitchener |first1=Caroline |last2=Marimow |first2=Ann |title=The Texas judge who could take down the abortion pill |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2023/02/25/texas-judge-abortion-pill-decision/ |access-date=April 13, 2023 |newspaper=[[Washington Post]] |date=March 14, 2023 |archive-date=February 25, 2023 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20230225185329/https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2023/02/25/texas-judge-abortion-pill-decision/#selection-1709.0-1717.128|url-status=live }} He graduated from [[Abilene Christian University]] in 1999 with a [[Bachelor of Arts]], ''[[summa cum laude]]''. He then attended the [[University of Texas School of Law]], where he was an executive editor of the conservative ''[[Texas Review of Law and Politics|Texas Review of Law & Politics]]''. He graduated with a [[Juris Doctor]] with honors in 2003.{{cite web|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2017/09/07/president-donald-j-trump-announces-seventh-wave-judicial-candidates|title=President Donald J. Trump Announces Seventh Wave of Judicial Candidates|date=September 7, 2017|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|access-date=September 8, 2017|archive-date=March 15, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210315195542/https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-seventh-wave-judicial-candidates/|url-status=live}}{{PD-notice}} From 2003 to 2008, he was an associate in the Dallas office of [[Baker Botts]], where he focused on commercial, constitutional, and intellectual property litigation. From 2008 through 2013, he was an [[assistant United States attorney]] in the Northern District of Texas where he was lead counsel in over 75 criminal appeals and co-counsel in high-profile criminal and terrorism trials. In 2013, Kacsmaryk received the attorney general's award for excellence in furthering the interests of U.S. national security for his work in ''United States v. Aldawsari''.{{cite web|url=https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/61st-year-doj-awards-program-attorney-general-holder-recognizes-department-employees-and|title=In 61st Year of DOJ Awards Program, Attorney General Holder Recognizes Department Employees and Others for Their Service|date=November 25, 2013|via=[[Department of Justice]]|access-date=January 18, 2022|archive-date=January 18, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220118183604/https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/61st-year-doj-awards-program-attorney-general-holder-recognizes-department-employees-and|url-status=live}} From 2014 to 2019, he worked for [[First Liberty Institute]], where he held the position of deputy general counsel.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Kacsmaryk%20SJQ.pdf|title=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees: Matthew J. He also described some of the defense arguments as supporting "eugenics." Josh Blackman, a conservative law professor at South Texas College of Law who knows Kacsmaryk, compared his judicial philosophy to that of two of the U.S. Supreme Court's most conservative justices, Justice Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito. "He's not a moderate," Blackman said.}} He insisted on using the terms "unborn human" or "unborn child" in place of '[[fetus]]', asserting: "Jurists often use the word 'fetus' to inaccurately identify unborn humans in unscientific ways." He further wrote that mifepristone is used "to kill the unborn human" and "starves the unborn human until death".{{cite news |last1=Atkins |first1=Chloe |last2=Arkin |first2=Daniel |title=Judge's abortion pill decision embraces extreme language and ideology of anti-abortion movement, experts say |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/abortion-pill-ruling-analysis-anti-abortion-terms-ideology-rcna78937 |access-date=April 22, 2023 |work=[[NBC News]] |date=April 11, 2023}} Kacsmaryk also called doctors who provide abortions "abortionists," and medication abortion "chemical abortion." On April 13, 2023, a three-judge panel of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]] granted an emergency stay on Kacsmaryk's restriction on the 2000 approval of mifepristone due to timeliness issues, stating that "it appears that the [[statute of limitations]] bars plaintiffs' challenges" to the 2000 approval; however, the panel, in a 2-1 vote, approved Kacsmaryk's restrictions on the FDA's actions expanding access to mifepristone from 2016.{{cite news |title=Federal appeals court preserves access to abortion pill for now but tightens rules |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/mifepristone-abortion-pill-federal-appeals-court-access-tighter-rules/ |access-date=April 23, 2023 |work=[[CBS News]] |agency=[[Associated Press]] |date=April 13, 2023}}{{cite news |last1=Weixel |first1=Nathaniel |title=Court preserves abortion pill access with limits |url=https://thehill.com/policy/healthcare/3946530-court-preserves-abortion-pill-access-with-limits/ |access-date=April 23, 2023 |work=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]] |date=April 13, 2023}} On April 21, 2023, a majority of the [[Supreme Court of the United States]], without comment, voted to indefinitely implement an emergency stay on all the restrictions against mifepristone while the lawsuit continued in the lower courts.{{cite news |last1=Kimball |first1=Spencer |title=Supreme Court says abortion pill mifepristone will remain broadly available during legal battle |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2023/04/21/supreme-court-says-abortion-pill-mifepristone-will-remain-broadly-available-during-legal-battle.html |access-date=April 22, 2023 |work=[[CNBC]] |date=April 21, 2023}}{{cite news |last1=Sherman |first1=Mark |title=Supreme Court preserves access to abortion pill for now |url=https://apnews.com/article/supreme-court-abortion-pill-mifepristone-access-f781488016640bf571faf36096339ea4 |access-date=April 22, 2023 |work=[[Associated Press]] |date=April 22, 2023}} On June 13, 2024, the Supreme Court of the United States issued a unanimous decision, ruling that the Alliance Defending Freedom lacked standing to challenge the FDA's approval or rule making. The decision reversed the ruling of the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit and lifted the injunction.{{Cite news |last=Hurley |first=Lawrence |date=June 13, 2024 |title=Supreme Court rejects bid to restrict access to abortion pill |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/supreme-court/supreme-court-rejects-bid-restrict-access-abortion-pill-rcna151308 |access-date=June 13, 2024 |work=[[NBC News]]}} === Disclosure controversies === ==== ''Texas Review of Law and Politics'' article ==== ''[[The Washington Post]]'' reported that in 2017, Kacsmaryk attempted to obscure his authorship of an article concerning issues he would potentially issue rulings on while under consideration for a federal judgeship. In early 2017, Kacsmaryk submitted a draft of an article arguing that physicians with religious objections should not be required to treat transgender patients or perform abortions to the ''Texas Review of Law and Politics.'' A timeline Kacsmaryk submitted to the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] stated that he was under consideration for a judicial nomination by early March and throughout April, meeting with Texas Senators [[Ted Cruz]] and [[John Cornyn]], as well as [[White House Counsel]]. On April 11, Kacsmaryk emailed an editor a subsequent draft of the article, titled "MJK First Draft". In late April 2017, Kacsmaryk asked his ''Texas Review of Law and Politics'' editor to remove his name from the article, citing: "reasons I may discuss at a later date," and stating that his First Liberty colleagues would "co-author the aforementioned article". After the co-authorship change, Kacsmaryk continued to offer minor edits to the article, and the article's final version "was almost identical to the one submitted under Kacsmaryk’s name". Trump nominated Kacsmaryk to the federal bench in September 2017, the same month the article was published. Kacsmaryk did not list the article on the Senate Judiciary Committee's questionnaire that requires judicial nominees to list all of their published works.{{cite news |last1=Kitchener |first1=Caroline |last2=Barnes |first2=Robert |last3=Marimow |first3=Ann E. |date=April 15, 2023 |title=The controversial article Matthew Kacsmaryk did not disclose to the Senate |newspaper=The Washington Post |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2023/04/15/matthew-kacsmaryk-law-review/ |access-date=15 April 2023}} ==== Financial holdings ==== On April 21, 2023, [[CNN]] reported that Kacsmaryk had "conceal[ed] the bulk of his personal fortune" on his 2020 and 2021 financial disclosures, redacting the name of a company in which he owned between $5 million and $25 million in stock. Federal law only allows for such redactions when the public disclosure of information could "endanger" a judge or their family, and the [[Free Law Project]]'s executive director Michael Lissner commented that while such redactions are not rare, the amount and concealment of the company name in this case was. CNN obtained Kacsmaryk's 2017 financial disclosures during his judicial nomination, which reported ownership of about $2.9 million in stock in [[Publix]], a Florida-based supermarket chain, noting that it was not clear whether the more recent redactions were the same as the disclosed stock ownership on the 2017 form. Kacsmaryk commented to CNN that the redaction was reviewed and approved by the Administrative Office of the United States Courts, and that the company has never had business before his district's court.{{Cite web |last=Chapman |first=Casey Tolan, Isabelle |date=2023-04-21 |title=Details about multimillion-dollar stock holding concealed in abortion pill judge's financial disclosures {{!}} CNN Politics |url=https://www.cnn.com/2023/04/21/politics/judge-kacsmaryk-financial-holdings-abortion-pill/index.html |access-date=2023-04-26 |website=CNN |language=en}} ==== Interviews ==== CNN reported on April 20, 2023, that during his Senate confirmation process, Kacsmaryk failed to disclose two interviews on [[Christian radio|Christian talk radio]] shows in which he discussed social issues likely to be relevant in potential cases, such as religious freedom law, anti-discrimination legislation, abortion, and contraception.{{Citation |title=Hear what judge who suspended abortion pill said in undisclosed radio interviews {{!}} CNN Politics |date=2023-04-20 |url=https://www.cnn.com/videos/politics/2023/04/20/federal-judge-kacsmaryk-fails-to-disclose-interviews-nomination-kfile-lead-vpx.cnn |access-date=2023-04-27 |language=en}}{{Cite web |date=2023-04-21 |title=Texas abortion judge didn't disclose interviews calling being gay 'a lifestyle' |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/americas/us-politics/texas-abortion-pill-judge-radio-interviews-gay-b2324282.html |access-date=2023-04-27 |website=The Independent |language=en}} Once made public, the interviews received subsequent media coverage given Kacsmaryk's comments linking the legalization of same-sex marriage to the [[sexual revolution]], liberalization of contraception access, and the legalization of [[no-fault divorce]]. The Senate confirmation process requires nominees to submit expansive disclosures of their public comments and publications. Kacsmaryk commented that the interviews were not disclosed due to a search error and that he had forgotten about the interviews, and additionally noted that he believed the interviews were consistent with materials in other disclosures.{{Cite web |last=Steck |first=Andrew Kaczynski, Em |date=2023-04-20 |title=Judge who suspended abortion pill failed to disclose interviews that discussed social issues {{!}} CNN Politics |url=https://www.cnn.com/2023/04/20/politics/kfile-judge-kacsmaryk-disclose-interviews-nomination/index.html |access-date=2023-04-26 |website=CNN |language=en}} ==Personal life== Kacsmaryk and his wife have five children.{{Cite web |last=Watkins |first=Matthew |date=2019-07-03 |title=New U.S. District Judge appointed to Amarillo Division of Northern District of Texas |url=https://abc7amarillo.com/news/local/new-us-district-judge-appointed-to-amarillo-division-of-northern-district-of-texas |access-date=2024-01-12 |website=KVII |language=en}} ==See also== *[[Donald He graduated from [[University of Notre Dame]] with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in 1978 and [[Harvard Law School]] with a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1981, where he was Executive Director of the [[Harvard Legal Aid Bureau]]. He served in private practice in [[Chicago]], [[Illinois]], from 1981 to 1982. He served as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Prentice Marshall]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois]] from 1982 to 1984. He reentered private practice in 1984 and served in that capacity until his appointment to the federal bench in 1999. ==Federal judicial service== On January 26, 1999, [[Bill Clinton]] nominated Kennelly to be a judge on the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois]] to a seat vacated by [[Paul Edward Plunkett]]. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on April 15, 1999, and received his commission on April 22, 1999. He assumed [[senior status]] on October 7, 2021. ==Notable rulings== {{See also|NSA warrantless surveillance (2001–2007)}} He gained widespread attention when he presided over the case of ACLU v. [[Harvard University]] ([[Master of Public Policy|MPP]])
[[Helsinki School of Economics]] }} '''Matthew Lane Garcia''' (born 1974){{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Garcia%20SJQ%20Public%20Final1.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=October 9, 2022}} is an American lawyer from [[New Mexico]] who is serving as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of New Mexico]]. == Education == Garcia received a [[Bachelor of Arts]], ''[[magna cum laude]]'', from the [[University of New Mexico]] in 1999, a [[Master of Public Policy]] from [[Harvard Kennedy School]] in 2003 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of New Mexico School of Law]] in 2005.{{Cite press release|title=President Biden Names Twenty-Third Round of Judicial Nominees|date=June 29, 2022|publisher=The White House|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/07/14/president-biden-names-twenty-third-round-of-judicial-nominees/|access-date=July 14, 2022}}{{PD-notice}} Garcia received a [[Fulbright Scholarship]] to study at the [[Helsinki School of Economics]] in [[Finland]].{{cite web | url=https://www.abqjournal.com/2516239/biden-nominates-matthew-garcia-for-federal-bench.html | title=Biden nominates governor's chief of staff to serve as a federal judge in New Mexico - Albuquerque Journal | date=14 July 2022 }} == Career == From 2006 to 2008, Garcia was an [[associate lawyer|associate]] at Freedman Boyd Daniels Hollander Goldberg & Ives in [[Albuquerque, New Mexico]]. From 2009 to 2012, he was a [[law firm partner|partner]] at Bach & Garcia in Albuquerque, New Mexico. From 2012 to 2018, he was a partner at Garcia Ives Nowara in Albuquerque. He was general counsel to [[New Mexico Governor]] [[Michelle Lujan Grisham]] from 2019 to 2020. He was appointed as interim chief of staff on October 5, 2020 by the governor,{{Cite web |title=Lujan Grisham's chief of staff to advise governor on Biden efforts |url=https://www.santafenewmexican.com/news/elections/lujan-grisham-s-chief-of-staff-to-advise-governor-on-biden-efforts/article_0b3b24e2-0f25-11eb-b36e-87738eef7ef6.html |access-date=July 14, 2022 |website=Santa Fe New Mexican |date=15 October 2020 |language=en}} and was named permanent chief of staff on November 12, 2020, after his predecessor, John Bingaman, resigned.{{Cite press release |title=Governor's Office shifts leadership |date=November 12, 2020 |publisher=Office of the Governor |url=https://www.governor.state.nm.us/2020/11/12/governors-office-shifts-leadership/ |access-date=July 14, 2022}} Garcia has worked as an [[adjunct professor]] at the [[University of New Mexico School of Law]]. === Notable cases === In 2006, Garcia represented state auditor candidate [[Hector Balderas]], who petitioned to replace the previous Democratic Party candidate on the ballot. Petitioners Barbara Johnson, Roger Gonzales, and the Republican Party of New Mexico made three separate challenges to the upcoming 2006 general election ballot. While each petitioner relied on different arguments, all three asserted that the Secretary of State erred in including or excluding certain candidates from the 2006 general election ballot. Balderas would later become the [[New Mexico Attorney General]].{{cite web | url=https://casetext.com/case/johnson-v-vigil-giron | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220908201512/https://casetext.com/case/johnson-v-vigil-giron | url-status=dead | archive-date=September 8, 2022 | title=Johnson v. Vigil-Giron, 140 N.M. 667 | Casetext Search + Citator }} In 2014, Garcia represented the [[American Civil Liberties Union|ACLU]] of New Mexico as ''[[amicus curiae]]'' in a suit against the [[New Mexico Department of Children, Youth, and Families]].{{Cite web |date=6 August 2014 |title=Ramirez vs. State of New Mexico Children Youth and Families Department, et al. |url=https://www.justice.gov/sites/default/files/crt/legacy/2014/08/13/ramireznewmexsctbrief.pdf |access-date=7 March 2026 |website=[[US Department of Justice]]}}{{cite web | url=https://vettingroom.org/2022/09/08/matthew-garcia/comment-page-1/#comment-37158 | title=Matthew Garcia – Nominee to the U.S. District Court for the District of New Mexico | date=8 September 2022 }} In 2016, Garcia argued before the [[New Mexico Supreme Court]] seeking to maintain a [[Whistleblower Protection Act]] claim against former secretary of state [[Mary Herrera]]; she served as the secretary of state from January 2007 until January 2011. On January 1, 2007, Herrera appointed Manny Vildasol as an office administrator. During his tenure, Vildasol suspected that secretary of state staff misused public funds and that Herrera violated election laws. Vildasol reported the suspected misconduct to the [[Federal Bureau of Investigation]] and the New Mexico Attorney General's Office. On September 4, 2010, Vildasol received a letter from Herrera terminating his employment.{{cite web | url=https://casetext.com/case/flores-v-herrera-2 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220908201512/https://casetext.com/case/flores-v-herrera-2 | url-status=dead | archive-date=September 8, 2022 | title=Flores v. Herrera, 384 P.3d 1070 | Casetext Search + Citator }} In 2020, Garcia successfully defended the state's emergency authority and pandemic restrictions before the [[New Mexico Supreme Court]] in response to the [[COVID-19 pandemic]].{{cite web | url=https://www.krqe.com/news/politics-government/governors-office-names-matthew-garcia-as-chief-of-staff/ | title=Governor's office names Matthew Garcia as chief of staff | date=13 November 2020 }} === Federal judicial service === On July 14, 2022, President [[Joe Biden]] nominated Garcia to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of New Mexico]]. President Biden nominated Garcia to the seat vacated by Judge [[Judith C. Herrera]], who assumed [[senior status]] on July 1, 2019.{{Cite web|date=July 14, 2022|title=PN2382 - Nomination of Matthew L. Garcia for The Judiciary, 117th Congress (2021-2022)|url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/117th-congress/2382|access-date=July 15, 2022|website=www.congress.gov}} On October 12, 2022, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web|title=Nominations|date=October 9, 2022|publisher=[[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]]|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/10/12/2022/nominations}} On December 1, 2022, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 12–10 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/EBM%20Results%20-%202022-12-011.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – December 1, 2022|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=December 1, 2022}} On January 3, 2023, his nomination was returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]]; he was renominated later the same day.{{Cite press release|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate|date=January 3, 2023|publisher=The White House|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2023/01/03/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-91/}} On February 2, 2023, his nomination was reported out of committee by an 11–9 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/EBM%20Results%20-%202023-02-021.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – February 2, 2023|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=February 2, 2023}} On February 14, 2023, the Senate invoked cloture on his nomination by a 54–45 vote.{{Cite web|date=February 14, 2023|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Matthew L. Garcia to be U.S. District Judge for the District of New Mexico)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00014.htm|access-date=February 14, 2023|website=United States Senate}} That same day, his nomination was confirmed by a 53–46 vote.{{Cite web|date=February 14, 2023|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Matthew L. Garcia, of New Mexico, to be U.S. District Judge for the District of New Mexico)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00015.htm|access-date=February 14, 2023|website=United States Senate}} He received his judicial commission on February 21, 2023.{{FJC Bio|nid=13261776|inline=yes}} He was sworn in on February 23, 2023.{{Cite web|date=February 23, 2023|title=Nomination of Matthew Garcia to Fill U.S. District Court Judicial Vacancy in the District of New Mexico Confirmed by the Senate|url=https://www.nmd.uscourts.gov/news/nomination-matthew-garcia-fill-us-district-court-judicial-vacancy-district-new-mexico-confirmed|website=nmd.uscourts.gov|access-date=May 27, 2023}} == See also == * [[List of Hispanic and Latino American jurists]] == References == {{Reflist}} == External links == *{{FJC Bio|nid=13261776}} *{{Ballotpedia|Matthew_Garcia}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Judith C. [[Washington University in St. Louis]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Matthew Paul Brookman''' (born 1968){{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Brookman%20SJQ%20Public.pdf |title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=January 24, 2023}} is an American [[lawyer]] from [[Indiana]] who serves as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Indiana]]. He previously served as a [[United States magistrate judge]] of the same court from 2016 to 2023. == Education == Brookman earned a [[Bachelor of Arts]] from [[DePauw University]] in 1990 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[Washington University School of Law]] in 1993.{{Cite press release |title=President Biden Names Twenty-Eighth Round of Judicial Nominees |date=December 21, 2022 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/12/21/president-biden-names-twenty-eighth-round-of-judicial-nominees/ |access-date=December 21, 2022}} {{PD-notice}}{{Cite web |last=Odendahl |first=Marilyn |title=Magistrate Judge Brookman to be nominated to Indiana Southern District Court |url=https://www.theindianalawyer.com/articles/magistrate-judge-brookman-to-be-nominated-to-indiana-southern-district-court |access-date=2022-12-27 |website=The Indiana Lawyer |date=December 21, 2022 |language=en-US}} Brookman also studied abroad at the [[University of Essex]] in [[Colchester|Colchester, England]]. == Career == Brookman began his legal career as an [[Associate lawyer|associate]] for Brown & James in [[St. Louis, Missouri]], from 1993 to 1994. From 1994 to 1997, he was a state court prosecutor in [[Jefferson County, Missouri]]. From 1997 to 1999, he was an [[Associate lawyer|associate]] at the law firm Herzog, Crebs & McGhee in St. Louis. From 1999 to 2002, he was a special [[assistant United States attorney]] in the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Western District of Missouri and from 2002 to 2016, he was an assistant United States attorney in the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Indiana. Brookman served as the chief of the office's drug and violent crime unit and lead organized crime and drug enforcement task force attorney. He has been a part-time [[adjunct professor]] at the [[University of Southern Indiana]] and the [[University of Evansville]]. === Notable cases === As an assistant U.S. Attorney, Brookman was involved in prosecuting the quadruple homicide case of ''United States v. Jarvis Brown, et al''. In 2010, Brookman received the Director's Award from Attorney General [[Eric Holder]] for his work on the case.{{cite web | url=https://www.theindianalawyer.com/articles/38212-brookman-selected-as-us-magistrate-judge | title=Brookman selected as U.S. Magistrate judge | date=September 15, 2015 }} === Federal judicial service === Brookman was appointed as a [[United States magistrate judge]] of the United States District Court for the Southern District of Indiana on September 14, 2015, to fill the vacancy left by the retirement of Judge William G. Hussmann, who retired on January 31, 2016.{{Cite press release|title=Matthew P. Brookman selected as United States Magistrate Judge|date=September 14, 2015|publisher=United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Indiana|url=https://www.justice.gov/usao-sdin/pr/matthew-p-brookman-selected-united-states-magistrate-judge|access-date=December 21, 2022}} He assumed office on February 1, 2016.{{Cite web|title=Magistrate Judge Matthew P. Brookman|url=https://www.insd.uscourts.gov/content/magistrate-judge-matthew-p-brookman|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220624221817/https://www.insd.uscourts.gov/content/magistrate-judge-matthew-p-brookman|archive-date=June 24, 2022|access-date=December 21, 2022|website=www.insd.uscourts.gov}}{{Cite web|title=Matthew P. Brookman|url=https://www.uscourts.gov/judicial-milestones/matthew-p-brookman|access-date=December 21, 2022|website=United States Courts|language=en}}{{Cite web |date=February 1, 2016 |title=Matthew P. Brookman sworn in as Magistrate Judge |url=https://www.insd.uscourts.gov/news/matthew-p-brookman-sworn-magistrate-judge |access-date=December 23, 2022 |website=www.insd.uscourts.gov}} His service as a magistrate judge ended on March 31, 2023 when he was elevated to district court judge.{{FJC Bio|nid=13481986|inline=yes}} On December 21, 2022, President [[Joe Biden]] announced his intent to nominate Brookman to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Indiana]]. On January 3, 2023, his nomination was sent to the Senate. President Biden nominated Brookman to the seat to be vacated by Judge [[Richard L. Young]], who announced his intent to assume [[senior status]] upon confirmation of a successor.{{Cite press release|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate|date=January 3, 2023|publisher=The White House|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2023/01/03/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-91/}} On January 25, 2023, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web|title=Nominations|date=January 24, 2023|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/01/25/2023/nominations}} On March 9, 2023, his nomination was reported out of committee by [[voice vote]].{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/2023-03-09%20-%20EBM%20-%20Results.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – March 9, 2023|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=March 9, 2023}} On March 29, 2023, the [[United States Senate]] confirmed his nomination by [[voice vote]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/118th-congress/98|title=PN98 — Matthew P. '''Matthew Walden McFarland''' (born 1967) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Ohio]] and former Judge of the Ohio Fourth District Court of Appeals.

==Education==

McFarland received his [[Bachelor of Arts]], ''cum laude'', from [[Capital University]], and his [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Capital University Law School]].<ref name="WHBio">[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-eighteenth-wave-judicial-nominees-eighteenth-wave-united-states-attorney-nominees-thirteenth-wave-united-states-marshal-nominees/ "President Donald J. Trump Announces Eighteenth Wave of Judicial Nominees, Eighteenth Wave of United States Attorney Nominees, and Thirteenth Wave of United States Marshal Nominees" White House, October 10, 2018] {{PD-notice}}</ref>

==Career==

Prior to joining the bench, McFarland was a [[Scioto County, Ohio|Scioto County]] assistant prosecutor and acted as special counsel for the [[Ohio Attorney General]]. He was also a Licking County assistant county prosecutor. He previously served as the magistrate in Scioto County Common Pleas Court Probate/Juvenile Division and as chairman of the Ohio Association of Magistrates, Juvenile Section.<ref name="WHBio" /> He is an adjunct professor for [[Shawnee State University]] and formerly taught constitutional law at [[Capital University]].<ref name="WHBio" />

=== Federal judicial service ===

On October 10, 2018, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to nominate McFarland to serve as a United States district judge of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Ohio]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.portsmouth-dailytimes.com/top-stories/31979/mcfarland-is-nominatednch|title=McFarland is nominated|last=Corrigan|first=Tom|newspaper=Portsmouth Daily Times|date=October 11, 2018|access-date=October 15, 2018|archive-date=October 16, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181016032636/https://www.portsmouth-dailytimes.com/top-stories/31979/mcfarland-is-nominatednch|url-status=dead}}</ref> On November 13, 2018, his nomination was sent to the Senate. President Trump nominated McFarland to the seat vacated by Judge [[Thomas M. Rose]], who assumed [[senior status]] on June 30, 2017.<ref>[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/twenty-six-nominations-sent-senate/ "Twenty Six Nominations Sent to the Senate", White House, November 13, 2018]</ref> On January 3, 2019, his nomination was returned to the president under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]].

On January 23, 2019, President Trump announced his intent to renominate McFarland for a federal judgeship.<ref>[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-intent-nominate-judicial-nominees/ "President Donald J. Trump Announces Intent to Nominate Judicial Nominees", White House, January 23, 2019]</ref> His nomination was sent to the Senate later that day.<ref>[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/nominations-sent-senate-2/ "Nominations Sent to the Senate", White House, January 23, 2019]</ref> On June 26, 2019, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].<ref>[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/06/26/2019/nominations United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Nominations for June 26, 2019]</ref> On July 18, 2019, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 12–10 vote.<ref>[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/071819%20Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting.pdf Results of Executive Business Meeting – July 18, 2019, Senate Judiciary Committee]</ref> On December 18, 2019, the Senate invoked [[cloture]] on his nomination by a 55–38 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=1&vote=00401|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Matthew Walden McFarland, of Ohio, to be U.S. District Judge for the Southern District of Ohio)|website=www.senate.gov|access-date=2019-12-18}}</ref> His nomination was confirmed later that day by a 56–38 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=1&vote=00402|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Matthew Walden McFarland, of Ohio, to be U.S. District Judge for the Southern District of Ohio)|website=www.senate.gov|access-date=2019-12-18}}</ref> He received his judicial commission on December 31, 2019.<ref>{{FJC Bio|nid=7539421|inline=yes}}</ref>

===Notable rulings===

In July 2022, McFarland ruled<ref>{{Cite news |last=Koeninger |first=Kevin |date=October 19, 2022 |title=Air Force urges panel to lift block on Covid vaccine mandate |work=Courthouse News Service |url=https://www.courthousenews.com/air-force-urges-panel-to-lift-block-on-covid-vaccine-mandate/}}</ref> that the [[United States Air Force|U.S. Air Force]]'s mandate of [[COVID-19]] vaccinations for its members violated the [[First Amendment to the United States Constitution|First Amendment's]] [[Free Exercise Clause|free exercise clause]]. Later, the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit|Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals]] upheld<ref>{{Cite web |title=Court Opinion |url=https://www.opn.ca6.uscourts.gov/opinions.pdf/22a0255p-06.pdf}}</ref> the decision. Not long after McFarland's ruling and the appellate decision upholding it, the [[United States Department of Defense|U.S. Department of Defense]] rescinded the mandate for all troops.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Pentagon ends coronavirus vaccine mandate that fueled political uproar |newspaper=The Washington Post |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/national-security/2023/01/10/pentagon-ends-covid-vaccine-mandate/}}</ref>

== Memberships ==

He has been a member of the [[Federalist Society]] since 2017.<ref name="Questionnaire">[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/McFarland%20SJQ.pdf United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees: Matthew McFarland]</ref>

The Cogburn family owns Pisgah View Ranch near [[Candler, North Carolina|Candler]], which will become [[Pisgah View State Park]].{{Cite web |date=2009-04-06 |title=Max O. Cogburn, Sr. - Groce Funeral Home |url=https://www.grocefuneralhome.com/obits/max-o-cogburn-sr/ |access-date=2025-10-04 |language=en-US}} Cogburn earned a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from the [[University of North Carolina]] in 1973 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[Samford University]] [[Cumberland School of Law]] in 1976.{{Cite web |url=http://m.whitehouse.gov/the-press-office/president-obama-names-two-united-states-district-court-52710 |title=President Obama Names Two to United States District Court, 5/27/10 |access-date=2011-03-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110719151345/http://m.whitehouse.gov/the-press-office/president-obama-names-two-united-states-district-court-52710 |archive-date=2011-07-19 |url-status=dead }}{{FJC Bio|nid=1393646|inline=yes}} ==Career== From 1976 until 1980, Cogburn worked as an [[Associate lawyer|associate]] and then as a [[Law firm partner|partner]] at an [[Asheville, North Carolina]] law firm. From 1980 until 1992, he worked in the United States Attorney's office in Asheville as an [[Assistant United States Attorney]], including as Chief Assistant United States Attorney from 1986 until 1988. From 1992 until 1995, Cogburn was a partner in a law firm in [[Charlotte, North Carolina]]. From 1995 until 2004, he served as a federal magistrate judge on the [[United States District Court for the Western District of North Carolina]]. He returned to private practice in 2004, working in Asheville, North Carolina. ===Federal judicial service=== On May 27, 2010, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Cogburn to a seat on the Western District of North Carolina. He was reported out of the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] on December 8, 2010, but his nomination lapsed at the end of 2010 and the end of the [[111th Congress]].{{Cite web |url=http://judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/Materials112thCongress.cfm |title=Judicial Nominations Materials: 112th Congress |access-date=2011-03-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110927191217/http://judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/Materials112thCongress.cfm |archive-date=2011-09-27 |url-status=dead }} Obama renominated Cogburn on January 5, 2011, and he was reported out of the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] on February 3, 2011. The [[United States Senate|Senate]] confirmed Cogburn by a 96–0 vote on March 10, 2011.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1121/vote_112_1_00038.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Max Oliver Cogburn, Jr., of North Carolina, to be U.S. District Judge)|publisher=[[United States Senate]]}} He received his commission on March 11, 2011. In February 2022, Cogburn announced his decision to move to senior status to take a reduced court caseload.{{cite news |last=Gordon |first=Michael |title=U.S. courts of Western NC have had only white male judges for 150 years. Is that changing? |work=[[Charlotte Observer]] |date=April 13, 2022 |url=https://www.charlotteobserver.com/news/local/article260343265.html}} In November 2024, Cogburn reversed his decision to take senior status and remain a full-time federal district court judge.Pandolfo, Chris. [https://www.foxnews.com/politics/mcconnell-criticizes-federal-judges-reversing-retirement-decisions-open-partisanship McConnell criticizes federal judges for reversing retirement decisions as 'open partisanship'], ''[[FOX News]]'', December 3, 2024. ===Notable rulings=== * On October 10, 2014, Cogburn struck down North Carolina's [[gay marriage ban]] as [[unconstitutional]], opening the way for same-sex marriages in North Carolina to begin immediately.{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2014/10/11/us/same-sex-couples-line-up-to-wed-and-courts-regroup-after-decisions.html|title=Same-Sex Couples Line Up to Wed, and Courts Regroup After Decisions|last=The New York Times|newspaper=The New York Times|date=10 October 2014|publisher=}} * Cogburn was a member of a three-judge panel that struck down the redistricting of certain North Carolina Congressional districts for relying too heavily on race. Cogburn also wrote a separate concurring opinion in that case. The case eventually made its way to the Supreme Court.{{cite news|last1=Gordon|first1=Michael|title=North Carolina Redistricting Fight Heads to Supreme Court|url=https://www.charlotteobserver.com/news/politics-government/article59299843.html|publisher=Charlotte Observer|date=February 9, 2016}} The case, ''[[Cooper v. Harris]]'', was upheld by a 5–3 decision of the Supreme Court on May 22, 2017.{{cite news|last1=Barnes|first1=Robert|title=Supreme Court rules race improperly dominated N.C. redistricting efforts|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/courts_law/supreme-court-rules-race-improperly-dominated-nc-redistricting-efforts/2017/05/22/c159fc70-3efa-11e7-8c25-44d09ff5a4a8_story.html|newspaper=Washington Post|date=May 22, 2017}} ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1393646}} *{{Ballotpedia|Max_O._Cogburn,_Jr.}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Lacy Thornburg]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of North Carolina]]}}|years=2011–present}} {{s-inc}} {{s-end}} {{United States 4th Circuit district judges}} {{authority control}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Cogburn, Max}} [[Category:1951 births]] [[Category:Living people]] [[Category:Assistant United States attorneys]] [[Category:Cumberland School of Law alumni]] [[Category:Judges of the United States District Court for the Western District of North Carolina]] [[Category:United States district court judges appointed by Barack Obama]] [[Category:University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill alumni]] [[Category:United States magistrate judges]]

'''Maxine Mackler Chesney''' (born October 29, 1942) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of California]].

==Early life and education==

Chesney was born on October 29, 1942, in [[San Francisco]], [[California]].<ref name=recorder_20030805>Jason Hoppin, [http://www.law.com/jsp/ca/PubArticleCA.jsp?hubtype=&id=900005391813&Judicial_Profile_Maxine_Chesney Judicial Profile: Maxine Chesney], ''The Recorder'' (August 5, 2003).</ref><ref name=fjc_chesney>{{cite web|url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/chesney-maxine-m.|title=Chesney, Maxine M. - Federal Judicial Center}}</ref> She received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from the [[University of California, Berkeley]] in 1964 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of California, Berkeley School of Law|University of California, Berkeley, Boalt Hall School of Law]] in 1967. She was an attorney, Office of the San Francisco District Attorney, California from 1968 to 1979. She was a trial attorney from 1968 to 1969. She was a senior trial attorney from 1969 to 1971. She was a Principal trial attorney from 1971 to 1976. She was a Head trial attorney in 1976. She was an Assistant chief deputy from 1976 to 1979.

==Judicial career==
===Municipal court judge===
Chesney was a judge on the San Francisco Municipal Court, California from 1979 to 1983. She was a judge on the Superior Court of California, City and County of San Francisco, appointed and subsequently elected from 1983 to 1995.

===Federal judicial service===
In 1994, Chesney was nominated by President [[Bill Clinton]] to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of California]] vacated by [[John P. Vukasin Jr.]], but the [[United States Senate]] took no action on the nomination. However, President Clinton successfully resubmitted the nomination on January 24, 1995, and Chesney was confirmed by the Senate on May 8, 1995, receiving her commission on May 10, 1995. She assumed [[senior status]] on June 30, 2009.<ref name=fjc_chesney />

In 2020, she was elected as judge of the Monroe County Court, becoming the only Asian American judge on the bench in the seventh judicial district.{{Cite web |last=Gandy |first=George |date=May 8, 2024 |title=Monroe County Judge recommended to serve in WNY Federal Court |url=https://www.rochesterfirst.com/local-politics/monroe-county-judge-recommended-to-serve-in-wny-federal-court/ |access-date=May 8, 2024 |website=RochesterFirst |language=en-US}} She was elected in 2021 to serve as a judge on the Monroe County Court.{{Cite web |title=Hon. He is a former [[United States magistrate judge]] of the same court. ==Biography== Shipp was born in October 1965 in [[Paterson, New Jersey]]. He received his [[Bachelor of Science]] from [[Rutgers University]] in 1987. He received his [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Seton Hall University School of Law]] in 1994. He served as a law clerk for Justice James H. Coleman of the [[New Jersey Supreme Court]] from 1994 to 1995. From 1995 to 2003, he worked as an associate at Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom LLP in [[Newark, New Jersey]]. From 2003 to 2007, he worked in the New Jersey Office of the Attorney General, first as an Assistant Attorney General in charge of Consumer Protection and later as Counsel to the Attorney General. In 2007, he was appointed as a [[United States magistrate judge]] of the United States District Court for the District of New Jersey (the first [[African American]] U.S. magistrate judge in that district)Congressional Record (Bound Edition), Volume 158 (2012), Part 9, [Senate], Pages 11847-11854, from the U.S. Government Publishing Office, available online at: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CRECB-2012-pt9/html/CRECB-2012-pt9-Pg11847.htm holding that position until his elevation to District Judge on that court.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2012/01/23/president-obama-nominates-judge-michael-shipp-serve-us-district-court|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Obama Nominates Judge Michael A. Shipp to Serve on the US District Court|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=23 January 2012}} He is the brother of former NFL player, [[Marcel Shipp]]. Justice Shipp is a member of [[Alpha Phi Alpha]] fraternity.{{FJC Bio|nid=1394031}} Shipp received his LLM in judicial studies from [[Duke Law School]] in 2020.{{cite web|url=https://judicialstudies.duke.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/2018-MJS-Bios-Photos.pdf|title=MASTER OF JUDICIAL STUDIES PROGRAM 2018‐2020 PARTICIPANT BIOGRAPHIES|publisher=Bolch Judicial Institute of Duke Law School|page=9|access-date=August 25, 2021}} ===Federal judicial service=== On January 23, 2012, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Shipp to be a United States District Judge for the United States District Court for the District of New Jersey to the seat vacated by Judge [[Mary Little Cooper]], who assumed senior status in 2011. He received a hearing before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] on March 14, 2012 and his nomination was reported to the floor on April 19, 2012, by a voice vote, with [[Mike Lee|Senator Lee]] recorded as voting no based on unrelated general principles. Despite the relatively uncontroversial nature of Shipp's nomination, Senator [[Rand Paul]] in July 2012 held up allowing an up-or-down, Senate floor vote on Shipp's nomination over an unrelated issue, involving Paul's desire to cut off all U.S. aid to [[Pakistan]] unless authorities there release Dr. [[Shakil Afridi]].{{cite web|url=http://www.rollcall.com/news/rand_paul_increases_pressure_to_halt_pakistan_aid-216311-1.html|title=Rand Paul Increases Pressure to Halt Pakistan Aid|date=20 July 2012|website=Roll Call}} In a Senate floor speech on July 19, 2012, Paul announced his intention to hold up all Senate business until receiving a satisfactory answer to his question about why a Pakistani judicial panel has delayed Afridi's appeal of his conviction on charges related to assistance he provided to the CIA in the capture of [[Osama bin Laden]]. Paul also said he intended to seek a vote to terminate all aid to Pakistan. On July 19, 2012, Senate Majority Leader [[Harry Reid]] moved to invoke [[cloture]] in order to confirm Shipp's nomination. The cloture vote was vitiated on July 23, 2012 when Paul consented to a confirmation vote on the nomination. Shipp's nomination was confirmed that same day by a 91–1 vote, with Senator [[Mike Lee]] again casting the sole no vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1122/vote_112_2_00182.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Michael A. Shipp, of New Jersey, to be U.S. District Judge for the District of New Jersey)|website=United States Senate}}{{cite web|url=http://legaltimes.typepad.com/blt/2012/07/amid-more-partisan-squabbling-senate-votes-to-approve-district-court-nominee.html|title=Amid More Partisan Squabbling, Senate Votes to Approve District Court Nominee|website=The BLT: The Blog of Legal Times}} He received his commission on July 26, 2012. == See also == * [[List of African-American federal judges]] * [[List of African-American jurists]] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1394031}} *{{Ballotpedia|Michael_Shipp}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Mary Little Cooper]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States District Court for the District of New Jersey]]}}|years=2012–present}} {{s-inc}} {{s-end}} {{United States 3rd Circuit district judges}} {{authority control}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Shipp, Michael Andre}} [[Category:1965 births]] [[Category:African-American judges]] [[Category:Judges of the United States District Court for the District of New Jersey]] [[Category:Living people]] [[Category:Rutgers University alumni]] [[Category:Seton Hall University School of Law alumni]] [[Category:United States district court judges appointed by Barack Obama]] [[Category:United States magistrate judges]]

'''Michael Morris Baylson''' (born May 29, 1939) is a [[United States federal judge|senior United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania|U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania]].

==Early life and education==
Baylson was born in [[Philadelphia]], on May 29, 1939. He attended [[Cheltenham High School]] in neighboring [[Cheltenham Township, Pennsylvania]], where he graduated in 1957.<ref>[http://cheltenhamalumni.org/BIOS/baylson-michael.htm Cheltenham Alumni]</ref> He received a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree from the [[University of Pennsylvania]] in 1961 and received his [[Bachelor of Laws]] from the [[University of Pennsylvania Law School]] in 1964.<ref name=FJC>{{FJC Bio|nid=1391541|inline=yes}}</ref>

==Career==
Baylson was a [[law clerk]] for Joseph Sloane in the Philadelphia [[Pennsylvania courts of common pleas|Court of Common Pleas]] in 1965. He was an assistant district attorney in Philadelphia from 1966 to 1970. From 1970 to 1988 Judge Baylson was in private practice in Philadelphia.<ref name=FJC/><ref name=about>{{cite web|url=https://www.duanemorris.com/site/past_and_present.html|title=Duane Morris LLP - Past and Present|website=www.duanemorris.com}}</ref> In 1988 he was appointed by President [[Ronald Reagan]] as the [[United States attorney]] for the Eastern District, a position he held until 1993.<ref name=FJC/> He returned to private practice as a partner with [[Duane Morris]] until 2002.<ref name="about"/>

===Federal judicial service===
On January 23, 2002, Baylson was nominated by President [[George W. Bush]] to a seat on the United States District Court for the Eastern District that had been vacated by Judge [[Robert F. Kelly]].<ref name=about/> He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on April 30, 2002, and received his commission on June 19, 2002. He assumed senior status on July 13, 2012.<ref name=FJC/>

==Other activities==
Baylson was a founder, and later counsel, to Gaudenzia, Inc., the largest non-profit provider of drug, alcohol and mental health rehabilitation services in [[Pennsylvania]].

Baylson is a member of the Advisory Committee on Civil Rules of the Committee on Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Judicial Conference of the United States, and is also [[adjunct professor]] at the [[University of Pennsylvania Law School]] and [[Temple University Beasley School of Law]].

[[Yale Law School|Yale University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Michael Etan Farbiarz''' (born 1973){{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Farbiarz%20SJQ%20Public.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=January 24, 2023}} is an American lawyer from [[New Jersey]] who is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of New Jersey]]. == Education == Farbiarz received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] from [[Harvard University]] in 1995 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Yale Law School]] in 1999.{{Cite press release |title=President Biden Names Twenty-Eighth Round of Judicial Nominees |date=December 21, 2022 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/12/21/president-biden-names-twenty-eighth-round-of-judicial-nominees/ |access-date=December 21, 2022}} {{PD-notice}} == Career == After graduating from law school, he served as a [[law clerk]] for then-Chief Judge [[Michael Mukasey]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]] from 1999 to 2000 and for Judge [[José A. Cabranes]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit]] from 2000 to 2001. From 2001 to 2004, Farbiarz was an [[associate lawyer|associate]] at [[Davis Polk|Davis Polk & Wardwell]] in [[New York City]]. From 2004 to 2014, he served as an [[assistant United States attorney]] in the [[United States Attorney for the Southern District of New York|U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York]], including as co-chief of the terrorism and international narcotics unit from 2010 to 2014. From 2014 to 2016, Farbiarz was a [[Fellow|senior fellow]] at the [[New York University School of Law]]. From 2016 to 2023, he served as [[general counsel]] of the [[Port Authority of New York and New Jersey]].{{cite web |date=August 31, 2016 |title=PORT AUTHORITY NAMES NEW CORPORATE COUNSEL TO OVERSEE THE AGENCY'S LAW DEPARTMENT |url=https://www.panynj.gov/port-authority/en/press-room/press-release-archives/2016_press_releases/port_authority_namesnewcorporatecounseltooverseetheagencyslawdep.html |access-date=December 21, 2022 |website=www.panynj.gov}} He has taught courses at [[Columbia Law School]] and New York University School of Law. === Notable cases as a federal prosecutor === In 2001, Farbiarz prosecuted [[Mokhtar Haouari]], who was convicted of conspiracy in a [[2000 millennium attack plots|plot]] to bomb [[Los Angeles International Airport]] shortly before New Year's Day 2000.{{cite web |title=LAX Bombing Plot Figure Is Convicted |date=2001-07-14 |website=[[Los Angeles Times]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230117192122/https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2001-jul-14-mn-22347-story.html |archive-date=2023-01-17 |url-status=live |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2001-jul-14-mn-22347-story.html}}{{cite web|url=https://vettingroom.org/2023/01/17/michael-farbiarz/ |title=Michael Farbiarz – Nominee to the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey |publisher=The Vetting Room |date=2023-01-17 |access-date=2023-01-28}}{{cite web|author=Phil Hirschkorn |url=http://www.cnn.com/2001/LAW/07/13/millennium.plot/ |title=Man found guilty in millennium bomb plot against LAX - July 13, 2001 |publisher=CNN.com |date= |access-date=2023-01-28}} In 2009, Farbiarz prosecuted [[Somali pirate]]s, including [[Abduwali Muse]], who had seized the American container ship [[Maersk Alabama hijacking|Maersk Alabama]] in the [[Indian Ocean]].{{cite web|url=https://newjerseyglobe.com/fr/biden-picks-top-port-authority-lawyer-superior-court-judge-as-federal-judges-in-n-j/|title=Biden picks top Port Authority lawyer, Superior Court judge, as federal judges in N.J.|first=David|last=Wildstein|date=December 21, 2022|website=New Jersey Globe}} The incident was portrayed in the 2013 film ''[[Captain Phillips (film)|Captain Phillips]]''.{{cite web|url=https://sofrep.com/specialoperations/navy-seals-rescue-captain-phillips-of-the-maersk-alabama-april-12-2009/|title=Navy SEALs Rescue Captain of the Maersk Alabama, April 12, 2009|website=SOFREP}}{{cite web|url=https://www.fbi.gov/newyork/press-releases/2009/nyfo042109.htm|title=Somalian Pirate Brought to U.S. to Face Charges for Hijacking the Maersk Alabama and Holding the Ship's Captain Hostage|website=FBI}} In 2010, Farbiarz was the lead prosecutor of eleven deep-cover Russian agents. [[Anna Chapman]], a Russian living in [[New York (state)|New York]], was one of the eleven prosecuted and was charged as a spy.{{cite web|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/anna-chapman-pictures-of-suspected-russian-spy-surface/|title=Anna Chapman: Pictures of Suspected Russian Spy Surface|website=www.cbsnews.com|date=29 June 2010 }} === Federal judicial service === Farbiarz was recommended by [[List of United States senators from New Jersey|Senator]] [[Cory Booker]].{{cite web |last=Wildstein |first=David |date=December 21, 2022 |title=Biden picks top Port Authority lawyer, Superior Court judge, as federal judges in N.J. |url=https://newjerseyglobe.com/judiciary/biden-picks-top-port-authority-lawyer-superior-court-judge-as-federal-judges-in-n-j/ |access-date=December 22, 2022 |website=New Jersey Globe |language=en-US}} On December 22, 2022, during [[Joe Biden]]'s presidency, Biden announced his intention to nominate Farbiarz as a [[United States district judge]] for the [[United States District Court for the District of New Jersey]]. On January 3, 2023, his nomination was sent to the Senate. Farbiarz was nominated to fill the seat vacated by Judge [[Noel Lawrence Hillman]], who assumed [[senior status]] on April 4, 2022.{{Cite press release |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |date=January 3, 2023 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2023/01/03/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-91/}} A hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] on January 25, 2023.{{cite web |date=January 24, 2023 |title=Nominations |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/01/25/2023/nominations |publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary |location=Washington, D.C.}} On April 20, 2023, the committee reported his nomination favorably by a 17–4 vote.{{cite web |title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – April 20, 2023 |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/2023-04-20%20-%20EBM%20-%20Results.pdf |accessdate=April 20, 2023 |publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary}} On May 2, 2023, the [[United States Senate]] invoked cloture on his nomination by a 65–34 vote,{{Cite web |date=May 2, 2023 |title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Michael Farbiarz to be U.S. District Judge for the District of New Jersey) |url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00102.htm |access-date=May 2, 2023 |website=United States Senate}} and was confirmed later that day by the same margin.{{cite web |date=May 2, 2023 |title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Michael Farbiarz, of New Jersey, to be United States District Judge for the District of New Jersey) |url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00104.htm |access-date=May 2, 2023 |website=United States Senate}} He received his judicial commission on He was appointed in 2011 by President [[Barack Obama]]. He previously served as a [[United States magistrate judge]] of the same court. ==Early life and education== Born in [[Livorno|Livorno, Italy]], where his father was stationed in the U.S. Army, Urbanski attended Denbigh High School in [[Newport News]], Virginia.{{cite web | url=https://www.virginiabusiness.com/article/law-the-hon-michael-f-urbanski/ | title=Law: THE HON. MICHAEL F. URBANSKI | date=30 August 2022 }} Urbanski earned an [[Bachelor of Arts|Artium Baccalaureus]] degree in 1978 from [[The College of William & Mary]] and a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1981 from the [[University of Virginia School of Law]].{{Cite web | author=The White House: Office of the Press Secretary | url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2010/12/01/president-obama-names-seven-united-states-district-court | title=President Obama Names Seven to United States District Court | date=December 1, 2010 | via=[[NARA|National Archives]] | work=[[whitehouse.gov]] | access-date=March 22, 2011}} From 1981 until 1982, Urbanski served as a law clerk to Judge [[James Clinton Turk]] of the United States District Court for the Western District of Virginia.{{FJC Bio|nid=1393706|inline=yes}} ==Career== From 1982 until 1984, Urbanski served as an associate in [[Washington, D.C.]] for the law firm [[Vinson & Elkins]]. From 1984 until 2004, practiced with the ''Woods Rogers'' law firm in [[Roanoke, Virginia]], serving first as an associate from 1984 until 1988, and then as a principal from 1989 until 2004. ===Federal judicial service=== In 2004, Urbanski was selected by the judges on the United States District Court for the Western District of Virginia to be a [[United States magistrate judge]]. On December 1, 2010, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Urbanski to a vacant seat on the United States District Court for the Western District of Virginia that had been created by the decision by Judge [[Norman K. Moon]] to assume [[senior status]] in July 2010.{{Cite web | author=The White House: Office of the Press Secretary | url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2010/12/01/presidential-nominations-sent-senate | title=Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate | date=December 1, 2010 | via=[[NARA|National Archives]] | work=[[whitehouse.gov]] | access-date=March 22, 2011}} The [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] reported Urbanski's nomination out of committee on March 10, 2011.{{Cite web |url=http://judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/Materials112thCongress.cfm |title=Judicial Nominations Materials: 112th Congress |access-date=2011-03-22 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110927191217/http://judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/Materials112thCongress.cfm |archive-date=2011-09-27 |url-status=dead }} The [[United States Senate]] confirmed him on May 12, 2011 by a 94–0 vote.{{Cite web |url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1121/vote_112_1_00070.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Michael Francis Urbanski, of Virginia, to be U.S. District Judge for the Western District of Virginia)|access-date=2022-11-03}} He received his judicial commission on May 13, 2011. He became chief judge on July 3, 2017 and served until July 4, 2024. In July 2023, Urbanski gave a one-year notice that he would be taking [[senior status]].{{Cite news |last=Gangloff |first=Mike |date=2023-07-18 |title=Applicants sought for federal judgeship as Urbanski gives one-year notice |url=https://roanoke.com/news/local/crime-courts/help-wanted-sign-hung-out-for-urbanskis-federal-judgeship/article_56e2b43a-2595-11ee-9fe2-9f20f57a62c5.html |access-date=2024-03-14 |work=The Roanoke Times |language=en}} Virginia's senators recommended [[Jasmine Yoon]] for Urbanski's position, and President [[Joe Biden]] nominated her in January 2024. She was confirmed in March 2024.{{Cite news |date=2024-03-13 |title=Senate Confirms First Asian American Judge for WDVA |url=https://www.vba.org/news/667294/Senate-Confirms-First-Asian-American-Judge-for-WDVA.htm |access-date=2024-03-14 |work=The Virginia Bar Association}} Urbanski assumed [[senior status]] on July 4, 2024. ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1393706}} *{{Ballotpedia|Michael_Urbanski}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Norman K. [[Harvard Law School|Harvard University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | footnotes = }} '''Michael Howard Simon''' (born December 1, 1956) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Oregon]]. == Early life and education == Simon was born in [[New York City]] in 1956 into a [[Jewish American]] family. He was the older of two children born to [[Danny Simon]] and Arlene Friedman.{{cite web | first=Cable | last=Neuhaus | url=http://www.people.com/people/archive/article/0,,20085362,00.html | title=Comedy Writer Danny Simon Nurses An Old Wound—the Frustration of Being Neil Simon's Brother | work=[[People (magazine)|People]] | date=June 27, 1983 | access-date=February 1, 2012}} Simon's father was a television comedy writer, and his uncle [[Neil Simon]] was an acclaimed playwright.{{cite news | first=Jeff | last=Mapes | url=https://blog.oregonlive.com/mapesonpolitics/2011/05/suzanne_bonamici_brings_financ.html | title=Suzanne Bonamici brings financial assets to potential congressional race | work=[[The Oregonian]] | date=May 27, 2011 | access-date=February 1, 2012}} Simon earned his [[Bachelor of Arts]], ''[[summa cum laude]]'', in 1978 from the [[University of California, Los Angeles]] and his [[Juris Doctor]], ''[[cum laude]]'', in 1981 from [[Harvard Law School]].{{Cite web |url=http://m.whitehouse.gov/the-press-office/president-obama-names-five-united-states-district-court-0 |title=President Obama Names Five to United States District Court |access-date=2011-06-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120323093811/http://m.whitehouse.gov/the-press-office/president-obama-names-five-united-states-district-court-0 |archive-date=2012-03-23 |url-status=dead }} He is married to Democratic [[United States House of Representatives|U. S. Representative]] [[Suzanne Bonamici]].{{cite news|last=Duin|first=Steve|title=In the wake of David Wu case, accusations fly in Oregon's First District|url=https://www.oregonlive.com/news/oregonian/steve_duin/index.ssf/2011/08/in_the_wake_of_david_wu_case_a.html|newspaper=[[The Oregonian]]|date=August 6, 2011|access-date=February 1, 2012}}{{FJC Bio|nid=1393726|inline=yes}} == Career == From 1981 until 1986, Simon served as a trial attorney at the [[United States Department of Justice Antitrust Division]], in [[Washington, D.C.]], where he handled both civil and criminal antitrust matters. During his time with the DOJ, Simon also served in 1985 as a [[assistant United States attorney|special assistant United States attorney]] for the Eastern District of Virginia. In 1986, Simon joined the law firm of [[Perkins Coie]], where he specialized in business litigation in both state and federal court and acted as head of litigation for the firm's [[Portland, Oregon|Portland]] office. After becoming a partner with the firm in 1990, he handled several high-profile [[First Amendment to the United States Constitution|First Amendment]] cases on a [[pro bono]] basis. === Federal judicial service === On July 14, 2010, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Simon to a seat on the United States District Court for the District of Oregon to fill the seat vacated by Judge [[Ancer L. Haggerty]], who assumed [[senior status]] in August 2009.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/president-obama-names-five-united-states-district-court-0|title=President Obama Names Five to United States District Court|date=July 14, 2010|access-date=16 August 2010|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170216171747/https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/president-obama-names-five-united-states-district-court-0|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|archive-date=16 February 2017}}{{Cite web |url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/presidential-nominations-and-withdrawal-sent-senate-71410 |title=Presidential Nominations and Withdrawal Sent to the Senate, 7/14/10 | the White House |access-date=2011-06-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120323093836/http://m.whitehouse.gov/the-press-office/presidential-nominations-and-withdrawal-sent-senate-71410 |archive-date=2012-03-23 |url-status=live }} Simon's nomination lapsed at the end of 2010, and Obama renominated him on January 5, 2011. On February 17, 2011, the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] reported Simon's nomination to the full United States Senate by a 14–4 vote.{{cite web|url=https://afjjusticewatch.blogspot.com/2011/02/obama-nominates-two-district-court.html|title=Justice Watch: Obama Nominates Two District Court Judges, Four Other Nominees Sent to the Senate Floor|first=Alliance For|last=Justice|date=17 February 2011}} In his committee questionnaire, Simon encountered questions from Republican senators about his past work as a volunteer lawyer for the [[American Civil Liberties Union]].{{cite web|url=http://judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/112thCongressJudicialNominations/upload/MichaelSimon-QFRs.pdf|title=Questions for the Record|access-date=June 21, 2011|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160404213859/http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/112thCongressJudicialNominations/upload/MichaelSimon-QFRs.pdf|archive-date=April 4, 2016}} On June 21, 2011, the United States Senate confirmed Simon by a 64–35 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1121/vote_112_1_00092.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Michael H. Simon, of Oregon, to be U.S. District Judge)|website=senate.gov}} He received his commission on June 22, 2011. === Notable rulings === * On November 2, 2019, Simon issued a [[temporary restraining order]] against a Trump administration rule requiring immigrants prove they will have health insurance.{{Cite web |url=https://news.yahoo.com/us-judge-blocks-trumps-health-222526673.html |title=US He received his [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[Ohio State University]] in 1983 and his [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Capital University Law School]] in 1987. He was a member of the [[United States Air Force]] from 1975 to 1978 and was in the [[Ohio Air National Guard]] from 1978 to 1984. He rose to the rank of E5. Watson was a [[bailiff]]/[[law clerk]] of the [[Franklin County, Ohio|Franklin County]] [[Ohio Courts of Common Pleas|Court of Common Pleas]] from 1983 to 1988. He was in [[Practice of law|private practice]] in [[Ohio]] from 1988 to 1991 and was chief legal counsel of the [[Ohio Department of Commerce]] from 1991 to 1992. He was a deputy chief legal counsel in the [[Governor of Ohio|Office of the Governor of Ohio]] from 1992 to 1994 and was chief legal counsel from 1994 to 1995. Watson was a judge to the Franklin County Court of Common Pleas from 1996 to 2003. He was a judge to the Tenth District [[Ohio District Courts of Appeal|Ohio Court of Appeal]] from 2003 to 2004. ===Federal judicial service=== President [[George W. Bush]] nominated Watson to the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Ohio]] on April 6, 2004,{{cite web |title=Presidential Nomination: Michael Harrison Watson |url=https://georgewbush-whitehouse.archives.gov/news/nominations/1773.html |website=White House Archives}} to the seat vacated by Judge [[James L. Graham]]. His nomination generated no controversy. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate|Senate]] on September 7, 2004, by a [[voice vote]] and he received his commission on September 10, 2004. He assumed [[senior status]] on November 1, 2025.{{cite web|title=Watson, Michael H.|url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/watson-michael-h.|publisher=[[Federal Judicial Center]]|access-date=November 2, 2025}} ==== Ohio State University abuse scandal lawsuits ==== Since 2018, Watson has presided over the [[Ohio State University abuse scandal]] lawsuits, which has stalled in [[mediation]] for over 3 years and favored OSU defendants{{cite news |last=Marshall |first=Colleen |title=Plaintiffs claim OSU bargaining in bad faith with Strauss victims |date=5 May 2021 |url=https://www.nbc4i.com/news/local-news/new-lawsuit-claims-osu-bargaining-in-bad-faith-with-strauss-victims/ |work=[[WCMH-TV|NBC4i]] |access-date= 23 September 2021}}{{cite web |last=Langer |first=Jessica |last2=Orozco |first2=Jessica |title=Strauss victims respond to Ohio State's proposed settlement program |date=6 May 2021 |url=https://www.thelantern.com/2021/05/strauss-victims-respond-to-ohio-states-proposed-settlement-program/ |website=[[The Lantern]] |access-date=14 September 2021}} In September 2021, it was revealed that Judge Watson failed to disclose that his wife has a licensing agreement with the university to sell OSU flags; the judge offered to hear arguments requesting his [[recusal]].{{cite news |last1=Kovac |first1= Marc |last2=Hendrix |first2=Sheridan |date=2021-09-13 |title=Judge gives plaintiffs in Ohio State Strauss case until Sunday to request his recusal |url=https://www.dispatch.com/story/news/2021/09/13/federal-judge-gives-plaintiffs-option-recuse-him-strauss-cases/8316905002/ |newspaper=[[The Columbus Dispatch]] |access-date=14 September 2021}} Watson is also an [[adjunct faculty]] member at OSU, which would typically be a disqualification from presiding over his employer. The plaintiffs and Strauss survivors in these lawsuits are frustrated with the Judge and OSU.{{cite web |last=Szilagy |first=Sarah |editor-last=Orozco |editor-first=Jessica |title=As deadline nears, Strauss victims seek accountability, not Ohio State's settlement program |date=2 September 2021 |url=https://www.thelantern.com/projects/project/as-deadline-nears-strauss-victims-seek-accountability-not-ohio-states-settlement-program/ |website=[[The Lantern]]}} However, the Sixth Circuit later ruled that none of these grounds required Judge Watson's recusal.{{multiref2 |{{cite news |last=Franko |first=Kantele |date=2022-09-14 |title=Court revives lawsuits against Ohio State over sex abuse |url=https://apnews.com/article/sports-health-education-ohio-lawsuits-8a3167b13035516f68d72dd29b13dee7 |work=[[AP News]] |access-date=2024-08-23}} |{{cite web |title=Appeal from the United States District Court for the Southern District of Ohio at Columbus. Nos. 18-cv-00692 (21-3972); 19-cv-04746 (21-3974); 19-cv-02462 (21-3982); 21-cv-02542 (21-4070); 21-cv-02562 (21-4128) —Michael H. [[University of Minnesota Law School|University of Minnesota]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | footnotes = }} '''Michael James Davis''' (born July 21, 1947) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Minnesota]]. ==Early life, education, and career== Davis was born to Chester Davis and Doris Ruth Smith in [[Cincinnati]], Ohio, and grew up in [[Aurora, Illinois]]. He is the great-great-grandson of Nathan Hughes, an escaped slave who joined the Union Army and fought with the [[29th United States Colored Infantry Regiment]], was wounded twice, and was the only African American member of the [[Grand Army of the Republic]] in [[Kendall County, Illinois]].History on the Fox https://historyonthefox.wordpress.com/tag/juneteenth/ Davis graduated from [[East Aurora High School]] in 1965, where he was a star basketball player, wrote for the school newspaper, and served on the student council. He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[Macalester College]] in 1969 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Minnesota Law School]] in 1972.{{FJC Bio|nid=1379851|inline=yes}} Davis served as a [[law clerk]] for the Legal Rights Center from 1971 to 1973. He was an attorney in the Office of Legal Counsel for the [[Social Security Administration]] in [[Baltimore]] in 1973, and a [[criminal defense]] lawyer for the Neighborhood Justice Center in 1974. He returned to the Legal Rights Center as an attorney from 1975 to 1978. He then served as an attorney and commissioner at the Minneapolis Civil Rights Commission from 1977 to 1982 and as an attorney for the [[Hennepin County, Minnesota]], [[Public defender|Public Defender's]] Office from 1978 to 1983. Davis served as a judge in Hennepin County Municipal Court from 1983 to 1984 and a judge of the [[Minnesota District Courts|Fourth Judicial District of Minnesota]] (Hennepin County) from 1984 to 1994. Davis served as an adjunct professor at the [[University of Minnesota Law School]] from 1982 to 2013 and at [[William Mitchell College of Law]] from 1977 to 1981. He was also an instructor at the Minnesota Institute of Legal Education in 1991 and 1992. ===Federal judicial service=== On November 19, 1993, President [[Bill Clinton]] nominated Davis to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the District of Minnesota]] vacated by Judge [[Harry H. MacLaughlin]]. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate|Senate]] on March 25, 1994, and he received his commission on March 28, 1994. In May 1999, Chief Justice [[William Rehnquist]] appointed Davis to serve as a judge on the [[Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court]]. His term on this court expired on May 18, 2006. He served as the chief judge of the district court from 2008 to 2015.
