[[University of California, Berkeley School of Law|University of California, Berkeley]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | signature = | signature_alt = | website = | footnotes = }} '''Miranda Mai Du''' (born 1969) is an American lawyer who has served as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Nevada]]. As a district judge, Du has presided over a number of noteworthy cases, including a number regarding [[voting rights]]. She served as the chief judge of the court 2019 to 2024. ==Early life and education== Du was born in [[Cà Mau]], [[Vietnam]], in 1969.[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/MirandaDu-PublicQuestionnaire.pdf Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees: Miranda Mai Du], United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary. During the [[Vietnam War]], her father had been a supporter of the U.S.-backed [[Army of the Republic of Vietnam]], and the family left to [[Vietnamese in Malaysia|seek asylum in Malaysia]] when Du was nine years old,{{cite web | first=Erin | last=Gulden | url=https://www.superlawyers.com/nevada/article/an-ocean-of-experience/cc1640a5-da0d-46ba-8f0c-6cded31a8b50.html| title=An Ocean of Experience | work=Mountain States Rising Stars 2009 | date=July 2009 | access-date=August 3, 2011}} fleeing the country [[Boat people|by boat]].Jennifer Smith-Pulsipher, [https://www.nvbar.org/wp-content/uploads/NevadaLawyer_May2020_Du-Trutanich-Profiles.pdf Miranda M. Du: Chief Judge of the U.S. District Court for the District of Nevada], ''Nevada Lawyer'' (May 2020), p. 20.Linh Hua, "Du, Miranda (1969-)" in ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=3AxIAgAAQBAJ Asian Americans: An Encyclopedia of Social, Cultural, Economic, and Political History]'' (ed. Ziaojian Zhao & Edward J. W. Park: Greenwood, 2013), pp. 352-53. Du's family spent nearly a year in Malaysian [[refugee camp]]s before ultimately being granted asylum in the United States, being sponsored by a family in [[Winfield, Alabama]].[https://capac-chu.house.gov/press-release/capac-commends-president-obama-nominating-miranda-du-and-promoting-judicial-diversity CAPAC Commends President Obama for Nominating Miranda Du and Promoting Judicial Diversity] (press release), Congressional Asian Pacific American Caucus (August 2, 2011).[https://capac-chu.house.gov/press-release/capac-praises-confirmation-miranda-du-us-district-court CAPAC Praises Confirmation of Miranda Du to U.S. District Court] (press release), Congressional Asian Pacific American Caucus (March 28, 2012). Growing up, Du and her family lived in a number of places across the United States, including [[Winfield, Alabama]], where her father worked on a dairy farm. The family also lived at various times in [[Tuscaloosa, Alabama]]; [[Seattle, Washington]]; and [[Oakland, California]]. Du participated in [[Upward Bound]] in high school. Du received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] from [[University of California, Davis]], in 1991,{{cite web|publisher=[[White House Office of the Press Secretary]]| url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2011/08/02/president-obama-nominates-miranda-du-united-states-district-court-bench|title=President Obama Nominates Miranda Du to the United States District Court Bench|date=August 2, 2011}}{{FJC Bio|nid=1393941|inline=yes}} graduating with honors in history and economics. She earned her [[Juris Doctor]] from [[University of California, Berkeley School of Law]] in 1994. == Career == Upon graduating from law school, Du was admitted to the bar in Nevada in 1994 and in California in 1995. She took a job as an associate at the law firm McDonald Carano Wilson LLP in 1994 and was promoted to partner in 2002. She practiced for about one year in [[Las Vegas]], before transferring to the firm's [[Reno, Nevada]] office. Du practiced employment law, serving as chair of her firm's employment and labor practice group. ===Federal judicial service=== [[File:Harry_Reid_and_Miranda_Du.jpg|thumb|Miranda Du in 2012 with [[Senate Majority Leader]] [[Harry Reid]].]] On August 2, 2011, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Du to replace Judge [[Roger L. Hunt]], who assumed [[senior status]]. A substantial majority of the [[American Bar Association]]'s [[Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary]], which rates the qualifications of judicial nominees, rated Du as "qualified" for the post, with a minority rating her "not qualified" (the committee rates on a three-tier scale: well qualified, qualified, and not qualified).{{cite web|url=http://www.americanbar.org/content/dam/aba/uncategorized/2011/ratings112.authcheckdam.pdf|publisher=American Bar Association [[Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary]]|title=Ratings of Article III Judicial Nominees: 112th Congress|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160628165220/http://www.americanbar.org/content/dam/aba/uncategorized/2011/ratings112.authcheckdam.pdf|archive-date=2016-06-28}} Du's nomination and confirmation were strongly supported by Nevada's two U.S. senators, [[Harry Reid]] (Democrat) and [[Dean Heller]] (Republican),[https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CHRG-112shrg74979/html/CHRG-112shrg74979.htm Confirmation Hearings on Federal Appointments], [[112th United States Congress|112th Cong.]], 1st Session, S. Hrg. 112-72, Pt. 4, Senate Committee on the Judiciary (September 7, 2011). as well as the [[Congressional Asian Pacific American Caucus]].{{cite web|url=http://www.rafu.com/2012/04/miranda-du-confirmed-as-nevadas-first-apa-federal-district-court-judge/|title=Miranda Du Confirmed as Nevada's First APA Federal District Court Judge|newspaper=[[Rafu Shimpo]]|date=April 2, 2012}} Her confirmation was opposed by some Republican senators, who viewed her as too inexperienced and cited a sanction against her in 2007 by a Nevada federal court. On November 3, 2011, the [[Senate Judiciary Committee]] reported her nomination to the [[United States Senate|Senate]] floor by a 10–8 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/executive-business-meeting-2011-11-03|title=Executive Business Meeting: Full Committee|date=November 3, 2011|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary}} On March 28, 2012, Du's nomination was confirmed by a 59–39 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=112&session=2&vote=00061|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Miranda Du, of Nevada, to be U.S. District Judge)|publisher=United States Senate}}{{cite web|last=Linehan |first=Lawren |url=http://www.lvrj.com/news/nevada-judicial-nominee-faces-senate-vote-another-nominee-s-future-complicated-144663285.html|title=Reno attorney Du confirmed as federal judge|newspaper=Las Vegas Review-Journal|date=March 28, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120626070309/http://www.lvrj.com/news/nevada-judicial-nominee-faces-senate-vote-another-nominee-s-future-complicated-144663285.html |archive-date=2012-06-26 }} She received her commission two days later. Du became the first [[Asian Pacific American]] to serve as an [[Article III judge]] in Nevada. As a new district judge, Du initially worked in Las Vegas, but after about a year transferred her chambers to Reno, where she remains based.Carri Geer Thevenot, [https://www.reviewjournal.com/crime/courts/nevada-inmate-sentenced-for-threatening-federal-judge-1965334/ Nevada inmate sentenced for threatening federal judge], ''Las Vegas Review-Journal'' (February 24, 2020). She became chief judge of the court on September 2, 2019,{{Cite web |url=https://mynews4.com/news/local/judge-miranda-m-du-becomes-new-chief-judge-for-us-district-court-district-of-nevada |title=Judge Miranda M. Du becomes new Chief Judge for US District Court, District of Nevada |date=August 27, 2019|publisher=KRNV}} after Judge [[Gloria Navarro]] finished her term as chief judge. Du served as chief judge of the court during the [[COVID-19 pandemic in Nevada|coronavirus pandemic]], during which all federal trials and naturalization ceremonies in the judicial district were postponed.Jeff German & David Ferrara, [https://www.reviewjournal.com/news/politics-and-government/nevada/nevada-court-trials-on-hold-were-taking-it-day-by-day-1982615/ Nevada court trials on hold: 'We're taking it day by day'], ''Las Vegas Review-Journal'' (March 16, 2020). Her term as chief judge ended in September or October 2024. Du is part of the court's Patent Pilot Program, which allows judges who are not part of the program to have new [[United States patent law|patent]] and [[plant variety protection]] cases randomly reassigned to a judge who is participating in the program.[https://www.nvd.uscourts.gov/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/go2011.03.pdf First Amended General Order No. 2011-03: Patent Pilot Program], U.S. District Court for the District of Nevada (August 24, 2012). In February 2020, a Nevada prison inmate was sentenced to four years in prison for making threats of violence against Du. ====Voting rights decisions==== In 2016, Du granted a [[preliminary injunction]] sought by members of two Nevada [[Native Americans in the United States|Native American]] tribes (the [[Pyramid Lake Paiute]] and [[Walker River Paiute]]), compelling the [[Washoe County, Nevada|Washoe County]] registrar to set up [[early voting]] polling places at the tribes' reservations (in [[Nixon, Nevada|Nixon]] and [[Schurz, Nevada|Schurz]]), and to set up an [[Election Day]] polling place at Nixon. In the absence of the ruling, many tribal members would have had to travel nearly 100 miles round trip to reach polling sites, and Du ruled that Section 2 of the [[Voting Rights Act of 1965]] required the state to take the location of their reservations into account when planning polling locations. Du denied the plaintiffs' request to require the state to set up in-person voter registration locations at the reservations, holding that the tribes lacked standing to seek that form of relief.{{Cite news|author=Seth A. Richardson|url=https://www.rgj.com/story/news/politics/2016/10/07/tribe-says-they-have-enough-registered-voters-require-polling-site/91733818/|title=Judge rules partially in favor of tribes in federal suit|work=Reno Gazette Journal|date=October 7, 2016}}''[https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=965423729227541877 Sanchez v. Cegavske]'', 214 F. Supp. 3d 961 (D. Nev. 2016). In April and May 2020, Du twice rejected requests made by the right-wing group [[True the Vote]] and Nevada Right to Life seeking to cancel Nevada's [[Postal voting in the United States|mostly all-mail]] [[Partisan primary|primary election]]s, which was put in place by [[Nevada Secretary of State]] [[Barbara Cegavske]] because in-person voting risked [[COVID-19 pandemic in Nevada|spreading COVID-19]].Riley Snyder, [https://thenevadaindependent.com/article/judge-rejects-conservative-groups-attempt-to-block-planned-all-mail-primary Judge rejects conservative group’s attempt to block planned all-mail primary], ''Nevada Independent'' (April 30, 2020).Riley Snyder, [https://thenevadaindependent.com/article/judge-again-blocks-conservative-groups-effort-to-block-mail-only-primary-election Judge again blocks conservative group's effort to stop mail-only primary election], ''Nevada Independent'' (May 27, 2020). Du held that the groups lacked standing to seek to block an all-mail election and that "Defendants' interests in protecting the health and safety of Nevada's voters and to safeguard the voting franchise in light of the COVID-19 pandemic far outweigh any burden on Plaintiffs' [[right to vote]], particularly when that burden is premised on a speculative claim of voter fraud resulting in dilution of votes." In May 2020, Du issued a decision granting Fair Maps Nevada (a [[political action committee]] backed by the Nevada [[League of Women Voters]]) additional time to collect voter signatures necessary to put a [[ballot question|question on the ballot]] to create an independent Nevada [[redistricting]] commission. Du held that because the COVID-19 [[stay-at-home order]] issued by the Nevada authorities effectively prevented Fair Maps Nevada from gathering signatures for the period that the order was in effect, the Nevada Secretary of State's decision to refuse to extend the deadline to collect signatures was unreasonable and violated the First Amendment.Colton Lochhead, [https://www.reviewjournal.com/news/politics-and-government/ballot-petition-for-redistricting-commission-gets-more-signature-gathering-time-2039324/ Ballot petition for redistricting commission gets more signature-gathering time], ''Las Vegas Review-Journal'' (May 29, 2020). Du therefore extended the deadline to August 2020. However, Du declined Fair Maps Nevada's request to allow [[electronic signature]] gathering. ====Environment and land use decisions==== In 2015, Du denied a request by a number of rural Nevada counties, mining companies, and ranchers seeking a preliminary injunction to block a [[U.S. Department of the Interior]] policy that restricted development on federal lands in Nevada and eastern California to protect the [[greater sage grouse]].Scott Sonner, [https://apnews.com/c5dd70b9e71b411d8640f40ac6aaa46c Nevada judge denies counties' bid for sage grouse injunction], Associated Press (December 9, 2015). Du held that the plaintiffs had failed to demonstrate imminent, [[irreparable harm]], a prerequisite for obtaining a preliminary injunction.Bob Conrad, [https://thisisreno.com/2015/12/judge-denies-request-for-preliminary-injunction-in-sage-grouse-lawsuit/ Judge Denies Request for Preliminary Injunction in Sage Grouse Lawsuit], ''The Is Reno'' (December 8, 2015). In 2020, Du sided with the [[U.S. Forest Service]] and conservationists in upholding the Forest Service's power to prohibit [[off-roading]] within a {{convert|4|miles|km}} "buffer area" in the [[Mono Basin]] along the California-Nevada border for a three-month period, to protect the greater sage grouse [[mating season|mating grounds]].Scott Sonner, [https://apnews.com/358e1241efd142d9d9f79276692e522d Judge denies Nevada off-road challenge to grouse protection], Associated Press (July 13, 2020). The Sierra Trail Dogs Motorcycle and Recreation Club sued the Forest Service over the rule, which forced the postponement of the club's annual [[dirt bike]] race; Du held that under the [[National Environmental Policy Act]], the Forest Service's prohibition was a minor variation of the previously issued [[environmental impact statement]], and therefore the agency was not required to conduct a supplemental environmental review. In 2019, Du rejected a request by the Nevada state government for a [[preliminary injunction]] to block the [[U.S. Department of Energy]] from shipping weapons-grade [[plutonium]] from South Carolina's [[Savannah River Site]] to the [[Nevada National Security Site]].Humberto Sanchez, [https://thenevadaindependent.com/article/nevada-to-appeal-ruling-against-state-request-barring-more-plutonium-shipments Nevada to appeal ruling against state request barring more plutonium shipments], ''The Nevada Independent'' (February 4, 2019).[https://www.ktnv.com/news/nevada-to-appeal-judges-decision-not-to-block-plutonium Nevada to appeal judge's decision not to block plutonium], Associated Press (February 4, 2020).''[https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=18280168704018075595 Nevada v. United States]'', 364 F. Supp. 3d 1146 (D. Nev. 2019). Du found that an injunction was unwarranted because Nevada "cannot demonstrate the likelihood of irreparable harm in the absence of preliminary injunctive relief or that the balance of hardships tips in its favor". Nevada's appeal to the Ninth Circuit was dismissed as [[Mootness|moot]] because the federal government completed the plutonium shipments to Nevada.''[https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=14015170840889221734 Nevada v. United States]'', 783 F. App'x 700 (9th Cir. 2019).{{cite news |last=Sonner |first=Scott |title=Court rules for US in fight over Nevada plutonium shipment |date=August 13, 2019 |work=Associated Press |url=https://abcnews.go.com/Technology/wireStory/court-rules-us-fight-nevada-plutonium-shipment-64950688|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190813212800/https://abcnews.go.com/Technology/wireStory/court-rules-us-fight-nevada-plutonium-shipment-64950688|url-status=dead|archive-date=August 13, 2019}} ====Criminal law decisions==== In 2015, Du granted the [[habeas petition]] of Jose Echavarria, a death row inmate convicted of killing an FBI agent during a [[bank robbery]] in 1991. Echavarria's attorneys argued that his trial was unfair because the presiding judge was also being investigated by the FBI – a fact the [[Criminal defense lawyer|defense]] did not learn until after the trial ended. Du agreed and ruled that Echavarria was entitled to a new trial.{{Cite news|url=https://www.reviewjournal.com/local/local-las-vegas/bias-finding-prompts-new-trial-in-vegas-fbi-agent-murder/|title=Bias finding prompts new trial in Vegas FBI agent murder|date=January 23, 2015|work=Las Vegas Review-Journal|access-date=July 19, 2020}}[https://apnews.com/2cd0397a1839437b9a71151a982462dc Ruling upholds order for new trial for death row inmate], Associated Press (July 25, 2018).''[https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=9234979685710075812 Echavarria v. Baker]'', Case No. 3:98-cv-00202-MMD-VPC (D. Nev. Jan. 16, 2015). Du's ruling was upheld by the [[U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]].''[https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=14214053178676159036 Echavarria v. Filson]'', 896 F.3d 1118 (9th Cir. 2018). Du also presided over the criminal case against a doctor and hospital executive from [[Winnemucca, Nevada|Winnemucca]] in rural Nevada who illegally wrote prescriptions for [[opioid]]s without a medical purpose. The executive pleaded guilty to distribution of a [[Controlled Substances Act|controlled substance]];[https://apnews.com/7d40603825c148f5bcbc0d9369fdc9d8 Rural Nevada hospital exec guilty of opioid charges], Associated Press (February 6, 2019). Du sentenced him to a [[Year and a day rule|year and a day]] in federal prison, a $125,000 fine, and three years of supervised release.[https://mynews4.com/news/local/winnemucca-doctor-sentenced-to-prison-for-illegal-drug-prescriptions Former Winnemucca doctor sentenced to prison for illegal drug prescriptions], [[KRXI-TV]] (August 26, 2019). ====Other notable decisions==== Du was assigned to preside over ''Walden v. State of Nevada [[ex rel.]] [[Nevada Department of Corrections]]'', a major employment suit brought by several hundred Nevada state prison guards against the state.''Walden v. State of Nevada ex rel. Nevada Department of Corrections'', Case No. 3:14-cv-00320-MMD-WGC (Mar. 26, 2018).James DeHaven, [https://www.rgj.com/story/news/politics/2019/10/17/lawyers-nevada-prison-guards-owed-millions-unpaid-wages/4008879002/ 9th Circuit issues Nevada another blow in long-running legal fight with prison guards], ''Reno Gazette-Journal'' (October 18, 2019).[https://lasvegassun.com/news/2019/oct/21/nevada-could-face-100m-in-damages-to-state-prison/ Nevada could face $100M in damages to state prison guards], Associated Press (October 21, 2019). The guards allege that they are entitled to payment for tasks (such as debriefings, equipment collection, and uniform inspections) completed just before their shifts officially begin. In 2018, Du found that the state of Nevada had waived its [[sovereign immunity]] from suit by [[Removal jurisdiction|removing]] the guards' case from state court to federal court; that the pre-shift activities were "integral and indispensable" to the guards' jobs; and that the guards could thus pursue federal [[Fair Labor Standards Act]] claims against the state relating to overtime pay. Du dismissed the guards' breach-of-contract claims. In 2019, Du dismissed a suit brought by three Texas women who argued that [[Prostitution in Nevada|Nevada's legal prostitution law]] (the only one of its kind in the United States) conflicted with federal [[sex trafficking]] laws and therefore violated the [[Supremacy Clause]] of the [[U.S. Constitution]]. The women alleged that they had been victims of sexual violence in Nevada attributable to Nevada's legal brothels.Jackie Valley, [https://thenevadaindependent.com/article/federal-court-dismisses-lawsuit-seeking-to-end-brothel-industry Federal court dismisses lawsuit seeking to end brothel industry], ''Nevada Independent'' (October 31, 2019).Ken Ritter, [https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/news/nation-world/story/2019-10-31/us-judge-dismisses-case-against-legal-brothels-in-nevada US judge dismisses case against legal brothels in Nevada], Associated Press (October 31, 2019).''[https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16539409823034565128 Charleston v. State of Nevada]'', Case No. 3:19-cv-00107-MMD-WGC (D. Nev. 2019). In dismissing the suit, Du wrote: "While the Court empathizes with Plaintiffs for their [[lived experiences]], the Court cannot adjudicate Plaintiffs' claims because Plaintiffs fail to establish [[Standing (law)|standing]] to confer jurisdiction upon this Court." In May 2020, during the [[COVID-19 pandemic in Nevada]], Du denied a church's request for an emergency injunction that would allow it to exceed a 50-person cap on religious gatherings imposed by Governor [[Steve Sisolak]] to slow the spread of [[Coronavirus disease 2019|COVID-19]]. The church asserted that the 50-person limit violated their [[Free Exercise Clause|right to free exercise of religion]] and sought a court order allowing the church to exceed the limit for [[Pentecost Sunday]] services. Du denied the motion, writing that although the church members undoubtedly had "sincerely held religious convictions" they had failed to demonstrate "the diligence required to warrant emergency relief" because they had waited until one business day before Pentecost Sunday to seek an emergency injunction.Scott Sonner, [https://apnews.com/8cc34003eea60a6c3ed99ec87d77200c US judge won't lift 50-person cap on Nevada church services], Associated Press (May 29, 2020). In September 2020, Du ruled that [[Tesla, Inc.]] could not be sued for defamation after falsely alleging to several news outlets that a former employee, Martin Tripp, may "come back and shoot people" at Tesla's Gigafactory in Nevada.{{cite web |url=https://www.theverge.com/2020/9/19/21446587/judge-dismiss-defamation-employee-tesla-leak-elon-musk-model-3 |title=Judge throws out defamation case against Tesla by former employee |author=Kim Lyons |date=19 September 2020 |website=[[The Verge]] |access-date=19 September 2020 }} In the same ruling, Du refused to dismiss Tesla's suit against Tripp for leaking a Tesla document. In April 2025, Du ruled that "a [[tower dump]] is a search and the warrant law enforcement used to get it is a general warrant forbidden under the Fourth Amendment" but that "the Court will not order any evidence suppressed".{{Cite web |last=Gault |first=Matthew |date=2025-04-18 |title=Judge Rules Blanket Search of Cell Tower Data Unconstitutional |url=https://www.404media.co/judge-rules-blanket-search-of-cell-tower-data-unconstitutional/ |archive-url=https://archive.today/20250418140827/https://www.404media.co/judge-rules-blanket-search-of-cell-tower-data-unconstitutional/ |archive-date=18 April 2025 |website=[[404 Media]] |language=en}}{{Cite web |last=Roth |first=Emma |date=2025-04-18 |title=Cops can't do cell tower mass surveillance 'dumps,' court rules |url=https://www.theverge.com/news/652036/cops-cell-tower-dumps-unconstitutional-court-ruling |website=[[The Verge]] |language=en-US}} ==See also== *[[List of Asian American jurists]] *[[List of first women lawyers and judges in Nevada]] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1393941}} *{{Ballotpedia|Miranda_Du}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Roger L. Monti Belot:
{{Short description|American judge (born 1943)}} {{Infobox officeholder | honorific_prefix = | name = Monti Belot | honorific_suffix = | image = | alt = | caption = | office = [[Senior status|Senior Judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Kansas]] | term_start = March 4, 2008 | term_end = | office1 = Judge of the [[United States District Court for the District of Kansas]] | term_start1 = November 25, 1991 | term_end1 = March 4, 2008 | appointer1 = [[List of federal judges appointed by George H. W. Bush|George H. W. Bush]] | predecessor1 = ''Seat established by 104 Stat. 5089'' | successor1 = [[Eric F. Melgren]] | pronunciation = | birth_name = Monti Louis Belot | birth_date = {{Birth date and age|1943|03|04}} | birth_place = [[Kansas City, Missouri]], U.S. | death_date = | death_place = | death_cause = | resting_place = | resting_place_coordinates = | citizenship = | party = | other_party = | height = | spouse = | partner = | relations = | children = | parents = | mother = | father = | relatives = | education = [[University of Kansas]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|BA]], [[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | footnotes = }} '''Monti Louis Belot''' (born March 4, 1943) is an inactive [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Kansas]]. ==Early life and career== Belot was born in [[Kansas City, Missouri]]. He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from the [[University of Kansas]] in 1965 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Kansas School of Law]] in 1968. He was a [[United States Naval Reserve]] Legal officer, in the JAG Corps, from 1968 to 1971. He was a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Wesley E. Brown]] of the United States District Court for the District of Kansas from 1971 to 1973. He was an [[assistant United States attorney]] in [[Topeka, Kansas]] from 1973 to 1976. He was a special assistant to the [[United States attorney]] in Topeka from 1976 to 1978. He was in private practice in [[Kansas City, Kansas]] from 1976 to 1983. He was in private practice in [[Coffeyville, Kansas]] from 1983 to 1991.{{FJC Bio|nid=1377726|inline=yes}} ===Federal judicial service=== On July 26, 1991, Belot was nominated by President [[George H. W. Bush]] to a new seat on the [[United States District Court for the District of Kansas]] created by 104 Stat. 5089. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on November 21, 1991, and received his commission on November 25, 1991. He assumed [[senior status]] on March 4, 2008. ===Schneider trial=== Belot presided over the trial of Stephen and Linda Schneider, charged with illegally distributing prescription painkillers.[[Adam Liptak|Liptak, Adam]] (2010-11-01) [https://www.nytimes.com/2010/11/02/us/02bar.html?_r=1 Outspoken Activist's Case Becomes Tangled in Secrets]. ''[[New York Times]]'' In that capacity, he threw out all but 4 of the 56 alleged patient overdose deaths Assistant [[United States Attorney]] Tanya Treadway attempted to link to the Schneiders, "sternly warned Treadway not to appeal his decision [and] also instructed the government not to use inflammatory descriptions like '[[pill mill]]' in front of the jury."[[Radley Balko|Balko, Radley]] (2009-05-06) [http://reason.com/blog/2009/05/06/tenth-circuit-to-hear-argument Tenth Circuit to Hear Arguments Today on the Science Behind Painkiller Prosecutions], ''[[Reason Magazine|Reason]]'' Belot also denied federal prosecutor Tanya Treadway's request for a gag order on [[Pain Relief Network]] founder and pain relief advocate [[Siobhan Reynolds]], as well as her request for a change of venue.[[Radley Balko|Balko, Radley]] (2010-12-21) [http://www.slate.com/id/2278244/pagenum/all/ The Worst Kind of Ham Sandwich], ''[[Slate.com]]'' However, by the time Belot sentenced the Schneiders to 30 years in prison in October 2010, "he was so irritated by Reynolds' advocacy on behalf of the couple that he could not contain himself."[[Jacob Sullum|Sullum, Jacob]] (2010-11-17) [http://reason.com/archives/2010/11/17/chilling-her-softly Chilling Her Softly], ''[[Reason Magazine|Reason]]'' In his sentencing opinion,{{cite web|url=http://reason.com/assets/db/1289232486248.pdf|title=Schneider Sentencing Opinion|publisher=}} "he digressed to take a swipe at Ms. Reynolds and her group, though he did not get its name quite right," saying "he hoped the prison sentences would 'curtail or stop the activities of the [[Bozo the Clown]] outfit known as the Pain Control Network, a [[ship of fools]] if there ever was one.' He added that the group and its leaders were 'stupid' and 'deranged.'" Journalist [[Jacob Sullum]] referred to these statements as "an extraordinary tirade against Reynolds and PRN, neither of which was a party to the case," adding:
Is Belot really saying that one function of the heavy sentences imposed on the Schneiders is to deter Reynolds and like-minded activists from speaking out against such prosecutions in the future? That's certainly what it sounds like. Reynolds seems to have a real talent for getting under the skin of people in power. But that is not a crime—or at least it shouldn't be.[[Jacob Sullum|Sullum, Jacob]] (2010-11-08) [http://reason.com/blog/2010/11/08/if-we-unsealed-the-brief-they If We Unsealed the Brief, You Might Talk About It], ''[[Reason Magazine|Reason]]''

Mustafa T. Kasubhai:
{{Short description|American judge (born 1970)}} {{Infobox judge | name = Mustafa T. Kasubhai | image = Judge Mustafa T. Kasubhai (cropped).jpg | alt = | office = Judge of the [[United States District Court for the District of Oregon]] | term_start = November 22, 2024 | term_end = | appointer = [[List of federal judges appointed by Joe Biden|Joe Biden]] | predecessor = [[Ann Aiken]] | successor = | office1 = Magistrate Judge of the [[United States District Court for the District of Oregon]] | term_start1 = September 21, 2018 | term_end1 = November 22, 2024 | predecessor1 = Jolie A. Russo | successor1 = | office2 = Judge for the [[Lane County, Oregon|Lane County]] Circuit Court | term_start2 = 2007 | term_end2 = 2018 | appointer2 = [[Ted Kulongoski]] | education = [[University of California, Berkeley]] ([[Bachelor of Sciences|BS]])
[[University of Oregon School of Law|University of Oregon]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | birth_name = | birth_date = {{Birth year and age|1970}} | birth_place = {{nowrap|[[Reseda, Los Angeles]], California, U.S.}} | known_for = | website = [https://www.ord.uscourts.gov/index.php/court-info/our-judges/judge-kasubhai District Court Webpage] | footnotes = }} '''Mustafa Taher Kasubhai''' (born 1970){{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/kasubhai_sjq2.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=October 4, 2023}} is an American lawyer who has served as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Oregon]] since 2024. He previously served as a [[United States magistrate judge]] of the same court from 2018 to 2024 as well as a judge on the [[Lane County, Oregon|Lane County]] [[Oregon Circuit Court|Circuit Court]] from 2007 to 2018. He is the first [[Islam|Muslim]] to serve as a federal judge in the United States.Kasubhai became the first Muslim to serve as a federal judge following his appointment as a Magistrate Judge for the [[United States District Court for the District of Oregon|District of Oregon]]. Kasubhai was not the first Muslim [[Article III judge]] however, as [[Zahid Quraishi]] was confirmed to the [[United States District Court for the District of New Jersey|District of New Jersey]] prior to Kasubhai's respective confirmation to the District of Oregon == Early life and career == Kasubhai was born in the [[Los Angeles]] suburb of [[Reseda, Los Angeles|Reseda]] in the [[San Fernando Valley]] in 1970, and grew up in the Los Angeles suburb of [[Canoga Park]]. His parents were [[Gujarati people|Gujarati]] [[Dawoodi Bohra]] [[Indian Americans|Indian]] immigrants, having moved to the United States from [[Mumbai]] in the 1960s.{{Cite news|last=Newton|first=Cynthia|date=2019|title=Multnomah Bar Lawyer, page 11|work=Multnomah Bar Association|url=https://mbabar.org/assets/MLs/2019/Mar2019-ML-Final_web.pdf}} Kasubhai graduated from the [[University of California, Berkeley]] in 1992 with a degree in business administration. He completed his [[Juris Doctor]] degree at the [[University of Oregon School of Law]] in 1996.{{cite news |last1=Voruganti |first1=Harsh |title=Mustafa Kasubhai – Nominee to the U.S. District Court for the District of Oregon |url=https://vettingroom.org/2023/10/23/mustafa-kasubhai/ |access-date=25 June 2024 |work=The Vetting Room |date=23 October 2023 |language=en}} Kasubhai began his private legal career in a small [[Civil law (legal system)|civil]] [[plaintiff]]'s firm until he opened his own practice, the Law Offices of Mustafa T. Kasubhai. He worked primarily between [[Klamath Falls, Oregon|Klamath Falls]] and [[Eugene, Oregon]], representing workers and unions in [[workers compensation]] cases and plaintiffs in civil cases primarily involving [[torts]] and [[Occupational injury|work-related injuries]].{{Cite journal|last=Bailey|first=Kirk|title=New judge brings changes to Lane County court.|url=https://scholarsbank.uoregon.edu/xmlui/bitstream/handle/1794/10018/OQ_Autumn09.pdf;jsessionid=C7AB2A44826CB05CEB58C517AA37286D?sequence=1|journal=Oregon Quarterly|volume=Fall 2009|pages=48}} In 2003, [[Oregon Governor]] [[Ted Kulongoski]] nominated Kasubhai to serve on the Oregon Workers' Compensation Board as one of its labor members in [[Salem, Oregon]]. He remained there until joining the state bench in 2007. == Judicial career == Governor Kulongoski appointed Kasubhai as a judge on the [[Lane County, Oregon|Lane County]] [[Oregon circuit courts|Circuit Court]] in 2007. He was re-elected to another six-year term in 2014. Kasubhai is the first [[South Asian Americans|South Asian]]-American and [[Muslim]] judge to be appointed to the Lane County Circuit Court.{{Cite web|title=Oregon Federal District Court Appoints First Muslim American to be a Federal Judge.|url=http://oapaba.org/oregon-federal-district-court-appoints-first-muslim-american-to-be-a-federal-judge/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190226170826/http://oapaba.org/oregon-federal-district-court-appoints-first-muslim-american-to-be-a-federal-judge/|url-status=dead|archive-date=February 26, 2019}} Following his appointment as a [[United States magistrate judge|magistrate judge]] for the District of Oregon in 2018, he became the first Muslim-American to serve as a federal judge in the United States.{{cite web |last1=Shumway |first1=Julia | url=https://www.corvallisadvocate.com/2024/oregons-newest-u-s-district-court-judge-was-the-first-muslim-american-to-serve-on-the-federal-bench/ | title=Oregon’s Newest U.S. District Court Judge was the First Muslim American to Serve on the Federal Bench | website=The Corvallis Advocate | date=November 27, 2024 |access-date=December 9, 2024}}{{cite web |last1=Shumway |first1=Julia | url=https://www.oregoncapitalinsider.com/news/u-s-senate-confirms-mustafa-kasubhai-as-oregon-district-judge/article_7e716a6e-a6bd-11ef-b25c-db2c5da170b7.html | title=U.S. Senate confirms Mustafa Kasubhai as Oregon district judge | website=[[Oregon Capital Insider]] | date=November 19, 2024 |access-date=December 9, 2024}} [[File:Mustafa Kasubhai.jpg|thumb|right|250px|Mustafa T. Kasubhai U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee hearing - October 4, 2023]] === Federal judicial service === On June 1, 2023, Kasubhai was one of six names U.S. senators [[Ron Wyden]] and [[Jeff Merkley]] submitted to the White House for a vacancy on the [[United States District Court for the District of Oregon]] created by [[Marco A. Hernandez]], who subsequently assumed [[senior status]] on August 21, 2024.{{Citation |title=Names of 6 finalists forwarded to White House for upcoming federal court vacancy in Oregon |url=https://www.oregonlive.com/crime/2023/06/names-of-6-finalists-forwarded-to-white-house-for-upcoming-federal-court-vacancy-in-oregon.html|language=en |access-date=2023-06-01}} On September 6, 2023, President [[Joe Biden]] announced his intent to nominate Kasubhai to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Oregon]].{{Cite press release |title=President Biden Names Thirty-Eighth Round of Judicial Nominees |date=September 6, 2023 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2023/09/06/president-biden-names-thirty-eighth-round-of-judicial-nominees/ |access-date=September 6, 2023}} {{PD-notice}} On September 18, 2023, his nomination was sent to the Senate. President Biden nominated Kasubhai to the seat being vacated by Judge [[Ann Aiken]], who subsequently assumed [[senior status]] on December 29, 2023.{{Cite press release|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |date=September 18, 2023 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2023/09/18/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-120/}} On October 4, 2023, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web|title=Nominations|date=October 3, 2023|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/committee-activity/hearings/09/27/2023/nominations}} During his confirmation hearing, Republican senators questioned him over a ruling that he made in 2020 regarding the [[George Floyd protests]] and his statements and writings about [[diversity, equity, and inclusion]].{{Cite news|last=Raymond|first=Nate|title=Senate Republicans question Oregon judicial nominee's support for diversity|url=https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/senate-republicans-question-oregon-judicial-nominees-support-diversity-2023-10-04/|website=Reuters|access-date=October 4, 2023}} Kasubhai was also questioned on guidance he created for the use of [[Preferred gender pronoun|preferred pronouns]] and honorifics in his courtroom, and whether he was a [[Marxism|Marxist]] based on his past writings.{{Cite web |date=November 2, 2023 |title=Judiciary Panel Unexpectedly Delays Votes on Biden Judge |url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/judiciary-panel-unexpectedly-delays-votes-on-biden-judge-picks?source=newsletter&item=read-text®ion=digest |language=en-US}} On November 9, 2023, his nomination was favorably reported out of committee by a party-line 11–10 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/2023-11-09_-_ebm_-_results.pdf|title=Results of Executive November 13, 2023, his nomination was returned to the Judiciary Committee because of issues regarding [[proxy voting]] in committee.{{Cite web|url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/ip-law/senate-returns-two-district-court-nominations-to-judiciary-panel|title=Senate Returns Two District Court Nominations to Judiciary Panel|publisher=Bloomberg an 11–10 [[party-line vote]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/2024-01-18_-_ebm_-_results1.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – January 18, 2024, a cloture vote to advance Kasubhai's nomination was set to take place in the U.S. Senate. Majority Leader [[Chuck Schumer]] cancelled the planned vote, citing attendance issues. According to ''Bloomberg Law'', "Kasubhai has faced intense opposition from GOP lawmakers who've said that he's too radical for the federal bench."{{cite news |last1=Headley |first1=Tiana |title=Senate Democrats Pull Vote on Trial Court Nominee Kasubhai (1) |url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/senate-democrats-pull-vote-on-us-trial-court-nominee-kasubhai |access-date=25 June 2024 |work=news.bloomberglaw.com |date=June 18, 2024 |language=en}} On November 19, 2024, the Senate invoked [[cloture]] on his nomination by a 51–43 vote.{{Cite web|date=November 19, 2024|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Mustafa Taher Kasubhai to be United States District Judge for the District of Oregon.)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1182/vote_118_2_00284.htm|access-date=November 19, 2024|website=United States Senate}} Later that day, his nomination was confirmed by a 51–44 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1182/vote_118_2_00285.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Mustafa Taher Kasubhai, of Oregon, to be United States District Judge for the District of Oregon)|website=United States Senate|date=November 19, 2024|access-date=November 19, 2024}} He received his judicial commission on November 22, 2024.{{FJC Bio|nid=13761892|inline=yes}} ===Notable cases=== In ''State of New York v. United States Department of Energy'' (2025), Kasubhai blocked a [[U.S. Department of Energy]] policy that limited reimbursement of indirect and employee-benefit costs for state and local government grants to 10 percent of the total award. He held that the policy conflicted with federal regulations requiring agencies to recognize negotiated indirect-cost rates, vacated the policy, and enjoined the department from implementing it. The Department of Energy subsequently rescinded the policy and voluntarily dismissed its appeal.{{cite news |last=Mills |first=Taylor |title=Energy Department’s Cap on Financial Assistance Blocked by Judge |url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/litigation/energy-departments-cap-on-financial-assistance-blocked-by-judge |work=Bloomberg Law |date=November 11, 2025 |access-date=July 18, 2026}} In ''United States v. Oregon'' (2026), Kasubhai dismissed a [[Department of Justice]] lawsuit seeking Oregon's unredacted statewide voter-registration records, which included information such as full dates of birth, driver's-license numbers, and partial Social Security numbers. He concluded that the [[National Voter Registration Act]], the [[Help America Vote Act]], and the [[Civil Rights Act of 1960]] did not authorize the federal government to compel production of the requested information.{{cite news |last=Rush |first=Claire |title=Federal judge dismisses Justice Department lawsuit seeking Oregon's voter rolls |url=https://apnews.com/article/f0a3477a5fa061cc71e9ee6ce652ff7a |agency=Associated Press |date=January 26, 2026 |access-date=July 18, 2026}} The decision is currently on appeal in the [[Ninth Circuit]].{{cite web |title=On Election Day, Attorney General Rayfield Defends Voter Privacy at Ninth Circuit |url=https://www.doj.state.or.us/media-home/news-media-releases/ag-rayfield-defends-voter-privacy-at-court-of-appeals/ |publisher=Oregon Department of Justice |date=May 19, 2026 |access-date=July 18, 2026}} In ''M-J-M-A- v. Wamsley'' (2026), Kasubhai issued a preliminary injunction restricting warrantless civil-immigration arrests in Oregon. Kasubhai's order required immigration officers making an arrest without a warrant to first make an individualized determination, supported by probable cause, that the person was likely to escape before a warrant could be obtained.{{cite news |title=ICE agents can't make warrantless arrests in Oregon unless there's a risk of escape, US judge rules |url=https://apnews.com/article/f21f3856e3c60e283e7be4bac1f04272 |agency=Associated Press |date=February 4, 2026 |access-date=July 18, 2026}} In ''Oregon v. Kennedy'' (2026), Kasubhai granted summary judgment to a coalition of states challenging a declaration issued by Secretary of Health and Human Services [[Robert F. Kennedy Jr.]] concerning gender-affirming medical care for minors. The declaration stated that such care did not meet professionally recognized standards and asserted that providers offering it could be excluded from federal programs including Medicare and Medicaid. Kasubhai held that the declaration exceeded the department's statutory authority, had been issued without required notice-and-comment procedures, and improperly displaced state-recognized standards of medical care. He vacated the declaration and enjoined the department from enforcing it or a materially similar policy against providers in the plaintiff states.{{cite news |title=Judge says he will bar RFK move aimed at cutting gender-affirming care for minors |url=https://www.reuters.com/business/healthcare-pharmaceuticals/judge-says-he-will-bar-rfk-move-aimed-cutting-gender-affirming-care-minors-2026-03-20/ |work=Reuters |date=March 20, 2026 |access-date=July 18, 2026}}{{cite web |last1=Merrill |first1=Monique |title=Federal judge blocks RFK declaration targeting gender-affirming care |url=https://www.courthousenews.com/federal-judge-blocks-rfk-declaration-targeting-gender-affirming-care/ |website=Courthouse News Service |date=March 19, 2026}} In ''Renshaw v. General Services Administration'' (2026), Kasubhai granted a preliminary injunction sought by [[Eugene, Oregon|Eugene]]-area activists challenging a security fence that prevented public access to much of the plaza surrounding the Eugene Federal Building. The building had been the site of recurring protests against immigration enforcement and the Trump administration. The [[General Services Administration]] announced plans for the fence after a January 30, 2026 protest was declared a riot by Eugene police following damage to the building, including broken windows. The agency said the fence barrier was necessary to protect federal employees, visitors, and the facility.{{cite news |last=Wilk |first=Nathan |title=Eugene builds new sidewalk at Federal Building in response to proposed fence |url=https://www.klcc.org/politics-government/2026-04-27/eugene-builds-new-sidewalk-at-federal-building-in-response-to-proposed-fence |work=KLCC |date=April 27, 2026 |access-date=July 18, 2026}}{{cite news |last=Ziegler |first=Zac |title=How much did the fence around Eugene’s federal building cost? Contract data gives an idea |url=https://www.klcc.org/politics-government/2026-05-07/how-much-did-the-fence-around-eugenes-federal-building-cost-contract-data-gives-an-idea |work=KLCC |date=May 7, 2026 |access-date=July 18, 2026}} Kasubhai concluded that the plaintiffs were likely to establish that the plaza was a traditional public forum and that closing nearly the entire area was not narrowly tailored to the government's security interests. Kasubhai ordered the General Services Administration to remove the fence, while permitting more limited security measures immediately surrounding the building's entrances and windows. After a brief administrative stay during appellate proceedings, the fence was removed in July 2026.{{cite news |last=Wilk |first=Nathan |title=Judge orders fence around Eugene Federal Building to be removed |url=https://www.klcc.org/breaking/2026-06-22/judge-orders-fence-around-eugene-federal-building-removed |work=KLCC |date=June 22, 2026 |access-date=July 18, 2026}}{{cite news |last=Adame |date=June 22, 2026 |access-date=July 18, 2026}}{{cite news |title=The Fence has Fallen |url=https://eugeneweekly.com/2026/07/02/the-fence-has-fallen/ |work=Eugene Weekly |date=July 2, 2026 '''Myron Herbert Thompson''' (born January 7, 1947) is a [[United States federal judge|senior United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Middle District of Alabama]].
In 2026, he was elected to the [[American Philosophical Society]].
==Education and career==

Born in [[Tuskegee, Alabama|Tuskegee]], [[Alabama]], Thompson received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[Yale University]] in 1969 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Yale Law School]] in 1972. He was an Assistant [[Attorney General of Alabama]] from 1972 to 1974, and the first African American to hold this position<ref>{{cite journal |title=Judge Myron H. Thompson |journal=United States District Court for the Middle District of Alabama |url=https://www.almd.uscourts.gov/judges/myron-h-thompson |access-date=12 June 2026}}</ref>, and then in private practice in [[Dothan, Alabama|Dothan]], Alabama until 1980.

==Federal judicial service==
[[File:Myron H. Thompson official.jpg|thumb|right|Judge Thompson's portrait.]]
On September 17, 1980, Thompson was nominated by President [[Jimmy Carter]] to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Middle District of Alabama]] vacated by Judge [[Frank Minis Johnson]]. Thompson was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on September 26, 1980, and received his commission on September 29, 1980. He served as Chief Judge from 1991 to 1998, and he was the first African American Chief Judge of any U.S. District Court in the State of Alabama.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Judge Thompson to Deliver Commencement Address |journal=University of Alabama |date=30 March 2016 |url=https://law.ua.edu/news/judge-thompson-to-deliver-commencement-address/ |access-date=12 June 2026}}</ref> He took [[senior status]] on August 22, 2013.<ref>[http://www.montgomeryadvertiser.com/article/20130824/NEWS02/308240040/Federal-judge-Myron-Thompson-moves-senior-status-Obama-appoint-successor?nclick_check=1 ''Montgomery Advertiser'', "Federal judge Myron Thompson moves to senior status; Obama to appoint successor," August 24, 2013] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130828072029/http://www.montgomeryadvertiser.com/article/20130824/NEWS02/308240040/Federal-judge-Myron-Thompson-moves-senior-status-Obama-appoint-successor?nclick_check=1 |date=August 28, 2013 }}</ref> As of 2025, he is the last Democratic appointee to serve on the District Court for the Middle District of Alabama, and also the last judge appointed by a Democratic president to that court.

==Notable cases==

In 2013, in a redistricting case heard by a three-judge panel, Thompson disagreed with its decision contending it was an illegal use of racial quotas. He wrote that Alabama's use of the [[Voting Rights Act]] was a "cruel irony," that as the state was simultaneously arguing before the Supreme Court in ''[[Shelby County v. Holder]]'', that Section 5 should be found unconstitutional, it was "relying on racial quotas…and seeking to justify those quotas with the very provision it was helping to render inert."<ref>[https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2014/11/alabama-supreme-court-racial-gerrymandering/After Gutting the Voting Rights Act, Alabama Cites It As an Excuse for Racial Gerrymandering], ''[[Mother Jones (magazine)|Mother Jones]]'', November 2014. Retrieved June 12, 2021.</ref> On October 29, 2019, Judge Thompson issued a preliminary injunction blocking the Human Life Protection Act from taking effect in Alabama as prescribed on November 15, 2019. The Alabama law "imposes criminal liability on abortion providers for nearly all abortions, completed or attempted, regardless of fetal viability." In essence," the Court said, "the Act imposes a near-total ban on abortion." Judge Thompson concluded, "The court is persuaded that the plaintiffs are likely to succeed in showing that the Act violates an individual’s constitutional right to obtain a pre-viability abortion, and thus that it violates her constitutional rights."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.scribd.com/document/432554248/Myron-Thompson-Order#from_embed|title=Myron Thompson Order | PDF | Justice | Crime & Violence}}</ref> In 2014,  in ''[[Planned Parenthood]] Southeast, Inc., v. [[Luther Strange|Strange]],'' (also known as ''Planned Parenthood Southeast, Inc., v. [[Robert J. Bentley|Bentley]]''), Thompson ruled an Alabama law regulating abortion unconstitutional, citing the [[undue burden standard]].<ref>[http://www.cnn.com/2014/08/05/justice/alabama-abortion-federal-court-ruling/index.html?hpt=hp_t2 CNN.com: Federal judge: Abortion like right to bear arms]</ref><ref>[https://ecf.almd.uscourts.gov/cgi-bin/show_public_doc?2013cv0405-238 Opinion, from U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Alabama]</ref>

'''Nancy Dell Freudenthal''' (née '''Roan''', born 1954) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Wyoming]]. She is the first female judge to serve in the District of Wyoming.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.afj.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/06/President-Obama-Female-Firsts.pdf |title=Making History: President Obama's Female Judicial Nominees |publisher=[[Alliance for Justice]] |date=June 11, 2013 |access-date=December 14, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180928205158/https://www.afj.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/06/President-Obama-Female-Firsts.pdf |archive-date=September 28, 2018 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Freudenthal was also the [[First Lady]] of [[Wyoming]] from January 6, 2003, to January 3, 2011, as the wife of Governor [[Dave Freudenthal]].

== Early life and education ==

Born in 1954, in [[Cody, Wyoming]],<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.lawyercentral.com/nancy-d-freudenthal-interactive-profile--20-706103.html |title=Attorney Nancy D Freudenthal – Lawyer in Sheridan WY |website=www.lawyercentral.com |access-date=2016-03-28 |archive-date=2016-04-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160408041602/http://www.lawyercentral.com/nancy-d-freudenthal-interactive-profile--20-706103.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> Freudenthal earned a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in 1976 from the [[University of Wyoming]] and a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1980 from the [[University of Wyoming College of Law]].<ref name=whgov_20091204>{{cite web |url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/president-obama-nominates-nancy-freudenthal-judge-d-price-marshall-jr-and-judge-ben |title=President Obama Nominates Nancy Freudenthal, Judge D. Price Marshall Jr. and Judge Benita Pearson to Serve on the District Court Bench |date=December 4, 2009 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170216173510/https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/president-obama-nominates-nancy-freudenthal-judge-d-price-marshall-jr-and-judge-ben |via=[[NARA|National Archives]] |work=[[whitehouse.gov]] |archive-date=February 16, 2017 }}</ref><ref name="fjc.gov">{{FJC Bio|nid=1393106}}</ref>

== Career ==

From 1980 until 1989, Freudenthal worked in the office of the Wyoming governor as an attorney for intergovernmental affairs.<ref name=whgov_20091204/> From 1985 to 1986, she was an [[adjunct professor]] at the University of Wyoming College of Law.<ref name="fjc.gov"/> From 1989 to 1991, she served on the Wyoming Tax Commission, and from 1989 until 1995, she was on the board of the Wyoming Board of Equalization.<ref name=whgov_20091204/> Freudenthal has spent much of her legal career working on energy and environmental issues.<ref name="Billings Gazette">{{cite news |url=http://billingsgazette.com/news/state-and-regional/wyoming/article_94911810-061b-11df-b6dd-001cc4c002e0.html |title=Smooth sailing in Senate for Nancy Freudenthal |agency=Associated Press |newspaper=Billings Gazette |date=January 20, 2010}}</ref> In 1995, she took a job as an associate at the [[Cheyenne, Wyoming]] law firm of Davis & Cannon. In 1998, she became a partner and held that post until her nomination as a federal judge.<ref name=whgov_20091204/><ref name="fjc.gov"/>

=== Federal judicial service ===

According to the questionnaire that Freudenthal submitted to the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]], after the election of [[Barack Obama]], Freudenthal's husband, Wyoming Gov. [[Dave Freudenthal]], asked her if she would be interested in serving as a federal district judge for Wyoming. Her husband subsequently—without telling her—submitted three possible nominees to the Obama administration for it to consider nominating: his wife, another attorney, Ford Bussart, and a state district court judge, Norman E. Young.<ref name=neary_20090514>{{cite news |first=Ben |last=Neary |url=http://www.trib.com/news/state-and-regional/article_76f75627-95c4-5449-84fa-ffb5f123255a.html |title=Gov nominates wife for federal court |newspaper=[[Casper Star-Tribune]] |date=May 14, 2009}}</ref> "I thought about that long and hard, and the question really came down to (was) should she be penalized for having married me," Dave Freudenthal told a local newspaper. "And the conclusion I came down to is that all three of them are qualified, and fortunately, it's up to the president and not me."<ref name=neary_20090514/><ref name="fjc.gov"/>

In August 2009, the [[United States Department of Justice]] contacted Nancy Freudenthal about the nomination and she was interviewed by Justice Department lawyers on October 5, 2009. Obama formally submitted her nomination to the [[United States District Court for the District of Wyoming]] on December 3, 2009.<ref name=whgov_20091204/> Freudenthal would fill the vacancy created in 2006 when Judge [[Clarence Addison Brimmer Jr.]] assumed [[senior status]].  President George W. Bush previously nominated [[Richard Honaker]] for the seat, but he never received a hearing on his nomination.<ref name=neary_20090514/> The [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]] held a hearing on Freudenthal's nomination on January 20, 2010.<ref name="Billings Gazette" /> On May 5, 2010, the [[United States Senate]] confirmed Freudenthal by a 96–1 vote.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1112/vote_111_2_00129.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Nancy D. Freudenthal, of Wyoming, to be U.S. District Judge)|publisher=United States Senate|date=May 5, 2010}}</ref> She received her judicial commission on May 6, 2010. Freudenthal served as Chief Judge from July 24, 2011, to May 31, 2018. She assumed [[senior status]] on June 1, 2022.<ref name="fjc.gov"/>

She previously served in the role of city attorney for the city of [[New Orleans]] from the time that Mayor [[Mitch Landrieu]] hired her in May 2010 until becoming a federal judge in 2011. As city attorney, Brown was responsible for all city contracts and oversaw all legal matters for the city. ==Early life and education== Brown received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[University of Louisiana at Lafayette|University of Southwestern Louisiana]] in 1985, and then attended [[Tulane Law School]], where she received a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1988 and a [[Master of Laws]] in Energy and Environment in 1998.{{cite web | url = https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2011/03/02/president-obama-names-three-united-states-district-court | title = President Obama Names Three to the United States District Court | date = 2 March 2011 | access-date = 2011-03-26 | publisher = The White House Office of the Press Secretary}}{{FJC Bio|nid=1393771}} ==Career== From 1988 to 1992, Brown practiced corporate and environmental litigation at the New Orleans office of the firm of Adams & Reese LLP, From 1996 to 1998 she was working for the Onebane Law Firm. From 2000 to 2003, Brown was employed by Milling, Benson, Woodward LLP. Between 2004 and 2007, she practiced at the firm Chaffe McCall LLP{{cite news | first = Jonathan | last = Tilove | title = President Barack Obama nominates Jolivette-Brown for federal court opening | date = March 2, 2011 | publisher = New Orleans Net LLC | url = http://www.nola.com/politics/index.ssf/2011/03/president_barack_obama_nominat.html | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110306172557/http://www.nola.com/politics/index.ssf/2011/03/president_barack_obama_nominat.html | url-status = dead | archive-date = March 6, 2011 | work = The Times-Picayune | access-date = 2011-04-07}} and again with this firm from 2009 until 2010. From 2007 to 2009, she was a visiting assistant clinical professor at [[Loyola University New Orleans College of Law]]. ===Federal judicial service=== Brown was nominated to fill the seat of Judge [[Stanwood Duval]] by President [[Barack Obama]] on March 2, 2011. {{nowrap|[[Columbia Law School|Columbia University]] ([[Bachelor of Laws|LLB]])}} | website = | footnotes = }} '''Naomi Lynn Reice Buchwald''' (born February 14, 1944) is a [[United States federal judge|senior United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]].{{Cite web |title=Buchwald, Naomi Reice {{!}} Federal Judicial Center |url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/buchwald-naomi-reice |access-date=2025-05-21 |website=www.fjc.gov}}{{Cite web |title=Hon. Naomi Reice Buchwald {{!}} U.S District Court |url=https://nysd.uscourts.gov/hon-naomi-reice-buchwald |access-date=2025-05-21 |website=nysd.uscourts.gov}} ==Early life and education== Naomi Reice was born in 1944 in [[Kingston, New York]],{{FJC Bio|nid=1391026|inline=yes}} to Mr. and Mrs. Albert Reice.[https://www.nytimes.com/1974/01/06/archives/naomi-reice-willbe-bride.html "Naomi Reice Will Be Bride," ''The New York Times,'' January 6, 1974, page 66] She graduated [[Phi Beta Kappa]] from [[Brandeis University]] in 1965 and then ''[[cum laude]]'' from [[Columbia Law School]] in 1968.{{cite book |title=Almanac of the federal judiciary |date=2025 |publisher=Wolters Kluwer |location=Chicago, Illinois |isbn=9780735568891 |page=47|volume=1|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1PW0pzLlL2cC&newbks=1&newbks_redir=0&lpg=RA13-PA3&pg=RA1-PA47#v=onepage&q&f=false}} == Career == Naomi Reice, as she was then known, practiced law in New York City from 1968 until 1973, when she became an [[Assistant United States Attorney]] in the Southern District of New York, rising to the position of Chief of the Civil Division. She held this position until she was named a [[United States magistrate judge]] in the same district in 1980. She served as chief United States magistrate judge from 1994 until 1999. === Federal judicial service === On February 12, 1999, Buchwald was nominated by President [[Bill Clinton]] to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]] vacated by [[Miriam G. Cedarbaum]]. Buchwald was [[Advice and consent#United States|confirmed by the Senate]] on September 13, 1999, and received her commission on September 22, 1999. She assumed [[senior status]] (a form of semi-retirement) on March 21, 2012. ==Notable cases == === ''SEC v. Dorozhko'' === In a 2008 civil case concerning [[insider trading]], Buchwald ordered{{Cite web |url=http://law.du.edu/images/uploads/corporate-governance/sec-governance-dorozhko.pdf |title=SEC v. Dorozhko, 606 F. Supp. 2d 321 (S.D.N.Y. 2008). Retrieved 2010-10-27. |access-date=2010-10-27 |archive-date=2020-08-30 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200830080006/https://www.law.du.edu/images/uploads/corporate-governance/sec-governance-dorozhko.pdf |url-status=dead }} the [[U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission]] (SEC) to unfreeze the ill-gotten profits of [[Ukraine|Ukrainian]] resident Oleksandr Dorozhko. Dorozhko was accused of [[Hacker (computer security)|hacking]] into a company database to access a then-unreleased earnings announcement. Based upon the undisclosed information, Dorozhko invested $41,671 in [[put options]], which he sold the following day for $328,571. The SEC froze the profits, but the judge ruled against the SEC, finding that while Dorozhko's conduct almost certainly was criminal, it did not fall within the relevant civil statute. Buchwald stayed her order pending appeal. The [[United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit]] reversed the judge's ruling.{{Cite web |url=http://law.du.edu/documents/corporate-governance/sec-and-governance/dorozhko/08-0201-cv-opn.pdf |title=SEC v. Dorozhko, 574 F.3d 42 (2d Cir. 2009). Retrieved 2010-10-27. |access-date=2010-10-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100623052633/http://law.du.edu/documents/corporate-governance/sec-and-governance/dorozhko/08-0201-cv-opn.pdf |archive-date=2010-06-23 |url-status=dead }} When Dorozhko later stopped participating in his defense, Buchwald granted the SEC summary judgement and ordered Dorozhko to pay nearly $580,000 in disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty.{{Cite web |url=http://law.du.edu/documents/corporate-governance/sec-and-governance/dorozhko/SEC-v-Dorozhko.pdf |title=SEC v. Dorozhko (S.D.N.Y. 2010). Retrieved 2010-10-27. |access-date=2010-10-27 |archive-date=2020-07-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200710100446/https://www.law.du.edu/documents/corporate-governance/sec-and-governance/dorozhko/SEC-v-Dorozhko.pdf |url-status=dead }} The SEC managed to seize $296,456 of this amount.[http://norris.blogs.nytimes.com/2010/03/29/common-sense-and-insider-trading/ "Common Sense and Insider Trading"] by Floyd Norris, ''The New York Times'' blog, March 29, 2010, 6:50 pm. Retrieved 2010-03-30. === ''Organic Seed Growers & Trade Ass'n v. Monsanto Co.'' === On February 24, 2012,[https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=9891874946309865887&q "Organic Seed Growers & Trade Ass'n v. Monsanto Co."], No. 11 Civ. 2163 (NRB) (S.D.N.Y. Feb. 24, 2012). Buchwald dismissed a lawsuit brought by [[Organic Seed Growers and Trade Association|a consortium of U.S. organic farmers and seed dealers]] aggrieved by Monsanto's [[genetically modified organism]] seeds. [[Monsanto]] denied that it had harmed anyone. After extensive briefing and oral argument, she held that the plaintiffs had no standing to sue, calling the case a "transparent effort to create a controversy where none exists."[https://www.reuters.com/article/us-monsanto-lawsuit-idUSTRE81Q1PN20120228 "Monsanto prevails in suit brought by organic growers"] by Carey Gillam, ''Reuters.com'' updated February 28th 2012, 2:17 AM. Retrieved 2012-02-29. The decision was appealed to the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit]] on March 28, 2012.[https://www.reuters.com/article/monsanto-lawsuit-idUSL2E8ESYK420120328 "Monsanto Lawsuit: Organic Farmers Appeal U.S. District Court Decision"] by Carey Gillam, ''Reuters.com'' updated March 28th 2012, 3:46 PM. Retrieved 2012-04-08. The [[Supreme Court of the United States|Supreme Court]] declined to hear an appeal by the organic farmers in January 2014.{{cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/usa-court-monsanto-idUSL2N0KN1CA20140113|title=Top U.S. court refuses to hear appeal of Monsanto seed case |date=Jan 13, 2014|publisher=Reuters|access-date=25 February 2015}} === ''In re LIBOR-Based Financial Instruments Antitrust Litigation'' === In March 2013, Buchwald dismissed much, though not all, of a class-action lawsuit directed at the banks that allegedly manipulated the [[London Interbank Offered Rate]] (LIBOR).{{cite web |url=https://dealbook.nytimes.com/2013/04/01/in-libor-ruling-a-big-win-for-the-banks |title=In Libor Ruling, a Big Win for the Banks |first=Peter J. |last=Henning |date=April 2013 }} In a 161-page memorandum of decision,''[https://www.scribd.com/doc/133360634/Judge-Naomi-Reice-Buchwald-s-ruling In re LIBOR-Based Financial Instruments Antitrust Litigation]'', no. 11-2262 (S.D.N.Y. Mar. 29, 2013) she held that U.S. antitrust law did not apply. She said that since the LIBOR-setting process was never meant to be competitive, the suppression of that process was not anti-competitive. In May 2016, the [[U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit]] reversed the dismissal order, reinstating the lawsuit.{{cite web |title=LIBOR Antitrust Claims Revived by Second Circuit |url=https://www.sidley.com/en/insights/newsupdates/2016/05/libor-antitrust-claims-revived-by-second-circuit |website=Sidley Austin LLP |access-date=May 24, 2018 |language=en |date=May 24, 2016 |archive-date=May 25, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180525063022/https://www.sidley.com/en/insights/newsupdates/2016/05/libor-antitrust-claims-revived-by-second-circuit |url-status=dead }}''[https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/ca2/13-3565/13-3565-2016-05-23.html In re LIBOR-Based Financial Instruments Antitrust Litigation]'', no. 13-3565 (2d Cir. May 23, 2016){{Update inline|date=May 2018}} === ''Knight First Amendment Institute v. Donald J. Trump'' === {{Update|section|date=May 2024}} On May 23, 2018, Buchwald held that President Trump's blocking of the plaintiffs from his [[Twitter]] account @realDonaldTrump was "because of their expressed political views violates the First Amendment."''[https://knightcolumbia.org/sites/default/files/content/Cases/Wikimedia/2018.05.23%20Order%20on%20motions%20for%20summary%20judgment.pdf Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University, et al. v. Donald J. Trump, et al.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190811045913/https://knightcolumbia.org/sites/default/files/content/Cases/Wikimedia/2018.05.23%20Order%20on%20motions%20for%20summary%20judgment.pdf |date=2019-08-11 }}'', No. 17 Civ. 5205 (S.D.N.Y. May 23, 2018). Buchwald differentiated between Twitter's muting and blocking functions, explaining that muting "vindicates the President's right to ignore certain speakers and to selectively amplify the voices of certain others . . . without restricting the right of the ignored to speak." Buchwald declined, however, to issue an injunction against the president and instead issued a declaratory judgment with the statement that "we must assume that the President and Scavino [ [[Dan Scavino]], the White House director of social media] will remedy the blocking we have held to be unconstitutional."The Volokh Conspiracy, ''[http://reason.com/volokh/2018/05/24/the-trump-twitter-declaratory-judgment The Trump Twitter Declaratory Judgment]'' (May 24, 2018).{{cite news |last1=Cullins |first1=Ashley |title=Donald Trump Can't Block Twitter Users Over Politics, Judge Rules |url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/thr-esq/donald-trump-cant-block-twitter-users-violating-first-amendment-1114349 |access-date=May 23, 2018 |work=The Hollywood Reporter |date=May 23, 2018 |language=en}} This decision stands in conflict with similar cases from other courts. For example, earlier in 2018, a Kentucky judge upheld a governor's decision to block commenters from his Twitter and Facebook feeds in Morgan v. Bevin (E.D. Ky. 2018).The Volokh Conspiracy, ''[http://reason.com/volokh/2018/05/23/blocking-of-twitter-users-from-realdonal Blocking of Twitter Users from @RealDonaldTrump Violates First Amendment]'' (May 23, 2018). Another example is Florida Democratic gubernatorial candidate [[Philip Levine (politician)|Philip Levine]], who is fighting a lawsuit for blocking Democratic activist and radio personality Grant Stern.Politico, ''[https://www.politico.com/states/florida/story/2018/05/18/levines-social-media-blocking-haunts-florida-gubernatorial-campaign-427254 Levine’s social media blocking haunts Florida gubernatorial campaign]'' (May 18, 2018). Buchwald's ruling was affirmed by the 2nd circuit on July 9, 2019,{{Cite web|url=https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/ca2/18-1691/18-1691-2019-07-09.html|title=Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University v. Trump, No. 18-1691 (2d Cir. 2019)|website=Justia|date=2019-07-09|access-date=2025-03-30}} and the 2nd circuit denied en banc rehearing on March 23, 2020 {{Cite web|url=https://knightcolumbia.org/documents/daa1a14eb1|title=Order (denying en banc petition): KNIGHT INSTITUTE V. TRUMP - A lawsuit challenging President Trump's blocking of critics on Twitter|website=knightcolumbia.org|date=2020-03-23|access-date=2025-03-30}} Then, on April 5, 2021, the Supreme Court ordered the case to be dismissed as moot.{{Cite web|url=https://knightcolumbia.org/cases/knight-institute-v-trump|title=Knight Institute v. Trump|website=knightcolumbia.org|access-date=2025-03-30}} === ''Chung v. Trump'' === On March 25, 2025, Buchwald granted a temporary restraining order blocking immigration officials from detaining or deporting Yunseo Chung, a 21-year old green card holder at Columbia University who participated in a pro-Palestine protest at Barnard College.{{Cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/mar/25/columbia-gaza-protester-deportation?CMP=oth_b-aplnews_d-1|title=Judge rules Columbia protester can't be detained as she fights deportation|website=The Guardian|date=March 25, 2025|access-date=March 25, 2025}} === Recent Cases Heard === United States ''v.'' Energy Wall, LLC, 1:25-cv-04875 - CourtListener.com |url=https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/70526273/arrow-electronics-inc-v-energy-wall-llc/ |access-date=2025-09-28 |website=CourtListener |language=en-us}} == Criticism by Preet Bharara == At a July 2014 roast for a departing prosecutor in his office, [[Preet Bharara]], then the [[U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York]], referred to Buchwald, who had just presided over his office’s first loss of a major insider trading case, as “the worst federal judge” he’d ever encountered.[https://www.nytimes.com/2015/04/17/business/preet-bharara-and-federal-judges-trade-barbs-and-some-fear-consequences.html "Some Fear Fallout From Preet Bharara’s Tension With Judges," ''The New York Times,'' April 16, 2015][https://www.foxbusiness.com/markets/wall-streets-top-cops-harsh-words-for-federal-judge-that-ended-his-win-streak "Wall Street's Top Cop's Harsh Words for Federal Judge that Ended His Win Streak," ''Fox Business,'' July 18, 2014][https://www.thenation.com/article/archive/will-preet-bharara-new-yorks-anti-corruption-crusader-run-higher-office/ "Will Preet Bharara, New York’s Anti-Corruption Crusader, Run for Higher Office?," ''The Nation,'' April 29, 2015] == Personal life == She was married on January 19, 1974, to Don David Buchwald of [[Jericho, New York]].
