[[New York University School of Law|New York University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Natasha Clarise Merle''' (born 1983) is an American lawyer from [[New York (state)|New York]] who serves as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York]]. == Education == Merle received her [[Bachelor of Arts]] in government and [[Spanish language|Spanish]], with honors, from the [[University of Texas at Austin]] in 2005 and she graduated, ''[[cum laude]]'', with a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[New York University School of Law]] in 2008.{{Cite press release |title=President Biden Names Thirteenth Round of Judicial Nominees |date=January 19, 2022 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/01/19/president-biden-names-thirteenth-round-of-judicial-nominees/ |access-date=January 19, 2022}} {{PD-notice}}{{Cite web |title=Natasha Merle |url=https://www.naacpldf.org/about-us/staff/natasha-merle/ |access-date=January 19, 2022 |website=NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund |language=en-US}} == Career == Merle began her legal career as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Robert L. Carter]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]] from 2008 to 2009. From 2009 to 2011, she was a staff attorney at the Gulf Region Advocacy Center.{{cite news |last1=Voruganti |first1=Harsh |title=Natasha Merle – Nominee to the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of New York |url=https://vettingroom.org/2022/03/03/natasha-merle/ |access-date=9 June 2022 |work=The Vetting Room |date=3 March 2022 |language=en}} Merle then became an [[federal public defender|assistant federal public defender]] at the [[Office of the Federal Public Defender]].{{cite web | url=https://www.peoplesparity.org/unrigthecourts/#list | title=Unrig the Courts }} She also served as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[John Gleeson (judge)|John Gleeson]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York]] from 2012 to 2013. From 2013 to 2015, Merle was a litigation associate and civil rights [[fellow]] at [[Fried, Frank, Harris, Shriver & Jacobson]] in [[New York City]]. From 2016 to 2021, she served as assistant counsel and then senior counsel for the [[NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund]] ("LDF"). From 2021 to 2023, she was the deputy director of litigation at LDF. From 2019 to 2021, Merle was a [[adjunct professor]] of clinical law at the [[New York University School of Law]] and from 2020 to 2021, she was a [[lecturer]] in law at [[Columbia Law School]].{{FJC Bio|nid=13720111|inline=yes}} === Notable cases === In 2017, Merle was a member of the petitioner team in ''[[Buck v. Davis]]''.{{cite news | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/02/22/us/politics/duane-buck-texas-death-penalty-case-supreme-court.html | title=Citing Racist Testimony, Justices Call for New Sentencing in Texas Death Penalty Case | work=The New York Times | date=22 February 2017 | last1=Liptak | first1=Adam }}{{cite web | url=https://www.theatlantic.com/politics/archive/2017/02/supreme-court-duane-buck/517542/ | title=Some Toxins Can Be Deadly in Small Doses | website=[[The Atlantic]] | date=23 February 2017 }}{{cite web | url=https://www.c-span.org/video/?415420-1/buck-v-davis-oral-argument | title=Buck v. Davis Oral Argument }} In 2017, Merle was lead counsel for ''[[NAACP LDF v. Trump]]''.{{cite web | url=https://www.naacpldf.org/case-issue/ldf-v-trump/ | title=LDF v. Trump }}{{cite web | url=https://www.naacpldf.org/about-us/staff/natasha-merle/ | title=Natasha Merle }}{{cite web | url=https://www.huffpost.com/entry/naacp-trump-lawsuit-voting-rights-act-violation_n_5fb8ca33c5b6cf1e0f085815 | title=NAACP LDF Lawsuit: Trump Violated Voting Rights Act | date=21 November 2020 }} === Federal judicial service === On January 19, 2022, President [[Joe Biden]] nominated Merle to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York]]. President Biden nominated Merle to a new seat created following the appointment of [[Roslynn R. Mauskopf]] as director of the [[Administrative Office of the United States Courts]].{{Cite press release |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |date=January 19, 2022 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/01/19/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-59/}} {{PD-notice}} On April 27, 2022, a hearing on her nomination was held before the Senate Judiciary Committee.{{Cite web|title=Nominations|date=April 25, 2022|publisher=[[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]]|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/04/20/2022/nominations}} During Merle's confirmation hearing, Republican senators criticized her over comments she made in 2017 in which she said that proposals for [[Voter identification laws in the United States|voter ID laws]] and a [[border wall]] were based in [[white supremacy]].{{cite news |last1=Lucas |first1=Fred |title=Meet Biden's most controversial judicial nominees stalled in Senate because of Feinstein's absence |url=https://www.foxnews.com/politics/meet-bidens-most-controversial-judicial-nominees-stalled-senate-because-feinsteins-absence |access-date=8 May 2023 |work=Fox News |date=3 May 2023}}{{Cite news|last=Headley|first=Tiana|title=Civil Rights Lawyer Who Drew GOP Ire Confirmed to NY Court (1)|url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/kamala-harris-breaks-tie-to-advance-ny-judge-on-senate-floor|website=Bloomberg Law|access-date=June 21, 2023}}{{cite news |title=Sen. Susan Collins' 'no' votes on judicial nominees have risen sharply under Biden |url=https://www.yahoo.com/news/sen-susan-collins-no-votes-163100389.html |date=June 25, 2023}} On May 26, 2022, her nomination was reported out of committee by a 12–10 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/EBM%20Results%20-%202022-05-262.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – May 26, 2022|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=May 26, 2022}} On January 3, 2023, her nomination was returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]]; she was renominated later the same day.{{Cite press release |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |date=January 3, 2023 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2023/01/03/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-91/}} On February 2, 2023, the committee failed to report her nomination by a 10–10 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/EBM%20Results%20-%202023-02-021.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – February 2, 2023|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=February 2, 2023}} On February 9, 2023, her nomination was reported out of committee by an 11–10 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/2023-02-09%20-%20EBM%20-%20Results.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – February 9, 2023|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=February 9, 2023}} On June 21, 2023, the Senate invoked cloture on her nomination by a 51–50 vote, with Vice President [[Kamala Harris]] [[List of tie-breaking votes cast by the vice president of the United States|voting in the affirmative]].{{Cite web|date=June 21, 2023|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Natasha C. Merle to be United States District Judge for the Eastern District of New York)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00168.htm|access-date=June 21, 2023|website=United States Senate}} Later that day, her nomination was confirmed by a 50–49 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00169.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Natasha C. W. Wilson Company }} His elder brother was [[Slade Gorton]], who later became a member of the [[United States Senate]] from [[Washington (state)|Washington]].{{FJC Bio|nid=1381406|inline=yes}} Gorton received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[Dartmouth College]] in 1960, and a [[Bachelor of Laws]] from [[Columbia Law School]] in 1966. He was in the [[United States Navy]] from 1960 to 1962, where he was a [[Lieutenant Junior Grade]], and an executive officer on the [[USS Banner (AKL-25)|USS ''Banner'']] (AKL-25) in the Western [[Pacific Ocean]].[https://www.lawdiary.com/docs/subscribers/MA_Judicial_Biographies.pdf "FEDERAL COURT JUDGES sitting in MASSACHUSETTS,"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141215045610/https://www.lawdiary.com/docs/subscribers/MA_Judicial_Biographies.pdf |date=2014-12-15 }} ''Biographies of Massachusetts Judges'', 2019.Charles Bruce Brownson (2011). [https://books.google.com/books?id=RCSMTJZrOBsC&q=nathaniel+gorton+%22uss+banner%22 "Gorton, Nathanial M.,"] ''Judicial Staff Directory''. Gorton worked in private practice in [[Boston]] from 1966 to 1992, where he was an associate in the trial and business departments at [[Nutter McClennen & Fish]] until 1969, an associate at Powers & Hall PC from 1970 to 1974 and a partner at the latter firm from 1975 until 1992, practicing civil business litigation.[https://www.bloomberg.com/profiles/people/1914423-nathaniel-m-gorton "Nathaniel Gorton, United States District Court of Massachusetts: Profile & Biography,"] Bloomberg.[https://masslawyersweekly.com/judicial-profiles/gorton-nathaniel-m/ GORTON, NATHANIEL M.,] Judicial Profiles, ''Massachusetts Lawyers Weekly'', August 1, 2001. ==Federal judicial service== On April 28, 1992, Gorton was nominated by President [[George H. W. Bush]] to a new seat on the [[United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts]] created by Section 203(a)(14) of the [[Civil Justice Reform Act]] of 1990 ({{USPL|101|650}}, {{USStat|104|5100}}). He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on September 23, 1992, and received his commission the following day. He assumed [[senior status]] on May 31, 2025. In 2015 Gorton received the [[Federal Bar Association]], Massachusetts chapter, Recognition Award for dedication and service. According to the ''USA Today'' in April 2019, Gorton "has a reputation for issuing stronger sentences than his peers," while [[Law360]] stated that he "has a reputation for being a no-nonsense, fairly conservative judge."Joey Garrison (April 11, 2019). [https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/nation/2019/04/11/college-admissions-case-parents-feds-accused-judge-shopping/3434061002/ "College admissions case: Parents, feds accused of judge shopping"], ''USA Today''.[https://www.law360.com/sports/articles/1148628/-varsity-blues-judge-tough-fair-and-a-good-draw-for-feds 'Varsity Blues' Judge Tough, Fair, And A Good Draw For Feds,] Law360, April 11, 2019. He presided over the sentencing of many parents indicted in the 2019 College admissions bribery scandal, most notably actress [[Lori Loughlin]] and her husband, fashion designer [[Mossimo Giannulli]], which saw the two of them sentenced to two months and five months in prison respectively.{{Cite web|url=https://www.justice.gov/usao-ma/pr/california-couple-college-admissions-case-sentenced-prison|title=California Couple in College Admissions Case Sentenced to Prison|date=21 August 2020}} ==Other activities== Gorton is a former Chair of the Board of Trustees of [[Buckingham Browne & Nichols School]], an independent co-educational day school in [[Cambridge, Massachusetts]], with students from pre-kindergarten through 12th grade. ==See also== * [[List of United States federal judges by longevity of service]] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== * {{FJC Bio|nid=1381406}} * [https://www.bna.com/know-judge-nathaniel-n57982091713/ "Know Your Judge: Nathaniel M. From 2001 to 2011, Ramos served as a judge of the 347th District Court.{{Cite news|first=Sara |last=Foley |url=http://www.caller.com/news/2011/jan/26/nelva-gonzales-ramos-nominated-federal-judge/ |title=Nelva Gonzales Ramos nominated for federal judgeship |work=[[Corpus Christi Caller-Times]] |date=January 26, 2011 |access-date=August 3, 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110303121109/http://www.caller.com/news/2011/jan/26/nelva-gonzales-ramos-nominated-federal-judge/ |archive-date=March 3, 2011 }} ===Federal judicial service=== During the [[111th Congress]], Ramos was one of three candidates recommended by Democrats from the [[Texas's congressional delegations#United States House of Representatives|Texas House delegation]] for a [[Corpus Christi, Texas|Corpus Christi]] vacancy on the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas]].{{Cite news|first1=Mary Ann |last1=Cavazos |first2=Jaime |last2=Powell |url=http://www.caller.com/news/2010/jun/09/democrats-select-three-finalists-federal-judgeship/ |title=Democrats select three finalists for federal judgeship |work=[[Corpus Christi Caller-Times]] |date=June 9, 2010 |access-date=August 3, 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120323081229/http://www.caller.com/news/2010/jun/09/democrats-select-three-finalists-federal-judgeship/ |archive-date=March 23, 2012 }} Ramos was the only candidate also supported by Republican Senators [[Kay Bailey Hutchison]] and [[John Cornyn]]. '''Nicholas George Garaufis''' (born September 28, 1948)<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3a2bgthMue0C&pg=PA430|title=Confirmation Hearings on Federal Appointments: February 22, March 23, April 27, and May 10, 2000|author=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|year=2001}}</ref> is a [[United States federal judge|senior United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York]].

==Early life and education==

Garaufis was born in [[Paterson, New Jersey]], to Demetria (1924–2011) and George Garaufis (1919–2007). His father was a civil engineer and his mother was the district office manager for Republican Congressman [[Seymour Halpern]].<ref name="wedding">{{cite news |title=WEDDINGS; Elizabeth Seidman, Nicholas Garaufis  |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2002/04/21/style/weddings-elizabeth-seidman-nicholas-garaufis.html |access-date=November 15, 2020 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=April 21, 2002}}</ref>  His grandparents were Greek immigrants.<ref name="nytimes2012">{{cite news |last1=Secret |first1=Mosi |title=For Judge in Firefighter Discrimination Case, an Evolving Opinion   |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/10/08/nyregion/for-judge-in-firefighter-discrimination-case-an-evolving-opinion.html |access-date=November 15, 2020 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=October 8, 2012}}</ref>

Garaufis graduated from [[Columbia College of Columbia University]] in 1969 with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree and received his [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Columbia Law School]] in 1974. He taught in the [[New York City]] public schools prior to receiving his Juris Doctor.

==Career==

Garaufis began his legal career in 1974 as an associate of [[Chadbourne & Parke]]. He also served as an Assistant Attorney General in the Litigation Bureau of the New York State Attorney General's office under [[United States Attorney General|Attorney General]] Louis J. Lefkowitz and has practiced law privately in [[Queens County, New York|Queens County]], [[New York (state)|New York]]. Garaufis served for more than five years as the Chief Counsel of the [[Federal Aviation Administration]] in [[Washington, D.C.]], overseeing a staff of 200 attorneys. Prior to his appointment to the Clinton Administration in June 1995, Garaufis served for nine years as counsel to Queens Borough President [[Claire Shulman]] in New York City.

==Federal judicial service==

Upon the recommendation of [[United States Senator]] [[Daniel Patrick Moynihan]], Garaufis was nominated by [[Bill Clinton|President Clinton]] on February 28, 2000, to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York]] vacated by [[Charles P. Sifton]] and [[Advice and consent|confirmed]] by [[unanimous consent]] by the [[United States Senate]] on May 24, 2000. Garaufis received his commission on May 25, 2000, and entered service on August 28, 2000. Garaufis took [[senior status]] on October 1, 2014.

===New York Fire Department hiring case===
In 2007, the United States Department of Justice, joined by the Vulcan Society, an organization of black firefighters, and three individual applicants, filed a lawsuit against New York City alleging that the city's written firefighter entrance exam excluded a disproportionate number of black and Hispanic applicants.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Newman |first1=Andy |title=Justice Dept. Sues New York City, Citing Bias in Hiring Firefighters |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/05/22/nyregion/22bias.html |work=New York Times |date=May 22, 2007}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Eligon |first1=John |last2=Cardwell |first2=Diane |title=Black and Hispanic Firefighter Applicants Have Doubled |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/11/28/nyregion/28fire.html |work=New York Times |date=November 28, 2007}}</ref> At that time, just three percent of the department's 11,000 firefighters were black and 4.5 percent were Hispanic despite the fact that over half the population of New York City was black or Hispanic.<ref name=Newman>{{Cite web|last=Newman|first=Andy|title= Justice Dept. Sues New York City, Citing Bias in Hiring Firefighters|work=[[The New York Times]]|date= May 22, 2007|url= https://www.nytimes.com/2007/05/22/nyregion/22bias.html }}</ref> On October 5, 2011, Garaufis ruled that a court-appointed monitor would be installed to oversee the New York City Fire Department's efforts to hire and retain more minorities.<ref name="Feuer">{{Cite web|last=Feuer|first=Alan|title= Monitor Must Oversee Fire Dept. Hiring Practices, Judge Rules|work=[[The New York Times]]|date= October 5, 2011|url= https://www.nytimes.com/2011/10/06/nyregion/monitor-must-oversee-ny-fire-dept-hiring-judge-rules.html}}</ref> While the ruling did not impose racial quotas, it explained that a systemic effort by the Fire Department was required.<ref name="Feuer"/> On September 28, 2012, Garaufis approved a new entrance exam for firefighters after the city submitted data showing that the test produced results more representative of the city's racial and ethnic makeup.<ref name="Secret2011">{{cite news |last1=Secret |first1=Mosi |title=Judge Approves New Entrance Exam for City Firefighters |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/09/29/nyregion/judge-approves-new-entrance-exam-for-city-firefighters.html |work=New York Times |date=September 28, 2011}}</ref> The first class of recruits after the ruling included some recruits that were older than had been typical of previous classes.<ref name="Schwirtz2013">{{cite news |last1=Schwirtz |first1=Michael |title=For New York City Fire Department, More Diversity Amid Tension |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2013/12/04/nyregion/for-new-york-city-fire-department-more-diversity-amid-tension.html|work=New York Times |date=December 4, 2013}}</ref> Injuries in that class were higher and the dropout rate, usually 10 percent, was 24 percent for that class.<ref name="Schwirtz2013"/>

On May 14, 2013, an appeals court disagreed with Garaufis's finding that the discrimination was intentional.<ref name="SecretWeiser">{{cite news |last1=Secret |first1=Mosi |last2=Weiser |first2=Benjamin |title=Appeals Court Says Judge Went Too Far in Forcing Fire Dept. to Revamp Its Hiring |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2013/05/15/nyregion/appeals-court-rules-judge-went-too-far-in-fire-dept-hiring-case.html |work=New York Times |date=May 14, 2013}}</ref> The appeals court determined that the question of intentionality, which was relevant to the amount of damages the city might have to pay, should go to trial under a different judge.<ref name="SecretWeiser"/> After the appeals court's ruling, the parties settled the remaining claims in the case, and the entire case was referred to Garaufis for oversight of the settlement.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Santora |first1=Marc |last2=Schwirtz |first2=Michael |title=New York City Settles Lawsuit Accusing Fire Dept. of Racial Bias |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2014/03/19/nyregion/new-york-settles-bias-lawsuit-against-fire-department.html |work=New York Times |date=March 18, 2014}}</ref>

The number of minority firefighters in the department doubled to 1,230 between 2002 and 2013.<ref name="Schwirtz2013"/>  On June 28, 2018, the Fire Department reported that forty-three percent of the nearly 2,300 top scorers on its most recent entrance exam were black or Hispanic.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Farinacci |first1=Amanda |title=FDNY reports progress in diversity recruitment efforts |url=https://www.ny1.com/nyc/all-boroughs/news/2018/06/29/fdny-reports-progress-in-diversity-recruitment-efforts- |work=Spectrum News NY1 |date=June 28, 2018}}</ref>   In October 2018, people of color comprised more than 40 percent of the class graduating from the training academy.<ref>{{cite news |title=FDNY Graduates Diverse Class of Firefighters |url=https://www.ny1.com/nyc/all-boroughs/news/2018/10/19/fdny-graduates-diverse-class-of-firefighters |work=Spectrum News NY1 |date=October 19, 2018}}</ref>

=== Bryant Neal Vinas terrorism case ===
On May 11, 2017, Garaufis sentenced [[Bryant Neal Vinas]] to [[time served]] for [[providing material support for terrorism]], giving the highly cooperative informant three months more in prison before beginning a life on [[probation]].<ref>{{cite news|last1=Hays|first1=Tom|title=Al-Qaida member who flipped and helped US gets time served|url=https://apnews.com/c24939d294424613aa0c77b7c06c8705|access-date=February 17, 2018|work=[[Associated Press]]|date=May 11, 2017}}</ref>

===Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals===
In 2016, Martín Batalla Vidal, a recipient of Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA), filed a federal lawsuit in the Eastern District of New York challenging the Department of Homeland Security (DHS)’s decision to revoke his work permit in connection with the [[nationwide injunction]] issued by the Southern District of Texas.<ref name="M&O Dkt. 104">{{Cite web|url=https://www.clearinghouse.net/chDocs/public/IM-NY-0051-0010.pdf|title=Memorandum & Order (Dkt. 104)}}</ref> The Texas case sought to block the implementation of the Deferred Action for Parents of Americans Lawful Permanent Residents (DAPA) and an expansion of DACA.<ref name="M&O Dkt. 104" /> On September 29, 2016, the advocacy organization Make the Road New York (MRNY) joined Batalla Vidal's lawsuit.<ref name="M&O Dkt. 104" />

On February 13, 2018, Garaufis issued a nationwide preliminary injunction enjoining rescission of the DACA program.<ref name="M&O Dkt. 255">{{Cite web|url=https://www.clearinghouse.net/chDocs/public/IM-NY-0051-0029.pdf|title=Amended Memorandum & Order & Preliminary Injunction (Dkt. 255)}}</ref> Garaufis found that Plaintiffs were entitled to a preliminary injunction.<ref name="M&O Dkt. 255"/> The government appealed Garaufis's decision to the Second Circuit, which heard oral argument on January 25, 2019.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Bishop |first1=Stewart |title=Gov't Defends DACA Rollback As Discretionary In 2nd Circ. |url=https://www.law360.com/articles/1122313 |website=Law360}}</ref>

On July 28, 2020, [[Chad Wolf]], who served as Acting Secretary of the Department of Homeland Security, issued a memorandum stating new DACA applicants would not be accepted, and renewals would be limited to one year instead of two.<ref>{{Cite web|author=Priscilla Alvarez and Geneva Sands|title=Trump administration to review DACA and reject new applications|url=https://www.cnn.com/2020/07/28/politics/daca-trump-administration/index.html|access-date=2020-11-15|website=CNN|date=28 July 2020 }}</ref> Garaufis ruled on November 14 that Wolf was not lawfully appointed as the Acting Secretary, and that the memorandum was invalid as a result of that.<ref>{{Cite web|author=Dan Berman, Priscilla Alvarez and Geneva Sands|title=Federal judge says new DACA rules are invalid|url=https://www.cnn.com/2020/11/14/politics/federal-judge-daca-rules-chad-wolf/index.html|access-date=2020-11-15|website=CNN|date=14 November 2020 }}</ref>

==Personal life==

Following the death of his first wife, writer and television producer Eleanor Prescott, Garaufis married New York-based nonprofit executive and board director Elizabeth Seidman in 2002 in [[Queens]], New York. Judge [[Robert Katzmann|Robert A. Katzmann]] officiated the ceremony.<ref name="wedding"/>

[[University of Michigan Law School|University of Michigan]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | party = }} '''Jagan Nicholas Ranjan''' (born 1978) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania]]. == Education == Ranjan graduated from [[Grove City College]] in 2000 with a [[Bachelor of Arts]], ''[[summa cum laude]]''. He then attended the [[University of Michigan Law School]], where he was a note editor of the ''[[Michigan Law Review]]''. He graduated in 2003 with a [[Juris Doctor]], ''[[cum laude]]''.{{Cite web|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-sixteenth-wave-judicial-nominees-sixteenth-wave-united-states-attorney-nominees-eleventh-wave-united-states-marshal-nominees/|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Donald J. Trump Announces Sixteenth Wave of Judicial Nominees, Sixteenth Wave of United States Attorney Nominees, and Eleventh Wave of United States Marshal Nominees}} == Career == Ranjan started his legal career by serving as a [[law clerk]] to Judge [[Deborah L. Cook]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit]]. Upon graduation from law school, Ranjan served as a Simon Karas Fellow with the [[Ohio Attorney General]]'s Office, working with the [[Solicitor General of Ohio|state solicitor general]] on the office's major appeals. From 2005 to 2019, Ranjan was an equity partner in the [[Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania]], office of [[K&L Gates]], where he litigated [[commercial law|commercial]], [[energy law|energy]], and [[appellate law|appellate]] matters. While at K&L Gates, he served on the firm's global [[pro bono]] and diversity committees, and directed his office's pro bono program—which was awarded "pro bono law firm of the year" in 2017 by the local bar association. He is active in the community, serving on legal diversity and symphony boards, as well as serving as a mentor to local middle school students. === Federal judicial service === On July 13, 2018, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to nominate Ranjan to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania]]. On July 24, 2018, his nomination was sent to the Senate. President Trump nominated Ranjan to the seat vacated by Judge [[Kim R. Gibson]], who assumed [[senior status]] on June 3, 2016.{{Cite web|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/two-nominations-one-withdrawal-sent-senate-today-2/|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Two Nominations and One Withdrawal Sent to the Senate Today}} On November 13, 2018, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/11/13/2018/nominations|title=Nominations | United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|website=www.judiciary.senate.gov|date=13 November 2018 }} On January 3, 2019, his nomination was returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]], which provides that nominations not acted upon during a session are considered to have expired.{{cite web|url=https://www.rules.senate.gov/rules-of-the-senate|access-date=2020-10-10|title=Rules of the Senate}} On January 23, 2019, President Trump announced his intent to renominate Ranjan for a federal judgeship.{{Cite web|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-intent-nominate-judicial-nominees/|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Donald J. Trump Announces Intent to Nominate Judicial Nominees}} His nomination was sent to the Senate later that day.{{Cite web|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/nominations-sent-senate-2/|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate}} On February 7, 2019, his nomination was reported out of committee by an 18–4 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/02.07.2019%20Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting1.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – February 7, 2019, Senate Judiciary Committee}} On July 9, 2019, the Senate invoked cloture on his nomination by an 83–15 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=1&vote=00194|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: J. Nicholas Ranjan to be U.S. District Judge for the Western District of Pennsylvania)|website=www.senate.gov}} On July 10, 2019, his nomination was confirmed by an 80–14 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=1&vote=00196|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation J. Nicholas Ranjan, of Pennsylvania, to be U.S. District Judge for the Western District of Pennsylvania)|website=www.senate.gov}} He received judicial commission on July 12, 2019.{{FJC Bio|nid=6731086|inline=yes}} ===Notable rulings=== * In August 2020, Ranjan ordered the Trump campaign to produce evidence of voter fraud in Pennsylvania by Friday, August 14. The Trump campaign must answer questions from Democratic groups, or admit to having no proof of election fraud. A hearing about the evidence was set for late September.{{Cite web|last=Polantz |first=Katelyn |date=13 August 2020 |title=Judge orders Trump campaign to produce evidence of voter fraud in Pennsylvania |url=https://www.cnn.com/2020/08/13/politics/trump-campaign-voter-fraud-lawsuit-pennsylvania/index.html |website=CNN |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200813191817/https://www.cnn.com/2020/08/13/politics/trump-campaign-voter-fraud-lawsuit-pennsylvania/index.html |archive-date=13 August 2020 |access-date=16 June 2025}} On August 23, 2020, Ranjan issued a stay on the Trump campaign's lawsuit, pending the result of a similar state-level lawsuit.{{Cite news|last=Renshaw |first=Jarrett |date=23 August 2020 |title=Federal judge issues stay in Trump challenge of mail balloting in Pennsylvania|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-usa-election-mail-ballot-lawwsuit-idUSKBN25J0VO|newspaper=Reuters |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200824053512/https://www.reuters.com/article/us-usa-election-mail-ballot-lawwsuit-idUSKBN25J0VO|archive-date=24 August 2020 |access-date=16 June 2025}} * On October 10, 2020, in the case of ''Donald J. Trump for President, Inc. v. Boockvar'', Ranjan granted judgment in favor of the Secretary of State of Pennsylvania, [[Kathy Boockvar]], and denied the Trump campaign's claims of voter fraud and allowed ballot dropboxes to remain in service.{{Cite web|url=https://www.cnn.com/2020/10/10/politics/pennsylvania-voting-policy-challenges-trump/index.html|title=Federal judge in Pennsylvania denies Trump campaign voting policy challenges in major ruling|date=October 10, 2020|via=[[CNN]]}} In his decision, Ranjan concluded that "the plain language of the [Pennsylvania State] Election Code imposes no requirement for signature comparison for mail-in and absentee ballots and applications," a reasoning that was approvingly cited by the Pennsylvania Supreme Court on 23 October.Supreme Court of Pennsylvania, No. 149 MM 2020. She was appointed by President [[Bill Clinton]] in 1996 at the recommendation of [[Daniel Patrick Moynihan|Senator Daniel Patrick Moynihan]].142 Cong. Rec. S 9312 She assumed [[senior status]] on October 16, 2008. ==Education and career== Born in [[Chicago]], Illinois, Gershon received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in English with honors from [[Cornell University]] in 1962 and a [[Bachelor of Laws]] from [[Yale Law School]] in 1965.{{cite web|url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/gershon-nina|title=Gershon, Nina - Federal Judicial Center|website=www.fjc.gov}} In 1965 and 1966, she was a [[Fulbright Scholar]] at the [[London School of Economics]]' Hampstead Clinic.{{Citation needed|date=October 2010}} She was a Staff attorney of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York, Mental Health Information Service from 1966 to 1968, and was then assistant corporation counsel with the Appeals Division of the New York City Law Department from 1968 to 1969, and from 1970 to 1972. She was a professor of law and political science at the [[University of California, San Diego]] from 1969 to 1970. She was an attorney for the New York City Law Department from 1972 to 1976, serving as Chief of the Federal Appeals Division from 1972 to 1975 and Chief of the Consumer Protection Division from 1975 to 1976. ==Federal judicial service== In 1976, Gershon became a [[United States magistrate judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York|Southern District of New York]], an office she would hold for twenty years. She was also an adjunct professor of law at the [[Cardozo School of Law]] from 1986 to 1988. On October 18, 1995, Gershon was nominated by President [[Bill Clinton]] to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York]] vacated by [[Leonard D. Wexler]]. She was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on July 30, 1996, and received her commission on August 1, 1996. She assumed [[senior status]] on October 16, 2008. ===Notable cases=== * In the 1970s, working as a lawyer for New York City, Gershon won a court ruling that rejected the building of Grand Central Tower on top of [[Grand Central Terminal]], which would have ruined the historical site. The ruling was later upheld in ''[[Penn Central Transportation Co. v. New York City]]''.''New York Times'', October 4, 1999, "In Museum Case, Judge Has Eye for Law, if Not Art". * In 1999, Gershon ruled that New York City mayor [[Rudolph Giuliani]] could not cut the Brooklyn Museum of Art's funding after it mounted an exhibit entitled [[Sensation exhibition|"Sensation"]]. Giuliani described the works in the exhibit as "sick" and "disgusting."''Brooklyn Inst. of Arts & Scis v. City of New York & Rudolph W. Giuliani'', 64 F. Supp. 2d 184, 205 (E.D.N.Y. 1999) * In 2000, Gershon ruled that New York's century-old kosher food laws violated the [[First Amendment to the United States Constitution|First Amendment]].{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2000/08/04/nyregion/judge-voids-law-certifying-kosher-food.html|title=Judge Voids Law Certifying Kosher Food|first=Robert D. Mcfadden With Joseph P.|last=Fried|work=The New York Times |date=4 August 2000|publisher=|via=NYTimes.com}} * In the spring of 2006, Gershon presided over the trial of [[Shahawar Matin Siraj]], a [[Pakistan]]i immigrant who was accused of plotting to blow up New York's [[Herald Square]] subway station. After a four-week trial, a jury found Siraj guilty of four crimes, including plotting to bomb a public transportation system.New York Times, May 25, 2006. On January 8, 2007, Gershon sentenced Siraj to 30 years imprisonment for his role in the plot.{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/world/americas/6243241.stm|work=BBC News|title=Man jailed over NY bombing plot|date=January 8, 2007}} * On December 11, 2009, Judge Gershon issued a [[preliminary injunction]] against the United States Government preventing the implementation of a law barring the [[Association of Community Organizations for Reform Now]] (ACORN) from receiving federal funds. Judge Gerson found that the law, passed as part of an [[Appropriation bill]], was an unconstitutional [[Bill of attainder]].{{cite web|url=http://ccrjustice.org/files/Judge%20Gershon%2012%2011%202009%20PI%20Order.pdf|title=ccrjustice.org|publisher=}} The [[United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit|Second Circuit Court of Appeals]] overturned this decision on August 13, 2010.{{cite web|url=https://www.google.com/hostednews/ap/article/ALeqM5goHmEoyYhLPQ7xhPuFBAM-gBjbUAD9HIOI900|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100817021846/http://www.google.com/hostednews/ap/article/ALeqM5goHmEoyYhLPQ7xhPuFBAM-gBjbUAD9HIOI900|url-status=dead|archive-date=August 17, 2010|title=Federal appeals court in NY rules against ACORN|publisher=Associated Press|date=|accessdate=2010-08-13}} ==See also== * [[List of Jewish American jurists]] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1381126}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Leonard D. [[Harvard Law School|Harvard University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Nina Nin-Yuen Wang''' (born 1972){{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Wang%20SJQ%20Public%20Final.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=May 24, 2022}} is a Taiwan-born lawyer serving as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Colorado]]. She previously served as a [[United States magistrate judge]] of the same court. == Early life== Nina Y. Wang is an immigrant from [[Taiwan]].{{Cite web |last=Karlik |first=Michael |date=January 19, 2022 |title=Biden names magistrate judge Nina Wang as judicial nominee |url=https://www.coloradopolitics.com/courts/biden-names-magistrate-judge-nina-wang-as-judicial-nominee/article_a8302638-7943-11ec-8ba0-7bc3f3b599d4.html |access-date=January 19, 2022 |website=Colorado Politics |language=en}} She earned a [[Bachelor of Arts]] from the [[Washington University in St. Louis]] in 1994 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Harvard Law School]] in 1997.{{Cite web|date=January 19, 2022|title=President Biden Names Thirteenth Round of Judicial Nominees|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/01/19/president-biden-names-thirteenth-round-of-judicial-nominees/|access-date=January 19, 2022|website=The White House|language=en-US}} {{PD-notice}} == Career == Wang began her career as an associate at [[Fried, Frank, Harris, Shriver & Jacobson]]. From 1999 to 2000, Wang served as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Peter J. Messitte]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Maryland]]. From 2000 to 2004, she served as an [[Assistant United States Attorney]] in the United States Attorney's Office for the District of Colorado. She was an associate at Faegre Drinker from 2004 to 2008 and partner until 2015. In private practice, Wang focused on [[copyright]] and [[intellectual property]] law.{{cite web | url=https://gazette.com/colorado_politics/bennet-hickenlooper-send-recommendations-to-white-house-for-court-vacancy/article_5bbb855a-bf11-11eb-806b-27dd91c03200.html | title=Bennet, Hickenlooper send recommendations to White House for court vacancy | date=May 30, 2021 }} Wang cofounded the Colorado Pro Bono Patent Initiative. {{nowrap|[[Notre Dame Law School|University of Notre Dame]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]])}} | alma_mater = | occupation = | profession = | known_for = | salary = | net_worth = | cabinet = | committees = | portfolio = | awards = | signature = | signature_alt = | website = | footnotes = }} '''Nora Barry Fischer''' (born in 1951){{cite web |url=http://www.pawd.uscourts.gov/Documents/Public/Reference/j_fischer.pdf |title=Biography of Honorable Nora Barry Fischer |author= |date= |publisher=U.S. District Court Western District Pennsylvania |accessdate=September 17, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130509192828/http://www.pawd.uscourts.gov/Documents/Public/Reference/j_fischer.pdf |archive-date=May 9, 2013 |url-status=dead }} is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania]]. ==Early life and education== Fischer was born Nora Barry in [[Homestead, Pennsylvania|Homestead]], [[Pennsylvania]], to Michael T. Barry and Olga Stipetich Barry, both first generation United States citizens. She is one of eight siblings, all of whom graduated from college.[http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/postgazette/obituary.aspx?pid=155748824 MICHAEL T. "RED" BARRY Obituary] Pittsburgh Post Gazette, February 2012 Fischer attended [[Saint Mary's College (Indiana)|Saint Mary's College]], where she studied history and humanistic studies. As part of her undergraduate education she attended L'Universite Catholique (see [[Catholic University of the West]]) located in Angers, France for one academic year. She graduated with her [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in 1973 and later from [[Notre Dame Law School]] with a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1976. ==Legal career== Following law school graduation, she worked as a legal editor at Callaghan & Company, in part working on revisions to McQuillin on Municipal Corporations and to Fletchers Cyclopedia on Corporations. Fischer returned to [[Pittsburgh]] in 1977 where she became the first female associate at Meyer Darragh Buckler Bebenek & Eck, an [[insurance]] defense [[Lawsuit|litigation]] firm. In 1980, Fischer was named the first female junior partner at Meyer Darragh Buckler Bebenek & Eck and in 1982, its first female senior partner. In 1992, she joined the firm of Pietragallo Bosick & Gordon as an [[equity partner]]. She served the firm as administrative partner and as a practice group leader. Her practice at both Meyer Darragh and PB&G was litigation based, as she handled [[product liability]], [[toxic tort]], insurance coverage and [[bad faith]] as well as municipal liability and [[Civil and political rights|civil rights]] litigation. ==Federal judicial career== On the recommendation of Senator [[Arlen Specter]], Fischer was nominated to the United States District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania by President [[George W. Bush]] on January 9, 2007, to a seat vacated [[Robert J. Cindrich]], who resigned. Fischer was confirmed by the [[United States Senate|Senate]] on February 14, 2007, on an unopposed 96-0 Senate vote and received her commission on April 2, 2007. She assumed [[senior status]] on June 13, 2019. ==Notable cases== In October 2010, Fischer sentenced a man from [[New Castle, Pennsylvania|New Castle]], Pennsylvania, to 30 years in prison for transporting and receiving child pornography.{{Citation needed|date=March 2026}} In 2012 and 2013, she upheld a verdict and damages award of $1.17 billion in a patent infringement suit against [[Marvell Technology Group]].{{Cite news |author= Bernard Vaughan |work= Reuters |title= Judge upholds $1.17 billion patent verdict against Marvell |date= August 23, 2013 |url= https://www.reuters.com/article/us-marvell-carnegiemellon-idUSBRE97N00V20130824 |accessdate=August 24, 2013 }}{{Cite news |author= Jonathan Stempel |title= Chipmaker Marvell loses $1.17 billion patent verdict |work= Chicago Tribune |date= December 26, 2012 |url= https://www.chicagotribune.com/2012/12/26/chipmaker-marvell-loses-117-billion-patent-verdict/ |access-date=August 24, 2013 }} ==Personal== Fischer is married to Dr. Donald R. '''Norman Kenneth Moon''' (born November 4, 1936)<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-OWsLwFBT9EC&dq=%22Norman+kenneth+moon%22+Judicial&pg=PA811|title=Confirmation Hearings on Federal Appointments: Hearings Before the Committee on the Judiciary, United States Senate, One Hundred Fifth Congress, First Session, on Confirmation of Appointees to the Federal Judiciary|page=811|year=1998}}</ref> is an American lawyer who has served as a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Virginia]].

==Education and career==

Moon was born in [[Lynchburg, Virginia]]. He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] from the [[University of Virginia]] in 1959 and his [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Virginia School of Law]] in 1962. He was in private practice in Lynchburg from 1962 to 1974. He was a judge on the Twenty-fourth Judicial Circuit of Virginia from 1974 to 1985, serving as Chief Judge from 1983 to 1984. He was a judge on the [[Court of Appeals of Virginia]] from 1985 to 1997, serving as Chief Judge from 1993 to 1997. He received a [[Master of Laws]] from the [[University of Virginia School of Law]] in 1988.<ref name="FJC">{{FJC Bio|nid=1390551|inline=yes}}</ref>

===Federal judicial service===

On October 8, 1997, Moon was nominated by President [[Bill Clinton]] to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Virginia]] vacated by Judge [[Jackson L. Kiser]]. Moon was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on November 7, 1997, and received his commission on November 12, 1997. He took [[senior status]] on July 1, 2010.<ref name="FJC"/>

==== Notable decisions ====
*In May 2019, Moon rejected constitutional challenges to the [[Anti-Riot Act]] by accused [[Rise Above Movement]] rioters and accepted their conditional guilty pleas for criminal offenses at the 2017 [[Unite the Right rally]].<ref>{{cite court |litigants=United States v. Daley|vol=378|reporter=F.Supp. 3d|opinion=539|court=W.D. Va.|date=2019|url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=5997160015164562386|accessdate=}}</ref> In August 2020, Moon's judgment was affirmed by the unanimous [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit]].<ref>{{Bluebook journal |first=|last=Note|title=Recent Case: Fourth Circuit Finds the Anti-Riot Act Partially Unconstitutional|volume=134 |journal=[[Harvard Law Review|Harv. L. Rev.]] |page=2614|url=https://harvardlawreview.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/134-Harv.-L.-Rev.-2614-1.pdf|year=2021}}</ref>
*In 2022 he dismissed the lawsuit brought by former [[Charlottesville]] police chief Rashall Brackney alleging racism had forced her out of her position.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-01-24 |title=Judge Moon throws out former Charlottesville Police Chief's suit against the city |url=https://infocville.com/2023/01/24/judge-moon-throws-out-former-charlottesville-police-chiefs-suit-against-the-city/ |access-date=2023-04-26 |website=Information Charlottesville |language=en}}</ref>
*In 2023 he reduced the $24 million punitive damages settlement against [[Unite the Right rally|Unite the Right]] demonstrators to $350,000. The law requires that jurors not be told of the $350,000 maximum, but that any amount demanded over that be reduced to $350,000.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Judge slashes millions owed by hate groups for 2017 Charlottesville rally |language=en-US |work=Washington Post |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/dc-md-va/2023/01/03/charlottesville-unite-the-right-damages/ |access-date=2023-04-26 |issn=0190-8286}}</ref>
*In 2023 he dismissed the lawsuit brought by [[Jason Kessler]] following the Unite The Right rally in Charlottesville.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Judge dismisses Kessler's civil rights lawsuit against the city |url=http://www.cbs19news.com/story/41769425/judge-throws-jason-kesslers-case-against-the-city-claiming-civil-rights-violated |access-date=2023-04-26 |website=www.cbs19news.com |language=en}}</ref>

'''Norwood Carlton Tilley Jr.''' (born December 16, 1943) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Middle District of North Carolina]].

==Education and career==
Tilley was born in [[Rock Hill, South Carolina]]. He received a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree from [[Wake Forest University]] in 1966 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Wake Forest University School of Law]] in 1969. He was a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Eugene Andrew Gordon]] of the [[United States District Court for the Middle District of North Carolina]] from 1969 to 1971. He was an [[assistant United States attorney]] of the Middle District of North Carolina from 1971 to 1974. He was the [[United States Attorney]] for the Middle District of North Carolina from 1974 to 1977. He was in private practice in [[Greensboro, North Carolina]] from 1977 to 1988.<ref name="auto">{{FJC Bio|nid=1388816}}</ref>

===Federal judicial service===
Tilley was nominated by President [[Ronald Reagan]] on April 26, 1988, to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Middle District of North Carolina]] vacated by Judge [[Hiram Hamilton Ward]]. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on October 14, 1988, and received his commission on October 17, 1988. He served as Chief Judge from 1999 to 2006. He assumed [[senior status]] on December 16, 2008.<ref name="auto"/>

===Notable cases===
Tilley was the judge who decided [[Yacovelli v. Moeser]] (2002).

'''Omar Antonio Williams''' (born 1977)<ref name="Questionnaire">[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/O.%20Williams%20SJQ%20Public%20Final.pdf United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees: Omar Antonio Williams]</ref> is an American attorney serving as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Connecticut]]. He previously served as a judge of the [[New London District Superior Court]] from 2016 to 2021.

== Early life and education ==

Williams was born in [[Rochester, New York]]. He earned a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from the [[University of Connecticut]] in 1998 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Connecticut School of Law]] in 2002.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|date=June 15, 2021|title=President Biden Announces 4th Slate of Judicial Nominations|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/06/15/president-biden-announces-4th-slate-of-judicial-nominations/|access-date=June 15, 2021|website=The White House|language=en-US}}</ref>

== Career ==

Williams began his career as an [[public defender|assistant public defender]]. In 2014, he was nominated by Governor [[Dannel Malloy]] to serve as a judge of the [[Connecticut Superior Court|New London District Superior Court]].<ref>{{Cite press release |title=Gov. Malloy nominates four Connecticut residents to superior court, five to board of pardons and paroles |date=October 8, 2014 |url=https://portal.ct.gov/Malloy-Archive/Press-Room/Press-Releases/2014/10-2014/Gov-Malloy-Nominates-Four-Connecticut-Residents-to-Superior-Court-Five-to-Board-of-Pardons-and-Parol |access-date=June 18, 2021}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=October 11, 2014|title=Bridgeport Man Appointed To Serve As Superior Court Judge|url=https://dailyvoice.com/connecticut/bridgeport/news/bridgeport-man-appointed-to-serve-as-superior-court-judge/498867/|access-date=June 15, 2021|website=Bridgeport Daily Voice|language=en}}</ref>  On January 30, 2015, he was unanimously confirmed by both chambers of the General Assembly.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Vote for HJ-45 Roll Call Number 3 |url=https://www.cga.ct.gov/2015/VOTE/H/2015HV-00003-R00HJ00045-HV.htm |website=Connecticut General Assembly}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=January 30, 2015 |title=Vote for HJ-45 Sequence Number 35 |url=https://www.cga.ct.gov/2015/VOTE/s/2015SV-00035-R00HJ00045-SV.htm |access-date=June 18, 2021}}</ref> Williams was involved with the New England Regional Judicial Opioid Initiative, the Sentence Review Division, and the Wiretap Panel.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://law.uconn.edu/2021/06/17/omar-a-williams-02-nominated-to-the-u-s-district-court-for-ct/ | title=Omar A. Williams '02 Nominated to the U.S. District Court for CT | School of Law | date=June 17, 2021 }}</ref> In 2020, Williams served on a task force that provided recommendations on reforming the way jurors are selected for trial in Connecticut.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.courant.com/politics/hc-pol-jury-trial-recommendations-20210406-c75xmxooqjeppoi3apzsv4pfmq-story.html|title=Democrats advance reforms designed by Connecticut judges, attorneys to reduce racial bias in jury selection|first=Zach|last=Murdock|website=courant.com|date=April 6, 2021 }}</ref>

=== Federal judicial service ===
On June 15, 2021, President [[Joe Biden]] nominated Williams to serve as a United States district judge for the [[United States District Court for the District of Connecticut]] to the seat vacated by Judge [[Alvin W. Thompson]], who assumed [[senior status]] on August 31, 2018.<ref>{{Cite }}</ref> On September 23, 2021, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 13–9 vote.<ref>{{cite [[Tulane University Law School|Tulane University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} ''' Orelia Eleta Merchant''' (born 1971){{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Merchant%20SJQ%20Public%20Final.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=January 24, 2023}} is an American lawyer who serves as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York]]. She previously served as chief deputy attorney general for state counsel in the [[Attorney General of New York|New York Attorney General's Office]]. == Education == Merchant earned a [[Bachelor of Science degree]] in [[physics]] and [[mathematics]] from [[Dillard University]] in 1992, a [[Master of Arts]] in [[marine science]] from the [[College of William & Mary]] in 1995, and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[Tulane University Law School]] in 1998.{{Cite web |title=Orelia E. In 2000 and 2001, Merchant served as a special assistant United States attorney in the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana|United States Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Louisiana]]. Merchant served as an assistant United States attorney in the United States Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of New York from 2002 to 2016 and executive assistant United States attorney from 2016 to 2019. She joined the New York Attorney General's Office in 2019 and left in 2023 when she became a district court judge.{{Cite web |date=September 2, 2022 |title=President Biden Names Twenty-Sixth Round of Judicial Nominees |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/09/02/president-biden-names-twenty-sixth-round-of-judicial-nominees/ |access-date=September 2, 2022 |website=The White House |language=en-US}} === Federal judicial service === Merchant was recommended to President [[Joe Biden]] by Senator [[Chuck Schumer]].{{Cite web |last=Balk |first=Tim |date=June 9, 2022 |title=Sen. She served as Chief Judge from 1999 to 2006, when Judge [[Jack Tarpley Camp Jr.]] became Chief Judge. Evans assumed [[senior status]] on December 31, 2008. '''Orlando Luis Garcia''' (born 1952) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Texas]] and former [[Texas]] [[Texas Legislature|state legislator]].

==Education and career==

Garcia was born in [[Jim Wells County, Texas]]. He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from the [[University of Texas at Austin]] in 1975 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Texas School of Law]] in 1978. He was in private practice in [[San Antonio, Texas]] from 1978 to 1990, and served in the [[Texas House of Representatives]] from 1983 to 1991. From 1991 to 1992 he was a judge of the Texas Fourth Court of Appeals.

===Federal judicial service===
Garcia was nominated by President [[Bill Clinton]] on November 19, 1993, to a seat vacated by Judge [[Emilio M. Garza]], who was elevated to the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]] in 1991. Garcia was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on March 10, 1994, and received his commission on March 11, 1994. He became chief judge on January 1, 2016, and served until November 18, 2022, when he turned 70 years old.<ref>{{FJC Bio|nid=1381036|inline=yes}}</ref>

On February 26, 2014, in San Antonio, Garcia [[De Leon v. Perry|overturned]] the [[Defense of Marriage Act (Texas)|Texas ban]] on [[same-sex marriage]], ruling that the prohibition is unconstitutional and stigmatizes the relationship of gay couples in the conservative state. He stayed his ruling pending appeal.<ref>{{cite news|author=Guillermo Contreras|url=http://www.mysanantonio.com/news/local/article/Texas-ban-on-gay-marriage-ruled-unconstitutional-5270099.php|newspaper=San Antonio Express-News|date=February 26, 2014|title=Texas' ban on gay marriage ruled unconstitutional}}</ref>

In August 2017, Garcia granted a preliminary injunction against [[Texas Senate Bill 4]], which imposed prohibitions against certain local policies relating to illegal immigration.<ref>{{cite court
|litigants=City of El Cenizo v. Texas
|vol=264
|reporter=F. Supp. 3d
|opinion=744
|court=W.D. Tex.
|date=2017
|url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=12929557267537567791}}</ref> That injunction was reversed in part by the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]] in May 2018.<ref>{{Bluebook journal |first=|last=Note|title=Recent Case: Fifth Circuit Reverses Injunction of Texas’s Sanctuary Cities Bill|volume=132 |journal=[[Harvard Law Review|Harv. L. Rev.]] | page=1738 | url=https://harvardlawreview.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/1738-1747_Online.pdf| year=2019}}</ref>

As chief judge, starting in 2020, the allegedly litigant-friendly behavior of Judge [[Alan Albright]] of the [[Waco]] division of the court led to a significant increase in [[patent]] filings in that division. Garcia ultimately responded to Albright's behavior by issuing a [[Docket (court)|docket]]-stripping order that ensured patent cases filed in Waco would be randomly assigned rather than assigned to Albright by default.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.law.com/texaslawyer/2022/07/25/the-western-district-of-texas-may-have-just-dethroned-the-king-of-patent-litigation/|title=The King of Patent Litigation Might Just Have Been Dethroned|website=Texas Lawyer|access-date=July 28, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web| title=Order assigning the business of the court as it relates tо patent cases | url=https://www.txwd.uscourts.gov/wp-content/uploads/Standing%20Orders/District/Order%20Assigning%20the%20Business%20of%20the%20Court%20as%20it%20Relates%20to%20Patent%20Cases%20072522.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220725222115/https://www.txwd.uscourts.gov/wp-content/uploads/Standing%20Orders/District/Order%20Assigning%20the%20Business%20of%20the%20Court%20as%20it%20Relates%20to%20Patent%20Cases%20072522.pdf | archive-date=2022-07-25}}</ref>

'''Patrick Casey Pitts''' (born 1980)<ref name="Questionnaire">{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Pitts%20SJQ%20Public%20Final1.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=December 12, 2022}}</ref> is an American lawyer from [[California]] who is serving as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of California]].

== Education ==

A native of [[Fargo, North Dakota]], Pitts graduated from [[Fargo South High School]].<ref>https://www.ndcourts.gov/news/federal-courts/related-courts/general-news/federal-practice-committee-sponsors-cle-speaker</ref> Pitts received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] from [[Yale University]] in 2003 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Yale Law School]] in 2008.<ref name="WHBio">{{Cite press release|title=President Biden Names Twenty-Sixth Round of Judicial Nominees|date=September 2, 2022|publisher=The White House|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/09/02/president-biden-names-twenty-sixth-round-of-judicial-nominees/|access-date=September 2, 2022}}{{PD-notice}}</ref>  While in law school, he was a director of the Rebellious Lawyering Conference, managing editor of the ''[[Yale Journal of Law and Feminism]]'', and a senior editor of the ''[[Yale Law Journal]]''.<ref name="altshulerberzon">{{Cite web |title=P. Casey Pitts |url=https://altshulerberzon.com/attorneys/p-casey-pitts/ |access-date=September 2, 2022 |website=Altshuler Berzon LLP |language=en-US}}</ref>{{failed verification|date=August 2023}}

== Career ==

Pitts served as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Stephen Reinhardt]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]] from 2008 to 2009. He was a [[law firm partner|partner]] at Altshuler Berzon LLP in [[San Francisco]], [[California]], where he worked from 2009 to 2023. Pitts was an [[law firm associate|associate]] at the firm from 2009 to 2017.<ref name="WHBio" />

=== Notable cases ===

In 2010, Pitts was part of the legal team that represented the [[United Teachers Los Angeles]] in ''Reed v. United Teachers Los Angeles''. The case involved the Education Code and the [[collective bargaining agreement]] between the district and its teachers, which generally requires that when the district reduces its teaching force for budgetary reasons, lay-offs must be based on seniority. In the summer of 2009, the district faced a budget shortfall and implemented a reduction in force (RIF) and laid-off temporary and probationary teachers. Other schools in the district did not suffer the same fate. For the 2009–2010 school year, vacancies at the Three Schools were filled with [[substitute teachers]]. In the spring of 2010, the district again faced a budget shortfall. It proposed a second RIF that would include permanent as well as probationary teachers.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://casetext.com/case/reed-v-united-teachers-la?q=P.%20Casey%20Pitts&sort=relevance&p=5&type=case | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220909014920/https://casetext.com/case/reed-v-united-teachers-la?q=P.%20Casey%20Pitts&sort=relevance&p=5&type=case | url-status=dead | archive-date=September 9, 2022 | title=Reed v. United Teachers Los Angeles, 208 Cal.App.4th 322}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.anylaw.com/case/sharail-reed-et-al-v-united-teachers-los-angeles/california-court-of-appeal/08-10-2012/SqQsSGYBTlTomsSBHYu3|title=Sharail Reed et al v. United Teachers Los Angeles |website=www.anylaw.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aclusocal.org/en/cases/reed-v-state-california|title=Reed v. State of California|date=April 19, 2005|website=ACLU of Southern California}}</ref>

In 2013, Pitts, Altshuler Berzon, Stephen Berzon and Scott Kronland represented the [[United Food and Commercial Workers Union]] Local 8. They filed an ''[[amicus curiae]]'' against plaintiff [[Ralphs Grocery Company]]. Beginning in October 2008, non-employee representatives of respondent, defendant United Food and Commercial Workers Union Local 8, began an informational [[picket line]] in front of the Foods Co store. Allegations included the picketing involved carrying placards, distributing leaflets, and attempting to engage Foods Co shoppers in conversations to inform them that Foods Co workers did not receive the benefits they would under a union contract. In addition, there were allegations of confrontations between picketers and store employees and of occasional aggressive efforts by picketers to give handbills to customers who were not willing to receive them. Alleging that the picketers refused to obey the rules appellant had established for presence on the property, and alleging that the police department was unwilling to remove the picketers from the property, appellant filed a complaint in February 2009 for declaratory and injunctive relief and for damages arising from respondent's picketers' continued presence.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://casetext.com/case/ralphs-grocery-co-v-united-food-commercial-workers-union-local-9/?q=P.%20Casey%20Pitts&sort=relevance&p=1&type=case | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220909014855/https://casetext.com/case/ralphs-grocery-co-v-united-food-commercial-workers-union-local-9/?q=P.%20Casey%20Pitts&sort=relevance&p=1&type=case | url-status=dead | archive-date=September 9, 2022 | title=Ralphs Grocery Co. V. United Food & Commercial Workers Union Local 8, No. F058716}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2012/s185544.html|title=Ralphs Grocery Co. v. United Food & Commercial Workers Union Local 8|website=Justia Law}}</ref>

In 2015, Pitts was part of the legal team that represented Tristan Broussard. Broussard is a [[transgender man]] who was employed with First Tower Loan, LLC, a [[consumer loan]] company, headquartered in Mississippi, with branches in five states, including Louisiana. Broussard's employment was terminated by the company.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://casetext.com/case/broussard-v-first-tower-loan-llc-5?q=P.%20Casey%20Pitts&sort=relevance&p=4&type=case | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220909014854/https://casetext.com/case/broussard-v-first-tower-loan-llc-5?q=P.%20Casey%20Pitts&sort=relevance&p=4&type=case | url-status=dead | archive-date=September 9, 2022 | title=Broussard v. First Tower Loan, LLC, 150 F. Supp. 3d 709}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nclrights.org/about-us/press-release/civil-rights-groups-sue-national-finance-company-for-illegally-firing-transgender-employee/|title=Civil Rights Groups Sue National Finance Company for Illegally Firing Transgender Employee|website=National Center for Lesbian Rights}}</ref>

In 2020, Pitts was part of the legal team that represented the defendant union in Jenni Chambers' case against the [[American Federation of State, County, and Municipal Employees]] International Union. The plaintiffs were public employees in Oregon, while the defendants were unions or their affiliates that exclusively represent Plaintiffs in the public workplace. The unions negotiated collective bargaining agreements ("CBAs") with the plaintiffs' public employers. These CBAs established the terms and conditions of employment for the relevant bargaining units. Although the plaintiffs were not members of the unions, Oregon law had previously required plaintiffs to pay compulsory union fees, often by automatic deduction from plaintiffs' wages, to the unions as a condition of plaintiffs' public employment. In addition, certain provisions in plaintiffs' respective CBAs reinforced this obligation. Plaintiffs did not consent to paying these fees to the Unions.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://casetext.com/case/chambers-v-am-fedn-of-state-cnty-mun-emps-intl-union?q=P.%20Casey%20Pitts&sort=relevance&p=2&type=case | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220909014852/https://casetext.com/case/chambers-v-am-fedn-of-state-cnty-mun-emps-intl-union?q=P.%20Casey%20Pitts&sort=relevance&p=2&type=case | url-status=dead | archive-date=September 9, 2022 | title=Chambers v. Am. Fed'n of State, Cnty., & Mun. Emps. Int'l Union, 450 F. Supp. 3d 1108}}</ref>

=== Federal judicial service ===

On September 2, 2022, President [[Joe Biden]] announced his intent to nominate Pitts to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of California]]. On September 6, 2022, his nomination was sent to the Senate. President Biden nominated Pitts to the seat vacated by Judge [[Lucy Koh]], who was elevated to the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]] on December 15, 2021.<ref>{{Cite press release|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate|date=September 6, 2022|publisher=The White House|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/09/06/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-80/}}</ref> On December 13, 2022, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Nominations|date=December 12, 2022|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/12/13/2022/nominations}}</ref> On January 3, 2023, his nomination was returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]]. He was renominated on January 23, 2023.<ref>{{Cite press release |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |date=January 23, 2023 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2023/01/23/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-92/}}</ref> On February 9, 2023, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 12–9 vote.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/2023-02-09%20-%20EBM%20-%20Results.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – February 9, 2023|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=February 9, 2023}}</ref> On June 14, 2023, the Senate invoked cloture on his nomination by a 53–46 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00159.htm|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: P. Casey Pitts to be United States District Judge for the Northern District of California)|website=United States Senate|date=June 14, 2023|access-date=June 14, 2023}}</ref> Later that day, his nomination was confirmed by a 53–46 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00161.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: P. Casey Pitts, of California, to be United States District Judge for the Northern District of California)|website=United States Senate|date=June 14, 2023|access-date=June 14, 2023}}</ref> He received his judicial commission on July 7, 2023.<ref>{{FJC Bio|nid=13705591|inline=yes}}</ref> Pitts became the only [[LGBT]] [[Federal tribunals in the United States#Article III courts|Article III judge]] actively serving on the United States District Court for the Northern District of California.<ref name="WHBio" /><ref>{{Cite web|last=Adler|first=Madison|date=September 2, 2022|title=Montana Law Professor Is Biden's Pick for Ninth Circuit Seat|url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/montana-law-professor-is-bidens-pick-for-ninth-circuit-seat-19|access-date=September 2, 2022|website=news.bloomberglaw.com|language=en}}</ref>

=== Notable rulings ===
On December 24, 2025, Pitts blocked ICE from conducting immigration arrests in northern California courthouses, agreeing with plaintiffs that ICE's presence presented noncitizens with a "Hobson's choice" between attending mandatory court hearings and risking arrest by ICE or not attending and risking a removal order.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://davisvanguard.org/2025/12/federal-judge-blocks-courthouse-arrests/|title=Federal Judge Pauses Trump Administration Policy Allowing Immigration Courthouse Arrests in Northern California|website=Vanguard|date=2025-12-26|access-date=2025-12-26}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2025-12-25/federal-judge-blocks-ice-from-arresting-immigrants-in-northern-california-courts|title=Federal judge blocks ICE from arresting immigrants in Northern California courts|website=Los Angeles Times|date=2025-12-24|access-date=2025-12-26}}</ref>
