'''Paul Adam Engelmayer''' (born 1961)<ref name="fjc.gov" /> is an American lawyer and jurist serving as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York|U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York]]. He was appointed in 2011 by President [[Barack Obama]].

== Early life and education ==
Engelmayer was born in 1961 in [[New York City]]. He graduated from [[Harvard University]] in 1983 with a [[Bachelor of Arts]], ''[[summa cum laude]]''.<ref name="whgov_20110202" /> After spending a year as a staff reporter for ''[[The Wall Street Journal]]'', he attended [[Harvard Law School]], where he was the treasurer of the ''[[Harvard Law Review]]''. He graduated in 1987 with a [[Juris Doctor]], ''magna cum laude''.<ref name=whgov_20110202>{{Cite web | author=The White House: Office of the Press Secretary | url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2011/02/02/president-obama-names-two-united-states-district-court | title=President Obama Names Two to the United States District Court | date=February 2, 2011 | via=[[NARA|National Archives]] | work=[[whitehouse.gov]] | access-date=March 26, 2011}}</ref>

After law school, Engelmayer was a [[law clerk]] to Chief Judge [[Patricia Wald]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit|U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia]] from 1987 to 1988,<ref name=whgov_20110202/> and then for Justice [[Thurgood Marshall]] of the [[Supreme Court of the United States|U.S. Supreme Court]] from 1988 to 1989.<ref name=whgov_20110202/><ref name="fjc.gov">{{FJC Bio|nid=1393736|inline=yes}}</ref>

== Career ==
From 1989 to 1994, Engelmayer served as a federal prosecutor for the [[United States Attorney for the Southern District of New York|United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York]]. He served as an [[assistant United States attorney]] from 1989 to 1994, and as the Deputy Chief Appellate Attorney in 1994.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Hon. Paul A. Engelmayer |url=https://www.pli.edu/faculty/hon.-paul-a.-engelmayer-i432241 |access-date=2023-11-26 |website=www.pli.edu}}</ref>

From 1994 to 1996, Engelmayer served as an assistant to the [[United States Solicitor General]] [[Drew S. Days, III|Drew S. Days III]] in Washington D.C.<ref name="whgov_20110202" /> In that role, he argued four cases before the [[Supreme Court of the United States|U.S. Supreme Court]]. As of taking the bench, he had argued over 20 appellate cases.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2011-08-03 |title=Partner Paul Engelmayer Confirmed to US District Court |url=https://www.wilmerhale.com/insights/news/partner-paul-engelmayer-confirmed-to-us-district-court-august-3-2011 |access-date=2023-11-26 |website=www.wilmerhale.com |language=en}}</ref>

In 1996, Engelmayer returned to the United States Attorney's Office in Manhattan, serving as the Chief of the Major Crimes Unit.<ref name="whgov_20110202" /> He led the prosecution of Lawrence X. Cusack III, who created and sold $7 million worth of [[John F. Kennedy document hoax|forged documents]] claiming that [[John F. Kennedy|President John F. Kennedy]] paid hush money to conceal a supposed affair with [[Marilyn Monroe]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=NHL lawsuit assigned to former federal prosecutor |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/nhl/2012/12/16/nhl-lawsuit-assigned-to-former-federal-prosecutor/1773543/ |access-date=2023-11-26 |website=USA TODAY |language=en-US}}</ref> Engelmayer also received the U.S. Attorney's Director's Award for Superior Performance in 1998 in connection with his prosecution of William F. Duker, a New York City lawyer who defrauded the FDIC and the Resolution Trust Corporation of $1.4 million in overbillings.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite news |last=Weiser |first=Benjamin |date=1997-12-11 |title=Prison Term for Lawyer Who Overcharged U.S. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1997/12/11/nyregion/prison-term-for-lawyer-who-overcharged-us.html |access-date=2023-11-26 |work=New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Engelmayer and [[Lewis Liman]], a future colleague on the Southern District of New York bench, also prosecuted three defendants for a scheme to extort $40 million from the actor [[Bill Cosby]] by using threats to publicly claim that one of them was Cosby's illegitimate daughter.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Weiser |first=Benjamin |date=1997-07-26 |title=3 Are Found Guilty Of Trying to Extort Money From Cosby |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1997/07/26/nyregion/3-are-found-guilty-of-trying-to-extort-money-from-cosby.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171229090730/http://www.nytimes.com/1997/07/26/nyregion/3-are-found-guilty-of-trying-to-extort-money-from-cosby.html |archive-date=2017-12-29 |access-date=2024-12-29 |work=New York Times |language=en |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 2000, Engelmayer joined the law firm [[Wilmer Cutler Pickering Hale and Dorr]] in Manhattan as a [[Law firm partner|partner]].<ref name="whgov_20110202" /> He was the partner in charge of the New York office from 2005 until he was appointed as a federal judge in 2011.<ref name="fjc.gov" />

Engelmayer is an elected member of the [[American Law Institute]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Paul A. Engelmayer |url=https://www.ali.org/profile/675 |access-date=2025-02-12 |website=The American Law Institute}}</ref> He has lectured or taught at numerous law schools and professional conferences.<ref name=":1" /> He is a trustee of the Harvard Law Review.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.foundationsearch.com/TopSP/HARVARD%20LAW%20REVIEW%20ASSOCIATION-042104292.HTML|title=Foundation Search ("Harvard Law Review")|website=Foundationsearch.com|access-date=October 14, 2026}}</ref> In a 2001 [[The Wall Street Journal|Wall Street Journal]] op-ed, he discussed the challenges prosecutors investigating President [[Bill Clinton]]'s pardons of Marc Rich and others faced.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Engelmayer |first=Paul A. |date=2001-03-02 |title=Proving Bribery Isn't Easy |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB983494389378921301 |access-date=2024-12-29 |work=Wall Street Journal |language=en-US |issn=0099-9660}}</ref> In a keynote speech in 2015, he called on Congress to pass an insider trading law.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Engelmayer |first=Paul A. |date=2015-10-23 |title=Congress: U.S. Needs an Insider Trading Law |url=https://www.law.com/newyorklawjournal/almID/1202740459962/ |access-date=2024-12-29 |website=New York Law Journal |language=en}}</ref>

=== Federal judicial service ===
{{excessive examples|section of cases|date=February 2025}}
On February 2, 2011, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Engelmayer to fill the judicial seat vacated by Judge [[Gerard E. Lynch]], who was elevated to the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit]].<ref>{{Cite web|author=The White House: Office of the Press Secretary|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2011/02/02/presidential-nominations-sent-senate| title=Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate|date=February 2, 2011|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|access-date=March 26, 2011}}</ref> The [[American Bar Association]] rated Engelmayer as Unanimously Well Qualified.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Paul A. Engelmayer |url=https://ballotpedia.org/Paul_A._Engelmayer |access-date=2023-11-26 |website=Ballotpedia |language=en}}</ref> On March 16, Engelmayer attended a hearing before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].<ref name=blt_20110316>{{Cite news| first=David|last=Ingram|url=http://legaltimes.typepad.com/blt/2011/03/sdny-nominees-breeze-through-senate-hearing.html|title=SDNY Nominees Breeze Through Senate Hearing|work=[[Legal Times|The Blog of Legal Times]]| date=March 16, 2011|access-date=March 26, 2011}}</ref> On March 31, Senator [[Charles Grassley]] placed Engelmayer's nomination on hold, along with two other nominations.<ref>{{cite news|last=Keen|first=Lisa|title=Grassley puts gay district court nominee's vote on hold|url=http://www.keennewsservice.com/2011/03/31/grassley-puts-gay-district-court-nominees-vote-on-hold/|access-date=1 April 2011|newspaper=Keen News Service|date=March 31, 2011}}</ref> Grassley later lifted the holds, and the Senate Judiciary Committee referred Engelmayer's nomination to the full Senate.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/Materials112thCongress.cfm |title=Judicial Nominations Materials: 112th Congress |access-date=2011-03-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110927191217/http://judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/Materials112thCongress.cfm |archive-date=2011-09-27 |url-status=dead }}</ref> On July 26, the Senate confirmed Engelmayer by a 98–0 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1121/vote_112_1_00117.htm|title=U.S. Senate: U.S. Senate Roll Call Votes 112th Congress - 1st Session|website=Senate.gov|access-date=October 14, 2026}}</ref> He received his commission on July 27, 2011.<ref name="fjc.gov"/>

==== Notable civil cases and rulings ====
===== NYC subway advertisements =====
In 2012, in ''American Freedom Defense Initiative v. Metropolitan Transit Authority,''<ref>880 F.Supp.2d 456 (S.D.N.Y. 2012).  </ref> Engelmayer held that the MTA violated the First Amendment in refusing to allow a pro-Israel advertisement to appear on New York City subways and buses. The plaintiff advocacy organization had sought to place, in response to ads it viewed as anti-Israel, an ad that read: "In any war between the civilized man and the savage, support the civilized man" and "Support Israel. Defeat Jihad." The MTA blocked the ad based on a policy banning ads that demeaned people based on specified characteristics, including race, color, religion, and national origin. Engelmayer held that the ad was protected political speech and that, because the MTA's demeaning-speech policy was selective, banning such speech aimed only at certain categories of people, it was content-based without justification.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Weiser |first=Benjamin |date=2012-07-20 |title=MTA Violated Rights of Group, Judge Says |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/07/21/nyregion/mta-violated-rights-of-pro-israel-group-judge-says.html |work=New York Times}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Haberman |first=Clyde |date=2012-07-23 |title=Protecting Speech, Even When It's Unpopular |url=https://archive.nytimes.com/cityroom.blogs.nytimes.com/2012/07/23/protecting-speech-even-when-its-unpopular/ |access-date=2025-01-19 |website=New York Times |language=en}}</ref> The MTA allowed the ad to run, with a disclaimer.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2012-09-27 |title=After 'Savage' Flap, Subway Ads Get Disclaimers |url=https://www.nbcnewyork.com/news/local/mta-disclaimer-subway-ad-controversial-jihad-religious-political-moral/2094495/ |work=NBCNew York}}</ref>

===== Emergency rescue of AIG =====
In 2012, in ''Starr Int’l Co. vs. Federal Reserve Bank of N.Y.'',<ref>906 F.Supp.2d 202 (S.D.N.Y. 2012), ''aff’d'', 742 F.3d 37 (2d Cir. 2014), ''cert. denied'', 573 U.S. 947 (2014).</ref> Engelmayer dismissed multi-billion-dollar damages claims brought against the [[Federal Reserve Bank of New York]] by a major stockholder in [[American International Group, Inc.]]<ref>{{Cite news |date=2012-11-19 |title=Case Against New York Fed in A.I.G. Rescue Is Rejected |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/11/20/business/case-against-new-york-fed-in-aig-rescue-is-rejected.html |work=New York Times}}</ref> The state-law claims, for breach of fiduciary duty, arose from FRBNY's exercise of emergency rescue powers during the [[2008 financial crisis]]. Engelmayer held that the claims were federally preempted and that the plaintiff had failed to plead that FRBNY had taken control of AIG.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Bray |first=Chad |date=2012-11-19 |title=Judge Tosses Suit Over AIG |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/11/20/business/case-against-new-york-fed-in-aig-rescue-is-rejected.html |work=The New York Times}}</ref>

===== Bridge and tunnel discounts =====
In 2013, Engelmayer upheld New York City's policy of awarding bridge and tunnel toll discounts to residents of certain neighborhoods.<ref>''Janes v.'' ''Triborough Bridge and Tunnel Authority'', 977 F.Supp.2d 320 (S.D.N.Y. 2013), ''aff’d'', 774 F.3d 1052 (2d Cir. 2014), ''cert. denied'', 577 U.S. 914 (2015).</ref> The plaintiffs, non-resident motorists, had claimed an infringement of the right to travel and of the dormant commerce clause.<ref>{{Cite news |date=October 5, 2015 |title=Supreme Court upholds discounts for Staten Island residents |url=https://abc7ny.com/staten-island-tolls-supreme-court-verrazano-narrows-bridge/1018303 |work=Eyewitness News 7}}</ref>

===== Exotic dancers' wage claims =====
In 2013 and 2014, in ''Hart v. Rick's Cabaret, Intern., Inc.'', Engelmayer issued pretrial decisions holding a Manhattan [[strip club]] liable to a class of more than 1,900 exotic dancers for minimum wage, overtime, and other labor law violations. He held that the dancers were employees, not independent contractors, and protected by the federal [[Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938]] and the New York Labor Law.<ref>967 F.Supp.2d 901 (S.D.N.Y. 2013) and 60 F.Supp.3d 447 (S.D.N.Y. 2014).  </ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=McGeehan |first=Patrick |date=September 10, 2013 |title=Strippers Are Protected by Labor Laws, Judge Says |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2013/09/11/nyregion/strippers-are-protected-by-labor-laws-judge-says.html |work=New York Times}}</ref> These decisions awarded the class $10.8 million in damages, with additional claims set for trial.{{Citation needed|date=February 2025}} The case settled shortly before trial for approximately $15.5 million.<ref>''Hart v. RCI Holdings, Inc.,'' 2015 WL 5577713 (S.D.N.Y. Sept. 22, 2015).</ref>

===== Beastie Boys v. Monster Energy =====
In 2014, Engelmayer presided over a two-week jury trial of copyright infringement and [[Lanham Act]] false-endorsement claims brought by the hip-hop group the [[Beastie Boys]] against the energy drink company [[Monster Energy]], which had used segments of five Beastie Boys songs to promote its products online. The jury found for the Beastie Boys and awarded $1.7 million in damages.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Itzhkoff |first=Dave |date=June 6, 2014 |title=Beastie Boys Win $1.7 Million in Suit Over Unauthorized Use of Music |url=https://archive.nytimes.com/artsbeat.blogs.nytimes.com/2014/06/06/beastie-boys-win-1-7-million-in-suit-over-unauthorized-use-of-music/ |work=New York Times}}</ref><ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Newman |first=Jason |date=June 5, 2014 |title=Beastie Boys Win $1.7 Million in Monster Copyright Lawsuit |url=https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/beastie-boys-win-1-7-million-in-monster-energy-copyright-lawsuit-194992/ |magazine=Rolling Stone}}</ref> Engelmayer's post-trial rulings upheld the verdict<ref>''Beastie Boys v. Monster Energy Co.'', 66 F.Supp.3d 424 (S.D.N.Y. 2014).</ref> and awarded the Beastie Boys an additional $668,000 in prevailing party legal fees.<ref>112 F.Supp.3d 31 (S.D.N.Y. 2015).</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=June 17, 2015 |title=Beastie Boys win fight for their right to $668,000 legal fees from Monster Energy |url=https://www.theguardian.com/music/2015/jun/17/beastie-boys-win-fight-for-their-right-to-legal-fees-from-monster-energy#:~:text=Beastie%20Boys%20win%20fight%20for,Energy%20%7C%20Beastie%20Boys%20%7C%20The%20Guardian |work=The Guardian}}</ref>

===== Music licensing antitrust litigation =====
In 2014, Engelmayer sustained conspiracy and monopolization claims under the [[Sherman Antitrust Act]] brought by a class of local television broadcast televisions against [[SESAC|SESAC, LLC]], the nation's third-largest music licensing organization.<ref>''Meredith Corp. v. SESAC, LLC'', 1 F.Supp.3d 180 (S.D.N.Y. 2014).</ref> The case later settled for $58.5 million, with SESAC agreeing to henceforth resolve disputes over royalty rates in arbitration.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Sisario |first=Ben |date=July 23, 2015 |title=SESAC Settles Antitrust Lawsuit Over Royalty Rates |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/07/24/business/media/sesac-settles-antitrust-lawsuit-over-royalty-rates.html |work=New York Times}}</ref> In approving the class settlement and fee award, Engelmayer equated its terms to the landmark antitrust consent decrees that for decades had bound [[ASCAP]] and [[Broadcast Music, Inc.|BMI]], the nation's two largest music licensing organizations.<ref>87 F.Supp.3d 650 (S.D.N.Y. 2015).</ref>

===== Off-label marketing =====
In 2015, in a closely watched action for injunctive relief, ''Amarin Pharma, Inc. v. U.S. Food & Drug Administration'', Engelmayer held that the First Amendment bars the [[Food and Drug Administration]] from prosecuting a pharmaceutical manufacturer for misbranding, where the manufacturer's conduct consisted only of truthful speech marketing an off-label use of an FDA-approved product.<ref>119 F.Supp.3d 196 (S.D.N.Y. 2015).  </ref> He held that the First Amendment protects truthful speech by a manufacturer about a product's off-label uses, much as it protects the same speech when made by other speakers, such as doctors.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Pollack |first=Andrew |date=August 7, 2015 |title=Court Forbids F.D.A. From Blocking Truthful Promotion of Drug |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/08/08/business/court-forbids-fda-from-blocking-truthful-promotion-of-drug.html |work=New York Times}}</ref> The FDA did not appeal.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Dennis |first=Brady |date=March 8, 2016 |title=FDA settles with drug company on promotion of fish-oil pill for unapproved uses |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/national/health-science/fda-settles-with-drug-company-on-promotion-of-fish-oil-pill-for-unapproved-uses/2016/03/08/0403a5ea-e57d-11e5-bc08-3e03a5b41910_story.html |newspaper=Washington Post}}</ref>

===== Bernard L. Madoff bankruptcy =====
Between 2016 and 2019, Engelmayer issued a series of decisions<ref>''In re Bernard L. Madoff Investment Securities, LLC'', 2016 WL 183492 (S.D.N.Y. 2016), ''aff’d'', 697 Fed. ===== Disabled group home settlement =====
Between 2016 and 2019, Engelmayer presided over litigation over claims on behalf of severely disabled adults of years of physical abuse and deficient care at the Union Avenue IRA, a state-run group home staff called the "Bronx Zoo". In 2019, after Engelmayer sustained the claims of constitutional, statutory, and state-law violations<ref>''D.K. v. Teams'', 260 F.Supp.3d 334 (S.D.N.Y. 2017)</ref> and strongly urged the state to settle, New York State agreed to pay the residents $6 million and to surrender control of the facility to a private nonprofit agency.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Weiser |first=Benjamin |date=2019-09-30 |title=$6 Million for Disabled Adults Who Were Punched and Spat At |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/09/30/nyregion/ny-abuse-lawsuit-group-home.html |access-date=2025-01-19 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

===== Mirena multi-district litigation =====
In 2019, Engelmayer granted summary judgment for the defense, ending a nationwide products liability [[Multidistrict Litigation]] spanning claims by 920 plaintiffs.<ref>''In re Mirena IUS Levonorgestrel-Related Prod. Liab. Litig. MDL (No. II)'', 387 F.Supp.3d 323 (S.D.N.Y. 2019), ''aff’d'', 982 F.3d 113 (2d Cir. 2020).</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Raymond |first=Nate |date=June 11, 2019 |title=Bayer wins dismissal of 920 Mirena products liability lawsuits |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/legal/bayer-wins-dismissal-of-920-mirena-products-liability-lawsuits-idUSL2N23I1VT/ |work=Reuters}}</ref> The plaintiffs claimed that the synthetic hormone secreted by Mirena, an [[Intrauterine device|intrauterine contraceptive product]] made and marketed by [[Bayer AG]] and affiliates, caused users to suffer [[idiopathic intracranial hypertension]] (IIH), a condition involving buildup of cerebrospinal fluid around the brain. Engelmayer held that the plaintiffs had not adduced evidence to establish general causation—the capacity of Mirena to cause IIH. He had earlier excluded plaintiffs' seven proposed general causation experts because their testimony did not satisfy ''Daubert v. Merrill Dow Pharmaceuticals, Inc.'' and Federal Rule of Evidence 702.<ref>''In re Mirena IUS Levonorgestrel-Related Prod. Liab. Litig. MDL (No. II)'', 341 F.Supp.3d 213 (S.D.N.Y 2018), ''aff’d'', 982 F.3d 113 (2d Cir. 2020).</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=December 15, 2020 |title=Second Circuit Affirms Mirena MDL Court's "Hard Look" at Plaintiffs' Experts' Methodology |url=https://www.jdsupra.com/legalnews/second-circuit-affirms-mirena-mdl-court-21810/ |work=JD Supra}}</ref>

===== Airbnb data ordinance =====
In 2019, in ''Airbnb, Inc. v. City of New York'',<ref>373 F.Supp.3d 467 (S.D.N.Y. 2019).</ref> Engelmayer enjoined a [[New York City]] ordinance that required home-sharing companies to turn over voluminous data monthly about hosts, finding it facially invalid under the [[Fourth Amendment to the United States Constitution|Fourth Amendment]].<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Weiser |first1=Benjamin |last2=Goodman |first2=J. David |date=January 3, 2019 |title=Judge Blocks New York City Law Aimed at Curbing Airbnb Rentals |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/01/03/nyregion/nyc-airbnb-rentals.html |work=The New York Times}}</ref> Calling the scale of the required monthly productions breathtaking and unprecedented, he wrote: "The city has not cited any decision suggesting that the governmental appropriation of private business records on such a scale, unsupported by individualized suspicion or any tailored justification, qualifies as a reasonable search and seizure." He added: "An attempt by a municipality in an era before electronic data storage to compel an entire industry monthly to copy and produce its records as to all local customers would have been unthinkable under the Fourth Amendment." New York City and [[Airbnb]] later settled the lawsuit.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Carville |first=Olivia |date=July 12, 2020 |title=Airbnb Agrees to Give Host Data to NYC in Settlement |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2020-06-12/airbnb-settles-lawsuit-with-nyc-over-providing-host-data |work=Bloomberg News}}</ref>

===== Khashoggi FOIA litigation =====
In 2019, in a ruling on a [[Freedom of Information Act (United States)|Freedom of Information Act]] request,<ref>''Open Society Justice Initiative v. Central Intelligence Agency et al.''., 399 F.Supp.3d 161 (S.D.N.Y. 2019)</ref> Engelmayer ordered the U.S. Departments of State and Defense each to process at least 5,000 pages per month of materials relating to the killing of Saudi journalist and U.S. resident [[Jamal Khashoggi]]. Rejecting the agencies' request for a slower pace of processing, he said the request concerned "a matter of exceptional public importance and obvious and unusual time sensitivity".<ref>{{Cite news |last=Gonzales |first=Richard |date=August 6, 2019 |title=Federal Judge Orders Release Of Khashoggi Records By U.S. Government |url=https://www.npr.org/2019/08/06/748877181/federal-judge-orders-release-of-khashoggi-records-by-u-s-government |work=NPR}}</ref>

===== Conscience rule =====
In 2019, Engelmayer invalidated a 2019 rule that the [[U.S. Department of Health and Human Services]] had promulgated to define the statutory conscience rights of federally funded health care entities and providers.<ref>''State of New York v. United States Department of Health and Human Services'', 414 F.Supp.3d 475 (S.D.N.Y. 2019).</ref> The rule superseded a narrower 2011 rule, adding broadened definitions, new compliance regulations, and a new enforcement mechanism. On a challenge brought by states and cities led by New York State, Engelmayer held that HHS had violated the [[Administrative Procedure Act]]. The agency had no authority to impose major portions of the rule, he held, and its stated justification for the new rule-making "in the first place—a purported 'significant increase' in civilian complaints relating to the conscience provisions—was factually untrue." Engelmayer enjoined the rule's enforcement nationwide.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Weiser |first1=Benjamin |last2=Sanger-Katz |first2=Margot |date=November 6, 2019 |title=Judge Voids Trump-Backed 'Conscience Rule' for Health Care Workers |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/11/06/upshot/trump-conscience-rule-overturned.html |work=The New York Times}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Abutaleb |first=Yasmeen |date=November 6, 2019 |title=Trump's 'conscience rule' for health providers blocked by federal judge |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/health/trumps-conscience-rule-for-health-providers-voided-by-federal-judge/2019/11/06/39aa9b74-00b1-11ea-9518-1e76abc088b6_story.html |newspaper=Washington Post}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Editorial Board |date=November 8, 2019 |title='Flatly untrue': The courts again see through the Trump administration's bogus claims |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/the-trump-administration-takes-its-lies-to-court-and-loses--again/2019/11/08/31e16ca4-0199-11ea-8bab-0fc209e065a8_story.html |newspaper=Washington Post}}</ref> Later the same month, courts in the [[Northern District of California]] and the [[Eastern District of Washington]] issued similar rulings. HHS later dismissed its appeal of the decision and, in 2024, proposed an alternative rule implementing the statutory conscience provisions.<ref>{{Cite web |date=January 9, 2024 |title=HHS Issues New Nondiscrimination Final Rule to Protect Conscience Rights |url=https://www.hhs.gov/about/news/2024/01/09/hhs-issues-new-nondiscrimination-final-rule-protect-conscience-rights.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240109145055/https://www.hhs.gov/about/news/2024/01/09/hhs-issues-new-nondiscrimination-final-rule-protect-conscience-rights.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=January 9, 2024 |website=Department of Health and Human Services}}</ref>

===== Nasdaq Exchange Traded Funds litigation =====
In 2019, after a 10-day bench trial, Engelmayer entered judgment in favor of [[Nasdaq, Inc.]], owner of the world's second-largest stock exchange, on breach-of-contract claims against Exchange Traded Funds Managers Group, LLC, a company that constructed and managed index funds.<ref>''Nasdaq, Inc. v. Exchange Traded Managers Group, LLC'', 431 F.Supp.3d 176 (S.D.N.Y. 2019).</ref> He held that ETFMG had unlawfully seized and claimed entitlement to the stream of profits generated by a series of index funds, including a successful cybersecurity index fund known as HACK. He awarded Nasdaq more than $78.4 million, plus prejudgment interest.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Osipovich |first=Alexander |date=December 20, 2019 |title=Nasdaq Prevails in Lawsuit Over Alleged ETF Theft |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/nasdaq-prevails-in-lawsuit-over-alleged-etf-theft-11576884078 |work=Wall Street Journal}}</ref>

===== Blind pedestrian access =====
In 2020, in ''American Council for the Blind of New York, Inc. v. City of New York'',<ref>495 F.Supp.3d 211 (S.D.N.Y. 2020).</ref> Engelmayer held that New York City's longstanding failure to make its pedestrian grid meaningfully accessible to blind and low-vision pedestrians violated the ADA and state and city law.<ref>{{Cite news |last=McGeehan |first=Patrick |date=December 1, 2020 |title=Why the Pandemic Has Made Streets More Dangerous For Blind People |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/12/01/nyregion/nyc-blind-pedestrian-signals.html |work=New York Times}}</ref> In 2021, he ordered a remedial plan for those violations.<ref>579 F.Supp.3d 539.</ref> It required the City to install accessible pedestrian signals (APS) at a pace that would result in 10,000 signalized intersections equipped with APS by the end of 2031.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Watkins |first=Ali |date=December 27, 2021 |title=Why New York City May Soon Be More Walkable for Blind People |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/12/27/nyregion/nyc-crosswalk-blind-people.html |work=New York Times}}</ref> In 2022 and 2023, the first two years the remedial plan was implemented, the City's Department of Transportation installed, respectively, 519 and 885 APSs at city intersections, exceeding the plan's targets of 400 and 500 APSs, respectively.<ref>{{Cite web |date=November 2024 |title=New York City DOT Accessible Pedestrian Signals Program Status Report |url=https://www.nyc.gov/html/dot/downloads/pdf/aps-program-status-report.pdf}}</ref>

In 2023, Engelmayer issued a pair of decisions addressing questions of first impression under the Ending Forced Arbitration of Sexual Assault and Sexual Harassment Act of 2021 (EFAA), enacted in 2022.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Karni |first=Annie |date=February 10, 2022 |title=Congress Passes Bill to Nullify Forced Arbitration in Sex Abuse Cases |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/02/10/us/politics/senate-bill-forced-arbitration-sexual-harassment-assault.html |work=New York Times}}</ref> In one, he held that the EFAA's invalidation of arbitration agreements in cases of sexual assault or harassment extends to the entirety of the case, not merely to the discrete claims that themselves allege or relate to such harassment.<ref>''Johnson v. ===== Solar Winds securities litigation =====
In 2024, in a closely watched case, Engelmayer dismissed most claims the SEC brought against cybersecurity company Solar Winds and its chief information security officer, Timothy Brown. In December 2020, Solar Winds disclosed that it had fallen victim to a large-scale cyberattack known as SUNBURST. Engelmayer dismissed the SEC's claim that Solar Winds's disclosures about the attack were inadequate. He also dismissed the SEC's claim that the company had inadequate cybersecurity controls, holding that the Securities Exchange Act's accounting controls provision does not give the SEC authority to regulate cybersecurity controls.<ref>''SEC v. Solar Winds Corp.'', 2024 WL 3461952, --- F.3d --- (S.D.N.Y. July 18, 2018).</ref> But Engelmayer sustained the securities fraud claims based on a "Security Statement" on the company's website. The SEC, he held, adequately pleaded that Solar Winds and Brown, in that statement, falsely and misleadingly touted the company's cybersecurity, including its password and access controls, as strong.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Menn |first=Joseph |date=July 18, 2024 |title=Judge in SolarWinds case rejects SEC oversight of cybersecurity controls |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2024/07/18/solarwinds-sec-cybersecurity-hack-disclosures/ |newspaper=Washington Post}}</ref>

===== White-collar crime =====
In 2014, Engelmayer sentenced Nelson Castro, a Bronx assemblyman who was a longtime secret government informant, making recordings of colleagues while twice winning reelection. Calling Castro's cooperation historic and noting that it resulted in successful prosecutions including of a fellow assemblyman, Engelmayer sentenced Castro to two years' probation and 500 hours of community service on his federal false statement charge. "[T]he good that you did by cooperating over a period of years exposed and put an end to far more official corruption and misconduct than you engaged in", Engelmayer said. Too often, he said, elected officials "talk a good game about fighting corruption and then they do nothing about it. For all your warts, for all your misdeeds, you did something about it."<ref>{{Cite news |last=Weiser |first=Benjamin |date=2013-08-28 |title=Legislator Who Informed on Others Admits Lying to Authorities |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2013/08/28/nyregion/legislator-who-informed-on-others-admits-lying-to-authorities.html?login=smartlock&auth=login-smartlock |access-date=2025-01-19 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Weiser |first=Benjamin |date=2014-09-12 |title=Former Assemblyman Turned Informer Avoids Prison |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2014/09/12/nyregion/former-assemblyman-turned-informant-avoids-prison.html |access-date=2025-01-19 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

In 2015, Engelmayer sentenced Dmitry Braverman, an IT employee at the law firm of Wilson Sonsini, to two years in prison on insider trading charges, based on his trading ahead of mergers underway at the law firm.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Randazzo |first=Sara |date=July 29, 2015 |title=Ex-Wilson Sonsini Employee Sentenced to Two Years for Insider Trading |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/BL-LB-51800 |work=Wall Street Journal}}</ref>

In 2016, Engelmayer sentenced Alonzo Knowles, a Bahamian man who hacked celebrities' email and attempted to sell unreleased movie and television scripts and personal images and videos, to 60 months in prison. The sentence was about twice as long as recommended by federal sentencing guidelines, in part because Knowles, while awaiting sentencing, had been caught sending emails plotting, upon his release, to sell the scripts and materials.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Weiser |first=Benjamin |date=December 6, 2016 |title=Benjamin Weiser, "Man Who Hacked Celebrities' Email Accounts Gets 5 Years in Prison |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/12/06/nyregion/alonzo-knowles-celebrity-hacker.html |work=New York Times}}</ref>

In 2016, Engelmayer presided over the trial of "Banana King" Thomas Hoey on charges that he embezzled nearly $800,000 from his banana-distribution company's employees' retirement fund. Hoey was convicted at trial<ref>{{Cite news |date=March 18, 2016 |title=New York banana mogul convicted of embezzling retirement funds |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/world/us/new-york-banana-mogul-convicted-of-embezzling-retirement-funds-idUSKCN0WK2TM/ |work=Reuters}}</ref> and sentenced to 84 months' imprisonment, 66 of which were to run largely consecutive to a separate federal sentence on narcotics and obstruction of justice charges.{{Citation needed|date=February 2025}}

In 2017, Engelmayer presided over the trial on insider trading charges of John Afriyie, a Wall Street investment analyst who used his employer's confidential information relating to a potential acquisition of ADT Corp. as the basis to buy call options, which gained him more than $1.5 million when the acquisition was announced. Afriyie fled on the day of trial but was found and convicted.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Berthelsen |first=Christian |date=January 30, 2017 |title=EX-MSD Capital Analyst Convicted of Insider Trading Charges |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2017-01-30/ex-msd-capital-analyst-convicted-of-insider-trading-charges?embedded-checkout=true |work=Bloomberg}}</ref> Engelmayer sentenced him to 45 months in prison.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Pierson |first=Brendan |date=July 26, 2017 |title=Ex-New York analyst gets three years and nine months for insider trading |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/world/us/ex-new-york-analyst-gets-three-years-and-nine-months-for-insider-trading-idUSKBN1AB304/ |work=Reuters}}</ref>

In 2021 and 2022, Engelmayer presided over the prosecution of five [[Long Island Rail Road]] officials for a scheme to inflate their overtime hours. Each, in 2018, reportedly received more than $200,000 in overtime pay, with one claiming to have worked 3,864 overtime hours on top of 1,682 regular hours. Engelmayer called the offense "an orgy of overtime fraud carried out on an epic scale". He imposed sentences ranging from two to eight months in prison.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Weiser |first=Benjamin |date=December 3, 2020 |title=Rail Worker Accused of Overtime Fraud Made $461,000 in One Year |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/12/03/nyregion/mta-overtime-fraud.html |work=New York Times}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-02-04 |title=Southern District of New York {{!}} Highest Paid MTA Employee In 2018 Sentenced To 8 Months In Overtime Fraud Scheme {{!}} United States Department of Justice |url=https://www.justice.gov/usao-sdny/pr/highest-paid-mta-employee-2018-sentenced-8-months-overtime-fraud-scheme |access-date=2025-01-19 |website=www.justice.gov |language=en}}</ref>

In 2022, Engelmayer sentenced Hollywood executive William Sadlier to six years' imprisonment for defrauding a [[BlackRock]] investment fund of more than $30 million, based on two wire fraud schemes in which he posed as an executive of a sham company.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Crane-Newman |first=Molly |date=September 10, 2022 |title=Hollywood executive who bought himself a mansion with stolen investments sentenced to 6 years in federal prison |url-access=limited |url=https://www.nydailynews.com/2022/09/09/hollywood-executive-who-bought-himself-a-mansion-with-stolen-investments-sentenced-to-6-years-in-federal-prison/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250817035727/https://www.nydailynews.com/2022/09/09/hollywood-executive-who-bought-himself-a-mansion-with-stolen-investments-sentenced-to-6-years-in-federal-prison/ |url-status=live |archive-date=August 17, 2025 |work=New York Daily News}}</ref>

In 2022, Engelmayer presided over the trial of Stefan Gillier, a Belgian national extradited to the U.S., on wire fraud conspiracy charges based on a scheme to obtain over $6 million in aircraft parts. Gillier was convicted at trial. In 2023, Engelmayer sentenced him to 84 months in prison.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Moreno |first=Ivan |date=March 9, 2023 |title=Plane Parts Exec Gets 7 Years For $15M Fraud On Honeywell |url=https://www.law360.com/articles/1584069/plane-parts-exec-gets-7-years-for-15m-fraud-on-honeywell |work=Law360}}</ref>

In 2024, Engelmayer presided over the trial of Jonathan Moynahan Larmore, who was convicted of orchestrating a $77 million tender offer fraud. It involved announcing a fake tender offer for shares of [[WeWork|WeWork Inc.]] by a company Larmore founded at a price that stood to drive up WeWork's stock price. Days earlier, Larmore had purchased thousands of WeWork options that stood to be worth millions of dollars had the scheme succeeded.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Dolmetch |first=Chris |date=October 22, 2024 |title=Strip Mall Mogul Convicted in Scam Tied to Fake WeWork Bid |url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/securities-law/strip-mall-mogul-convicted-in-scam-tied-to-fake-bid-for-wework |work=Bloomberg Law}}</ref>

Magnuson was born and raised on a farm near [[Carthage, South Dakota]]. He is the product of a one-room schoolhouse and graduated in a class of 13 from high school.  Magnuson received his Bachelor of Arts degree in (1959) from [[Gustavus Adolphus College]] where he was active in athletics and student government, having served as Class President and Student Body President.  He received his Juris Doctor (1963) from [[William Mitchell College of Law]] (again Class President) where he attended night law school while employed as assistant registrar, casualty claim adjuster, and law clerk. == Career == === Attorney and lecturer === Magnuson served as a private practicing attorney for 18 years in the firm of Levander, Gillen Miller and Magnuson, South Saint Paul, Minnesota, where his endeavors emphasized eminent domain and municipal law. Magnuson served as a lecturer at [[William Mitchell College of Law]] and [[Hamline University School of Law]] from 1982 to 1989.  From 1986 to 1991, Magnuson also served as Jurist in Residence at a number of undergraduate college liberal arts campuses in Minnesota.  In 2010, Magnuson was a Fulbright Scholar at United International College, Zhuhai, China. === Federal judicial service === Magnuson was nominated by President [[Ronald Reagan]] and, upon confirmation, entered judicial service on November 16, 1981. During his judicial career, Magnuson has served on the Judicial Conference of the United States as a Member and Chair of the Bankruptcy Committee, and International Judicial Relations Committee, and a member of the Inter-Circuit Assignment Committee. He also served the [[Federal Judicial Center]] as a Member of the District Judges Education Committee.  Magnuson was also a longtime member of the Board of Directors of the Federal Judges Association, where he held numerous executive offices. In addition, Magnuson has traveled to some 50 countries where he has encouraged the development of independent, ethical judiciaries in emerging democracies. This work has primarily been in Eastern Europe, Central Asia, Asia, and Africa.{{citation needed|date=September 2021}} Magnuson served as Chief Judge from 1994 to 2001.{{cite web|url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/magnuson-paul-arthur|title=Magnuson, Paul Arthur - Federal Judicial Center|website=www.fjc.gov}} In 2002, he assumed senior status where he continues to carry an active case load.{{cite news|title=National Briefing {{!}} Washington: Stay Of Ruling On River Level|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2003/07/26/us/national-briefing-washington-stay-of-ruling-on-river-level.html|accessdate=17 December 2010|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=26 July 2003}} In 2009, Magnuson presided over a wrongful death civil suit over the [[killing of Fong Lee]] by a Minneapolis police officer.{{Cite news |last=Hanners |first=David |date=2009-05-27 |title=Tears, satisfaction after Fong Lee verdict favors city, police over family |work=[[St. Paul Pioneer Press]] |url=https://www.twincities.com/2009/05/27/tears-satisfaction-after-fong-lee-verdict-favors-city-police-over-family/ |access-date=2023-02-19}} In the early 2020s, he presided over the federal civil rights cases of the four Minneapolis police officers—[[Derek Chauvin]], Tou Thao, J. In July 2016, he was appointed by Chief Justice Roberts as the chair of the executive committee of the Judicial Conference of the United States.{{Cite web|url=http://www.uscourts.gov/news/2016/07/13/chief-justice-names-new-executive-committee-members|title=Chief Justice Names New Executive Committee Members|access-date=2016-07-19}} == Early life and education == Barbadoro was born in [[Providence, Rhode Island|Providence]], [[Rhode Island]], and grew up in [[Acton, Massachusetts|Acton]], [[Massachusetts]]. He graduated from [[Gettysburg College]] with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in 1977 and earned a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Boston College Law School]] in 1980.{{cite web|url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/barbadoro-paul-j.|title=Barbadoro, Paul J. - Federal Judicial Center|website=www.fjc.gov}} == Legal career == He was a New Hampshire Assistant Attorney General from 1979 to 1984,[https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=uc1.c050174085&view=1up&seq=810&q1=Paul%20James%20Barbadoro Confirmation hearings on federal appointments : hearings before the Committee on the Judiciary, United States Senate, One Hundred Second Congress, first session, on confirmation hearings on appointments to the federal judiciary pt.10 (1993)] and was counsel to [[United States Senator]] [[Warren Rudman]] from 1984 to 1986. After a brief stint in private practice in [[Concord, New Hampshire|Concord]], [[New Hampshire]], he served as Deputy Chief Counsel to the United States Senate investigative Committee on Secret Military Assistance to Iran and the Nicaraguan Opposition, during the [[Iran-Contra]] affair in 1987. He returned to private practice in [[Concord, New Hampshire]] from 1986 until he was appointed to the federal bench in 1992. He is also an [[adjunct Professor]] of Business Law at the [[Tuck School of Business]] at [[Dartmouth College]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.tuck.dartmouth.edu/faculty/faculty-directory/the-honorable-paul-barbadoro|title=Tuck School of Business {{!}} The Honorable Paul Barbadoro|website=www.tuck.dartmouth.edu|access-date=2016-07-19}} == Federal judicial service == At the time of his appointment, Barbadoro was the youngest candidate to ever be appointed as a federal judge.{{Cite web|url=http://abcolonialclub.com/barbadoro.html|title=Acton Boxborough Colonial Club|website=abcolonialclub.com|access-date=2016-07-19}} He was nominated by President [[George H. W. Bush]] on September 9, 1992, to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the District of New Hampshire]] vacated by Judge [[Shane Devine]]. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on October 8, 1992, and received his commission the next day. He served as Chief Judge from 1997 to 2004. He assumed [[senior status]] on March 1, 2021. ==Other service== More recently, in March 2008, Barbadoro was brought in from New Hampshire as a visiting judge to handle the case of former [[governor of Puerto Rico]] [[Aníbal Acevedo Vilá]]. The governor was indicted on 21 federal charges and due to the extensive coverage of case in the local media it was thought that Barbadoro would be a better choice for the case.{{Citation needed|date=March 2009}} On July 13, 2016, [[Supreme Court of the United States|United States Supreme Court]] Chief Justice John Roberts appointed Barbadoro to serve as chair of the [[Judicial Conference of the United States|Executive Committee of the Judicial Conference of the United States]]. Borman|publisher=University of Michigan Law School}} Borman was earlier an assistant United States attorney, and Special Counsel to the Mayor of Detroit. For 15 years thereafter, he was chief federal defender of the [[National Legal Aid & Defender Association|Legal Aid & Defender Association]] of Detroit from 1979 to 1994.{{cite web|url=http://detroitcenter.umich.edu/hall-of-fame/paul-d-borman|title=Paul D. Borman|publisher=University of Michigan Hall of Fame|access-date=2014-11-17|archive-date=2014-11-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141129032624/http://detroitcenter.umich.edu/hall-of-fame/paul-d-borman|url-status=dead}} When he was appointed to be a federal judge, he became the first federal defender to be appointed to the federal bench. He was also a professor and assistant dean at [[Wayne State University Law School]], and an adjunct lecturer at the [[University of Michigan Law School]]. ==Early life and education== Borman was a native of [[Detroit]], [[Michigan]], and his father – Tom Borman – was president of Borman Food Stores, Inc.{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1964/01/19/paul-d-borman-becomes-fiance-of-susan-cohen.html?_r=0|work=The New York Times|title=Paul D. Borman Becomes Fiance of Susan Cohen; Graduate Law Student to Wed Daughter of S.E.C. Commissioner|date=19 January 1964}} Borman graduated from [[Mumford High School]] in 1956.{{cite web|url=http://mumfordhighschool.org/class-of-1956.html|title=Mumford HS class of 1956|author=Mumford High School}} He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in economics from the [[University of Michigan]] in 1959.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ndTmAAAAMAAJ&q=%22paul+d.+borman%22%7Ctitle%3DMichiganensian%7Cpublisher%3D&pg=PA425|title=Michiganensian|year=1959}} He later received a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Michigan Law School]] in 1962, and a [[Master of Laws]] from [[Yale Law School]] in 1964. Borman became engaged to Susan Cohen, daughter of [[Manuel F. Cohen]], Commissioner of the [[Securities and Exchange Commission]], in early 1964, and married her in June of that year.{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1964/07/11/man-in-the-news.html|work=The New York Times|title=Man in the News; New Wall St. Watchdog; Manuel Frederick Cohen|date=11 July 1964}} ==Career== Borman was a staff attorney of the [[United States Commission on Civil Rights]] from 1962 to 1963. He was then an [[assistant United States attorney]] for the [[United States Department of Justice]] from 1964 to 1965.{{cite web|url=https://www.mied.uscourts.gov/index.cfm?pageFunction=chambers&judgeid=15|title=Judge Paul D. Borman |publisher=United States District Court – Eastern Michigan District}} He later acted as Vice President and house counsel for Borman Food Stores, Inc. Borman was a Special Counsel, Mayor's Development Team, Detroit, in 1967. He was also Special Counsel to the Mayor of Detroit, [[Jerome Cavanagh]], from 1967 to 1968. He was an Assistant County Prosecutor, [[Wayne County, Michigan|Wayne County]], Michigan, from 1974 to 1975. He was Chief Federal Defender, [[National Legal Aid & Defender Association|Legal Aid & Defender Association]] of Detroit, from 1979 to 1994. When he was appointed to be a federal judge, he became the first federal defender to be appointed to the federal bench.{{cite web|url=http://scholarship.law.duke.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=4266&context=lcp|title=FEDERAL DEFENDER SERVICES: SERVING THE SYSTEMOR THE CLIENT?}} ===Academic career=== Borman was a professor at [[Wayne State University Law School]] from 1968 to 1979. He was an assistant dean at Wayne State University Law School from 1968 to 1973. He was an adjunct lecturer at the University of Michigan Law School from 1981 to 1994. ===Federal judicial service=== On March 24, 1994, Borman was nominated by President [[Bill Clinton]] to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan]] vacated by Judge [[Stewart Albert Newblatt]]. Borman was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on August 9, 1994, and received his commission on August 10, 1994. He assumed [[senior status]] on August 1, 2023.{{FJC Bio|nid=1378051|inline=yes}} ===Notable cases=== Judge Borman presided over the [[Trial of Geoffrey Fieger|trial]] of famed lawyer [[Geoffrey Fieger]] from April 14, 2008 to June 2, 2008, on charges of violations of the [[Federal Election Campaign Act]], making [[Making false statements|false statements]], and [[Obstruction of justice in the United States|obstruction of justice]]. Fieger was represented by [[Gerry Spence]] and was found not guilty on all charges.{{Cite news |last=Carter |first=Terry |date=2008-06-02 |title=Spence's No-Loss Record Stands with Fieger Acquittal |url=https://www.abajournal.com/news/article/spences_no_loss_record_stands_with_fieger_acquittal |access-date=2024-10-05 |work=[[ABA Journal]]}} On December 26, 2009, Judge Borman presided over the arraignment of [[Umar Farouk Abdulmuttalab]], who was charged with an attempt to destroy an aircraft and with placing a destructive device in proximity to an aircraft, in connection with [[Northwest Airlines Flight 253]].{{cite news|author=Shane, Scott, Schmitt, Eric and Lipton, Eric|title=U.S. Charges Suspect, Eyeing Link to Qaeda in Yemen|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/12/27/us/27terror.html|date=December 26, 2009|work=The New York Times|access-date=December 26, 2009}} On October 5, 2012, Borman issued an injunction against Secretary of State Ruth Johnson's "citizenship checkbox" as a violation of the [[Equal Protection Clause]] of the 14th amendment. In his ruling, Borman stated that the checkbox “will create chaos” and cause “irreparable injury to the voting process.” https://www.aclumich.org/en/press-releases/citizenship-checkbox-ordered-november-ballot-application ''ACLU Michigan.'' October 5, 2012. Retrieved February 23, 2021. On September 14, 2018, Borman ruled that the ACLU's lawsuit against Michigan could move forward. The ACLU sued Michigan over its decision to allow faith-based agencies which receive federal funding to deny services to same-sex couples, arguing that Michigan's decision violated the [[Establishment Clause]] of the [[First Amendment]]. "The plaintiffs have adequately alleged injury in fact for both their [[Establishment Clause]] and [[equal protection]] claims," wrote Borman. "This injury is at least 'fairly traceable' to the state defendants based on the allegations before the court."{{cite news|title=Judge rules against faith-based agency in landmark case over LGBT rights and religious liberty|url=https://www.deseret.com/2018/9/14/20653582/judge-rules-against-faith-based-agency-in-landmark-case-over-lgbt-rights-and-religious-liberty#married-couple-kristy-and-dana-dumont-with-great-danes-penny-left-and-pixie-right-walk-along-the-grand-river-near-their-home-in-dimondale-mich-on-tuesday-june-19-2018-the-dumonts-hope-to-be-able-to-adopt-children-together|date=September 14, 2018|work=Deseret News|access-date=February 23, 2021}} ==Publications== Borman is the co-author, with Professors Peter Henning, Jerold Israel, and [[Ellen Podgor]], of the casebook ''White Collar Crime: Law and Practice''. ==Awards== Borman is a member of the University of Michigan Hall of Fame. He was given the [[Jewish Federation]]’s Fred M. Butzel Award for Distinguished Community Service in 2007. ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|217|nid=1378051|name=Paul D. Gardephe''' (born 1957) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]]. ==Education and career== Born in [[Fitchburg, Massachusetts]], Gardephe received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from the [[University of Pennsylvania]] in 1979, a [[Master of Arts]] degree from the [[University of Pennsylvania]] in 1979, and a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Columbia Law School]] in 1982. He was a [[law clerk]] to Judge [[Albert J. Engel Jr.]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit]] from 1982 to 1983. He was in private practice in [[New York City]] from 1983 to 1987. He was an [[Assistant United States Attorney]] of the U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York from 1987 to 1992, and served as Chief of the Appeals Unit, Criminal Division in that office from 1992 to 1995. From 1995 to 1996, Gardephe held the position of Senior litigation counsel, in the U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York. He worked in the [[Time Inc.]] Law Department from 1996 to 2003, first as associate general counsel until 1998, then deputy general counsel for litigation from 1998 to 2000, then vice president and deputy general counsel from 2000 to 2003. He was also a consultant (special counsel) for the Office of the Inspector General of the [[United States Department of Justice]] from 1996 to 2000 and from 2001 to 2003. He returned to private practice from 2003 to 2008 as partner at [[Patterson Belknap Webb & Tyler|Patterson Belknap]], eventually heading the litigation department.{{cite web|title=Faculty profile|url=http://www.law.columbia.edu/faculty/paul-gardephe|website=Columbia Law School|accessdate=16 January 2018}} ===Federal judicial service=== On April 29, 2008, Gardephe was nominated by President [[George W. Bush]] to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]] vacated by [[Charles L. Brieant]]. Gardephe was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on July 17, 2008, and received his commission on August 8, 2008. He assumed [[senior status]] on August 9, 2023.{{FJC Bio|nid=1392751|inline=yes}} ==Notable cases== *In 2014, he presided over the trial of [[Mathew Martoma]], a former [[portfolio manager]] for [[hedge fund]] SAC Capital Advisers, who was convicted by a unanimous jury verdict on 6 February 2014 for carrying out what federal prosecutors called the most profitable insider-trading scheme in U.S. history. On 8 September 2014, Gardephe sentenced Martoma to 9 years in prison, and ordered him to pay nearly $9.4 million. The judge acknowledged Martoma's community charitable work and history of helping others, and the filing of more than 100 letters to the court from supporters, but said he had gone for "one big score" and now had "to deal with the fallout." Martoma's lawyers said they would be appealing the February 6, 2014 conviction.{{cite news|title=Nine years prison term given to ex SAC manager|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2014/09/08/martoma-ordered-to-forfeit-938-million.html|date=8 September 2014|access-date=8 September 2014|publisher=CNBC}} In August 2017, a divided panel of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit]] upheld the conviction.{{Bluebook journal |first=|last=Note|title=Recent Case: Second Circuit Redefines Personal Benefit Requirement for Insider Trading|volume=132 |journal=[[Harvard Law Review|Harv. L. Rev.]] | page=1730 | url=https://harvardlawreview.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/1730-1737_Online.pdf| year=2019}} *"Months before his arrest in late 2012, [[Gilberto Valle]], then a New York police officer, sat at his computer, hiding behind fictional online identities and exchanging messages about abducting, torturing, killing and eating women... There may not have been a more sensational trial in Manhattan in recent years than that of Mr. Valle, who came to be widely known as the cannibal cop. He was convicted of kidnapping conspiracy in March 2013 after prosecutors persuaded a jury that he was plotting actual abductions with others in one of the darkest corners of the Internet... In June, the judge, Paul G. Gardephe of Federal District Court, overturned Mr. Valle's conspiracy conviction, saying the evidence supported his contention that he was engaged in only "fantasy role-play." The government appealed, asking that the conviction be reinstated; but the Court ruled 2-1 on December 3, 2015 to uphold Judge Gardephe's ruling overturning the guilty verdict.{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/04/17/nyregion/gilberto-valle-ex-new-york-police-officer-talks-about-his-cannibalism-fantasies-in-film.html?_r=0 |title=Gilberto Valle, Ex-New York Police Officer, Talks About His Cannibalism Fantasies in Film |first=BENJAMIN |last=WEISER |date=April 16, 2015 |newspaper=New York Times}} ==References== {{Reflist}} ==Sources== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1392751}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Charles L. Holmes, III – Lawyer Profile | work=[[LexisNexis Martindale-Hubbell|Martindale]] }}{{failed verification|date=August 2021}} Holmes earned a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[Westminster College (Missouri)|Westminster College]] in [[Fulton, Missouri]], in 1973 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Arkansas School of Law]] in 1978.{{Cite news | url=http://www.magnoliareporter.com/news_and_business/regional_news/article_18c28888-fd99-11df-8bef-001cc4c03286.html | title=Pryor, Lincoln push for Holmes' confirmation as new federal judge | work=Magnolia Reporter | date=December 1, 2010}}{{Cite news | last=White House: Office of the Press Secretary | url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/president-obama-names-three-united-states-district-court | work=[[whitehouse.gov]] | title=President Obama Names Three to the United States District Court | via=[[NARA|National Archives]] | date=April 28, 2010}}{{Cite news | last=The City Wire staff | url=http://www.thecitywire.com/index.php?q=node/7352 | title=P.K. Holmes recommended for Western District Federal Judge | work=The City Wire | date=December 16, 2009}}{{FJC Bio|nid=1393601|inline=yes}} == Career == From 1973 to 1974 he served as a [[Trainee|management trainee]] for the United National Bank in [[Little Rock, Arkansas]].[https://web.archive.org/web/20181228161549/https://www.congress.gov/111/chrg/shrg66817/CHRG-111shrg66817.pdf Holmes' Testimony] In 1974 he served as a campaign aide to David Pryor when he ran for [[Governor of Arkansas]]. In 1975 he served as an [[Account executive]] for an advertising agency in Little Rock. In 1976 he served as a law clerk for a private law firm in Little Rock. From 1976 to 1978 he served as a part-time investigator for the Washington County Public Defender's Office in [[Fayetteville, Arkansas]]. From 1978 until 1993, Holmes worked in private legal practice in [[Fort Smith, Arkansas]]. From 1993 until 2001, Holmes was the [[United States Attorney]] for the Western District of Arkansas. From 2001 until his appointment to the federal bench, Holmes worked in private legal practice in Fort Smith. === Federal judicial service === In December 2009, Arkansas senators [[Mark Pryor]] and [[Blanche Lincoln]] recommended Holmes to become a federal district judge. On April 28, 2010, President Obama nominated Holmes to the seat on the Western District of Arkansas that was vacated when Judge [[Robert T. Dawson]] assumed [[senior status]] on August 14, 2009.{{Cite news|first=Steve|last=Tetreault|url=http://www.swtimes.com/news/article_67c2b348-2fbe-11e0-81a0-001cc4c03286.html|title=Senate Committee Advances P.K. Holmes|work=[[Southwest Times Record]]|date=February 3, 2011|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110209214118/http://swtimes.com/news/article_67c2b348-2fbe-11e0-81a0-001cc4c03286.html| archive-date=February 9, 2011}} Holmes' nomination lapsed at the end of 2010, and he was renominated by Obama on January 5, 2011. The [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]] voted to advance Holmes' nomination to the full [[United States Senate]] on February 3, 2011. The United States Senate confirmed Holmes' nomination on February 7, 2011, by a 95–0 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1121/vote_112_1_00013.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Paul Kinloch Holmes III, of Arkansas, to be U.S. District Judge)|website=senate.gov}} He received his commission on February 8, 2011. He served as Chief Judge on February 14, 2012, until February 14, 2019. [[University at Buffalo Law School|University at Buffalo]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Paul Lawrence Friedman'''{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GAZ5g4J8xDoC&pg=PA1138|page=1138|title=Hearings before the Committee on the Judiciary, United States Senate, One Hundred Third Congress, Second Session, on Confirmation of Appointees to the Federal Judiciary, March 25; April 21, 22, 29; May 12 and 25, 1994|publisher=U.S. Government Printing Office|year=1996}} (born February 20, 1944) is a [[United States federal judge|senior United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Columbia]]. He serves as secretary of the [[American Law Institute]].{{cite web|url=https://www.ali.org/about-ali/governance/officers-council/|title=Officers and Council - The American Law Institute|publisher=American Law Institute|accessdate=November 24, 2019}} == Education and career == Friedman was born in [[Buffalo, New York]]. He received his [[Bachelor of Arts]] from [[Cornell University]] in 1965, where he was president of the [[Quill and Dagger]] society and a member of ''[[Zeta Beta Tau]]''. He received his [[Juris Doctor]] from [[University at Buffalo Law School]] in 1968. He began his legal career as a [[law clerk]] to Judge [[Aubrey Eugene Robinson Jr.]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Columbia]] from 1968 to 1969, and then for Judge [[Roger Robb]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit]] from 1969 to 1970. He was an [[Assistant United States Attorney]] for the District of Columbia from 1970 to 1974. He was an Assistant [[Solicitor General of the United States|United States Solicitor General]] from 1974 to 1976.{{cite web|url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/friedman-paul-l|title=Friedman, Paul L. - Federal Judicial Center|accessdate=November 24, 2019}} He was in private practice of law at the firm of [[White & Case]] in [[Washington, D.C.]] from 1976 to 1994. In June 1984, Friedman was elected to the [[American Law Institute]] and was elected to the ALI Council in October 1998. He began his first three-year term as ALI Secretary in 2013. == Federal judicial service == Friedman was nominated by President [[Bill Clinton]] on March 22, 1994, to a seat vacated by [[Gerhard A. Gesell]]. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on June 15, 1994, and received his commission on June 16, 1994. He assumed [[senior status]] on December 31, 2009. === Notable cases === Among Friedman's notable cases is the continuing supervision of [[John Hinckley Jr.]], the would-be assassin of President [[Ronald Reagan]]. Friedman has issued rulings that relaxed the restrictions on Hinckley by allowing him to leave the grounds of [[St. Elizabeths Hospital]] to spend more days each month visiting his mother's home town of [[Williamsburg, Virginia]].{{cite news|author1=Zapotosky, Matt|author2=Marimow, Ann E.|date=December 20, 2013|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/crime/federal-judge-grants-more-freedom-to-reagans-would-be-assassin/2013/12/20/efdd2c60-68e9-11e3-8b5b-a77187b716a3_story.html|title=Federal judge grants more freedom to John Hinckley Jr., Reagan's would-be assassin|accessdate=November 24, 2019}} On July 27, 2016, it was announced that Hinckley would be allowed to permanently reside there. Friedman also presides over ''In re: Rail Freight Fuel Surcharge Antitrust Litigation'', an ongoing MDL ([[multidistrict litigation]]) that saw multiple appeals to the [[D.C. Circuit]] in a battle for class certification that lasted over a decade.{{cite web|url=https://www.railwayage.com/freight/it-aint-over-till-the-fat-lady-sings/|title=It Ain't Over 'Till The Fat Lady Sings|date=August 18, 2019|website=Railway Age|accessdate=November 24, 2019}}{{cite web|url=https://www.hausfeld.com/case-studies/rail-freight?lang_id=1|title=In re Rail Freight Fuel Surcharge Antitrust Litigation|accessdate=November 24, 2019|archive-date=August 11, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200811030055/https://www.hausfeld.com/case-studies/rail-freight?lang_id=1|url-status=dead}} Friedman also notably dismissed a lawsuit filed by 26 members of Congress who contended that [[President Clinton]] has had no legal authority to continue U.S. participation in the airstrikes against Yugoslavia. The bipartisan lawsuit sought to enforce timetables in the largely ignored Vietnam-era War Powers Act, which would have required Clinton to obtain congressional approval or terminate U.S. involvement in Kosovo by May 25, two months after the start of the action.{{Citation needed|date=November 2026}} In 2026, Friedman ruled against a US [[Department of Defense]] policy restricting the press credentials of journalists who declined new reporting restrictions, in a case brought by ''[[The New York Times]]''. He ordered [[the Pentagon]] to reinstate seven of the newspaper's journalists' credentials and refused its request to stay the ruling pending appeal.{{cite news |title=Judge sides with New York Times in challenge to Pentagon policy limiting reporters' access |publisher=PBS NewsHour |date=March 2026 |url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/judge-sides-with-new-york-times-in-challenge-to-pentagon-policy-limiting-reporters-access}} == Speech deploring attacks on judges == Delivering the annual [[Thomas Aquinas Flannery|Judge Thomas A. Flannery]] Lecture on November 6, 2019, Friedman entered the political fray by deploring President [[Donald Trump]]'s rhetorical attacks on judges, saying they “violate all recognized democratic norms" and are starting to "undermine faith in the rule of law itself."{{cite news|url=https://www.newsweek.com/federal-judge-slams-trump-attacks-judiciary-1470674|title=Federal Judge says Donald Trump's Attacks "Undermine Faith in the Rule of Law Itself"|author=Hutzler, Alexandra|date=November 8, 2019|work=Newsweek|accessdate=November 24, 2019}}
“We are witnessing a chief executive who criticizes virtually every judicial decision that doesn’t go his way and denigrates judges who rule against him, sometimes in very personal terms. He seems to view the courts and the justice system as obstacles to be attacked and undermined, not as a coequal branch to be respected even when he disagrees with its decisions.”{{cite news|author=Shepherd, Katie|title=Trump 'violates all recognized democratic norms,' federal judge says in biting speech on judicial independence|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/nation/2019/11/08/judge-says-trump-violates-democratic-norms-judiciary-speech/|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=November 8, 2019|accessdate=November 24, 2019}}

[[University of Pennsylvania Law School|University of Pennsylvania]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | footnotes = }} '''Paul Steven Diamond''' (born January 2, 1953) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania]] and a former federal judicial nominee to be a judge on the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit]]. He was appointed a federal judge by [[George W. Bush]] in 2004. ==Education== Diamond was born in [[Brooklyn]]. He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[Columbia University]] in 1974 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Pennsylvania Law School]] in 1977.{{Cite book |last1=Columbia College (Columbia University). Office of Alumni Affairs and Development |url=http://archive.org/details/ldpd_12981092_050 |title=Columbia College today |last2=Columbia College (Columbia University) |date=September 2008 |publisher=New York, N.Y. : Columbia College, Office of Alumni Affairs and Development |others=Columbia University Libraries}} ==Career== Diamond was an assistant district attorney in the [[Philadelphia County]] [[District Attorney]]'s Office from 1977–1979. In 1980 he served as a [[law clerk]] to [[Pennsylvania Supreme Court]] Justice [[Bruce W. Kauffman]], who would later also be appointed as a judge on the Eastern District by President [[Bill Clinton]]. Diamond returned to the District Attorney's Office from 1981 to 1983. He worked in private practice in Philadelphia from 1983 to 2004, when he was appointed by [[President of the United States|President]] [[George W. Bush]] to the Eastern District. Diamond also has worked as an [[adjunct professor]] of law at [[Temple University Beasley School of Law]] from 1990–1992.{{cite web |url=http://www.instablogs.com/entry/bush-nominates-judge-for-3rd-us-appeals-court/ |title=Bush Nominates Judge for 3rd US Appeals Court |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20081017093307/http://www.instablogs.com/entry/bush-nominates-judge-for-3rd-us-appeals-court/ |archivedate=2008-10-17 }} From 1993 until 1995, Diamond worked as the treasurer and as the counsel for the failed 1996 presidential campaign of United States Senator [[Arlen Specter]].{{cite web|url=http://www.law.com/jsp/article.jsp?id=1202422708639 |title=Sources: Senators Agree on New Federal Judges Package |first=Shannon P. |last=Duffy |work=The Legal Intelligencer |date=July 2, 2008 |publisher=[[Law.com]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080707050034/http://www.law.com/jsp/article.jsp?id=1202422708639 |archive-date=July 7, 2008 }} ===Federal judicial service=== On January 20, 2004, President [[George W. Bush]] nominated Diamond to a seat on the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania vacated by [[Herbert J. Hutton]]. Diamond was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on June 16, 2004 and received his commission on June 22, 2004.{{FJC Bio|nid=1392156|inline=yes}} ===Third Circuit nomination under Bush=== On July 2, 2008, the ''Legal Intelligencer'' reported that as part of a package of judicial nominees, President Bush had agreed to withdraw his then nominee to the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit]], [[Gene E. K. Pratter]] and replace her with Diamond. On July 24, 2008, President Bush formally nominated Diamond to the United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit, in conjunction with Pratter's withdrawal.{{cite news |url-status=dead |last=Duffy |first=Shannon P. |url=http://www.law.com/jsp/article.jsp?id=1202423251503 |title=Five Tapped for Federal Bench Openings in Pennsylvania |work=The Legal Intelligencer |date=July 25, 2008 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20080803201204/http://www.law.com/jsp/article.jsp?id=1202423251503 |archivedate=August 3, 2008 |access-date=July 25, 2008 }} Since Diamond was nominated after July 1, 2008, the unofficial start date of the [[Thurmond Rule]] during a presidential election year, no hearings were scheduled on his nomination, and the nomination was returned to Bush at the end of his term. === Presidential election cases === * In 2016, Judge Diamond rejected [[Jill Stein]]'s request for a recount of Donald Trump's victory in Pennsylvania.{{Cite web|url=https://www.cnn.com/2016/12/12/politics/pennsylvania-recount-blocked-jill-stein/index.html|title=Wisconsin, Pennsylvania certify Trump wins, ends Stein's recount push|first=Eric |last=Bradner |date=2016-12-12 |website=CNN}} * During the [[2020 United States presidential election|2020 presidential election]], Judge Diamond [[Hearing (law)|heard]] arguments from the [[Donald Trump 2020 presidential campaign|Trump campaign]] who were seeking to stop Philadelphia's election board from counting remaining ballots. He advised the two parties to reach an agreement and he then dismissed the case [[Prejudice (legal term)|without prejudice]].{{cite web |last1=Briggs |first1=Ryan |title=Federal judge dismisses Trump's attempt to stop vote counting in Philadelphia |url=https://whyy.org/articles/trump-asks-federal-court-to-stop-vote-counting-in-phiadelphia/ |website=[[WHYY-FM|WHYY]] |accessdate=6 November 2020 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20201105231227/https://whyy.org/articles/trump-asks-federal-court-to-stop-vote-counting-in-phiadelphia/ |archivedate=5 November 2020 |date=5 November 2020}} ==References== {{Reflist}} ==Sources== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1392156}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Herbert J. [[Yale Law School|Yale University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | occupation = | profession = | known_for = | salary = | net_worth = | cabinet = | committees = | portfolio = | awards = | signature = | signature_alt = | website = | footnotes = }} '''Paula Xinis''' ({{IPAc-en|E|k|'|s|i:|n|@|s}}; born '''Panagiota Xinis''' in 1968) is an American lawyer and jurist serving as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Maryland|U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland]]. She was appointed in 2016 by President [[Barack Obama]]. She is best known for her role as judge in [[Deportation of Kilmar Abrego Garcia|the deportation case of Kilmar Abrego Garcia]], receiving national and worldwide attention. ==Biography== Xinis is of Greek ancestry.{{cite news |last1=Blackburn |first1=Piper Hudspeth |title=Who is Judge Paula Xinis? What to know about the judge in the case of a man mistakenly deported to El Salvador |url=https://edition.cnn.com/2025/04/17/politics/paula-xinis-judge-kilmar-abrego-garcia/index.html |access-date=24 April 2025 |work=CNN |date=17 April 2025}} She received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree, summa cum laude, in 1991 from the [[University of Virginia]]. She received a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1997 from [[Yale Law School]]. She began her legal career as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Diana Gribbon Motz]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit]], from 1997 to 1998. From 1998 to 2011, she served as an [[Federal public defender|assistant federal public defender]], serving as director of Training for the office from 2006 to 2011. She served at the law firm of Murphy, Falcon & Murphy in [[Baltimore]], Maryland, as a senior trial attorney from 2011 and as a partner from 2013 to 2016. She practiced both civil and criminal litigation.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2015/03/26/president-obama-nominates-two-serve-united-states-district-courts|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Obama Nominates Two to Serve on the United States District Courts|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=26 March 2015}}{{FJC Bio|nid=1394851|inline=yes}} ===Federal judicial service=== On March 26, 2015, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Xinis to serve as a United States district judge of the United States District Court for the District of Maryland, to the seat vacated by Judge [[Deborah K. Chasanow]], who assumed [[senior status]] on October 3, 2014. Her nomination was reported from the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] on September 17, 2015, by a [[voice vote]].{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2015/03/26/presidential-nominations-sent-senate-0|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=26 March 2015}}{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/executive-business-meeting-09-17-15|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – September 17, 2015|website=www.judiciary.senate.gov}} On May 16, 2016, the Senate confirmed her nomination by a 53–34 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=114&session=2&vote=00072|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Paula Xinis, of Maryland, to be U.S. District Judge)|website=www.senate.gov}}{{cite news|date=May 16, 2016|access-date=May 16, 2016|work= Associated Press News|title=The Senate has confirmed lawyer Paula Xinis to be a federal judge in Maryland|url= https://apnews.com/article/6d2bb02ae384491f9c1ad4317aa2d35b|first=Mary Clare|last=Jalonick}} She received her judicial commission on May 18, 2016. ====Notable rulings==== {{Expand section|date=April 2025}} In ''[[Deportation of Kilmar Abrego Garcia|Abrego Garcia v. Noem]]'', No. 25-cv-951 (Apr. 4, 2025), after the United States government described Kilmar Abrego Garcia's deportation as being due to an "administrative error", Judge Xinis ordered the government to "facilitate" and "effectuate" Garcia's return to the United States. Parts of this ruling were later affirmed by the [[Supreme Court of the United States]], though it stopped short of requiring the government to "effectuate" Garcia's return.{{Cite web| title=Kristi Noem, Secretary of homeland security, et al. v. Kilmar Armando Abrego Garcia, et al | url=https://www.supremecourt.gov/DocketPDF/24/24A949/354843/20250407103341248_Kristi%20Noem%20application.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250407161208/https://www.supremecourt.gov/DocketPDF/24/24A949/354843/20250407103341248_Kristi%20Noem%20application.pdf | archive-date=2025-04-07}}{{Cite web| title=Kristi Noem, Secretary of homeland security, et al. v. Kilmar Armando Abrego Garcia, et al | url=https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/24pdf/24a949_lkhn.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250410225644/https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/24pdf/24a949_lkhn.pdf | archive-date=2025-04-10}} He was returned on June 6, 2025, but held in custody pending other removal efforts by the government, with a brief release in August, until December 11, 2025, when Xinis granted Garcia's habeas petition to release him from custody, and he was released.{{cite news|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/kilmar-abrego-garcia-immediate-release-ice-custody/|title=Federal judge in Maryland orders Abrego Garcia's immediate release from ICE custody|first1=Jacob|last1=Rosen|first2=Melissa|last2=Quinn|first3=Kathryn|last3=Watson|publisher=CBS News|date=December 11, 2025|accessdate=December 11, 2025}} ==See also== *[[James Boasberg]], the Federal judge in the concurrent deportation case of Venezuelan nationals. ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1394851}} *{{Ballotpedia|Paula_Xinis}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Deborah K.
