Reed O'Connor, U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas |website=FedSoc.org |date=September 15, 2018 |publisher=[[The Federalist Society]] |location=Washington, DC |access-date=March 30, 2023}} According to his critics, O'Connor has become a "go-to" favorite for conservative lawyers, because, they claim, he reliably rules against Democratic policies and for Republican policies.{{Cite web|first=Bob|last=Bryan|date=December 17, 2018|url=https://www.businessinsider.com/obamacare-repeal-lawsuit-supreme-court-overturn-odds-2018-12|title=Experts think the ruling that declared Obamacare unconstitutional is 'insanity in print' and will likely be overturned|website=[[Business Insider]]|access-date=December 22, 2018}}{{Cite web|date=December 20, 2018|first=Julie |last=Moreau|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/feature/nbc-out/texas-judge-who-struck-down-aca-weigh-transgender-health-case-n950501|title=Texas judge who struck down ACA to weigh in on trans health case|website=[[NBC News]]|language=en|access-date=December 22, 2018}} Attorneys General in Texas appear to strategically file cases in O'Connor's jurisdiction so that he will hear them.{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/12/15/us/judge-obamacare-reed-oconnor.html|title=In Weaponized Courts, Judge Who Halted Affordable Care Act Is a Conservative Favorite|last=Fernandez|first=Manny|date=December 15, 2018|work=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=December 22, 2018|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}} On February 11, 2015, O'Connor held that a portion of the federal [[Gun Control Act of 1968]] was unconstitutional.''Mance v. Holder'', 74 F. Supp. 3d 795 (N.D. Tex. 2015). This ruling was reversed on appeal.''Mance v. Sessions'', 896 F.3d 699 (5th Cir. 2018). On March 26, 2015, O'Connor enjoined the federal government's definition of marriage as it relates to the [[Family and Medical Leave Act of 1993]].''Texas v. United States'', 95 F. Supp. 3d 965 (N.D. Tex. 2015). He dissolved the injunction following the Supreme Court's decision in ''[[Obergefell v. Hodges]]''.''Texas v. United States'', No. 7:15-CV-00056-O, 2015 WL 13424776 (N.D. Tex. June 26, 2015). On August 21, 2016, O'Connor issued a ruling against the [[Obama administration]] dealing with the government's interpretation of [[Title IX]] rules. The guidance from the White House was issued in May 2016, and addresses the Title IX requirement that schools receiving federal funding not discriminate against students on the basis of sex. The guidance required that [[transgender]] students be allowed to use the bathroom that corresponds to their [[gender identity]]. O'Connor ruled that the new guidelines did not receive proper notice and comment prior to publication, and that Title IX and its implementing regulation are "not ambiguous" as to the "plain meaning of the term sex as used". He then issued a [[nationwide injunction]] preventing them from being enforced with respect to students' access to "intimate facilities."{{cite web|url=https://www.npr.org/sections/thetwo-way/2016/08/22/490915833/u-s-judge-grants-nationwide-injunction-blocking-white-house-transgender-policy|title=U.S. Judge Grants Nationwide Injunction Blocking White House Transgender Policy|first=Camila|last=Domonoske|website=[[NPR]]|date=August 22, 2016|access-date=January 2, 2017}} The Obama administration appealed the decision, but the [[First presidency of Donald Trump|Trump administration]] rescinded the guidance and moved to dismiss the appeal.{{Cite web|url=https://www.npr.org/sections/thetwo-way/2017/02/22/516664633/trump-administration-rescinds-obama-rule-on-transgender-students-bathroom-use|title=Trump Administration Rescinds Obama Rule on Transgender Students' Bathroom Use|website=[[NPR]]|date=February 22, 2017|last1=Hersher|first1=Rebecca|last2=Johnson|first2=Carrie}}Texas v. United States, No. 16-11534, 2017 WL 7000562 (5th Cir. Mar. 3, 2017). On December 31, 2016, in a separate case, O'Connor issued a [[preliminary injunction]] against enforcement of the Obama administration's regulations implementing Section 1557 of the [[Affordable Care Act]] (prohibiting sex discrimination in federally funded health programs) as a likely violation of the [[Religious Freedom Restoration Act]] and what he said was an improper inclusion of [[gender identity]] discrimination.{{cite web|author=Zaveri, Mihir|url=http://www.houstonchronicle.com/news/houston-texas/houston/article/Texas-judge-blocks-transgender-policy-10829078.php?t=59e46d2b06438d9cbb|title=Texas judge blocks transgender policy|work=[[Houston Chronicle]]|date=December 31, 2016|access-date=January 2, 2017}} In early 2018, O'Connor held the Certification Rule of the Affordable Care Act unconstitutional in ''Texas v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue'', concluding that it violated the [[nondelegation doctrine]].{{cite court |litigants=State of Texas, et al. v. United States of America, et al.|vol=.4:20-cv-00283-O |reporter= |opinion= |pinpoint= |court=UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT FOR THE NORTHERN DISTRICT OF TEXAS, WICHITA FALLS DIVISION |date=August 4, 2016 |url=https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.txnd.265817/gov.uscourts.txnd.265817.34.0.pdf|access-date=March 30, 2023 |quote= |postscript=}} This ruling was reversed on appeal.''Texas v. Rettig'', 987 F.3d 518 (5th Cir. 2021) In 2018, O'Connor ruled that the [[Indian Child Welfare Act]] was unconstitutional.{{cite web|url=http://www.indianz.com/News/2018/10/05/judge-strikes-down-indian-child-welfare.asp| title=Texas judge strikes down Indian Child Welfare Act in contested ruling |work=Indianz.com|date=October 5, 2018|access-date=October 8, 2018}} The Fifth Circuit reversed O'Connor's ruling on appeal, and the reversal was upheld by the Supreme Court in ''[[Haaland v. Brackeen]]'' (2023).''Haaland v. Brackeen'', No. 21-376. On October 31, 2021, O'Connor ruled that the First Amendment and the [[Religious Freedom Restoration Act]] provide religious employers an exemption from Title VII of the Civil Rights Act's ban on discrimination "on the basis of...sex".{{cite web|url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/social-justice/religious-businesses-shielded-from-lgbt-bias-claims-judge-rules|title=Religious Businesses Shielded From LGBT Bias Claims, Judge Rules|date=October 31, 2021|first=Erin|last=Mulvaney|website=[[Bloomberg Law]]}}''Bear Creek Bible Church v. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission'', No. 4:18-CV-00824-O, 2021 WL 5052661 (N.D. Tex. Oct. 31, 2021). In 2022, O'Connor issued a preliminary injunction blocking the Pentagon from enforcing a COVID-19 vaccine requirement for its Navy Seals. O'Connor said the U.S. government had "no license" to abrogate the freedoms of the Navy SEALs.{{Cite news|last=Whitcomb|first=Dan|date=2022-01-04|title=U.S. judge blocks Pentagon from punishing Navy SEALs who refused COVID-19 vaccine|language=en|work=[[Reuters]]|url=https://www.reuters.com/world/us/us-judge-blocks-pentagon-punishing-navy-seals-who-refused-covid-19-vaccine-2022-01-04/|access-date=2022-01-04}} The preliminary injunction was partially stayed by the Supreme Court on March 25, 2022.''LLOYD J. AUSTIN, III, SECRETARY OF DEFENSE, ET AL. v. U. S. NAVY SEALS 1–26, ET AL.'', No. 21A477. In October 2022, O'Connor ruled that the Boeing Company committed criminal acts when not disclosing the MCAS system of the FAA. This contradicted the previous settlement the federal government made with Boeing, and opened the door for new legal action by victims families.{{cite news | url=https://www.reuters.com/world/us/us-judge-passengers-fatal-boeing-737-max-crashes-crime-victims-2022-10-21/ | title=U.S. Judge: Passengers in fatal Boeing 737 MAX crashes are 'crime victims' | work=[[Reuters]] | date=October 22, 2022 | last1=Shepardson | first1=David }} In ''VanDerStok v. By classifying receiver blanks as firearms, the ATF rule required such receiver blanks to have serial numbers, required manufacturers of such receiver blanks to be licensed, and required commercial sellers to conduct background checks for purchasers. O'Connor determined that the ATF rule exceeded the agency's authority, ruling that receiver blanks were not firearms or firearm receivers. The U.S. appealed to the Fifth Circuit, and O'Connor's injunction was administratively stayed by the [[U.S. Supreme Court]] pending further proceedings.Ariane de Vogue, [https://www.cnn.com/2023/07/28/politics/ghost-guns-alito-supreme-court/index.html Federal ghost gun regulations temporarily revived by Justice Alito], CNN (July 28, 2023).[https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=1761874998091319695 ''Garland v. Vanderstock''], Order, July 28, 2023. The Supreme Court later reversed O'Connor's opinion in ''[[Bondi v. VanDerStok]]'', in an opinion written by Trump appointee [[Neil Gorsuch]].{{Cite news |last=Howe |first=Amy |date=2025-03-26 |title=Supreme Court upholds regulation on 'ghost guns' |url=https://www.scotusblog.com/2025/03/supreme-court-upholds-regulation-of-ghost-guns/ |access-date=2025-03-26 |website=[[SCOTUSblog]] |language=en-US}} On remand, in ''[[Defense Distributed v. A judge with Tesla stock keeps hearing them |url=https://www.npr.org/2024/08/09/g-s1-16087/elon-musk-lawsuits-texas-same-judge-hears-them-tesla-stock |access-date= |work=National Public Radio}} On August 13, 2024, Judge O'Connor recused himself from one of those cases — the lawsuit against the World Federation of Advertisers.{{Cite web |last=Kolodny |first=Lora |date=2024-08-13 |title=Texas judge who owned Tesla stock recuses himself in Elon Musk's X case against advertisers |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2024/08/13/judge-in-x-lawsuit-against-advertisers-recuses-he-owned-tesla-stock.html |access-date=2024-08-16 |website=CNBC |language=en}} {{See also|Legal affairs of the second Trump presidency#Subpoenas}} In May 2026, while the [[United States Department of Justice|Department of Justice]] prosecutors were still in talks with [[Rhode Island Hospital]] for access to medical records of juveniles who sought treatment for gender dysphoria, the DOJ filed an enforcement action before O'Connor's court in Texas. The DOJ then attempted to seek enforcement of the order, but was denied by Rhode Island's Judge [[Mary S. McElroy|Mary McElroy]] on May 14, who concluded O'Connor's subpoena "lacks a congressionally authorized purpose" and was issued "for an improper purpose in bad faith."{{Cite web |title=Rhode Island fights DOJ over trans youth health records {{!}} Advocate.com |url=https://www.advocate.com/politics/national/rhode-island-trans-records-texas |access-date=2026-05-29 |website=www.advocate.com |language=en}}{{Cite web |title=Trump judge calls DOJ conduct 'appalling' in trans care case {{!}} Advocate.com |url=https://www.advocate.com/politics/national/rhode-island-judge-torches-doj |access-date=2026-05-29 |website=www.advocate.com |language=en}} On May 18, O'Connor then issued an injunction "claiming to prohibit the hospital from seeking relief in the federal courts that oversee Rhode Island under threat of contempt" and forced the hospital to turn over the records.{{Cite news |last=Stern |first=Mark Joseph |date=2026-05-19 |title=A MAGA Judge’s Shocking Power Grab Crosses Over Into an Impeachable Offense |url=https://slate.com/news-and-politics/2026/05/texas-maga-judge-trump-gender-affirming-care-case.html |access-date=2026-05-29 |work=Slate |language=en-US |issn=1091-2339}} The injunction had been characterized as an "abuse of power" and was largely successful as the [[First Circuit]] refused to hear a request from the hospital to issue an order to allow the hospital not to hand over the records to anyone.{{Cite web |last=Strikes |first=Balls & |date=2026-05-20 |title=The Right's Favorite District Court Judge Is Delivering For Trump's Anti-Trans Agenda |url=https://ballsandstrikes.org/law-politics/reed-oconnor-rhode-island-judge-shopping/ |access-date=2026-05-29 |website=Balls and Strikes |language=en-US}} In June 2026, O'Connor joined Judge [[Mark T. Texas}} On December 14, 2018, O'Connor [[Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act#Texas et al v. United States of America et al|ruled that the Affordable Care Act]] was unconstitutional.{{cite web |title= Federal judge in Texas strikes down ObamaCare |last= Sullivan |first=Peter |url=https://thehill.com/policy/healthcare/421511-federal-judge-in-texas-strikes-down-obamacare |website=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]] |date= December 14, 2018 |access-date=December 15, 2018}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/federal-judge-rules-affordable-care-act-is-unconstitutional-11544838743|title=Federal Judge Rules Affordable Care Act Is Unconstitutional Without Insurance-Coverage Penalty|last=Armour|first=Stephanie|date=December 14, 2018|website=[[The Wall Street Journal]]}} O'Connor ruled that the [[Health insurance mandate|individual mandate]] was unconstitutional by saying "[the] Individual Mandate can no longer be fairly read as an exercise of Congress's Tax Power and is still impermissible under the [[Interstate Commerce Clause]]—meaning the Individual Mandate is unconstitutional."{{Cite web|url=https://www.cnn.com/2018/12/14/politics/texas-aca-lawsuit/index.html|title=Federal judge in Texas strikes down Affordable Care Act|first1=Ariane|last1=de Vogue|first2=Tami |last2=Luhby|date=December 14, 2018|website=[[CNN]]}} This is in reference to ''[[National Federation of Independent Business v. Sebelius]]'' (2012) which ruled that the individual mandate was constitutional because of the tax penalty. The penalty was reduced to $0 by [[Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017|the 2017 tax bill]] starting in 2019.{{cite web |last1=Blackman |first1=Josh |title=Understanding the New Obamacare Decision, Texas v. United States: Part II |url=http://reason.com/volokh/2018/12/17/understanding-the-new-obamacare-decision |website=Reason.com |access-date=19 December 2018 |language=en |date=17 December 2018}} The ruling was deemed likely to be appealed, with both Republican and Democratic legal experts saying that the legal challenge to the Affordable Care Act was unlikely to succeed.{{Cite news|first=Devlin|last=Barrett|date=December 15, 2018|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/national-security/legal-experts-rip-judges-rationale-for-declaring-obamacare-law-invalid/2018/12/15/9cab3bb8-0088-11e9-83c0-b06139e540e5_story.html|title=Legal experts rip judge's rationale for declaring Obamacare law invalid|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]}}{{Cite web|url=https://politi.co/2CdkwaC|title=Judge rules Obamacare unconstitutional, endangering coverage for 20 million|last1=Demko|first1=Paul|last2=Cancryn|first2=Adam|website=[[Politico]]|date=December 14, 2018|language=en|access-date=December 18, 2018}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.vox.com/policy-and-politics/2018/6/8/17441512/obamacare-lawsuit-texas-trump|title=The new anti-Obamacare lawsuit heads to court today. Scholars think it's 'absurd.'|last=Scott|first=Dylan|date=June 8, 2018|website=[[Vox (website)|Vox]]|access-date=December 18, 2018}}{{Cite journal|url=https://www.healthaffairs.org/do/10.1377/forefront.20181215.617096/full/|title=Federal Judge Strikes Down Entire ACA; Law Remains In Effect|website=www.healthaffairs.org|year=2018|language=en|doi=10.1377/forefront.20181215.617096|url-access=subscription}} The Affordable Care Act would remain in effect throughout the appeals process. President [[Donald Trump]] commended the ruling on Twitter.{{Cite tweet|url=https://twitter.com/realDonaldTrump/status/1073763695807877120|title=Wow, but not surprisingly, ObamaCare was just ruled UNCONSTITUTIONAL by a highly respected judge in Texas. Great news for America!|last=Trump|first=Donald J.|authorlink=Donald Trump|user=realDonaldTrump|number=1073763695807877120|date=December 14, 2018|language=en|access-date=December 15, 2018}}{{Cite tweet|url=https://twitter.com/realDonaldTrump/status/1073761497866747904|title=As I predicted all along, Obamacare has been struck down as an UNCONSTITUTIONAL disaster! Now Congress must pass a STRONG law that provides GREAT healthcare and protects pre-existing conditions. Mitch and Nancy, get it done!|last=Trump|first=Donald J.|authorlink=Donald Trump|date=December 14, 2018|user=realDonaldTrump|number=1073761497866747904|language=en|access-date=December 15, 2018}}{{Cite news|first=Robert|last=Barnes|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/national/health-science/federal-judge-in-texas-rules-obama-health-care-law-unconstitutional/2018/12/14/9e8bb5a2-fd63-11e8-862a-b6a6f3ce8199_story.html|title=Federal judge in Texas rules Obama health-care law unconstitutional|date=December 14, 2018|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]}} Legal experts who both support and oppose the Affordable Care Act harshly criticized O'Connor's ruling, with ''[[The Washington Post]]'' noting that legal scholars considered O'Connor's ruling "as a tortured effort to rewrite not just the law but congressional history." Ted Frank, director of litigation at the conservative [[Competitive Enterprise Institute]] said the ruling was "embarrassingly bad." Nicholas Bagley said O'Connor's ruling was "about as naked a piece of [[judicial activism]] as I have ever seen; I don't even think it's close." [[Jonathan H. Adler]] and Abbe R. Gluck, who were on opposing sides of the 2012 and 2015 Supreme Court challenges to the Affordable Care Act, wrote a joint opinion editorial in ''[[The New York Times]]'' where they described the ruling as "lawless", "a mockery of the rule of law and basic principles of democracy" and "an exercise of raw judicial power."{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/12/15/opinion/obamacare-ruling-unconstitutional-affordable-care-act.html|title=Opinion {{!}} What the Lawless Obamacare Ruling Means|last1=Adler|first1=Jonathan H.|date=December 15, 2018|work=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=December 18, 2018|last2=Gluck|first2=Abbe R.|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}{{Cite news|first=Robert |last=Barnes|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/courts_law/controversial-ruling-on-health-care-law-could-face-a-skeptical-supreme-court--if-it-gets-there/2018/12/17/81e40476-020f-11e9-b6a9-0aa5c2fcc9e4_story.html|title=Controversial ruling on health care law could face a skeptical Supreme Court — if it gets there|date=December 17, 2018|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]}} While O'Connor's ruling was upheld on appeal to the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]], O'Connor and the Fifth Circuit were reversed by the [[Supreme Court of the United States]] in a 7-2 [[California v. Texas|ruling]] issued on June 17, 2021, which stated that the parties involved in the lawsuit did not have standing to bring the suit.{{Cite web|url=https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/20pdf/19-840_6jfm.pdf|title=California et al, petitioners v. Texas, et al (Case 19–840)|publisher=The Supreme Court of the United States|author=Stephen Breyer (majority opinion), Clarence Thomas (concurring opinion with the majority), and Samuel Alito (dissenting opinion)|date=June 17, 2021}} Associate Justice [[Stephen Breyer]] was joined in the majority by Chief Justice [[John Roberts]] and Associate Justices [[Clarence Thomas]], [[Sonia Sotomayor]], [[Elena Kagan]], [[Brett Kavanaugh]], and [[Amy Coney Barrett]]. Thomas wrote a concurring opinion while Associate Justice [[Samuel Alito]] wrote a dissenting opinion and was joined by Associate Justice [[Neil Gorsuch]]. In ''[[Kennedy v. Braidwood Management, Inc.]]'', on March 30, 2023, O'Connor sided with a group of employers and individuals in Texas who argued that the Affordable Care Act's provision mandating that businesses provide their employees with free coverage of preventative services including [[mammogram]]s, [[colonoscopy|colonoscopies]], mental health screenings, and the [[HIV]] prevention drug [[Pre-exposure prophylaxis|PrEP]] was unconstitutional.{{cite court |litigants= Braidwood Management Inc., et al. v. [[Xavier Becerra]], et al. |vol=.4:20-cv-00283-O |reporter= |opinion= |pinpoint= |court=United States District Court Northern District of Texas Fort Worth Division |date=March 30, 2023 |url=https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.txnd.330381/gov.uscourts.txnd.330381.113.0_2.pdf |access-date=March 30, 2023 |quote= |postscript= }} Coverage recommendations are driven by the volunteer [[U.S. Preventive Services Task Force]]; O'Connor ruled that enforcing these recommendations was "unlawful" and violated the [[Appointments Clause]] of the [[U.S. Constitution]].{{cite web|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/obamacare-affordable-care-act-preventive-care-mandate-judge-ruling/|title=Judge undercuts preventive care mandate in Affordable Care Act|website=[[CBS News]]|date=March 30, 2023|accessdate=March 30, 2023}} He also wrote that the coverage requirements violate employers' religious beliefs "by making them complicit in facilitating [[homosexual]] behavior, drug use, and sexual activity outside of marriage between one man and one woman."{{cite web|first=Alice Miranda|last=Ollstein|title=Texas judge strikes down free HIV drugs, cancer screenings under Obamacare|url=https://www.politico.com/news/2023/03/30/texas-judge-obamacare-00089641|website=[[Politico]]|date=March 30, 2023|accessdate=March 30, 2023}} The Supreme Court later reversed his ruling in 2025. ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1392661}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[A. [[American University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Reggie Barnett Walton''' (born February 8, 1949) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Columbia]]. He is a former presiding judge of the [[Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court]]. {{cite news | url = https://www.reuters.com/article/usa-security-fisa-judges-idUSL2N0EV1TG20130621 | title = The judges who preside over America's secret court | publisher = Reuters |author1=Shiffman, John |author2=Cooke, Kristina | date = 2013-06-21 | access-date = 2013-07-01 | archive-date = 2013-06-23 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20130623010333/https://www.reuters.com/article/2013/06/21/usa-security-fisa-judges-idUSL2N0EV1TG20130621 | url-status = live | quote = Twelve of the 14 judges who have served this year on the most secret court in America are Republicans and half are former prosecutors. }} {{cite news | url = https://www.theguardian.com/world/2013/jun/06/fisa-court-judge-verizon-records-surveillance?guni=Network%20front:network-front%20main-5%20Eds%20picks%201:Network%20front%20-%20all-purpose%20editable%20trailblock:Position1:sublinks | title = Fisa chief judge defends integrity of court over Verizon records collection | work = The Guardian | author = Ackerman, Spencer | author-link = Spencer Ackerman | date = 2013-06-06 | location = [[Washington DC]] | access-date = 2013-07-01 | quote = In the wake of the Guardian's revelations, Reggie Walton, presiding judge of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court (Fisa), said claims that the body was unduly acquiescent to the government's requests for surveillance orders were "absolutely false". }} ==Early life and education == Walton won a football scholarship to get his [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[West Virginia State University|West Virginia State College]] in 1971, and then a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[Washington College of Law]] at [[American University]] in 1974.{{Cite web |title=Judge Reggie B. Walton |url=https://cleoinc.org/jhof/hof/judge-reggie-b-walton/ |access-date=July 19, 2024 |website=CLEO Judges Hall of Fame |language=en-US}} Walton is a member of the [[Alpha Phi Alpha]] fraternity. ==Career== Walton served as an associate judge of the [[Superior Court of the District of Columbia]] from 1981 to 1989 and from 1991 to 2001. He also served as associate director of the [[Office of National Drug Control Policy]].{{Cite web |title=Senior Judge Reggie B. Walton {{!}} District of Columbia {{!}} United States District Court |url=https://www.dcd.uscourts.gov/content/senior-judge-reggie-b-walton |access-date=July 20, 2024 |website=www.dcd.uscourts.gov}} ===Federal judicial service=== In 2001, he was nominated to the federal bench by President [[George W. Bush]], and subsequently confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on September 21, 2001. He received his commission on September 24, 2001.{{FJC Bio|nid=1391301|inline=yes}} In 2004, Bush appointed him to chair the [[National Prison Rape Elimination Commission]], investigating ways to curb [[prison rape]]. In May 2007, Chief Justice [[John Roberts]] appointed him to a seat on the [[United States Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court]]. His term on the FISA Court ended May 18, 2014. He assumed [[senior status]] on December 31, 2015. During his FISC tenure, Judge Walton was "exceptionally concerned" about the [[NSA]]'s "flagrant violation" of the court orders regarding privacy, and he accused the agency of "misinterpretations."{{Cite journal|last=Bamford|first=James|date=September 7, 2016|title=Every Move You Make|url=https://foreignpolicy.com/2016/09/07/every-move-you-make-obama-nsa-security-surveillance-spying-intelligence-snowden/|journal=Foreign Policy}} ''[[The Washington Post]]'' reported, "fellow judges and lawyers who appear before him say Walton's decisions do not appear to be guided by politics but by a tough-on-crime mentality." Walton is known by local defense attorneys as a "long ball hitter" – a judge willing to impose long sentences in order to deter future crimes. In fall 2005, the judge was driving his wife and daughter to the airport for a vacation when he came across an assailant attacking a cab driver on the side of the road. Walton tackled the assailant and subdued him until police arrived. The D.C. police spokesperson noted in response, "God bless Judge Walton. I surely wouldn't want to mess with him."[https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2007/06/04/AR2007060401601.html "Libby Jurist's Career Built on Toughness"], ''The Washington Post'', June 5, 2007. === Notable cases === [[File:Judge-walton-pic.jpg|thumb|right|Walton in his office]] ====''United States v. Libby''==== {{Main|United States v. Libby}} Walton also presided over the trial of Vice President [[Dick Cheney]]'s former chief of staff, [[Scooter Libby]]. On March 6, 2007, the jury convicted Libby of four of the five counts with which he was charged: two counts of perjury, one of obstruction of justice, and one of [[making false statements]] to federal investigators.[https://www.nytimes.com/ref/washington/LIBBYDIARY.html "Diary of the Leak Trial"], ''[[The New York Times]]'', accessed June 23, 2007. On June 5, 2007, Walton sentenced Libby to 30 months in federal prison and a fine of US$250,000, and, subsequently, he ordered that Libby report to jail without bail pending any appeals.Lewis, Neil A.; [[David Stout|Stout, David]]. [https://www.nytimes.com/2007/06/14/washington/14cnd-libby.htm "Judge Won't Delay Libby Prison Term"], ''The New York Times'', June 14, 2007, accessed June 16, 2007. On June 20, 2007, Libby appealed Walton's ruling in federal appeals court.[[Associated Press]], [https://www.nytimes.com/2007/06/20/washington/20brfs-libby.htm "Libby Appeals Sentencing Ruling"], ''The New York Times'', June 20, 2007, accessed June 20, 2007. The next day, Walton filed a 30-page expanded ruling, in which he explained his decision to deny Libby bail in more detail.Gerstein, Josh. [http://www.nysun.com/article/57156?page_no=1 "Libby Judge Files Expanded Opinion:] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070929111704/http://www.nysun.com/article/57156?page_no=1 |date=2007-09-29 }} Details Decision Not Allowing Libby to Remain Free", ''[[New York Sun]]'', June 22, 2007, accessed June 22, 2007. Walton received several threatening letters after pronouncing sentence on Libby.{{cite news |first=Jerry |last=Markon |title=Threats to Judges, Prosecutors Soaring |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2009/05/24/AR2009052402931.html |newspaper=The Washington Post |page=A01 |quote=The judge in the CIA leak case got threatening letters when he ordered Vice President Richard B. Cheney's former chief of staff to prison. |date=2009-05-25 |access-date=May 25, 2009}} ====Rocket propellant case==== Walton was the presiding judge in ''[[Tripoli Rocketry Association]], Inc. and [[National Association of Rocketry]] v. United States Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives'', a long-running case brought by the two largest hobby rocketry organizations, which challenged the inclusion of certain types of solid fuel rocket propellant on the list of "explosives" regulated by the [[Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives|ATF]]. On March 16, 2009, Walton ruled in favor of the rocketry organizations.{{cite web |url=http://www.v-serv.com/usr/ATFE-03-16-09.pdf |title=Tripoli Rocketry Association and National Association of Rocketry v. Bureau of Alcohol Tobacco and Firearms |publisher=United States District Court for the District of Columbia |date=March 16, 2009 |access-date=2013-07-08 |archive-date=2014-07-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140726174731/http://www.v-serv.com/usr/ATFE-03-16-09.pdf |url-status=dead }} ====''United States v. Roger Clemens''==== On August 30, 2010, ''[[USA Today]]'' reported that Walton arraigned former major-league pitcher [[Roger Clemens]] on charges of lying to Congress (three counts of making false statements, two counts of [[perjury]], and one count of obstruction of Congress) about the use of [[performance-enhancing substance]]s. Pre-trial prosecutors brought a motion of conflict of interest against defense attorney [[Rusty Hardin]] for having briefly represented [[Andy Pettitte]], who was an important witness for the government.Thomas, Katie. [https://www.nytimes.com/2011/02/03/sports/baseball/03clemens.html?_r=0 "Clemens's Co-Counsel to Question Pettitte"] ''The New York Times''. February 2, 2011. On July 14, 2011, Walton declared a mistrial over inadmissible evidence shown to jurors. The judge said Clemens could not be assured a fair trial after prosecutors showed jurors evidence against his orders in the second day of testimony. Following the mistrial, the US Attorneys Office brought Clemens to trial once more for perjury. On June 18, 2012, Judge Walton accepted the jury's unanimous verdict of acquittal.{{cite web|last=Brady |first=Erik |url=http://content.usatoday.com/communities/dailypitch/post/2012/06/roger-clemens-verdict/1#.T-ABAWC8GSA |title=Roger Clemens acquitted on all counts: 'You are free to go' |publisher=USA Today |date=2012-06-18 |access-date=2013-07-08}} ====Whitewater==== {{Main|Whitewater controversy}} On October 4, 2016, Walton rejected the release of [[Hillary Clinton]] criminal indictment drafts prosecutors prepared, but never issued, during the Whitewater investigation in the 1990s. He ruled that Clinton had a "substantial privacy interest" when he rejected a [[Freedom of Information Act (United States)|FOIA]] lawsuit filed by [[Judicial Watch]].{{cite web|last=Gerstein |first=Josh |url=https://www.politico.com/story/2016/10/hillary-clinton-whitewater-indictment-drafts-229093 |title=Judge won't release drafts of Hillary Clinton Whitewater indictment |publisher=[[Politico]] |date=2016-10-04 |access-date=2016-10-07}}{{cite web|last=Dinan |first=Stephen |url=http://m.washingtontimes.com/news/2016/oct/4/judge-shields-clinton-draft-indictments-release/ |title=Judge won't release Clinton draft indictments: Privacy outweighs public debate |publisher=[[The Washington Times]] |date=2016-10-04 |access-date=2016-10-07}} ====''Mohammon v. Bush''==== Walton presided over ''[[Mohammon v. Bush]]'', a set of amalgamated [[habeas corpus]] petitions, submitted on behalf of [[Guantanamo captives]].{{cite news | url=http://www.pegc.us/archive/In_re_Gitmo/gov_mot_to_dismiss_20070419.pdf | title=Exhibit C: List of No Longer Enemy Combant Detainees With Pending Habeas Corpus Petitions Who Have Been Released From United States Custody | page=64 | publisher=[[United States Department of Justice]] | date=April 17, 2007 | access-date=2008-05-05 | archive-date=2009-03-27 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090327090515/http://www.pegc.us/archive/In_re_Gitmo/gov_mot_to_dismiss_20070419.pdf | url-status=dead }} ====''Hatfill v. John Ashcroft et al.''==== {{Further|Steven Hatfill#Hatfill v. John Ashcroft, et al.}} Walton presided over the lawsuit that [[Steven Hatfill]] filed against former US Attorney General [[John Ashcroft]].[http://www.cnn.com/2003/LAW/08/26/lawsuit.hatfill/ "Anthrax 'person of interest' sues Ashcroft, FBI"], ''[[CNN]]'', 27 August 2003. Ashcroft publicly described Hatfill as a "[[person of interest]]" in the FBI's investigations into the [[2001 anthrax attacks]]. On March 30, 2007, Walton issued an order warning Hatfill that he may lose his lawsuit over the leaks if he did not compel journalists to name their sources and giving Hatfill until April 16, 2007, to decide whether to do so.Gerstein, Josh. [http://www.nysun.com/article/51808 "Judge Urges Hatfill To Compel Outing of Sources"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070417094513/http://www.nysun.com/article/51808 |date=2007-04-17 }}, ''[[The New York Sun]]'', April 4, 2007, accessed June 23, 2007. Hatfill's lawyers complied with the order, as reported on April 18 by Gerstein, who warns that a "free press battle looms," as
The reporters in jeopardy now are expected to defy Hatfill's subpoenas and any court order to name their sources. ... one critical issue will be whether Judge Walton imposes fines on the news organizations involved. ... A First Amendment battle could possibly be avoided: The government and Dr. Hatfill's lawyers asked Walton to name a mediator to explore a possible settlement of the case. ... No one has been charged in the anthrax attacks, which killed at least five people.Josh Gerstein, [http://www.nysun.com/article/52682 "Free Press Battle Looms in Hatfill Case"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070629172645/http://www.nysun.com/article/52682? |date=2007-06-29 }}, ''[[The New York Sun]]'', April 18, 2007, accessed June 23, 2007.
====Guantanamo captives' habeas petitions==== On August 21, 2009, [[Reuters]] reported that Walton issued a ruling about "[[hearsay|hearsay evidence]]" that applied to all the [[Guantanamo detainees' appeals in Washington, D.C. courts|Guantanamo detainees' habeas petitions]] before him. {{cite news | author=Pelofsky, Jeremy | url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-usa-guantanamo-idUSTRE57I5ZZ20090819 | title=Obama Admin to Transfer Six Guantanamo Prisoners | publisher=Reuters | date=2009-08-19 | access-date=2013-07-08 }} Much of the evidence the Department of Justice presented in the habeas petitions was hearsay evidence. Walton wrote: {{blockquote|Even the most widespread rumors are often inaccurate in part if not in whole. The court's only point is that otherwise unreliable hearsay cannot be deemed reliable because there is other unreliable hearsay to the same effect.}} ====Mueller Report redactions==== On August 5, 2019, [[Politico]] reported that while hearing arguments regarding lawsuits by [[BuzzFeed]] and the nonprofit [[Electronic Privacy Information Center]], as they sought to reveal the approximately 1,000 redacted items in the publicly-released edition of former special counsel Robert Mueller's report, Walton indicated that he would review the redactions before determining whether to make them public.Samuelsohn, Darren, ''[https://www.politico.com/story/2019/08/05/judge-signals-interest-in-removing-mueller-report-redactions-1448331 Judge signals interest in removing Mueller report redactions]'', Politico, August 5, 2019. On March 5, 2020, Walton described Attorney General William Barr's public statements about the Mueller report as "misleading," and said that Barr's representations regarding DOJ redactions from the report could not be credited. He directed the DOJ to submit the unredacted version of the Mueller Report to the Court for [[In camera|in camera review]].Hsu, Spencer S. & Barrett, Devlin ''[https://www.washingtonpost.com/national-security/mueller-report-attorney-general-william-barr/2020/03/05/3fa7afce-5f2c-11ea-b29b-9db42f7803a7_story.html Judge cites Barr's 'misleading' statements in ordering review of Mueller report redactions]'' On October 6, 2020, President Trump, referencing the Mueller report, tweeted "I have fully authorized the total Declassification of any & all documents pertaining to the single greatest political CRIME in American History, the Russia Hoax".{{Cite news |last=González |first=Oriana |title=Mark Meadows confirms in court Trump's tweets "declassifying" Russia documents were false |url=https://www.axios.com/2020/10/20/mark-meadows-trump-tweets-russia |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260222161109/https://www.axios.com/2020/10/20/mark-meadows-trump-tweets-russia |archive-date=2026-02-22 |access-date=2026-02-27 |work=Axios |language=en}} In response to the President's statement, BuzzFeed requested an unredacted version of the report; however, BuzzFeed's request was denied by the DOJ. The DOJ told Walton that "the President's statements on Twitter were not self-executing declassification orders..." To clear up the position of the President, Walton ordered a continuance until October 21, 2020 so, "I can get something from White House counsel saying that they conferred with the president, and the president, in fact, did not intend to declassify the information..."{{Cite web|url=https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/politics/judge-orders-doj-to-find-out-if-trump-s-declassification-tweets-mean-entire-mueller-report-should-be-released/ar-BB1a6zDv|title = Judge orders DOJ to find out if Trump's declassification tweets mean entire Mueller report should be released|website = [[MSN]]}} ====''United States v. Bergdahl''==== On July 25, 2023, the [[Associated Press]] reported that Walton vacated the sentence due to Judge Jeffery Nance's failure to report an application to the executive branch as an immigration judge; however, Judge Walton rejected the defense's claim of undue command influence due to [[Donald Trump]]'s comments during his campaign in 2016.Barakat, Matthew, ''[https://apnews.com/article/bowe-bergdahl-court-martial-overturned-12da397af78384788a6a09d6499936c0]'', Associated Press, July 25, 2023. [[University of Colorado, Boulder]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Regina Marie Rodriguez''' (born 1963)[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Rodriguez%20Senate%20Questionnaire.pdf United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees: Regina Rodriguez] is the [[United States federal judge|chief United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Colorado]]. == Early life and education == Rodriguez was born in 1963 in [[Gunnison, Colorado]], to a [[Mexican Americans|Mexican-American]] father and [[Japanese Americans|Japanese-American]] mother.{{Cite web |url=http://www.lawyercentral.com/regina-m-rodriguez-interactive-profile--20-840463.html |title=Lawyer Central profile |access-date=2016-04-29 |archive-date=2016-05-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160504234721/http://www.lawyercentral.com/regina-m-rodriguez-interactive-profile--20-840463.html |url-status=live }}{{cite web | url=https://www.denverpost.com/2016/04/28/obama-nominates-denver-lawyer-regina-rodriguez-to-federal-bench/ | title=Obama nominates Denver lawyer Regina Rodriguez to federal bench | work=[[The Denver Post]] | first=John | last=Ingold | date=April 28, 2016 | access-date=April 4, 2021}} Her late father, [[Pete Rodriguez (American football)|Pete Rodriguez]], played football for [[Western Colorado University|Western State Colorado University]] and went on to serve as an assistant coach in the [[National Football League]], which made him one of the league's first Hispanic coaches.{{cite web | url=https://amp.usatoday.com/amp/72709946 | title=Pioneer for Hispanics in NFL nominated for Hall of Fame | work=[[KUSA]] | first=Victoria | last=Sanchez | date=September 23, 2015 | access-date=April 4, 2021 | archive-date=April 15, 2021 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210415170759/https://amp.usatoday.com/amp/72709946 | url-status=dead }} Rodriguez received a [[Bachelor of Science]] from the [[University of Iowa]] in 1985 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Colorado School of Law]] in 1988. == Career == Rodriguez began her legal career as an [[Associate lawyer|associate]] in the law firm of Cooper & Kelly, P.C. (now defunct) from 1988 to 1995. She served as an [[assistant United States attorney]] for the United States Attorney's Office for the District of Colorado from 1995 to 2002, during which time she served as the deputy chief of the Civil Division from 1998 to 1999 and as chief of the civil division from 1999 to 2002. In addition, from 1997 to 1998, she served a four-month detail as deputy senior counsel for [[alternative dispute resolution]] in the [[United States Department of Justice]]. Previously, from 2002 to 2016, she worked in the Denver office of [[Faegre & Benson]] LLP (now Faegre Baker Daniels LLP) as a special counsel until she was elevated to partner in 2005. She was a partner in the [[Denver]] office of [[Hogan Lovells]] from 2016 to 2019, where she specialized in [[mass tort]] and [[product liability]] defense.{{Cite web |url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2016/04/28/president-obama-nominates-eight-serve-united-states-district-courts |title="President Obama Nominates Eight to Serve on the United States District Courts" White House, April 28, 2016 |date=28 April 2016 |access-date=March 3, 2021 |archive-date=February 29, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200229121741/https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2016/04/28/president-obama-nominates-eight-serve-united-states-district-courts |url-status=live }} She was a partner at [[Wilmerhale|WilmerHale]] from 2019 until she was commissioned as a federal judge.{{Cite web|title=Accomplished Litigator Regina M. Rodriguez Joins WilmerHale|url=https://www.wilmerhale.com/en/insights/news/20190513-accomplished-litigator-regina-m-rodriguez-joins-wilmerhale|access-date=2021-08-23|website=www.wilmerhale.com|date=13 May 2019 |language=en}} == Federal judicial service == === Expired nomination to district court under Obama === On April 28, 2016, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Rodriguez to serve as a United States district judge of the United States District Court of the District of Colorado, to the seat vacated by Judge [[Robert E. Blackburn]], who assumed [[senior status]] on April 12, 2016. Her nomination expired on January 3, 2017, with the end of the [[114th United States Congress|114th Congress]].{{Cite web |url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2016/04/28/presidential-nominations-sent-senate-0 |title="Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate" White House, April 28, 2016 |date=28 April 2016 |access-date=March 3, 2021 |archive-date=August 6, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200806080142/https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2016/04/28/presidential-nominations-sent-senate-0 |url-status=live }} === Renomination to district court under Biden === On March 30, 2021, President [[Joe Biden]] announced his intent to nominate Rodriguez to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Colorado]].[https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/03/30/president-biden-announces-intent-to-nominate-11-judicial-candidates/ "President Biden Announces Intent to Nominate 11 Judicial Candidates", White House, March 30, 2021] {{PD-notice}} On April 19, 2021, her nomination was sent to the Senate. President Biden nominated Rodriguez to the seat vacated by Judge [[Marcia S. Krieger]], who assumed [[senior status]] on March 3, 2019.[https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/04/19/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-11/ "Nominations Sent to the Senate", White House, April 19, 2021] On April 28, 2021, a hearing was held on her nomination before the Senate Judiciary Committee.[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/04/21/2021/nominations United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Nominations for April 28, 2021] On May 20, 2021, her nomination was reported out of committee by a 17–5 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%20May%2020,%202021.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – May 20, 2021|website=Senate Judiciary Committee}}{{cite news|last1=Lacey|first1=Hank|title=Senate Judiciary Committee Advances Regina Rodriguez Nomination|url=https://lawweekcolorado.com/article/senate-judiciary-committee-advances-rodriguez-nomination/|access-date=9 June 2021|agency=Law Week Colorado|publisher=Circuit Media|date=21 May 2021}} On June 8, 2021, the [[United States Senate]] invoked [[cloture]] on her nomination by a 72–28 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=117&session=1&vote=00221|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Regina M. Rodriguez to be U.S. District Judge for the District of Colorado)|website=United States Senate|date=June 8, 2021}} She was confirmed later that day by a 72–28 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=117&session=1&vote=00222|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Regina M. Rodriguez, of Colorado, to be U.S. District Judge for the District of Colorado)|date=June 8, 2021|website=United States Senate|access-date=June 8, 2021}}{{Cite web|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/06/08/statement-by-president-joe-biden-on-the-first-confirmations-of-his-judicial-nominees/|title=Statement by President Joe Biden on the First Confirmations of His Judicial Nominees|date=June 8, 2021|website=The White House}} She received her judicial commission on July 1, 2021. Hinojosa''' (born January 24, 1950) is a [[senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas]] and served as the chairman of the [[United States Sentencing Commission]]. ==Education and career== Hinojosa was born in [[Rio Grande City, Texas]]. He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from the [[University of Texas, Austin]] in 1972, and a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Harvard Law School]] in 1975. He was a [[law clerk]] to the [[Texas Supreme Court]] from 1975 to 1976. He was then in private practice in [[McAllen, Texas]], until 1983.{{FJC Bio|nid=1382201|inline=yes}} In 2015, he received the Presidential Citation from UT Austin.{{Cite web |date=2016-01-10 |title=Presidential Citation |url=https://president.utexas.edu/awards-fellowships/presidential-citation |access-date=2024-07-01 |website=Office of the President |language=en}} ===Federal judicial service=== On April 12, 1983, Hinojosa was nominated by President [[Ronald Reagan]] to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas]] vacated by Judge [[Woodrow Bradley Seals]]. Hinojosa was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on May 4, 1983, and received his commission on May 5, 1983. He was appointed as a commissioner on the [[United States Sentencing Commission]] by then President [[George W. Bush]] in 2003. He served as chief judge from 2009 to 2016. He assumed [[senior status]] on May 21, 2025, by which time Hinojosa was the longest-serving federal judge remaining in active service.{{cite web|last=Bublé|first=Courtney|title=Longest-Serving Federal Judge To Take Senior Status|url=https://www.law360.com/pulse/articles/2329792/longest-serving-federal-judge-to-take-senior-status |website=Law360 Pulse|publisher=Portfolio Media, Inc.}} Hinojosa left the court on October 1, 2025.{{Cite web|url=https://www.txs.uscourts.gov/page/history-district-judges|title=History of District Judges|website=Southern District of Texas|access-date=December 3, 2025}} ==See also== * [[George W. He previously served as a deputy prosecuting attorney for [[King County, Washington]], attorney for the [[Port of Seattle]], and assistant United States attorney in the region, in addition to private practice. ==Early life and education== Born in [[Seattle]] in 1950, Jones is the son of Quincy Delight Jones Sr., who worked as a semi-professional baseball player and carpenter, and his second wife. He is 17 years younger than his half-brother [[Quincy Jones]], a musician and producer.{{Cite news | first=Peter | last=Lattman | url=https://blogs.wsj.com/law/2007/10/09/law-blog-famous-family-member-fraternity-richard-jones/ | title=Law Blog Famous Family Member Fraternity: Richard Jones | work=Wall Street Journal Law Blog | date=October 9, 2007 | access-date=July 16, 2011}}{{Cite news | first=Jim | last=Brunner | url=https://www.seattletimes.com/seattle-news/federal-bench-nominee-jones-wins-high-praise-from-both-parties/ | title=Federal bench nominee Jones wins high praise from both parties | work=[[The Seattle Times]] | date=March 25, 2007 | archive-date=2007-03-29 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070329052155/http://seattletimes.nwsource.com/html/localnews/2003634951_jones25m.html | url-access=limited | url-status=live | access-date=July 16, 2011}} After attending Seattle public schools, Richard Jones received a Bachelor of Public Administration degree from [[Seattle University]] in 1972 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Washington School of Law]] in 1975. He was admitted to the [[Washington State Bar Association]] in 1977. ==Career== Jones was a community liaison officer, Office of King County Prosecuting Attorney, Washington from 1975 to 1977. He was a deputy prosecuting attorney of the Office of King County Prosecuting Attorney from 1977 to 1978. He was a staff attorney of the [[Port of Seattle]] from 1978 to 1983. After being in private practice with the major law firm of Bogle & Gates in Seattle from 1983 to 1988, he became an [[Assistant United States Attorney]] of the United States Attorney's Office, Western District of Washington. He served there from 1988 to 1994. ===Judicial service=== Jones served as a judge on the King County Superior Court, Washington from 1994 to 2007. During this period, he presided over several high-profile cases, including the prosecution of [[Gary Ridgway]], the notorious "Green River Killer" who was known to have killed 48 women. Jones was recommended by a bipartisan panel in Washington and nominated by President [[George W. Bush]] on March 19, 2007, to a seat vacated by [[John C. Coughenour]]. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on October 4, 2007, and received his commission on October 29, 2007. He assumed senior status on September 5, 2022.{{FJC Bio|nid=1392636|inline=yes}} In April 2024, Jones sentenced [[Changpeng Zhao]], founder of the [[cryptocurrency exchange]] [[Binance]], to only four months in prison over Zhao's guilty plea to [[money laundering]] charges, despite federal prosecutors seeking a three-year term.{{Cite news |last=Yaffe-Bellany |first=David |date=2024-04-30 |title=Binance Founder Sentenced to 4 Months in Prison |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/04/30/technology/binance-founder-changpeng-zhao-sentenced.html |access-date=2024-05-05 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} Dennis Kelleher of the non-profit Better Markets criticized the sentence as insufficient to dissuade similar corporate behavior.{{Cite web |date=2024-04-30 |title='Crime Pays!' Is The Message Sent by DOJ's Actions Reflected in Today's Sentencing of Binance's Former CEO CZ To Just 4 Months in Prison |url=https://bettermarkets.org/newsroom/crime-pays-is-the-message-sent-by-dojs-actions-reflected-in-todays-sentencing-of-binances-former-ceo-cz-to-just-4-months-in-prison/ |access-date=2024-05-05 |website=Better Markets |language=en-US}} ====Privacy/surveillance==== Some of Jones's decisions expanding state surveillance powers have been controversial, including one in 2017 to allow unfettered [[Warrantless search|warrantless camera surveillance]] by the City of Seattle by barring the public release, in response to a [[public records request]], of information regarding cameras installed by the [[FBI]].{{cite news |title=City Councilmember Blasts FBI's 'Warrantless' Surveillance in Seattle |url=https://www.securitysales.com/news/city_councilmember_blasts_fbis_warrantless_surveillance_in_seattle/ |work=Security S & I |date=27 January 2017 |language=en}} In a 2016 case also narrowing the scope of a citizen's [[reasonable expectation of privacy]], he ruled that users of the [[Tor (anonymity network)|Tor]] anonymity network, the purpose of which is to provide privacy, do not have a reasonable expectation of privacy and was criticized for not understanding the technology.{{cite news |last1=Mimoso |first1=Michael |title=Judge Confirms DoD Funded Research to Decloak Tor Users |url=https://threatpost.com/judge-confirms-dod-funded-research-to-decloak-tor-users/116464/ |access-date=16 February 2020 |work=threatpost.com |date=February 25, 2016 |language=en}} ==Personal== He is married to Leslie Jones, diversity program manager for [[Sound Transit]]. Jones has been active on the board of the [[YMCA]]. '''Richard Alexander Schell''' (born 1950) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Texas]].

==Education and career==

Schell was born in [[Dallas]]. He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[Southern Methodist University]] in 1972 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[Dedman School of Law]] at Southern Methodist University in 1975. He was an instructor at the Dedman School of Law from 1975 to 1976. He was an assistant district attorney of [[Collin County, Texas]] in 1976. He was in private practice in [[McKinney, Texas]] from 1977 to 1982. He was a Judge of the County Court at Law in Collin County from 1982 to 1986. He was a Judge of the 219th Judicial District Court of Texas from 1986 to 1988.<ref name="fjc.gov">{{FJC Bio|nid=1387446|inline=yes}}</ref>

=== Federal judicial service ===

On April 13, 1988, Schell was nominated by President [[Ronald Reagan]] to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Texas]] vacated by Judge [[William Steger]]. Schell was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on May 27, 1988, and received his commission on June 6, 1988. He served as Chief Judge from 1994 to 2001. He took [[senior status]] on March 10, 2015.<ref name="fjc.gov"/> Schell took inactive senior status on June 13, 2023.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.txed.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/judgeFiles/standing%20order.Schell_.pdf|title=STANDING ORDER FOR UNITED STATES SENIOR DISTRICT JUDGE RICHARD A. SCHELL|website=txed.uscourts.gov|date=2023-06-13|access-date=2025-12-31}}</ref>

[[Villanova University School of Law|Villanova University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | footnotes = }} '''Richard Joseph Arcara''' (born June 6, 1940) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of New York]]. == Early life and education == Arcara was born in [[Buffalo, New York]]. He graduated from [[Canisius High School]] in 1958, received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] from [[St. Bonaventure University]] in 1962, and received a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Villanova University School of Law]] in 1965. He was a captain in the [[United States Army]], Military Police Corps from 1966 to 1967.{{FJC Bio|nid=1377241|inline=yes}} == Career == He was in private practice in Buffalo from 1968 to 1969. He joined the office of the [[United States Attorney]] of the Western District of New York in 1969, first as an [[Assistant United States Attorney]] until 1973, then as a First Assistant United States Attorney from 1973 to 1974, finally becoming the district's United States Attorney from 1975 to 1981. He was then [[Erie County, New York|Erie County]], New York District Attorney from January 1, 1982 to May 31, 1988. === Federal judicial service === On August 7, 1987, Arcara was nominated by President [[Ronald Reagan]] to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Western District of New York]] vacated by Judge [[John T. Elfvin]], who assumed senior status. Arcara was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on February 19, 1988, and received his commission on February 22, 1988. He served as [[Chief judge (United States)|Chief Judge]] of the district from 2003 to 2010. He assumed [[senior status]] on January 3, 2015. ===Notable rulings=== Arcara presided over the 2007 trial of [[James Charles Kopp]], who was charged with violating the Freedom of Access to Clinic Entrances Act. Kopp had previously been convicted in 2003 in New York State court by Judge Pigott for the 1998 sniper-style murder of Dr. Barnett Slepian, an American physician from Amherst, New York who performed [[abortion]]s. Judge Arcara also presided over the internationally significant Robert Rhodes trial in 2005. Rhodes, a United States Customs and Border Protection Officer, was arrested and indicted for beating a Chinese National on the US-Canada border in Niagara Falls, NY. The incident was addressed by then Secretary of State Colin Powell and Secretary of Homeland Security Thomas Ridge when the Chinese Foreign Minister accused the United States of human rights violations by Rhodes' actions. Rhodes was acquitted after a high-profile trial in August 2005, presided over by Chief Judge Arcara.{{cite web|url=http://news.newamericamedia.org/news/view_article.html?article_id=2096531dd16c14d6693109e895dc2082|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080306091640/http://news.newamericamedia.org/news/view_article.html?article_id=2096531dd16c14d6693109e895dc2082|url-status=usurped|archive-date=March 6, 2008|title=New America Media|website=news.newamericamedia.org}}{{cite web|url=http://www.taipeitimes.com/News/world/archives/2005/09/01/2003269973|title=Chinese businesswoman sees US assaulter in court - Taipei Times|website=www.taipeitimes.com|date=September 2005 }}{{cite web|url=http://english.peopledaily.com.cn/200407/26/eng20040726_150855.html|title=People's Daily Online -- FM urges US to punish officer for beating|last=|website=english.peopledaily.com.cn}} ==References== {{Reflist}} ==Sources== * {{FJC Bio|nid=1377241}} * {{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20080306091640/http://news.newamericamedia.org/news/view_article.html?article_id=2096531dd16c14d6693109e895dc2082 Article title]}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[John T. Bennett''' (born August 12, 1947) is a [[United States federal judge|United States Senior District Judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Maryland]]. Born in Maryland, Bennett is a graduate of [[Severn School]], the [[University of Pennsylvania]], and the [[University of Maryland Francis King Carey School of Law]].{{Cite web |title=Richard D. Bennett, U.S. District Court Judge (Maryland) |url=https://msa.maryland.gov/msa/mdmanual/39fed/02usd/senior/html/msa14072.html |access-date=2023-07-20 |website=msa.maryland.gov}}{{Cite web |title=Richard D. Bennett, District Judge {{!}} District of Maryland {{!}} United States District Court |url=https://www.mdd.uscourts.gov/richard-d-bennett-district-judge |access-date=2023-07-20 |website=www.mdd.uscourts.gov}}{{cite news |title=Register |url=https://www.bizjournals.com/baltimore/news/2021/05/14/whos-who-in-law-judge-bennett-us-district-court-md.html |website=www.bizjournals.com |access-date=26 August 2023 |language=en |url-access=limited}} He previously served as an [[Assistant United States Attorney]] and the [[United States Attorney]] for Maryland, and was awarded multiple commendations for his service. In private practice, Bennett was a partner in a major Maryland law firm, where he specialized in [[white collar criminal defense]]. Appointed to the federal bench in 2003, he took [[senior status]] in 2021.{{Cite web |date=2003-01-30 |title=Legal Community Praises Nomination of Bennett for U.S. District Court Bench |url=https://cnsmaryland.org/2003/01/30/legal-community-praises-nomination-of-bennett-for-u-s-district-court-bench/ |access-date=2023-07-20 |website=CNS Maryland |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/bennett-richard-d |access-date=27 August 2023 |title=Bennett, Richard D. |website=www.fjc.gov}} While maintaining an active trial docket in the District of Maryland, Bennett has increasingly been [[Visiting judge|sitting by designation]] with the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]]. ==Education and career== Born in [[Baltimore, Maryland]], Bennett grew up in [[Severna Park, Maryland|Severna Park]] near Annapolis, and attended [[Severn School]]. In 1969, he received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from the [[University of Pennsylvania]], where he majored in [[Political science|Political Science]] with a study in the Russian language. At Penn, he was selected to the [[Sphinx Senior Society|Sphinx Senior Honor Society]], one of the oldest societies at the University, and was elected as one of four officers for his graduating class. Following a period of military service, Bennett returned home to Maryland, and pursued the practice of law. In 1973, he received a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Maryland School of Law]], where he served as a member of the [[Maryland Law Review]] and won academic awards. In 1976, Bennett was appointed to serve as an [[Assistant United States Attorney]] of the District of Maryland. He remained in that position until 1981, when he returned to private practice. In 1991, Bennett was unanimously confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] as the [[United States Attorney]] for the District of Maryland. In that position he received the Outstanding Service Award from the Maryland State's Attorneys Association, and an award from the [[Governor of Maryland]] for outstanding contributions in the field of victim rights. In 1993, Bennett returned to private practice as a partner at the Maryland law firm of Miles and Stockbridge, PC, where he spearheaded that firm's white collar criminal defense and government investigations practice.{{Cite web |last=Gibson |first=Gail |date=April 30, 2003 |title=State gains U.S. District judge today |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2003/05/01/state-gains-us-district-judge-today/ |work=[[The Baltimore Sun]]}} Bennett would remain at the firm until his appointment to the federal bench in 2003. During his tenure, Bennett defended several high-profile clients, including Democratic [[Maryland Delegate|State Delegate]] [[Tony Fulton (Maryland politician)|Tony E. Fulton]], who was acquitted in 2000 of federal fraud and conspiracy charges. He was also retained by the [[United States House of Representatives]] as [[Special counsel|Special Counsel]] to investigate foreign campaign contributions in the [[1996 United States presidential election|1996 United States Presidential Election]]. He was recognized by a respected national publication as one of the "Best Lawyers in America." In addition to his active federal trial practice, Bennett was a leading figure in the Maryland Republican Party. He was the 1994 Republican candidate for [[Attorney General of Maryland]] and the 1998 Republican candidate for [[Lieutenant Governor of Maryland|Lieutenant Governor]], having been selected by [[Ellen R. Sauerbrey]] as her running mate in her gubernatorial campaign. He was selected as a delegate to the [[Republican National Convention]]s in 1988, 1996, and 2000. At a Maryland state Republican Party convention in 1998, he was elected by acclamation to serve as the Chairman of the [[Maryland Republican Party]]. In that capacity, he represented Maryland on the Republican National Committee until 2000, when he resigned out of his determination to represent Democratic State Delegate Tony E. Fulton in a high-profile federal corruption case.{{Cite news |title=GOP Slow to Weigh In Formally on Fulton |language=en-US |newspaper=Washington Post |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/1999/12/30/gop-slow-to-weigh-in-formally-on-fulton/4177d051-a1c6-4ff0-a77b-83ae38440df2/ |access-date=2023-07-20 |issn=0190-8286}} Outside of his legal practice, Bennett served over 20 years in the [[United States Army Reserve]] and the [[Maryland National Guard]], and is a [[Major (rank)|Major]] in the Retired Reserve. During his service, he received the Maryland Commendation Medal for Outstanding Service, the Maryland Distinguished Service Cross for Service Beyond the Call of Duty, and the Meritorious Service Medal. Bennett is also a Life Fellow of the [[American Bar Foundation]] and the [[Maryland State Bar Foundation]]. He has served on the board of the Kennedy-Krieger Institute for Disabled Children, and the Board of Trustees of Severn School, where he has been inducted to that school’s athletic Hall of Fame, and received the school’s Distinguished Alumnus Award.  He has also served on the Board of Visitors of the University of Maryland Francis King Carey School of Law which has awarded him the prestigious Barbera Judicial Excellence Award in recognition of his exemplifying the highest standards of judicial excellence and extraordinary courage in the handling of complex and difficult cases.{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=k8MEaVPyr3s |title=2024 Mary Ellen Barbera Judicial Excellence Award - Richard Bennett |language=en |access-date=2024-05-01 |via=www.youtube.com}} ==Federal Judicial Service== On January 29, 2003, Bennett was nominated by [[President of the United States|President]] [[George W. Bush]] to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the District of Maryland]] vacated by [[Frederic N. Smalkin]]. Bennett's nomination received the strong, bipartisan support of Democratic Senators [[Paul Sarbanes|Paul S. Sarbanes]] and [[Barbara Mikulski|Barbara A. Mikulski]], and was praised by prominent members of the Maryland legal community. He was unanimously confirmed with a vote of 99-0 by the [[United States Senate]] on April 9, 2003, received his commission on April 10, 2003, and took his oath of office on April 29, 2003. After more than eighteen years on the federal bench, Bennett assumed [[senior status]] on June 30, 2021.{{FJC Bio|nid=1391816|inline=yes}} Since taking senior status, Bennett has continued to maintain an active trial docket. Additionally, Bennett has been frequently [[Visiting judge|sitting by designation]] with the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]]. In October 2009, Judge Bennett was appointed by [[Chief Justice of the United States|Chief Justice]] [[John Roberts|John G. Roberts, Jr.]] to serve on the International Judicial Relations Committee of the [[Judicial Conference of the United States|United States Judicial Conference.]] He has traveled extensively in Central and [[Eastern Europe]] participating in judicial exchange programs in [[Russia]], [[Estonia]], [[Bulgaria]], [[Turkey]], [[Ukraine]] and the [[Czech Republic]]. ==Notable Cases== {{BLP unreferenced section|date=September 2021}} In 2011 he presided in the case of [[National Security Agency]] [[Whistleblower]] [[Thomas Andrews Drake]]. He was also the trial judge in [[Snyder v. Phelps]], in which case he was reversed by the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit]], and ultimately by the [[United States Supreme Court]]. In National Federation of the Blind v. Lamone, 2014 WL 4388342 Bennett held that the State of Maryland's refusal to provide an online ballot marking tool to enable blind residents to vote privately and independently violated the Americans With Disabilities Act, 42 U.S.C. §1201. This ruling, called "historic" by the President of the National Federation of the Blind, was affirmed by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit in National Federation of the Blind v. Lamone, 813 F.3d 494 (4th Cir. 2016). ''Henson v. Santander Consumer USA, Inc., 2014 WL 1806915,'' Bennett held that a company may collect debts that it purchased for its own account without therefore being classified as a debt collector within the ambit of the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act.  15 U.S.C. §1692(a)(6).  His opinion was affirmed by the United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit, 817 F.3d 131 (2016), and by the United States Supreme Court in a unanimous ruling, 137 S. Ct. 1718 (2017), affirming Bennett’s initial ruling that the federal statue applies to debt collectors who regularly seek to collect debts and not a debt owner seeking to collect debts for itself. ''Mayor and City of Baltimore v. Azar, 392 F. Supp 3d 602,'' Bennett issued preliminary and permanent injunctions halting the implementation of a U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Rule that would prohibit physicians from referring patients for an abortion, even if that is the patient’s desire ( a so-called “gag rule”). He was affirmed by the United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit in an en banc ruling, 973 F.3d 258 (2020).  Bennett declined to issue a nationwide injunction, limiting his ruling to the State of Maryland. ''Leaders of a Beautiful Struggle v. Baltimore Police Department, 456 F. Supp. 3d 699,'' a case that received nationwide attention addressing Baltimore’s six-month Aerial Investigation Research (“AIR”) program in light of ''United States v. Carpenter, 138 S. [[University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Richard Ernest Myers II''' (born 1967){{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Richard%20Myers%20SJQ%20-%20PUBLIC.pdf|title=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees: Richard Myers}} is an American lawyer and jurist serving as the chief [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of North Carolina]]. He was appointed in 2019 by President [[Donald Trump]], and he has been the chief judge of the district court since 2021. Before his appointment, Myers was a professor at the [[University of North Carolina School of Law]]. == Early life and education == Myers was born in 1967 in [[Kingston, Jamaica]]. He moved with his family to [[Wilmington, North Carolina]], as a child.{{cite web | title=Trump nominates law professor for judicial vacancy | url=https://www.apnews.com/858d3a46c016451cad351b24eb1cc292 | date=August 15, 2019 | publisher=[[Associated Press]] | access-date=August 17, 2019}}{{cite web | last1=Murphy | first1=Brian | title= Trump picks UNC law professor for long-vacant judge post, ending push for Thomas Farr| url=https://www.newsobserver.com/news/politics-government/article234007197.html | date=August 14, 2019 | publisher=[[The News & Observer]] | access-date=August 17, 2019}} His voter registration states that he belongs to "two or more races." Myers graduated from the [[University of North Carolina at Wilmington]] in 1989 with a [[Bachelor of Arts]], ''[[summa cum laude]]'', followed by a [[Master of Arts]] in 1994. He worked as a reporter for the ''[[Star-News]]'' from 1991 to 1995, where he covered the murder of [[James R. Jordan Sr.]], the father of [[Michael Jordan]]. He then attended the [[University of North Carolina School of Law|University of North Carolina School]] of Law, where he was an articles editor for the ''[[North Carolina Law Review]]''.{{Cite web|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-judicial-nominees-united-states-attorney-nominees-united-states-marshal-nominees/|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Donald J. Trump Announces Judicial Nominees, United States Attorney Nominees, and United States Marshal Nominees}} He graduated in 1998 with a [[Juris Doctor]], ''magna cum laude'', and [[Order of the Coif]] membership. == Career == Upon graduation from law school, Myers served as a law clerk to Judge [[David B. Sentelle]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit]]. He then worked in private practice at [[O'Melveny & Myers]]. He previously served as an [[Assistant United States Attorney]] for the [[United States District Court for the Central District of California|Central District of California]] and later the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of North Carolina|Eastern District of North Carolina]]. While a federal prosecutor, Myers prosecuted a wide variety of crimes including counterfeiting, narcotics, and firearms offenses. Myers was the Henry Brandis Distinguished Professor of Law and Director of Trial Advocacy at the [[University of North Carolina School of Law]], where his teaching and scholarship focused on criminal law. He joined UNC as a faculty member in 2004, and left in 2019 upon becoming a judge. At UNC, Myers served as the advisor to the law school's [[Federalist Society]] chapter. === Federal judicial service === On August 14, 2019, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to nominate Myers to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] for the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of North Carolina]]. On September 9, 2019, his nomination was sent to the Senate. He has been nominated to the seat vacated by [[Malcolm Jones Howard]], who assumed senior status on December 31, 2005.{{Cite web|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/seventeen-nominations-two-withdrawals-sent-senate/|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Seventeen Nominations and Two Withdrawals Sent to the Senate}} Myers was nominated to a seat that had been vacant since December 31, 2005, at the time was the longest federal judicial vacancy.{{cite web | last1=Ruger | first1=Todd | title=Trump names new nominee to oldest federal judicial vacancy | url=https://www.rollcall.com/news/congress/oldest-federal-judicial-vacancy-gets-new-nominee | date=August 14, 2019 | archive-date=August 15, 2019 | url-status=dead }} On September 11, 2019, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/09/11/2019/nominations|title=Nominations | United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|website=www.judiciary.senate.gov|date=September 11, 2019 }} On October 31, 2019, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 16–6 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=1&vote=00375 |title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Richard Ernest Myers II to be U.S. District Judge for the Eastern District of North Carolina) |last=|first=|date=December 4, 2019|website=[[United States Senate]]|access-date=December 4, 2019|language=en}} On December 5, Senate]]|access-date=December 6, 2019|language=en}} He received his judicial commission on December 10, 2019. Myers became chief judge in January 2021.{{FJC Bio|nid=7470666}} He maintains chambers in Wilmington.{{Cite web|url=https://www.starnewsonline.com/opinion/20191212/our-view-ex-starnews-reporter-returns-to-wilmington----as-federal-judge|title=OUR VIEW: Ex-StarNews reporter returns to Wilmington – as a federal judge|first=StarNews Editorial|last=Board|website=Wilmington Star News|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191213005028/https://www.starnewsonline.com/opinion/20191212/our-view-ex-starnews-reporter-returns-to-wilmington----as-federal-judge|archive-date=December 13, 2019|url-status=dead|access-date=December 13, 2019}} == Memberships == Myers has been a member of the [[Federalist Society]] since 2004. He has been a member of the [[National Rifle Association of America]] since 2010. He has been a member of the [[Christian Legal Society]] since 2004, of which he serves as a faculty advisor. == Review of judicial rulings == In 2022, Myers concluded that a Civil War amnesty law passed by Congress in 1872 essentially repealed the 14th Amendment's "disqualification clause," which prohibited officeholders from returning to elected positions if they supported an insurrection.{{Cite web |author=Marshall Cohen |title=Judge shuts down January 6-based challenge to Rep. Madison Cawthorn's candidacy |url=https://www.cnn.com/2022/03/04/politics/madison-cawthorn-north-carolina/index.html |access-date=2022-03-05 |website=CNN|date=March 4, 2022 }} Myers agreed that the Amnesty Act of 1872 applied not only retroactively to Confederate officials, but also in perpetuity regarding future rebellions. This interpretation was later rejected by an appeals court, which ruled that this law applied only to people who committed "constitutionally wrongful acts" before 1872.{{Cite news |last=Weiner |first=Rachel |date=May 24, 2022 |title=Insurrectionists can be barred from office, appeals court says |newspaper=The Washington Post |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/dc-md-va/2022/05/24/madison-cawthorn-insurrectionist-challenge/ |access-date=May 25, 2022}}{{Cite news |last=Weiner |first=Rachel |date=May 4, 2022 |title=Cawthorn fights ballot challenge accusing him of being 'insurrectionist' |newspaper=The Washington Post |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/dc-md-va/2022/05/04/cawthorn-insurrectionist-ballot/ |access-date=May 4, 2022}}{{Cite web |last1=Wynn |last2=Richardson |last3=Heytens |date=May 24, 2022 |title=MADISON CAWTHORN v.
