[[Columbia Law School|Columbia University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | footnotes = }} '''Richard Warren Roberts''' (born June 21, 1953){{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TRqYw7uA7BoC&pg=PA153|page=153|title=Hearings before the Committee on the Judiciary, United States Senate, One Hundred Fifth Congress, Second Session, on Confirmations of Appointees to the Federal Judiciary, May 14; June 18; July 16; July 30, 1998|publisher=U.S. Government Printing Office|year=1999}} is an inactive [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Columbia]]. ==Early life and education== Roberts was born in [[New York City]], and is [[African American]]. Both of Roberts's parents were public school teachers. His mother was involved as a chorister at the [[Metropolitan Opera]], and his father was avidly involved with the [[NAACP]] and participated in the [[March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom]] in 1963. His father also participated in the 1968 march in [[Memphis, Tennessee]], following the [[assassination of Martin Luther King Jr.]] Roberts attended the [[The High School of Music and Art|High School of Music and Art]] in [[New York City]] and was a 1970 graduate.{{cite web|url=http://www.jtb.org/index.php?src=directory&view=biographies&srctype=detail&refno=152|title=Richard W. Roberts|work=Just The Beginning Foundation|accessdate=17 March 2016|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20160318000545/http://www.jtb.org/index.php?src=directory&view=biographies&srctype=detail&refno=152|archivedate=18 March 2016|url-status=live}} Roberts studied [[mathematics]] at [[Vassar College]], graduating in 1974 with a [[Bachelor of Arts|Artium Baccalaureus]] degree ''[[Latin honors#United States|cum laude]]''. He continued his education at both the [[SIT Graduate Institute|School for International Training]] in [[Brattleboro, Vermont]], and [[Columbia Law School]] in [[New York City]]. In 1978, he received a [[Master of International Administration]] from the School for International Training, and a [[Juris Doctor]] from Columbia Law School. ==Organization membership and other titles== In 1983, Roberts helped found the Washington, D.C., chapter of Concerned Black Men, Inc.{{cite web|url=http://www.thehistorymakers.com/biography/honorable-richard-w-roberts|title=The Honorable Richard W. Roberts|accessdate=17 March 2016|work=The HistoryMakers}} The vision of this organization is to help provide more black male role models for children in various communities across the United States. Roberts held the positions of secretary and deputy general counsel for the Washington, D.C., chapter. He is a Master of the Edward Bennett Williams Inn of Court; an Archon in [[Sigma Pi Phi]], Epsilon boulé; and a member of The DePriest 15 and of the Judicial Council of the Washington Bar Association. He was earlier a member of the National Black Prosecutors Association and of the National Conference of Black Lawyers, Washington, D.C. Chapter.{{Cite web |title=Hon. Richard Roberts Biographical Sketch |url=https://dcchs.org/sb_pdf/hon-richard-roberts-biographical-sketch/ |website=Historical Society of the District of Columbia Circuit}} According to the Biography by the National Conference on Citizenship, Roberts has held various academic, community, and legal positions. In academic settings, he served for four terms on the board of trustees of Vassar College, has been a visiting faculty member of the Harvard Law School Trial Advocacy Workshop for over 37 years, and was an adjunct professor of trial practice at Georgetown University Law Center. He also served on the faculty of the Department of Justice National Advocacy Center, and has been a writing coach for first year students at Howard Law School. Roberts has also held positions on the board of directors for the Abramson Scholarship Foundation, as well as the Council for Court Excellence and their executive committee. Roberts was a term member of the Council on Foreign Relations and co-chaired a local public school restructuring team.{{cite web|url=http://ncoc.net/RichardRoberts|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303225809/http://ncoc.net/RichardRoberts|url-status=dead|archive-date=3 March 2016|title=Hon. Richard W. Roberts|accessdate=17 March 2016|work=National Conference on Citizenship}} He has served on the board of directors of the Historical Society of the D.C. Circuit; the steering committee of the African-American Alumnae/i of Vassar College; and the board of directors of the Alumnae and Alumni of Vassar College. ==Pre-judicial career== The first position that Roberts held was as a Trial Attorney position for the Civil Rights Division of the United States Department of Justice. He held this position from 1978 to 1982. In this position, Roberts prosecuted{{cite web|url=http://www.courtexcellence.org/news-events/a-conversation-with-chief-judge-richard-w-roberts|title=A Conversation with Chief Judge Richard W. Roberts|work=Council for Court Excellence|accessdate=17 March 2016|archive-date=24 September 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160924233833/http://www.courtexcellence.org/news-events/a-conversation-with-chief-judge-richard-w-roberts|url-status=dead}} the murder of two black Salt Lake City joggers who were killed for racial reasons by [[Joseph Paul Franklin]], a white supremacist. While prosecuting Franklin, the 27-year-old Roberts met Terry Mitchell, a 16-year-old wounded survivor of Franklin's attack on the joggers and one of two key eyewitnesses at his trial. Mitchell alleged 35 years later that Roberts raped her repeatedly, "nearly every day for several weeks", before and after the trial. She says he obtained her silence by telling her that if their sexual relationship ever came to light it would surely result in a mistrial for Franklin and his subsequent release.{{cite news|url=http://www.thedailybeast.com/articles/2016/03/17/witness-against-racist-serial-killer-says-prosecutor-raped-her.html|title=Serial Killer's Survivor: Prosecutor Raped Me During the Trial|work=The Daily Beast|date=17 March 2016|last1=Nestel|first1=M. L.}} After his tenure as a trial attorney for the Department of Justice, Roberts joined the international law private practice, Covington & Burling. He was an attorney at Covington & Burling for four years until 1986.{{cite web|url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/roberts-richard-w.|title=Roberts, Richard W. - Federal Judicial Center|website=www.fjc.gov}} In 1986, Roberts was then appointed as an [[assistant United States attorney]] for the Southern District of New York He served underneath United States Attorney [[Rudy Giuliani]], who later served as Mayor of New York City. He held the position of assistant United States attorney for two years until he was appointed as an assistant United States attorney for the District of Columbia, underneath United States Attorney Jay B. Stephens. In 1993, when President Bill Clinton appointed [[Eric Holder]] as United States attorney for the District of Columbia, Roberts was picked as the principal assistant United States attorney. Roberts held the position of principal assistant U.S. attorney for two years until 1995. One of the most notable cases that Roberts prosecuted was Washington, D.C., Mayor [[Marion Barry]]. https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/1990/08/01/the-prosecutors-who-didnt-rest/d31ec92f-e00f-4972-b507-2dc5bf8128f0/ Mayor Barry was arrested after a sting at the Vista Hotel involving crack cocaine. Attorney General Janet Reno appointed Roberts to the position of Criminal Section Chief of the United States Department of Justice, Civil Rights Division, in 1995. He served in this position for three years until 1998. ==Federal judicial service== President [[Bill Clinton]] nominated Roberts to the [[United States District Court for the District of Columbia]] on January 27, 1998, to a seat vacated by Judge [[Charles R. Richey]]. He was then confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on June 5, 1998, received his commission on June 23, 1998 and sworn in on July 31, 1998. He served as chief judge and a member of the Judicial Conference of the United States from 2013 until March 16, 2016, when he took inactive senior status. On February 20, 2025, the Duke Ellington School of the Arts in Washington, D.C. hosted the virtual unveiling of his judicial portrait that was painted by renowned portrait artist Simmie Knox. https://drive.google.com/file/d/1WbxVgHhrh_wBe5U1WVG5TaXXOORipl8r/view?usp=drivesdk. ===Barring CIA destruction of torture tapes=== Roberts issued a [[court order]] prohibiting the [[CIA]] destroying evidence of its use of interrogations in July 2005. [[CIA Director]] [[Michael V. Hayden]] acknowledged in December 2007 that the CIA had subsequently destroyed hundreds of hours of tapes of the use of "[[extended interrogation techniques]]", including the technique known as "[[waterboarding]]", where subjects's lungs are filled with water, so they experience the first stages of drowning. Many commentators have described the CIA's destruction of this evidence as a violation of Roberts's court order. On January 24, 2008, Roberts demanded an explanation from the CIA for the tapes destruction. On March 25, 2008 [[Charles Carpenter (American lawyer)|Charles Carpenter]], a lawyer for a Guantanamo captive from [[Yemen]] named [[Hani Abdullah]] brought suit against the CIA, before Roberts, arguing that the evidence the CIA destroyed would have helped prove his client's innocence. ===Citizens United=== Roberts signed on to the unanimous three-judge district court opinion against Citizens United that recognized as constitutional the federal legislation that was designed to purge national politics of the pernicious influence of big money campaign contributions by restricting corporate speech advocating the defeat of a candidate. Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission, 530 F. Supp. 2d 274 (D.D.C. 2008). The Supreme Court later retreated from its own precedents that the district court had followed and issued its controversial split decision favoring Citizens United and reversing the district court. 558 U.S. 310 (2010). ===Abu Zubaydah=== Roberts oversaw a lawsuit by [[Abu Zubaydah]] challenging his detention at [[Guantanamo Bay detention camps]] which was filed in July 2008 after the ''[[Boumediene v. Bush]]'' ruling. {{As of|2015}}, the judge had failed to rule on any motions related to the case, even the preliminary ones. This led Zubaydah's lawyers to file motion asking Roberts to recuse himself for "nonfeasance" in January 2015. ==Inactive senior status and sexual assault allegation== On March 16, 2016, Roberts took inactive [[senior status]], citing unspecified health issues.{{Cite web|url=http://www.ksl.com/?sid=38932400&nid=148|title=D.C. judge resigns on same day Utahn accuses him of decades-old rape|website=[[KSL.com]]|date=Mar 17, 2016 |author=Romboy, Dennis}}{{cite web |title= Richard W. Roberts |publisher=[[Federal Judicial Center]]|url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/roberts-richard-w. |access-date=2018-04-21|location=[[Washington, D.C.]]}} Judge [[Karen L. Henderson]] signed Roberts's certificate of disability, allowing him to take early senior status.{{Cite web|url=https://www.npr.org/2016/03/18/470852225/federal-judge-retires-as-bad-lapse-in-judgment-with-16-year-old-surfaces|title = Federal Judge Retires as 'Bad Lapse in Judgment' with 16-Year-Old Surfaces|website = NPR|date = 18 March 2016|last1 = Johnson|first1 = Carrie}} That same day, Terry Mitchell, the eyewitness from the Franklin trial, filed a federal suit against him, accusing him of repeatedly raping her when she was a witness in a high-profile Utah murder case 35 years earlier.{{Cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2016/mar/27/terry-mitchell-richard-roberts-prosecutor-alleged-rape-interview|title=Murder trial witness on alleged 1981 rape by prosecutor: 'He derailed my life'|website=[[TheGuardian.com]]|date=27 March 2016|access-date=2017-12-08}} Roberts said that her accusations “are perplexing and demonstrably false” and “flat wrong.” Mitchell v. Roberts, U.S. District Court, District of Utah, Case No. 2:16-cv-00843, Document 9 at 4. Roberts's lawyers told members of the press that their client, who was 27 and unmarried at the time, did indeed have a brief consensual sexual relationship with Mitchell but that it occurred after the trial ended.{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/public-safety/chief-judge-of-the-districts-federal-court-retires/2016/03/16/2ff09bf0-ebc1-11e5-b0fd-073d5930a7b7_story.html|title=Chief judge of the District's federal court retires as lawsuit accuses him of sexual assault|author=Ann E. Marimow|date=16 March 2016|newspaper=The Washington Post}} Mitchell also filed a judicial misconduct complaint, and the ensuing extensive investigation found that neither the facts nor the law supported her claims, conclusions that Mitchell did not challenge.https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/c.c.d._no._17-02_november_30_2017.pdf [uscourts.gov]. Her lawsuit was dismissed with prejudice in 2021.Mitchell v. Roberts, U.S. District Court, District of Utah, Case No. 2:16-cv-00843, Document 54. That order was affirmed on appeal,{{Cite web| title=Terry Mitchell, v. Richard Warren Roberts | url=https://ca10.uscourts.gov/sites/ca10/files/opinions/010110722059.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220810000432/https://www.ca10.uscourts.gov/sites/ca10/files/opinions/010110722059.pdf | archive-date=2022-08-10}} a decision Mitchell did not challenge. ==Sibley suit== [[Montgomery Blair Sibley]], the last lawyer for the late [[Deborah Jeane Palfrey]], sued Roberts for his refusal to file Sibley's request to have a prior judge's gag order lifted, that forced Sibley to keep Palfrey's customer list private. Palfrey was a prominent arranger of trysts with high class [[call girls]], and Sibley alleged her client list was packed with highly placed Washington insiders. In April 2016, the U.S. Supreme Court denied the request to lift the lower court order, in place since 2007, that bars Sibley from releasing any information about her records.{{Cite web|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/scotus-denies-request-dc-madam-s-attorney-release-info-n551121?cid=sm_twitter_feed_politics|title=SCOTUS Denies Request from D.C. Madam's Attorney to Release Info|website=NBC News|date=5 April 2016 |access-date=2016-04-05}}. ==Awards and honors== For Roberts's prosecutorial efforts against Joseph Paul Franklin, the U.S. Attorney General awarded him with a special commendation. Roberts also graduated cum laude from Vassar College in 1974 with a bachelor's degree.{{cite web|url=http://www.dcd.uscourts.gov/roberts|work=U.S. District Court, District of Columbia|title=Chief Judge Richard W. Roberts|accessdate=17 March 2016|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20160313133856/http://www.dcd.uscourts.gov/roberts|archivedate=13 March 2016}} When Roberts was a civil rights prosecutor in the Justice Department, he was hired into the Attorney General's Honors Program. Roberts was inducted into the Hall of Fame of the Council on Legal Education Opportunity.{{Cite web|url=https://cleoinc.org/jhof/hof/judge-richard-w-roberts/|title = Judge Richard W. Roberts| work=CLEO Judges Hall of Fame }} He was bestowed the Outstanding Service to Vassar Award.{{Cite web|url=https://www.vassar.edu/alums/aavc/awards/outstanding-service|title = Alums - AAVC - Awards - Outstanding Service to Vassar College Award Archive | Vassar College}} == See also == * [[List of African-American federal judges]] * [[List of African-American jurists]] ==References== {{Reflist|refs= {{cite news | url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2007/12/21/AR2007122101392.html | title=Detainee Evidence Probe Weighed: Judge Told Guantanamo Information May Have Been Destroyed | page=A02 | newspaper=[[Washington Post]] | author=[[Carol D. '''Rita Faye Lin''' (born 1978)<ref name="Questionnaire">{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Lin%20SJQ%20Public%20Final1.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=November 29, 2022|archive-date=November 29, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221129185356/https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Lin%20SJQ%20Public%20Final1.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> is an American lawyer and jurist serving as a [[United States federal judge|U.S. district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of California|U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California]]. She was appointed in 2023 by President [[Joe Biden]]. She served as a California state court judge on the [[San Francisco County Superior Court]] from 2018 to 2023.

== Early life and education ==

Lin was born in 1978 in [[Oakland, California]], to a [[Taiwanese American]] family.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Rita Lin |url=https://afj.org/nominee/judge-rita-lin/ |access-date=2024-12-06 |website=Alliance for Justice |language=en-US}}</ref> She earned a [[Bachelor of Arts]], ''[[magna cum laude]]'', from [[Harvard University]] in 2000 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Harvard Law School]] in 2003.<ref name="WHBio">{{Cite press release |title=President Biden Names Twenty-Fourth Round of Judicial Nominees |date=July 29, 2022 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/07/29/president-biden-names-twenty-fourth-round-of-judicial-nominees/ |access-date=July 29, 2022}} {{PD-notice}}</ref>

== Career ==

From 2003 to 2004, Lin served as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Sandra Lynch]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit]]. She joined [[Morrison & Foerster]] in [[San Francisco]] as an associate in 2004 and later became a partner at the firm. From 2014 to 2018, she served as an [[assistant United States attorney]] for the Northern District of California. She was appointed to serve as a judge of the [[San Francisco County Superior Court]] by Governor [[Jerry Brown]] in 2018.<ref>{{Cite web |title=MOFO ALUMNA SPOTLIGHT: JUDGE RITA F. LIN |url=https://together.mofo.com//topics/mofo-alumna-spotlight-judge-rita-f-lin |access-date=July 29, 2022 |website=together.mofo.com |language=en}}</ref><ref name="DiFeliciantonio">{{Cite web |last=DiFeliciantonio |first=Chase |date=July 29, 2022 |title=Biden selects two judicial nominees for Northern District bench, continuing streak of diverse appointments |url=https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Biden-judicial-nominees-Northern-District-diverse-17337341.php |access-date=July 29, 2022 |website=San Francisco Chronicle |language=en-US}}</ref> Lin was an [[adjunct professor]] of law at the [[University of California, Hastings College of the Law]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Rita Lin |url=https://www.uchastings.edu/people/rita-lin/ |access-date=July 29, 2022 |website=UC Hastings Law {{!}} San Francisco |language=en-US |archive-date=July 29, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220729183637/https://www.uchastings.edu/people/rita-lin/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> where in the fall 2021 semester she co-taught a course on [[criminal procedure]].<ref name="Questionnaire" />

Lin worked ''[[pro bono]]'' as co-counsel against the [[Defense of Marriage Act]], which was declared [[unconstitutional]] on February 22, 2012, in U.S. District Court in California.<ref name="Law.com">{{Cite web |title=Rita Lin |url=https://www.law.com/therecorder/almID/1202555674057/ |access-date=August 1, 2022 |website=The Recorder |language=en}}</ref>

=== Federal judicial service ===

On July 29, 2022, President [[Joe Biden]] announced his intent to nominate Lin to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of California]].<ref name="WHBio" /> On August 1, 2022, her nomination was sent to the Senate. President Biden nominated Lin to the seat vacated by Judge [[Edward M. Chen]], who assumed [[senior status]] on May 17, 2022.<ref>{{Cite press release|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate|date=August 1, 2022|publisher=The White House|location=Washington, D.C.|url= https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/08/01/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-78/}}</ref> On November 30, 2022, a hearing on her nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].<ref name="Hearing">{{Cite web|title=Nominations|date=November 30, 2022|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/11/30/2022/nominations}}</ref>

On January 3, 2023, her nomination was returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]]. She was renominated on January 23, 2023.<ref>{{Cite press release |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |date=January 23, 2023 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2023/01/23/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-92/}}</ref> On February 9, 2023, her nomination was reported out of committee by a 12–9 vote.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/2023-02-09%20-%20EBM%20-%20Results.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – February 9, 2023|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=February 9, 2023}}</ref> On September 19, 2023, the Senate invoked [[cloture]] on her nomination by a 52–45 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Rita F. Lin to be United States District Judge for the Northern District of California)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00231.htm|access-date=September 19, 2023|website=United States Senate}}</ref> Later that day, her nomination was confirmed by a 52–45 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00232.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Rita F. Lin, of California, to be United States District Judge for the Northern District of California)|website=United States Senate|date=September 19, 2023|access-date=September 19, 2023}}</ref> She received her judicial commission on October 4, 2023.<ref>{{FJC Bio|nid=13761006|inline=yes}}</ref>
Lin is the second [[Asian Pacific American]] woman—and first [[Chinese American]] woman—to serve on the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California.<ref name="DiFeliciantonio"/>

Six judges discuss why it matters. | newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] | date=August 6, 2024 |access-date=August 10, 2024}}</ref><ref name="Hearing" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Arken |first=James |url=https://www.law360.com/pulse/articles/1553302/gop-sens-question-judge-picks-on-crime-2nd-amendment|title=GOP Sens. [[Georgetown University Law Center|Georgetown University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | footnotes = }} '''Robert Neil Chatigny''' (born October 17, 1951) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Connecticut]]. ==Education== Chatigny received a Bachelor of Arts degree from [[Brown University]] in 1973 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Georgetown University Law Center]] in 1978, where he was Case and Note Editor of the ''[[Georgetown Law Journal]]''.{{Citation needed|date=April 2026}} ==Career== Chatigny served as a [[law clerk]] to three different judges: [[Samuel Conti]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of California]] from 1979 to 1980; [[José A. Cabranes]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Connecticut]] in 1980; and [[Jon O. Newman]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit]] from 1980 to 1981. He was in the private practice of law in [[Washington, D.C.]], from 1981 to 1983 and in [[Hartford, Connecticut]], from 1984 to 1994.{{Citation needed|date=April 2026}} ===Federal judicial service=== Chatigny was nominated to the court by President [[Bill Clinton]] on August 5, 1994, to a seat vacated by Judge [[Warren William Eginton]], confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on September 28, 1994, and received his commission on September 29, 1994. He served as chief judge of the court from 2003 to September 2009. He assumed [[senior status]] on December 31, 2016.{{Citation needed|date=April 2026}} ===Consideration for Second Circuit=== Chatigny was nominated by President [[Barack Obama]] to a seat on the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit]].{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/president-obama-nominates-goodwin-liu-united-states-court-appeals-ninth-circuit-jud|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Obama Nominates Goodwin Liu for the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, Judge Robert N. Chatigny for the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit|date=24 February 2010|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|access-date=1 July 2015}} The nomination received a unanimous rating of "well qualified" from the American Bar Association's [[Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary]], and the U.S. Judiciary Committee approved the nomination on June 10, 2010, on an 11–7 party-line vote.{{Citation needed|date=April 2026}} No date was set for full Senate consideration. ====Support for the nomination==== Supporters included three Republican former appointees as United States Attorney for the District of Connecticut who said in a letter to the Judiciary Committee in April 2010 that they "support, without any reservation," this nomination. They wrote: "While each of us has dealt with Judge Chatigny under different circumstances, we have found him to be even tempered, thorough and without agenda. We believe that he is a fair minded and impartial judge, who has appropriate fitness and temperament for the appellate court.... We believe that a close examination of Judge Chatigny's record in sentencing federal criminal defendants shows that he is appropriately sensitive to the facts of the person before him and the rights of victims of the crimes that have been committed. Indeed, it is our understanding that the government has never filed an appeal from Judge Chatigny's sentencings and that there has only been one defendant who has appealed from an upward departure. We are of the strong opinion that Judge Chatigny's record on the bench makes him an outstanding and very qualified candidate."[http://www.ctpost.com/news/article/Three-state-Republican-lawyers-support-Democratic-456835.php Mayko, Michael. "Three state Republican lawyers support Democratic judge." '''''The Connecticut Post'''.'' 2010-04-22.] Seventeen former federal prosecutors who have worked with Judge Chatigny wrote to the Senate Judiciary Committee that "in criminal as well as civil matters Judge Chatigny has proven himself over the course of 15 years on the bench to be unbiased, compassionate and temperate."{{cite web|url=http://judiciary.senate.gov/hearings/testimony.cfm?id=4548&wit_id=2629|title=Leahy, Patrick. U.S. Senate Committee on the Judiciary. Statement. 2010-04-28.|publisher=|access-date=2010-06-14|archive-date=2010-06-13|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100613053434/http://judiciary.senate.gov/hearings/testimony.cfm?id=4548&wit_id=2629|url-status=dead}} ====Opposition to the nomination==== Opposition has centered upon judicial restraint and attitude toward sexual offenders.{{cite web|url=http://hatch.senate.gov/public/index.cfm?FuseAction=PressReleases.Detail&PressRelease_id=22e0b8c8-1b78-be3e-e07f-b574cb72b183|title=United States Senator Orrin Hatch|work=senate.gov|access-date=1 July 2015}}{{Dead link|date=February 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }} On March 5, 2010, one of the prosecutors in the Michael B. Ross case, Michael E. O'Hara, Supervisory Assistant State's Attorney for the State of Connecticut, wrote a 12-page letter to the U. S. Senate Judiciary Committee to elaborate upon the complaint that was filed and dismissed in 2005/2006, stating that Judge Chatigny's actions "certainly call into questions {{sic}} Judge Chatigny's fitness to serve on the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit."{{Cite letter|first=Michael E.|last=O’Hare|recipient=Senator Patrick J. Leahy, Senator Jeff Sessions|subject=Nomination of Judge Robert N. Chatigny to the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit|date=2010-03-05|url=https://pdfserver.amlaw.com/nlj/O%27Hare%20letter.pdf}} A May 26, 2010 ''Washington Times'' editorial enumerated 1) that Chatigny served as co-counsel for director [[Woody Allen]] when he unsuccessfully complained against a prosecutor who had publicly stated he had probable cause grounds for Allen's reportedly abusing a minor stepchild; 2) that Judge Chatigny was reversed by the U.S. Supreme Court in 2001 "when the judge tried to rule against one aspect of his [[Sex offender registries in the United States|state's sex-offender registry]]"; 3) that the sentences imposed by Judge Chatigny in 12 child-pornography cases were "either at or more lenient than the recommended minimum - with most downward departures involving sentences less than half as long"; and 4) that, in the Ross case, Judge Chatigny "threatened to take away an attorney's law license if the lawyer failed to appeal the death sentence of an eight-time murderer of girls and young women. The judge claimed the killer's 'sexual sadism' was a mental disorder that made the murderer himself a victim."{{cite news| title =Editorial: Sexual sadism, unleaded| newspaper =[[The Washington Times]]| date =2010-05-26| url =http://www.washingtontimes.com/news/2010/may/26/sexual-sadism-unleaded/| access-date =2010-05-26 }} ===Notable rulings=== {{Update|section|date= August 2016}} He gained national attention in 2005 when he delayed the execution of [[Michael Bruce Ross]] in order to determine if he was competent to waive challenges to his death sentence and potentially prevent a violation of the [[Eighth Amendment to the United States Constitution|Eighth Amendment's]] prohibition on [[cruel and unusual punishment]]. Ross was subsequently found competent to waive his rights and was executed. The prosecution filed a complaint against Judge Chatigny that was dismissed by the Second Circuit Judicial Council in a 24-page decision on July 26, 2006. In its 2006 dismissal of charges in the Ross case, the Second Circuit Judicial Council found that Judge Chatigny's actions "were not motivated by any bias in favor of Ross [the prisoner] or against the death penalty, but only by the judge's reasonable perception that the discharge of his own judicial duty...required that he take forceful steps on Ross's behalf.... While the judge used strong language, there was no misconduct....[I]n the judge's reasonable view, the circumstances thrust on him called for unusual action in discharge of judicial duty to ensure the fair resolution of the important proceeding before him."{{cite web|url=http://judiciary.senate.gov/hearings/testimony.cfm?id=4548&wit_id=2629|title=Quoted by Leahy, Patrick. U.S. Senate Committee on the Judiciary. 1972-1977 (CAANG) | rank = [[Staff Sergeant]] }} '''Robert Clive Jones''' (born July 21, 1947) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Nevada]]. He served as the [[United States federal judge|Chief United States District Judge]] from 2011 to 2014. ==Biography== Jones was born in [[Las Vegas]]. He graduated with a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree from [[Brigham Young University]] where he majored in English, accounting and economics in 1971, becoming a [[Certified Public Accountant|CPA]] soon after graduation. Jones attended [[UCLA School of Law]], where he was an editor of the ''[[UCLA Law Review]]'', receiving a [[Juris Doctor]].{{cite news|last=Cannon|first=Mark W.|title=LDS federal judges raising the bar|url=http://www.ldschurchnewsarchive.com/articles/46430/LDS-federal-judges-raising-the-bar.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140517152613/http://www.ldschurchnewsarchive.com/articles/46430/LDS-federal-judges-raising-the-bar.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=May 17, 2014|access-date=November 30, 2012|newspaper=Church News|date=November 6, 2004}} He served in the [[United States Army National Guard]] from 1971 to 1972, and then in the [[United States Air National Guard]] from 1972 to 1977. ==Career== In 1975, Jones was a [[law clerk]] to Judge [[J. Clifford Wallace]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]]. From 1976 to 1982, he was in private practice. ===Bankruptcy judge=== Jones was appointed by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit as a bankruptcy judge from 1983 to 1999, serving as Chief Judge from 1984 to 1993.{{cite web|url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/jones-robert-clive|title=Jones, Robert Clive - Federal Judicial Center|website=www.fjc.gov}} He was also appointed to the [[Bankruptcy Appellate Panel|Bankruptcy Appellate Panel for the Ninth Circuit]] from 1986 to 1999. For six years, he served on the national Judicial Conference Committee on codes of conduct, handling ethics issues for federal judges throughout the nation. ===Federal district judge=== On June 9, 2003, Jones was nominated by President [[George W. Bush]] to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the District of Nevada]] vacated by [[David Warner Hagen]]. Jones was unanimously confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on October 2, 2003, and received commission on November 30, 2003. He assumed [[senior status]] on February 1, 2016. Jones was still hearing cases as of 2022.{{Cite web|url=https://www.njchs.org/wp-content/uploads/Oral-History-Interview-Judge-Jones.pdf|title=Oral History Interview Of Ninth Circuit Judge Robert Clive Jones|website=Ninth Judicial Circuit Historical Society|date=2022-04-08|access-date=2025-12-20}}{{Primary source inline|date=January 2026}} However, Jones appears to be inactive as of December 2025.{{Cite web|url=https://www.nvd.uscourts.gov/court-information/judges/|title=Judges|website=nvd.uscourts.gov|access-date=2025-12-20}}{{Original research inline|date=January 2026}} ====Notable cases==== {{BLP primary sources|section|date=October 2023}} In August 2012, Jones held that Nevada's election law giving voters the ability to select "[[None of These Candidates]]" was unconstitutional. The following month, a three-judge panel of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]] blocked the [[preliminary injunction]] issued by Jones, granting an emergency stay.Debra Cassens Weiss, [http://www.abajournal.com/news/article/in_remarkable_smackdown_9th_circuit_allows_nevadans_to_vote_for_none_of_the/ In 'Remarkable Smackdown,' 9th Circuit Allows Nevadans to Vote for None of the Above], ''ABA Journal'' (September 6, 2012).[https://www.fjc.gov/sites/default/files/materials/52/EE-NV-3-12-cv-310-Townley.pdf "None of These Candidates": Townley v. Nevada (Robert C. Jones, D. Nev. 3:12-cv-310)], ''Case Studies in Emergency Election Litigation'', [[Federal Judicial Center]]. One member of that panel, Judge [[Stephen Reinhardt]], criticized Jones' handling of the case: "His dilatory tactics appear to serve no purpose other than to seek to prevent the state from taking an appeal of his decision before it prints the ballots.... Such arrogance and assumption of power by one individual is not acceptable in our judicial system."{{cite news|title=Nevadans to keep "none of the above" ballot option|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/nevadans-to-keep-none-of-the-above-ballot-option/|access-date=November 30, 2012|newspaper=CBS News|date=September 5, 2012}} The case was ultimately dismissed for lack of [[Standing (law)|standing]]. In November 2012, in the case of ''[[Sevcik v. Sandoval]]'', Jones ruled that Nevada's denial of marriage rights to same-sex couples does not violate the [[Equal Protection Clause]] of the U.S. Constitution.Sevcik v. Sandoval, 911 F. Supp. 2d 996 (D. Nev. 2012).{{cite news|last=Geidner|first=Chris|title=Federal Judge Rules Nevada Can Ban Same-Sex Couples From Marriage|url=https://www.buzzfeed.com/chrisgeidner/federal-judge-rules-the-nevada-can-ban-same-sex-co|access-date=November 30, 2012|newspaper=BuzzFeed Politics|date=November 29, 2012}} Jones stated that,"a meaningful percentage of heterosexual persons would cease to value the civil institution as highly as they previously had and hence enter into it less frequently." He also wrote that adoption is "not an alternative means of creating children, but rather a social backstop for when traditional biological families fail." In October 2014, a unanimous panel of the Ninth Circuit reversed Jones's ruling and directed him to promptly enjoin the state of Nevada from "preventing otherwise qualified same-sex couples from marrying".Latta v. Otter, 771 F.3d 456, [https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4722258604110231177#p476 476–77] (2014). However, instead of issuing the order, Jones issued an order recusing himself the next day.Sevcik v. Sandoval, No. 2:12-cv-578 (October 8, 2014) ([https://cases.justia.com/federal/district-courts/nevada/nvdce/2:2012cv00578/86894/117/0.pdf R. 117]). In August 2013, Jones did not sign a letter to the leaders of the United States Congress urging them to avoid further [[Budget sequestration in 2013|sequestration]] related budget cuts. The letter explained that further cuts would have a "devastating and long-lasting impact" on federal courts.{{cite news| url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/judges-urge-congress-to-avoid-more-sequestration-cuts/2013/08/15/64c4c30c-05f4-11e3-a07f-49ddc7417125_story.html?wprss=rss_politics&wpisrc=nl_wonk_b | newspaper=The Washington Post | first=Mark | last=Sherman | title=Judges urge Congress to avoid more sequestration cuts | date=August 16, 2013}} In September 2015, having cited case law that raised concerns about "exhibit[ing] personal bias," the Ninth Circuit identified Jones as having "well established and inappropriately strong" feelings against out-of-state attorneys and directed reassignment of one of his cases to a different judge in order "to maintain the appearance of justice".Nat'l Council of La Raza v. Cegavske, 800 F.3d 1032, [https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=8446321588638622254#p1045 1045, 1046] (9th Cir. 2015). In January 2016, the Ninth Circuit reversed a decision by him in a case involving a claim for damages by the federal government against ranchers who grazed their cattle on federal property without a permit.United States v. Estate of Hage, [http://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2016/01/15/13-16974.pdf No. 13-16974], 2016 U.S. App. LEXIS 733 (9th Cir. January 15, 2016). The Ninth Circuit stated that Judge Jones's rulings in the case were "plainly" and "clearly" contrary to law;United States v. Estate of Hage, [http://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2016/01/15/13-16974.pdf No. 13-16974], 2016 U.S. App. LEXIS 733 (9th Cir. January 15, 2016)., slip op. at 20 ("Rather than simply resolving the fact-specific inquiries as to when and where the cattle grazed illegally, the district court applied an 'easement by necessity' theory that plainly contravenes the law. The district court also encouraged Defendants to file a counterclaim that was clearly time barred."). that he had "grossly abused the power of contempt";United States v. Estate of Hage, [http://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2016/01/15/13-16974.pdf No. 13-16974], 2016 U.S. App. LEXIS 733 (9th Cir. January 15, 2016)., slip op. at 21 ("[T]he court grossly abused the power of contempt by holding two federal agency officials in contempt of court for taking ordinary, lawful actions that had no effect whatsoever on this case." (citation omitted)). that he had "harbored animus" against federal agencies; that his "bias" was a "matter of public record"; and that he had engaged in "improper treatment of government officials" in a previous case.United States v. Estate of Hage, [http://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2016/01/15/13-16974.pdf No. 13-16974], 2016 U.S. App. LEXIS 733 (9th Cir. January 15, 2016)., slip op. at 23. The Ninth Circuit stated that it had "expressed concern about Judge Jones' conduct in several other recent cases".United States v. Estate of Hage, [http://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2016/01/15/13-16974.pdf No. 13-16974], 2016 U.S. App. LEXIS 733 (9th Cir. January 15, 2016)., slip op. at 24. In remanding the case to the district court for further proceedings, the panel ordered the assignment of the case to a different judge due to the appearance of bias created by Judge Jones' conduct during the case.United States v. Estate of Hage, [http://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2016/01/15/13-16974.pdf No. 13-16974], 2016 U.S. App. LEXIS 733 (9th Cir. January 15, 2016)., slip op. at 25. In March 2016, the Ninth Circuit removed Jones from hearing a case between [[Burning Man]] and [[Pershing County, Nevada]]. In its ruling, the Ninth Circuit stated the judge had no legal basis to reject a settlement the parties had entered into and expressed concern about how Jones conducted the proceedings.{{cite news|url=http://www.sacbee.com/news/nation-world/national/article63827782.html|first=Scott|last=Sonner|title=9th Circuit Rules on Burning Man, Slaps Judge in Reno Again|date=March 3, 2016|newspaper=[[Sacramento Bee]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304104841/http://www.sacbee.com/news/nation-world/national/article63827782.html |archive-date=March 4, 2016 |url-status=dead}}Block Rock City, LLC v. Pershing Cnty. Bd. of Comm'rs, No. 14-15221 (9th Cir. Mar. 2, 2016) (unpublished), ''available via'' [http://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/memoranda/2016/03/02/14-15221.pdf USCourts.gov] ''or'' [https://web.archive.org/web/20160304224453/http://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/memoranda/2016/03/02/14-15221.pdf Archive.org]. ==Personal life== Jones is married to Michele Bunker and is a member of [[the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints]] and has served in several positions in the church including bishop. He then worked as a partner at another Scranton law firm from 1979 until 1993.{{Cite web | title=President Obama Names Seven to United States District Court {{!}} whitehouse.gov | url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2010/12/01/president-obama-names-seven-united-states-district-court | access-date=2025-06-29 | website=obamawhitehouse.archives.gov}} From 1993 until his confirmation, Mariani was a lawyer in sole private practice in Scranton, specializing in labor and employment law. === Labor representation === Mariani spent the majority of his career representing unions and employees in labor and employment matters.{{Cite web| title=Hon. Robert D. Mariani - U.S. District Judge, Middle District of Pennsylvania | url=https://www.fedbar.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/Mariani-June13-pdf-3.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230809052204/https://www.fedbar.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/Mariani-June13-pdf-3.pdf | archive-date=2023-08-09}} In his practice, he represented the Teamsters, food workers, stagehands, iron workers, and steel workers.{{Cite web| title=Hon. Robert D. Mariani - U.S. District Judge, Middle District of Pennsylvania | url=https://www.fedbar.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/Mariani-June13-pdf-3.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230809052204/https://www.fedbar.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/Mariani-June13-pdf-3.pdf | archive-date=2023-08-09}} Mariani was inspired by his personal experiences with organized labor through his father's work as a carpenter and grandfather's work as a coal miner.{{Cite web| title=Hon. Robert D. Mariani - U.S. District Judge, Middle District of Pennsylvania | url=https://www.fedbar.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/Mariani-June13-pdf-3.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230809052204/https://www.fedbar.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/Mariani-June13-pdf-3.pdf | archive-date=2023-08-09}} === Federal judicial service === On December 1, 2010, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Mariani to a vacant judicial seat on the United States District Court for the Middle District of Pennsylvania that previously had been held by Judge [[James Martin Munley]], who assumed [[senior status]] in January 2009.{{Cite press release|publisher=White House Office of the Press Secretary|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2010/12/01/presidential-nominations-sent-senate|title=Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate|date=December 1, 2010}} Mariani never received a Judiciary Committee hearing before the end of 2010, and his nomination lapsed at the end of the year. Obama renominated Mariani on January 5, 2011. The American Bar Association rated Mariani Unanimously Qualified for the nomination.{{Cite web | title=Robert David Mariani - Ballotpedia | url=https://ballotpedia.org/Robert_David_Mariani | access-date=2025-06-29 | website=ballotpedia.org}} On July 21, 2011, the Senate Judiciary Committee reported his nomination out of committee. On October 19, 2011, the [[United States Senate]] confirmed his nomination by an 82–17 vote.{{Cite web|publisher=United States Senate|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1121/vote_112_1_00169.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Robert David Mariani, of Pennsylvania, to be United States District Judge)|date=October 19, 2011}} He received his commission that same day. [[University of Colorado Law School]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | footnotes = }} '''Robert Edward Blackburn''' (born April 12, 1950) is a [[United States federal judge|senior United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Colorado]]. == Early life and education == Blackburn was born in [[Lakewood, Colorado]]. He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[Western State College of Colorado]] in 1972. He received a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Colorado Law School]] in 1974. == Career == Blackburn was in private practice in [[Las Animas, Colorado]], from 1975 to 1980. He was a deputy district attorney of Sixteenth Judicial District Attorney's Office, Colorado from 1980 to 1986. He was a [[county attorney]] of [[Bent County, Colorado|Bent County]], Colorado, from 1980 to 1988. He was a Municipal judge, Town of [[Kim, Colorado|Kim]], Colorado, from 1985 to 1988. He was a judge on the Sixteenth Judicial District of Colorado from 1988 to 2002. === Federal judicial service === Blackburn was nominated to be a United States district judge of the [[United States District Court for the District of Colorado]] by President [[George W. Bush]] on September 10, 2001, to a seat vacated by [[Zita Leeson Weinshienk]]. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on February 26, 2002, and received his commission on March 6, 2002. He assumed [[senior status]] on April 12, 2016. == Jurisprudence in practice == ===Individual rights=== {{See also|United States v. Fricosu}} Blackburn has argued that the [[Fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution|Fifth Amendment]] protection from individuals being compelled to testifying against themselves does not apply to testimony which is required to decrypt a protected data source in order to provide prosecutors with evidence. He suggests that the convenience of prosecutors in acquiring evidence in this manner overrules the otherwise inalienable right to avoid being "compelled in any criminal case to be a witness against himself". {{Citation | title = Judge: Americans can be forced to decrypt their laptops | publisher=cnet.com | date = January 23, 2012 | url = http://news.cnet.com/8301-31921_3-57364330-281/judge-americans-can-be-forced-to-decrypt-their-laptops/ | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20120124012557/http://news.cnet.com/8301-31921_3-57364330-281/judge-americans-can-be-forced-to-decrypt-their-laptops | url-status = dead | archive-date = January 24, 2012 | accessdate =January 24, 2010 }} Critics have argued that since the password to an encrypted data source is a part of the defendant's mind, compelled testimony to reveal it is a direct violation of the Fifth Amendment.{{Citation | title = BRIEF OF AMICUS CURIAE ELECTRONIC FRONTIER FOUNDATION IN SUPPORT OF DEFENDANT FRICOSU'S OPPOSITION TO GOVERNMENT'S APPLICATION UNDER THE ALL WRITS ACT REQUIRING DEFENDANT TO ASSIST IN THE EXECUTION OF PREVIOUSLY ISSUED SEARCH WARRANTS | publisher=eff.org | date = July 8, 2011 | url = https://www.eff.org/files/filenode/us_v_fricosu/fricosuamicus7811.pdf | accessdate =January 24, 2010 }} == References == {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1391446}} *[http://www.cod.uscourts.gov/JudicialOfficers/ActiveArticleIIIJudges/HonRobertEBlackburn.aspx Robert E. In the summers of 1967 and 1968, he served as the director of the Spirit Lake Girl Scout Camp in [[Toutle, Washington]]. ===Military service and legal career=== Whaley was in the [[United States Marine Corps]] in 1968, and in private practice of law in [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]] from 1968 to 1969. '''Robert Jensen Bryan''' (born October 29, 1934) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Washington]].

==Education and career==

Bryan was born in [[Bremerton, Washington]]. He was in the [[United States Army]] Reserve from 1955 to 1957, and received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from the [[University of Washington]] in 1956, where he was a member of the [[Delta Upsilon]] fraternity. He earned a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Washington School of Law]] in 1958. He was in private practice in Bremerton from 1959 to 1967. He was then a judge on the Superior Court of Washington from 1967 to 1984, including service as a judge pro tem, [[Washington State Court of Appeals]] in 1975 and as a judge pro tem on the [[Washington State Supreme Court]] from 1979 to 1982. He was in private practice in [[Seattle, Washington]] from 1984 to 1986.<ref name="fjc.gov">{{FJC Bio|nid=1378466|inline=yes}}</ref>

===Federal judicial service===

On February 3, 1986, Bryan was nominated by President [[Ronald Reagan]] to a new seat on the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Washington]] created by 98 Stat. 333. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on April 24, 1986, and received his commission on May 7, 1986. He assumed [[senior status]] on November 1, 2000.<ref name="fjc.gov"/>

On August 30, 2021, Bryan dismissed a lawsuit challenging Washington's ban on conversion therapy for minors.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/washington/wawdce/3:2021cv05359/299341/47/|title=Tingley v. Ferguson et al, No. 3:2021cv05359 - Document 47 (W.D. Wash. 2021)|website=Justia|date=August 30, 2021|access-date=January 21, 2024}}</ref> The 9th circuit affirmed Bryan in September 2022, and the Supreme Court denied certiorari on December 11, 2023.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2022/09/06/21-35815.pdf|title=BRIANTINGLEY, Plaintiff-Appellant, v. ROBERT W. FERGUSON|website=ca9.uscourts.gov|date=September 6, 2022|access-date=January 21, 2024}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.vox.com/scotus/2023/12/11/23889129/supreme-court-conversion-therapy-washington-lgbtq-tingley-ferguson|title=The Supreme Court hands down a small but unexpected victory for LGBTQ people|website=Vox|date=December 11, 2023|access-date=January 21, 2024}}</ref>

[[University of Oxford]] ([[Master of Studies|MSt]]) }} '''Robert Lee Pitman''' (born 1962) is an American attorney who serves as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Texas]]. He is a former [[United States attorney]] for the Western District of Texas. He was previously a [[United States magistrate judge]] of the same court. ==Early life and education== Pitman was born in [[Fort Worth, Texas]], in 1962, the youngest of five children.{{cite news | first=Samuel | last=Knight | url=http://www.mainjustice.com/2011/09/13/meet-robert-pitman/ | title=Meet Robert Pitman | work=Main Justice | date=September 13, 2011 | access-date=September 29, 2011 | url-status=dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110927072529/http://www.mainjustice.com/2011/09/13/meet-robert-pitman/ | archive-date=September 27, 2011 }}{{cite web|url=http://www.dallasvoice.com/law-west-pecos-10105703.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304041904/https://dallasvoice.com/law-west-pecos-10105703.html|archive-date=March 4, 2016|title=The law west of the Pecos|date=March 29, 2012|first=Anna|last=Waugh|work=[[Dallas Voice]]}} He received a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree from [[Abilene Christian University]], where he was student body president.{{cite news | first=Steven | last=Kreytak | url=http://www.statesman.com/news/content/news/stories/local/archive/120103_pitman.html | title=Behind the bench, a man to be counted on: New judge won praise for fairness, kindness in 13 years as U.S. prosecutor | work=[[Austin American-Statesman]] | date=December 1, 2003 | access-date=September 29, 2011 | url-status=dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110303172937/http://www.statesman.com/news/content/news/stories/local/archive/120103_pitman.html | archive-date=March 3, 2011 }} Pitman then obtained a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Texas School of Law]]. After completing law school, Pitman served as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[David Owen Belew Jr.]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Texas]] in Fort Worth. Pitman holds a [[Master of Studies]] degree in legal research from the [[University of Oxford]].{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/06/26/president-obama-nominates-four-serve-united-states-district-courts|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Obama Nominates Four to Serve on the United States District Courts|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=June 26, 2014}}{{FJC Bio|nid=1394761|inline=yes}} ==Career== [[File:Robert L Pitman US Attorney.jpg|thumb|right|Pitman as U.S. Attorney]] Following his judicial clerkship, Pitman began his career at the international law firm of [[Fulbright & Jaworski]] in [[Houston]]. In 2001, Pitman briefly served as interim [[United States attorney]] for the Western District of Texas. As United States attorney on September 11, 2001, he formed the first [[anti-terrorism]] task force in the district, uniting local, state, and federal law enforcement agencies in their counter-terrorism efforts and in their work to better secure Texas' international border. He was replaced by [[George W. Bush]] appointee [[Johnny Sutton]], who asked Pitman to remain in the office as his chief deputy. In October 2003, Pitman was selected to serve as a [[United States magistrate judge]] for the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Texas]]. As magistrate judge, Pitman consistently ranked highest among all local, state, and federal judges in the judicial poll conducted annually by the Austin Bar Association.{{cite news|last=Kreytak|first=Steven|title=Pitman most "excellent" among Austin judges, poll says|url=http://www.statesman.com/blogs/content/shared-gen/blogs/austin/courts/entries/2009/02/20/pitman_mos|newspaper=Austin American-Statesman|date=February 20, 2009}}{{dead link|date=April 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} In 2009, [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] Senators [[John Cornyn]] and [[Kay Bailey Hutchison]] sent Pitman's name to [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] President [[Barack Obama]] as one of two candidates for United States attorney for the Western District of Texas.{{cite news | first=Andrew | last=Ramonas | url=http://www.mainjustice.com/2009/11/02/texas-republican-senators-advanced-gay-u-s-attorney-candidate/ | title=Texas GOP Senators Advanced Gay U.S. Attorney Candidate | work=Main Justice | date=November 2, 2009 | access-date=September 29, 2011 | url-status=dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110905073433/http://www.mainjustice.com/2009/11/02/texas-republican-senators-advanced-gay-u-s-attorney-candidate/ | archive-date=September 5, 2011 }}{{cite news | first=Todd J. | last=Gilman | url=http://www.dallasnews.com/sharedcontent/dws/news/washington/columnists/tgillman/stories/DN-texwatch_01nat.ART.State.Edition1.4f62253.html | title=Hutchison irks right by including gay judge as U.S. attorney pick | work=[[The Dallas Morning News]] | date=November 1, 2009 | access-date=October 10, 2010}} The recommendation of Pitman, who is [[openly gay]], was publicly opposed by a [[social conservative]] group in Texas. On June 27, 2011, almost two years after Pitman was recommended for the post, Obama notified members of Congress that he would nominate Pitman to be United States attorney for the Western District of Texas.{{cite news | first=Gary | last=Martin | url=http://www.mysanantonio.com/news/local_news/article/Austin-magistrate-judge-to-get-U-S-attorney-nod-1442668.php | title=Austin magistrate judge to get U.S. attorney nod | work=[[San Antonio Express-News]] | date=June 27, 2011 | access-date=September 29, 2011}} He was formally nominated the following day.{{cite web | author=The White House: Office of the Press Secretary | url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2011/06/28/president-obama-nominates-four-serve-united-states-attorneys | title=President Obama Nominates Four to Serve as United States Attorneys | date=June 28, 2011 | via=[[NARA|National Archives]] | work=[[whitehouse.gov]] | access-date=September 29, 2011}} Citing his credentials and experience, and expressing a desire to fill the position with the most qualified candidate, he was supported by Texas' two United States Senators, both Republicans. With their support, the United States Senate confirmed Pitman to be the chief federal law enforcement officer in the Western District of Texas on September 26, 2011. He took office on October 3, 2011. He left office on December 19, 2014, upon receiving his judicial commission. He is currently an adjunct professor at the [[University of Texas School of Law]]. === Federal judicial service === On June 26, 2014, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Pitman to serve as a United States district judge of the United States District Court for the Western District of Texas, to the seat vacated by Judge [[William Royal Furgeson Jr.]], who assumed [[senior status]] on November 30, 2008.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/06/26/presidential-nominations-sent-senate|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=June 26, 2014}} He received a hearing before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]] for September 9, 2014.{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/judicial-nominations-2014-09-09|title=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|website=www.judiciary.senate.gov}} On November 20, 2014, his nomination was reported out of committee by [[voice vote]].{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%2011-20-14.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – November 20, 2014 United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary}} On Saturday, December 13, 2014, [[Senate Majority Leader]] [[Harry Reid]] filed a motion to invoke [[cloture]] on the nomination. On December 16, 2014, Reid withdrew his cloture motion on Pitman's nomination, and the Senate proceeded to vote to confirm Pitman by a [[voice vote]]. He received his judicial commission on December 19, 2014. === Notable rulings === * On October 6, 2021, Pitman ordered Texas to suspend the [[Texas Heartbeat Act]], a law which banned most [[Abortion in Texas|abortions]], calling it an "offensive deprivation of such an important right."Weber, Paul J. "[https://apnews.com/article/abortion-us-supreme-court-business-texas-courts-5eb085acee67615da3623212953220c9 Judge orders Texas to suspend new law banning most abortions]", [[Associated Press]]. October 6, 2021. Retrieved October 7, 2021.{{Cite web|last=Swanson|first=Ian|date=October 7, 2021|title=Texas to appeal ruling blocking abortion law|url=https://thehill.com/regulation/court-battles/575717-texas-to-appeal-ruling-blocking-abortion-law|access-date=October 8, 2021|website=The Hill|language=en}} Two days later the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]] reversed Pitman's suspension order, permitting the law to be enforced again.{{cite news|url=https://thehill.com/regulation/court-battles/576048-judge-issues-stay-of-preliminary-injunction-on-texass-6-week|title=Appeals court temporarily reinstates Texas abortion law|last=Vakil|first=Caroline|date=October 8, 2021|work=The Hill|access-date=October 10, 2021}} * On December 1, 2021, Pitman struck down a Texas law which attempted to censor social media platforms, in the case, NetChoice, LLC. v. Paxton.{{cite web|author=[[Eric Goldman]]|access-date=December 2, 2021|title=Court Enjoins Texas' Attempt to Censor Social Media, and the Opinion Is a Major Development in Internet Law-NetChoice v. Paxton|url=https://blog.ericgoldman.org/archives/2021/12/court-enjoins-texas-attempt-to-censor-social-media-and-the-opinion-is-a-major-development-in-internet-law-netchoice-v-paxton.htm|date=December 2, 2021|website=Technology & Marketing Law Blog}} * On March 30, 2023, Pitman ordered the return of books containing [[LGBT|LGBTQ]] content to shelves after they were removed from public libraries, saying "...the First Amendment prohibits the removal of books from libraries based on either viewpoint or content discrimination"{{Cite web |last=Schrader |first=Adam |date=April 1, 2023 |title=Federal judge orders books with LGBTQ content to return to library shelves in Texas - UPI.com |url=https://www.upi.com/Top_News/US/2023/04/01/federal-judge-orders-books-lgbtq-content-return-library-shelves-texas/7861680388879/ |access-date=June 20, 2023 |website=UPI |language=en}} Pittman's decision was subsequently reversed by the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals en banc which held that there is no First Amendment right to receive information and library catalog decisions are government speech not subject to free speech challenges.{{Cite web |title=Fifth Circuit Holds That Government Speech Doctrine Applies to Public Library Book Removals, Creating Circuit Split With Eighth Circuit {{!}} Cahill Gordon & Reindel LLP |url=https://www.cahill.com/publications/client-alerts/2025-09-22-fifth-circuit-holds-that-government-speech-doctrine-applies-to-public-library-book-removals-creating-circuit-split-with-eighth-circuit |access-date=2026-09-23 |website=www.cahill.com |language=en}} * On August 30, 2024, he enjoined a section of the [[SCOPE Act]] because they were preempted by [[Section 230]] and violated the [[First Amendment to the United States Constitution|First Amendment]] in the case [[Computer and Communications Industry Association]] et al v. [[Ken Paxton|Paxton]]. The section of the [[SCOPE Act]] that was blocked required the monitoring and filtering of content that promoted suicide, self-harm, eating disorders, substance abuse, stalking, bullying, or harassment, grooming, trafficking, child pornography, or other sexual exploitation or abuse. He stated it was from clear that [[Texas]] had a compelling interest in some of the categories of content [[Texas]] was looking to filter with the law. He also stated that the laws use of the word's promotion, grooming, harassment or substance abuse were vague and that [[LGBTQ|Pro-LGBTQ]] content could be seen as promotion of grooming, he however would let the rest of the law take effect as their wasn't enough evidence that the rest of the law violated the [[Constitution of the United States|Constitution]] or was preempted by federal law.[https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.txwd.1172798016/gov.uscourts.txwd.1172798016.25.0_1.pdf gov.uscourts.txwd.1172798016.25.0_1.pdf][https://abc13.com/post/texas-scope-act-blocked-robert-pitman-social-media-filters-blocked/15261423/ Federal judge blocks portion of Texas SCOPE Act that cracks down on minors and social media - ABC13 Houston] ==Personal life== Pitman is a sixth-generation Texan and lives in Austin. McKinney School of Law|Indiana University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | footnotes = }} '''Robert Lowell Miller Jr.''' (born November 21, 1950){{cite book|url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=pst.000011806349&seq=1161|title=Confirmation Hearings on Federal Appointments: Hearings before the Committee on the Judiciary, United States Senate, Ninety-Ninth Congress|volume=2|year=1986|page=1143}} is an inactive [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Indiana]]. ==Education and career== Miller was born in [[South Bend, Indiana]]. He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[Northwestern University]] in 1972. He received a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Indiana University Robert H. McKinney School of Law]] in 1975. He was a [[law clerk]] for the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Indiana]] in 1975. He was a judge of the [[St. Joseph County, Indiana|St. Joseph County]] Superior Court in South Bend from 1975 to 1985.{{FJC Bio|nid=1385161|inline=yes}} ===Federal judicial service=== Miller was nominated by President [[Ronald Reagan]] on October 23, 1985, to the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Indiana]], to a new seat created by 98 Stat. 333. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on December 16, 1985, and received his commission on December 17, 1985. He served as Chief Judge from February 3, 2003, to February 2, 2010.{{Cite web |date=January 28, 2022 |title=General Order 2022-02 |url=https://www.innd.uscourts.gov/sites/innd/files/2022-02.pdf |access-date=August 5, 2024 |website=United States District Court for the Northern District of Indiana}} He assumed [[senior status]] on January 11, 2016. On July 8, 2020, Miller was appointed to the [[United States Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court of Review]] by Chief Justice [[John Roberts]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.fisc.uscourts.gov/fiscr_membership|title=Current Membership - Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court of Review|website=United States Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court}} On August 3, 2023, it was announced that would assume inactive senior status in August 2023.{{Cite press release|date=August 3, 2023|title=Retirement of The Honorable Robert L. {{nowrap|[[Boston College]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]])}} }} '''Robert Nichols Scola Jr.'''{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/RobertScola-PublicQuestionnaire.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|work=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|date=June 22, 2011}} (born October 30, 1955){{Cite web |url=http://www.lawdiary.com/docs/subscribers/FL_Judicial_Biographies.pdf |title=BIOGRAPHIES OF FEDERAL COURT JUDGES SITTING IN FLORIDA |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170730052812/http://www.lawdiary.com/docs/subscribers/FL_Judicial_Biographies.pdf |archive-date=July 30, 2017 |access-date=May 9, 2018}} is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida]]. == Early life and education == Scola earned a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in 1977 from [[Brown University]] and a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1980 from [[Boston College School of Law]].{{Cite web | author=The White House: Office of the Press Secretary | url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2011/05/04/president-obama-nominates-six-judges-united-states-district-courts | title=President Obama Nominates Six Judges to United States District Courts | date=May 4, 2011 | via=[[NARA|National Archives]] | work=[[whitehouse.gov]] | access-date=May 7, 2011}}{{FJC Bio|nid=1393831|inline=yes}} == Career == From 1980 until 1986, Scola worked in the Miami-Dade Office of the State Attorney. From 1986 until 1995, he worked in private legal practice, both as a sole legal practitioner and also as a criminal defense attorney. In 1995, Scola became a judge on Florida's Eleventh Judicial Circuit presiding over criminal, civil and family law matters. === Federal judicial service === On May 4, 2011, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Scola to serve as a judge on the United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida. Scola would fill the seat vacated by Judge [[Paul Huck]], who took [[senior status]] in August 2010.{{Cite web | author=The White House: Office of the Press Secretary | url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2011/05/04/nomination-s-sent-senate | title=Nominations Sent to the Senate | date=May 4, 2011 | via=[[NARA|National Archives]] | work=[[whitehouse.gov]] | access-date=May 7, 2011}} The United States Senate confirmed Scola in a [[voice vote]] on October 19, 2011; he received his commission the following day. He assumed [[senior status]] on October 31, 2023. Scola retired on October 3, 2025.{{Cite web|url=https://www.flsd.uscourts.gov/sites/flsd/files/25-10-03%20ADDENDUM%20to%20Administrative%20Procedures%20-%20Removing%20Judge%20Scola%20due%20to%20retirement.pdf|title=ADDENDUM to Case Management Electronic Case Files (CM/ECF) Administrative Procedures October 3, 2025|website=flsd.uscourts.gov|date=2025-10-03|access-date=2026-05-11}} ===Notable cases=== On April 29, 2019, Scola, a cancer survivor, recused himself from a case against [[healthcare insurance]] company [[UnitedHealth Group#UnitedHealthcare]], stating, that the company's denial of treatment was "immoral and barbaric" and that his opinions regarding would prevent him from "deciding this case fairly and impartially."{{Cite news|title='Immoral and barbaric': Cancer-surviving judge blasts insurer for denying treatment|language=en-US|newspaper=Washington Post|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/nation/2019/05/01/immoral-barbaric-cancer-surviving-judge-blasts-insurer-denying-therapy-before-recusing-himself/|date=May 1, 2019|author =Megan Flynn|access-date=2023-01-12|issn=0190-8286}} == References == {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1393831}} *{{Ballotpedia|Robert_N._Scola,_Jr.}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Paul Huck]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida]]}}|years=2011–2023}} {{s-aft|after=[[Ed Artau]]}} {{s-end}} {{United States 11th Circuit senior district judges}} {{authority control}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Scola, Robert N. '''Robert Porter Chamberlin''' (known professionally as '''Bobby Chamberlin''') (born April 6, 1965) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Mississippi]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Vance |first1=Taylor |date=3 September 2025 |title=Trump federal judge nominees for Mississippi testify to Senate committee - Mississippi Today |url=https://mississippitoday.org/2025/09/03/trump-mississippi-federal-judge-nominees-chamberlin-maxwell-senate/ |access-date=30 September 2025 |publisher=Mississippi Today}}</ref> He previously served as an associate justice of the [[Supreme Court of Mississippi]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.themississippimonitor.com/justice-robert-p-bobby-chamberlin-awarded-northwest-alumni-professional-achievement-award/|title=Justice Robert P. "Bobby" Chamberlin Awarded Northwest Alumni Professional Achievement Award|first=Mississippi|last=Monitor|date=January 22, 2025|access-date=August 13, 2025|archive-date=December 19, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251219065945/https://www.themississippimonitor.com/justice-robert-p-bobby-chamberlin-awarded-northwest-alumni-professional-achievement-award/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.martindale.com/attorney/robert-p-chamberlin-1018882/|title=Robert P Chamberlin Judge Profile on Martindale.com|website=www.martindale.com}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==

Chamberlin was born on April 6, 1965.<ref name="OfficialBio" /><ref name="Questionnaire">{{cite web |last=Chamberlin |first=Robert Porter |date=September 3, 2025 |title=Chamberlin's Senate Judiciary Committee Questionnaire |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/chamberlin_sjq.pdf |website=www.judiciary.senate.gov |location= |publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary |access-date=September 3, 2025 |archive-date=October 10, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251010180444/https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/chamberlin_sjq.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> Chamberlin received his [[Bachelor of Arts]] from the [[University of Mississippi]] in 1987 and his [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Mississippi School of Law]] in 1990. He was admitted to the bar in 1990.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.martindale.com/jackson/mississippi/robert-p-chamberlin-1018882-a/ |title=Robert P. Chamberlin |website=martindale.com |access-date=January 16, 2018 |archive-date=January 17, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180117012018/https://www.martindale.com/jackson/mississippi/robert-p-chamberlin-1018882-a/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Questionnaire"/>

== Career ==

'''Political and legal career in Mississippi'''

Chamberlin began his career as a municipal judge for [[Hernando, Mississippi]], from 1991 for 1999, including a stint as municipal prosecutor for [[Horn Lake, Mississippi]], in 1992.<ref name="CABA" /><ref name="Questionnaire" />

In 1999, he entered state politics and was elected to the [[Mississippi State Senate]], serving Senate District 1 of [[DeSoto County, Mississippi|DeSoto County]] for five years.<ref name="OfficialBio" /><ref name="Questionnaire" />

On November 24, 2004, he was appointed to the 17th Circuit District by Governor [[Haley Barbour|Haley Babour]]<ref name="OfficialBio">{{Cite web |url=https://courts.ms.gov/newsite2/appellatecourts/sc/bios/justicechamberlin.php |title=Associate Justice Robert P. Chamberlin District 3, Place 1 |website=courts.ms.gov |access-date=January 16, 2018 |archive-date=January 17, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180117131158/https://courts.ms.gov/newsite2/appellatecourts/sc/bios/justicechamberlin.php |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Questionnaire" />

On November 29, 2016, Chamberlin was elected to [[Supreme Court of Mississippi]], winning a runoff election, when he received around 55% of the vote for District 3, Place. On January 3, 2017, he took the oath of office at the Court and took the seat last held by Justice [[Ann Hannaford Lamar]].<ref name="CABA">{{Cite web |url=http://caba.ms/articles/features/meet-robert-p-chamberlin.html |title=Meet Newly Elected Mississippi Supreme Court Justice Robert P. Chamberlin |last=Smith |first=Blake |date=March 2017 |publisher=Capital Area Bar Association |access-date=January 16, 2018 |archive-date=January 17, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180117070322/http://caba.ms/articles/features/meet-robert-p-chamberlin.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Questionnaire" />

=== Federal judicial service ===

On August 12, 2025, President Donald Trump announced his intention to nominate Chamberlin to the United States District Court for the Northern District of Mississippi. On September 3, 2025, Chamberlin testified before the U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee. On November 20, 2025, the Senate Judiciary Committee voted to send his nomination to the full U.S. Senate by a [[Party line (politics)|party line]] 12–10 vote. On December 8, 2025, the U.S. Senate invoked [[cloture]] on his nomination by a 52–44 vote. The following day, his nomination was confirmed by a 51–46 vote. Chamberlin received his judicial commission on December 16, 2025.<ref>{{FJC Bio|nid=13762093|inline=yes}}</ref>

==Personal life==

Chamberlin is married to his wife, Kim, with whom he has one son.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://votesmart.org/candidate/biography/20686/robert-chamberlin#.Wl4p4qinHIU |title=Robert Chamberlin's Biography PrintTrack This Politician |publisher=[[Project Vote Smart]] |access-date=January 16, 2018 |archive-date=January 17, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180117131327/https://votesmart.org/candidate/biography/20686/robert-chamberlin#.Wl4p4qinHIU |url-status=live }}</ref> He lives in Hernando.<ref name="Questionnaire"/>
