She received a [[Bachelor of Science in Nursing]] degree from the [[University of Oklahoma]] in 1986. After graduating from nursing school, she worked as a [[registered nurse]] at Lindsay Municipal Hospital, [[North Kansas City Hospital]], and as a temporary nurse for a nurse staffing organization in [[Kansas City]]. In 1990, She received a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Kansas School of Law]].{{FJC Bio|nid=1394796|inline=yes}}{{cite web|url=http://www.courts.mo.gov/file.jsp?id=38836|title=Missouri Judgeship Application|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304223513/http://www.courts.mo.gov/file.jsp?id=38836|archive-date=March 4, 2016|url-status=dead}} ==Career== She began her career as an assistant prosecutor in [[Jackson County, Missouri|Jackson County]], from 1990 to 1995. From 1995 to 2001, she was first assistant prosecutor in [[Platte County, Missouri|Platte County]]. From 2001 to 2015, she served as an assistant United States attorney in the Western District of Missouri. She served as first assistant United States attorney from 2001 to 2006 and again from 2009 to 2010. She served as executive assistant United States attorney from 2006 to 2007 and again in 2010. She served in the [[Fraud]] and [[Corruption]] Unit.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/11/20/president-obama-nominates-three-serve-united-states-district-courts|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Obama Nominates Three to Serve on the United States District Courts|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=November 20, 2014}} ===Federal judicial service=== On November 20, 2014, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Ketchmark to serve as a United States district judge of the United States District Court for the Western District of Missouri, to the seat vacated by Judge [[Gary A. Fenner]], who at the time was going to assume [[senior status]] on a date to be determined. He eventually assumed [[senior status]] after Ketchmark was confirmed on September 8, 2015.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/11/20/presidential-nominations-sent-senate|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=November 20, 2014}} On December 16, 2014, her nomination was returned to the President due to the [[sine die]] adjournment of the [[113th United States Congress|113th Congress]]. On January 7, 2015, President Obama renominated her to the same position.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2015/01/07/presidential-nominations-sent-senate|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=January 7, 2015}} She received a hearing on her nomination on March 11, 2015.{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/nominations|title=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|website=www.judiciary.senate.gov}} On April 23, 2015, her nomination was reported out of committee by a [[voice vote]].{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%20-%20April%2023,%202015.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – April 23, 2015|publisher=}} On September 8, 2015, the [[United States Senate]] confirmed her by a 96–0 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=114&session=1&vote=00263|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Roseann A. Ketchmark, of Missouri, to be U.S. District Judge for the Western District)|website=www.senate.gov}} She received her judicial commission on September 14, 2015.{{cite web|url=http://www.mow.uscourts.gov/judges/ketchmark.html,|title=United States District Court for the Western District of Missouri, U.S. District Judge Roseann Ketchmark|publisher=}} ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== * {{FJC Bio|nid=1394796}} * {{Ballotpedia|Roseann_A._Ketchmark}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Gary A. She served as a Chief Judge for the district from 2011 to 2013. ==Early life and education== She was born '''Roslyn Elaine Olson''' in [[Phoenix, Arizona]] in 1946. She received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from the [[University of California, Santa Barbara|University of California at Santa Barbara]] in 1968 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Sandra Day O'Connor College of Law]] at [[Arizona State University]] in 1971.{{cite web|url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/silver-roslyn-o.|title=Silver, Roslyn O. - Federal Judicial Center}} ==Career== Silver was a [[law clerk]] for Justice [[Lorna Lockwood]] of the [[Supreme Court of Arizona]] from 1971 to 1972. She was in private practice in Phoenix from 1972 to 1974. Silver then served as an adviser and litigator for the Education Division of the [[Navajo Nation]]'s [[Native American Rights Fund]] from 1974 to 1976. She was an in house labor counsel for the [[Greyhound Corporation]] from 1976 to 1978. Silver returned to private practice in Phoenix in 1978 before becoming a trial attorney for the [[Equal Opportunity Commission]] in 1979. She was an [[Assistant United States Attorney]] for the District of Arizona from 1980 to 1984. Silver became an assistant Arizona attorney general in 1984 and served until she returned to the United States Attorney's office in 1986. In 1989, she was promoted to Chief of the criminal division. ===Federal judicial service=== Silver was nominated by President [[Bill Clinton]] on September 14, 1994, to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the District of Arizona]] vacated by [[Earl H. Carroll]]. She was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on October 7, 1994, and received her commission on October 11, 1994. She took [[senior status]] on September 3, 2013. Silver became Chief Judge in January 2011 after the shooting death of previous Chief Judge [[John Roll]] during the [[2011 Tucson shooting|2011 assassination attempt]] of Congresswoman [[Gabby Giffords]], serving until she took senior status. She was appointed to the court under the name of '''Roslyn O. Moore-Silver'''.{{cite news|last=Markon|first=Jerry|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2011/01/16/AR2011011604721.html|title=Federal court authorities plan to move trial of Tucson shooting suspect|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|date=January 17, 2011|access-date=January 18, 2011}} ==Awards and recognition== In 2013 Judge Silver was recognized, for outstanding service to Veterans’ Program, Arizona Army National Guard, Arizona Coalition for Military Families, and Arizona Veterans Magazine, and for outstanding achievement, Federal Bar Association, Phoenix Chapter[http://www.ce9.uscourts.gov/publications/AnnualReport2013.pdf United States Courts for the Ninth Circuit 2013 Annual Report] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161227074638/http://www.ce9.uscourts.gov/publications/AnnualReport2013.pdf |date=2016-12-27 }} ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{Ballotpedia|Roslyn_Silver|Roslyn Silver}} *{{FJC Bio|nid=1385321}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Earl H. [[North Carolina Central University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | party = | spouse = Carol Miller | allegiance = {{flag|United States}} | branch = {{army|United States|size=23px}} | unit = | service_years = 1975 | rank = [[File:Army-USA-OR-03.svg|15px]] [[Private First Class]] | battles = | mawards = {{collapsible list |titlestyle= background:transparent;text-align:left;font-weight:normal; |title= See list |}} }} '''Rossie David Alston Jr.''' (born May 31, 1957) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia]]. He was appointed by President [[Donald Trump]] in 2019. He was formerly a Judge of the [[Court of Appeals of Virginia]] after having previously been a judge in the Prince William County [[Virginia Circuit Court|Circuit Court]] and the Prince William County [[Juvenile and Domestic Relations District Court]]. == Biography == Alston graduated with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[Averett University]] in 1979 and obtained his [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[North Carolina Central University School of Law]] in 1982.{{cite news|title=Rossie Alston Jr. appointed state judgeship |url=http://www.insidenova.com/isn/news/local/article/rossie_alston_jr._appointed_state_judgeship/29829/ |first=Keith |last=Walker |date=February 12, 2009 |newspaper=Virginia Lawyers Weekly |location=Richmond, Virginia |access-date=August 17, 2015 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090224025149/http://www.insidenova.com/isn/news/local/article/rossie_alston_jr._appointed_state_judgeship/29829/ |archive-date=February 24, 2009 }} He worked as a staff attorney for the [[National Labor Relations Board]] for two years before going into private practice. He was elected by the [[Virginia General Assembly]] to be a judge of the Juvenile and Domestic Relations District Court for the 31st [[Virginia General District Court|Judicial District]], encompassing [[Prince William County, Virginia|Prince William County]], in 1998. He was elected to the [[Prince William County, Virginia|Prince William County]] [[Virginia Circuit Court|Circuit Court]] in 2001. While on the circuit court, he presided over the case of [[John Allen Muhammad]], the mastermind of the [[D.C. sniper attacks]], which brought him national attention.{{Cite news |url=http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2007/11/27/AR2007112702905.html |title=County Judges on Rise at Circuit, Appeals Courts |last=Vargas |first=Theresa |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |date=2007-11-29 |language=en-US |access-date=2019-05-26}} He was selected by his colleagues to be Chief Judge of the circuit court in 2007, when that position became vacant upon the elevation of [[LeRoy F. Millette Jr.]] to the Court of Appeals.{{cite news | title = County Judges on Rise at Circuit, Appeals Courts | url = https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2007/11/27/AR2007112702905.html | first = Theresa | last = Vargas | date = November 29, 2007 | newspaper = The Washington Post | location = Washington, D.C. | access-date = August 17, 2015}} Alston was elevated to the [[Court of Appeals of Virginia|Virginia Court of Appeals]] in 2009 to fill the vacancy created upon the retirement of [[Jean Harrison Clements]].{{Cite web |url=https://scvahistory.org/rossie-d-alston-jr-march-2009-present/ |title=Rossie D. Alston, Jr., March 1, 2009–present |date=2014-11-25 |website=Virginia Appellate Court History |language=en-US |access-date=2018-07-18}} Alston was known to be tough on violent criminals and those he thought had squandered second chances. He is quoted as saying "If you deserve the hammer, you're getting the hammer." In another case a man whose 21-month-old child died in a sweltering van, the jury recommended a one-year prison sentence. However Alston instead ordered the father to spend a day in jail for seven years on the anniversary of his daughter's death and run an annual blood drive in her name.{{cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/public-safety/judge-rossie-alston-will-be-nominated-to-federal-bench-in-virginia/2018/01/12/9602ccf6-f7c2-11e7-a9e3-ab18ce41436a_story.html |title=Judge Rossie Alston expected to be nominated to federal bench in Virginia |date=2018-01-14 |author1=Rachel Weiner |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |place=Washington, D.C. |issn=0190-8286 nominated him to be elected to a twelve-year term.{{cite news | last = Nolan | first = Jim | title = Senate panel certifies Alston as qualified for Supreme Court | work = The Richmond Times-Dispatch | |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/public-safety/judge-rossie-alston-will-be-nominated-to-federal-bench-in-virginia/2018/01/12/9602ccf6-f7c2-11e7-a9e3-ab18ce41436a_story.html?noredirect=on |access-date=8 June 2018 |newspaper=Washington Post |date=January 14, 2018}} === Federal judicial service === On June 7, 2018, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to nominate Alston to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia]].[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-fifteenth-wave-judicial-nominees-fourteenth-wave-united-states-attorney-nominees-ninth-wave-united-states-marshal-nominees/ "President Donald J. Trump Announces Fifteenth Wave of Judicial Nominees, Fourteenth Wave of United States Attorney Nominees, and Ninth Wave of United States Marshal Nominees" White House, June 7, 2018] {{PD-notice}} He was Trump's second [[African-American people|African American]] federal judicial nominee. On June 18, 2018, his nomination was sent to the [[United States Senate]]. Trump nominated Alston to the seat on the vacated by [[Gerald Bruce Lee]], who retired on September 30, 2017.{{Cite news|last=Weiner|first=Rachel|date=9 June 2018|title=Rossie Alston nominated as judge for Eastern District of Virginia|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/public-safety/rossie-alston-nominated-as-judge-for-eastern-district-of-virginia/2018/06/09/d8d5d3a6-6a91-11e8-9e38-24e693b38637_story.html|access-date=|newspaper=The Washington Post}} On October 10, 2018, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=10 October 2018|title=Circuit Court Nominee Chad Readler Quizzed on DOJ's Defense of Trump Policies|url=https://finance.yahoo.com/news/circuit-court-nominee-chad-readler-072045734.html|access-date=2020-10-19|website=Yahoo! Finance|language=en-US}} On January 3, 2019, his nomination was returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the Senate. On January 23, 2019, President Trump announced his intent to renominate Alston Jr. for a federal judgeship.{{Cite web|title=President Donald J. Trump Announces Intent to Nominate Judicial Nominees|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-intent-nominate-judicial-nominees/|access-date=2020-10-19|via=[[NARA|National February 7, 2019, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 20–2 vote.{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=|title=Results of Executive Business was confirmed by a 75–20 vote.{{Cite web|date=June 10, 2019|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Rossie David Alston, Jr., of Virginia, to be United States District Judge for the Eastern District of Virginia)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=1&vote=00146|access-date=2020-10-19|website=United States Senate}}{{Cite web|last1=Kargie|first1=Andrew|last2=Hoover|first2=Jimmy|date=12 September 2019|title=Law360's Guide To Trump's Judicial Picks – Law360|url=https://www.law360.com/articles/963060/law360-s-guide-to-trump-s-judicial-picks|access-date=2020-10-19|website=Law360|language=en}} He received his judicial commission on June 12, 2019.{{FJC Bio|nid=6586021|inline=yes}} In December 2023, Alston issued a [[temporary restraining order]] (TRO) preventing the U.S. Army from removing the [[Confederate Memorial (Arlington National Cemetery)|1914 Confederate Monument]] at [[Arlington National Cemetery]], pending a hearing. This memorial was commissioned in 1914 by the [[United Daughters of the Confederacy]] and is dedicated "To our dead heroes"; in 2022, the [[Naming Commission|Renaming Commission]] recommended in a report to Congress the removal of the statuary, along with other [[Confederate monuments and memorials]] on Defense Department property. However, some Republican politicians had expressed opposition to removing the memorial, expressing the belief that this Monument, the work of sculptor and Confederate veteran [[Moses Jacob Ezekiel|Sir Moses Ezekiel]], commemorates the reconciliation of the North and South post-Appomattox and not the Confederate States of America.{{Cite news|date=11 Dec 2023|title=GOP lawmakers demand Pentagon stop removal of Confederate memorial in Arlington National Cemetery|url=https://www.foxnews.com/politics/gop-lawmakers-demand-pentagon-stop-removal-confederate-memorial-arlington-national-cemetery|access-date=2023-12-19|website=Fox News|language=en}}{{Cite news|author=Olivia Diaz, Justin Wm. Moyer & Gregory S. Schneider|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/dc-md-va/2023/12/19/arlington-confederate-memorial-removal-ruling/|title=Judge says removal of Confederate statue at Arlington can proceed|newspaper=Washington Post|date=December 19, 2023}} Alston's order was issued after a group called Defend Arlington, the plaintiffs seeking to halt the memorial's removal, alleged that Ezekiel's headstones was damaged during the removal.{{Cite web |date=2023-12-18 |title=Judge issues order keeping Confederate memorial at Arlington Cemetery for now |url=https://apnews.com/article/confederate-memorial-arlington-cemetery-restraining-order-65a00f0e3b49b22547059ee021ec3e82 |work=Associated Press News|language=en}} However, one day after issuing the TRO, Alston allow the removal to go forward, denying the plaintiff's request for a [[preliminary injunction]]; during a hearing and in an order, Alston wrote that Defend Arlington had not come forward with evidence of any disturbance of graves, and during a site visit he had seen nothing supporting the group's claims. Silverstein | children = 2 | profession = {{hlist|Judge|lawyer|writer}} }} '''Roy Kalman Altman''' (born 1982) is a Venezuelan-American jurist, lawyer, and author who serves as a [[United States district court#Judges|United States district judge]] for the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida]]. Altman graduated from [[Columbia University]] in 2004, and [[Yale Law School]] in 2007 where he was an editor of the ''[[Yale Law Journal]]''. He served as a law clerk to Judge [[Stanley Marcus]] of the [[U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit]], and then as a federal criminal prosecutor from 2008 to 2014. From 2014 to 2019 he was an attorney in private practice. When he was appointed in 2019 at 36 years of age, he became the youngest federal district court judge in the United States. ==Early life and education== Altman was born in 1982 in [[Caracas]], Venezuela, and is Jewish.{{cite web |title=Altman, Roy Kalman |url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/altman-roy-kalman |website=Federal Judicial Center}}{{cite web |last=Silverstein |first=Rachel |title=Spotlight on the Honorable Roy K. Altman |url=https://www.fba-sdfla.org/post/spotlight-on-the-honorable-roy-k-altman |website=Federal Bar Association South Florida Chapter |date=March 3, 2021}} His paternal grandparents had previously fled [[Eastern Europe]] during World War II, finding refuge in Venezuela, while his maternal grandparents migrated from Poland to Mexico.{{cite news |title=Federal Judge Roy K. Altman named School of Law 2026 commencement speaker |url=https://news.miami.edu/law/stories/2026/04/federal-judge-roy-k-altman-named-school-of-law-2026-commencement-speaker.html |work=University of Miami School of Law |date=April 28, 2026 }} During [[the Holocaust]], his maternal grandfather's first wife and their five children were killed by the [[Nazi]]s in the [[gas chamber]]s in the [[Auschwitz concentration camp]].{{cite web |title="Facts vs. Narratives: A Legal Lens on Israel" with Roy K. Altman |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CmjwZ4gGW14 |website=Aish / YouTube |date=April 27, 2026}} His paternal great-grandfather, a police officer in [[Romania]], was exiled by Soviet forces to the [[Gulag]] [[Correctional labour camp|labor camps]] in [[Siberia]] in 1939/40, where he was ultimately killed.{{cite web |title=From Holocaust Survival to Generational Legacy: Roy K. Altman |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=B1bqP4Miy1k |website=Tikvah Open University / YouTube |date=May 11, 2026}} His paternal grandfather escaped [[Prague]] in 1938 [[History of the Jews in Venezuela|to Venezuela]], worked as a hotel general manager in Caracas, and later returned to Europe in 1945 after the war to rescue his sister, who had survived incarceration in the [[Mogilev]] [[concentration camp]]. His paternal grandmother evaded wartime capture in Europe by hiding, during which time she killed a [[Nazi soldier]]; she later was a flight attendant for [[Air France]]. Altman's father grew up in Venezuela, but relocated to Israel at the age of 18 in 1970, where he served as an officer and engineer in the [[Israeli Air Force]]. His mother was a nurse who grew up in Mexico and relocated to Israel as a teenager, where she met his father. Following their marriage, his parents returned to Venezuela, where they lived until increasing civil instability prompted them to immigrate to and settle in Miami, Florida, in 1984, when Altman was two years old. ===Education=== Altman attended high school at [[Miami Country Day School]], graduating in 2000.{{cite web |title=Spartan Athletics Hall of Fame: Roy Altman |url=https://www.miamicountryday.org/athletics/spartan-hall-of-fame/ |website=Miami Country Day School |date=September 30, 2026}} There, he competed as a four-year member of both the varsity football team, and of the varsity baseball team as a [[pitcher]] and [[outfielder]], and played varsity basketball at guard for two seasons. In football, Altman played [[quarterback]] and was named to the ''[[Miami Herald]]'' First Team All-Dade squad twice, and was named the ''Miami Herald'''s Class 3A-1A Football Player of the Year during his senior season. In baseball, he was named First Team All-Conference honors during his senior season. For his academic and athletic performance, he was named a finalist for the ''Miami Herald'' Scholar Athlete of the Year in 2000. He attended [[Columbia College (New York)|Columbia College]] of [[Columbia University]], where he studied the Core Curriculum and graduated with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] with honors in 2004.{{cite web |title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees: Roy Kalman Altman |url=https://senate.gov |website=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary}}{{Cite web|title=AitN: April 8, 2019|url=https://www.college.columbia.edu/cct/latest/alumni-news/aitn-april-8-2019|access-date=December 21, 2020|website=Columbia College Today|date=April 8, 2019 }}{{Cite web |date=July 8, 2019 |title=Newsmakers |url=https://www.college.columbia.edu/cct/issue/summer19/article/newsmakers |access-date=June 14, 2022 |website=Columbia College Today |language=en}}{{cite web |title=Roy Altman |url=https://ballotpedia.org/Roy_Altman |website=Ballotpedia}}{{cite web |title=Hon. Roy K. Altman |url=https://igp.sipa.columbia.edu/distinguished-fellows/hon-roy-k-altman |website=Institute of Global Politics, Columbia University SIPA }} While at Columbia, Altman was a dual student-athlete, playing as a quarterback on the [[Columbia Lions football|Columbia Lions football team]] and as a pitcher on the [[Columbia Lions baseball|Columbia Lions baseball team]], earning All-[[Ivy League|Ivy]] honors in baseball.{{cite web |title=Hon. Roy Kalman Altman |url=https://fedsoc.org/bio/roy-altman |website=The Federalist Society |date=November 7, 2025}} In his senior season in 2004, pitching for the baseball team in 19 games he had four [[Save (baseball)|save]]s, tied for fifth-most in a season in school history.{{cite web |title=Columbia Baseball Single-Season Records |url=https://gocolumbialions.com/sports/2010/7/9/204966909 |website=Columbia University Athletics |date=July 9, 2010 }} Altman earned his [[Juris Doctor]] in 2007 from [[Yale Law School]]. There, he was Projects Editor of volume 116 of the ''[[The Yale Law Journal|Yale Law Journal]]''.{{cite web |title=The Yale Law Journal: Volume 116, Number 1 |url=https://yalelawjournal.org |website=The Yale Law Journal |date=October 2006}} ==Early legal career== ===Law clerk=== He began his legal career as a [[law clerk]] to Judge [[Stanley Marcus (judge)|Stanley Marcus]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit]] from 2007 to 2008.{{cite web |url=http://www.podhurst.com/our-team/roy-kalman-altman/ |title=Roy Kalman Altman bio |website=Podhurst Orseck |access-date=February 13, 2018 }}{{cite web|url=http://www.sun-sentinel.com/news/florida/fl-reg-trump-nominations-federal-judges-20180213-story.html|title=Trump names his top three picks for federal judge in South Florida|first=Paula|last=McMahon|date=February 13, 2018|website=[[Sun-Sentinel]]|access-date=April 13, 2018}} === Federal prosecutor === Altman served for six years as an [[assistant United States attorney]] for the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida|Southern District of Florida]], from 2008 to 2014. He prosecuted hundreds of criminal cases and tried more than 20 cases to jury verdict, arguing several of them before the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit]], advancing to Deputy Chief of Special Prosecutions.{{cite web |title=Podhurst Orseck Attorney Recognized as "Rising Star" by Daily Business Review |url=https://www.podhurst.com/news/daily-business-review-professional-excellence-rising-star/ |website=Podhurst Orseck |date=December 12, 2015}} He was designated the Federal Prosecutor of the Year in 2012 by the [[Miami-Dade County]] Association of Chiefs of Police and the Law Enforcement Officers Charitable Foundation, and received the [[Federal Bar Association]] 2013 Young Federal Lawyer Award, the Director of the [[Executive Office for United States Attorneys|Executive Office of U.S. Attorneys]] Award for Superior Litigation Team in ''United States v. Mentor'' in 2014, and the Director of the Executive Office of U.S. Attorneys Award for Superior Litigation Performance in ''United States v. Flanders'' in 2015.{{cite web |url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-thirteenth-wave-judicial-nominees-seventh-wave-united-states-marshal-nominees/ |title=President Donald J. Trump Announces Thirteenth Wave of Judicial Nominees and Seventh Wave of United States Marshal Nominees |date=April 26, 2018 |via=[[NARA|National Archives]] |work=[[whitehouse.gov]] |access-date=April 26, 2018 }} {{PD-notice}} === Private practice === In 2014, Altman joined the trial and appellate law firm of Podhurst Orseck in Miami, Florida, as a [[law firm partner|partner]], a position that he held until 2019. He specialized in [[commercial litigation]], [[mass tort]]s, and international [[aviation law]].{{cite report |title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees: Roy Kalman Altman |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Altman%20SJQ.pdf |publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary}} He represented families affected by the disappearance of [[Malaysia Airlines Flight 370]], handled cross-border fraud and tobacco [[product liability]] cases, and served on the [[Florida Third District Court of Appeal]] [[Judicial Nominating Commission]].{{cite web |last=Altman |first=Roy K. |title=Roy K. Altman: books, biography, latest update |url=https://www.amazon.com/stores/author/B0GM1XKM5Z |website=Amazon Author Central |date=January 15, 2026}} ==Federal judicial service== === Confirmation; youngest U.S. federal district court judge === Altman was mentioned as a potential judicial nominee in February 2018, when he emerged as a leading candidate recommended by Florida's bipartisan [[judicial nominating commission]].{{cite news |last=Ovalle |first=David |title=Miami lawyer, a former federal prosecutor, considered for federal judgeship |url=https://law.com |work=Daily Business Review |date=February 12, 2018}}{{cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/states/florida/story/2018/02/13/trump-taps-3-new-judges-in-federal-district-overseeing-mar-a-lago-250044|title=Trump taps 3 new judges in federal district overseeing Mar-a-Lago|first=Marc|last=Caputo|date=February 13, 2018|website=[[Politico]]|access-date=February 15, 2018}} On April 26, 2018, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to nominate Altman to serve as a [[United States District Judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida]]. On May 7, 2018, his nomination was sent to the [[U.S. Senate]]. He was nominated to fill the seat vacated by Judge [[Joan A. Lenard]], who assumed [[senior status]] on July 1, 2017.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/fifteen-nominations-sent-senate-today-2/ "Fifteen Nominations Sent to the Senate Today" White House, May 7, 2018] On June 20, 2018, a confirmation hearing on his nomination was held by the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/06/20/2018/nominations United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Nominations for June 20, 2018] On July 19, 2018, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 17–4 vote.[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%2007-19-18.pdf Results of Executive Business Meeting – July 19, 2018, Senate Judiciary Committee] However, the full Senate did not act on his nomination before the conclusion of the Congressional term, and on January 3, 2019, his nomination was returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the Senate. On January 23, 2019, President Trump announced his intent to renominate Altman for a federal judgeship.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-intent-nominate-judicial-nominees/ "President Donald J. Trump Announces Intent to Nominate Judicial Nominees", White House, January 23, 2019] His nomination was sent to the Senate later that day.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/nominations-sent-senate-2/ "Nominations Sent to the Senate", White House, January 23, 2019] On February 7, 2019, his nomination was reported out of committee without a new hearing by a 16–6 vote.[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/02.07.2019%20Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting1.pdf Results of Executive Business Meeting – February 7, 2019, Senate Judiciary Committee] On April 3, 2019, the Senate invoked [[cloture]] on his nomination by a 66–33 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=1&vote=00060|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture on Roy Kalman Altman, of Florida, to be U.S. District Judge for the Southern District of Florida)|date=April 3, 2019|website=[[United States Senate]]|access-date=April 3, 2019|language=en}} The following day, on April 4, 2019, Altman was confirmed by a 66–33 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=1&vote=00062|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Roy Kalman Altman, of Florida, to be U.S. District Judge for the Southern District of Florida)|date=April 4, 2019|website=[[United States Senate]]|access-date=April 4, 2019|language=en}} He received his lifetime judicial commission on April 9, 2019.{{FJC Bio|nid=6244926|inline=yes}} At 36 years of age, he was the youngest federal district court judge in the United States, and the youngest-ever appointed judge in the [[Southern District of Florida]]. === Notable cases === Altman has presided over civil actions involving complex corporate, constitutional, and political matters.{{cite news |title=Trump lawsuits reach key stages after pair of recent setbacks |url=https://www.theindianalawyer.com/articles/trump-lawsuits-reach-key-stages-after-pair-of-recent-setbacks |work=The Indiana Lawyer |date=July 20, 2026}} * '''''Donald J. Trump v. British Broadcasting Corporation'':''' Altman is the presiding trial judge in a $10 billion [[defamation lawsuit]] filed by Donald Trump against the [[British Broadcasting Corporation]] (BBC). The suit stems from the broadcaster's editing of Trump's January 6, 2021 speech in a 2024 ''[[Panorama (British TV programme)|Panorama]]'' documentary, which Trump alleges created a false impression that he incited violence.{{cite news |title=Trump's lawyers in BBC lawsuit open the door to exposing all of his financial records — and scramble to close it |url=https://fortune.com/2026/08/08/trump-bbc-lawsuit-reputation-election-contradiction/ |work=Fortune |date=August 8, 2026}} Altman drew legal media attention for admonishing Trump's counsel over missed procedural filing deadlines.{{cite news |title=Judge Might Sanction Trump's Miami Lawyers in BBC Case |url=https://www.law.com/dailybusinessreview/2026/06/09/judge-might-sanction-trumps-miami-lawyers-in-bbc-case/ |work=Daily Business Review |date=June 9, 2026}} * '''''Trump Organization v. Capital One'':''' Altman presided over a major commercial lawsuit in which the [[Trump Organization]] accused the bank of politically motivated "[[de-banking]]" by abruptly closing hundreds of the Trump Organization's corporate accounts after the conclusion of Trump's first presidential term. Altman originally dismissed the case due to a lack of initial sufficient evidence, but granted the plaintiffs leave to refile, overseeing subsequent heavily redacted [[amended complaint]]s and court-ordered evidence exchanges. * '''Generative AI misuse admonitions:''' Altman has issued formal warnings to litigating counsel appearing in his court concerning the unchecked use of [[artificial intelligence]] in drafted filings, noting that failing to personally verify AI-generated [[case citation]]s stunts attorney development and causes severe professional harm to clients.{{cite news |title=Judge warns AI could stunt lawyers' training and harm their clients |url=https://www.reuters.com/legal/litigation/judge-warns-ai-could-stunt-lawyers-training-harm-their-clients-2026-10-02/ |work=Reuters |date=October 2, 2026}} === International judicial fact-finding missions === In March 2024, Altman, U.S. District Judge [[Lee Rudofsky]], and litigator Matthew Solomon organized a one-week fact-finding mission to Israel of 14 U.S. federal judges to examine legal issues.{{cite news |last=Ghermezian |first=Shiryn |title=US federal judges visit Israel on fact-finding mission to examine legal issues from Oct. 7 attacks |url=https://jpost.com |work=The Jerusalem Post |date=March 28, 2024}} The mission examined the impact of the [[October 7 attacks]] on the [[Israeli legal system]], specifically [[international humanitarian law]] and the [[law of armed conflict]] from the Israeli perspective. During the visit, the delegation conducted high-level legal consultations with Israeli Foreign Ministry legal advisor [[Tal Becker]], military justice representatives of the [[IDF]], and Palestinian [[human rights activist]]s.{{cite news |last1=Starr |first1=Michael |title=US federal judge delegation explores Oct 7 challenge to Israeli legal system |url=https://www.jpost.com/israel-hamas-war/article-791830 |access-date=July 30, 2026 |work=[[Jerusalem Post]] |date=March 13, 2024}} Since then, Altman has brought three judicial education missions of U.S. federal judges to Israel, to study cross-border [[evidentiary]] and [[humanitarian]] legal dynamics, sponsored by the [[World Jewish Congress]].{{cite news |last=Raymond |first=Nate |title=US judge cleared of misconduct over pro-Israel book, advocacy |url=https://reuters.com |work=Reuters |date=September 2, 2026}}{{cite news |last1=Wagenheim |first1=Mike |title=Federal judge says many lessons can be learned from Jerusalem's judiciary |url=https://www.jns.org/u.s.-news/federal-judge-says-many-lessons-can-be-learned-from-jerusalems-judiciary |access-date=July 30, 2026 |work=[[Jewish News Syndicate]] |date=July 9, 2025}} === University of Miami School of Law commencement address === On May 14, 2026, Altman delivered the keynote commencement address to the graduating class at the [[University of Miami School of Law]]'s spring graduation ceremony.{{cite news |last=Miami Law Staff Report |title=Federal Judge Roy K. Altman named School of Law 2026 commencement speaker |url=https://miami.edu |work=University of Miami School of Law |date=April 28, 2026}} In his address, he detailed his experiences on the federal bench, emphasized the ethical obligations of young lawyers entering highly polarized civic environments, and discussed how adhering to foundational legal methodology helps safeguard factual truth in modern public discourse.{{cite news |last1=Valencia |first1=Michelle |title=A century of excellence: School of Law commencement celebrates graduates and 100-year anniversary |url=https://news.miami.edu/law/stories/2026/05/a-century-of-excellence-school-of-law-commencement-celebrates-graduates-and-100-year-anniversary.html |access-date=July 30, 2026 |date=May 9, 2026}} ==Works== In 2026, Altman published his debut book, ''[[Israel on Trial|Israel on Trial: Examining the History, the Evidence, and the Law]]'', a 304-page historical and legal text addressing legal and historical debates surrounding [[Israel]], [[antisemitism]], and the [[Israeli–Palestinian conflict]] after the [[October 7 attacks]].{{cite web|title=Israel on Trial: Examining the History, the Evidence, and the Law|url=https://www.simonandschuster.com/books/Israel-on-Trial/Roy-K-Altman/9798891886360|website=Simon & Schuster|author=Roy K. Altman|access-date=May 19, 2026}}{{cite web |title=Israel on Trial: Examining the History, the Evidence, and the Law |url=https://www.indigo.ca/products/israel-on-trial-examining-the-history-the-evidence-and-the-law |website=Indigo |publisher=Advantage Media |date=April 28, 2026}} The book achieved national commercial success, placing on both [[The New York Times Best Seller list|''The New York Times'' Best Seller List]] and the [[USA Today Best-Selling Books|''USA Today'' bestseller list]].{{cite news |title=Advantage Celebrates Multiple National Bestseller List Placements Across Its Publishing Portfolio |url=https://natlawreview.com/press-releases/advantage-celebrates-multiple-national-bestseller-list-placements-across-its |work=The National Law Review |date=May 8, 2026}} ==Memberships== Altman was a member of the [[Federalist Society]] from 2004 during his studies at Yale Law School to 2007. He rejoined the organization in 2015 while working in private practice.[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Altman%20SJQ.pdf United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees: Roy Kalman Altman] Since rejoining, Altman frequently speaks at events hosted by the Federalist Society to various audiences, including law school students.{{Cite web |date=September 8, 2017 |title=Hon. Roy Kalman Altman |url=https://fedsoc.org/bio/roy-altman |access-date=October 4, 2025 |website=The Federalist Society}} His presentations span a wide variety of [[constitutional]] and professional topics, including modern [[originalism]], [[free speech]] legal frameworks, and Western civilizational protections of open discourse.{{cite news |title=Commencement speaker preview - University of Miami News |url=https://miami.edu |work=University of Miami News |date=May 1, 2026}}{{cite video |title=Judge Roy Altman on Free Speech and Western Civilization at National Free Speech Week |url=https://www.facebook.com/Federalist.Society/videos/we-dont-censor-one-side-just-because-its-got-the-facts-or-the-law-right-we-let-t/1818204765488744/ |date=October 24, 2025 |publisher=The Federalist Society}} He has partnered with the society's metropolitan networks to host interactive book forums exploring how rigorous [[Evidence (law)|evidentiary principles]] apply to highly polarized global issues.{{cite video |title=Israel on Trial with U.S. District Judge Roy Altman and U.S. Court of Appeals Judge Don Willett |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2hwNL6EHaSs |date=April 16, 2026 |publisher=The Federalist Society Austin Lawyers Chapter}}{{cite web |title=Atlanta Lawyer Chapter – Israel on Trial: A Conversation with Judge Roy Altman |url=https://fedsoc.org/chapters/GA/atlanta-lawyer-chapter |website=The Federalist Society |date=September 10, 2026}}{{cite web |title=Orange County Lawyer Chapter – Israel on Trial: A Conversation with Judge Roy Altman |url=https://fedsoc.org/chapters/CA/orange-county-lawyer-chapter |website=The Federalist Society |date=September 15, 2026}} == Personal life == Altman is married to Rachel N. Silverstein, Ph.D., who serves as the executive director of the environmental [[non-profit organization]] Miami Waterkeeper. The couple resides in Miami, and has two children.{{cite web |last=Johannes |first=Vanessa Singh |title=Athena Rising S2 E9: Honorable Roy K. '''Roy Bale "Skip" Dalton Jr.''' (born July 9, 1952) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States Federal Judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Middle District of Florida]].

==Early life and education==
Dalton was born on July 9, 1952, in [[Jacksonville, Florida]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.lawyercentral.com/roy-b-skip-dalton-jr-interactive-profile--20-175401.html|title=Attorney Roy B Skip Dalton Jr – Lawyer in Orlando FL|website=www.lawyercentral.com|access-date=2016-03-28|archive-date=2018-10-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181029191619/https://www.lawyercentral.com/roy-b-skip-dalton-jr-interactive-profile--20-175401.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> He earned a [[Bachelor of Arts]] in 1974 from the [[University of Florida]] and a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1976 from the [[University of Florida Levin College of Law]].<ref name=whgov_20101117>{{Cite web | author=The White House: Office of the Press Secretary | url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2010/11/17/president-obama-nominates-six-united-states-district-court-111710 | title=President Obama Nominates Six to the United States District Court, 11/17/10 | date=November 17, 2010 | via=[[NARA|National Archives]] | work=[[whitehouse.gov]] | access-date=March 22, 2011 | archive-date=January 18, 2017 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170118124332/https://www.whitehouse.gov/the-press-office/2010/11/17/president-obama-nominates-six-united-states-district-court-111710 | url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="fjc.gov">{{FJC Bio|nid=1393681|inline=yes}}</ref>

==Career==
From 1977 until 2011, Dalton worked as a [[civil litigator]] for a variety of different law firms. From 1977 until 1980, he was an [[Associate lawyer|associate]] for an [[Orlando, Florida]], law firm, Dean, Ringers, Morgan and Lawton, PA, and from 1980 until 1982, he was a principal at that firm. From 1982 until 1984, Dalton was in solo private practice in Orlando, and he was part of a larger law firm in Orlando as a principal from 1984 until 1986. He was part of a different Orlando law firm from 1986 until 1989, and then from 1989 until 1998, he was part of an Orlando law firm where one of his fellow partners was future United States Senator [[Mel Martinez]]. From 1999 until 2001, Dalton was again in solo legal practice in Orlando, and he was a principal in an Orlando firm in partnership with another lawyer from 2001 until 2003. From 2004 to 2011, Dalton had been of counsel to The Carlyle Appellate Law Firm in [[The Villages, Florida]]. He also served as a counsel to Martinez in 2005 and 2006.<ref name=whgov_20101117/><ref name="fjc.gov"/>

===Federal judicial service===
On November 17, 2010, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Dalton to fill a judicial vacancy on the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Florida that was created by the transition to [[senior status]] by Judge [[Henry Lee Adams Jr.]] in April 2010.  His nomination lapsed at the end of 2010, and Obama renominated him on January 5, 2011.  On March 2, 2011, the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] held a hearing on his nomination. Pursuant to an agreement of April 14, 2011, the [[United States Senate|Senate]] deemed his nomination confirmed by unanimous consent during executive proceedings that were held on May 2, 2011. He received his commission on May 3, 2011. He assumed [[senior status]] on July 9, 2022, his 70th birthday.<ref name="fjc.gov"/>

'''Royce Charles Lamberth''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|l|æ|m|b|ər|θ}}; born July 16, 1943) is a [[United States federal judge|senior judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Columbia]], who formerly served as its [[Chief judge (United States)#United States district courts|chief judge]]. Since 2015, he has sat as a [[visiting judge]] on the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Texas]] in [[San Antonio]].<ref name=CongressionalDirectory2005-2006>{{cite news|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Kl_GqvpDelsC|title=Official Congressional Directory, 2005-2006: 109th Congress|publisher=[[United States Government Publishing Office|Government Printing Office]]|year=2005|isbn=9780160724671|page=843|access-date=2012-09-09}}</ref>

==Education and career==

Lamberth was born in 1943 in [[San Antonio]], [[Texas]]. He graduated with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from the [[University of Texas]], where he was a member of the [[Tejas Club]], and from the [[University of Texas School of Law]], receiving a [[Bachelor of Laws]] in 1967. He served as a captain in the [[United States Army Judge Advocate General's Corps]] from 1968 to 1974, including one year in [[Vietnam War|Vietnam]]. After that, he became an Assistant [[United States Attorney]] for the District of Columbia. In 1978, Lamberth became chief of the civil division of the United States Attorney's Office, a position he held until his appointment to the federal bench.<ref name="fjc.gov">{{cite web|url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/lamberth-royce-c.|title=Lamberth, Royce C. - Federal Judicial Center|website=www.fjc.gov}}</ref>

==Federal judicial service==
Lamberth was nominated by President [[Ronald Reagan]] on March 19, 1987, to the seat on the [[United States District Court for the District of Columbia]] vacated by Judge [[Barrington D. Parker]]. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on November 13, 1987, and commissioned on November 16, 1987. He served as chief judge from 2008 to 2013. He assumed [[senior status]] on July 15, 2013.<ref name="fjc.gov"/> He also served as presiding judge of the [[United States Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court]] from 1995 to 2002.<ref name=RoyceCLamberth>{{cite news|url=http://www.dcd.uscourts.gov/lamberth-bio.html|title=Chief Judge Royce C. Lamberth|publisher=[[United States Department of Justice]]|access-date=2008-10-04|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081002150356/http://www.dcd.uscourts.gov/lamberth-bio.html|archive-date=2008-10-02}}</ref><ref name="Reuters2013-06-21">{{cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/usa-security-fisa-judges-idUSL2N0EV1TG20130621|title=The judges who preside over America's secret court|publisher=Reuters|author1=John Shiffman|author2=Kristina Cooke|date=2013-06-21|access-date=2013-07-01|archive-date=2013-06-23|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130623010333/https://www.reuters.com/article/2013/06/21/usa-security-fisa-judges-idUSL2N0EV1TG20130621|url-status=live|quote=Twelve of the 14 judges who have served this year on the most secret court in America are Republicans and half are former prosecutors.}}</ref> Since becoming a senior judge, Lamberth has been assigned as a visiting judge in San Antonio for several months per year at the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Texas]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.txwd.uscourts.gov/JudgesInfo/Lists/Judges Bios/DispForm.aspx?ID=27&Source=http://www.txwd.uscourts.gov/JudgesInfo/SitePages/JudgeDirectoryBio.aspx&ContentTypeId=0x0100A21A2D68A91AD8479639817C3091CCAF|title=Senior U.S. District Judge Royce C. Lamberth}}{{Dead link|date=April 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

==Notable cases==
===''Cobell v. Kempthorne''===
Lamberth presided over ''[[Cobell v. Kempthorne]]'', a case in which a group of [[Native Americans in the United States|Native Americans]] sued the [[U.S. Department of the Interior]] for allegedly mismanaging a trust intended for their benefit.<ref name=FoxNews2006-05-06>{{cite news|url=https://www.foxnews.com/story/disputes-continue-over-royalties-owed-to-american-indians|title=Disputes Continue Over Royalties Owed to American Indians|publisher=[[Fox News]]|date=2006-05-06|access-date=2008-10-04}}</ref> Lamberth, appointed to the bench by President [[Ronald Reagan]], was known for speaking his mind and repeatedly ruled for the Native Americans in their [[class-action lawsuit]]. His opinions condemned the government and found Interior secretaries [[Gale Norton]] and [[Bruce Babbitt]] in [[contempt of court]] for their handling of the case. The appellate court reversed Lamberth several times, including the contempt charge against Norton. After a particularly harsh opinion in 2005, in which Lamberth lambasted the Interior Department as [[racist]], the government petitioned the Court of Appeals to remove him, alleging that he was too biased to continue with the case. On July 11, 2006, the [[U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit]], siding with the government, removed Judge Lamberth from the case.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Weiss |first=Eric |date=July 12, 2006 |title=At U.S. Urging, Court Throws Lamberth Off Indian Case |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/politics/2006/07/12/at-us-urging-court-throws-lamberth-off-indian-case/72b9f5cd-e668-4d9f-98f9-10d83e5052b7/ |access-date=July 21, 2023}}</ref>

===1983 Beirut barracks bombing case===
In May 2003, in a case brought by families of the two hundred forty-one servicemen who were killed in the [[1983 Beirut barracks bombing]], Lamberth ordered the [[Islamic Republic of Iran]] to pay US$2.65 billion for the actions of [[Hezbollah]], a [[Shia]] [[militia]] group determined to be involved in the bombing in [[Beirut]], [[Lebanon]].<ref name=MarineCorpsTimes>{{cite news | access-date = 2007-09-07 | url = http://www.marinecorpstimes.com/news/2007/09/ap_beirutfine_070907/ | title = Iran is fined $2.65 billion in Marine deaths | author = Matt Apuzzo | date = September 7, 2007 | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070912133808/http://www.marinecorpstimes.com/news/2007/09/ap_beirutfine_070907/ | archive-date = September 12, 2007 | author-link = Matt Apuzzo }}</ref>

=== Guantanamo cases ===

Lamberth has presided over [[Guantanamo captive]]s ''[[habeas corpus]]'' petitions.<ref name=Reuters2008-06-18>{{cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/topNews/idUSN1829920120080618?feedType=RSS&feedName=topNews|title=U.S. judge meets lawyers to discuss Guantanamo cases|publisher=[[Reuters]]|author=James Vicini|date=2008-06-18|access-date=2008-10-04}}</ref><ref name=Reuters2008-07-02>{{cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/topNews/idUSN0235993420080702|title=Judges assigned to decide Guantanamo cases|publisher=[[Reuters]]|author=James Vicini|date=2008-07-02|access-date=2008-10-04}}</ref>

On December 29, 2016, Lamberth ordered the preservation of the full classified [[United States Senate]] [[United States Senate Intelligence Committee|Intelligence Committee]] [[Senate Intelligence Committee report on CIA torture|report on CIA torture]].<ref name=MiamiHerald2016-12-29>{{cite news|url=http://www.miamiherald.com/news/nation-world/world/americas/guantanamo/article123591209.html|title=Federal judge preserves CIA 'Torture Report' after Guantánamo war court wouldn't do it|publisher=[[Miami Herald]]|author=Carol Rosenberg|date=2016-12-29|location=[[Miami]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161230160356/http://www.miamiherald.com/news/nation-world/world/americas/guantanamo/article123591209.html|archive-date=2016-12-30|access-date=2017-01-03|url-status=live|quote=U.S. District Court Judge Royce Lamberth issued the two-page order Wednesday in Washington, in the mostly dormant federal court challenge of the Guantánamo detention of former CIA prisoner Abd al Rahim al Nashiri. The Saudi, who was [[waterboarding|waterboarded]] and rectally abused while a captive of the spy agency, is awaiting trial by military commission as the alleged architect of al-Qaida's Oct. 12, 2000, [[USS Cole bombing]] off Yemen that killed 17 U.S. sailors.|author-link=Carol Rosenberg}}</ref>
The six thousand–page report had taken Intelligence Committee staff years to prepare. A six hundred–page unclassified summary was published in December 2014, when Democratic Senator [[Dianne Feinstein]] chaired the committee, against objections of the Committee's Republican minority. Its publication stirred controversy. Limited copies of the classified report had been made, and human rights workers were concerned that the CIA would work to have all copies of the document destroyed.{{citation needed|date=March 2020}}

===James Rosen search warrants===
In 2010, two federal magistrate judges approved a warrant sought by the Justice Department to search personal e-mails and phone records of Fox News reporter [[James Rosen (journalist)|James Rosen]] related to a story about the North Korean nuclear program. In May 2010, Judge Lamberth overruled Magistrate Judge John Facciola's determination that the Justice Department needed to directly notify Rosen of the issuance of the warrant.<ref>{{cite magazine|url=http://www.newyorker.com/online/blogs/newsdesk/2013/05/how-justice-fought-to-keep-rosens-warrant-secret.html |title=How Prosecutors Fought to Keep Rosen's Warrant Secret |magazine=The New Yorker |date=2013-05-24 |access-date=2014-08-02}}</ref> In May 2013, Lamberth issued an apology from the bench for the clerk's office failure to unseal the search warrant docket entries as Lamberth had ordered in November 2011.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20130609063344/http://articles.washingtonpost.com/2013-05-22/world/39440575_1_federal-court-documents-search-and-arrest-warrants Judge apologizes for lack of transparency in James Rosen leak probe], Ann E. Marimow, Washington Post, May 22, 2013</ref>

===''Sherley v. Sebelius''===
In August 2010, Lamberth issued a temporary injunction blocking an executive order by President [[Barack Obama]] that expanded [[stem cell]] research. He indicated the policy violated a ban on federal money being used to destroy embryos,<ref>{{cite news|last=Harris|first=Gardiner|title=U.S. Judge Rules Against Obama's Stem Cell Policy|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/08/24/health/policy/24stem.html?_r=1|access-date=25 August 2010|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=August 23, 2010}}</ref> called the [[Dickey–Wicker Amendment]].<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2010/08/23/AR2010082303448.html?nav%3Demailpage&sub=AR |author= Rob Stein and Spencer S. Hsu |title=NIH cannot fund embryonic stem cell research, judge rules |date=August 24, 2010 |newspaper=Washington Post}}</ref> [[Susan Jacoby]] complained that his decision was more a reflection of his politics than a rigorous interpretation of the Dickey–Wicker Amendment.<ref>{{cite news| url=http://newsweek.washingtonpost.com/onfaith/spirited_atheist/2010/08/one_judge_and_christian_right_throw_stem_cell_research_into_chaos.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100906133003/http://newsweek.washingtonpost.com/onfaith/spirited_atheist/2010/08/one_judge_and_christian_right_throw_stem_cell_research_into_chaos.html | url-status=dead | archive-date=2010-09-06 | newspaper=The Washington Post | first=Susan | last=Jacoby | title=One Judge And Christian Right Throw Stem Cell Research Into Chaos}}</ref>

Judge Lamberth refused to lift the injunction forbidding the research pending the appeal of his ruling, and the [[United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit]] issued an order on September 9, 2010, providing for an emergency temporary lifting of the injunction in the case that had forbidden the research, at the request of the Justice Department. A three-judge panel from that court overturned Lamberth's decision in August 2012, and the Supreme Court denied the plaintiff's request for an appeal.<ref name="Nature">{{cite journal|last1=Wadman|first1=Meredith|title=High court ensures continued US funding of human embryonic-stem-cell research|url=http://www.nature.com/news/high-court-ensures-continued-us-funding-of-human-embryonic-stem-cell-research-1.12171|journal=Nature|year=2013|doi=10.1038/nature.2013.12171|s2cid=87211791|access-date=30 March 2016|doi-access=free|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

===''In re Kutler''===
In July 2011, Judge Lamberth ordered the release of Richard Nixon's testimony concerning the [[Watergate]] scandal. The Justice Department reviewed the decision after an objection from the administration insisting on the continued need for privacy of those involved.<ref name=NYT2011-07-29>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/07/30/us/30brfs-JUDGEORDERSR_BRF.html|title=Judge Orders Release of Nixon's Watergate Testimony|work=[[New York Times]]|author=John Schwartz|date=2011-07-29|access-date=2011-08-01|author-link=John Schwartz}}</ref>

===''Royer v. Federal Bureau of Prisons''===
On January 15, 2014, Judge Lamberth issued an order<ref name=Emptywheel>{{cite web|url=http://www.emptywheel.net/wp-content/uploads/2014/01/Royer-v-Federal-Bureau-of-Prisons-Order-on-Discovery-Motions.pdf|title=Royer Order}}</ref> harshly criticizing the [[United States Department of Justice|Department of Justice]] for what he described as its "sneering argument" that a federal prisoner had not been prejudiced by the Department's repeated failure to comply with [[Discovery (law)|discovery]] "because he remains incarcerated."<ref name=SimpleJustice>Greenfield, Scott (2014-01-30) [http://blog.simplejustice.us/2014/01/30/when-judge-lamberth-smacks-the-doj-hides/ When Judge Lamberth Smacks, The DOJ Hides], ''Simple Justice''</ref> Judge Lamberth went on to write that "[t]he whole point of this litigation is whether defendant can continue to single out plaintiff for special treatment as a terrorist during his continued period of incarceration. Did any supervising attorney ever read this nonsense that is being argued to this Court?"<ref name=Emptywheel/><ref name=SimpleJustice/> Judge Lamberth proceeded "to grant the inmate plaintiff pretty much all his discovery motion and hammer[ed] the DOJ by telling plaintiff to submit its request for sanctions in the form of award of attorney fees and costs."<ref name=SimpleJustice/> In response to the Order, the Justice Department moved to substitute new counsel "and remove the appearances of all prior counsel for Defendant in the above-captioned case," [[United States Attorney|Assistant United States Attorneys]] Charlotte Abel, Laurie Weinstein, Rhonda Campbell and Rhonda Fields.<ref name=SimpleJustice/><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.emptywheel.net/wp-content/uploads/2014/01/RoyerSubstCounsel.pdf|title=Royer Substitution Order}}</ref> This led one legal commentator to note that "[i]t appears that the government is seeking the clerk’s assistance in fundamentally altering the record, to intentionally conceal the identities of the assistants" who had been reprimanded by Judge Lamberth.<ref name=SimpleJustice/>

|last=Niedzwiadek |first=Nick |date=2022-01-04 |title=Hundreds of crimes, little punishment: Inside the sentences since the Capitol attack cases, 1 judge stands out as the toughest punisher |url=https://www.tampabay.com/news/nation-world/2022/06/12/in-jan-6-cases-1-judge-stands-out-as-the-toughest-punisher/ |access-date=2023-07-21 |website=Tampa Bay Times |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Tillman |first=Zoe |date=2021-11-22 |title=A Judge Who Felt Burned After Giving A Capitol Rioter Probation Threw The Book At Another In 2021, Lamberth controversially ordered a DC jail to provide Jacob Chansley the [[Organic food|organic]] food he had requested as a [[Reasonable accommodation|religious accommodation]], after Chansley refused to eat for days while awaiting trial.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Leonard |first=Ben |date=2021-02-03 |title='QAnon shaman' granted organic food in jail after report of deteriorating health |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2021/02/03/qanon-shaman-organic-food-465563 |access-date=2023-07-21 |website=POLITICO |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Carrega |first=Nicole Chavez, Christina |date=2021-02-08 |title='QAnon Shaman' rioter will eat organic food, while most prisons and jails have reputation for serving food that is unhealthy |url=https://www.cnn.com/2021/02/08/us/prison-meals-qanon-shaman-organic-food/index.html |access-date=2023-07-21 |website=CNN |language=en}}</ref> Lamberth eventually ordered Chansley moved to a new jail that would provide him with organic food.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-02-05 |title="QAnon Shaman" Jake Angeli transferred to another jail so he can eat organic meals - In October 2021, Lamberth held D.C. corrections officials in contempt, citing treatment and [[civil rights]] abuses of January 6 participant [[Christopher John Worrell|Christopher Worrell]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Neidig |first=Harper |date=2021-10-13 |title=Judge holds DC corrections officials in contempt over treatment of Jan. 6 defendant |url=https://thehill.com/regulation/court-battles/576561-judge-holds-dc-corrections-officials-in-contempt-over-treatment-of/ |access-date=2023-07-21 |website=The Hill |language=en-US}}</ref>

By 2023, after several hundred participants had been jailed, tried and convicted for their activities, some House Republicans such as [[Marjorie Taylor Greene]] sought to characterize them as "political prisoners." Donald Trump and [[House Republican Conference]] chair [[Elise Stefanik]] characterized them as "hostages." Lamberth, who had presided over dozens of the cases, remarked in a January 2024 court filing, in part:<blockquote>I have been shocked to watch some public figures try to rewrite history, claiming rioters behaved "in an orderly fashion" like ordinary tourists, or martyrizing convicted January 6 defendants as "political prisoners" or even, incredibly, "hostages." That is all preposterous. But the Court fears that such destructive, misguided rhetoric could presage further danger to our country.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Mascaro |first1=Lisa |title=Marjorie Taylor Greene's jail visit pulls GOP closer to Jan. 6 rioters |url=https://apnews.com/article/marjorie-taylor-greene-jan-6-capitol-attack-20f06d75072a563d56a86b0ecf2d89b8 |publisher=Associated Press |date=March 25, 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Cheney |first1=Kyle |title='Preposterous': Federal judge decries efforts to downplay Jan. 6 violence, label perpetrators 'hostages' |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2024/01/25/judge-lamberth-jan-6-trump-00137960 |work=Politico |date=January 25, 2024}}</ref></blockquote>During one trial, supporters of Taylor James Johnatakis—a participant in the attack Lamberth sentenced to more than 7 years in prison<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-04-03 |title=Man who used megaphone to lead attack on police during Capitol riot gets more than 7 years in prison |url=https://apnews.com/article/taylor-johnatakis-capitol-riot-sentencing-f97acd68b8860d36b212e408ac80abd4 |access-date=2024-04-13 |website=AP News |language=en}}</ref>—wrote letters to the court in Johnatakis's support.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Hsu |first=Spencer |date=April 4, 2024 |title=Judge to backers of Jan. 6 rioter: Don't condone political violence |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/dc-md-va/2024/04/04/jan6-riot-judge-letter/ |newspaper=The Washington Post}}</ref> In response, Lamberth published a written version of his sentencing remarks in an unusual public court filing he styled as “Notes for Sentencing,” and ordered the court clerk to send a copy to those who had written in support of Johnatakis.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Barber |first=C. Ryan |title=The Burly Texas-Born Judge Fighting Efforts to Play Down Jan. 6 |url=https://www.wsj.com/us-news/law/the-burly-texas-born-judge-fighting-efforts-to-play-down-jan-6-ef24dfb1 |access-date=2024-04-13 |work=WSJ |language=en-US}}</ref> “In any angry mob, there are leaders and there are followers. Mr. Johnatakis was a leader,” Lamberth said. “He knew what he was doing that day.”<ref>{{Cite web |last=Lamberth |first=J. |date= |title=Notes for Sentencing |url=https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.dcd.227212/gov.uscourts.dcd.227212.272.0.pdf |website=Court Listener}}</ref>

=== Revolution Wind offshore wind farm ===
Danish energy company [[Ørsted]] has almost finished [[Revolution Wind]], a large [[Offshore wind power|wind farm]] off the [[US East Coast]]. In August 2025, the [[Second presidency of Donald Trump|Trump administration]] ordered a temporary halt to construction.<ref>25 August 2025: [https://www.tagesschau.de/wirtschaft/unternehmen/orsted-windpark-usa-100.html ''Trump stoppt Windpark - und ein dänischer Konzern leidet''] (translated: ''Trump halts wind farm project, causing difficulties for a Danish corporation'')</ref> 
On 22 December 2025, the [[United States Department of the Interior|US Department of the Interior]] suspended five<ref>[[Vineyard Wind|Vineyard Wind 1]] off the coast of Massachusetts, [[Sunrise Wind]] and [[Empire Wind]] in New York, [[Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind]] and 'Revolution Wind'.</ref> offshore wind leases over what it said were 'national security concerns'.<ref name=guardian /><ref>[https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/dec/22/trump-wind-farms ''Trump officials halt offshore wind-farm projects over ‘national security risks’ '']</ref>
Ørsted filed a lawsuit.<ref>[https://orsted.com/en/media/news/2026/01/revolution-wind-llc-to-file-preliminary-injunction-1473856511 orsted.com] 2 January 2026.</ref> 
On 12 January 2026, US district judge Lamberth has overturned the construction freeze. He said the 'Revolution Wind' project is likely to succeed in the ongoing legal dispute.<ref name=guardian />

Lamberth stated that without a preliminary injunction, the project would suffer “irreparable harm” and that the company's request was “in the [[public interest]].”<ref name=guardian>[[theguardian.com]] 12 January 2026: [https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/jan/12/orsted-rhode-island-wind-project-trump ''US judge lets Danish firm resume Rhode Island offshore wind project halted by Trump'']</ref>
<!---The order allows for the “immediate resumption of the affected activities,” according to the project's website. Construction work will “resume as soon as possible.” --->

She was assistant county counsel for Imperial County from 2011 to 2012 and also served as a deputy county counsel IV in 2000. == Judicial career == === State judicial service === From 2012 to 2013 and again from 2015 to 2018, Montenegro served as a judge on the [[Imperial County Superior Court]] in California.{{Cite web |title=Governor Appoints Ruth Bermudez Montenegro to Imperial County Superior Court |url=https://www.ca.gov/archive/gov39/2012/02/29/news17432/index.html |access-date=November 3, 2021 |website=California State Portal}} She served as the Imperial County Superior Court's Family Support Commissioner from 2013 to 2015. === Federal judicial service === ==== United States magistrate judge tenure ==== She was appointed as a [[United States Magistrate Judge]] for the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of California]] on August 15, 2018.{{Cite web |title=Ruth Bermudez Montenegro |url=https://www.uscourts.gov/judicial-milestones/ruth-bermudez-montenegro |access-date=November 3, 2021 |website=United States Courts |language=en}} Her service as a magistrate terminated on March 30, 2022 when she was commissioned as a district judge.{{FJC Bio|nid=11690371}} ==== District court service ==== On November 3, 2021, President [[Joe Biden]] nominated Montenegro to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of California]]. President Biden nominated Montenegro to the seat vacated by Judge [[John A. Houston]], who assumed [[senior status]] on February 6, 2018.{{Cite press release |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |date=November 3, 2021 |website=[[Whitehouse.gov]] |publisher=The White House |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/11/03/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-43/}} {{PD-notice}} On December 15, 2021, a hearing on her nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web |title=Nominations |date=December 8, 2021 |website=[[Senate.gov]] |publisher=[[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]] |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/12/08/2021/nominations}} On January 3, 2022, her nomination was returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]];{{Cite web |date=January 3, 2022 |title=PN1503 - Nomination of Ruth Bermudez Montenegro for The Judiciary, 117th Congress (2021–2022) |url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/117th-congress/1503 |access-date=January 4, 2022 |website=[[Congress.gov]]}} she was later renominated the same day.{{Cite press release |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |date=January 3, 2022 |website=[[Whitehouse.gov]] |publisher=The White House |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/01/03/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-53/}} {{PD-notice}} On January 20, 2022, her nomination was reported out of committee by a 14–8 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/EBM%20Results%201.20.222.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – January 20, 2022|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=January 20, 2022}} On March 16, 2022, the Senate invoked cloture on her nomination by a 57–42 vote.{{Cite web|date=March 16, 2022|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Ruth Bermudez Montenegro to be U.S. District Judge for the Southern District of California)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1172/vote_117_2_00084.htm|access-date=March 17, 2022|website=United States Senate}} On March 22, 2022, her nomination was confirmed by a 55–41 vote.{{Cite web|date=March 22, 2022|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Ruth Bermudez Montenegro, of California, to be U.S. District Judge for the Southern District of California)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1172/vote_117_2_00098.htm|access-date=March 22, 2022|website=United States Senate}} She received her judicial commission on March 30, 2022. == See also == * [[List of Hispanic and Latino American jurists]] == References == {{Reflist}} == External links == *{{FJC Bio|nid=11690371}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[John A. [[University of Texas Law School|University of Texas]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | footnotes = }} '''Sam Allen Lindsay''' (born October 16, 1951){{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Cmlw3xWy5EQC&pg=PA516|page=516|title=Hearings before the Committee on the Judiciary, United States Senate, One Hundred Fifth Congress, Second Session, on Confirmations of Appointees to the Federal Judiciary, February 4; February 25; March 18; March 24; April 29, 1998|publisher=U.S. Government Printing Office|year=1998}} is an American attorney who serves as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Texas]], with chambers in [[Dallas]], [[Texas]]. ==Early life and education== Lindsay was born in [[San Antonio, Texas|San Antonio]], [[Texas]] and raised in South Texas. He received his [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in History and Government from [[St. Mary's University, Texas|St. Mary’s University]] in 1974, graduating [[magna cum laude]]. In 1977, he earned his [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Texas School of Law]] in Austin. == Career == After graduating from law school, Lindsay served as a staff attorney for the Texas Aeronautics Commission from 1977 to 1979. In 1979, he joined the Dallas City Attorney's office, where he progressed through various posts until being named City Attorney in 1992. He was the head of the Federal Litigation Section from 1979 to 1986, a Chief of litigation division/executive assistant city attorney from 1986 to 1990, a first assistant city attorney from 1990 to 1991, an Acting city attorney in 1991, and finally a City Attorney from 1992 to 1998. === Federal judicial service === On November 8, 1997, Lindsay was nominated by President [[Bill Clinton]] to be a United States District Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Texas]], to a new seat created by 104 Stat. 5089. He was [[unanimous]]ly confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on March 11, 1998, and received commission on March 17, 1998. Lindsay was the first [[African American]] to serve on the federal District Court in Dallas. === Notable cases === *In October 2006 Lindsay presided over the case against [[InfoCom Corporation]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.justice.gov/archive/usao/txn/PressRel06/elashi_bayan_ghassan_basman_infocom_sent_pr.html|title = Bayan Elashi, Ghassan Elashi, Basman Elashi and Infocom Corporation Sentencing Press Release}} *On May 21, 2007, Lindsay issued an order blocking enforcement of an [[by-law|ordinance]] approved by the citizens of [[Farmers Branch, Texas]].Stephanie Sandoval [http://www.dallasnews.com/sharedcontent/dws/news/localnews/stories/DN-fbimmigration_05met.ART.State.Edition1.433f282.html 2 sides in FB case are dealt minor setbacks: Hearing is today on preliminary injunction against city's rental ban,"] ''The Dallas Morning News'', June 5, 2007 The ordinance would have authorized fines against property managers who rented to [[illegal immigration|illegal immigrants]]. *On January 22, 2015, Lindsay sentenced journalist [[Barrett Brown]] for his role in a December 2011 [[Anonymous (group)|Anonymous]] hack of Texas-based [[Stratfor]]. Brown pleaded guilty to accessory after the fact, interfering with an FBI investigation, and threatening an FBI agent. At the time of sentencing, he had been in jail about 2.5 years. Lindsay sentenced Brown to a total of 63 months in jail and fined him almost $1 million, with the money to be paid to Stratfor and other companies targeted by Anonymous. [[Jeremy Hammond]], who was responsible for the Stratfor breach, pleaded guilty to one count, illegally accessing computer systems. In 2013, Judge [[Loretta Preska]], sentenced Hammond to 10 years, the maximum allowed; news reports make no mention of Preska imposing a fine. {{cite news | last = Coleman | first = Gabriella | title = Bad, Bad Barrett Brown | newspaper = Slate.com | date = 23 January 2015 | url=http://www.slate.com/articles/technology/future_tense/2015/01/barrett_brown_sentencing_the_u_s_government_overreaction_to_hackers.single.html | accessdate = 25 January 2015 }} {{cite news | last = Rogers | first = Tim | title =Barrett Brown Sentenced to 63 Months in Prison, Looks Horrible in Mustard Yellow Jail Togs | newspaper = Frontburner | date = 23 January 2015 | url=http://frontburner.dmagazine.com/2015/01/23/barrett-brown-sentenced-to-63-months-in-prison-looks-horrible-in-mustard-yellow-jail-togs/ | accessdate = 25 January 2015 }} {{cite news | last = Nicks | first = Denver | title =Activist Defiant After Sentencing Over Stratfor Hacking | newspaper = TIME | date = 23 January 2015 | url=https://time.com/3680594/barrett-brown-sentencing/ | access-date = 25 January 2015 }} {{cite news | last = Woolf | first = Nicky | title =Barrett Brown sentenced to 63 months for 'merely linking to hacked material' | newspaper = The Guardian | date = 23 January 2015 | url=https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2015/jan/22/barrett-brown-trial-warns-dangerous-precedent-hacking-sentencing | accessdate = 25 January 2015 }} {{cite news | last = Pilkington | first = Ed | title =Jailed Anonymous hacker Jeremy Hammond: 'My days of hacking are done' | newspaper = The Guardian | date = 15 November 2013 | url=https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2013/nov/15/jeremy-hammond-anonymous-hacker-sentenced | accessdate = 25 January 2015 }} ==Personal life== Lindsay's daughter, [[Rachel Lindsay (television personality)|Rachel Lindsay]], is an attorney and television personality who first appeared as a contestant on [[The Bachelor (American TV series) season 21|''The Bachelor'']], coming in third place. [[Columbia University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Samantha Dowd Elliott''' (born 1975){{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Elliott%20SJQ%20Public%20Final.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=November 2, 2021}} is an American lawyer from [[New Hampshire]] serving as the [[United States federal judge|chief United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of New Hampshire]]. == Education == Elliott received a [[Bachelor of Arts]], ''[[cum laude]]'', from [[Colgate University]] in 1997 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Columbia Law School]] in 2006.{{Cite press release |title=President Biden Names Eighth Round of Judicial Nominees |date=September 30, 2021 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/09/30/president-biden-names-eighth-round-of-judicial-nominees/ |access-date=September 30, 2021}} {{PD-notice}} == Career == From 2006 until 2021, Elliott was a [[Law firm partner|partner]] and vice president at Gallagher, Callahan & Gartrell, P.C., in [[Concord, New Hampshire]]. While at the law firm, she served as president from 2015 to 2020 and as a hiring partner from 2014 to 2019. She has been a member of New Hampshire Legal Assistance and the Legal Advice Referral Center. In June 2021, she became co-chair of the founding board of directors for 603 Legal Aid, an entity created by merging two other statewide legal aid groups. == Federal judicial service == On September 30, 2021, President [[Joe Biden]] nominated Elliott to serve as a [[federal district judge]] of the [[U.S. District Court for the District of New Hampshire]]. Biden nominated Elliott to the seat vacated by Judge [[Paul Barbadoro]], who assumed [[senior status]] on March 1, 2021.{{Cite press release |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |date=September 30, 2021|publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/09/30/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-37/}} {{PD-notice}} On November 3, 2021, a hearing on her nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web |title=Nominations |date=October 27, 2021 |publisher=[[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]] |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/10/27/2021/nominations}} On December 2, 2021, her nomination was reported out of committee by a 15–7 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%2012.2.21.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – December 2, 2021|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=December 3, 2021}} On December 14, 2021, the [[United States Senate]] invoked [[cloture]] on her nomination by a 59–40 vote.{{Cite web|date=December 14, 2021|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Samantha D.
