'''Theodore David Chuang''' (born 1969) is a  [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Maryland]] and former deputy general counsel of the [[United States Department of Homeland Security]].

==Early life and education==
Chuang was born to a [[Taiwanese American]] family in [[Media, Pennsylvania]], in 1969.<ref name="Questionnaire">[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Theodore-Chuang-Senate-Judiciary-Questionnaire-Final.pdf Questionnaire: Theodore Chuang], [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]].</ref> His parents are immigrants from [[Taiwan]].<ref name="Duncan">{{cite news|url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2017/03/16/who-is-the-maryland-judge-in-the-trump-travel-ban-ruling/|title=Who is the Maryland judge in the Trump travel ban ruling?|last=Duncan|first=Ian|date=March 16, 2017|work=Baltimore Sun}}</ref> Chuang graduated ''[[summa cum laude]]'' with his [[Bachelor of Arts]] from [[Harvard University]] in 1991 and was elected to [[Phi Beta Kappa]].<ref name="Questionnaire" /> As an undergraduate, he wrote for ''[[The Harvard Crimson]]'' and won the Endicott Peabody Saltonstall Prize as a top senior at [[Harvard College]]''.''<ref name="Duncan" /> He went on to earn a [[Juris Doctor]], ''magna cum laude'', from [[Harvard Law School]] in 1994.<ref name="Questionnaire"/> As a law student, he served as an editor of the ''[[Harvard Law Review]]''.<ref name="Questionnaire"/><ref name="fjc.gov">{{FJC Bio|nid=1394471|inline=yes}}</ref>

==Career==
Chuang began his legal career as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Dorothy Wright Nelson]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]], from 1994 to 1995. From 1995 to 1998, he served as a trial attorney in the [[United States Department of Justice Civil Rights Division|Civil Rights Division]] of the [[United States Department of Justice]]. From 1998 to 2004, he served as an [[assistant United States attorney]] in the District of Massachusetts.<ref name="Questionnaire"/> He served as counsel at the law firm of [[Wilmer Cutler Pickering Hale and Dorr|Wilmer, Cutler, Pickering, Hale and Dorr LLP]] in [[Washington, D.C.]] from 2004 to 2007. From 2007 to 2009, he was deputy chief investigative counsel for the [[United States House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform|House Oversight and Government Reform Committee]]. In 2009, he was chief investigative counsel for the [[United States House Committee on Energy and Commerce|House Committee on Energy and Commerce]].<ref name="Questionnaire"/> From 2009 until his confirmation as a federal judge in 2014, he served as deputy general counsel of the [[United States Department of Homeland Security]].<ref name="Questionnaire"/><ref name="Whitehouse">{{cite press release|title=President Obama Nominates Two to Serve on the United States District Courts|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2013/09/25/president-obama-nominates-two-serve-united-states-district-courts|publisher=White House Office of the Press Secretary|date=September 25, 2013}}</ref><ref name="fjc.gov"/>

In 2024, Chuang was elected to serve a six-year term on [[Harvard Board of Overseers|Harvard's Board of Overseers]], a governing body that ensures "the University remains true to its charter as a place of learning."<ref>{{Cite web |last=harvardgazette |date=2024-05-21 |title=Five alumni elected to the Board of Overseers |url=https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2024/05/five-alumni-elected-to-the-board-of-overseers-2/ |access-date=2024-11-03 |website=Harvard Gazette |language=en-US}}</ref>

===Federal judicial service===
On September 25, 2013, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Chuang to serve as a United States district judge of the United States District Court for the District of Maryland, to the seat being vacated by Judge [[Roger W. Titus]], who assumed [[senior status]] on January 17, 2014.<ref name="Whitehouse" /> Chuang's nomination was strongly supported by Maryland's two U.S. senators, [[Ben Cardin]] and [[Barbara Mikulski]].<ref name="Duncan"/> He was rated "well-qualified" by the [[American Bar Association]]'s [[Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary]].<ref>[http://www.americanbar.org/content/dam/aba/uncategorized/GAO/WebRatingChart.authcheckdam.pdf Rating of Article III Judicial Nominees: 113th Congress: Adjourned December 16, 2014], American Bar Association Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary.</ref> On January 16, 2014, his nomination was reported out of the [[Senate Judiciary Committee]] by a 10–8 vote.<ref>{{cite web |title=Executive Business Meeting|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/ExecutiveBusinessMeetingResults-01-16-2014.pdf|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|date= January 16, 2014}}</ref> On April 29, 2014, Senate Majority Leader [[Harry Reid]] filed for [[cloture]] on Chuang's nomination. On May 1, 2014, the Senate invoked [[cloture]] on his nomination by a 54–43 vote.<ref>{{cite web|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture on Theodore David Chuang, of Maryland, to be U.S. District Judge for the District of Maryland)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1132/vote_113_2_00124.htm|publisher=United States Senate}}</ref> Later that day, Chuang was confirmed by a 53–42 vote.<ref>{{cite web|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Theodore David Chuang, of Maryland, to be U.S. District Judge for the District of Maryland)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=113&session=2&vote=00127|publisher=United States Senate}}</ref> He received his judicial commission on May 2, 2014.<ref name="fjc.gov"/> Chuang sits in [[Greenbelt, Maryland]].<ref name="Duncan"/>

=== Notable rulings ===

==== Mifepristone (2020) ====
On July 13, 2020, Chuang suspended the in-person requirement for women wanting to obtain the abortion pill [[mifepristone]] during the [[COVID-19]] epidemic due to public health risks.<ref>{{cite web|last=Kunzelman|first=Michael|date=July 13, 2020|title=Judge: Women can get abortion pill without doctor visit|url=https://www.abc12.com/2020/07/13/judge-women-can-get-abortion-pill-without-doctor-visits/|access-date=July 13, 2020|website=[[WJRT-TV]]}}</ref> Chuang affirmed the decision in December 2020 when the [[First presidency of Donald Trump|Trump administration]] requested to reinstate that requirement.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Kunzelman|first=Michael|date=December 11, 2020|title=Federal judge in Maryland rejects Trump administration bid to reinstate rule for dispensing abortion pill|work=[[The Baltimore Sun]]|agency=[[Associated Press]]|url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2020/12/11/federal-judge-in-maryland-rejects-trump-administration-bid-to-reinstate-rule-for-dispensing-abortion-pill/|access-date=}}</ref> However, the [[Supreme Court of the United States]] subsequently overruled Chuang's decision 6-3, therefore requiring women to obtain the pills in person until at least the end of the Trump presidency.<ref>{{Cite news|last=|first=|date=January 12, 2021|title=Supreme Court justices say women must obtain abortion pill in person|work=[[PBS NewsHour]]|agency=[[Associated Press]]|url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/justices-say-women-must-obtain-abortion-pill-in-person|access-date=}}</ref>

==== USAID and DOGE (2025–2026) ====
In March 2025, Chuang ruled that President [[Donald Trump]] and [[Elon Musk]]'s dismantling of the [[United States Agency for International Development]] (USAID) was likely unconstitutional and blocked Musk and [[Department of Government Efficiency]] from continuing the process of shutting down USAID.<ref name="Pierson_20250319">{{Cite news| last = Pierson| first = Brendan| title = US judge finds Musk's USAID cuts likely unconstitutional, blocks him from making more cuts| work = Reuters| access-date = 2025-03-19| date = 2025-03-19| url = https://www.reuters.com/world/us/us-judge-bars-musk-doge-further-efforts-shut-down-usaid-2025-03-18/}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last1=Thompson |first1=Steve |last2=Judkis |first2=Maura |last3=Rodriguez |first3=Sabrina |last4=McDaniel |first4=Justine |last5=Vazquez |first5=Maegan |last6=Marimow |first6=Ann |last7=Svitek |first7=Patrick |last8=Zakrzewski |first8=Cat |last9=Patel |first9=Kasha |date=2025-03-18 |title=Maryland judge orders DOGE to stop efforts to dismantle USAID |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/dc-md-va/2025/03/18/maryland-judge-blocks-doge/ |access-date=2025-03-18 |newspaper=The Washington Post |language=en-US |issn=0190-8286}}</ref> Chuang ruling was in response to a lawsuit filed by employees of USAID, whose workforce had been reduced by 98 percent through DOGE cuts.<ref name="Olmsted_20250318">{{Cite magazine| issn = 0028-6583| first = Edith |last=Olmsted| title = Elon Musk Dealt Huge Blow as Judge Rules USAID Cuts Unconstitutional| magazine = [[The New Republic]]| access-date = 2025-03-19| date = 2025-03-18| url = https://newrepublic.com/post/192889/elon-musk-doge-judge-rules-usaid-unconstitutional}}</ref> This is the first ruling to constrain Musk personally as well as DOGE.<ref name="Olmsted_20250318"/> The 70-page ruling said that DOGE violated the separation of powers clause by attempting to shut down USAID without congressional approval.<ref name="Olmsted_20250318"/>

On March 28, 2025, a three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit set aside Judge Chuang's order and allowed Elon Musk and his team of analysts to resume their work in helping to dismantle USAID.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/03/28/us/politics/trump-musk-usaid.html | title=Appeals Court Allows Musk to Keep Pushing Steep Cuts at U.S.A.I.D. | work=The New York Times | date=29 March 2025 | last1=Montague | first1=Zach }}</ref>

In the same case, which Chuang certified as a [[class action]] in August 2025,<ref>{{Cite news |last=Wagner |first=Erich |date=August 19, 2025 |title=Judge certifies class in lawsuit on behalf of ex-USAID workers, contractors |url=https://www.govexec.com/workforce/2025/08/judge-certifies-class-lawsuit-behalf-ex-usaid-workers-contractors/407551/ |work=[[Government Executive]] |access-date=November 14, 2026}}</ref> he ruled in February 2026 that Musk could be deposed about his role in shutting down USAID.<ref>{{Cite news |issn=0028-6583 |title=Elon Musk Will Be Deposed Over What He Did With DOGE |work=[[The New Republic]] |url=https://newrepublic.com/post/206223/elon-musk-will-deposed-doge |access-date=November 14, 2026}}</ref> On March 4, 2026, a divided Fourth Circuit panel granted the Trump administration's petition for a [[writ of mandamus]] 2–1 and directed Chuang to issue a protective order barring the depositions of Musk and other officials, holding that he had abused his discretion because the plaintiffs had not first sought the information through other means.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Tillman |first=Zoe |date=March 4, 2026 |title=Elon Musk Deposition Blocked by Appeals Court in DOGE Fight |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-03-04/elon-musk-deposition-blocked-by-appeals-court-in-doge-fight |work=[[Bloomberg News]] |url-access=subscription |access-date=November 14, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=April 13, 2026 |title=Will Elon Musk ever be forced to explain what he did inside DOGE? |url=https://www.cnn.com/2026/04/13/politics/elon-musk-doge-lawsuits-avoid-deposition-questions |work=CNN |access-date=November 14, 2026}}</ref>

==== Prosecution of John Bolton (2025–2026) ====
{{Main|Prosecution of John Bolton}}
Chuang presided over the prosecution of former [[National Security Advisor (United States)|national security advisor]] [[John Bolton]], who was indicted in October 2025 on 18 counts of unlawfully transmitting and retaining national defense information.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Gallagher |first1=Fallon |last2=Rubin |first2=Lisa |date=October 16, 2025 |title=John Bolton indicted by federal grand jury in national security case |url=https://www.msnbc.com/msnbc/news/john-bolton-indictment-trump-doj-charges-rcna237354 |access-date=November 14, 2026 |website=MSNBC.com |language=en}}</ref> On June 26, 2026, Bolton pleaded guilty before Chuang to one count of retaining national defense information. Under the plea agreement, he faces up to five years in prison and a $2.25 million fine.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Diaz |first=Jaclyn |date=June 26, 2026 |title=John Bolton, former Trump national security adviser, pleads guilty in classified documents case |url=https://www.npr.org/2026/06/26/nx-s1-5871292/john-bolton-national-security-classified-documents |work=[[NPR]] |access-date=November 14, 2026}}</ref> Sentencing, originally scheduled for October 28, 2026, was moved to December 4, 2026.<ref>{{Cite web |title=United States v. Bolton, 8:25-cr-00314 |url=https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/71668443/united-states-v-bolton/ |website=CourtListener |access-date=November 14, 2026}}</ref>

==== FBI headquarters (2026) ====
On August 17, 2026, in a lawsuit brought by the state of [[Maryland]] and [[Prince George's County, Maryland|Prince George's County]], Chuang blocked the Trump administration's plan to move [[Federal Bureau of Investigation|FBI]] headquarters into the [[Ronald Reagan Building and International Trade Center|Ronald Reagan Building]] in Washington, D.C. He ruled that the FBI and the [[General Services Administration]] had exceeded their statutory authority, because Congress had directed that the headquarters be built at one of three sites (Greenbelt or Landover, Maryland, or Springfield, Virginia), and he reinstated [[Greenbelt, Maryland]] as the selected location.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Baehr |first=Jasmine |date=August 18, 2026 |title=Federal judge blocks Trump admin plan to move FBI headquarters to Reagan Building |url=https://www.foxnews.com/politics/federal-judge-blocks-trump-administration-plan-move-fbi-headquarters-reagan-building |work=[[Fox News]] |access-date=November 14, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Rothstein |first=Ethan |date=August 18, 2026 |title=Judge Rules FBI Can't Scrap Maryland Headquarters Plan |url=https://www.bisnow.com/news/washington-dc/office/judge-rules-fbi-cant-scrap-maryland-headquarters-plan |work=Bisnow |access-date=November 14, 2026}}</ref>

{{nowrap|[[Notre Dame Law School|University of Notre Dame]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]])}} | footnotes = }} '''Theresa Lazar Springmann''' (born January 23, 1956) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Indiana]]. ==Early life and education== Born in [[Gary, Indiana]], as the third of four children and the granddaughter of immigrants from Ireland and Russia.[http://indianalawblog.com/archives/2008/03/ind_courts_fede_13.html Federal Judge Theresa Lazar Springmann is the 2008 recipient of the Nancy A. Maloley Outstanding Public Servant Award]. Retrieved 2010-02-08. In 1977, Springmann graduated summa cum laude from [[Indiana University Northwest]] with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree and later from [[Notre Dame Law School]] with a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1980. ==Career== Following law school graduation, she worked as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[James Tyne Moody]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Indiana]] from 1980 to 1983. She was in private practice in Indiana from 1984 to 1995. She served as a [[United States magistrate judge]] of the Northern District of Indiana from 1995 to 2003. ===Federal judicial service=== On the recommendation of Senator [[Richard Lugar]], Springmann was nominated to the United States District Court for the Northern District of Indiana by President George W. Bush on January 29, 2003, to a seat vacated by Judge [[James Tyne Moody]]. Springmann was confirmed by the [[United States Senate|Senate]] on March 31, 2003, on a Senate vote and received her commission on June 24, 2003. She served as chief judge from February 3, 2017, to May 31, 2020.[http://www.innd.uscourts.gov/sites/innd/files/2017-1.pdf IN THE MATTER OF DESIGNATING A CHIEF JUDGE FOR THE UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT, NORTHERN DISTRICT OF INDIANA, General Order No. 2017-1, February 10, 2017] She assumed [[senior status]] on January 23, 2021, her 65th birthday. ===Notable rulings=== In May 1997, a John M. Stephenson received a guilty verdict and death sentence for killing three people in [[Warrick County, Indiana]]. He appealed his case to the [[Indiana Supreme Court]] on the basis of "ineffective counsel" because his attorney didn't object to him wearing a [[stun belt]] in front of the jury that convicted him. In April 2007, the Indiana Supreme Court unanimously rejected his appeal. After the Indiana Supreme Court rejected Stephenson's appeal, he took it to the [[United States federal courts|federal level]], where Judge Springmann overturned his guilty sentence and the [[Capital punishment|death penalty]] in a 26-page ruling. She noted, "Due process mandates that John M. Stephenson is entitled to what he was denied: a trial without restraints".[http://www.wthr.com/Global/story.asp?S=10639254&nav=menu188_2 ''WTHR'' "US judge vacates verdict in Indiana triple slayings", July 2, 2009] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110629132125/http://www.wthr.com/Global/story.asp?S=10639254&nav=menu188_2 |date=June 29, 2011 }} The Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals reversed and remanded. On remand, Judge Springmann ruled that Stephenson had not been prejudiced by his lawyer's failure to object to his having to wear a stun belt visible to jurors in the penalty phase of the litigation. In 2017, on appeal for the second time, Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed in part and reversed in part. The appellate court ruled that Stephenson was not entitled to habeas relief with respect to his murder conviction, but that he was entitled to a new sentencing hearing because his attorney was ineffective for failing to object to his having to wear a stun belt.[https://www.leagle.com/decision/infco20170804093 Stephenson v. '''Thomas Edward Johnston''' (born September 8, 1967) is an American lawyer who serves as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of West Virginia]].

==Education and career==

Johnston was born in [[Charleston, West Virginia]]. He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[West Virginia University]] in 1989 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[West Virginia University College of Law]] in 1992. {{Citation needed|date=August 2020}} He was a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Frederick Pfarr Stamp Jr.]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of West Virginia]] from 1992 to 1994. He was in private practice in [[Wheeling, West Virginia|Wheeling]], West Virginia, from 1994 to 2001. He was the [[United States attorney]] for the Northern District of West Virginia from 2001 to 2006.<ref name="FJCBio">{{FJC Bio|nid=1392356}}</ref>

===Federal judicial service===

Johnston was nominated by President [[George W. Bush]] on September 28, 2005, to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of West Virginia]]. He was nominated to a seat vacated by [[Charles Harold Haden II]]. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on March 6, 2006, and received his commission on April 17, 2006. He became chief judge on September 5, 2017 and served a seven-year-term until September 5, 2024.<ref name="FJCBio" />

'''Thomas Francis Hogan''' (born 1938) is a [[Senior status|Senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Columbia]], who served as director of the [[Administrative Office of the United States Courts]] from October 17, 2011, until June 30, 2013.

==Education==

Hogan was born in [[Washington, D.C.]] He graduated from the [[Georgetown Preparatory School]] in 1956, receiving a [[Bachelor of Arts]] from [[Georgetown University]] in 1960.  He attended [[George Washington University]]’s masters program in American and English [[literature]] from 1960 to 1962, and he graduated with a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[Georgetown University Law Center]] in 1966, where he was the St. Thomas More Fellow. Following law school, Hogan [[law clerk|clerked]] for Judge [[William Blakely Jones]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Columbia]] from 1966 to 1967.<ref name="fjc.gov">{{cite web|url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/hogan-thomas-francis|title=Hogan, Thomas Francis - Federal Judicial Center|website=www.fjc.gov}}</ref>

==Experience==

Hogan served as counsel to the National Commission for the Reform of Federal Criminal Laws from 1967 to 1968, and was engaged in private practice from 1968 to 1982, in [[Rockville, Maryland|Rockville]], [[Maryland]], [[Chevy Chase, Maryland|Chevy Chase]], Maryland and [[Washington, D.C.]] He was an assistant professor at Potomac School of Law from 1977 to 1979. He was an adjunct professor of law at the Georgetown University Law Center from 1986 to 1992, and has also been a Master of the Prettyman-Leventhal Inn of Court. He served as a member of the executive committee of the [[United States Judicial Conference]] and served as the Judicial Conference's chair of the Courtroom Technology Subcommittee. Additionally he served as a member of the board of the  [[Federal Judicial Center]].<ref name="fjc.gov"/>

==Federal judicial service==

Hogan was nominated by President [[Ronald Reagan]] on August 10, 1982, to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the District of Columbia]] vacated by Judge [[William B. Bryant]]. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on August 20, 1982, and received commission on August 20, 1982. He served as chief judge from June 19, 2001 to May 1, 2008. He assumed [[senior status]] on May 1, 2008.<ref name="fjc.gov"/> He served from 2009 to 2016 on the [[United States Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court]] and served as Presiding Judge of that court from 2014 to 2016.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court: 2013 Membership |url=http://www.fas.org/irp/agency/doj/fisa/court2013.html |work=[[Federation of American Scientists]] |accessdate=June 9, 2013}}</ref><ref name=Reuters2013-06-21>
{{cite news 
| url         = https://www.reuters.com/article/usa-security-fisa-judges-idUSL2N0EV1TG20130621
| title       = The judges who preside over America's secret court
| publisher   = [[Reuters]]
| author      = John Shiffman, Kristina Cooke
| date        = 2013-06-21
| accessdate  = 2013-07-01
| archivedate = 2013-06-23
| archiveurl  = https://web.archive.org/web/20130623010333/https://www.reuters.com/article/2013/06/21/usa-security-fisa-judges-idUSL2N0EV1TG20130621
| url-status     = live
| quote       = Twelve of the 14 judges who have served this year on the most secret court in America are Republicans and half are former prosecutors.
}}</ref>

==Notable cases==

In 1986, Judge Hogan decided that the blind have a Constitutional right to have Playboy magazine provided to them in braille for free at the expense of the federal Government.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Halting Braille Playboy Ruled Unconstitutional |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/politics/1986/08/29/halting-braille-playboy-ruled-unconstitutional/f052263a-8dd7-47ce-b8bf-59e6cd34bf74/ |access-date=2023-07-17 |newspaper=The Washington Post}}</ref>

Congress passed the [[Line Item Veto Act]] of 1996 to control "[[pork barrel spending]]" that favors a particular region rather than the nation as a whole. [[President of the United States|President]] [[Bill Clinton]] used the [[line item veto]] 11 times, striking spending on 82 items.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cnn.com/ALLPOLITICS/1998/06/25/scotus.lineitem/|title=CNN|website=[[CNN]]|publisher=}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.access.gpo.gov/nara/nara004.html|title=History of Line Item Veto Notices|website=www.access.gpo.gov|access-date=2010-02-09|archive-date=2012-02-04|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120204040511/http://www.access.gpo.gov/nara/nara004.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> The first case challenging the line-item veto was ordered dismissed by the Supreme Court for lack of standing, vacating the trial court's decision finding that the veto was unconstitutional. ''[[Raines v. Byrd]],'' <!--the preceding link is a redirect, ergo the following external link--> {{ussc|521|811|1997}}. In the second case, Hogan ruled February 12, 1998, that such unilateral amendment or repeal of only parts of statutes violated the U.S. Constitution. This ruling was affirmed on June 25, 1998, in a 6–3 decision of the [[Supreme Court of the United States]] in the case [[Clinton v. City of New York]].

In 2001, Judge Hogan sentenced an 82-year-old man to five years' imprisonment for drug possession.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Miller |first=Bill |date=2001-02-02 |title=82-Year-Old Gets 5 Years in Prison |language=en-US |newspaper=Washington Post |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/2001/02/02/82-year-old-gets-5-years-in-prison/9d0c7942-a4ab-4ec7-b980-4388642f44b1/ |access-date=2023-07-17 |issn=0190-8286}}</ref>

In 2005, Judge Hogan jailed New York Times reporter [[Judith Miller]] for failing to reveal her confidential sources, a decision that Reporters Without Borders termed "a dark day for freedom of the press."<ref>{{Cite web |date=2005-07-07 |title=Prison for Judith Miller: a dark day for freedom of the press {{!}} RSF |url=https://rsf.org/en/prison-judith-miller-dark-day-freedom-press |access-date=2023-07-17 |website=rsf.org |language=en}}</ref>

In United States v. TANIOS, No. 21-3034 (D.C. Cir. Aug. 9, 2021), the Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit found that Judge Hogan had erred in ordering the indefinite pre-trial detention of George Tanios, who Judge Hogan had believed had the intent to use pepper-spray during the January 6, 2021 Capitol riot. The Court of Appeals stated: "[Judge Hogan] clearly erred in [hi]s individualized assessment of appellant's dangerousness. The record reflects that Tanios has no past felony convictions, no ties to any extremist organizations, and no post-January 6 criminal behavior that would otherwise show him to pose a danger to the community within the meaning of the Bail Reform Act."

[[University of San Diego]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Thomas Lamson Ludington''' (born December 28, 1953){{Cite web|url=https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/005272900|title=Confirmation hearings on federal appointments: hearings before the Committee on the Judiciary, United States Senate, One Hundred Ninth Congress, first session.|date=February 24, 2006|publisher=U.S. G.P.O. : For sale by the Supt. of Docs., U.S. G.P.O.|via=HathiTrust}} is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan]]. Although the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan|Eastern District of Michigan]]'s other 14 judges cover the Southern Division, Ludington is the only judge for the entire Northern Division,{{Cite web|title=Bay City Federal Court|url=https://www.amberglaw.net/bay-city-federal-court|access-date=2021-12-29|website=Amberg & Amberg|language=en-US}}{{dead link|date=February 2026}} which covers nearly a quarter of [[Michigan]]'s land mass.{{Cite journal|last1=Lawson|first1=David|last2=Ludington|first2=Thomas|date=July 2011|title=A Proposal for Restructuring the Eastern District of Michigan|url=https://www.michbar.org/file/barjournal/article/documents/pdf4article1879.pdf|journal=Michigan Bar Journal|volume=July 2011|pages=2}} ==Education and career== Born in [[Midland, Michigan]], Ludington received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[Albion College]] in 1976 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of San Diego School of Law]] in 1979. During the summers of 1976 and 1977, he directed the water-ski school for [[Culver Academies]] in [[Culver, Indiana]]. He was in private practice in [[Michigan]] from 1980 to 1994. He was a judge on the [[Judiciary of Michigan|Midland County Circuit Court]] from 1994 to 2006, serving as Chief Judge of that court from 1999 to 2006. ==Federal judicial service== Ludington was originally nominated through President [[George W. Bush]] on September 12, 2002, to a federal judgeship in the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan]] vacated by [[Paul V. Gadola]]. During this time the judicial nomination process was blocked by [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrats]] in the [[United States Senate]], and Ludington's appointment was delayed for 1,365 days. Ludington was later confirmed [[unanimously]] on June 8, 2006, and received his commission on June 12, 2006. === Notable opinions === In Al-Sadoon v. Lynch, 586 F. Supp. 3d 713 (E.D. Mich. 2022),{{Cite web|last=Ludington|first=Thomas|date=February 17, 2022|title=Al-Sadoon v. Lynch|url=https://casetext.com/case/al-sadoon-v-lynch|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220928020549/https://casetext.com/case/al-sadoon-v-lynch|url-status=dead|archive-date=September 28, 2022|access-date=September 27, 2022|website=casetext.com}} Ludington granted [[habeas relief]]—for the first time in his nearly 30-year tenure as a judge—to Ali Najim Al-Sadoon, who was forgotten in detention as a result of the [[Biden Administration]]'s February 18, 2021 reprioritization of removable immigration detainees.{{Cite web |last=U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement |date=February 18, 2021 |title=Interim Guidance: Civil Immigration Enforcement and Removal Priorities |url=https://www.ice.gov/doclib/news/releases/2021/021821_civil-immigration-enforcement_interim-guidance.pdf }} Ludington found that the government had detained Al-Sadoon "not charged with any crime, for 757 days—more than 17% of his life," which was "longer than any other [habeas] petitioner—ever." ==Awards and recognition== In 2023, the [[American Bar Association]] awarded Ludington the Honorable William D. Missouri Civility Award,{{Cite web |title=William D. Missouri Civility Award |url=https://www.americanbar.org/groups/judicial/awards/missouri-civility-award/ |access-date=2025-01-10 |website=www.americanbar.org |language=en}} which recognizes judges with "exceptional qualities of civility, courtesy, and professionalism toward colleagues, litigants, and the public."{{Cite web |title=Michigan Federal Judge to Receive ABA Civility Award |url=https://www.michbar.org/journal/Details/Michigan-Federal-Judge-to-Recieve-ABA-Civility-Award?ArticleID=4664 |access-date=2025-01-10 |date=August 2023 |website=www.michbar.org |language=en-US}} Ludington was nominated by his chambers staff and law clerks, supported by letters of recommendation from fellow judges in [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan|Michigan's Eastern District]] and a judge with the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit|6th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals]].{{Cite web |title=Michigan federal judge Thomas Ludington to receive ABA civility award |url=https://www.americanbar.org/news/abanews/aba-news-archives/2023/06/judge-ludington-civility-award/ |access-date=2025-01-10 |date=2023-06-30 |website=www.americanbar.org |language=en}} ==Arrest== Ludington was arrested October 4, 2025, in [[Emmet County, Michigan]] after allegedly crashing a car into two road signs. He was charged with Operating While Intoxicated with a high BAC.{{Cite web |title=Federal Judge Couldn’t Recite Alphabet in Field Sobriety Test |url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/business-and-practice/federal-judge-couldnt-recite-alphabet-in-field-sobriety-test |language=en |first1=Eric |last1=Heisig |accessdate=2026-02-26 |date=2026-02-19 |website=Bloomberg Law}} In police body-cam footage of his arrest, Ludington is asked to complete a series of field sobriety tests while soaked in urine. When asked to choose a number between 19 and 21, Ludington chose the number 15.{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5_xQe2EAjiY |title=Traffic stop of U.S. District Judge Thomas Ludington |date=2026-02-25 |last=MLive |access-date=2026-02-27 |via=YouTube}}{{Cite web |last=Jaworowski |first=Matt |date=2026-02-05 |title=Formal complaint filed against Michigan judge charged with "super drunk" OWI |url=https://www.woodtv.com/news/michigan/formal-complaint-filed-against-michigan-judge-charged-with-super-drunk-owi/}} Effective February 23, 2026, he is on an indefinite paid leave of absence.{{Cite web|url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/business-and-practice/us-judge-goes-on-paid-leave-while-awaiting-drunken-driving-trial|title=US Judge Goes on Leave While Awaiting Drunken-Driving Trial (1) |first1=Eric |last1=Heisig |accessdate=2026-02-26 |date=2026-02-23 |website=Bloomberg Law}} On April 8, 2026, Ludington agreed to a plea deal, pleading no contest to misdemeanor operating while intoxicated, with the charge of operating with a high BAC to be dismissed at sentencing.{{Cite web|url=https://upnorthlive.com/news/local/federal-judge-facing-super-drunk-charge-takes-plea-deal-drunk-driving-emmet|title=Federal judge facing 'super drunk' charge takes plea deal|first=Maryjane|last=Glynn|date=April 8, 2026|website=WPBN}} On May 13, 2026, Ludington was sentenced to 6 months of probation, plus court costs and fees and must undergo twice weekly alcohol screening during his probation. He will not return to judicial duties until pending disciplinary proceedings against him are complete.{{Cite web|url=https://www.detroitnews.com/story/news/local/michigan/2026/05/13/federal-judge-tom-ludington-sentenced-in-super-drunk-driving-case/89975593007/|title=Federal judge Tom Ludington sentenced in 'super drunk' driving case|first=Robert|last=Snell|website=The Detroit News}} In early June 2026, Ludington was ordered to appear in court on June 8, 2026, for probation violations stemming from his failure to complete mandated twice weekly alcohol screenings. If convicted of probation violation, Ludington could be ordered to complete any or all of his potential 93 days of jail time, in addition to possible extension of his period of probation.{{cite news |last=Snell |first=Robert |date=June 2, 2026 |title=Federal judge Tom Ludington back in trouble in 'super drunk' scandal |url=https://www.detroitnews.com/story/news/local/michigan/2026/06/02/federal-judge-tom-ludington-back-trouble-super-drunk-scandal/90368293007/ |work=The Detroit News |location= |publisher= |access-date=June 2, 2026}} Ludington pleaded not guilty to probation violation on June 8, 2026, and a further hearing is scheduled for June 22, 2026, for which Ludington has been ordered to appear in person.{{Cite web|url=https://upnorthlive.com/news/local/federal-judge-thomas-ludington-back-in-court-on-probation-violation|title=Federal Judge Thomas Ludington back in court on probation violation|first=Maryjane Glynn | Roxanne|last=Werly|date=June 8, 2026|website=WPBN}} == References == {{Reflist}} ==Sources== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1392431}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Paul V. [[Cornell Law School|Cornell University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | footnotes = }} '''Thomas Samuel Zilly''' (born 1935) is a [[United States federal judge|senior United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Washington]].{{cite book |title=Confirmation Hearings on Federal Appointments |date=1989 |publisher=United States. Congress. Senate. Committee on the Judiciary |page=908 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GjfFeq-91SoC&dq=Thomas+Samuel+Zilly++January+1+1935&pg=PA908 |access-date=14 August 2021}} ==Education and career== Zilly was born in [[Detroit]]. He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from the [[University of Michigan]] in 1956 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Cornell Law School]] in 1962. He was a [[United States Naval Reserve]] Lieutenant (J.G.) from 1956 to 1962, serving on [[Reserve components of the United States Armed Forces|active duty]] from 1956 to 1959. He entered private practice in [[Seattle]], [[Washington (state)|Washington]], working from 1962 to 1988 at the law firm Lane Powell Moss & Miller. He was a Judge pro tem of the Seattle Municipal Court from 1972 to 1980.{{FJC Bio|nid=1390281}} Zilly served as president of the Seattle-King County Bar Association in 1986-1987 and on multiple Washington State Bar Association committees, including as a hearing officer for its disciplinary board and as a bar examiner.{{citation needed|date=December 2021}} ===Federal judicial service=== On February 16, 1988, Zilly was nominated by President [[Ronald Reagan]] to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Washington]] vacated by Judge [[Walter T. McGovern]]. A hearing on his nomination was held on March 28, 1988, and the Senate Judiciary Committee approved it on April 14, 1988.{{cite web |title=PN850 — Thomas S. Zilly — The Judiciary |url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/100th-congress/850 |website=Congress.gov |publisher=U.S. Government |access-date=9 June 2021}} Zilly was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on April 19, 1988, and received his commission the following day. He assumed [[senior status]] on January 1, 2004. === Notable rulings === In November 1988 Zilly ruled that the [[US Fish and Wildlife Service]] had unlawfully failed to list the [[northern spotted owl]] under the [[Endangered Species Act]].{{cite news |last1=Egan |first1=Timothy |title=Ruling on Owl Stirs New Hope for Trees |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1988/11/18/us/ruling-on-owl-stirs-new-hope-for-trees.html |access-date=27 April 2021 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=18 November 1988}} In August 1997, Zilly certified a [[class-action]] [[lawsuit]] by 64 prison inmates who alleged they had been subjected to [[X-ray]] bombardment of their [[testes]] during a [[Cold War]] experiment conducted at the [[Washington State Penitentiary]] at [[Walla Walla, Washington|Walla Walla]] during the 1960s.{{cite news |last1=Steele |first1=Karen |title=Judge Throws Out Oregon Man's Suit On Cold War Tests Rules He Waited Too Long; Local Case Still Active |url=https://www.spokesman.com/stories/1997/aug/14/judge-throws-out-oregon-mans-suit-on-cold-war/ |access-date=27 April 2021 |agency=The Spokesman-Review |date=14 August 1997}} In June 2002, Zilly ruled that the [[University of Washington]] had not engaged in "[[reverse discrimination]]" against white [[law school]] admission aspirants who had not been admitted to the class entering in fall 1994.{{cite web |title=Law School Admissions Legal, Judge Rules in 'Reverse Discrimination' Lawsuit |url=https://www.washington.edu/alumni/columns/sept02/briefings_lawschool.html |website=Columns: The University of Washington Alumni Magazine |publisher=University of Washington |access-date=27 April 2021}} On January 28, 2017, Zilly ordered{{cite web |last1=Zilly |first1=Thomas |title=Order Granting Emergency Motion for Stay of Removal, John Doe I et al. v. Trump et ux. |url = https://web.pdx.edu/~pcooper/JohnDoe1vTrumpWDWA01282017.pdf |publisher=U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington |access-date=27 April 2021 |date=28 January 2017}} a temporary injunction preventing the removal from the [[United States]] of two [[Yemeni]] citizens under [[Donald Trump]]'s order to ban all immigration from seven predominantly Muslim nations.{{citation needed|date=December 2021}} In February 2019, Zilly ordered the [[Department of Defense]] not to discriminate against U.S. armed forces members who are naturalized citizens by requiring them to undergo periodic security checks. The plaintiffs in the case were 17 individuals who had enlisted via the [[Military Accessions Vital to the National Interest]] (MAVNI) program.{{cite news |title=Judge Orders Pentagon To Stop Discriminating Against Naturalized Citizen Soldiers |url=https://www.cpr.org/2019/02/02/judge-orders-pentagon-to-stop-discriminating-against-naturalized-citizen-soldiers/ |access-date=27 April 2021 |agency=National Public Radio |date=2 February 2019}} In September 2020, Zilly denied a government motion to dismiss a civil rights lawsuit filed by the family of Che Andre Taylor, who had been shot dead by [[Seattle]] police officers in 2016.{{cite news |last1=Carter |first1=Mike |title='They said, he's dead': Judge in Seattle won't dismiss civil rights lawsuit by family of Che Taylor |url=https://www.seattletimes.com/seattle-news/they-said-hes-dead-judge-wont-dismiss-civil-rights-lawsuit-by-family-of-che-taylor/ |access-date= April 27, 2021 |work=[[The Seattle Times]] |date=September 5, 2020}} Zilly presided over the first trial in the Western District of Washington ever conducted via the online platform Zoom during October 2020.{{cite news |last1=Alder |first1=Madison |title=Zoom Trial Judge Recommends Jurors Get Time for Virtual Chitchat |url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/zoom-trial-judge-recommends-jurors-get-time-for-virtual-chitchat |access-date=27 April 2021 |agency=Bloomberg Law |publisher=Bloomberg |date= October 9, 2020}} ==References== {{Reflist}} ==Sources== * {{FJC Bio|nid=1390281}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Walter T. McGovern]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Washington]]}}|years=1988–2004}} {{s-aft|after=[[James Robart]]}} {{s-end}} {{United States 9th Circuit senior district judges}} {{Authority control}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Zilly, Thomas Samuel}} [[Category:1935 births]] [[Category:Living people]] [[Category:21st-century American judges]] [[Category:Cornell University alumni]] [[Category:Judges of the United States District Court for the Western District of Washington]] [[Category:Lawyers from Detroit]] [[Category:United States district court judges appointed by Ronald Reagan]] [[Category:United States Navy officers]] [[Category:University of Michigan alumni]]

Conrad]] | successor = | office1 = [[United States Attorney]] for the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Virginia|Western District of Virginia]] | president1 = [[Donald Trump]] | term_start1 = March 30, 2018 | term_end1 = September 15, 2020 | predecessor1 = [[John P. [[William & Mary Law School|College of William & Mary]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | party = | father = [[Richard Cullen (attorney)|Richard Cullen]] }} '''Thomas Tullidge Cullen''' (born 1977) is an American attorney who has served as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Virginia]] since 2020. He served as a [[United States attorney]] for the same district from 2018 to 2020. == Education and legal career == Cullen is a 1996 graduate of [[Collegiate School (Richmond, Virginia)|Collegiate School]] in Richmond, Virginia. He attended [[Furman University]], where he was a four-year member of its Division I Track and Field team,https://eweb.furman.edu/athletics/track_mens/archives/roster.html and received his [[Bachelor of Arts]] ''[[cum laude]]'' in 2000. He received his [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[William & Mary School of Law]] in 2004, where he was inducted into the [[Order of the Coif]]. He was a [[law clerk]] to Judge [[Robert E. Payne]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia]] from 2004 to 2005 and for Judge [[Roger Gregory]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit]] from 2005 to 2006. Cullen served as an [[assistant United States attorney]] for the [[United States District Court for the Western District of North Carolina|Western District of North Carolina]] from 2006 to 2010 and for the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Virginia|Western District of Virginia]] from 2010 to 2013, where he was Deputy Criminal Chief. Before becoming U.S. Attorney, he was a principal/partner at Woods Rogers PLC in [[Roanoke, Virginia]], from 2013 to 2018, representing clients in complex civil and criminal litigation.{{Cite web |date=February 16, 2018 |title=President Donald J. Trump Announces Eleventh Wave of United States Attorney Nominees |url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-eleventh-wave-united-states-attorney-nominees/ |access-date=February 16, 2018 |work=[[whitehouse.gov]] |via=[[NARA|National Archives]]}} {{PD-notice}}{{Cite web |title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Thomas%20Cullen%20SJQ%20-%20PUBLIC.pdf |access-date=December 11, 2022 |website=U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee}} === U.S. Attorney === Cullen was recommended as a candidate for [[United States attorney]] by Virginia [[United States Senate|Senators]] [[Mark Warner]] and [[Tim Kaine]].{{Cite web |date=July 21, 2017 |title=Cullen's son among two that Warner, Kaine recommend for top U.S. prosecutor in Roanoke |url=http://www.richmond.com/news/virginia/government-politics/cullen-s-son-among-two-that-warner-kaine-recommend-for/article_920753c5-1217-560d-a13d-c1a8198a8a09.html |access-date=February 16, 2018 |newspaper=[[Richmond Times-Dispatch]]}} On March 22, 2018, his nomination was reported out of committee by [[voice vote]].{{Cite web |title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – March 22, 2018, Senate Judiciary Committee |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%2003-22-18.pdf}} He was confirmed by [[voice vote]] later the same day.{{Cite web |date=March 22, 2018 |title=PN1656 - Nomination of Thomas T. Cullen for Department of Justice, 115th Congress (2017-2018) | Congress.gov | Library of Congress |url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/115th-congress/1656?r=21}} He was sworn in on March 30, 2018. As U.S. Attorney, Cullen directed the federal response to the deadly "Unite the Right" rally in Charlottesville, Virginia, successfully prosecuting several white supremacists who committed hate crimes and other acts of violence.{{cite news |last1=Jaffe |first1=Harry |date=August 7, 2019 |title=The Trump appointee who's putting white supremacists in jail |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/magazine/wp/2019/08/07/feature/the-trump-appointee-whos-putting-white-supremacists-in-jail/ |access-date=October 11, 2025 |newspaper=Washington Post |language=en}} His tenure as U.S. Attorney ended on September 15, 2020, when he became a federal district judge.{{Cite press release |title=U.S. Attorney Thomas T. Cullen Announces Departure |date=September 10, 2020 |publisher=United States Attorney's Office for the Western District of Virginia |location=[[Roanoke, Virginia]] |url=https://www.justice.gov/usao-wdva/pr/us-attorney-thomas-t-cullen-announces-departure |access-date=October 14, 2020}} === Federal judicial service === On December 18, 2019, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to nominate Cullen to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Virginia]].{{Cite web |title=President Donald J. Trump Announces Judicial Nominees and United States Marshal Nominees – The White House |url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-judicial-nominees-united-states-marshal-nominees/ |website=trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov}} The ABA Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary rated Cullen as a "well-qualified" nominee, its highest possible rating.{{Cite web |last=ABA Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary |date=December 15, 2020 |title=Ratings of Article III and Article IV Judicial Nominees |url=https://www.americanbar.org/content/dam/aba/administrative/government_affairs_office/webratingchart-trump116.pdf}} On February 4, 2020, his nomination was sent to the Senate. President Trump nominated Cullen to the seat vacated by Judge [[Glen E. Conrad]], who assumed [[senior status]] on December 11, 2017.{{Cite web |title=Eleven Nominations Sent to the Senate – The White House |url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/eleven-nominations-sent-senate/ |website=trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov}} On March 4, 2020, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web |title=Nominations | United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/committee-activity/hearings/03/04/2020/nominations |website=www.judiciary.senate.gov}} On May 14, 2020, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 17–5 vote.{{Cite web |title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – May 14, 2020 |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/051420%20Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting.pdf |publisher=Senate Judiciary Committee}} On September 9, 2020, the [[United States Senate]] invoked cloture on his nomination by a 77–18 vote.{{Cite web |date=September 9, 2020 |title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Thomas T. Cullen to be U.S. District Judge for the Western District of Virginia) |url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1162/vote_116_2_00163.htm |website=United States Senate}} On September 10, 2020, his nomination was confirmed by a 79–19 vote.{{Cite web |date=September 10, 2020 |title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Thomas T. Cullen, of Virginia, to be U.S. District Judge for the Western District of Virginia) |url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=2&vote=00166 |website=United States Senate}} He received his judicial commission on September 15, 2020.{{FJC Bio|nid=8869816|inline=yes}} === Notable rulings === In July 2025, the chief judge of the United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit appointed Cullen to preside over ''[[United States v. Russell (2025)|United States v. Russell]], et al.'', the Trump administration's lawsuit against all of the active and semi-retired federal district judges in Maryland.{{Cite web |last=Thomsen |first=Jacqueline |date=July 3, 2025 |title=Trump Appointee and Ex-Prosecutor to Hear DOJ's Judges Lawsuit |url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/trump-appointee-and-ex-prosecutor-to-hear-dojs-judges-lawsuit |website=[[Bloomberg Law]]}} On August 26, 2025, Cullen issued a 39-page opinion dismissing the case in favor of the judges.{{cite news |last=Rizzo |first=Salvador |date=August 26, 2025 |title=Judge dismisses DOJ lawsuit against Maryland judges over deportations |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/national-security/2025/08/26/judge-dismisses-unprecedented-doj-lawsuit-against-maryland-federal-court/ |work=[[Washington Post]]}} He concluded that the administration's suit violated the separation of powers, was prohibited by the doctrine of judicial immunity, and was not otherwise authorized by law.{{cite news |last=Feuer |first=Alan |date=August 26, 2025 |title=Judge Dismisses Trump Administration Suit Against Federal Bench in Maryland |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/08/26/us/politics/trump-suit-maryland-judges.html |website=[[The New York Times]]}} Cullen also cited numerous instances in which administration officials had publicly criticized federal judges, noting that "[a]lthough some tension between the coordinate branches of government is the hallmark of our constitutional system, this concerted effort by the Executive to smear and impugn individual judges who rule against it is both unprecedented and unfortunate."{{cite web |date=August 26, 2025 |title=United States v. Russell, et al. |url=https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.mdd.584990/gov.uscourts.mdd.584990.58.0_3.pdf |website=[[Court Listener]] |type=Memorandum Opinion}}{{Cite news |last=Cheney |first=Kyle |last2=Gerstein |first2=Josh |date=August 26, 2025 |title=Trump-appointed judge rebukes White House for 'smear' of judiciary |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2025/08/26/trump-judge-rebukes-white-house-smear-00525450 |website=Politico}} ==Book== In 2025, Cullen's debut novel, ''Charlie-Man'', was published.{{cite news |last1=McBroom |first1=Kimberly |date=October 9, 2025 |title=Federal Judge Thomas Cullen is author of coming-of-age novel |url=https://www.wdbj7.com/2025/10/09/here-home-federal-judge-thomas-cullen-is-now-author-coming-age-novel/ |access-date=October 10, 2025 |work=WDBJ7 |language=en}}{{cite news |last1=Yancey |first1=Dwayne |date=May 16, 2025 |title=Federal judge in Roanoke has a new side hustle: Author of a young adult novel. |url=https://cardinalnews.org/2025/05/16/federal-judge-in-roanoke-has-a-new-side-hustle-author-of-a-young-adult-novel/ |access-date=October 10, 2025 |work=Cardinal News}} ==Awards and honors== In 2022, Cullen was named a [[trustee]] at his alma mater, Furman University.{{Cite web |title=Board of Trustees |url=https://www.furman.edu/about/leadership/trustees/}} In 2024, he was named the Carter O. [[Harvard Law School|Harvard University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | occupation = | profession = | known_for = | salary = | net_worth = | cabinet = | committees = | portfolio = | awards = | signature = | signature_alt = | website = | footnotes = }} '''Thomas Woodrow Thrash Jr.''' (born May 8, 1951) is a [[Senior status|Senior Judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Georgia]]. == Biography == Thrash was born in [[Birmingham, Alabama|Birmingham]], [[Alabama]] in 1951. He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from the [[University of Virginia]] in 1973 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Harvard Law School]] in 1976. He was in private practice in [[Atlanta]], [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]] from 1976 to 1977. He was then an assistant district attorney of Fulton County District Attorney's Office until 1980. He resumed his private practice in Atlanta from 1981 to 1997. He was a Law professor at [[Georgia State University]] from 1986 to 1997 teaching a trial practice class. During this time, he also served as counsel to the Democratic Party of Georgia and authored ''Handbook of Georgia Campaign Finance and Disclosure Law''.{{Cite web |url=https://www.fedbar.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/ThrashAugust2007-pdf-3.pdf |title=Judicial Profile |website=[[Federal Bar Association]] |access-date=June 14, 2026}} == Federal judicial service == On January 7, 1997, Thrash was nominated by President [[Bill Clinton]] to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Georgia]] vacated by [[Robert L. Vining Jr.]] Thrash was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on July 31, 1997, and received his commission on August 1, 1997. He became Chief Judge on July 31, 2014. He assumed [[senior status]] on May 8, 2021. == Notable cases == In November 1997, Thrash ruled in favor of the Upper Chattahoochee Riverkeeper Fund in their lawsuit against the City of Atlanta for violating the Clean Water Act and the Georgia Water Quality Control Act in polluting the Chattahoochee river. As a result, the City of Atlanta paid over $3 billion to clean up the city's sewer system.{{Cite web |url=https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2013-10/documents/atlanta1998-cd.pdf |title=1998 Consent Degree |website=[[Environmental Protection Agency]] |access-date=June 14, 2026}} In June 2011, Thrash issued an injunction preventing some of an immigration law in Georgia from going into effect. The case was brought by the Georgia Latino Alliance for Human Rights and others against the Governor of Georgia, Nathan Deal, et al. Thrash struck down the portions of the law that prevented the knowing transport or shelter of illegal aliens, and allowing police to investigate the immigration status of suspects without identification.{{Cite web |url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=558742135664795508&q=NO.+1:11-CV-1804-TWT&hl=en&as_sdt=2,5 |title=Georgia Latino Alliance for Human Rights v. Deal, 793 F. Supp. 2d 1317 - Dist. Court, ND Georgia 2011 |website=[[Google Scholar]] |access-date=June 14, 2026}} Thrash oversaw the case resulting from the [[2017 Equifax data breach]] resulting in the largest settlement to date from a U.S. data breach. On January 13, 2020, Thrash granted final approval of a $1.5 billion dollar settlement that included $425 million in consumer relief and over $1 billion in mandated security upgrades.{{Cite web |url=https://www.cohenmilstein.com/case-study/re-equifax-inc-customer-data-security-breach-litigation/ |title=In Re Equifax, Inc. Customer Data Security Breach Litigation |access-date=June 14, 2026}} == Personal life == Thrash has been married since 1981 to Meg Thrash, a former practicing lawyer. They have a son and a daughter who are both writers. In 2025, Thrash published a book titled ''Shakespeare Legally Speaking: The Law in Shakespeare's Plays'' that draws upon his five decades in the legal profession to explore the law in Shakespeare's plays.{{Cite web |url=https://books.google.com/books/about/Shakespeare_Legally_Speaking.html?id=MJ6Z0QEACAAJ |title=Shakespeare Legally Speaking: The Law in Shakespeare's Plays |website=[[Google Books]] |access-date=June 14, 2026}} == Undisclosed luxury travel == In May 2024, [[NPR]] revealed that Thrash had received free travel in December 2021 to the Breakers Colloquium, a privately funded legal seminar hosted at [[The Breakers (hotel)|The Breakers]] resort in [[Palm Beach, Florida|Palm Beach]], Florida, but had failed to disclose this on his required annual financial disclosure report for that year, in violation of federal law.{{Cite web |last=Dreisbach |first=Tom |last2=Johnson |first2=Carrie |date=2024-05-01 |title=When judges get free trips to luxury resorts, disclosure is spotty |url=https://www.npr.org/2024/05/01/1247512187/federal-judges-disclosures-luxury-trips |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240501093641/https://www.npr.org/2024/05/01/1247512187/federal-judges-disclosures-luxury-trips |archive-date=2024-05-01 |access-date=2024-05-06 |website=[[NPR]]}} In response, a representative of Thrash told NPR, "No comment." In other years, Thrash did disclose reimbursements for travel to judicial conferences suggesting that the failure to report the trip to the legal seminar in 2021 was an oversight.{{Cite web |url=https://www.courtlistener.com/person/3225/disclosure/8583/thomas-w-thrash-jr/ |title=Financial Disclosures for J. '''Tiffany Mae Cartwright''' (born 1985)<ref name="Questionnaire" /> is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Washington]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.khq.com/news/president-biden-nominates-tiffany-cartwright-to-serve-as-us-district-court-judge-for-western-district/article_98376a0a-7936-11ec-ac37-8f35d06078ca.html|title=President Biden nominates Tiffany Cartwright to serve as US District Court judge for Western District of Washington|first=Bradley|last=Warren|website=KHQ Right Now|date=January 19, 2022 }}</ref>

== Early life and education ==

Cartwright was born in [[Lansing, Michigan]], and grew up in [[Kitsap County]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.afj.org/document/tiffany-m-cartwright-fact-sheet/|title=Tiffany M. Cartwright Fact Sheet|publisher=Alliance for Justice}}</ref> She earned a [[Bachelor of Arts]] from [[Stanford University]] in 2007, where she was elected to [[Phi Beta Kappa]], and a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Stanford Law School]] in 2010, where she was a member of the Stanford Supreme Court Litigation Clinic.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Warren|first=Bradley|title=President Biden nominates Tiffany Cartwright to serve as US District Court judge for Western District of Washington|url=https://www.khq.com/news/president-biden-nominates-tiffany-cartwright-to-serve-as-us-district-court-judge-for-western-district/article_98376a0a-7936-11ec-ac37-8f35d06078ca.html|access-date=January 19, 2022|website=KHQ Right Now|date=January 19, 2022 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="Questionnaire" /> She was co-editor in chief of ''Stanford Law & Policy Review'' in 2009 and 2010.<ref name="Questionnaire">{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Cartwright%20SJQ%20Public%20Final%20for%20OneDrive.pdf|title=QUESTIONNAIRE FOR JUDICIAL NOMINEES|date=January 19, 2022|publisher=[[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]]|access-date=January 19, 2026|archive-date=May 24, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220524234341/https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Cartwright%20SJQ%20Public%20Final%20for%20OneDrive.pdf|url-status=bot: unknown}}</ref> During law school, Cartwright worked at the [[federal public defender]] office in [[Seattle]] and at the [[United States Department of Justice]] [[corruption|Public Integrity]] Unit.<ref name=":0" /> She also worked as a [[research assistant]] for [[Michael W. McConnell]].<ref name="Questionnaire" />

== Career ==

From 2010 to 2012, Cartwright served as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Dana Fabe]] of the [[Alaska Supreme Court]] and for [[Betty Binns Fletcher]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]].<ref name="MHB">{{Cite web |title=Tiffany M. Cartwright | MacDonald Hoague & Bayless, Seattle Civil Rights and Immigration Attorneys |url=https://www.mhb.com/who-we-are/tiffany-m-cartwright |access-date=June 29, 2022 |website=www.mhb.com}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://got.law/attorney/tiffany-mae-cartwright/ | title=Lawyer Tiffany Mae Cartwright - Seattle, Washington | Got.Law }}</ref> From 2012 to 2014, she was an [[Associate attorney|associate]] at [[Jenner & Block]] in [[Chicago]].<ref name="Questionnaire" /><ref>{{Cite news |last=Arkin |first=James |date=May 25, 2022 |title=1st, 2nd Circ. Noms Face Few Questions From Judiciary Panel |work=Law360 |url=https://www.law360.com/articles/1496395/1st-2nd-circ-noms-face-few-questions-from-judiciary-panel}}</ref> In 2014, she joined the law firm MacDonald Hoague & Bayless in [[Seattle]], became a [[Law firm partner|partner]] in 2018 until she was commissioned as a federal judge.<ref>{{Cite web|date=January 19, 2022|title=President Biden Names Thirteenth Round of Judicial Nominees|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/01/19/president-biden-names-thirteenth-round-of-judicial-nominees/|access-date=January 19, 2022|website=The White House|language=en-US}} {{PD-notice}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-01-19 |title=President Biden nominates Tiffany Cartwright to serve as US District Court judge for Western District of Washington {{!}} FOX 28 Spokane |url=https://www.fox28spokane.com/president-biden-nominates-tiffany-cartwright-to-serve-as-us-district-court-judge-for-western-district-of-washington/ |access-date=2022-03-22 |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Notable cases ===

In 2017, Cartwright represented the family of Leonard Thomas in connection with claims that he had been wrongfully killed by the [[Lakewood, Washington|Lakewood]] police department. Following trial, a jury sided with Thomas and awarded Thomas's family $15 million in damages.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://apnews.com/article/ba24abde58bc4aa68b34e53fe0a218e3|title=$15M awarded to family of unarmed black man killed by sniper|date=July 15, 2017|website=AP NEWS}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Fowler |first=Lilly |title=After $15 million verdict, a Q&A about police shootings {{!}} Crosscut |url=https://crosscut.com/2017/07/fife-police-shooting-15-million-lawsuit-lawyers-talk |access-date=2022-07-01 |website=crosscut.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Carter |first=Mike |date=July 14, 2017 |title=Jury awards more than $15M to family of unarmed black man killed by SWAT sniper in Fife |url=https://www.seattletimes.com/seattle-news/law-justice/jury-awards-nearly-15m-to-family-of-unarmed-black-man-killed-by-swat-sniper-in-fife/ |access-date=July 12, 2022 |website=The Seattle Times |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Moreno |first=Joel |date=July 14, 2017 |title=A son remembers a dad hours after jury awards $15M in his police-shooting death |url=https://komonews.com/news/local/a-son-remembers-a-dad-hours-after-jury-awards-15m-in-his-police-shooting-death |access-date=July 12, 2022 |website=KOMO |language=en}}</ref>

In 2020, Cartwright represented the family of 17 year-old MiChance Dunlap-Gittens, who was killed by [[King County, Washington|King County]] police in a case of mistaken identity, and won a $2.25 million settlement.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://kuow.org/stories/lawsuit-settled-king-county-sheriff-s-office-and-family-of-dunlap-gittens-reach-agreement|title=King County, family of teen killed during botched sting operation reach $2.25 million settlement|first1=Ashley|last1=Hiruko|first2=Gil|last2=Aegerter|date=May 4, 2020|website=kuow.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.seattletimes.com/seattle-news/times-watchdog/deadly-sting-wrong-target-how-the-death-of-a-cops-son-led-king-county-deputies-to-kill-a-des-moines-teen/|title=Deadly sting, wrong target: How the death of a cop's son led King County deputies to kill a Des Moines teen|date=April 28, 2019|website=The Seattle Times}}</ref><ref name=":0" />

In 2021, Cartwright served as ''[[pro bono]]'' Washington state counsel for the [[Campaign Legal Center]] in ''Aguilar v. Yakima County'', a case litigated under the Washington Voting Rights Act.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Smith |first=Kate |date=October 29, 2021 |title=Judge OKs new map, rules in Yakima County voting rights settlement |url=https://www.yakimaherald.com/news/local/judge-oks-new-map-rules-in-yakima-county-voting-rights-settlement/article_d63a5522-e32e-543c-99cf-8edab7d4cf58.html |access-date=2022-02-09 |website=Yakima Herald-Republic |language=en}}</ref>

Cartwright represented several [[Exoneration|exonerees]]: a group of men in [[Fairbanks, Alaska]], known as [[The Fairbanks Four]], who spent seventeen years in prison before their exoneration for murder in 2015;<ref name=":0" /> Paul Browning, a [[capital defendant]], obtaining his release in 2019 after 33 years on Nevada's death row; and Rodney Wheeler, who was wrongfully accused of homicide and received a $500,000 settlement from King County in 2021.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-04-23 |title=King County pays $500,000 to man acquitted of murder charge |url=https://apnews.com/article/homicide-trials-lawsuits-crime-seattle-8d1faeceb47ef33b0cc8469ebcf762f1 |access-date=2022-10-25 |website=AP NEWS |language=en}}</ref>

=== Federal judicial service ===
[[File:Tiffany Cartwright (Judge).jpg|thumb|Tiffany Cartwright]]
On January 19, 2022, President [[Joe Biden]] nominated Cartwright to serve as a United States district judge of the United States District Court for the Western District of Washington.<ref name="auto">{{Cite web |last=Harrison |first=Joey |date=January 19, 2022 |title=Biden nominates Muslim woman to the federal bench, a first in US history as he diversifies the judiciary|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/2022/01/19/biden-nominate-first-muslim-woman-federal-judge/6571815001/|access-date=July 25, 2022 |website=[[USA Today]]|language=en}}</ref> The nomination came as part of the Biden administration's larger push to nominate judges with diverse backgrounds and identities.<ref name="auto"/><ref>{{Cite web |last=Brown |first=Matthew |date=March 30, 2021 |title=Biden judicial nominees represent diverse professional backgrounds, identities
|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/2021/03/30/bidens-first-judicial-nominees-bring-diverse-experiences/7058774002/|access-date=July 25, 2022 |website=[[USA Today]]|language=en}}</ref> President Biden nominated Cartwright to the seat vacated by Judge [[Benjamin Settle]], who assumed [[senior status]] on January 1, 2020.<ref>{{Cite press release |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |date=January 19, 2022 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/01/19/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-59/}}</ref> At the time she was nominated she was President Biden's youngest judicial nominee, but between her initial nomination and confirmation she was surpassed by [[Brad Garcia]] ([[United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit|D.C. Cir.]]) and [[Jamar K. Walker]] ([[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia|E.D. Va.]]).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.huffpost.com/entry/tiffany-cartwright-civil-rights-judge-biden_n_64aec337e4b03d308d98c41e|title=Senate Confirms 38-Year-Old Civil Rights Attorney To Be A Federal Judge|first=Jennifer|last=Bendery|date=July 12, 2023|accessdate=July 19, 2023|website=[[HuffPost]]}}</ref>

On May 25, 2022, a hearing on her nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Nominations |date=May 23, 2022 |publisher=[[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]] |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/05/25/2022/nominations}}</ref> On June 16, 2022, her nomination was reported out of committee by a 12–10 vote.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/EBM%20Results%20-%202022-06-16.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – June 16, 2022|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=June 16, 2022}}</ref> In addition to all Democrats on the committee, Cartwright received the support of Republican Senator [[Lindsey Graham]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Raymond |first=Nate |date=June 16, 2022 |title=U.S. Senate panel advances public defender vets up for judgeships |url=https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/us-senate-panel-advances-public-defender-vets-up-judgeships-2022-06-16/|access-date=July 25, 2022 |website=[[Reuters]]|language=en}}</ref> On January 3, 2023, her nomination was returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the Senate; Cartwright to be United States District Judge for the Western District of Washington)|website=United States Senate|date=July 11, 2023|access-date=July 11, 2023}}</ref> On July 12, 2023, her nomination was confirmed by a 50–47 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00180.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Tiffany M. [[Wake Forest University School of Law|Wake Forest University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Tiffany Rene Johnson''' (born 1986){{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/johnson_sjq.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=September 24, 2024}} is an American lawyer who serves as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Georgia]]. == Education == Johnson received a [[Bachelor of Arts]], ''[[magna cum laude]]'', from [[Princeton University]] in 2009 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Wake Forest University School of Law]] in 2012.{{Cite press release |title=President Biden Names Fifty-Third Round of Judicial Nominees |date=July 31, 2024 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2024/07/31/president-biden-names-fifty-third-round-of-judicial-nominees/ |access-date=July 31, 2024}} {{PD-notice}} == Career == From 2012 to 2017, Johnson worked as a litigation associate at the [[Atlanta]] law firm of Parker, Hudson, Rainer & Dobbs, LLP. Chase College of Law|Northern Kentucky University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | footnotes = }} '''Timothy Seymour Black''' (born August 30, 1953) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Ohio]]. == Education == Black earned a [[Bachelor of Arts]] from [[Harvard College]] in 1975 and then earned a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1983 from the [[Salmon P. Chase College of Law]] of [[Northern Kentucky University]].[http://cincinnati.com/blogs/politics/2009/12/24/obama-nominates-local-lawyer-for-judgeship "Obama nominates local lawyer for judgeship"], ''[[The Cincinnati Enquirer]]'', December 24, 2009.{{FJC Bio|nid=1393131|inline=yes}} == Career == Black practiced law as a civil litigator for the [[Cincinnati]] law firm of Graydon Head & Ritchey from 1983 until 1993. In 1991, Black unsuccessfully ran in a judicial election for the [[Hamilton County, Ohio|Hamilton County]] [[Hamilton County Courthouse (Ohio)|Municipal Court]] as a Republican.Emily Foster and Linda Vaccariello, "Rating the Judges: Municipal Court", ''[[Cincinnati Magazine]]'', September 1997. In 1993, he ran as a Democrat and defeated sitting judge David Albanese. He served as a Hamilton County Municipal Court judge from 1994–2004. He ran unsuccessfully for a seat on the Ohio Supreme Court in 2000 and 2002. === Federal judicial service === In 2004, the judges of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Ohio selected Black as a [[United States magistrate judge]].Dan Horn, [http://news.cincinnati.com/article/20091224/NEWS0107/91224013/Obama-taps-local-lawyer-for-fed-judge Obama taps local lawyer for fed judge], ''[[The Cincinnati Enquirer]]'', December 24, 2009. In July 2009, a bipartisan commission in Ohio selected Black from a list of three finalists and recommended him to President [[Barack Obama]] to fill a vacancy on the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Ohio]]. On December 24, 2009, Obama formally nominated Black to fill the district court vacancy, which was created by Judge [[Sandra Beckwith]] taking [[senior status]] on January 1, 2009. On May 11, 2010, the United States Senate confirmed Black in a unanimous voice vote. He received his commission on May 13, 2010. He assumed [[senior status]] on May 18, 2022. ==== Recognition of same-sex married couple ==== On July 22, 2013, Black ruled that Ohio must recognize the same sex marriage of John Arthur and [[James Obergefell]]. Arthur, who died on October 22, 2013,[http://www.cincinnati.com/article/20131022/NEWS0104/310220031 John Arthur and James Obergefell marriage lawsuit], cincinnati.com, October 22, 2013; accessed June 26, 2015. of [[Lou Gehrig's disease]], and Obergefell were married in Maryland, where same-sex marriage is recognized, in a ceremony on an airplane on the airport tarmac. The ruling meant the pair can be buried next to each other in Arthur's family plot, located at a cemetery that only allows descendants and spouses. Black reasoned that because Ohio recognizes out-of-state heterosexual marriages that would be prohibited in Ohio, such as marriages between first cousins or minors – including those who married outside Ohio for the sole purpose of evading its marriage laws – the state cannot single out homosexual marriages as the sole category of out-of-state marriages to which it will not grant recognition.[http://www.huffingtonpost.com/2013/07/23/ohio-gay-marriage-ruling-_n_3639296.html "Ohio Gay Couple's Marriage Must Be Recognized In State, Judge Rules"], HuffingtonPost.com, July 23, 2013; accessed June 26, 2015. In September 2013, Ohio State Representative [[John Becker (politician)|John Becker]] sent a letter to a member of the Ohio Congressional delegation asking him to initiate impeachment proceedings against Black.[https://www.advocate.com/politics/marriage-equality/2013/09/23/impeach-judge-who-ordered-ohio-recognize-gay-marriages-says], advocate.com; accessed June 26, 2015. On December 23, 2013, Black ordered Ohio to recognize same-sex marriages from other states on death certificates, deeming Ohio's ban on same-sex marriage unconstitutional.{{cite news |last=Sewell |first=Dan |date=December 23, 2013 |title=Ohio gay marriage ban is rejected in narrow ruling |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/national/ap-narrow-ruling-rejects-ohio-gay-marriage-ban/2013/12/23/3d940e7a-6bf5-11e3-a5d0-6f31cd74f760_story.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131223230741/http://www.washingtonpost.com/national/ap-narrow-ruling-rejects-ohio-gay-marriage-ban/2013/12/23/3d940e7a-6bf5-11e3-a5d0-6f31cd74f760_story.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=December 23, 2013 |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |access-date=June 26, 2015}} == Personal life == On June 17, 2017, Black's daughter, Emily, married [[Jon Favreau (speechwriter)|Jon Favreau]], a political [[podcast]]er and former [[speechwriter]] for President [[Barack Obama]], at the Black family's vacation home in [[Biddeford Pool]], [[Maine]].{{cite magazine|title=Jon Favreau's Summer Wedding in Maine|url=http://www.brides.com/story/jon-favreau-wedding-in-maine|magazine=Brides|date=July 4, 2017|last=Price Olsen|first=Anna}} == References == {{Reflist}} == Sources == *{{FJC Bio|nid=1393131}} *{{Ballotpedia|Timothy_S._Black}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Sandra Beckwith]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Ohio]]}}|years=2010–2022}} {{s-aft|after=[[Jeffery P.
