[[Harvard University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Andrew Lynn Brasher''' (born May 20, 1981{{cite web|url=https://vettingroom.org/2019/12/02/judge-andrew-brasher/ |title=Judge Andrew Brasher – Nominee to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit |publisher=The Vetting Room |date=2019-12-02 |access-date=2020-04-17}}) is a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit]] and a former [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Middle District of Alabama]]. He is a former solicitor general of Alabama. == Early life and career == Brasher received a [[Bachelor of Arts]], ''summa cum laude'', from [[Samford University]] in 2002, and a [[Juris Doctor]], ''cum laude'', from [[Harvard Law School]] in 2006, where he was a member of the ''[[Harvard Law Review]]'' and earned the Victor Brudney Prize. While in law school, Brasher was a summer associate at [[Gibson Dunn|Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher]] in 2005.{{cite web |title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees: Andrew Lynn Brasher |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/download/brasher-sjq |publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary |format=PDF |access-date=June 26, 2026}} After law school, served as a [[law clerk]] to Judge [[William H. Pryor Jr.]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit]] from 2006 to 2007. He then worked in the [[Birmingham, Alabama|Birmingham]] office of [[Bradley Arant Boult Cummings]] from 2007 to 2011. From 2011 to 2014, Brasher became Deputy Solicitor General of Alabama under state [[Attorney General of Alabama|Attorney General]] [[Luther Strange]]. He was promoted to Solicitor General in February 2014 and continued to serve in that role until his appointment as a federal district judge in 2019.{{cite web |url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-twelfth-wave-judicial-nominees-twelfth-wave-united-states-attorneys-sixth-wave-united-states-marshals/ |title=President Donald J. Trump Announces Twelfth Wave of Judicial Nominees, Twelfth Wave of United States Attorneys, and Sixth Wave of United States Marshals |date=April 10, 2018 |via=[[NARA|National Archives]] |work=[[whitehouse.gov]] |access-date=April 10, 2018 }} {{PD-notice}} == Federal judicial service == === District court service === On April 10, 2018, President [[Donald Trump]] nominated Brasher to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Middle District of Alabama]]. He was nominated to the seat vacated by Judge [[Mark Fuller (judge)|Mark Fuller]], who resigned under the threat of impeachment on August 1, 2015.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/ten-nominations-sent-senate-today-2/ "Ten Nominations Sent to the Senate Today", The White House, April 10, 2018] On June 6, 2018 a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/06/06/2018/nominations United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Nominations for June 6, 2018] On June 28, 2018, his nomination was reported out of committee by an 11–10 vote.[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%2006-28-18.pdf Results of Executive Business Meeting – June 28, 2018, Senate Judiciary Committee] On January 3, 2019, his nomination was returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]], of the [[United States Senate]]. On January 23, Trump announced his intent to renominate Brasher for a federal judgeship.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-intent-nominate-judicial-nominees/ "President Donald J. Trump Announces Intent to Nominate Judicial Nominees", White House, January 23, 2019] His nomination was sent to the Senate later that day.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/nominations-sent-senate-2/ "Nominations Sent to the Senate", White House, January 23, 2019] On February 7, 2019, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 12–10 vote.[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/02.07.2019%20Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting1.pdf Results of Executive Business Meeting – February 7, 2019, Senate Judiciary Committee]. Accessed September 7, 2022. On May 1, 2019, the Senate invoked cloture on his nomination by a 52–47 vote.[https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1161/vote_116_1_00086.htm On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture Andrew Lynn Brasher to be U.S. District Judge for the Middle District of Alabama)], United States Senate, May 1, 2019 His nomination was confirmed that same day by a 52–47 vote.[https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=1&vote=00087 On the Nomination (Confirmation Andrew Lynn Brasher, of Alabama, to be U.S. District Judge for the Middle District of Alabama)], United States Senate, May 1, 2019 He received his judicial commission on May 3, 2019.{{FJC Bio|nid=6383991|inline=yes}} He was sworn into office on May 7, 2019.{{cite web|url=http://www.almd.uscourts.gov/news/andrew-brasher-sworn-us-district-judge|title=Andrew Brasher Sworn in as US District Judge|date=May 9, 2019|website=almd.uscourts.gov|access-date=August 6, 2019|archive-date=August 7, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190807020424/http://www.almd.uscourts.gov/news/andrew-brasher-sworn-us-district-judge|url-status=dead}} His district court service terminated on June 30, 2020, when he was elevated to the court of appeals. === Court of appeals service === On November 6, 2019, President Donald Trump announced his intent to nominate Brasher to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit]].[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-judicial-nominees-8/ "President Donald J. Trump Announces Judicial Nominees" White House, November 6, 2019] {{PD-notice}} On November 21, 2019, his nomination was sent to the Senate. Trump nominated Brasher to the seat to be vacated by Judge [[Edward Earl Carnes]], who had announced his intention to assume [[senior status]] upon confirmation of a successor.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/nine-nominations-sent-senate-5/ "Nine Nominations Sent to the Senate Today", White House, November 21, 2019] A hearing on his nomination before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] was held on December 4, 2019.[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/12/04/2019/nominations Nominations for December 4, 2019] On January 3, 2020, his nomination was returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]].{{cite web|url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/116th-congress/1297|title=PN1297 - Nomination of Andrew Lynn Brasher for The Judiciary, 116th Congress (2019–2020)|date=2020-01-03|website=www.congress.gov|access-date=2020-01-04}} Later that day, he was renominated to the same seat.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/four-nominations-sent-senate-2/ "Four Nominations Sent to the Senate", White House, January 3, 2020] On January 16, 2020, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 12–10 vote.[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/011620%20Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting.pdf Results of Executive Business Meeting – January 16, 2020, Senate Judiciary Committee] On February 10, 2020, the Senate invoked [[cloture]] on his nomination by a 46–41 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=2&vote=00035|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Andrew Lynn Brasher to be United States Circuit Judge for the Eleventh Circuit)|website=www.senate.gov|access-date=2020-02-10}} On February 11, 2020, his nomination was confirmed by a 52–43 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=2&vote=00036|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Andrew Lynn Brasher, of Alabama, to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the Eleventh Circuit)|website=www.senate.gov|access-date=2020-02-11}} He received his judicial commission June 30, 2020, and he was sworn in the same day.{{cite web|url=http://www.ca11.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/courtdocs/general/ALB%20new%20judge%20press%20release.pdf|title=NEWS RELEASE|publisher=United States Court of Appeals Eleventh Judicial Circuit|date=June 30, 2020|access-date=July 1, 2020}} == Memberships == He was a member of the [[Federalist Society]] from 2003 to 2006 and again since 2008.[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Brasher%20SJQ.pdf United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees: Andrew L. [[University of Cambridge]] ([[Master of Philosophy|MPhil]])
[[Harvard University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Andrew Stephen Oldham''' (born 1978)[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Oldham%20SJQ1.pdf United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees: Andrew Oldham] is an American lawyer and jurist serving as a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]]. He was appointed in 2018 by President [[Donald Trump]]. Prior to his appointment, Oldham was the [[general counsel]] to [[Texas Governor]] [[Greg Abbott]] and an associate at the law firm [[Kellogg, Hansen, Todd, Figel & Frederick]]. == Early life and education == Oldham was born in 1978 in [[Richmond, Virginia]]. He graduated from the [[University of Virginia]] in 2001 with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] with highest honors. He then studied at the [[University of Cambridge]] on a [[Harry S. Truman Scholarship]], receiving a [[Master of Philosophy]] with [[first-class honours]] in 2002. He then attended [[Harvard Law School]], where he was an editor of the ''[[Harvard Journal of Law and Public Policy]]'' and a semi-finalist in the [[Ames Moot Court Competition]]. He graduated in 2005 with a [[Juris Doctor]], ''[[Latin honors#United States|magna cum laude]]''. == Career == After law school, Oldham was a [[law clerk]] to judge [[David B. Sentelle]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit]] from 2005 to 2006. He worked as an attorney-adviser in the [[United States Department of Justice]]'s [[Office of Legal Counsel]] from 2006 to 2008, as part of the [[George W. Bush Administration]]. He then clerked for Justice [[Samuel Alito]] of the [[Supreme Court of the United States|United States Supreme Court]] from 2008 to 2009, where he was a co-clerk with future federal judge [[Michael H. Park]].Ryan, Tim. [https://www.courthousenews.com/trump-nominates-nine-for-judicial-seats-including-four-appellate-slots/ "Trump Nominates Nine for Judicial Seats, Including Four Appellate Slots"], Courthouse News Service ([[Pasadena, California]]), February 12, 2018. Oldham entered private practice in 2009 at the law firm Kellogg, Hansen, Todd, Figel & Frederick in Washington, D.C. His practice focused on appellate litigation in federal courts of appeals throughout the country. He then served in the [[Solicitor General of Texas|Office of the Solicitor General of Texas]] as Deputy Solicitor General, where he represented Texas in federal courts across the country. In 2015, Oldham wrote an [[amicus curiae]] brief in support of Abbott's successful challenge of President [[Barack Obama]]'s [[Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals]] executive order.{{Cite web|last=Diaz|first=Kevin|date=2018-07-18|title=Gov. Abbott staffer Andrew Oldham confirmed to 5th Circuit Court of Appeals|url=https://www.houstonchronicle.com/politics/texas/article/Gov-Abbott-staffer-Andrew-Oldham-confirmed-to-13085789.php|access-date=2022-02-17|website=Houston Chronicle|language=en-US}} Prior to becoming a judge, Oldham served as general counsel to Texas governor [[Greg Abbott]],{{Cite web | url=https://gov.texas.gov/news/post/governor-abbott-names-andrew-oldham-general-counsel |title = Governor Abbott Names Andrew Oldham General Counsel}} where he advised Abbott on a range of issues under federal and state law and managed litigation in which the Governor was an interested party.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-eleventh-wave-judicial-nominees/ "President Donald J. Trump Announces Eleventh Wave of Judicial Nominees" White House, February 12, 2018] {{PD-notice}} Abbott appointed Oldham as general counsel to replace [[Jimmy Blacklock]], who left to take a seat on the [[Supreme Court of Texas]]. Oldham has been an [[adjunct professor]] at the [[University of Texas School of Law]] since 2019.[https://law.utexas.edu/faculty/andrew-s-oldham/ Andrew S Oldham, Adjunct Professor] He has been a member of the [[Federalist Society]] since 2002. == Federal judicial service == On February 12, 2018, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to nominate Oldham to an undetermined seat on the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]]. On February 15, 2018, his nomination was sent to the Senate. President Trump nominated Oldham to the seat vacated by Judge [[Edward C. Prado]], who became the [[United States Ambassador to Argentina]].Platoff, Emma. [https://www.texastribune.org/2018/02/12/donald-trump-nominates-texas-gov-greg-abbott-advisor-andrew-oldham-5th/ "Trump to nominate Abbott adviser Oldham to the 5th Circuit Court of Appeals"], ''[[Texas Tribune]]'', February 12, 2018. On April 25, 2018, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/04/25/2018/nominations United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Nominations for April 25, 2018] On May 24, 2018, his nomination was reported out of committee by an 11–10 vote.[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/05-24-18%20Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting.pdf Results of Executive Business Meeting – May 24, 2018, Senate Judiciary Committee] On July 17, 2018, the Senate invoked [[cloture]] on his nomination by a 50–49 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=115&session=2&vote=00159|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture Andrew S. Oldham, of Texas, to U.S. Circuit Judge for the Fifth Circuit)|website=www.senate.gov|access-date=July 19, 2018}} On July 18, 2018, his nomination was confirmed by a 50–49 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1152/vote_115_2_00160.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Andrew S. Oldham, of Texas, to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the Fifth Circuit)|website=www.senate.gov|access-date=July 19, 2018}} He received his judicial commission on July 19, 2018.{{FJC Bio|nid=4947641|inline=yes}} === Notable opinions === ==== ''Consumers' Research v. FCC'' (2024) ==== In July 2024, Oldham wrote the majority opinion for the Fifth Circuit, sitting [[en banc]], in ''Consumers' Research v. FCC'', holding that the funding mechanism for the [[Universal Service Fund]] violated the [[nondelegation doctrine]] because Congress had delegated taxing authority to the [[Federal Communications Commission]], which had in turn sub-delegated it to a private nonprofit administrator.{{cite web|url=https://www.ca5.uscourts.gov/opinions/pub/22/22-60008-CV2.pdf|title=Consumers' Research v. FCC, No. 22-60008 (5th Cir. July 24, 2024) (en banc)|publisher=[[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]]|date=July 24, 2024|access-date=May 28, 2026}} The ruling deepened a circuit split with the Sixth and Eleventh Circuits, which had rejected similar challenges. In a March 21, 2025, ''[[The Washington Post|Washington Post]]'' column, [[George Will]] praised the opinion and wrote that Oldham "merits promotion to a higher court."{{cite news|last=Will|first=George|title=Opinion: Congress needs a Supreme Court jolt to rein in a rampant presidency|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/2025/03/21/congress-supreme-court-fcc-trump/|access-date=May 3, 2025|work=[[The Washington Post]]|date=March 21, 2025}} On June 27, 2025, the Supreme Court reversed 6–3 in ''[[FCC v. Consumers' Research]]'', upholding the funding mechanism and rejecting Oldham's nondelegation analysis.{{cite news|last=Walker|first=Christopher J.|url=https://www.yalejreg.com/nc/what-fcc-v-consumers-research-means-for-the-future-of-the-nondelegation-doctrine/|title=What FCC v. Consumers' Research Means for the Future of the Nondelegation Doctrine|work=[[Yale Journal on Regulation]]|date=June 28, 2025|access-date=October 12, 2025}} ==== ''United States v. Sanders'' (2025) ==== In March 2025, Oldham wrote a concurring opinion in ''United States v. Sanders'', the direct criminal appeal of Thomas Sanders, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering a 12-year-old child and sentenced to death on two counts. The panel majority, written by Judge [[Priscilla Owen|Priscilla Richman]] and joined by Judge [[Leslie H. Southwick]], vacated one of the two sentences on [[double jeopardy]] grounds and otherwise affirmed. President [[Joe Biden]] had commuted Sanders' death sentences to life without parole on December 23, 2024, as part of a broader grant of clemency to 37 of the 40 inmates on federal death row.{{cite web|url=https://www.ca5.uscourts.gov/Opinions/pub/15/15-31114-CR0.pdf|title=United States v. Sanders, No. 15-31114 (5th Cir. March 27, 2025)|publisher=[[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]]|date=March 27, 2025|access-date=May 28, 2026}} In his concurrence, Oldham wrote that "questions have arisen about the flurry of last-minute pardons issued by the Biden Administration," noting that "at least one was issued by mistake" and that "some or all were allegedly effectuated via [[autopen]]." He cited [[William Blackstone]]'s ''[[Commentaries on the Laws of England]]'' for the proposition that pardons obtained when a sovereign was "deceived" or "misinformed" were historically void, and surveyed the history of the [[Federal pardons in the United States|pardon power]] dating to Anglo-Saxon practice. Oldham also questioned whether the [[Federal Death Penalty Act]] permitted the president to commute a death sentence to life without parole, as opposed to imposing some other authorized sentence on remand.{{cite web|url=https://www.ca5.uscourts.gov/Opinions/pub/15/15-31114-CR0.pdf|title=United States v. Sanders, No. 15-31114 (5th Cir. March 27, 2025) (Oldham, J., concurring)|publisher=[[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]]|date=March 27, 2025|access-date=May 28, 2026}} The concurrence drew attention because it raised the baseless autopen and competency theories then being pressed publicly by President [[Donald Trump]]{{Cite web |last=Farley |first=Robert |date=2025-03-21 |title=Trump's Baseless Autopen Claim |url=https://www.factcheck.org/2025/03/trumps-baseless-autopen-claim/ |access-date=2026-11-19 |website=FactCheck.org |language=en-US}} and acting U.S. Attorney [[Ed Martin (Missouri politician)|Ed Martin]], who had sent letters to former Biden aides questioning whether Biden was competent when he issued clemency in his final days in office.{{cite news|last=Dennie|first=Madiba K.|url=https://ballsandstrikes.org/law-politics/andrew-oldham-biden-death-penalty/|title=This Trump Judge Sure Sounds Like He Wants to Help the White House Start Executing People Again|publisher=Balls and Strikes|date=April 2, 2025|access-date=May 28, 2026}} A 2005 [[Office of Legal Counsel]] opinion under President [[George W. Bush]] had concluded that a president's use of an autopen to sign a document does not affect its legal validity. Biden later told ''[[The New York Times]]'' that he had made every clemency decision personally and that aides used the autopen to execute pre-approved lists.{{cite news|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/joe-biden/biden-defends-pardons-clemency-orders-rcna218856|title=Biden defends pardons signed by autopen: 'I made every decision'|publisher=NewsNation|date=July 13, 2025|access-date=May 28, 2026}} The Fifth Circuit denied panel rehearing on July 29, 2025.{{cite web|url=https://www.supremecourt.gov/DocketPDF/25/25A445/379500/20251014105006796_App%20B%20300-1%20Denial%20of%20Panel%20Rehearing.pdf|title=United States v. Arianna J. Freeman:
{{Short description|American judge (born 1978)}} {{Use mdy dates|date=October 2022}} {{Infobox officeholder | name = Arianna Freeman | image = Arianna Freeman.jpg | office = Judge of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit]] | appointer = [[Joe Biden]] | term_start = October 20, 2022 | term_end = | predecessor = [[Theodore McKee]] | successor = | birth_name = Arianna Julia Freeman | birth_date = {{birth year and age|1978}} | birth_place = [[Boston]], [[Massachusetts]], U.S. | death_date = | death_place = | education = [[Swarthmore College]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|BA]])
[[Yale University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Arianna Julia Freeman''' (born 1978) is an American lawyer from [[Pennsylvania]] who serves as a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit]]. == Early life and education == Freeman was born in 1978 in [[Boston]].{{cite web |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Freeman%20SJQ%20Public%20Final1.pdf |title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees |publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary |access-date=February 28, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220228185920/https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Freeman%20SJQ%20Public%20Final1.pdf |archive-date=February 28, 2022 |url-status=dead}} She received her [[Bachelor of Arts]] with honors from [[Swarthmore College]] in 2001 and earned her [[Juris Doctor]] (J.D.) in 2007 from [[Yale Law School]], where she was an editor of ''[[The Yale Journal of International Law]]''.{{Cite press release |title=President Biden Names Thirteenth Round of Judicial Nominees |date=January 19, 2022 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/01/19/president-biden-names-thirteenth-round-of-judicial-nominees/ |access-date=January 19, 2022}} {{PD-notice}} == Career == Freeman served as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[James T. Giles]] from 2007 to 2008 and Judge [[C. Darnell Jones II]] from 2008 to 2009, both on the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania]]. From 2009 to 2022, she worked at the Federal Community Defender Office including as an [[federal public defender|assistant federal defender]] as a research and writing specialist from 2009 to 2014 and in the Non-Capital Habeas Unit from 2014 to 2016. From 2016 to 2022, she was a managing attorney with the Federal Community Defender office for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania in [[Philadelphia]]. Freeman was part of the legal team handling the [[Habeas corpus in the United States|federal ''habeas corpus'']] challenge of the death sentence of [[Terry Williams (murderer)|Terrance Williams]]; the appeal prevailed at the [[United States Supreme Court]].{{Cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/legal/litigation/gop-criticizes-biden-judicial-nominees-defense-death-row-inmate-2022-03-02/|title=GOP criticizes Biden judicial nominee's defense of death row inmate|first1=Nate|last1=Raymond|newspaper=Reuters |date=March 2, 2022|via=www.reuters.com}} === Federal judicial service === On January 19, 2022, President [[Joe Biden]] announced his intent to nominate Freeman to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] for the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit]]. President Biden nominated Freeman to the seat vacated by Judge [[Theodore McKee]], who on July 29, 2021, notified the White House that he intended to assume [[senior status]] upon confirmation of his successor.{{Cite press release|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate|date=January 19, 2022 |publisher=The White House|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/01/19/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-59/}} On January 28, 2022, following Justice [[Stephen Breyer]]'s announcement of his intention to retire as an [[Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States]], Freeman was mentioned as one of the potential nominees for a Supreme Court appointment by President [[Joe Biden]].{{Cite web|last=de Vogue|first=Ariane|title=White House considering wider list of Supreme Court nominees|url=https://www.cnn.com/2022/01/29/politics/growing-supreme-court-nominee-list/index.html|access-date=January 30, 2022|website=CNN|date=January 29, 2022 }} On March 2, 2022, a hearing on her nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web|title=Nominations|date=February 28, 2022|publisher=[[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]]|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/03/02/2022/nominations}} During her confirmation hearing, Republican senators criticized her work as a public defender.{{cite news|last=Wagner|first=Rose|title=Four tapped for federal courts advance, but 3rd Circuit nominee is stuck|url=https://www.courthousenews.com/four-tapped-for-federal-courts-advance-but-3rd-circuit-nominee-is-stuck/}} On April 4, 2022, the committee failed to report her nomination by an 11–11 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/EBM%20Results%20-%202022-04-04.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – April 4, 2022|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=April 4, 2022}} On June 22, 2022, the [[United States Senate]] discharged the committee from further consideration of her nomination by a 50–48 vote.{{Cite web|date=June 22, 2022|title=On the Motion to Discharge (Motion to Discharge: Arianna J. Freeman, to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the Third Circuit from the Committee on the Judiciary)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1172/vote_117_2_00236.htm|access-date=June 23, 2022|publisher=United States Senate}} On September 6, 2022, Majority Leader [[Chuck Schumer]] filed [[cloture]] on her nomination.{{Cite web |title=PN1684 — Arianna J. Freeman — The Judiciary |url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/117th-congress/1684 |access-date=2023-07-24 |website=Congress.gov}} On September 12, 2022, the Senate invoked cloture on her nomination by a 45–44 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1172/vote_117_2_00332.htm|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Arianna J. Freeman to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the Third Circuit)|date=September 12, 2022|website=[[United States Senate]]|access-date=September 12, 2022}} On September 13, 2022, the Senate rejected her nomination by a 47–50 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1172/vote_117_2_00333.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Arianna J. Freeman, of Pennsylvania, to be United States Circuit Judge for the Third Circuit)|date=September 13, 2022|website=[[United States Senate]]|access-date=September 13, 2022}} Freeman was the first Biden judicial nominee to be rejected by the Senate.{{Cite web|url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/us-senate-fails-to-confirm-biden-appellate-pick-freeman|title=Confirmation Failure a First for Biden on Judicial Nominees (2)|website=news.bloomberglaw.com}} On September 29, 2022, upon reconsideration, her nomination was confirmed by a 50–47 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1172/vote_117_2_00350.htm|title= On the Nomination (Upon Reconsideration, Confirmation: Arianna J. Freeman, of Pennsylvania, to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the Third Circuit)|date=September 29, 2022|website=[[United States Senate]]|access-date=September 29, 2022}} She received her judicial commission on October 20, 2022.{{FJC Bio|nid=12588691|inline=yes}} She is the first [[African-American]] woman to serve on the Third Circuit.{{Cite web|last=Alder|first=Madison|date=January 19, 2022|title=Biden Nominee Would be First Black Woman on Third Circuit (Corrected)|url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/biden-to-tap-naacp-ldf-gibson-dunn-lawyers-for-judgeships|access-date=January 19, 2022|website=news.bloomberglaw.com|language=en}}{{Cite web|last=DeJesus|first=Ivey|date=January 19, 2022|title=Biden nominates first Black woman, a Philadelphia public defender, to federal appeals court serving Pennsylvania|url=https://www.mcall.com/news/pennsylvania/mc-nws-pa-black-woman-judge-nomination-20220119-drc2ue5fg5gargithypo7ckzi4-story.html|access-date=January 19, 2022|website=mcall.com}} ====Notable rulings==== On July 17, 2026, Freeman authored the majority opinion in ''Association of New Jersey Rifle and Pistol Clubs Inc. v. Davenport'', which held that New Jersey's bans on [[semi-automatic rifle]]s and [[large capacity magazine]]s violated the [[Second Amendment to the United States Constitution]].{{cite news |last1=Schonfeld |first1=Zach |title=Appeals court says NJ’s AR-15, high-capacity magazine bans violate Second Amendment |url=https://thehill.com/regulation/court-battles/5975022-3rd-circuit-new-jersey-assault-weapons-magazine-ban/amp/ |access-date=July 19, 2026 |agency=The Hill |date=July 17, 2026}} == See also == * [[List of African American federal judges]] * [[List of African American jurists]] * [[Joe Biden judicial appointment controversies]] * [[Joe Biden Supreme Court candidates]] == References == {{Reflist}} == External links == *{{FJC Bio|nid=12588691}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Theodore McKee]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit]]}}|years=2022–present}} {{s-inc}} {{s-end}} {{United States courts of appeals judges}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Freeman, Arianna J.}} [[Category:1978 births]] [[Category:Living people]] [[Category:21st-century African-American lawyers]] [[Category:21st-century American lawyers]] [[Category:21st-century American women judges]] [[Category:African-American judges]] [[Category:Judges of the United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit]] [[Category:Lawyers from Boston]] [[Category:Pennsylvania lawyers]] [[Category:Public defenders]] [[Category:Swarthmore College alumni]] [[Category:United States court of appeals judges appointed by Joe Biden]] [[Category:Yale Law School alumni]]

[[Columbia University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Barbara Lagoa''' (born November 2, 1967){{cite web |url=https://www.mynews13.com/content/dam/News/static/FL/pdfs/Lagoa-Barbara-Application.pdf |title=Application of Barbara Lagoa to the Florida Supreme Court Judicial Nominating Commission |date=2018 |work=Florida Supreme Court Judicial Nominating Commission |access-date=September 24, 2020}} is an American attorney and jurist serving as a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit]]. Prior to becoming a [[federal judge]], she was the first [[Latino (demonym)|Latina]] and [[Cuban American]] woman appointed to serve as a justice of the [[Supreme Court of Florida]].{{cite news|first=David|last=Ovalle|url=https://www.miamiherald.com/news/politics-government/article224069530.html|title=Miami's Barbara Lagoa is the next Florida Supreme Court justice|newspaper=[[The Miami Herald]]|date=January 9, 2019}}{{cite web |url= https://fedsoc.org/contributors/barbara-lagoa|title=Federalist Society Contributor: Barbara Lagoa|website=fedsoc.org|date=December 13, 2021 }} In 2020, Lagoa was a finalist to succeed [[Ruth Bader Ginsburg]] as an [[Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States|associate justice]] of the [[Supreme Court of the United States]], which ultimately went to [[Amy Coney Barrett]].{{cite web |url=https://www.cnn.com/2020/09/26/politics/trump-supreme-court-barrett-lagoa/index.html|title=How Trump picked Amy Coney Barrett over Barbara Lagoa for the Supreme Court | CNN Politics |website=[[CNN]] |date=September 26, 2020 }}{{cite web |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/news/latino/barbara-lagoa-cuban-american-federal-judge-potential-trump-supreme-court-n1240588|title=In Miami, buzz over Cuban American judge Barbara Lagoa as potential Trump Supreme Court pick |website=[[NBC News]] |date=September 21, 2020 }} == Early life and education == Lagoa was born in [[Miami]], Florida, in 1967.{{cite web |last1=Voruganti |first1=Harsh |title=Justice Barbara Lagoa – Nominee to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit |url=https://vettingroom.org/2019/11/15/justice-barbara-lagoa/ |website=Vetting Room |date=November 15, 2019|access-date=21 September 2020}} Her parents, Antonio and Araceli Lagoa, were [[Cuba]]n immigrants who fled Cuba following the [[Cuban Revolution]] and the assumption of power by [[Fidel Castro]].{{Cite news|first=Michael|last=Van Sickler|url=https://www.tampabay.com/news/florida-politics/2020/09/19/trump-considering-this-florida-justice-to-replace-ruth-bader-ginsburg/|title=Trump considering this Florida justice to replace Ruth Bader Ginsburg|newspaper=[[Tampa Bay Times]]|date=September 19, 2020}} She grew up in the majority [[Cuban-American]] city of [[Hialeah, Florida]].{{Cite web |url=http://wusfnews.wusf.usf.edu/post/desantis-picks-female-cuban-american-states-high-court|title=DeSantis Picks Female Cuban-American For State's High Court|website=wusfnews.wusf.usf.edu|date=January 9, 2019 }} She is bilingual in [[English language|English]] and [[Spanish language|Spanish]].{{cite news |last1=Kelley |first1=Eileen |title=Five things to know about Barbara Lagoa, rumored to be on Trump's short list for Supreme Court |url=https://www.sun-sentinel.com/news/politics/fl-ne-five-things-you-should-know-barbara-lagoa-20200920-biurrw7w4najrnrjwifeyztinm-story.html |access-date=21 September 2020 |newspaper=Florida Sun Sentinel |date=September 20, 2020}} Lagoa studied [[English literature]] at [[Florida International University]], graduating in 1989 with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] ''[[Latin honors#United States|cum laude]]'' and [[Phi Kappa Phi]] membership. She then attended [[Columbia Law School]], where she was an associate editor of the ''[[Columbia Law Review]]''. She graduated with a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1992. == Career == === Early career === After law school, Lagoa returned to Miami and entered private practice at the law firm [[Morgan, Lewis & Bockius]]. From 1998 to 2003, she was an associate at [[Greenberg Traurig]]. In 2000, Lagoa was one of a dozen lawyers who mostly ''[[pro bono]]'' represented the Miami family of [[Elián González]].{{cite news|first1=Alfonso|last1=Chardry|first2=Jay|last2=Weaver|url=http://www.latinamericanstudies.org/elian/rival.htm|title=Rival campaigns helping to pay for lawyers in Elian case |newspaper=[[The Miami Herald]]|date=May 5, 2000|via=[[Latin American Studies]]}} In 2003, Lagoa became an [[assistant United States attorney]] for the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida|Southern District of Florida]], working in the Civil, Major Crimes, and Appellate Sections. === Florida Supreme Court === Lagoa was appointed to the Third District Court of Appeal by Governor [[Jeb Bush]] in June 2006, and became chief judge on January 1, 2019.{{cite web|url=https://www.3dca.flcourts.org/Judges/31-Lagoa.shtml|title=Biography of Judge Barbara Lagoa|website=www.3dca.flcourts.org|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070728085316/https://www.3dca.flcourts.org/Judges/31-Lagoa.shtml|archive-date=July 28, 2007}}{{cite web|url=https://www.floridasupremecourt.org/Justices/Former-Justices/Justice-Barbara-Lagoa|title=Justice Barbara Lagoa|website=floridasupremecourt.org|access-date=September 24, 2020}} On January 9, 2019, she was appointed to the Supreme Court of Florida by Governor [[Ron DeSantis]]. She was the first Hispanic woman and the first Cuban-American woman to sit on the Florida Supreme Court.{{Cite web|first1=Devan|last1=Cole|first2=Ariane|last2=de Vogue|first3=Katelyn|last3=Polantz|title=Meet Barbara Lagoa, one of Trump's top contenders for the Supreme Court|url=https://www.kctv5.com/news/us_world_news/meet-barbara-lagoa-one-of-trumps-top-contenders-for-the-supreme-court/article_7379d60c-dd40-5171-a648-3dcbd75a1f0d.html|access-date=2020-09-22|website=KCTV Kansas City|language=en}} In April 2019, Lagoa wrote for the unanimous court when it found that DeSantis had acted within his authority by suspending Sheriff [[Scott Israel]] for his response to the [[Stoneman Douglas High School shooting]].{{cite news |last1=Fineout |first1=Gary |last2=Atterbury |first2=Rew |title=Florida Supreme Court upholds suspension of embattled Broward sheriff |url=https://www.politico.com/states/florida/story/2019/04/23/florida-supreme-court-upholds-suspension-of-embattled-broward-sheriff-985820 |date=April 23, 2019|access-date=September 21, 2020 |work=[[Politico]] |language=en}}{{cite court |litigants=Israel v. DeSantis |vol=269 |reporter=So. 3d |opinion=491 |court=Fla. |date=2019 |url= https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=13362342622779053401 }} In November 2019, Lagoa participated in oral arguments concerning an [[advisory opinion]] on whether the governor could require felons whom voters had re-enfranchised through [[2018 Florida Amendment 4]] to pay fines before being allowed to vote.{{cite news | author-link = Mark Joseph Stern | last = Stern |first1=Mark Joseph |title=Two Trump Judges Broke Ethics Rules to Stop Up to 1 Million Floridians From Voting in November |url=https://slate.com/news-and-politics/2020/07/11th-circuit-florida-fines-fees-judicial-ethics.html |access-date=21 September 2020 |work=[[Slate Magazine]] |date=22 July 2020 |language=en}}{{cite web |title=SC19-1341 Advisory Opinion to the Governor Re: Implementation of Amendment 4, (Voting Restoration) |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jbsNFmdZnEk |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211221/jbsNFmdZnEk |archive-date=2021-12-21 |url-status=live|website=[[YouTube]] | date=November 12, 2019 |publisher=Florida Supreme Court |access-date=21 September 2020}}{{cbignore}} Lagoa resigned her position when she was appointed to the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit]].{{cite web|url=https://www.flgov.com/2019/01/09/what-they-are-saying-florida-leaders-react-to-governor-ron-desantis-appointment-of-barbara-lagoa-to-the-florida-supreme-court/|title=What They Are Saying: Florida Leaders React to Governor Ron DeSantis' Appointment of Barbara Lagoa to the Florida Supreme Court|date=January 9, 2019|website=flgov|access-date=January 10, 2019|archive-date=October 20, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201020231611/https://www.flgov.com/2019/01/09/what-they-are-saying-florida-leaders-react-to-governor-ron-desantis-appointment-of-barbara-lagoa-to-the-florida-supreme-court/|url-status=dead}} === Federal judicial service === On September 12, 2019, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to nominate Lagoa to a seat on the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit]].{{Cite web|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-judicial-nominees-5/|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Donald J. Trump Announces Judicial Nominees}} She was nominated to the seat being vacated by Judge [[Stanley Marcus (judge)|Stanley Marcus]].{{Cite web|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/twenty-five-nominations-three-withdrawals-sent-senate/|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Twenty-five Nominations and Three Withdrawals Sent to the Senate}} On October 15, 2019, her nomination was sent to the Senate.{{cite web |title=Pres. Nom. 1171 |date=November 20, 2019 |url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/116th-congress/1171 |publisher=116th Cong. (2019)}} On October 16, 2019, a hearing on her nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/10/16/2019/nominations|title=Nominations | United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|website=www.judiciary.senate.gov|date=October 16, 2019 }} On November 7, 2019, her nomination was reported out of committee by an 18–4 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%20November%207%202019.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business – November 7, 2019, Senate Judiciary Committee}} On November 19, 2019, the [[United States Senate|Senate]] invoked [[cloture]] on her nomination by an 80–15 vote,{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=1&vote=00359|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Barbara Lagoa to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the Eleventh Circuit)|date=November 19, 2019|website=[[United States Senate]]|access-date=November 19, 2019|language=en}} and on November 20, 2019, her nomination was confirmed by an 80–15 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=1&vote=00360|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Barbara Lagoa to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the Eleventh Circuit)|date=November 20, 2019|website=[[United States Senate]]|access-date=November 20, 2019|language=en}} She received her judicial commission on December 6, 2019.{{FJC Bio|nid=7395471|inline=yes}} In July 2020, Democratic members of the Senate Judiciary Committee wrote directly to Lagoa to urge her to [[recuse]] herself from a challenge to [[felon disenfranchisement in Florida]] because of her earlier participation in a related matter on the Florida Supreme Court. Lagoa and her fellow Judge [[Robert Luck]] declined to recuse themselves: "An objective, disinterested lay person, knowing that we asked questions in a different proceeding (advisory vs. case-and-controversy), in a different court (Florida Supreme Court vs. federal court), with different issues (interpreting the state constitution vs. federal constitutional questions), and with different participants (“interested persons” vs. parties), would not reasonably entertain a significant doubt about our impartiality in this case."{{Cite web|last=Moline|first=Michael|date=July 27, 2020|title=Judges Lagoa, Luck refuse to withdraw from appeal affecting felon voting rights in FL|url=https://www.floridaphoenix.com/2020/07/27/judges-lagoa-luck-refuse-to-withdraw-from-appeal-affecting-felon-voting-rights-in-fl/|website=Florida Phoenix}}{{Cite web|title=Order|url=https://www.ca11.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/enbanc_cases/20-12003%20Order%20%28Recusals%29.pdf}} In September 2020, Lagoa joined the majority when the ''[[en banc]]'' circuit by a 6-4 vote upheld the constitutionality of the law that the Florida legislature had passed, which required re-enfranchised felons to pay all financial obligations, including fines, fees, and restitution before being allowed to vote.{{cite news |last1=Mazzei |first1=Patricia |title=Ex-Felons in Florida Must Pay Fines Before Voting, Appeals Court Rules |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/09/11/us/florida-felon-voting-rights.html |access-date=21 September 2020 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=11 September 2020}} Lagoa joined Chief Judge [[William H. Pryor Jr.]]'s majority opinion, joined Pryor's additional concurrence, and authored her own concurrence.{{cite news |last1=Kennedy |first1=John |last2=Wolf |first2=Richard |title=Trump eyes Cuban American judge from Florida for Supreme Court |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/2020/09/19/supreme-court-latina-judge-barbara-lagoa-eyed-possible-nominee/5840189002/ |access-date=21 September 2020 |work=[[USA Today]]}}{{cite web |title=''Jones v. Governor of Florida'' |url=https://media.ca11.uscourts.gov/opinions/pub/files/202012003.enb.pdf |publisher=No. 20-12003 (11th Cir. Sept. 11, 2020).}} In December 2022, Lagoa wrote the en banc court's majority opinion finding that a high school's bathroom policy, which separated bathrooms on the basis of biological sex, does not violate the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment or Title IX.{{cite web |title=''Adams v. School Board of St. Johns County'' |url=https://media.ca11.uscourts.gov/opinions/pub/files/201813592.2.pdf |publisher=No. 18-13592 (11th Cir. Dec. 30, 2022).}} Lagoa separately wrote a special concurrence to "discuss the effect that a departure from a biological understanding of 'sex' under Title IX—i.e., equating 'sex' to 'gender identity' or 'transgender status'—would have on girls’ and women's rights and sports." On August 21, 2023, Lagoa authored an opinion vacating a district court's preliminary injunction and allowing section 4(a)(1)-(3) of Alabama's Vulnerable Child Compassion and Protection Act to go into effect.{{cite web |title=''Eknes-Tucker v. Governor'' |url=https://media.ca11.uscourts.gov/opinions/pub/files/202211707.pdf |publisher=No. 22-11707 (11th Cir. Aug. 21, 2023)}} Section 4(a)(1)-(3) makes it a crime in Alabama to "engage in or cause" the prescription or administration of puberty blockers or cross-sex hormones to individuals under the age of 19 "for the purpose of attempting to alter the appearance of or affirm the minor's perception of his or her gender or sex, if that appearance or perception is inconsistent with the minor's sex." In allowing the law to take effect, Lagoa found it unlikely that the Constitution protects an unenumerated right of parents to treat their children with transitioning medications. She also held that the law does not amount to sex discrimination. ==== Potential Supreme Court nomination ==== On September 9, 2020, Trump included Lagoa on a list of [[Donald Trump Supreme Court candidates|potential nominees]] to the [[United States Supreme Court]].{{Cite web|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefings-statements/remarks-president-trump-judicial-appointments/|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Remarks by President Trump on Judicial Appointments}} After the death of [[Ruth Bader Ginsburg]] on September 18, 2020, Lagoa was mentioned as one of several frontrunners to fill the vacancy created by Ginsburg's death.{{Cite web|first1=Carrie|last1=Johnson|first2=Tamara|last2=Keith|title=Sources: Trump Considers Barrett, Lagoa, Rushing For Supreme Court Spot|url=https://www.npr.org/sections/death-of-ruth-bader-ginsburg/2020/09/19/914829456/sources-trump-considers-coney-barrett-lagoa-thapar-for-supreme-court-spot|date=September 19, 2020|access-date=September 20, 2020|website=[[NPR]]|language=en}}{{Cite web|first1=Richard|last1=Wolf|first2=John|last2=Kennedy|title=Trump eyes Cuban American judge from Florida for Supreme Court|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/2020/09/19/supreme-court-latina-judge-barbara-lagoa-eyed-possible-nominee/5840189002/|date=September 19, 2020|access-date=September 20, 2020|newspaper=[[USA Today]]|language=en-US}}{{Cite web|last=Semones|first=Evan|title=What you need to know about Barbara Lagoa|url=https://www.politico.com/news/2020/09/19/what-you-need-to-know-about-barbara-lagoa-418437|date=September 19, 2020|access-date=September 20, 2020|website=[[Politico]]|language=en}} ''[[The Washington Post]]'' reported that colleagues, friends, and scholars who have followed Lagoa's career describe her as "quiet and collegial, with shrewd political instincts." Her potential nomination to the United States Supreme Court was supported by a broad cross-section of Florida Republicans. Lagoa and her husband have built up "years of goodwill... in Florida's legal and political circles." Had she been successfully nominated, she would have been the first Supreme Court justice from Florida. On September 26, 2020, President Trump nominated [[Amy Coney Barrett]] to the United States Supreme Court.[https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-us-canada-54312699 BBC News, report published 26 September 2020] Barrett was confirmed in October of that year. == Personal life == Lagoa is married to lawyer Paul C. Huck Jr., and her father-in-law is [[United States federal judge|United States District Judge]] [[Paul Huck]], a [[Bill Clinton]] appointee. She and her husband have three daughters, including a set of twins.{{cite web |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2020/09/19/what-you-need-to-know-about-barbara-lagoa-418437 |title=What you need to know about Barbara Lagoa |first=Evan |last=Semones |date=September 19, 2020 |website=[[Politico]]}}{{cite news |last1=Stanley-Becker |first1=Isaac |last2=Davis |first2=Aaron |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/barbara-lagoa-supreme-court/2020/09/20/364d73e4-fb50-11ea-b555-4d71a9254f4b_story.html |title=Barbara Lagoa, Cuban American judge, rises on Trump's Supreme Court list as allies emphasize Florida campaign edge |access-date=21 September 2020 |newspaper=Washington Post |date=September 20, 2020}} Lagoa is a practicing [[Roman Catholic]], and cites [[Catholic [[University of Chicago]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Benjamin Michael Flowers''' (born March 19, 1987) is an American lawyer who served as the 10th [[Solicitor General of Ohio]]. He is known for his work in appellate litigation and has represented several cases before the [[Supreme Court of the United States]]. Flowers has been recognized for his legal writing and has received awards including the Best Brief Award from the [[Ohio State Bar Association]] and from the National Association of Attorneys General. He is a judge on the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit]]. == Early life and education == Flowers was born on March 19, 1987, and raised in [[Harwinton, Connecticut]]. He graduated from [[Lewis S. Mills High School]] in 2005. He earned a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[Ohio State University]] in 2009, graduating [[Latin honors|''summa cum laude'']] in the arts and sciences with research distinction in philosophy. In 2012, he received his [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Chicago Law School]], graduating [[Order of the Coif]].{{Cite web |last=By |date=2005-06-22 |title=LEWIS S. MILLS HIGH SCHOOL CLASS OF 2005 |url=https://www.courant.com/2005/06/22/lewis-s-mills-high-school-class-of-2005/ |access-date=2025-04-15 |website=Hartford Courant |language=en-US}}{{cite web|url=https://www.ohioattorneygeneral.gov/About-AG/Service-Divisions/Appeals/Who-We-Are/Benjamin-Flowers|title=Benjamin M. Flowers|publisher=ohioattorneygeneral.com|access-date=June 26, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190823192723/https://www.ohioattorneygeneral.gov/About-AG/Service-Divisions/Appeals/Who-We-Are/Benjamin-Flowers|archive-date=2019-08-23|url-status=dead}}{{cite web |last=Flowers |first=Benjamin Michael |date=April 16, 2026 |title=Senate Judiciary Committee Questionnaire |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/flowers_sjq.pdf |website=www.judiciary.senate.gov |location= |publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary |access-date=April 23, 2026}} == Career == === Early career === Following law school, Flowers served as a [[law clerk]] to Judge [[Sandra Segal Ikuta]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]] and later to Justice [[Antonin Scalia]] of the [[Supreme Court of the United States]]. After his clerkships, Flowers joined the law firm [[Jones Day]] at its [[Columbus, Ohio|Columbus]] office,{{Cite web|url=https://www.martindale.com/attorney/benjamin-m-ben-flowers-168828544/|title=Benjamin Michael Flowers | Lawyer at Jones Day|website=martindale.com}} where he focused on [[appellate]] [[litigation]]. === Solicitor General of Ohio === In 2019, Flowers was appointed [[Solicitor General of Ohio]]. In this role, he represented the state in [[appellate court]]s, including the Supreme Court of the United States, the [[Supreme Court of Ohio|Ohio Supreme Court]], and the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit]]. His work frequently involved matters of [[federalism]] and state sovereignty.{{Cite web |date=2023-09-29 |title=Ohio's solicitor general moves on after arguing big cases involving abortion, other state policy |url=https://www.statenews.org/government-politics/2023-09-29/ohios-solicitor-general-moves-on-after-arguing-big-cases-involving-abortion-other-state-policy |access-date=2025-04-15 |website=The Statehouse News Bureau |language=en}} One of his most high-profile cases was ''[[National Federation of Independent Business v. Occupational Safety and Health Administration]]'' (commonly referred to in Ohio filings as ''Ohio v. OSHA''), in which the Supreme Court stayed a federal rule requiring large employers to mandate [[COVID-19]] vaccinations or testing for employees, holding that [[Occupational Safety and Health Administration|OSHA]] lacked the authority to impose such a requirement.{{Cite web |date=2022-01-07 |title=Justice Sotomayor Claims Not to Understand the Distinction Between State and Federal Powers |url=https://www.nationalreview.com/news/justice-sotomayor-claims-not-to-understand-the-distinction-between-state-and-federal-powers/ |access-date=2025-04-15 |website=National Review |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |date=2022-01-07 |title=Ohio solicitor general makes anti-vax mandate case to Supreme Court remotely after getting Covid |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/supreme-court/ohio-solicitor-general-makes-anti-vax-case-supreme-court-remotely-n1287158 |access-date=2025-04-15 |website=NBC News |language=en}}{{Cite web |last=Sabrina Eaton |first=cleveland com |date=2022-01-07 |title=U.S. Supreme Court hears Ohio challenge to Biden administration workplace coronavirus mandates |url=https://www.cleveland.com/news/2022/01/us-supreme-court-hears-ohio-challenge-to-biden-administration-workplace-coronavirus-mandates.html |access-date=2025-04-15 |website=cleveland |language=en}} Flowers also argued on behalf of the state in other notable cases, including ''[[Shoop v. Twyford]]'' and ''Ohio Adjutant General v. FLRA''. In ''Preterm-Cleveland v. McCloud'', he defended an Ohio law prohibiting abortions based on a diagnosis of [[Down syndrome]]. The United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit upheld the law, marking the first time a federal [[appellate court]] deemed such a restriction constitutional.{{Cite web |title=Supreme Court Hears Arguments in Death Penalty Cases that Could Limit Access to Federal Court Review |url=https://deathpenaltyinfo.org/supreme-court-hears-arguments-in-death-penalty-cases-that-could-limit-access-to-federal-court-review |access-date=2025-04-15 |website=Death Penalty Information Center |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |title=Administrative Deference in Ohio, by John Kerkhoff |url=https://www.yalejreg.com/nc/administrative-deference-ohio/ |access-date=2025-04-15 |website=Yale Journal on Regulation |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |last=Tebben |first=Susan |date=2023-09-28 |title=Should abortion law be paused while court case continues? Ohio Supreme Court weighs arguments. • Ohio Capital Journal |url=https://ohiocapitaljournal.com/2023/09/28/should-abortion-law-be-paused-while-court-case-continues-ohio-supreme-court-weighs-arguments/ |access-date=2025-04-15 |website=Ohio Capital Journal |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |date=2023-09-27 |title=Ohio wants to revive a strict abortion law. Justices are weighing the legal arguments |url=https://apnews.com/article/abortion-ohio-b4c582e669c70bddafb29f5b65b19810 |access-date=2025-04-15 |website=AP News |language=en}} In ''TWISM Enterprises, LLC v. State Board of Registration for Professional Engineers & Surveyors'', Flowers represented the [[Ohio Attorney General]] as [[amicus curiae]], arguing that Ohio courts are not required to defer to state administrative agencies' interpretations of statutes. The Supreme Court of Ohio agreed, establishing a precedent regarding [[judicial review]] of administrative agency interpretations.{{Cite web |last=Shows |first=Casemine |date=2024-10-16 |title=Twism Enterprises v. State Board: Ohio Supreme Court Limits Agency Deference in Statutory Interpretation |url=https://www.casemine.com/commentary/us/twism-enterprises-v.-state-board:-ohio-supreme-court-limits-agency-deference-in-statutory-interpretation/view |access-date=2025-04-15 |website=Casemine |language=en}} In 2020, Flowers received the [[Ohio State Bar Association]]'s "Best Brief Award" for outstanding [[legal writing]]{{Cite web |title=Litigation Section Best Brief Award - Ohio Law {{!}} OSBA |url=https://www.ohiobar.org/about-us/awards-scholarships/litigation-section-best-brief-award/ |access-date=2025-04-15 |website=www.ohiobar.org}} and in 2023, the National Association of Attorneys General's Best Brief Award for excellence in work before the [[Supreme Court of the United States]].{{Cite web |last=Schneider |first=Staci |date=2023-10-11 |title=National Association of Attorneys General Announces Winners for 2023 Supreme Court Best Brief Awards |url=https://www.naag.org/press-releases/national-association-of-attorneys-general-announces-winners-for-2023-supreme-court-best-brief-awards/ |access-date=2025-04-15 |website=National Association of Attorneys General |language=en-US}} === Return to private practice === In October 2023, Flowers stepped down as Ohio Solicitor General and joined the law firm Ashbrook Byrne Kresge LLC,{{Cite web |date=2023-10-02 |title=Solicitor General Chat: Ohio SG Ben Flowers Talks Departure |url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/litigation/solicitor-general-chat-ohio-sg-ben-flowers-talks-departure |access-date=2025-06-26 |website=Bloomberg Law |language=en}} which is now known as Ashbrook Byrne Kresge Flowers LLC.{{Cite web |date=2025-06-25 |title=These Small Conservative Law Firms Are Raking In Business |url=https://www.wsj.com/us-news/law/trump-small-conservative-maga-law-firms-2e7b29e7?gaa_at=eafs&gaa_n=ASWzDAjCfHElrZAVfqF0FVi53I3MW3v_M_L2epSjXu75jA35Ntyd1TSdOoiQ&gaa_ts=685d8b5f&gaa_sig=Q3N6o1R_fHGiaK1xCRKqqI2NG-InYGBE8u_ZkZ0egbbFy8kMOba7Vtvyal5eb5F4PHlAbS_0itldT05rkVym1Q%3D%3D |access-date=2025-06-26 |website=Wall Street Journal |language=en}} === Federal judicial service === On April 9, 2026, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intention to nominate Flowers to an unspecified seat on the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit]].{{Cite web|url=https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/116377358457034052|title=Donald J. Trump (@realDonaldTrump)|website=Truth Social}} On April 27, 2026, Trump nominated Flowers to the seat on the Sixth Circuit being vacated by [[Jeffrey Sutton]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/119th-congress/938/1|title=PN938-1 - Nomination of Benjamin M. Flowers for The Judiciary, 119th Congress (2025-2026)|date=April 27, 2026|website=www.congress.gov}} On June 18, 2026, the Judiciary Committee advanced his nomination on a 12–10 party line vote. On July 20, 2026, the Senate invoked cloture on his nomination by a 43–40 vote. On July 22, 2026, the Senate confirmed his nomination by a 49–46 vote. He received his judicial commission on October 2, 2026.{{FJC Bio|nid=13762147|inline=yes}} ==Personal== Flowers is married to Denise Vendeland and has three children.{{Cite web|url=https://fedsoc.org/bio/benjamin-flowers|title=Benjamin M. [[University of Chicago]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Beth Robinson''' (born 1965) is an American lawyer and judge from [[Vermont]]. She is a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit]] and is the first openly lesbian judge to serve on any federal court of appeals. Robinson served as an associate justice of the [[Vermont Supreme Court]] from 2011 to 2021. Robinson was born in [[Karachi]], Pakistan, and she was raised and educated in [[Indiana]]. She graduated from [[Dartmouth College]] ([[Bachelor of Arts]], 1986) and the [[University of Chicago Law School]] ([[Juris Doctor]], 1989). After serving as a law clerk for a federal judge, Robinson joined [[Vermont]]'s Langrock, Sperry & Wool law firm, where she was active on cases related to workers' compensation, personal injury, and constitutional law. Robinson became active in the movement for expanded rights for gays and lesbians, and served as co-counsel in the case of ''[[Baker v. State]]'', the 1999 decision that led to Vermont passing the first [[civil unions in Vermont|civil unions]] law. As chair of the Vermont Freedom to Marry organization, Robinson was a high-profile supporter of [[same-sex marriage]], and worked with leaders of the [[Vermont General Assembly]] on passage of the 2009 [[Marriage Equality Act (Vermont)|Marriage Equality Act]]. After working on [[Peter Shumlin]]'s successful campaign for governor in 2010, Robinson joined his staff as legal counsel, a position which included drafting and analyzing proposed legislation and regulations, making recommendations on whether to approve requests for pardons, and ensuring compliance with ethics rules. In 2011, Shumlin appointed Robinson as an associate justice of the [[Vermont Supreme Court]]. She served until 2021, when she resigned after having been confirmed as a judge on the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit]]. == Early life and education == Robinson was born in [[Karachi]], [[Pakistan]], in 1965, the daughter of Dr. Robert D. Robinson Jr. and Cynthia (Pittenger) Robinson.{{cite news |date=August 7, 1952 |title=Robert Robinson To Wed Cynthia Pittenger August 24 |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/89977129/robinson-pittenger/ |work=[[Indianapolis News]] |location=Indianapolis, IN |page=24 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}{{cite news |date=January 23, 1972 |title=Hospital Ball Promises To Be An Adventure: Mrs. Robert (Cynny) Robinson |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/89976820/cynny-robinson/ |work=The Times-Mail |location=Bedford, IN |page=13 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}{{cite web |url=https://vettingroom.org/tag/justice-beth-robinson/ |title=Justice Beth Robinson – Nominee to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit |date=August 16, 2021 |website=The Vetting Room |publisher=Harsh Voruganti |location=Arlington, VA}}{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Robinson%20SJQ%20Public%20FINAL.pdf |title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees |publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|location=Washington, D.C. |access-date=September 13, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210914021919/https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Robinson%20SJQ%20Public%20FINAL.pdf |archive-date=September 14, 2021 |url-status=dead}} Robinson's father worked in Pakistan at the time of her birth, and she was raised in [[Indiana]].{{cite journal |last1=Robinson |first1=Robert D. Jr. |display-authors=et al. |date=October 1966 |title=Acute Rheumatic Fever in Karachi, Pakistan |url=https://ur.booksc.eu/book/15777140/beb398 |journal=The American Journal of Cardiology |volume=18 |issue=4 |pages=548–551 |doi=10.1016/0002-9149(66)90009-9|pmid=5923981 |url-access=subscription }} In 1982, she graduated from [[Brebeuf Jesuit Preparatory School]] in [[Indianapolis]].{{cite news |date=May 28, 1982 |title=County's No. 1 Seniors Planning Careers |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/86161914/seniors-robinson/ |work=[[Indianapolis News]] |location=Indianapolis, IN |page=8 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}{{cite magazine |editor-last=Fitzgerald |editor-first=Jennifer (Infanger) |date=Spring 2010 |title=Alumni Notes: Beth Robinson '82 |url=https://issuu.com/brebeufjesuit/docs/bylines_spring_2010/34 |magazine=Brebeuf Bylines |location=Indianapolis, IN |publisher=Brebeuf Jesuit Preparatory School |page=32 |via=Issuu.com}} While at Brebeuf, Robinson was a member of the basketball and tennis teams, the French club, and the orchestra. She won honors in mathematics contests and won the Optimist's Club's oratorical contest. At graduation, Robinson was named a [[National Merit Scholarship Program|National Merit Scholar]]. In 1986, Robinson received her [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in [[philosophy]] and [[government]] from [[Dartmouth College]], and she graduated ''[[summa cum laude]]'' and [[Phi Beta Kappa]].{{cite magazine |last1=Bonauto |first1=Mary |last2=Murray |first2=Susan M. |last3=Robinson |first3=Beth |date=1999 |title=The Freedom to Marry for Same-Sex Couples: The Opening Appellate Brief of Plaintiffs Stan Baker Et Al. In Baker Et Al. V. State of Vermont |url=https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/232697976.pdf |magazine=Michigan Journal of Gender & Law |location=Ann Arbor, MI |publisher=University of Michigan Law School Scholarship Repository |page=1}}{{cite magazine |date=May–June 2019 |title=Words of Wisdom: Eighteen alums offer new graduates advice to live by |url=https://dartmouthalumnimagazine.com/articles/words-wisdom |magazine=Dartmouth Alumni Magazine |location=Hanover, NH |publisher=Dartmouth College}}{{cite news |last=Olinick |first=Michael |date=January 1, 2010 |title=Vermonter of the Year nominations for Beth Robinson |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/86191296/vermonter-robinson/ |work=[[The Burlington Free Press]] |location=Burlington, VT |page=4A |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} During 1985, she spent a semester abroad as a student at the [[University of Edinburgh]]. Robinson graduated from the [[University of Chicago Law School]] with a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1989, and was admitted to the [[Order of the Coif]].{{cite news |last=Galloway |first=Anne |date=October 18, 2011 |title=Gay marriage activist named to Vermont Supreme Court |url=https://vtdigger.org/2011/10/18/robinson_appointed_vt_supreme_court/ |work=VT Digger |location=Montpelier, VT}}{{cite web |url=https://lawreview.vermontlaw.edu/wp-content/uploads/2012/02/lawday.pdf |title=Dartmouth College Law Day Panel: Introduction, Beth Robinson |last=Donin |first=Robert |date=December 15, 2009 |website=Vermontlaw.edu |publisher=Vermont Law School |location=South Royalton, VT |access-date=October 4, 2021 |page=1}} She was a recipient of the [[Floyd R. Mechem House|Mechem]] Prize, a full merit scholarship. While in law school, Robinson was a member of the ''[[University of Chicago Law Review]]''{{cite journal |editor-last1=Eisgruber |editor-first1=Christopher L. |date=Winter 1988 |title=Front Matter |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1599768 |journal=The University of Chicago Law Review |volume=55 |issue=1 |page=Title |jstor=1599768 |jstor-access=free}} and then served as an associate editor.{{cite journal |editor-last1=Barry |editor-first1=James T. |date=Winter 1989 |title=Front Matter |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1599685 |journal=The University of Chicago Law Review |volume=56 |issue=1 |page=Title |jstor=1599685 |jstor-access=free}} == Legal career == After graduating from law school, Robinson was a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[David B. Sentelle]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit]] from 1989 to 1990.{{cite news |last1=Heintz |first1=Paul |last2=Duffort |first2=Lola |date=August 5, 2021 |title=Biden names Justice Beth Robinson, a champion of marriage equality, to federal appellate court |url=https://vtdigger.org/2021/08/05/biden-names-justice-beth-robinson-to-federal-appellate-court/ |work=VT Digger |location=Montpelier, VT}} She was an [[associate attorney]] at [[Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom]] of [[Washington, D.C.]] from 1990 to 1991 and self employed as an attorney under contract by [[Philip Hirschkop|Hirschkop]] & Associates of [[Alexandria, Virginia]] from 1992 to 1993. Robinson was employed for 18 years at Langrock, Sperry & Wool, a law firm with offices in [[Burlington, Vermont|Burlington]] and [[Middlebury, Vermont|Middlebury]]. While there, she worked on issues of workers' compensation, personal injury, constitutional law and, most prominently, gay and lesbian rights.{{cite news|url=http://www.addisonindependent.com/201011miller-gets-post-shumlin-cabinet|title=Miller gets post in Shumlin cabinet|date=November 24, 2010|work=[[Addison County Independent]]|access-date=November 2, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190103065656/http://www.addisonindependent.com/201011miller-gets-post-shumlin-cabinet|archive-date=January 3, 2019|url-status=dead}} Robinson served as co-counsel in the case of ''[[Baker v. State]]'', the landmark 1999 decision that led to Vermont becoming the first state to enact [[civil unions in Vermont|civil unions]].{{cite news|url=http://www.legalnewsline.com/news/234200-vermont-gov-appoints-counsel-to-supreme-court|title=Vermont gov appoints counsel to supreme court|date=October 24, 2011|work=Legal Newsline}} She was subsequently involved in the 2009 legislative battle to enact [[same-sex marriage]], chairing the Vermont Freedom to Marry advocacy organization and working closely with [[Peter Shumlin]], a prominent supporter of same-sex marriage, who was then [[President pro tempore of the Vermont Senate|President ''pro tempore'']] of the [[Vermont Senate]].{{cite news|url=http://www.wcax.com/story/15721381/governor-appoints-beth-robinson-to-vt-supco|title=Governor appoints Beth Robinson to Vt SupCo|work=[[WCAX]]|date=October 18, 2011|access-date=November 2, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111020053841/http://www.wcax.com/story/15721381/governor-appoints-beth-robinson-to-vt-supco|archive-date=October 20, 2011|url-status=dead}} In addition to practicing law, Robinson has also taught at the college level. She was a senior lecturer at Dartmouth College during the 2006 summer term and again during the 2009 spring term. Robinson served as a [[Justice of the peace#Vermont|justice of the peace]] for the town of Ferrisburgh from 2003 to 2011. In 2008, she was a delegate to the [[2008 Democratic National Convention|Democratic National Convention]] and pledged to support [[Hillary Clinton]]. From 1999 to 2010, Robinson served on the Vermont Board of Bar Examiners. She was an associate member from 1999 to 2003, and an examiner from 2003 to 2009. From 2009 to 2010 she served as the board's vice chair, and she served as chair in 2010. Robinson was active in Shumlin's successful [[2010 Vermont gubernatorial election|2010 gubernatorial campaign]], then joined his administration as his general counsel. == Judicial career == === Vermont Supreme Court === On October 18, 2011, Shumlin announced he was appointing Robinson to the [[Associate Justice]]'s seat on the [[Vermont Supreme Court]] that had been vacated by [[Denise R. Johnson]]'s retirement in August 2011.{{cite news |date=October 19, 2011 |title=Beth Robinson Appointed to Vermont Supreme Court|url=https://vtbarfoundation.org/news/beth-robinson-appointed-to-vermont-supreme-court/|work=Vermont Bar Foundation News|publisher=Vermont Bar Foundation|location=Montpelier, VT}} Since the Senate was not in session at the time, Robinson's appointment was considered interim until the Senate convened and acted upon her nomination.{{cite web|url=http://www.leg.state.vt.us/statutes/const2.htm|title=Vermont Constitution, Section 33}} She was sworn in as an interim member of the court on November 28, 2011.{{cite news|url=http://www.burlingtonfreepress.com/article/20111128/NEWS03/111128020/Same-sex-marriage-advocate-joins-Vermont-Supreme-Court|archive-url=https://archive.today/20130118162949/http://www.burlingtonfreepress.com/article/20111128/NEWS03/111128020/Same-sex-marriage-advocate-joins-Vermont-Supreme-Court|url-status=dead|archive-date=January 18, 2013|title=Same-sex marriage advocate joins Vermont Supreme Court|date=November 28, 2011|work=[[The Burlington Free Press]]}} The Senate voted on her nomination on February 7, 2012, and approved [[Harvard University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Bradley Nelson Garcia''' (born 1986){{cite web |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Garcia%20SJQ%20Public%20Final.pdf |title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees |publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary |access-date=July 26, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220726193703/https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Garcia%20SJQ%20Public%20Final.pdf |archive-date=July 26, 2022 |url-status=dead}} is an American lawyer and jurist serving as a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit]]. He was an official at the [[United States Department of Justice]] from 2022 to 2023. == Education == Garcia was born in 1986 in [[Gaithersburg, Maryland]]. He graduated from [[Johns Hopkins University]] in 2008 with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] in [[international relations|international studies]] and [[economics]],{{Cite web|title=2017 Washington DC Career Conference|url=https://www.practicepro.cc/2017-washington-dc-career-conference/|access-date=June 15, 2022|website=PracticePro|archive-date=July 26, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220726194045/https://www.practicepro.cc/2017-washington-dc-career-conference/|url-status=live}} where he also was president of the university's chapter of the [[Pi Kappa Alpha]] fraternity.{{Cite news|last=Cushing|first=Marie|date=February 22, 2008|title=Wawa, Pike may be forced to relocate - University repeals sophomore housing exemption for fraternity members|work=[[The Johns Hopkins News-Letter]]|url=https://www.jhunewsletter.com/article/2008/02/wawa-pike-may-be-forced-to-relocate-university-repeals-sophomore-housing-exemption-for-fraternity-me|access-date=June 15, 2022|archive-date=July 26, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220726193956/https://www.jhunewsletter.com/article/2008/02/wawa-pike-may-be-forced-to-relocate-university-repeals-sophomore-housing-exemption-for-fraternity-me|url-status=live}} Garcia then attended [[Harvard Law School]], where he was an editor of the ''[[Harvard Law Review]]''. He graduated in 2011 with a [[Juris Doctor]], [[Latin honors#United States|''magna cum laude'']].{{Cite news |date=June 15, 2022|title=President Biden Names Nineteenth Round of Judicial Nominees|work=[[The White House]]|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/06/15/president-biden-names-nineteenth-round-of-judicial-nominees/|access-date=June 15, 2022|archive-date=June 15, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220615143117/https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/06/15/president-biden-names-nineteenth-round-of-judicial-nominees/|url-status=live}} == Career == After law school, Garcia was a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Thomas B. Griffith]] of the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit from 2011 to 2012 and for Associate Justice [[Elena Kagan]] of the [[Supreme Court of the United States|United States Supreme Court]] from 2012 to 2013. After his clerkships, Garcia entered private practice at the law firm [[O'Melveny & Myers]] in 2013, becoming a [[partner (business rank)|partner]] in 2020. Garcia practiced [[appellate law]] with a client list that included [[Google]], [[Warner Bros.]], and the [[Ford Motor Company]].{{Cite news|last=Rubin|first=Jordan S.|date=March 24, 2021|title=They've Got Next: Appellate Fresh Face Brad Garcia|work=[[Bloomberg Law]]|url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/theyve-got-next-appellate-fresh-face-brad-garcia|access-date=June 15, 2022}}{{cite news|first=|last=|title=Appointments|newspaper=[[Washington Post]]|page=A11|date=December 28, 2020}} Garcia argued more than a dozen times before federal and state appeals courts, including before the United States Supreme Court in a 2021 immigration case, ''[[United States v. Palomar-Santiago]]''.{{Cite web|url=https://www.law.com/nationallawjournal/2022/06/15/latest-biden-nominees-would-be-first-latino-on-dc-circuit-first-women-of-color-on-5th-circuit/|title=Latest Biden Nominees Would Be First Latino on DC Circuit, First Women of Color on 5th Circuit|website=National Law Journal|access-date=2022-06-15}}{{Cite web |title=United States v. Palomar-Santiago |url=https://www.oyez.org/cases/2020/20-437 |access-date=2023-11-30 |website=Oyez |language=en}} Other cases he practiced included the fields of [[criminal law]], [[corporate law]], [[insurance law|insurance coverage]], [[patent rights]], and [[federal jurisdiction]].{{cite web | url=https://www.omm.com/news/press-releases/former-o-melveny-partner-brad-garcia-nominated-to-us-court-of-appeals-for-the-dc-circuit/ | title=Former O'Melveny Partner Brad Garcia Nominated to U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit - O'Melveny }} In February 2022, Garcia left private practice to serve as a deputy assistant attorney general in the [[United States Department of Justice]]'s [[Office of Legal Counsel]].{{Cite news |last=Scarcella |first=Mike |date=February 4, 2022 |title=Appellate law veteran at O'Melveny leaves for DOJ legal counsel post |work=[[Reuters]] |url=https://www.reuters.com/legal/litigation/appellate-law-veteran-omelveny-leaves-doj-legal-counsel-post-2022-02-04/ |access-date=June 15, 2022 |archive-date=June 15, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220615144658/https://www.reuters.com/legal/litigation/appellate-law-veteran-omelveny-leaves-doj-legal-counsel-post-2022-02-04/ |url-status=live }} He left in 2023 when he became a federal judge. === Notable cases === Garcia was part of the legal team representing [[El Paso County, Texas]], in a suit challenging the diversion of [[United States Department of Defense]] funds to build a [[border wall]].{{cite web | url=https://www.law360.com/articles/1399938/high-court-vacates-border-wall-case-after-construction-halt | title=High Court Vacates Border
