represented a man seeking better mental health treatment in a [[Pennsylvania]] prison.{{cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/dc-md-va/2022/06/15/dc-circuit-bradley-garcia/ |title=Biden nominee would be first Latino on federal appeals court in D.C. |date=2022-06-15 |author1=Rachel Weiner |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |place=Washington, D.C. |issn=0190-8286 |oclc=1330888409 |access-date=2022-06-15 |archive-date=2022-06-16 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220616132254/https://www.washingtonpost.com/dc-md-va/2022/06/15/dc-circuit-bradley-garcia/ |url-status=live }} A unanimous panel of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit]] ruled in favor of the prisoner.{{cite web|url=https://www2.ca3.uscourts.gov/opinarch/191684p.pdf|title=CASEY DOOLEY v. JOHN WETZEL; KEVEN KAUFMAN; RICHARD A. GOSS|website=2.ca3.uscourts.gov|access-date=July 24, 2022|archive-date=March 4, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220304184631/https://www2.ca3.uscourts.gov/opinarch/191684p.pdf|url-status=live}} In 2019, Garcia was co-counsel for Jason Daniel Sims, who pleaded guilty to being a felon in possession of a firearm, in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1). Sims was sentenced as an armed [[career criminal]], and he appealed. The [[Armed Career Criminal Act]] ("ACCA") imposes a mandatory fifteen-year minimum sentence on a defendant convicted of being a felon in possession of a firearm or ammunition who has three or more previous convictions for violent felonies or serious drug offenses. 18 U.S.C. § 924(e)(1). The district court designated Sims an armed career criminal based on four convictions: two [[Arkansas]] residential [[burglaries]] and two serious drug offenses. Sims appealed, arguing that his previous Arkansas burglary convictions do not qualify as violent felonies and that he therefore lacks the three or more convictions necessary to qualify as an armed career criminal.{{cite web | url=https://casetext.com/case/united-states-v-sims-156?q=Bradley%20N%20Garcia&sort=relevance&p=2&type=case&tab=keyword&jxs= | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220911223058/https://casetext.com/case/united-states-v-sims-156?q=Bradley%20N%20Garcia&sort=relevance&p=2&type=case&tab=keyword&jxs= | url-status=dead | archive-date=September 11, 2022 | title=United States v. Sims, 933 F.3d 1009 | Casetext Search + Citator }}{{Cite web|url=https://www.courthousenews.com/supreme-court-backs-expansive-burglary-definition-in-career-criminal-case/|title=Supreme Court Backs Expansive Burglary Definition in Career-Criminal Case|website=www.courthousenews.com}} In 2020, Garcia was the counsel of record in ''[[June Medical Services, LLC v. Russo]]'', challenging [[Louisiana]]'s law requiring doctors who perform abortions to have [[admitting privilege]]s at a local hospital.{{cite web | url=https://thehill.com/homenews/senate/3847743-graham-under-fire-for-voting-for-biden-judicial-nominees/ | title=Graham under fire for voting for Biden judicial nominees | date=7 February 2023 }}{{cite web | url=https://abcnews.go.com/Politics/louisiana-abortion-case-day-supreme-court/story?id=69366374 | title=Louisiana abortion case may hinge on Supreme Court Chief Justice Roberts | website=ABC News }}{{cite web |title=The Louisiana Clinic At The Center Of Abortion Case Before Supreme Court |website=[[NPR]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230413185405/https://www.npr.org/2019/12/29/791514162/the-louisiana-clinic-at-the-center-of-abortion-case-before-supreme-court |archive-date=2023-04-13 |url-status=live |url=https://www.npr.org/2019/12/29/791514162/the-louisiana-clinic-at-the-center-of-abortion-case-before-supreme-court}} In 2022, Garcia was co-counsel for Bel Air Auto Auction, Inc. in their lawsuit against Great Northern Insurance Company. Bel Air's claims stemmed from Great Northern's denial of insurance benefits Bel Air asserts Great Northern owed it to cover business loss Bel Air incurred during the [[COVID-19 pandemic]].{{cite web | url=https://casetext.com/case/bel-air-auto-auction-inc-v-great-n-ins-co-1?q=Bradley%20N%20Garcia&sort=relevance&p=1&type=case&tab=keyword&jxs= | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220911223057/https://casetext.com/case/bel-air-auto-auction-inc-v-great-n-ins-co-1?q=Bradley%20N%20Garcia&sort=relevance&p=1&type=case&tab=keyword&jxs= | url-status=dead | archive-date=September 11, 2022 | title=Bel Air Auto Auction, Inc. Great Northern Insurance Company|website=www.law360.com}} === Federal judicial service === On June 15, 2022, President [[Joe Biden]] nominated Garcia to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] for the [[United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit]]. he was renominated later the same day.{{Cite press release |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |date=January 3, 2023 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2023/01/03/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-91/}} On February 2, 2023, his nomination was reported out of committee by an 11–9 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/EBM%20Results%20-%202023-02-021.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – February 2, 2023|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=February 2, 2023}} On May 9, 2023, Majority Leader [[Chuck Schumer]] filed [[cloture]] on his nomination.{{Cite web |title=PN93 - Nomination of Bradley N. '''Bridget Anne Shelton Bade''' ({{nee|'''Shelton'''}}; born 1965)<ref>{{cite book |last=Hubbell |first=Martindale |date=April 1997 |title=Martindale-Hubbell Law Directory |url=https://archive.org/details/martindalehubbel01newp |publisher=[[Martindale-Hubbell]] |page=AZ162B |isbn=9781561602223}}</ref><ref name="Questionnaire">[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Bade%20SJQ.pdf United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees: Bridget Shelton Bade]</ref><ref>Hubbell, p. AZ162B</ref> is an American lawyer and jurist from [[Arizona]]. She is a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]]. She was formerly a [[United States magistrate judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Arizona]].

== Early life and career ==

Bade earned her [[Bachelor of Arts]], ''[[summa cum laude]]'', from the [[Arizona State University]] in 1987, and her [[Juris Doctor]], ''[[cum laude]]'', from its [[Sandra Day O'Connor College of Law]] in 1989. She served as an articles editor of the ''Arizona State Law Journal''. 

After graduating from law school, Bade clerked for Judge [[Edith Jones]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]] from 1990 to 1991. Bade served for four years as a trial attorney in the Environmental Torts Section of the [[United States Department of Justice Civil Division]] from 1991 to 1995. She was later a [[shareholder]] at Beshears Wallwork Bellamy in [[Phoenix, Arizona]], where her practice focused on [[civil litigation]]. Bade then spent a year as special counsel in the [[Phoenix, Arizona]] office of [[Steptoe & Johnson]]. Following her years in private practice, Bade was an [[Assistant United States Attorney]] for the [[United States District Court for the District of Arizona|District of Arizona]] for six years from 2006 to 2012.<ref name="WHBio">{{cite web |url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-seventeenth-wave-judicial-nominees/ |title=President Donald J. Trump Announces Seventeenth Wave of Judicial Nominees |date=August 27, 2018 |via=[[NARA|National Archives]] |work=[[whitehouse.gov]] |access-date=August 27, 2018 }} {{PD-notice}}</ref>

== Federal judicial service ==
=== Magistrate judge tenure ===
Bade served as a [[United States magistrate judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Arizona]], a position she was appointed to in 2012, and left in 2019 when she became a circuit judge.<ref name="WHBio" /><ref>{{cite web |title=United States Court for the Ninth Circuit - 2012 Annual Report |url=https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/judicial-council/publications/AnnualReport2012.pdf#page=19}}</ref>

=== Court of appeals service ===
On August 27, 2018, President [[Donald Trump]] nominated Bade to serve as a United States circuit judge of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]].<ref name="WHBio" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/115th-congress/2449|title=PN2449 — Bridget S. Bade — The Judiciary|date=August 27, 2018|website=[[United States Senate]]|access-date=August 27, 2018|language=en}}</ref> She was nominated to the seat vacated by [[Barry G. Silverman]], who assumed senior status on October 11, 2016. On October 24, 2018, a hearing on her nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].<ref>[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/10/24/2018/nominations United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Nominations for October 24, 2018]</ref>

On January 3, 2019, her nomination was returned to the president under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]]. On January 23, 2019, President Trump announced his intent to renominate Bade for a federal judgeship.<ref>[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-intent-nominate-judicial-nominees/ "President Donald J. Trump Announces Intent to Nominate Judicial Nominees", White House, January 23, 2019]</ref> Her nomination was sent to the Senate later that day.<ref>[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/nominations-sent-senate-2/ "Nominations Sent to the Senate", White House, January 23, 2019]</ref> On February 7, 2019, her nomination was reported out of committee by a 17–5 vote.<ref>[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/02.07.2019%20Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting.pdf Results of Executive Business Meeting – February 7, 2019, Senate Judiciary Committee]</ref> On March 25, 2019, the Senate invoked cloture on her nomination by a 77–20 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=1&vote=00050|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture on the Nomination of Bridget S. Bade, of Arizona, to be United States Circuit Judge for the Ninth Circuit)|date=March 25, 2019|website=[[United States Senate]]|access-date=March 25, 2019|language=en}}</ref> On March 26, 2019, her nomination was confirmed by a 78–21 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=1&vote=00051|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Bridget S. Bade, of Arizona, to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the Ninth Circuit)|date=March 26, 2019|website=[[United States Senate]]|access-date=March 26, 2019|language=en}}</ref> She received her judicial commission on April 1, 2019.<ref>{{FJC Bio|nid=6202901|inline=yes}}</ref> 

In September 2020, President Trump included Bade on his list of potential nominees to the [[United States Supreme Court]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Castaneda Perez |first1=Jose-Ignacio |title=Who is Bridget Bade, the Phoenix native on Trump's list of potential Supreme Court picks? |url=https://www.azcentral.com/story/news/politics/arizona/2020/09/11/bridget-bade-trump-list-possible-supreme-court-nominees/3470481001/ |access-date=1 December 2020 |work=The Arizona Republic |date=September 11, 2020}}</ref>

=== Notable rulings ===
On March 30, 2021, Bade and [[Milan Smith]] held in a 2-1 ruling that [[California Governor]] [[Gavin Newsom]]'s restrictions on private gatherings, which limited indoor and outdoor gatherings to three households at a time, were constitutional. A [[Bible study group]] had sued Newsom on account of religious discrimination, but the majority held that religious gatherings were not being treated any differently than non-religious gatherings.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/politics/newsom-s-restrictions-on-private-gatherings-pass-court-s-muster/ar-BB1f8xVb|title=Newsom's restrictions on private gatherings pass court's muster|website=San Francisco Chronicle|date=March 30, 2021}}</ref>

'''William Earl Britt''' (born December 7, 1932) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of North Carolina]].

==Education and career==

Britt was born in [[McDonald, North Carolina]]. He is the younger brother of [[David M. Britt]]. He received a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree from [[Wake Forest University]] in 1956 and a [[Bachelor of Laws]] from [[Wake Forest University School of Law]] in 1958. He was in the [[United States Army]] (SP-4) from 1953 to 1955. He was a [[law clerk]] for Justice [[Emery B. Denny]] of the [[North Carolina Supreme Court]] from 1958 to 1959. He was in private practice of law in [[Fairmont, North Carolina|Fairmont]] and [[Lumberton, North Carolina|Lumberton]], North Carolina from 1959 to 1980.<ref name="auto">{{FJC Bio|265|nid=1378291|name=William Earl Britt<!--(1932–)-->}}</ref>

===Federal judicial service===
Britt was nominated by President [[Jimmy Carter]] on April 14, 1980, to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of North Carolina]] vacated by Judge [[John Davis Larkins Jr.]] He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on May 21, 1980, and received his commission on May 23, 1980. He served as chief judge from 1983 to 1990. Britt assumed [[senior status]] on December 7, 1997.<ref name="auto"/> As of 2020, Britt is the last judge for the Eastern District of North Carolina to be appointed by a Democratic president.{{citation needed|date=May 2024}}

Urbana-Champaign]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''William Frederic Jung''' (born 1958) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Middle District of Florida]]. == Early life, education, and career == Jung was born in 1958 in [[Fort Belvoir]], [[Virginia]].{{Cite web |url=http://www.lawyercentral.com/william-f-jung-interactive-profile--20-181995.html |title=Lawyer Central profile |access-date=April 29, 2016 |archive-date=September 1, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180901080550/https://www.lawyercentral.com/william-f-jung-interactive-profile--20-181995.html |url-status=dead }} He received a [[Bachelor of Arts]], [[magna cum laude]], in 1980 from [[Vanderbilt University]], where he was elected to [[Phi Beta Kappa]] and was a member of [[Kappa Sigma]] fraternity (Kappa chapter). He received a [[Juris Doctor]], [[summa cum laude]] in 1983 from the [[University of Illinois College of Law]], where he was editor in chief of the ''Illinois Law Review'', [[Order of the Coif]], and class [[valedictorian]]. He began his legal career as a [[law clerk]] to Judge [[Gerald Bard Tjoflat]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit]], from 1983 to 1984. From 1984 to 1985, he served as a [[law clerk]] to [[Associate Justice]] [[William Rehnquist]] of the [[Supreme Court of the United States]].[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Jung%20Senate%20Questionnaire.pdf Judicial Questionnaire for William Jung], Committee on the Judiciary, U.S. Senate. No date. Retrieved January 10, 2017. In 1983, he became a member of the Florida Bar with the highest score in the First Appellate District. From 1985 to 1987, he was an associate in the [[Tampa, Florida|Tampa]], [[Florida]], office of [[Carlton Fields]]. Jung served as an [[Assistant United States Attorney]] for six years, first in the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida|Southern District of Florida]], from 1987 to 1990, and subsequently in the [[United States District Court for the Middle District of Florida|Middle District of Florida]], from 1990 to 1993. Before becoming a judge, he was a partner at the law firm of Jung & Sisco, P.A. (formerly Black & Jung, P.A.) in Tampa, Florida, which he co-founded in 1993. He specialized in [[white-collar criminal]] defense and complex [[civil litigation]].[https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2016/04/28/president-obama-nominates-eight-serve-united-states-district-courts "President Obama Nominates Eight to Serve on United States District Courts" White House, April 28, 2016] In 2017 Florida Trend Magazine inducted Jung into its "Florida Legal Elite Hall of Fame."digital.floridatrend.com/publication/?m=28897&i=417354&p=80&ver=html5 Jung has published approximately thirty articles in [[legal publications]].{{cite journal|last1=Jung|first1=William F.|title=The Last Unlikely Hero: Gerald Bard Tjoflat and the Jacksonville Desegregation Crisis — 35 Years Later|journal=Florida Bar Journal|date=March 2006|volume=80|issue=3|page=10|url=https://www.floridabar.org/divcom/jn/jnjournal01.nsf/Author/A0D88491D60EFD6B8525712300520F30|access-date=January 10, 2017}} == Federal judicial service == === Expired district court nomination under Bush === On July 10, 2008, President [[George W. Bush]] nominated Jung to serve as a [[United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Middle District of Florida]], to the seat vacated by [[Susan C. Bucklew]], who assumed [[senior status]] on August 1, 2008. No action was taken on his nomination and it expired on January 2, 2009, with the end of the [[110th United States Congress|110th Congress]].{{cite web|url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/110th-congress/1846|title=PN1846 — William Frederic Jung — The Judiciary|last=|first=|date=July 10, 2008|website=[[United States Senate]]|access-date=August 31, 2018|language=en}} === Expired district court nomination under Obama === On April 28, 2016, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Jung to serve as a United States District Judge of the United States District Court for the Middle District of Florida, to the seat vacated by Judge [[Anne C. Conway]], who assumed [[senior status]] on August 1, 2015. His nomination expired on January 3, 2017, with the end of the [[114th United States Congress|114th Congress]].[https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2016/04/28/presidential-nominations-sent-senate-0 "Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate" White House, April 28, 2016] === Renomination to district court under Trump === On December 20, 2017, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to nominate Jung to serve as a United States district judge of the United States District Court for the Middle District of Florida.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-ninth-wave-judicial-nominees-tenth-wave-united-states-attorney-nominees/ "President Donald J. Trump Announces Ninth Wave of Judicial Nominees and Tenth Wave of United States Attorney Nominees" White House, December 20, 2017] {{PD-notice}} On December 21, 2017, his nomination was sent to the [[United States Senate]]. '''William Francis Kuntz II''' (born June 24, 1950) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York]].

== Early life and education ==
Born in [[New York City]], Kuntz graduated from [[Fordham Preparatory School]] in 1968, and earned an [[Bachelors of Arts|Artium Baccalaureus]] in 1972 from [[Harvard College]].<ref name=whgov_20110309>{{cite web | author=The White House: Office of the Press Secretary | url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2011/03/09/president-obama-nominates-william-francis-kuntz-ii-united-states-distric | title=President Obama Nominates William Francis Kuntz, II to the United States District Court | date=March 9, 2011 | via=[[NARA|National Archives]] | work=[[whitehouse.gov]] | access-date=March 27, 2011}}</ref> He then earned an [[Master of Arts|Artium Magister]] in 1974 and a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] in 1979 from [[Harvard University]] and a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1977 from [[Harvard Law School]].<ref name=whgov_20110309/><ref name="fjc.gov">{{FJC Bio|nid=1393776|inline=yes}}</ref>

== Career ==
From 1978 until 1986, Kuntz was an associate in the New York law firm [[Shearman & Sterling]].<ref name=whgov_20110309/> From 1986 until 1994, Kuntz was a partner in the New York law firm Milgrim Thomajan Jacobs & Lee, and from 1994 until 2001, Kuntz was a partner in the New York law firm [[Seward & Kissel]].<ref name=whgov_20110309/> From 2001 until 2004, he was a partner in the New York office of the Canadian law firm [[Torys LLP]], and from 2004 until 2005, he was counsel at the New York law firm Constantine & Cannon.<ref name=whgov_20110309/> From 2005 until becoming a federal judge, Kuntz was a partner in the New York office of the law firm [[Baker Hostetler]].<ref name=whgov_20110309/> His specialty is commercial and labor litigation.<ref name=whgov_20110309/> Prior to his appointment to the EDNY, Kuntz was the New York City Council's designee from Kings County to the [[New York City Civilian Complaint Review Board|Civilian Complaint Review Board]] from October 1993 through 2010.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nyc.gov/html/ccrb/pdf/ccrbann2010.pdf |title=Archived copy |website=www.nyc.gov |access-date=17 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111214071316/http://www.nyc.gov/html/ccrb/pdf/ccrbann2010.pdf |archive-date=14 December 2011 |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="fjc.gov"/>

=== Federal judicial service ===
On March 9, 2011, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Kuntz to fill a seat on the United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York that became vacant when Judge [[Nina Gershon]] took [[senior status]] on October 16, 2008.<ref>{{cite web | author=The White House: Office of the Press Secretary | url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2011/03/09/nominations-sent-senate | title=Nominations Sent to the Senate | date=March 9, 2011 | via=[[NARA|National Archives]] | work=[[whitehouse.gov]] | access-date=March 27, 2011}}</ref> The United States Senate confirmed Kuntz by [[unanimous consent]] on October 3, 2011.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/112thCongress.cfm |title=Judicial Nominations and Confirmations: 112th Congress |website=judiciary.senate.gov |access-date=17 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110108213625/http://judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/112thCongress.cfm |archive-date=8 January 2011 |url-status=dead}}</ref> He received his judicial commission the following day. Kuntz assumed [[senior status]] on January 1, 2022.<ref name="fjc.gov"/>

== Personal ==
Kuntz's wife, Dr. Alice Beal, is the director of palliative care for the New York Harbor Healthcare System Veterans Administration. They live in [[Brooklyn, New York]], where they are members of the parish of the Brooklyn Oratory of St. Boniface. Their son Will is the General Manager of the [[LA Galaxy]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.lagalaxy.com/news/la-galaxy-name-will-kuntz-general-manager|title=LA Galaxy Name Will Kuntz General Manager|date=December 5, 2023|website=lagalaxy.com}}</ref> and one daughter, Katharine Meleney is a physician, trained in infectious diseases, and another daughter, Elizabeth, is a librarian.

Wolf]] | office2 = Judge of the [[United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts]] | term_start2 = April 4, 1985 | term_end2 = July 1, 2021 | appointer2 = [[List of federal judges appointed by Ronald Reagan|Ronald Reagan]] | predecessor2 = ''Seat established by 98 Stat. 333'' | successor2 = [[Julia Kobick]] | pronunciation = | birth_name = William Glover Young | birth_date = {{Birth date and age|1940|9|23}}{{Cite web|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Xy3zQIW4DW8C&pg=PA508|title=Confirmation Hearings on Federal Appointments: February 22; March 7,14, 20; April 11, 25; May 9, 23; June 7, 13, 26; July 26; August 7, 8; September 5, 18, 19, 26; and October 2, 1984|first=United States Congress Senate Committee on the|last=Judiciary|date=October 1, 1985|publisher=U.S. Government Printing Office|via=Google Books}} | birth_place = [[Huntington, New York|Huntington]], [[New York (state)|New York]], U.S. | death_date = | death_place = | death_cause = | education = [[Harvard University]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|BA]], [[Bachelor of Laws|LLB]]) }} '''William Glover Young''' (born September 23, 1940) is an American attorney and jurist serving as a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|U.S. district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts]]. He was appointed in 1985 by President [[Ronald Reagan]], and he served as chief judge of the district from 1999 to 2005. Young was a judge of the [[Massachusetts Superior Court]] from 1978 to 1985. ==Early life and career== Born in [[Huntington, New York|Huntington]], [[New York (state)|New York]], Young received a [[Bachelor of Arts|B.A.]] degree from [[Harvard University]] in 1962.{{Cite news |last=Montague |first=Zach |date=2025-06-18 |title=William G. Young, a Reagan-Appointed Judge, Is Fast-Tracking Trump to Trial |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/06/18/us/politics/judge-william-g-young-trump.html |access-date=2025-06-19 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} He received a [[Bachelor of Laws]] from [[Harvard Law School]] in 1967. He was a Captain in the [[United States Army]] from 1962 to 1964. He was a [[law clerk]] for Chief Justice Raymond S. Wilkins of the [[Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court]] from 1967 to 1968. Young was in private practice of law in [[Boston]], [[Massachusetts]], from 1968 to 1972. Young was a special assistant attorney general of Massachusetts from 1970 to 1972 and chief counsel to the Governor of Massachusetts, [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] [[Francis Sargent]], from 1972 to 1974. He was in private practice of law in Boston from 1975 to 1978. He was an associate justice of the Massachusetts Superior Court from 1978 to 1985. Young was a lecturer in law for [[Boston College Law School]] from 1968 to the present and at [[Boston University Law School]] from 1979 to the present. He was a lecturer in law at [[Harvard Law School]] from 1979 to 1990.{{FJC Bio|2678|nid=1390241|name=William G. Young}} ==Federal judicial service== Young was first nominated by President [[Ronald Reagan]] on September 11, 1984, to the United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts, to a new seat created by 98 Stat. 333, but the nomination lapsed without a Senate vote. Reagan renominated him on March 8, 1985. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on April 3, 1985, and received his commission on April 4, 1985. He served as chief judge from 1999 to 2005. On March 10, 2021, Young advised President [[Joe Biden]] that he intended to retire from regular active service on July 1, 2021, and would serve as a [[senior judge]] thereafter.{{cite web|url= https://www.mad.uscourts.gov/general/pdf/announce/03102021%20Press%20Release%20-%20Judge%20Young%20senior%20status.pdf |title= Press Release| publisher= United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts| work= Office of the Clerk|date= March 10, 2021| access-date= July 1, 2021}} In January 2024, Young blocked the $3.8 billion merger of [[Spirit Airlines]] and [[JetBlue]], saying that it would violate the [[Clayton Antitrust Act of 1914|Clayton Act]], which "was designed to prevent anticompetitive harms for consumers". Ten months later, Spirit Airlines announced plans to file for bankruptcy. On May 2, 2026, it ceased operations.{{Cite news |first1=Aamer |last1=Madhani |first2=Rio |last2=Yamat |first3=Jeff |last3=Amy |first4=Mike |last4=Catalini |url=https://apnews.com/article/spirit-airlines-trump-bailout-bankruptcy-37a4818e1b71c0905d022f669d85948c |title=Spirit Airlines shuts down as company says it can't keep up with higher oil prices |publisher=[[Associated Press]] |date=May 2, 2026}} == Notable cases == === Patent cases === As a federal judge, Young has heard [[patent]] cases relating to [[biotechnology]] and [[pharmaceuticals]]480 F.Supp.2d 462 and also heard computer-related patent cases, including a [[patent infringement]] suit by a small company against [[RealNetworks]].462 F.Supp.2d 131 The jury found that the patents were invalid and the case was affirmed upon appeal.223 Fed.Appx. 986 === Criminal cases === Young has heard many criminal cases both as a Massachusetts state judge and as a federal judge, including the "Big Dan" rape case, the [[shoe bomber]] case, and the [[Boston Strangler]] case.{{Cite web |url= http://www.trutv.com/library/crime/serial_killers/notorious/boston/19.html |title= TruTV | Funny Because it's tru |access-date= 2008-12-04 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20081204114541/http://www.trutv.com/library/crime/serial_killers/notorious/boston/19.html |archive-date= 2008-12-04 |url-status= dead }} He was the trial judge in Massachusetts state court for the highly publicized{{cite news| url= http://findarticles.com/p/articles/mi_m1282/is_v36/ai_3230920 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20070128073331/http://www.findarticles.com/p/articles/mi_m1282/is_v36/ai_3230920 |url-status= usurped | archive-date= 2007-01-28 | work= National Review | volume= 36 |title= Big Dan's tavern - rape case in New Bedford }} [[Cheryl Araujo|"Big Dan" rape case]]401 Mass. 843, 519 N.E.2d 1328, Mass., March 10, 1988 which was the inspiration for the movie ''[[The Accused (1988 film)|The Accused]]''. He sentenced [[Richard Reid (shoe bomber)|Richard Reid]], better known as the [[shoe bomber]], to three life terms plus 110 years in prison.{{cite news|url= http://www.cnn.com/2003/LAW/01/30/shoebomber.sentencing/ |work= CNN |title= Exchange between Reid, judge follows life sentence |date= January 30, 2003}} === Constitutional law cases === ==== Singer v. City of Newton - drones ==== Young heard [[Regulation of UAVs in the United States#State-level regulation|''Singer v. City of Newton'']], the first case in the United States on the constitutionality of state and local regulation of drones (unmanned aerial vehicles). He partially invalidated the city ordinance because it was [[federal preemption|preempted]] by [[Federal Aviation Administration]] regulations.{{Bluebook journal |first= |last=Note |title= Recent Case: Massachusetts District Court Finds Portion of Local Drone Ordinance Preempted by FAA Regulation| volume= 131 |journal= [[Harvard Law Review]] |page= 2057 |url= https://harvardlawreview.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/2057-2064_Online.pdf |year= 2018}}{{cite court| litigants= Singer v. City of Newton |vol= 284 |reporter= F. Supp. 3d |opinion= 125 |court= D. Mass. |date= Sept. 21, 2017|url= https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=7213100011129767991 }} ==== AAUP v. Rubio - free speech ==== {{Further|AAUP et al v. Marco Rubio}} Young heard ''American Association of University Professors et al. v. Marco Rubio'', which he called "perhaps the most important to fall within the jurisdiction of this district court". In his decision, he addressed the question "whether non-citizens lawfully present here in United States actually have the same free speech rights as the rest of us".AAUP v. Rubio, District of Massachusetts. Case 1:25-cv-10685-WGY, filed June 19, 2025, available at:https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.mad.282460/gov.uscourts.mad.282460.261.0.pdf, p.3 Young answered, "unequivocally 'yes, they do.' 'No law' means 'no law.' The First Amendment does not draw President Trump's invidious distinction and it is not to be found in our history or jurisprudence."Id., pp. 3-4. Young further addressed ICE agents' practice of wearing masks: {{blockquote|text=Can you imagine a masked marine? It is a matter of honor—and honor still matters. To us, masks are associated with cowardly desperados and the despised [[Ku Klux Klan]]. In all our history we have never tolerated an armed masked secret police. Carrying on in this fashion, ICE brings indelible obloquy to this administration and everyone who works in it.Id., p. 98.}} Young's decision concluded: {{blockquote|text=[T]his Court finds as fact and concludes as matter of law that Secretaries Noem and Rubio and their several agents and subordinates acted in concert to misuse the sweeping powers of their respective offices to target noncitizen pro-Palestinians for deportation primarily on account of their First Amendment protected political speech. They did so in order to strike fear into similarly situated non-citizen pro-Palestinian individuals, pro-actively (and effectively) curbing lawful pro-Palestinian speech and intentionally denying such individuals (including the plaintiffs here) the freedom of speech that is their right. Moreover, the effect of these targeted deportation proceedings continues unconstitutionally to chill freedom of speech to this day.Id., p. 147}} ===American Public Health Association v. National Institutes of Health=== In ''[[American Public Health Association v. National Institutes of Health]]'', [[United States Supreme Court]] Justices [[Neil Gorsuch]] and [[Brett Kavanaugh]] accused Young of defying its [[shadow docket]] orders. Justice [[Stephen Breyer]] defended Young, and Young apologized.{{cite news |last1= Liptak |first1= Adam |author1-link= Adam Liptak |title= Justice Breyer Defends Judge Accused of Defying Supreme Court Order |url= https://www.nytimes.com/2025/09/06/us/politics/justice-breyer-boston-judge.html |work= [[The New York Times]] |date= September 6, 2025 |archive-url= https://archive.today/20250907002306/https://www.nytimes.com/2025/09/06/us/politics/justice-breyer-boston-judge.html |archive-date= September 7, 2025}}{{cite news |last1= Montague |first1= Zach |title= Judge Apologizes to Conservative Justices in Case Over N.I.H. He grew up in the [[South Shore, Chicago|South Shore]] community of [[Chicago]] and graduated from [[Lyons Township High School]] in [[La Grange, Illinois]].Ameet Sachdev, [https://www.chicagotribune.com/2011/01/11/new-colorado-federal-judge-has-chicago-roots/ New Colorado federal judge has Chicago roots], ''[[Chicago Tribune]]'' (January 11, 2011). Martínez earned a [[Bachelor of Arts]] and [[Bachelor of Science]] degree from the [[University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign]] in 1977, followed by a [[Juris Doctor|J.D.]] degree from the [[University of Chicago Law School]] in 1980.[http://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/ws/index.php?pid=122144 President Obama Nominates Three for District Court Bench], [[White House Office of the Press Secretary]] (February 24, 2010).{{FJC Bio|nid=1393576|inline=yes}} == Career == From 1980 until 1984, Martínez served as a staff attorney for the Legal Assistance Foundation of Metropolitan Chicago, and from 1984 until 1987, he served as a staff attorney for the foundation's Employment Law Project. From 1988 until 1992, Martínez served as a senior litigation associate for a Denver law firm. From 1992 until 1996, he served as a Denver-based regional attorney for the United States [[Equal Employment Opportunity Commission]]. From 1997 until 2001, Martínez worked as a sole law practitioner in Denver, and from 2001 until 2010 he was a partner at the Denver firm of McNamara & Martínez (later known as McNamara, Roseman, Martínez & Kazmierski), where he specialized in employment and civil rights law. === Federal judicial service === On February 24, 2010, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Martínez to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the United States District Court for the District of Colorado, to fill the seat that Judge [[Edward Nottingham]] vacated in 2008 when he resigned. Martínez was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on December 21, 2010 by a 58–37 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1112/vote_111_2_00291.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation William Joseph Martinez, of Colorado, to be United States District Judge for the District of Colorado)}}Mark Harden, [http://www.bizjournals.com/denver/news/2010/12/21/martinez-confirmed.html Martínez confirmed as Colorado federal judge], ''[[American City Business Journals|Denver Business Journal]]'' (December 21, 2010). He received his commission the same day. '''William J. Zloch''' (born September 16, 1944)<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.lawdiary.com/docs/subscribers/FL_Judicial_Biographies.pdf |title=BIOGRAPHIES OF FEDERAL COURT JUDGES SITTING IN FLORIDA |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170730052812/http://www.lawdiary.com/docs/subscribers/FL_Judicial_Biographies.pdf |archive-date=July 30, 2017 |access-date=May 9, 2018}}</ref> is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida]], as well as a former [[American football]] [[quarterback]] and [[wide receiver]] for the [[Notre Dame Fighting Irish football|University of Notre Dame]].

==College football==
Following the departure of [[Heisman Trophy]] winner [[John Huarte]] in 1965, [[University of Notre Dame|Notre Dame]] [[College football|football]] coach [[Ara Parseghian]] was faced with a wide-open competition for the [[quarterback]] position. He opted to move senior Bill Zloch from wide receiver to quarterback for the 1965 season.<ref>{{cite web|title=QB Battles And Results|publisher=Blue and Gold|url=http://www.blueandgold.com/content/?aid=3363|access-date=2007-12-17}}</ref> Directing a team that was heavily run-oriented, Zloch finished the season completing 36 of 88 passes for 558 yards and three touchdowns.<ref>{{cite web|title=Yearly Leaders|publisher=UND.com|url=http://und.cstv.com/sports/m-footbl/archive/nd-m-fb-a-yl.html|access-date=2007-12-17}}</ref> The team finished 7-2-1 and ranked 8th nationally.

==Education and career==
Zloch graduated from the [[University of Notre Dame]] with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in 1966. After graduation, he spent three years in the [[United States Navy]], achieving the rank of [[lieutenant]] and played football for the [[Pensacola Navy Goshawks]] with [[Roger Staubach]].<ref>Cope, Jay. [https://www.navy.mil/Press-Office/News-Stories/Article/2254588/hall-of-fame-quarterback-remembers-goshawks-playing-time/ "Hall of Fame Quarterback Remembers Goshawks Playing Time"], Naval Air Station Whiting Field Public Affairs, ''[[Navy.mil]] website'', August 28, 2017. Retrieved October 9, 2025.</ref> He then returned to [[Notre Dame Law School]], completing a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1974. He returned to [[Fort Lauderdale, Florida|Fort Lauderdale]], Florida where he practiced law from 1974 to 1985.<ref name="auto">{{FJC Bio|2688|nid=1390291|name=William J. Zloch<!--(1944–)-->}}</ref>

===Federal judicial service===
On October 9, 1985, President [[Ronald Reagan]] nominated Zloch to a new seat on the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida]] created by 98 Stat. 333. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on November 1, 1985, and received his commission on November 4, 1985.<ref name="auto"/> On July 1, 2000, he began a seven-year term as chief judge of the district, ending on June 30, 2007. He was succeeded as chief judge by Judge [[Federico A. Moreno]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Judge Federico A. Moreno Succeeds Judge William J. Zloch|publisher=Florida Southern District Court|url=http://www.flsd.uscourts.gov/default.asp?file=press.asp|access-date=2007-12-17 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20071206144840/http://www.flsd.uscourts.gov/default.asp?file=press.asp |archive-date = 2007-12-06}}</ref> He assumed [[senior status]] on January 31, 2017.<ref name="auto"/> As of April 29, 2026, Zloch appears to be inactive.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.flsd.uscourts.gov/sites/flsd/files/adminorders/2026-30.pdf|title=IN RE: AMENDED MAGISTRATE JUDGE PAIRING ASSIGNMENT PLAN FOR MIAMI, FORT LAUDERDALE, WEST PALM BEACH, FORT PIERCE, AND KEY WEST|website=flsd.uscourts.gov|date=2026-04-29|access-date=2026-05-12}}</ref>

==Notable case==
On August 21, 2009, Judge Zloch sentenced [[UBS]] [[whistleblower]] [[Bradley Birkenfeld]] to 40 months in prison with 3 years probation and a $30,000 fine, a term that was harsher than the prosecutors wanted. "Assistant U.S. attorney Jeffrey A. Neiman recommended that Birkenfeld get 30 months in prison for his conviction on one count of conspiracy to defraud the government—down from the 60-month maximum sentence he is exposed to—because of his extensive cooperation," the ''Miami Herald'' reported.<ref>[http://www.miamiherald.com/business/international/story/1196559.html "UBS whistle-blower gets 40-month sentence"] by Martha Brannigan, ''Miami Herald'', 8/21/09. Retrieved 8/31/09.</ref><ref>[https://www.nytimes.com/2010/01/09/business/global/09whistle.html Ex-UBS Banker Reports to Prison], By BLOOMBERG NEWS, JAN. 8, 2010</ref>

On August 25, 2017, Federal Judge William Zloch, dismissed the class-action lawsuit the DNC rigged primary elections against presidential candidate [[Bernie Sanders]] after several months of litigation during which DNC attorneys argued that the DNC would be well within their rights to select their own candidate. “In evaluating Plaintiffs’ claims at this stage, the Court assumes their allegations are true—that the DNC and Wasserman Schultz held a palpable bias in favor Clinton and sought to propel her ahead of her Democratic opponent,” "The Observer" reported.<ref>[https://observer.com/2017/08/court-admits-dnc-and-debbie-wasserman-schulz-rigged-primaries-against-sanders/], By The Observer, AUG. 26, 2017</ref>

[[George Washington University Law School|George Washington University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | footnotes = }} '''William Kenneth Sessions III'''{{cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/middleburyCourseCatalogs_a10-3_1970/page/n145/mode/2up|page=144|title=Middlebury College Bulletin 1970-71|year=1970|publisher=Middlebury College}} (born February 9, 1947){{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qgDQT4am8doC&pg=PA442|page=442|title=Hearings before the Committee on the Judiciary, United States Senate, One Hundred Fourth Congress, First Session, on Confirmations of Appointees to the Federal Judiciary, July 18; August 3; September 28; October 24; November 30; December 19, 1995|publisher=U.S. Government Printing Office|year=1997|isbn=978-0-16-047149-0 }} is serving as a [[United States federal judge|senior United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Vermont]] and has served as the Vice Chair and eventually as Chair of the [[United States Sentencing Commission]]. He was confirmed on October 21, 2009, as Chair of the United States Sentencing Commission, and served until December 22, 2010.{{cite web|title=Former Commissioner Information|date=28 October 2013|url=http://www.ussc.gov/about/commissioners/former-commissioner-information|publisher=United States Sentencing Commission|access-date=16 June 2014|archive-date=23 May 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150523001120/http://www.ussc.gov/about/commissioners/former-commissioner-information|url-status=dead}} ==Education and career== Sessions was educated at [[Middlebury College]] where he earned a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in 1969. He earned a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1972 from the [[George Washington University Law School]]. Sessions served as a [[United States Army]] First Lieutenant. He was a [[law clerk]] for Judge Hilton Dier in Addison County District Court in 1973. He later worked for the [[Addison County, Vermont|Addison County]] Public Defender before entering private practice in 1978. He also worked as an adjunct professor at [[Vermont Law School]] from 1978 until 1995. In 1992 he managed the successful reelection campaign of Senator [[Patrick Leahy]], who defeated [[Jim Douglas]].{{Citation needed|date=May 2025}} ===Federal judicial service=== Sessions was nominated by President [[Bill Clinton]] on June 30, 1995, to a seat vacated by Judge [[Fred I. Parker]]. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate|Senate]] on August 11, 1995, and received his commission on August 14, 1995. Sessions served as chief judge from 2002 to 2010. He assumed [[senior status]] on June 15, 2014.{{FJC Bio|nid=1387601|inline=yes}} ===Notable cases=== On September 12, 2007, Judge Sessions ruled in favor of the [[Sierra Club]], the states of [[Vermont]] and [[New York (state)|New York]], and other environmental groups in rejecting the auto industry's attempt to block states from regulating emissions from cars. Sessions' ruling opens the doors for New York and Vermont to proceed with enacting the California Clean Car (Pavley) Standards, pending [[United States Environmental Protection Agency]] approval. These standards, adopted by California and at least 11 other states, aim to reduce emissions from cars by 30 percent when fully implemented in 2016. This precedent will likely have an important impact on similar cases pending in California and Rhode Island.{{cite web|url=http://www.sierraclub.org/environmentallaw/lawsuits/0303.asp|title=Sierra Ray |website=[[Georgia Court of Appeals]] |access-date=July 14, 2017}} He received his [[Bachelor of Business Administration]] from the [[University of Georgia]]'s [[Terry College of Business]] in 1985, ''magna cum laude'', his [[Master of Business Administration]] from the [[Terry College of Business]] in 1986, and his [[Juris Doctor]], ''cum laude'', from the [[University of Georgia School of Law]] in 1990. Upon graduation he joined the law firm of Andersen, Davidson & Tate, P.C. in [[Gwinnett County, Georgia]]. He ran for the [[Georgia State Senate]] in 1996 and spent six years representing the [[Georgia's 48th Senate district|48th District]]. He served on the Judiciary, Special Judiciary, Rules, Appropriations, Natural Resources, and Transportation Committees. On January 14, 2002, he took the oath of office to be a Superior Court Judge on the Gwinnett Judicial Circuit, a position in which he served for ten years.{{cite web|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2017/07/13/president-donald-j-trump-announces-fifth-wave-judicial-candidates|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Donald J. Trump Announces Fifth Wave of Judicial Candidates}} On July 30, 2012, Governor [[Nathan Deal]] appointed Ray to serve as the 76th Judge of the Court of Appeals of Georgia, where he succeeded [[Keith R. web|url=https://gov.georgia.gov/press-releases/2012-07-25/deal-names-two-georgia-court-appeals|archive-url=https://archive.today/20121213073013/http://gov.georgia.gov/press-releases/2012-07-25/deal-names-two-georgia-court-appeals|url-status=dead|archive-date=December Court for the Northern District of Georgia]], to the seat vacated by Judge [[Harold Lloyd Murphy]], who assumed [[senior status]] on March 31, 2017.{{cite web|url=https://www.whitehouse.gov/the-press-office/2017/07/13/ten-nominations-sent-senate-today|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170714065923/https://www.whitehouse.gov/the-press-office/2017/07/13/ten-nominations-sent-senate-today|url-status=dead|archive-date=2017-07-14|title=" Judiciary Committee]].{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/09/20/2017/nominations|title=Nominations – United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|website=www.judiciary.senate.gov|date=September 20, 2017 }} On October 19, 2017, his nomination was reported out of committee by an 11–9 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%2010-19-17.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – October 19, 2017, Senate Judiciary Committee}} On January 3, 2018, his nomination was returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]].{{cite web|url=https://www.congress.gov/congressional-record/2018/1/3/daily-digest|title=Congressional Record|website=www.congress.gov}} On January 5, 2018, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to renominate Ray to a federal judgeship.{{cite web|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-renomination-21-judicial-nominees/|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Donald J. Trump Announces Renomination of 21 Judicial Nominees}} On January 8, 2018, his renomination was sent to the [[United States Senate|Senate]].{{cite web|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/nominations-sent-senate-today-2/|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate Today}} On January 18, 2018, his nomination was reported out of committee by an 11–10 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%2001-18-181.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – January 18, 2018, Senate Judiciary Committee}} On October 11, 2018, his nomination was confirmed by a 54–41 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=115&session=2&vote=00234|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation William M. Ray II, of Georgia, to be U.S. District Judge for the Northern District of Georgia)|date=October 11, 2018|website=[[United States Senate]]|access-date=October 11, 2018|language=en}} He received his judicial commission on October 25, 2018.{{FJC Bio|nid=5373556|inline=yes}} == Notable cases == During the [[2020 Georgia (U.S. state) elections|2020 Georgia elections]], to protect voting rights during the [[COVID-19 pandemic in Georgia (U.S. state)|COVID-19 pandemic]], the [[Georgia Secretary of State|secretary of state of Georgia]] [[Brad Raffensperger]] directed the mailing of [[Postal voting in the United States|absentee (mail-in) ballot]] applications to all of Georgia's 6.9 million active registered voters for the state's June 2020 primary. The Georgia Association of Latino Elected Officials and other civil rights groups sued the Office of the Secretary of State of Georgia, and the [[Gwinnett County, Georgia|Gwinnett County]] elections board in Federal District Court, arguing that the mailing of mail-in ballot applications for the 2020 general election (which were only in English) should also have been sent in the [[Spanish language]] in [[Gwinnett County, Georgia|Gwinnett County]], which has a significant Spanish-speaking population. Judge Ray dismissed the suit in October 2020, ruling that the plaintiffs lacked [[Standing (law)|standing]] and the English-only mailings did not violate the [[Voting Rights Act]].[https://apnews.com/article/georgia-lawsuits-voting-rights-elections-voting-2020-82efaa4765e3c8e7be71c5194980b5d3 Judge dismisses request to send Spanish ballot applications], Associated Press (October 5, 2020). == Personal life == Ray has been married since 1989 to Dr. Kelle Chandler Ray, who is a clinical psychologist who practices in Lawrenceville, Georgia. They have three sons and reside in [[Norcross, Georgia]]. One of Ray's uncles was [[Richard Ray]], a Democratic [[United States House of Representatives|United States Congressman]] from [[Perry, Georgia|Perry]], [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]] and served as Senator [[Sam Nunn]]'s Chief of Staff in Washington, D.C. for 12 years, and another uncle was [[Robert Ray (Georgia politician)|Robert Ray]] of [[Fort Valley, Georgia|Fort Valley]] who served in the [[Georgia House of Representatives]] for 24 years. == References == {{Reflist}} == External links == * {{FJC Bio|nid=5373556}} * {{Ballotpedia|William_M._Ray,_II|William M. He received an [[Bachelor of Arts|Artium Baccalaureus]] degree from [[Canisius College]] in 1966, a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Howard University School of Law]] in 1969, and a [[Master of Laws]] from [[Northwestern University School of Law]] in 1972. He was a Fellow at the [[Ford Foundation]]. He was an [[assistant United States attorney]] of the Northern District of Illinois from 1971 to 1973. He was an assistant United States attorney of the Western District of New York from 1973 to 1975. He was a first assistant United States attorney of Western District of New York from 1975 to 1981. He was a special counsel for the Attorney General's Advocacy Institute in [[Washington, D.C.]] in 1979. He was a staff attorney of Office of Special Prosecutor of the Department of Justice in Washington, D.C. in 1980. He was in private practice in Buffalo from 1981 to 1983. He was a first deputy district attorney of [[Erie County, New York|Erie County]], New York from 1983 to 1988. He was in private practice in Buffalo from 1988 to 1990.{{FJC Bio|nid=1387901|inline=yes}} ===Federal judicial service=== Skretny was nominated by President [[George H. W. Bush]] on June 12, 1990, to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Western District of New York]] vacated by Judge [[John Thomas Curtin]]. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on August 3, 1990, and received his commission on August 7, 1990. He served as Chief Judge from 2010 to 2015. [[Boston College Law School|Boston College]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | footnotes = }} '''William Horsley Orrick III''' (born 1953) is an American lawyer who serves as a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of California]].{{citation|title=District Judge William H. Orrick|url=https://www.cand.uscourts.gov/judges/orrick-william-h-who/|access-date=2023-03-08|website=U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California website|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230220234115/https://www.cand.uscourts.gov/judges/orrick-william-h-who/|archive-date=2023-02-20|url-status=live|quote=Nominated by Barack Obama on June 11, 2012 and renominated on January 3, 2013, to a seat vacated by Charles Breyer. Confirmed by the Senate on May 15, 2013, and received commission on May 16, 2013.}} He had a long career as a lawyer in private practice in San Francisco, and served as a [[Deputy Assistant Attorney General]] in the [[United States Department of Justice Civil Division|Civil Division]] of the [[United States Department of Justice]] during the [[Obama administration]]. ==Early life and education== Orrick was born in [[San Francisco]] in 1953.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/William-Orrick-Senate-Questionnaire-Public-Final.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees: William Horsley Orrick, III|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary}}Julia Cheever, [http://sfappeal.com/2013/05/sf-lawyer-follows-fathers-footsteps-into-federal-judgeship/ "SF Lawyer Follows Father's Footsteps in Federal Judgeship], ''Bay City News'' (May 15, 2013). His father, [[William H. Orrick Jr.]] (1915–2003), was a United States District Judge for the Northern District of California and served as Assistant Attorney General for the Civil Division in the [[John F. Kennedy administration]].{{cite web|url=https://www.law360.com/articles/559414/the-scion-of-san-francisco-judge-william-h-orrick-iii|work=Law360|author=Gavin Broady|title=The Scion of San Francisco: Judge William H. Orrick III}}Reynolds Holding, [https://www.sfgate.com/bayarea/article/William-Orrick-U-S-district-judge-2595886.php William Orrick – U.S. district judge], ''San Francisco Chronicle'' (August 16, 2003). His mother, Marion Naffziger Orrick ({{Abbr|d.|died}} 1995), was active in San Francisco civic life.[https://www.sfgate.com/news/article/Marion-Naffziger-Orrick-3043619.php Marion Naffziger Orrick], ''San Francisco Chronicle'' (February 25, 1995). Orrick's uncle, [[Andrew Downey Orrick]], was acting chairman of the [[U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission]] in San Francisco.Bob Egelko, [https://www.sfgate.com/bayarea/article/S-F-lawyer-Andrew-Downey-Orrick-dies-3228575.php S.F. lawyer Andrew Downey Orrick dies], ''San Francisco Chronicle'' (February 2, 2008). Orrick received his [[Bachelor of Arts]], ''[[Latin honors|cum laude]]'', from [[Yale University]] in 1976. He received his [[Juris Doctor]], ''cum laude'', from [[Boston College Law School]] in 1979.{{cite press release|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2012/06/11/president-obama-nominates-two-serve-us-district-court|publisher=White House Press Office|date=June 11, 2012|title=President Obama Nominates Two to Serve on the US District Court}} ==Career== From 1977 to 1979 he was a student attorney for the Boston College Legal Assistance Bureau. After graduating, Orrick worked from 1979 to 1984 at the [[Georgia Legal Services Program]] in [[Savannah, Georgia|Savannah]],{{FJC Bio|nid=1394201|inline=yes}} providing [[legal aid]] services to low-income Georgians. Upon returning to [[San Francisco]], he chose to join [[William Coblentz (attorney)|William Coblentz]]'s Coblentz, Patch, Duffy & Bass LLP, rather than the law firm co-founded by his grandfather William Orrick Sr., [[Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe]]. Orrick practiced at the Coblentz firm for about 25 years, from 1984 to 2009. He joined as an associate in 1984 and was promoted to partner in 1988. Orrick then served in the [[United States Department of Justice Civil Division|Civil Division of the U.S. Department of Justice]], first as counselor (June 2009 – June 2010) and then as deputy assistant attorney general (June 2010 – 2013), heading the [[Office of Immigration Litigation]].Ryan J. Reilly, [https://web.archive.org/web/20100614072924/http://www.mainjustice.com/2010/06/09/new-office-of-immigration-litigation-chief-named/ New Office of Immigration Litigation Chief Named], ''Main Justice'' (June 9, 2010). Orrick returned to Coblentz, Patch, Duffy & Bass for ten months while his nomination to the district court was pending in the Senate. ===Federal judicial service=== On June 11, 2012, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Orrick to be a United States district judge of the United States District Court for the Northern District of California, to the seat vacated by Judge [[Charles Breyer]], who assumed [[senior status]] on December 31, 2011. The [[American Bar Association]]'s [[Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary]], which rates the qualifications of federal judicial nominees, unanimously rated Orrick "well qualified" for the judgeship (the committee's highest rating).[https://www.americanbar.org/content/dam/aba/uncategorized/2011/ratings112.pdf Ratings of Article III Judicial Nominees, 112th Congress], [[American Bar Association]] [[Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary]]. The [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] held a hearing on Orrick's nomination on July 11, 2012.[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/nominations-2012-07-11 Nominations: Full Committee] (July 11, 2012), United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary. His nomination was reported out of committee on August 2, 2012, by a 12–6 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/ExecutiveBusinessMeetingResults-08-02-2012.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – August 2, 2012|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary}} However, his nomination was blocked by Senate [[Republican Party (United States)|Republicans]], and on January 2, 2013, his nomination was returned to the President, due to the [[Adjournment sine die|adjournment ''sine die'']] of the Senate at the end of the [[112th Congress]].[https://www.congress.gov/nomination/112th-congress/1729 PN1729 — William H. Orrick III — The Judiciary, 112th Congress (2011–2012)], Congress.gov. The next day, January 3, 2013, he was renominated to the same office.{{cite press release|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2013/01/03/president-obama-re-nominates-thirty-three-federal-judgeships|title=President Obama Re-nominates Thirty-Three to Federal Judgeships|date=January 3, 2013|publisher=White House Press Office}} His nomination was reported by the Senate Judiciary Committee on February 28, 2013, by a 11–7 vote.[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/ExecutiveBusinessMeetingResults-02-28-2013.pdf Results of Executive Business Meeting – February 28, 2013], United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary. The U.S. Senate confirmed his nomination on May 15, 2013, by a 56–41 vote, with three senators not voting.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=113&session=1&vote=00125|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation William H. Orrick, III, of the District of Columbia, to be U.S. District Judge for the Northern District of California)|publisher=United States Senate}} The confirmation vote was mostly on party lines, with all Democrats and three Republican Senators ([[Jeff Flake]], [[Susan Collins]], and [[Lisa Murkowski]]) voting to confirm Orrick and all other Republicans voting against confirmation.{{cite web|title=Senate confirms Orrick as federal judge|author=Bob Egelko|date=May 15, 2013|url=https://www.sfgate.com/bayarea/article/Senate-confirms-Orrick-as-federal-judge-4520478.php}} He received his commission the following day. He assumed [[senior status]] on May 17, 2023. As a federal judge, Orrick established chambers in the [[Phillip Burton Federal Building]] in San Francisco. ===Notable cases=== In 2014, Orrick upheld California state legislation that banned the possession and sale of [[Shark fin soup|shark fin]], a prohibition aimed at stopping the practice of [[shark finning]]. Orrick rejected the claim of a group of [[San Francisco Bay Area]] [[Chinese American]] businesses and shark fin suppliers that the ban was unconstitutionally discriminatory. Orrick wrote that although "people of Chinese origin or culture undoubtedly overwhelmingly comprise the market for shark fin,{{nbsp}}... a law is not unconstitutional simply because it has a racially disparate impact."Bob Egelko, [https://www.sfgate.com/science/article/California-shark-fin-ban-upheld-by-federal-judge-5348461.php California shark fin ban upheld by federal judge], ''San Francisco Chronicle'' (March 26, 2014).''[https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=14976155598669763328 Chinatown Neighborhood Ass'n v. Harris]'', 33 F. Supp. 3d 1085 (N.D. Cal. 2014). Orrick's dismissal of the case was affirmed on appeal.''[https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2568626277348529266 Chinatown Neighborhood Ass'n v. Harris]'', 794 F.3d 1136 (9th Cir. 2015). In 2015, Orrick denied a motion filed by [[Pacific Gas and Electric Co.]] (PG&E) to dismiss the case against it arising from pollution discharges into [[San Francisco Bay]] by PG&E's [[History of manufactured fuel gases|manufactured fuel gas]] (oil and coal) power plants decades earlier. Orrick held that PG&E's refusal to test for [[groundwater contamination]] at the former plants gave rise to a continuing "imminent and substantial endangerment" to the environment and human health, particularly in the [[Marina District, San Francisco|Marina District]] and [[Fisherman's Wharf, San Francisco|Fisherman's Wharf]] neighborhoods.Bob Egelko, [https://m.sfgate.com/bayarea/article/PG-E-agrees-to-clean-up-pollution-from-power-13267112.php?t=84c26ed49d PG&E settles lawsuit over pollution from old power plants in San Francisco], ''San Francisco Chronicle'' (September 28, 2018).''[https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=14024338758348168103 San Francisco Herring Ass'n v. Pacific Gas & Electric Co.]'', 81 F. Supp. 3d 847 (N.D. Cal. 2015). In 2018, Orrick approved a settlement of the case, in which PG&E agreed to monitor and potentially clean up pollution from its old sites and agreed to make payments to a conservation organization and habitat restoration efforts. Orrick is the judge assigned to oversee the reforms of the [[Oakland Police Department]] mandated by the department's 2003 settlement of ''[[Allen v. City of Oakland]]'', a long-running case involving systemic [[police misconduct]].[https://www.sfgate.com/news/bayarea/article/Mayor-Says-She-Shares-Judge-s-Concerns-About-14372124.php Mayor Says She Shares Judge's Concerns About Police Department], Bay City News Service (August 22, 2019). In hearings, Orrick has pushed the department to make more progress on reforms. [[Robert Warshaw]] is the court-appointed monitor of the Oakland Police Department reforms.[https://www.sfgate.com/news/bayarea/article/Judge-Appoints-Attorney-To-Investigate-Fatal-13666062.php Judge Appoints Attorney To Investigate Fatal Shooting By Officers], Bay City News Service (March 5, 2019). In March 2019, Orrick appointed an attorney to serve as an independent investigator to probe the killing of a homeless man with mental health problems who was shot by Oakland police in 2018. At an August 2019 court conference, Orrick criticized the city for not making sufficient progress in eliminating racial disparities in policing.Bob Egelko & Megan Cassidy, [https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Federal-judge-blasts-Oakland-for-losing-ground-in-14369346.php Federal judge criticizes Oakland for losing ground in court-ordered policing reforms], ''San Francisco Chronicle'' (August 22, 2019). In 2015, Orrick issued a [[temporary restraining order]] (TRO) blocking the [[Center for Medical Progress]] (CMP), an anti-abortion group, from releasing [[Planned Parenthood 2015 undercover videos controversy|secretly recorded videos]] of the [[National Abortion Federation]] (NAF). CMP had earlier released [[Planned Parenthood 2015 undercover videos controversy|heavily edited videos]], which purported to show that [[Planned Parenthood]] had been inappropriately selling fetal tissue. In his decision granting a restraining order, Orrick wrote that a TRO was necessary to prevent irreparable harm to NAF "in the form of harassment, intimidation, violence, invasion of privacy, and injury to reputation, and the requested relief is in the public interest."{{cite news |last=Scott |first=Eugene |url=http://www.cnn.com/2015/08/01/politics/court-restraining-order-center-for-medical-progress/ |title=Judge issues restraining order against anti-abortion group |publisher=CNN|date=August 15, 2015}} In subsequent proceedings, Orrick reviewed hundreds of hours of videos and found no evidence of wrongdoing on NAF's behalf, and concluded that the CMP, led by anti-abortion activist [[David Daleiden]], had "misleadingly edited videos to make it appear as though abortion providers were breaking the law."{{cite news|author=Nicholas Iovino|url=https://www.courthousenews.com/ninth-circuit-lets-contempt-sanctions-of-abortion-foe-stand/|publisher=[[Courthouse News Service]]|title=Ninth Circuit Lets Contempt Sanctions of Abortion Foe Stand|date=June 5, 2019}} In 2016, Orrick subsequently issued a [[preliminary injunction]] against CMP blocking the release of their videos; after Daleiden violated the injunction, Orrick found Daleiden and his two attorneys in [[civil contempt]] and fined them $195,000. The contempt finding was upheld on appeal. In April 2017, Orrick stayed the implementation of the [[First presidency of Donald Trump|Trump administration]]'s [[Executive Order 13768]] to withhold funding from [[sanctuary cities]] that limit cooperation with [[U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement]] authorities, saying Trump had no authority to attach new conditions to [[Government spending|federal spending]].{{cite news |last=Kopan |first=Tal |url=http://www.cnn.com/2017/04/25/politics/sanctuary-cities-injunction/ |title=Judge blocks part of Trump's sanctuary cities executive order |publisher=CNN|date=April 25, 2017 Cities|last=Yee|first=Vivian|date=April 25, 2017|work=The New York Times|access-date=April 25, 2017|issn=0362-4331}} In November 2017, Orrick ruled in favor of the [[City and County of San Francisco]] and [[County of Santa Clara]] (who challenged the order), finding that Section 9(a) of the Executive Order was [[Facial challenge|unconstitutional on its face]] as a violation of the [[Separation of Amendment]] rights and issuing a nationwide [[permanent injunction]] against its implementation.{{cite news|newspaper = [[Huffington Post]]|title = Judge Permanently Blocks Trump's Executive Order On Trump|court =9th Cir.|volume=897|reporter=F.3d|opinion=1225|date=2018}} In February 2018, Orrick issued a [[preliminary injunction]] ordering the Trump administration to enforce limits on [[methane emissions]] from oil and gas wells on federal and tribal land. Orrick's order directed the [[U.S. Bureau of Land Management]] to halt the Trump administration's suspension of an Obama administration-era regulations that required fossil-fuel extractors on federal lands to take steps to reduce [[Gas flare|flaring]] and [[Gas venting|venting]], and thus prevent [[methane leakage]].Bob Egelko, [https://www.sfgate.com/nation/article/Trump-administration-ordered-to-enforce-limits-on-12704732.php Trump administration ordered to enforce limits on methane gas emissions], ''San Francisco Chronicle'' (February 23, 2018).''[https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2625995240954337811 State of California v. Bureau of Land Management]'', 286 F. Supp. 3d 1054 (N.D. 2018). In April 2022, Orrick cut the jury award for a former Black contractor in a racial discrimination lawsuit against Tesla from $137 million to $15 million. Diaz' lawyer told NPR that "it wasn't because [Orrick] found anything wrong with what Mr. Diaz said or that Mr. Diaz wasn't injured", suggesting that the decision was "just based on a comparison."{{Cite news|url=https://www.npr.org/2022/04/14/1092804493/telsa-racial-discrimination-lawsuit-15-million |title=Judge cuts the payout in a Black former Tesla contractor's racial discrimination suit |last=Torchinsky |first=Rina |date=April 14, 2022 |work=[[NPR]]}} In July 2023, he denied [[Sarah Andersen]], [[Kelly McKernan]], and Karla Ortiz's [[copyright infringement]] lawsuit against [[Stability AI]], [[Midjourney]], and [[DeviantArt]]. Orrick stated would dismiss most of the case, requesting they elaborate on issues and "provide more facts".{{cite news |last1=Brittain |first1=Blake |title=US judge finds flaws in artists' lawsuit against AI companies |url=https://www.reuters.com/legal/litigation/us-judge-finds-flaws-artists-lawsuit-against-ai-companies-2023-07-19/ |work=[[Reuters]] |date=19 July 2023}} ====San Francisco Public Works corruption scandal==== Since 2020, Orrick has been involved in the plea deals, trials and sentencing of people guilty of fraud and bribery in the ongoing [[San Francisco Department of Public Works corruption scandal]]. '''William Quinn Hayes''' (born April 14, 1956) is a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of California]].

==Early life and education==
Born in [[Bronxville, New York]], Hayes received a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree from [[Syracuse University]] in 1978, a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Syracuse University School of Law]] in 1983, and a [[Master of Business Administration]] from the [[Martin J. Whitman School of Management]] at Syracuse University in 1983.

==Career==
Hayes was in private practice from 1983 to 1986. He was an adjunct faculty member at [[National American University|National College]] from 1984 to 1985. He was adjunct faculty at the [[University of Colorado Denver]] from 1985 to 1986. He was Chief of the Criminal Division for the Southern District of California's [[United States Attorney]]'s Office from 1987 to 2003. He served as adjunct faculty at [[Thomas Jefferson School of Law]] from 1989 to 1996. He was an adjunct faculty member at the [[University of San Diego School of Law]] in 1998.

===Federal judicial service===
On May 1, 2003, Hayes was nominated by President [[George W. Bush]] to serve as a United States district judge of the United States District Court for the Southern District of California, to a new seat created by 116 Stat. 1758. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on October 2, 2003, and received his commission on October 6, 2003. He assumed senior status on August 1, 2021.<ref>{{FJC Bio|nid=1392031|inline=yes}}</ref>

'''William Shaw Stickman IV''' (born 1979) is a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania]].

== Education ==

Stickman earned his [[Bachelor of Arts]], ''[[summa cum laude]]'', in 2002 and his [[Juris Doctor]] in 2005 from [[Duquesne University]] in [[Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania]]. He was a member of the ''Duquesne Law Review'' during law school.<ref name="WHBio">[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-judicial-nominees-united-states-attorney-nominee-united-states-marshal-nominees-3/ "President Donald J. Trump Announces Judicial Nominees, United States Attorney Nominee, and United States Marshal Nominees" White House, May 3, 2019] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210120202328/https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-judicial-nominees-united-states-attorney-nominee-united-states-marshal-nominees-3/ |date=January 20, 2021 }} {{PD-notice}}</ref>

== Legal career ==

From 2006 to 2007, Stickman served as a [[law clerk]] to [[Chief Justice]] [[Ralph Cappy]] of the [[Pennsylvania Supreme Court]]. He was then hired as an associate with Del Sole Cavanaugh Stroyd LLC in 2007 and became a partner in 2013, where his practice focused on [[commercial litigation]], [[appellate]] matters, and [[personal injury law]]. From 2011 to 2017, he served on the Pennsylvania Civil Procedural Rules Committee.<ref name="WHBio" />

== Federal judicial service ==

On May 3, 2019, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to nominate Stickman to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] for the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania]]. [[University of Virginia School of Law|University of Virginia]] ([[Master of Laws|LLM]]) | website = | footnotes = }} '''Willis Beverly Hunt Jr.''' (born December 10, 1932) is an inactive [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|United States district judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Georgia]]. ==Education and career== Hunt was born in [[Malden, Massachusetts]]. He graduated from [[Emory University]] in 1954 with a [[Bachelor of Laws]]. While a student at Emory, Hunt became a brother of the [[Alpha Tau Omega]] fraternity. After completing his degree, Hunt served in the [[United States Army]] from 1955 to 1957, after which he was a special agent with the [[Federal Bureau of Investigation]] from 1957 to 1959. Leaving the Bureau, he practiced law privately for thirteen years: in [[Clearwater, Florida|Clearwater]], [[Florida]], from 1959 to 1960; in [[Atlanta]], [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]], from 1960 to 1967; and in the [[Houston County, Georgia|Houston County]], Georgia cities of [[Perry, Georgia|Perry]] and [[Warner Robins, Georgia|Warner Robins]], from 1967 to 1971. At this time, Hunt re-entered government service, being a judge on the Houston County Superior Court from 1971 to 1986. He unsuccessfully ran for a seat on the Georgia Supreme Court in 1982, finishing fifth out of six in a statewide election. He was appointed by Governor [[Joe Frank Harris]] to the [[Supreme Court of Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia Supreme Court]] in 1986, to a seat vacated by the elevation of [[Thomas O. Marshall]] to chief justice, following the resignation of former Chief Justice [[Harold N. Hill]]. During his time on the Georgia Supreme Court, Hunt earned a [[Master of Laws]] from the [[University of Virginia School of Law]] in 1990. ===Federal judicial service=== On January 23, 1995, Hunt was nominated by President [[Bill Clinton]] to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Georgia]] vacated by [[Horace Ward]]. Hunt was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on March 24, 1995, and received his commission the same day. Hunt assumed [[senior status]] on June 30, 2005.{{FJC Bio|nid=1382566|inline=yes}} His courtroom is located in the [[Richard B. Russell Federal Building and United States Courthouse]] in [[downtown Atlanta]].[http://www.gand.uscourts.gov/directory/district-judges.php District Judges] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150509042021/http://www.gand.uscourts.gov/directory/district-judges.php |date=2015-05-09 }}, [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Georgia]], 2008-09-08. Accessed 2008-11-24. ===Notable cases=== Among Hunt's leading cases since his appointment to the federal bench was a major corruption trial in early 2001, in which the ''Atlanta Business Chronicle'' saw a connection to the scandals of the late Clinton administration.[http://www.bizjournals.com/atlanta/stories/2001/02/05/editorial1.html Atlanta corruption trial part of the enduring Bill Clinton curse], ''[[American City Business Journals|Atlanta Business Chronicle]]'', 2001-02-02. Accessed 2008-11-24. Hunt assumed [[senior status]] on June 30, 2005, but continues to hear cases in that capacity; and received some media coverage when he dismissed a lawsuit as "[[Frivolous litigation|farcical]]" by prisoner [[Jonathan Lee Riches]] against NFL Quarterback [[Michael Vick]].Rankin, Bill. [http://www.ajc.com/falcons/content/sports/falcons/stories/2007/08/17/vicklawsuit_0817.html Inmate's bizarre lawsuit against Vick thrown out of court] ''[[The Atlanta Journal-Constitution]]''.
