{{Short description|American federal judge (born 1973)}} {{Use American English|date=March 2026}} {{Use mdy dates|date=November 2026}} {{Infobox officeholder | name = James Ho | image = James Ho (Judge) (cropped).jpg | office = Judge of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]] | appointer = [[Donald Trump]] | term_start = January 4, 2018 | term_end = | predecessor = [[Carolyn Dineen King]] | successor = | office1 = 4th [[Solicitor General of Texas]] | governor1 = [[Rick Perry]] | term_start1 = May 12, 2008 | term_end1 = December 9, 2010 | predecessor1 = [[Ted Cruz]] | successor1 = [[Jonathan F. Mitchell]] | birth_name = Ho Chiun-Yue | birth_date = {{birth date and age|1973|2|27}} | birth_place = [[Taipei]], [[Taiwan]] | death_date = | death_place = | spouse = {{marriage|Allyson Newton|April 17, 2004}} | children = 2 | education = [[Stanford University]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|BA]])
[[University of Chicago]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) |module = {{Infobox Chinese |child = yes |c = 何俊宇 |p = Hé Jùnyǔ |w = Ho2 Chün4-yü3 |tl = Hô Tsùn-ú |mi = {{IPAc-cmn|h|e|2|-|j|ün|4|.|yu|3}}}} }} '''James Chiun-Yue Ho''' ([[Chinese language|Chinese]]: 何俊宇; [[pinyin]]: ''Hé Jùnyǔ''; born February 27, 1973) is an American lawyer and jurist serving as a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]]. He was appointed in 2018 by President [[Donald Trump]], becoming the Fifth Circuit's only [[Asian Americans|Asian-American]] judge and the only judge to be an immigrant.{{Cite web |last=Kass |first=John |date=March 31, 2021 |title=Column: Asian American judge challenges racism inherent in 'equity' |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2021/03/31/column-asian-american-judge-challenges-racism-inherent-in-equity/ |access-date=October 22, 2024 |website=[[Chicago Tribune]] |language=en-US}} Born in [[Taiwan]], Ho immigrated to the United States as a child and graduated from [[Stanford University]] and the [[University of Chicago Law School]]. He served as the [[Solicitor General of Texas]] from 2008 to 2010, becoming the first Asian-American to hold the position.{{Cite web |last=Severino |first=Carrie Campbell |date=September 28, 2017 |title=Who is James Ho? |url=https://www.nationalreview.com/bench-memos/who-james-ho/ |access-date=October 23, 2024 |website=[[National Review]] |language=en-US}} He has been identified as a potential Supreme Court nominee for Donald Trump's second term.{{Cite news |last=Jauregui |first=Phillip |date=May 8, 2024 |title=A shortlist of Supreme Court picks Donald Trump should consider |url=https://www.washingtontimes.com/news/2024/may/8/shortlist-of-supreme-court-picks-donald-trump-shou/ |work=Washington Examiner}}{{Cite web |last=McCormack |first=John |date=June 25, 2024 |title=Will Donald Trump Release a 2024 SCOTUS Short List? |url=https://thedispatch.com/article/will-donald-trump-release-a-2024-scotus-short-list/ |access-date=July 26, 2024 |website=The Dispatch |language=en-US}}{{Cite news |last=Willis |first=Jay |date=July 9, 2024 |title=Opinion {{!}} Trump's Next Supreme Court Picks Would Break the Mold |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/07/09/opinion/trump-supreme-court.html |access-date=July 26, 2024 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} == Early life and education == Ho was born on February 27, 1973, in [[Taipei]], [[Taiwan]], to So-Hwa and Steve Song-Shan Ho.{{FJC Bio|nid=4025386|inline=yes}} His father was a doctor who specialized in [[obstetrics and gynaecology|obstetrics and gynecology]]. The family immigrated to the United States when Ho was a child, moving first to [[Long Island]] before settling in [[San Marino, California]].{{Cite web |last=Hall |first=Michael |date=August 15, 2024 |title=Is James Ho Too Brash for Even Trump to Make Him a Supreme Court Justice? |url=https://www.texasmonthly.com/news-politics/james-ho-supreme-court/ |access-date=October 23, 2024 |website=[[Texas Monthly]] |language=en}} He became a [[United States nationality law#Naturalization|naturalized]] United States citizen at age nine.{{Cite web |last=Platoff |first=Emma |date=October 11, 2017 |title=Texas nominee for federal court at odds with Trump on birthright citizenship |url=https://www.texastribune.org/2017/10/11/jim-ho-5th-circuit-nominee-at-odds-Trump-birthright-citizenship/ |access-date=August 21, 2024 |website=[[The Texas Tribune]] |language=en}} Ho was educated at the [[Polytechnic School (California)|Polytechnic School]], a rigorous private school in [[Pasadena, California|Pasadena]], where he became the editor-in-chief of the school newspaper, ''The Paw Print''.{{Cite web |last=Mathews |first=Joe |date=October 27, 2020 |title=Two Would-Be Supreme Court Justices and Me |url=https://www.zocalopublicsquare.org/2020/10/27/leondra-kruger-jim-ho-supreme-court-high-school-memories/ideas/connecting-california/ |access-date=February 18, 2022 |website=Zócalo Public Square |publisher=[[Arizona State University]] |language=en-US}} He was a high school classmate of [[Leondra Kruger]], who would later become a justice of the [[Supreme Court of California]].{{Cite news |last=Wilson |first=Scott |date=February 18, 2022 |title=On the California Supreme Court, Leondra Kruger is known for her 'persuasive powers' among the justices |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/nation/2022/02/17/leondra-kruger-supreme-court/ |access-date=July 24, 2024 |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |language=en-US |issn=0190-8286}} Ho volunteered as an actor and dancer for school plays and briefly served as a football [[Lineman (gridiron football)|lineman]]. A classmate described Ho as "super-intense; he walked fast, laid out pages fast, and drove too fast, in a [[Ford Probe]]". After high school, Ho attended [[Stanford University]], where he studied [[public policy]], wrote for ''[[The Stanford Daily]]'', and graduated with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] with honors in 1995. From 1995 to 1996, Ho was a [[California Senate Fellows|California Senate Fellow]] at [[California State University, Sacramento]], and worked as a legislative aide to California state senator [[Quentin L. Kopp]]. He then attended the [[University of Chicago Law School]], where he became an editor of the ''[[University of Chicago Law Review]]'', joined the [[Federalist Society]], and also served as an editor for [[The Green Bag (1997)|''The Green Bag'']]. In 1998, Ho served as the executive editor of the ''[[Harvard Journal of Law & Public Policy]]''. He graduated in 1999 with a [[Juris Doctor]] with high honors and membership in the [[Order of the Coif]].{{cite news |last=Council |first=John |date=December 14, 2017 |title=Senate Confirms Former Texas Solicitor General James Ho to Fifth Circuit |url=https://www.law.com/texaslawyer/sites/texaslawyer/2017/12/14/senate-confirms-former-texas-solicitor-general-james-ho-to-fifth-circuit/ |access-date=December 14, 2017 |work=[[ALM (company)|Texas Lawyer]] |location=[[New York City]]}} Upon graduation, the law school awarded him its Ann Watson Barber Outstanding Service Award, given for "exceptional contributions to the quality of life at the Law School".{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=May 28, 2021 |title=Graduating Student Awards |url=https://www.law.uchicago.edu/news/class-2021-graduating-student-awards |access-date=October 24, 2024 |website= |publisher=[[University of Chicago Law School]] |language=en}} == Career == After law school, Ho was a [[law clerk]] to Fifth Circuit judge [[Jerry Edwin Smith]] from 1999 to 2000. From 2000 to 2001, he was in private practice at the [[Washington, D.C.]] office of the law firm [[Gibson Dunn]], where he assisted partner [[Theodore Olson]] with his representation of [[George W. Bush]] in ''[[Bush v. Gore]]''. From 2001 to 2003, Ho was an attorney in the [[United States Department of Justice]]'s [[United States Department of Justice Civil Rights Division|Civil Rights Division]] and [[Office of Legal Counsel]]. He was chief counsel to subcommittees of the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] from 2003 to 2005 under Republican Senator [[John Cornyn]].{{cite web | last1=Johnson | first1=Carrie | title=Legal Opinions Or Political Commentary? A New Judge Exemplifies The Trump Era | url=https://www.npr.org/2018/07/26/632005799/legal-opinions-or-political-commentary-a-new-judge-exemplifies-the-trump-era | date=July 26, 2018 | publisher=[[NPR]] | access-date=October 18, 2018}} From 2005 to 2006, Ho was a law clerk to Supreme Court justice [[Clarence Thomas]]. Ho returned to private practice at Gibson Dunn in its [[Dallas, Texas|Dallas]] office from 2006 to 2008 and 2010 to 2017. From 2008 to 2010, he was the [[Solicitor General of Texas]] in the Office of the [[Attorney General of Texas]], replacing [[Ted Cruz]] in that position. As Texas solicitor general, Ho led the state's lawsuits against the [[Obama administration]]. Ho has worked as a volunteer attorney with the [[First Liberty Institute]], a religious legal advocacy organization.{{cite press release|url=https://globenewswire.com/news-release/2017/12/14/1262269/0/en/First-Liberty-Institute-Congratulates-Its-Former-Volunteer-Attorney-James-C-Ho-on-His-Judicial-Confirmation.html|title=First Liberty Institute Congratulates Its Former Volunteer Attorney James C. Ho on His Judicial Confirmation|date= December 14, 2017|access-date=December 16, 2017}}{{cite web | last1=Marcus | first1=Ilana | last2=Eaton | first2=Joshua | last3=Timms | first3=Ed | title=Federal judges: From political players to lifetime appointments | url=https://www.rollcall.com/2020/03/20/federal-judges-from-political-players-to-lifetime-appointments/ | date=March 20, 2020 | work=[[Roll Call]] | access-date=May 24, 2020}} He has held multiple positions as a member of the [[Federalist Society]] since 1996.{{Cite web |last=Ho |first=James |date=2017 |title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/James%20Ho%20SJQ.pdf |access-date=June 30, 2018 |website=[[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]]}} === Federal judicial service === On September 28, 2017, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to nominate Ho as a United States circuit judge to an undetermined seat on the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]].{{cite news |first1=Patrick |last1=Svitek |first2=Emma |last2=Platoff |url=https://www.texastribune.org/2017/09/28/trump-taps-2-texans-willett-and-ho-5th-circuit/ |title=Trump taps two Texans — Willett and Ho — for judicial posts |work=[[The Texas Tribune]] |date=September 28, 2017}} Cruz had promoted Ho as a candidate for a vacancy on the court. On October 16, 2017, Trump sent Ho's nomination to the Senate. He was nominated to the seat vacated by Judge [[Carolyn Dineen King]], who assumed [[senior status]] on December 31, 2013.[https://www.congress.gov/nomination/115th-congress/1108 PN1108 — James C. Ho — The Judiciary], 115th Congress (2017-2018), Congress.gov. On November 15, 2017, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/committee-activity/hearings/11/15/2017/nominations|title=Nominations | United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|website=www.judiciary.senate.gov|date=November 15, 2017}} On December 7, 2017, his nomination was reported out of committee by an 11–9 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%2012-07-17.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – December 7, 2017|publisher=Senate Judiciary Committee}} On December 13, 2017, the [[United States Senate]] invoked [[cloture]] on his nomination by a 53–44 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1151/vote_115_1_00316.htm|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: James C. Ho to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the Fifth Circuit)|website=United States Senate|date=December 13, 2017}} On December 14, 2017, Ho's nomination was confirmed by a 53–43 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=115&session=1&vote=00317|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation James C. Ho, of Texas, to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the Fifth Circuit)|website=United States Senate|date=December 14, 2017}} He received his judicial commission on January 4, 2018. He was sworn in by Justice [[Clarence Thomas]] at the private library of Texan real estate billionaire and Republican donor [[Harlan Crow]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.propublica.org/article/clarence-thomas-scotus-undisclosed-luxury-travel-gifts-crow|title=Clarence Thomas and the Billionaire|website=ProPublica|date=April 6, 2023|access-date=April 6, 2023}} On September 9, 2020, Trump included Ho on a list of potential nominees to the Supreme Court.{{Cite web|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefings-statements/remarks-president-trump-judicial-appointments/|title=Remarks by President Trump on Judicial Appointments – The White House|website=trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov}} Trump nominated [[Amy Coney Barrett]], who was confirmed. Ho has again been identified as a potential Supreme Court nominee should a vacancy arise during Donald Trump's second term.{{Cite web |author-first1=Shannon |author-last1=Bream |author-first2=Bill |author-last2=Mears |date=June 10, 2024 |title=Potential candidates for Supreme Court under a second Donald Trump term |url=https://www.foxnews.com/politics/potential-candidates-supreme-court-under-second-donald-trump-term |access-date=June 24, 2024 |website=Fox News |language=en-US}} Senator [[Josh Hawley]] (R-MO) stated in June 2024 that he believes Ho "has done a terrific job on the 5th [Circuit]" and that Ho is "principled" and "will be immune to the [[Greenhouse effect (United States Supreme Court)#:~:text=Notable affected justices-,Origins of the theory,Fellow at Yale Law School.|Greenhouse effect]].” Senator [[Ted Cruz]] (R-TX) has also expressed support for Ho's elevation to the Supreme Court.{{Cite web |last=Svitek |first=Patrick |date=September 14, 2020 |title=Ted Cruz says he doesn't want to join the Supreme Court after being shortlisted by Trump |url=https://www.texastribune.org/2020/09/14/ted-cruz-supreme-court/ |access-date=July 26, 2024 |website=The Texas Tribune |language=en}} Ho was named to the shortlist of presidential candidate [[Vivek Ramaswamy 2024 presidential campaign|Vivek Ramaswamy]].{{Cite web |date=July 17, 2023 |title=GOP presidential hopeful Vivek Ramaswamy lists Senators Cruz, Lee as possible Supreme Court picks |url=https://apnews.com/article/ramaswamy-supreme-court-cruz-lee-ho-aaac0090149fd389d0b5466f4e13a501 |access-date=July 26, 2024 |website=AP News |language=en}} On September 29, 2022, Ho delivered a speech at a Federalist Society conference in Kentucky and said he would no longer hire law clerks from [[Yale Law School]], which he said was plagued by "[[cancel culture]]" and students disrupting conservative speakers. Ho said Yale "not only tolerates the cancellation of views — it actively practices it", and he urged other judges to likewise boycott the school.{{cite news | url=https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/trump-appointed-judge-boycotts-yale-law-clerks-over-cancel-culture-2022-09-29/ | title=Trump-appointed judge boycotts Yale for law clerks over 'cancel culture' | newspaper=Reuters | date=September 30, 2022 | last1=Raymond | first1=Nate }}{{cite web | last1=Alder | first1=Madison | title=US Judge Won't Hire Yale Law Clerks Citing 'Cancel Culture' (1) | url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/fifth-circuits-ho-wont-hire-from-yale-citing-cancel-culture | date=September 30, 2022 | work=[[Bloomberg Law]] | access-date=November 6, 2022}} United States Circuit Judge [[Elizabeth L. Branch]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit]] confirmed her participation in the Yale boycott in a statement to [[National Review]]. Branch told the National Review that Ho raised "legitimate concerns about the lack of free speech on law school campuses, Yale in particular," and that she would not consider students from Yale for clerkships in the future.{{cite news | url=https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/2nd-trump-appointed-judge-publicly-says-she-will-not-hire-yale-clerks-2022-10-07/ | title=2nd Trump-appointed judge publicly says she will not hire Yale clerks | newspaper=Reuters | date=October 7, 2022 | last1=Raymond | first1=Nate }} [[File:James Ho (federal judge) and Rebecca Bradley (Wisconsin justice) during an event at Wisconsin Law School on February 22, 2024.jpg|thumb|Ho (left), accompanied by Wisconsin Justice [[Rebecca Bradley]], speaking during a 2024 event at the [[University of Wisconsin Law School]]]] On May 6, 2024, Ho cosigned a letter alongside twelve federal judges, which he shared with [[CNN]], vowing not to hire [[Columbia University]] law students or undergraduates for concerns that the university is not doing enough to counter students protesting the war in Gaza.{{Cite web |last=Pazmino |first=Gloria |date=May 7, 2024 |title=Trump-appointed judges say they'll boycott Columbia grads over university's handling of protests {{!}} CNN Business |url=https://www.cnn.com/2024/05/07/business/columbia-protests-federal-judges-boycott/index.html |access-date=July 26, 2024 |website=CNN |language=en}} Ho asked in the letter that the university should identify "students who engage in such conduct so that future employers can avoid hiring them. If not, employers are forced to assume the risk that anyone they hire from Columbia may be one of these disruptive and hateful students."{{Cite web |date=May 6, 2024 |title=Trump-appointed judges say they'll boycott Columbia grads over university's handling of protests|url=https://www.cnn.com/2024/05/07/business/columbia-protests-federal-judges-boycott/index.html | newspaper=CNN |access-date=May 8, 2024}} Ho has been outspoken defender of [[consular nonreviewability]] against illegal immigration, suggesting "a sovereign isn’t a sovereign if it can't control its borders" and that "[o]ur national objectives are undercut when states encourage illegal entry into the United States."Platero-Rosales v. Garland (5th Cir. 2022), https://www.ca5.uscourts.gov/opinions/pub/20/20-60707-CV0.pdf{{Cite news |last=Thomsen |first=Jacqueline |date=February 12, 2024 |title=Fifth Circuit Chides Judge for Quick Trial in Texas Border Case |url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/fifth-circuit-chides-judge-for-quick-trial-in-texas-border-case |work=Bloomberg Law}} He has stated that "[i]f only 'the political branches of the federal government' can decide if a state has been invaded, it effectively prohibits states from exercising their sovereign right of self-defense without federal permission."{{Cite web |title=United States v. Abbott, 92 F.4th 570 {{!}} Casetext Search + Citator |url=https://casetext.com/case/united-states-v-abbott-61 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240726223611/https://casetext.com/case/united-states-v-abbott-61 |url-status=dead |archive-date=July 26, 2024 |access-date=July 26, 2024 |website=casetext.com}} Ho has also defended the use of the term "[[Alien (law)|alien]]", arguing it should not be seen as offensive, noting that "[i]t's a centuries-old legal term found in countless judicial decisions."{{Cite news |last=Umanah |first=Ufonobong |date=May 31, 2023 |title=Conservative Judge Offers Defense of 'Alien' in Immigration Case |url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/immigration/conservative-judge-offers-defense-of-alien-in-immigration-case |work=Bloomberg Law}} Ho was for many years a prominent defender of [[Birthright citizenship in the United States|birthright citizenship]] for the children of undocumented immigrants, but shifted his views on the topic after Donald Trump was elected in 2024.{{Cite news |last=Mark |first=Julian |date=May 30, 2026 |title=There are no Supreme Court vacancies, but some judges are acting like there might be |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/05/30/with-flashy-opinions-judges-may-be-auditioning-supreme-court/ |work=The Washington Post |language=en-US |issn=0190-8286}} In a 2006 article in ''[[The Green Bag (1997)|The Green Bag]]'', he wrote that the [[Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution|Fourteenth Amendment's]] Citizenship Clause protected "no less for children of undocumented persons than for descendants of Mayflower passengers," and he restated this position in a 2011 ''[[The Wall Street Journal|Wall Street Journal]]'' op-ed and a 2008 ''[[University of Richmond Law Review]]'' article.{{Cite journal |last=Ho |first=James C. |date=Summer 2006 |title=Defining "American": Birthright Citizenship and the Original Understanding of the 14th Amendment |url=https://www.gibsondunn.com/wp-content/uploads/documents/publications/Ho-DefiningAmerican.pdf |journal=[[The Green Bag (1997)|The Green Bag]] |volume=9 |issue=4 |pages=366–378}}{{Cite news |url=https://thehill.com/regulation/court-battles/5292906-supreme-court-birthright-citizenship/ |title=Birthright citizenship debate erupts as Supreme Court arguments near |date=May 11, 2025 |work=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]] |access-date=May 28, 2026}} In a November 11, 2024, interview with law professor [[Josh Blackman]] at ''[[The Volokh Conspiracy]]'', published a week after Trump's reelection, Ho qualified that position. He told Blackman: "No one to my knowledge has ever argued that the children of invading aliens are entitled to birthright citizenship," analogizing the situation to that of "unlawful combatants" after 9/11.{{Cite web |last=Blackman |first=Josh |author-link=Josh Blackman |url=https://reason.com/volokh/2024/11/11/an-interview-with-judge-james-c-ho/ |title=An Interview with Judge James C. Ho |date=November 11, 2024 |work=[[The Volokh Conspiracy]] |access-date=May 28, 2026}} The remark connected the birthright citizenship question to Ho's earlier concurrence in ''United States v. Abbott'', in which he had written that the southern border was the site of an "invasion." The shift was characterized by ''[[Slate (magazine)|Slate]]'' as a walkback of his previous position, with commentator [[Mark Joseph Stern]] writing that Ho was "framing immigrants who lack permanent legal status as 'invading aliens.'"{{Cite news |last=Stern |first=Mark Joseph |url=https://slate.com/news-and-politics/2024/11/trump-scotus-supreme-court-short-list-flip-flop-james-ho.html |title=A SCOTUS Short-Lister Has Flip-Flopped to Embrace One of Trump's Worst Positions |date=November 12, 2024 |work=[[Slate (magazine)|Slate]] |access-date=May 28, 2026}} Originalist legal scholar [[Michael Ramsey (legal scholar)|Michael Ramsey]], writing at the [[Tenth Amendment Center]], said he was sympathetic to Ho's earlier writings on birthright citizenship and disagreed with Ho's new framing.{{Cite web |url=https://blog.tenthamendmentcenter.com/2024/11/invasion-and-birthright-citizenship/ |title=Invasion and Birthright Citizenship |publisher=[[Tenth Amendment Center]] |date=November 18, 2024 |access-date=May 28, 2026}} The interview was subsequently cited by the Trump administration in its [[Supreme Court of the United States|Supreme Court]] briefing in defense of the January 20, 2025, executive order restricting birthright citizenship.{{Cite web |url=https://www.supremecourt.gov/DocketPDF/24/24A884/354214/20250328091910316_Washington%20v.%20Trump%20-%20SCOTUS%20Amicus%20-%20For%20Filing.pdf |title=Brief in Washington v. Trump |date=March 28, 2025 |publisher=[[Supreme Court of the United States]] |access-date=May 28, 2026}} ''The Washington Post'' covered Ho's shift on birthright citizenship in an article on conservative judges who appeared to bringing attention to himself and auditioning to President Donald Trump to be appointed to the Supreme Court. === Notable opinions === On April 18, 2018, in his first written opinion as a Fifth Circuit judge, Ho dissented from a denial of a rehearing ''[[en banc]]'' in a case regarding a [[Campaign finance in the United States|limit on campaign contributions]]. The Fifth Circuit three-judge panel upheld the constitutionality of a [[Austin, Texas|City of Austin]] ordinance setting an individual campaign contribution limit of $350 per election for candidates for mayor and city council, rejecting the plaintiff's claim that the limit violated the [[First Amendment of the United States Constitution|First Amendment]]. In his dissent, Ho argued the court "should have granted rehearing [[en banc]] and held that the Austin contribution limit violates the First Amendment" and asserted that "if there is too much money in politics, it's because there's too much government."''[https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4269082086850393014 Zimmerman v. City of Austin]'', 881 F.3d 378 (5th Cir. 2018).{{Cite web |url=https://slate.com/news-and-politics/2018/04/james-ho-shows-the-presidents-court-packing-strategy-is-working.html |title=Trump Judge Judges Trumpily |author-link=Mark Joseph Stern|last=Stern |first=Mark Joseph |date=April 24, 2018 |website=slate.com |access-date=May 6, 2018}}{{cite magazine |url=https://www.washingtonexaminer.com/opinion/trump-appointed-judge-delivers-fantastic-campaign-finance-opinion-in-first-ruling |title=Trump-appointed judge delivers fantastic campaign finance opinion in first ruling |last=Smith |first=Bradley |date=May 2, 2018 |magazine=[[The Washington Examiner]] |access-date=May 6, 2018}} In 2020, Ho was a member of a panel that stayed a preliminary injunction entered by United States District Judge [[Samuel Frederick Biery Jr.]] that expanded the right to use a [[Postal voting in the 2020 United States elections|mail-in ballot]] to all Texas voters during the ongoing [[COVID-19 pandemic in Texas|COVID-19 pandemic]] (allowing broader use of mail-in voting than under the Texas Election Code, which entitled only Texas voters over age 65 to vote absentee without an excuse). Ho wrote a separate concurring opinion favoring the state officials.{{Cite web |url=https://static.texastribune.org/media/files/4c6a8f8249814314d7e84258c0d2ca37/5thCircuitVBMMotionPendingAppeal.pdf?_ga=2.249116679.1297343671.1591317896-1711246450.1590118534 |title=IN THE UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE FIFTH CIRCT No. 20-50407: Texas Democratic Party, et al. v. Greg Abbott, et al. |date=June 4, 2020 |access-date=June 4, 2020}}{{Cite web|date=June 4, 2020|title=Federal appeals court extends block on voting-by-mail expansion in Texas|url=https://www.texastribune.org/2020/06/04/federal-appeals-court-extends-block-voting-mail-expansion-texas/|access-date=June 4, 2020}}{{Cite web|title=Texas Democratic Party v. Abbott, 961 F.3d 389 (5th Cir. June 4, 2020) - Google Scholar|url=https://scholar.google.co.uk/scholar_case?case=8934111846629613891|access-date=October 13, 2020|website=scholar.google.co.uk}}{{Cite web|title=Texas Democratic Party v. Abbott, No. 20-50407 (5th Cir. Sep. 10, 2020) - Google Scholar|url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=9985145995200608910|access-date=October 13, 2020|website=scholar.google.co.uk}}{{Cite web|last=Ura|first=Alexa|date=June 16, 2020|title=Texas Democrats ask U.S. Supreme Court to weigh in on voting by mail|url=https://www.texastribune.org/2020/06/16/texas-vote-by-mail/|access-date=June 18, 2020|website=The Texas Tribune|language=en}} On September 9, 2021, Ho authored the majority opinion for an en banc panel in ''[[Helix Energy Solutions Group, Inc. v. Hewitt]]'', interpreting a provision of the [[Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938]]. Ho was affirmed by the United States Supreme Court in an opinion authored by Justice [[Elena Kagan]].{{Cite web |date=February 23, 2023 |title=Justices decide a day-rate is not a salary |url=https://www.scotusblog.com/2023/02/helix-energy-supreme-court-opinion/ |access-date=July 26, 2024 |website=SCOTUSblog |language=en-US}} == Personal life == Ho's wife, Allyson Paix Newton Ho (née Newton, formerly Heidelbaugh), is a lawyer who is a partner in the Dallas office of Gibson Dunn and serves as co-chair of the firm's appellate practice group. The two met when Ho was a law clerk for Judge Jerry Edwin Smith in [[Houston|Houston, Texas]], and Newton was a law student working for a Houston firm. They married on April 17, 2004.{{Cite journal |date=Spring 2004 |editor-last=Davies |editor-first=Ross E. |editor2-last=Gossett |editor2-first=David M. |editor3-last=Kosma |editor3-first=Montgomery N. |title=Front Matter |url=http://greenbag.org/v7n3/v7n3_front_matter.pdf |journal=[[The Green Bag (1997)|The Green Bag]] |series=2D |volume=7 |issue=3 |pages=1–4}} Newton earned a Ph.D. in English from [[Rice University]] and served as a law clerk to Justice [[Sandra Day O'Connor]]. She has argued four cases before the United States Supreme Court. They have twins, a daughter and a son.{{Cite web |date=2018 |title=Biography of Judge James C. Jane L. Kelly:
{{Short description|American judge (born 1964)}} {{Infobox officeholder |name = Jane Kelly |image = Judge Jane Kelly (cropped).jpg |caption = Kelly in 2013 |office = Judge of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit]] |appointer = [[Barack Obama]] |term_start = April 25, 2013 |term_end = |predecessor = [[Michael Joseph Melloy]] |successor = |birth_name = Jane Louise Kelly |birth_date = {{birth date and age|1964|10|28}} |birth_place = [[Greencastle, Indiana]], U.S. |death_date = |death_place = |education = [[Duke University]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|BA]])
[[Harvard University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Jane Louise Kelly''' (born October 28, 1964) is an American lawyer and jurist serving as a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit]]. ==Early life and education== Kelly was born in 1964 in [[Greencastle, Indiana]],{{cite web|url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/kelly-jane-louise|title=Kelly, Jane Louise|publisher=Federal Judicial Center|work=History of the Federal Judiciary}} to Richard and Judith C. Kelly.{{cite web |last=Bernsee |first=Eric |title=Greencastle native in line to be Justice Scalia successor? |url=https://www.bannergraphic.com/story/2277730.html|website=Banner Graphic |date=February 15, 2016 |access-date=March 2, 2016}} She graduated from Greencastle High School in 1983 as co-[[valedictorian]]. She received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree, ''summa cum laude'', in 1987, from [[Duke University]], and a [[Juris Doctor]], ''[[cum laude]]'', from [[Harvard Law School]], in 1991. She studied pediatrics for one year in [[New Zealand]] under a [[Fulbright Program|Fulbright Scholarship]] in between Duke and Harvard.{{cite web |last=Hopson |first=Thomas |title=Potential nominee: Judge Jane Kelly, former public defender |url=http://www.scotusblog.com/2016/03/potential-nominee-judge-jane-kelly-former-public-defender/ |website=SCOTUSblog |date=March 7, 2016 |access-date=March 8, 2016}} Her graduating class included [[Barack Obama]]. ==Career== After graduation, Kelly was a [[law clerk]] for [[Donald J. Porter]], chief judge of the [[United States District Court for the District of South Dakota]] in [[Sioux Falls, South Dakota|Sioux Falls]], [[South Dakota]].{{cite web|last1=Lynch|first1=James Q.|title=Cedar Rapids attorney Jane Kelly nominated to federal appeals court|url=https://www.thegazette.com/2013/01/31/cedar-rapids-attorney-jane-kelly-nominated-to-federal-appeals-court|website=The Gazette|date=January 31, 2013}} She then clerked for [[David R. Hansen]], a judge of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit]]. During the 1993–94 academic year, Kelly taught as a visiting instructor at the [[University of Illinois College of Law]].{{cite web|title=Jane Kelly Judge, United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/profiles/people/18030154-jane-louise-kelly|website=Bloomberg Business|access-date=2 March 2016}} In 1994, Kelly became an [[Federal public defender|assistant federal public defender]] in [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Iowa|the Northern District of Iowa]]. From 1999 to 2013, she served as the supervising attorney in the [[Cedar Rapids, Iowa|Cedar Rapids]], [[Iowa]] office.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2013/01/31/president-obama-nominates-two-serve-us-court-appeals|title=President Obama Nominates Two to Serve on the US Court of Appeals|publisher=[[White House Office of the Press Secretary]]|date=January 31, 2013}}{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/113thCongressJudicialNominations/upload/Kelly-Senate-Questionnaire-Final.pdf|title=Senate Judiciary Committee Nomination Questionnaire|access-date=2013-02-11|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160223232634/http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/nominations/113thCongressJudicialNominations/upload/Kelly-Senate-Questionnaire-Final.pdf|archive-date=2016-02-23|url-status=dead}} === Federal judicial service === On January 31, 2013, [[President of the United States|President]] [[Barack Obama]] nominated Kelly to serve as a United States Circuit Judge of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit]], to the seat vacated by Judge [[Michael Joseph Melloy]], who assumed [[senior status]] on February 1, 2013. Her nomination was reported on a voice vote of the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] on March 22. The Senate confirmed Kelly by a 96–0 vote on April 24.{{cite web|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Jane Kelly, of Iowa, to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the Eighth Circuit)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=113&session=1&vote=00108|publisher=United States Senate}} She received her commission on April 25. In March 2016, Kelly was reported to be a potential nominee for the [[Supreme Court of the United States|Supreme Court]] to replace the vacancy caused by the death of Justice [[Antonin Scalia]].{{cite news |title=Here are judges the White House is considering for the Supreme Court |date=March 7, 2016 |newspaper=[[Washington Post]] |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/here-are-the-five-judges-the-white-house-is-considering-for-the-supreme-court/2016/03/06/2e785858-e0a4-11e5-9c36-e1902f6b6571_story.html }} The conservative [[Judicial Crisis Network]] ran ads against her to forestall the nomination.{{Cite web|url=https://thehill.com/opinion/judiciary/595960-ketanji-brown-jackson-and-the-job-of-a-public-defender?rl=1|title = Ketanji Brown Jackson and the job of a public defender|date = 27 February 2022}} ==Notable cases== * In July 2017, Kelly dissented when the ''[[en banc]]'' Eighth Circuit found, by a vote of 7–2, that the [[National Labor Relations Act]] did not protect [[Jimmy John's]] employees from being fired for putting up [[Industrial Workers of the World]] posters seeking [[sick leave]].{{Bluebook journal |first=|last=Note| title=Recent Case: Eighth Circuit Holds Employee Organizing Activity Unprotected for Disloyalty Despite Lack of “Malicious Motive”| volume=131 | journal=[[Harvard Law Review|Harv. L. Rev.]] | page=1820 | url=https://harvardlawreview.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/1820-1827_Online.pdf| year=2018}} *On August 23, 2019, Kelly dissented when the Eighth Circuit ruled in favor of a religious exemption from a state's anti-discrimination law.{{Cite web |url=http://www.adfmedia.org/files/TelescopeMediaOpinion8thCircuit.pdf/ |title=Archived copy |access-date=2019-12-12 |archive-date=2019-10-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191015190415/http://www.adfmedia.org/files/TelescopeMediaOpinion8thCircuit.pdf |url-status=dead }} *Five days before Election Day 2020, the 8th circuit ruled that all Minnesota ballots received after Election Day should be set aside, leaving it to the district court whether those ballots should be thrown out. Kelly strongly dissented, noting that Minnesota voters had already been informed that ballots received by Election Day could be counted as long as they were postmarked by Election Day.{{Cite web|url=https://ecf.ca8.uscourts.gov/opndir/20/10/203139P.pdf|title=James Carson; Eric Lucero v. Steve Simon|website=ecf.ca8.uscourts.gov|date=October 29, 2020|access-date=October 6, 2021}} As state officials urged voters to turn in ballots sooner rather than later as a result of this ruling, only 2,447 ballots arrived after Election Day, causing the plaintiffs to drop their case.{{Cite web|url=https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/politics/minnesota-received-just-2447-mail-ballots-after-election-day/ar-BB1aZQKu|title=Minnesota received just 2,447 mail ballots after Election Day|website=MSN|date=November 13, 2020|access-date=October 6, 2021}} *Kelly authored a June 9, 2021, order that blocked part of a Missouri abortion law that would ban abortion after 8 weeks.{{Cite web|url=https://s3.documentcloud.org/documents/20804881/6-9-21-8th-circuit-opinion-planned-parenthood-v-parson-missouri.pdf|title=Reproductive Health Services of Planned Parenthood of the St. Louis Region, Inc., et al v. Governor Michael L. Parson, et al|website=s3.documentcloud.org|date=June 9, 2021|access-date=October 6, 2021}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.jurist.org/news/2021/06/federal-appeals-court-blocks-missouri-abortion-restrictions/|title=Federal appeals court blocks Missouri abortion restrictions|website=Jurist|date=June 10, 2021|access-date=October 6, 2021}} ==Personal life== In 2004, Kelly was attacked while jogging in a park in Cedar Rapids, brutally beaten and left barely conscious; her assailant was never identified.{{cite news|last1=Hirschfield Davis|first1=Julie|title=White House Said to Be Vetting Iowa Judge for Supreme Court Seat|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/03/03/us/politics/white-house-vetting-jane-kelly-judge-supreme-court.html |work=The New York Times|date=2 March 2016|access-date=2 March 2016}}"[http://wcfcourier.com/news/breaking_news/public-defender-attacked-while-jogging-in-c-r/article_2ba33a48-3420-50dd-bff5-04b9835c2ec4.html Public defender attacked while jogging in C.R.]", ''The Courier'' (June 30, 2004). ==See also== *[[Barack Obama Supreme Court candidates]] ==References== {{Reflist|30em}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1394186}} *{{Ballotpedia|Jane_Kelly|Jane Kelly}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Michael Joseph Melloy]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit]]}}|years=2013–present}} {{s-inc}} {{s-end}} {{USCourtsOfAppealsJudges}} {{Authority control}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Kelly, Jane L.}} [[Category:1964 births]] [[Category:21st-century American women judges]] [[Category:Duke University alumni]] [[Category:Harvard Law School alumni]] [[Category:Iowa lawyers]] [[Category:Judges of the United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit]] [[Category:Living people]] [[Category:People from Greencastle, Indiana]] [[Category:Public defenders]] [[Category:United States court of appeals judges appointed by Barack Obama]] [[Category:University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign faculty]] [[Category:Lawyers from Sioux Falls, South Dakota]]

[[Ohio State University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Jeffrey Stuart Sutton''' (born 1960) is an American lawyer and jurist serving as a [[Senior status|senior]] [[United States federal judge|judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit]]. Sutton was appointed to the Sixth Circuit in 2003 by President [[George W. Bush]] and served as its chief judge from 2021 to 2026. ==Early life and career== Sutton received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in history from [[Williams College]] in 1983.{{cite web |title=1983, Jeff Sutton – Judge, United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit |url=https://history.williams.edu/history-majors-past/1983-jeff-sutton-judge-united-states-court-of-appeals-for-the-sixth-circuit/ |website=Williams College History Majors, Past and Present |access-date=April 9, 2022}} Sutton worked as a [[paralegal]] in [[Washington, D.C.]], and spent a summer at an [[archaeological dig]] site in [[Jordan]] as part of a [[United States Department of State]] [[Cultural diplomacy|cultural exchange]] program, then returned to Ohio to be a high school history teacher and varsity soccer coach at the [[Columbus Academy]], a private school in [[Gahanna, Ohio]]. Sutton received his [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Ohio State University]]'s [[Moritz College of Law]] in 1990. He then clerked for Judge [[Thomas Meskill]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit]] from 1990 to 1991. Next he clerked at the [[United States Supreme Court]] for Justice [[Lewis F. Powell Jr.]], who had assumed senior status, then for Justice [[Antonin Scalia]] from 1991 to 1992. Scalia later said that Sutton was "one of the very best law clerks [he] ever had".{{Cite web |last=Dish |first=The Daily |date=August 31, 2010 |title=Justice Scalia and How Elites Are Hired |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/daily-dish/archive/2010/08/justice-scalia-and-how-elites-are-hired/182958/ |access-date=May 20, 2022 |website=The Atlantic |language=en}} Sutton was in private practice in Columbus at the law firm [[Jones Day]] from 1992 to 1995 and 1998 to 2003, serving as [[Solicitor General of Ohio]] from 1995 to 1998. He has also served as an adjunct professor of law at the [[Ohio State University]] [[Moritz College of Law]][http://moritzlaw.osu.edu/faculty/bios.php?ID=120 Moritz College of Law – Faculty: The Honorable Jeffrey S. Sutton] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120222064243/http://moritzlaw.osu.edu/faculty/bios.php?ID=120 |date=February 22, 2012 }}. Moritzlaw.osu.edu. Retrieved on June 25, 2012. since 1994 and more recently as a visiting lecturer at [[Harvard Law School]].[http://www.law.harvard.edu/faculty/directory/index.html?id=1014 Harvard Law School - Faculty: Jeffrey S. Sutton]. Law.harvard.edu. Retrieved January 14, 2013. He teaches state constitutional law, a subject in which he is particularly interested and about which he has written extensively.''See, e.g.'', Holland, McAllister, Shaman, and Sutton, State Constitutional Law: The Modern Experience (2010); [http://www.law.ku.edu/sites/law.drupal.ku.edu/files/docs/law_review/v59/01-Sutton_Final.pdf ''What Does—and Does Not—Ail State Constitutional Law''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170808183144/https://law.ku.edu/sites/law.drupal.ku.edu/files/docs/law_review/v59/01-Sutton_Final.pdf |date=August 8, 2017 }}, 59 U. Kan. L. Rev. 687 (2011). ==Federal judicial service== Sutton was first nominated by President [[George W. Bush]] on May 9, 2001, to a seat on the Sixth Circuit vacated by [[David A. Nelson]], who assumed [[senior status]] on October 1, 1999. That nomination, made during the [[107th United States Congress]], never received a floor vote in the [[United States Senate]]. Sutton was not confirmed until almost two years later, on April 29, 2003, when the Senate of the [[108th United States Congress]] confirmed him by a 52–41 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1081/vote_108_1_00135.htm?congress=108&session=1&vote=00135|title=U.S. Senate: U.S. Senate Roll Call Votes 108th Congress - 1st Session|website=Senate.gov}} He received his commission on May 5, 2003.{{FJC Bio|nid=1391886|inline=yes}} He became Chief Judge on May 1, 2021.{{Cite web|date=May 3, 2021|title=The Honorable Jeffrey S. Sutton assumed the position of Chief Judge|url=https://www.ca6.uscourts.gov/news/honorable-jeffrey-s-sutton-assumed-position-chief-judge|access-date=May 3, 2021|website=Ca6.uscourts.gov}} On February 20, 2026, Sutton announced that he would be taking [[senior status]].{{Cite web|url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/sixth-circuit-judge-sutton-to-step-back-hand-trump-a-vacancy|title=Sixth Circuit Judge Sutton to Step Back, Hand Trump Vacancy |website=News.bloomberglaw.com|date=February 20, 2026|access-date=July 29, 2026}} ===Notable opinions=== In 2007, Sutton dissented in part when the Sixth Circuit held that a police officer did not have [[qualified immunity]] for arresting a speaker for using foul language at a town meeting.[https://harvardlawreview.org/wp-content/uploads/pdfs/leonard_v_robinson.pdf ''Recent Case: Sixth Circuit Denies Qualified Immunity to Police Officer for Arrest for Speech at Public Meeting''], 120 Harv. L. Rev. 2238 (2007) In June 2011, Sutton became the first judge appointed by a Republican to [[National Federation of Independent Business v. Sebelius|rule]] in favor of the [[Health care in the United States|health care]] mandate in President [[Barack Obama]]'s [[Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act|Health Care law]].[https://www.politico.com/story/2011/06/6th-circuit-panel-upholds-mandate-058040 6th Circuit Court of Appeals panel upholds individual mandate – Jennifer Haberkorn]. Politico.Com. Retrieved on June 25, 2012. In November 2014, Sutton authored the 2–1 [[Obergefell v. Hodges|opinion]] ruling upholding same-sex marriage bans in Michigan, Kentucky, Ohio, and Tennessee in the Sixth Circuit reversing six previous federal district court rulings. The ruling was the second federal court ruling and the only Federal Court of Appeals ruling{{cite web|last1=Denniston|first1=Lyle|title=Puerto Rico ban on same-sex marriage upheld|url=http://www.scotusblog.com/2014/10/puerto-rico-ban-on-same-sex-marriage-upheld/|website=SCOTUSblog|date=October 21, 2014 |access-date=November 12, 2014}} to uphold same-sex marriage bans after the U.S. Supreme Court struck down a portion of the [[Defense of Marriage Act]] in ''[[United States v. Windsor]]'' in June 2013. This [[Circuit split|ran counter]] to rulings by the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the 4th, 7th, 9th and 10th circuits, which then led the U.S. Supreme Court to grant [[writ of certiorari]] to review same-sex marriage bans when it previously declined to do so.{{cite news|last1=Wolf|first1=Richard|title=Gay marriage bans in four states upheld, Supreme Court review likely|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/nation/2014/11/06/gay-marriage-appeals-court-ohio-michigan-kentucky-tennessee/15712319/|access-date=November 7, 2014|work=USA Today|publisher=Gannett|date=November 7, 2014}}{{cite news|last1=Wolf|first1=Richard|title=Supreme Court agrees to rule on Gay Marriage|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/nation/2015/01/16/supreme-court-gay-marriage/21867355/|access-date=May 7, 2015|work=USA Today|date=January 16, 2015}} In ''[[Obergefell v. Hodges]]'' the Supreme Court reversed the decision of the Sixth Circuit. {{See also|Jonathan Skrmetti#VUMC investigation|LGBT rights in Tennessee#Medical care}} On December 17, 2021, in ''[[National Federation of Independent Business v. Occupational Safety and Health Administration|In re MCP No. 165, OSHA, Interim Final Rule: COVID-19 Vaccination & Testing]]'', 20 F.4th 264 (6th Cir. 2021), Chief Judge Sutton dissented from the denial of initial hearing [[en banc]]. The case concerned a rule issued by the Secretary of Labor requiring “roughly 80 million workers to become vaccinated or face a weekly self-financed testing requirement and a daily masking requirement.” Chief Judge Sutton’s opinion argues that the Secretary of Labor lacks “authority to impose this vaccine-or-test mandate.”{{Cite web | url=https://www.opn.ca6.uscourts.gov/opinions.pdf/21a0287p-06.pdf | title=In Re: MCP no. 165, occupational safety and health administration, interim final rule: Covid-19 vaccination and testing; emergency temporary standard 86 fed. reg. 61402 | website=Opn.ca6.uscourts.gov}} On April 12, 2022, in ''[[United States v. Biden]]'' (6th Cir. 2022), Judge Sutton wrote a concurrence suggesting that [[nationwide injunctions]] "seem to take the judicial power beyond its traditionally understood uses, permitting district courts to order the government to act or refrain from acting toward nonparties in the case."{{Cite web | url=https://www.opn.ca6.uscourts.gov/opinions.pdf/22a0074p-06.pdf | title=State of Arizona, Montana, Ohio v. [[Yale University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Jennifer Sung''' (born 1972) is a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]]. == Early life and education == Sung was born in 1972 in [[Edison, New Jersey]], to a Chinese-American family.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Sung%20SJQ%20Public%20Final.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=September 7, 2021|archive-date=December 25, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211225171831/https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Sung%20SJQ%20Public%20Final.pdf|url-status=bot: unknown}} She graduated from [[Oberlin College]] in 1994 with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] in politics with honors. From 1994 to 2001, Sung worked as a [[union organizer]] for the [[Service Employees International Union]].{{cite news |last1=Campbell |first1=Braden |title=Who Is Jennifer Sung, Biden's Labor-Side 9th Circ. Pick? - Law360 |url=https://www.law360.com/employment-authority/articles/1399156 |access-date=28 September 2021 |work=www.law360.com |date=June 30, 2021 |language=en}} She then attended [[Yale Law School]], graduating in 2004 with a [[Juris Doctor]].{{Cite web|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/06/30/president-biden-names-fifth-round-of-judicial-nominees/|title=President Biden Names Fifth Round of Judicial Nominees|date=30 June 2021|website=The White House|access-date=10 December 2021}} == Career == After law school, Sung served as a [[law clerk]] to Ninth Circuit judge [[Betty Binns Fletcher]] from 2004 to 2005. From 2005 to 2007, she was a [[Skadden#Skadden Fellowship Foundation|Skadden Fellow]] at the [[Brennan Center for Justice]] at the [[New York University School of Law]]. From 2007 to 2013, she worked at Altshuler Berzon LLP in [[San Francisco]]. From 2013 to 2017, she was a partner at McKanna Bishop Joffe in Portland, Oregon. From July 1, 2017 to December 20, 2021, she was a member of the Oregon Employment Relations Board.{{cite news|last1=Bernstein|first1=Maxine|title=Oregon labor lawyer, former union organizer nominated to serve as judge on federal appellate court|url=https://www.oregonlive.com/crime/2021/06/oregon-labor-lawyer-former-union-organizer-nominated-to-serve-as-judge-on-federal-appellate-court.html|access-date=28 September 2021|work=oregonlive|date=30 June 2021|language=en}} === Federal judicial service === On June 30, 2021, President [[Joe Biden]] announced his intent to nominate Sung to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] for the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]]. On July 13, 2021, her nomination was sent to the Senate. President Biden nominated Sung to the seat to be vacated by Judge [[Susan P. Graber]], who announced her intent to assume senior status upon confirmation of a successor.{{Cite web|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/07/13/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-24/|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate|date=13 July 2021|website=The White House|access-date=10 December 2021}} On September 14, 2021, a hearing on her nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/09/07/2021/nominations|title=Nominations | United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|website=Judiciary.senate.gov|date=14 September 2021 |access-date=10 December 2021}} During the hearing, senators questioned her about her decision to sign a letter regarding [[Brett Kavanaugh]]'s [[Brett Kavanaugh Supreme Court nomination|nomination to the United States Supreme Court]]. The letter accused Kavanaugh of being an "intellectually and morally bankrupt ideologue" and claimed that "people will die if he is confirmed".{{cite news|title=Law students, alumni condemn Kavanaugh in open letter|first1=Adelaide|last1=Feibel|first2=Hailey|last2=Fuchs|date=10 July 2018|work=[[Yale Daily News]]|url=https://yaledailynews.com/blog/2018/07/10/law-students-criticize-kavanaugh-in-open-letter/}} Sung said she recognized that much of the letter's rhetoric "was overheated," but she did not disavow the letter or say "whether she thought Kavanaugh was indeed 'intellectually and morally bankrupt.'"{{Cite web|title=Circuit Pick Apologizes Over Kavanaugh Opposition Letter (1)|url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/circuit-pick-apologizes-for-signing-kavanaugh-opposition-letter|access-date=2021-09-14|website=Bloomberg 2021}} On November 3, 2021, the [[United States Senate]] discharged the committee from further consideration of her nomination by a 49–49 vote, with Vice President [[Kamala Harris]] [[List of Circuit Judge for the Ninth Circuit)|date=December 15, 2021|website=United States Senate|access-date=December 15, 2021}} She received her judicial commission on December 20, 2021.{{FJC Will more follow in 2022?|url=https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article256630236.html|access-date=December 24, 2021|website=[[The Sacramento Bee]]}} === Notable rulings === On September 26, 2022, Sung dissented on an [[en banc]] panel in a 8–3 decision that held that California AB 32, a law that banned private, for-profit prison and immigration detention centers within the state, was unconstitutional.{{cite web |last1=Pazanowski |first1=Bernie |title=California Ban on Private Prisons in State Held Unconstitutional |url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/california-ban-on-private-prisons-in-state-held-unconstitutional |website=[[Bloomberg Law]] |date=September 26, 2022}} Sung joined a unanimous decision of a three-judge panel, ruling that the [[Second presidency of Donald Trump|Trump administration]] could deploy the National Guard to curb riots in [[Los Angeles]], in spite of the objections of [[California Governor]] [[Gavin Newsom]].{{cite web |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/06/19/us/california-national-guard-trump.html |title=Appeals Court Lets Trump Keep Control of California National Guard in L.A. |work=The New York Times |last1=Savage |first1=Charlie |last2=Rosenhall |first2=Laurel }} On August 1, 2025, Sung ruled that [[United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement|ICE]] cannot detain people based on their race, language, accent, occupation, or location.{{Cite web|url=https://voiceofoc.org/2025/08/9th-circuit-judges-uphold-block-on-southern-california-ice-sweeps/|title=9th Circuit Judges Uphold Block on Southern California ICE Sweeps|website=Voice of OC|date=2025-08-02|access-date=2025-08-06}}{{Cite web|url=https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2025/08/01/25-4312.pdf|title=Pedro Vasquez Perdomo v. [[Harvard University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Jennifer Walker Elrod''' ([[née]] '''Walker'''; 1966) is an American lawyer and jurist serving as the [[United States federal judge|chief United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]]. She previously served as a state court judge on the [[Texas District Courts|190th District Court of Texas]] from 2002 to 2007. ==Background== Elrod was born Jennifer Leigh Walker in 1966 in [[Port Arthur, Texas]], and grew up in [[Baytown, Texas]]. After high school, Elrod studied [[economics]] at [[Baylor University]], graduating in 1988 with a [[Bachelor of Arts]], ''[[Latin honors|magna cum laude]]''. At Baylor, she was the Outstanding Graduating Senior of the Honors Program and was eventually named Outstanding Young Alumna. She went to [[Harvard Law School]] in 1989 and received her [[Juris Doctor]] in 1992, graduating ''[[cum laude]]''. At Harvard Law School, she was a member of the [[Board of Student Advisers]], an active member of the Harvard Federalist Society, and a finalist in the Ames Moot Court competition. She became a member of the [[State Bar of Texas]] in 1992. After law school, Elrod was a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Sim Lake]] of the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas]] from 1992 to 1994. She then entered private practice at the law firm [[Baker Botts]]. == Judicial career == === State judicial service === In 2002, Governor [[Rick Perry]] appointed Elrod to be a judge on the 190th District Court in [[Harris County, Texas|Harris County]]. She was elected to the judgeship in the 2002 general election, and again in 2006 when she ran unopposed. As a state district court judge, she presided over jury and bench trials involving civil litigation. Elrod remained on the Harris County bench until her confirmation to the Fifth Circuit. === Federal judicial service === President [[George W. Bush]] nominated Elrod to a vacancy on the New Orleans-based [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]], the primary court of appeals for all federal trial court cases in Texas, Mississippi and Louisiana, on March 29, 2007, She succeeded Judge [[Patrick Higginbotham]], who assumed [[senior status]] on August 26, 2006. Elrod received a hearing before the [[Senate Judiciary Committee]] on July 19, 2007, and was voted out of committee on September 20, 2007. She was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] by [[voice vote]] on October 4, 2007.{{Cite web|title=PN402 — Jennifer Walker Elrod — The Judiciary|date=March 29, 2007|publisher=United States Senate|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/110th-congress/402}} She received her commission on October 19, 2007.{{FJC Bio|nid=1392631|inline=yes}} She maintains chambers in [[Houston|Houston, Texas]]. She has authored significant rulings against abortion rights, gun control and Obamacare. In 2022, Elrod ruled that the SEC's in-house adjudication of securities fraud charges was unconstitutional under the Seventh Amendment, Article I, and Article II of the Constitution.Jarkesy v. Sec. & Exch. Comm'n, 34 F.4th 446 (5th Cir. 2022), cert. granted, 143 S. Ct. 2688, 216 L. Ed. 2d 1255 (2023), and cert. denied, 143 S. Ct. 2690, 216 L. Ed. 2d 1256 (2023), and aff'd and remanded, No. 22-859, 2024 WL 3187811 (U.S. June 27, 2024). The Supreme Court affirmed her ruling on Seventh Amendment grounds in a 6–3 decision in 2024.Sec. & Exch. Comm'n v. Jarkesy, 603 U.S. ___ (2024). On October 4, 2024, Elrod was named chief judge of the Fifth Circuit. Scarcella, Mike [https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/conservative-5th-circuit-judge-takes-helm-key-us-appeals-court-2024-10-04/ "Conservative 5th Circuit judge takes helm at key US appeals court"] ''Reuters'', October 4, 2024. Retrieved October 6, 2024.{{Cite press release|title=Press Release - New Chief Judge|url=https://www.ca5.uscourts.gov//docs/default-source/default-document-library/press-release-new-chief-judge-fith-circuit|website=ca5.uscourts.gov|access-date=October 3, 2024}} Elrod has served on the [[Judicial Conference of the United States]] in multiple capacities. From 2018 to 2024, Elrod was a member of the Committee on Codes of Conduct, serving as Chair from 2021 to 2024.{{Cite web |date=2017-09-08 |title=Hon. Jennifer Walker Elrod |url=https://fedsoc.org/bio/jennifer-elrod |access-date=2026-11-08 |website=The Federalist Society}} She also previously served on the Committee on Judicial Security. [[Harvard University]] ([[Master of Public Administration|MPA]]) }} '''Jerome A. Holmes''' (born November 18, 1961) is an American lawyer serving as the [[United States federal judge|Chief United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit]]. He is the [[List of African-American firsts|first]] [[African American]] to serve on the Tenth Circuit. == Early life and education == Holmes graduated from [[Wake Forest University]] in 1983 with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree. He then attended the [[Georgetown University Law Center]], where he was an editor of the ''Georgetown Immigration Law Journal''. He graduated with a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1988. Later in his career, Holmes studied at [[Harvard University]]'s [[John F. Kennedy School of Government]], receiving a [[Master of Public Administration]] in 2000. ==Legal career== Holmes began his legal career as a [[law clerk]] for judge [[Wayne Alley]] of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Oklahoma]] from 1988 to 1990. Holmes then clerked for judge [[William Judson Holloway Jr.]] of the Tenth Circuit from 1990 to 1991. After his clerkships, Holmes entered private practice with the law firm [[Steptoe & Johnson]] in its [[Washington, D.C.]] office. He practiced at the firm as an [[Associate lawyer|associate]] from 1991 to 1994. He then returned to Oklahoma to serve as an [[assistant United States attorney]] for the Western District of Oklahoma, where he became deputy chief of the Criminal Division. During that time, Holmes worked on the prosecution team for the [[Oklahoma City bombing]] that secured the convictions of death for [[Timothy McVeigh]] and a life sentence for [[Terry Nichols]]. In the aftermath of the [[September 11 terrorist attack]], Holmes served for two and a half years as the Anti-Terrorism Coordinator in the Western District of Oklahoma, coordinating the federal, state, and local domestic and international terrorism initiatives until 2005.{{Cite web | title=Jerome A. Holmes (1961- ) | date=16 November 2020 | url=https://blackpast.org/african-american-history/people-african-american-history/jerome-a-holmes-1961/ | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201125045607/https://www.blackpast.org/african-american-history/people-african-american-history/jerome-a-holmes-1961/ | access-date=2026-08-13 | archive-date=2020-11-25}} Holmes re-entered private practice in 2005 as a Director of the Oklahoma firm [[Crowe & Dunlevy]], where his practice was focused on [[white collar criminal defense]], complex [[civil litigation]], and [[corporate law]]. == Federal judicial service == Holmes was initially nominated for a federal judgeship in the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Oklahoma]], having been chosen from group of finalists that included Tulsa attorneys Lane Wilson and [[John M. O'Connor]] (Wilson would later serve as U.S. Magistrate Judge for the Northern District before leaving to become General Counsel at the [[Williams Companies]]).{{cite news|last1=Myers|first1=Jim|title=OKC lawyer gets federal judge nod|url=http://www.tulsaworld.com/archives/okc-lawyer-gets-federal-judge-nod/article_ff278bf5-ff01-5382-b06c-0e9e6102ebbb.html|access-date=25 August 2017|work=Tulsa World|date=15 February 2006}} While his nomination for a United States District Court seat was pending, Holmes was nominated by President [[George W. Bush]] on May 4, 2006, to fill a seat vacated by Judge [[Stephanie Kulp Seymour]].[https://www.congress.gov/nomination/109th-congress/1536 Pres. Nom. 1536], 109th Cong. (2006). Bush's previous pick to replace Judge Seymour, United States District Judge [[James H. Payne]], withdrew over criticism of his handling of cases in which he allegedly had a [[conflict of interest]]. The [[United States Senate]] confirmed his nomination less than three months later on July 26, 2006, by a 67–30 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=109&session=2&vote=00213|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Jerome A. Holmes, of Oklahoma, to be US Circuit Judge)}} He received his commission on August 9, 2006.{{FJC Bio|nid=1392476|inline=yes}} He became the chief judge on October 1, 2022.{{cite web|url=https://www.ca10.uscourts.gov/ce/news/honorable-jerome-holmes-elevated-chief-judge|title=Honorable Jerome A. Holmes Elevated to Chief Judge}} ===Notable cases=== * Holmes' first published opinion for the court, [http://www.ca10.uscourts.gov/opinions/06/06-2056.pdf ''United States v. Ahidley''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304043944/http://www.ca10.uscourts.gov/opinions/06/06-2056.pdf |date=2016-03-04 }}, was released on May 25, 2007. Holmes wrote for a unanimous three-judge panel holding that a criminal defendant was improperly ordered to pay immediate restitution to the victim of his crime. * Holmes was on the first federal appellate court panel to weigh affirmatively on the constitutional right of same-sex couples to marry. He penned an important concurrence on the role of [[Animus (law)|animus]] in the ban of [[same-sex marriage in Oklahoma]].{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2014/07/29/us/politics/ruling-poses-potential-obstacle-at-supreme-court-for-same-sex-marriage.html|title=Opinion May Pose Obstacle for Same-Sex Unions|first=Adam|last=Liptak|newspaper=The New York Times |date=28 July 2014}} * In 2017, Holmes found that the [[Indian Gaming Regulatory Act]] did not permit the [[United States Department of the Interior]] to force a state to participate in mediation with a tribe after the state had asserted its [[sovereign immunity]].{{Bluebook journal |first=|last=Note| title=Recent Case: Tenth Circuit Holds that Severability Analysis Cannot Extend to Construing Indian Gaming Regulatory Act to Support an Administrative Remedy| volume=131 | journal=[[Harvard Law Review|Harv.
