'''Jerry Edwin Smith''' (born November 7, 1946) is an American lawyer and jurist serving as a [[United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]] since December 1987.

==Early life and education==
Smith was born on November 7, 1946, in [[Del Rio, Texas|Del Rio]], Texas.<ref>{{cite book|title=Who's who in the South and Southwest|date=2005|publisher=Marquis Who's Who|isbn=9780837908359|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=paFmAAAAMAAJ|access-date=April 13, 2015}}</ref> After high school, he graduated from [[Yale University]] with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in 1969 and earned a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Yale Law School]] in 1972.<ref name="fjc.gov" /> At Yale, he was a member of the [[Calliopean Society]].{{citation needed|date=April 2026}}

== Career ==
Smith clerked for Judge [[Halbert O. Woodward]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Texas]] from 1972 to 1973. After his clerkship, he joined the law firm Fulbright & Jaworski (now [[Norton Rose Fulbright]]), where he became a [[Law firm partner|partner]] in 1981.<ref>{{cite web |title=Hon. Jerry E. Smith |date=November 16, 2018 |url=https://fedsoc.org/contributors/jerry-smith |publisher=The Federalist Society}}</ref>

Smith was Director of the [[Harris County, Texas|Harris County]] Housing Authority in Texas from 1978 to 1980. He was a special assistant attorney general of Texas from 1981 to 1982. He was Chairman of the Houston Civil Service Commission from 1982 to 1984. He was the City Attorney for the City of Houston from 1984 to 1987.<ref name="fjc.gov">{{cite web |url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/smith-jerry-edwin |title=Smith, Jerry Edwin |website=[[Biographical Directory of Federal Judges]] |publisher=[[Federal Judicial Center]]}}</ref>

== Federal judicial service ==
Smith was nominated to the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]] by President [[Ronald Reagan]] on June 2, 1987, to a new seat created by 98 Stat. 333. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on December 19, 1987, and received his judicial commission on December 21, 1987.<ref name="fjc.gov" />

===Notable cases===
==== 1991 on EPA regulation ====
In ''Corrosion Proof Fittings v. EPA'', Smith wrote a panel opinion that required the [[United States Environmental Protection Agency]] to use [[cost-benefit analysis]] when deciding whether to ban a toxic substance.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Corrosion Proof Fittings v. EPA, 947 F.2d 1201 (5th Cir. 1991) |url=https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F2/947/1201/153685/ |access-date=2026-04-15 |website=Justia Law |language=en}}</ref>

==== 2010 on deep water drilling ====
Smith was one of three judges on a panel that heard the appeal to ''[[Hornbeck Offshore Services LLC v. Salazar]]'',{{Citation needed|date=April 2026|reason=I can't find any source specifically stating that Judge Smith was on any of these panels.}} a case challenging the [[United States Department of the Interior|U.S. Department of the Interior's]] six-month [[2010 United States deepwater drilling moratorium|moratorium on exploratory drilling in deep water]] that was adopted in the wake of the [[Deepwater Horizon explosion]] and the [[Deepwater Horizon oil spill|subsequent oil spill]]. The lower court had struck down the [[United States Department of the Interior]]'s moratorium as arbitrary and capricious government action, and the Fifth Circuit panel denied the government's emergency request to stay the lower court's decision pending appeal.<ref>Pelofsky, Jeremy.; Doggett, Tom. [https://web.archive.org/web/20100709115646/http://ca.reuters.com/article/topNews/idCATRE65O5TA20100709 Court refuses stay in deepwater drilling case.] ''Reuters Canada.'' July 8, 2010.</ref>

==== 2012 on Obamacare ====
In April 2012, during oral argument in a Fifth Circuit case involving the [[Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act]] (ACA), Smith ordered the [[United States Department of Justice]] to provide his panel of three judges with a three-page, single-spaced report explaining President [[Barack Obama]]'s views on [[judicial review]]. Smith's order was prompted by Obama's recent press conference remarks on the then-pending case ''[[National Federation of Independent Business v. Sebelius]]'' before the Supreme Court in which the Court was considering, among other things, whether to strike down the entire ACA as unconstitutional. Obama had stated that if the Supreme Court overturned the ACA, it would be "an unprecedented, extraordinary step of overturning a law that was passed by a strong majority of a democratically elected Congress," and that a law that was passed by Congress on an economic issue had not been overturned by the court "going back to the '30s, pre [[New Deal]]."<ref>{{Cite web |title=President Obama Speaks at the Associated Press Luncheon |url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/node/137797 |access-date=2026-04-15 |website=The White House |language=en}}</ref> These remarks were criticized by many as historically and legally inaccurate.<ref>Brooks Jackson, Factcheck.org, [https://www.usatoday.com/news/washington/story/2012-04-04/fact-check-obama-court-unprecedented/54004040/1 Fact check: Obama's Supreme Court remarks] USAToday, April 5, 2012</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2012-04-04 |title=Jerry Smith’s Obama rebuke questioned by legal experts |url=https://www.yahoo.com/news/blogs/lookout/jerry-smith-obama-rebuke-questioned-legal-experts-213822371.html |access-date=2026-04-15 |website=Yahoo News |language=en-US}}</ref> Though Judge Smith's response and order were criticized by some legal scholars and members of the press,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kerr |first=Orin |date=2012-04-03 |title=Fifth Circuit Panel of GOP-Nominated Judges Orders DOJ to Say Whether President Obama Believes in Judicial Review |url=https://volokh.com/2012/04/03/fifth-circuit-panel-of-gop-nominated-judges-orders-doj-to-say-whether-president-obama-believes-in-judicial-review/ |access-date=2026-04-15 |website=The Volokh Conspiracy |language=en-US}}</ref> [[Presidency of George W. Bush|George W. Bush administration]] U.S. Attorney General and former judge [[Michael Mukasey]] defended Smith, stating that Obama's remarks had called judicial review "into question", so that "the court has, it seems to me, every obligation to sit up and take notice of Mr. Obama."<ref>{{Cite news |last=Baker |first=Sam |date=2012-04-04 |title=Bush attorney general defends judge’s probe of Obama healthcare comments |url=https://thehill.com/policy/healthcare/110649-bush-attorney-general-defends-judges-probe-of-obama-healthcare-comments/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251225112225/https://thehill.com/policy/healthcare/110649-bush-attorney-general-defends-judges-probe-of-obama-healthcare-comments/ |archive-date=2025-12-25 |access-date=2026-04-15 |work=The Hill |language=en-US}}</ref> U.S. Attorney General Eric Holder said that the Justice Department would respond "appropriately" to Smith's request<ref>{{Cite web | title=News from The Associated Press | url=http://hosted.ap.org/dynamic/stories/U/US_OBAMA_HEALTH_CARE_JUDGE?SITE=AP&SECTION=HOME&TEMPLATE=DEFAULT | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120408022333/http://hosted.ap.org/dynamic/stories/U/US_OBAMA_HEALTH_CARE_JUDGE?SITE=AP&SECTION=HOME&TEMPLATE=DEFAULT | access-date=December 26, 2024 | archive-date=April 8, 2012 | url-status=live }}</ref> and filed a short response, conceding that the federal courts have the power to strike down laws passed by Congress but citing Supreme Court precedent for the proposition that those laws are presumed constitutional and should only be overturned "sparingly".<ref name="letter">{{Cite news |date=2012-04-05 |title=In letter to Texas judge, Holder defends Obama’s comments urging Supreme Court to uphold health-care law |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/in-letter-to-texas-judge-holder-defends-obamas-comments-urging-supreme-court-to-uphold-health-care-law/2012/04/05/gIQAxEH1xS_story.html |access-date=2026-04-15 |work=The Washington Post |language=en-US |issn=0190-8286}}</ref>

==== 2012 on the scope of Congress's power ====
In July 2012, Smith authored the majority opinion for the ''en banc'' Fifth Circuit in ''United States v. Kebodeaux'', holding that, once a former federal convict has fully served his sentence and been unconditionally released from prison, the federal government cannot regulate his purely intrastate conduct merely because he was once convicted of a federal crime. Smith's majority opinion further held that the mere possibility that a person may move interstate in the future is an insufficient basis for the federal government to regulate that person under the Interstate Commerce Clause.<ref>{{Cite web |title=United States v. Kebodeaux, No. 08-51185 (5th Cir. 2012) |url=https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/ca5/08-51185/08-51185-2012-07-06.html |access-date=2026-04-15 |website=Justia Law |language=en}}</ref> The decision was reversed 7–2 by the Supreme Court in ''[[United States v. Kebodeaux]]'' (2013), on the grounds that Kebodeaux himself was not unconditionally released from federal custody because a law in effect at the time of his offense required him to register as a sex offender after his release from prison. However, a concurring opinion by Chief Justice Roberts agreed with Judge Smith's ''en banc'' opinion on the core issue that "[t]he fact of a prior federal conviction, by itself, does not give Congress a freestanding, independent, and perpetual interest in protecting the public from the convict's purely intrastate conduct."<ref>{{Cite web |title=United States v. Kebodeaux, 570 U.S. 387 (2013) |url=https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/570/387/ |access-date=2026-04-15 |website=Justia Law |language=en}}</ref>

==== 2019 on qualified immunity ====
In 2019, Smith wrote the majority opinion in ''Taylor v. Williams'', a civil rights case filed by a prisoner against several correctional officers for their treatment of him, during which he subjected to six days' seclusion in cells covered in feces, with no water or toilet available. Smith granted [[qualified immunity]] to the officers because he ruled that it "wasn't clearly established" that "prisoners...housed in cells teeming with human waste [for] a time period so short violated the Constitution," holding that the illegality of such actions was not "beyond debatable."<ref>{{Cite web |title=Taylor v. Stevens, No. 17-10253 (5th Cir. 2019) |url=https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/ca5/17-10253/17-10253-2019-12-20.html |access-date=2026-04-15 |website=Justia Law |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Trent Taylor v. Marion Williams – CourtListener.com|url=https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4689562/trent-taylor-v-marion-williams/|access-date=August 8, 2020|website=CourtListener|language=en-us}}</ref>

==== 2021 on 2020 election ====
On January 2, 2021, Smith, along with Judges [[Patrick Higginbotham]] and [[Andrew Oldham]], affirmed the dismissal for lack of jurisdiction of a lawsuit filed by [[Louie Gohmert]] against Vice President [[Mike Pence]] aimed at empowering the latter to overturn President-elect [[Joseph Biden]]'s [[United States Electoral College|Electoral College]] win.<ref>{{Cite web| title=Case: 21-40001 | publisher=United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit | date=January 2, 2021 | url=http://www.ca5.uscourts.gov/opinions/unpub/21/21-40001.0.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210103033756/http://www.ca5.uscourts.gov/opinions/unpub/21/21-40001.0.pdf | archive-date=January 3, 2021}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Gohmert v. Pence, No. 21-40001 (5th Cir. 2021) |url=https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/ca5/21-40001/21-40001-2021-01-02.html |access-date=2026-04-15 |website=Justia Law |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/politics/appeals-court-dismisses-gohmerts-election-suit-against-pence/ar-BB1cqrMf|title = Appeals court dismisses Gohmert's election suit against Pence|website = [[MSN]]}}</ref>

==== 2022 on vaccine mandates ====
On February 9, 2022, Smith and Judge [[Don Willett]] formed the majority of a panel that declined to rule on a request to stay a preliminary injunction against Biden's [[COVID-19]] vaccine mandate for federal employees. Judge [[Stephen A. Higginson]] dissented from the ruling, arguing that the government was entitled to an immediate stay while it appealed.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.ca5.uscourts.gov/opinions/pub/22/22-40043-CV0.pdf|title=Feds for Medical Freedom et al. vs. Joseph R. Biden Jr. et al.|website=ca5.uscourts.gov|date=February 9, 2022|access-date=February 18, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Feds for Medical Freedom v. Biden, No. 22-40043 (5th Cir. 2022) |url=https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/ca5/22-40043/22-40043-2022-02-09.html |access-date=2026-04-15 |website=Justia Law |language=en}}</ref>

On February 17, Smith dissented when the panel majority consisting of Judges [[Jennifer Walker Elrod]] and [[Andrew Oldham]] reversed the district court's order denying a preliminary injunction to employees challenging United Airlines' vaccine mandate.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Sambrano v. United Airlines, No. 21-11159 (5th Cir. 2022) |url=https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/ca5/21-11159/21-11159-2022-08-18.html |access-date=2026-04-15 |website=Justia Law |language=en}}</ref> Smith's nearly 60-page dissent accused the majority of flouting "fifty years of precedent and centuries of Anglo-American remedies law" and ignoring the text of the relevant statute "to extract its desired result." He also criticized the majority for hiding its "made-up" legal theory in an unsigned and unpublished opinion. Judge Smith concluded, quoting the late Supreme Court Justice [[Antonin Scalia]], "if I ever wrote an opinion authorizing preliminary injunctive relief for plaintiffs without a cause of action, without a likelihood of success on the merits (for two reasons), and devoid of irreparable injury, despite the text, policy, and history of the relevant statute, despite the balance of equities and the public interest, and despite decades of contrary precedent from this circuit and the Supreme Court, all while inventing and distorting facts to suit my incoherent reasoning, 'I would hide my head in a bag.'"<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://www.ca5.uscourts.gov/opinions/unpub/21/21-11159.0.pdf|title=David Sambrano et al. v. United Airlines|website=ca5.uscourts.gov|date=February 17, 2022|access-date=February 18, 2022}}</ref> [[Slate (magazine)|''Slate'' magazine]] described Smith's dissent as a "60-page burst of fury" and "one of the angriest dissents of his career".<ref>{{cite web |last=Stern |first=Mark Joseph|date=February 18, 2022 |title=Thursday Was One of the Most Radical Days for the Federal Courts in Years |url=https://slate.com/news-and-politics/2022/02/united-vaccine-vra-trumpiest-court-rulings.html  |url-access=subscription |website=Slate|location= |publisher= |access-date=November 18, 2025}}</ref>

==== 2023 on death penalty ====
On October 9, 2023, Smith dissented from an order upholding a stay of execution for convicted murderer Jedidiah Murphy. Smith attached a fake majority opinion to his otherwise brief dissent, demonstrating what he thought the majority opinion should have been.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Murphy v. Nasser, No. 23-70005 (5th Cir. 2023) |url=https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/ca5/23-70005/23-70005-2023-10-10.html |access-date=2026-04-15 |website=Justia Law |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ballsandstrikes.org/ethics-accountability/jerry-smith-fake-opinion-dont-be-polite-to-hacks/|title=Federal Judges Shouldn't Be Polite to Unserious Hacks|website=Balls and Strikes|date=October 13, 2023|access-date=May 25, 2024}}</ref>

==== 2025 on redistricting ====
On November 18, 2025, Smith filed a 104-page dissent from a three-judge mixed-level court ruling invalidating [[2025 Texas redistricting|Texas' mid-decade redistricting]] of the state's congressional map written by [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas]] judge [[Jeff Brown (judge)|Jeff Brown]], a Trump appointee.<ref>{{Cite web |title=League of United Latin American Citizens et al v. Abbott et al, No. 3:2021cv00259 - Document 1437 (W.D. Tex. 2025) |url=https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/texas/txwdce/3:2021cv00259/1150387/1437/ |access-date=2026-04-15 |website=Justia Law |language=en}}</ref> Smith argued that "the main winners from Judge Brown's opinion are [[George Soros]] and [[Gavin Newsom]]. The obvious losers are the People of Texas and the Rule of Law."<ref>{{Cite web |title=League of United Latin American Citizens et al v. Abbott et al, No. 3:2021cv00259 - Document 1439 (W.D. Tex. 2025) |url=https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/texas/txwdce/3:2021cv00259/1150387/1439/ |access-date=2026-04-15 |website=Justia Law |language=en}}</ref> Various sources described the dissent, which described Judge Brown as an "unskilled magician" conducting "pernicious judicial misbehavior", as "extraordinary", "unusual", a personal attack on Brown, and "berserk".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cnn.com/2025/11/19/politics/dissent-texas-redistricting-case-judge-jerry-smith-all-about-eve|title='I dissent,' judge says 16 times in 100-page broadside against colleagues in Texas redistricting case | CNN Politics|first=Devan|last=Cole|date=November 19, 2025|website=CNN}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Rubin |first=Jordan |date=November 19, 2025 |title=Judge issues berserk dissent from ruling blocking Texas congressional maps |url=https://www.ms.now/deadline-white-house/deadline-legal-blog/judge-dissent-texas-ruling-congressional-map-redistricting-rcna244875 |website=MS NOW |location= |publisher= |access-date=December 16, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/news/2025/11/19/texas-redistricting-case-dissent-00660625|title=Jerry's jeremiad: A wild dissent roils Texas redistricting debate|date=November 19, 2025|website=POLITICO}}</ref>

Reyna''' (born November 11, 1952) is an American lawyer, former president of the [[Hispanic National Bar Association]], and a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit]].[https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2010/09/29/president-obama-names-two-us-circuit-courts-0 President Obama Names Two to U.S. Circuit Courts] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170216171217/https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2010/09/29/president-obama-names-two-us-circuit-courts-0 |date=2017-02-16 }}, White House press release (September 29, 2010). Reyna's appointment to the federal bench had two historical distinctions: he became both the first Latino and first international trade practitioner to be appointed to the Federal Circuit. ==Early life and education== Jimmie Reyna was born on November 11, 1952, in [[Tucumcari, New Mexico]],[http://www.martindale.com/Jimmie-V-Reyna/348392-lawyer.htm Jimmie V. Reyna - Lawyer Profile] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110616194422/http://www.martindale.com/Jimmie-V-Reyna/348392-lawyer.htm |date=2011-06-16 }} ''[[LexisNexis Martindale-Hubbell|Martindale]]''. to Julian Calano Reyna and Consuelo Valdenebro Reyna,[http://www.williamsmullen.com/reyna-receives-ohtli-9-8-2009/ Jimmie V. Reyna Receives Highest Recognition from the Government of Mexico] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210222193118/https://www.williamsmullen.com/news/jimmie-v-reyna-receives-highest-recognition-government-mexico |date=2021-02-22 }}, ''Williams Mullen Press Release'' (September 8, 2009). who were [[Baptist]] [[missionaries]].Alan Cooper, [http://valawyersweekly.com/blog/2006/09/25/dcs-reyna-to-lead-national-hispanic-bar/ DC's Reyna to lead national Hispanic bar], ''[[Virginia Lawyers Weekly]]'' (September 25, 2006). He grew up in [[Clovis, New Mexico|Clovis]], New Mexico, and graduated as [[valedictorian]] of his high school class.[http://lawschool.unm.edu/news/archives/2010/september/reyna.pdf Alumni News, Profiles: Jimmie Reyna Prospers in International Trade Career] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110718004540/http://lawschool.unm.edu/news/archives/2010/september/reyna.pdf |date=2011-07-18 }} ''UNM Law'' (Spring 2002). He was also senior [[class president]], a [[Letterman (sports)|letterman]], and participated in the speech and drama clubs. Throughout high school, Reyna held after-school jobs and worked at night with his father, cleaning offices. Reyna received his [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from the [[University of Rochester]] in 1975 and his [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of New Mexico School of Law]] in 1978. In 1971, Reyna entered the University of Rochester on scholarship where he majored in history. During his freshman year, Reyna married classmate Dolores Ramirez from the [[Bronx, New York]]; they had their first child during their sophomore year. While in college, during their summers, he sold books door-to-door in various cities and regions around the country. As a WRUR campus [[disc jockey]], he created Rochester's first [[Spanish language]] radio program, which he operated as a community program for several hours each Saturday morning. Both Dolores and Reyna graduated from the University of Rochester in 1975. In 1975, Reyna entered the [[University of New Mexico School of Law]]. During his third year of law school, he participated in the Centro Legal Clinical Law Program and the Felony Prosecution Program and clerked for Ortega & Snead. He received his [[Juris Doctor]] in 1978 and was admitted to the New Mexico State Bar in 1979. ==Professional career== Reyna's legal career has included work as a solo practitioner, firm associate, law firm partner, and the federal bench. His practice has involved jury and bench trials, representation of companies, individuals and children, and appearances before municipal, state, and federal courts as well as a wide variety of U.S. administrative and agencies and governmental departments. His bar admissions include the Supreme Court of the United States, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, the U.S. Court of International Trade, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit, the U.S. District Court for the District of New Mexico, the District of Columbia Court of Appeals, and the Supreme Court of the State of New Mexico. After completing law school, Reyna stayed in [[New Mexico]] to work as an associate for the law firm of Shaffer, Butt, Thornton & Baer. From 1981 to 1986, Reyna had a solo practice in [[Albuquerque, New Mexico]]. In 1984, he was a founder of the Hispanic Culture Foundation and for the next several years served on its board and as its legal counsel. The Hispanic Culture Foundation was the predecessor organization to the National Hispanic Cultural Center (and Foundation) located in Albuquerque, New Mexico. In 1985, he attended the National Security Forum of the Air War College in Montgomery, Alabama. Throughout their time in Albuquerque, both Reyna and Dolores were actively engaged in the area's mental health community. In 1986, Reyna started as an associate in [[Washington, D.C.]], with the law firm of Stewart & Stewart, where he specialized in trade policy and international trade regulation. In 1993, he was made partner at Stewart and Stewart. By then his work had expanded to international trade policy as he developed expertise and an international reputation in matters involving multilateral and regional trade arrangements, including representation of client interests in international trade negotiations. Since 1994, Reyna has served as a U.S. [[Judicial panel|panelist]] for disputes arising under Chapter 19 of the [[North American Free Trade Agreement]] (NAFTA), addressing [[antidumping]] claims and [[countervailing duties]]. In addition, in 1995, he was nominated by the U.S. government and confirmed by the World Trade Organization (WTO) to serve on the U.S. roster of non- governmental panelists for the World Trade Organization (WTO), Dispute Settlement Mechanism for disputes involving both trade in goods and trade in services, one of a few individuals worldwide who at that time received that distinction. He served on both the NAFTA and the WTO rosters up to his appointment to the federal bench. In 1998, Reyna joined Williams Mullen as a partner, and directed the firm's Trade and Customs Practice Group and its Latin America Task Force.Joint Committee on Printing, ''[https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CDIR-2014-02-18/html/CDIR-2014-02-18-JUDICIARY.htm Official Congressional Directory] , 2013-2014'' (February 2014), p. 863. In 2006, he was elected to serve on the firm's board of directors for a two-year term, and then reelected in 2008 to a three-year term. Judge Reyna has authored two books, ''Passport to North American Trade: Rules of Origin and Customs Procedures Under the NAFTA'' (Shepards 1995), and ''The GATT Uruguay Round, A Negotiating History: Services, 1986-1992'' (Kluwer 1993). He has also authored a number of articles on international trade and customs issues. For over 25 years, Reyna worked as an international trade practitioner. His legal work has focused on laws, regulations, and governmental measures that affect cross-border movement of goods and services. He advised clients on foreign investment; U.S. and foreign trade policy; international treaties, pacts, and accords; trade negotiations; international trade agreements; and multilateral trade-related organizations. He provided representation on U.S. trade relief cases (antidumping, countervailing duty, and safeguard actions), including trade cases involving U.S. interests that are brought before foreign governments. In addition, he provided extensive representation in business regulation matters including compliance, export controls, FCPA, customs, trade in services, rules of origin, customs audits/compliance, product standards, food safety, and homeland and border security issues. He represented clients before the Court of International Trade, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, and assisted with the representation of U.S. clients before foreign governmental, administrative and judicial bodies. On three separate occasions, the Court of International Trade commended him for his pro bono work before that court. ==Federal judicial service== Reyna was originally nominated to fill a seat on the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit]] on September 29, 2010. His nomination was returned to the President after the adjournment of Congress and he was renominated on January 5, 2011. The [[United States Senate|Senate]] confirmed his nomination on April 4, 2011, by a 86–0 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=112&session=1&vote=00047|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Jimmie V. Reyna, of Maryland, to be United States Circuit Judge for the Federal Circuit)|access-date=2018-02-16}} He received his commission on April 5, 2011.{{FJC Bio|nid=1393666|inline=yes}} Reyna's appointment to the federal bench had two historical distinctions: he became both the first Latino and first international trade practitioner to be appointed to the Federal Circuit.{{citation needed|date=October 2018}} As of January 11, 2019, Reyna has heard 1,325 cases and authored 272 opinions, including 125 precedential opinions and 3 en banc opinions; Reyna authored the en banc opinions in ''Wi-Fi One, LLC v. Broadcom Corporation'', 878 F.3d 1364 (Fed. Cir. 2018) (en banc), ''Suprema, Inc. v. Int'l Trade Comm'n'', 796 F.3d 1338 (Fed. Cir. 2015) (en banc) and ''Cloer v. Sec'y of Health & Human Servs.'', 675 F.3d 1358 (Fed. Cir. 2012) (en banc order). In 2018, Judge Reyna authored the most precedential opinions by the Federal Circuit at fifteen opinions.{{Cite web |url=https://www.law360.com/articles/1114963/fed-circ-patent-decisions-in-2018-an-empirical-review |title=Fed. Circ. Patent Decisions in 2018: An Empirical Review - Law360 |access-date=2019-01-17 |archive-date=2021-02-22 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210222193118/https://www.law360.com/articles/1114963/fed-circ-patent-decisions-in-2018-an-empirical-review |url-status=live }} Notable cases authored by Judge Reyna include ''Monk v. Shulkin'', 855 F.3d 1312 (Fed. Cir. 2017) and his dissent in ''Kingdomware Technologies, Inc. v. United States'', 754 F.3d 923 (Fed. Cir. 2014). In ''Monk'', the Federal Circuit ruled for the first time that veterans may bring class actions against the [[United States Department of Veterans Affairs|Department of Veterans Affairs]].{{Cite web |url=https://www.law.com/litigationdaily/2018/08/27/daily-dicta-in-seismic-decision-court-says-veterans-can-bring-class-actions/?slreturn=20190015113433 |title=Expert Perspectives on Biggest Court Cases |access-date=2019-01-17 |archive-date=2021-02-22 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210222193125/https://www.law.com/litigationdaily/2018/08/27/daily-dicta-in-seismic-decision-court-says-veterans-can-bring-class-actions/?slreturn=20210122143133 |url-status=live }} In ''Kingdomware Technologies, Inc. v. United States'', 136 S. Ct. 1969 (2016), the [[Supreme Court of the United States|Supreme Court]] adopted Judge Reyna's dissenting position{{Cite web |url=https://www.bna.com/judge-reynas-devotion-n73014447123/ |title=Bloomberg Industry Group |access-date=2019-01-17 |archive-date=2019-01-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190115234741/https://www.bna.com/judge-reynas-devotion-n73014447123/ |url-status=live }} that 38 U.S.C. § 8127(a) of the Veterans Benefits, Health Care and Information Technology Act of 2006 requires the Department of Veterans Affairs to apply the "Rule of Two" in all contracting decisions. Until the Supreme Court's decision, the department applied the Rule of Two only when it needed contracts to satisfy its annual goals for contracting with service-disabled and other veteran-owned small businesses. ==Awards== Judge Reyna has been nationally recognized as a leader and jurist. In 2009, Judge Reyna received the [[Ohtli Award]], the highest honor bestowed by the Mexican government on non-Mexican citizens for work in the U.S. (and other countries) assisting Mexican citizens and promoting Mexican culture.[[Ohtli Award]]{{Circular reference|date=July 2019}} He has consistently been named to Top 100 lists as one of the most influential Latino leaders by ''Hispanic Business Magazine'' (2011), ''Latino Leaders Magazine'' (2011, 2012, 2015, 2016 and 2017), and ''Washington Business Journal'' (2010). In 2018, Judge Reyna received the Hon. William C. Conner Inn Excellence Award. This award is given to judges of certain federal courts for their "dedication to the promotion of excellence in the legal profession."{{Cite web|url=https://www.connerinn.org/excellenceaward|title = Hon. William C. Conner Inn of Court - Excellence Award}} In 2017, Judge Reyna delivered the commencement speech at the University of Rochester.{{Cite web |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FKsKTCq6rlM |title=2017 Commencement: Jimmie Reyna AS&E Commencement Address Highlight - YouTube |website=[[YouTube]] |date=21 May 2017 |access-date=2019-01-17 |archive-date=2021-02-22 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210222193346/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FKsKTCq6rlM |url-status=live }} The University of Rochester also awarded Reyna the Charles Force Hutchison and Marjorie Smith Hutchison Medal in 2017 for outstanding achievement and notable service.{{Cite web |url=https://www.rochester.edu/provost/honorsandawards/hutchisonmedal.html |title=Hutchison Medal :: Honors and Awards :: Office of the Provost :: University of Rochester |access-date=2019-01-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180904220911/http://www.rochester.edu/provost/honorsandawards/hutchisonmedal.html |archive-date=2018-09-04 |url-status=dead }}{{Cite web|url=http://www.rochester.edu/newscenter/2017-commencement-honorary-degree-award-recipients-announced/|title = 2017 Commencement honorary degree, award recipients announced|date = 27 April 2017}} Reyna also delivered the 2017 commencement address to graduates of the [[South Texas College of Law Houston]], where he was introduced as "One of the most influential Hispanic lawyers - and people - in our country."{{Cite web |url=https://www.stcl.edu/news/stcl-houston-grants-diplomas-to-213-at-may-2017-commencement-ceremony/ |title=STCL Houston grants diplomas to 213 at May 2017 commencement ceremony – South Texas College of Law Houston |date=16 May 2017 |access-date=2019-01-17 |archive-date=2021-02-22 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210222193125/https://www.stcl.edu/news/stcl-houston-grants-diplomas-to-213-at-may-2017-commencement-ceremony/ |url-status=live }} Judge Reyna is heavily involved in the Hispanic National Bar Association where he has provided nearly twenty years of leadership, including serving as its National President from 2006 to 2007.{{Cite web |url=http://www.cafc.uscourts.gov/judges/jimmie-v-reyna-circuit-judge |title=JIMMIE V. REYNA, Circuit Judge | US Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit |access-date=2019-01-17 |archive-date=2021-02-22 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210222193125/http://www.cafc.uscourts.gov/judges/jimmie-v-reyna-circuit-judge |url-status=live }} He also help found the U.S.-Mexico Law Institute, where he has served as a member of its board of directors. ==Personal== Reyna married his wife, Dolores Ramirez, during his freshman year at the University of Rochester. They left New Mexico for [[Rockville, Maryland]] in 1986 in search of specialized care facilities for their [[autistic]] son. In 1989, he was ordained as a Deacon, First Baptist Church of Wheaton, Maryland, where for over ten years he taught a Sunday School Class for senior men (ages 60 and over). Reyna's professional career reflects his belief that an attorney owes a duty to improve the profession and to be of service to the community. He first joined the American Bar Association and the Hispanic National Bar Association in 1981. Reyna's work in the American Bar Association included: Section on International Law (vice-chair Mexican Law Committee, 1990–92; co-chair of the Mexican Law Committee 1993–94, 2003–05; chair of the U.S.-Mexico Foreign Trade Subcommittee, 1989–90, 1994; Section on Dispute Resolution, International Committee (co-chair of the Subcommittee on MERCOSUR 1999–01, co-chair Subcommittee on WTO 2001–06)). Reyna's work for the Hispanic National Bar Association (HNBA) began in earnest in 1998. In 1999 he started the HNBA International Law Committee and served as its chair for several years. In 2004, he was elected to the HNBA Board of Governors as a Regional President for Region V (MD, DC, VA, WVA). In 2005 he was elected HNBA Vice President of Regional Affairs. From October 2005 through September 2006, he served as HNBA President Elect. In September 2006-October 2007, he served as HNBA National President. He devoted countless hours and many resources to the HNBA and in time became a sought after mentor for lawyers and judges of all ages. He also created and instituted the HNBA Legislative Day program and the Office of the HNBA Historian. In 2006, he established the first HNBA LGBT Committee. He created the HNBA first community outreach program called La Promesa en el Derecho ("The Promise in the Law"), a program designed to instill trust and confidence within the Latino community in the U.S. legal and government institutions. He continues his work in the HNBA and speaks throughout the country on the responsibilities of lawyers in America, in particular before local and state Hispanic bar associations. In 2010, he was a recipient of the Ohtli Medal Award (the highest honor bestowed by the Mexican government for non-Mexican citizens). The Ohtli is awarded to persons that have been dedicated to opening pathways for Latinos living in the United States. Reyna has authored two books and a large number of articles on international trade topics and issues. In addition, he was the founder, and served as the Senior Editor, of the Hispanic National Bar Association Journal of Law and Policy. Reyna is a noted speaker. He developed his own speaker program that takes him throughout the country speaking before America's youth and, in particular, the many local and state Hispanic bar associations. His messages are inspirational and move audiences to seek excellence in their work and diligence towards meeting life goals. In addition, he is a frequent keynote speaker before local, state and national bar associations that are devoted to intellectual property law. In February 2016, the Minnesota IP Inn of Court voted to change its name to the Honorable Jimmie V. {{Short description|American judge (born 1971)}} {{Use mdy dates|date=December 2017}} {{Infobox officeholder | name = Joel Carson | image = Joel M Carson III.png | office = Judge of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit]] | appointer = [[Donald Trump]] | term_start = May 17, 2018 | term_end = | predecessor = [[Paul Joseph Kelly Jr.]] | successor = | birth_name = Joel McElroy Carson III | birth_date = {{birth year and age|1971}} | birth_place = [[Artesia, New Mexico]], U.S. | death_date = | death_place = | education = [[Texas Tech University]] ([[Bachelor of Business Administration|BBA]])
[[University of New Mexico]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Joel McElroy Carson III''' (born 1971) is an American lawyer and jurist serving as a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit]].{{cite web|title=PN1330 — Joel M. Carson III — The Judiciary|url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/115th-congress/1330|website=Congress.gov|publisher=Library of Congress|access-date=9 January 2018}} == Biography == Carson graduated from [[Texas Tech University]] in [[Lubbock]] in 1994 with a [[Bachelor of Business Administration]] degree. He then attended the [[University of New Mexico School of Law]] in [[Albuquerque]], where he was an editor of the ''Natural Resources Journal''. He graduated in 1997 with a [[Juris Doctor]].{{cite web |title=SJC Questionnaire |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Carson%20SJQ.pdf |access-date=20 July 2023}} After law school, Carson served as a [[law clerk]] to Judge [[Bobby Baldock]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit]] from 1997 to 1999. He then went on to be a [[Law firm partner|partner]] at the [[Roswell, New Mexico]]-based law firm of Hinkle, Hensley, Shanor & Martin, LLP, where he practiced for nine years and focused on [[natural resources law]], [[mining law]], and [[regulatory law]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.hinklelawfirm.com/services|title=Services (List)|website=Hinkle Shanor LLP.}} He served for five years as [[General Counsel]] of Mack Energy Corporation, an independent oil and gas company in [[Artesia, New Mexico]].{{Cite web|url=https://mec.com/about/|title=About}} He started his own law firm in 2014, Carson Ryan LLC.{{Cite web|url=https://vettingroom.org/tag/joel-carson/|title=Joel Carson|first=Harsh|last=Voruganti|date=February 12, 2018|website=The Vetting Room}} where he practiced until becoming a Circuit Judge.{{Cite web|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-ninth-wave-judicial-nominees-tenth-wave-united-states-attorney-nominees/|title=President Donald J. Trump Announces Ninth Wave of Judicial Nominees and Tenth Wave of United States Attorney Nominees – The White House|website=trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov}} Carson served on [[List of governors of New Mexico|New Mexico Governor]] [[Susana Martinez]]'s energy and environment transition teams following her election in 2010. He is a member of the New Mexico Judicial Performance Evaluation Commission.{{cite news|title=Carson III nominated by president for U.S. Court of Appeals|url=http://www.artesianews.com/1534729/carson-iii-nominated-by-president-for-u-s-court-of-appeals.html|access-date=18 January 2018|publisher=Artesia Daily Press|date=December 21, 2017|archive-date=January 19, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180119120333/http://www.artesianews.com/1534729/carson-iii-nominated-by-president-for-u-s-court-of-appeals.html|url-status=dead}} == Federal judicial service == === Magistrate judge tenure === Carson served as a part-time [[United States magistrate judge]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of New Mexico]] from 2015 to 2018. === Court of Appeals service === In 2017, Carson was recommended to the [[White House Counsel]]'s Office by [[Congressman]] [[Steve Pearce (politician)|Steve Pearce]]. On December 20, 2017, President [[Donald Trump]] nominated Carson to serve as a United States Circuit Judge of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit]], to the seat that was vacated by Judge [[Paul Joseph Kelly Jr.]], who subsequently assumed [[senior status]] on December 31, 2017.{{Cite web|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/eight-nominations-sent-senate-today-3/|title=Eight Nominations Sent to the Senate Today – The White House|website=trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov}} On February 14, 2018, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/committee-activity/hearings/02/14/2018/nominations|title=Nominations | United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|website=www.judiciary.senate.gov}} On March 15, 2018, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 15–6 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/03-15-18%20Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – March 15, 2018, Senate Judiciary Committee}} On May 11, 2018, the [[United States Senate]] invoked [[cloture]] on his nomination by a 71–24 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1152/vote_115_2_00090.htm|title= On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture on Joel M. Carson III to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the Tenth Circuit)|date=May 10, 2018|website=[[United States Senate]]|access-date=May 10, 2018|language=en}} On May 15, 2018, his nomination was confirmed by a 77–21 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=115&session=2&vote=00094|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Joel M. Carson III, of New Mexico, to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the Tenth Circuit)|date=May 15, 2018|website=[[United States Senate]]|access-date=May 15, 2018|language=en}} He received his commission on May 17, 2018.{{FJC Bio|nid=4625001|inline=yes}} He was sworn in on May 18, 2018.{{Cite web|date=May 18, 2018|title=Honorable Joel M. Carson Joins the Tenth Circuit Court of Appeals|url=https://www.ca10.uscourts.gov/ce/news/honorable-joel-m-carson-joins-tenth-circuit-court-appeals|website=United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit|access-date=May 27, 2023}} == Notable cases == === First Amendment === Writing for the panel in ''Vogt v. Rodebush'', Carson recognized that the First Amendment prevents public employers from conditioning employment on political beliefs, affiliation, or non-affiliation. Carson held that the First Amendment enables employees to refuse "a candidate all support, or only some forms of support," because, whether the refusal is "partial or complete," the employee is choosing to exercise her First Amendment right of political affiliation by refusal.{{Cite web |last=United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit |date=April 15, 2024 |title=Vogt v. Rodebush |url=https://www.ca10.uscourts.gov/sites/ca10/files/opinions/010111031799.pdf |website=}} === Fourteenth Amendment === In ''Doe v. Rocky Mountain Classical Academy'', the Defendant suspended and disenrolled the Plaintiff because he wore earrings at school, violating school's dress code which permitted girls (but not boys) to wear earrings. Plaintiff argued that the school violated his right to equal protection under the Fourteenth Amendment. The district court held that the school did not violate Plaintiff's equal protection rights because the dress code imposed "comparable burdens" on both boys and girls. Carson, writing for a unanimous panel of the Tenth Circuit, reversed, holding that the district court had erred "by applying the comparable burdens test instead of intermediate scrutiny." But Carson noted that the opinion did not "address whether comparable burdens are relevant to a proper intermediate scrutiny analysis."{{Cite web |last=United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit |date=April 30, 2024 |title=Doe v. Rocky Mountain Classical Academy |url=https://cases.justia.com/federal/appellate-courts/ca10/22-1369/22-1369-2024-04-30.pdf?ts=1714493072 }} == References == {{Reflist}} == External links == * {{FJC Bio|nid=4625001}} * {{Ballotpedia|Joel_Carson|Joel M. [[Stanford University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''John Byron Owens''' (born 1971) is an American judge and lawyer who serves as a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]]. ==Early life and education== Owens was born in [[Washington, D.C.]] in 1971, and grew up in [[Northern California]].{{cite news | first=Maura | last=Dolan | url=https://www.latimes.com/local/lanow/la-me-ln-9th-circuit-appointees-20130801,0,7565477.story | title=Two lawyers from same California firm nominated for 9th Circuit | work=[[Los Angeles Times]] | date=August 1, 2013 | access-date=August 2, 2013}}{{cite news|title=New 9th Circuit judge's local roots|url=https://blogs.mercurynews.com/internal-affairs/2014/07/17/new-9th-circuit-judges-local-roots/|access-date=22 August 2014|work=San Jose Mercury News|date=July 17, 2014}} He is the grandson of [[Harold Agnew]].{{cite journal|last1=Mulkin|first1=Barb|journal=The Atom|date=March 1979|volume=15|issue=2|page=9|url=https://library.lanl.gov/cgi-bin/getfile?00847112.pdf|title=Beverly J Agnew|access-date=22 August 2014}}{{cite web |title=SJC Questionnaire |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/John-Owens-Senate-Questionnaire-Final.pdf}} Owens graduated from the [[University of California, Berkeley]] in 1993 with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] with high distinction. While an undergraduate, Owens worked as a marketing assistant for the [[Golden State Warriors]]. He then attended [[Stanford Law School]], where he was an editor of the ''[[Stanford Law Review]]''. He graduated in 1996 ranked first in his class with a [[Juris Doctor]] degree with distinction. == Career == After law school, Owens was a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[J. Clifford Wallace]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]] from 1996 to 1997 and for Justice [[Ruth Bader Ginsburg]] of the [[Supreme Court of the United States|U.S. Supreme Court]] from 1997 to 1998.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2013/08/01/president-obama-nominates-three-serve-united-states-courts-appeals|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Obama Nominates Three to Serve on the United States Courts of Appeals|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=1 August 2013}} Owens then worked as a trial attorney for the [[United States Department of Justice]]'s Office of Consumer Litigation. From 2000 until 2001, he served as a litigation associate at the law firm [[O'Melveny & Myers]] in Washington, D.C. From 2001 until 2004, he served in the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Central District of California as an [[Assistant United States Attorney]]. In 2004, he transferred to the U.S. Attorney's Office in the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of California|Southern District of California]], where he served until 2012, serving first as an Assistant United States Attorney from 2004 until 2008, then as the deputy chief of the major frauds section from 2008 until 2010 and finally as the chief of the criminal division from 2010 until 2011. He has appeared on the television show [[American Greed]].{{cite web|url=http://www.afj.org/our-work/nominees/john-b-owens#fn2-3113|title=» John B. Owens}} From January 2012 until April 2014, Owens was a litigation partner in the Los Angeles office of [[Munger, Tolles & Olson LLP]]. ===Federal judicial service=== [[File:Owens Taking Oath.jpg|thumb|Owens taking oath of office; Being sworn in as circuit judge of the Ninth Circuit ''(April 25, 2014)'']] On August 1, 2013, President Barack Obama nominated Owens to a seat on the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit. He filled the seat that was vacated by Judge [[Stephen S. Trott]], who assumed [[senior status]] on December 31, 2004.{{cite news|first=Howard|last=Mintz|url=https://www.mercurynews.com/crime-courts/ci_23778654/white-house-names-san-francisco-la-lawyers-powerful|title=White House names S.F., L.A. lawyers to powerful federal appeals court|work=[[San Jose Mercury News]]|date=August 1, 2013|access-date=August 2, 2013}} On January 16, 2014 his nomination was reported out of committee by a [[voice vote]].{{cite web|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting - January 16, 2014|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/ExecutiveBusinessMeetingResults-01-16-2014.pdf|access-date=16 January 2014}} On March 26, 2014, Senate Majority Leader [[Harry Reid]] filed for cloture on the nomination. On March 27, 2014, the [[United States Senate]] invoked cloture on Owens' nomination by a 54–44 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=113&session=2&vote=00089|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture on the Nomination of John B. Owens, of California, to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the Ninth Circuit)|publisher=United States Senate|access-date=27 March 2014}} On March 31, 2014, Owens’ nomination was confirmed by a 56–43 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1132/vote_113_2_00091.htm| title= On the Nomination (Confirmation John B. Owens, of California, to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the Ninth Circuit)|publisher=United States Senate|access-date=31 October 2022}}{{cite web|title=Senate Vote Could End Feud Over Ninth Circuit Seat|url=https://www.nationallawjournal.com/legaltimes/id=1202649038021/Senate-Vote-Could-End-Feud-Over-Ninth-Circuit-Seat|publisher=Legal Times|access-date=31 March 2014}} He received his judicial commission on April 2, 2014.{{cite web|url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/owens-john-byron|title=Owens, John Byron |website=Federal Judicial Center}} Owens was officially seated and sworn in on April 25, 2014. == See also == * [[List of law clerks for the sixth seat of the Supreme Court of the United States]] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1394431}} *{{Ballotpedia|John_B._Owens|John B. [[Harvard University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''John Kenneth Bush''' (born August 24, 1964) is an American attorney and [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit]].{{cite web|url=http://www.lawyercentral.com/john-k-bush-interactive-profile--20-269719.html|title=Attorney John K Bush - Lawyer in Louisville KY|website=www.lawyercentral.com|access-date=May 9, 2017|archive-date=July 5, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180705092312/https://www.lawyercentral.com/john-k-bush-interactive-profile--20-269719.html|url-status=dead}}{{cite news | publisher = NPR |url=https://www.npr.org/2017/07/20/538363825/conservative-political-blogger-confirmed-for-seat-on-federal-appeals-court | title = Conservative Political Blogger Confirmed For Seat On Federal Appeals Court | first = Nina | last = Totenberg | author-link = Nina Totenberg | date = July 20, 2017}} Bush graduated from [[Harvard Law School]] and practiced in [[Washington, D.C.]], and [[Louisville, Kentucky]], where he served as president of the local branch of the [[Federalist Society]]. In 2017, he was nominated to a seat on the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit|Sixth Circuit]] by President [[Donald Trump]]. Bush's confirmation hearings were controversial as it was revealed that he had authored pseudonymous blog posts in which he opposed [[gay rights]] and [[abortion]] and cited [[alt-right]] websites promoting [[Barack Obama citizenship conspiracy theories|birtherism]] and other false right-wing conspiracy theories. He was confirmed in the Senate by the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] majority on a 51–47 vote in July 2017.{{cite news|work=USA Today|title=Louisville attorney John Bush confirmed 51-47 for seat on federal court of appeals|date=July 20, 2017|first=Andrew|last=Wolfson|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/2017/07/20/louisville-attorney-john-bush-confirmed-51-47-seat-federal-court-appeals/494904001/#}} == Education and career == Bush received his [[Bachelor of Arts]], ''[[summa cum laude]]'', in 1986 from [[Vanderbilt University]], where he was a member of [[Phi Beta Kappa]]. He received his [[Juris Doctor]], cum laude, in 1989 from [[Harvard Law School]], where he was Executive Editor of the ''[[Harvard Journal of Law and Public Policy]]'' and an [[Ames Moot Court Competition|Ames Moot Court]] Finalist.{{cite news|last1=Severino|first1=Carrie|author-link1=Carrie Severino|title=Bench Memos: Who is John K. Bush?|url=http://www.nationalreview.com/bench-memos/447405/who-john-k-bush|date=May 7, 2017|work=[[National Review]]|access-date=May 10, 2017}}{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1990/04/08/style/bridget-maloney-engaged-to-john-bush.html|title=Bridget Maloney Engaged to John Bush|date=1990-04-08|work=The New York Times|access-date=2019-05-01|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}} After graduating from law school, Bush served as a [[law clerk]] to Judge [[J. Smith Henley]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit]]. He practiced law at the firm of [[Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher]] in [[Washington, D.C.]], before taking a job at Bingham Greenebaum Doll in [[Louisville, Kentucky]]. He was a partner at the firm and co-chair of the firm's litigation department before becoming a judge. Bush specialized in complex litigation, including antitrust, securities, financial institutions, insurance, intellectual property, and product liability disputes.{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/05/07/us/politics/trump-lower-court-nominees-conservatives.html|title=Trump to Announce Slate of Conservative Federal Court Nominees|first=Adam|last=Liptak|work=The New York Times |date=May 7, 2017|via=NYTimes.com}}{{cite web |url=https://www.whitehouse.gov/the-press-office/2017/05/08/president-donald-j-trump-announces-judicial-candidate-nominations|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170509012131/https://www.whitehouse.gov/the-press-office/2017/05/08/president-donald-j-trump-announces-judicial-candidate-nominations|url-status=dead|archive-date=May 9, 2017|title=President Donald J. Trump Announces Judicial Candidate Nominations|date=May 8, 2017|publisher=White House, Office of Press Secretary}}{{cite web |url=https://www.martindale.com/louisville/kentucky/john-kenneth-bush-581191-a/|title=John Kenneth Bush Lawyer Profile on Martindale.com |website=www.martindale.com}} Bush was chairman of the Louisville chapter of the [[Federalist Society]] before becoming a judge.{{cite news |last1=Wolfson |first1=Andrew |title=President Trump taps Louisville conservative John K. Bush for court|url=http://www.courier-journal.com/story/news/politics/2017/05/08/donald-trump-taps-louisville-conservative-john-k-bush-court/101426196/|access-date=May 10, 2017|work=Louisville Courier-Journal|date=May 9, 2017}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Bush%20SJQ.pdf?smid=nytcore-ios-share|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees: John Kenneth Bush|last=U.S. Senate Committee on the Judiciary|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180705003543/https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Bush%20SJQ.pdf?smid=nytcore-ios-share|archive-date=2018-07-05|url-status=dead|access-date=July 4, 2018}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Bush%20Responses%20to%20QFRs.pdf|title=Questions from Senator Feinstein|last=U.S. Senate Committee on the Judiciary|date=June 21, 2018}} == Federal judicial service == === Nomination and confirmation === On May 8, 2017, President [[Donald Trump]] nominated Bush to the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit]] seat vacated by Judge [[Danny Julian Boggs]], who assumed [[senior status]] on February 28, 2017.{{cite web|url=https://www.whitehouse.gov/the-press-office/2017/05/08/nine-nominations-sent-senate-today|title=Nine Nominations Sent to the Senate Today|date=May 8, 2017|publisher=[[The White House]]|access-date=May 9, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170515081524/https://www.whitehouse.gov/the-press-office/2017/05/08/nine-nominations-sent-senate-today|archive-date=May 15, 2017|url-status=dead|df=mdy-all}} A hearing on his nomination before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]] was held on June 14, 2017.{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/06/14/2017/nominations|title=Nominations | United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|website=www.judiciary.senate.gov|date=June 14, 2017 }} On a tragedies'|url=http://www.courier-journal.com/story/news/local/2017/05/24/blog-posts-could-dog-trump-judicial-nominee-and-louisville-lawyer-john-k-bush/340746001/|access-date=August 8, 2017|publisher=The Courier-Journal|date=May 24, 2017}} His blog posts expressed opposition to gay marriage, the [[Affordable Care Act]], public financing of political campaigns, and the idea of trying terrorists in civilian courts.{{cite news|last1=Tillman|first1=Zoe|title=One Of Trump's Judicial Nominees Blogged Under A Pen Name That Ted Cruz Was A "Sore Loser"|url=https://www.buzzfeed.com/zoetillman/one-of-trumps-judicial-nominees-blogged-under-a-pen-name|access-date=August 8, 2017|publisher=BuzzFeed|date=May 19, 2017}}{{cite posts|url=http://www.courier-journal.com/story/news/2017/06/28/judicial-nominee-louisville-john-k-bush-ducks-questions-controversial-blog-posts/433160001/|access-date=August 8, 2017|publisher=The Courier-Journal|date=June 28, 2017}} Bush also compared [[abortion]] to [[slavery]], and cited media reports containing [[Barack Obama citizenship conspiracy theories|"birther"]] falsehoods about [[Barack Obama]]'s citizenship.{{cite news|last1=Min Kim|first1=Seung|title=Trump's judge picks: 'Not qualified,' prolific bloggers|url=https://www.politico.com/story/2017/10/17/trump-judges-nominees-court-picks-243834|access-date=16 August 2018|publisher=Politico|date=November 17, 2017}}{{cite news|title=Senate Confirms Judge Who Equated Abortion With Slavery|url=http://fortune.com/2017/07/20/judge-bush-abortion-slavery/|access-date=16 August 2018|agency=Associated Press|publisher=Fortune|date=July 20, 2017}} When questioned about his blogging during his judicial nomination process, Bush said that "my personal views are irrelevant to the position for which I have been nominated" and that "blogging is a political activity. It is not appropriate to bring politics to the bench."{{cite web|url=https://www.npr.org/2017/06/15/533014228/senators-grill-trump-judicial-nominees-on-provocative-blog-posts|title=Senators Grill Trump Judicial Nominees On Provocative Blog Posts|website=NPR.org}} On July 13, 2017, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 11–9 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%2007-13-17.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – July 13, 2017|website=judiciary.senate.gov}} On July 19, 2017, the [[United States Senate]] invoked [[cloture]] on his nomination by a 51–48 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1151/vote_115_1_00163.htm|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture on the Nomination of John Kenneth Bush, of Kentucky, to be United States Circuit Judge for the Sixth Circuit)|website=senate.gov}} The following day, he was confirmed by a 51–47 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1151/vote_115_1_00164.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation John Kenneth Bush, of Kentucky, to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the Sixth Circuit)|website=senate.gov}} He received his judicial commission on July 21, 2017.{{FJC Bio|nid=3114866|inline=yes}} === Notable cases === ==== Abortion ==== Bush authored the opinion in ''EMW Women's Surgical Center v. Beshear'' (2019), in which the Sixth Circuit upheld, 2–1, a Kentucky law compelling physicians to show and describe a fetal ultrasound to patients before performing an abortion.{{cite court|litigants=EMW Women's Surgical Center v. Beshear|vol=920|reporter=F.3d |opinion=421|court=6th Cir.|date=2019|url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=17190567350642465169}}{{cite news | work = The Hill | title = Appeals court upholds Kentucky ultrasound abortion law | url = https://thehill.com/policy/healthcare/437459-appeals-court-upholds-kentucky-ultrasound-abortion-law | date = April 4, 2019 | first = Nathaniel | last = Weixel}} The law, part of a years-long effort to restrict abortion access in Kentucky,{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/03/16/us/kentucky-fetal-heartbeat-abortion-law.html|title=Judge Blocks Kentucky Fetal Heartbeat Law That Bans Abortion After 6 Weeks|last=Mervosh|first=Sarah|date=2019-03-16|work=The New York Times|access-date=2019-05-02|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}} had previously been deemed unconstitutional by a lower court. Bush wrote that the law "provides truthful, non-misleading, and relevant information aimed at informing a patient about her decision to abort unborn life". Judge [[Alan Eugene Norris]] joined Bush's opinion; Judge [[Bernice B. Donald]] dissented, writing that the Kentucky law "has coopted physicians' examining tables, their probing instruments, and their voices in order to espouse a political message, without regard to the health of the patient or the judgment of the physician". On December 9, 2019, the [[Supreme Court of the United States|Supreme Court]] declined to review the case, leaving in place Bush's opinion.{{Cite web|url=https://www.supremecourt.gov/orders/courtorders/120919zor_ihdj.pdf|title=ORDER LIST: 589 U.S.|date=2019-12-09|website=www.SupremeCourt.gov|language=en-US|access-date=2019-12-09}}{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/12/09/us/supreme-court-kentucky-abortion-ultrasound.html|title=Supreme Court Lets Kentucky Abortion Ultrasound Law Take Effect|last=Liptak|first=Adam|date=2019-12-09|work=The New York Times|access-date=2019-12-10|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}} ==== ADA ==== Bush authored the court's opinion in ''McDonald v. UAW-GM Center for Human Resources''{{Cite web|url=https://caselaw.findlaw.com/us-6th-circuit/1900286.html|title=FindLaw's United States Sixth Circuit case and opinions.|website=Findlaw}} finding that the [[Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990|Americans with Disabilities Act]] did not require the defendant to extend the employee's lunch break for her to exercise. The plaintiff requested an extended lunch break for doctor-required exercise. The employer was in the decision-making process regarding the accommodation when the employee was suspended for [[insubordination]] and use of profanity toward her superior. During the suspension, the plaintiff voluntarily quit her job. The court found that the doctor did not require that the employee work out during her lunch break and that it was only the employee's preference. Furthermore, the employer was engaged in an interactive process regarding the requested accommodation when the employee quit voluntarily, therefore no ADA violation was found.{{Cite web|url=https://www.employerlawreport.com/2018/08/articles/labor-relations/sixth-circuit-holds-that-employer-was-not-required-to-extend-lunch-breaks-for-exercise-as-reasonable-accommodation/|title=Sixth Circuit holds that employer was not required to extend lunch breaks for exercise as reasonable accommodation|date=2018-08-21|website=Employer Law Report|language=en-US|access-date=2019-05-01}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.shrm.org/resourcesandtools/legal-and-compliance/employment-law/pages/court-report-extra-lunchtime.aspx|title=Vague Doctor's Note Did Not Prove the Need for Extra Lunchtime|date=2018-09-18|website=SHRM|language=en-US|access-date=2019-05-01}} ==== Separation of powers ==== Bush joined the court's opinion in ''Hagy v. Demers & Adams, LLC''{{Cite web|url=https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/ca6/17-3696/17-3696-2018-02-16.html|title=Hagy v. Demers & Adams, No. 17-3696 (6th Cir. 2018)|website=Justia Law|language=en|access-date=2019-05-01}} involving a letter sent from an attorney discharging the plaintiffs' debts following a mortgage foreclosure. The letter failed to include language disclosing that it came from a debt collector as required under the Fair Debt Collections Protections Act (FDCPA). Despite the fact that no injury or harm came from the failure to disclose, nor was the letter unfair, deceptive, or harassing as the FDCPA aims to prevent, the district court awarded $1,000 in statutory penalties and over $74,000 in attorneys fees to the plaintiffs. The circuit court reversed, finding that the plaintiffs had no standing in court because no harm had occurred outside of a bare procedural violation. Citing the Supreme Court in ''[[Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins]],'' the circuit court found that Congress had overstepped its congressional authority by creating injuries that satisfy Article III standing requirements where no actual harm had occurred. The court found that Congress may not "simply enact an injury into existence, using its lawmaking power to transform something that is not remotely harmful into something that is".{{Cite web|url=https://www.natlawreview.com/article/dismissing-fdcpa-lawsuit-sixth-circuit-calls-out-congress-creating-statutory|title=Dismissing FDCPA Lawsuit, Sixth Circuit Calls Out Congress for Creating Statutory Remedies Where No Harm Has Occurred|website=The National Law Review|language=en|access-date=2019-05-01}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.jdsupra.com/legalnews/applying-spokeo-6th-circuit-dismisses-92383/|title=Applying Spokeo, 6th Circuit Dismisses FDCPA Suit|website=JD Supra|language=en|access-date=2019-05-01}} ==== Qualified immunity ==== Bush wrote a concurrence in the case ''Yates v. Davis''{{Cite web|url=https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/ca6/17-6120/17-6120-2019-08-23.html|title=Yates v. Davis, No. 17-6120 (6th Cir. 2019)|website=Justia Law|language=en|access-date=2019-09-07}} regarding former Rowan County, Kentucky court clerk Kim Davis, who refused to marriage licenses following the U.S. Supreme Court's decision recognizing a constitutional right to same-sex marriage in ''[[Obergefell v. Hodges]]''. The court found that Davis was not entitled to [[Sovereign immunity in the United States|sovereign]] or [[qualified immunity]] and allowed the case to move forward. Bush authored a concurrence, agreeing that Davis did not qualify for sovereign or qualified immunity, but using a different level of scrutiny to evaluate the question of qualified immunity.{{Cite web|url=https://www.courthousenews.com/ex-kentucky-clerk-kim-davis-must-face-suit/|title=Ex-Kentucky Clerk Kim Davis Must Face Suit|last=Kelly|first=Joe|date=23 August 2019|website=Courthouse News Service}}{{Cite web|url=https://reason.com/2019/08/28/no-qualified-immunity-for-kim-davis/|title=No Qualified Immunity for Kim Davis|date=2019-08-28|website=Reason.com|language=en-US|access-date=2019-09-07}} On June 18, 2020, in ''Wright v. City of Euclid'', Bush reversed the district court's decision to grant qualified immunity for police officers who tased, pepper-sprayed, and arrested Lamar Wright, a black man who had his hands raised and was cooperating with the officers but had trouble exiting his vehicle due to a colostomy bag from a recent surgery.{{Cite web|title=Wright v. City of Euclid, No. 19-3452 (6th Cir. 2020)|url=https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/ca6/19-3452/19-3452-2020-06-18.html|access-date=2020-06-19|website=Justia Law|language=en}}{{Cite web|last=Allard|first=Sam|title=Court OKs Reopening Euclid Police Lawsuit Where Cops Tased, Pepper-Sprayed Black Man with Colostomy Bag|url=https://www.clevescene.com/scene-and-heard/archives/2020/06/19/court-oks-re-opening-euclid-police-lawsuit-where-cops-tased-pepper-sprayed-black-man-with-colostomy-bag|access-date=2020-06-19|website=Cleveland Scene|language=en|archive-date=June 20, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200620183510/https://www.clevescene.com/scene-and-heard/archives/2020/06/19/court-oks-re-opening-euclid-police-lawsuit-where-cops-tased-pepper-sprayed-black-man-with-colostomy-bag|url-status=dead}} The circuit court's unanimous decision to remand for a jury trial on unconstitutional use of force, false arrest, extended detention, and malicious prosecution claims was authored by Bush. The court also reversed the dismissal of Wright's ''[[Monell v. Department of Social Services of the City of New York|Monell]]'' claims based on police training that notably included a [[Chris Rock]] video and a cartoon of a police officer beating a figure lying on the ground.{{Cite web|url=https://www.opn.ca6.uscourts.gov/opinions.pdf/20a0185p-06.pdf|title=Lamar Wright v. Rogers]] | successor = | birth_name = John Baylor Nalbandian | birth_date = {{birth year and age|1969}} | birth_place = [[Fort Ord]], [[California]], U.S. | death_date = | death_place = | party = [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] | spouse = {{marriage|Caroline May|1994}} | children = 2 | education = [[University of Pennsylvania]] ([[Bachelor of Science|BS]])
[[University of Virginia]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''John Baylor Nalbandian''' (born 1969) is a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit]]. He was previously a partner in the [[Cincinnati]] office of [[Taft Stettinius & Hollister]]. == Biography == Nalbandian received his [[Bachelor of Science]] from the [[Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania]] and his [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Virginia School of Law]] with the [[Order of the Coif]] honor.{{cite web |url=https://www.law.virginia.edu/uvalawyer/spring-2019/article/5101525-hows-life-after-law-school |title=5/10/15/25: How's Life After Law School? | University of Virginia School of Law |date=May 22, 2019}} At the start of his legal career Nalbandian served as a [[law clerk]] to Judge [[Jerry Edwin Smith]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]]. He then went on to be an [[Associate attorney|associate]] at [[Jones Day]], where he practiced for five years. In 2000, he joined [[Taft Stettinius & Hollister]] in [[Cincinnati]] and eventually became a [[Law firm partner|partner]], where he continued to work until becoming a judge.{{cite web|url=https://www.natlawreview.com/author/john-b-nalbandian |title=John B. Nalbandian | The National Law Review |website=[[The National Law Review]] |date=October 4, 2010 |access-date=January 26, 2018}} Nalbandian was appointed by [[Governor of Kentucky|Kentucky Governor]] [[Ernie Fletcher]] to serve as a Special Justice of the [[Kentucky Supreme Court]] in 2007. In June 2010, he was nominated by President [[Barack Obama]] and confirmed by the [[United States Senate|Senate]] to be a board member of the [[State Justice Institute]] to fill [[Keith McNamara]]'s seat, serving until July 11, 2018.{{cite web|url=http://www.sji.gov/about-sji/board-of-directors/ |title=State Justice Institute |access-date=January 26, 2018}} He resigned his seat on the Board of Directors on July 11, 2018.{{Cite web |url=http://www.sji.gov/sji-honors-judge-john-nalbandian-for-his-service-on-the-board-of-directors/ |title=SJI Honors Judge John Nalbandian for His Service on the Board of Directors |website=www.sji.gov |access-date=2019-11-08}} He was a member of the Magistrate Judge Merit Selection Panel for the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Kentucky]].[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-tenth-wave-judicial-nominees/ "President Donald J. Trump Announces Tenth Wave of Judicial Nominees" White House, January 23, 2018] {{PD-notice}} He has been a member of the [[Federalist Society]] since 1991.{{Cite web |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Nalbandian%20SJQ.pdf |title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees |website=judiciary.senate.gov |access-date=June 30, 2018}} == Federal judicial service == On January 23, 2018, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to nominate Nalbandian to an undetermined seat on the United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit. On January 24, 2018, his nomination was sent to the [[United States Senate]]. He was nominated to the seat being vacated by Judge [[John M. Rogers]], who announced his intention to assume [[senior status]] on a date to be determined.{{cite web|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/eight-nominations-sent-senate-today-4/|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Eight Nominations Sent to the Senate Today}} On March 7, 2018, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/03/07/2018/nominations|title=Nominations – United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|website=www.judiciary.senate.gov|date=March 7, 2018 }} On April 19, 2018, his nomination was reported out of committee by an 11–10 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%2004-19-18.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – April 19, 2018, Senate Judiciary Committee}} On May 11, 2018 the Senate invoked [[cloture]] on his nomination by a 52–43 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1152/vote_115_2_00091.htm|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture on John B. Nalbandian, of Kentucky, to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the Sixth Circuit)|date=May 15, 2018|website=[[United States Senate]]|access-date=May 15, 2018|language=en}} On May 15, 2018, his nomination was confirmed by a 53–45 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=115&session=2&vote=00095|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation John B. Nalbandian, of Kentucky, to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the Sixth Circuit)|date=May 15, 2018|website=[[United States Senate]]|access-date=May 15, 2018|language=en}} He received his commission on May 17, 2018.{{FJC Bio|nid=4625006|inline=yes}} == Personal life == Nalbandian's mother was born in a [[Internment of Japanese Americans|Japanese American internment camp]] during [[World War II]].{{cite web|url=https://www.justice.gov/opa/speech/assistant-attorney-general-beth-williams-delivers-remarks-judicial-nominations-american|title=Assistant Attorney General Beth Williams Delivers Remarks on Judicial Nominations to American Academy of Appellate Lawyers' 2018 Spring Meeting|website=[[United States Department of Justice]]|date=April 14, 2018|access-date=April 16, 2018}} He married Caroline May in 1994. == Notable Cases == Judge Nalbandian has notable cases in the areas of federal sentencing, civil procedure, and class actions. * ''CIC Services LLC v. IRS'', 925 F.3d 247 (6th Cir. 2019) (Nalbandian, J., dissenting), rev'd, 593 U.S. 209 (2021). * ''Crawford v. Tilley'', 15 F.4th 752 (6th Cir. 2021). * ''United States v. Tomes'', 990 F.3d 500 (6th Cir. 2021). * ''United States v. McCall'', 56 F.4th 1048 (6th Cir. 2022). * ''Allstates Refractory Contractors, LLC v. Su'', 79 F.4th 755 (6th Cir. 2023) (Nalbandian, J., dissenting). * ''Tennessee v. Dep't of Educ.'', 104 F.4th 577 (6th Cir. 2024). * ''Bowles v. Sabree'', 121 F.4th 539 (6th Cir. 2024). * ''Friends of George's, Inc. v. Mulroy'', 108 F.4th 431 (6th Cir. 2024). * ''United States v. Sittenfeld'', 128 F.4th 752 (6th Cir. 2025). * ''Salazar v.
