[[University of the Pacific (United States)|University of the Pacific]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]])
[[Duke University]] ([[Master of Laws|LLM]]) }} '''Johnnie Mae Blakeney Rawlinson'''{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vZPLQiWklXIC&pg=PA377|page=377|title=Hearings before the Committee on the Judiciary, United States Senate, One Hundred Sixth Congress, Second Session, on Confirmations of Appointees to the Federal Judiciary, May 25, June 15, July 12, and July 25, 2000|publisher=U.S. Government Printing Office|year=2001}} (born December 16, 1952) is a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]] and a former United States district judge of the [[United States District Court for the District of Nevada]]. ==Early life and career== Rawlinson was born in [[Concord, North Carolina]]. Rawlinson received most of her education in [[North Carolina]], where she earned her [[Bachelor of Science]] degree ''[[summa cum laude]]'' from [[North Carolina Agricultural and Technical State University]] in 1974. She graduated with distinction from the [[McGeorge School of Law]] at the [[University of the Pacific (United States)|University of the Pacific]], receiving her [[Juris Doctor]] in 1979. In 1980, Rawlinson and [[Viveca Monet Woods]] became the first African American women admitted to practice law in Nevada.{{Cite web |last=Anderson |first=Rachel J. |date=2013 |title=Blacks in the Nevada Legal Profession |url=https://scholars.law.unlv.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1856&context=facpub |website=University of Nevada, Las Vegas -- William S. Boyd School of Law}}{{Cite web |last=Anderson |first=Rachel J. |date=February 2012 |title=Timeline of African-American Legal History in Nevada (1861-2011) |url=http://scholars.law.unlv.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1706&context=facpub}} She had served as deputy district attorney and chief deputy for over 17 years in the office of the Clark County District Attorney in [[Las Vegas, Nevada|Las Vegas]], [[Nevada]], as well as receiving law practice as a clerk at Kiefer Clark & O'Reilly and other legal services throughout the [[United States]] prior to her appointments. She served as a United States district judge after being nominated by President Clinton and confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] in 1997. She was the first female judge to serve on the [[United States District Court for the District of Nevada]].{{cite journal |last1=Anderson |first1=Rachel J. |title=Timeline of African-American Legal History in Nevada (1861-2011) |journal=University of Nevada, Las Vegas -- William S. Boyd School of Law |date=2012 |url=https://scholars.law.unlv.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?date=1361818084&article=1706&context=facpub&preview_mode= |access-date=14 December 2025}} In 2016, Judge Rawlinson received a Master of Judicial Studies degree from [[Duke University School of Law]].{{cite web|url=http://law.duke.edu/video/duke-law-graduation-2016-judge-johnnie-b-rawlinson |title=Duke Law Graduation 2016 {{!}} Judge Johnnie B. Rawlinson |publisher=Duke University School of Law |date=May 14, 2016 |access-date=February 5, 2017}} ==Federal judicial service== ===District court service=== Rawlinson was a federal judge to the [[United States District Court for the District of Nevada]]. Rawlinson was nominated by President [[Bill Clinton]] on January 27, 1998, to a seat vacated by [[Lloyd D. George]]. She was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on April 2, 1998, and received commission on April 7, 1998. Rawlinson's service was terminated on July 26, 2000, due to elevation to the court of appeals.{{FJC Bio|nid=1390671|inline=yes}} ===Court of appeals service=== Rawlinson was nominated by President [[Bill Clinton]] on February 22, 2000, to a seat on the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]] after being recommended for the post by United States Senator [[Harry Reid]]. Rawlinson was nominated to a seat vacated by [[Melvin T. Brunetti]]. Rawlinson was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] by a voice vote on July 21, 2000, making her the final appeals-court nominee to be confirmed during Clinton's presidency. She received her commission on July 26, 2000.{{FJC Bio|nid=1390671|inline=yes}} Rawlinson subsequently took the oath of office on the same day, becoming the first African American woman to sit on the Ninth Circuit. On April 14, 2022, news reports stated Rawlinson suggested she would consider assuming senior status, creating a vacancy for her seat on the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]], if Berna Rhodes-Ford, former law clerk and wife of [[Aaron D. Ford]], would be nominated as her successor.{{cite news | url=https://www.reuters.com/legal/litigation/9th-circuit-judge-urges-biden-nevada-senators-pick-state-ags-wife-successor-2022-04-14/ | title=9th Circuit judge urges Biden, Nevada senators to pick state AG's wife as successor | newspaper=Reuters | date=14 April 2022 | last1=Raymond | first1=Nate }}{{cite web | url=https://davidlat.substack.com/p/bidens-judicial-nominees-turnabout?s=w | title=Biden's Judicial Nominees: Turnabout is Fair Play | date=15 April 2022 }} ==Personal life== Rawlinson resides in [[Las Vegas]]. Her husband of 40 years, Dwight Rawlinson, died of cancer in August 2016.{{cite web | url = http://obits.reviewjournal.com/obituaries/lvrj/obituary.aspx?pid=181360008 | title = Dwight Rawlinson Obituary | publisher = Las Vegas Review Journal | access-date = May 12, 2017}} ==See also== * [[Barack Obama Supreme Court candidates]] * [[List of African-American federal judges]] * [[List of African-American jurists]] * [[List of first women lawyers and judges in Nevada]] ==References== {{Reflist |refs= {{cite web |url= http://www.appellate-counsellor.com/profiles/rawlinsn.htm |title= Profile of Judge Johnnie B. Winter Jr.]] | office2 = Judge of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit]] | appointer2 = [[Jimmy Carter]] | term_start2 = June 21, 1979 | term_end2 = July 1, 1997 | predecessor2 = Seat established | successor2 = [[Robert Katzmann]] | office3 = Judge of the [[United States District Court for the District of Connecticut]] | appointer3 = [[Richard Nixon]] | term_start3 = December 15, 1971 | term_end3 = June 21, 1979 | predecessor3 = [[William H. [[Yale University]] ([[Bachelor of Laws|LLB]]) }} '''Jon Ormond Newman''' (born May 2, 1932) is a [[United States federal judge|senior United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit]].{{cite book |title=Hearings - Volume 5 |date=1961 |publisher=U.S. Government Printing Office |page=90 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gGyyzhJlT7kC&dq=Jon+O.+Newman++may+1932&pg=PA90 |access-date=25 March 2021}} ==Early life and career== Born in [[New York City]], Newman earned his [[Bachelor of Arts|Artium Baccalaureus]] degree from [[Princeton University]] in 1953 and his [[Bachelor of Laws]] from [[Yale Law School]] in 1956. After Yale, he [[Law clerk|clerked]] for Judge [[George Thomas Washington]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit]] and then clerked for [[United States Supreme Court]] Chief Justice [[Earl Warren]] from 1957 to 1958. Additionally, he was in the [[United States Army Reserve]] from 1954 to 1962.{{FJC Bio|1755|nid=1385686|name=Jon Ormond Newman|accessdate=October 15, 2025}} He was in private practice from 1958 to 1960 in [[Hartford|Hartford, Connecticut]], and served as a graduate instructor at [[Trinity College (Connecticut)|Trinity College]].{{cite web|title=US Attorney Bulletin|url=https://www.justice.gov/usao/eousa/foia_reading_room/usab1626.pdf|publisher=DOJ|access-date=22 June 2011}} He also served as special counsel to the [[Governor of Connecticut]] in 1960. He was executive assistant to the [[United States Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare]] from 1961 to 1962 and then joined the staff of [[United States Senator]] [[Abraham Ribicoff]] as administrative assistant from 1963 to 1964.{{cite web |url=https://www.justice.gov/usao-ct/office |title=About the Office |date=18 March 2015}} He was the [[United States Attorney]] for the District of Connecticut from 1964 to 1969 when [[Richard Nixon]] took office. He entered private practice in Hartford again until 1971 when he was nominated to a federal district judgeship. ==Federal judicial service== Newman was nominated by President [[Richard Nixon]] on December 2, 1971, to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the District of Connecticut]] vacated by Judge [[William H. Timbers]]. He was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on December 11, 1971, received his commission on December 15, 1971, and began serving as a judge on January 17, 1972. His service as a District Judge terminated on June 25, 1979, due to his elevation to the Second Circuit. Newman was nominated by President [[Jimmy Carter]] on April 30, 1979, to the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit]], to a new seat created by 92 Stat. 1629. He was confirmed by the Senate on June 19, 1979, and received his commission on June 21, 1979. He served as Chief Judge from 1993 to 1997. He assumed [[senior status]] on July 1, 1997. ==Honor== On December 8, 2016, at a special ceremony at the [[Supreme Court of the United States]], Justice [[Elena Kagan]] presented to Judge Newman, on behalf of the federal judiciary, the 2016 [[Edward J. Devitt]] Distinguished Service to Justice Award.{{cite web|url=https://www.uscourts.gov/news/2016/12/07/judge-jon-o-newman-receive-2016-devitt-award|title=Judge Jon O. Newman to Receive 2016 Devitt Award}} The Devitt Award honors an Article III judge who has achieved a distinguished career and made significant contributions to the administration of justice, the advancement of the rule of law, and the improvement of society as a whole. == Noteworthy decisions == * ''Abele v. Markle'', 351 F. Supp. 224 (D. Conn. 1972) - Connecticut statute prohibiting abortions, except to save life of mother, was unconstitutional. * ''SCM Corp. v. Xerox Corp.'', 463 F. Supp. 983 (D. Conn. 1978) - After 14-month jury trial, probably the longest federal civil jury trial, Xerox Corp. did not violate antitrust laws by maintaining its plain paper copying monopoly.[http://www.ca2.uscourts.gov:8080/isysnative/RDpcT3BpbnNcT1BOXDA2LTI0ODAtYWdfb3BuLnBkZg==/06-2480-ag_opn.pdf#xml=http://www.ca2.uscourts.gov:8080/isysquery/irlcb26/1/hilite] * ''[[Salinger v. Random House]]'' 811 F.2d 90 (2d Cir.1987) - J.D. Salinger's biographer used too many of the author's letters to be exempted from copyright infringement by the doctrine of "[[fair use]]" * ''Kadic v. Karadzic'', 70 F.3d 232 (2d Cir. 1996) – There was [[subject matter jurisdiction]] under the [[Alien Tort Statute|Alien Tort Claim Act]], 28 U.S.C.S. § 1350, to pursue an action for war crimes against a private individual * ''[[American Geophysical Union v. Texaco]]'', 60 F.3d 913 (2nd Cir., 1994) – Texaco's bulk photocopying of articles from scientific journals for its researchers was not fair use since it was in support of the company's commercial goals and not the public good. The first Second Circuit copyright case to consider [[transformative use]]. * ''[[Leibovitz v. Jonathan A. Kobes:
{{Short description|American judge (born 1974)}} {{Use mdy dates|date=June 2018}} {{Infobox officeholder | name = Jonathan Kobes | image = Jonathan Kobes (Judge) (cropped).jpg | office = Judge of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit]] | appointer = [[Donald Trump]] | term_start = December 12, 2018 | term_end = | predecessor = [[Roger Leland Wollman]] | successor = | birth_name = Jonathan Allen Kobes | birth_date = {{birth date and age|1974|8|25}} | birth_place = [[Sioux City, Iowa]], U.S. | death_date = | death_place = | party = [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] | education = [[Dordt University]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|BA]])
[[Harvard University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Jonathan Allen Kobes''' (born August 25, 1974) is a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit]]. == Education == Kobes received his [[Bachelor of Arts]] from [[Dordt University]] and his [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Harvard Law School]], where he was an editor and the business manager of the ''[[Harvard Journal of Law and Public Policy]]''. During law school, Kobes worked at the [[Massachusetts Attorney General|Massachusetts Attorney General's Office]], the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]], the United States Attorney's Office for the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Iowa|Northern District of Iowa]], and the [[Chicago]] office of [[McDermott Will & Emery]]. == Legal career == After graduating from law school, Kobes served as a [[law clerk]] to Judge [[Roger Leland Wollman]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit]]. He then worked from 2002 to 2003 as litigation attorney at the [[Central Intelligence Agency]] and from 2003 to 2005 as [[Assistant United States Attorney]] for the [[United States Attorney for the District of South Dakota|District of South Dakota]]. Kobes was an associate at the [[Sioux Falls, South Dakota]], office of Murphy, Goldammer & Prendergast from 2005 to 2008. Kobes was then senior counsel to [[POET]] in Sioux Falls, senior regulatory counsel to [[DuPont Pioneer]] in [[Johnston, Iowa]], and Director of Corporate Compliance at [[Raven Industries]]. From 2014 to 2018, Kobes worked as General Counsel to U.S. Senator [[Mike Rounds]]. He was also a member of the Central Committee of the [[Lincoln County, South Dakota|Lincoln County]] [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]].{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/12/11/us/politics/republicans-judges-confirmation-votes.html|title=Trump's Judicial Nominees Take Heat but Largely Keep Marching Through Senate|last=Edmondson|first=Catie|date=2018-12-11|work=The New York Times|access-date=2018-12-11|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}} == Federal judicial service == On June 7, 2018, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to nominate Kobes to serve as a United States Circuit Judge of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit]].{{cite press release|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-fifteenth-wave-judicial-nominees-fourteenth-wave-united-states-attorney-nominees-ninth-wave-united-states-marshal-nominees/|title=President Donald J. Trump Announces Fifteenth Wave of Judicial Nominees, Fourteenth Wave of United States Attorney Nominees, and Ninth Wave of United States Marshal Nominees|date=June 7, 2018|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|access-date=June 7, 2018}} {{PD-notice}} On June 11, 2018, his nomination was sent to the Senate. Trump nominated Kobes to the seat being vacated by Judge [[Roger Leland Wollman]], who previously announced his intention to assume [[senior status]] upon confirmation of a successor.{{cite web|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/seventeen-nominations-sent-senate-today-3/|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Seventeen Nominations Sent to the Senate Today}} On August 22, 2018, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/08/22/2018/nominations|title=Nominations - United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|website=www.judiciary.senate.gov|date=August 22, 2018 }} On September 14, 2018, the [[American Bar Association]]'s [[Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary]] rated Kobes "Not Qualified."{{cite news |last1=Gregory |first1=Patrick |title=ABA Rates Another Trump 8th Circuit Nominee 'Not Qualified' |url=https://www.bna.com/aba-rates-trump-n73014482574/ |access-date=18 September 2018 |publisher=Bloomberg BNA |date=September 17, 2018}} The ABA's report said that Kobes was "a very accomplished, competent, and capable person, but his career path has not resulted in sufficient evidence of a developed ability to do the written work of a United States circuit court judge."{{cite news |last1=Silverstein |first1=Jason |title=Federal judge becomes first in U.S. history confirmed by tiebreaker in the Senate |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/jonathan-kobes-becomes-first-federal-judge-in-u-s-history-confirmed-by-tiebreaker-in-the-senate/ |access-date=26 December 2018 |website=[[CBS News]] |date=December 11, 2018}}{{cite magazine |last1=Weiss |first1=Debra Cassens |title=Pence breaks tie to confirm 8th Circuit nominee with 'not qualified' rating from ABA committee |url=http://www.abajournal.com/news/article/pence_breaks_tie_to_confirm_8th_circuit_nominee_with_not_qualified_rating |access-date=26 December 2018 |magazine=ABA Journal |date=December 12, 2018}} The ABA report questioned Kobes' understanding of "complex legal analysis" and "knowledge of the law". At the time of his nomination, Kobes had tried six cases during his legal career, cases that the ABA considered straightforward and not "legally complex". On October 11, 2018, Kobes' nomination was reported out of the Senate Judiciary Committee by a 11–10 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/10-11-18%20Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting1.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – October 11, 2018, Senate Judiciary Committee}} On November 29, 2018, the [[United States Senate]] invoked [[cloture]] on Kobes' nomination by a 50–49 vote, with Vice President [[Mike Pence]] [[List of tie-breaking votes cast by the vice president of the United States|breaking the tie]].{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=115&session=2&vote=00251|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Jonathan A. Kobes to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the Eighth Circuit)|website=www.senate.gov}} On December 11, 2018, he was confirmed by a 51–50 vote, with Pence casting his vote in the affirmative.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1152/vote_115_2_00258.htm|title= On the Nomination (Confirmation Jonathan A. Kobes, of South Dakota, to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the Eighth Circuit)|website=www.senate.gov}}{{cite news | last1=Ellis | first1=Jonathan | title=Trump judicial nominee, Sioux Falls lawyer Jonathan Kobes, wins confirmation | url=https://www.argusleader.com/story/news/2018/12/11/jonathan-kobes-trump-nominee-sioux-falls-lawyer-wins-confirmation/2280025002/ | date=December 11, 2018 | newspaper=[[Sioux Falls Argus Leader]] | access-date=December 12, 2018}}{{cite news | last1=Carney | first1=Jordain | title=Pence casts tie-breaking vote for Trump appeals court judge | url=https://thehill.com/homenews/senate/420848-pence-casts-tie-breaking-vote-for-trump-appeals-court-judge | date=December 11, 2018 | newspaper=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]] | access-date=December 12, 2018}} He was the first federal judicial nominee ever confirmed by a tie-breaking vote.{{cite web | last1=Silverstein | first1=Jason | title=Federal judge becomes first in U.S. history confirmed by tiebreaker in the Senate | url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/jonathan-kobes-becomes-first-federal-judge-in-u-s-history-confirmed-by-tiebreaker-in-the-senate/ | date=December 11, 2018 | website=[[CBS News]] | access-date=December 12, 2018}} Kobes received his judicial commission on December 12, 2018.{{FJC Bio|nid=5675191|inline=yes}} ==Notable cases== In December 2021, Kobes upheld the 20-year prison sentence of a doctor at the [[United States Department of Veterans Affairs]] who misdiagnosed a patient, resulting in the patient's death.{{Cite web|url=https://www.military.com/daily-news/2021/12/02/appeals-court-upholds-sentence-of-former-va-pathologist.html|title=Appeals Court Upholds Sentence of Former VA Pathologist|website=Military.com|date=December 2, 2021|access-date=December 5, 2021}}{{Cite web|url=https://ecf.ca8.uscourts.gov/opndir/21/12/211296P.pdf|title=United States of America v. Robert Levy|website=ecf.ca8.uscourts.gov|date=December 1, 2021|access-date=December 5, 2021}} == Memberships == Kobes was a member of the [[Federalist Society]] from 1999 to 2004.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Kobes%20SJQ.pdf|title=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees: Jonathan A. Kobes}} == See also == * [[Donald Trump judicial appointment controversies]] == References == {{Reflist}} == External links == * {{FJC Bio|nid=5675191}} * {{Ballotpedia|Jonathan_Kobes|Jonathan Kobes}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Roger Leland Wollman]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit]]}}|years=2018–present}} {{s-inc}} {{s-end}} {{United States courts of appeals judges}} {{Authority control}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Kobes, Jonathan A.}} [[Category:1974 births]] [[Category:Living people]] [[Category:20th-century American lawyers]] [[Category:21st-century American lawyers]] [[Category:Assistant United States attorneys]] [[Category:Dordt University alumni]] [[Category:Harvard Law School alumni]] [[Category:Judges of the United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit]] [[Category:People from Sioux City, Iowa]] [[Category:People of the Central Intelligence Agency]] [[Category:South Dakota lawyers]] [[Category:South Dakota Republicans]] [[Category:United States court of appeals judges appointed by Donald Trump]] [[Category:United States Senate lawyers]]

'''Julie G. Rikelman'''<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Rikelman%20SJQ%20Public%20Final.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|date=September 21, 2022|work=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary}}</ref> (born June 16, 1972)<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.thefocus.news/celebrity/julie-rikelman |title=Who is attorney Julie Rikelman as SCOTUS vote on Roe v Wade looms? |date=December 2, 2021 |website=The Focus}}</ref> is a Ukrainian-born American lawyer who is serving as a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit]]. She represented the [[Mississippi]] abortion clinic in ''[[Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization]]'', the United States Supreme Court case that overturned the constitutional right to abortion.<ref name=bloomberg>{{cite news |last1=Alder |first1=Madison |title=Dobbs Lawyer Says She'd Apply Abortion Ruling as US Judge (1) |url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/dobbs-lawyer-says-shed-apply-abortion-ruling-as-circuit-judge |access-date=1 October 2022 |work=news.bloomberglaw.com |date=September 21, 2022 |language=en}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==

Rikelman was born in [[Kyiv, Ukraine]], to [[Jewish]] parents,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://courtsmatter.org/nominees/julie-rikelman/|title=Julie Rikelman | CourtsMatter|date=September 1, 2022|website=courtsmatter.org}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine|title=The Fate of Roe v. Wade May Rest on This Woman's Shoulders|author=Abigail Abrams|date=October 21, 2021|magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]]|url=https://time.com/6108402/julie-rikelman-supreme-court-abortion-rights/}}</ref> immigrating to the United States with her family in 1979.<ref name="CNN">{{Cite web |last1=de Vogue |first1=Ariane |last2=Klein |first2=Betsy |date=July 29, 2022 |title=Biden nominates lawyer who represented Mississippi abortion clinic at Supreme Court for federal judgeship |url=https://www.cnn.com/2022/07/29/politics/julie-rikelman-nomination-dobbs/index.html |access-date=July 29, 2022 |website=CNN }}</ref> She received a [[Bachelor of Arts]], ''[[magna cum laude]]'', from [[Harvard College]] in 1993, and a [[Juris Doctor]], ''[[cum laude]]'', from [[Harvard Law School]] in 1997.<ref name="WHBio">{{Cite press release|title=President Biden Names Twenty-Fourth Round of Judicial Nominees|date=July 29, 2022|publisher=The White House|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/07/29/president-biden-names-twenty-fourth-round-of-judicial-nominees/|access-date=July 29, 2022}} {{PD-notice}}</ref>

== Career ==

From 1997 to 1998, Rikelman served as a [[law clerk]] for Justice [[Dana Fabe]] of the [[Alaska Supreme Court]] and from 1998 to 1999, was a law clerk for Judge [[Morton Ira Greenberg]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit]]. From 1999 to 2001, she was a [[Harry Blackmun|Blackmun Fellow]] at the [[Center for Reproductive Rights]]. From 2001 to 2004, she was an [[associate lawyer|associate]] at Feldman & Orlansky in [[Anchorage, Alaska]]. From 2004 to 2006, she was a senior associate at [[Simpson Thacher & Bartlett]] in [[New York City]]. From 2006 to 2011, Rikelman held various positions at [[NBC Universal, Inc.]], including vice president of litigation.<ref name="WHBio" /> From 2011 to 2023, she was the senior litigation director for the [[Center for Reproductive Rights]].<ref name="WHBio" /><ref name="CNN" />

=== Notable cases ===

Rikelman is well known for her representation and advocacy for [[abortion provider]]s in federal court challenges such as in ''[[June Medical Services LLC v. Russo]]'' (2020) and ''[[Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization]]'' (2022).<ref name="CNN" /><ref name="Bloomberg">{{Cite web |last=Adler |first=Madison |date=July 29, 2022 |title=Biden Taps Abortion Lawyer From Dobbs Case for First Circuit (1) |url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/biden-taps-abortion-lawyer-from-dobbs-case-for-first-circuit |access-date=July 29, 2022 |website=news.bloomberglaw.com |language=en}}</ref><ref name="Reuters">{{Cite web |last=Raymond |first=Nate |date=July 29, 2022 |title=Biden nominates abortion rights lawyer in U.S. Supreme Court case to federal judgeship |url=https://www.reuters.com/legal/world/us/biden-nominates-abortion-rights-lawyer-us-supreme-court-case-federal-judgeship-2022-07-29/ |access-date=July 29, 2022 |website=Reuters |language=en}}</ref>

In 2012, Rikelman represented [[Texas]] Medical Providers Performing Abortion Services when they sued the commissioner of the Texas Department of State Health Services and the executive director of the Texas Medical Board. The plaintiffs alleged constitutional violations resulting from the newly enacted Texas House Bill 15 ("the Act"), an Act "relating to informed consent to an abortion." H.B. 15, 82nd Leg. Reg. Sess. (Tex.2011).<ref>{{cite web | url=https://casetext.com/case/texas-med-providers-performing-abortion-servs-v-lakey | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150710034939/https://casetext.com/case/texas-med-providers-performing-abortion-servs-v-lakey | url-status=dead | archive-date=July 10, 2015 | title=Texas Med. Providers Performing Abortion Servs. V. Lakey, 667 F.3d 570 | Casetext Search + Citator }} {{PD-notice}}</ref> 

In December 2014, Rikelman argued in the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit]] for plaintiffs, who included an abortion provider and her patients seeking abortions. At issue was a North Carolina statute that required physicians to perform an [[ultrasound]], display the [[ultrasonogram|songram]], and describe the fetus to women seeking abortions. In July 2011, the [[North Carolina]] General Assembly passed the Woman's Right to Know Act over a gubernatorial veto. The act amended Chapter 90 of the North Carolina General Statutes, which governs medical and related professions, adding a new article regulating the steps that must precede an abortion. Physicians and abortion providers filed suit after the act's passage but before its effective date, asking the court to enjoin enforcement of the act and declare it unconstitutional.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://casetext.com/case/stuart-v-camnitz-1?q=Julie+Rikelman&sort=relevance&p=2&type=case|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220923133633/https://casetext.com/case/stuart-v-camnitz-1?q=Julie+Rikelman&sort=relevance&p=2&type=case|url-status=dead|archive-date=September 23, 2022|title=Stuart v. Camnitz, 774 F.3d 238 | Casetext Search + Citator|website=casetext.com}}</ref>

In October 2020, Rikelman was co-counsel representing [[Whole Woman's Health v. Jackson|Whole Woman's Health]], Planned Parenthood Center for Choice, Planned Parenthood of Greater Texas Surgical Health Services, Planned Parenthood South Texas Surgical Center, Alamo City Surgery Center, P.L.L.C. and Southwestern Women's Surgery Center on behalf of itself, its staff, physicians, and patients. The case challenged the constitutionality of Texas Senate Bill 8, a statute that requires a woman to undergo an additional and medically unnecessary procedure to cause fetal demise before she may obtain a dilation and evacuation abortion. This case was argued in the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://casetext.com/case/whole-womans-health-v-paxton-8?q=Julie+Rikelman&sort=relevance&p=2&type=case|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220923133632/https://casetext.com/case/whole-womans-health-v-paxton-8?q=Julie+Rikelman&sort=relevance&p=2&type=case|url-status=dead|archive-date=September 23, 2022|title=Whole Woman's Health v. Paxton, 978 F.3d 896 | Casetext Search + Citator|website=casetext.com}}</ref>

In 2021, Rikelman argued in the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit]] for several abortion providers and their patients seeking abortions. The North Carolina abortion providers brought this action to challenge as unconstitutional the state's criminalization of pre-viability abortions.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://casetext.com/case/bryant-ex-rel-gray-v-woodall?q=Julie+Rikelman&sort=relevance&p=2&type=case|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220923133631/https://casetext.com/case/bryant-ex-rel-gray-v-woodall?q=Julie+Rikelman&sort=relevance&p=2&type=case|url-status=dead|archive-date=September 23, 2022|title=Bryant ex rel. Gray v. Woodall, No. 19-1685 | Casetext Search + Citator|website=casetext.com}}</ref>

=== Federal judicial service ===
On July 29, 2022, President [[Joe Biden]] announced his intent to nominate Rikelman to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] for the [[United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit]].<ref name="WHBio" /> On August 1, 2022, her nomination was sent to the Senate. President Biden nominated Rikelman to the seat vacated by Judge [[Sandra Lynch]], who announced her intent to assume [[senior status]] upon confirmation of a successor.<ref>{{Cite press release|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate|date=August 1, 2022|publisher=The White House|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/08/01/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-78/}}</ref> Rikelman was unanimously rated "well qualified" for the judgeship by the [[American Bar Association]]'s [[Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary]].<ref>[https://www.americanbar.org/content/dam/aba/administrative/government_affairs_office/webratingchart-117.pdf Ratings of Article III and Article IV Judicial Nominees: 117th Congress], [[American Bar Association]]'s [[Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary]] (last updated December 2022).</ref>
On September 21, 2022, a hearing on her nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Nominations |date=September 21, 2022 |publisher=[[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]] |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/09/21/2022/nominations}}</ref> During her confirmation hearing, she was questioned by several Republican senators over her advocacy for abortion rights.<ref name="bloomberg" /> Rikelman was also questioned about a law review article she authored discussing appellate decisions permitting mandatory blood collection for [[DNA test]]ing under the [[Fourth Amendment to the United States Constitution|Fourth Amendment]], arguing that such mandatory collection was prohibited by the [[United States Constitution]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.baylor.edu/content/services/document.php/116868.pdf |title=JUSTIFYING FORCIBLE DNA TESTING SCHEMES UNDER THE SPECIAL NEEDS EXCEPTION TO THE FOURTH AMENDMENT: A DANGEROUS PRECEDENT |publisher=[[Baylor University]] |accessdate=2022-09-27 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://vettingroom.org/2022/09/26/julie-rikelman/|title=Julie Rikelman – Nominee to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit|date=26 September 2022 }}</ref> On December 1, 2022, the committee failed to report her nomination by an 11–11 vote.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/EBM%20Results%20-%202022-12-011.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – December 1, 2022|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=December 1, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Stern|first1=Seth|title=Senate Judiciary Deadlocks on Dobbs Lawyer for First Circuit|url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/senate-judiciary-deadlocks-on-dobbs-lawyer-for-first-circuit|access-date=1 December 2022|work=Bloomberg Law|date=1 December 2022|language=en}}</ref> On January 3, 2023, her nomination was returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]]; she was renominated later the same day.<ref>{{Cite press release |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |date=January 3, 2023 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2023/01/03/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-91/}}</ref>

On February 9, 2023, her nomination was reported out of committee by an 11–10 vote.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/2023-02-09%20-%20EBM%20-%20Results.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – February 9, 2023|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=February 9, 2023}}</ref> On June 12, 2023, Majority Leader [[Chuck Schumer]] filed [[cloture]] on her nomination.<ref>{{Cite web |title=PN90 — Julie Rikelman — The Judiciary |url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/118th-congress/90 |access-date=2023-07-07 |website=Congress.gov}}</ref> On June 15, 2023, the Senate invoked cloture on Rikelman's nomination by a 53–45 vote.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00165.htm|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Julie Rikelman to be United States Circuit Judge for the First Circuit)|website=United States Senate|date=June 15, 2023|access-date=June 15, 2023}}</ref> On June 20, 2023, her nomination was confirmed by a 51–43 vote.<ref>{{Cite web|date=June 20, 2023|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Julie Rikelman, of Massachusetts, to be United States Circuit Judge for the First Circuit)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00166.htm|access-date=June 20, 2023|website=United States Senate}}</ref> She received her judicial commission on June 23, 2023.<ref>{{FJC Bio|nid=13718106|inline=yes}}</ref>

Julius N. Richardson:
{{Short description|American judge (born 1976)}} {{Use mdy dates|date=July 2018}} {{Infobox judge | name = Jay Richardson | image = Julius N. Richardson (cropped).jpg | caption = Richardson in 2022 | office = Judge of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit]] | appointer = [[Donald Trump]] | term_start = August 20, 2018 | term_end = | predecessor = [[Dennis Shedd]] | successor = | birth_name = Julius Ness Richardson | birth_date = {{birth year and age|1976|}} | birth_place = {{nowrap|[[Columbia, South Carolina]], U.S.}} | death_date = | death_place = | party = [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] | relatives = [[Julius B. [[University of Chicago]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Julius Ness "Jay" Richardson''' (born 1976) is an American judge and lawyer who serves as a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit]]. He was formerly an [[Assistant United States Attorney]] for the [[United States District Court for the District of South Carolina|District of South Carolina]]. == Early life and career == Richardson was born and raised in [[Barnwell, South Carolina]]. He graduated from [[Vanderbilt University]] with a [[Bachelor of Science]] in 1999. He then attended the [[University of Chicago Law School]], where he served as articles editor of the ''[[University of Chicago Law Review]]'' and graduated in 2003 with a [[Juris Doctor]] with high honors. After graduating from law school, Richardson served as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Richard Posner]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit]] from 2003 to 2004 and for [[Chief Justice of the United States|Chief Justice]] [[William Rehnquist]] of the [[Supreme Court of the United States]] from 2004 to 2005.{{FJC Bio|nid=5090921|inline=yes}} Richardson then worked for three years at [[Kellogg, Hansen, Todd, Figel & Frederick]] in [[Washington, D.C.]], where he handled complex [[civil litigation]].{{Cite journal|last=May|first=James Hunter|date=July–August 2020|title=Judicial Profile: Hon. Julius Ness "Jay" Richardson|url=https://www.fedbar.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/JudicialProfile-Richardson.pdf|journal=Federal Lawyer}} In 2009, he became an [[Assistant United States Attorney]] for the [[United States District Court for the District of South Carolina|District of South Carolina]], where he prosecuted criminal cases and was Deputy Criminal Chief before becoming a judge. Richardson notably prosecuted the mass murderer [[Dylann Roof]] for his actions during the [[Charleston church shooting]].{{cite web |url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-thirteenth-wave-judicial-nominees-seventh-wave-united-states-marshal-nominees/ |title=President Donald J. Trump Announces Thirteenth Wave of Judicial Nominees and Seventh Wave of United States Marshal Nominees |date=April 26, 2018 |via=[[NARA|National Archives]] |work=[[whitehouse.gov]] |access-date=April 26, 2018 }} {{PD-notice}}{{cite web |url=http://www.thestate.com/news/local/crime/article209875319.html |title=Trump nominates Dylann Roof prosecutor Jay Richardson to top 4th Circuit court |last=Monk |first=John |date=April 26, 2018 |website=The State |access-date=April 26, 2018 }}{{cite web |url=https://www.postandcourier.com/church_shooting/trump-nominates-dylann-roof-prosecutor-jay-richardson-to-th-circuit/article_d559e874-495e-11e8-9b9a-5b0435d3523f.html |title=Trump nominates Dylann Roof prosecutor Jay Richardson to 4th Circuit Court of Appeals |last=Hawes |first=Jennifer Berry |date=April 26, 2018 |website=[[The Post and Courier]] |access-date=April 26, 2018 }} In ten years as a prosecutor, Richardson handled other high-profile prosecutions, including the [[public corruption]] case of a 42-year sheriff, an [[MS-13]] murder for hire, and a substantial [[RICO]] case against a chapter of the [[Hells Angels]]. Richardson and his wife Macon have four daughters. == Federal judicial service == [[File:Julius Ness Richardson (Judge) (cropped).jpg|thumb|right|250px|U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee hearing]] On April 26, 2018, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to nominate Richardson to serve as a United States Circuit Judge of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit]]. On May 7, 2018, his nomination was sent to the [[United States Senate|Senate]]. He was nominated to the seat vacated by Judge [[Dennis Shedd]], who assumed [[senior status]] on January 30, 2018.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/fifteen-nominations-sent-senate-today-2/ "Fifteen Nominations Sent to the Senate Today" White House, May 7, 2018] On June 20, 2018, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/06/20/2018/nominations United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Nominations for June 20, 2018] On July 19, 2018, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 20–1 vote.[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%2007-19-18.pdf Results of Executive Business Meeting – July 19, 2018, Senate Judiciary Committee] On August 16, 2018, the Senate invoked cloture on Richardson's nomination by an 80–10 vote{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=115&session=2&vote=00184|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Julius Ness Richardson, of South Carolina, to be U.S. Circuit Court Judge for the Fourth Circuit)|date=August 16, 2018|website=[[United States Senate]]|access-date=August 16, 2018|language=en}} and confirmed his nomination 81–8.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=115&session=2&vote=00185|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Julius Ness Richardson, of South Carolina, to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the Fourth Circuit)|date=August 16, 2018|website=[[United States Senate]]|access-date=August 16, 2018|language=en}} He received his judicial commission on August 20, 2018.{{FJC Bio|nid=5090921|inline=yes}} While Richardson served on the Fourth Circuit, the Court affirmed Dylann Roof's conviction and death sentence. As Richardson served as the lead prosecutor, all of the judges on the Fourth Circuit recused themselves from reviewing Roof’s case. The case was thus decided by three judges from other courts of appeal: Judges [[Duane Benton]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit]], [[Ronald Lee Gilman]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit]] and [[Kent A. Jordan]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit]].{{Cite news|last=Marimow|first=Ann|date=August 25, 2021|title=Appeals court affirms Dylann Roof's death sentence in Charleston church slayings|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/courts_law/dylann-roof-execution-upheld/2021/08/25/6797c53a-05b8-11ec-a266-7c7fe02fa374_story.html|access-date=September 8, 2021}} == Notable cases== {{importance section|date=October 2021}} *''Hirschfeld v. Bureau of Alcohol, Firearms, Tobacco & Explosives'', No. 19-2250, 2021 WL 2934468 (4th Cir. July 13, 2021). Judge Richardson held that several federal laws and regulations prohibiting federally licensed firearms dealers from selling handguns to those 18-to 20-years-old violated the Second Amendment. Judge Wynn dissented.{{Cite web|date=2021-07-13|title=Appeals court rules firearms dealers can sell handguns to 18-year-olds|url=https://nypost.com/2021/07/13/appeals-court-rules-handguns-can-be-sold-to-18-year-olds/|access-date=2021-09-08|website=[[New York Post]]|language=en-US}}{{Cite web|last=Schnell|first=Mychael|date=2021-07-13|title=Appeals court rules 21-year minimum age for handgun purchases is unconstitutional|url=https://thehill.com/regulation/court-battles/562834-appeals-court-rules-21-year-minimum-age-for-handgun-purchases-is|access-date=2021-10-05|website=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]]|language=en}} The panel subsequently vacated the decision as moot after the plaintiff turned 21.{{Cite web|last=Adler|first=Jonathan|date=September 22, 2021|title=Fourth Circuit Decision Affirming Second Amendment Rights of 18-20 Year Olds Vacated as Moot|url=https://reason.com/volokh/2021/09/22/fourth-circuit-moots/|access-date=October 5, 2021}}{{Cite news|last=Stempel|first=Jonathan|date=2021-09-22|title=U.S. appeals court erases ruling allowing gun sales to people under 21|language=en|work=[[Reuters]]|url=https://www.reuters.com/world/us/us-appeals-court-erases-ruling-allowing-gun-sales-people-under-21-2021-09-22/|access-date=2021-10-05}} *''Harley v. Wilkinson'', 988 F.3d 766 (4th Cir. 2021). The Fourth Circuit held that an as-applied Second Amendment challenge to the prohibition against possessing a firearm for a misdemeanor-domestic-violence conviction was categorically barred. Judge Richardson dissented, arguing that individuals should be allowed to bring as-applied challenges.{{Cite web|date=February 25, 2021|first=Elliot|last=Mincberg|title=Trump Judge Tries to Create "Good Behavior" Exception to Federal Law Prohibiting Those Convicted of Domestic Violence from Possessing Firearms: Confirmed Judges, Confirmed Fears|url=https://www.pfaw.org/blog-posts/trump-judge-tries-to-create-good-behavior-exception-to-federal-law-prohibiting-those-convicted-of-domestic-violence-from-possessing-firearms-confirmed-judges-confirmed-fears/|access-date=2021-09-08|website=People For the American Way|language=en-US}} *''Gonzalez v. Cuccinelli'', 985 F.3d 357 (4th Cir. Jan. 14, 2021). A group of immigrants seeking U-Visas sued for unreasonable delay to compel agency action. Judge Richardson rejected the challenge for the pre-waiting-list work authorizations but permitted the claims of unreasonable delay in adjudicating the U-Visa petitions to go forward.{{Cite web|title=4th Circ. Revives Claims In Crime Victim Visa Delay Fight - Law360|url=https://www.law360.com/articles/1345300/4th-circ-revives-claims-in-crime-victim-visa-delay-fight|access-date=2021-09-08|website=www.law360.com|language=en}} *''N. Carolina State Conf. of the NAACP v. Raymond'', 981 F.3d 295, 298 (4th Cir. 2020). After a federal district court enjoined North Carolina’s voter-ID law, Judge Richardson reversed the district because it had improperly flipped the burden of proof and failed to afford the General Assembly the required presumption of legislative good faith. Using the proper burden, the evidence in the record failed to meet the Challengers’ burden to show intentional race discrimination.{{Cite web|date=2020-12-03|title=4th Circuit: Federal judge was wrong to block voter ID|url=https://www.bladenjournal.com/news/34889/4th-circuit-federal-judge-was-wrong-to-block-voter-id|access-date=2021-09-08|website=Bladen Journal|language=en-US}}{{Cite web|last=Williams|first=Erika|date=December 2, 2020|title=Fourth Circuit Upholds North Carolina Voter ID Law|url=https://www.courthousenews.com/fourth-circuit-upholds-north-carolina-voter-id-law/|access-date=2021-10-05|website=www.courthousenews.com}} *''Mayor of Baltimore v. Azar'', 973 F.3d 258 (4th Cir. 2020). The Fourth Circuit on an initial en banc held that the Trump administration's rules barring programs receiving funds under Title X from making abortion referrals and requiring separation from abortion providers exceeded HHS’s authority and were arbitrary and capricious. Judge Richardson dissented, relying on the Supreme Court’s decision in Rust v. Sullivan that rejected similar challenges to similar regulations.{{Cite web|date=2020-10-30|title=Judicial Winning: Jay Richardson|url=https://www.nationalreview.com/bench-memos/judicial-winning-jay-richardson/|access-date=2021-09-08|website=National Review|language=en-US}}{{Cite news|last=Buchman|first=Brandi|date=September 3, 2020|title=En Banc Fourth Circuits Blocks Abortion Gag Rule in Maryland|work=Courthouse News Service|url=https://www.courthousenews.com/en-banc-fourth-circuits-blocks-abortion-gag-rule-in-maryland/|access-date=September 8, 2021}} The Supreme Court granted cert in the case but dismissed the case after the Biden administration indicated that it would change the challenged rules.{{Cite web|last=Lington|first=Jace|title=U.S. Supreme Court dismisses case challenging regulations related to abortion under Title X family planning program – Ballotpedia News|date=May 19, 2021 |url=https://news.ballotpedia.org/2021/05/19/u-s-supreme-court-dismisses-case-challenging-regulations-related-to-abortion-under-title-x-family-planning-program/|access-date=2021-09-08|language=en-US}} *''Maryland Shall Issue, Inc. v. Hogan'', 963 F.3d 356 (4th Cir. 2020). The Fourth Circuit held that Maryland's bump-stock ban that required citizens to forfeit their bump stocks or face up to three years in prison did not require just compensation under the Fifth Amendment's Takings Clause because the law required the bump stocks to be forfeited, not given to a third-party. In dissent, Judge Richardson explained that this was a distinction without a difference so compensation should be required.{{Cite web|last=Kunzelman|first=Michael|title=Federal appeals court upholds Maryland's ban on bump stocks|url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2020/06/29/federal-appeals-court-upholds-marylands-ban-on-bump-stocks/|access-date=2021-09-08|website=baltimoresun.com|date=June 29, 2020 }}{{Cite news|last=Williams|first=Erika|date=June 29, 2020|title=Fourth Circuit Upholds Maryland's Ban on 'Rapid Fire Trigger' Devices|work=Courthouse News|url=https://www.courthousenews.com/4th-circuit-upholds-maryland-ban-on-rapid-fire-trigger-devices/|access-date=October 5, 2021}} * ''United States v. Curry'', 965 F.3d 313 (4th Cir. 2020). An en banc court of the Fourth Circuit found that officers violated the Fourth Amendment when they stopped and asked a group of men to show that they were unarmed after hearing gunshots near their location. The Court held the stop was unconstitutional. Judge Richardson dissented, arguing that the exigent-circumstances doctrine justified the stop.{{Cite web|date=2020-07-16|title=En Banc Fourth Circuit Divides Sharply on Fourth Amendment 'Exigent Circumstances'|url=https://www.nationalreview.com/bench-memos/en-banc-fourth-circuit-divides-sharply-on-fourth-amendment-exigent-circumstances/|access-date=2021-09-08|website=National Review|language=en-US}}{{Cite web|first=Frank|last=Green|title=Full federal appeals court upholds Richmond judge in contentious search and seizure case|url=https://richmond.com/news/local/crime/full-federal-appeals-court-upholds-richmond-judge-in-contentious-search-and-seizure-case/article_1c1517f0-2a0d-5a20-9adc-0bc0a9b8b373.html|access-date=2021-09-08|website=Richmond Times-Dispatch|date=July 15, 2020 |language=en}} *''In re: Emerson Stevens'', 956 F.3d 229 (4th Cir. 2020). Judge Richardson authorized a successive federal habeas application to address newly discovered evidence. But he also focused on the executive's power and responsibility to address contested convictions. A year later, the Governor pardoned Mr. Stevens.{{Cite web|date=2021-08-16|title=Virginia Governor Pardons Man Wrongly Convicted of 1985 Northern Neck Murder {{!}} Washingtonian (DC)|url=https://washingtonian.com/2021/08/16/virginia-governor-pardons-man-wrongly-convicted-of-1985-northern-neck-murder/|access-date=2021-09-08|website=Washingtonian|language=en-US}} * ''United States v. Aigbekaen'', 943 F.3d 713 (4th Cir. 2019). The Fourth Circuit held a border search of the cell phone of a foreign national known to be engaged in interstate sex trafficking was unconstitutional (while affirming the conviction under the good-faith exception). The search was held unlawful because it lacked the requisite “nexus” to the purposes of the border-search doctrine. Judge Richardson concurred in the judgment, arguing that the majority’s newly-created “nexus” test was inconsistent with Supreme Court precedent.{{Cite thesis|last=Bode|first=Aaron|date=December 2020|title=Electronic Border Searches After Riley|url=https://www.hsdl.org/?view&did=850261|publisher=Naval Postgraduate School}} *''Guzman Chavez v. Hott'', 940 F.3d 867 (4th Cir. 2019). The Fourth Circuit found that the Immigration and Nationality Act required individualized bond hearings for detained immigrants awaiting withholding of removal proceedings. Judge Richardson dissented, finding that a different section governed and did not require individualized bond hearings. The Supreme Court reversed the Fourth Circuit in ''Johnson v. Guzman Chavez'', 141 S. Ct. 2271 (2021), citing Judge Richardson's dissent.{{Cite web|title=Johnson v. Guzman Chavez, 141 S. Ct. 2271 (2021)|url=https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/20pdf/19-897_c07d.pdf}} *''Casa De Maryland v. U.S. Dep't of Homeland Sec.'', 924 F.3d 684 (4th Cir. 2019). The Fourth Circuit held that the Trump administration's rescission of DACA was reviewable and arbitrary and capricious. Judge Richardson dissented, arguing that the rescission was part of the executive's discretion over enforcement and thus unreviewable under the APA. Judge Richardson also found that the rescission did not violate due process or equal protection.{{Cite news|last=Marimow|first=Ann|date=May 17, 2019|title=Appeals court finds Trump administration's move to end DACA 'arbitrary and capricious'|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/legal-issues/appeals-court-finds-trump-administrations-move-to-end-daca-arbitrary-and-capricious/2019/05/17/580d2c04-5ba1-11e9-842d-7d3ed7eb3957_story.html|access-date=September 8, 2021}} == Memberships == Richardson is a member of the [[Federalist Society]] and regularly speaks to the group. == See also == * [[List of law clerks for the chief justice of the United States]] == References == {{Reflist}} == External links == * {{FJC Bio|nid=5090921}} * {{Ballotpedia|Julius_Richardson|Julius Richardson}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Dennis Shedd]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit]]}}|years=2018–present}} {{s-inc}} {{s-end}} {{United States courts of appeals judges}} {{Authority control}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Richardson, Julius N.}} [[Category:1976 births]] [[Category:Living people]] [[Category:21st-century American lawyers]] [[Category:Assistant United States attorneys]] [[Category:Judges of the United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit]] [[Category:Law clerks of the Supreme Court of the United States]] [[Category:People from Columbia, South Carolina]] [[Category:South Carolina lawyers]] [[Category:United States court of appeals judges appointed by Donald Trump]] [[Category:University of Chicago Law School alumni]] [[Category:Vanderbilt University alumni]]

Kara Farnandez Stoll:
{{Short description|American judge (born 1968)}} {{Infobox officeholder | name = Kara Farnandez Stoll | image = Judge-Farnandez-Stoll-Photo.jpg | caption = Farnandez Stoll in 2015 | office = Judge of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit]] | appointer = [[Barack Obama]] | term_start = July 8, 2015 | term_end = | predecessor = [[Randall Ray Rader]] | successor = | birth_name = Kara Ann Farnandez | birth_date = {{birth year and age|1968|11}} | birth_place = [[Wilmington, Delaware]], U.S. | death_date = | death_place = | education = [[Michigan State University]] ([[Bachelor of Science|BS]])
[[Georgetown University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Kara Ann Farnandez Stoll''' (born November 1968) is a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit]]. ==Biography== ===Early life and education=== Farnandez Stoll received a [[Bachelor of Science in Electrical Engineering]] degree, in 1991, from [[Michigan State University]]. She worked as a [[patent examiner]] at the [[United States Patent and Trademark Office]] from 1991 to 1997. She received a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1997, from [[Georgetown University Law Center]]. From 1997 to 1998, she served as a [[law clerk]] to Judge [[Alvin Anthony Schall]] of the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/11/12/president-obama-nominates-two-serve-united-states-courts-appeals|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Obama Nominates Two to Serve on the United States Courts of Appeals|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=12 November 2014}} ===Legal career=== From 1998 to 2015, she worked at the law firm of [[Finnegan, Henderson, Farabow, Garrett & Dunner]] and was a partner at that firm. Her practice focused on patent litigation, primarily in the consumer electronics, computers, software and medical device industries. She represented clients at both the trial and appellate levels and served as lead counsel on a number of cases before the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit. Among her prominent cases, she represented [[Akamai]] in en banc rehearing on issues of [[divided infringement]] in ''Akamai Technologies, Inc. v. Limelight Networks, Inc.'' (Fed. Cir.) and she successfully represented [[i4i]] in the largest ($290 million) patent verdict sustained on appeal in ''i4i Ltd. v. Microsoft'' (Fed. Cir.). In 2013, she was recognized as a Washington, D.C. "Super Lawyer" in Intellectual Property Litigation by the ''Super Lawyers Magazine''.{{Cite web|title=Kara Farnandez Stoll {{!}} Attorneys {{!}} Finnegan |url=http://www.finnegan.com/karastoll |date=2015-04-25 |access-date=2016-02-22 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150425215811/http://www.finnegan.com/karastoll |archive-date=April 25, 2015 }} She served as an adjunct professor at [[Howard University School of Law]], from 2004 to 2008, and has served as a Distinguished Adjunct Professor at [[George Mason University Law School]], from 2008 to 2015. From 2013 to 2015, she served as co-chair of the Rules Committee of the [[Federal Circuit Bar Association]] and served as Vice Chair of that committee, from 2012 to 2013. ==Federal Circuit service== On November 12, 2014, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Farnandez Stoll to serve as a United States Circuit Judge of the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, to the seat vacated by Judge [[Randall Ray Rader]], who retired on June 30, 2014.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/11/12/presidential-nominations-sent-senate|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=12 November 2014}} On December 16, 2014, her nomination was returned to the President due to the [[sine die]] adjournment of the Senate. On January 7, 2015, President Obama renominated her to the same position.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2015/01/07/presidential-nominations-sent-senate|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=7 January 2015}} She received a hearing on her nomination on March 11, 2015.{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/nominations|title=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|date=11 March 2015 }} On April 23, 2015, her nomination was reported out of committee by a [[voice vote]].{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%20-%20April%2023,%202015.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – April 23, 2015}} On July 7, 2015, the [[United States Senate|Senate]] confirmed her by a 95–0 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=114&session=1&vote=00221|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Kara Farnandez Stoll, of Virginia, to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the Federal Circuit)}} She received her judicial commission on July 8, 2015.{{cite web|url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/stoll-kara-farnandez|title=Stoll, Kara Farnandez – Federal Judicial Center|website=www.fjc.gov}} She took the oath of office on July 17, 2015.{{cite web|url=http://www.cafc.uscourts.gov/judges/kara-farnandez-stoll-circuit-judge|title=KARA FARNANDEZ STOLL, CIRCUIT JUDGE – US Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit}} ==Notable opinions== Farnandez Stoll authored ''Advanced Steel Recovery v. X-Body Equipment'', 808 F.3d 1313 (Fed. Cir. 2015), which is highly cited for elaborating on the doctrine of equivalents, to include requiring the infringing patented product to "perform in substantially the same way as the claimed invention."{{Cite web|title = ADVANCED STEEL RECOVERY, LLC v. X-BODY EQUIPMENT, INC. [OPINION] {{!}} US Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit|url = http://www.cafc.uscourts.gov/node/19719|website = www.cafc.uscourts.gov|access-date = 2016-02-23|archive-date = 2016-03-04|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160304010413/http://www.cafc.uscourts.gov/node/19719|url-status = dead}} She authored ''Data Engine Techs. LLC v. Google LLC'', 906 F.3d 999 (Fed. Cir. 2018), which affirmed-in-part and reversed-in-part a district court’s holding that claims of several patents are ineligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, explaining that, when read as a whole, certain of the claims are directed to a specific improved method for navigating through three-dimensional electronic spreadsheets and thus are directed to eligible subject matter, while other claims reciting methods for tracking changes to data in spreadsheets are directed to the abstract idea of collecting, recognizing, and storing changed information.{{Cite web |title=Data Engine Techs. LLC v. Google LLC |url=https://www.cafc.uscourts.gov/opinions-orders/17-1135.opinion.10-9-2018.pdf |url-status=live |access-date=2026-04-13 |website=www.cafc.uscourts.gov}} She authored ''University of Southern Floridia Research Foundation, Inc. v. Fujifilm Medical Systems U.S.A., Inc.'', 19 F.4th 1315 (Fed. Cir. 2021), which clarified that under 35 U.S.C. § 281, if a license does not explicitly transfer the right to sue to the licensee, that licensee may not be considered the “patentee” and thus may not have the right to sue on its own without joining the patent owner to a lawsuit.{{Cite web |title=University of Southern Floridia Research Foundation, Inc. v. Fujifilm Medical Systems U.S.A., Inc. |url=https://www.cafc.uscourts.gov/opinions-orders/20-1872.OPINION.10-22-2021_1869580.pdf |url-status=live |access-date=2026-04-13 |website=www.cafc.uscourts.gov}} She authored the majority opinion in ''LKQ Corp. v. GM Glob. Tech. Operations LLC'', 102 F.4th 1280 (Fed. Cir. 2024) (en banc), which changed the obviousness standard for design patents by overruling the prior test and replacing it with the obviousness inquiry used for utility patents.{{Cite web|title = LKQ Corp. v. GM Glob. Tech. '''Karen LeCraft Henderson''' (born July 11, 1944) is an American lawyer and jurist serving since 1990 as a [[United States federal judge|U.S. circuit judge]] on the [[United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit|U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit]]. She was previously a district judge on the [[United States District Court for the District of South Carolina|U.S. District Court for the District of South Carolina]] from 1986 to 1990.

==Early life and education==
Henderson was born and raised in [[Oberlin, Ohio]]. She received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[Duke University]] in 1966 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of North Carolina School of Law]] in 1969. 

==Career==
Following law school, Henderson entered private practice in [[Chapel Hill, North Carolina]]. From 1973 to 1983, she was with the Office of the [[South Carolina Attorney General]], ultimately in the position of deputy attorney general. In 1983, she returned to private practice as a member of the firm of Sinkler, Gibbs & Simons of Charleston and Columbia, South Carolina.<ref name="fjc.gov">{{FJC Bio|nid=1382051|inline=yes}}</ref>

On June 3, 1986, Henderson was nominated by President [[Ronald Reagan]] to a seat on the [[U.S. District Court for the District of South Carolina]] vacated by Judge [[William Walter Wilkins]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=June 13, 1986 |title=Pres. Nom. 1140 |url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/99th-congress/1140 |publisher=99th Cong. (1986)}}</ref> She was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on June 13, 1986, and received her commission on June 16, 1986. Her service terminated on July 11, 1990, due to her elevation to the court of appeals.<ref name="fjc.gov" />

On May 8, 1990, President [[George H. W. Bush]] nominated Henderson to a seat on the [[U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit]] that had been vacated by the resignation of [[Kenneth Starr]] to become [[Solicitor General of the United States]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=June 29, 1990 |title=Pres. Nom. 1239 |url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/101st-congress/1239 |publisher=101st Cong. (1990)}}</ref> The Senate confirmed Henderson on June 28, 1990, by [[unanimous consent]], and she received her commission on July 5, 1990.<ref name="fjc.gov" />

===Notable cases and opinions===
===Second Amendment===
In ''[[Parker v. District of Columbia]]'' (2007) Henderson authored a dissent in which she wrote "the right of the people to keep and bear arms relates to those Militia whose continued vitality is required to safeguard the individual States."<ref>{{Cite web |title=D.C.'s Ban On Handguns In Homes Is Thrown Out |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2007/03/09/AR2007030902416_pf.html |website=www.washingtonpost.com}}</ref> She also wrote that "the Constitution, case law and applicable statutes all establish that the District is not a state within the meaning of the Second Amendment".<ref>[https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2007/03/28/AR2007032801879.html The Seat Congress Can't Offer].</ref>

===National security===
In ''[[Rasul v. Rumsfeld|Rasul v. Myers]]'' (2008), Henderson wrote for the majority when it found that British detainees at the [[Guantanamo Bay detention camp]] could not sue the government under the [[Alien Tort Statute]], the [[Geneva Conventions]], and the [[Religious Freedom Restoration Act]] for alleged torture, abuse, and denial of religious free expression.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Fassbender |first=B. |date=May 1, 2008 |title=Can Victims Sue State Officials for Torture?: Reflections on Rasul v. Myers from the Perspective of International Law |journal=[[Journal of International Criminal Justice]] |volume=6 |issue=2 |pages=347–369 |doi=10.1093/jicj/mqn009 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite court|litigants=Rasul v. Myers|vol=512|reporter=F. 3d|opinion=644|court=D.C. Cir.|date=2008|url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16980182709081911955}}</ref> The case was reportedly the first federal appeals court decision involving the treatment of terrorism suspects in the wake of the [[September 11 attacks]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Denniston |first=Lyle |date=January 11, 2008 |title=Detainees barred from challenging torture, abuse |language=en |work=[[SCOTUSblog]] |url=https://www.scotusblog.com/2008/01/detainees-barred-from-challenging-torture-abuse/ |access-date=February 29, 2020}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Vicini |first=James |date=January 11, 2008 |title=U.S. appeals court dismisses Guantanamo torture suit |language=en |work=[[Reuters]] |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-guantanamo-ruling/u-s-appeals-court-dismisses-guantanamo-torture-suit-idUSN1129837820080111 |access-date=February 29, 2020}}</ref>

In March 2017, Henderson found that the [[Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act]] prevented an Ethiopian dissident living with [[asylum in the United States]] from suing the Ethiopian government for infecting his home computer with [[FinSpy]] spyware and then surveilling him in Maryland.<ref>{{Bluebook journal |first=|last=Note| title=Recent Case: D.C. Circuit Finds Ethiopia Immune in Hacking Suit| volume=131 | journal=[[Harvard Law Review|Harv. L. Rev.]] | page=1179 | url=https://harvardlawreview.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/1179-1186_Online.pdf| year=2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite court |litigants=Doe v. Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia|vol=851 |reporter=F.3d |opinion=7|court=D.C. Cir.|date=2017|url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=12016984034191000630}}</ref>

In August 2018, Henderson wrote for the unanimous panel when it again rejected Guantanamo Bay detainee [[Moath Hamza Ahmed al Alawi]]'s petition for [[habeas corpus]], reasoned that the [[Authorization for Use of Military Force of 2001]] had not expired, that the [[National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2012]] had further authorized detentions, and that the international [[law of war]] permitted detention of [[enemy combatants]] as long as "active combat" continued.<ref>{{Bluebook journal |first=|last=Note|title=Recent Case: D.C. Circuit Holds the Government's Authority Has Not Unraveled|volume=132 |journal=[[Harvard Law Review|Harv. L. Rev.]] | page=1542 | url=https://harvardlawreview.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/1542-1549_Online.pdf| year=2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite court|litigants=Al-Alwi v. Trump|vol=901|reporter=F3d|opinion=294|court=D.C. Cir.|date=2018|url= https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=6967637316143379488 }}</ref>

===Immigration===

In October 2017, Henderson dissented in the ''en banc''-stage of ''[[Azar v. Garza]]'', arguing that an undocumented immigrant is not a "person" under the [[United States Constitution]] and so does not have rights under the [[Due Process Clause]].<ref>{{Bluebook journal |first=|last=Note| title=Recent Case: En Banc D.C. Circuit Upholds Order Requiring HHS to Allow an Undocumented Minor to Have an Abortion | volume=131 | journal=[[Harvard Law Review|Harv. L. Rev.]] | page=1812 | url=https://harvardlawreview.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/1812-1819_Online.pdf| year=2018}}</ref>{{rp|1815}}

===Cases involving Donald Trump===

In November 2019, Henderson indicated she wanted to revisit a 3-panel ruling allowing Congress to access [[Tax returns of Donald Trump|Trump's tax records]]. The DC Circuit rejected her view by an 8–3 vote. She was the only judge to dissent who was not appointed by Trump.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Trump's tax records can be sought by Congress, appeals court orders |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/legal-issues/congress-can-seek-eight-years-of-trumps-tax-records-appeals-court-rules/2019/11/13/b4fc8002-fc07-11e9-8906-ab6b60de9124_story.html}}</ref>

In February 2020, Henderson joined the opinion of Circuit Judge [[Thomas B. Griffith]] when the majority held that the [[United States House Committee on the Judiciary]] could not enforce a [[subpoena]] upon President Trump's former White House Counsel, [[Don McGahn]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=House Judiciary Committee v. McGahn |url=https://www.cadc.uscourts.gov/internet/opinions.nsf/29F7900862BA6CD68525851C00784758/$file/19-5331-1831001.pdf |access-date=February 28, 2020 |website=www.cadc.uscourts.gov |archive-date=February 29, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200229233539/https://www.cadc.uscourts.gov/internet/opinions.nsf/29F7900862BA6CD68525851C00784758/$file/19-5331-1831001.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> Henderson wrote a concurrence arguing that the House did not have [[standing (law)|standing to sue]] here, while Circuit Judge [[Judith W. Rogers]] wrote a dissent.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Savage |first=Charlie |author-link=Charlie Savage (author) |date=February 29, 2020 |title=Court Rules Congress Cannot Sue to Force Executive Branch Officials to Testify |page=A1 |work=[[The New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/02/28/us/mcgahn-subpoena-trump.html |access-date=February 29, 2020}}</ref> The full D.C. Circuit rejected this position on August 8, 2020.<ref>{{Cite web |title=En Banc DC Circuit Rules for House's Power to Sue Over Don McGahn Subpoena {{!}} Law.com |url=https://www.law.com/2020/08/07/en-banc-dc-circuit-rules-for-houses-power-to-sue-over-don-mcgahn-subpoena/}}</ref>

In June 2020, Henderson joined the opinion of fellow Circuit Judge [[Neomi Rao]] issuing a [[Mandamus|writ of mandamus]] ordering a district court judge to grant a motion brought by federal prosecutors asking that the criminal charges against [[Michael Flynn]] be dismissed.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Appeals court orders judge to dismiss Michael Flynn case – The Washington Post |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/legal-issues/appeals-court-orders-judge-to-dismiss-criminal-case-against-michael-flynn/2020/06/24/7f2caba4-b0c1-11ea-8758-bfd1d045525a_story.html}}</ref> The district judge appealed<ref>{{Cite web |title=A key federal appeals court will reexamine case on Michael Flynn's guilty plea |url=https://www.businessinsider.com/michael-flynn-loses-washington-dc-circuit-court-of-appeals-2020-7 |website=[[Business Insider]]}}</ref> and after hearing the case ''en banc'', the appeals court on August 31, 2020, ruled 8–2 against issuing the writ of mandamus, with Rao and Henderson joining each other's dissents.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Michael Flynn case does not have to be immediately dismissed, appeals court rules |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/legal-issues/appeals-court-michael-flynn/2020/08/31/24ce93f0-e0b1-11ea-b69b-64f7b0477ed4_story.html}}</ref>

On November 30, 2021, Henderson authored a unanimous ruling requiring the DOJ hand over more of the Mueller report, citing the [[Freedom of Information Act (United States)|Freedom of Information Act]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=November 30, 2021 |title=Appeals court orders release of more from Mueller report |url=https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/politics/appeals-court-orders-release-of-more-from-mueller-report/ar-AARjAGJ |access-date=December 5, 2021 |website=MSN}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=November 30, 2021 |title=Electronic Privacy Information Center, Appellee, Jason Leopold and Buzzfeed, Inc., Appellants v. United States Department of Justice, et al., Appellees |url=https://www.cadc.uscourts.gov/internet/opinions.nsf/8892DBE6CD1083448525879D00535C80/$file/20-5364-1924504.pdf |access-date=December 5, 2021 |website=cadc.uscourts.gov}}</ref>

==Criticism of hiring practices==

On May 16, 2022, the ''Washington Post'' published an article reporting that Henderson "hires only men among the three or four people she selects each year for clerkships." Specifically, the article stated that of "more than 70 clerks" Henderson hired since 1990, all but one were men. Henderson responded in a statement: "I give equal treatment and consideration to all applicants and hire law clerks based only on their credentials. To the extent any contrary impression exists, I regret that such impression exists and I will use my best efforts to address it."<ref>{{Cite news |title=Judges accused of sex discrimination, bullying, internal survey shows – The Washington Post |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2022/05/16/judges-accused-discrimination-bullying/}}</ref>

[[Harvard University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Karen Mary Nelson Moore''' ([[née]] '''Nelson'''; born 1948){{Cite book |last=Judiciary |first=United States Congress Senate Committee on the |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Bto1hy9MjBcC&pg=PA253 |title=Confirmation Hearings on Federal Appointments: Hearings Before the Committee on the Judiciary, United States Senate, One Hundred Fourth Congress, First Session, on Confirmation of Appointees to the Federal Judiciary |date=1996 |publisher=U.S. Government Printing Office |pages=253 |language=en}} is an American attorney and jurist serving as a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit]]. Her chambers are in [[Cleveland, Ohio]]. ==Education== Moore received her [[Bachelor of Arts|Artium Baccalaureus]] from [[Radcliffe College]] in 1970, graduating [[Phi Beta Kappa]] and [[magna cum laude]].{{Cite journal |last=Entin |first=Jonathan |date=August 2016 |title=Hon. Karen Nelson Moore: U.S. Circuit Judge for the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals |journal=[[The Federal Lawyer]] |pages=57–59}} She received her [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Harvard Law School]], also ''magna cum laude'', in 1973.{{cite web|url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/moore-karen-nelson|title=Moore, Karen Nelson - Federal Judicial Center|website=www.fjc.gov}}[http://www.ibiblio.org/pub/archives/whitehouse-papers/1994/Sep/1994-09-14-President-Nominates-Eight-Federal-Judges President Names Eight to Federal Bench], ''The White House: Office of the Press Secretary'' (September 14, 1994). During her time at Harvard, Moore served as an editor for the Harvard Law Review, during which time she was the Law Review's only female member.{{Cite web |title=Vol. 85, No. 1, Nov., 1971 of Harvard Law Review on JSTOR |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/i257443 |access-date=2025-03-11 |website=www.jstor.org |language=en}}{{Cite web |title=Vol. 86, No. 1, Nov., 1972 of Harvard Law Review on JSTOR |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/i257452 |access-date=2025-03-11 |website=www.jstor.org |language=en}} Moore also served as an instructor for the International Tax Law Program at [[Harvard Law School]] from 1972 to 1973. == Career == Moore [[Law clerk|clerked]] for Judge [[Malcolm Richard Wilkey]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit]] from 1973 to 1974 and was his first female law clerk. She then clerked for Justice [[Harry Blackmun]] of the [[United States Supreme Court]] during the October 1974 term. Moore was one of the first women to clerk on the Supreme Court and Blackmun's first female clerk.{{Cite journal |last=Moore |first=Karen |date=1998-01-01 |title=Justice Harry A. Blackmun: The Model Judge |url=https://repository.uclawsf.edu/hastings_constitutional_law_quaterly/vol26/iss1/1/ |journal=UC Law Constitutional Quarterly |volume=26 |issue=1 |pages=5 |issn=0094-5617}} From 1975 to 1977, Moore was an associate at [[Jones Day]] in Cleveland. From 1977 to 1995, she was a faculty member at [[Case Western Reserve University|Case Western Reserve University Law School]]. Moore was the school's first tenured female professor and the first woman to hold an endowed chair. She won awards for her teaching at Case Western, including its inaugural Teacher of the Year Award. She taught courses in civil procedure, federal income tax, complex litigation, conflict of laws, and International law. Moore was a visiting professor at [[Harvard Law School]] from 1990 to 1991. She has also served as director and vice president of the [[Harvard Alumni Association]] and as a presiding judge for the [[Ames Moot Court Competition]].{{Cite web |title=Ames Moot Court Competition Archive |url=https://hls.harvard.edu/ames-moot-court/ames-moot-court-competition-archive/ |access-date=2025-03-11 |website=Harvard Law School |language=en-us}} Most recently, Moore served a six-year term for Harvard's Board of Overseers, and was elected to serve as the President of the Overseers during the 2015–16 academic year.{{Cite web|url=https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2015/03/karen-moore-to-lead-board-of-overseers/|title = Karen Moore to lead Board of Overseers|date = 26 March 2015}} === Federal judicial service === On January 24, 1995, President [[Bill Clinton]] nominated Moore to a seat on the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit]] vacated by Judge [[Robert B. Krupansky]]. On March 24, 1995, the [[United States Senate]] confirmed her by [[voice vote]], and she received her commission the same day. Moore has been recognized as an academic feeder judge, with several of her former clerks on the faculty at U.S. law schools.{{Cite web |last=Wasserman |first=Howard M. |date=2021-04-12 |title=Do lawyers need clerkships to become law professors? |url=https://judicature.duke.edu/articles/academic-feeder-judges-are-clerkships-the-key-to-academia/ |access-date=2025-03-11 |website=judicature.duke.edu |language=en-US}} She was also considered a contender for nomination to the [[Supreme Court of the United States|United States Supreme Court]] in the early 2000s.{{Cite journal |first1=Stephen J. |last1 = Choi | first2 = G.
