{{Short description|American judge (born 1975)}} {{Family name hatnote|Lee|lang=Korean}} {{Use mdy dates|date=October 2018}} {{Infobox judge | name = Kenneth Lee | native_name = {{small|{{nobold|이기열}}}} | image = KennethKLee.jpg | office = Judge of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]] | appointer = [[Donald Trump]] | term_start = June 12, 2019 | term_end = | predecessor = [[Stephen Reinhardt]] | successor = | birth_name = Lee Kiyul | birth_date = {{nowrap|{{birth date and age|1975|8|30}}}} | birth_place = [[Seoul]], [[South Korea]] | death_date = | death_place = | education = [[Cornell University]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|BA]])
[[Harvard University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) | module = {{Infobox Korean name/auto | child = yes | hangul = %이기열 | hanja = 李氣熱}} }} '''Kenneth Kiyul Lee''' ({{Korean|이기열}};{{cite web|url=https://koreatimes.net/ArticleViewer/Article/118992|title=美 연방항소법원에 또 한인판사|work=Korea Times|date=May 17, 2019|access-date=May 26, 2020|language=ko}} born August 30, 1975){{Cite web |url=https://vettingroom.org/2019/05/15/kenneth-lee/ |title=Kenneth Lee – Nominee to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit |last=Voruganti |first=Harsh |date=2019-05-15 |website=The Vetting Room |language=en |access-date=2019-10-18}} is a South Korean-born American lawyer who serves as a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]]. == Early life and education == Lee was born in 1975 in [[Seoul]], [[South Korea]]. Lee's family immigrated to the United States when he was four years old, following the [[Coup d'état of December Twelfth|1979 military coup]] in South Korea.{{cite web |last1=Severino |first1=Carrie Campbell |title=Smears Against Judicial Nominees Continue |url=https://www.nationalreview.com/bench-memos/senate-democrats-smear-judicial-nominees-ken-lee/ |website=National Review |access-date=May 26, 2020 |date=March 4, 2019}} Lee grew up in the [[Koreatown, Los Angeles|Koreatown]] neighborhood of [[Los Angeles]].{{cite web |last1=Mullich |first1=Joe |title=A quintessential American story |url=https://jenner.com/system/assets/assets/8789/original/Ken_20Lee_20Super_20Lawyers_20Cover_206_202015.pdf |website=Super Lawyers Magazine |access-date=May 27, 2020 |date=2015 |via=Jenner & Block |archive-date=September 6, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180906015546/https://jenner.com/system/assets/assets/8789/original/Ken_20Lee_20Super_20Lawyers_20Cover_206_202015.pdf |url-status=dead }} His father operated a [[spray paint]] equipment repair shop, and his mother was a [[pharmacist]] and [[acupuncturist]]. Neither of Lee’s parents spoke [[English language|English]], but they insisted that he understand the language and did not allow him to attend a Korean church for that reason. After high school, Lee studied [[government]] at [[Cornell University]], where he wrote for the conservative and libertarian campus newspaper ''[[The Cornell Review]]''. He graduated in 1997 with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree ''[[Latin honors#United States|summa cum laude]]'' and was elected to [[Phi Beta Kappa]]. Lee then attended [[Harvard Law School]], graduating in 2000 with a [[Juris Doctor]] ''magna cum laude''.{{cite web |title=Kenneth K. Lee – Senate Judiciary Committee Questionnaire |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Kenneth%20Lee%20SJQ%20-%20PUBLIC.pdf}}{{cite web|url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/lee-kenneth-kiyul|title=Lee, Kenneth Kiyul|publisher=Federal Judicial Center|access-date=May 27, 2020}} {{PD-notice}} ==Early legal career== After graduating from law school, Lee served as a [[law clerk]] to Judge [[Emilio M. Garza]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]] from 2000 to 2001. Lee then worked as an [[associate lawyer|associate]] at [[New York City]] law firm [[Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz]] from 2001 to 2006. At Wachtell, following the [[September 11 attacks]], Lee served as second chair, deposed witnesses, and wrote briefs as part of the legal team representing real estate mogul [[Larry Silverstein]], whose 99-year lease of the [[World Trade Center (1973–2001)|World Trade Center]] provided a $3.5 billion insurance policy for an act of [[terrorism]]. The court ruled that the separate plane crashes in the World Trade Center represented 1.4 occurrences of terrorism. In 2005, Lee served as a [[special counsel]] on the [[United States Senate Judiciary Committee]]. From 2006 to 2009, Lee was Associate Counsel and Special Assistant to [[President of the United States|President]] [[George W. Bush]]. After Bush left office in 2009, Lee joined the [[Los Angeles]] office of the law firm [[Jenner & Block]] as a [[law firm partner|partner]].{{cite web |url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-eighteenth-wave-judicial-nominees-eighteenth-wave-united-states-attorney-nominees-thirteenth-wave-united-states-marshal-nominees/ |title=President Donald J. Trump Announces Eighteenth Wave of Judicial Nominees, Eighteenth Wave of United States Attorney Nominees, and Thirteenth Wave of United States Marshal Nominees |date=October 10, 2018 |via=[[NARA|National Archives]] |work=[[whitehouse.gov]] |access-date=October 10, 2018 }} {{PD-notice}} From 2010 to 2011, Lee served as an [[adjunct professor|adjunct faculty]] member at [[Pepperdine University School of Law]]. Lee has litigated consumer [[class action lawsuit]]s across the United States in the [[regulation of the food industry|food]], [[technology law|technology]], and [[health care law|health care]] sectors. He has argued appeals before a number of federal circuit courts. In his [[pro bono]] practice, Lee has represented a number of [[indigent]] and [[prisoners|incarcerated individuals]]. He is a member of the Food Law Committee of the Litigation Section of the [[State Bar of California]].{{cite web|last=Severino |first=Carrie Campbell |url=https://www.nationalreview.com/bench-memos/who-is-ken-lee/ |title=Who is Ken Lee? |work=National Review |date=2018-10-10 |access-date=2019-02-18}} In 2018, Lee was named one of the "Most Influential Minority Attorneys" by the ''[[Los Angeles Business Journal]].''{{cite web |title=Most Influential Minority Attorneys: Kenneth K. Lee |date=January 25, 2018 |url=http://labusinessjournal.com/news/2018/jan/25/most-influential-minority-attorneys-kenneth-k-lee/ |publisher=Los Angeles Business Journal |access-date=18 February 2019}} == Federal judicial service == [[File:Kenneth Kiyul Lee at confirmation hearing (cropped).jpg|thumb|Lee at his confirmation hearing on March 13, 2019]] On October 10, 2018, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to nominate Lee to serve as a United States Circuit Judge of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]]. Both California Senators [[Dianne Feinstein]] and [[Kamala Harris]] announced their opposition to his nomination.{{cite web |url=http://www.latimes.com/politics/la-na-pol-9th-circuit-nominees-20181011-story.html |title=California senators will try to block White House judicial nominees for the 9th Circuit - Los Angeles Times |last=Wire |first=Sarah D. |date=2018-10-11 |website=[[Los Angeles Times]] |access-date=2018-10-16}} On November 13, 2018, his nomination was sent to the Senate. President Trump nominated Lee to the seat vacated by Judge [[Stephen Reinhardt]], who died on March 29, 2018.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/twenty-six-nominations-sent-senate/ "Twenty Six Nominations Sent to the Senate", White House, November 13, 2018] On January 3, 2019, his nomination was returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]]. On January 30, 2019, President Trump indicated that he would renominate Lee to a Ninth Circuit vacancy.{{cite web |url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-intent-nominate-judicial-nominees-2/ |title=President Donald J. Trump Announces Intent to Nominate Judicial Nominees |date=2019-01-30 |language=en-US |via=[[NARA|National Archives]] |work=[[whitehouse.gov]] |access-date=2019-01-31}} On February 6, 2019, his nomination was sent to the Senate.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/twelve-nominations-sent-senate/ "Twelve Nominations Sent to the Senate", The White House, February 6, 2019] On March 13, 2019, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/nominations-hearing United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Nominations for March 13, 2019] During the hearing, he was questioned about college writings covering [[HIV/AIDS|AIDS]], [[political correctness]], and feminism. He apologized for some of the writings, saying he regretted them and was embarrassed by them.{{cite news |last1=Levine |first1=Marianne |title=Trump judicial pick expresses regret for college writings |url=https://www.politico.com/story/2019/03/13/trump-judicial-pick-college-writings-1220259 |access-date=March 15, 2019 |publisher=Politico |date=March 13, 2019}} ''[[The Wall Street Journal]]'' editorial board responded to the questioning about Lee's college writings: "...what Mr. Lee wrote in college is of no relevance to how he’d behave as a jurist. ... What liberals really don’t like is that Mr. Lee dissented from progressive doctrines on racial preferences, among other issues."{{cite web |title=Kenneth Kiyul Lee's White Privilege |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/kenneth-kiyul-lees-white-privilege-11551741146 |website=The Wall Street Journal |access-date=May 27, 2020 |date=March 4, 2019|archive-url=https://archive.today/20200101115456/https://www.wsj.com/articles/kenneth-kiyul-lees-white-privilege-11551741146|archive-date=January 1, 2020|url-status=dead}} On April 4, 2019, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 12–10 vote.[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/04.04.2019%20Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting.pdf Results of Executive Business Meeting – April 4, 2019, Senate Judiciary Committee] On May 14, 2019, the Senate invoked [[cloture]] on his nomination by a 50–45 vote.[https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=1&vote=00109 On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Kenneth Kiyul Lee to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the Ninth Circuit), United States Senate, May 14, 2019] On May 15, 2019, his nomination was confirmed by a 52–45 vote.[https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=1&vote=00110 On the Nomination (Confirmation Kenneth Kiyul Lee, of California, to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the Ninth Circuit), United States Senate, May 15, 2019] He received his judicial commission on June 12, 2019.{{FJC Bio|nid=6453086|inline=yes}} Lee is the nation's first Article III judge who was born in the Republic of Korea and the second Korean American to serve on the Ninth Circuit.{{cite news |last1=Tae-hee |first1=Lee |title=Korean-American judges gaining presence in US |url=http://www.koreaherald.com/view.php?ud=20181211000462 |access-date=18 February 2019 |publisher=The Korea Herald |date=December 11, 2018}}[http://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/ce9/2019/05/16/Lee_Confirmed.pdf "Senate Confirms L.A. Attorney Kenneth Kiyul Lee to Seat on Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals", United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, May 15, 2019] In August 2020, Lee was part of a three-judge panel who held that California's "[[large capacity magazine]] ban" was unconstitutional.{{Cite web|last=Romo|first=Vanessa|date=August 14, 2020|title=Federal Appeals Court Throws Out California Ban On Large-Capacity Gun Magazines|url=https://www.npr.org/2020/08/14/902676422/federal-appeals-court-throws-out-california-ban-on-large-capacity-gun-magazines|access-date=2020-08-19|website=NPR.org|language=en}}{{Cite web|date=August 14, 2020|title=Federal court throws out California's ban on high-capacity ammunition magazines|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/nation/2020/08/14/californias-ban-high-capacity-ammunition-magazines-tossed-court/5585205002/|access-date=2020-08-19|website=USA TODAY|publisher=Associated Press|language=en-US}} == Memberships == Lee is listed as an expert for the [[Federalist Society]] and has been a speaker and panelist on the topics of Food & Drug Law, [[Class action|Class Action]] lawsuits, and the Constitutionality of the [[Affordable Care Act]]. == See also == * [[List of Asian American jurists]] == References == {{Reflist}} == External links == * {{FJC Bio|nid=6453086}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Stephen Reinhardt]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]]}}|years=2019–present}} {{s-inc}} {{s-end}} {{United States courts of appeals judges}} {{Authority control}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Lee, Kenneth Kiyul}} [[Category:1975 births]] [[Category:Living people]] [[Category:21st-century American lawyers]] [[Category:American academics of Korean descent]] [[Category:American jurists of Korean descent]] [[Category:Asian conservatism in the United States]] [[Category:California Republicans]] [[Category:Cornell University alumni]] [[Category:George W. [[Harvard University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Kevin Christopher Newsom''' (born September 22, 1972){{cite web|title=AFJ Nominee Report: Kevin Newsom|url=https://www.afj.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/AFJ-Newsom-Report.pdf|publisher=Alliance for Justice|access-date=December 2, 2017|archive-date=December 2, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171202203404/https://www.afj.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/AFJ-Newsom-Report.pdf|url-status=dead}} is an American attorney and jurist serving as a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit]]. == Early life and education == Kevin Newsom was born in [[Birmingham, Alabama]], to Susan and Michael Alan Newsom. His father was an attorney. Newsom attended [[Homewood High School]] in Birmingham. Both of his parents had issues with [[alcoholism]].{{Cite web |date=2018-02-21 |title=Finding Your Voice: A Sitdown with Judge Newsom |url=https://www.lawweekly.org/features/2018/2/21/finding-your-voice-a-sitdown-with-judge-newsom |access-date=2024-04-14 |website=[[Virginia Law Weekly]] |language=en-US}} In 1994, Newsom received a [[Bachelor of Arts]], ''[[summa cum laude]]'', from [[Samford University]], graduating first in his class. In 1997, he graduated from [[Harvard Law School]] with a [[Juris Doctor]], ''[[magna cum laude]]'', where he was an articles editor of the ''[[Harvard Law Review]]''.{{cite web|title=Kevin C. Newsom|url=https://www.bradley.com/people/n/newsom-kevin-c|publisher=[[Bradley Arant Boult Cummings]] LLP|access-date=May 8, 2017|archive-date=May 8, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170508080404/https://www.bradley.com/people/n/newsom-kevin-c|url-status=dead}} == Career == After graduation, Newsom served as a [[law clerk]] to Judge [[Diarmuid O'Scannlain]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]] from 1997 to 1998. He then clerked for Justice [[David Souter]] of the [[Supreme Court of the United States]] from 1998 to 1999.{{cite book|last1=Peppers|first1=Todd C.|title=Courtiers of the Marble Palace|date=2006|publisher=Stanford University Press|location=Palo Alto, CA|isbn=0804753822|page=231|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NxiMWr730EcC&q=Kevin+C.+Newsom&pg=PA231}} Between and after his clerkships, he worked for [[Covington & Burling]] in [[Washington, D.C.]] In December 2003, he was appointed the State of Alabama's second [[Solicitor General]], replacing Nathan A. Forrester, and served for three and a half years under state [[Attorney General of Alabama|Attorneys General]] [[William H. Pryor Jr.]] and [[Troy King]].{{cite web|last1=Lat|first1=David|author-link1=David Lat|title=Articles on Kevin Newsom|url=http://abovethelaw.com/kevin-newsom/|publisher=[[Above the Law (website)|Above the Law]]|access-date=May 8, 2017}} {{Dead link|date=November 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}{{cite journal|last1=Gibeut|first1=John|title=It's All in the Execution|journal=American Bar Association Journal|date=August 11, 2006|url=http://www.abajournal.com/magazine/article/its_all_in_the_execution|access-date=May 8, 2017}}{{cite news|last1=Mahoney|first1=Ryan|title=Ex-state solicitor general |url=https://www.americanbar.org/groups/litigation/committees/appellate-practice/articles/2013/winter2013-0313-state-solicitor-general-boom/ |access-date=June 30, 2020 |website=www.americanbar.org '''Kim Anita McLane Wardlaw''' (born 1954) is an American lawyer and jurist serving as a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]] since 1998. She is the first [[Hispanic American]] woman to be appointed to a federal appeals court.<ref name="msjd_wardlaw">{{cite web|url=https://ms-jd.org/blog/article/profile-judge-kim-wardlaw|title=Profile: Judge Kim Wardlaw|publisher=ms-jd.org |first=Amelia |last=Hansen |date=March 7, 2007 |access-date=August 26, 2019}}</ref> Wardlaw was considered as a [[Barack Obama Supreme Court candidates|possible candidate to be nominated]] by [[Barack Obama]] to the [[Supreme Court of the United States]].<ref>Jess Bravin, [https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB122333844642409819?mod=googlenews_wsj Barack Obama: The Present Is Prologue], ''[[The Wall Street Journal]]'' (October 7, 2008).</ref><ref>Manu Raju, [https://www.politico.com/story/2009/05/feinstein-pushes-two-hispanic-judges-022421 Feinstein pushes two Hispanic judges], ''[[The Politico|Politico]]'' (May 12, 2009).</ref>

== Early life and education ==
In 1954, Wardlaw was born as Kim Anita McLane in [[San Francisco]], California. Wardlaw's father was a salesman of [[Scotch-Irish Americans|Scotch Irish]] lineage. Wardlaw's mother was Soledad Jiménez, an accountant of Mexican descent.<ref name="msjd_wardlaw"/><ref name="appellatestrategist_wardlaw">{{cite web |url=https://www.appellatestrategist.com/2010/04/articles/employment/supreme-court-short-list-profiles-judge-kim-mclane-wardlaw-of-the-9th-circuit-court-of-appeals/ |title=Supreme Court Short List Profiles: Judge Kim McLane Wardlaw of the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals |publisher=appellatestrategist.com |date=April 19, 2010 |access-date=August 26, 2019}}</ref><ref name="votesmart_wardlaw">{{cite web |url=https://votesmart.org/candidate/biography/119802/kim-wardlaw |title=Judge Kim Wardlaw's Biography |publisher=[[Vote Smart]] |access-date=August 26, 2019}}</ref>

In 1976, Wardlaw earned a bachelor's degree in communications, ''[[summa cum laude]]'' and [[Phi Beta Kappa]], from [[University of California, Los Angeles|UCLA]]. In 1979, Wardlaw earned a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[UCLA School of Law]].<ref name="msjd_wardlaw"/><ref name="appellatestrategist_wardlaw"/><ref name="votesmart_wardlaw"/><ref>{{cite web |title=Two UCLA School of Law Alumni Appointed to the U.S. Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals |url=https://law.ucla.edu/news-and-events/in-the-news/2012/06/two-ucla-school-of-law-alumni-appointed-to-the-us-ninth-circuit-court-of-appeals/ |publisher=UCLA Law School |access-date=August 25, 2019 |date=June 18, 2012 |archive-date=August 27, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190827033632/https://law.ucla.edu/news-and-events/in-the-news/2012/06/two-ucla-school-of-law-alumni-appointed-to-the-us-ninth-circuit-court-of-appeals/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Career==
===Early career===
Wardlaw worked as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[William P. Gray]] of the [[United States District Court for the Central District of California]] and a legal extern for Judge [[Joseph Tyree Sneed III]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]]. Wardlaw joined the law firm of [[O'Melveny & Myers]] in 1980 as an associate, and worked at the firm for sixteen years, the final ten as a partner in the litigation department.

===Political campaigning===
Wardlaw volunteered for [[Bill Clinton presidential campaign, 1992|Bill Clinton's presidential campaign]] in California during the 1991–1992 election season, and later served on the Clinton-Gore [[United States presidential transition|presidential transition]] team, working with the [[United States Department of Justice]].<ref name=FJC>{{FJC Bio|nid=1389371|inline=yes}}</ref> She was an elected delegate from the [[California's 27th congressional district]] to the 1992 [[Democratic National Convention]]. In 1993, Wardlaw served on the Executive Committee on Debate Preparation for [[Richard Riordan]]'s campaign for [[Mayor of Los Angeles]].<ref name=FJC /> After volunteering for Riordan's successful campaign, she worked as his Government Liaison during the mayoral transition.<ref name=FJC />

===Federal judicial service===
President Clinton nominated Wardlaw to the [[United States District Court for the Central District of California]] on August 10, 1995. The [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Judiciary Committee]] unanimously approved her nomination, and the Senate confirmed Wardlaw on December 22, 1995, by [[unanimous consent]]. She received her judicial commission on December 26, 1995. She served on the district court until August 3, 1998 when she was elevated to the court of appeals.<ref name=FJC />

Clinton nominated Wardlaw to the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]] on January 27, 1998. The Judiciary Committee approved her nomination by a 17–1 vote, and the Senate again confirmed her nomination by unanimous consent on July 31, 1998. She received her judicial commission on August 3, 1998.<ref name=FJC />

==Notable cases==
{{BLP unreferenced section|date= December 2019}}

=== Jones v. City of Los Angeles ===
In 2006, Judge Wardlaw held that homeless plaintiffs could challenge an ordinance banning sleeping on the street, over the dissent of Judge [[Pamela Ann Rymer]].<ref>{{cite journal|title=Recent Case: Ninth Circuit Holds That "Involuntary" Conduct Cannot Be Punished|journal=[[Harvard Law Review]]|date=2006|volume=120|page=829|url=https://harvardlawreview.org/wp-content/uploads/pdfs/jones_v_losangeles.pdf|access-date=30 October 2017|archive-date=7 November 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171107004540/https://harvardlawreview.org/wp-content/uploads/pdfs/jones_v_losangeles.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>

=== Redding v. Safford Unified School District ===
On July 11, 2008, Wardlaw ruled in favor of Savannah Redding, a 13-year-old girl who was strip searched because she was wrongly suspected of having drugs on her. Wardlaw, joined by Judges Pregerson, Fisher, Paez, M. Smith, and N.R. Smith, ruled that the strip search of Redding violated the 4th amendment and denied individuals conducting the strip search qualified immunity.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=8356948863210998128&hl=en&as_sdt=6&as_vis=1&oi=scholarr|title=April REDDING, legal guardian of minor child, Plaintiff-Appellant, v. SAFFORD UNIFIED SCHOOL DISTRICT # 1; Kerry Wilson, husband; Jane Doe Wilson, wife; Helen Romero, wife; John Doe Romero, husband; Peggy Schwallier, wife; John Doe Schwallier, husband, Defendants-Appellees.|website=Google Scholar|date=July 11, 2008|access-date=February 11, 2024}}</ref> In [[Safford Unified School District v. Redding]], the Supreme Court affirmed the 9th circuit on the strip search violating the 4th amendment, but granted [[qualified immunity]] to the individuals conducting the strip search. Justices [[Ruth Bader Ginsburg]] & [[John Paul Stevens]] dissented from the qualified immunity ruling and voted to affirm Wardlaw's ruling in full.

=== Bryan v. McPherson ===
Wardlaw wrote the majority opinion in [[Bryan v. MacPherson]], a case where police officers tasered a man at a traffic spot because he was not wearing a seatbelt. Wardlaw concluded that the police violated the man's 4th amendment rights, and that use of a taser can be considered [[excessive force]]. Wardlaw also wrote a concurrence in denying en banc, joined by judges Pregerson, Reinhardt, and W. Fletcher, defending her initial decision to rule against the officers.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.leagle.com/decision/infco20101130227|title=BRYAN v. MacPHERSON|website=Leagle|date=November 30, 2010|access-date=January 5, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://casetext.com/case/bryan-v-macpherson|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190808034419/https://casetext.com/case/bryan-v-macpherson|url-status=dead|archive-date=August 8, 2019|title=Bryan v. MacPherson (2)|website=casetext|date=November 30, 2010|access-date=January 29, 2024}}</ref>

=== Bringas-Rodriguez v. Sessions ===
On March 8, 2017, Wardlaw ruled that Carlos Bringas-Rodriguez, a gay Mexican, must be given protection from persecution, overruling ''Castro-Martinez v. Holder''. She ruled that Bringas-Rodriguez had suffered past prosecution, as he was abused as a child based on his sexual orientation, and that the Mexican police would not investigate the abuse because of Bringas-Rodriguez's sexual orientation. Wardlaw was joined by Chief Judge [[Sidney Runyan Thomas]], Judge [[William A. Fletcher]], [[Milan Smith]], [[Morgan Christen]], [[John B. Owens]], [[Michelle T. Friedland]], and Senior Judge [[Barry G. Silverman]], over the dissent of [[Carlos Bea]] who was joined by [[Diarmuid O'Scannlain]]. [[Richard R. Clifton]] concurred in the judgement but would not overrule Castro-Martinez v. Holder.

=== Ibrahim v. Department of Homeland Security ===
On January 2, 2019, Wardlaw ruled that Dr. Rahinah Ibrahim had experienced sex discrimination, and Wardlaw remanded for a recalculation of Ibrahim's fees. Wardlaw also ruled that the government may have acted in bad faith. Wardlaw was joined by [[Sidney Runyan Thomas]], [[M. Margaret McKeown]], [[William A. Fletcher]], [[Marsha Berzon]], [[Milan Smith]], [[Morgan Christen]], and [[Paul J. Watford]], over the partial dissent of [[Consuelo Callahan]] who was joined by [[N. Randy Smith]] and [[Jacqueline Nguyen]]. In October 2019, the Supreme Court declined to hear the case, with Justice [[Samuel Alito]] commenting that he voted to take up the case.

=== City of Los Angeles v. Barr (Sanctuary Cities) ===
On July 12, 2019, in ''City of Los Angeles V. Barr,'' the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]] overturned a [[nationwide injunction]] issued in 2018, thus upholding preferential treatment in awarding community policing grants to cities that cooperate with immigration authorities. In the opinion, Judge [[Sandra Segal Ikuta|Sandra Ikuta]] wrote, "Cooperation relating to enforcement of federal immigration law is in pursuit of the general welfare, and meets the low bar of being germane to the federal interest in providing the funding to "address crime and disorder problems, and otherwise... enhance public safety... one of the main purposes for which” the grant is intended. In her dissent,  Judge Wardlaw wrote, "[The Department of Justice's] decision to implement both the illegal immigration focus area and the Cooperation Certification is foreclosed by the text, structure, and purpose of the Community Policing Act."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2019/07/12/18-55599.pdf|author=United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit|title=Opinion No. 18-55599|publisher=[[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]]|date=2019-07-12}}</ref>

In July 2019, Wardlaw dissented when the 9th circuit en banc upheld Trump's gag rule which defunded abortion providers from Title X funds.

=== Tresóna v. Burbank High School ===

In March 2020, Wardlaw authored the opinion of the court on Tresóna Multimedia v. [[Burbank High School (Burbank, California)|Burbank High School]] Vocal Music Ass'n,<ref name=17-56006>{{cite court |litigants=Tresóna Multimedia, LLC v. Burbank High School Vocal Music Ass'n |vol= |reporter= |opinion=17-56006 |pinpoint= |court=9th Cir. |date=2020 |url=https://propertyintangible.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/03/Tresor-Multimedia-v.-Burbank-High-School.pdf |access-date= |quote=}}</ref> which held the school choir's usage of the song ''[[Magic (Olivia Newton-John song)|Magic]]'' was [[fair use]], and that the school should be awarded [[attorney's fee]]s due to Tresóna's "overreaching claims of copyright infringement".<ref>{{cite web|access-date=2020-03-30|title=Don't Sue a High School Choir for Copyright Infringement in the Ninth Circuit|url=https://propertyintangible.com/2020/03/template-17.html|date=2020-03-30|author=Pam Chestek|quote=The panel affirmed the district court's summary judgment in favor of the vocal music director at Burbank High School and other defendants in a copyright suit and reversed the district court's denial of attorneys' fees to defendants.}}{{Dead link|date=February 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref>

Wardlaw wrote that
{{blockquote|Tresóna did more than simply pursue an aggressive litigation strategy. It sued a public school teacher, a not-for-profit Boosters Club, and parent volunteers. [...] None of these actions furthers the purposes of the [[1976 Copyright Act|Copyright Act]]. Courts have a legitimate interest in deterring the type of litigation conduct in which Tresóna engaged, and in compensating those who have been harmed by such conduct. [...] Awarding Defendants their attorneys' fees insures that they are properly compensated for defending against overreaching claims of copyright infringement and pressing a defense that benefits those educating our youth. An award of attorneys' fees here assures that "an overzealous monopolist [cannot] use his copyright to stamp out the very creativity that the [Copyright] Act seeks to ignite," allowing for greater breathing room for classroom educators and those involved in similar educational extracurricular activities.|<ref name=17-56006/>}}

=== Center for Investigative Reporting v. DOJ ===

On September 23, 2021, Wardlaw, joined by Milan Smith, ordered the DOJ to publicize records regarding the number of weapons that were formerly owned by law enforcement. The basis for this decision was the [[Freedom of Information Act]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2021/09/23/18-17356.pdf|title=CIR v. DOJ|website=ca9.uscourts.gov|date=September 23, 2021|access-date=January 22, 2024}}</ref>

=== Okonowsky v. Garland ===

On July 25, 2024, Wardlaw reinstated a hostile work environment lawsuit. The lawsuit had been filed by a staff psychologist working for a federal prison who discovered that a corrections lieutenant was sexually harassing her via social media.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2024/07/25/23-55404.pdf|title=LINDSAY OKONOWSKY, Plaintiff-Appellant, v. MERRICK B. GARLAND, Attorney General, United States Attorney General, Defendant-Appellee.|website=ca9.uscourts.gov|date=July 25, 2024|access-date=December 23, 2024}}</ref>

=== Election Integrity Project v. Weber ===

On August 15, 2024, Wardlaw wrote for a unanimous panel ruling that California's vote-by-mail system was constitutional.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2024/08/15/23-55726.pdf|title=Election Integrity Project v. Weber|website=ca9.uscourts.gov|date=August 15, 2024|access-date=December 23, 2024}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/litigation/california-vote-by-mail-upheld-in-rebuke-of-vote-dilution-suit|title=California Vote-By-Mail Upheld in Rebuke of 'Vote Dilution' Suit|website=Bloomberg Law|date=August 15, 2024|access-date=December 23, 2024}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Wardlaw's husband is William Wardlaw. They have two children, William, Jr. and Katherine Ann. Since 2009, Wardlaw and her family have resided in Pasadena, California.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.kevinroderick.com/wardlaw.html |title=Reign Maker |publisher=kevinroderick.com |first=Kevin |last=Roderick |date=January 2005 |access-date=August 26, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://ms-jd.org/blog/article/first-woman-judge-kim-mclane-wardlaw|title=First Women Series: Judge Kim McLane Wardlaw|publisher=ms-jd.org |date=March 10, 2009 |access-date=August 26, 2019}}</ref>

Wardlaw established the Soledad Jiménez McLane Scholarship Fund, in honor of her mother, for disadvantaged Latino children in the [[San Gabriel Valley]] at the [[Mayfield Senior School|Mayfield School]], in [[Pasadena, California]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://issuu.com/mayfieldjuniorschool/docs/mjs-annualreport2015|title=Mayfield Junior School Annual Report 2014-2015|date=7 March 2016 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.legacy.com/obituaries/mercurynews/obituary.aspx?pid=15647057 |title=Soledad Jimenez McLane |publisher=legacy.com |date=November 8, 2005 |access-date=August 26, 2019}}</ref>

[[Tulane University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Luis Felipe Restrepo''', known commonly as '''L. Felipe Restrepo''', is a [[United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit|United States Court of Appeals Judge for the Third Circuit]] and a former [[United States federal judge|United States District Court Judge]] for the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania|Eastern District of Pennsylvania]]. He is also a member of the [[United States Sentencing Commission]], where he currently serves as Vice Chair.{{cite web | url=https://www.ussc.gov/commissioners | title=About the Commissioners }} ==Biography== [[File:L. Felipe Restrepo senate judiciary hearing.jpg|thumb|Judge Restrepo and Senator [[Pat Toomey|Toomey]] at Judge Restrepo's Senate Judiciary Hearing|306x306px]] Judge Restrepo has served as a [[United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit|United States Court of Appeals Judge for the Third Circuit]] since 2016.{{Cite web |date=2014-11-12 |title=President Obama Nominates Two to Serve on the United States Courts of Appeals |url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/11/12/president-obama-nominates-two-serve-united-states-courts-appeals |access-date=2025-10-29 |website=whitehouse.gov |language=en}} Judge Restrepo previously served as a [[United States district court|United States District Court Judge]] for the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania|Eastern District of Pennsylvania]] from 2013 to 2016, and as a [[United States magistrate judge|United States Magistrate Judge]] for the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania|Eastern District of Pennsylvania]] from 2006 to 2013, where he presided over a variety of criminal and civil matters.{{Cite web |date=2012-11-27 |title=President Obama Nominates Three to the United States District Court |url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2012/11/27/president-obama-nominates-three-united-states-district-court |access-date=2025-10-29 |website=whitehouse.gov |language=en}} He was a partner at the Philadelphia law firm of Krasner & Restrepo (with current [[District Attorney of Philadelphia|Philadelphia District Attorney]] [[Larry Krasner]]) from 1993 to 2006. From 1990 to 1993, he served as an Assistant Federal Defender in the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania|Eastern District of Pennsylvania]], and from 1987 to 1990 as an Assistant Defender with the [[Defender Association of Philadelphia]]. Judge Restrepo has served in a variety of teaching positions. Since 1993, he has been an [[Adjunct professor|Adjunct Professor]] teaching [[Trial advocacy|Trial Advocacy]] at [[Temple University Beasley School of Law]]. From 1997 to 2009, he also served as an [[Adjunct professor|Adjunct Professor]] teaching [[Trial advocacy|Trial Advocacy]] at the [[University of Pennsylvania Law School]]. Judge Restrepo received his B.A. from the [[University of Pennsylvania]] in 1981 and his J.D. from [[Tulane University School of Law|Tulane Law School]] in 1986. Judge Luis Felipe Restrepo was born in [[Medellín|Medellín, Colombia]], and was raised in [[Northern Virginia]]. He was sworn in as a United States Citizen on September 7, 1993. ==Federal judicial service== === District court service === [[File:Felipe Restrepo (cropped).jpg|thumb|right|Judge Restrepo]] On November 27, 2012, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Judge Restrepo to serve as a United States District Judge of the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, to the seat vacated by Judge [[Anita B. Brody]], who assumed senior status on June 8, 2009.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2012/11/27/president-obama-nominates-three-united-states-district-court|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Obama Nominates Three to the United States District Court|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=27 November 2012}} On January 2, 2013, his nomination was returned to the President, due to the sine die adjournment of the Senate. On January 3, 2013, Obama renominated Restrepo to the same office.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2013/01/03/president-obama-re-nominates-thirty-three-federal-judgeships|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Obama Re-nominates Thirty-Three to Federal Judgeships|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=January 3, 2013}} The [[United States Senate|Senate]] confirmed his nomination on June 17, 2013, by a [[voice vote]].{{cite web|url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/113th-congress/26/actions?q=%7B%22search%22%3A%5B%22Restrepo%22%2C%22Restrepo%22%5D%7D&s=1&r=12&overview=closed|title=PN26 — Luis Felipe Restrepo — The Judiciary|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=January 4, 2013}} He received his commission on June 19, 2013. On January 7, 2015, President Obama renominated him to the same position.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2015/01/07/presidential-nominations-sent-senate|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=January 7, 2015}} He received a hearing before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] on June 10, 2015.{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/nominations-06-10-15|title=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|website=www.judiciary.senate.gov|date=June 10, 2015 }} On July 9, 2015, his nomination was reported out of committee by a [[voice vote]].{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%20-%20July%209,%202015.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – July 9, 2015}} On January 11, 2016, the [[United States Senate]] confirmed him by an 82–6 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=114&session=2&vote=00001|title=On the Nomination (Nomination Luis Felipe Restrepo, of Pennsylvania, to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the Third Circuit)|website=www.senate.gov}} Judge Restrepo was President [[List of federal judges appointed by Barack Obama|Obama]]'s last appellate court judge to be confirmed by the Senate. '''Leonard Steven Grasz''' (born November 1, 1961)<ref name=":1">{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Grasz%20SJQ.pdf|title=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees: Leonard Steven Grasz}}</ref> is an American attorney and jurist serving as a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit]].

A graduate of the [[University of Nebraska–Lincoln]] and the [[University of Nebraska College of Law]], Grasz spent eleven years as the state of Nebraska's Chief Deputy Attorney General. He was a senior partner at the law firm of Husch Blackwell prior to his appointment to the federal judiciary.

At the time of his 2017 nomination for the United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit, the [[American Bar Association]]'s [[Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary]] unanimously voted to give Grasz a "not qualified" rating for the position. Grasz was the first circuit court nominee to receive a unanimous "not qualified" rating from the ABA since 2006. Republican Senators accused the ABA of political bias and Grasz, in his testimony, claimed that the ABA's review process was unprofessional.

==Early life and education==
Grasz was born in [[Chappell, Nebraska]], to farmers. As a child, he showed steers and lambs, belonged to [[4-H]], and was a state officer for [[National FFA Organization|Future Farmers of America]]. He played basketball and was on the track team in high school, graduating in a class of 33 students.<ref name=omahamag>{{cite news |last1=Simonson |first1=Kevin |title=Steve Grasz Takes the Bench |url=http://omahamagazine.com/articles/steve-grasz-takes-the-bench/ |access-date=25 January 2019 |work=Omaha Magazine |date=March 2, 2018}}</ref>

Grasz received his [[Bachelor of Science]], ''[[cum laude]]'', in agriculture from the [[University of Nebraska–Lincoln]] in 1984. He received his [[Juris Doctor]] degree from the [[University of Nebraska College of Law]] in 1989, where he was inducted into the [[Order of the Coif]], served as the executive editor of the ''Nebraska Law Review'', and received the Roscoe Pound Award for his selection as top oral advocate in his class.<ref name=whitehouse>[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2017/08/03/president-donald-j-trump-announces-sixth-wave-judicial-candidates-and "President Donald J. Trump Announces Sixth Wave of Judicial Candidates and Fifth Wave of U.S. Attorney Candidates", White House, August 3, 2017]{{PD-notice}}</ref>

==Career==

=== Early career ===
Grasz began his career as an [[intern]] and legislative assistant to [[Virginia Smith (politician)|Virginia D. Smith]], a Republican member of the [[United States House of Representatives]] who represented [[Nebraska's 3rd congressional district]] from 1975 to 1991 and was the first woman from Nebraska to hold a seat in the U.S. House.<ref name=omahamag/> Grasz went on to spend two years as an [[Associate lawyer|associate]] at [[Kutak Rock]].<ref name=whitehouse/> 

Grasz then spent eleven years as the state of Nebraska's chief deputy attorney general, where he oversaw the [[Nebraska Attorney General]]'s Office's civil and appellate practice in state and federal courts, the state's official Attorney General's opinions, and the representation of state constitutional officers and legislators.<ref name=whitehouse/> While serving as chief deputy attorney general, Grasz authored nine briefs in the U.S. Supreme Court and served as counsel of record before the Supreme Court in ''[[Stenberg v. Carhart]]'' (2000), in which he defended a state statute prohibiting [[partial-birth abortion]].<ref name="memo">{{cite news|last1=Severino|first1=Carrie|author-link=Carrie Severino|title=Who is Steve Grasz?|url=http://www.nationalreview.com/bench-memos/450160/who-steve-grasz|access-date=September 25, 2017|website=[[National Review]]|date=August 4, 2017}}</ref> 

In 2002, Grasz joined the Omaha office of Husch Blackwell. He was named senior partner in 2013. While in private practice, Grasz challenged a state constitutional provision restricting ownership of agricultural land under the [[Commerce Clause]].<ref name=memo/> He worked as a [[Lobbying|lobbyist]] in addition to maintaining a legal practice.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Voruganti|first=Harsh|date=October 31, 2017|title=L. Steven Grasz|url=https://vettingroom.org/2017/10/31/steve-grasz/|website=The Vetting Room}}</ref> From 2007 to 2013, he served as general counsel to the [[Nebraska Republican Party]]. From 2013 to 2017, he worked as legal counsel, treasurer, and secretary to [[Pete Ricketts]]'s gubernatorial campaigns.<ref name=":1" />

Grasz has also written numerous op-eds, including one in 2012 criticizing [[John Roberts]] as "the one who ushered in the ultimate transfer of limitless power to the federal government" for his decision in [[National Federation of Independent Business v. Sebelius]], which he described as "unsupportable in terms of its legal reasoning and adherence to longstanding rules of constitutional interpretation or construction".<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite news|last=Grasz|first=Steve|date=July 9, 2012|title=Local View: Roberts jeopardized legitimacy of high court|work=Lincoln Journal-Star|url=https://journalstar.com/news/opinion/editorial/columnists/local-view-roberts-jeopardized-legitimacy-of-high-court/article_e6de9051-3758-5c30-af0b-3659f94fbecd.html}}</ref>

In 2017, Grasz was part of the state chapter of the [[Federalist Society]], joining the Nebraska Lawyers Chapter Steering Committee.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite news|last=Harloe|first=Kate|date=October 31, 2017|title=Senate Republicans Set to Move Forward with Judicial Nominee Rated "Not Qualified"|work=Mother Jones|url=https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2017/10/senate-republicans-set-to-move-forward-with-judicial-nominee-rated-not-qualified/}}</ref> He was on the board of the conservative advocacy group [[Nebraska Family Alliance]] during the year in which he was nominated by Trump.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Ruiz |first1=Rebecca R. |last2=Gebeloff |first2=Robert |last3=Eder |first3=Steve |last4=Protess |first4=Ben |date=March 14, 2020 |title=A Conservative Agenda Unleashed on the Federal Courts |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/03/14/us/trump-appeals-court-judges.html |work=The New York Times }}</ref> He served on the board of and as legal counsel to Nebraskans for the Death Penalty.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite news|last=Tillman|first=Zoe|date=September 17, 2017|title=One Of Trump's Judicial Nominees Sits On The Board Of A Group That Defends "Conversion" Therapy|work=BuzzFeed News|url=https://www.buzzfeednews.com/article/zoetillman/one-of-trumps-judicial-nominees-sits-on-the-board-of-a}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|last=Silva|first=Christianna|date=November 1, 2017|title=Who Is Steve Grasz, Trump's Newest Federal Judge Nominee With Anti-LGBT History?|work=Newsweek|url=https://www.newsweek.com/who-steve-grasz-trumps-newest-anti-lgbt-nominee-who-isnt-qualified-8th-circuit-698846}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|last=Pilger|first=Lori|date=May 25, 2016|title=Attorneys battle over whether death penalty should end up on November ballot|work=Lincoln Journal-Star|url=https://journalstar.com/news/local/article_b1607fb5-d931-5004-9eaa-06f4e2df066a.html}}</ref>

===Federal judicial service===

On August 3, 2017, President [[Donald Trump]] nominated Grasz to serve as a United States Circuit Judge of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit]], to the seat vacated by Judge [[William J. Riley]], who assumed [[senior status]] on June 30, 2017.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2017/08/03/eighteen-nominations-sent-senate-today|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|publisher=[[White House]]|title=Eighteen Nominations Sent to the Senate Today – The White House}}</ref> On November 1, 2017, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/11/01/2017/nominations|title=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|website=judiciary.senate.gov|date=November 2017 }}</ref>

In October 2017, the [[American Bar Association]]'s Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary, an entity which rates judicial nominees, unanimously voted to give Grasz a "not qualified" rating for the position. In a statement, the chair of the ABA's standing committee that reviews nominees said that Grasz's "temperament issues, particularly bias and lack of open-mindedness, were problematic".<ref>{{cite news|last1=Min Kim|first1=Seung|title=ABA deems another Trump judicial nominee 'not qualified'|url=https://www.politico.com/story/2017/10/30/aba-trump-judicial-nominee-not-qualified-244327|access-date=October 30, 2017|work=[[Politico]]|date=October 30, 2017}}</ref><ref>Lawrenz Fare, [http://www.jurist.org/paperchase/2017/11/aba-committee-gives-8th-circuit-nominee-not-qualified-rating.php ABA committee gives 8th Circuit nominee 'not qualified' rating], ''Jurist'' (November 1, 2017).</ref><ref>Debra Cassens Weiss, [http://www.abajournal.com/news/article/aba_committee_explains_its_not_qualified_rating_for_8th_circuit_nominee ABA committee explains its 'not qualified' rating for 8th Circuit nominee], ''ABA Journal'' (October 31, 2017).</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.law360.com/articles/985753?sidebar=true|title=ABA Judicial Ratings Remain In GOP Senators' Crosshairs – Law360|website=law360.com}}</ref> Grasz was the first circuit court nominee to receive a unanimous "not qualified" rating since 2006.<ref name=":0">{{cite news |last=Ryan|first=Tim|date=December 7, 2017|title=Senate Panel Advances Nominations of 10 Federal Judges|url=https://www.courthousenews.com/senate-panel-advances-nominations-of-10-federal-judges/|work=[[Courthouse News Service]]|access-date=December 12, 2017}}</ref> Nebraskan Senators [[Ben Sasse]] and [[Deb Fischer]] defended Grasz's reputation and accused the ABA of conducting a biased evaluation "based on limited facts".<ref>{{cite web |last1=Sasse |first1=Ben |author-link1=Ben Sasse |last2=Fischer |first2=Deb |author-link2= Deb Fischer |url=http://www.omaha.com/opinion/deb-fischer-and-ben-sasse-grasz-deserves-seat-on-court/article_6c4bf54c-9648-50df-a8e6-b02763760106.html |title=Deb Fischer and Ben Sasse: Grasz deserves seat on court |work=Omaha World-Herald |date=November 5, 2017 |access-date=December 12, 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.law360.com/articles/994010/senate-oks-trump-s-8th-circ-pick-despite-aba-rating|title=Senate OKs Trump's 8th Circ. Pick Despite ABA Rating – Law360|website=law360.com}}</ref> Grasz's nomination carried the support of former [[U.S. Senator]] and [[Governor of Nebraska|Governor]] [[Ben Nelson]] and former [[U.S. Attorney]] for the District of Nebraska [[Deborah R. Gilg]], both [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrats]].<ref name=omahamag/> 

On November 15, 2017, Pamela Bresnahan, the chair of the ABA's Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary, testified before the U.S. Senate in order to explain the organization's vetting of Grasz. In his confirmation hearing, Grasz had testified that the ABA's review process was unprofessional.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Schneier|first1=Cogan|title=Cruz Rails Against ABA Vetting Amid Confusion About 8th Circuit Nominee|url=https://www.law.com/nationallawjournal/sites/nationallawjournal/2017/11/15/cruz-rails-against-aba-vetting-amid-confusion-about-8th-circuit-nominee/|access-date=December 3, 2017|work=The National Law Journal|date=November 15, 2017}}</ref> On November 30, 2017, [[Senate Judiciary Committee]] Chairman [[Chuck Grassley]] stated that follow-up materials from Grasz "appear to indicate that the ABA relied on faulty information in their evaluation". Upon the request of the Senate Judiciary Committee Ranking Member [[Dianne Feinstein]], the committee vote on Grasz's nomination was delayed for one week.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/11-30-17%20Grassley%20Statement.pdf|title=Prepared Statement by Senator Chuck Grassley of Iowa, Chairman, Senate Judiciary Committee, Executive Business Meeting, November 30, 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Morton|first1=Joseph|title=Senate panel delays consideration of Omaha attorney Steve Grasz's nomination|url=http://www.omaha.com/news/politics/senate-panel-delays-consideration-of-omaha-attorney-steve-grasz-s/article_e25e0aee-d5e3-11e7-9a95-5755d003c0e4.html|access-date=December 3, 2017|work=Omaha World-Herald|date=November 30, 2017}}</ref>

On December 7, 2017, his nomination was reported out of committee by an 11–9 vote.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%2012-07-17.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – December 7, 2017, Senate Judiciary Committee}}</ref> On December 11, 2017, the [[United States Senate]] invoked [[cloture]] on his nomination by a 48–47 vote.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=115&session=1&vote=00312|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Leonard Steven Grasz to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the Eighth Circuit)|website=senate.gov}}</ref> On December 12, 2017, his nomination was confirmed by a 50–48 vote, with Senators [[John McCain]] and [[Thad Cochran]] absent.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=115&session=1&vote=00313|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Leonard Steven Grasz, of Nebraska, to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the Eighth Circuit)|website=senate.gov}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/leonard-steven-grasz-trump-judicial-pick-not-qualified-okd-senate/|title=Leonard Steven Grasz, Trump judicial pick rated as "not qualified," OK'd by Senate|publisher=[[CBS News]] |date=December 13, 2017 }}</ref> He received his judicial commission on January 3, 2018.<ref>{{FJC Bio|nid=4025236|inline=yes}}</ref>

==Notable cases==

* On November 15, 2021, Grasz, writing for a unanimous panel, denied [[qualified immunity]] to a police officer who shot service dogs.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ecf.ca8.uscourts.gov/opndir/21/11/202632P.pdf|title=Jennifer L.M. LeMay, personally, and as guardian of CLE, VE, minors; Courtney J. Livingston v. Michael B. Mays; City of Minneapolis|website=ecf.ca8.uscourts.gov|date=November 15, 2021|access-date=December 5, 2021}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.abajournal.com/news/article/8th-circuit-rejects-qualified-immunity-for-officer-who-shot-service-dogs/|title=Officer who shot service dogs not entitled to qualified immunity, 8th Circuit says|website=ABA Journal|date=November 16, 2021|access-date=December 5, 2021}}</ref> 

* On December 15, 2022, Grasz authored a unanimous opinion of the Court reversing a lower court jury's veredict that a man who had secretly video recorded his underage niece was guilty of two counts of production of child pornography. Grasz wrote that covertly filming an underage child in a state of undress does not necessarily constitute production of child pornography because "the videos were not intended or designed to elicit a sexual response in the viewer." Grasz's opinion did not suggest what alternative, non-sexual motivation might have existed for the man to have made the secret recordings.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Brantley |first=Max |date=2022-12-15 |title=8th Circuit reverses child porn convictions of Rison man who secretly filmed women in bathroom |url=https://arktimes.com/arkansas-blog/2022/12/15/8th-circuit-reverses-child-porn-convictions-of-rison-man-who-secretly-filmed-women-in-bathroom |access-date=2022-12-15 |website=Arkansas Times |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>United States Court of Appeals For the Eighth Circuit. ''U.S. v. Matthew McCoy''. December 15, 2022. </ref>

* On December 31, 2025, Grasz, writing for a unanimous panel, reversed a jury award of over $158 million awarded against [[Amtrak]] in a wrongful death case involving a passenger who was shot by another passenger. The jury had awarded $8.8 million in compensatory damages and $100 million in punitive damages for Amtrak's conduct. In reversing the jury and district court, Grasz reasoned that the railroad had no duty to protect passengers from criminal acts of other passengers under Missouri law and that the plaintiff had failed to establish causation as a matter of law.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Grasz |first=Steven |date=2025-12-31 |title=Aaron v. Nat'l Railroad Passenger Corporation |url=https://public.fastcase.com/ppbqSQpNDaJE%2F8PlIk0b8A%2Fsi8%2BmC9GnLJT2j9tpeVl9AA3Ix9GgT1tQ5rI2WfoM |access-date=2026-01-02 |website=Fast Case |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>United States Court of Appeals For the Eighth Circuit. ''Steven v. Amtrak''. December 31, 2025. </ref>

[[Boston College]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Lara Elizabeth Montecalvo''' (née '''Ewens'''; born 1974) is an American lawyer from [[Rhode Island]] who has served as a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit]] since 2022. == Early life and education == Born Lara Elizabeth Ewens in 1974 in [[Syracuse, New York]],{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Montecalvo%20SJQ%20Public%20Final.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=May 24, 2022}} Montecalvo received her [[Bachelor of Arts]] from [[Swarthmore College]] in 1996 and her [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Boston College Law School]] in 2000.{{Cite press release |title=President Biden Names Seventeenth Round of Judicial Nominees |date=April 27, 2022 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/04/27/president-biden-names-seventeenth-round-of-judicial-nominees/ |access-date=April 27, 2022}} {{PD-notice}} She is married to Craig Montecalvo, and they have one child.{{cite web |url=https://news.yahoo.com/president-biden-names-ri-public-124851967.html |title=President Biden names RI public defender Lara Montecalvo to federal appeals court |website=news.yahoo.com |date=27 April 2022 }} == Career == Montecalvo started her legal career as a trial attorney in the [[United States Department of Justice Tax Division]] from 2000 to 2004. From 2004 to 2020, she served as an assistant [[public defender]] in the Rhode Island Public Defender's Office; she served in multiple roles within the office including as a trial attorney from 2004 to 2010, as an appellate attorney from 2010 to 2014 and as chief of the appellate division from 2014 to 2020. In March 2020, Montecalvo was nominated by [[Rhode Island Governor]] [[Gina Raimondo]] to serve as the Public Defender of Rhode Island.{{Cite web |last=Raimondo Nominates Lara Montecalvo for Rhode Island Public Defender |date=March 5, 2020 |title=RIGOV |url=https://www.ri.gov/ |access-date=April 27, 2022 |website=www.ri.gov |language=en}} === Federal judicial service === On April 27, 2022, President [[Joe Biden]] announced his intent to nominate Montecalvo to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] for the [[United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit]].{{Cite web |last=Mulvaney |first=Katie |date=April 27, 2022 |title=President Biden names RI public defender Lara Montecalvo to federal appeals court|url=https://www.providencejournal.com/story/news/courts/2022/04/27/president-joe-biden-appointment-lara-montecalvo-1st-u-s-circuit-court-of-appeals/9551349002/|access-date=April 27, 2022|website=The Providence Journal |language=en-US}} Her nomination was praised by Senators [[Jack Reed (Rhode Island politician)|Jack Reed]] and [[Sheldon Whitehouse]]. On May 19, 2022, her nomination was sent to the Senate. President Biden nominated Montecalvo to the seat to be vacated by Judge [[O. Rogeriee Thompson]], who announced her intent to assume [[senior status]] upon confirmation of a successor.{{Cite press release |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |date=May 19, 2022 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url= https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/05/19/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-67/}} On May 25, 2022, a hearing on her nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web |title=Nominations |date=May 23, 2022 |publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/05/25/2022/nominations}} On June 16, 2022, her nomination was reported out of committee by a 12–10 vote.{{cite web|url= https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/EBM%20Results%20-%202022-06-16.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – June 16, 2022|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=June 16, 2022}} On September 13, 2022, the [[United States Senate]] invoked cloture on her nomination by a 51–45 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1172/vote_117_2_00334.htm |title= On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Lara E. Montecalvo to be United States Circuit Judge for the First Circuit)|date=September 13, 2022|website=United States Senate|access-date=September 13, 2022}} On September 14, 2022, her nomination was confirmed by a 52–47 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1172/vote_117_2_00335.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Lara E. Montecalvo, of Rhode Island, to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the First Circuit)|date=September 13, 2022|website=United States Senate|access-date=September 13, 2022}} Montecalvo was the sixth public defender nominated by President Biden to be confirmed as a United States circuit judge, handing Biden the record for placing the most nominees with that kind of experience onto the circuit courts.{{cite news |last=Raymond |first=Nate |title=U.S. Senate vote gives Biden record for most public defenders on appeals courts |url=https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/us-senate-vote-gives-biden-record-most-public-defenders-appeals-courts-2022-09-14/}}{{cite news |last=Alder |first=Madison |title=Biden Sets Record for Public Defenders on Circuit Courts (1) |url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/montecalvos-circuit-confirmation-hits-mark-for-public-defenders?usertype=External&bwid=00000183-3c7f-d71b-af97-feff4d930001&qid=7353537&cti=&uc=&et=NEWSLETTER&emc=blnw_nl%3A8&source=newsletter&item=read-text®ion=digest&access-ticket=eyJjdHh0IjoiTFdOVyIsImlkIjoiMDAwMDAxODMtM2M3Zi1kNzFiLWFmOTctZmVmZjRkOTMwMDAxIiwic2lnIjoiSXVDdUlnWENneGpPRVpnZW5mSnlGMGdTeXk0PSIsInRpbWUiOiIxNjYzMTgwMTg3IiwidXVpZCI6IklSMjJGL1JJZEhuS2ZBVGp4K3pZVWc9PWtDVHJqWURjekpyZG5SUkVWZlNGNHc9PSIsInYiOiIxIn0%3D}} She received her judicial commission on September 20, 2022.{{FJC Bio|nid=12588656|inline=yes}} == Personal life == Montecalvo lives in [[Barrington, Rhode Island]], with her husband, Craig V. [[Harvard University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Lawrence James Christopher VanDyke''' (born 1972){{cite news |last=Johnson |first=Charles S. |title=VanDyke seeks to bring appellate law background to Supreme Court |url=https://helenair.com/news/local/vandyke-seeks-to-bring-appellate-law-background-to-supreme-court/article_e7f2f476-aa75-11e3-876e-0019bb2963f4.html |newspaper=[[Independent Record]] |location=Helena, Montana |date=March 13, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190924225948/https://helenair.com/news/local/vandyke-seeks-to-bring-appellate-law-background-to-supreme-court/article_e7f2f476-aa75-11e3-876e-0019bb2963f4.html|archive-date=2019-09-24 |url-status=live |url-access=subscription |access-date=2026-04-03}} is an American lawyer and jurist serving as a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]] since 2020. He previously served as the [[solicitor general]] of [[Nevada]] from 2015 to 2019 and of [[Montana]] from 2013 to 2014. == Early life and education == VanDyke was born in 1972 in [[Midland, Texas]], and grew up in [[Bozeman, Montana]].{{cite web |url=https://helenair.com/news/local/vandyke-seeks-to-bring-appellate-law-background-to-supreme-court/article_e7f2f476-aa75-11e3-876e-0019bb2963f4.html |title=VanDyke seeks to bring appellate law background to Supreme Court |date=March 13, 2014 |website=Independent Record |language=en-US |access-date=October 19, 2019}} After attending [[Oklahoma Christian University]] from 1992 to 1995, he studied [[civil engineering]] at [[Montana State University]], graduating in 1997 with a [[Bachelor of Science]] with highest honors. He worked for his family's construction company and did graduate study at Montana State for the next three years, receiving a Master of Construction Engineering Management degree in 2000.{{cite web |url=https://www.nationalreview.com/bench-memos/who-is-lawrence-vandyke/ |title=Who Is Lawrence VanDyke? |date=September 20, 2019 |website=National Review |language=en-US |access-date=September 21, 2019}} VanDyke graduated from Bear Valley Bible Institute, a [[Bible college]] in [[Denver]], Colorado, in 2002 with a [[Bachelor of Theology]] degree, [[Latin honors#United States|''summa cum laude'']]. He then attended [[Harvard Law School]], where he was an editor of the ''[[Harvard Law Review]]'' and the ''[[Harvard Journal of Law & Public Policy]]''. He graduated in 2005 with a [[Juris Doctor]], ''magna cum laude''.{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=2019|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Lawrence%20VanDyke%20SJQ%20-%20PUBLIC.pdf|access-date=|website=}} == Legal career == VanDyke worked for the law firm [[Gibson Dunn]] from 2005 to 2006, then served as a [[law clerk]] to judge [[Janice Rogers Brown]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit]] from 2006 to 2007. He returned to Gibson Dunn from 2007 to 2012. While in private practice, VanDyke performed ''pro bono'' legal work for groups including the [[American Civil Liberties Union]], the [[Free Market Foundation]], and the [[Alliance Defending Freedom]].{{cite news |last1=Severino |first1=Carrie |title=Who Is Lawrence VanDyke? |url=https://www.nationalreview.com/bench-memos/who-is-lawrence-vandyke/ |access-date=November 1, 2019 |work=[[National Review]] |date=September 20, 2019}}{{Cite web|first=Matt|last=Volz|url=https://www.greatfallstribune.com/story/news/local/2014/10/26/colleague-questions-vandykes-experience/17947963/|title=Colleague questions VanDyke's experience|website=[[Great Falls Tribune]]|date=October 25, 2014}} In 2010, VanDyke filed an [[amicus brief|''amicus'' brief]] in the Supreme Court case ''[[Christian Legal Society v. Martinez]]'' on behalf of the organization Gays and Lesbians for Individual Liberty, in which he argued that a college student group had a [[First Amendment to the United States Constitution|First Amendment]] right to exclude from membership students whose sexual conduct violated the group's stated beliefs.{{cite web|first1=Dahlia |last1=Lithwick |first2=Mark Joseph |last2=Stern |url=https://slate.com/news-and-politics/2019/11/lawrence-vandyke-aba-trump-judge-9th-circuit-unqualified.html |title=The latest 'unqualified' Trump judicial nominee thinks he's the real victim |date=November 1, 2019 |website=[[Slate (magazine)|Slate]] |access-date=November 2, 2019}} From 2012 to 2013, VanDyke was an assistant to the [[Solicitor General of Texas]]. He was then appointed Solicitor General of Montana but resigned in 2014, citing strain in the workplace.{{cite news|first=Matt |last=Volz |title=Colleague questions VanDyke's experience |url=https://www.greatfallstribune.com/story/news/local/2014/10/26/colleague-questions-vandykes-experience/17947963/ |newspaper=Great Falls Tribune |date=October 25, 2014 |access-date=April 3, 2026}}{{cite web|author=Charles S. Johnson |url=https://helenair.com/news/state-and-regional/vandyke-resigning-as-state-solicitor-general/article_88184036-d740-11e3-9c55-0019bb2963f4.html |title=VanDyke resigning as state solicitor general | State and Regional |date=May 9, 2014 |publisher=helenair.com |access-date=October 30, 2019}} In that role, he submitted numerous ''amicus'' briefs filed in other states. He recommended signing on to other states' challenges to state and federal gun laws, co-wrote a brief supporting an Arizona law prohibiting abortions after 20 weeks, and recommended that Montana file a brief in a New Mexico case involving a photographer who refused to photograph a lesbian commitment ceremony.{{cite web|author=John S. Adams|url=https://www.greatfallstribune.com/story/news/local/2014/09/17/vandyke-politician-nature/15812491/ |title=Montana Supreme Court: VanDyke takes the spotlight |publisher=Great Falls Tribune|date=September 18, 2014 |access-date=November 1, 2019}} VanDyke unsuccessfully ran for a seat on the [[Montana Supreme Court]] in 2014, losing to incumbent Justice [[Mike Wheat]].{{cite news|url = https://missoulacurrent.com/lawrence-vandyke/|title = Trump to nominate former Montana solicitor general to 9th Circuit Court|last = Dennison|first = Mike|date = September 23, 2019|accessdate = January 12, 2026|work = Missoula Current}} He then became Solicitor General of Nevada under Attorney General [[Adam Laxalt]] in 2015, where he served until 2019 when he became a deputy Assistant Attorney General for the [[United States Department of Justice Environment and Natural Resources Division]].{{cite web |url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-judicial-nominees-united-states-marshal-nominee-5/ |title=President Donald J. Trump Announces Judicial Nominees and United States Marshal Nominee |date=September 20, 2019 |via=[[NARA|National Archives]] |work=[[whitehouse.gov]] |access-date=September 20, 2019 }} {{PD-notice}} Since graduating law school, VanDyke has been a member of the [[Federalist Society]]. == Federal judicial service == On September 20, 2019, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to nominate VanDyke to serve on the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]]. Nevada Senators [[Jacky Rosen]] and [[Catherine Cortez Masto]], both Democrats, announced their opposition in the nomination.{{cite news|last1=Sanchez|first1=Humberto|title=Nevada senators raise concerns about Trump's intention to tap ex-Nevada solicitor general for Ninth Circuit|url=https://thenevadaindependent.com/article/cortez-masto-and-rosen-raise-concerns-about-trumps-intention-to-tap-lawrence-vandyke-for-ninth-circuit-court-of-appeal|access-date=September 23, 2019|publisher=Nevada Independent|date=September 20, 2019}} He was appointed to the seat being vacated by Judge [[Jay Bybee]], who had previously announced his intention to take [[senior status]] on December 31, 2019.{{Cite web|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/twenty-five-nominations-three-withdrawals-sent-senate/|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Twenty-five Nominations and Three Withdrawals Sent to the Senate}} Six retired justices of the Montana Supreme Court publicly opposed VanDyke's nomination.{{Cite web|url=https://mtstandard.com/opinion/columnists/guest-view-vandyke-unqualified-for-judgeship/article_0b842f96-4792-5f5a-90e5-ae96c131f011.html|title=Guest view: VanDyke unqualified for judgeship|last=Nelson|first=James C.|date=November 2, 2019|website=[[Montana Standard]]|language=en|access-date=December 21, 2019}} VanDyke received a "not qualified" rating from the [[American Bar Association]] (ABA). An ABA evaluator conducted 60 anonymous interviews with lawyers, judges, and others who had worked with VanDyke. In unusually personal terms, the ABA sent and later published a letter to the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] criticizing VanDyke asserting that some interviewees described VanDyke as "arrogant, lazy, an ideologue, and lacking in knowledge of the day-to-day practice" of law.{{Cite news|url=https://www.latimes.com/opinion/story/2019-12-18/donald-trump-judges-federal-courts-conservatives|title=Opinion: Trump is packing courts with right-wing ideologues. Democrats, what's your plan?|last1=Hardy|first1=Nathan R.|last2=Jolly|first2=Richard L|date=December 18, 2019|newspaper=[[Los Angeles Times]]|language=en-US|access-date=December 21, 2019}} The ABA added that "there was a theme that the nominee lacks humility, has an 'entitlement' temperament, does not have an open mind, and does not always have a commitment to being candid and truthful."{{Cite web|url=https://www.foxnews.com/politics/trump-judicial-nominee-hearing|title=Trump judicial pick breaks down in tears at hearing over legal group's attack|first=Ronn|last=Blitzer|date=October 30, 2019|website=[[Fox News]]}} Finally, the letter raised "concerns about whether Mr. VanDyke would be fair to persons who are part of the [[LGBTQ people|LGBTQ community]], claiming that "Mr. VanDyke would not say affirmatively that he would be fair to any litigant before him, notably members of the LGBTQ community."{{cite news|last1=Knowles|first1=Hannah |title=Trump judicial nominee cries over scathing letter from the American Bar Association |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2019/10/30/trump-judicial-nominee-cries-over-scathing-letter-american-bar-association |access-date=November 1, 2019 |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |date=October 30, 2019}} On October 30, 2019, a hearing on VanDyke's nomination before the Senate Judiciary Committee became contentious.{{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/10/30/2019/nominations|title=Nominations | United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|website=www.judiciary.senate.gov|date=October 30, 2019 }} Much of the two-hour hearing was focused on VanDyke's record on LGBTQ issues.{{cite web|last=Keen |first=Lisa |url=https://www.ebar.com/news/latest_news//283860 |title=Bay Area Reporter :: Online Extra: Trump judicial nominee defends himself against anti-LGBT claims |website=Ebar.com |access-date=November 2, 2019}} VanDyke was asked by Senator [[Josh Hawley]] (R-[[Missouri|MO]]), "Did you say that you wouldn't be fair to members of the LGBTQ community?" VanDyke broke down in tears, denying the accusation: "I did not say that. I do not believe that. It is a fundamental belief of mine that all people are created in the image of God and they should all be treated with dignity and respect."{{cite news |last1=McCormack |first1=John |title=The ABA's Attack on Lawrence VanDyke Doesn't Make Sense |url=https://www.nationalreview.com/2019/10/american-bar-association-attack-on-lawrence-vandyke-doesnt-make-sense/ |access-date=November 1, 2019 |publisher=National Review |date=October 31, 2019}} Senator [[Patrick Leahy]] (D-[[Vermont|VT]]) questioned VanDyke about an opinion editorial he wrote in 2004 while a student at Harvard Law claiming that [[same-sex marriage]] may be harmful for children on average. VanDyke stated generally that some of his personal views had changed since that time,{{r|Fox tears}} and added that his ABA evaluator told him that she was in a "hurry" and did not give him the opportunity to fully respond to concerns. The ABA acknowledged that its lead evaluator assigned to VanDyke, Montana attorney Marcia Davenport, had contributed $150 to VanDyke's opponent in a 2014 Montana Supreme Court election.{{cite news |last1=de Vogue |first1=Ariane |last2=Rogers |first2=Alex |title='Not qualified' rating and accusation from American Bar Association moves Trump nominee to tears |url=https://www.cnn.com/2019/10/30/politics/american-bar-association-nominees-vandyke/index.html |access-date=October 30, 2019 |website=[[CNN]] |date=October 30, 2019}} The ABA's handling of VanDyke was widely denounced by conservative commentators. Writing for ''[[National Review]]'', John McCormack asked: "Were VanDyke's comments to the ABA twisted or taken wildly out of context in order to paint him as a bigot? It is hard to believe any judicial nominee would suggest during an interview with the ABA that he might not be 'fair' to all litigants." McCormack asked the ABA for a transcript of the relevant portion of its interview with VanDyke, but the association declined to provide one. Legal scholar Adam White, a former member of the ABA's Administrative Law Section, wrote a ''[[Wall Street Journal]]'' op-ed arguing that there was "no basis on which to evaluate any of the broad-brush descriptions of Mr. VanDyke. We don't know what basis, if any, his critics have for these judgments, or even who they are. We're expected to take the ABA's disparagement at face value."{{cite news |last1=White |first1=Adam |title=Another Smear Campaign From the American Bar Association |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/another-smear-campaign-from-the-american-bar-association-11572475391 |access-date=November 2, 2019 |newspaper=[[Wall Street Journal]] |date=October 30, 2019}} The ''Wall Street Journal'' editorial board also published a critique of the ABA's treatment of VanDyke.{{cite news |title=The ABA Strikes Again |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/the-aba-strikes-again-11572475604 |access-date=November 2, 2019 |newspaper=[[Wall Street Journal]] |date=October 30, 2019}} Writing in ''[[The Atlantic]]'', law professor [[Josh Blackman]] suggested that "going forward, when a nominee is rated as unqualified, the transcript should be released, and the recording should be posted publicly online."{{cite web
