news|date=2021-03-25|title=In barbed dissents, Trump appointees call out 9th Circuit colleagues in immigration case|language=en|work=Reuters|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/legal-us-otc-9thcircuit-idUSKBN2BH34V|access-date=2021-10-13}}{{Cite web|last=Journal|first=A. B. A.|title=Dissenting judge says 9th Circuit took habeas dysfunction to new level with 'hypothetical dicta'|url=https://www.abajournal.com/news/article/dissenting-judge-says-9th-circuit-took-habeas-dysfunction-to-new-level-with-hypothetical-dicta|access-date=2021-10-13|website=ABA Journal|language=en}}{{Cite web|title=Trump Appointee Accuses Ninth Circuit of 'Judge-Jitsu' and 'Mischief' in Immigration Ruling|url=https://www.law.com/therecorder/2021/03/24/trump-appointee-accuses-ninth-circuit-of-judge-jitsu-and-mischief-in-immigration-ruling/|access-date=2021-10-13|website=The Recorder|language=en}} === ''McDougall v. County of Ventura'' === In January 2022, VanDyke wrote a majority opinion holding that two California counties had violated the [[Second Amendment to the United States Constitution|Second Amendment]] when they shut down gun and ammunition stores in 2020 as nonessential businesses during the [[COVID-19 pandemic]].{{Cite web|first=Jacob|last=Cullum|date=January 21, 2022|title=9th Circuit Panel Says Pandemic-Inspired Shutdowns of Gun Stores Were Unconstitutional|url=https://reason.com/2022/01/21/9th-circuit-panel-says-pandemic-inspired-shutdowns-of-gun-stores-were-unconstitutional/|access-date=January 22, 2022|website=[[Reason (magazine)|Reason]]|language=en-US}} VanDyke unusually filed a concurrence to his own opinion, predicting that the case would be heard ''en banc'' and claiming that "no firearm-related ban or regulation ever ultimately fails" in the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit|Ninth Circuit]]. He criticized the court's approach to Second Amendment challenges as "exceptionally malleable". In his attached 13-page concurrence, VanDyke asserted that he would rule in favor of the California counties—the opposite conclusion of his own majority opinion for the panel—and explained: "I figure there is no reason why I shouldn’t write an alternative draft opinion that will apply our test in a way more to the liking of the majority of our court. That way I can demonstrate just how easy it is to reach any desired conclusion under our current framework, and the majority of our court can get a jumpstart on calling this case en banc. Sort of a win-win for everyone." He ended the alternate opinion with "You’re welcome."{{Cite web|first=Avalon|last=Zoppo|title='You're Welcome': 9th Circuit Judge Writes Alternative Opinion for Ruling on COVID Gun Shop Closures|url=https://www.law.com/nationallawjournal/2022/01/20/youre-welcome-9th-circuit-judge-writes-alternative-opinion-for-ruling-on-covid-gun-shop-closures/|date=January 20, 2022|access-date=January 22, 2022|website=[[National Law Journal]]|language=en}} ===''Anita Green v. Miss United States of America''=== In November 2022, VanDyke held in ''Anita Green v. Miss United States of America'' that beauty pageant companies may exclude [[trans women]] as part of their [[freedom of speech]] rights. In this case, he wrote that "it is commonly understood that beauty pageants are generally designed to express the 'ideal vision of American womanhood'."{{Cite web|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/nbc-out/out-news/us-beauty-pageant-can-exclude-transgender-contestants-court-rules-rcna55448|title=U.S. beauty pageant can exclude transgender contestants, court rules|website=[[NBC News]]|agency=[[Reuters]]|date=November 3, 2022 }}{{cite web |title=Anita Green v. Miss United States of America (21-35228) |url=https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/66687053/anita-green-v-miss-united-states-of-america/ |website=[[CourtListener]] |access-date=March 15, 2026}} ===''United States v. Idaho''=== On September 28, 2023, VanDyke upheld [[Idaho]]'s abortion law despite its lack of exceptions for medical emergencies.{{Cite web|url=https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2023/09/28/23-35450.pdf|title=United States v. Idaho|website=ca9.uscourts.gov|date=September 28, 2023|access-date=February 18, 2024}} On November 13, 2023, the Ninth Circuit reversed VanDyke in voting 7–4 ''en banc'' to temporarily block the state abortion ban due to its lack of exceptions for medical emergencies.{{Cite web|url=https://www.scotusblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/20231120154722276_2023-11-20-Motion-with-Appendix-copy.pdf|title=UNITED STATES OF AMERICA vs. STATE OF IDAHO|website=SCOTUSBlog|date=November 13, 2023|access-date=February 18, 2024}} On January 5, 2024, the Supreme Court said that it would take up the case and dissolved the Ninth Circuit's temporary injunction.{{Cite magazine|url=https://time.com/6552689/supreme-court-idaho-abortion-ban-pending-hearing/|title=Supreme Court Allows Idaho to Enforce Its Strict Abortion Ban, Even in Medical Emergencies|magazine=Time|date=January 6, 2024|access-date=February 18, 2024}}{{Dead link|date=August 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} On June 27, 2024, the Supreme Court dismissed the case on the grounds that its review would be premature, reinstated the injunction, and returned the case to the Ninth Circuit to decide the case on the merits.{{Cite web|url=https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/23pdf/23-726_6jgm.pdf|title=MOYLE vs. UNITED STATES OF AMERICA|website=SupremeCourt.gov|date=June 27, 2024|access-date=August 7, 2024}} ===''Duncan v. Bonta''=== [[File:Lawrence VanDyke dissent video in 23-55805 Duncan v. Bonta.webm|thumb|right|300px|Dissent video released by Lawrence VanDyke in relation to Duncan v. Bonta.]] In November 2021, an ''en banc'' panel of the Ninth Circuit upheld a California law that limited gun magazine capacity to 10 bullets,{{Cite web|url=https://www.huffpost.com/entry/ninth-circuit-court-california-ban-magazines-guns_n_61a682f6e4b044a1cc1b5115|title=Court Upholds California's Ban On High-Capacity Gun Magazines|website=[[Huffington Post]]|date=November 30, 2021|access-date=November 30, 2021}} and VanDyke accused the majority of "distrust[ing] gun owners and think[ing] the [[Second Amendment]] is a [[vestigial organ]] of their living constitution." He concluded his dissenting opinion by saying that the ruling meant that "at most, you might get to possess one janky handgun and 2.2 rounds of ammunition, and only in your home under lock and key. That's it. That’s ridiculous, and so I must respectfully dissent."{{Cite web|url=https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2021/11/30/19-55376.pdf|title=Virginia Duncan et al. v. Rob Bonta|website=ca9.uscourts.gov|date=November 30, 2021|access-date=November 30, 2021}}{{Primary source inline|date=October 2026}} VanDyke later went on to record a video dissent to more easily demonstrate the reasoning for his dissent, with a focus on the insistence of the state that magazines were not an 'arm' protected by the Second Amendment and instead were an 'accessory' due to them being a part of a firearm that could be changed. He argued that that reasoning by the state could be used to effectively ban any 'protected arm' they wished, as the vast majority of the parts that make up any modern firearm could then be classified as an 'accessory' due to the fact that almost every single part can be changed.{{cite web|title= Dissent video in 23-55805 Duncan v. Bonta |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DMC7Ntd4d4c|website=United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit Youtube Page|date=March 20, 2025}}{{Primary source inline|date=October 2026}} ===''Olympus Spa v. Armstrong''=== In March 2026, VanDyke issued a dissenting opinion in ''Olympus Spa v. Armstrong'', a Ninth Circuit case regarding the admittance of trans women to a gender-separated Korean spa in Washington. He wrote that the case under examination was about "swinging dicks" and that "woke regulators and complicit judges seem entirely willing, even eager, to ignore the consequences that their [[Frankenstein]] social experiments impose on real women and young girls."{{cite news |last1=Libby |first1=Sara |title=A Trump-appointed judge used a vulgar term to attack trans women. His colleagues hit back |url=https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/van-dyke-trans-dissent-22075048.php |access-date=March 15, 2026 |work=[[San Francisco Chronicle]] |date=March 13, 2026}} VanDyke's opinion drew written rebukes by 29 of the 51 judges on the Ninth Circuit, who asserted that his "crude and vitriolic language" made them "sound like juveniles, not judges, and it undermines public trust in the courts."{{cite news |last1=Monyak |first1=Suzanne |title=VanDyke Uses Crude Phrase in Case Over Spa’s Transgender Policy |url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/vandyke-uses-crude-phrases-in-case-over-spas-transgender-policy |access-date=March 15, 2026 |work=[[Bloomberg Law]] |date=March 13, 2026}}{{cite web |title=Olympus Spa, et al. v. Armstrong, et al. Document #65 |url=https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/69162936/65/olympus-spa-et-al-v-armstrong-et-al/ |website=[[CourtListener]] |access-date=March 15, 2026 |date=March 12, 2026}} ''[[The Washington Post]]'' covered his remarks in a piece on conservative judges who appeared to be bringing attention to themselves and auditioning to President Donald Trump to be appointed to the Supreme Court.{{Cite news |last=Mark |first=Julian |date=2026-05-30 |title=There are no Supreme Court vacancies, but some judges are acting like there might be |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/05/30/with-flashy-opinions-judges-may-be-auditioning-supreme-court/ |work=The Washington Post |language=en-US |issn=0190-8286}} == See also == * [[Donald Trump judicial appointment controversies]] * [[Donald Trump Supreme Court candidates]] == References == {{Reflist}} == External links == * {{FJC Bio|nid=7504281}} * {{Ballotpedia|Lawrence_VanDyke|Lawrence VanDyke}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Jay Bybee]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]]}}|years=2020–present}} {{s-inc}} {{s-end}} {{United States courts of appeals judges}} {{Authority control}} {{DEFAULTSORT:VanDyke, Lawrence}} [[Category:1972 births]] [[Category:Living people]] [[Category:21st-century American lawyers]] [[Category:Harvard Law School alumni]] [[Category:Judges of the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]] [[Category:Montana lawyers]] [[Category:Montana State University alumni]] [[Category:Nevada lawyers]] [[Category:People associated with Gibson Dunn]] [[Category:People from Midland, Texas]] [[Category:Solicitors general of Montana]] [[Category:Solicitors general of Nevada]] [[Category:Texas lawyers]] [[Category:United States court of appeals judges appointed by Donald Trump]] [[Category:United States Department of Justice lawyers]] [[Category:Candidates in the 2014 United States elections]]

[[United States Army Reserve]]
[[Mississippi National Guard]] | battles = [[Iraq War]] }} '''Leslie Harburd Southwick'''{{cite web |url=https://mississippiencyclopedia.org/entries/leslie-harburd-southwick |title=Southwick, Leslie Harburd}} (born 1950) is a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]] and a former judge of the [[Mississippi Court of Appeals]]. == Early life and education == Born in [[Edinburg, Texas|Edinburg]], [[Texas]], Southwick graduated with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree ''[[cum laude]]'' from [[Rice University]] in 1972 and received his [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Texas School of Law]] in 1975. ==Career== Following law school, Southwick [[law clerk|clerked]] for the Presiding Judge, John F. Onion, Jr., of the [[Texas Court of Criminal Appeals]] from 1975 to 1976, and then, in [[Mississippi]], for Judge [[Charles Clark (judge)|Charles Clark]] of the United States Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals from 1976 to 1977.{{cite web|url=https://georgewbush-whitehouse.archives.gov/infocus/judicialnominees/southwick.html|title=Judicial Nominations - Judge Leslie H. Southwick}} Southwick was in private practice as an attorney in [[Jackson, Mississippi|Jackson]], Mississippi with the firm Brunini, Grantham, Grower & Hewes from 1977 to 1989, serving as a partner from 1983 to 1989. In 1989, Southwick entered government service as a Deputy Assistant Attorney General for the [[United States Department of Justice Civil Division]]. There he supervised the one hundred and twenty-five lawyers of the Federal Programs Branch, which defends suits brought against the United States. He also supervised the Office of Consumer Litigation, a twenty-five lawyer division charged with civil and criminal enforcement of federal consumer laws. Southwick was elected one of the first ten judges of the [[Mississippi Court of Appeals]] in 1994. He was a candidate for a seat on the [[Supreme Court of Mississippi]] in 1996, coming in third out of five candidates in the general election.Leslie Southwick, [https://dc.law.mc.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1410&context=lawreview Mississippi Supreme Court Elections: A Historical Perspective 1916-1996], 18 Miss. C. L. Rev. 115 (1997-1998). He thereafter remained on the court of appeals until the end of 2006 when, with a nomination to a lifetime position in the federal judiciary pending, he did not run for re-election. He attended The [[Judge Advocate General's Legal Center and School]] at the [[University of Virginia]] and entered the [[United States Army Judge Advocate General's Corps]] from 1992 to 1997. Southwick was on a leave of absence from the court from August 2004 to January 2006. In 2005, he served in [[Iraq]] in support of [[Operation Iraqi Freedom]] as a Judge Advocate General with the [[155th Brigade Combat Team (United States)|155th Brigade Combat Team]] of [[Mississippi Army National Guard]]. Southwick also taught law as an adjunct professor at the [[Mississippi College School of Law]] and was a member of the [[American Inns of Court]], [[Charles Clark (judge)|Charles Clark]] Chapter. === Federal judicial service === [[File:Trent Lott and Leslie Southwick.jpg|thumb|right|Southwick with [[Trent Lott]] in October 2007]] On January 9, 2007, President [[George W. Bush]] nominated Southwick to fill a seat on the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]] vacated by Judge [[Charles W. Pickering]], who retired in 2004.{{Cite web |date=2007-01-09 |title=Press Release: Nominations Sent to the Senate |url=https://georgewbush-whitehouse.archives.gov/news/releases/2007/01/20070109-4.html}} Bush had previously elevated Pickering to the Fifth Circuit with a [[recess appointment]] in January 2004, after [[United States Democratic Party|Senate Democrats]] blocked two previous attempts to appoint Pickering in 2001 and 2003.{{Cite web |title=CNN.com - Pickering appointment angers Democrats - Jan. 17, 2004 |url=https://www.cnn.com/2004/ALLPOLITICS/01/17/bush.pickering/ |access-date=2022-09-25 |website=www.cnn.com}}{{Cite web |title=Pickering retires from federal bench |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/id/wbna6688768 |access-date=2022-09-25 |website=NBC News |date=9 December 2004 |language=en}} In December 2004, Pickering announced that he would retire from the federal bench and would not seek a nomination for a permanent seat on the Fifth Circuit. Originally, Bush nominated Mississippi attorney [[Michael Wallace (lawyer)|Michael B. Wallace]] in the [[109th Congress]] to replace Pickering,{{Cite web |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |url=https://georgewbush-whitehouse.archives.gov/news/releases/2006/02/20060208-11.html |access-date=2022-09-25 |website=georgewbush-whitehouse.archives.gov}} but his nomination also became stalled due to fierce opposition from Senate Democrats.{{Cite news |title=Lawyer Asks Bush to Revoke His Nomination to the Bench |language=en-US |newspaper=Washington Post |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/politics/2006/12/27/lawyer-asks-bush-to-revoke-his-nomination-to-the-bench/b325af2c-bd83-48c0-a833-f177b74bbcae/ |access-date=2022-09-25 |issn=0190-8286}} Upon the Democratic takeover of Congress in the November 2006 elections, Wallace asked President Bush not to re-nominate him in the [[110th Congress]]. Finding itself without a nominee to a judgeship that had already sat vacant for two years, the White House turned to Southwick, then a nominee to a vacancy on the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Mississippi]]. Bush had nominated him on June 9, 2006 to fill a vacancy on that court left by Judge [[William H. Barbour Jr.]], who retired on February 4, 2006.{{Cite web |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |url=https://georgewbush-whitehouse.archives.gov/news/releases/2006/06/20060606-8.html |access-date=2022-09-25 |website=georgewbush-whitehouse.archives.gov}} Southwick had a hearing before the [[Senate Judiciary Committee]] on September 19, 2006 and was reported favorably to the floor of the Senate by the Committee on September 29, 2006. However, Southwick, like many other judicial nominees, failed to receive a vote by the full Senate before the 109th Congress adjourned for good on December 9, 2006. Pursuant to Senate rules of procedure, his nomination, along with many others, was returned to the President. Southwick's successive federal nominations within seven months of each other, though unusual, were not unprecedented. In May 2006, the Bush White House similarly nominated [[Jerome A. Holmes]] to a vacancy on the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit]] after nominating him to a vacancy on the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Oklahoma]] in February 2006.{{Cite web |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |url=https://georgewbush-whitehouse.archives.gov/news/releases/2006/02/20060214-4.html |access-date=2022-09-25 |website=georgewbush-whitehouse.archives.gov}}{{Cite web |title=Nominations and Withdrawal Sent to the Senate |url=https://georgewbush-whitehouse.archives.gov/news/releases/2006/05/20060504-13.html |access-date=2022-09-25 |website=georgewbush-whitehouse.archives.gov}} The Senate Judiciary Committee of the 110th Congress held a hearing on Southwick's nomination to the Fifth Circuit on May 10, 2007. The hearing was chaired by [[Rhode Island]] Democrat [[Sheldon Whitehouse]]. Just prior to the hearing, controversy arose over the nomination. Southwick's nomination was opposed by the [[People for the American Way]],{{cite web |url=http://www.pfaw.org/pfaw/general/default.aspx?oid=24117 |title=People for the American Way - Senators Should Reject Bush's Latest Nominee to 5th Circuit |access-date=2007-08-16 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070807004652/http://www.pfaw.org/pfaw/general/default.aspx?oid=24117 |archive-date=2007-08-07 }} ''Senators Should Reject Bush's Latest Nominee to 5th Circuit''; People for the American Way; May 30, 2007 the [[Human Rights Campaign]],{{cite web |url=http://www.hrcactioncenter.org/campaign/southwick/ |title=Take Action: Take Action! Don't Let Prejudice Trump Justice |access-date=2007-08-16 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070825211250/http://www.hrcactioncenter.org/campaign/southwick |archive-date=2007-08-25 }} ''Take Action! Don't Let Prejudice Trump Justice''; Human Rights Campaign; August 15, 2007 and the [[Congressional Black Caucus]],[http://www.congressionalblackcaucus.net/] ''The Congressional Black Caucus Denounces Appointment of Southwick''; Congressional Black Caucus; August 2, 2007 who alleged that Southwick was racially intolerant and homophobic. Two cases that Southwick participated in as a state judge formed the primary basis for the groups' charges. In the first case, ''Richmond v. Mississippi Department of Human Services'', Southwick joined the majority opinion upholding the decision of the Mississippi Employee Appeals Board to reinstate a white state employee (Richmond) who was fired for a single incident of referring to a black co-worker as a "good ole nigger" outside of the co-worker's presence. When the black co-worker was informed of Richmond's comment, Richmond immediately apologized, and her apology apparently was accepted. The Appeals Board's decision to reinstate Richmond was based, in part, on a hearing officer's opinion that the slur was only "somewhat derogatory" and "was in effect calling the individual a 'teacher's pet.'".{{cite web |url=http://www.andrewhyman.com/confirmthem/nword.pdf |title=Archived copy |access-date=2007-08-16 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070928020509/http://www.andrewhyman.com/confirmthem/nword.pdf |archive-date=2007-09-28 }} ''Richmond v. Mississippi Dept of Human Services'' (Miss. Ct. App. 1998) Retrieved October 31, 2007 Bound by law to affirm a decision of the Appeals Board supported by substantial factual evidence, the court held it had no authority to set aside the findings in this case, even though Richmond's remark was "undoubtedly ill-advised and indicative of a rather remarkable insensitivity.".Southwick4 On [[writ of certiorari]], the [[Mississippi Supreme Court]] agreed that "the unique circumstances of this case do not warrant imposition of the ultimate penalty of dismissal." However, the court found the record was insufficient to uphold the Employee Appeals Board's decision that Richmond effectively receive no penalty whatsoever. It decided to remand the case "in order for the board to impose an appropriate penalty less than dismissal, or to make detailed findings as to why no penalty should be imposed."[http://www.mssc.state.ms.us/Images/Opinions/Conv7856.pdf] ''Richmond v. Mississippi Dept of Human Services'' (Miss. 1999) Retrieved August 20, 2007 The second case often cited by Southwick's critics is ''S.B. v. L.W.'', an 8-2 decision upholding a chancellor's decision to grant sole custody of an eight-year-old girl to her father, in part because the mother was a lesbian who had lived with several different partners during the child's life. Southwick joined the majority opinion as well as a concurrence written by Judge Payne which states, in part:
¶ 33. I do recognize that any adult may choose any activity in which to engage; however, I also am aware that such person is not thereby relieved of the consequences of his or her choice. It is a basic tenet that an individual's exercise of freedom will not also provide an escape of the consequences flowing from the free exercise of such a choice. As with the present situation, the mother may view her decision to participate in a homosexual relationship as an exertion of her perceived right to do so. However, her choice is of significant consequence, as described before in the discussion of our State's policies, in that her rights to custody of her child may be significantly impacted.{{cite web |url=http://www.andrewhyman.com/confirmthem/CustodyCase.pdf |title=Archived copy |access-date=2007-08-20 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070928020524/http://www.andrewhyman.com/confirmthem/CustodyCase.pdf |archive-date=2007-09-28 }} ''S.B. v. L.W.'' (Miss. Ct. App. 1999), Retrieved August 20, 2007
After intense Democratic opposition, Southwick was reported out of Committee by a 10-9 vote on August 2, 2007 when Democratic [[California]] Senator [[Dianne Feinstein]] voted with the Committee's nine Republicans to send Southwick to the full Senate with a favorable report. Southwick was confirmed by a 59–38 vote on October 24, 2007.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=110&session=1&vote=00393|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Leslie Southwick, of Mississippi, to be U.S. Circuit Judge)}} Southwick's confirmation came almost ten months after his nomination to the Fifth Circuit and over a year after he was first nominated to a federal judgeship. He received his commission on October 29, 2007.{{FJC Bio|nid=1392651|inline=yes}} Southwick was sworn in as judge of the Fifth Circuit on October 30, 2007.{{citation needed|date=June 2023}} His first published opinion for the Fifth Circuit was [http://www.ca5.uscourts.gov/opinions/pub/07/07-30089-CV0.wpd.pdf ''Anthony v. United States''], which was released on March 4, 2008. Southwick wrote for a unanimous three judge panel on an issue involving the valuation of private annuities for estate tax purposes. His first published dissent was in ''Louisiana ex rel. Caldwell v. [[Allstate|Allstate Insurance]] Co.'', 536 F.3d 418 (5th Cir. 2008) in which Southwick dissented from the assumption of federal jurisdiction under the Class Action Fairness Act. In August 2018, Southwick found that the [[Texas Medical Board]] was entitled to [[qualified immunity]] for its unconstitutional warrantless search of a doctor's patient records, drawing an unusual concurrence ''[[dubitante]]'' from Circuit Judge [[Don Willett]].{{Bluebook journal |first=|last=Note| title=Recent Case: Fifth Circuit Holds Medical Board Investigators Are Protected by Qualified Immunity in Warrantless Search of Records| volume=132 | journal=[[Harvard Law Review|Harv. L. Rev.]] | page=2042 | url=https://harvardlawreview.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/2042-2049_Online.pdf| year=2019}}{{cite court |litigants=Zadeh v. Robinson|vol=902 |reporter=F.3d|opinion=483 |court=5th Cir.|date=2018|url= https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11429370861168916271 }} == Personal == Southwick is married, and is [[Roman Catholic]]. ([[Bachelor of Arts|BA]], [[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Lucy Haeran Koh''' (born August 7, 1968) is an American lawyer serving as a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]]. Koh previously served as a United States district judge of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of California]] from 2010 to 2021. She also served as a California state court judge of the [[Santa Clara County Superior Court]] from 2008 to 2010. She is the first [[Korean Americans|Korean American]] woman to serve on a federal appellate court in the United States.{{cite news |last1=Egelko |first1=Bob |title=Local judge becomes first Korean American woman to serve on a federal appellate court |url=https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Local-judge-becomes-first-Korean-American-woman-16699588.php |access-date=December 16, 2021 |work=San Francisco Chronicle |date=December 14, 2021}} == Early life and education == Born on August 7, 1968,{{Cite web |last=Voruganti |first=Harsh |date=September 30, 2021 |title=Judge Lucy Koh – Nominee to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit |url=https://vettingroom.org/2021/09/30/judge-lucy-koh/ |access-date=February 7, 2022 |website=The Vetting Room |language=en}} in [[Washington, D.C.]], Koh was the first member of her family to be born in the United States. Her mother, a refugee from [[North Korea]], had escaped the country at the age of ten after walking two weeks to [[South Korea]]. Her father was a veteran of the [[Korean War]], where he fought Communist forces.{{Cite web|last1=Deakin|first1=Michelle|date=January 1, 2011|title=Stepping Up: Lucy Koh '93|url=https://hls.harvard.edu/today/stepping-up-lucy-koh-93/|publisher=Harvard Law School|work=Harvard Law Today|language=en-US}} Koh spent most of her childhood in [[Mississippi]], where her mother was an academic at [[Alcorn State University]]. She also spent parts of her youth in [[Maryland]] and [[Oklahoma]]. In 1986, Koh graduated from [[Norman High School]] in 1986 in [[Norman, Oklahoma]]. She attended [[Harvard College]], where she was awarded a [[Harry S. Truman Scholarship]] and graduated in 1990 with a [[Bachelor of Arts]], ''[[Latin honors#North America|magna cum laude]]'', in [[social studies]]. She then attended [[Harvard Law School]], where she was a semifinalist in the [[Ames Moot Court Competition]] and graduated in 1993 with a [[Juris Doctor]].{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Koh%20Senate%20Questionnaire%20Final.pdf|title=United States Senate Judiciary Committee Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|date=2021|publisher=[[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|United States Senate Judiciary Committee]]}}{{Cite web|url=http://www.law.harvard.edu/news/2010/01/29_koh.nomination.html|title=Lucy Koh '93 nominated to serve as federal district court judge|date=December 14, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131214183848/http://www.law.harvard.edu/news/2010/01/29_koh.nomination.html|access-date=December 11, 2021|archive-date=December 14, 2013}}[https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/president-obama-nominates-five-serve-united-states-district-court-bench President Obama Nominates Five to Serve on the United States District Court Bench] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170216173233/https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/president-obama-nominates-five-serve-united-states-district-court-bench |date=February 16, 2017 }}, ''whitehouse.gov'' (January 20, 2010).{{FJC Bio|nid=1393231|inline=yes}}{{cite web |title=Senate Judiciary Committee Questionnaire – Lucy Koh |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/download/lucy-koh-public-questionnaire}} == Legal career== From 1993 to 1994, Koh worked for the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]] as a Women's Law and Public Policy Fellow. From 1994 to 1997, she worked for the [[United States Department of Justice]], first as a Special Counsel in the Office of Legislative Affairs (1994{{ndash}}1996) and then as a Special Assistant to the [[United States Deputy Attorney General|Deputy Attorney General]] (1996–1997).[https://web.archive.org/web/20080128175850/http://gov.ca.gov/press-release/8613/ Governor Schwarzenegger Appoints Lucy Koh to Santa Clara County Superior Court] (January 25, 2008) (press release). From 1997 to 2000, Koh served as an [[assistant United States attorney]] in the United States Attorney's Office for the Central District of California. From 2000 to 2002, she worked as a senior associate at [[Wilson Sonsini Goodrich & Rosati]], a [[Palo Alto, California|Palo Alto]] law firm. From 2002 to 2008, Koh worked as a litigation partner at the [[Silicon Valley]] office of the law firm [[McDermott Will & Emery]] representing technology companies in [[patent]], [[trade secret]], and commercial civil matters.{{cite news|title=Senate Confirms Lucy Haeran Koh as Federal Judge in California's Northern District|url=http://www.metnews.com/articles/2010/koh060810.htm|date=June 8, 2010|work=Metropolitan News Company|access-date=June 8, 2010}} == Judicial service == === California state court service === In January 2008, California Governor [[Arnold Schwarzenegger]] appointed Koh to the [[Santa Clara County Superior Court]], a position she held until 2010, when she became a federal judge. === Federal judicial service === ==== District court service ==== On January 20, 2010, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Koh on the recommendation of California Senators [[Barbara Boxer]] and [[Dianne Feinstein]] to a seat on the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of California]] vacated by Judge [[Ronald M. Whyte]], who assumed [[senior status]] in 2009. On February 11, the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] held a hearing on her nomination.{{Cite web |title=PN1363 — Lucy Haeran Koh — The Judiciary |url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/111th-congress/1363 |access-date=2023-07-07 |website=Congress.gov}} On March 4, the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] favorably reported her nomination.{{cite news|url=https://www.sfgate.com/nation/article/San-Jose-judge-one-step-away-from-federal-bench-3197094.php|title=San Jose judge one step away from federal bench|work=San Jose Mercury News|date=March 4, 2010|access-date=March 4, 2010|first=Bob|last=Egelko}} The Senate confirmed Koh by a 90–0 vote on June 7{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1112/vote_111_2_00178.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Lucy Haeran Koh, of California, to be United States District Judge for the Northern District of California)|website=United States Senate|date=June 7, 2010|access-date=November 8, 2022}}{{cite web|url=http://legaltimes.typepad.com/blt/2010/06/elena-kagan-nomination-not-stopping-other-nominees.html|title=Kagan Nomination Not Stopping Other Nominees|publisher=The BLT: The Blog of Legal Times|date=June 7, 2010|access-date=December 24, 2012}} and she received her commission on June 9. Her service as the district court judge was terminated on December 15, 2021, when she was elevated to the court of appeals. As a district judge, Koh presided over litigation including ''[[Apple Inc. v. Samsung Electronics Co.]]'', ''[[High-Tech Employee Antitrust Litigation|In re High-Tech Employee Antitrust Litigation]]'', ''FTC v. Qualcomm'' (finding antitrust liability for conduct in licensing [[Essential patent|standard-essential patents]], later reversed), and multi-district litigation, including the [[Yahoo! data breaches|Yahoo]] and [[Anthem data breach|Anthem]] data breaches and Apple and Google privacy litigation.{{Cite news|date=August 23, 2019|title=Federal Trade Commission v. Qualcomm Inc., No. 19-16122 (9th Cir. 2020)|newspaper=Justia Law |url=https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/ca9/19-16122/19-16122-2020-08-11.html|page=9|access-date=October 26, 2021}} In 2020, Koh presided over a case in which a coalition of local governments, activist groups, and [[Federally recognized tribes|American Indian tribes]] sued the [[United States Department of Commerce|Commerce Department]] over the Trump administration's intention to end the [[2020 United States Census|2020 Census]] early. She issued a ruling that resulted in extending the once-a-decade count from September 30 to October 15.{{cite news|last1=Wang|first1=Hansi Lo|title=Appeals Court Rejects Push To End Census Early By Trump Administration|url=https://www.npr.org/2020/09/30/916291712/appeals-court-rejects-push-to-end-census-early-by-trump-administration|access-date=October 3, 2020|agency=[[NPR]]|date=September 30, 2020}}{{cite news|last1=Wang|first1=Hansi Lo|title=Supreme Court Allows Trump Administration To End Census Counting On Oct. 15|url=https://www.npr.org/2020/10/13/921428056/supreme-court-allows-trump-administration-to-end-census-early|work=[[All Things Considered]]|publisher=NPR|date=October 13, 2020}} Koh presided over ''[[Tandon v. Newsom]]'', a challenge brought by plaintiffs' challenging [[California]] restrictions on gatherings during the [[COVID-19 pandemic]].[http://www.metnews.com/articles/2021/EmergencyRelief_04012021.htm Ninth Circuit Denies Emergency Relief Permitting In-Home Bible Studies], ''Metropolitan News-Enterprise'' (April 1, 2021). Koh denied the plaintiffs' request for an injunction seeking to block the restrictions "insofar as they (1) ban indoor religious gatherings at their homes, including Bible studies, theological discussions, collective prayer, and musical prayer; and (2) limit outdoor religious gatherings at their homes to three households"; in February 2021, she ruled that the restrictions did not violate the [[Free Exercise Clause]] because "the State's private gatherings restrictions treat religious and secular gatherings alike and make no reference to religion."''Tandon v. Newsom'', 517 F. Supp. 3d 922 (N.D. 2021). The Ninth Circuit affirmed Koh's decision but its ruling was overturned by the United States Supreme Court, which issued an order, on a 5–4 vote, determining that the restriction on religious gatherings in private homes was unconstitutional.{{cite news|last1=Scarcella|first1=Mike|title=9th Circuit nominee Lucy Koh defends COVID-19, antitrust rulings|url=https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/9th-circuit-pick-lucy-koh-defends-covid-19-antitrust-rulings-2021-10-06/|work=Reuters|date=October 6, 2021}}{{cite news|last1=Savage|first1=David|title=In 5–4 vote, Supreme Court lifts California's COVID ban on group Bible study in homes|url=https://www.latimes.com/world-nation/story/2021-04-09/high-court-halts-calif-virus-rules-limiting-home-worship|access-date=October 6, 2021|agency=[[Los Angeles Times]]|date=April 9, 2021}}{{cite court|litigants=Tandon v. Newsom|vol=593|reporter=U.S.|opinion=20A151|date=2021|url=https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/20pdf/20a151_4g15.pdf}} ==== Expired nomination to court of appeals under Obama ==== On February 25, 2016, President Obama nominated Koh to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] for the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]], to the seat vacated by Judge [[Harry Pregerson]], who assumed [[senior status]] on December 11, 2015.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2016/02/25/president-obama-nominates-judge-lucy-haeran-koh-serve-united-states|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Obama Nominates Judge Lucy Haeran Koh to serve on the United States Court of Appeals|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=February 25, 2016}}{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2016/02/25/presidential-nominations-sent-senate|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Presidential Nominations Sent to the Senate|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=February 25, 2016}} On July 13, 2016, a hearing on her nomination was held before the Senate Judiciary Committee.{{cite web|url=http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/07/13/2016/nominations|title=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|website=Judiciary.senate.gov|date=July 13, 2016 }} On September 15, her nomination was reported out of committee by a 13–7 vote,{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%20-%2009-15-16.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – September 15, 2016|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=October 12, 2022}} but the Senate did not act upon her nomination, and it expired on January 3, 2017, at the end of the [[114th United States Congress|114th Congress]]. President [[Donald Trump]] nominated [[Daniel P. Collins]] to that seat on February 6, 2019, and he was confirmed on May 21. ==== Renomination to court of appeals under Biden ==== On September 8, 2021, President [[Joe Biden]] announced his intention to renominate Koh to serve as a United States circuit judge for the Ninth Circuit.{{Cite press release|title=President Biden Names Seventh Round of Judicial Nominees|date=September 8, 2021|publisher=The White House|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/09/08/president-biden-names-seventh-round-of-judicial-nominees/|access-date=September 8, 2021}} On September 20, her nomination was sent to the Senate. Biden nominated Koh to the seat to be vacated by Judge [[Richard Paez]], who had announced his intent to assume [[senior status]] upon confirmation of a successor.{{Cite press release|title=Nominations and Withdrawal Sent to the Senate|date=September 20, 2021|publisher=The White House|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/09/20/nominations-and-withdrawal-sent-to-the-senate-3/}} Koh was unanimously rated "well qualified" for the circuit judgeship by the [[American Bar Association]]'s [[Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary]].[https://www.americanbar.org/content/dam/aba/administrative/government_affairs_office/webratingchart-117.pdf Ratings of Article III and Article IV Judicial Nominees: 117th Congress], [[American Bar Association]]'s [[Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary]] (last updated December 12, 2022). On October 6, 2021, the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] held a confirmation hearing on her nomination.{{Cite web|title=Nominations|date=October 6, 2021|publisher=[[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]]|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/09/29/2021/nominations}} During her hearing, Republican senators criticized Koh for her ruling in the ''Tandon'' case.{{cite news|last=Raymond|first=Nate|title=U.S. Senate confirms Koh to 9th Circuit, with Sung vote looming|url=https://www.reuters.com/legal/litigation/us-senate-confirms-koh-9th-circuit-with-sung-vote-looming-2021-12-13/|date=December 13, 2021|work=Reuters}}Jacqueline Thomsen, [https://www.law.com/nationallawjournal/2021/10/06/biden-9th-circuit-pick-draws-republican-ire-over-covid-19-religious-gathering-ruling/ Biden 9th Circuit Pick Draws Republican Ire Over COVID-19 Religious Gathering Ruling],''National Law Journal'' (October 6, 2021). At least one Republican senator accused her of hostility to people of faith; Koh noted that she is a person of faith. Another Republican senator, [[Tom Cotton]], suggested that Koh should have disregarded circuit precedent in the ''Tandon'' case; Koh responded that she was bound to follow higher court precedents.Madison Alder, [https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/ninth-circuit-pick-says-diverse-bench-has-role-modeling-function Religious Freedom Tension Spills Into Circuit Pick Hearing (1)], Bloomberg Law (October 6, 2021). Democrats defended Koh, and her nomination was also supported by former California Governor [[Arnold Schwarzenegger]], a Republican who appointed Koh to the state court earlier in her career. California Senator [[Alex Padilla]] criticized Republicans' attacks on Koh and other Biden judicial nominees, suggesting that they had singled out nonwhite judicial nominees for disparaging treatment.Tal Kopan, [Padilla calls out treatment of judicial nominees of color ahead of Supreme Court fight], ''San Francisco Chronicle'' (February 11, 2022). On October 28, Koh's nomination was favorably reported by the committee by a 13–9 vote.{{Cite web|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/EBM%20Results%2010.28.21.pdf|date=October 28, 2021|publisher=[[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]]}}Bob Egelko, [https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Judiciary-panel-sends-Lucy-Koh-appeals-court-16572579.php Judiciary panel sends Lucy Koh appeals court nomination to Senate floor], ''San Francisco Chronicle'' (October 28, 2021). On December 7, 2021, Majority Leader [[Chuck Schumer]] filed [[cloture]] on Koh's nomination.{{Cite web |title=PN1167 — Lucy Haeran Koh — The Judiciary |url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/117th-congress/1167 |access-date=2023-07-07 |website=Congress.gov}} On December 9, the Senate invoked cloture on her nomination by a 51–38 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1171/vote_117_1_00492.htm|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Lucy Haeran Koh to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the Ninth Circuit)|date=December 9, 2021|website=[[United States Senate]]|access-date=December 9, 2021}} On December 13, Koh was confirmed by a 50–45 vote{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1171/vote_117_1_00494.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Lucy H. Koh, of California, to be United States Circuit Judge for the Ninth Circuit)|date=December 13, 2021|website=[[United States Senate]]|access-date=December 13, 2021}}{{Cite web|title=Senate Confirms First Korean-American Woman Appeals Court Judge|url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/senate-confirms-first-korean-american-woman-appeals-court-judge-1|access-date=December 14, 2021|publisher=Bloomberg Law|date=December 13, 2021|author=Jordan S. Rubin}} and she received her judicial commission on December 14. Koh is the first [[Korean Americans|Korean-American]] woman to serve as a federal appellate judge and the second [[Asian Pacific American]] woman to serve on the Ninth Circuit from California, after [[Jacqueline Nguyen]].{{Cite web |date=September 8, 2021 |title=President Biden Makes Judges Koh And Thomas First Korean-American And African American Female Appeals Court Judges In California |url=https://oaklandnewsnow.com/president-biden-makes-judges-koh-and-thomas-first-korean-american-and-african-american-female-appeals-court-judges-in-california/ |access-date=September 8, 2021 |website=Oakland News Now |language=en-US}} ====Cases as a circuit judge==== On November 13, 2023, Koh was in a 7-4 majority that temporarily blocked Idaho's abortion ban due to its lack of exceptions for medical emergencies.{{Cite web|url=https://www.scotusblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/20231120154722276_2023-11-20-Motion-with-Appendix-copy.pdf|title=UNITED STATES OF AMERICA vs. STATE OF IDAHO|website=SCOTUSBlog|date=November 13, 2023|access-date=February 18, 2024}} On January 5, 2024, the Supreme Court said it would take up the case and dissolved the 9th Circuit's temporary injunction.{{Cite web|url=https://time.com/6552689/supreme-court-idaho-abortion-ban-pending-hearing/|title=Supreme Court Allows Idaho to Enforce Its Strict Abortion Ban, Even in Medical Emergencies|website=Time|date=January 6, 2024|access-date=February 18, 2024}} On June 27, 2024, the Supreme Court dissolved the stay in ''[[Moyle v. United States]]'', reinstating the 9th circuit's injunction against the ban. On January 11, 2024, Koh struck down a San Francisco ordinance that prohibited homeless people from "sleeping, lodging or camping on public property".{{Cite web|url=https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2024/01/11/23-15087.pdf|title=COALITION ON HOMELESSNESS v. CITY AND COUNTY OF SAN FRANCISCO|date=January 11, 2024|access-date=February 18, 2024}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.pfaw.org/blog-posts/biden-judges-uphold-injunction-against-citys-actions-punishing-homeless-people/?|title=Biden Judges Uphold Injunction Against City’s Actions Punishing Homeless People|website=People for the American Way|date=January 16, 2024|access-date=February 18, 2024}} On May 14, 2025, Koh upheld a federal district court's order blocking the Trump administration from cutting legal aid funding for migrants.{{Cite web|url=https://amicacenter.org/app/uploads/2025/05/17.1-panel-denial-of-govt-motion-to-stay-PI.pdf|title=Case: 25-2808, 05/14/2025, DktEntry: 17.1|website=amicacenter.org|date=2025-05-14|access-date=2025-08-06}}{{Cite web|url=https://justiceactioncenter.org/news/ninth-circuit-upholds-legal-protections-for-immigrant-children/|title=Ninth Circuit Upholds Legal Protections for Immigrant Children|website=Justice Action Center|date=2025-05-15|access-date=2025-08-06}} In October 2025, Koh and [[William A. Fletcher]] wrote a concurring opinion when the full 9th circuit declined to visit their previous ruling.{{Cite web|url=https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2025/10/10/25-2808.pdf|title=CMTY. LEGAL SERVICES V. U.S. HHS|website=ca9.uscourts.gov|date=2025-10-10|access-date=2025-12-21}} ==Personal life== Koh is married to [[Mariano-Florentino Cuéllar]], the former president of the [[Carnegie Endowment for International Peace]] and a former justice of the [[California Supreme Court]] and professor at [[Stanford Law School]].Howard Mintz, [https://www.mercurynews.com/2010/06/07/santa-clara-county-judge-becomes-first-asian-american-federal-judge-in-bay-area-history/ Santa Clara County judge becomes first Asian-American federal judge in Bay Area history], ''Mercury News''/Bay Area News Group (June 7, 2010). [[Cornell University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Mark Jeremy Bennett''' (born February 24, 1953) is a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]]. == Career == In 1976, Bennett obtained his [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in [[political science]] from [[Union College]] in [[Schenectady, New York|Schenectady]]. He attended [[Cornell Law School]] in [[Ithaca, New York|Ithaca]] where he sat on the Board of Editors of the ''[[Cornell Law Review]]''. There, he received his [[Juris Doctor]] in 1979. After leaving law school, Bennett became a law clerk to Chief Judge [[Samuel Pailthorpe King]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of Hawaii]]. Completing his clerkship, Bennett served as an [[Assistant United States Attorney]] for the [[United States District Court for the District of Columbia|District of Columbia]] from 1980 to 1982 and for the [[United States District Court for the District of Hawaii|District of Hawaii]] until 1990. In 1991, Bennett went into private legal practice as a partner at the firm of McCorriston Miller Mukai MacKinnon LLP. At the same time, he worked pro-bono for the attorney general's office and taught at the [[William S. Richardson School of Law]].{{cite web|url=http://hawaii.gov/ag/main/about_us/ag_bio|title=Attorney General Mark J. Bennett|publisher=Hawaii Department of the Attorney General|access-date=April 13, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081004150831/http://hawaii.gov/ag/main/about_us/ag_bio|archive-date=October 4, 2008 |url-status=dead}} He served as [[Attorney General of Hawaii]] from 2003 to 2010 in the two-term administration of [[Hawaii Republican Party|Republican]] [[Governor of Hawaii|Governor]] [[Linda Lingle]]. Bennett served as [[acting governor|Acting Governor of Hawaii]] from August 25 to September 3, 2004, upon the absence of Governor Linda Lingle and [[Lieutenant Governor of Hawaii|lieutenant governor]] [[Duke Aiona]].{{cite web|url=http://www.votesmart.org/bio.php?can_id=32250|title=Profile of Mark J. Bennett|publisher=Project Vote Smart|url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081028082736/http://www.votesmart.org/bio.php?can_id=32250 |archive-date=28 October 2008 |access-date=16 June 2025}} The executives left the Hawaiian Islands to attend the [[2004 Republican National Convention]] in [[New York City]]. == Federal judicial service == On February 12, 2018, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to nominate Bennett to an undetermined seat on the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]]. On February 15, 2018, his nomination was sent to the Senate. Bennett was nominated for the seat vacated by Judge [[Richard Clifton]], who assumed [[senior status]] on December 31, 2016. On April 11, 2018, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web|title=Nominations | United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/04/11/2018/nominations-1|access-date=2023-01-12|website=www.judiciary.senate.gov|date=April 11, 2018 |language=en}} On May 10, 2018, his nomination was reported out of committee by an 18–2 vote.[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%2005-10-18.pdf "Results of Executive Business Meeting – May 10, 2018, Senate Judiciary Committee"]. On July 9, 2018, the [[United States Senate]] invoked cloture on his nomination by a 72–25 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=115&session=2&vote=00144|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture on Mark Jeremy Bennett, of Hawaii, to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the Ninth Circuit)|website=www.senate.gov |access-date=2018-07-10}} On July 10, 2018, his nomination was confirmed by a 72–27 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1152/vote_115_2_00145.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Mark Jeremy Bennett, of Hawaii, to be United States Circuit Judge for the Ninth Circuit)|website=www.senate.gov |access-date=2018-07-10}} Most of the 27 votes against his confirmation came from Republican Senators due to his defense of Hawaii's restrictive firearms laws in court.{{cite news |last1=Swoyer |first1=Alex |title=27 Republicans vote against Trump pick for 9th Circuit |url=https://www.washingtontimes.com/news/2018/jul/10/27-republicans-vote-against-trumps-judge-9th-circu/ |access-date=15 May 2019 |work=Washington Times |date=July 10, 2018}} He received his judicial commission on July 13, 2018.{{FJC Bio|nid=4908101|inline=yes}} On August 16, 2019, Bennett was in the majority of a split panel for the Ninth Circuit which blocked new asylum restrictions by the Trump administration within its own jurisdiction but declined to block the new asylum rules across the entire nation.{{cite news |last1=Thomsen |first1=Jacqueline |title=Ninth Circuit Panel Fractures Over National Injunctions With Trump's Latest Asylum Order |url=https://www.law.com/therecorder/2019/08/16/ninth-circuit-panel-fractures-over-national-injunctions-with-trumps-latest-asylum-order/ |access-date=22 August 2019 |publisher=Law.com |date=August 16, 2019}} In September 2020, Bennett dissented when the panel majority found that a [[robocall]] defendant could not use the [[Federal Arbitration Act]] to compel enforcement of a customer agreement the plaintiff had signed years earlier with a separate company that had subsequently been acquired by the holding company that now also owned the defendant.{{Bluebook journal |first=|last=Note |title=Recent Case: Ninth Circuit Refuses to Enforce Infinite Arbitration Agreement |volume=134 |journal=[[Harvard Law Review|Harv. L. Rev.]] |page=2871 |url=https://harvardlawreview.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/134-Harv.-L.-Rev.-2871.pdf |year=2021}}{{cite court |litigants=Revitch v. DIRECTV, LLC |vol=977 |reporter=F.3d |opinion=713 |court=9th Cir. |date=2020 |url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=12949644032048028028 |accessdate=}} On December 4, 2021, Bennett was one of two judges who declined to halt San Diego Unified School District's requirements that students be vaccinated by December 20.{{Cite web|url=https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2021/12/04/21-56259.pdf|title=John Doe v. San Diego Unified School District|website=ca9.uscourts.gov|date=December 4, 2021|access-date=December 5, 2021}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/us/vaccine-mandate-for-san-diego-unified-students-moves-forward-after-federal-court-lifts-injunction/ar-AARuZQ0|title=Vaccine mandate for San Diego Unified students moves forward after federal court lifts injunction|website=MSN|date=December 5, 2021|access-date=December 5, 2021}} On September 6, 2022, Bennett wrote a concurring opinion in the 9th circuit decision upholding Washington's ban on [[conversion therapy]] for minors.{{Cite web|url=https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2022/09/06/21-35815.pdf|title=BRIANTINGLEY, Plaintiff-Appellant, v. ROBERT W. FERGUSON|website=ca9.uscourts.gov|date=September 6, 2022|access-date=January 21, 2024}} The Supreme Court denied ''certiorari'' on December 11, 2023.{{Cite web|url=https://www.vox.com/scotus/2023/12/11/23889129/supreme-court-conversion-therapy-washington-lgbtq-tingley-ferguson|title=The Supreme Court hands down a small but unexpected victory for LGBTQ people|website=Vox|date=December 11, 2023|access-date=January 21, 2024}} In June 2025, Bennett ruled that President Trump can keep control of the California National Guard in the wake of ICE raids.{{Cite web|url=https://calmatters.org/justice/2025/06/9th-circuit-los-angeles-national-guard/|title=Trump can keep troops in LA for now, appeals court rules|website=Cal Matters|date=2025-06-19|access-date=2025-08-06}} == Personal life == Bennett is married to Honolulu attorney Patricia Tomi Ohara. He has been a member of the [[Federalist Society]] since 2016.{{Cite web |title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Bennett%20SJQ13.pdf |access-date=June 30, 2018 |website=judiciary.senate.gov}} == References == {{Reflist|30em}} == External links == * {{FJC Bio|nid=4908101}} * [https://www.oyez.org/advocates/mark_j_bennett Appearances at the U.S. Supreme Court] from the [[Oyez Project]] * {{Ballotpedia|Mark_Bennett_(Hawaii)|Mark J. Mary H. Murguia:
{{Short description|American judge (born 1960)}} {{Use American English|date=June 2026}} {{Use mdy dates|date=June 2026}} {{Infobox officeholder |name = Mary Murguia |image = Judge Mary Murguia.jpg |office = Chief Judge of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]] |term_start = December 1, 2021 |term_end = |predecessor = [[Sidney R. Thomas]] |successor = |office1 = Judge of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]] |appointer1 = [[Barack Obama]] |term_start1 = January 4, 2011 |term_end1 = |predecessor1 = [[Michael Daly Hawkins]] |successor1 = |office2 = Judge of the [[United States District Court for the District of Arizona]] |appointer2 = [[Bill Clinton]] |term_start2 = October 13, 2000 |term_end2 = January 4, 2011 |predecessor2 = Seat established |successor2 = [[Diane Humetewa]] |birth_name = Mary Helen Murguia |birth_date = {{birth date and age|1960|9|6}} |birth_place = [[Kansas City, Kansas]], U.S. |death_date = |death_place = |relatives = [[Janet Murguía]] (sister)
[[Carlos Murguia]] (brother) |education = [[University of Kansas]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|BA]], [[Bachelor of Science|BS]], [[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Mary Helen Murguia''' (born September 6, 1960) is an American lawyer and jurist serving as the [[United States federal judge|Chief United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]]. She previously served as a U.S. district judge of the [[United States District Court for the District of Arizona]] from 2000 to 2011. == Early life and education == Murguia is one of seven children of Alfred and Amalia Murguia, who [[emigration|emigrated]] from [[Mexico]] in 1950.Manny Lopez, [http://www.bizjournals.com/kansascity/stories/2001/02/12/focus1.html Raising the Bar], ''[[American City Business Journals|Kansas City Business Journal]]'' (February 11, 2001). She was born in 1960 in [[Kansas City, Kansas|Kansas City]], [[Kansas]].{{cite web|url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/murguia-mary-helen|title=Murguia, Mary Helen – Federal Judicial Center|website=www.fjc.gov}} Murguia was raised in the Kansas City community of [[Argentine, Kansas|Argentine]]. Murguia earned two bachelor's degrees (a [[Bachelor of Arts]] and a [[Bachelor of Science]]) from the [[University of Kansas]] in 1982. She then earned a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Kansas Law School]] in 1985. == Professional career == Murguia served as an assistant district attorney of [[Wyandotte County, Kansas|Wyandotte County]], Kansas, from 1985 until 1990. From 1990 until 2000, Murguia served as an [[assistant United States attorney]] in the United States Attorney's Office for the District of Arizona, and concurrently served in the Executive Office for U.S. Attorneys from 1998 until 2000. She was counsel to the director's staff from 1998 until 1999, and the principal deputy director in 1999. She was a director from 1999 until 2000. == Federal judicial service == === District court service === On July 21, 2000, President [[Bill Clinton]] nominated Murguia to a new seat on the [[United States District Court for the District of Arizona]] that was created by 113 Stat. 1501. The [[United States Senate]] confirmed Murguia on October 3, 2000, and she received her commission on October 13, 2000. Her service as a district court judge was terminated on January 4, 2011 when she was elevated to the court of appeals. === Court of appeals service === On March 25, 2010, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Murguia to a fill a vacancy on the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]] that was created when Judge [[Michael Daly Hawkins]] assumed [[senior status]].{{cite web|url=http://legaltimes.typepad.com/blt/2010/03/former-doj-official-picked-for-9th-circuit.html |title=Former DOJ Official Picked for 9th Circuit |publisher=Legal Times |date=2010-03-25 |access-date=2010-03-26}} On December 22, 2010, she was confirmed by the United States Senate by a 89–0 vote.[https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=111&session=2&vote=00299 On the Nomination (Confirmation Mary Helen Murgia, of Arizona to be U.S. Circuit Judge)], ''senate.gov'' (December 22, 2010). On January 4, 2011, she received her commission and took the oath of office.{{cite web |title=Court's Newest Judge Takes Oath of Office |date=January 5, 2011 |work=US Courts for the Ninth Circuit Announcements |url=https://www.ca9.uscourts.gov/content/view.php?pk_id=0000000514 }} She became Chief Judge on December 1, 2021.{{cite web|url=https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/ce9/2021/12/Gavel_Passing.pdf|title=Gavel Passing Brings New Chief Judge to the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals|publisher=[[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]]|work=Public Information Office|date=December 1, 2021|accessdate=December 2, 2021}} She had been suggested as a [[Barack Obama Supreme Court candidates|potential nominee to the Supreme Court]] in Obama's second term.{{cite news |last1=Greg |first1=Stohr |title=Obama's Victory Creates New Chance to Mold U.S. Supreme Court |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2012-11-09/obama-s-victory-creates-new-chance-to-mold-u-s-supreme-court |access-date=July 8, 2014 |agency=Bloomberg |date=November 8, 2012}} == Notable rulings == === Elton Simpson case === {{see also|Curtis Culwell Center attack}} On March 14, 2011, Murguia [[Acquittal|acquitted]] acquitted Elton Simpson of making a false statement to federal agents involving terrorism, and released him on [[probation]] with a minor fine for lesser charges.{{cite news |first=Eugene |last=Volokh |author-link=Eugene Volokh |title=Why Elton Simpson, one of the Texas shooters, had been acquitted of an earlier terrorism-related offense |newspaper=[[Washington Post]] |date=May 4, 2015 |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/volokh-conspiracy/wp/2015/05/04/why-elton-simpson-one-of-the-texas-shooters-had-been-acquitted-of-an-earlier-terrorism-related-offense/ }} Simpson had allegedly lied to FBI agents about his intent to travel to [[Somalia]] to join up with terrorist groups to kill non-Muslims, but Murguia declined to enhance his sentence based on the government's evidence. Four years later, Simpson was one of two terrorists who attacked a free speech event in Texas, injuring an unarmed security guard and being killed in the process. Evidence indicated that after Murguia released him, Simpson became involved with the terrorist organization [[Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant]], who immediately after the attack claimed Simpson was a "soldier for the caliphate".{{cite news |title=Texas Attacker Left Trail of Extremist Ideas on Twitter |first=Scott |last=Shane |date=May 5, 2015 |work=[[New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/05/06/world/middleeast/isis-texas-muhammad-cartoons.html }} === ''Melendres v. Arpaio'' === Murguia [[Recusal|recused]] herself from the federal racial profiling case against [[Maricopa County]] Sheriff [[Joe Arpaio]] in February 2009. Arpaio's attorneys alleged Murguia had, "...a natural, personal bias in favor of the Plaintiffs," based upon her sister's leadership of National Council of La Raza, which has been highly critical of Arpaio.{{cite web|last1=Lemons|first1=Stephen|title=Joe Arpaio Scores: Judge Mary Murguia Recuses Self From Racial Profiling Lawsuit Against Joe Arpaio|url=http://www.phoenixnewtimes.com/blogs/joe-arpaio-scores-judge-mary-murguia-recuses-self-from-racial-profiling-lawsuit-against-joe-arpaio-6498674|website=Phoenix New Times|publisher=Village Voice Media|access-date=11 June 2016}} The Melendres case was reassigned. In May 2013, Judge [[G. Murray Snow]] ruled that Arpaio had indeed engaged in racial profiling. In 2014, Snow found Arpaio had violated court orders addressing cessation of racial profiling, and began proceedings to hold Arpaio in [[contempt of court]]. Arpaio has also accused Snow of bias, and initiated previously-secret investigations into the alleged bias.{{cite web|last1=Kiefer|first1=Michael|title=Murray Snow: The man judging Sheriff Joe|url=http://www.azcentral.com/story/news/local/phoenix/2015/06/05/judge-murray-snow-sheriff-joe-arpaio/28554351/|website=AZCentral.com|publisher=The Arizona Republic|access-date=11 June 2016}} === ''The United States of America v. Victor Manuel Raya-Vaca'' === In 2014, a case was brought by the United States of America against Raya-Vaca, on the grounds of illegal entry, but the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit|9th Circuit Court of Appeals]] deemed that the defendant was judged with bias and therefore reversed the lower court’s opinion.{{Cite web|title=UNITED STATES OF AMERICA v. VICTOR MANUEL RAYA-VACA § (2014)|url=https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2014/11/10/13-50129.pdf|website=cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov}} Judge Murguia wrote in the opinion that Raya-Vaca was the victim of bias and that the government had acted without due process of his rights and therefore the legal grounds for his ejection were not a solid legal basis for his removal. === ''Jesse James Andrews v. Ron Davis'' === In 2018, this ''[[en banc]]'' case held that Jesse Andrew did not receive proper constitutionally granted counsel during the first phase of the legal system.{{Cite web|title=JESSE JAMES ANDREWS v. RON DAVIS § (2018)|url=https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2019/12/16/09-99012_.pdf|website=cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov}} Initially, Andrews was raised in a segregated and poverty-stricken area of Mobile, Alabama at a school that has since been shuttered based on their violations of the [[Eighth Amendment to the United States Constitution|Eighth Amendment]]. Because of this, Murguia wrote that mitigating information was not told to the court and therefore the death penalty should not be judged by those standards. === ''Grigoryan v. Barr'' === In 2019, Judge Murguia and the panel of judges ruled that the [[Board of Immigration Appeals]] violated the petitioners’ rights as immigrants.{{Cite web|title=ELEN GRIGORYAN; SIRUN HARUTYUNYAN; ARTAVAZD GRIGORYAN; KAREN GRIGORYAN v. WILLIAM P. BARR § (2019)|url=https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2020/06/02/16-73652.pdf|website=cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov}} The violation concerned the actions that the government took that disabused the plaintiffs’ rights of due process before their status was terminated. The basis of this decision was supported by the fact that the Board did not provide “sufficient” information to the Plaintiffs. Judge Murguia wrote that even though they were in the U.S. for fourteen years, they were not judged fairly and given the proper information and denied their relief of deportation based on a single page that didn’t hold up under scrutiny. === ''Ashley Judd v. Harvey Weinstein'' === In the 2020 opinion written by Judge Murguia for the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit|9th Circuit Court of Appeals]], she and her fellow judges overturned the lower court’s ruling since they deemed an incorrect application of statutes since her case was thrown out.{{Cite web|title=ASHLEY JUDD v. HARVEY WEINSTEIN § (2020)|url=https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2020/07/29/19-55499.pdf|website=cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov}} Based on statute. Cal. Civ. Code § 51.9(a)(1)(F) (1996), the panel headed by Murguia ruled that their relationship constituted by the statute and therefore Weinstein was suited to use his leverage to allegedly abuse the plaintiff. This ruling and the following opinion reversed the ruling from the [[Supreme Court of California]]. This case was also instrumental to the cohesion of the [[Me Too movement|Me Too]] movement as well. == Personal life== Murguia's twin sister is noted civil rights leader [[Janet Murguía]], while her older brother, [[Carlos Murguia]], was a United States district judge.{{cite web |title=106 Senate Hearings |work=From the U.S. Government Printing Office via GPO Access |url=http://ftp.resource.org/gpo.gov/hearings/106s/73475.txt |archive-date=March 10, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120310143938/http://ftp.resource.org/gpo.gov/hearings/106s/73475.txt }} == See also == *[[Barack Obama Supreme Court candidates]] *[[List of first women lawyers and judges in Arizona]] *[[List of Hispanic and Latino American jurists]] == References == {{Reflist}} ==Sources== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1391261}} *{{Ballotpedia|Mary_Murguia|Mary Murguia}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-new|seat}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States District Court for the District of Arizona]]}}|years=2000–2011}} {{s-aft|after=[[Diane Humetewa]]}} |- {{s-bef|before=[[Michael Daly Hawkins]]}} {{s-ttl|title=Judge of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]]|years=2011–present}} {{s-inc|rows=2}} |- {{s-bef|before=[[Sidney R. Thomas]]}} {{s-ttl|title=Chief Judge of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]]|years=2021–present}} {{s-end}} {{United States Judicial Conference}} {{USCourtsOfAppealsJudges}} {{Authority control}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Murguia, Mary Helen}} [[Category:1960 births]] [[Category:Living people]] [[Category:20th-century American judges]] [[Category:20th-century American women judges]] [[Category:21st-century American women judges]] [[Category:Assistant United States attorneys]] [[Category:Hispanic and Latino American judges]] [[Category:Hispanic and Latino American lawyers]] [[Category:Judges of the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]] [[Category:Judges of the United States District Court for the District of Arizona]] [[Category:People from Kansas City, Kansas]] [[Category:United States court of appeals judges appointed by Barack Obama]] [[Category:United States district court judges appointed by Bill Clinton]] [[Category:University of Kansas School of Law alumni]]

Hurwitz]] | birth_date = {{birth date and age|1940|12|04}} | birth_place = [[Boulder, Colorado]], U.S. | death_date = | death_place = | education = [[Swarthmore College]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|BA]])
[[University of Chicago]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Mary Murphy Schroeder''' ([[née]] '''Murphy'''; born December 4, 1940) is an American attorney and jurist serving as a [[United States federal judge|senior United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]]. == Early life and education == [[File:Mary M. Schroeder.jpg|thumb|left|Schroeder with her Ninth Circuit predecessor, [[Procter Ralph Hug Jr.|Procter Hug]] (2012)]] Born on December 4, 1940, in [[Boulder, Colorado]], Schroeder received her [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[Swarthmore College]] in 1962 and her [[Juris Doctor|J.D.]] degree from the [[University of Chicago Law School]] in 1965, one of six women in her class.{{cite web|url=http://207.41.19.15/Web/OCELibra.nsf/3cf90a23430db5a9852562840073ae37/ed6034c6e95f169d882569a700695274?OpenDocument |title=Judge Mary M. Schroeder becomes Chief Judge of the Ninth Circuit. News release |access-date=2008-11-21 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110529223510/http://207.41.19.15/Web/OCELibra.nsf/3cf90a23430db5a9852562840073ae37/ed6034c6e95f169d882569a700695274?OpenDocument |archive-date=2011-05-29 }} She received an honorary [[Doctor of Laws]] (Legum Doctor (LL.D.) from Swarthmore in May 2006. == Career == Schroeder practiced as a trial attorney with the [[United States Department of Justice Civil Division]] from 1965 until 1969. She served as a [[law clerk]] to Justice [[Jesse Addison Udall]] of the [[Arizona Supreme Court]] in 1970. She joined the law firm of [[Lewis & Roca]] in [[Phoenix, Arizona]], in 1971 and became a partner in 1973. She was appointed to the [[Arizona Court of Appeals]] in 1975 and served until 1979.{{FJC Bio|2119|nid=1387476|name=Mary Murphy Schroeder}} Schroeder was elected to the [[American Law Institute]] in 1974 and was elected to the ALI Council in 1993.[http://www.ali.org/index.cfm?fuseaction=about.officerslist American Law Institute - Officers and Council] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120925021943/http://www.ali.org/index.cfm?fuseaction=about.officerslist|date=2012-09-25}} She served as an Adviser on the Restatement Third of Agency and serves as an adviser on the Restatement Third, The Law of Consumer Contracts[http://www.ali.org/index.cfm?fuseaction=projects.members&projectid=25 Restatement Third, the Law of Consumer Contracts - Project Participants] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140106180027/http://www.ali.org/index.cfm?fuseaction=projects.members&projectid=25|date=2014-01-06}} and Principles of Government Ethics.[http://www.ali.org/index.cfm?fuseaction=projects.members&projectid=22 Principles of Government Ethics - Project Participants] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140407080351/http://www.ali.org/index.cfm?fuseaction=projects.members&projectid=22|date=2014-04-07}} She served as president of the National Association of Women Judges in 1998-99.{{Cite web |title=Past Presidents {{!}} National Association of Women Judges |url=https://www.nawj.org/about-nawj/past-presidents |access-date=2023-06-26 |website=www.nawj.org}} ===Federal judicial service=== Schroeder was nominated by President [[Jimmy Carter]] on May 3, 1979, to the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]], to a new seat authorized by 92 Stat. 1629. She was confirmed by the [[United States Senate]] on September 25, 1979, and received her commission on September 26, 1979. She served as the first female chief judge of the Ninth Circuit from 2000 to 2007. She assumed [[senior status]] on December 31, 2011. === Awards === Schroeder has received numerous prestigious awards, including but not limited to: * the American Law Institute's [https://www.ali.org/news/articles/john-minor-wisdom-award-margaret-h-marshall-and-mary-m-schroeder/ John Minor Wisdom Award in 2023] * the Arizona State Bar Association's James A. Walsh Outstanding Jurist Award * the American Bar Association's [https://www.americanbar.org/groups/diversity/women/margaret-brent-awards/pasthonorees/ Margaret Brent Award] * the Joan Dempsey Klein NAWJ Honoree of the Year Award In addition, the Arizona State University Law School has [https://law.asu.edu/newsroom/asu-law-honors-faculty-students-graduation-awards named two awards after Schroeder]: * the Mary M. Schroeder Public Interest Prize * the Judge Mary M. Schroeder Federal Practice Award == Notable cases == * The northern [[spotted owl]], a case related to the [[Endangered Species Act]] * The [[Napster]] file trading software [[copyright infringement]] appeal. * ''[[Hirabayashi v. United States]]'' [[coram nobis]] in which the opinion authored by Schroeder vacated the infamous convictions of Gordon Hirabayashi for refusing to report to a control center and breaking curfew during the [[internment of Japanese Americans]] during World War II * In CAPEEM v. Torlakson, Schroeder rejected a claim that California schools inaccurately portrayed Hinduism.{{cite web |title=Ninth Circuit Tosses Claims of Anti-Hindu Bias in California Schools |url=https://www.courthousenews.com/ninth-circuit-tosses-claims-of-anti-hindu-bias-in-california-schools/ |website=[[Courthouse News Service]] |access-date=21 May 2021 |language=en}} * ''[[Jespersen v. Harrah's Operating Co.]]'' holding an employer's grooming standards that appropriately discriminate by gender (here requiring women to wear makeup to work) are not facially discriminatory under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e et seq. * In August 2015, Schroeder found that the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of California]]'s policy of indiscriminately shackling criminal defendants in all pretrial hearings violated the Constitution's [[Due Process Clause]].{{Bluebook journal |first=|last=Note| title=Recent Case: Ninth Circuit Deems Unconstitutional Routine Shackling in Pretrial Proceedings| volume=131 | journal=[[Harvard Law Review|Harv. L. Rev.]] | page=1163 | url=https://harvardlawreview.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/1163-1170_Online.pdf| year=2018}}{{cite court |litigants=United States v. Sanchez-Gomez|vol=798 |reporter=F.3d |opinion=1204|court=9th Cir.|date=2015|url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11286111609155867842}} Her judgment was affirmed by the narrowly divided circuit ''[[en banc]]'', before being vacated by the unanimous [[Supreme Court of the United States]].{{cite court |litigants=United States v. Sanchez-Gomez|vol=859 |reporter=F.3d |opinion=649|court=9th Cir.|date=2017) (en banc|url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=10428058978903876951}}{{cite web |title=United States v. Sanchez-Gomez |url=https://www.oyez.org/cases/2017/17-312 |website=[[Oyez Project]] |access-date=11 March 2019 |language=en}} * On December 14, 2016, Schroeder in a unanimous opinion upheld California's 10-day waiting period for firearm purchases under the now-abrogated intermediate scrutiny.{{Cite web |date=December 14, 2016 |title=Silvester v. Harris Appellate Opinion |url=https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.ca9.261012/gov.uscourts.ca9.261012.9028615265.1.pdf |access-date=February 3, 2024 |website=CourtListener}} *{{Cite web|url=https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2021/05/14/19-71930.pdf|title=A Community Voice v. USEPA|website=cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov|date=May 14, 2021|access-date=May 20, 2021}} (May 14, 2021): Schroeder ruled that the EPA failed to properly examine lead standards, and that it must reconsider those standards.{{Cite web|url=https://www.law360.com/productliability/articles/1384971|title=9th Circ. Says EPA Must Revisit Lead-Related Standards|website=Law360|date=May 14, 2021|access-date=May 20, 2021}} Schroeder concluded her opinion by writing "Consistent with our holding in this opinion that the EPA must reconsider the DLHS, we direct the EPA to reconsider the clearance levels as well in the same proceeding. Both sets of standards must work together to effectuate Congress's intent to end the hazards of [[lead poisoning]] in our children." == Personal life == She was married to Milton Schroeder (d. 2025), a professor at the [[Sandra Day O'Connor College of Law]], and has two children, Katherine and [[Caroline T.
