[[Seton Hall University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Michael Arthur Chagares'''[https://books.google.com/books?id=eOsnflnvvCEC&pg=PA424 Confirmation Hearings on Federal Appointments: Hearings Before the Committee on the Judiciary, United States Senate, One Hundred Ninth Congress, First Session, Part 3] (born May 1, 1962) is an American lawyer who has served as the chief judge of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit]] since 2020. He was appointed to the court by President [[George W. Bush]] in 2006. ==Education== Chagares received his [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[Gettysburg College]] in 1984 and his [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Seton Hall University School of Law]] in 1987. ==Legal career== Chagares began his legal career as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Morton Ira Greenberg]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit]] from 1987 to 1988. Chagares was in private practice the next two years before joining the [[United States Department of Justice]] as an [[assistant United States attorney]] in 1990. He rose to become chief of the Civil Division for the [[U.S. Attorney for the District of New Jersey|U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of New Jersey]] in 1999, but left the Justice Department in 2004 to return to private practice at Cole Schotz in [[Hackensack, New Jersey]]. Since 1991, Chagares has been an [[adjunct professor]] at [[Seton Hall University School of Law]].{{cite web|title=Adjunct Faculty|url=http://law.shu.edu/Faculty/adjunct-faculty.cfm|publisher=Seton Hall School of Law|access-date=April 21, 2017}} ==Federal judicial service== Chagares was nominated to the Third Circuit by President [[George W. Bush]] on January 25, 2006, to fill the seat vacated by [[Michael Chertoff]], who resigned to become [[Secretary of Homeland Security]].{{cite web|title=Judicial Nominations-Michael Chagares|url=https://georgewbush-whitehouse.archives.gov/infocus/judicialnominees/chagares.html|publisher=The White House-G.W. Bush|access-date=April 21, 2017}} Chagares's nomination generated no controversy and moved unusually swiftly through the [[United States Senate]], and he was confirmed just over two months later on April 4, 2006, by a 98–0 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=109&session=2&vote=00086|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Michael A. Chagares, of New Jersey, to be U.S. Circuit Judge)}} He received his commission on April 20, 2006.{{FJC Bio|nid=1392371|inline=yes}} On November 17, 2021, it was announced that Chagares will become the next Chief Judge of the Third Circuit, effective on December 4, 2021.{{cite web|url=https://www.ca3.uscourts.gov/sites/ca3/files/Judge%20Chagares%20Press%20Release.pdf|title=Judge Chagares Press Release|publisher=[[United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit]]|date=November 17, 2021|accessdate=December 2, 2021}} ==Writings== Chagares co-authored the non-fiction book ''New Jersey Federal Civil Procedure''.{{cite web|url=https://www.law.columbia.edu/sites/default/files/2020-06/2019_hfs_moot_court_judge_bios.pdf |title=Court Judge Bios |website=[[Columbia Law School|law.columbia.edu]] |access-date=December 18, 2023}} ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1392371}} *[https://web.archive.org/web/20140907191704/http://articles.philly.com/2006-01-26/news/25411344_1_mayor-milton-milan-camden-federal-bench "Prosecutor Bumb picked for U.S. bench; The assistant U.S. attorney's big wins include Milton Milan's conviction"], ''[[The Philadelphia Inquirer]]'', January 26, 2006 {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Michael Chertoff]]}} {{s-ttl|title=Judge of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit]]|years=2006–present}} {{s-inc|rows=2}} |- {{s-bef|before=[[D. {{Short description|American judge (born 1976)}} {{pp-semi-protected|small=yes}} {{Use mdy dates|date=October 2018}} {{Infobox officeholder | name = Michael Park | image = Michael H. Lynch]] | successor = | birth_name = Michael Hun Park | birth_date = {{birth date and age|1976|4|1}} | birth_place = [[Saint Paul, Minnesota]], U.S. | death_date = | death_place = | spouse = Sarah Seo | education = [[Princeton University]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|BA]])
[[Yale University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Michael Hun Park''' (born April 1, 1976){{Cite web |url=https://vettingroom.org/2019/03/06/michael-park/ |title=Michael Park – Nominee to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit |last=Voruganti |first=Harsh |date=2019-03-06 |website=The Vetting Room |language=en |access-date=2019-05-20}} is an American lawyer who serves as a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit]].{{cite web |title=Michael H. Park |url=https://www.ca2.uscourts.gov/judges/bios/mhp.html |website=United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit |access-date=June 19, 2024}} Prior to becoming a judge, Park was a named partner at Consovoy McCarthy (originally Consovoy McCarthy Park), a prominent law firm in the conservative legal movement.{{cite web |title=Hon. Michael Park |url=https://fedsoc.org/contributors/michael-park |website=The Federalist Society |access-date=June 19, 2024}} Park was appointed by [[Donald Trump]] and is a member of the [[Federalist Society]].{{cite web |title=Nomination of Michael H. Park to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit Questions for the Record |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Park%20Responses%20to%20QFRs.pdf |website=judiciary.senate.gov |access-date=June 19, 2024}} == Early life and education == Park is a graduate of the [[Thomas Jefferson High School for Science and Technology]].[http://ny.koreatimes.com/article/20181015/1208637 Korea Times] Park earned his [[Bachelor of Arts]], ''magna cum laude'', from [[Princeton University]], and his [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Yale Law School]] in 2001, where he served as managing editor of the ''[[Yale Law Journal]]''.{{cite web |title=Masthead-Board of editors |url=https://www.yalelawjournal.org/masthead/volume-110 |publisher=Yale Law Journal |access-date=October 11, 2018 |date=2000–2001}} == Early career == After graduating from law school, Park served as a [[law clerk]] to then-Judge [[Samuel Alito]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit]]. From 2002 to 2006, he was an associate in the [[New York City]] office of [[Wilmer Cutler Pickering Hale and Dorr]]. Park was an attorney-advisor in the [[United States Department of Justice]] [[Office of Legal Counsel]] for two years, and then again clerked for Alito during the 2008–2009 term after he became an associate justice of the [[Supreme Court of the United States]].{{cite web |title=Opinions of the Office of Legal Counsel, Vol 32, 2008 |url=https://www.justice.gov/olc/file/477051/download |publisher=United States Department of Justice |access-date=October 11, 2018 |page=iv |date=2014}}{{cite book |title=Confirmation Hearing on the Nomination of Samuel A. Alito, Jr. to be an Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States before the Judiciary Committee of the United States Senate |date=2006 |publisher=Diane Publishing |isbn=9781422332429 |page=1026 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cQPWT1nb6soC&q=%22michael+h.+park%22&pg=PA1027 |access-date=October 11, 2018}} There, he was a co-clerk with [[Andy Oldham]]. He was counsel at [[Dechert]] from 2009 to 2011 and a partner from 2012 to 2015.{{cite web |title=Press release: Dechert's Michael H. Park Named Among 'Best Lawyers Under 40' by National Asian Pacific American Bar Association |url=https://www.dechert.com/knowledge/news/2013/11/dechert-s-michael-h-park-named-among-best-lawyers-under-40-by-n.pdf |publisher=Dechert |date=November 19, 2013 |access-date=October 11, 2018}} From 2015 to 2019, he practiced as a name partner at the boutique litigation firm Consovoy McCarthy Park PLLC.{{cite news |last1=Lat |first1=David |author-link1=David Lat |title=Prominent Young Partners Leave Biglaw For A High-Powered Boutique |url=https://abovethelaw.com/2015/05/prominent-young-partners-leave-biglaw-for-a-high-powered-boutique/ |work=Above The Law |date=May 28, 2015 |access-date=October 12, 2018}}{{cite web |title=AABANY in the News |url=https://www.aabany.org/page/536 |publisher=Asian American Bar Association of New York |date=2015 |access-date=October 11, 2018}}{{cite web |url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-eighteenth-wave-judicial-nominees-eighteenth-wave-united-states-attorney-nominees-thirteenth-wave-united-states-marshal-nominees/ |title=President Donald J. Trump Announces Eighteenth Wave of Judicial Nominees, Eighteenth Wave of United States Attorney Nominees, and Thirteenth Wave of United States Marshal Nominees |date=October 10, 2018 |via=[[NARA|National Archives]] |work=[[whitehouse.gov]] |access-date=October 10, 2018 }} {{PD-notice}} In 2016, Park represented the [[Kansas Department of Health and Environment]] in its effort to cut off [[Medicaid]] funding to [[Planned Parenthood]].{{cite news |last1=Margolies |first1=Dan |title=Kansas Retains High-Powered Law Firm In Planned Parenthood Battle |url=http://www.jcpost.com/2016/06/12/kansas-retains-high-powered-law-firm-in-planned-parenthood-battle/ |access-date=October 11, 2018 |work=Junction City Post |date=June 12, 2016}} In 2017, Park led efforts to challenge a [[United States Environmental Protection Agency]] (EPA) rule under the [[Clean Water Act]] that sought to expand the statute's protection of wetlands.{{cite web |title=Brief for the Chamber of Commerce |url=https://www.scotusblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/16-299-amicus-pet-chamber.pdf |website=scotusblog.com |access-date=June 19, 2024}} In 2018, Park worked on behalf of Project on Fair Representation to defend the Trump Administration's efforts to insert a citizenship question into the [[2020 United States census]].{{cite web |title=MOTION FOR LEAVE TO FILE BRIEF AMICUS CURIAE OF PROJECT ON FAIR REPRESENTATION IN SUPPORT OF DEFENDANTS’ MOTION TO DISMISS |url=https://www.brennancenter.org/sites/default/files/legal-work/New-York_v_Dept-of-Commerce_Motion-for-Leave-to-File-Amicus-Brief_Project-on-Fair-Representation.pdf |website=Brennan Center: Copy of Filing in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York |access-date=June 19, 2024}} Park is an adjunct professor at the [[Antonin Scalia Law School]], where he teaches the Supreme Court Clinic.{{cite web |title=Legal Clinic – Supreme Court |url=https://www.law.gmu.edu/academics/clinics/supreme_court_legal_clinic/ |publisher=Antonin Scalia Law School, George Mason University |access-date=October 11, 2018}} He is also an adjunct professor at [[Columbia Law School|Columbia Law School.]]{{Cite web |title=Michael Park |url=https://www.law.columbia.edu/faculty/michael-park |access-date=January 27, 2023 |website=[[Columbia Law School]]}} He is a member of the Board of Trustees of the [[Supreme Court Historical Society]], the Board of Directors of Operation Exodus Inner City, the Asian American Bar Association of New York and the [[Federalist Society]].{{cite web |title=Michael H. Park bio |date=September 17, 2015 |url=https://fedsoc.org/contributors/michael-park |publisher=The Federalist Society |access-date=October 11, 2018}} == Federal judicial service == On October 10, 2018, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to nominate Park to serve as a United States Circuit Judge of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit]]. Park became the second Asian Pacific American and the first Korean American to serve on the Second Circuit.{{cite news |last1=Tae-hee |first1=Lee |title=Korean-American judges gaining presence in US |url=http://www.koreaherald.com/view.php?ud=20181211000462 |access-date=18 February 2019 |publisher=The Korea Herald |date=December 11, 2018}} On November 13, 2018, his nomination was sent to the Senate. President Trump nominated Park to the seat vacated by Judge [[Gerard E. Lynch]], who took [[senior status]] on September 5, 2016.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/twenty-six-nominations-sent-senate/ "Twenty Six Nominations Sent to the Senate", White House, November 13, 2018] Park was on a list the Trump White House sent to New York Senators [[Chuck Schumer]] and [[Kirsten Gillibrand]] in July that included three other names for the Second Circuit, where there were two vacancies - the other names were then-United States District Judge [[Richard J. Sullivan]]; Matthew McGill, a partner at the law firm [[Gibson Dunn]] in [[Washington, D.C.]] and [[Nicholas Quinn Rosenkranz]], a professor at [[Georgetown University Law Center]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.buzzfeednews.com/article/zoetillman/the-white-house-has-pitched-a-nominee-for-manhattans|title = The White House Has Pitched a Nominee for Manhattan's Powerful US Attorney Opening| website=[[BuzzFeed News]] | date=August 7, 2017 }} On January 3, 2019, his nomination was returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]]. On January 23, 2019, [[Donald Trump|President Trump]] announced his intent to renominate Park for a federal judgeship.[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-intent-nominate-judicial-nominees/ "President Donald J. Trump Announces Intent to Nominate Judicial Nominees", White House, January 23, 2019] His nomination was sent to the Senate later that day [https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/nominations-sent-senate-2/ "Nominations Sent to the Senate", White House, January 23, 2019] On February 13, 2019, a hearing on Park's nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/02/13/2019/nominations United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Nominations for February 13, 2019] Schumer and Gillibrand, the two Democratic Senators from Park's home state, refused to return [[Blue slip (U.S. Senate)|blue slips]] for his nomination.{{cite web |title=Judges Confirmed to Second Circuit Despite ‘Blue Slip’ Objections |url=https://www.leadershipconnect.io/courts/judges-confirmed-to-second-circuit-despite-blue-slip-objections/ |website=leadershipconnect.io |access-date=June 19, 2024}} Despite this, on March 7, 2019, the committee proceeded with the nomination and reported out it by a party-line 12–10 vote.[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/03.07.2019%20Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting.pdf Results of Executive Business Meeting – March 7, 2019, Senate Judiciary Committee] On May 8, 2019, the U.S. Senate invoked [[Cloture]] on his nomination by a vote of 51–43.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=116&session=1&vote=00105|title=U.S. Senate: U.S. Senate Roll Call Votes 116th Congress - 1st Session}} On May 9, 2019, Park's nomination was confirmed by a vote of 52–41.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1161/vote_116_1_00106.htm|title=U.S. Senate: U.S. Senate Roll Call Votes 116th Congress - 1st Session}} He received his judicial commission on May 13, 2019.{{FJC Bio|nid=6420566|inline=yes}} == Personal life == Park is married to Sarah Seo,[https://blog.aabany.org/2019/07/15/robing-ceremony-of-the-hon-michael-h-park/ AABANY blog] a legal historian and Professor of Law at [[Columbia Law School]].{{Cite web|title=Sarah A. Seo|url=https://www.law.columbia.edu/faculty/sarah-seo|website=Columbia Law School}} == See also == * [[Donald Trump Supreme Court candidates]] * [[List of Asian American jurists]] * [[List of law clerks for the eighth seat of the Supreme Court of the United States]] == References == {{Reflist}} == Select publications == * {{cite news |last1=Park |first1=Michael H. |title=Court's 'No-Action' Clause Holding May Surprise Bond Issuers |url=https://www.dechert.com/content/dam/dechert/uploads/documents/Litigation/Court’s%20‘No-Action’%20Clause%20Holding%20May%20Surprise%20Bond%20Issuers.pdf |work=New York Law Journal |date=September 8, 2014}} (posted at Dechert) == External links == * {{FJC Bio|nid=6420566}} * {{Ballotpedia|Michael_Park|Michael Park}} * [https://www.nationalreview.com/bench-memos/who-is-michael-park/ Bio], National Review {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Gerard E. Michael Y. Scudder:
{{Short description|American judge (born 1971)}} {{Infobox judge | name = Michael Scudder | image = Michael Scudder (Judge) (cropped).jpg | caption = Scudder in 2018 | office = Judge of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit]] | appointer = [[Donald Trump]] | term_start = May 21, 2018 | term_end = | predecessor = [[Richard Posner]] | successor = | birth_name = Michael Yale Scudder Jr. | birth_date = {{birth year and age|1971|}} | birth_place = [[Fort Wayne, Indiana|Fort Wayne]], [[Indiana]], U.S. | death_date = | death_place = | spouse = {{marriage|Sarah Schoenle|July 3, 1993}} | education = [[Saint Joseph's College (Indiana)|Saint Joseph's College]] ([[Bachelor of Business Administration|BBA]])
[[Northwestern University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Michael Yale Scudder Jr.''' (born 1971) is a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit]]. == Education and legal career == In 1989, Scudder graduated from Bishop Dwenger High School in [[Fort Wayne, Indiana|Fort Wayne]], [[Indiana]].{{Cite web|url=http://journalgazette.net/news/local/20180213/dwenger-grad-tapped-for-7th-circuit|title=Dwenger grad tapped for 7th Circuit | Local | Journal Gazette|date=13 February 2018 }} Scudder received his [[Bachelor of Business Administration]] from [[Saint Joseph's College (Indiana)|Saint Joseph's College]] as co-[[valedictorian]], and his [[Juris Doctor]] in 1998 ''[[magna cum laude]]'' from the [[Northwestern University Pritzker School of Law]], where he was inducted into the [[Order of the Coif]].{{cite web|title=Campaign Cabinet-Motion to Lead: The Campaign for Northwestern Pritzker School of Law|url=https://www.law.northwestern.edu/campaign/cabinet/|publisher=Pritzker School of Law, Northwestern University|access-date=February 14, 2018}}{{cite web|title=Major Gifts-Motion to Lead: The Campaign for Northwestern Pritzker School of Law|url=https://www.law.northwestern.edu/campaign/major-gifts/|publisher=Pritzker School of Law, Northwestern University|access-date=February 14, 2018}} Scudder worked as an auditor for [[Ernst and Young]] before attending law school and is a [[Certified Public Accountant]]. Following law school, Scudder served as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Paul V. Niemeyer]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit]] from 1998 to 1999, and then for Justice [[Anthony Kennedy]] of the [[Supreme Court of the United States]] from 1999 to 2000.{{cite web| title=Michael Yale Scudder Jr| url=https://lawyers.justia.com/lawyer/michael-yale-scudder-jr-452659| website=justia.com| access-date=March 3, 2022}} Following his clerkships, he first worked as an attorney for two years at [[Jones Day]] in [[Cleveland, Ohio]]. He then served as: [[Assistant United States Attorney]] for the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York|Southern District of New York]] from 2002 to 2006; counsel to the [[United States Department of Justice National Security Division|National Security team]] of the [[U.S. Department of Justice]] in 2006;{{cite news|last1=Meisner|first1=Jason|last2=Skiba|first2=Katherine|title=4 finalists for U.S. attorney's job in Chicago emerge|url=http://www.chicagotribune.com/news/local/politics/ct-chicago-us-attorney-search-met-20170622-story.html|access-date=February 13, 2018|work=Chicago Tribune|date=June 23, 2017}} associate counsel to President [[George W. Bush]] in the [[White House Counsel]]'s office in 2007; and as the [[general counsel]] of the [[United States National Security Council|National Security Council]] from 2007 to 2009. He served as a partner of [[Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom]] in [[Chicago]], [[Illinois]] from 2009 to 2018. Additionally, he has taught at the [[Northwestern Pritzker School of Law]] and at the [[University of Chicago Law School]].[https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-eleventh-wave-judicial-nominees/ "President Donald J. Trump Announces Eleventh Wave of Judicial Nominees" White House, February 12, 2018] {{PD-notice}} == Federal judicial service == On February 12, 2018, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his intent to nominate Scudder to a seat on the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit]].{{cite news|title=Morning Spin: Cullerton throws budget shade at Rauner ahead of big speech|url=http://www.chicagotribune.com/news/local/politics/ct-bruce-rauner-john-cullerton-budget-20180213-story.html|access-date=February 13, 2018|work=Chicago Tribune|date=February 13, 2018}}{{cite news|last1=Sweet|first1=Lynn|title=Trump taps Scudder, St. Eve for Chicago based seats on Court of Appeals|url=https://chicago.suntimes.com/2018/2/14/18394795/trump-taps-scudder-st-eve-for-chicago-based-seats-on-court-of-appeals|access-date=February 14, 2018|work=[[Chicago Sun-Times]]|date=February 12, 2018}} On February 15, 2018, his nomination was sent to the Senate. Scudder — The Judiciary, congress.gov] On March 21, 2018, a hearing on his nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/03/21/2018/nominations United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Nominations for March 21, 2018] On April 19, 2018, his nomination was reported out of committee by a 21–0 vote.[https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting%2004-19-18.pdf Results of Executive Business Meeting – April 19, 2018, Senate Judiciary Committee] On May 14, 2018, the [[United States Senate]] confirmed his nomination by a 90–0 vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=115&session=2&vote=00092|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Michael Y. Scudder, of Illinois, to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the Seventh Circuit)|date=May 14, 2018|website=[[United States Senate]]|access-date=May 14, 2018|language=en}} Scudder received his commission on May 21, 2018.{{FJC Bio|nid=4622996|inline=yes}} == Personal life == On July 3, 1993, Scudder married Sarah Rose Schoenle in [[Allen County, Indiana]].{{cite web|title=Allen County Marriage Records from State Indexes, 1958–1991, 1993–2004, 2006–2017|url=https://www.acgsi.org/marriage2/sc.asp|website=ACGSI.org|publisher=Allen County Genealogical Society of Indiana}} Scudder once served as vice chairman of the Board of Advisors of the Catholic Charities, [[Archdiocese of Chicago]].{{cite web|title=Board of Advisors|url=https://catholiccharities.net/AboutUs/Governance/BoardofAdvisors.aspx|publisher=Catholic Charities, Archdiocese of Chicago|access-date=February 14, 2018}} == See also == * [[List of law clerks for the first seat of the Supreme Court of the United States]] == References == {{Reflist}} == External links == * {{FJC Bio|nid=4622996}} * {{Ballotpedia|Michael_Scudder|Michael Scudder}} * [https://www.skadden.com/professionals/s/scudder-michael-y Biography at Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom] {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Richard Posner]]}} {{s-ttl|title={{nowrap|Judge of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit]]}}|years=2018–present}} {{s-inc}} {{s-end}} {{United States courts of appeals judges}} {{Authority control}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Scudder, Michael Y.}} [[Category:1971 births]] [[Category:Living people]] [[Category:20th-century American lawyers]] [[Category:21st-century American lawyers]] [[Category:American accountants]] [[Category:Assistant United States attorneys]] [[Category:George W. Michelle Friedland:
{{Short description|American judge (born 1972)}} {{Infobox officeholder | name = Michelle Friedland | image = 2022 Judge Michelle Friedland.png | caption = Friedland in 2022 | office = Judge of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]] | appointer = [[Barack Obama]] | term_start = April 29, 2014 | term_end = | predecessor = [[Raymond C. Fisher]] | successor = | birth_date = {{birth year and age|1972|}} | birth_place = [[Berkeley, California|Berkeley]], [[California]], U.S. | death_date = | death_place = | spouse = {{marriage|Daniel Kelly|June 17, 2000}} | education = [[Stanford University]] ([[Bachelor of Science|BS]], [[Juris Doctor|JD]])
[[Wolfson College, Oxford]] (attended) }} '''Michelle Taryn Friedland''' (born in 1972) is a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]]. ==Biography== ===Early life and education=== Friedland was born in [[Berkeley, California|Berkeley]], [[California]].{{cite news | first=Maura | last=Dolan | url=https://www.latimes.com/local/lanow/la-me-ln-9th-circuit-appointees-20130801,0,7565477.story | title=Two lawyers from same California firm nominated for 9th Circuit | work=[[Los Angeles Times]] | date=August 1, 2013 | access-date=August 2, 2013}} She graduated from [[The Pingry School]] in [[Basking Ridge, New Jersey|Basking Ridge]], [[New Jersey]].[https://www.pingry.org/uploaded/Student_Life/Publications/Review/review-mar2014.pdf#page=53 "Class Notes"], ''Pingry Review'', March 2014. Accessed March 14, 2022. "1990: Michelle Friedland has been nominated by President Obama to serve on the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit." She received a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree in biology in 1995 from [[Stanford University]], graduating [[Phi Beta Kappa]].{{cite web |title=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary: Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Michelle-Friedland-Senate-Questionnaire-Final.pdf |website=judiciary.senate.gov |access-date=June 13, 2024}} She then studied philosophy at [[Wolfson College, Oxford]], as a [[Fulbright Scholar]], returning to California for law school. She received a [[Juris Doctor]] in 2000 from [[Stanford Law School]], graduating [[Order of the Coif]] and second in her class.{{cite web|url=http://www.mto.com/lawyers/Michelle-T-Friedland|title=Biography at Munger, Tolles and Olsen LLP|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130814063138/http://mto.com/lawyers/Michelle-T-Friedland|archive-date=2013-08-14}} She served as a law clerk to Judge [[David Tatel]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit]] and then served as a law clerk to Justice [[Sandra Day O'Connor]] of the [[United States Supreme Court]]. She completed a two-year lectureship at [[Stanford Law School]] before entering private practice.{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2013/08/01/president-obama-nominates-three-serve-united-states-courts-appeals|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Obama Nominates Three to Serve on the United States Courts of Appeals|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|date=1 August 2013}} She has been married to Daniel Kelly since June 17, 2000.{{cite web |title=Weddings; Michelle Friedland, Daniel Kelly |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2000/06/18/style/weddings-michelle-friedland-daniel-kelly.html |access-date=November 7, 2024 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=June 18, 2000}} ===Professional career=== Before her confirmation, Friedland served as a litigation partner in the San Francisco office of [[Munger, Tolles & Olson LLP]]. She joined the firm in 2004 as an associate, becoming a partner in January 2010. She has extensive litigation experience at the state and federal trial court and appellate levels, including litigating before the United States Supreme Court. During her legal career, Friedland represented a number of corporate clients in cases involving a wide range of legal issues, including antitrust, tax, patent, copyright, and consumer class actions. She also frequently represented the [[University of California]] in cases involving constitutional issues. She maintained an active ''pro bono'' practice. The State Bar of California named a Munger team including Friedland a recipient of the 2013 President's Pro Bono Service Award.{{cite web |url=http://www.calbar.ca.gov/AboutUs/Awards/PresidentsProBonoService/2013.aspx |title=President's Pro Bono Service 2013 |publisher=The State Bar of California}} Friedland also has served as an adjunct professor at the [[University of Virginia Law School]], teaching a course on constitutional issues in higher education. ==Federal judicial service== [[File:Friedland Applauded by Justice O'Connor (Ret).jpg|thumb|Friedland being applauded by Justice [[Sandra Day O'Connor]] (Ret.) after being administered the oath of office on June 13, 2014]] On August 1, 2013, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Friedland to a seat on the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]]. She filled the seat that was vacated by Judge [[Raymond C. Fisher]], who assumed [[senior status]] on March 31, 2013. On January 16, 2014, the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] reported her nomination out of committee by a 14–3 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/ExecutiveBusinessMeetingResults-01-16-2014.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting - January 16, 2014|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=November 1, 2022}} On April 10, 2014, the [[United States Senate]] invoked cloture on her nomination by a 56–41 vote.{{cite web|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture on the Nomination of Michelle T. Friedland, of California, to be U.S. Circuit Judge)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=113&session=2&vote=00106|publisher=United States Senate|access-date=10 April 2014}} On April 28, 2014, her nomination was confirmed by a 51–40 vote.{{cite web|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Michelle T. Friedland, of California, to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the Ninth Circuit)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=113&session=2&vote=00108|publisher=United States Senate|access-date=28 April 2014}} She received her judicial commission on April 29, 2014.{{cite web|url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/friedland-michelle-taryn|title=Friedland, Michelle Taryn – Federal Judicial Center|website=www.fjc.gov}} Justice [[Sandra Day O'Connor]] administered the oath of office to Friedland at her formal investiture on June 13, 2014, in the [[James R. Browning United States Court of Appeals Building]] in [[San Francisco]]. At the time of her appointment Friedland, then 41, ranked fourth among the youngest appointees to the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit|Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals]].{{cite web|url=http://www.ce9.uscourts.gov/absolutenm/articlefiles/698-Friedland_Confirmed.pdf|title=Senate Confirms Michelle T. Friedland to Seat on Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals|publisher=United States Courts for the Ninth Circuit|work=Public Information Office|access-date=30 April 2014}} [[File:Friedland Sitting on Bench.jpg|thumb|Friedland taking her seat as Circuit Judge for the Ninth Circuit]] ==Notable cases== On February 4, 2017, Friedland and Judge [[William Canby]] rejected{{Cite web|url=http://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/general/2017/02/05/17-35105.pdf|title=Order denying immediate administrative stay pending full consideration of the emergency motion for stay and setting schedule|last1=Canby|first1=William|last2=Friedland|first2=Michelle|date=February 4, 2017|access-date=February 6, 2017}} the [[First presidency of Donald Trump|Trump administration]]'s request for an administrative stay{{Cite web|url=http://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/general/2017/02/04/17-35105%20motion.pdf|title=Emergency Motion Under Circuit Rule 27–3 for Administrative Stay and Motion for Stay Pending Appeal|last=Francisco|first=Noel|date=February 4, 2017|access-date=February 6, 2017}} of the district court's temporary restraining order in [[Washington v. Trump (2017)|State of Washington v. Trump]], part of the ongoing court cases related to [[Executive Order 13769]], pending full review in the Ninth Circuit. On February 7, Friedland, Canby, and Judge [[Richard Clifton]] heard oral arguments on the emergency motion to stay, with an audio feed{{Citation|last=United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit|title=17-35105 State of Washington, et al. v. Donald J. Trump et al.|date=2017-02-07|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RPOFowWqFGU|access-date=2017-02-09}} of the telephonic argument broadcast nationwide.{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/02/06/us/politics/trump-travel-ban-court.html|title=Justice Department Urges Appeals Court to Reinstate Trump's Travel Ban|last=Liptak|first=Adam|date=2017-02-06|newspaper=The New York Times|access-date=2017-02-07|issn=0362-4331}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.ca9.uscourts.gov/content/motionspanel.php|title=Motions Panel|website=www.ca9.uscourts.gov|language=en-us|access-date=2017-02-07}} On February 9, the three judges denied the request for a stay of the temporary restraining order.{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/02/09/us/politics/appeals-court-trump-travel-ban.html|title=Court Refuses to Reinstate Travel Ban, Dealing Trump Another Legal Loss|last=Liptak|first=Adam|date=2017-02-09|newspaper=The New York Times|access-date=2017-02-09|issn=0362-4331}}{{Cite web|url=https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2017/02/09/17-35105.pdf|title=Published Order Denying Stay|date=February 9, 2017|website=Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals|access-date=February 9, 2017}} The case was notably parodied by [[Saturday Night Live]], with Judge Friedland being portrayed by [[Vanessa Bayer]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dLYfwprjtog|title = Trump People's Court - SNL|website = [[YouTube]]| date=12 February 2017 }} On July 3, 2019, in another high-profile ruling, Friedland and [[Richard R. Clifton]] upheld a district court's halting of parts of [[Donald Trump]]'s wall. [[N. Randy Smith]] issued a dissent, and on July 26, the Supreme Court overturned Friedland and Clifton by a 5–3 vote, with [[Stephen Breyer]] saying he would temporarily block the construction of the wall but allow funding to be set aside for it.{{Cite web| title=Sierra club; Southern border communities coalition, v. Donald J. Trump, in his official capacity as President of the United States; et al. | url=http://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2019/07/03/19-16102.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190704034421/http://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2019/07/03/19-16102.pdf | archive-date=2019-07-04}}{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/07/26/us/politics/supreme-court-border-wall-trump.html|title=Supreme Court Lets Trump Proceed on Border Wall|first=Adam|last=Liptak|newspaper=The New York Times|date=July 26, 2019}} On August 16, 2021, Friedland (joined by Ronald Gould & Jill Otake) upheld an EPA ruling that the Sacketts' property contained wetlands that were protected by the Clean Water Act. {{Cite web|url=https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2021/08/16/19-35469.pdf|title=MICHAEL SACKETT; CHANTELL SACKETT, Plaintiffs-Appellants, v. U.S. ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AGENCY; MICHAEL S. REGAN, Administrator, Defendants-Appellees.|website=ca9.uscourts.gov|date=August 16, 2021|access-date=February 11, 2024}} The 9th circuit was reversed by the Supreme Court in [[Sackett v. Environmental Protection Agency (2023)]], which held that only wetlands with a "continuous surface connection" to waters of the United States were protected by the Clean Water Act. In ''Garcia v. City of Los Angeles'', decided on September 2, 2021, Friedland ruled that the city of Los Angeles cannot seize and discard the "bulky items" of homeless individuals.{{Cite web|url=https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2021/09/02/20-55522.pdf|title=No. 20-55522 Garcia v. City of Los Angeles|website=cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov|date=September 2, 2021|access-date=September 5, 2021}} On January 2, 2024, Friedland wrote a dissent from denial of en banc in ''California Restaurant Association v. City of Berkeley'', a case where the original panel overturned the City of Berkeley's ban on natural gas in new buildings. Friedland was joined by Chief Judge Murguia, Judges Wardlaw, Gould, Koh, Sung, Sanchez, & Mendoza. In Friedland's nearly 10 years on the bench, this is the first time she has written a dissent from denying en banc.{{Cite web|url=https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2024/01/02/21-16278.pdf|title=CALIFORNIA RESTAURANT ASSOCIATION, a California nonprofit mutual benefit corporation, Plaintiff-Appellant, vs. CITY OF BERKELEY, Defendant-Appellee.|website=ca9.uscourts.gov|date=January 2, 2024|access-date=January 2, 2024}} ==Personal life== Friedland is married to Daniel Kelly.{{cite news |title=WEDDINGS; Michelle Friedland, Daniel Kelly |date=June 18, 2000 |work=New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2000/06/18/style/weddings-michelle-friedland-daniel-kelly.html }} ==See also== * [[List of Jewish American jurists]] * [[List of law clerks for the eighth seat of the Supreme Court of the United States]] * [[Joe Biden Supreme Court candidates]] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1394436}} *{{Ballotpedia|Michelle_T._Friedland|Michelle T. [[University of Chicago]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Milan Dale Smith Jr.''' (born 1942) is an American attorney and jurist serving as a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]].{{cite book|title=Who's Who in American Law|author=Marquis Who's Who, Inc|date=1977|publisher=Marquis Who's Who, LLC|isbn=9780837935010|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=z41DAQAAIAAJ|access-date=2015-04-13}} Smith's brother, [[Gordon H. Smith]], was a [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] U.S. [[United States Senate|Senator]] from 1997 to 2009. Milan Smith is neither a Republican nor a Democrat, and he considers himself to be a political independent.{{Cite web|url=https://www.deseret.com/2022/6/27/23171027/a-good-judge-of-character-milan-smith-jr-george-w-bush-court-partisanship-school-prayer|title=A good judge of character|website=Deseret News|date=June 27, 2022|access-date=July 21, 2022}} Smith is married to Kathleen Denise Crane, a trust and estates attorney.{{Cite web |title=Steady Wins the Race |url=https://www.torrancememorialfoundation.org/news/steady-wins-race |access-date=2025-10-01 |website=Torrance Memorial Foundation |language=en}} == Early life and education == Smith was born in [[Pendleton, Oregon|Pendleton]], [[Oregon]]. He is the son of Milan D. Smith, Sr., who served as chief of staff of the [[United States Department of Agriculture|Department of Agriculture]] under [[United States Secretary of Agriculture|Secretary]] [[Ezra Taft Benson]]. Smith received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[Brigham Young University]] in 1966. Smith attended the [[University of Chicago Law School]] on a full-tuition scholarship, graduating in 1969 with a [[Juris Doctor|J.D.]] degree. == Career == After law school, Smith became an associate attorney at the Los Angeles firm of [[O'Melveny & Myers]]. In 1972, Smith left O'Melveny to co-found his own law firm, Smith & Hilbig, which eventually became Smith, Crane, Robinson & Parker. He was a President-General Counsel of the Los Angeles State Building Authority from 1983 to 2006. Smith was a Vice Chairman of the California Fair Employment and Housing Commission from 1987 to 1991. === Federal judicial service === Smith was nominated by President [[George W. Bush]] on February 14, 2006, to fill a seat vacated by Judge [[A. Wallace Tashima]].{{cite web|url=https://georgewbush-whitehouse.archives.gov/news/releases/2006/02/20060214-4.html |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |publisher=georgewbush-whitehouse.archives.gov|access-date=2015-04-13}} The Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary of the [[American Bar Association]] rated him "well qualified," the highest possible rating.{{Cite web |date=January 10, 2008 |title=Ratings of Article III Judicial Nominees for the 109th Congress |url=https://www.americanbar.org/content/dam/aba/administrative/federal_judicary/ratings109.pdf}} He was confirmed just over three months later by the [[United States Senate]] on May 16, 2006, by a 93–0 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=109&session=2&vote=00120 |title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Milan D. Smith, Jr., of California, to be U.S. Circuit Judge) |publisher=senate.gov|date=January 27, 2015|access-date=2015-04-13}} He was the fifth judge appointed to the Ninth Circuit by Bush, and the first since [[Carlos Bea]] was confirmed in 2003. He received his commission on May 18, 2006.{{FJC Bio|nid=1392401|inline=yes}} In 2022, Smith told the [[Deseret News]] that he has no plans to retire and wishes to "die with my boots on."{{cite web | url=https://www.deseret.com/2022/6/27/23171027/a-good-judge-of-character-milan-smith-jr-george-w-bush-court-partisanship-school-prayer | title=Confidence in the Supreme Court is falling. This conservative judge thinks he knows why | date=28 June 2022 }} == Notable cases == Smith has been one of the Ninth Circuit's most prolific writers. According to one periodical, he authored the most majority opinions of any judge on the Ninth Circuit in the three-year period ending on May 10, 2013.Scott Graham, The Recorder, "At the Ninth Circuit, Moderates Do the Talking." May 10, 2013 === First Amendment === * {{cite court |litigants=United States v. Alvarez|vol=617 |reporter=F.3d|opinion=1198 |court=9th Cir.|date=2010|url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=3332503989513069132&q=617+F.3d+1198&hl=en&as_sdt=6,48}} Smith wrote the majority opinion, which struck down the [[Stolen Valor Act of 2005]]. The panel ruled 2 to 1 that the law violated the [[First Amendment]]. "The right to speak and write whatever one chooses—including, to some degree, worthless, offensive and demonstrable untruths—without cowering in fear of a powerful government is, in our view, an essential component of the protection afforded by the First Amendment," Smith wrote in the majority opinion. The [[U.S. Supreme Court]] affirmed the judgment in a [[United States v. Alvarez|6–3 decision]]. * {{cite court |litigants=Comite de Jornaleros v. City of Redondo Beach|vol=657 |reporter=F.3d|opinion=936 |court=9th Cir.|date=2011|url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=15901930064674762628&q=657+F.3d+936&hl=en&as_sdt=6,48}} Smith, writing for the majority of an 11-judge [[en banc]] panel, concluded that an ordinance of the City of [[Redondo Beach, California]], that barred day laborers from soliciting work from occupants of motor vehicles violated the Free Speech Clause of the First Amendment. * {{cite court |litigants=Protectmarriage.com-Yes on 8 v. Bowen|vol=752 |reporter=F.3d|opinion=827 |court=9th Cir.|date=2014|url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=17065231173382667412&q=752+F.3d+827&hl=en&as_sdt=6,48}} Smith, writing for a divided panel, rejected an effort by contributors to California's anti-gay marriage ballot measure, [[Proposition 8]], to shield their identities from disclosure. The opinion rejected a Free Speech Clause challenge to the California requirement that committees report donations made before the election but after the pre-election reporting deadline, and that certain other aspects of the donors' challenges were either moot or not ripe because the information the donors sought to keep confidential had already been published across the internet. * {{cite court |litigants=Kennedy v. Bremerton School District|vol=869 |reporter=F.3d|opinion=813 |court=9th Cir.|date=2017|url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=9409884593517831860&q=869+F.3d+813&hl=en&as_sdt=6,48}} Writing on behalf of an undivided panel, Smith held that a high school football coach spoke as a public employee when he would kneel and pray on the 50-yard line immediately after games, in full school apparel, while in view of students and parents. Because the coach's demonstrative conduct was made in his capacity as a public employee, the school did not illegally retaliate against him when the school ordered the coach not to speak in the manner that he did. Smith also noted that the school district's action was justified in order to avoid violating the [[Establishment Clause]]. The 9th circuit denied en banc on July 19, 2021, with Smith writing a concurring opinion.{{Cite web |date=2021-07-19 |title=JOSEPH A. KENNEDY, Plaintiff-Appellant, v. BREMERTON SCHOOL DISTRICT, Defendant-Appellee.|url=https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2021/07/19/20-35222.pdf|access-date=2024-12-23 |website=ca9.uscourts.gov |language=en-US}} Certiorari was granted in the case on January 14, 2022.{{Cite news |title=Kennedy v. Bremerton School District |url=https://www.scotusblog.com/case-files/cases/kennedy-v-bremerton-school-district-2/ |website=SCOTUSblog}} The U.S. Supreme Court reversed the judgment in a [[Kennedy v. Bremerton School District|6–3 decision]]. In her dissent, [[Sonia Sotomayor|Justice Sonia Sotomayor]] echoed Smith's observation that the coach's argument that he only wanted to conduct his own private prayer while seeking no attention from his players or the public was flatly contradicted by the facts in the record.{{Cite web |date=2022-06-27 |title=Neil Gorsuch 'Misconstrues The Facts' In School Prayer Case |url=https://www.huffpost.com/entry/bremerton-school-prayer-joseph-kennedy_n_62ba18c2e4b0326883a8a9b8 |access-date=2024-03-13 |website=HuffPost |language=en}}{{Cite news |last=Blake |first=Aaron |date=2022-06-29 |title=Analysis {{!}} Gorsuch and Sotomayor’s extraordinary factual dispute |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2022/06/29/gorsuch-sotomayor-praying-coach/ |access-date=2024-03-13 |work=Washington Post |language=en-US |issn=0190-8286}}{{Cite web |date=2022-06-27 |title=Justices side with high school football coach who prayed on the field with students |url=https://www.scotusblog.com/2022/06/justices-side-with-high-school-football-coach-who-prayed-on-the-field-with-students/ |access-date=2024-03-13 |website=SCOTUSblog |language=en-US}} * {{cite court |litigants=Herring Networks, Inc. v. Maddow|vol=8 |reporter=F.4th|opinion=1148 |court=9th Cir.|date=2021|url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=5290404362576241359&q=8+F.4th+1148&hl=en&as_sdt=2003}} Smith dismissed a defamation lawsuit against [[Rachel Maddow]]. He ruled that Maddow's words that [[One America News Network|OAN]] “really literally is paid Russian propaganda" could not amount to defamation and that her speech is protected by the First Amendment. * {{cite court |litigants=Tucson v. City of Seattle|vol=91 |reporter=F.4th|opinion=1318 |court=9th Cir.|date=2024|url=https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2024/02/02/23-35449.pdf}} Smith wrote the majority opinion, which reversed the district court’s order preliminarily enjoining the City of [[Seattle]] from enforcing its anti-graffiti ordinance. Writing for an undivided panel, Smith criticized the district court for enjoining the ordinance as overbroad without acknowledging “the numerous applications of the ordinance that would not implicate any protected speech, such as spray-painting an individual’s private home, vehicle, or other private property, or chalking messages on an individual’s private driveway.” [[The Seattle Times]] characterized the ruling as “a victory for [[Seattle City Attorney]] [[Ann Davison (politician)|Ann Davison]], who made public disorder and specifically graffiti crackdowns central to her campaign two years ago.”{{Cite web |date=2024-02-02 |title=Seattle’s graffiti law reinstated by Court of Appeals |url=https://www.seattletimes.com/seattle-news/politics/seattles-graffiti-law-reinstated-by-court-of-appeals/ |access-date=2024-03-13 |website=The Seattle Times |language=en-US}} * ''NetChoice v. Bonta'', 113 F.4th 1101 (9th Cir. 2024). Writing for a unanimous panel, Smith partially upheld and partially vacated a preliminary injunction issued by [[Beth Labson Freeman|Judge Beth Labson Freeman]] that had previously blocked the enforcement of California's Age-Appropriate Design Code Act ("CAADCA"). Smith agreed with Judge Freeman that the CAADCA likely violated the First Amendment insofar as it required online companies to assess and report on potential content-related harms to children. However, Smith vacated the rest of the district court's injunction, finding that it was unclear whether the other provisions of the CAADCA, such as those related to default privacy settings and the prohibition of using children's data in harmful ways, also violated the First Amendment. * ''Hunter v. U.S. Dep't of Educ.'', 115 F.4th 955 (9th Cir. 2024). Writing for an undivided panel, Smith affirmed a lower court's dismissal of a constitutional challenge to [[Title IX]]'s exemption for sex-based discrimination at religious post-secondary institutions that receive federal funding. Smith held that Congress, “within its constitutional boundaries,” adequately balanced the interests of religious freedom and gender-based equality, both of which are protected under the American Constitution. * ''X Corp. v. Bonta'', 116 F.4th 888 (9th Cir. 2024). Smith, writing for a unanimous panel, blocked the state of California from enforcing a law that requires large social media platforms to report how they moderate especially controversial categories of speech, finding that certain provisions of the law violate the First Amendment. === Second Amendment === * {{cite court |litigants=United States v. Henry|vol=688 |reporter=F.3d|opinion=637 |court=9th Cir.|date=2012|url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=9122864920515362069&q=688+F.3d+637&hl=en&as_sdt=6,48}} Smith, writing for a unanimous three-judge panel, upheld a conviction for the possession of a homemade machine gun. Rejecting the defendant's [[Second Amendment]] claim based on ''[[District of Columbia v. Heller]]'', 554 U.S. 570 (2008), Smith wrote that machine guns are "dangerous and unusual weapons" that are not "typically possessed by law-abiding citizens for lawful purposes," and that their possession is not protected by the Second Amendment. * ''United States v. Duarte'' (9th Cir. 2024). Smith dissented from the majority opinion, which held that the felon-in-possession statute, 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1), violates the [[Second Amendment to the United States Constitution|Second Amendment]] as applied to non-violent offenders who have served their time in prison and reentered society. Smith urged the court to rehear the case en banc. === Fourth Amendment === * {{cite court |litigants=Estate of Lopez v. Gelhaus|vol=871 |reporter=F.3d|opinion=998 |court=9th Cir.|date=2017|url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=10022886165218899631&q=871+F.3d+998&hl=en&as_sdt=6,48}} Smith authored the majority opinion affirming the denial of summary judgment based on [[qualified immunity]], where a deputy sheriff fatally shot a 13-year-old boy. Viewing the facts in the light most favorable to the plaintiffs, the panel concluded that the deputy deployed deadly force within seconds after exiting his vehicle while the boy was walking in the opposite direction on an adjacent sidewalk, holding what appeared to be a gun pointed at the ground, without warning about the amount of force that would be used, and without observing any aggressive behavior by the boy. Because the boy did not pose an immediate threat to law enforcement officials or anyone else, the law clearly established that the deputy's conduct was unconstitutional and the deputy was not entitled to qualified immunity. The U.S. Supreme Court later [[certiorari|denied cert]].{{Cite web |title=June 25, 2018 Orders List |url=https://www.supremecourt.gov/orders/courtorders/062518zor_g3bh.pdf}} * {{cite court |litigants=Snitko v. United States|vol=90 |reporter=F.4th|opinion=1250 |court=9th Cir.|date=2024|url=https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2024/01/23/22-56050.pdf}} Writing for a unanimous panel, Smith rebuked the FBI for its March 2021 raid on US Private Vaults in Beverly Hills, California, in which it seized over 700 safe deposit boxes and attempted to civilly forfeit each box's contents.{{Cite web |last=Rector |first=Kevin |last2= |last3= |last4= |date=2024-01-24 |title=Appeals court finds FBI did violate rights of some Beverly Hills safe-deposit box holders |url=https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2024-01-23/appeals-court-finds-fbi-did-violate-rights-of-some-beverly-hills-safe-deposit-box-holders |access-date=2024-03-13 |website=Los Angeles Times |language=en-US}} Smith also wrote a separate concurrence indicating his view that the inventory search doctrine should categorically not extend to searches of safe deposit boxes in a locked vault. Many observers celebrated the ruling as a crucial win for individuals' Fourth Amendment rights.{{Cite web |last=Boehm |first=Eric |date=2024-01-23 |title=Appeals Court: FBI's safe-deposit box seizures violated Fourth Amendment |url=https://reason.com/2024/01/23/appeals-court-fbis-safe-deposit-box-seizures-violated-fourth-amendment/ |access-date=2024-03-13 |website=Reason.com |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |last=Wimer |first=Andrew |date=January 23, 2024 |title=Federal Appeals Court Slams FBI’s Actions In Security Deposit Box Raid |url=https://ij.org/press-release/federal-appeals-court-slams-fbis-actions-in-security-deposit-box-raid/}} === Environmental law === * {{cite court |litigants=Karuk Tribe of California v. U.S. Forest Service|vol=681 |reporter=F.3d|opinion=1006 |court=9th Cir.|date=2012|url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11771938237862345250&q=681+F.3d+1006&hl=en&as_sdt=6,48}} Smith dissented from an en banc decision of the court holding that a federal agency's decision to refrain from acting triggered the [[Endangered Species Act]]'s interagency consultation process. The dissent began with a reproduction of a woodcut and excerpt from [[Jonathan Swift]]'s ''[[Gulliver's Travels]]'', depicting and describing the eponymous traveler's capture by the [[Lilliputians]]—an unusual sight in the [[Federal Reporter]]. * {{cite court |litigants=Cottonwood Env't L. Ctr. v. Edwards|vol=86 |reporter=F.4th|opinion=1255 |court=9th Cir.|date=2023|url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=9093708394420992214&q=86+F.4th+1255&hl=en&as_sdt=2003}} Writing for an undivided panel, Smith held that the passage of pollutants through natural groundwater before reaching navigable waters necessarily triggered application of the Supreme Court's "functional equivalent" test from its decision in {{cite court |litigants=Cnty. of Maui, Hawaii v. Hawaii Wildlife Fund|vol=140 |reporter=S. Ct.|opinion=1462 |court=|date=2020|url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=375141810380080689&q=140+S.Ct.+1462&hl=en&as_sdt=2003}} === Intellectual property === * {{cite court |litigants=Williams v. Gaye|vol=885 |reporter=F.3d|opinion=1150 |court=9th Cir.|date=2018|url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=8791668563997281436&q=885+F.3d+1150&hl=en&as_sdt=6,48}} Smith wrote the majority opinion for a divided panel, which upheld a [[Pharrell Williams v. Bridgeport Music|jury verdict]] finding that the 2013 song "[[Blurred Lines]]" infringed on [[Marvin Gaye]]'s estate's [[copyright]] to the 1977 song "[[Got To Give It Up]]." The decision rested on narrow grounds based on the procedural posture of the case. * ''Gray v. Hudson'', 28 F.4th 87 (9th Cir. 2022). Writing for a unanimous panel, Smith wrote an opinion upholding the district court's [[Gray v. Perry|decision]] to overturn a $2.78 million award in a copyright lawsuit against the singer [[Katy Perry]] and several other defendants. In the lawsuit, the plaintiffs alleged that Perry's song "[[Dark Horse (Katy Perry song)|Dark Horse"]] impermissibly copied an [[ostinato]] (i.e., repeated musical figure) from their song "Joyful Noise." Smith agreed with the district court that the plaintiffs failed to show that Perry or her co-defendants had copied elements of "Joyful Noise" that were sufficiently original to be protectable under copyright law, stating: "The portion of the 'Joyful Noise' ostinato that overlaps with the 'Dark Horse' ostinato consists of a manifestly conventional arrangement of musical building blocks. Allowing a copyright over this material would essentially amount to allowing an improper monopoly over two-note pitch sequences or even the minor scale itself." Smith's opinion did not comment on other issues decided by the district court, concluding that it was unnecessary to "reach any other issue in this case." Smith's ruling was recognized within the legal community as one of the most important copyright decisions of 2022.{{Cite web |date=8 July 2022 |title=The Biggest Copyright Rulings Of 2022: A Midyear Report |url=https://www.kirkland.com/news/in-the-news/2022/07/the-biggest-copyright-rulings-of-2022 |website=Kirkland & Ellis}}{{Cite web |title=The Biggest Copyright Rulings Of 2022 |url=https://www.cozen.com/news-resources/news/2022/the-biggest-copyright-rulings-of-2022 |access-date=2024-07-17 |website=www.cozen.com |language=en}} === Labor, employment, and antitrust === * {{cite court |litigants=Tibble v. Edison International|vol=843 |reporter=F.3d|opinion=1187 |court=9th Cir.|date=2016|url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=12428205595963450636&q=843+F.3d+1187&hl=en&as_sdt=6,48}} On remand from the U.S. Supreme Court, Smith authored an opinion on behalf of a unanimous en banc panel that vacated the district court's judgment in favor of an employer and its benefits plan administrator on claims of breach of [[fiduciary duty]] in the selection and retention of certain mutual funds for a benefit plan governed by [[ERISA]]. Smith reasoned that federal law imposes on fiduciaries an ongoing duty to monitor investments, even absent a change in circumstances. Looking to the law of trusts, the duty of prudence requires fiduciaries to reevaluate investments periodically and to take into account their power to obtain favorable investment products, particularly when those products were substantially identical—other than their lower cost—to products they had already selected. * {{cite court |litigants=In re Nat'l Collegiate Athletic Ass'n Athletic Grant-in-Aid Cap Antitrust Litig.|vol=958 |reporter=F.3d|opinion=1239 |court=9th Cir.|date=2020|url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=8955059460304581980&q=958+F.3d+1239&hl=en&as_sdt=2003}} Smith authored a concurring opinion in which he largely joined the majority's finding that rules implemented by the [[National Collegiate Athletic Association]] capping the amount of grant-in-aid that [[student-athletes]] are permitted to receive from their school as part of an [[athletic scholarship]] was in violation of antitrust law as an illegal restraint of trade. Smith wrote separately to argue that the majority's use of cross-market analysis to assign a procompetitive benefit to benefit of the NCAA's amateurism restrictions in developing a separate and distinct market for amateur college sports was against the legislative purpose of the Sherman Antitrust Act. Writing that the treatment of student-athletes "is the result of a cartel of buyers acting in concert to artificially depress the price that sellers could otherwise receive for their services"—exactly the "sort of distortion" that the antitrust laws were designed to prohibit—Smith argued that the majority's analysis "seems to erode the very protections a Sherman Act plaintiff has the right to enforce" by limiting the extent of the relief afforded to student-athletes despite their being "quite clearly deprived of the fair value of their services." After the case was appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court, [[Brett Kavanaugh|Justice Brett Kavanaugh]] shared the same concerns as Smith, stating that antitrust laws "should not be a cover for exploitation of the student athletes."{{Cite web |last=Quinn |first=Melissa |date=2021-06-21 |title=Supreme Court rules for student-athletes in battle over NCAA limits on certain benefits - CBS News |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/supreme-court-ncaa-ruling-student-athletes-benefits/ |access-date=2024-03-13 |website=www.cbsnews.com |language=en-US}} * {{cite court |litigants=Epic Games, Inc. v. Apple, Inc.|vol=67 |reporter=F.4th|opinion=946 |court=9th Cir.|date=2023|url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4412900701356352496&q=67+F.4th+946&hl=en&as_sdt=2003}} Smith authored the majority opinion, which affirmed the district court’s conclusion that [[Apple Inc.|Apple]]’s [[App Store (Apple)|App Store]] anti-steering rules violated California’s Unfair Competition Law and upheld the nationwide injunction against those rules.  The panel also affirmed the district court’s conclusion that Epic had failed to provide sufficient evidence showing that Apple’s prohibition on app distribution outside of the App Store and its related requirement that developers exclusively use Apple’s In-App Purchase payment system for purchases within an app violate federal antitrust laws. The U.S. Supreme Court later denied cert.{{Cite web |last=Robertson |first=Adi |date=2024-01-16 |title=Supreme Court rejects Epic v. Apple antitrust case |url=https://www.theverge.com/2024/1/16/24039983/supreme-court-epic-apple-antitrust-case-rejected |access-date=2024-03-13 |website=The Verge |language=en}} === Other notable cases === * {{cite court |litigants=United States v. California|vol=921 |reporter=F.3d|opinion=865 |court=9th Cir.|date=2019|url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4151096663030776370&q=921+F.3d+865&hl=en&as_sdt=6,48}} Smith, writing for a unanimous panel, largely upheld a district court's denial of the federal government's motion to enjoin California's [[sanctuary city|sanctuary state]] laws, including SB 54, the [[California Senate Bill 54 (2017)|California Values Act]]. The panel mostly rejected the government's [[Intergovernmental immunity (United States)|intergovernmental immunity]] and preemption arguments, concluding instead that the [[Tenth Amendment to the United States Constitution|Tenth Amendment's]] anticommandeering doctrine precluded the government's attempt to force state and local officials to assist with immigration enforcement efforts. The panel concluded: "SB 54 may well frustrate the federal government's immigration enforcement efforts. However, whatever the wisdom of the underlying policy adopted by California, that frustration is permissible, because California has the right, pursuant to the anticommandeering rule, to refrain from assisting with federal efforts." The U.S. Supreme Court later denied cert.{{Cite web |title=U.S. Supreme Court, Proceedings and Orders, No. 19-532 |url=https://www.supremecourt.gov/search.aspx?filename=/docket/docketfiles/html/public/19-532.html}} * ''State of California v. Azar'' (9th Cir. 2020). On February 24, 2020, Smith was in a 7-4 majority that upheld a gag rule that prohibited funding to programs that included abortion in family planning.{{Cite web|url=https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2020/02/24/19-15974.pdf|title=STATE OF CALIFORNIA V. AZAR|website=ca9.uscourts.gov|date=February 24, 2020|access-date=February 18, 2024}} * {{cite court |litigants=McGill v. Shinn|vol=16 |reporter=F.4th|opinion=666 |court=9th Cir.|date=2021|url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=7732535272747689516&q=16+F.4th+666&hl=en&as_sdt=2003}} Smith dissented when the Ninth Circuit permitted Arizona to execute someone despite the fact that Arizona's death penalty statute at the time was declared unconstitutional by the U.S. Supreme Court in ''[[Ring v. Arizona]]''.{{Cite web |date=October 28, 2021 |title=Trump Judge Casts Deciding Vote to Uphold Retroactive Death Sentence: Our Courts, Our Fight |url=https://www.pfaw.org/blog-posts/trump-judge-casts-deciding-vote-to-uphold-retroactive-death-sentence-our-courts-our-fight/ |access-date=November 2, 2021 |website=People for the American Way}} Although Arizona updated its death penalty statute afterwards, Smith argued that the execution violates the [[Ex Post Facto Clause|ex post facto clause]]. * ''United States v. Idaho'' (9th Cir. 2023). On November 13, 2023, Smith was in a different 7-4 majority that temporarily blocked Idaho's abortion ban due to its lack of exceptions for medical emergencies.{{Cite web|url=https://www.scotusblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/20231120154722276_2023-11-20-Motion-with-Appendix-copy.pdf|title=UNITED STATES OF AMERICA vs. STATE OF IDAHO|website=SCOTUSBlog|date=November 13, 2023|access-date=February 18, 2024}} On January 5, 2024, the Supreme Court said it would take up the case and dissolved the 9th circuit's temporary injunction.{{Cite web|url=https://time.com/6552689/supreme-court-idaho-abortion-ban-pending-hearing/|title=Supreme Court Allows Idaho to Enforce Its Strict Abortion Ban, Even in Medical Emergencies|website=Time|date=January 6, 2024|access-date=February 18, 2024}} The Supreme Court dissolved the stay, reinstating the injunction in ''[[Moyle v. United States]]'' on June 27, 2024. On December 10, 2024, the same 11-judge panel heard oral arguments for a merits ruling.{{Cite web|url=https://www.courthousenews.com/en-banc-ninth-circuit-takes-up-idahos-total-abortion-ban/|title=En banc Ninth Circuit takes up Idaho’s ‘total abortion ban’|website=Courthouse News|date=December 10, 2024|access-date=December 23, 2024}} * ''State of Washington v. Trump'' (9th Cir. 2025). On February 19, 2025, Smith was one of three judges to reject the Trump administration's attempt to end birthright citizenship.{{Cite web|url=https://www.courthousenews.com/ninth-circuit-rejects-trump-administration-attempt-to-end-birthright-citizenship/|title=Ninth Circuit rejects Trump administration’s attempt to enforce birthright citizenship order|website=Courthouse News|date=February 19, 2025|access-date=February 19, 2025}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.courthousenews.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/washington-trump-birthright-ninth-circuit-block.pdf|title=State of Washington, et al. vs. Donald J. [[Golden Gate University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Morgan Brenda Christen''' (born December 5, 1961) is an American lawyer and jurist who serves as a [[United States federal judge|U.S. circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit|U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]]. She previously served as a state court judge on the [[Alaska Supreme Court]] from 2009 to 2012 and on the [[Judiciary of Alaska|Alaska Superior Court]] from 2002 to 2009.{{cite news |url=http://www.juneauempire.com/stories/030809/sta_406743982.shtml |title=Palin pick to be 2nd female on Alaska court |last=Sutton |first=Anne |date=March 8, 2009 |work=Juneau Empire |agency=Associated Press |access-date=2010-07-26}} ==Early life, education, and legal career== Christen was born in 1961 in [[Chehalis, Washington]].{{cite news |last1=Williams |first1=Carol J. |title=After 202-day delay, Senate confirms judge for appeals-court seat |url=https://www.seattletimes.com/nation-world/after-202-day-delay-senate-confirms-judge-for-appeals-court-seat/ |access-date=August 22, 2024 |work=The Seattle Times |publisher=[[The Los Angeles Times]]}} She graduated from the [[University of Washington]] in 1983 with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in international studies. She then attended the [[Golden Gate University School of Law]], graduating with a [[Juris Doctor]] in 1986. She is married to James Torgerson and has one child.{{cite web |title=Judge Morgan Christen Welcomed to Ninth Circuit |url=https://www.ca9.uscourts.gov/ninth-circuit-news/judge-morgan-christen-welcomed-to-ninth-circuit/ |website=ca9.uscourts.gov |publisher=United States Courts for the Ninth Circuit |access-date=21 January 2024}} After graduating from law school, Christen was a [[law clerk]] to Alaska Superior Court judge Brian Shortell from 1986 to 1987. From 1987 to 2002, she was in private practice at the law firm [[Preston Gates & Ellis]], becoming a [[partner (business rank)|partner]] in 1993. == Judicial career == === Alaska state judicial service === Christen was a judge on the Alaska Superior Court from 2002 to 2009. In 2009, she was one of two candidates recommended by the seven-member Alaska Judicial Council to replace Justice [[Warren Matthews]] on the [[Alaska Supreme Court]].{{cite news|url=http://www.adn.com/2009/03/04/711378/palin-bucks-pressure-in-supreme.html|title=Palin bucks pressure in Supreme Court appointment|last=Demer|first=Lisa|date=March 4, 2009|work=[[Anchorage Daily News]]|access-date=2010-07-26}} Christen was opposed by [[Opposition to the legalization of abortion|anti-abortion advocacy]] groups due to her service as a [[Planned Parenthood]] board member in the mid-1990s. Nonetheless, on March 4, 2009, Governor [[Sarah Palin]] selected Christen to fill the vacancy on the Alaska Supreme Court. === Federal judicial service === On May 18, 2011, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated Christen to the seat on the Ninth Circuit vacated by [[Andrew Kleinfeld]], who assumed [[senior status]] on June 12, 2010.{{cite web |title=President Obama Nominates Justice Morgan Christen for the United States Court of Appeals |date=May 18, 2011 |work=White House Press Release |url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2011/05/18/president-obama-nominates-justice-morgan-christen-united-states-court-ap }} On September 8, 2011, the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] reported her nomination out of committee by a [[voice vote]]. The Senate confirmed Christen by a 95–3 vote on December 15, 2011.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=112&session=1&vote=00231|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Morgan Christen, of Alaska, to be U.S. Circuit Judge)}} She received her commission on January 11, 2012{{FJC Bio|nid=1393881|inline=yes}} and maintains her chambers in [[Anchorage, Alaska|Anchorage]].{{cite web |title=The Judges of this Court in Order of Seniority |url=https://www.ca9.uscourts.gov/judicial-council/judges-seniority-list/ |website=www.ca9.uscourts.gov |access-date=11 May 2022}} ==See also== *[[List of first women lawyers and judges in Alaska]] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{FJC Bio|nid=1393881}} *{{Ballotpedia|Morgan_Christen}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Warren Matthews]]}} {{s-ttl|title=[[List of justices of the Alaska Supreme Court|Associate Justice of the Alaska Supreme Court]]|years=2009–2012}} {{s-aft|after=[[Peter J. [[Tulane University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Nancy Gbana Abudu''' (born 1974){{cite web |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Abudu%20SJQ%20Public%20Final.pdf |title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees |publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary |access-date=May 10, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220823220221/https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Abudu%20SJQ%20Public%20Final.pdf |archive-date=August 23, 2022 |url-status=dead}} is an American lawyer from [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]] who serves as a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit]]. == Early life and education == Abudu was born and raised in [[Alexandria, Virginia]], the daughter of [[Ghanaian Americans|immigrants from Ghana]].{{Cite web|date=2021-05-13|title=Nancy Abudu '92: Voting and Working for Fairness|url=https://www.mercersburg.edu/nancy-abudu-%E2%80%9992-voting-and-working-fairness|access-date=2021-12-23|website=Mercersburg Academy|language=en|archive-date=2021-12-23|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211223212633/https://www.mercersburg.edu/nancy-abudu-%E2%80%9992-voting-and-working-fairness|url-status=dead}} Abudu was influenced by the [[Pan-Africanism|Pan-Africanist]] movement politics of her parents, including her father's [[Internal resistance to apartheid|anti-apartheid]] activism in [[South Africa]].{{Cite news|title=Nancy Abudu Confirmed as First Black Woman on Eleventh Circuit|url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/nancy-abudu-confirmed-as-first-black-woman-on-eleventh-circuit|website=Bloomberglaw|access-date=May 18, 2023}} After graduating from [[Mercersburg Academy]] in 1992, she earned a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from [[Columbia University]] in 1996 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Tulane University Law School]] in 1999.{{Cite press release |title=President Biden Names Twelfth Round of Judicial Nominees |date=December 23, 2021 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/12/23/president-biden-names-twelfth-round-of-judicial-nominees/ |access-date=December 23, 2021}} {{PD-notice}}{{Cite web|date=2020-10-07|title=Voting-Themed School Meeting Features Two Alumni|url=https://www.mercersburg.edu/voting-themed-school-meeting-features-two-alumni|access-date=2021-12-23|website=Mercersburg Academy|language=en|archive-date=2021-12-23|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211223213007/https://www.mercersburg.edu/voting-themed-school-meeting-features-two-alumni|url-status=dead}} == Career == After law school, Abudu entered private practice at the law firm [[Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom]] from 1999 to 2001. From 2002 to 2004, she served as a staff attorney for the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit]], where she focused on [[international law]] and [[public interest law]].https://www.martindale.com/attorney/ms-nancy-gbana-abudu-504015/ From 2005 to 2013, she was a staff attorney at the [[American Civil Liberties Union|ACLU]] Voting Rights Project. From 2013 to 2019, she was the legal director for the American Civil Liberties Union of Florida. During her time with the ACLU, Abudu specialized in [[Voting rights in the United States|voting rights]] law.{{Cite web|title=Q&A: ACLU attorney Nancy Abudu focused on voting rights|url=https://www.postandcourier.com/politics/q-a-aclu-attorney-nancy-abudu-focused-on-voting-rights/article_58b5d843-d8f3-5101-8db3-ef5613d44f1f.html|access-date=2021-12-23|website=Post and Courier|date=5 October 2011 |language=en}} From 2019 to 2023, she worked as the deputy legal director and interim director for strategic litigation at the [[Southern Poverty Law Center]].{{Cite web|title=Challenging Regressive Voting Rights Policies: A discussion with Nancy Abudu, Interim Director of Strategic Litigation & Deputy Legal Director for the Voting Rights Program for the Southern Poverty Law Center|url=https://hls.harvard.edu/event/challenging-regressive-voting-rights-policies-a-discussion-with-nancy-abudu-interim-director-of-strategic-litigation-deputy-legal-director-for-the-voting-rights-program-for-the-southern-poverty-la/|access-date=2021-12-23|publisher=Harvard Law School|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211223212625/https://hls.harvard.edu/event/challenging-regressive-voting-rights-policies-a-discussion-with-nancy-abudu-interim-director-of-strategic-litigation-deputy-legal-director-for-the-voting-rights-program-for-the-southern-poverty-la/|archive-date=2021-12-23|url-status=dead}} === Notable cases === * In 2009, Abudu was co-counsel for Debra L. Harvey and Catherine M. Beddard, who challenged [[Arizona]]'s felon-restoration statute. Arizona's Constitution provides: "No person who is adjudicated an incapacitated person shall be qualified to vote at any election, nor shall any person convicted of treason or felony, be qualified to vote at any election unless restored to civil rights." The plaintiffs brought suits challenging Arizona's disenfranchisement scheme, arguing the law violated the [[Equal Protection Clause]] of the [[Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution]].{{Cite web|url=https://casetext.com/case/harvey-v-brewer?q=Myrna+P%C3%A9rez&sort=relevance&p=5&type=case&tab=keyword&jxs=|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220916005413/https://casetext.com/case/harvey-v-brewer?q=Myrna+P%C3%A9rez&sort=relevance&p=5&type=case&tab=keyword&jxs=|url-status=dead|archive-date=September 16, 2022|title=Harvey v. Brewer, 605 F.3d 1067 | Casetext Search + Citator|website=casetext.com}}{{cite web | url=http://www.metnews.com/articles/2010/ariz052810.htm | title=Court: Disenfranchisement Not Limited to Felonies at Common Law }} * In 2016, Abudu was co-counsel for [[The League of Women Voters]] of Florida in a lawsuit, claiming that the congressional redistricting plan adopted by the [[Florida]] Legislature violated Article III, Section 20 of the Florida Constitution, by "favoring the Republican Party and its incumbents." Article III, Section 20 was added to the Florida Constitution on November 2, 2010, following the general election and provides in subsection (a) that "[n]o apportionment plan or individual district shall be drawn with the intent to favor or disfavor a political party or an incumbent...."{{Cite web|url=https://casetext.com/case/league-of-women-voters-of-fla-v-detzner-4?q=Nancy+Abudu&sort=relevance&p=2&type=case&tab=keyword&jxs=|title=League of Women Voters of Fla. v. Detzner, 188 So. 3d 68 | Casetext Search + Citator|website=casetext.com|access-date=2022-09-16|archive-date=2022-09-16|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220916005413/https://casetext.com/case/league-of-women-voters-of-fla-v-detzner-4?q=Nancy+Abudu&sort=relevance&p=2&type=case&tab=keyword&jxs=|url-status=dead}}{{cite web | url=https://campaignlegal.org/cases-actions/league-women-voters-florida-v-detzner | title=League of Women Voters of Florida v. Detzner | date=17 May 2016 }} * In 2017, Abudu was co-counsel for The Gainesville Woman Care LLC in a case against the state of Florida. They challenged the 2015 amendment to Florida's [[informed consent]] law for abortion that created a 24–hour waiting period.{{Cite web|url=https://casetext.com/case/state-v-gainesville-woman-care-llc-2?q=Nancy+Abudu&sort=relevance&p=1&type=case&tab=keyword&jxs=|title=State v. Gainesville Woman Care LLC, 213 So. 3d 1141 | Casetext Search + Citator|website=casetext.com|access-date=2022-09-16|archive-date=2022-09-16|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220916005412/https://casetext.com/case/state-v-gainesville-woman-care-llc-2?q=Nancy+Abudu&sort=relevance&p=1&type=case&tab=keyword&jxs=|url-status=dead}}{{cite web | url=https://www.law.cornell.edu/women-and-justice/resource/gainesville_woman_care_llc_et_al_v_florida_et_al | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210115212948/https://www.law.cornell.edu/women-and-justice/resource/gainesville_woman_care_llc_et_al_v_florida_et_al | url-status=dead | archive-date=January 15, 2021 | title=Gainesville Woman Care LLC, et al.
