Florida, et al }} === Federal judicial service === On December 23, 2021, President [[Joe Biden]] announced his intent to nominate Abudu to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] for the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit]]. On January 10, 2022, her nomination was sent to the Senate. President Biden nominated Abudu to the seat vacated by Judge [[Beverly B. Martin]], who retired on September 30, 2021.{{Cite press release |title=Nominations Sent to the Senate |date=January 10, 2022 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/01/10/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-56/}} {{PD-notice}} On April 27, 2022, a hearing on her nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web |title=Nominations |date=April 25, 2022 |publisher=[[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]] |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/04/20/2022/nominations}} Her nomination attracted intense Republican opposition due to Abudu's work for the [[Southern Poverty Law Center]], which has labeled some of the Judiciary Committee's Republican members as "white supremacists".{{cite news|last1=Headley|first1=Tiana|title=Biden Eleventh Circuit Pick Advances Out of Senate Judiciary (1)|url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/biden-eleventh-circuit-pick-advances-out-of-senate-judiciary-1|access-date=26 April 2023|work=news.bloomberglaw.com|date=February 9, 2023|language=en}} [[Fox News]] reported on an article{{Cite web |last=Abudu |first=Nancy |date=2020-06-12 |title=On the 57th anniversary of Medgar Evers' assassination, the march for voting rights continues |url=https://www.splcenter.org/news/2020/06/12/57th-anniversary-medgar-evers-assassination-march-voting-rights-continues |access-date=2023-05-28 |website=Southern Poverty Law Center |language=en}} she had written for the Southern Poverty Law Center in 2020, in which she compared [[Felony disenfranchisement in the United States|felon disenfranchisement]] with the political disenfranchisement of slaves.{{cite news |last1=Lucas |first1=Fred |title=Meet Biden's most controversial judicial nominees stalled in Senate because of Feinstein's absence |url=https://www.foxnews.com/politics/meet-bidens-most-controversial-judicial-nominees-stalled-senate-because-feinsteins-absence |access-date=8 May 2023 |work=Fox News |date=3 May 2023}} On May 26, 2022, the committee failed to report her nomination by an 11–11 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/EBM%20Results%20-%202022-05-262.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – May 26, 2022|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=May 26, 2022}}{{cite news|date=May 26, 2022|last=Wagner|first=Rose|title=One nominee left in lurch at Senate committee vote on judicial picks|url=https://www.courthousenews.com/one-nominee-left-in-lurch-at-senate-committee-vote-on-judicial-picks/|website=Courthouse News|language=en}} On January 3, 2023, her nomination was returned to the President under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]] of the [[United States Senate]]; she was renominated later the same day.{{Cite press release|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate|date=January 3, 2023|publisher=The White House|location=Washington, D.C.|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2023/01/03/nominations-sent-to-the-senate-91/}} On February 9, 2023, her nomination was favorably reported by the committee by a [[Party line (politics)|party line]] 11–10 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/2023-02-09%20-%20EBM%20-%20Results.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – February 9, 2023|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=February 9, 2023}} Abudu did not receive any Republican support in the committee because Republicans questioned whether her advocacy work would prevent her from being impartial on the bench. On May 15, 2023, Majority Leader [[Chuck Schumer]] filed [[cloture]] on her nomination.{{Cite web |title=PN95 — Nancy G. Abudu — The Judiciary |url=https://www.congress.gov/nomination/118th-congress/95 |access-date=2023-07-07 |website=Congress.gov}} On May 17, 2023, the Senate invoked cloture on her nomination by a 50–48 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00131.htm|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Nancy G. Abudu to be United States Circuit Judge for the Eleventh Circuit)|website=United States Senate|date=May 17, 2023|access-date=May 17, 2023}} On May 18, 2023, her nomination was confirmed by a 49–47 vote, with Senator [[Joe Manchin]] being the only Democrat to vote against confirmation.{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00132.htm|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Nancy G. Abudu, of Georgia, to be United States Circuit Judge for the Eleventh Circuit)|website=United States Senate|date=May 18, 2023|access-date=May 18, 2023}}{{Cite news|last=Headley|first=Tiana|title=Nancy Abudu Confirmed as First Black Woman on Eleventh Circuit|url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/nancy-abudu-confirmed-as-first-black-woman-on-eleventh-circuit|website=news.bloomberglaw.com|access-date=May 18, 2023|language=en}} Senator Manchin's no vote was the first time any Democrat had voted against one of President Biden's judicial nominees.{{Cite news|last=Cohen|first=Zach|title=Manchin For First Time Bucks Biden Judge, Narrowing Nominee Path|url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/ip-law/manchin-for-first-time-bucks-biden-judge-narrowing-nominee-path|website=Bloomberg Law News|access-date=May 18, 2023|language=en}}{{Cite news|title=Second Biden judicial pick in one month withdraws from consideration|url=https://www.politico.com/news/2023/05/23/second-biden-judicial-pick-withdraws-00098469|website=Politico|access-date=May 23, 2023}} She received her judicial commission on May 26, 2023.{{FJC Bio|nid=13651551|inline=yes}} Abudu is the first [[African Americans|African American]] woman to sit on the Eleventh Circuit.{{Cite web|last=Long|first=Colleen|date=December 23, 2021|title=40 federal judges confirmed in 2021; Biden nominates 2 more|url=https://apnews.com/article/joe-biden-bill-clinton-race-and-ethnicity-voting-rights-district-of-columbia-80830dd1e0687173a0d3927952ed4a8b|work=Associated Press}} == See also == * [[Joe Biden judicial appointment controversies]] * [[Joe Biden Supreme Court candidates]] * [[List of African American federal judges]] * [[List of African American jurists]] == References == {{Reflist}} == External links == *{{FJC Bio|nid=13651551}} * {{C-SPAN|129082}} {{s-start}} {{s-legal}} {{s-bef|before=[[Beverly B. Nancy L. Maldonado:
{{Short description|American judge (born 1975)}} {{Use mdy dates|date=July 2024}} {{Infobox judge | name = Nancy Maldonado | image = Nancy Maldonado (Judge) (cropped).jpg | office = Judge of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit]] | appointer = [[Joe Biden]] | term_start = July 11, 2024 | term_end = | predecessor = [[Ilana Rovner]] | successor = | office1 = Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois]] | appointer1 = [[Joe Biden]] | term_start1 = August 10, 2022 | term_end1 = July 11, 2024 | predecessor1 = [[Matthew Kennelly]] | successor1 = [[April Perry]] | birth_date = {{birth year and age|1975|}} | birth_place = [[Skokie, Illinois]], U.S. | death_date = | death_place = | education = [[Harvard University]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|BA]])
[[Columbia University]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Nancy Lee Maldonado''' (born 1975) is an American lawyer from [[Chicago]] who has served as a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit]] since 2024. She previously served as a United States district judge of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois]] from 2022 to 2024. == Early life and education == Maldonado was born in 1975,{{Cite web |last=Voruganti |first=Harsh |date=April 28, 2022 |title=Nancy Maldonado – Nominee to the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois |url=https://vettingroom.org/2022/04/28/nancy-maldonado/ |access-date=May 1, 2022 |website=The Vetting Room |language=en}} in [[Skokie, Illinois]].{{cite web |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Maldonado%20SJQ%20Public%20Final.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary |access-date=May 13, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220513205941/https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Maldonado%20SJQ%20Public%20Final.pdf |archive-date=May 13, 2022 |url-status=dead}} She received a [[Bachelor of Arts]], ''[[cum laude]]'', from [[Harvard College]] in 1997 and a [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Columbia Law School]] in 2001.{{Cite press release |title=President Biden Names Sixteenth Round of Judicial Nominees |date=April 13, 2022 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/04/13/president-biden-names-sixteenth-round-of-judicial-nominees/ |access-date=April 13, 2022}} {{PD-notice}} == Career == Maldonado previously served as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Rubén Castillo (judge)|Rubén Castillo]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois]] from 2001 to 2003. In 2003, she joined the law firm of Miner, Barnhill & Galland in [[Chicago]] as an associate until 2009 when she was elevated to partner in 2010. She went on to work as partner until 2022 when she was appointed as a district judge. === Federal judicial service === ==== District court service ==== In December 2021, Maldonado was recommended to the president by Senators [[Dick Durbin]] and [[Tammy Duckworth]].{{Cite web |last=Thomas |first=David |date=December 16, 2021 |title=Democrats recommend judges for Chicago federal court |url=https://www.reuters.com/legal/legalindustry/democrats-recommend-judges-chicago-federal-court-2021-12-16/ |access-date=January 18, 2023 |website=Reuters |language=en}} On April 13, 2022, President [[Joe Biden]] announced his intent to nominate Maldonado{{Cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/legal/legalindustry/democrats-recommend-judges-chicago-federal-court-2021-12-16/|title=Democrats recommend judges for Chicago federal court|first1=David|last1=Thomas|newspaper=Reuters |date=December 16, 2021|via=www.reuters.com}} to serve as a United States District Judge of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois]]. On April 25, 2022, her nomination was sent to the Senate. President Biden nominated Maldonado to the seat vacated by Judge [[Matthew Kennelly]], who assumed [[senior status]] on October 7, 2021.{{Cite press release |title=Nominations and Withdrawals Sent to the Senate |date=April 25, 2022 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/04/25/nominations-and-withdrawals-sent-to-the-senate-64/}} {{PD-notice}} On May 11, 2022, a hearing on her nomination was held before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]].{{Cite web |title=Nominations |date=May 10, 2022 |publisher=[[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary]] |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/meetings/05/11/2022/nominations}} On June 9, 2022, her nomination was reported out of committee by a 13–9 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/EBM%20Results%20-%202022-06-09.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – June 9, 2022|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|accessdate=June 9, 2022}} On July 19, 2022, the [[United States Senate]] invoked cloture on her nomination by a 53–41 vote.{{Cite web|date=July 19, 2022|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture: Nancy L. Maldonado to be U.S. District Judge for the Northern District of Illinois)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1172/vote_117_2_00258.htm|access-date=July 19, 2022|website=United States Senate}} She was confirmed on the same day by a 53–45 vote.{{Cite web|date=July 19, 2022|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation: Nancy L. Maldonado, of Illinois, to be U.S. District Judge for the Northern District of Illinois)|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1172/vote_117_2_00259.htm|access-date=July 19, 2022|website=United States Senate}} She received her judicial commission on August 10, 2022.{{FJC Bio|nid=12282101|inline=yes}} She was sworn in on October 3, 2022.{{Cite press release|date=October 3, 2022|title=Judge Nancy L. Maldonado Sworn in as District Judge for the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois|url=https://www.ilnd.uscourts.gov/_assets/_news/JudgeMaldonadoSwornIn.pdf|website=ilnd.uscourts.gov|access-date=May 28, 2023}} She became the first Hispanic woman to serve as a federal judge on the Court for the Northern District of Illinois.{{Cite web |last=Meisner |first=Jason |title=Biden taps Judge John Z. Lee, attorney Nancy Maldonado for federal judgeships in Chicago |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/news/criminal-justice/ct-judge-john-lee-nancy-maldonado-federal-court-nominations-chicago-20220413-duyvezwll5c7ta6f3xlkhs6jte-story.html |access-date=April 13, 2022 |website=chicagotribune.com|date=April 13, 2022 }} Her service as a district judge was terminated on July 11, 2024, when she was elevated to the court of appeals. ==== Court of appeals service ==== On February 21, 2024, President [[Joe Biden]] announced his intent to nominate Maldonado to serve as a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit]].{{Cite press release |title=President Biden Names Forty-Sixth Round of Judicial Nominees and Announces Two New Nominees to Serve as U.S. Attorney |date=February 21, 2024 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2024/02/21/president-biden-names-forty-sixth-round-of-judicial-nominees-and-announces-two-new-nominees-to-serve-as-u-s-attorney/ |access-date=February 21, 2024}} {{PD-notice}} On February 27, 2024, her nomination was sent to the Senate. '''Nancy Louise Moritz''' (born 1960)<ref>{{cite web |date=November 13, 2013 |title=CONFIRMATION HEARINGS ON FEDERAL APPOINTMENTS |url=https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CHRG-113shrg24007/pdf/CHRG-113shrg24007.pdf |access-date=July 24, 2021 |publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary |page=32}}</ref> is a  [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit]] and former justice of the [[Kansas Supreme Court]].

==Biography==

Moritz (formerly Caplinger) was born in [[Beloit, Kansas|Beloit]], [[Kansas]]. She grew up in [[Tipton, Kansas|Tipton]], Kansas, before her family moved to [[Salina, Kansas|Salina]], Kansas, when Moritz was 15 years old.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.afj.org/our-work/nominees/nancy-l-moritz |title=Nancy L. Moritz |access-date=December 27, 2013 |work=Alliance for Justice |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181026025033/https://www.afj.org/our-work/nominees/nancy-l-moritz |archive-date=October 26, 2018 |url-status=dead }}</ref> She graduated [[valedictorian]] of her class from Sacred Heart High School in Salina. She received her [[Bachelor of Business Administration]] degree from [[Washburn University]] in 1982 and her [[Juris Doctor]] from [[Washburn Law School]] in 1985. She has two daughters.<ref name="bio">{{cite web|url=http://www.kscourts.org/kansas-courts/Supreme-Court/Justice-Bios/moritz.asp|title=Kansas Judicial Branch – Supreme Court – Hon. Nancy Moritz|access-date=2011-01-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181125212011/http://www.kscourts.org/kansas-courts/supreme-court/justice-bios/moritz.asp|archive-date=2018-11-25|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Career==
Moritz began her legal career in 1985 as a research attorney for Justice [[Harold S. Herd]] of the [[Kansas Supreme Court]]. In 1987, she became a [[law clerk]] to Judge [[Patrick F. Kelly]] with the [[United States District Court for the District of Kansas]]. From 1989 to 1995, she was an [[Associate lawyer|associate]] with the law firm Spencer, Fane, Britt and Browne in [[Overland Park]], where she primarily defended businesses and municipalities against federal claims.<ref name="auto">{{Cite web|url=https://afj.org/nominee/nancy-l-moritz/|title=Nancy L. Moritz|website=Afj.org|accessdate=July 29, 2026}}</ref> She then became an [[assistant United States attorney]] in Kansas City, focusing on [[medical malpractice]] and [[employment discrimination law]]. until 1999, when she became an [[Appellate]] Coordinator for the United States Attorney's office. As Appellate Coordinator, Moritz wrote more than 170 briefs in both [[Civil law (common law)|civil]] and [[Criminal law|criminal]] matters, and personally argued about 25 cases before the Tenth Circuit.<ref name="auto"/> She held this position until her appointment to the [[Kansas Court of Appeals]] by [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] [[Kansas Governor|Governor]] [[Kathleen Sebelius]] in 2004.<ref name="bio"/> [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrat]] Governor [[Mark Parkinson (Kansas politician)|Mark Parkinson]] appointed her to the [[Kansas Supreme Court]] in November 2010, and she was sworn in on January 7, 2011, replacing former Chief Justice [[Robert E. Davis (judge)|Robert E. Davis]], serving until July 29, 2014.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www2.ljworld.com/news/2011/jan/04/kansas-supreme-court-justice-nancy-moritz-caplinge/?kansas_legislature |title=Kansas Supreme Court Justice Nancy Moritz Caplinger to be sworn in Friday |date=January 4, 2011 |access-date=January 29, 2011 |work=LJWorld.com (by Associated Press)}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www2.ljworld.com/news/2010/nov/01/parkinson-names-judge-nancy-moritz-caplinger-kansa/ |title=Parkinson names Judge Nancy Moritz Caplinger to Kansas Supreme Court |date=November 1, 2010 |access-date=January 29, 2011 |work=LJWorld.com (by Associated Press)}}</ref>

=== Federal judicial service ===
In August 2013, President [[Barack Obama]] tapped Moritz for a seat on the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://cjonline.com/news/2013-11-14/law-professor-moritz-gliding-toward-confirmation |title=Law professor: Moritz gliding toward confirmation |date=November 14, 2013 |access-date=December 27, 2013 |website=Cjonline.com }}</ref>  Moritz was nominated after the nomination of former [[Kansas Attorney General]] [[Stephen Six]] was defeated by strong Republican opposition.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nationalreview.com/bench-memos/six-nomination-deep-sixed-jonathan-h-adler/|title=Six Nomination Deep Sixedwebsite=Nationalreview.com|date=July 28, 2011|access-date=July 29, 2026}}</ref>  In contrast to Six, Moritz generated little controversy. On April 29, 2014, Senate Majority Leader [[Harry Reid]] filed for [[cloture]] on Moritz's nomination On May 1, 2014, the Senate invoked cloture on her nomination by a 60–38 vote.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1132/vote_113_2_00126.htm|title=On the Cloture Motion (Motion to Invoke Cloture on Nancy L. Moritz, to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the Tenth Circuit)|publisher=United States Senate|date=1 May 2014}}</ref> On May 5, 2014, her nomination was confirmed by a 90–3 vote.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_lists/roll_call_vote_cfm.cfm?congress=113&session=2&vote=00130|title=On the Nomination (Confirmation Nancy L. Moritz, of Kansas, to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the Tenth Circuit)|publisher=United States Senate|date=5 May 2014}}</ref> She received her commission on July 29, 2014.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.fjc.gov/history/judges/moritz-nancy-louise|title=Moritz, Nancy Louise – Federal Judicial Center|website=www.fjc.gov}}</ref>

{{Short description|American judge (born 1973)}} {{use mdy dates|date=June 2020}} {{Infobox officeholder | name = Neomi Rao | image = Neomi Rao official photo (cropped).jpg | caption = Official portrait, 2018 | office = Judge of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit]] | appointer = [[Donald Trump]] | term_start = March 18, 2019 | term_end = | predecessor = [[Brett Kavanaugh]] | successor = | office1 = Administrator of the [[Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs]] | president1 = Donald Trump | term_start1 = July 18, 2017 | term_end1 = March 18, 2019 | predecessor1 = Dom Mancini (acting) | successor1 = Dom Mancini (acting) | birth_name = Neomi Jehangir Rao | birth_date = {{birth year and age|1973|}} | birth_place = [[Detroit]], Michigan, U.S. | death_date = | death_place = | spouse = Alan Lefkowitz | children = 2 | education = [[Yale University]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|BA]])
[[University of Chicago]] ([[Juris Doctor|JD]]) }} '''Neomi Jehangir Rao''' (born 1973) is an American jurist and legal scholar serving as a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit]]. She was appointed in 2019 by President [[Donald Trump]], having served in the [[First presidency of Donald Trump|Trump administration]] from 2017 to 2019 as administrator of the [[Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs]].{{cite news|last1=Adler|first1=Jonathan|title=White House names Neomi Rao as next 'regulatory czar'|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/volokh-conspiracy/wp/2017/04/07/white-house-names-neomi-rao-as-next-regulatory-czar/|access-date=18 May 2017|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=April 7, 2017}} She was previously a professor of law at the [[Antonin Scalia Law School]] of [[George Mason University]]. ==Early life and education== Rao was born in 1973 in [[Detroit]]. Her parents, Zerin and Jehangir Narioshang Rao, were [[Parsis|Parsi]] physicians from [[India]] who immigrated to the United States in 1972.{{cite news|url=http://parsi-times.com/2017/07/neomi-rao-lead-oira-us/|title=Neomi Rao To Lead OIRA In US|publisher=Parsi Times|access-date=June 16, 2018}} She grew up in [[Bloomfield Hills, Michigan]], and attended [[Detroit Country Day School]], graduating in 1991.{{cite journal|title=Alumni Class Notes|journal=Bee Hive, for Alumni, Friends and Family of Detroit Country Day School|date=2005|issue=Winter|page=39|url=http://www.dcds.edu/uploaded/alumni/beehive/winter_05_beehive.pdf|access-date=November 15, 2017}} She has since converted to [[Judaism]].{{cite news|url=https://www.jpost.com/diaspora/senate-confirms-jewish-nominee-to-dc-court-after-abortion-views-hiccup-583528|title=Senate confirms Jewish nominee|publisher=The Jerusalem Post|access-date=November 7, 2024}} After high school, Rao studied ethics, politics, economics and philosophy at [[Yale University]], graduating in 1995 with a [[Bachelor of Arts]], ''[[Latin honors|cum laude]]''. From 1995 to 1996, Rao was a [[reporter]] for ''[[The Weekly Standard]]''. She then attended the [[University of Chicago Law School]], where she was a comment editor of the ''[[University of Chicago Law Review]]'' and executive editor of a symposium issue of the ''[[Harvard Journal of Law and Public Policy]]''. She graduated in 1999 with a [[Juris Doctor]] with high honors and [[Order of the Coif]] membership. == Career == After law school, Rao was a [[law clerk]] to Judge [[J. Harvie Wilkinson III]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit]] from 1999 to 2000. She was legal counsel to the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] from 2000 to 2001, then clerked for Justice [[Clarence Thomas]] of the [[Supreme Court of the United States|United States Supreme Court]] from 2001 to 2002. In 2002, Rao entered private practice in [[London]] with the British law firm [[Clifford Chance]], where she practiced [[public international law]] and [[arbitration]]. From 2005 to 2006, during the presidency of [[George W. Bush]], Rao was an associate with the [[White House Counsel]]. In 2006, she became a [[professor of law]] at the George Mason University School of Law (now [[Antonin Scalia Law School]]),{{Cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/07/09/business/the-scholar-who-will-help-lead-trumps-assault-on-rules.html |title=Neomi Rao, the Scholar Who Will Help Lead Trump's Regulatory Overhaul |last=Eder |first=Steve |date=2017-07-09 |work=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=2017-11-15 |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} where she received tenure in 2012. In 2015, she founded the Center for the Study of the Administrative State.{{cite web|first=Steven|last=Mufson|date=April 20, 2017|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/amphtml/business/economy/trumps-pick-for-rules-czar-is-expected-to-hand-over-more-power-to-trump/2017/04/19/8b33b176-206f-11e7-a0a7-8b2a45e3dc84_story.html |title=Pick for rules czar would hand more power to Trump|website=[[The Washington Post]]|accessdate=July 10, 2017}}{{cite magazine|last1=Waddell|first1=Melanie|date=April 11, 2017|title=Scalia Law's Neomi Rao Picked for Trump Regulatory Chief|url=http://www.nationallawjournal.com/id=1202783476710/Scalia-Laws-Neomi-Rao-Picked-for-Trump-Regulatory-Chief|magazine=[[National Law Journal]]|access-date=18 May 2017}} She is a member of the [[Administrative Conference of the United States]] and the governing council of the [[American Bar Association]]'s Section of [[Administrative Law]] and [[Regulatory law|Regulatory Practice]], where she co-chairs the section's regulatory policy committee.{{cite news|title=Indian-American Neomi Rao nominated as Trump's regulatory czar|url=https://www.deccanchronicle.com/world/america/080417/indian-american-neomi-rao-nominated-as-trumps-regulatory-czar.html|access-date=18 May 2017|newspaper=Deccan Chronicle|date=April 8, 2017}} She is a member of the [[Federalist Society]].{{cite web|last1=McDonald|first1=Laughlin|last2=Dudley|first2=Susan E.|url=https://fedsoc.org/commentary/blog-posts/president-nominates-neomi-rao-to-head-oira|title=President nominates Neomi Rao to head OIRA|publisher=[[Federalist Society]]|date=April 12, 2017|access-date=October 17, 2018}} ===Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs=== On April 7, 2017, President [[Donald Trump]] nominated Rao to become the administrator of the [[Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs]] (OIRA) within the [[Office of Management and Budget]]. Former OIRA Administrator [[Susan Dudley]], who served under President [[George W. Bush]], called Rao "an excellent choice to lead OIRA...In addition to a sharp legal mind, she brings an openness to different perspectives and an ability to manage the competing demands of regulatory policy."{{cite news|last1=Devaney|first1=Tim|title=Trump nominates regulatory chief|url=https://origin-nyi.thehill.com/regulation/administration/327912-trump-nominates-regulatory-chief|access-date=18 May 2017|newspaper=The Hill|date=April 7, 2017}} [[File:National Space Council meeting 180221-D-SW162-1244 (39511229035) (cropped).jpg|thumb|Rao (far left) at a [[National Space Council]] meeting in 2018]] Legal commentator and law professor [[Jonathan H. Adler]] wrote, "Trump's selection of Rao suggests the administration is serious about regulatory reform, not merely reducing high-profile regulatory burdens." Opposition to Rao came from groups such as the [[League of Conservation Voters]] (LCV), which said she had "led efforts to roll back fundamental environmental protections" and "misuse[d] the regulatory review process for partisan political purposes."{{Cite web|title=Re: Oppose the judicial nomination of Neomi Rao to the United States Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit|url=https://www.lcv.org/article/re-oppose-judicial-nomination-neomi-rao-united-states-court-appeals-d-c-circuit/|access-date=2021-10-23|website=League of Conservation Voters|language=en}} The [[United States Senate]] confirmed Rao to the position on July 10, 2017.{{cite magazine|last1=Siegel|first1=Josh|title=Senate confirms Neomi Rao to lead White House office overseeing regulations|url=http://www.washingtonexaminer.com/senate-confirms-neomi-rao-to-lead-white-house-office-overseeing-regulations/article/2628230|access-date=9 August 2017|magazine=[[Washington Examiner]]|date=July 10, 2017}} === Federal judicial service === On November 13, 2018, Trump announced his intent to nominate Rao to serve on the [[United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit]] upon Judge [[Brett Kavanaugh]]'s elevation to the [[Supreme Court of the United States]].{{cite web|url=https://edition.cnn.com/2018/11/13/politics/trump-neomi-rao-brett-kavanaugh/|title=Trump nominates Neomi Rao to replace Kavanaugh on DC Circuit|work=[[CNN]]|last=Gray|first=Noah|date=November 13, 2018|access-date=November 13, 2018}} Her nomination was sent to the Senate that day.{{Cite web |url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/two-nominations-sent-senate-2/ |title=Two Nominations Sent to the Senate |language=en-US |via=[[NARA|National Archives]] |work=[[whitehouse.gov]] |access-date=2018-11-16}} Upon the expiration of the congressional session on January 3, 2019, Rao's nomination was returned to the president under [[Standing Rules of the United States Senate, Rule XXXI|Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6]], of the [[United States Senate]]. On January 23, 2019, Trump announced his intent to resubmit Rao's nomination.{{cite web|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-intent-nominate-judicial-nominees/|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=President Donald J. Trump Announces Intent to Nominate Judicial Nominees}} Her nomination was sent to the Senate that day.{{cite web|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/nominations-sent-senate-2/|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Nominations Sent to the Senate}} Rao's nomination attracted opposition due to articles she wrote on race, [[sexual assault]], [[feminism]], [[multiculturalism]], and people with disabilities.{{cite journal|url=http://www.abajournal.com/news/article/dc-circuit-nominee-under-fire-for-college-writings-on-race-feminism-and-date-rape/|journal=[[ABA Journal]] |publisher=[[American Bar Association]] |location=Chicago, Illinois |title=DC Circuit nominee under fire for college writings on race, feminism, date rape|first=Debra|last=Cassesn Weiss|date=January 16, 2019|access-date=October 7, 2019}} Rao was criticized by disability rights activists such as [[Rebecca Cokley]] for a 2011 law review article{{cite web | url=https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1838597 | ssrn=1838597 | title=Three Concepts of Dignity in Constitutional Law | date=May 11, 2011 }} and a blog post in which she expressed opposition to bans on [[dwarf-tossing]].{{Cite news|last=Nover|first=Scott|date=January 22, 2019|title=How a Trump judicial nominee reignited the debate over dwarf tossing|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/magazine/how-a-trump-judicial-nominee-reignited-the-debate-over-dwarf-tossing/2019/01/22/65fd885a-0d21-11e9-8938-5898adc28fa2_story.html|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]}} Rao's confirmation hearing before the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] was held on February 5, 2019. Asked by several senators about her college writings, some of which they viewed as sexual assault [[victim blaming]], Rao responded: "A victim of a horrible crime is not to blame and the person who commits those crimes should be held responsible."{{cite web |last1=Homan |first1=Timothy R. |title=Trump's pick for Kavanaugh's old court seat grilled over date-rape comments |url=https://thehill.com/homenews/senate/428553-trumps-pick-for-kavanaughs-old-court-seat-grilled-over-date-rape-comments |website=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]] |access-date=February 6, 2019 |language=en |date=February 5, 2019}} Democrats expressed concern that rules Rao worked to repeal in her role as administrator of the White House [[Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs]] could face legal challenges and wind up before the District of Columbia Circuit Court of Appeals, which is considered the second-most powerful appeals court. Rao said she would "look carefully at the standards for recusal, consult with my colleagues, and follow the precedent and practices of the D.C. Circuit." Senator [[Josh Hawley]] questioned whether she was sufficiently socially conservative about abortion rights but voted for her confirmation.{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/02/26/us/politics/josh-hawley-neomi-rao-abortion.html|title=Senator Josh Hawley Raises Questions About Neomi Rao's Abortion Stance|first1=Annie|last1=Karni|first2=Maggie|last2=Haberman|authorlink2=Maggie Haberman|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=26 February 2019}} On February 28, 2019, the Senate Judiciary Committee advanced Rao's nomination by a 12–10 vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/02.28.2019%20Results%20of%20Executive%20Business%20Meeting.pdf|title=Results of Executive Business Meeting – February 28, 2019, Senate Judiciary Committee}} On March 12, the Senate invoked [[cloture]] on her nomination by a 53–46 vote.{{Cite web |title=U.S. Senate: U.S. Senate Roll Call Votes 116th Congress - 1st Session |url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1161/vote_116_1_00043.htm |access-date=2024-03-16 |website=www.senate.gov}} On March 13, Rao was confirmed by a 53–46 vote.{{Cite web |title=U.S. Senate: U.S. Senate Roll Call Votes 116th Congress - 1st Session |url=https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1161/vote_116_1_00044.htm |access-date=2024-03-16 |website=www.senate.gov}} She received her judicial commission on March 18, 2019.{{FJC Bio|nid=6135386|inline=yes}} === Notable opinions === ==== ''Trump v. Mazars'' (2019) ==== In an October 11, 2019, opinion of a three-judge panel of the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, Rao was the dissenter in a 2–1 ruling to affirm a district court ruling supporting a congressional subpoena for President Trump's records from the accounting firm [[Mazars]].{{Cite web|url=https://talkingpointsmemo.com/news/appeals-court-rules-against-trump-for-house-subpoena-for-financial-records|title=Appeals Court Upholds House Subpoena Of Trump Financial Records|last=Shuham|first=Matt|date=October 11, 2019|website=[[Talking Points Memo]]|language=en-US|access-date=October 11, 2019}} She wrote, "allegations of illegal conduct against the president cannot be investigated by Congress except through impeachment."{{Cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/11/18/us/politics/trump-supreme-court-tax-returns.html|title=Chief Justice Gives Trump Temporary Reprieve in Financial Records Case|last=Liptak|first=Adam|date=November 18, 2019|website=[[The New York Times]]|language=en-US|access-date=November 18, 2019}} ==== ''United States v. Flynn'' (2020) ==== Rao participated in the May 2020 appeal of Judge [[Emmet G. Sullivan]]'s actions appointing ''[[amicus curiae]]'' in response to the [[United States Department of Justice]] moving to dismiss charges in ''[[United States v. Flynn]]''. The appeals court initially ordered Sullivan to file a response to the appeal within ten days.{{cite web|url=https://www.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.dcd.191592/gov.uscourts.dcd.191592.211.0_5.pdf|title=USCA ORDER as to MICHAEL T. FLYNN re: Emergency Petition for a Writ of Mandamus|publisher=[[United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit|D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals]]|date=May 21, 2020}}{{cite web|url=https://www.cadc.uscourts.gov/internet/orders.nsf/14CA50587730CED08525856F006906EF/$file/20-5143LDSN.pdf|title=DC Circuit Court Of Appeals Order|date=May 21, 2020}}{{cite web|url=https://www.cadc.uscourts.gov/internet/opinions.nsf/79798A0FA0633B7985258591004DD3E7/$file/20-5143-1848728.pdf|title=DC Circuit Court Of Appeals Opinions|date=June 24, 2020}} On June 24, 2020, Rao, joined by Judge [[Karen L. Henderson|Karen Henderson]], wrote the 2–1 decision to dismiss Flynn's conviction. Judge [[Robert L. Wilkins|Robert Wilkins]] dissented.{{cite web|first1=Katelyn|last1=Polantz|first2=Marshall|last2=Cohen|url=https://www.cnn.com/2020/06/24/politics/michael-flynn-dismiss/index.html|title=Appeals court orders judge to dismiss Michael Flynn case|website=[[CNN]]|date=June 24, 2020}} Observers were surprised because Henderson had expressed skepticism of the government's position during the hearing, saying, "I don't see why we don't observe regular order and allow him to rule".{{cite web|url=https://www.law.com/nationallawjournal/2020/06/12/dc-circuit-didnt-sound-eager-to-force-dismissal-of-case-against-michael-flynn/|title=DC Circuit Didn't Sound Eager to Force Dismissal of Case Against Michael Flynn|website=[[National Law Journal]]|first=C. Ryan|last1=Barber|date=June 12, 2020|accessdate=August 3, 2020}} Flynn's lawyer, [[Sidney Powell]], argued there was no longer any case or controversy, and the trial judge must dismiss the case against Flynn at the Justice Department's request. After vacating Rao's decision, the full court heard the case on August 11, with many judges expressing skepticism about upholding the ruling.{{Cite web|first1=Josh|last1=Gerstein|first2=Kyle|last2=Cheney|url=https://www.politico.com/news/2020/08/11/federal-appeals-court-michael-flynn-dismissal-393638|title=Federal appeals court skeptical of Michael Flynn's effort to immediately dismiss criminal charge|website=[[Politico]]|date=August 11, 2020 }}{{Cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-usa-trump-flynn-idUSKCN2571BA|title=Judges appear reluctant to immediately end case against Trump ex-aide Flynn|agency=[[Reuters]]|date=August 11, 2020|last1=Wolfe|first1=Jan}} On August 31, 2020, the appeals court ''en banc'' ruled 8–2 in favor of denying the [[writ of mandamus]] and not reassigning the case to a different district court judge, and remanded the case to Sullivan, with Rao writing in dissent, joined by Henderson.{{Cite web|url=https://www.cnn.com/2020/08/31/politics/read-flynn-appeals-ruling/index.html|title=READ: Appeals court ruling in Michael Flynn case|website=[[CNN]]|date=August 31, 2020 |access-date=September 19, 2020}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/legal-issues/appeals-court-michael-flynn/2020/08/31/24ce93f0-e0b1-11ea-b69b-64f7b0477ed4_story.html|title=Michael Flynn case does not have to be immediately dismissed, appeals court rules|first1=Ann E.|last1=Marimow|first2=Spencer S.|last2=Hsu|access-date=September 19, 2020|website=[[The Washington Post]]}} ==== ''Frederick Douglass Foundation, Inc. v. D.C.'' (2023) ==== In August 2023, Rao wrote the decision in ''Frederick Douglass Foundation, Inc. v. D.C.'', No. 21-7108 (D.C. Cir. 2023), overturning Judge [[James Boasberg]]'s dismissal of a lawsuit against the District of Columbia and holding that the [[First Amendment]] prohibits government discrimination on the basis of viewpoint and that the protection for freedom of speech applies not only to legislation but also to enforcement of the law. The [[Frederick Douglass]] Foundation had filed suit following the arrest of two of its members for defacing government property by writing on the sidewalk in chalk without first obtaining a permit from the City. The Foundation claimed [[viewpoint discrimination]] because the City had routinely ignored unpermitted chalk and paint by other protest groups but arrested the Frederick Douglass Foundation members when they wrote [[anti-abortion]] messages. For the court, Rao wrote: "The government may not enforce the laws in a manner that picks winners and losers in public debates. It would undermine the First Amendment's protections for free speech if the government could enact a content-neutral law and then discriminate against disfavored viewpoints under the cover of prosecutorial discretion. Neutral regulations may reasonably limit the time, place, and manner of speech, but such regulations cannot be enforced based on the content or viewpoint of speech."{{Cite web |title=Frederick Douglass Foundation, Inc. v. DC, No. 21-7108 (D.C. Cir. 2023) |url=https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/cadc/21-7108/21-7108-2023-08-15.html |access-date=August 17, 2023 |website=[[Justia Law]] |language=en}}{{Cite news |date=August 16, 2023 |title=Opinion {{!}} Progressives for Speech Discrimination |language=en-US |work=[[The Wall Street Journal]] |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/frederick-douglass-foundation-v-d-c-neomi-rao-protesters-defacement-law-washington-muriel-bowser-b6cb39af |access-date=2023-08-17 |issn=0099-9660}} ==== ''J.G.G. v. Trump'' (2025–2026) ==== In August 2025, Rao joined a [[per curiam decision]] in ''J.G.G. v. Trump'', 147 F.4th 1044 (D.C. Cir. 2025), that granted the Trump administration's petition for a writ of [[mandamus]] and vacated Judge [[James Boasberg]]'s probable cause order finding the administration in criminal contempt. The contempt proceedings arose from the government's March 15, 2025, deportation of more than 130 Venezuelan men to the [[CECOT]] prison in El Salvador under the [[Alien Enemies Act]], in what Boasberg concluded was willful disregard of his oral order to turn the planes around. The D.C. Circuit unanimously dismissed the government's interlocutory appeal for lack of jurisdiction, but Rao and Judge [[Gregory G. Katsas|Gregory Katsas]] wrote separate concurrences agreeing that mandamus was warranted, with Judge [[Cornelia Pillard]] dissenting. Rao concluded that the legal error was the district court's use of criminal contempt to force compliance with an order the Supreme Court had since vacated.{{cite web|url=https://media.cadc.uscourts.gov/opinions/docs/2026/04/25-5452-2168528.pdf|title=J.G.G. v. Trump, On Petition for Writ of Mandamus|publisher=[[United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit|D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals]]|date=April 14, 2026}}{{cite web|url=https://reason.com/volokh/2025/08/08/divided-d-c-circuit-panel-nixes-judge-boasbergs-criminal-contempt-order-against-trump-administration/|title=Divided D.C. Circuit Panel Nixes Judge Boasberg's Criminal Contempt Order Against Trump Administration|website=[[Reason (magazine)|Reason]]|date=August 8, 2025|access-date=May 28, 2026}}{{cite web|url=https://clearinghouse.net/case/46232/|title=J.G.G. v. Trump 1:25-cv-00766 (D.D.C.)|publisher=Civil Rights Litigation Clearinghouse|access-date=May 28, 2026}} On November 14, 2025, the D.C. Circuit denied rehearing en banc, though six of eleven active judges wrote separately to say Boasberg's contempt inquiry had been appropriate.{{cite web|url=https://www.acludc.org/cases/jgg-v-trump-challenging-unlawful-use-alien-enemies-act-1789-deport-immigrants-without-due/|title=J.G.G. v. Trump|publisher=[[ACLU of the District of Columbia]]|access-date=May 28, 2026}} After Boasberg resumed the contempt inquiry on remand and ordered live testimony from government lawyers, the same panel of Rao, [[Justin Walker (judge)|Justin Walker]], and [[J. Michelle Childs]] issued an administrative stay in December 2025. On April 14, 2026, Rao wrote a 2–1 majority opinion ordering Boasberg to terminate the renewed inquiry, joined by Walker. Rao held that the administration had a "clear and indisputable" right to relief because the March 15, 2025, order had not been clear and specific enough to support criminal contempt, and because the government had already identified former Homeland Security Secretary [[Kristi Noem]] as the official who allowed the flights to proceed. Rao wrote that the district court "proposes to probe high-level Executive Branch deliberations about matters of national security and diplomacy" and that the proceedings were "a clear abuse of discretion", posing what she called a "judicial intrusion into the autonomy of a co-equal department."{{cite news|last=Polantz|first=Katelyn|url=https://www.cnn.com/2026/04/14/politics/court-criminal-contempt-trump-officials-deportation|title=Court orders DC judge to end criminal contempt inquiry into Trump officials involved in deportation flights|publisher=[[CNN]]|date=April 14, 2026|access-date=May 28, 2026}}{{cite news|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/alien-enemies-act-deportations-criminal-contempt-appeals-court/|title=Appeals court shuts down criminal contempt probe over deportation flights of Venezuelan migrants|publisher=[[CBS News]]|date=April 14, 2026|access-date=May 28, 2026}}{{cite news|url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/appeals-court-orders-judge-to-end-contempt-investigation-of-deportation-flights|title=Appeals court orders judge to end contempt investigation of deportation flights|publisher=[[PBS NewsHour]]|date=April 14, 2026|access-date=May 28, 2026}} Childs dissented, writing that "contempt of court is a public offense, and the fate of our democratic republic will depend on whether we treat it as such" and warning that the majority's reasoning would let "any litigant" argue against contempt based on a preferred reading of a court's order before findings are even made.{{cite news|url=https://www.foxnews.com/politics/dc-appeals-court-orders-judge-boasberg-halt-trump-contempt-probe-over-deportation-flights|title=DC appeals court orders Judge Boasberg to halt Trump contempt probe over deportation flights|publisher=[[Fox News]]|date=April 14, 2026|access-date=May 28, 2026}}{{cite news|url=https://thehill.com/regulation/court-battles/5830552-trump-administration-james-boasberg-appeals-court-contempt-ruling/|title=Appeals court halts Boasberg contempt inquiry over Venezuelan deportation flights|newspaper=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]]|date=April 14, 2026|access-date=May 28, 2026}} [[American Civil Liberties Union]] attorney Lee Gelernt said the plaintiffs would seek en banc review.{{cite news|url=https://www.courthousenews.com/judge-ordered-to-end-contempt-probe-over-deportation-flights/|title=Judge ordered to end contempt probe over deportation flights|publisher=[[Courthouse News Service]]|date=April 14, 2026|access-date=May 28, 2026}} '''''National Trust for Historic Preservation v. National Park Service (2026)''''' In April 2026, Rao dissented from a 2–1 D.C. Circuit ruling that remanded ''National Trust for Historic Preservation v. National Park Service'' to the district court for further factual development on the security implications of halting construction of a White House ballroom. The litigation arose after the Trump administration demolished the [[East Wing]] in October 2025 to make way for a 90,000-square-foot, roughly $300–400 million ballroom funded largely by private donations from corporations and individuals, with some public money for underground bunkers and security upgrades.{{cite news|url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2025/10/24/who-are-the-private-donors-funding-trumps-white-house-ballroom|title=Who are the private donors funding Trump's White House ballroom?|publisher=[[Al Jazeera English|Al Jazeera]]|date=October 24, 2025|access-date=May 28, 2026}}{{cite news|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/federal-appeals-court-white-house-ballroom-construction-lawsuit/|title=Federal appeals court sends White House ballroom construction lawsuit back to lower court|publisher=[[CBS News]]|date=April 12, 2026|access-date=May 28, 2026}} The [[National Trust for Historic Preservation]], a congressionally chartered nonprofit, sued in December 2025, arguing the project required congressional authorization and federal review.{{cite news|last=Ramaswamy|first=Swapna Venugopal|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/2025/12/12/national-trust-files-lawsuit-stop-trumps-ballroom-construction/|title=National Trust files lawsuit to stop Trump's ballroom construction|newspaper=[[USA Today]]|date=December 12, 2025|access-date=May 28, 2026}} On March 31, 2026, Judge [[Richard J. Leon]] entered a preliminary injunction, concluding that no statute authorized the president to demolish a wing of the White House and replace it with a privately funded ballroom and that the action was likely [[ultra vires]].{{cite web|url=https://clearinghouse.net/case/47494/|title=National Trust for Historic Preservation in the United States v. National Park Service 1:25-cv-04316 (D.D.C.)|publisher=Civil Rights Litigation Clearinghouse|access-date=May 28, 2026}} The panel of Judges [[Patricia Millett]] and [[Bradley Garcia]] returned the case to Leon to clarify how the injunction's "necessary for safety and security" exception would operate, citing an inadequate record on the asserted security need for the ballroom.{{cite news|url=https://thehill.com/regulation/court-battles/5827374-appeals-court-white-house-ballroom/|title=White House ballroom construction can continue, federal appeals court says|newspaper=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]]|date=April 11, 2026|access-date=May 28, 2026}} Rao dissented: she would have stayed the injunction outright. She wrote that the district court had "halted construction based on the alleged aesthetic injury of one individual residing in Washington, D.C." and that the government had shown a strong likelihood of success on the merits both because the National Trust lacked Article III standing and because 3 U.S.C. § 105(d)(1) authorizes the president to undertake "improvement[s]" to the White House.{{cite web|url=https://media.cadc.uscourts.gov/orders/docs/2026/04/26-5101LDSN2.pdf|title=National Trust for Historic Preservation v. National Park Service, No. 26-5101, Order|publisher=[[United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit|D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals]]|date=April 11, 2026}} According to Rao, the government had presented "credible evidence of ongoing security vulnerabilities at the White House that would be prolonged by halting construction" and that those concerns outweighed the "generalized aesthetic harms" claimed in the suit.{{cite news|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2026/04/11/judge-told-to-reconsider-national-security-implications-of-halting-trumps-white-house-ballroom.html|title=Judge told to reconsider national security implications of halting Trump's White House ballroom|publisher=[[CNBC]]|date=April 11, 2026|access-date=May 28, 2026}} == Personal life == Rao is married to Alan Lefkowitz, a law school classmate,{{Cite web|title=Neomi Rao, '99: Serving the Public from the Executive Branch to the Bench {{!}} University of Chicago Law School|url=https://www.law.uchicago.edu/news/neomi-rao-99-serving-public-executive-branch-bench|access-date=2021-10-23|website=www.law.uchicago.edu|date=October 23, 2020 }} with whom she has two Nicole Berner:
{{Short description|American-Israeli judge (born 1965)}} {{Use mdy dates|date=December 2023}} {{Infobox judge | name = Nicole Berner | image = Nicole G Berner.jpg | office = Judge of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit]] | appointer = [[Joe Biden]] | term_start = March 19, 2024 | term_end = | predecessor = [[Diana Gribbon Motz]] | successor = | birth_name = Nicole Gina Berner | birth_date = {{birth year and age|1965}} | birth_place = [[Woking]], England, UK | death_date = | death_place = | citizenship = Israel
United Kingdom
United States | spouse = [[Debra Katz]] | children = 3 | education = [[University of California, Berkeley]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|BA]], [[Juris Doctor|JD]], [[Master of Public Policy|MPP]]) }} '''Nicole Gina Berner''' (born 1965){{Cite web|url=https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/berner_sjq.pdf|title=Questionnaire for Judicial Nominees|publisher=United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|access-date=December 13, 2023}} is an American-Israeli lawyer who serves as a [[United States federal judge|United States circuit judge]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit]]. She served as general counsel for the [[Service Employees International Union]] (SEIU) from 2017 to 2024 and a partner at the law firm of James & Hoffman.{{cite web |title=Nicole G. Berner |url=https://www.jamhoff.com/attorneys/nicole-g-berner/ |website=James & Hoffman, P.C. |access-date=November 14, 2023 |language=en}} ==Early life and education== Berner was born in [[Woking]], Surrey, England to American parents.{{cite web |title=Meet the Berner-Kadish Family |url=https://www.nif.org/stories/human-rights-democracy/meet-the-berner-kadish-family/ |website=[[New Israel Fund]] |access-date=November 28, 2023 |date=June 11, 2015}} During her childhood, her family moved to the United States, settling in [[Oakland, California]].{{cite news |last1=Goldsmith |first1=Aleza |title=Top court in Israel rules ex-Berkeley lesbians are moms |url=https://jweekly.com/2000/06/02/top-court-in-israel-rules-ex-berkeley-lesbians-are-moms/ |access-date=November 28, 2023 |work=[[J. The Jewish News of Northern California]] |date=June 2, 2000}} She earned a Bachelor of Arts degree in [[women's studies]] from the [[University of California, Berkeley]]. During her studies, she spent a semester in Israel studying at the [[University of Haifa]], and decided to move there. After completing her degree, she moved to Israel. In 1990 in [[Tel Aviv]], she founded the Bat Adam organization, an advocacy group for victims of sexual assault and domestic violence.[https://www.ynetnews.com/article/skgkbe00r6 First Israeli American confirmed as U.S. federal judge] Berner returned to the United States in 1992 to attend [[UC Berkeley School of Law|Berkeley School of Law]] at the University of California, Berkeley. She completed a [[Juris Doctor]] from Berkeley School of Law and a [[Master of Public Policy]] from the [[Goldman School of Public Policy]] at the University of California, Berkeley.{{cite news |last1=Weiner |first1=Rachel |title=Biden nominates labor lawyer Nicole Berner to 4th Circuit |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/dc-md-va/2023/11/15/fourth-circuit-judicial-nomination-biden-berner/ |access-date=November 28, 2023 |newspaper=[[Washington Post]] |date=November 18, 2023}} Berner is a citizen of the United States, Israel, and the United Kingdom.{{Cite web |date=2024-08-15 |title=Nicole G. Berner |url=https://afj.org/nominee/nicole-g-berner/ |access-date=2026-10-18 |website=Alliance for Justice |language=en-US}} ===''Berner-Kadish v. Minister of Interior''=== In 2000, as a dual American-Israeli citizen, represented by the [[Association for Civil Rights in Israel]], Berner and her then-wife Ruti Kadish prevailed in a landmark civil rights case before the [[Israeli Supreme Court]]. Berner had legally adopted their son in California, but when the family moved to Israel, attempts to register their son with two mothers were refused by the [[Ministry of Interior (Israel)|Ministry of Interior]] in Israel.{{cite news |last1=Segal |first1=Naomi |title=Court lets lesbian couple be co-moms |url=https://www.jta.org/2000/06/01/lifestyle/court-lets-lesbian-couple-be-co-moms |access-date=November 28, 2023 |work=[[Jewish Telegraphic Agency]] |date=June 1, 2000}}{{Cite book |last=Agigian |first=Amy |url=http://archive.org/details/babystepshowlesb0000agig |title=Baby steps : how lesbian alternative insemination is changing the world |date=2004 |publisher=Middletown, Conn. : Wesleyan University Press |others=Internet Archive |isbn=978-0-8195-6629-4 |pages=85–86}}{{Cite book |last1=Minot |first1=Leslie Ann |url=http://archive.org/details/conceivingparent00mino |title=Conceiving parenthood : parenting and the rights of lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender people and their children |last2=Long |first2=Scott |last3=International Gay and Lesbian Human Rights Commission |date=2000 |publisher=San Francisco, Calif. : International Gay and Lesbian Human Rights Commission |pages=164–165}} The subsequent legal case, ''Berner-Kadish v. Minister of Interior'', challenged the refusal to register Kadish and Berner's second parent adoption of their son. The Israel Supreme Court ruled that the Ministry of Interior must register the adoption decree, accepting legally that the child has two mothers.{{cite news |last1=Sontag |first1=Deborah |title=Matan Has Two Mommies, and Israel Is Talking |work=The New York Times |date=June 4, 2000 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2000/06/04/world/matan-has-two-mommies-and-israel-is-talking.html |access-date=November 14, 2023}}{{cite web |last1=Izenberg |first1=Dan |title=High Court: Recognize lesbian parents |url=https://www.jpost.com/israel/high-court-recognize-lesbian-parents |website=[[The Jerusalem Post]] |access-date=November 14, 2023 |date=December 9, 2007 |issn=0792-822X}}{{cite news |title=Israels lesbian mothers contributing to the gaybe boom |url=https://jweekly.com/2001/09/14/israel-s-lesbian-mothers-contributing-to-the-gaybe-boom/ |access-date=November 28, 2023 |work=[[J. The Jewish News of Northern California]] |date=September 14, 2001}} ==Career== From 1996 to 1997, Berner worked as a [[law clerk]] for Judge [[Betty Binns Fletcher]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]], and from 1997 to 1998, she worked as a [[law clerk]] for Chief Judge [[Thelton Henderson]] of the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of California]].{{Cite press release |title=President Biden Names Forty-Second Round of Judicial Nominees |date=November 15, 2023 |publisher=The White House |location=Washington, D.C. |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2023/11/15/president-biden-names-forty-second-round-of-judicial-nominees/ |access-date=November 15, 2023}} {{PD-notice}} She was a visiting attorney at [[Yigal Arnon & Co.]] in Israel from 1999 until 2000, and was a litigation associate at [[Jenner & Block]] from 2000 through 2004. From 2004 to 2006, Berner worked as a staff attorney at [[Planned Parenthood]].{{cite web |title=Biden's Latest Picks Include Top Labor Atty For 4th Circ. - Law360 |url=https://www.law360.com/ip/articles/1766853 |website=www.law360.com |publisher=LexisNexis |language=en}} Berner joined the SEIU's legal department as an [[in-house counsel]] in 2006 and was named [[General Counsel]] in 2017.{{cite web |title=SEIU Appoints New General Counsel |url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/daily-labor-report/seiu-appoints-new-general-counsel |website=news.bloomberglaw.com |access-date=November 14, 2023 |language=en}} Her work with the SEIU has included legal efforts to support the [[Affordable Care Act]], to oppose the [[Defense of Marriage Act]], and to oppose an effort to end the [[Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals]] (DACA) program during the Trump administration.{{cite web |title=BRIEF OF SERVICE EMPLOYEES INTERNATIONAL UNION, AMERICAN FEDERATION OF TEACHERS, AMERICAN FEDERATION OF STATE, COUNTY AND MUNICIPAL EMPLOYEES, COMMUNICATIONS WORKERS OF AMERICA, INTERNATIONAL BROTHERHOOD OF TEAMSTERS, INTERNATIONAL UNION OF PAINTERS AND ALLIED TRADES, AND UNITED FARM WORKERS OF AMERICA AS AMICI CURIAE IN SUPPORT OF PLAINTIFFS |url=https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/general/2018/03/28/18-15068-seiu-amicus-brief.pdf |website=cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov |access-date=November 28, 2023 |date=March 20, 2018}} She was the lead attorney on the ''[[amicus curiae]]'' brief filed on behalf of the SEIU in ''[[California v. Texas]]''.{{cite web |title=BRIEF OF AMICI CURIAE SERVICE EMPLOYEES INTERNATIONAL UNION, MARILYN RALAT-ABERNAS, R.N., MARCUS SANDLING, M.D., ET AL., IN SUPPORT OF PETITIONERS IN NO. 19-840 AND CROSS-RESPONDENTS IN NO. 19-1019 |url=https://www.supremecourt.gov/DocketPDF/19/19-840/143409/20200513122409554_Brief%20of%20Amici%20Curiae%20SEIU%20et%20al.%20iso%20Petitioners.pdf |website=www.supremecourt.gov |access-date=November 28, 2023 |date=May 13, 2020}} She was also involved with the [[Fight for $15]] movement.{{cite news |last1=Kullgren |first1=Ian |title=Biden's Planned Fourth Circuit Pick Is Steadfast Union Ally |url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/daily-labor-report/biden-plans-to-nominate-steadfast-union-ally-to-fourth-circuit |access-date=November 28, 2023 |work=[[Bloomberg Law]] |date=November 16, 2023 |language=en}} In 2019, liberal group [[Demand Justice]] included Berner on their list of suggested Supreme Court nominees for any future Democratic president.{{Cite news |last=Kim |first=Seung Min |date=October 15, 2019 |title=Democratic presidential candidates come under pressure to release Supreme Court picks |language=en-US |access-date=November 27, 2023 |issn=0190-8286}} In 2023, Berner was named an [[adjunct professor]] of law at [[Vanderbilt Law School]].{{cite web |title=Biography |url=https://law.vanderbilt.edu/bio/?pid=nicole-berner |website=Vanderbilt University |access-date=November 14, 2023}} Berner is an elected member of the [[American Law Institute]].{{cite web |title=Ten Fellows Named New Members of American Law Institute |url=https://www.americanbarfoundation.org/ten-fellows-named-new-members-of-american-law-institute/ |website=[[American Bar Foundation]]
